11506-the-old-bell-of-independence-or-ph:
Henry C. Watson's 1851 Old Bell of Independence, or Philadelphia in 1776, in the Young American's Library, aims to awaken veneration for Revolutionary patriots and emulation of their example. Its preface warns that freedom's enjoyment makes Americans underrate the toils and sufferings that secured it, and argues knowledge of the fathers is the best cure for falling off. War's horrors are condemned, but generous devotion, resolution, and skill are commended wherever displayed.

Stories of Washington, a spy's fate, a sermon, a prayer, Lydia Darragh, and a dead man's lake cluster around the old bell as rallying point for veteran story-tellers. Watson, author of Camp-Fires of the Revolution, writes for young readers. The book shows mid-century patriotic education in story form.
23174-a-good-for-nothing-1876:
Hjalmar Hjorth Boyesen published A Good for Nothing in 1876, a work of fiction centred on a boy named Ralph. The opening follows Ralph from babyhood into early childhood. His mother reads deep meaning into small habits, taking his thumb-sucking and quiet corner-sitting as signs of a poet's brooding mind.

By age five, Ralph has become the ruling force in his own home. Boyesen tells this with gentle irony, letting the mother's proud reading sit beside the plain facts of a spoiled small child. Readers get a wry portrait of family pride, early character, and how adults can build large hopes on very small evidence.
25536-history-of-the-english-people-volu:
John Richard Green closes his History of the English People with this eighth volume, Modern England from 1760 to 1815, in the 1896 Eversley edition. The full index to the eight volumes once stood at its end, and now circulates as a separate volume.

Chapters cover the independence of America from 1767 to 1782, industrial England, England and revolutionary France, and England and Napoleon. Green follows a nation remade by lost colonies, new mills, and long wars, in the readable narrative style that made his history popular. Macmillan issued the volume in London and New York.
28010-bacon-s-rebellion-1676:
Thomas J. Wertenbaker published Bacon's Rebellion, 1676 as Jamestown 350th Anniversary Historical Booklet Number 8, issued by the Virginia 350th Anniversary Celebration Corporation in Williamsburg in 1957, with later printings in 1959 and 1964. The booklet also opens with omens: a great comet, vast flights of pigeons, and swarms of cicadas.

Wertenbaker also traces the disaster to Charles I naming Sir William Berkeley Governor of Virginia, a member of the Privy Chamber whose intense loyalty shaped his rule. The booklet still remains a clear, concise, plain account today of the greatest catastrophe in the colony's history, written for the Jamestown anniversary audience.
30557-lilrc-interlibrary-loan-manual-jan:
The Long Island Library Resources Council publishes its Interlibrary Loan Manual in January 1976, from Box 31, Bellport, New York. Eight sections cover introduction, loan policies and procedures, direct access to other libraries, the INS system, request forms, good borrowing, good lending, and appendices.

Loan procedures detail what may be borrowed, placing requests, form of request, verification, photocopying, and expenses. Direct access adds location service and a research loan program, while INS covers billing, cancellations, delivery, pickup, microforms, recalls, renewals, and returns. The manual serves librarians and borrowers who share books across Long Island libraries. Staff can use it day to day to move books, check forms, and keep loans on track.
32222-felicitas-a-tale-of-the-german-mig:
Felix Dahn's Felicitas, a tale of the German migrations in the year 476, translated from the German by M. A. C. E., was published in London by Macmillan in 1883. Its introduction places the author in Salzburg, studying old records and Roman antiquities. His studies concerned the fifth century, when Germanic tribes invaded those regions and Roman garrisons retired, with or without resistance.

Many settlers, Dahn writes, remained in the land: peasants, tradespeople, and mechanics who would not forsake their homes, lucrative occupations, or valued, long-cherished plots of ground. They stayed under the rule of the barbarian, who, once conquest's storm and battle had ended and the country was divided, did not molest them. Readers get a migration-era romance grounded in Salzburg records, about ordinary settlers under a new rule.
45850-theism-being-the-baird-lecture-of-:
Theism, by Robert Flint, holds the Baird Lecture for 1876. William Blackwood and Sons printed it in Edinburgh and London in 1877. Flint taught divinity at the University of Edinburgh. The lectures were given at Glasgow, St Andrews, and Edinburgh. A second volume on anti-theistic theories was to follow, from the lectures of 1877. Ten lectures make up this book. The first asks whence and how we get the idea of God.

Later lectures weigh polytheism and pantheism against theism. The nature and limits of proof for God get a lecture. The argument from order takes two. Conscience and history supply a moral argument. Flint closes by calling mere theism not enough. Notes in an appendix treat design in astronomy, chemistry, and geology.
4824-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
This twenty-second volume of The Rise of the Dutch Republic covers 1574 to 1576. Its file header numbers it as the twenty-fourth Gutenberg volume. Chapter three opens with latter days of the Blood Council, and informal, insincere negotiations for peace. Characteristics of negotiators and their diplomatic correspondence are weighed, with Dr. Junius prominent among them.

Secret conferences between Dr. Leoninus and Orange follow, with steadfastness of the Prince amid shifting talks. Changes in internal government of the northern provinces, generosity and increasing power of municipalities, and incipient jealousies among them shape the chapter's second half. Peace talks that neither side trusts, a prince who will not bend, and towns growing strong enough to govern themselves carry the narrative on. Readers get Motley's account of diplomacy without trust, in the years before the provinces united.
4825-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
By 1576 the revolt has outgrown single provinces, and John Lothrop Motley shows Orange pulling them into closer union. A new act joins Holland and Zealand, defines the prince's authority, and sets out a provincial polity built around towns that now fund and govern much of the war.

At Brussels, a state council tries to run affairs while Madrid hesitates, and Orange watches every move with care. Letters from the king, talks with Elizabeth of England, and secret dealings with France and Alencon fill the background. The volume explains how a rebellion became a state, held together by law, money, and Orange's steady leadership.
50295-reconstruction-and-the-constitutio:
Reconstruction and the Constitution, 1866 to 1876, is a history by John Burgess, professor of political science and constitutional law at Columbia University. Scribner published it at New York in the American History Series, with a copyright of 1902. Burgess inscribes it to the memory of his pupil, colleague, and lifelong friend Richmond Mayo Smith, with grief too deep for words.

Chapter one sets out the theory of reconstruction. Then come Lincoln's views and acts, and Johnson's plan of reconstruction and his course in carrying it out. Four chapters follow the congressional plan step by step to its completion. Burgess asks what a state is in a federal system, and whether a state can destroy itself by renouncing its allegiance. His book treats the rebuilding of the Union as a question of constitutional law. It long stood as a standard scholarly account of the era,.
53725-from-palmerston-to-disraeli-1856-1:
From Palmerston to Disraeli, covering the years 1856 to 1876, is a volume in Bell’s English History Source Books. That series gave students the raw words of history in small cheap volumes. Each book sold at a shilling net in the list. Other volumes treated the welding of the English race and the Normans in England.

Source books let a class read the past in its own documents. Letters, speeches, acts, and reports replaced a bare summary of events. The Palmerston to Disraeli volume covers twenty years of Victorian politics. Two great rivals head that age, and the title names them both. Editors chose the extracts and linked them for school and college use. The book shows how history teaching turned to first hand texts in that period.
54537-musical-instruments-1876:
Carl Engel wrote Musical Instruments, number five in the South Kensington Museum art handbooks. William Maskell edited the series, the note dated August 1875 says. These handbooks reprint the essays set before the large museum catalogues. Each is trimmed to a portable shape for the public. They were meant to serve other collections as well as South Kensington's own. At a trifling cost, a visitor could grasp the history of the subject.

Woodcuts crowd the book, showing instruments of many lands and ages. The large catalogues hold the full details of the museum's examples. Engel treats music as a fine art known, in some stage, to all nations. The origin of vocal music opens his account of the art. From voice he passes to the tools men made to bear the tune. The book stays a neat ground plan of the instrument family.
66607-story-of-the-automobile-its-histor:
H. L. Barber wrote this tale of the car, printed at Chicago in 1917. He was a man of funds and wrote on how funds are made. The full head of the book sets its span: the tale of the car and its growth from 1760 to 1917. To the tale is added a look at the stand and the hopes of the trade of the car. A plate at the front names three men of the theme: Franklin, Duryea, and Ford.

Franklin is called the first great teach of thrift in America. Duryea is named as the maker of the first car of America that ran on the fumes of oil. Ford is named the sire of the make of cars in great count. The word at the front states the gap the book fills.
76915-motion-pictures-1976:
The Copyright Office of the Library of Congress issued a catalog of copyright entries for motion pictures covering January to June 1976. The volume, printed in Washington in 1977, is volume thirty, parts twelve and thirteen, number one of the third series. It is sold by the Superintendent of Documents. Codes at the front sort works by origin and class.

Published works of foreign origin under a waiver of fee, and domestic published and unpublished works, each take a mark. Each entry records the films registered for copyright in that half year, with claimants, dates, and credits as filed. Film researchers and rights holders use such a catalog to trace who claimed a picture and when, in the official record of the United States.
9072-life-of-johnson-volume-2-1765-1776:
This second volume of Boswell's Life of Johnson, in the Hill edition, covers the years 1765 to 1776. Johnson, now famous for his Dictionary, works on his edition of Shakespeare and writes for friends, while Boswell records his talk, letters, and quarrels with care. The volume adds notes on Johnson's views of America and his own records.

Readers meet Johnson in his prime: witty, learned, dogmatic, and kind in turns, holding court in London coffee houses and clubs. Boswell's eye for small detail makes the man live on the page. For lovers of biography, this stretch of the Life is among its richest, full of talk that still sparks.
9112-the-dare-boys-of-1776:
Stephen Angus Cox wrote this boys' adventure novel, published in New York in 1910. It opens on July 4, 1776, as Philadelphia weighs the Declaration of Independence. Two brothers, Dick and Tom Dare, join the patriot cause and take on dangerous work as spies. Their deeds soon please General Washington himself.

Chapters move from road ambushes and night attacks to camps of the foe, a haunted house, and the Battle of Long Island. The pace is swift and the heroes brave. The book is a fine sample of the patriotic dime-novel spirit that once fired young readers.
a-general-history-and-collection-of-voya: Volume eleven of Robert Kerr's voyages continues George Shelvocke's voyage round the world from 1719 to 1722. Its sections follow Shelvocke from California to Canton in China and his residence there. The voyage then returns from China to England. Kerr's volume adds a lively privateering circumnavigation to his collection. The tale is lively, bold, and full of the sea and strange lands.
abridgement-of-elements-of-phrenology-18: Abridgement of Elements of Phrenology, dated 1876 and credited to B H Webb, is a shortened version of a phrenology textbook's elements. By the eighteen seventies phrenology had a long shelf of elementary treatises. An abridgement served readers who wanted the system in brief: the faculties, the organs on the skull, and the rules for reading them. The record for this entry gives little beyond its title, author, and date. The piece survives as a late, small brick in the large popular literature of head reading.
account-of-an-alchemical-roll-on-parchme: Account of an Alchemical Roll on Parchment, dated 1876, describes a remarkable object: a parchment roll presented by the Earl of Cromarty in 1707 to the Royal College of Physicians of Edinburgh. Alchemical rolls carry the work of the philosophers in pictures and text along a long strip. This account records the Edinburgh roll for learned readers. The copy preserved here comes through the University of Glasgow Library and the Ferguson collection, whose name stands on the record.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
Volume V of the Encyclopaedia of Pure Materia Medica appeared in 1876, the halfway point of Allen's ten. The symptoms of each remedy stand in strict anatomical order, a habit that lets a busy reader land on the right page fast. Sources are cited, so claims can be traced.

Some entries run for pages, proof of how often a drug was tested in that busy age of provings. Others stay brief. All of it feeds the same craft: choosing one remedy whose proved picture matches the sick person's signs. The volume keeps the archive's standard of full record over fine writing.
arxiv-2412-00176:
Hui Ren and co-authors ask if an image model needs paintings in its training to learn a painting style, in a 2024 paper. Their test model learned from photos alone, with no art of any kind in its diet. The question bears on consent, since art sets are often scraped without leave.

Given just a few sample works, the photo-trained model took on new art styles well. In user tests and scored checks, its art matched that of top models raised on huge mixed sets. Tracing where outputs draw from showed both art and photo data play roles. The team frames the result as an opt-in path: style can come from a small, picked set.
arxiv-2412-00676:
The XRISM Collaboration presents a 2024 astronomy paper on the supernova remnant Sagittarius A East, which sits beside the Milky Way's central black hole. The remnant's X-ray glow was suspected to come from overionized plasma, gas whose atoms were stripped further than its current temperature allows, hinting at a strange history. The team's new space telescope paired a high-resolution spectrometer with a wide-field imager for the first detailed look.

Iron emission lines were resolved into fine structure for the first time. Their intensity pattern strongly confirms overionized plasma. Before the shift, the gas must have been hotter than four kiloelectronvolts, and the change happened fast. The iron ions move slowly, ruling out violent expansion now. The authors weigh two triggers: rapid cooling as the gas expanded out of dense surrounding material, or a past blaze of radiation from the black hole next door.
arxiv-2412-01576:
Isufi and co-authors survey topological signal processing and learning, a young field that handles data living on structures richer than graphs. Graphs model pairwise links, which suits gene, brain, power, and social networks, and graph methods for signals and learning are well developed. But many systems involve group interactions that pairs cannot express. Simplicial and cell complexes can capture those, and this survey explains how signal methods extend to them.

The paper lays out the core ideas through Hodge theory, then reviews progress in representing, filtering, and sampling signals on such structures, plus ways to infer the structure itself from data. It covers time-varying signals and links to machine learning, and it closes with applications: flows over networks, geometry processing, ranking, biology, and semantic communication. Open problems and future directions round out the survey.
arxiv-2412-01676: Robert Auffarth, Angel Carocca, and Rubí Rodríguez count distinguishing structures on abelian varieties in this 2024 mathematics paper. An abelian variety can carry principal polarizations, extra structures that shape its geometry, and the variety's own symmetries act on the set of them. On a very general member of a whole family of singular such varieties, one might expect exactly one polarization up to symmetry. The authors show the count is not always one.
arxiv-2412-02076:
Bo Wen, Haochen Zhang, Dirk-Uwe Bartsch, William Freeman, Truong Nguyen, and Cheolhong An wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. It keeps the topology of tube-like forms true when software cuts them out of biomedical images.

A cut that breaks a vessel or drops a loop can ruin later work, even if most pixels are right. Past loss rules match lasting features in a pure topology space, which can pair the wrong features. The new loss also uses where features sit in the image, so matches are guided by place. Tests on many kinds of tube images beat top rivals on topology accuracy. Code is public.
arxiv-2412-02276:
Mbewe, Mekuria, Sahlu, and Abebe study a cosmology where the cosmic fluids are slightly sticky, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. With the right conditions, their viscous interacting model mimics the standard ΛCDM universe at the background level, expanding the same way while telling a different microphysical story.

The authors derive the background equations for the multifluid system. They then fit the model to Type Ia supernova data using Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. Best-fit parameters are compared against the standard picture. Next they perturb the model in a dust-dominated frame, using a covariant formalism that tracks how inhomogeneities grow. The perturbation results carry a warning: bound structures in the late universe tend to disintegrate in this model. That prediction gives observers a handle to test viscous cosmologies against the large-scale structure we actually see.
arxiv-2412-02676:
Li and five co-authors teach two robot arms touch-rich tasks from plan-made drills in this twenty twenty-four paper. Two-arm work needs fine sync of grips, pushes, and turns on one thing. Real drill sets for such work are scant and hard to grow by hand.

Inside, a plan tool breeds drill paths in a rich fake world for the arms. Those paths span things of all shapes, sizes, and stuff traits in the set. A spread-style net then learns the drill paths by copy in the lab. Craft picks in marks, task code, and drill mix help cross to real arms. Tests in fake and real rooms show the arms work on new things well.
arxiv-2412-02776:
Rustem Turtayev and three colleagues test how well plain language model agents can hack in capture-the-flag contests, in a 2024 paper. These contests pose graded security puzzles, and the test set they use targets a high school level.

With simple prompting, tool use, and repeat attempts, the agents solved ninety-five percent of the benchmark tasks. That score far beats earlier results of twenty-nine and seventy-two percent. Many tasks fell in just one or two rounds of the agent's plan-and-act loop. The authors argue that today's models already pass the high school level in attack skills. The skill was there all along, they say, waiting for simple methods to draw it out.
arxiv-2412-02876:
Weiguang Jiang and co-authors teach a neural network to read nuclear responses in a 2024 paper. When photons strike a nucleus, the strength of its dipole response shapes many reactions. Measured curves exist for some nuclei but not others. The team trained a network on measured curves for 216 nuclei across the chart. They then tested it on ten more nuclei with known data.

The trained model matched known curves well. It also flagged some measured sets as suspect, hinting they may need review or rejection. Where data run thin or missing, its guesses backed up theory based curves. The work gives nuclear physics a fast guide for where fresh measures would pay off most.
arxiv-2412-03076:
Francesc Wilhelmi and four co-authors tackle Wi-Fi crowding in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Nearby networks often talk over each other. A method called spatial reuse lets devices send at the same time if they tune their power and sensing levels well. The authors let each network learn its own settings through trial and reward. They call this a multi-agent multi-armed bandit setup.

The agents act under a coordination scheme planned for future Wi-Fi. The team tested several learning rules and ways to share rewards. They ran the tests in Komondor, a known Wi-Fi simulator. Their results show that learned settings can beat fixed ones. The work speaks to engineers shaping the next Wi-Fi standards, where smart control will be built in.
arxiv-2412-03176:
León-Paul Schaub Torre, Pelayo Quirós, and Helena García-Mieres wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It builds a system that reads Spanish clinical notes and names the skin disease a patient likely has, by pairing a large language model with medical reference structures.

The hybrid system learns in a set order: first the type of skin problem, then its severity, then where on the body it sits. Teaching the model that order, and grounding it in medical ontologies, lifted accuracy a great deal. The system reached precision of 0.84 on disease classification, with strong balance scores. The authors report the best results to date for this task. They release both the method and the dataset, so other teams can test and extend the approach for Spanish medical text.
arxiv-2412-03676:
Francesco Innocenti and five co-authors set out JPC, a library for training networks that learn by foretelling their own input, built on a fast code base. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

Such networks, drawn from how the brain may work, learn by a flow of error through their layers. The library gives a plain, fast, and loose face for many forms: sorting, making, and mixed nets. In place of the plain step rule past libraries used, it solves the flow with true equation solvers. A second-order solver runs far faster, at like scores, across tasks and depths. The library adds theory tools to study such nets. The code is shared.
arxiv-2412-03776:
Stephen Lack and Shay Tobin characterize the category of Hilbert spaces using only abstract category theory, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Hilbert spaces are the stage of quantum mechanics, and knowing that a category must consist of them, from structural clues alone, is a deep kind of recognition.

Earlier characterizations by Heunen and Kornell leaned on a monoidal structure, and that assumption shut out quaternionic Hilbert spaces. The new approach drops the monoidal assumption entirely. Behind it stands Solèr's theorem, which forces a space satisfying certain symmetry conditions to be a Hilbert space over the reals, the complexes, or the quaternions. Lack and Tobin recover the real and complex cases and gain the quaternionic one as well. Their result widens the categorical fingerprint of Hilbert spaces. It also speaks to the foundations of quantum theory, where such recognition theorems matter.
arxiv-2412-03876:
Peng and co-authors tackle a safety problem in text-to-image models, which can produce harmful pictures despite built-in filters, in a 2024 paper. Existing guards are easily bypassed by crafted prompts. Their method, called prompt-noise optimization, needs no retraining of the model.

Instead, at generation time the method adjusts both the prompt's internal representation and the random noise that seeds the image, steering the output away from unsafe content. Tests show the approach blocks toxic generations at the level of the best current methods and resists attack prompts designed to break it. It runs at a comparable speed and keeps images faithful to safe prompts.
arxiv-2412-04376:
David Billington and co-authors measure magnetic noise in a material called spin ice in a 2024 paper. In spin ice, magnetic moments can act like free magnetic charges, called monopoles, that wander through the crystal. Past noise studies found a pink noise pattern and odd motion at low temperatures, but results at higher temperatures clashed.

The team used a magnetic response method that reaches far higher frequencies than past noise work. They measured the key exponent between two and twenty degrees above absolute zero. Their values show real departures from plain random motion up to about twenty degrees, larger than past noise studies found. Results varied by sample, which points to a role for crystal defects. The work refines the picture of monopole motion in a dense, strongly linked fluid.
arxiv-2412-04576:
Brandon Jaipersaud, Zining Zhu, Frank Rudzicz, and Elliot Creager use large language models to uncover how fiction shows character through action. Most tools rely on explicit statements about a character, such as a direct claim that someone is kind or bold. Stories often reveal character through deeds instead. The team first builds a story dataset with more varied topics, richer word choice, and longer narratives than standard sets. Their framework, LIIPA, then prompts models to infer the hidden portrayal.

The framework can use word lists or chain-of-thought steps as intermediate work. It beats earlier methods and holds up as the number of characters grows, because it reads the whole story. The team also finds a fairness and accuracy tradeoff. Some versions judge sex and race with bias. Even so, every version beats non-model baselines on fairness and accuracy together.
arxiv-2412-04876:
Pramesh Gautam and colleagues forecast interference for dense future factory networks, in work from 2024. Sixth generation sub networks must hit extreme delay and trust targets in tight spaces. Crowded links with fast channel shifts make interference the core threat to those targets.

Link tuning needs sharp forecasts, so the team models interference as hidden states. A state space model folds in model error plus signal and protocol delays. A Kalman filter variant then predicts values from channel quality reports alone. Tests beat the classic baseline by a clear margin on forecast accuracy. Scores matched a supervised learning rival despite far less input data.
arxiv-2412-05176:
Edoardo Loru and co-authors studied how ideology sets the agenda on social media in a 2024 paper. Feeds overflow with takes, and what a crowd talks about is no longer set by newsrooms alone. The team mined large X data sets from three global fights: climate change, COVID-19, and the war in Ukraine.

They found that talk sorts by shared ideology more than by actor type. Users form polarized camps, and a user's stance in one fight forecasts their camp in the next. Media and activists matter less than the camp pull itself. The result reframes how online agendas form.
arxiv-2412-05376:
Tali Palma and co-authors present a 2024 catalogue of star clusters that form pairs or groups in the Milky Way. Such systems show how clusters form and change through pull on each other. The team started from a database of 7,167 clusters. They kept only near neighbors, within a set span, and gauged the tidal pull on each one.

In all, 2,170 clusters took part in double or larger systems. The team sorted 617 paired systems into bound pairs, captured pairs, and pairs that only look close. They also found 261 groups with three or more members. Motion, age, and color data drove the sorting. The catalogue gives a firmer base for cluster studies.
arxiv-2412-05476:
Carlos Budde, Pedro D'Argenio, and Arnd Hartmanns model an open-pit mine in their 2024 case study. They want to find the best way to run trucks and loaders so the mine earns the most in a set time. Their model treats each choice and delay as a chance event in a formal network.

Exact checking of the model proved hopeless, since the number of states explodes even for a small mine. So the team sampled strategies at random and also tried a learning method that builds a score table. They added a way to turn the best strategies into decision trees, which people can read and trust. Tests showed the learning method has limits, but the trees made the winning plans clear.
arxiv-2412-06076: Kiyoshi Sogo generalizes Jacobi's theta relations in a 2024 paper. The old relations tie quartic products of theta functions. Sogo extends them to products of any length. An older way to derive them is stretched to prove the general case. A new notion, the cycle number, is key to the proof. General addition formulas and theta constant identities fall out along the way. The cubic case is worked through in full as a check.
arxiv-2412-06176:
Pranjal Aggarwal, Bryan Parno, and Sean Welleck build a system that writes code with proof that the code is right, in work from twenty twenty-four. Language models now write code fast, but they give no proof of correctness. Formal proof could supply that proof, yet proof data is scarce. Proofs are also hard for models to write from scratch. The team aims to grow proof skill with no human help.

Their system, AlphaVerus, works in three looping phases. First it tries translations of programs from a data-rich language. Next a tree search, called Treefinement, refines drafts with feedback from a checker. Last it filters out drafts whose specs and code do not match. That loop lets a large open model produce checked code on its own. Tests on two known coding sets show the path works. The work lays a base for code agents users can trust.
arxiv-2412-06276:
Yuanyang Zhou and co-authors use a trial-and-tune method to design three-qubit gates in semiconductor quantum dots, in a 2024 paper. Quantum dots are small traps that can hold spin qubits, the basic units of a quantum computer. Good three-qubit gates are a key step toward machines that can grow in size and still work well.

The design uses only terms that match real physical interactions, with no change over time. The gates built this way include two well-known types, the Toffoli and Fredkin gates. Both show high fidelity in tests. They also hold up well when noise is added, both from charge shifts and from nuclear spins. The method can be used for other systems too, such as superconducting qubits and trapped ions.
arxiv-2412-06576:
Timon Eichhorn and co-authors link a lone speck of doped crystal to a tiny light trap in a 2024 paper. The specks may one day host quantum bits in their long-lived core spins. A good link must steer the speck's glow into the trap so the bits can be read.

Cold tests show the trap boosts two glow lines of the doped ions at once. One line's life span halved, a boost of well over a hundred-fold for that line. A slim glow width for a few ions hints at clean reads, a step toward single-ion quantum nodes.
arxiv-2412-06776:
Fadini and Coros wrote this 2024 robotics paper on measuring and then maximizing how gracefully the motion of a robot resists perturbation. Stability is usually judged qualitatively, yet design optimization needs a number. Their metric is the Lyapunov exponent spectrum, computed through differentiable simulation run over long horizons, which naturally extends to the limit cycles of walking and other rhythmic tasks.

A gradient-based optimizer built on JAX then tunes designs and controllers against the exponent objective. The test bench spans simple systems up to high-degree-of-freedom machines in contact-rich settings where parts collide and grip. Across the board the optimization stiffened robustness in ways cruder metrics miss. The authors pitch exponent-guided design as a general tool for robots that must not fall over, in simulation or on the floor.
arxiv-2412-06876:
Emilio Santos presents a cosmology essay, printed in 2024, asking whether the quantum vacuum itself helps push the universe apart. The standard model of cosmology leans on dark energy to explain the accelerating expansion. Santos applies Einstein's equation, in a semiclassical form, to a spherical patch of universe filled with the standard model's matter plus the restless energy of empty space.

Expanding the math in powers of Newton's constant, the vacuum's contribution appears at second order, small but not nothing. The calculation suggests at least part of the observed acceleration could come from quantum vacuum fluctuations rather than a separate dark energy. Santos offers the result as a provocation to the standard picture, from a career spent on the quantum vacuum.
arxiv-2412-07176:
Yang Gao and co-authors report the first check of how mid-infrared glow tracks cold gas in early-type galaxies. These smooth, old galaxies hold less gas than spirals, so cheap gas gauges are prized. The team uses public WISE satellite data beside carbon monoxide line readings, the standard gas tracer.

The sample holds three hundred fifty-two early-type galaxies with both kinds of data. Glow at twelve microns tracks both main CO lines very tightly, with scatter under a tenth of a dex. Slopes here run steeper than in star-forming galaxies, and the CO line ratio shows no link to the glow. Shifts from the trend may stem from glow by old stars or from gas traits. A fixed glow gauge could thus speed gas surveys of old galaxies.
arxiv-2412-07776:
Alexander Pondaven and co-authors present a method in 2024 that copies the motion of one video onto a freshly made video. Their tool is built for the newest class of video generators, which use transformer blocks to clean up noise step by step. Motion copy lets a creator keep the action of a reference clip while the scene and actors change.

First they run the reference through a pre trained generator and read its cross frame attention maps. From those maps they extract a patch level motion signal. Then they steer the new video's hidden state so its motion matches that signal, with no training at all. They also tune the model's position codes for a further boost. Tests against recent rival methods favor theirs on several scores and in human judgments.
arxiv-2412-08176:
Jingjing Xie, Yuxin Zhang, and their co-authors present TextRefiner, a 2024 add on that sharpens prompt tuning for vision language models. Prompt learning adapts such models cheaply, but the learned prompts are usually shared across all classes, so they blur fine visual differences between similar classes. Other fixes borrow descriptions from large language models at some running cost.

TextRefiner instead mines the vision model's own image branch. A local cache module gathers fine visual concepts from image tokens. Those concepts are pooled and aligned with the text branch's output, enriching the prompts from within the model itself. The module plugs into existing prompt methods without outside knowledge. Tests showed better class separation at no added inference burden from external models.
arxiv-2412-08476:
Mangesh Daspute and co-authors model the interiors and habitability of four super-Earth exoplanets, in a research paper from 2024. The planets orbit dwarf stars in the habitable zone and sit within forty parsecs, which makes them prime targets for follow-up study. Their inner make-up decides whether surfaces could hold liquid water.

Bayesian modeling of interiors is paired with tidal heating and air heating estimates. Two planets look likely to be water worlds if air is thin. The other two may have rocky surfaces. Tidal heating alone cannot warm surfaces enough, but greenhouse heating can. With thick air and strong heat transport, some planets may run too hot for liquid water.
arxiv-2412-08576:
Alaa Ibrahim and Bruno Salvy give a way to prove that recurrence-made number lists stay positive, in a 2024 arXiv paper. Such lists grow by a rule that reuses past terms with polynomial weights. Telling if all terms stay above zero is hard in general. For fixed weights, a full answer is known only for short rules.

Their method works for a wide class of rules of any length. It builds a cone that the rule shrinks into itself, so positivity follows step by step. Starts outside one flat set can thus be proved positive. The cone build leans on a classic result on maps that keep a cone in place.
arxiv-2412-08876:
Jakob Robnik, Reuben Cohn-Gordon, and Uroš Seljak make a fast sampling method practical by removing its guesswork, in a 2024 paper. The head title calls it practical and scalable Hamiltonian Monte Carlo without the usual acceptance test. That test removes the small bias caused by rough numerical steps, but it also slows mixing and raises noise.

Skipping the test trades a little bias for much lower variance, yet few used the shortcut because picking the step size was an art. The authors tie the size of energy errors to the bias, then tune the step automatically to meet a bias limit the user sets. On hard test problems, including one with over a million parameters, the tuned shortcut beat the standard method clearly.
arxiv-2412-08976:
Lianrui Mu, Xingze Zou, Wenjie Zheng, Jiangnan Ye, and Haoji Hu wrote a 2024 computer vision paper on animating a character's photo with someone else's movements without losing the face. Pose guided animation copies motion from a driving video onto a still portrait. In lively scenes like dancing, the face often drifts or warps, because the driver's facial landmarks do not fit the reference face's geometry.

Their fix passes the landmarks through three dimensions. A morphable face model lifts the flat points into a 3D face, reshapes that face to match the reference identity, then flattens it back to guide the animation. Experiments showed identity held up far better through complex motion. The method targets games, film, and virtual avatars that must stay recognizably themselves.
arxiv-2412-09476:
Lee Mitchell and four co-authors report how the SIRI-2 instrument caught the extraordinary gamma-ray burst GRB 221009A without being blinded by it. Most detectors saturated on this record-breaking burst and needed pile-up corrections. SIRI-2, a set of strontium iodide detectors in geosynchronous orbit, stayed clean.

Its measured energetics agree with other instruments, and its spectral fits match the unsaturated Insight and GECAM results. The total fluence came out lower than elsewhere, likely because rising background forced a shorter counting window. Extrapolating from known bursts, the authors estimate events this bright should occur roughly once every four thousand years. The paper documents a rare unsaturated record of an extreme event.
arxiv-2412-09576:
Irakli Giorgadze and four co-authors study how to gauge the entanglement of states of many fermions, the class of parts that make up matter. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

Such states sit at the heart of quantum chemistry, a top use case for near-term quantum machines. Plain qubits pay a high cost to hold fermion traits. New fermion-based gear may cost less. The team reads entanglement through trimmed states, for cuts of the full space at many sizes. One gauge, the von Neumann disorder of the trimmed state, needs no base choice. It stretches the old one-part gauge of chemistry. They map the top bounds such gauges can reach.
arxiv-2412-09676:
A large survey team reports a planet smaller than Jupiter around a very light star or brown dwarf. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, rests on a microlensing event from twenty fifteen. In such events, a front star's gravity bends light from a back star and briefly brightens it. A planet near the front star adds a short extra blip.

Two survey telescopes, OGLE and MOA, each caught the blip cleanly. That double catch makes the planet claim firm, which is rare for survey-only finds. The host is so light that it may not be a true star at all. Such finds help count planets around the smallest hosts.
arxiv-2412-10276: Sergey Bobkov and Friedrich Götze prove a math result in a 2024 paper on chance distributions. The topic is the Kantorovich transport distance, a way to measure how far apart two chance patterns lie. They give an upper bound for that distance between patterns in many dimensions. The bound rests on the same distances between flat, one-line shadows of the patterns. Their result puts hard numbers on a classic theorem by Cramér and Wold about how chance patterns settle.
arxiv-2412-10376:
Vladimir Sluchak studies how to bend a repeating signal on purpose in a 2024 paper. Some filtration processes take in a smooth periodic signal, and only certain of its harmonics, the pure tones in its Fourier makeup, shape what comes out.

One case is the sound made by a spinning body in steady fluid flow. That sound can be steered through the strength of chosen harmonics of the inflow pattern around the circle. The author states the aims of such steering as soft targets. He then proves the needed inequalities that link broad traits of the signal to the sizes of its Fourier parts. The results give engineers bounds they can design against when shaping such sounds.
arxiv-2412-10476:
Tao Li and seven colleagues survey, in a 2024 preprint, a decade of research on testing web applications. Web apps run in browsers and build pages on the fly from user actions. Their mix of shifting content, background operations, and varied user setups makes testing hard. Yet quality matters more as user counts grow. The survey gathers what the field has produced over twelve years of fast change.

It walks through the main steps of testing: making test cases, running them, and judging the results. Tools built for each step are catalogued and compared. The authors sort the many approaches by the web traits they target. They close with open problems, such as keeping tests valid as apps change weekly. The paper aims to give new researchers a map of the area and veterans a view of where it should go next.
arxiv-2412-10876:
Weinan Lin, Guozhen Wang, and Zhouli Xu report machine proofs for Adams differentials in two thousand twenty-four. Adams computations decide deep facts about stable homotopy groups. Their dataset covers forty nine CW spectra and many maps. Sixty one cofiber sequences enter the records as well.

The document explains how the machine results were obtained. Detailed proofs back the computed differentials and extensions. Human insight adds ad hoc steps where the machine stops. Together they settled the Last Kervaire Invariant Problem in dimension one two six. The dataset sits on Zenodo for others to inspect.
arxiv-2412-11376:
Chengsen Wang and co-authors build ChatTime, a base model that treats time series as a foreign tongue, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Human experts blend numbers with text when reading series, but most forecast tools take numbers alone. Fixed windows and one-set training also cramp older tools.

ChatTime takes both series and text in, and returns both as well. It forecasts on fresh sets with no new training. The team built four mixed datasets to close data gaps and ran wide task checks. Results back the model's range across tasks and scenes. Readers get one model for series work where words and numbers meet.
arxiv-2412-11476:
Mengde Han and co-authors build a way to erase one client's data from a shared model in a 2024 arXiv paper. In split federated learning, firms train one model while each keeps its own data columns. Privacy law now grants a right to be forgotten, so a model must be able to drop one client's mark. Full retraining is costly and needs all data at hand.

Their method runs learning in reverse, climbing the loss slope under a bound model. A planted backdoor then proves the drop worked. Scores land close to retraining from scratch. The method stores no past updates and touches no raw data.
arxiv-2412-11576:
Interpretable image classifiers often explain themselves with a checklist of concepts, fur, stripes, beak, but building that checklist usually needs huge text or image collections. Katharina Prasse and co-authors design a leaner version in a 2024 paper: data-efficient concept bottleneck models.

Instead of borrowing concepts from a language model, their system cuts each image into regions with segmentation or detection tools and treats those regions, at several sizes, as the concepts. Every image thus supplies its own vocabulary, tuned to the dataset at hand. The approach suits fine-grained sorting and strange, out-of-distribution cases where canned concepts fail. Heat-map checks show the chosen regions really do sit on the object in new images. The authors frame the method as interpretability that travels light.
arxiv-2412-11776:
Clémentine Phung-Ngoc and five co-authors jointly reconstruct activity and attenuation in positron emission tomography using diffusion posterior sampling. Estimating both maps at once suffers crosstalk, above all without time of flight data. Diffusion models offer a prior that can separate the two quantities more cleanly.

Two dimensional phantom data from the XCAT model test the framework. The sampling approach significantly outperforms the traditional maximum likelihood method for joint estimation. Reconstructions stay consistent and high quality even with no time of flight information. Work in progress extends the method to real three dimensional data with encouraging early findings. Better joint maps could sharpen scans on scanners that lack timing hardware.
arxiv-2412-11876:
Anna Lentz studies measures that can sit on wild sets yet vanish where a space is too thin to hold them. These capacitary measures tie to relaxed edge problems, where the best edge value may not exist in plain form. Her 2024 work moves a key tightness result from smooth spaces to rougher ones.

The rough spaces allow fractional smoothness, a dial between plain and smooth. Lentz proves the measures stay tight under a matching form of convergence there too. That proof then sharpens the best-possible terms for a class of minimization problems in those spaces. The work is pure theory, aimed at readers in analysis. It rounds out a picture that was known only for the smooth case.
arxiv-2412-11976:
Elena Poli and co-authors studied a strange state of matter in 2024 that acts as both a solid and a fluid at once. Such a state is called a supersolid. When the team set their supersolid spinning, its crystal part fell into step with an outside rhythm. That match was sparked by the birth of tiny whirlpools in the fluid part.

By checking their model against lab results, the team turned this match into a probe. It can show the spin rate at which the whirlpools first form. The work gives physicists a fresh way to test how such mixed states react when they are set in motion.
arxiv-2412-12776:
Maese, Caballero, and Merino build a simulator for a flying and ground robot pair tied by a hanging cable, in a 2024 robotics paper. In these marsupial systems, the drone rides or deploys from the ground vehicle, and a winch adjusts the tether length. Tether sway and pull shape how both robots move, above all in tight spaces. The simulator models the drone, the vehicle, and the winch together.

Extensive tests compared the simulated motion with real-world deployments. The match was close, especially where tether effects dominate. A trusted simulator lets teams rehearse missions that would be risky or slow to test live. The authors offer the tool for studying control strategies in tethered robot teams, from inspection to rescue work.
arxiv-2412-13376:
Christian Green, Mehmet Ergezer, and Abdurrahman Zeybey present a 2024 paper on attacks that fool systems which recognize three-dimensional objects. Such systems often view an object from many angles. A weak spot is a small, crafted noise pattern that makes the system name the wrong object.

Their method, called VIAP, builds one noise pattern that works from many viewpoints. It can also be aimed, forcing the system to output a chosen wrong label. They tested it on 1,210 images of 121 rendered objects. The untargeted version held up under rotations and other changes of view. The targeted version reached top accuracy above 95 percent in their tests. The work offers a way to stress-test vision systems before real-world use.
arxiv-2412-13576:
Wenbo Liu, Akang Wang, and Wenguo Yang present a 2024 mathematics paper on solving hard whole-number optimization problems. One known strategy improves a current answer step by step along special directions drawn from a set called the Graver basis. The catch is that finding those directions is itself very hard.

The authors build a heavily parallel shortcut that hunts for promising directions by solving smooth stand-in problems with fast first-order methods on many processors at once. They test the approach on two public problem libraries used to benchmark solvers. Their method matched the performance of advanced solvers, which suggests the step-by-step strategy could become practical for larger nonlinear problems.
arxiv-2412-13676:
Drones that ferry computing tasks to edge servers must save energy without wobbling off course. Bin Li, Xiao Zhu, and Junyi Wang tackle that joint problem in a 2024 paper on drone-assisted mobile edge computing with data compression.

Shrinking data before sending cuts the energy cost of offloading tasks. The team frames flight path and task scheduling as a learning problem and applies an ensemble Q-learning method that can learn more from each batch of experience. In simulations, the scheme cut user energy use while keeping flight stable. It beat two rival learning methods by roughly a fifth and a third in energy terms. The authors see promise for real drone networks in messy settings.
arxiv-2412-13776:
Kaihong Lu, Huanshui Zhang, and Long Wang study games where the shared aggregate that players react to is itself chosen by an inner optimization. In these aggregative games with bilevel structure, a virtual leader's objective sets the aggregation. Each player sees only a local piece of that objective.

The authors propose a distributed algorithm using second-order gradient information, including Hessian matrices of the leader's costs. Players update their actions while jointly estimating the aggregation through neighbor communication on a connected graph. Under mild assumptions, the actions converge to the Nash equilibrium. A second part of the paper treats the case where Hessian information is unavailable.
arxiv-2412-13876:
Simon Badger and co-authors compute a key scattering quantity for top-quark pair plus jet production at particle colliders, at two-loop precision. Such numbers let physicists compare collider data with theory at matching sharpness. The gluon channel with leading color is their target.

Their new trick re-bases the hard integrals on special functions so that the divergent parts cancel cleanly on paper, even with elliptic integrals in play. The elliptic parts survive only in the final finite answer, which they expand as series and evaluate in real event conditions. Finite-field algebra and projectors built the amplitudes. The result is a first benchmark for this process.
arxiv-2412-13976:
Louie Corpe, Thomas Chehab, and Andreas Goudelis vet the kit that lets outsiders re-read a CERN hunt for long-lived exotic parts. The hunt sought pairs of such parts that die late into sprays of normal bits in the heat gauge zone. Its re-read kit is a map from true part paths to the odds a spray makes the cut. Their note runs the map on fake events and checks the bounds it gives.

The map won back the bounds the first hunt post in the test. Soft spots in the kit are named, from lost facts to thin zones of the map. The vet steps themselves draw fire for gaps in what the first post shared. Re-cast hunts live or die on such kits, the note warns.
arxiv-2412-14276:
Shaina Raza, Drai Paulen-Patterson, and Chen Ding grade fake-news spotters in a 2024 paper. Fake tales sway crowds and shake trust, so sound spotting tools count. Which kind of model spots best, small tuned readers or big chat models, was not fairly weighed on one set.

Their set of news tales was tagged with a top chat model's aid, then checked by human eyes. Both model kinds were tuned on it, and a taught chat model with vote-count calls joined the race. Small readers won the clean calls, while big models held up better under noise. Each kind earns its place.
arxiv-2412-14776:
Dimitar Garkov, Tommaso Piselli, and their co-authors tested whether working in pairs inside mixed reality helps people solve graph problems together. Their 2024 study compares lone workers, working pairs, and nominal pairs, a benchmark in which two solo results are combined after the fact. Seventy two people took part across two countries and three languages.

Tasks involved reading and reasoning about visual graphs in a three dimensional mixed reality space. A complexity measure rated how demanding each task instance was. True pairs did not beat the nominal benchmark, which the authors stress as the right yardstick for judging shared virtual spaces. Three dimensional graph views alone, they conclude, are not enough to make collaboration pay off.
arxiv-2412-14876:
Kevin Marc Seja, Niclas Wall-Wennerdal, Tomas Löfwander, Annica Black-Schaffer, Mikael Fogelström, and Patric Holmvall wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four, with fuller names in its text. It maps how dirt, in the form of impurities, fights a phase crystal state at the edge of a nodal d-wave superconductor.

Phase crystals are ground states with built-in phase slopes that drive rings of current and break time symmetry. The team uses a t-matrix method with full self-consistency to chart the state against impurity strength and heat. The crystal holds up to a large share of the strength that would kill superconductivity outright, in both weak and strong scattering. In small samples a rival edge state with even currents competes.
arxiv-2412-15176:
Lukas Aichberger, Kajetan Schweighofer, and Sepp Hochreiter rethink uncertainty scores for language models in this 2024 paper. Knowing when a model is unsure is key to trusting its text. Leading methods sample many outputs and compare them, which is costly at scale. The authors inspect the theory behind those methods.

Proper scoring rules point to a simpler measure. The negative log likelihood of the most likely output is itself a principled uncertainty score. Their method, G-NLL, estimates it from one greedy output sequence. No repeated sampling is needed. Tests across varied scenarios matched the best prior methods. The result challenges the need for complex multi sample scoring in routine use.
arxiv-2412-15476:
Iiro Kumpulainen, Sebastian Dalleiger, Jilles Vreeken, and Nikolaj Tatti ask, in a 2024 paper, how to find structure shared across many networks at once. The classic stochastic block model sorts a graph's nodes into blocks with similar linking patterns. Real work, though, often hands us several graphs of different sizes whose nodes do not line up. The authors define the shared version of the problem.

They prove that fitting such a shared model exactly is NP-hard, then give two workable routes. One searches directly with a sampling algorithm. The other fits each graph on its own and then picks which blocks to share, by exact optimization or by a fast greedy rule. On synthetic and real data, both routes recovered shared structure well. The work serves anyone comparing networks across sites or times.
arxiv-2412-15676:
Jahnavi Kumar and Sridhar Chimalakonda test one shared model for three code review jobs, trained without pooling private code, in a 2024 study. Reviewers must judge if a change needs review, write comments, and fix the code. Past tools treated each job alone. The authors join them in one multi-task model, then train it across owners with federated learning, so code stays home.

They tried five ways to run the joint training: two step-by-step schemes, one parallel scheme, and two that stack skills over time. Step-by-step training fared worst, since the model forgot early skills as it learned new ones. Stacked training beat even single-job models. Sharing a model across firms also held up on unseen code. The authors call for more work on how such shared models should be tuned.
arxiv-2412-15776:
Self-amplifying web structures are hunted with math tuning by Víctor Blanco, Gabriel González, and Praful Gagrani in a 2024 arXiv paper. The head gives that title, while the catalog title names top growth of such subnetworks. A score, the maximal amplification factor, gauges how well a sub-web feeds its own growth. The team casts the hunt as a hard mixed number problem.

An exact step method solves it with proof it settles. Wide tests on fake but fair cases show the method works. A case study on chemical webs, from a sugar-making loop to gut germ core paths, found known and new self-feeding sub-webs.
arxiv-2412-16076:
Hesham El Faham and five co-authors wrote this 2024 paper on how to sharpen the search for new physics at high-energy colliders. The team works within a framework that extends the Standard Model with added terms, and they focus on contact interactions among four fermions. At very high energies, weak-force effects grow large, so the team asks how those effects change the added terms.

The authors work out the needed corrections and apply them to top quark pair production and to the Drell-Yan process, at both a current collider and a planned muon collider. They find that the correction factors differ from the plain model case and depend on both the process and the term chosen. The team also shows that these corrections can help pin down directions in the parameter space that lower-order work leaves flat.
arxiv-2412-16176:
Emergency calls often break up just when clear speech matters most. Danush Venkateshperumal, Rahman Abdul Rafi, Shakil Ahmed, and Ashfaq Khokhar wrote a 2024 paper on fixing weak internet voice calls used by emergency services. Packet loss, low bandwidth, poor signal, delay, and jitter all hurt call quality. Panic, speech problems, and loud noise make callers harder to understand, and short staffing adds more delay.

The authors propose large language models to rebuild broken speech and fill gaps in what was said. Their plan pairs live transcription with search-based generation and uses Twilio and AssemblyAI tools. Tests gave high precision and good text match scores. The work points to faster sorting of the most urgent calls first.
arxiv-2412-16276:
Yingxu Wang and co-authors built this 2024 classifier for antimicrobial peptides, short proteins that kill microbes and could seed new antibiotics. Mining them from metagenomic data is promising, but known examples are rare next to non-examples, and sequence-only methods miss shape, which decides function. The team predicted each peptide's three-dimensional form with a fast folding tool and built a graph from its backbone atoms.

Their graph network learned structural features from that lean representation. Two weighting tricks fought the class imbalance: one sharpened contrast between similar and dissimilar peptides, another distilled knowledge from confidently guessed labels. The design aims at accuracy where data are both scarce and skewed, the normal state of antibiotic discovery.
arxiv-2412-16676:
Yihui Tong and co-authors study, in a 2024 math paper, a family of diffusion equations proposed to clean a speckled form of noise from images. Multiplicative noise, common in radar and medical scans, is harder to remove than plain grain. Their equations flow forward in some places and backward in others, with an added source term.

Using a step-by-step time method, a relaxation result, and a fixed-point theorem, the authors prove that solutions of a generalized kind exist for the model. They also show results on how solutions depend on the starting image. Computer tests then compare the model's cleaning power with rival methods, showing clear gains on test images.
arxiv-2412-16776:
Sanghyun Son and co-authors introduce DMesh++, a faster way to work with triangular meshes whose connections themselves can shift and learn. Recent probabilistic mesh methods capture varied shapes by making connectivity differentiable, but they slow down badly as shapes grow detailed. The new method cuts the time cost from linear to logarithmic in the number of elements and uses far less memory.

On top of it, the team builds a reconstruction algorithm that turns point clouds or sets of photos into complex two- and three-dimensional shapes. The approach targets the intricate structures that older methods could not afford to represent. Code and extra material are posted on the project page.
arxiv-2412-17076:
Benjamin Aymard studies how order and chaos emerge in a spreading, reacting system in this 2024 mathematics paper. The model tracks two species that diffuse and react, with extra terms for self-diffusion and cross-diffusion. Such systems are known for Turing patterns, the regular stripes and spots that appear when diffusion destabilizes a uniform state.

Aymard builds a Fourier spectral method to follow the system's steady states and orbits with high accuracy. That accuracy matters when tracing periodic orbits and testing their stability. Varying one control parameter across four diffusion regimes, he finds new kinds of Turing patterns and oscillating patterns born through Hopf bifurcations. Further changes trigger period doubling that ends in chaos. The paper closes by reporting new strange attractors, the tangled sets that chaotic orbits trace in phase space.
arxiv-2412-17176:
Md Mahmuddun Nabi Murad, Mehmet Aktukmak, and Yasin Yilmaz wrote a 2024 paper on forecasting long stretches of time series data. Forecasts of weather, power demand, and prices all depend on spotting patterns at several scales at once. Recent mixer models, built from simple layers, rival fancy attention models at this task but had not reached their full strength.

Their model, WPMixer, splits the series with wavelets into layers of detail, from slow trends to fast wiggles. It then cuts the series into patches and mixes information within and across patches. Tests showed it beat leading mixer and attention models on long-range forecasts. The design keeps the cost low, which matters when forecasts run every few minutes.
arxiv-2412-17576:
Senne Vervoort and co-authors, in a 2024 paper, show how arrays of Josephson junctions can make and sense microwave signals right on a cold chip. Circuits that work at very low temperatures now need bulky, costly cables to carry radio signals in from room temperature gear. A junction array runs on plain direct current, and sits inside the chip itself.

The team built arrays from thin superconductor islands joined by gold links, using two kinds of base material. They varied heat, magnetic fields, current, and design to steer the signals the arrays give off. The signals reached the C band range and beyond. Since such arrays can also detect microwaves, the authors propose a full on chip platform run by direct current alone. That would shrink cold measurement setups.
arxiv-2412-17776:
Davide Bilò and co-authors design data structures that answer network questions fast after links fail. A network may lose a few nodes or links, and planners still need sound answers at once. Such a structure pre-reads the network and a failure bound. It then answers for any small set of failures without a full re-run.

Three questions are covered: short paths with few links, paths of a set length, and tight groups of a set size. The core tool is a family of backup subnetworks that keep at least one good path. The new build queries that family far faster than past builds, at near the same size. Oracles for all three questions flow from it, with a clear speed gain for path queries.
arxiv-2412-17876:
Elgammal reads the spin of a proposed Z-prime boson from the angles of muon pairs in simulated collider data. The paper from twenty twenty-four uses electron-positron runs at the planned International Linear Collider. Low-mass muon pairs there come mostly from the Drell-Yan process, which leans forward-backward in a set way. New physics models bend that angular shape in their own ways.

The study tracks one angle in the Collins-Soper frame. A mono-Z-prime model, with fermionic dark matter in tow, interprets the mock data. No new signal is assumed found. Upper limits at a set confidence level then bound the masses of the model's particles. The spin-one nature of the Z-prime is the trait under the lens. The work shows how angular shapes can sort rival models before any discovery lands.
arxiv-2412-18376:
Raven Adam and Marie Lisa Kogler introduce a way to compare the themes of two text collections, in this 2024 paper. Their method, Bidirectional Topic Matching, trains a topic model on each corpus and then runs each model on the other corpus. That two-way pass reveals both the themes the collections share and the ones each holds alone.

The framework accepts several topic toolkits, from classic allocation models to modern embedding-based ones. Checks against similarity-based methods showed strong agreement. A case study on climate news separated shared ground from split angles between climate change and climate action coverage.
arxiv-2412-18676:
Bor, Hernández-Lamoneda, and Tabachnikov study the tracks a bicycle leaves when its front wheel steers a closed loop, in a 2024 paper. A bike's rear wheel traces a second curve; riding the loop again applies a transformation, the bicycling monodromy, to that trace. The question is when this transformation is hyperbolic, stretching one direction and squeezing another.

Their main tool reimagines the process as a hyperbolic development of the curve. With it they prove fresh necessary and sufficient conditions for hyperbolicity. Computer experiments on strictly convex loops then suggest two conjectures. Recreational geometry here touches deep dynamics: a plaything becomes a lens on surface theory.
arxiv-2412-19076:
Dima Galat reports a 2024 study of methods to spot AI-written text, done for a shared task at a language tech meeting. The task was to judge text sentence by sentence inside mixed articles, where human and machine lines sit side by side. Good spotting tools are in rising demand as made text spreads.

One model's output showed distinct, repeating chance patterns that allowed steady spotting within its own domain. Light edits such as rewording barely dented the scores. The paper sets out the methods tried and what the results mean for building stronger detectors of made text.
arxiv-2412-19176:
Le and co-authors compare tuning methods for a quantum algorithm that estimates ground-state energies, in this 2024 paper. The algorithm, called VQE, splits work between a quantum chip and a classical optimizer. Which optimizer steers it best on today's noisy hardware is an open question.

Using a magnetism model as the test bed, the team ran classical and quantum-aware optimizers side by side. They also built a hybrid scheme that pairs a natural-gradient method with cheap gradient guesses and exact checks. The hybrid improved stability and speed per step while staying light on resources. The findings may sharpen optimization across quantum learning tasks.
arxiv-2412-19776:
Habibi, Kocvara, and Stingl tackle in 2024 the numeric solution of Lasserre relaxations for binary quadratic optimization. Such relaxations grow into large semidefinite programs that standard solvers handle poorly. Their approach uses an interior point method whose inner systems are solved by a gradient method with preconditioning.

The preconditioner exploits the low rank form of relaxation solutions, after a rewrite of the moment form. An exact penalty handles the equality constraints inside the solver. Tests on max cut and random problems beat a leading semidefinite solver and an alternating method in their runs. A hybrid of the two methods also proved efficient for some classes.
arxiv-2412-19876:
Ninad Jadhav, Meghna Behari, Robert Wood, and Stephanie Gil explore unknown spaces with robots that share no maps, in work from 2024. Teams must cover new ground fast while link bandwidth stays tight in the field. Signal pings alone can give rough partner positions without full data exchange.

Their method uses only local partner range guesses from onboard radio signals. Each robot picks its next goal to cut overlap with nearby partners by that clue. Teams can end at split times with no shared map held in common. Tests cut overlap by over half versus a no sharing baseline method. Hardware runs with full onboard sensing backed the simulation gains.
arxiv-2501-00576:
Antoni Kijowski, Sebastiano Nicolussi Golo, and Ben Warhurst wrote this mathematics paper on when two curved spaces share the same diffusion geometry. The catalog dates it 2025, while the paper itself says 2024. On sub-Riemannian Lie groups, the sub-Laplacian plays the role the ordinary Laplacian plays in flat space, spreading heat along allowed directions only. The trio ask which smooth maps between such groups respect that operator.

Their answer is sharp: exactly the maps that are sub-Riemannian conformal submersions, a rigid class that stretches space evenly while projecting it down. The result tidies earlier work begun on Carnot groups. A striking corollary follows: on a Carnot group, the sub-Laplacian alone determines the whole sub-Riemannian structure, so sound, in effect, reveals the shape of the space.
arxiv-2501-00776:
Priya, Simran Arora and B. Chauhan wrote a 2025 paper on the masses of neutrinos, the lightest known matter particles. Some models set one entry of the mass matrix to zero. The team added a broad symmetry rule to those models. That pairing yields mass patterns that can be tested.

Their work draws links between key values, such as the mixing angle that future beam tests will measure. They also weigh a rare decay that labs are hunting for. One mass order, they find, clashes with limits from space data on total neutrino mass. New survey limits may rule out more of the model cases.
arxiv-2501-01076:
Niraj Inamdar gives exact algebra answers to a classic locating problem: finding a sound or signal source from the delays between its arrivals at several sensors, in a 2025 paper. Rescue beacons, gunshots, and underwater calls are all pinned down this way. Standard solutions lean on approximations, repeated refinement, or least-squares fitting. Inamdar's versions use nothing but the arrival delays and plain vector algebra, with no fitting step at all.

Solutions are given for five sensors and for four. The five-sensor answer is clean outright, while the four-sensor answer needs one sign choice resolved. Tests without noise show the maths lands exactly, within computing error. The rare failures come from picking the wrong sign in the four-sensor case. The paper offers engineers formulas that are exact, transparent, and quick to run.
arxiv-2501-01876:
Pengzhou Chen, Jingzhi Gong, and Tao Chen ran a huge empirical study in 2025 asking whether a more accurate surrogate model really tunes software configurations better. Tuning is costly because each trial means measuring a real system, so a learned stand-in model is used to guess performance cheaply. The field's working belief is that accuracy is all: build a truer model, get a better tune.

Their study ran for thirteen months around the clock and covered ten models, seventeen tuners, and twenty-nine systems under four settings, in the scale reported. That scale lets them test whether small accuracy gains matter to the tuner at all, and what role accuracy plays in tuning quality. Readers get a challenge to a stereotype, backed by one of the largest tuning studies to date.
arxiv-2501-02676:
Penrose and Yang count parts in chance shape graphs at the dense edge. Points fall at chance in a tight zone with a smooth rim. A set span ties which points join by line in the graph. Three counts lead: whole parts, off-giant points, and lone points. Picks of the span make one count grow but at a slow pace. Mean lone counts grow vast in that pick frame as well.

All three counts then run near one mark in chance terms. That mark takes a closed form for flat zones of two parts. For three or more parts, a rim term joins the closed form. Spread and bell claims cap the counts for the high case. A Poisson in-feed case gets the same care in the work. Off-flat point spreads join the claim set in the close.
arxiv-2501-02776: Kohki Iba studies what happens to a one-dimensional Lévy process when it is forced to avoid a bounded set. In this short 2025 paper, Iba looks at the limit of the process as the time window grows without bound, with the condition that the path never enters the forbidden set. Several kinds of bounded set are treated, each paired with its own random clock.
arxiv-2501-03076:
Levine and Friedman test in 2025 a deep idea about how quantum systems settle into balance. The eigenstate thermalization hypothesis says a small part of an excited system should look thermal on its own. They study free fermions linked to a reservoir through only a few narrow channels, called quantum point contacts.

With so few links, the small system's entanglement grows only with its edge length, not its volume, unlike a normal thermal system. At low energies the entropy followed the pattern of a one-dimensional system. Each added channel contributed a fixed, quantized share. The result shows that connection geometry can change even equilibrium properties, not just the time needed to reach them.
arxiv-2501-03276:
Yoel Zeldes and co-authors built ComMer in 2025, a way to personalize big language models on a budget. Feeding a user's documents into every prompt is capped by context size and costs at each call. Fine-tuning the model per user costs even more and ages fast.

ComMer instead squeezes each user's documents into a compact code. Codes from many sources merge into one, which feeds a frozen model. The squeeze happens once, offline, and the merged code rides along cheaply. Personal answers then draw on the user's own material without retraining. The frame suits services with millions of users and little compute to spare.
arxiv-2501-03376:
Dora Medgyesy and co-authors test how a social robot's personality changes what users feel, in work from 2025. Robots now work in homes, schools, and clinics. Designers need to know whether a warm manner helps or harms trust.

Twelve students took part in a study at a university in Amsterdam. Each student met a small robot that asked health questions in two modes. One mode showed a clear personality, while the other stayed flat and task-focused. Speech tools let the robot talk and listen. After both rounds, students rated their feelings and views of the robot. The contrast helps designers choose a tone that fits care settings.
arxiv-2501-03476:
Jiangshan Lan, Jialin Chen, Zhimin Zhu, Chandan Mondal, Xingbo Zhao, and James Vary compute strange meson spectra in a 2025 physics paper. Their tool is a light-front Hamiltonian fed with QCD input. It includes quark-antiquark pairs plus a dynamical gluon component. A three-dimensional confinement force completes the setup.

One set of states describes many kaon traits at once. Charge shape, decay rate, and internal share plots all fit. Quark and gluon share curves evolve with energy scale as QCD demands. The team also forecast a kaon-nucleus collision cross section. A CERN program is expected to measure that rate soon. The work ties meson structure to testable predictions.
arxiv-2501-03676:
Zheng Chun builds on an offline reinforcement learning method, TD7, by adding ensemble Q-networks and a gradient diversity penalty drawn from another method. Offline learning trains from logged data alone, where out of sample acts can skew values. The work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The base method learns state action codes and replays key past steps first. Ensembles punish the actor for stray acts, which keeps it near the data. The diversity penalty spreads Q gradients, which further damps over high values for stray acts. A cloning term guides early training, then fades as the ensemble sharpens. Tests on robot control benchmarks beat past methods in speed and score.
arxiv-2501-04276:
Yichao Zhong and co-authors, the full byline given in the head, teach legged robots to run fast without hitting things, even when the ground rules change. Real floors can be slick, loads can shift, and a robot must stay both quick and safe as those facts vary.

Their system, BAS, pairs a fast policy that dodges with a rescue policy that stops a crash. A judge network, trained on control theory, picks which policy runs. A third part guesses the physical facts, like friction and load, and both policies adapt to the guess. In tests the system was safer and faster than rivals, in sim and on real floors.
arxiv-2501-04376:
Xinghe Fu and colleagues investigated why deepfake detectors fail on new material in 2025. The usual explanation blames differences between forgery techniques. Their investigation showed failures also appear when factors unrelated to forgery change, and they traced the problem to two biases detectors pick up during training.

The first bias is positional: detectors lean on where a suspicious region sits in the image, even in spots with no forgery. The second is content bias: detectors use irrelevant details such as background or hair to decide. To fight both, the authors add two branches that shuffle and mix the image tokens inside a transformer's hidden space, scrambling positions and content while keeping local structure. The aim is a detector that judges the forgery itself and generalizes more honestly.
arxiv-2501-04476:
Patrick Bastian, writing alone in 2025, argues for a different measuring stick when hunting change points in curve data. Many data sets arrive as whole curves over time, one per subject or day. A change point is where the average curve suddenly shifts. Past tests measured that shift with two common norms. Bastian proposes a test based on the L1 norm, which sums absolute gaps. He proves the test is valid for classic and for broader hypotheses.

Theory and experiments both favor the new stick in many settings. Its edge is widest across a broad range of cases, he shows. A power booster is added for cases where the shift is sparse. The method is shown on made-up data and on real data as well. Choosing the right norm turns out to matter a great deal. The paper is a methods piece for statisticians who work with curve data.
arxiv-2501-04676:
Álvaro Castañeda, Claudio Gallegos, and Néstor Jara study systems that change from step to step, in a 2025 math paper. Such step-by-step systems appear in models where the rules themselves shift over time. The team looks at spectra, sets of growth rates that sort the system's behavior into stable and unstable parts.

Their focus is a flexible kind of split behavior, where growth is measured against a chosen pace function. They prove spectrum theorems for both even and uneven cases.
