The uneven case hides odd behavior that earlier work used without fully facing. The authors name two new traits of such systems and propose a fresh spectrum concept that sits between known ones. They also show, against recent belief, that one classic spectrum can break when two systems are loosely alike.
arxiv-2501-04776:
Erik Recio-Armengol and Joseph Bowles present a software package called IQPopt in a 2025 paper. The package helps researchers tune a class of quantum circuits known as IQP circuits on normal computers. Such circuits are thought to be hard for normal computers to copy once they run on real quantum hardware. Finding good settings before that step can save time and point to the most useful designs.

IQPopt uses a fast simulation method to estimate what a circuit will output. It can handle circuits with thousands of qubits and millions of gates when the goal can be stated in simple terms. The package builds on the JAX library, so it can use graphics cards for speed. It also includes tools to train and test quantum models that learn to generate data.
arxiv-2501-05376:
A rare class of insulators breaks the standard chart of matter states. Konstantinos Ladovrechis and Shouvik Sur ask what happens when such a state is pushed by linked particle play, in work from twenty twenty-five. Their study circles the edge point where the rare state meets a plain state. Past that point, fresh states can bloom.

Two fresh states emerge in their math: a gap-free state with odd cones, and a fresh insulator state. The gap-free state can host one-way superflow and a ghost sheet of particles, a mix that may explain a known diode-like effect in superflow gear. The work ties the rare insulators to two known gap-free families in one frame.
arxiv-2501-05876:
Leandro Arosio and Matteo Fiacchi wrote a survey in two thousand twenty-five on a property of paths in curved spaces. In a well-behaved space, shortest paths that head toward the boundary should approach each other in a controlled way. That approaching geodesics property links the geometry of a space to maps of its edge at infinity.

The authors gather recent results and open questions on the property. They cover its use in studying two ways of adding a boundary to a space, and new results on how symmetries of the space move. They also give an example of a well-behaved complex domain where the property fails.
arxiv-2501-06076:
Melissande Machefer and co-authors build, in a 2025 paper, an open data set that joins the main world food security gauges in one file. Food crises need fast, full data to track and to foretell, yet the gauges sit in split stores with split place codes. Their set, HFID, merges four sources: two phase scales for crisis grade, and two survey scores on what homes eat and how they cope. It is updated each month and uses one shared list of local units, so places line up across sources.

The set spans wide ground and long time, at the level below the nation. Aid groups can use it to watch risk and to plan help. The team also shows where data are thin, so gaps can be closed. Model builders gain a clean base for forecast tools.
arxiv-2501-06276:
Shaozuo Zhang, Ambuj Mehrish, Yingting Li, and Soujanya Poria give a speech forge a heart in a 2025 paper. A forge can read text in a clean voice, yet joy, grief, and zeal are hard to dial at will.

Their frame takes a word cue for the feel and a knob for its strength, across many voice kinds. Big word tools bend the tune of the speech while the words stay the same. Feel cues are set in the frame's own space, so a cue can blend or swap mid-line. Tests of the dials show each one bites as meant. The authors say cue-led feel gives speech craft a near-man range of voice.
arxiv-2501-06376:
Filippo Lazzati and Alberto Maria Metelli study robustness when a target reward can only be partly identified from feedback, in a research paper from 2025. Reward learning tries to recover an unknown reward from human or system feedback. When feedback is thin, many rewards fit the data, and picking the wrong one can break the planned use.

Their framework measures the performance drop caused by that uncertainty. A robust method then plans for the worst reward in the feasible set. Their algorithm applies the idea to choosing between two policies, with guarantees on sample and step counts. A small proof-of-concept test illustrates the setting and the gain.
arxiv-2501-06476:
Xing Li, Ying-ying Sun, and Da-jun Zhang build a direct route to solutions of a classic wave equation. Their 2025 paper treats the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equation, a model for shallow water waves. Their scheme is elliptic, built around the Lamé function from the theory of elliptic curves. It pairs an integral equation with a formula for wave solutions.

They check the scheme against the equation's known symmetry pairs. Careful study of real-valuedness leads to a Marchenko equation for the elliptic waves. A mechanism in the scheme yields smooth, real wave trains on a repeating background. Reductions then carry the results to two cousin equations, for water waves and long waves. Pictures of the solutions show solitons crossing on the periodic swell.
arxiv-2501-06576:
Many hard problems in math ask for a point that stays fixed under a mapping while also solving an inclusion. Furmose Mendy and John Mendy present an iterative method for such problems in a 2025 paper, working in Hilbert space with maps that may take many values and only mildly shrink distances. Their process adds a viscosity term, a gentle pull that steadies the iteration, plus an extra sequence of iterates.

Each round blends the fixed-point step with that steadying pull. The authors prove the sequence converges strongly to a true solution, which they argue makes the method dependable for this class of problems.
arxiv-2501-06676:
Azeef Muhammed and Gomes build, in a 2025 algebra paper, a structure theory for a class of semigroups called left reductive regular semigroups. Semigroups model sets with a combining rule but no undo button. In this class, the right ideal structure hides inside the left one, so one object can seed a full build.

The authors upgrade a classic category tool from Nambooripad into what they call a connected category. Their main theorem sets up a two-way match between these semigroups and connected categories. They then specialize the match to unipotent semigroups, bands, inverse semigroups, and regular monoids. Concrete cases cover finite transformation semigroups, linear ones, and symmetric inverse monoids. The frame unifies many older build recipes.
arxiv-2501-06976:
Demetris Chrysostomou, Jose Luis Rueda Torres, and Jochen Lorenz Cremer release a Python package that maps flexibility in power grids in 2025. Grid operators need to know how much slack local networks can offer. That slack must be used without breaking local limits. No open package existed for mapping it.

Their package ships four estimation methods, from fast math to full power flow checks. It can adapt maps across working states. Providers that offer fixed step changes are handled as well. The aim is wider uptake by operators and researchers. Open code lets others test and extend the methods. The paper frames flexibility maps as a daily tool for modern grids.
arxiv-2501-07076:
Tongxu Zhang and Bei Wang teach point cloud tools to learn from whole and part views at once in a 2025 paper. Point clouds are dot sets that trace a 3D form; upsampling fills their gaps. Sparse, noisy zones oft break past builds. Their frame, ReLPU, cuts each cloud two ways: even chunks for whole form and patches for local grain. Twin coders read both feeds, then fuse them for one shared build.

The frame plugs into top coder-based nets. Tests on set data banks show firm gains in form truth and noise grit. Saliency maps show the twin feeds sharpen what the nets heed. Thin zones gain most, the team find. The paper serves 3D build and sight work.
arxiv-2501-07176:
Jan Tristram Acuña, Kuan-Yen Chou, and Po-Yan Tseng (2025) ask whether axion clumps could betray themselves by bending radio signals. Axions are particles proposed as dark matter. Theory says they can gather into axion stars, dense balls held together by gravity and their self-interactions. If such stars make up part of the dark matter, light passing near one would be bent. This effect is called lensing. The bend changes when the star's finite size is counted, and again through its coupling to light.

The team calculates how often fast radio bursts would be lensed by these stars. These bursts are brief flashes from distant galaxies. Because coupling depends on frequency, low-frequency radio is the best probe. Their predicted event counts turn into limits on the axion's properties. They also limit how much dark matter can sit inside such stars.
arxiv-2501-07276:
Sartipi and co-authors benchmark in 2025 methods for filling gaps in smart meter data. Missing values from sensor faults and transmission errors bias energy analysis and forecasts. Classic methods struggle with the nonlinear, shifting patterns of meter data as volume grows.

Two general language models and five time series foundation models were tested against machine learning and statistical baselines. Fake gaps from thirty minutes to a day were cut into a public anonymized dataset. Foundation models won on accuracy in certain cases thanks to context reading. Cost though may outweigh the gain, a trade off the study keeps in view.
arxiv-2501-08276:
Pulkit Arora, Akbar Karimi, and Lucie Flek wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on whether language models handle reworded text evenly across social groups. Models can be thrown off by small changes to their input. Most robustness work twists single words, while real variation follows the style of whole communities.

The team extended a question data set with paraphrases shaped by age and gender. They tested both whether models can write such paraphrases and whether they still understand the results. Checks covered word variety, fluency scores, and human judgment. Rewriting by demographic style changed model performance markedly, which the authors flag as a fairness concern.
arxiv-2501-08376:
Arpita Roy and co-authors argue that clumpy winds of massive stars can light up helium lines in galaxies in a 2025 paper. Many galaxies glow in ionized helium far more than standard starlight explains. Rival suspects, from X-ray binaries to hidden black holes, each leave gaps in the story.

The team couples star evolution tracks with population and gas cloud models. If the winds of the hottest stars are clumpy enough to turn nearly transparent, their hardest photons escape and ionize helium around them. Metal-poor, fast-spinning populations do the job best. The match holds across a wide span of observed glow ratios. Starlight alone may solve the helium puzzle.
arxiv-2501-08476:
Kuban, Nemitz, and Chahine build a simulation of quantum key distribution to check NASA's quantum communications software, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Sharing entangled particles over long distances could power future air and space links. NASA's analysis suite models such systems, but little measured data exists to confirm its predictions.

Key distribution experiments, by contrast, offer a rich published record. The team's simulation takes the suite's own input parameters and produces a link budget: key rates, error rates, and a correlation measure. Early comparisons with published experiments line up well, supporting the model's soundness. A verified suite will guide experiments at NASA's Glenn laboratory and possible future missions.
arxiv-2501-08676:
Anant Khandelwal published this study in 2025. It introduces FlexiClip, a tool for animating clipart characters with smooth, faithful motion. Earlier tools warp clip art well in single frames but stumble across time, giving jerky moves and bent shapes. Video generators trained on real footage also mishandle the flat clipart style. FlexiClip starts from curve-based motion paths, then adds three fixes.

Temporal corrections adjust the motion step by step to keep it smooth. Continuous-time modeling with flow equations cuts timing noise. A flow-matching loss, borrowed from generative network theory, polishes the transitions. Tests across many clipart types, people and animals included, show clean, natural movement. The author claims a new quality bar for free-form clipart animation, especially in fast or stretchy scenes.
arxiv-2501-08776:
Ahmed Hussain and co-authors unite sensing and communication in one near-field wireless design, in a 2025 paper. Future networks at very high frequencies use huge antenna arrays, and at close range their wavefronts curve, letting beams aim by angle and distance at once. The team designs a shared codebook that serves both jobs: a standard set gives rough angle and range, and a polar set refines them.

Those estimates then feed a trimmed signal-processing method that spots slow targets while cutting background clutter. Simulations show the pairing slashes the processing load by about a thousandfold, trims the time spent training beams, and sharpens the estimates. The authors offer it as a path to networks that sense as they communicate.
arxiv-2501-08876:
Every dying star in history has shed a faint spray of neutrinos, and those sprays sum to a glow across the sky. Andrew Santos sums up the hunt for that glow in 2025. It encodes the tale of star birth through time, and the share of dying stars that end as black holes.

No detector has caught it yet. The best limits come from a giant water tank in Japan. Two new giants, one in Japan and one in China, will soon take up the watch with keener eyes. The glow could also betray new physics, if its shape bends from the forecast. The review gathers the latest bounds and the odds for the next few years of data.
arxiv-2501-09076:
Felipe Espinoza-Arancibia and Bogumił Pilecki weigh a pulsing star that seems to be the product of a stellar merger. The Cepheid in question orbits a companion every 59 days, far faster than any known pair of its kind. Its expected low mass also hinted at a merged past.

Their new method blends the measured mass ratio, the pulsation period, evolution models, and the known distance. It gives a Cepheid of 3.41 solar masses beside a lighter companion. The pair's apparent age gap of nearly a billion years supports the merger story. If common, merged Cepheids could skew age estimates across astronomy.
arxiv-2501-09276:
The IceCube Collaboration reports a search for closely timed neutrino pairs and triples in a 2025 paper. IceCube is a huge detector buried in Antarctic ice that watches for neutrinos from space. Pairs or triples arriving close together could signal brief cosmic events, such as flares from distant objects.

The search uses eleven point four years of IceCube data, the longest run applied to this question by the team. Events are checked for clustering in time and direction beyond what random background would produce. A huge author list reflects the scale of running the observatory. Such searches test whether any cosmic sources flash repeatedly on short time scales in neutrinos.
arxiv-2501-09476:
Geonwoo Kang and Jounghun Lee propose reading the spin of cosmic voids in a 2025 paper. Voids are the vast empty bubbles between galaxy webs. A key number for cosmology, called sigma-eight, measures how clumpy matter is, but it is tangled with other unknowns in most probes.

The pair ran fifteen simulated universes, each tweaked in just one ingredient, and found the giant voids in each. The spread of void spin strengths followed a two-parameter curve, and both parameters answered almost only to sigma-eight, shrugging off dark matter density, neutrino mass, and dark energy's push. The hold stayed firm under different cuts. A real sky survey could use void spin as a clean ruler.
arxiv-2501-09676:
D Jaffino Stargen, a physicist, studies how long a sped-up detector must run before it feels a steady heat bath. The Unruh effect says a detector that speeds up at a fixed rate should sense warmth where a still one senses none. Real runs are finite, so stray wobble terms muddy that pure heat read at the start. Stargen splits the finite-time rate into clean heat terms and fading wobble terms in exact math form.

The wobble terms swing with the run length and wash out when the run is long in one set sense. He then sets a gauge for how much wobble is too much and solves for the wait time to reach it. For mild speed-up, the wait has a neat form in the gauge. The work tells labs how long a run buys a true heat read.
arxiv-2501-09976:
Ten authors, led by Changze Lv, present a 2025 paper on a learning method for neural networks that copies the brain more closely. Backpropagation, the standard training method, works well but does not look like real brain learning. Critics point to three flaws: it needs symmetric weights, it uses one global error signal, and it trains in two separate phases.

The team's method, called Dendritic Localized Learning, takes its cues from pyramidal neurons and the branch-like dendrites they use to take in signals. It is built to fix all three flaws at once. Past attempts fixed some flaws but lost accuracy. In wide tests, the new method met all three brain-like criteria. It also reached top-level results among methods of its kind. The work shows that a more brain-like rule need not mean weaker performance.
arxiv-2501-10276:
Garcilazo and Valcarce argue that triple systems of a rare heavy baryon cannot bind together, in this 2025 paper. Lattice simulations had found the pair version of this baryon, built from three heavy quarks, attracts its twin strongly. That raised hopes for bound states of three or more as the quark grows heavier.

The authors trace the block to the Pauli principle acting twice over. At the level of whole baryons, it spoils the quietest pairing wave. At the level of the quarks inside, it spoils a second wave. Together the two effects close every door, for strange, charm, and bottom versions alike. The paper tempers expectations for exotic heavy matter.
arxiv-2501-10376:
Waleed El-Geresy, Christos Papavassiliou, and Deniz Gündüz study how to store data on memristors whose resistance drifts over time, in work the text dates to 2024. The catalog lists 2025. Memristors promise dense analog memory, but their stored values wander. The team proves a basic trade-off: longer-lived states cost more energy to write. They then treat storage as sending a message over a noisy, power-limited channel.

Their scheme codes images jointly for source and channel, trained end to end with a learned model of the drift. A new normalization layer lets the coder adapt to the starting resistance and the expected delay. The delay-aware network learned to spend energy wisely, keeping image quality high and even across delays. The authors frame the result as a design rule for analog memory.
arxiv-2501-10476:
Katherine Collins and co-authors revisit a classic learning puzzle for the age of AI in a 2025 paper. People learn alone by trial, or socially by copying others, and each route has its own costs and odds. Alan Rogers once simulated such a population and found, oddly, that cheap social learning added no fitness gain over learning alone.

That paradox drove decades of follow-up work. Now the mix changes again: humans can learn socially from AI systems that themselves learned from humans. The authors rebuild the network model with both kinds of learners inside. They test strategies open to the human user, the model builder, and regulators, and grade each by the quality of the shared world model the society settles into. Feedback loops, where each side copies the other's errors, get close attention.
arxiv-2501-10776:
Marin Šako and co-authors study how tiny surface defects trigger bubbles in stretched water, in this 2025 paper. Cavitation, the birth of vapor bubbles in a liquid under tension, matters for pumps, propellers, and medicine. Using molecular simulations joined with classic nucleation theory, they show that water sealed by flawless walls can bear far stronger tension than experiments ever see.

Water-hating surfaces lower the limit, but not enough to match practice. A single defect just one or two nanometers wide, able to cradle a bubble, collapses the strength. The team concludes that the largest defect, not the count of them, rules cavitation.
arxiv-2501-10876:
Jens Agerberg and five co-authors build neural networks that read the shape of data and can prove they will not be easily fooled, in this 2025 paper. Their input is the persistence diagram, topological data analysis's fingerprint of holes and loops at every scale. Turning those diagrams into features a network can learn from, without losing their stability, is the craft.

The architecture they propose learns discriminative geometric representations from such diagrams. The key property is Lipschitz stability with a controllable constant: small wiggles in the input can only move the representation by a bounded amount. In adversarial settings that bound becomes a certificate, a proof that no perturbation within a set size can flip the classification of a given sample. They demonstrate the certification on ORBIT5K, a data set of orbits from a discrete dynamical system. Robustness, here, is a theorem rather than a hope.
arxiv-2501-11076:
Christopher Atherfold wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on random number-theoretic functions. A Rademacher random multiplicative function assigns each whole number a value built from fair coin flips at the primes. Analysts study weighted sums of such a function to understand how cancellation behaves. The paper pins down how large those sums can typically grow.

For almost every such random function, the author proves the sum up to any point stays below a modest power of a slowly growing log term. Yet he also shows that somewhere along the way, the sum must sometimes exceed a smaller threshold in the other direction. This mix differs from a cousin case studied before, because here a product over primes dominates the behavior. A sharper bound is proved for sums restricted to numbers with a large prime factor. The results refine the theory of random models for arithmetic functions.
arxiv-2501-11176:
Shahid Sattar, Daniel Hedman, and Canali study what happens when the surface of a magnetic topological insulator rebuilds itself. Thin films of MnBi2Te4 are prized for exotic states like the quantum anomalous Hall effect, which need a clean magnetic gap at the surface. Real surfaces, though, shuffle their atoms, and the shuffle's cost was unexplored.

Simulations mixing first-principles math with machine-learned molecular dynamics compare two rebuild styles. The buried, interstitial pattern wins on energy and reshapes the exchange gap and the topological character. The peripheral pattern may explain odd photoemission signals seen in labs. Side-wall edge channels, the workhorses of quantum transport here, shift with the rebuild too.
arxiv-2501-11276:
Xiangyang Hu and ten colleagues build a network that predicts which patients with mild cognitive impairment will progress to Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 paper. Combining brain scans and other data types improves prediction, but PET scans are often missing and the data types differ wildly. Their network, ITCFN, works with three data types even when one is absent.

A generator module synthesizes the missing PET features from MRI scans, and dedicated encoders extract features from each source. Attention modules then merge the streams while trimming redundancy, guided by a loss designed for missing data and cross-type alignment. On two standard Alzheimer's data sets the method beat both single-type and rival multi-type models.
arxiv-2501-11376:
Marko Pesut, a solo author, presents a study from twenty twenty-five on a twist to the standard model of particle physics. In his take, force groups act in unlike ways on light quarks and on the heavy third family. The Higgs boson is not a basic field here. It forms as a light relic of a new strong force that breaks a larger symmetry.

He shows how the Higgs field's energy shape can arise from loops of the new particles. That shape holds the tuning needed to split the weak scale from the strong scale. New flavoured force carriers must sit near the TeV scale. Colliders in the near term can hunt for their marks.
arxiv-2501-11576:
The true capacity of a noisy quantum channel hides behind a hard optimization, and a 2025 arXiv paper by Chengkai Zhu and co-authors recasts it as a walk on curved spaces. The Holevo capacity, the channel's one shot classical limit, becomes a climb over a product of two manifolds: one of probabilities, one of input states.

Their Riemannian gradient method follows the slope on that curved ground. In numerical tests it beat existing methods on both speed and size of problem handled, returning firm lower bounds on capacity. Lower bounds matter here because the full regularized capacity may stay out of reach for years.
arxiv-2501-11676:
Tristan Daus and Elena Kozlikin computed the growth of cosmic structure in twenty twenty-five. They used Newtonian particle dynamics. They ran no simulation to do it. Their analytical framework treats gravitating particles in phase space as a field theory. It is a perturbative solution of the kinetic hierarchy. Its loop expansion has a natural truncation rule built in. From it they derived the nonlinear power spectrum of density fluctuations.

On big scales the analytic spectrum matches numeric simulations to very high precision. On mid and small scales it is off by about ten percent. The pair argue the gap is diagnostic, not fatal. If the perturbation theory is restructured, the fit on small scales should get much better. A firm analytic grip on how structure forms would add to brute-force cosmology simulations. It would show which physics drives each scale of the cosmos.
arxiv-2501-11976:
Michal Bizzarri, Miroslav Lávička, Rafael Sendra, and Jan Vršek ask when a spun surface admits a polynomial description. A surface of revolution comes from rotating a plane curve around an axis. Modelers want parametrizations built from polynomials, not messier functions. The team ties the surface's polynomiality to that of its generating curve.

When the curve qualifies, the surface does too, and the paper gives formulas to compute its polynomial parametrization over the complex numbers. Real parametrizations are harder, and the authors take first steps on existence and computation there. Quadrics, the simplest curved surfaces, get a complete real classification as a payoff. A conjecture covers the general case. The work serves geometric modeling, where polynomial patches are the currency of design tools.
arxiv-2501-12076:
Jacopo Nudo, Matteo Cinelli, Andrea Baronchelli, and Walter Quattrociocchi study how community size shapes talk on social media in a 2025 paper. Platforms now host public debate at a huge scale. The team asks whether the size of a platform or a thread changes how people join in and how long they stay.

They tracked user behavior across six platforms over more than three decades. Smaller platforms held richer, longer exchanges, while larger ones drew wider but briefer input. As communities grew, users were less likely to return to a thread. Niche spaces broke that rule, keeping strong repeat input. The authors link these patterns to how each platform is built.
arxiv-2501-12276:
Milan Ding and co-authors teach a neural net to find lines in dense atomic light spectra in a 2025 paper. Some atoms give off tens of thousands of lines, and hand work to list them eats years. The net reads the spectrum point by point with a two-way memory design, then calls line spots through a plain output layer.

Trained on fake spectra, the net was tried on true nickel and neodymium reads across wide ranges. It beat classic ways most on noisy, merged, or ringing lines. Lines it newly found let the team pin two nickel energy levels that had long been marked as out of reach.
arxiv-2501-12576:
Yunshu Liu and Lingjie Duan studied blockchain order books in twenty twenty-five, where miners match trades and may act selfishly. In these systems, buyers and sellers post trades with fees, and miners choose which to include in blocks. Selfish miners chase high fees and skip matches that would help overall welfare.

The authors give the first analytic study of fee choices and miner strategies here, proving the welfare loss can be unboundedly bad. Their fix is an adjustable block size mechanism that needs no change to the decentralized protocol and leaves fees and matching free. Despite missing information and mixed strategies, the mechanism keeps welfare loss well bounded, and hits the optimum for uniform-quantity trades like NFTs. Tests on a local Ethereum setup and real data confirm the gains.
arxiv-2501-13076:
Kon'kov, Shishkov, and Surnachev wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on when a class of differential inequalities has solutions that exist across all of space. The inequalities are of second order and quasilinear, and they involve an elliptic operator written in divergence form. The authors look for positive solutions defined on the whole space, in two or more dimensions.

The operator is built from a Carathéodory function, a kind of function that is well behaved in each of its inputs. The paper sets growth and sign conditions on that function, tied to a power p greater than one. Under such conditions, the authors study whether global positive solutions exist. Results of this kind mark the border between problems that admit whole-space solutions and problems where any solution must break down. The work sits in the theory of nonlinear partial differential equations.
arxiv-2501-13376:
Five authors, Gabrielle Hoyer, Michelle Tong, Rupsa Bhattacharjee, Valentina Pedoia, and Sharmila Majumdar, wrote this 2025 paper on AI tools for muscle and joint MRI scans. Precision care in this field needs measures that can be taken at scale. The team built a modular system that turns routine MRI scans into standard numbers for use in care choices.

The system fine-tuned promptable segmentation models, including SAM, SAM2, and MedSAM, on varied scan sets. Auto detection feeds prompts to the models, so no hand input is needed. The resulting measures of cartilage, bone, and soft tissue matched expert marks closely. The team then showed two uses. One is a three-stage knee triage chain that cuts checking work while keeping sensitivity. The other forecasts knee replacement and new osteoarthritis over 48 months, with sound calibration.
arxiv-2501-13576:
Majid Rafiei, Mahsa Pourbafrani, and Wil van der Aalst tackle process checking across firms in a 2025 paper. Process mining compares how work actually runs against a model of how it should run. Doing that across company borders can expose miscommunication, but firms guard their data. Their method checks the shared process while keeping each firm's records private.

They test the idea on a simulated supply chain with three firms. Each firm runs one part, from buying to shipping, and fake event logs are made for each part and the whole chain. The method finds planted miscommunications and puts a cost on them, showing the approach can work without pooling raw data.
arxiv-2501-13676:
Elias Abad Rocamora, Grigorios Chrysos, and Volkan Cevher work on proof of safety for text classifiers in a 2025 paper. Small edits to a text, such as swapping or dropping letters, can flip a model's verdict if chosen with malice. Proof methods exist, but their cost explodes when edits are counted by a standard distance measure.

Their method, LipsLev, first estimates how sharply the model can react to such edits. That estimate guides training of models whose reactions are capped by design. Safety proof then takes a single pass through the model. On a news dataset the method certified solid accuracy at one and two edits, while running far faster than past approaches. The authors see a path to practical proof for text systems.
arxiv-2501-13776:
Lorenz Kummer, Samir Moustafa, Wilfried Gansterer, and Nils Kriege present Crossfire, a defense for graph neural networks in 2025. Bit flip attacks alter a few stored bits to sabotage a network. Such attacks, built for vision models, now hit graph models too, and no defense existed for them.

Older tricks from vision work, like hashing and honeypots, fall short on graphs when tested alone. Crossfire blends both with bit-level repair of odd weights, exploiting natural weight sparsity. It needs no retraining and no labeled data. Across 2,160 trials, it restored attacked networks to their prior state far more often than rivals, and lifted post-repair accuracy as well.
arxiv-2501-14176:
Micah Rentschler and Jesse Roberts show that a pre-trained Transformer, fine-tuned with reinforcement learning, can learn to solve new problems on its own, in a paper from 2025. The model practices across many episodes of varied tasks. Over time it gains a skill the authors call in-context reinforcement learning.

The trained model solved tasks it had never seen, using few attempts. It also did well on tasks outside its training range. Its gains did not depend much on the quality of its training examples. It could stitch together behaviors shown in its context and adapt when the rules of a task changed mid-stream. The authors present it as a general-purpose problem solver that improves its own answers.
arxiv-2501-15176:
Tristan van der Vlugt studies a counting question about infinite series in a 2025 mathematics paper. A conditionally convergent series can be thinned to a subseries that diverges, a classic fact. The subseries numbers ask how few index sets one must choose in advance so that every such series diverges on at least one of them.

Van der Vlugt turns the question around. Taking only index sets that are endless in both directions, he asks how the answer changes when the chosen sets must make every such series converge instead. That number turns out to be a cardinal characteristic of the continuum, one of the standard gauges of infinity's fine structure. He links his new numbers to several known ones and proves matching dual results.
arxiv-2501-15276:
Yue Fu and co-authors study novices making music with AI in a 2025 paper. Nine undergraduates in one class made three songs with AI tools in 10 weeks. Songs went from first spark to a Spotify release. AI helped with tunes, words, cover art, and the release path. Logs and talks caught how the work flow bent.

AI sped the spark stage and shrank the prep stage of old craft. Pick and proof of raw outputs then grew hard for new hands. A new stage rose: collage and refine, where parts fuse to wholes. Roles in the group shifted with the tools as well. Two models of the co-work close the paper.
arxiv-2501-15476:
Flambaum explores whether tiny bound systems of ordinary particles, held by extra strong gravity at short range, could serve as dark matter. The setting is the ADD model, where extra compact dimensions make gravity grow far stronger at small distances than in daily life. His 2025 paper asks what that force can bind.

Quarks, neutrinos, axions, and other Standard Model particles could form small composite states under such a pull, he argues. These states have a small cross section for their mass, which is just what dark matter needs: heavy enough to shape galaxies, yet shy enough to dodge detection. The paper sizes up this path as a candidate account of the missing mass.
arxiv-2501-15676:
Tuhin Paul, Aishee Chakraborty, Souvik Ghose, and Tapas Das study how matter falling into a black hole can mimic gravity itself. When gas streams steadily onto a black hole, small ripples in the flow travel like sound waves in a medium. Under the right conditions those ripples face their own horizon, a point they cannot cross, much like light at a real black hole.

The team builds steady, faster-than-sound inflow solutions for a hot, multi-species gas, using stand-in potentials for the black hole's pull, then nudges the flow to test stability. The nudges reveal an acoustic metric, a geometry for sound, with horizons they map using causal diagrams. They also track how the analogue surface gravity of that horizon shifts as the flow's settings change. The work feeds analogue gravity, the effort to study black hole physics through look-alike systems.
arxiv-2501-16176:
Tyler Sterling explains the physics of light from snapping shrimp in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. When these shrimp snap, they make bubbles that collapse and flash with light. The effect is a shrimp version of sonoluminescence, the light emitted by a collapsing bubble in a fluid.

Sterling studies the dynamics of such a bubble in detail. The collapse is so fast that no heat escapes, and the trapped gas grows hot enough to ionize. Light then comes from electrons striking ions and atoms, and from electrons rejoining ions. He shows how to compute the spectrum of the emitted light. That calculation explains the physical steps behind the shrimp's flash.
arxiv-2501-16276:
Long Nguyen and Tho Quan present URAG, a unified hybrid retrieval framework for university admission chatbots. Their 2025 arXiv paper serves educational question answering. Language models power such chatbots, but they can invent facts. Wrong admission answers mislead applicants in harmful ways. Retrieval-augmented generation grounds answers in university data.

Standard retrieval setups can be costly and complex to run. They often need training of specialized extra modules. URAG blends retrieval routes into one leaner hybrid design. Accuracy gains were strongest on critical queries in tests. The framework aims for precise answers without heavy operations. Admission offices need dependable tools that staff can maintain. The work targets that practical deployment gap.
arxiv-2501-16476:
Robert O'Shea and Bipin Rajendran propose a way to train neural networks with no feedback at all. Their 2025 paper works in the hardest corner of backpropagation-free learning, where a layer cannot hear anything back from the layers above it while it sets its own weights.

Their method, Forward Projection, needs a single pass through the data. Random projections of inputs and labels create targets for each layer's activity, and each layer fits those targets by closed-form regression. A bonus is clarity: each layer's activity reads as its own guess at the label. On biomedical data sets the method matched local learning rivals, learned faster, and in few-shot tests generalized better than backpropagation.
arxiv-2501-16676:
Mingzhe Yang, Linli Pan, and Jiang Zhang propose a measure of living system flexibility in a 2025 paper. Many theories try to state what sets living systems apart. Few give a number for how alive-like a system is.

Their indicator sits at the level of dynamic mechanisms. It gauges how flexibly a system responds to its environment. The measure is proven to fit the rules of partial information decomposition. System and environment contributions are split into shared and unique parts. Readers get a formal tool for comparing self-organization across very different systems.
arxiv-2501-17076:
Muhammad Shahbaz and co-authors train roadside laser scanners to spot vehicles and people without any hand-labeled data, in a 2025 paper. Labeling point clouds by hand is slow and costly, which holds back traffic safety systems.

Their framework, DINOSTAR, uses rule-based teacher models that filter background, cluster points, and fit boxes to rough objects. A student detector then learns from the combined noisy labels of several teachers, which forces it to handle varied views of the same objects. On public roadside data sets, the self-taught detectors matched ones trained on human labels. The authors present the system as a scalable way to deploy roadside detection without a labeling budget.
arxiv-2501-17176:
Marc Ballestero-Ribo and Daniel Ortiz Martinez test chatbots as programming teaching assistants in a 2025 paper. Large language models promise near one to one tutoring, with help on demand for students stuck on basic coding tasks. Two well known models were judged on the feedback they give beginners, and their cost in real use was weighed.

The stronger model far outperformed the weaker one, yet still produced wrong information that novices may not catch, so it is not classroom ready alone. A carefully built prompt with worked examples automated much of the grading of feedback and set a floor estimate for the share of wrong comments, saving staff time and money.
arxiv-2501-17276:
Angelica Babei, Andrew Fiori, and Cameron Franc study representations of the modular group in this 2025 math paper. A representation maps group elements to matrices, here inside the exceptional group G2. The space of all such maps, the moduli space, has two main parts.

One part is one-dimensional and holds rigid examples that Katz studied. The authors focus on the larger four-dimensional part, whose members are not rigid. They build a big family there as an etale cover of degree ninety-six over an open set. They also give algebra tests that ensure the maps cover G2 over a finite field for primes at least five. New congruence subgroups result.
arxiv-2501-17476:
Laura Crosara, Mahtab Mirmohseni, and Stefano Tomasin propose a hybrid way to verify wireless senders at the signal level, in work from 2025. Faking a sender is a core risk in wireless links. Checks that use both the channel and a shared secret can be stronger than either alone.

The receiver partly steers the channel, for instance with a smart reflecting surface. It then sends a random channel setup as a challenge. A valid sender must answer with a coded key that fits that exact channel state. Coding hides the key from eavesdroppers at the same time. The letter weighs how pilot signals for channel reading trade against key length.
arxiv-2501-17576:
Patricia Bouyer, Srivathsan, and Vaishnavi Vishwanath wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It revisits model-checking for real-time systems through alternating timed automata, machines that track clocks and can flip between states in a game-like way.

Timed logics such as Metric Temporal Logic can be turned into one-clock versions of these automata, and checking a formula comes down to checking if the automaton is empty. Past emptiness tests rest on region builds that suit theory more than code. The authors add a deactivation move that switches a clock off in plain sight, sharpen the logic swap, and build zone-based tests. They give a fast entailment check and show the general check is NP-hard.
arxiv-2501-17776:
Diluka Galappaththige and co-authors speed up multi-target sensing in a 2025 letter. Huge antenna arrays at high frequencies can talk and sense at once. They must form many beams to serve users and spot targets. Classic methods are slow: one past run took two weeks for a mid-size array.

The joint problem is non-convex, with rate goals, sensing targets, and power caps. Their method searches on a curved manifold so the rules hold by design. A stochastic gradient method with an augmented Lagrangian drives the search. The result runs far faster than standard benchmarks on large arrays. The work makes real-time use of giant arrays more plausible.
arxiv-2501-17876:
Hao Mo and co-authors propose a 2025 method to clean noise from digital messages that carry meaning, not just raw bits. Their model borrows from score-based diffusion, a family of tools first built to make images. Past work of this kind did not match how digital channel noise truly behaves.

Their design shapes the training noise to fit real channel noise. Once trained, the model cleans received symbols across a range of signal strengths and makes the decoder's job easier. Tests beat the base model on three quality scores, most at low signal strength. It also needs far less storage, which helps real use.
arxiv-2501-18176:
Chen-Xun Weng and eight co-authors test asymmetric relativistic zero knowledge proofs in two thousand twenty-five. Such proofs build trust with privacy, with no assumptions on compute limits. Past quantum sound forms needed too many rounds to run. Their cost in time and randomness blocked real use.

The new protocol uses relativistic bit commitments for its base. Its soundness ties to a known nonlocal game, CHSH. Rounds grow in a line with the edge count of the graph. A lab run finished all rounds in a flash of time. Randomness cost was large but far more sane than past forms.
arxiv-2501-18276:
Ming Hui Xu and Patrick Charlot check how steady the sky positions of distant galaxies are when read at four radio bands at once, in a 2025 study. The galaxies, all with active centers, serve as fixed markers that define the sky grid used to track Earth’s shape and tilt. If a marker wanders, the grid suffers.

The team used position time series from special geodetic solutions of very long baseline data. For markers high in the sky, the main cause of wander was the marker’s own shifting structure. For lower markers, the limits of the method itself dominated, since it reads one sky coordinate less sharply. Knowing which cause rules where helps grid keepers weight each marker fairly.
arxiv-2501-18476:
Aditya Banerjee (2025) asks whether part of an isolated quantum system forgets its past as it settles. The standard picture treats each part as an open system bathed by the rest. If that bath erased memory steadily, the part's motion would be Markovian. Banerjee tested this on a mixed-field Ising chain pushed far from equilibrium. He followed the distances between a small subsystem's states at different times.

The distances did not decay in the clean, memory-free way. They carried clear signatures of memory, meaning the surroundings feed information back. The effect depended on the direction of the sudden change that started the motion. Jumps from the disordered side into the ordered side showed much stronger memory than the reverse. The classical distance measure behaved in a strikingly regular way. Banerjee offers rough arguments for the asymmetry. The work warns against assuming simple forgetting inside closed quantum systems.
arxiv-2501-19276:
Scattering X-rays off a crystal can reveal how its electrons move, but the reading depends on the angle of the setup. Gawne and co-authors measure that effect in single crystal silicon in a 2025 study at a European X-ray laser site. Their setup lets the scattering direction turn through the crystal as the shot runs.

With fine resolution, they saw strong shifts in the scattered spectrum at low angles. Top computer models of electron motion matched those shifts well. The match backs the models for use on other hard materials. Data also came in far faster than in a prior run on the same rig. Fast, sharp reads widen what such lasers can probe.
arxiv-2502-00076:
Bidossessi Agossou and co-authors test how color fixes in capsule camera images affect AI disease spotting, in a 2025 paper. Patients swallow a tiny camera that films the gut. Deep learning models scan that film for disease. Color quality in training data can sway those models.

The team made two color-corrected versions of a known data set. They trained two detection models on the raw and fixed versions. Color fixes led the models to draw larger boxes that overlapped the true marks more. For some diseases, fixes also raised false alarms. The mixed result warns that image cleanup is not free of cost. Clinics should test such steps before adopting them in screening tools.
arxiv-2502-00176: Benedek Kovács, Zoltán Lóránt Nagy, and Dávid Szabó settle a century-old puzzle in 2025 for the case where the banned line length is not small. The puzzle asks how many points of a square lattice can be picked with no set count of them in a line. When the ban length passes a threshold tied to the grid's size, the team prove the best pick is the ban length times the grid's side. Their proof leans on random two-sided graphs and bunching bounds.
arxiv-2502-00376:
Abdul Rehman, Ilona Heldal, and Jerry Chun-Wei Lin detect ADHD from brain signals during attention tasks in a 2025 paper. The team first learns representations from unlabeled EEG with self supervision, then transfers them into a sequence model mixing two recurrent designs. Two lighter rivals, a plain deep network and a random forest, serve as comparisons.

Signals came from children performing visual attention tasks, cleaned by normalization, filtering, and class balancing. The full model reached about eighty one percent accuracy, the best of the three. The authors admit dataset imbalance and feature choice remain hard. They frame the work as a step toward objective, signal based screening support rather than a stand alone diagnosis.
arxiv-2502-00576:
Sydney Vach and co-authors found a young super-Neptune planet in a 2025 survey paper. The planet is just 16 million years old, a baby by planet standards, in a young star group near Scorpius and Centaurus. Planets under 50 million years old are rare finds, and each one tests how planets form and change.

NASA's TESS telescope watched nearly the whole group for passing planets. This world showed up as a dip in its star's light as it crossed. The team also ran a first survey of the group's transiting planets. Young worlds like this show what giant planets look like before they settle.
arxiv-2502-00976:
Wentao Tang learns the size of a control model's error from flight data instead of theory, in a 2025 paper. Robust control needs a bound on how far the real plant strays from its model, but for tangled nonlinear systems that bound is guesswork.

Tang frames the mismatch with integral quadratic constraints, flexible inequalities used in control theory. Their unknown parameters are fitted to sampled trajectories using a one-class support vector machine, a method that learns the shape of normal behavior. Statistical learning theory backs the method's generalization. Two tests, a time-delay system and a two-phase chemical reactor, recovered the true frequency-domain uncertainty well. Data, in this account, can certify what analysis cannot.
arxiv-2502-01276:
Marcel Wever and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on explaining the tuning knobs of a learning algorithm with fair-share math. Tuning those knobs, called hyperparameters, decides much of a model's skill. Yet which knob matters, and how knobs interact, stays opaque, and black-box tuners give users little reason to trust them. The team borrows Shapley values from game theory, which split a team's payoff fairly among its players.

Their frame, named HyperSHAP, splits a model's score among the knobs that produced it. It also prices how pairs of knobs amplify or cancel each other. The split works knob by knob for one run, or pooled across many runs. Users can read it as an ablation guide, a measure of how much tuning headroom an algorithm holds, or a window on the tuner's own behavior. Tests across tuning benchmarks showed the readings are stable and usable.
arxiv-2502-01576:
Malik and co-authors test whether image encoders hardened on large datasets can shield multi-modal language models from visual attacks. Such models answer questions about images, but tiny crafted changes can fool them. Attacks can trigger false claims or slip past safety checks. Current defenses fine-tune the vision part on modest data with limits that cap gains. The team instead borrows classifiers already hardened at large scale.

Large, diverse attack training gave these encoders stronger resistance across many threat types. They held up where narrower defenses thinned out. The analysis weighs robustness against keeping general vision skill. Borrowing proven parts may beat training small defenses from scratch.
arxiv-2502-01676:
Man Luo and seven co-authors create the first benchmark for detecting toxic language in scientific peer review. Harsh feedback discourages authors and slows science, yet toxicity in reviews had no agreed definition or dataset. The team split the concept into four categories and had experts annotate reviews from the OpenReview platform.

They then benchmarked a dedicated toxicity model, a sentiment model, open-source language models, and two commercial ones. Prompt detail mattered enormously: leading models aligned poorly with human judgments under simple instructions but improved with detailed ones. Model confidence proved a useful filter, raising agreement when only confident calls were kept. The dataset and findings give the community a starting point.
arxiv-2502-01776:
Haocheng Xi and co-authors speed up video-making models in a 2025 study. These models can take tens of minutes to make a few seconds of video, since each frame must check against all others. The team found that most of that checking follows two simple patterns.

Some attention heads care only about spots within one frame, while others care only about the same spot across frames. Their system, Sparse VideoGen, spots which pattern each head uses and skips the rest of the checks. On two known video models it ran more than twice as fast with no clear loss in quality. The code is shared in public, so other teams can build on the gain.
arxiv-2502-01876:
Teaching an agent by rewards works best when every step earns a score, but real feedback often arrives in chunks. Yihan Du and co-authors study that middle ground in a 2025 theory paper on reinforcement learning with segment feedback.

Each episode of action is cut into segments, and the agent learns its score only at each segment's end. The team studies two forms: a simple pass-fail mark, and the summed reward for the segment. They design algorithms and prove bounds on the cost of learning for both. With pass-fail marks, more segments cut the cost sharply. With summed rewards, more segments barely help, a surprise the proofs confirm. Tests back the theory.
arxiv-2502-02076:
Krishan Agyakari Raja Babu and co-authors argue, in a 2025 position paper, that synthetic medical data will only enter clinical AI use if clinicians learn to trust it. Computer-made data promise relief from privacy worries, bias, and scarce real data sets, and research on them has boomed. Yet adoption in clinics lags, held back by doubts about whether fake data behave like the real thing.

The authors bring evidence from brain tumor segmentation showing that the quality, variety, and share of synthetic data in training directly move model performance. From that base they draw lessons for building, testing, and presenting synthetic data so care teams can judge it fairly. Trust, they say, must be earned with proof, not assumed.
arxiv-2502-02176:
Juma Kamulali, Benard Nsamba, and their colleagues introduce MAISTEP, a machine learning tool for dating stars, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The tool reads a star's age, mass, and size from its air alone. Knowing host star ages matters because the census of planets depends on the stars they orbit.

Most planet hosts come with only atmospheric measures: surface heat, iron content, and brightness. MAISTEP trains four tree-based learning methods on a grid of star models, then blends their answers. Fed those three measures, it infers radius, mass, and age together. The authors run a detailed statistical check of how trustworthy the inferences are. They then apply the tool to stars that host giant planets and study how those ages spread out. The work offers planet hunters a sturdier way to date the stars behind their finds.
arxiv-2502-02276:
Marcelino Agúndez and co-authors rebut a claimed phosphine detection around a carbon star, in their 2025 arXiv paper. A recent article used ALMA telescope data on the envelope of IRC +10216 to confirm interstellar phosphine there. Checking the spectrum, the authors find the key emission feature is misassigned.

The feature matches a rotational transition of hydrogen cyanide in a highly excited vibrational state, supported by companion components at the expected relative strengths. Phosphine itself remains genuinely detected toward this star, they stress, but from earlier single-dish telescope lines, not from this ALMA feature. The note is a careful correction of a molecular identification.
arxiv-2502-02576:
Mun Jung Jung and three co-authors propose a rare neutrino reaction as a yardstick for the DUNE experiment, in a 2025 physics paper. DUNE will shoot neutrinos through the Earth to study their shifts. Knowing the beam's strength well is key, and the muon neutrino share is the hardest part. In the reaction they study, a neutrino knocks a pion out of a nucleus in one clean piece, so the beam energy can be read back from the debris.

The cross section for the reaction can be tied to pion-argon scattering data by a known relation. That data could even be taken in DUNE's own near detector at the same time. Their fits suggest the beam peak could be pinned to within a few percent. The authors list the lab and theory work still needed to make the yardstick trustworthy.
arxiv-2502-03276:
Bezuglov, Kniehl, Onishchenko and Veretin present a method for computing Lauricella functions to high precision. The functions here have indices tied in a linear way to a parameter, and the values sought are Laurent series around zero. Older routes build analytic continuations from multi-dimensional sums or integral forms, which are clumsy for precise numeric work.

Their route uses Frobenius generalized power series, which are one-dimensional and far better suited to high-precision sums. The parameter dependence is rebuilt from values at chosen numeric points, which also lets the work run in parallel with ease. The method is built into a Wolfram Mathematica package called PrecisionLauricella.
arxiv-2502-03576:
Damien Berriaud and Roger Wattenhofer ask how to weight items so that near-duplicates cannot hijack the total. The problem shows up when tasks are pooled into a benchmark, when data points drive domain adaptation, and when opinions feed a voting advice tool. In each case, clones of one item can stack the deck. Their 2025 paper builds a theory for weights that resist this.

Clone-proof weighting makes similar items share importance instead of each claiming a full share. The framework grows out of the maximum uncertainty principle, extended to general metric spaces. Three axioms guide the design: symmetry, continuity, and clone-proofness. The authors then tackle when such weights exist. Benchmark designers get a principled defense against redundancy dressed as consensus.
arxiv-2502-03876:
Juan Du and co-authors set out a position paper in 2025 on finding flaws in 3D point cloud data with no trained model at all. Point clouds are sets of points that map a surface in three dimensions. Factories that make one off custom parts may have just one good sample, with no labels and no past data to learn from.

The authors define this untrained problem in formal terms, and set it apart from the usual untrained by label methods, which still learn from past data. Their route leans on prior knowledge about surfaces and flaws instead. They propose three frames for the work. One uses chance based models, one splits a cloud into clean, flawed, and noise parts, and one reads local shape. Each is meant to spot flaws from a single sample.
arxiv-2502-04176:
Qinhan Yu and co-authors build a benchmark for AI systems that answer questions with both text and images pulled from a source collection. Standard retrieval systems fetch outside facts but answer in words alone. The new task demands mixed answers, which are richer but harder to grade.

Their benchmark holds 4,346 documents, over 14,000 images, and 4,800 human-checked question pairs across web, academic, and lifestyle sets. Scoring mixes classic statistics with model-based grades. They also propose a generation framework and report results for eleven popular models, all public for reuse.
arxiv-2502-04276:
Xin Li, Markus Lange-Hegermann, and Bogdan Raiţă present a study from twenty twenty-five on solving inverse tasks for linear partial differential equations with Gaussian processes. A Gaussian process can serve as a prior guess for the unknown field. Here the prior is built from deep algebra, not from a plain smooth kernel. That build is turned into code with an algebra package.

Their test task reads the wave speed from noisy data for the classic wave equation. The method hits high truth while it runs fast. The authors frame the gain as a blend of system theory and algebra based priors. Such tasks are core in physics, where the rules are known but key dials hide.
arxiv-2502-04476:
Soham Deshmukh and co-authors teach machines to explain, in words, how two sounds differ. Spotting and describing audio differences matters for forensics, quality checks, and sound generation. Their 2025 paper is the first to frame that task fully, with datasets, benchmarks, and a working model.

The team built two datasets from existing audio-caption collections. Large language models wrote the difference reports at three depths. The shallowest list the events and objects heard, while the deepest add scenes, signal traits, and listener feelings. A simple baseline that feeds two sound embeddings into a frozen language model stumbled on similar sounds. Their ADIFF model adds a cross-projection module, position captioning, and a three-step training plan. It wrote fuller, sharper explanations, judged by both scoring metrics and human raters. The work opens a new corner of audio understanding.
arxiv-2502-04576:
So Yeon Min and six co-authors teach AI agents to ask for help at the right time. Their twenty twenty-five paper starts from a human trait: we know our limits and seek aid only when needed. Language model agents lack that sense, and they either fail boldly or ask so often that they waste time.

The team trains a helper policy offline, with a fixed budget of interventions, like calls to a stronger model. Process reward models score the best moments to step in, using past trajectories. Tabular reinforcement learning then trains the helper on those labels. The offline design avoids costly calls during training and holds up on off-policy data.
arxiv-2502-04776:
Bo-Yang Zhang and four co-authors gauge how well future gravitational wave detectors can test two deep rules of gravity, in a 2025 arXiv paper. The rules are parity, a mirror like balance, and Lorentz symmetry, a core of Einstein's theory. New detectors on the ground and in space will hear far more waves than today's set.

The team fed sample waves from pairs of dense dead stars into five planned detectors. They then fit the waves with forms that allow the two rules to bend, in both loudness and phase. The ground pair, used jointly, set far tighter caps on the bend scale than today's network. Space detectors won in some bend cases and matched the ground pair in strength. The work maps where each fleet shines.
arxiv-2502-05076:
Liang Ze Wong presents a 2025 paper on how much fact knowledge a single attention layer can hold. Attention is the core part of the transformer models behind modern AI. Wong studies a simple form with one layer only. Facts from a database are cast as a three-way array, and its rank gauges the size of that database.

A matched array stands for the attention layer itself. Tests on toy models and random data show the two ranks move together. The work picks out which weight parts matter most for recall. It also shows how two math steps shape that rank. The finds suggest a way to raise layer capacity with no extra size. That could help future model design.
arxiv-2502-05176:
Chung-Ho Wu and co-authors fill holes in full-circle 3D scenes with a guide view in a 2025 paper. Cutting an object from a round scene must keep views in step and shapes true, a hard bar. Their method works on scenes built from soft specks that can be viewed from any side.

Three steps drive it: depth-aware masks that find hidden zones, a depth spread step that seeds new points with no training, and a polish step for cross-view match. A new bench set with true answers backs the tests, where the method tops past rivals.
arxiv-2502-05276:
Dennis Sweeney presents a 2025 math paper on the shapes hidden inside small semigroups. A semigroup is a set with an associative combining rule, like numbers under addition. Each finite one has a classifying space, a shape whose holes encode its algebra.

Sweeney built software that computes the integral homology of finite ones quickly, by using structure in projective resolutions. Running it over semigroups and monoids of small orders gave a trove of counterexamples. One finite aperiodic one carries large torsion in its homology. Two have Moore spaces as classifying shapes. Another has nonzero rational homology in infinitely many dimensions, which refutes conjectures by William Nico. The set of such shapes is also closed under suspension.
arxiv-2502-05376:
Shrinking a large language model to four-bit numbers for both its weights and its working values can slash cost, but keeping accuracy is hard without retraining. Reena Elangovan, Charbel Sakr, Anand Raghunathan, and Brucek Khailany propose a method for that task in this 2025 paper. Their approach, named LO-BCQ in the text, first chops each data block into groups of neighboring values.

Groups with alike statistics are clustered together, and each cluster gets its own tuned codebook for rounding values. A loop alternates between regrouping and retuning to squeeze the rounding error down. Counting the small extra cost of storing scales and codebook choices, the method held accuracy losses under one percent across several models and tasks. The authors present it as a new best for this grade of compression.
arxiv-2502-05676:
Lars van der Laan and Ahmed Alaa generalize a calibration method for prediction models in this 2025 paper. A model is calibrated when its stated confidence matches reality, and the classic distribution free tools only promise that match in the long run.

Their unified framework extends Venn and Venn-Abers calibration beyond yes or no classification to any problem set by a loss function. It turns a predictor that is calibrated on its own training data into one that, on finite samples, offers at least one honest point prediction inside a shrinking set. A multicalibration version aims the same guarantee at subpopulations, and for quantile loss it recovers conformal prediction as a special case.
arxiv-2502-05776:
A seller who posts prices over time learns what buyers will pay from the bids that fall through the cracks. Yet the data are censored: a deal struck early hides the prices never tried. Daniele Bracale and co-authors built a pricing method in 2025 that needs no hand-set knobs. It leans on isotonic regression, a shape-fitting method, under a mild smoothness assumption on the unknown noise in buyers' values.

For that weaker assumption they prove a bound on the money left on the table. In simulations and on real data from a large healthcare property firm, the method consistently lost less than rival approaches. Being free of tuning choices is its practical selling point.
arxiv-2502-06076:
Daksh Mittal and co-authors set out a 2025 plan for choosing which data to label when labels are costly. True labels drive tests of new treatments and of prediction models alike. Random sampling for labels can waste a lot of money and effort. Their framework shifts effort in batches as results come in. Each batch of new labels updates what the team believes. The next batch is then chosen to cut doubt the most by the end.

The problem is framed as a sequence of choices under changing beliefs. Their computing method works with many kinds of doubt measure, including deep learning ones. A policy that looks just one step ahead already beat common rules of thumb by a lot. They also add a smoother way to train the policy, which trades a bit of bias for much steadier learning. Tests on real and made-up data back the gain.
arxiv-2502-06176:
Thi Thanh Mai Ta, Quang Huy Nguyen, and Dinh Nho Hào analyze the accuracy of a numerical method for finding a hidden source term, in a 2025 paper. The setting is an advection-diffusion equation, the workhorse model of spreading substances, posed on domains whose internal boundaries move. Recovering the source from measurements is an inverse problem, prone to instability.

The authors recast the recovery as an optimization task steadied by Tikhonov regularization. Their solver fits its mesh to the moving interfaces in space and time together. They prove two second-order error bounds for the forward solver. The unknown source is then discretized three ways: variationally, as a constant per element, and with a post-processing step. The first two reach optimal accuracy, the third converges faster than linear. Rules for choosing the regularization strength from mesh size and noise level guarantee convergence to the true source.
arxiv-2502-06276:
Kasun Weerasekara and co-authors simulate how uneven dust spread changes explosion strength in the standard twenty-liter test sphere, in this 2025 paper. Labs worldwide use this sphere to rate dust explosion hazards for industry. Inflow eddies push dust toward the wall before ignition, breaking the assumed even spread. The team modeled lycopodium dust blasts and checked the model against real data.

They define a simple score, Phi, for wall crowding, from zero for all-at-wall to one for perfectly even. As Phi drops from one, blast pressure first dips, then climbs. With heavy wall crowding, peak pressure rose slightly and its rise rate jumped a tenth over the even case. Middling crowding gave the weakest blasts. The authors warn test standards should account for distribution.
arxiv-2502-06376:
Vasileios Tsouvalas, Tanir Ozcelebi, and Nirvana Meratnia propose, in a 2025 paper, a federated fine-tuning method for clients who each juggle many tasks. Classic federated learning assumes every client does the same job. Real clients specialize, and some handle several tasks at once.

Older fixes group clients or give each a private model layer, burdening the server. Their method instead learns task vectors jointly across clients. A new merging rule weighs tasks by the direction of their vectors and builds one unified vector. That design drops clustering and per-client storage entirely. Many-task federation could let hospitals, phones, and firms train together without flattening their differences.
arxiv-2502-06476:
Vlad Hosu and co-authors define the natural size at which a photo looks its best, in this 2025 paper. Shrinking or enlarging an image changes how good it looks, yet quality tools mostly ignore scale. The authors name that best size the image's intrinsic scale: the largest size at which it still shows its highest perceived quality. Beyond it, flaws grow faster than detail.

To study the idea, they built a data set of seven hundred eighty-five images, each labeled with its intrinsic scale by experts. They also set out how such labels should be gathered, so the measure stays consistent. A predictor trained on the set could tell platforms when to stop upscaling a photo. The concept links two topics, quality and resolution, that tools have long treated apart.
arxiv-2502-06876:
A well-aligned language model should be helpful, honest, and harmless at once, but those three goals can pull against each other. Jinluan Yang and co-authors compared two ways to build such a model in 2025: mixing training data, or merging models that each specialize in one goal. Merging works at the level of model weights, where conflicts can be resolved directly.

The team map where the three goals help and hurt each other, then propose a merging method called RESM that reweights unusual values and adapts to sparse layers. In tests it beat both data mixing and earlier merging methods by small but consistent margins. The merged models were released for further study.
arxiv-2502-06976:
Upasana Biswas and co-authors ask a fresh question about human and machine teams: who leans on whom? Most past tests score such teams on task points alone and skip how the pair works as a team. Their 2025 study sets a measure for that lean, built from how each side's acts set up the other's acts in a shared plan. High task scores, they argue, can hide weak teamwork.

Tests pair trained agents with both learned human stand-ins and real people in a cooking game world. Agents that rack up high task points still fail to spark true joint work with their human mates. The gap shows in the lean scores, not the point tallies. The team offers the measure as a way to judge aid tools by teamwork, not just output.
arxiv-2502-07476:
Shiquan Ren wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on bundles that persist over spaces of hard spheres. A configuration space lists all ways a set of spheres can sit in a region without overlap. As the spheres grow, some layouts vanish, and the space changes in steps.

Ren builds bundle structures that survive across these steps. Classic markers of such bundles, called characteristic classes, then give tests for embedding problems. One use is deciding when a space can sit inside another in a regular way. The Stiefel-Whitney and Chern classes serve as the main tools. The work links topology with hard questions in geometry and robotics paths.
arxiv-2502-07776:
Chenchen Gu, Xiang Lisa Li, Rohith Kuditipudi, Percy Liang, and Tatsunori Hashimoto audit commercial language model APIs for a side channel hiding in their speed. Prompt caching makes repeated prompts answer faster. If a cache is shared across users, timing becomes a leak: an attacker can probe what others asked by watching response times. The team built statistical audits to detect caching in the wild.

Seven providers, including the largest, show evidence of globally shared caches. The privacy implication is direct: strangers' prompts leave timing fingerprints. Timing also betrayed architecture: one provider's embedding model shows the signature of a decoder-only transformer, previously undisclosed. The authors press for transparency about caching policies. Efficiency features, they show, are never merely efficiency features when a service is shared.
arxiv-2502-07876:
Sean Benevedes, Ameen Ismail, and Thomas Steingasser propose solving the Higgs hierarchy problem by letting cosmology delete the universes that get it wrong. In their landscape, regions scan over Higgs mass values. Where the mass takes its natural large value, the Higgs potential has only a deep negative-energy minimum, and that region crunches out of existence.

Where the mass falls below a critical value, a metastable minimum with an ordinary cosmic history survives. The critical value is set by where the quartic coupling runs negative. The mechanism needs new TeV-scale physics, such as vector-like fermions, to work. Two example models are worked out, and proposed colliders could probe the relevant parameter space.
arxiv-2502-08176:
Mamin and co-authors wrote this 2025 physics paper on a spectral puzzle at a defect in hexagonal boron nitride. A missing boron atom in this two-dimensional crystal is a favorite qubit candidate, and its electron-nuclear double resonance spectrum shows lines shifted away from the nitrogen Larmor frequency, where they should sit. The team blame the hyperfine embrace between the electron of the defect and nearby nitrogen-14 nuclei.

Second-order perturbation theory gave them correction formulas for the line positions. Plugging in numbers, the predicted shifts matched the experimental spectrum well. The mixing is tiny: nuclear character blends into the electron states at only about 0.04 to 0.07 percent. Small as it is, that admixture matters for reading the quantum state of the defect faithfully.
arxiv-2502-08276:
Shaoxuan Cui and co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on how groups of agents settle to shared states when they act in groups, not just in pairs. On plain networks, friendly links pull agents to one shared value. On signed networks, agents can split into two camps with values of the same size but opposed signs.

The team extends this study to hypergraphs, where one link can join many agents at once. They define a new form of the dynamics for unsigned hypergraphs. Then they work out when the group settles, when it splits in two, and when mixed friendly and hostile links change the result.
arxiv-2502-08376:
Ugochukwu Orji, Çiçek Güven, and Dan Stowell forecast electricity demand with a hybrid model that reads the power grid as a graph. Renewable energy has made demand swing harder, and grid operators need sharper forecasts to plan. Their model, GAT-LSTM, pairs an attention network that weighs links between grid nodes with a memory network that follows demand over time. Line capacities and efficiency figures feed straight into the attention step, so the model's sense of closeness follows physics, not just geography.

Spatial and time features are fused early, letting the model learn how place and rhythm interact. On Brazilian grid data the hybrid beat the best rival models by wide margins, cutting three error measures by roughly a fifth each. The authors present it as a sturdy tool for grid management and energy planning.
arxiv-2502-08476:
The five authors introduce low rank MSO, a fragment of monadic second-order logic in which set quantification is limited to vertex sets of bounded cutrank. They compare its expressive power with several other logics built for graph properties. Separator logic extends first-order logic with connectivity checks, while flip-connectivity and flip-reachability logic are analogues suited to dense graphs, proposed in this work.

Three results anchor the paper. On weakly sparse graph classes, low rank MSO matches separator logic, though not on all graphs. On classes of bounded VC dimension, it matches flip-connectivity logic, again not everywhere. On all graphs, it matches flip-reachability logic. That last result implies every undirected graph property expressible in low rank MSO can be decided in polynomial time, a concrete payoff for pinning down what the logic can say.
arxiv-2502-08776:
Christopher Tosh, Boyuan Zhang, and Wesley Tansey treat treatment response as a latent variable. Their 2025 arXiv paper helps scientists find who truly responds to a treatment. Natural variation blurs responders and non-responders in trial data. Refining hypotheses needs that split made cleanly. The team builds a causal two-groups model for the job.

Treated samples may or may not experience an effect. A prior probability governs that hidden response status. Two empirical Bayes procedures handle semi-parametric and nonparametric cases. The additive-effects version is identifiable from observed data. The flexible version can still test response per sample. Both control false discoveries near the target level. Power stays close to optimal in their checks.
arxiv-2502-08876:
Matilde Abreu and Michael Turner probe a major survey claim that dark energy may be changing over time, in work from 2025. A large sky survey reported hints that dark energy is not simple vacuum energy. If true, the claim would reshape basic cosmology.

The best-fit models behind the claim behave oddly, peaking near a single era and falling fast on both sides. The authors show the fitting form itself forces such shapes, since it allows only four basic patterns. Simpler field models with one free dial fit the data no better than the standard model. Data from the early universe and exploding stars are also weighed. Their verdict urges caution.
arxiv-2502-08976:
Robin Bowers, Elias Lindgren, and Bo Waggoner study costly search over many options in a theory paper from 2025.
