A decision maker can spend resources probing options, then pick one or a feasible set and collect the rewards. Each option hides its value behind a step-by-step search process modeled as a Markov chain on a graph.

Even simple cases of this problem are provably hard in the worst case. Still, the authors prove prophet-style guarantees for a simple sequential rule: probe each option fully as it arrives, keep it or drop it, then move on. For matroid limits the rule secures about half the best possible reward, and it yields fair mechanisms.
arxiv-2502-09176:
Gerhard Hiss and Caroline Lassueur write a 2025 pure math paper, the second part of a series on blocks of finite groups. A block is a chunk of a group's algebra, and the goal is to sort blocks by when their source algebras match. For blocks whose defect group runs in a cycle, an earlier scholar tied each block to a special module and a tree graph.

This part sorts the modules that arise from one family of groups, those close to simple groups of Lie types B, C, and D. The authors reduce that task to the same task for the general linear and unitary groups. For those two groups, they finish the sorting in full.
arxiv-2502-09276:
Carlos Melo and nine co-authors modeled transaction flow in a club-run blockchain to tune its speed, in a paper published in 2025. Such chains, run by known clubs, serve banks and trade, but waste and pace worry their keepers. Their model is a chance-based net that tracks each transaction step. It gives reply time bands at high confidence for a known chain build, Fabric.

Change tests show which dials move pace most. Block size alone could swing pace and reply times by up to three times. Keepers can thus test a change in the model before they touch the live network. The authors stress pace with lean resource use. The network serves as a what-if laboratory for chain administrators.
arxiv-2502-09376:
Junsu Kim, Jaeyeon Kim, and Ernest Ryu study why low-rank adaptation training works, in a research paper from 2025. The method, known as LoRA, fine-tunes large models by learning small low-rank updates. It is now standard, yet past theory relied on simple linear views or narrow setups that miss real training.

The authors sort training into a special regime and a generic, more realistic regime. In the generic case, training ends at a low-rank global best fit, or at a clearly distinct high-rank result. Starting at zero and shrinking weights bias the search toward the good region. The work explains why the method usually succeeds.
arxiv-2502-09576:
Xinqi Huang, Hong Liu, Mingyuan Rong, and Zixiang Xu wrote a 2025 graph theory paper unifying two threshold problems. The chromatic threshold asks how large the minimum degree of a graph must be before graphs avoiding a fixed pattern have bounded color numbers. The homomorphism version asks for more: the small image the graph maps into must also avoid the pattern.

The authors define a general threshold that interpolates between the two, using VC-dimension as the dial. Their main result shows a smooth transition as the restriction on the image tightens. For clique free graphs with enough minimum degree, a bounded size image free of a larger clique always exists. Matching constructions prove the degree condition cannot be improved. Earlier results from several groups fall out as special cases.
arxiv-2502-09776:
Ananya Bhattacharjee and eight co-authors studied in 2025 why people drift away from digital mental health tools. Most fixes tinker with the app itself. This team looked outward, at the user's life, during an eight-week texting program for well-being with twenty participants.

Life kept interrupting: family duties, work crunches, sudden illness. The authors call these situational disruptors. Workshops with twenty-five more people brainstormed answers, from gentler goal setting to kinder ways to frame a missed week. The lesson for designers: plan for messy lives, not ideal users who never get busy or sick.
arxiv-2502-09876:
Sanchez-Salcedo and Santillan simulate a small moon-like body that orbits backward inside a gas disc around a young star. Their 2025 paper asks what gap such a backward orbiter carves, and how the gap shifts with body mass, disc thickness in flow terms, and edge rules. Flat two-dimensional runs form the core, with one three-dimensional check.

A rule for when a gap opens matches the runs well. Depth grows as the disc flows more freely, and a scaling law ties depth to mass and flow. Unlike forward orbiters, the body sits at the gap's inner edge, where gas piles up to twenty times the gap floor. Roaming bodies may gain bent orbits from the uneven setting.
arxiv-2502-10076:
Samrik Chowdhury and co-authors present a 2025 method for sorting graphs that change over time. The hosted text lays out a way to layer such a graph by patterns that repeat across time, called temporal motifs. That layering turns a moving graph into a stack of still views at many scales, from fine to broad.

With that stack in place, tools built for still graphs can be used on time-based ones. The tools include persistent homology, which tracks how shapes in the data appear and vanish across scales, and recent kernel methods for layered graphs. The team shows the approach works on tasks that ask which class a time-based graph belongs to. The frame opens a new path for studying networks such as message traffic or contact patterns.
arxiv-2502-10376:
Nicolás Angelini and Ursula Molter study the size of slices cut through fractal sets. Their 2025 paper uses intermediate dimensions, a family of measures that sits between two classic ones. They ask how the dimension of a set relates to the dimension of its slices by flat subspaces. That question has known answers for the classic measures.

The authors prove upper bounds that match the classic pattern. They also draw side results on how these measures behave as their tuning value nears zero. For lower bounds that give equality for almost all slices, they state which conditions suffice. A new type of Frostman measure is built for this setting. The work extends slice theory to the in-between measures.
arxiv-2502-10476:
Pulkit Rustagi and co-authors plan robot moves under shifting goal ranks in a 2025 paper. A lone agent may face goals whose rank order flips by place or state. Past planners fix one rank order for the whole map.

Their frame ties both rank order and payoffs to a hidden context at each state. A Bayesian step learns that context map from expert paths. The solver builds one plan per rank order, then joins them into one loop free plan. Tests in software and on a real mobile robot check the plan. Context aware ranks suit homes and wards where aims shift by room.
arxiv-2502-10576:
Jan-Philip Joost and Michael Bonitz wrote a 2025 physics paper on charge separation in graphene nanoribbons, narrow strips of carbon sheet. Head title and text focus on these ribbons, and the study uses computer simulations. A laser pulse with even light across the strip can still spark charges in just one small spot.

The effect rests on the odd electronic structure of the ribbons, which comes from their shape rules. With the right light energy, direction, and phase, the pulse made local charges and excitons in a few femtoseconds. The spot size was below one nanometer. Such fast, local control could aid tiny electronics and brings petahertz switching, far faster than current speeds, within reach.
arxiv-2502-11776:
Koki Yanagida's paper from 2025 defines a new invariant for links, loops of knotted string sitting in the three-sphere. An invariant is a value that stays fixed while the link is bent, so it can tell links apart. The new one, the parabolic Dijkgraaf-Witten invariant, widens a reduced form set out earlier by Karuo.

Yanagida computes it for several links whose double covers match lens spaces, a well-known family of shapes. The paper also gives a way to read part of the invariant straight from a link diagram, the flat drawing of the knot. That shortcut makes the new tool usable without heavy machinery, and it ties knot theory to gauge-style counting methods.
arxiv-2502-12176:
Tao Fan and co-authors list ten hard problems for federated foundation models, in work from 2025. Large models can now learn across many sites without pooling private data. A big central model and small local models teach each other in turn.

The ten problems span five broad themes, from basic theory to fair rewards. Topics include learning from private data, forgetting on demand, and skewed local data. Moving knowledge both ways between center and edge is another core issue. Marking model ownership and cutting cost round out the list. The paper gives labs a shared map of what blocks real deployment of these systems.
arxiv-2502-12476:
Elnaz Rahmati, Alireza Ziabari, and Morteza Dehghani tackle a flaw in large language models in their 2025 paper. Such models learn tasks across tongues, yet they often reply in English or another big language when asked in a smaller one.

The team builds a score that checks if both the idea and the language of a reply are right. Tests in seven languages show that skill moves across tongues while the choice of tongue stays biased. The last layers of the model seem to pick the tongue. Training only those layers matched full training at far less cost, and helped small languages most.
arxiv-2502-12576:
Geetanjali Bihani and Julia Rayz test sentence encoders on grooming risk in chats, in a 2025 paper. Online grooming puts children at risk, yet predators rarely speak plainly at first. They build trust slowly and hide intent in coded, indirect words. Models tuned to spot grooming may miss those soft signals.

The authors use a fuzzy framework that maps human judgments to degrees of risk. Three groups supplied the judgments: law officers, real victims, and decoys. Fine-tuned encoders failed most where predators used indirect speech paths. Those same samples held more words outside the model's known vocabulary. The gap shows why coded language needs direct attention in safety tools.
arxiv-2502-13176:
Gulhan and co-authors wrote a paper in 2025 on BaKlaVa, a budgeted allocation approach for the key-value cache used by large language models processing long texts. The cache stores past computations so the model need not redo them, but it grows linearly with the length of the input, consuming scarce graphics memory. Earlier shortcuts treated the cache's many attention heads uniformly, clearing or compressing them by a single fixed rule.

BaKlaVa instead estimates the importance of each cache individually. A one-time profiling step then assigns each cache a share of a total memory budget. Important caches retain more of their data, while unimportant ones are trimmed harder. The team tested the approach on two widely used open models. It compressed the cache by up to seventy percent while keeping baseline performance, and at higher compression rates it improved accuracy by as much as tenfold over uniform methods.
arxiv-2502-13376:
Ameesh Shah and co-authors teach multi-agent teams to split big tasks into symbolic sub-tasks on their own. Their 2025 paper works with reward machines, a formal way to write tasks that can be broken into parts. Splitting work can make joint learning far more sample-efficient, but the best split is usually designed by hand.

Their framework learns the split and each agent's policy at the same time, guided by a task-aware network design. No prior knowledge of the setting is needed. Tests in several deep reinforcement learning worlds showed the method working well. It even handled settings where agents' actions depend on each other, allowing synced joint learning that earlier methods could not reach.
arxiv-2502-13976: Roberto Beraldo and Ricardo Suyama reflect on ill posed problems and the regularization method in a 2025 book written in Portuguese. Ill posed problems, whose answers swing wildly with tiny data changes, sit at the heart of inverse problems. In question and answer form, the book traces where regularization came from and where it may go. It also compares what the word means across fields that share it: inverse problems, statistics, machine learning, and deep learning. The authors frame the shared idea as a bridge between disciplines.
arxiv-2502-14076:
Li Wu and seven co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on cutting carbon from edge computing by moving work short distances. Edge data centers serve nearby users, so shifting work usually means breaking speed promises. But the team found that the carbon cost of electricity swings sharply even within one state or between neighboring countries.

Their system, CarbonEdge, places each job at the nearby site with the cleanest current power, while guarding response-time promises. On a real testbed in central Europe it cut emissions by nearly four-fifths. Simulations at content-delivery scale suggested savings near half in the US and two-thirds in Europe, with added delay under six milliseconds. The study shows green routing does not need continent-scale jumps: local contrasts in power mix are enough to matter.
arxiv-2502-14276:
Hanlin Wang and co-authors present STeCa in a 2025 paper on training language-model agents. Such agents act step by step in a live setting, but on long tasks one weak choice can pull the whole run off course.

STeCa fixes drift at the step where it starts. During exploration, it scores each action and flags the weak ones by comparing step-level rewards. A model then reflects on the flagged steps and writes better paths, which become training data next to the clean successful runs. Tests showed STeCa beat rival training methods by a clear margin. The lesson is that quick, small corrections teach agents more than end-of-task feedback alone.
arxiv-2502-14376:
Fangming Cui and co-authors presented SPTR in 2025, a prompt learning method that does not forget. Prompt learning adapts vision-language models to new tasks by tuning text prompts. Tuned prompts often overfit the task at hand and lose the broad knowledge held in hand-crafted prompts. The team's method guards that knowledge in two ways.

First, optimal transport acts as a textual regularizer, keeping tuned features close to hand-crafted ones. Second, a similarity paradigm blends natural and adversarial alignment scores from several hand-crafted prompts. The two parts share one aim: stronger generalization. Across four task types and eleven datasets, SPTR beat existing prompt learning methods. The gains covered few-shot learning, base-to-novel transfer, cross-dataset use, and domain shifts.
arxiv-2502-14476:
Irina Nikishina and co-authors build a yardstick for answers that compare two things, in a 2025 paper. Comparative questions, such as which phone or policy is better, need answers that argue both sides fairly. The team wrote fifteen criteria for judging such summaries, then scored answers from people and from six large language models across two datasets.

Human and model judges agreed closely under several setups. Llama-3 70B proved the best judge of summaries, while GPT-4 wrote the best comparative answers. All data and code are public. The benchmark gives builders of question-answering systems a shared way to grade a tricky answer style.
arxiv-2502-14976:
Nastaran Darabi and colleagues shielded vision-language models from adversarial images in a 2025 paper. These models read pictures and text together, and tiny crafted changes to a picture can flip their answers. Older defenses cost heavy retraining, depend on one model's shape, or break when attackers adapt, so the team sought a filter that runs at use time with no retraining.

Their EigenShield uses random matrix theory to spot structured distortions in the model's internal features. A scoring rule separates feature directions that carry real meaning from those prone to carry attack noise, and the input is projected onto the clean directions. Attack success dropped sharply in tests, with no model changes needed. The method works across model designs.
arxiv-2502-15076:
Five authors wrote a computer vision paper in two thousand twenty-five on training self-driving systems with fake data. Real road data are costly to label, so simulators make scenes instead. The catch is that models trained on fake scenes often fail on real streets, a gap between the virtual and real worlds.

Using the CARLA simulator, the team built a pipeline that makes LiDAR point cloud scenes for finding objects in three dimensions. Random variation in the scenes helped the model transfer. A detector trained only on fake data did well on the real KITTI benchmark. A little real data for fine-tuning nearly matched full real training.
arxiv-2502-15476:
Anton Ayzenberg and co-authors survey in 2025 how sheaf theory, a branch of deep geometry, is used in deep learning and data science. The catalog creator field is blank, so the byline in the text governs here. Sheaves track how local data fit together into a global whole.

The main text gives a friendly tour of ideas shared by theorists and practitioners. The authors note that notions from cellular sheaves extend to sheaves on general posets. They present a new algorithm for sheaf cohomology on finite posets. Appendices supply a rigorous path from basic diagrams to Laplacians and diffusion.
arxiv-2502-15676:
Zhining Zhang and co-authors present AutoToM in 2025, a method that helps machines guess what people think and want. Reading minds from acts is key for social machines that work with people. Prompting large models can work but brings steady errors, while hand-built models are firm yet narrow.

AutoToM builds its own model of the person in each task, then reasons backward from acts to beliefs. When doubt runs high, it adds more inner states or more steps of context and tries again. Across five test sets it beat older methods and even large reasoning models. It also gave trust scores much like human ones and aided live choices for a robot.
arxiv-2502-15876:
Michael Unger and Glennys Farrar wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, per the author line in its text. It studies how our galaxy's magnetic field bends the paths of the most energetic cosmic rays, a bend that must be undone to find where they were born.

The authors first sum up how unsure the back-tracked paths are under a recent set of field models. They then give a fresh fit that adds glow from the Local Bubble, a nearby cavity, using a shell model for its field. They also show why two well-known field maps differ, tracing it to the halo part. Last, they back-track the top events seen by two big observatories. None points to a clear steady source, which hints that some came from brief, one-off blasts.
arxiv-2502-15976:
Luca Battaglia and Francisco Reyes-Sánchez published a 2025 mathematics paper on shaping surfaces to order. A classic problem asks: given a surface, can it be stretched so its curvature matches a prescribed pattern? Their version is knottier: the surface has a boundary, cone-like singular points, and corners. Both the surface's own curvature and the boundary's bending are prescribed at once.

The authors solve it with a variational method, recasting the geometry as the search for a best function, an approach built for smooth surfaces and extended here to the singular case. They state this is the first result of its kind for surfaces with singularities. Prescribed-curvature problems sit at the junction of geometry and partial differential equations, with uses from materials to relativity. Handling cones and corners matters because surfaces are rarely perfectly smooth. The paper widens the map of what can be shaped to order.
arxiv-2502-16276:
Vu Hong Quan and two co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on best choices when goals clash and data is unsure. Their problem has many aims at once, range based values, and rough, non-smooth terms. Facts in the rules may also be off. They work with the robust twin of the problem, the form that guards against the worst data shifts.

They set out kinds of near best answers for that twin, in near and near regular forms. With a penalty trick, they show one kind exists and meets a key set of terms to a set level of truth. They then give terms that suffice for such answers. A dual form of the problem is built and its links to the primal are checked.
arxiv-2502-16976:
An-Lan Wang, Nuo Chen, Kun-Yu Lin, Yuan-Ming Li, and Wei-Shi Zheng tackled task-oriented grasping in clutter in 2025. A robot hand should grip a knife by the handle to cut, but by the blade to hand it over, so the right grasp depends on the task. Past work handled only simple grippers or tidy scenes, which limits help in real homes.

The team defines the fuller problem, with six degrees of freedom for the grasp pose in multi-object scenes. They built a large data set of 4,391 cluttered scenes holding more than two million grasp poses, each labeled for its task. Readers get both a benchmark and a problem statement that match daily assistance: many objects, full pose freedom, and a purpose behind every grip.
arxiv-2502-17676:
Anbajagane and a large team validate the analysis pipeline for a major weak lensing data set, in work from 2025. The DECADE catalog holds 107 million galaxies imaged by one camera. Its sky coverage is patchier than past surveys, since many programs fed it.

Cosmic shear measures how gravity bends galaxy shapes across the sky. Uneven data depth can fake or hide that faint signal. The team therefore stress-tested every pipeline stage on uneven mock data. Simulated data vectors checked that the methods recover known inputs cleanly. Passing those tests licenses the real catalog for cosmology. The paper is the third in the project series.
arxiv-2502-18276:
Pinaki Mondal revisits a classic counting problem in algebra in a solo twenty twenty-five paper. When a system of polynomial equations has more solutions bunched together than expected, we must assign each bunch a weight, called a multiplicity. Old fixes by Severi and Lazarsfeld treated all bunches alike.

Mondal breaks that symmetry and defines an ordered multiplicity, where the order in which equations are used matters. He gives an explicit form for this new weight. The payoff is a step-by-step route to count lone solutions, with bounds in the style of Bernstein and Kushnirenko. As a test, he counts the lines that touch four general spheres in space, and gets the known count of twelve.
arxiv-2502-18376:
Martirosyan and a large team of co-authors pinned down in 2025 the atomic layout of a thin oxide film whose properties hinge on tiny distortions. The film, a vanadium oxide perovskite fifty nanometers thick, was grown on a scandate crystal that strains it into a set pattern. The team combined X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, and 3D electron diffraction with first-principles math. Each method checked a different scale of the structure.

The film kept its bulk crystal system but grew locked to the substrate across all 140 unit cells. Maps of the reciprocal space fixed its orientation and lattice sizes. Imaging resolved the rare-earth atoms' sideways shifts, a signature distortion of this family. The authors say such maps guide the design of oxide stacks with tailored electronic states.
arxiv-2502-18576:
Jaemarie Solyst and seven co-authors study teens as AI auditors in twenty twenty-five. Young people use AI daily yet are shut out of responsible AI practice. Auditing, the hunt for problematic system behavior, is one place their perspective is missing. The authors ran a workshop study with seventeen teens.

The teens audited AI tools they actually meet: image generators, search autocomplete, and image search. Support came from critical AI literacy scaffolding. Guided discussion of AI ethics and a dedicated auditing tool backed their work. The teens produced quality insights, the authors found. Their hobbies, identities, and age-specific experience shaped what they caught. Readers in responsible AI get proof that youth can audit meaningfully, not just be studied.
arxiv-2502-18676:
Xingyu Bruce Liu, Haijun Xia, and Xiang Anthony Chen propose a new way for people and AI to work together in a 2025 position paper. In most systems today, the AI waits for a prompt, answers, and stops, taking turns with the user.

The authors call their idea Thoughtful AI. In this picture, the system keeps thinking between turns, growing and sharing its own train of thought as the talk goes on. They argue this would let the AI act on its own initiative and stay in step with the user's thinking. Example projects show what such systems might look like. The paper sets out the idea and its base concepts, and looks ahead to what it could change.
arxiv-2502-18776:
Sara Issaoun and co-authors present a 2025 astronomy paper reporting the first transfer of phase calibration from the three-millimetre band to the one-millimetre band across an Earth-sized baseline. Short wavelengths promise the sharpest black hole images, but the atmosphere scrambles their phase quickly. Frequency phase transfer borrows the steadier phase measured at a longer wavelength to correct the shorter one.

The team demonstrated the trick between distant radio telescopes spanning the planet. Longer coherence at one millimetre means fainter targets and sharper pictures become reachable. The result is a milestone for the global arrays that photograph black holes, extending their reach to the band where the finest detail lives.
arxiv-2502-19076:
Youval Klioui builds fast neural networks that pinpoint where signals come from. Direction-of-arrival estimation guides radar, sonar, and wireless systems. Classic solvers like ADMM work well but carry heavy memory and compute costs.

The new networks unfold that solver into layers built from circulant matrices, a structured form with a tiny footprint. Memory drops from the square of the problem size to roughly the size itself. Each layer costs far less to run. In tests, the lean networks matched bulkier rivals on detection rate and angle error, opening the door to sharp sensing on small hardware.
arxiv-2502-19176:
Amirhossein Azarbahram and four co-authors tune wireless power beaming with smart wall panels in a 2025 paper. Radio power transfer could charge tiny devices with no cords, but most of the sent power is lost on the way. Panels that steer radio waves can help, and a new kind links its cells in a web rather than one by one.

They study one sender, one panel, and one charger unit. Their task joins aim of the beam with the shape of a multi tone signal to lift the harvested power most. Two solvers are offered, one exact but heavy and one light loop. More tones or more panel cells raised the take in tests, and the best split of power swung with the charger's load state.
arxiv-2502-20076: Angus McCowan, a solo author writing in 2025, disputes a claim about the origin of the virus behind the recent pandemic. A prominent report said data strongly backed two separate jumps of the virus into humans. McCowan inspects that calculation and finds the test was not even-handed. The single-jump model faced stricter conditions than the two-jump model. When the two-jump model is held to the same conditions, he shows, the claimed support disappears.
arxiv-2502-20176:
Xinran Liu, Zhenhua Feng, Diptesh Kanojia, and Wenwu Wang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It makes full-body dance from music with a diffusion model fed by a music foundation model.

Past dance makers lean on hand-made music traits. The new method blends the deep traits of a foundation model with the hand traits, so high sense and fine timing both guide the steps. The team checks four foundation models and two hand trait sets. Their blend makes the most true-to-life dance and the best match to the beat and mood of the track. The work was shown at a NeurIPS workshop.
arxiv-2502-20476:
Yankai Li and Mo Chen unify three popular planning methods under one gradient view, in a paper from 2025. Path integral control, reinforcement learning, and diffusion models each excel at trajectory tasks, yet they were treated as separate worlds with separate math. A shared lens could transfer gains between them.

They show the first method performs gradient ascent on a smoothed energy over a probability law. Policy gradient learning then reduces to the same update after an exponential change of the objective. Diffusion sampling in reverse follows the identical rule as well. One Gibbs-measure frame thus covers all three.
arxiv-2502-20976:
Cadamuro and co-authors improve a reweighting method for Higgs pair studies in a 2025 note. Making two Higgs bosons at once probes how the Higgs interacts with itself. New physics effects are framed through effective theories that reshape event rates.

Old reweighting used only the pair's combined mass, which misses shifts in sideways momentum. That flaw bites hardest where signals cancel strongly. The new method blends several reference samples with weights set by a distance measure across key variables. Built for two effective theories at top collider energies, it tracks momentum variation far better. The approach could extend to other processes with fit samples.
arxiv-2502-21276:
Yuan Bian and co-authors work on a prediction problem where some answers are missing in a tricky way. In many datasets the missing values are not random: the chance of a gap depends on the unseen answer itself. Standard boosting methods, which build predictions by adding many small models, assume full data and can go wrong here.

The team adapts boosting by reshaping the loss it chases, using tools from a branch of statistics built for incomplete data. They give two ways to make that fix and prove the method settles down and stays consistent as data grows. Tests on sample data show the new approach predicts well in practice. The work adds theory that boosting has often lacked.
arxiv-2503-00076:
Eva Brucherseifer, Marco Marquard, Martin Hellmann, and Andrea Tundis sort data sources for disaster twins in a 2025 paper. A digital twin mirrors key systems like power, water, and traffic to guide crisis response. In a disaster, main data feeds may die from damage, overload, or attack.

Their taxonomy grades sources by traits and by weakness to crisis events. A likeness score then finds backup sources that can step in fast. A data source manager is sketched as an add-on to twin frames. A city traffic case shows the method at work. The aim is twins that bend under stress rather than go blind.
arxiv-2503-00176:
Xin Chen and Zhibin Ye sketch a workable receiver for quantum illumination, a radar-like trick that uses entanglement to spot faint targets, in a 2025 paper. The method beats classic sensing even in heavy noise, and its edge survives the loss of entanglement en route. The hard part is the receiver, which must turn faint linked signals into a readable shift across a vast number of modes.

Their design pairs three parts. A source makes linked light across frequency modes with matched photon counts. A heterodyne read takes in the returned light across all those modes at once. A cavity-boosted gate then processes the modes on command. Joined, the parts chart a path from lab demos to field-ready quantum sensors. The authors stress the mode handling, long the choke point, as the core advance.
arxiv-2503-00276:
Haoxin Li and co-authors taught a system in 2025 to animate a still photo into a video of a delicate human action, learning from very few example videos. Making fine actions, such as subtle hand moves, is hard for video generators, above all for rare actions with little training data.

Their method, called FLASH, forces the model to rebuild one video using the motion of another video that shows the same action with a different look. That push makes the motion lessons transfer to new images and stops the model from memorizing the few examples. Extra decoder layers carry detail from the photo into each frame. Human judges preferred its videos in about two thirds of comparisons.
arxiv-2503-00776:
Yun Min Song, Kangmin Lee, and Jae Kyoung Kim review a shortcut in cell modeling in this 2025 paper. Modelers of chemical networks inside cells often shrink big models with a steady-state shortcut. The total version of that shortcut is trusted for its accuracy in smooth, average models. Random, molecule-by-molecule models are another matter.

The review shows the shortcut can warp behavior in random models. The warp appears even where the shortcut is strictly valid in the smooth setting. False conclusions about cell dynamics can follow. The authors urge modelers to check the shortcut case by case in random simulations. Ease of use, they argue, is no proof of safety.
arxiv-2503-00876:
Zijian Dong and five co-authors tackle imbalanced regression, where some target values appear far more often than others and learned features crowd toward the common cases. Older fixes came from classification, clustering features into groups. That ignores the continuous, ordered nature of regression targets. The authors instead shape the feature space geometrically, asking features to spread evenly over a sphere.

Two losses do the shaping. An enveloping loss pushes the induced trace to cover the sphere's surface uniformly. A homogeneity loss keeps the spacing smooth and even. Both plug into a surrogate-driven representation learning framework. Tests on real regression and operator learning tasks show the geometry-based losses help rare values get fair representation. The paper argues uniformity, handled with care for ordering, is the missing ingredient for fair regression features.
arxiv-2503-01576:
Mojtaba Safari and co-authors present a 2025 paper on sharpening MRI scans with a diffusion model that works in very few steps. Diffusion models can rebuild crisp images from blurry ones, but they usually need long sampling chains. Their trick shifts the residual error inside the diffusion process itself, aligning blurry and sharp distributions early.

The framework, Res-SRDiff, rebuilt test images in only four sampling steps. It was tried on ultra-high-field brain maps and on prostate scans. Against four rival methods, it won on signal quality, structural likeness, and edge fidelity, with strong statistical support. Fine anatomy survived the speedup. Faster reconstruction could widen access to high-grade MRI analysis in busy clinics.
arxiv-2503-01676:
Elahe Delavari and co-authors presented a learning frame in 2025 for keeping self-driving cars in lane. Their frame joins perception and action, in the way human motor learning does. Standard driving stacks can struggle to adapt, generalise, and run cheaply.

The frame uses active inference, where a model tries to cut prediction error, or surprise. That model shapes steering from learned links between sensing and motion. The car can learn lane keeping with little data and no large retraining for new settings. Tests in a driving simulator matched standard methods, with no extra computing load. The authors see a robust option for real-world use.
arxiv-2503-02076:
Shanting Wang, Panagiotis Typaldos, and Andreas Malikopoulos present CorrA for obstacle avoidance in two thousand twenty-five. Self driving cars must dodge moving blocks in real time. CorrA pairs a large language model with model predictive control. The model sets the bounds of a safe corridor around each block.

Sigmoid shaped bounds define that corridor in a smooth way. Real time car data reshape the bounds as the scene shifts. That trims the state space the controller must search. An optimal control solver then finds a crash free, near best path. Tests in simulation and real runs beat a plain control baseline.
arxiv-2503-02176:
Kaoru Teranishi and Takashi Tanaka designed a way in 2025 to outsource control calculations without revealing them. A dynamic controller, the algorithm steering a machine in real time, may be run on remote servers for power or convenience, but its parameters, state, and signals can be sensitive. Their protocol splits the computation between two servers using secret sharing, so neither server ever sees the secrets it helps compute with.

Earlier encrypted control schemes worked with a single server and needed periodic decryption of the controller state or re-encryption of inputs, which caps how long they can run. The two-party design runs indefinitely with no such resets. The authors show its control performance can be made arbitrarily close to an unencrypted controller's, present refinements that cut communication costs, and demonstrate the protocol numerically on proportional-integral-derivative and observer-based controllers.
arxiv-2503-02276:
Immanuel Ben-Porat, José Carrillo, and Pierre-Emmanuel Jabin extend mean-field theory to swarms of particles whose interactions are singular and whose weights change over time. Earlier landmark work handled Coulomb-like repulsion with fixed weights. Time-varying weights break parts of that machinery, so new estimates are needed.

The authors combine the known commutator estimates with a new functional inequality to control the error between the particle system and its limiting equation. They also prove that the limiting partial differential equation and its trajectory system are well posed. The results apply to models where each particle's importance or mass evolves, such as opinion dynamics and biological aggregation with growth.
arxiv-2503-02676:
Park, Cho, Kim, and Lee assess the Electron-Ion Collider as a facility for pentaquark measurements, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Pentaquarks are exotic particles made of five quarks. The collider offers high energy plus polarized beams for precision study. One heavy pentaquark, Pc forty-three twelve, serves as the test case.

Production rates are computed under different spin-parity guesses. A vector meson dominance model keeps the approach parameter-free. Beam spin asymmetry and decay polarization can pin down spin and parity. The ePIC detector can measure both quantities accurately. Other heavy pentaquarks and nuclear matter studies extend the program.
arxiv-2503-03076:
The Raychaudhuri equation tracks how a bundle of paths through spacetime spreads or focuses, and it anchors much of cosmic evolution theory. The five authors extend it with a non-affine parametrization inside the k-essence framework, which lets the flow curves stray from geodesics. Working with a DBI-type k-essence Lagrangian, they derive a modified equation that produces emergent repulsive effects in the expansion of the universe.

Their Bayesian analysis, checked against cosmological data, supports the scaling link between the k-essence field's rate of change and the cosmic scale factor. The modified equation can address the Hubble tension and predicts a naturally evolving dark energy equation of state. Read as an anti-damped harmonic oscillator, it shows a caustic avoidance signature that may hint at classical or quantum-like effects. The authors present the work as a bridge between scalar field dynamics and modified gravity.
arxiv-2503-03276:
Jiayi Zhang and seven co-authors present a hybrid neural model for city traffic in a paper from 2025. Classic routing algorithms work on static maps but struggle with the shifting, tangled flow of real streets. Their model joins graph convolutional networks, which learn the street network's shape, with Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, which flex to fit curved patterns in the flow data.

Tests used real traffic data from the Baltimore area. The model matched rival methods on accuracy and handled noisy, irregular data better. It also rerouted flow in ways that eased congestion and adapted to a shock event, the collapse of a major bridge.
arxiv-2503-03376:
Grzegorz Centała and Jarosław Kłos examine a subtle coupling between magnetism and rotation in a tiny magnetic strip set in an elastic base, in this 2025 physics paper. When surface waves ripple the base, the strip's magnetization feels not only strain but the local rotation of the material. That rotational contribution can be tuned by the strip's own shape based magnetism.

The authors compute the coupling coefficients for a strip and fold them into the effective magnetic field the waves create. Two wave families are considered, Rayleigh and Love waves. The rotational share grows or shrinks with the thickness to width ratio and with the magnetization direction, and for one wave type it fades as the cross section nears a square. The results guide designs of magnonic devices that ride on sound.
arxiv-2503-03576:
Juha Harviainen, Frank Sommer, Manuel Sorge, and Stefan Szeider revisit a basic question in machine learning, in a paper published in 2025. Decision trees are prized because people can read them, and pruning trims a tree down without losing much accuracy. Two trims are common: swapping a subtree for a leaf, and raising a subtree in place of its parent.

Their analysis maps how hard each trim is to do perfectly. Swapping can be optimized in fast, polynomial time. Raising, surprisingly, is NP-complete, meaning no fast general method is likely. They then chart which limits on features or values make raising manageable, with matching fast and hard cases. Early experiments back the theory. The map helps builders know when to trust pruning tools.
arxiv-2503-04276:
Julius Reinhard, Felix Wiesner, and co-workers showed soft X-ray depth imaging driven by a tabletop light source in a 2025 paper. High-harmonic making produces coherent extreme ultraviolet light in the lab, but its speed falls toward higher photon energies. Blocking use in the soft X-ray water window. The band where carbon absorbs strongly and water stays transparent, ideal for imaging living and layered samples. The team pushed a high-flux harmonic source across that whole band anyway.

With it they performed soft X-ray coherence tomography, adapted from the optical technique, reading depth shapes inside a layered heterostructure without destroying it. The broadband, noise-resistant method reached an axial resolution of about twelve nanometers. Lab-scale sources that image in the water window could bring such analysis to plain facilities.
arxiv-2503-04576:
Emily Vorderwülbeke and Isabella Graßl compare how queer students fare in software engineering versus the humanities, in a 2025 study. Queer students often meet bias and weak belonging at university. Software engineering is male-dominated and heteronormative, while humanities draw more queer students and a more open culture.

Surveying 165 queer software engineering students and 119 in the humanities, the authors found stark gaps. Engineering students were less open about their sexuality, felt they belonged less, and hit more study hurdles. Yet they showed greater determination to finish their degrees. The authors urge computing programs to borrow the humanities' inclusive classroom habits so talent is not pushed out by climate.
arxiv-2503-04676:
Ferri-Cortés, Henriques, and Fernández-Rossier wrote this 2025 physics paper on testing a prized quantum magnet model with a microscope. The AKLT model describes spins linked in a lattice, and its ground state is a prized resource for a style of quantum computing. Real materials may or may not match the model, and the team ask how a tunneling microscope could tell.

For a simple two-spin unit, they show how current-based spectroscopy, run out of equilibrium, reveals every excited level, fixing both the plain and the curved parts of the spin coupling. For a sheet of spins of size three-halves, they turn to the edge. Loose half-spins dangle there in the ideal model, and their faint signals could betray a true AKLT match.
arxiv-2503-04876:
Comparing two groups by risk ratio or odds ratio is routine in medicine, but a study can end with error bars wider than planned. Luis Mendo designs sampling plans that promise a set accuracy in this 2025 paper. The data are yes-no outcomes from two groups, such as recovery or no recovery. The promise must hold no matter what the true rates are.

His plans sample in two stages for each group. The size of the second stage depends on what the first stage showed. That adaption keeps the error measure under a chosen target for any true rates. It also holds the average sample sizes of the two groups near a chosen ratio. A batch version lets both groups be sampled together in fixed lots. The paper weighs how close the plans come to the best possible efficiency.
arxiv-2503-05076:
Christopher Lombardi, Alexander Kosovichev, and Keitarou Matsumoto listen to a Sun-like star, KIC 6106415, for hints of its inner life. Stars ring like bells, and shifts in their tones track inner structure and surface activity. The team pairs two decades of solar tone data with Kepler's measures of the star.

They compare tone patterns and tone lifetimes between the star and the Sun. The star's spot count came out much like the Sun's, peaking near 175, which fits its faster spin. The data hint that its activity cycle may run shorter than the Sun's eleven years. Such checks sharpen the known link between a star's spin and its magnetic moods.
arxiv-2503-05176:
Shuxiang Xu and a team of co-authors study a nickel-based material under high pressure, in two thousand twenty-five. The material belongs to a rare family that can carry current with no resistance. Pressure is applied with diamond tools, which makes close study of its states hard.

The team used fast light pulses to watch the material as pressure rose. A wave pattern in the material faded with pressure and vanished near a point where its structure changed. Two forms of that wave stayed locked together as pressure grew. Past that point, a small energy gap appeared at low heat, in line with pairing for the no-resistance state. The two states seem to compete strongly.
arxiv-2503-05276:
Green fuel gas made from sun and wind comes in gusts, while its call runs its own clock, so its store and road plan must bend by the day. Hasturk and co-authors school a plan tool for that bend in a 2025 study. Their tool learns with the bars built in, not pasted on: stock caps and road rules sit in the school sums.

A state worth read past each choice sharpens the tool's aim. A wide look form then reads more days at once, and beats the plain form by a tenth on the mean, at more cost. Small sets sit near the best known. Stock school rules and plain rolls fall short of both forms.
arxiv-2503-05376:
Jiaoyi Zhang and co-authors present Femur, a framework for fast and secure queries to a public key-value store. Their 2025 paper starts from a privacy need: user query data must be protected when a public database is accessed.

Private information retrieval gives full security but scales poorly. The authors argue that many users would rather set their own privacy level, guided by theory, and trade some security for speed. They define distance-based indistinguishability to give provable guarantees for such relaxed settings. Femur then uses that idea to query public stores with flexible trade-offs. The design aims at large-scale use where full private retrieval is too slow.
arxiv-2503-05576:
Florent Mertens and co-authors set tighter upper bounds in 2025 on a faint signal from the early universe, when the first stars lit up gas between galaxies. A radio array in Europe listens for that signal at a set wavelength. Foreground noise and tool flaws have long swamped the real signal.

Better calibration, sky models, noise removal, and a learning-based split of signals cut leftover error a great deal. Results at three distances back in time improved two to four times over past bounds from the same array. Checks with added fake signals supported the method. Leftover glow from far sources and beam flaws still limit the search.
arxiv-2503-06076:
Sydney Anuyah and co-authors report a 2025 study on teaching computers to pull cause-and-effect links out of text. Such extraction helps search and question tools, but models trained on one source often fail on another. The team tested which network designs and data mixes carry over best between sources with different writing and labeling styles.

A fairly simple model, pairing a biomedical language model with a two-way memory network, generalized better than fancier designs. The team also built a scoring metric that rewards finding the right noun phrases, not just exact tag matches. Mixing training data from varied domains and label styles improved transfer. Gains were largest when the mix held a fair share of both stated and implied cause sentences.
arxiv-2503-06676:
Chenyu Huang and co-authors present Delta-DCT in a 2025 paper on shrinking the extra weights of fine-tuned models. Modern practice pretrains one large model, then fine-tunes a copy per task, and storing every copy is costly. Delta compression trims the gap between each copy and the base, but older methods need training data or extra training.

The trick borrows from JPEG image compression. Weight gaps are cut into patches, each patch is scored for importance, and patches move into the discrete cosine transform domain for quantization at matched bit widths. No training or calibration data is needed at any step. Tests span large language models, smaller text models, vision transformers, and a multimodal model. Even at very tight compression, scores matched or beat the uncompressed fine-tuned models in many cases.
arxiv-2503-06776:
Kai Ren, Giulio Salizzoni, Mustafa Emre Gürsoy, and Maryam Kamgarpour tackle safe robot teamwork under uncertainty in this 2025 paper. Robots that interact must respect shared safety limits even when sensing and motion are noisy. The authors cast the problem as a game where each robot optimizes its own cost.

Chance constraints cap the risk of violating the shared limits. They find a tractable reformulation of the game and a dual ascent algorithm to solve it. The algorithm provably settles at a feedback equilibrium that honors the chance constraints. In driving simulations and real robot tests, the method kept robots safe under uncertainty. Its paths were less conservative than a single-agent predictive controller's. The authors offer it for close multi-robot work.
arxiv-2503-07076:
Zhihao Huang and co-authors ordered image generation by frequency in two thousand twenty-five. Autoregressive models build images step by step. Standard ones draw pixels in a fixed spatial order. Real images carry structure in layers of fine detail. Broad shapes live in low frequencies, texture in high ones. The new framework, NFIG, follows that natural order.

Generation starts with the low-frequency parts of the picture. Those few tokens fix the global layout cheaply. Higher-frequency stages then add detail step by step. Quality rose while inference cost fell in their tests. Fewer tokens spent on layout means faster images. The method aligns the model's process with image structure. It may extend to other media with layered spectra.
arxiv-2503-07276:
Guilherme Silva and co-authors audit a decade of machine learning studies that classify heart rhythm faults from ECG traces, in a 2025 review. Automatic classification promises early warning of arrhythmias, and papers claim high accuracy. Yet many ignore the field’s evaluation standards, making results hard to compare or trust.

The review covers studies from 2017 to 2024. It checks three gaps: adherence to standard protocols, fair evaluation practice, and whether the models could run on real devices like monitors and patches. Hardware limits are often forgotten in papers but decide bedside value. The audit gives researchers a checklist and gives clinicians a reason to ask harder questions before adopting a model.
arxiv-2503-07576:
Raphael Gerlach and Sören von der Gracht analyze the symmetries of robot swarms with tools from dynamics in this 2025 paper. Their robots are forgetful, sight-only machines that move in lockstep rounds. The question is which mirror and spin patterns a swarm's motion can keep.

The swarm's update rule commutes with rotations and reflections of the plane. Swapping robot labels also leaves the rule unchanged. Those two facts pin down the full symmetry group of the system. From it, a ladder of possible symmetric behaviors can be derived. Designers can use the ladder to rule out formations a swarm cannot hold. The math serves swarms that must self-organize without a leader.
arxiv-2503-08676:
Jinchang Zhang and co-authors merge heat and light images into a single picture that also knows depth. Thermal cameras see in darkness but lose texture, while normal cameras fail in the dark; fused views serve robots and rescue teams better than either alone. Most fusion work serves detection tasks and throws depth away.

Their network leans on written prompts: a vision-language model reads the scene description and steers a diffusion process that blends the two feeds into a color image. Two side branches then estimate depth from the fused result, and depth errors flow back to sharpen the fusion itself. The loop is meant to give machines richer scene sense for driving, navigation, and search missions in murky settings.
arxiv-2503-09576:
Philippe Chlenski and co-authors present Manify, a free Python library for learning from data that lives on curved spaces rather than flat ones. Some data fit better on such spaces, and tools for that work have been spread out and hard to use.

The library gives tools to place data in single curved spaces or mixes of them. It can also sort and predict with such data, and guess how curved a space is. Code, samples, and guides are posted in public. The authors aim to make this branch of machine learning easier to try and to use in real work.
arxiv-2503-09776:
Aaron Welch and Mariam Kiran stress-test a quantum network simulator in a 2025 paper. Quantum networks are hard to build, and access to real testbeds is scarce, so researchers lean on simulators. Most run serially, which caps the size of networks they can model. One simulator had been parallelized, but its scaling across machines and at larger sizes was unproven.

The team ran the parallel version on Frontier, a top supercomputer, and charted how performance grows with problem size and processor count. Their results expose where the parallel strategy holds up and where it strains, with concrete ideas for improving it. The study is short and practical: simulator builders learn whether the parallel design deserves trust, and users learn what scale of quantum network they can honestly model today. Scaling evidence, the authors argue, matters as much as features.
arxiv-2503-09876:
Chaoming Song proves a new circle theorem for two-dimensional Ising spin glasses, in work from 2025. The classic Lee-Yang theorem places the zeros of a ferromagnet's partition function on the unit circle, but disorder breaks that pattern and blocks the theory's reach. Song shows that for the spin glass, the square of the partition function has zeros packed densely along the unit circle.

Simulations on the square lattice back the claim for quenched disorder. The angular spread of the zeros also shows a finite-temperature crossover marked by a gap opening. The result extends the Lee-Yang frame to disordered systems and gives a fresh angle on spin-glass criticality.
arxiv-2503-09976:
Mingyu Liu and Xian Shi built a frame in a 2025 paper to measure two quantum resources at once. Coherence, the wave-like overlap of states, and true multipartite entanglement, a deep link across many parts, both power quantum tools. Gauging them in the lab is costly, so cheap bounds with sound grounds are prized.

Their method leans on witness operators, tests that flag a resource when it is present. A distance measure between states turns those flags into lower bounds for the gauges. The frame stays light on computing and works across many setups. Labs can use it to size up states without full state mapping.
arxiv-2503-10276:
Linking quantum computers into networks needs a way to steer single photons between nodes on demand. Juan Cumbrado and Ricardo Puebla propose quantum switches for that job in 2025. Each switch is an extra qubit tied to the resonators that connect a node to its waveguide. Close the switch and an excitation leaves fully as a traveling photon. Open it and only part transfers, without warping the photon's shape.

With that control, the authors lay out step-by-step recipes for prized shared states across a network: Bell pairs, and the larger GHZ and W states. Simulations of a three-node network include noise and photon loss. The results still reach high fidelity, which the authors take as a sign the scheme fits today's hardware.
arxiv-2503-10376:
The MIT CompGeom Group with Hugo Akitaya and co-authors count in a 2025 paper the closed quasigeodesics on a cube. Such a curve keeps at most a half plane of surface on each side at every point. Unlike true geodesics, these may pass through corners of the solid.

Every convex solid holds at least three such closed loops, a known result. Beyond the tetrahedron, counts were open until this cube study. The cube holds exactly 15 simple closed quasigeodesics past the three known geodesics. Fifteen examples are built by hand for the lower bound in the paper. A matching upper bound, the main feat, closes the count for the cube.
arxiv-2503-11076:
Pinghui Huang and Xue-Ning Bai wrote a 2025 astronomy paper on how dust clumps in the outer parts of planet-forming disks. Clumping dust is the first step toward building planetesimals, the seeds of planets, yet the process is uncertain. A famous mechanism, the streaming instability, can gather dust, but the outer disk stirs its gas with other instabilities.

The authors ran a three-dimensional global simulation with a leading fluid code, refined enough to hold all four instabilities at work. Shear in the gas set the overall motion, with a breathing pattern strengthened by the dust itself. Dust settled into a thin midplane layer crowded with small vortices. Strong clumps appeared, likely where the streaming effect and a wavy instability acted together. Only a small share of vortices held clumps dense enough to form planetesimals. Finer grids made clumping stronger still, so the process had not settled.
arxiv-2503-11276:
Edward Pearce-Crump builds neural networks whose outputs respect the symmetries of symmetric tensors. The paper from twenty twenty-five notes that such tensors fill statistics, machine learning, and graph theory. They also serve physics, chemistry, and materials work. Past symmetry-aware models chased Euclidean motions and skipped symmetric tensor inputs. Permutation symmetry, where swapping indices changes nothing, is the trait here.

Pearce-Crump gives two full accounts of all linear maps with this trait between symmetric power spaces. No other linear maps qualify. Tests on two tasks show the maps learn from far less data than plain multilayer networks. They also hint at skill transfer to tensors of new sizes. The work hands modelers a complete parts list for this symmetry class.
arxiv-2503-11376:
Panggih Kusuma Ningrum and co-authors present a system for spotting uncertainty in science writing in a 2025 paper. Scientists often hedge claims with words that show doubt, and finding those spots helps search and text mining. Their system, called UnScientify, uses a weakly supervised method, so it needs little hand-labeled data.

The system matches word patterns, parses complex sentences, and checks who a claim is tied to. In tests, it scored higher on accuracy than modern large language models, reaching a score of about zero point eight one. The authors stress the trade-offs in the result. A plain rule-based tool can be cheap, clear, and easy to adapt to a field. For this narrow task, they argue, the older style still has real strengths.
arxiv-2503-11576:
Ahmed Nassar and co-authors present a tiny model that converts documents in a 2025 paper. Page conversion must catch text, tables, code, and layout at once. Past tools lean on huge models or on chains of narrow parts.

Their model, SmolDocling, reads a full page and writes a new markup that keeps content, structure, and place. At a quarter-billion parameters, it is far smaller than rivals. Yet tests show it matches models many times its size across business, science, and form pages. New public sets for charts, tables, equations, and code came with the work. Small size cuts the cost of bulk conversion.
arxiv-2503-11676:
Take two coprime integers p and q, and count how many ways a large number n can be written as a sum of distinct powers built from them. Erdős conjectured, and Birch proved, that at least one such expression exists once n is large enough. Yuchen Ding and co-authors now pin down how many expressions there are. The count grows roughly like two raised to a power set by the squared logarithm of n, divided by the logarithms of p and q.

They also show that stepping from n to n+1 barely changes the count for large n, so the function grows smoothly rather than jumping. The note connects the count to the classical topic of m-ary partitions. It is a short, sharp sharpening of a known theorem: where Birch guaranteed one representation, the authors give the asymptotic size of the whole family.
arxiv-2503-11776:
Paula Benaglia and five co-authors present radio observations of a rare pair of giant stars in a 2025 paper. The two stars in HD 93129A blow strong winds that crash into each other. That crash zone glows at radio wavelengths and speeds up tiny particles. The pair recently passed their closest point in a very long orbit.

The team watched the system for over a year at three radio bands, and added older data. Brightness rose about fourfold over fifteen years, then fell again. Their fits suggest the magnetic field grew stronger near the closest pass. They also measured radio glow from other giant star pairs in the same field.
arxiv-2503-11876:
Manav Kohli and co-authors present a wireless engineering paper, published in 2025, built on a large measurement campaign in New York City. Millimeter wave links at high frequency promise fast next generation networks, but heavy signal loss limits them to dense city areas. The team measured an urban testbed across four sites, gathering tens of millions of power readings over thousands of sidewalk links.

From those readings they model how signal strength fades with distance and how beam aiming loses gain, noting effects of transmitter height and season. They then build spectrum consumption models that show what signal quality users on a city block can expect. The results give planners grounded tools for placing such networks.
arxiv-2503-11976:
Patrick Martin and Radmila Sazdanović study hidden twists, called torsion, inside two related algebraic tools for measuring the shape of networks, in a 2025 paper. The tools are magnitude homology and its Eulerian variant, which sort the paths in a graph into algebraic groups. Torsion in those groups signals subtle structure that plain counting misses.

Building on three lines of earlier work, the authors give two proofs that torsion does occur in the Eulerian version. They also describe what kinds of torsion appear and what orders it can take. Worked computations for several families of graphs make the abstract claims concrete. The paper ties the two homology theories closer together and gives researchers a sharper picture of what these invariants can detect in a finite graph.
arxiv-2503-12176:
Deren Han, Min Tao, and Zihao Xia present a 2025 paper on algorithms for a class of ratio-based optimization problems. In these problems, the goal is to shrink a fraction whose top and bottom parts each mix smooth and rough terms. Such problems show up in CT scan rebuilding, sparse signal recovery, and picking a stock portfolio with a good risk-to-reward ratio.

The authors design an algorithm that runs in a single loop, splitting the work so a costly linear step is kept apart from the rough part. They prove it settles at an exact answer point under a standard assumption. A practical version with a flexible line search runs faster still. In tests on the three named tasks, the method beat leading rivals.
arxiv-2503-12476:
Daniel Majaess and co-authors add proof in 2025 that some dark bands in starlight come from a cage shaped carbon molecule. The bands have puzzled astronomers for a century, since no one knew what made most of them. Two bands were tied to the charged form of this molecule, but some doubted that the two bands share one source.

The team widened the range of band strengths they tested by a factor of ten and added new sight lines, corrected for a metal's own bands. Across that range, the two bands rise and fall together very tightly. They also point to more bands that match lab values for two larger charged forms of the molecule. Each firm match cuts the list of unknown bands and helps map the chemistry of space.
arxiv-2503-12676:
Ayoub Ammar Boudjelal, Rania Yasmine Bir, and Huseyin Arslan propose a mother waveform for future wireless networks in a 2025 paper. Networks from the fifth generation onward must mix many signal shapes for varied tasks, from calls to sensing. Swapping shapes usually means rebuilding the radio design each time.

Their candidate shape, built on interleaved frequency division, can morph into all common Fourier based shapes by setting index and phase values. Those shapes serve data links, radar like sensing, and joint use of both. Simulations show gains in data performance, sensing strength, and smooth coexistence of shapes on shared spectrum. The unified frame could ease design of sixth generation radios.
arxiv-2503-12776:
Rico Pohle and Nic Shannon explore exotic magnetism in a spin-1 pyrochlore in a 2025 paper. Spin liquids, magnets that refuse to freeze into ordinary patterns, were long hunted in spin-half materials, but spin-one magnets may host even richer versions.

Simulating a minimal model on the pyrochlore lattice, a network of corner-sharing tetrahedra, the pair found seven distinct spin liquid phases. One carries nematic correlations, order in direction without order in the arrows themselves. Matched against neutron scattering data, that nematic liquid fits the real material NaCaNi2F7 strikingly well. The match suggests the spin-one pyrochlore on lab shelves already hosts a liquid stranger than the classic picture.
arxiv-2503-12976:
Yan Kim and three co-authors shrink real-time multi-agent systems to a checkable size without breaking their verified properties, in this 2025 paper. The catalog title carries conference footnote text; the head's clean title governs. Model checking proves temporal properties of systems with many interacting agents, but only if the model stays small enough to analyze.

The team extends a variable-based abstraction method to systems with real time. Agents are described by an enriched graph, and irrelevant variables are folded away by a defined procedure. The authors prove the shrinking sound for the universal fragment of a timed temporal logic. Anything proven on the small model then holds of the large one. Complexity gains are estimated, and a simplified model of the Estonian internet voting system, checked with the Uppaal tool, demonstrates the pipeline. They pitch the abstractions as practical, not just theoretical.
arxiv-2503-13076:
Some crystals are chiral: their atoms spiral in a way no mirror image can match. Fernando Gómez-Ortiz, Aldo Romero, and Eric Bousquet build an algorithm that hunts for gentle phase changes linking a plain parent crystal to a chiral one. The method pairs a near-symmetry search with first-principles physics calculations.

The workflow checks candidate parents across the 22 space groups that allow handedness. It then looks for a soft vibration mode that could carry the parent into the chiral form through tiny shifts. Applied to six known chiral materials, the search sorts them into three fates. Some have no valid parent. Some have a parent but no soft mode. A few have both, giving a true pathway. The tool streamlines the search for switchable chiral materials.
arxiv-2503-13176:
Rui Wang, Quentin Lohmeyer, Mirko Meboldt, and Siyu Tang rebuild clean three-dimensional scenes from messy real captures in a 2025 computer vision study. People walking through a scan, objects that move, and other clutter end up baked into ordinary reconstructions, ruining them for design or measurement. Their framework separates the scene into a static part and a dynamic part inside a Gaussian splatting representation, the current fast standard for photo-real scenes.

The split is learned self-supervised, without hand labels for what moves. Distractor-free models from ordinary walkthrough videos suit product design review and robot mapping.
arxiv-2503-13276:
Manfred Borzechowski and co-authors settle a long-open question: a logic of programs does enjoy the Craig interpolation property. Their 2025 paper proves the claim for Propositional Dynamic Logic. Three past proof tries were later criticized or withdrawn, so a sound proof was still missing.

The proof builds a cyclic tableau system with a loading trick that spots good repeats. Soundness and completeness come through a game reading of the system. Interpolation adapts a classic method to tableaux with repeats, solving fixed-point equations cluster by cluster. The method is constructive: it tells how to compute the in-between formula. Code in Haskell ships with the work, and a formal check in Lean is under way.
arxiv-2503-13576:
Ziqiang Li and four co-authors survey how researchers teach image generators specific visual concepts, in a 2025 paper. Text prompts alone cannot pin down a particular face, style, or object. So a field has grown around mining concepts from reference images and feeding them to diffusion models alongside words.

The survey sorts the field into four pursuits. Concept learning captures a new idea from a few pictures. Concept erasing removes unwanted notions, from copyrighted styles to unsafe content. Decomposition splits a pictured concept into parts, and combination merges several learned concepts into one scene. For each, the authors explain the core techniques. They close with open challenges, offering newcomers a map of a fast-moving corner of generative AI.
arxiv-2503-13676:
Minoru Kusaba, Megumi Iwayama, and Ryo Yoshida give a model for cases where the thing to be predicted is a whole curve, like a spectrum, not a single number. Most past methods train a split model for each point of the curve, which wastes the links between points.

Their kernel based model uses those links, much as multitask learning does, which lifts both speed and accuracy. It gives not just a curve but a spread of doubt around it, worked out in closed form from a Bayesian view. Tests on fake data and on a materials task, the density of states, show the gains of the method.
arxiv-2503-13776:
Nicolas Augier, Milan Korda, and Rodolfo Rios-Zertuche probe a gap in control theory in a 2025 paper. Optimal control asks for the cheapest path that obeys a system's rules. A relaxed form swaps paths for spread measures, and the two may not agree.

The team build a case where a true gap opens, even in a smooth, fully steerable system kept inside a unit ball. The running cost bends the wrong way, and one odd path resists close copies that obey the bound. That resistance blocks a classic closeness result. The case also shows a gap for occupation measures. State bounds, the work warns, can break tidy theory.
arxiv-2503-13976:
Nipuni Ginige, Nandana Rajatheva, and Matti Latva-aho present a learning-based design for wireless links aided by smart surfaces in a 2025 paper. Such surfaces, placed in the environment, can bounce signals in helpful ways and lift performance in next-generation networks. Tuning the sender, the receiver, and the surface together is a complex task.

Their design uses a neural network shaped as an autoencoder, which learns the whole chain end to end. It handles coding, channel estimation, surface phase tuning, and signal shaping in one system. In numerical tests, the error rate beat the theoretical rate of conventional designs for the same setup. The letter suggests learned designs can outdo hand-built ones for surface-aided links.
arxiv-2503-14276:
Two famous conjectures in harmonic analysis turn out to lean on each other. Changkeun Oh proves in a solo 2025 note that the restriction conjecture for a hyperbolic paraboloid implies the decoupling theorem for the same surface in doubled dimension.

Restriction theory asks how waves can concentrate on curved surfaces; decoupling asks how a wave breaks into nearly independent pieces. Linking them means progress on one front pays off on the other. As a payoff, the note gives a notably simple proof of the decoupling result for the three-dimensional case, a result that once took heavy machinery. Short bridge results like this one quietly reorganize a field's map of what remains to prove.
arxiv-2503-14376:
Maximilian Beck and co-authors present faster software kernels for linear recurrent networks in this 2025 paper. Such networks scale gently with sequence length and now rival transformers at language modeling. In practice, though, speed needs hand-tuned kernels like the famous Flash Attention. A prior kernel for linear networks split sequences into chunks, but small chunks forced many states into memory.

Their Tiled Flash Linear Attention adds a second level of splitting inside each chunk. That lifts chunk size limits and keeps the chip's math units busy. They apply it to the xLSTM network with matrix memory, plus a slimmed variant with a simpler gate. Benchmarks beat Flash Attention, plain linear attention, and Mamba kernels. The authors claim a new speed mark for long-context building blocks.
arxiv-2503-14776:
Parameshwar Pasnoori, Ari Mizel, and Patrick Azaria solve a one-dimensional model in twenty twenty-five. The massive Thirring model is equivalent to the sine-Gordon model, a classic pair in quantum physics. They solve it under two kinds of Dirichlet boundary conditions: open, and twisted open. A duality symmetry links the two setups.

The symmetry swaps the sign of the bare mass while swapping the boundary type. For negative mass with open boundaries, the system sits in a trivial phase with a unique ground state. With twisted boundaries at the same mass, it enters a topological phase. That phase hosts zero energy modes pinned at each end. Positive mass reverses the pairing, as the duality demands. Readers get a full boundary spectrum for a textbook model.
arxiv-2503-14876:
Samuel Klein and co-authors train particle classifiers without simulated background in a 2025 paper. Supervised learning in high energy physics feeds on simulator labels, but as inputs grow rawer and higher dimensional, simulators drift from reality and poison the training. The classification without labels trick learns from mixed real samples instead.

Their strong version of the method removes the need for background simulation while training supervised style classifiers. Because real collisions supply the background, the domain shift that plagues simulation trained models disappears. Tests show the resulting classifiers can beat simulation trained rivals on real data. The authors pitch the method as the field's inputs keep getting lower level and harder to fake.
arxiv-2503-15076:
Lynnyngs Kelly Arruda and Dmitry E. Pelinovsky wrote a math paper in two thousand twenty-five on wave patterns in a nonlinear equation. The equation is the defocusing modified Korteweg-de Vries equation, used for waves in some physical settings. They study a wave that travels and repeats as it moves.

The authors describe that wave with special functions based on theta functions, and they derive the linked functions for the Lax system behind the equation. Their main result is a new solution. It describes a kink breather, a sharp step joined to a pulsing wave, moving on the traveling wave background. The work adds exact forms for a class of complex wave motion.
arxiv-2503-15276:
Near the ground, turbulence is rarely the same in all directions, and that unevenness, called anisotropy, shapes how weather models should treat the air layer. Mosso, Lapo, and Stiperski use machine learning to find out what drives it.

They trained random forest models on measurements from flat and mountainous sites, feeding them both raw variables and scaled, non-dimensional groups. A new feature-selection method pruned overlapping inputs. Against expectations, the terrain itself did not rank as a strong driver. The scaled groups proved sturdier, and a ratio of two length scales, the turbulence memory length against the integral scale, tracked anisotropy in day and night alike. By day a refined stability measure led; by night, measures of rapid distortion took over.
arxiv-2503-15376:
Tetsuo Hyodo reviews hadron interactions and the idea of compositeness in work from 2025. Hadrons are particles built from quarks, and exotic forms beyond the usual types may be loose pairs of hadrons bound like tiny nuclei.

Learning how hadrons interact is hard from scattering tests alone, above all at low energy. New tools include precise pair measurements, correlation methods from particle collisions, and first-principles lattice calculations. The review shows how correlation methods probe one key pair, uses compositeness to gauge the molecular share of one particle, and looks ahead to future facilities.
arxiv-2503-15476:
Suchismita Das and Raghunath Chelakkot run computer tests in 2025 on self-driven particles near a wall. Such particles can coat a wall fully, form drops, or leave it dry, states known as wetting. The team kept the particles inside flat, hard walls and turned one dial: how fast particles spin at the wall.

Faster wall spinning undid full coating in steps, they found. The coat first split unevenly, then broke into drops, then dried off. In the drop state they measured the contact angle as drive and spin changed. The shifts tied to wild swings in particle energy and bubbles in the dense layer. The neat result is that a local spin rule alone can flip a whole surface state.
arxiv-2503-15576:
Mics left in wild places can log bird song for months, but the flood of sound is too big to sort by ear. Alba Márquez-Rodríguez and co-authors build a sort chain in 2025 for a famed Spanish marsh. A famed bird tool works well in broad use, yet its train data skews to some places and sounds.

The team first runs a song spot step, which cuts clips to parts where birds sing. Then local models, tuned on hand marked marsh sound, name the kind. The spot step lifted every model, and a tuned form of the famed tool with the step beat the plain tool. The chain helps track marsh health through its birds.
arxiv-2503-15776:
Alice Chen, Phil Halper, and Niayesh Afshordi surveyed physicists about black holes and fundamental physics in two thousand twenty-five. The poll was taken at a two thousand twenty-four conference in Copenhagen called Black Holes Inside and Out. It aimed to snapshot expert attitudes for historians and sociologists of science.

Eighty-five completed surveys came back from one hundred fifty-one registered participants. Questions covered contested topics like black holes and dark energy. Leading ideas such as the cosmological constant, inflation, and string theory each won less than a majority. The only majority view, at sixty-eight percent, was that the Big Bang means the universe evolved from a hot dense state, not an absolute beginning.
arxiv-2503-15976:
Dondoglio and co-authors present a 2025 astronomy study of star clusters that host more than one generation of stars.
