Globular clusters mix an older first group, much like field stars, with a younger group rich in odd light elements. Light measures can sort the groups, while spectra give exact chemistry. The team merged both kinds of data across thirty-eight clusters.

Their tagged sample is the largest yet for six light elements, from carbon to aluminum. Cluster mass tracks how wide the element spread runs, backing earlier light-based work. Iron differences among first-group stars showed up in nineteen clusters. In eight, iron levels matched a star's place on iron-sensitive diagrams.
arxiv-2503-16076:
Boris Houska and co-authors present a 2025 control paper on building control Lyapunov functions for linear systems that face limits on their states and inputs. Their method uses a recent form of polyhedral computing, where the shape of the safe region is fixed in advance by a chosen configuration.

The authors show how this setup yields piecewise affine convex Lyapunov functions through one convex optimization problem. The same design also covers uncertain systems hit by both additive and multiplicative disturbances. It can stand in for the cost of long-run optimal control, which makes it useful for explicit controller design and for model predictive control. Worked examples show the method performs well.
arxiv-2503-16476:
Tsvetomila Mihaylova and colleagues staged traffic conflicts between self-driving cars and human drivers in a 2025 paper. Shared roads force automated and human drivers to negotiate, and misunderstandings at that interface cause the riskiest moments. Using the CARLA driving simulator, the team built a set of exemplary conflict scenarios that arise under shared autonomy.

The scenarios probe how driver behavior and split-second decisions affect safety and traffic flow when both kinds of driver must react. The toolkit is deliberately simple and extendable, so other groups can add conflicts and rerun them. Situation awareness researchers gain a shared stage for testing how machines and people read each other's intentions.
arxiv-2503-16776:
Valentin Bieri and co-authors asked in 2025 what vision-language models know about whole cities when shown three-dimensional reconstructions built from aerial photos. Such models usually work indoors or on roads. Their OpenCity3D approach points them at urban scale and asks high-level questions instead of tracing outlines.

The models estimated population density, guessed building ages, predicted property prices, and assessed crime and noise, all with little or no task-specific training. Zero-shot and few-shot results impressed the team. The authors claim a new paradigm: language-driven urban analytics, where a planner can interrogate a city model in words. Planning, policy, and environmental monitoring are the named beneficiaries. The project page hosts the materials for others to try.
arxiv-2503-17376:
Douglas Plummer and five co-authors review brain-like computing hardware in twenty twenty-five. Demand for computing keeps rising fast with AI, machine learning, and connected devices. That growth calls for new building blocks that save energy and scale well. Neuromorphic computing, modeled on the brain, is one such path.

The review covers two-dimensional spintronics, which uses electron spin in atom-thin materials. Methods discussed include spin-orbit torque, magnetic tunnel junctions, and skyrmions. New layered materials can join memory and logic at the atomic scale. The authors stress both how far the field has come and what still blocks real use. Readers get a survey aimed at scale and energy efficiency above all.
arxiv-2503-17476:
Kubendran Amos wrote this 2025 education paper on a fairness problem in team-based learning. In this teaching method, students work in small teams on class tasks. Amos found that when students pick their own teams, they tend to group with peers from similar income backgrounds, even when all sides say they value fairness.

The paper offers a simple fix. Students reflect in numbers on their background and on how prepared they feel. Teachers then use those numbers to form more balanced teams. When the fix was used, teams came out balanced and class performance improved. Without it, teams skewed toward one background and performance fell. The author argues that good intent needs structure behind it to produce fair results.
arxiv-2503-17576:
Zeynab Aghabazaz, Michael Daniels, Donald Lloyd-Jones, and Juned Siddique build a joint statistical model of cardiovascular risk in a two thousand twenty-five biostatistics paper. Risk factors, medications, and fatal events evolve as one, and modeling them apart loses information.

Their Bayesian approach links longitudinal trajectories of risk factors with medication use over time and with time-to-death results. It handles missing medication status and treatment switching as explicit uncertainties rather than nuisances. Applied to a cardiovascular cohort study, the model captures detailed temporal dynamics and improves prediction of events. The authors aim at personalized intervention plans grounded in how risk and treatment in fact unfold.
arxiv-2503-17676:
Jingyu Zheng and Baoyindureng Wu study spanning trees where every vertex has odd degree in a 2025 paper. Such odd trees are elusive: some dense graphs have none at all. The pair maps out exactly when they exist.

Every highly connected graph with an even number of vertices contains a connected odd factor, they show. Yet complete bipartite graphs with both parts even never have an odd spanning tree, yielding dense counterexamples at minimum degree half the graph size. Push the minimum degree one higher and an odd tree is guaranteed. Split graphs and triangle-free graphs get full characterizations too. An application shows the complement of any wide graph holds a spanning odd double star. Open problems close the paper.
arxiv-2503-17776:
Zewen Zhang, Qinyuan Zheng, and colleagues study a lattice model with three internal flavors in a 2025 physics study. Ultracold alkaline-earth atoms in optical lattices let experimenters tune such models closely. The Fermi-Hubbard model describes particles that hop between sites and repel when sharing one, and extra symmetry across flavors enriches its behavior.

Most theory assumes equal flavor populations and strong coupling limits. Real experiments drift from both, so the authors examine flavor imbalance away from those limits. Their ground-state results show how the model's phases respond to imbalance. That response tells experimenters which effects are robust and which are artifacts of ideal settings.
arxiv-2503-18076:
Somnath Roy and co-authors adapt, in twenty twenty-five, speculative decoding from text generation to classification. Speculative decoding uses small draft models to propose answers that a big model checks. Their framework flips that idea: up to three lightweight worker models predict class labels independently. When a majority agree, the label is accepted, skipping the expensive judge model. When they disagree, the judge decides. This balances efficiency and accuracy, they argue.

They found small three-billion-parameter chat models align with judges about as well as larger seven-billion models after tuning. The best small worker pair agreed with judges on eighty to eighty-three percent of sentiment cases. Harder ticket-similarity cases ranged from fifty to eighty percent. The design confines costly judging to hard cases.
arxiv-2503-18476:
Wei Deng, Mengshi Qi, and Huadong Ma generate 3D indoor scenes with a vision language model guided by global local tree search. Large vision language models excel in many fields, yet few studies apply them to indoor scene generation. The task is a planning problem bound by spatial and layout common sense.

Globally, objects are placed one by one, with multiple placements explored in a tree search. The scene is decomposed by room, region, floor objects, and supported objects to cut tree depth. Locally, each placement splits into steps. The model reads a top down grid whose cells carry distinct emojis and names a cell as the object location. Experiments show more plausible scenes than state of the art approaches.
arxiv-2503-18576:
Etienne Wamba and co-authors map instabilities in ultracold atom mixtures in a 2025 paper. Two Bose gases sit in a lattice of light, feeling both long-range dipole forces and a contact strength that pulses in time. Quantum corrections beyond the average picture also enter. The team reduced the system to a discrete wave equation and probed its stability.

Two kinds of instability, one from pattern formation and one driven by the pulsing, were charted in parameter diagrams. Long-range forces and quantum fluctuations each shifted the borders strongly. Direct simulations confirmed the charts and showed the tangled dance the three effects perform together. Knowing where the lattice gas breaks up helps experimenters steer it toward useful states instead of chaos.
arxiv-2503-18676:
Deep networks can approximate almost anything, which paradoxically makes it hard to say which features of the data do the work. Feilong Cao and Shao-Bo Lin take a constructive route in 2025. Rather than probing a trained network, they build one by hand. Their linear operator, made of deep sigmoid nets, is tuned to expose feature quality. Its product gates and local fitting power do the heavy lifting.

The built operator approximates smooth and radial functions at the best possible rate. Better, it can certify several features at once, smoothness and radialness among them. The authors offer the construction as a theoretical yardstick for judging what a target function demands.
arxiv-2503-18776:
Antonio Capolupo and co-authors argue that experiments built to catch the faint relic neutrinos from the early universe can also test a specific idea about neutrino mixing. In the flavor Fock space model, mixing creates a condensed flavor vacuum with unusual traits. That condensate might even account for part of dark matter.

A planned experiment called PTOLEMY aims to capture low-energy neutrinos on tritium. The authors show its results would be sensitive to which neutrino model is correct. A signature of the flavor vacuum in its data would support the model and its dark matter claim. The work links a tabletop-scale search to deep questions about neutrinos and the cosmos.
arxiv-2503-19076:
Distorting a six-iron molecule can tune its quantum links, Hamid Arian Zad and co-authors show in a 2025 paper. The molecule holds two iron triangles whose exchange forces compete. A classic distortion effect makes those forces uneven, lifting a ground-state tie and creating rich quantum behavior.

The team maps the ground-state phases and magnetization under an outside field. Measures of three-way entanglement and conditional entropy track how links shift. Distortion strengthens links inside each triangle while reshaping links between them, they find. Such molecules could serve as tunable building blocks for quantum devices. The work shows a chemical knob for dialing quantum correlations up or down.
arxiv-2503-19176:
Yizhu Wen and co-authors test how well hidden marks in AI-made audio hold up against attack in a 2025 survey. Such marks, called watermarks, can prove where a sound clip came from, expose fake speech, and guard music rights. Makers claim their marks resist removal, but each claim is usually tested against only a few attacks.

The team sorted twenty-two marking schemes, rebuilt nine of them from open code, and hit them with twenty-two kinds of attack in more than a hundred setups. They found eight new attacks that work very well. No scheme survived every distortion across three public data sets. The study gives builders a clear map of where current marks break and what real-world use demands.
arxiv-2503-19476:
Chuqin Geng, Ziyu Zhao, Zhaoyue Wang, Haolin Ye, Yuhe Jiang, and Xujie Si explain graph neural networks with logical rules that stay tied to real data, in a 2025 paper. Rule-based explanations promise global clarity about a model. Many are scored in an abstract concept space, though. Their final form, a highlighted subgraph, may mislead users. The team's framework builds rules from predicates matched to message passing. That structure keeps explanations grounded by design.

They also define a grounded fidelity score. It judges explanations in their final graph form, not the abstract one. Coverage and validity measures join it. Across experiments, the method beat rivals on grounded fidelity by over twenty percent. It also ran ten to one hundred times faster. Scaling held up on larger graphs. The authors release their code openly. They argue faithfulness must be checked where users actually look. The work targets explainable AI practice.
arxiv-2503-19576:
Dhananjaya Jayasundara and co-authors compress neural signal codes by exploiting patterns in their weights, in a 2025 paper. Implicit neural representations store images, shapes, and scenes as small networks that answer at any resolution. Older squeezes either quantize the trained net or bolt on a learned code, and both hinge on the coding scheme.

Their method, SINR, rewrites the weight space as a sparse code over a shared dictionary, and the dictionary itself needs no learning or sending. Plugged into existing pipelines, it cut storage sharply across images, occupancy fields, and radiance scenes while keeping decoding quality high.
arxiv-2503-20276:
Taku Nishino, Yoshiyuki Onishi, and Takayuki Ishizaki derive a stability test for power grids rich in inverters in a 2025 paper. As solar and battery units join the grid, grid staff need a clear rule for when small shakes will die out rather than grow.

Their rule uses only steady facts: part reactances, the network layout, and the resting power flow. It takes the form of matrix tests that each part can check in a shared way. A three bus test case shows the split in action: one kind of inverter load steadies the grid, while another kind upsets it.
arxiv-2503-20376:
Dun Zhang, Panxiang Zou, and Yudong Zhou give a 2025 technical report on Dewey, a text embedding model. Embedding models turn text into numbers that search systems can compare. Long documents strain most models, which lose coherence past short lengths and hurt search quality.

Dewey is built to handle very long inputs and still keep local and global meaning. Its training aligns chunks of a document with the whole through a teaching method called distillation. The open model scores well on standard English and long-text tests. Teams that build search over large files may find it a useful base, and the release notes are shared in the report.
arxiv-2503-20476:
Holovatch and co-authors study a one dimensional billiard in a 2025 paper: a row of resting point particles on a half line, struck by the leftmost one. The masses alternate between two values, and each crash is fully elastic.

As the system wakes, motion spreads both ways. A shock wave pushes into the filled side while a splash region grows on the empty side. Past work showed the key measures follow universal power laws at long times. But real runs are finite, so the laws only emerge slowly. Using effective scaling exponents, a tool from phase transition theory, the team tracks how the front, crash counts, and energies lean toward their universal values.
arxiv-2503-20776:
A single phone video shows a scene from one angle, yet AI tools increasingly need to act inside scenes that move through time. Shijie Zhou and ten co-authors present Feature4X in a 2025 paper, a framework that lifts skills from 2D vision models into four-dimensional scenes. It starts from ordinary monocular video, the kind users already record in huge amounts.

At the core sits a feature field built with Gaussian splatting, a way of storing a scene as soft 3D blobs that can carry learned features. The team distills features from video foundation models into that field, so tasks done in flat images can run in the moving scene. Those tasks include finding objects from open-ended words, editing by language, cutting out regions from a prompt, and answering questions about the scene. One shared representation holds all these skills at once.
arxiv-2503-21076:
Yusong Hu and five co-authors swap the final layer of continual learning models for a spline-based classifier, in a 2025 paper. Continual learning teaches a model task after task without erasing old skills, and the plain linear classifier is a weak link.

Their classifier borrows the structure of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, whose bendable spline curves had kept regression learning stable. Radial basis functions were mixed in for compatibility with the continual setting. Plugged into several recent methods, the new head improved results across benchmarks. Gains held across different continual scenarios. The code is public. The authors argue the classifier, long treated as an afterthought, deserves design attention of its own.
arxiv-2503-21176:
Machine learning potentials are usually built in Python, but most molecular dynamics software is written in lower-level languages, which makes the two awkward to combine. Learning potentials also tend to skip long-range electrostatics, a gap that hurts accuracy when flexible charges matter. Charge equilibration models fix that, yet they need iterative solvers with tight convergence, which costs time and threatens stability.

The five authors present a scalable Python version of a shadow molecular dynamics scheme built on charge equilibration. It avoids the convergence problem while keeping long-term energy stability and accurate properties. They add a fast neighbor list, Particle Mesh Ewald, and classic Ewald summation, powered on GPUs by Triton and PyTorch. The library runs fast charge equilibration for systems with hundreds of thousands of atoms, aiming to be friendly for users building learning potentials.
arxiv-2503-21276:
Naritaka Oshita, Emanuele Berti, and Vitor Cardoso probe a wobble in black hole ringdown math in this 2025 paper. A black hole's ringing tones shift when the underlying potential is nudged even slightly. The team computed tone strengths from first principles to see what that wobble does to waveform fits.

Small nudges spawn fresh tone sets that can fit the early ringdown better, even catching the late tail. Near-miss tone pairs can flare up but cancel each other in the full signal. So the waveform itself stays stable, they show. The work clarifies how much trust ringdown decompositions deserve.
arxiv-2503-21376:
Sangeeta Sharma and four co-authors show that saddle points in the electronic structure of graphene can be used to write information with laser light. Their paper came out in 2025. Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms, and its energy landscape has both valleys and saddle points, which are passes between peaks.

Valleys were already known as carriers of binary information states. The team shows that light with a set polarization excites two of the three saddle points, creating three possible excited configurations. Which configuration appears depends on the direction of the light's polarization. The effect proved robust, working both for very short strong pulses and for longer pulse trains. The same idea should apply to related single-layer materials.
arxiv-2503-21576:
Tobias Fritz and co-authors rebuild two classic laws of chance inside a neat abstract frame, in a study from 2025. The laws say that a long run of fair draws mirrors the true odds, and that the whole shape of past draws homes in on the true shape. Category theory gives a tongue to state those laws sans numbers.

The team sets two rules that a map must meet to count as a draw from the past-draw shape. Since not all strings of draws have such a shape, the maps may be partial. From those rules, they prove crisp forms of three big results, plus a law on shared odds. Worked cases on plain spaces give back the classic laws as a free gain. One proof thus covers ground that books split in two.
arxiv-2503-21676:
Nicolas Zucchet, Soham De and their co-authors study how language models learn facts during training in 2025. Models store vast knowledge, yet the steps by which they gain it are still poorly understood.

On a made-up recall task, learning came in three phases, with a flat stretch before exact facts clicked into place. That flat phase matched the forming of attention circuits that support recall. Uneven training data shortened the flat phase. False claims, or hallucinations, arose at the same time as true knowledge. Adding new facts later by fine-tuning also quickly harmed old stored facts.
arxiv-2503-21876:
Edward Zhang and a large mission team forecast what the SPHEREx space telescope will reveal about a key dust molecule family in nearby galaxies. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons glow at specific infrared wavelengths, and their shortest band sits inside SPHEREx's all-sky spectrophotometric survey range. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team simulated galaxy spectra to test how well the mission can measure the band. Galaxies out to moderate redshifts are covered. Detectability depends on stellar mass and star formation rate.

For massive, actively star-forming galaxies nearby, the band flux should be measurable to about thirty percent accuracy. More distant systems need to be bigger and busier to register. The thresholds are tabulated across redshift slices. The work tells the mission team which galaxy populations will yield dust chemistry, and where stacking or follow-up will be needed.
arxiv-2503-22276:
Calvin Kammerlander and co-authors train machine learning models to predict soil nutrients from satellite images and other farm data, with no lab test of the soil. Sharp nutrient calls let farmers feed crops with care and keep yields up in a lasting way.

A base model built on a European soil set and satellite views is enriched with weather, harvest, and clay data and learned image features. Tree based and neural methods were tuned for the task. The report lays out the data steps and pipelines, and the errors met tight targets. The project aims at regions where lab tests are scarce, such as parts of Africa.
arxiv-2503-22576:
Modern software leans on third-party libraries, and composition analysis tools exist to say which ones a program contains. Lyuye Zhang and co-authors note that those tools are only as good as the feature database they check against, and databases cannot keep up with the flood of open-source code. Their framework drops the database. A language model plays the analyst instead, hunting the open internet for evidence about a component and confirming its identity from what it finds.

The team tested the approach on two jobs: naming native libraries inside Android apps, and spotting copied library reuse in C and C++ code. Results were favorable, especially on components that older tools tend to miss or underrate. The authors present database-free analysis, riding on language models, as a promising direction for keeping software inventories accurate.
arxiv-2503-22676:
Yu, Ramamoorthi, Balakrishnan and their co-authors present TranSplat, a fast way to relight objects in Gaussian Splatting scenes in 2025. Older relighting needs costly inverse rendering or retraining, which slows editing work.

TranSplat works as a post step and shifts the light data of each small surface piece using ratios from source and target light maps. A dual path handles glossy, view-dependent looks, and a light module adds self-shadowing without mesh tracing. Tests on fake and real objects beat recent methods in most settings. Each relight took under one second, the authors report.
arxiv-2503-22876:
Kushagra Srivastava and co-authors build a flight simulator for drone students that cannot crash, in a 2025 paper. Hands-on courses in aerial robotics need testbeds where learners can experiment without smashing hardware. Their framework, VizFlyt, feeds a real drone's motion, tracked by an external positioning system, into a photorealistic virtual world built with 3D Gaussian splatting. The drone flies physically in a safe space while seeing a rich simulated scene.

The loop updates faster than one hundred times per second, quick enough for perception algorithms to react naturally. The team draws on their own teaching experience to propose an open-source, open-hardware curriculum built around the system. Trials in real course projects showed students could stress-test autonomy code stress-free. The paper packages the code, datasets, and build guides for other instructors.
arxiv-2503-23076:
Chip designers rely on cycle-level simulators to test new processors, but those tools are far too slow to explore many designs. A team from Google, MIT, and partner universities presents Concorde in a 2025 paper, a model that blends simple analytical formulas with machine learning. Instead of replaying each instruction, it summarizes a program by how each processor part limits it.

The model runs more than a hundred thousand times faster than the reference simulator while missing true cycle counts by only about two percent. That speed let the team run a first-of-its-kind study assigning performance losses to specific processor parts across millions of evaluations.
arxiv-2503-23176:
Adiesha Liyanage and co-authors wrote a 2025 computer science paper on the hard core of feature matching for malware hunting. Low level malware checks can be cast as a search for a pattern of colored blocks inside a program. Each block holds one key instruction, and a match must line up colors while the key signs form a reshuffle of each other.

The authors name three forms of the problem, from the loose general one to a strict form that demands a full pattern match. The strict form, they prove, is NP-complete, and so is the general one. Even ruling that no part of a pattern shows up is hard in a dual sense. Their upshot is blunt: feature matching tools face hard limits in theory.
arxiv-2503-23476:
Janmejoy Sarkar and a large team of co-authors describe the testing and tuning of a solar telescope flown on India's Aditya-L1 mission, in a 2025 paper. The telescope takes pictures of the Sun in ultraviolet light, a band that reveals the Sun's lower atmosphere. Ground and in-flight checks were needed before its data could be trusted.

The team compares test results with the design targets and explains how raw readings are turned into clean data. Nearly every target was met. The one miss was sharpness: fine detail came out at a scale a bit coarser than hoped, which limits only the finest brightness measures. Even so, the authors say the telescope opens a fresh window on the Sun.
arxiv-2503-23576:
Many speakers swap between two languages mid-sentence, and speech tools must cope with that mix. Injy Hamed, Ngoc Thang Vu, and Nizar Habash study a cheap fix: train the tools on fake mixed data. The open question is whether the quality of that fake data decides how much it helps.

The team tests a wide set of ways to build such data, from word swaps to theory-guided builds and round-trip translation. They check the effect on three tasks: text translation, speech-to-text, and speech translation that chains the two. Past work covered the first task, and this study asks whether its lessons hold for the rest. Their answer is that the payoff of good data shifts with the task at hand.
arxiv-2503-23676:
Chenguang Wan and co-authors build a plasma turbulence surrogate cheaply by fine-tuning on plentiful low-grade simulations, in work from twenty twenty-five. Tokamak turbulence models need costly high-grade runs for training data. One gyrokinetic code is heavy, another far lighter to run. Their trick pre-trains on many light runs, then fine-tunes lightly. The target instability drives heat loss in fusion plasmas.

High-grade data needs drop by about eighty percent overall. A surrogate trained mostly on light data matches the pure one. Performance stays nearly identical across the test comparisons made. Heavy simulation campaigns could shrink across fusion modelling broadly. Digital twins of tokamaks move a step closer with this recipe. Data thrift, not data hunger, is the headline lesson.
arxiv-2503-23876:
Xu and fifteen co-authors predict what paired massive stars become in the Small Magellanic Cloud, in a 2025 paper, the first of a series. Most massive stars are born with a close companion, and the pairing shapes their lives, above all where metals are scarce.

The team ran nearly 53,300 detailed simulations of binary evolution with the MESA code. The models cover a wide span of starting masses, mass ratios, and orbits, and follow the pair through mass transfer and the first star's death. In their standard population, 8 percent of the cloud's bright blue stars are post-transfer systems and 7 percent are mergers. The models match the count of one rare binary type but undercount X-ray binaries with a Be star.
arxiv-2503-23976:
Yongqiang Liu and Masahiko Yoshinaga settle when a twisted cohomology reaches its largest possible size in a 2025 paper. The setting is the space left after removing a family of hyperplanes, a classic arrangement complement. Earlier work capped the dimension of its local system cohomology by the ordinary Betti numbers.

For arrangements that come from real hyperplanes, the authors prove the cap is attained for some degree exactly when the local system is the constant one. Their proof reads the cohomology through the arrangement's chambers. A clean if-and-only-if statement closes a question left open by the earlier bound.
arxiv-2503-24376:
Yi Chen and co-authors test whether reinforcement learning beats plain fine-tuning for video AI in this 2025 paper. Their benchmark holds real-world clips with everyday planning questions in multiple-choice form. Models must both see the video well and reason over what they see.

Tests run at three levels of novelty, from familiar settings to fresh settings with fresh tasks. A mid-size open model was trained both ways. Reinforcement learning learned from less data and scored higher at every level. It even beat the fine-tuned model on outside video tests. A close read found a catch: its reasoning chains grew less coherent, and it sometimes ignored visual clues it had used well before.
arxiv-2504-00176:
Marco Canducci and six co-authors ask which traits split two groups in twenty twenty-five. A class task is hard when the training set is small, the traits are many, and the class scores overlap a lot. When two split groups share the same task, the aim of the work shifts. What counts most is which traits best split how the task plays out in each group.

Their tool, Discriminative Subspace Emersion, grows subspace learning into a broad trait rank plan. It finds the traits that count most to tell how the two groups make their class calls. The plan builds on clear learners with near straight cut lines. Careful tuning and trait rank scores do most of the hard work. The tool lets you set side by side how a choice is made in each group, and not just how right that choice is.
arxiv-2504-00676:
Anthony Yazdani, Ihor Stepanov, and Douglas Teodoro present GLiNER-BioMed for spotting biomedical terms in this 2025 paper. Medical text hides new entity names faster than fixed label lists can track. Standard taggers fail when a type was never in their training set.

Their models take plain language labels and find matching spans with no prior examples. A big teacher model first wrote synthetic labels across many texts. Two lean student designs then learned from that data at several sizes. On test sets the suite beat prior best scores in zero-shot and few-shot runs. Gains held across datasets, and all data and code are public for reuse.
arxiv-2504-00876:
Klaus Kraßnitzer reports on AutoAppendix, a summer project that tried to rerun other people's supercomputing artifacts with as little friction as possible. Conferences now ask authors to submit the code behind their results, and reviewers must judge whether it actually runs elsewhere. His 2025 technical report evaluates artifact submissions to a major supercomputing conference on a shared cloud testbed.

The findings catalog what breaks in transit: missing pieces, brittle setup scripts, quiet assumptions about the home machine. Patterns repeat enough to become advice. The project also ships notebook templates that walk authors and reviewers through evaluation in the same environment. Reproducibility advocates get field notes from the artifact trenches, plus tooling to make the next round less heroic.
arxiv-2504-01076:
Chiu and co-authors weigh galaxy clusters found by an X-ray sky survey and study their central galaxies, in a research paper from 2025. The clusters come from the first data release of the eROSITA survey, taken with a telescope aboard the SRG space observatory. The team used images from the Hyper Suprime-Cam program on the Subaru telescope.

Weak lensing, the slight bending of light by mass, let the team weigh 96 clusters from the shape changes in background galaxies. They also fit the light of the brightest central galaxy in 101 clusters to get its star mass. The central galaxy's star mass at a fixed cluster mass has grown only modestly since early times, by about 20 percent. That pattern fits a view where most of those stars formed very early.
arxiv-2504-01176:
Krzysztof Szczygielski, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, spells out covariant decomposable maps between C-star algebras. Such maps are the math backbone of quantum moves that respect a symmetry.

The main result is a dilation theorem for covariant positive decomposable maps, building on a classic nineteen seventy-nine result of Scutaru. As a case study, Szczygielski spells out the operator sum form of maps on complex matrix algebras that commute with the maximal commutative subgroup of the unitary group. The paper then links to how quantum systems change over time, giving needed and enough settings for decomposably divisible quantum evolution families to be covariant.
arxiv-2504-01376:
Kazuo Takatsuka lays out a twin frame for the core wave law of quantum acts, in a 2025 paper. First he builds the real form of the law from scratch with no lean on past mech or wave tales. Plain terms on split crowd parts, such as space shift faith and flux hold, drive the build.

Next he adds chance path acts that fit the wave law like jiggle fits spread laws. Each path is a lone track, as in slit tests where spots land one by one. Piled spots give the fringe the wave law calls. Self tied loops close the tale.
arxiv-2504-01876:
Ed Bennett sets out how the TELOS Collaboration, a lattice physics research group, works so that others can reproduce and reuse its results. The document serves two purposes at once: a public statement of policy and a practical guide for new members. It describes the collaboration's habits for producing and analyzing lattice data and for sharing research openly.

Some advice is local, such as funder requirements in the United Kingdom, but most of it is offered as a template other collaborations can adopt. Topics run from data handling to analysis workflows, with pointers to fuller tutorials elsewhere rather than attempts to teach everything in one place. Bennett also marks where current practice falls short and how the group plans to improve. The paper is a working blueprint for reproducible, open science in a mid-sized physics collaboration.
arxiv-2504-02376:
Yutao Chen and Wei Chen design a better way for many devices to ask for a shared radio channel. Their twenty twenty-five paper serves dense machine traffic, a key use for next wave wireless nets and Wi-Fi. When too many devices ask at once, they clash and waste time.

Their plan splits clashes in a tree-like way, step by step. A learning method tunes how bold each device should be when it tries again. The aim is high use of the channel while still meeting service needs. Readers see how a classic splitting idea and modern learning can work as one protocol.
arxiv-2504-02476:
Nativ Ben-Yeda, Kfir Blum, and Inbar Havilio wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It uses the spread of globular clusters, dense balls of stars, as a probe of the dark matter halos around their host galaxies.

Clusters are heavy test particles that plow through the halo. Drag from the halo matter, called dynamical friction, shrinks their orbits over time, which gives a test of cold dark matter past mean-field checks. The team ran body simulations and quick models across many starts. Data from two diffuse galaxies and the Fornax dwarf show halos are there, in line with star motion data. One galaxy is too spread out to bind the answer.
arxiv-2504-02676:
Tong introduces Snow, a broadcast protocol that lets cloud computers share messages without a fixed tree of senders. Tree broadcasts wobble when machines join or leave, and gossip methods waste bandwidth while only promising probable delivery. Cloud clusters churn constantly, so both flaws bite.

Snow lets each node forward messages based on its own view of the membership. A balanced multi-way tree then forms on its own, with leaf depths differing by at most one. Tests under churn showed reliable delivery and steady delay. The protocol adds no redundant copies to get there. Tong offers Snow as a fit for large distributed applications that cannot pause for repairs.
arxiv-2504-02876:
Finding an object in a photo from a written hint gets hard when look-alike objects sit side by side, like two kinds of soda can. Yangxiao Lu and co-authors define a new task in their 2025 paper: the model also gets reference photos of the candidate objects, and must use them to pick the right one. They built a dataset for this task and a method that pairs fast few-example detection with a large language model that matches candidates.

Their method beat very large rival models on the new benchmark. The authors say reference photos could help robots and other vision systems tell similar objects apart.
arxiv-2504-03276:
Daniele Proverbio and Giulia Giordano wrote this 2025 paper on the toughness of a gene circuit that boosts its own production. A transcription factor that switches on its own gene forms a loop meant to hold its level steady through noise and shocks. The authors model that loop as a chance process and measure how well it keeps its resting state.

They find that when the factor works in larger clusters, the loop grows tougher. Clustering sharpens the on-off curve of the regulation, and the resting state holds even near the edge where it could tip. A second lens on toughness, built from the spread of the system's states, backs the first. Computer runs match the theory. The lesson may guide the design of hardy synthetic gene circuits.
arxiv-2504-03676:
Four authors tackle a memory problem in chips built to run neural networks. Such chips use layered, software-managed memory, and the standard trick of tiling splits each network layer into pieces that fit. Tiling shrinks memory use but forces extra trips to slow off-chip memory, which wastes energy and creates bottlenecks. Their method, Fused-Tiled Layers, instead fuses tiled pieces of neighboring layers so data moves less.

The team built the method into an open-source deployment framework tuned for a RISC-V chip with mixed processor types. On a typical stage of a vision transformer, the fused approach cut runtime by up to 60.1 percent. Data movement fell by 47.1 percent across off-chip transfers and on-chip shuffling combined. The authors present the method as a general fix for accelerators with managed caches.
arxiv-2504-04276:
Keerthi Devireddy compares two families of tools that explain image classifier decisions, in a 2025 paper. One family probes any model from outside. The other reads a specific network's inner activations. A standard fifty-layer network supplied the predictions. Test images ranged from dogs and birds to insects.

Outside methods gave broad feature credit that transfers across designs. Inside methods pinpointed exact activation regions more cheaply. Each family exposed different parts of the decision story. No single method won across the board. Combining methods gave the fullest picture in the tests. The stakes are highest in medicine, driving, and finance, the author notes. A selection guide matches methods to needs and budgets. Transparency, the paper argues, is a toolbox rather than a switch.
arxiv-2504-04476:
Deepika Gill and four co-authors explore in 2025 how femtosecond laser pulses entangle excitons and free carriers in a one-atom-thick semiconductor. Ultrafast light can tailor matter on the fastest scales, opening new condensed matter physics. The interplay of bound and free charges under such pulses was poorly mapped.

First-principles pump-probe modeling on monolayer tungsten diselenide yields a surprise. Light tuned to the exciton boosts the early free carrier count massively. Carrier count and exciton peak height then swing in a locked oscillation that persists. The team dubs the coupled entities femto-excitons. Pulse design may thus steer both exciton and carrier behavior at once, a fresh control knob for ultrafast devices.
arxiv-2504-04676:
Bo Li and Jing Yun propose a new method for multi-view clustering in a 2025 paper. Clustering data seen from several angles can reveal shared meaning, but most methods chase only what the views agree on and drop what each view alone can add.

Their framework splits each view into shared and private parts using a disentangled variational autoencoder. Contrastive learning pulls the shared parts together, and two consistency checks then put the private parts to work through within-view and cross-view rebuilding. The design forces the model to keep both the common story and each view's extra detail. Tests in the paper show the fuller picture sharpens the clusters that come out.
arxiv-2504-04876: Peter Danchev, Brendan Goldsmith, and Patrick Keef characterize two recently defined classes of abelian groups in a 2025 math paper. The classes, co-Bassian groups and their generalized form, were introduced by the third author in 2024. The paper asks which of these groups keep their defining property in two stronger senses: hereditarily, under subgroups, and in the super form. The authors find necessary and sufficient conditions for both cases. The result sharpens the picture of how these classes are structured.
arxiv-2504-05176:
Mohamed Benzaghta and three colleagues design mobile networks that serve drones flying along set air corridors, in a 2025 paper. Ground networks aim their signals down, so drones above often get weak and patchy coverage.

The team used data-driven search methods that tune antenna tilt and beam width together. Some methods raised the median signal quality along drone routes by over twenty decibels, with little harm to ground users. Knowledge from one scene sometimes carried to a new scene, and sometimes failed. A test on a real network more than doubled data rates along the drone routes. The search also mapped trade-offs between drone coverage and ground speed.
arxiv-2504-05376:
Neutrino beams striking atoms shed light on how quarks turn into hadrons, Leonardo Bonino and co-authors calculate in a 2025 paper. The team computes charged pion output from neutrino and antineutrino hits with high precision, to second order in the strong force math. Such hits probe quark maps and splitting rules in blends that charged-lepton hits cannot reach.

Predictions are compared with precise older fixed-target data. The data prove sharply sensitive to how splitting rules are set, which helps tune those rules. Future neutrino facilities at the Large Hadron Collider could extend these probes. Better splitting rules feed into all collider forecasts that involve hadron formation.
arxiv-2504-05676:
William Hutchins and co-authors predict a new route by which heat can cross the border between a metal and a non-metal, in a 2025 paper. When a metal film is driven hard, its electrons can run far hotter than its lattice. In that state, the team argues, heat may leap the border as faint near-field radiation stirred by the hot electrons, without passing through the lattice at all.

Using the standard theory of fluctuating fields, they compute the radiated heat flow across a tungsten film on a boron nitride base. At an electron temperature of 5,000 degrees, the radiated conductance passed 300 units and rivaled the normal conducted flow. The size of the effect depends on how the electrons scatter. The authors say heat models for fast, hot electronics should count this channel alongside the usual ones.
arxiv-2504-06076:
Dhruv Mubayi and Nicholas Spanier pin down a Ramsey number for triple systems, confirming a conjecture posed by six researchers. Ramsey numbers measure how large a structure must be before a chosen pattern or its complement's pattern becomes unavoidable. Here the pattern is a small four-vertex triple system with three edges, and the complement pattern is a star: many triples sharing one common vertex.

The team proves the Ramsey number grows like the square of the star's size divided by its logarithm. The result generalizes a famous bound for the graph Ramsey number of a triangle against a star. That link is structural: fixing one vertex in a triple system avoiding the small pattern leaves a triangle-free graph. The proof adapts a pseudorandom refinement of the classic graph argument, following a route opened by Guo and Warnke.
arxiv-2504-06276:
Jasper Kyle Catapang asks a practical question in a 2025 paper: can models built to answer multiple-choice questions also rank search results? Search systems first pull a set of documents, then rank them by how well each one fits the query. A good ranker matters for search and for chat tools that read retrieved text before they answer.

Catapang points to a math parallel between picking the right answer choice and judging how relevant a document is. On that basis he built a small proof-of-concept model that joins the two ideas. Tests showed the model improved ranking accuracy while staying lightweight. The paper is early work, offered as a sign that question-answering models hold untapped value for ranking tasks.
arxiv-2504-06776:
Future space telescopes hope to photograph Earth-like planets and read their air for signs of life, but a nearby planet or moon can pollute the signal. Drinor Cacaj and co-authors study this photobombing risk for LIFE, a planned interferometer that cancels starlight to reveal faint planets. The usual sharpness rule for telescopes does not apply to such an instrument, so the team built new criteria based on keeping explanations simple.

Their measure covers two failure modes: two sources blending into one, and a source canceling itself out through interference. On paper, LIFE's sharpness rivals a 600-meter telescope working in the mid-infrared. Surveying likely target systems, they find that of about 73 habitable planets it might detect, roughly 71 would stay free of contamination.
arxiv-2504-07076: Junaid Razzaq, Rita Fioresi, and Maria Lledo prove basic theorems of invariant theory for a supergroup in a 2025 paper. Invariant theory asks which quantities stay fixed when a symmetry group acts, and classic results name generators and relations for those quantities. The authors carry that program to the special linear supergroup over complex numbers, and discuss the resulting algebra of invariants through super versions of the Plücker relations.
arxiv-2504-07276:
Gunnar Peng and Ory Schnitzer present a 2025 physics paper on why some drops in an electric field start spinning only after a jump. A drop in a strong field can break into rotation, a Quincke effect, when charge drains slower inside the drop than outside. Low-viscosity drops switch on with a snap and show hysteresis, a behavior theory had not explained.

The authors simulate a round drop in two dimensions across all viscosity ratios and field strengths. As the drop's viscosity falls, the onset fork flips from gentle to abrupt. A band of bistability opens, where spinning and still states both persist. In that band the starting state already shows charge piling up without bound at the equator. The finding ties the snap to that charge blowup.
arxiv-2504-07376:
Chen and co-authors present a theory study, published in 2025, on measuring rotation with a trapped-ion quantum oscillator. Ordinary oscillators measure force, acceleration, and spin in instruments like gyroscopes. The team's version uses a crystal of calcium ions held in an electric trap. One swirling motion of the crystal serves as the driver. When the device rotates, a sideways force couples that swirl into a vibration along the trap's axis.

The size of that axial vibration reveals the rotation rate. It can be read with great precision because the ions' spins are entangled with the motion. Quantum entanglement sharpens the readout beyond classical limits. The authors work out the theory for the sensor step by step. Compact, precise gyroscopes of this kind could serve navigation where satellite signals cannot reach.
arxiv-2504-07576:
Bernard Julia wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author, per its byline. It traces the road from general relativity to maximal supergravity, and the web of symmetry and duality that links them.

The tale runs through ten and eleven dimensions and down again by torus cuts. At each stage large exceptional duality groups appear, in a strikingly even pattern. Plain general relativity sits as the plainest case, tied to the real world. Shrunk to two dimensions, affine Kac-Moody groups rule and the theory turns integrable. At one dimension, hyperbolic groups bring chaos. Borcherds forms then let all matter laws be written as twisted self-duality. Seven open challenges close the piece.
arxiv-2504-07976:
Many physics tasks span two scales at once, and a full sim at fine scale costs far too much for repeat runs. Hamidreza Eivazi and co-authors build a fast stand in in 2025 that keeps one law by design: force balance. Their tool, EquiNO, learns from data yet can never break that law.

The trick is to build each answer from a set of flow free base shapes, drawn from past sims. Since each base shape is free of net force, any mix of them is too. The team sets the tool in a frame that weds grid maths with learned maps. On stiff solid tasks, it stayed true on small train sets and ran more than eight thousand times faster than the old route.
arxiv-2504-08076:
Thomas Varnish and co-authors probe the faintest galaxies in the deepest image from the Herschel space telescope, in a 2025 paper. The SPIRE instrument mapped the submillimetre sky at three long wavelengths. Its dark field pushes below the confusion limit, where galaxies blur together. Normal source-finding tools fail in such crowded images.

The team turned to a statistical method that studies the spread of pixel brightness. They compared the central patch of the field with current galaxy models. None of the recent models matched the data well. Their fit yields new counts of faint galaxies by brightness. Those counts feed into estimates of the cosmic infrared background, which agree with Planck satellite values.
arxiv-2504-08176:
Vahid Babaey and Arun Ravindran build an AI framework that attacks web firewalls so it can teach them to defend better. Their 2025 paper, GenXSS, targets cross-site scripting, where hostile scripts are slipped into web pages. Rule-based firewalls miss heavily disguised attacks because their rules need hand updates.

The system first uses a large language model to invent sophisticated attack scripts, then fires them at a test application behind a firewall. Attacks that slip through are sorted, and new firewall rules are drafted to stop them. With GPT-4o, the team generated 264 attack samples, most of them valid, and a large share challenged the defense. The loop turns offense into patch.
arxiv-2504-08376:
Shay Golan and Matan Kraus present, in a 2025 paper, fast parallel algorithms for classic string tasks in the congested clique model. In that model, n computers solve a problem together, swapping short messages with every other machine in each round. Rounds are the scarce resource.

Their first result sorts strings of any length in a constant number of rounds. The second matches patterns against text combinatorially, also in constant rounds. The third builds a suffix array, with its longest-common-prefix companion, in about log log n rounds. These are core tools wherever huge texts meet many processors, from search engines to genome pipelines. Shaving rounds cuts both time and coordination cost in real clusters.
arxiv-2504-08776:
Gautam Kishore Shahi, Oshani Seneviratne, and Marc Spaniol present SemCAFE in a 2025 paper on spotting unreliable news online. Readers often cannot tell whether an unfamiliar source can be trusted, and fake stories can copy the style of real ones. The problem grew worse after the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, when false reports spread fast.

SemCAFE judges an article by the named people, places, and groups inside it. It cleans the text, picks out those entities, and checks how they relate in a large knowledge base called YAGO. That check builds a kind of fingerprint for the article. On a test set of tens of thousands of articles about the invasion, the method beat leading rivals by a clear margin. The team shares its data and code openly.
arxiv-2504-09276:
Xiyue Han and Alexander Schied study how fast a roughness gauge settles to the truth, in work from twenty twenty-five. The gauge, called the Hurst parameter, sums up how rough a price path is. Rough volatility models use it to mimic the jagged moves of real markets. A past study built a simple scale-free gauge from the running sum of a noisy path. That gauge was shown to work for a plain rough path.

Han and Schied extend the proof to paths bent by a broad class of smooth maps. The gauge still hits the true Hurst value in that wider setting. They also prove a near-sure speed for how fast the error shrinks. The result covers rough volatility models read from spaced sums of past variance. It includes the well-known rough fractional model as one case.
arxiv-2504-09376:
Talk of echo chambers suggests that social media users speak only to their own side, yet Yusuf Mücahit Çetinkaya and co-authors find plenty of contact across the political divide. They studied three million tweets from the United States in 2020 to learn how cross-partisan exchanges start, which topics draw them, and when they stay civil or turn hostile. Their dataset lets them compare cross-party replies with same-party ones side by side.

Hot political events pulled users across party lines most strongly. Democrats crossed over slightly more often than Republicans, but their cross-party exchanges leaned more negative than their same-party talk. Republicans kept a steadier tone in both settings. The authors argue that spotting low-toxicity topics could guide efforts to cool online conflict.
arxiv-2504-09476:
Sacheendra Talluri and co-authors build an open archive of service failures in 2025. Cloud and web services run much of daily life, yet how often they fail is poorly known. The archive gathers failure reports from both users and operators. Reports cover cloud, web, and gaming services from many vantage points.

The team compares the new data with older failure records and cluster traces. They study how often services fail, how long repairs take, and what symptoms each side reports. High level services fail less often than base layers, likely due to backup design. The open data should help builders plan for real world breakdowns.
arxiv-2504-09676:
Jaya Maithil and eleven colleagues study jets of matter blasting from two quasars seen as they were when the universe was young, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Jets with clear X-ray extent are well studied nearby but barely explored at such distances.

Using data from the Chandra X-ray telescope, the team confirms extended jets, thousands of light-years long, in both quasars. Radio follow-up observations then pin down how fast and how angled the jets are. Those details let the authors estimate the energy the jets carry. The main goal is to test what makes the jets glow in X-rays. One candidate is X-rays produced when fast electrons in the jet bounce photons of the cosmic microwave background up to high energies. Distant jets, where that background was denser, are the natural place to check.
arxiv-2504-09876:
Tran Quoc Khanh Le and seven co-authors present a 2025 paper on segmenting fetal ultrasound images when labeled examples are scarce. Outlining the cervix in these scans is hard: contrast is low, shadows intrude, and borders blur. Fully supervised networks need large annotated sets that clinics rarely have. Their framework, HDC, learns from unlabeled scans too, using a single teacher model rather than several.

A hierarchical distillation scheme guides the student with two losses. One aligns feature representations between teacher and student. The other uses mutual information to steady the student against noisy guidance. The design cuts computing cost while fighting the confirmation bias that plagues teacher-student setups. On two fetal ultrasound data sets the method matched multi-teacher rivals with less overhead. The authors target practical semi-supervised segmentation for clinical imaging.
arxiv-2504-09976:
David Arcoya and four co-authors proved that a class of nonlocal equations has exactly one weak solution, in a 2025 mathematics paper. The equations use an operator that spreads influence across a region rather than acting point by point. The input data are rough: they are only assumed to be integrable, with a size bound, so standard tools do not apply.

The team built custom estimates and formulas to handle the rough data. They also showed that as a key parameter rises toward one, their solution settles onto the solution of the matching local problem. That limit recovers the classical theory as a special case. The operator they use comes from reshaping a uniform kernel, and in the limit it can stand in for any classical operator of the same form.
arxiv-2504-10076:
Georgios Makrygiorgos, Joshua Hang Sai Ip, and Ali Mesbah make Bayesian optimization scale better by teaching its surrogate model with gradients. Their 2025 paper explains that Bayesian optimization searches for the best design by modeling the objective from few trials. Gaussian processes are the usual surrogate, but Bayesian neural networks promise more flexibility at large scale.

Gradients, when they can be had, sharpen Gaussian process models, yet no one had fed them into network surrogates. Automatic differentiation makes that easy: the training loss can reward matching the gradient as well as the value. Tests on known benchmarks showed better surrogate predictions and faster convergence of the search. The method suits costly design problems where each gradient comes nearly free.
arxiv-2504-10276:
Lauren Olson and colleagues surveyed who carries the flag for ethics in software teams in 2025. Ethical concerns compete with profit-first market pressures inside companies, and the industry's demographic imbalance makes it important to know whether a practitioner's own background changes what they notice and push for. The team surveyed over two hundred software practitioners across roles, industries, and countries about the concerns they see, rank, and try to address.

The results show sharp demographic disparities. Practitioners from marginalized groups, including women, Black, Indigenous, and people of color, and disabled practitioners, reported ethical concerns more often than their peers. They also showed heightened sensitivity to how ethics is implemented in practice. The authors use these findings to identify the critical barriers to weaving ethics into development and to assess how much capacity practitioners actually have to push back.
arxiv-2504-10376:
Rafael Díaz Fuentes proves solution results for a math model of tumor and immune cells in a 2025 paper. The model tracks three fields: immune cells, a chemical signal, and tumor cells. Each spreads, drifts toward signals, and grows or dies by set rules.

The system is fully parabolic, which makes the math stiff. Fuentes asks when smooth solutions exist for all time, in domains of three or more dimensions. For growth power above one, mild assumptions on the constants suffice for bounded solutions. For power equal to one, an extra condition links the constants and the start data. The work extends two older models, adding the immune-tumor fight in full. Such proofs anchor later numeric studies of cancer growth.
arxiv-2504-11076:
Tom Hochsprung, Jakob Runge, and Andreas Gerhardus present a way to estimate cause-and-effect sizes from time series alone. Their 2025 paper targets settings with hidden confounders, where most methods lean on extra helper variables such as instruments or control series. Their setting needs none of those helpers. The data are assumed to follow a structural vector process, a standard model where each series reacts to past values and fresh shocks.

Direct effects come from solving sets of linear equations built from covariances and model parameters. The authors give graph conditions under which those equations have exactly one solution, and total effects follow by a classic path rule. The method turns the time structure itself into the source of identification.
arxiv-2504-11576:
Luca Albieri, Sergei Kucherenko, Stefano Scoleri, and Marco Bianchetti cut the cost of pricing risk measures in a 2025 paper. The measures, called Greeks, gauge how option prices react. Barrier and Asian options monitored at set dates are the test cases. Their simulation spaces carry many dimensions.

Global sensitivity analysis reveals each space's effective dimension. Chebyshev interpolation and a conditional pathwise method both shrink it. Smoother estimates then suit quasi Monte Carlo sampling well. Randomized runs converge faster and cost less as a result. Importance sampling adds gains with some of the methods. The low effective dimension explains which approach wins.
arxiv-2504-11876:
Giacomo Colombo proves smoothness results for the Stefan problem, a classic model of melting and freezing. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The model tracks a moving boundary between phases, such as ice and water. That free boundary can have singular points where it kinks. Colombo asks how bad those points can be over time. The setting here is four space dimensions plus time.

He shows the boundary is a smooth three-dimensional surface at almost every time. The singular set splits into two parts with distinct shapes. One part lies on a single smooth surface whose bad times form a tiny set. The other part is thin in a parabolic counting sense. The proof extends known results to this higher dimension. It sharpens the picture of phase change geometry.
arxiv-2504-12476:
Andreas Jungherr and Adrian Rauchfleisch survey what people in Germany and the United States expect from AI moderation. Their 2025 paper asks how well AI systems should match public values. Generative AI has raised public hopes and worries alike. Little was known about which alignment goals people actually back.

About eighteen hundred Germans and seventeen hundred fifty-six Americans answered. They rated four goals: accuracy, safety, bias reduction, and uplifting visions of society. Americans used AI more and backed every goal more strongly. Accuracy and safety won the widest support in both lands. Fairness and vision goals drew cooler backing, above all in Germany, where speech attitudes split views.
arxiv-2504-12676:
Yu Song and co-authors track cell nuclei in growing plant roots in a 2025 paper. Arabidopsis is a model plant, and live imaging lets scientists watch growth and cell division as they happen. Tracking each nucleus in three dimensions over time is key, but common software struggles when cells sit in dense rows, as root cells do.

Their method works from coarse to fine. It first tracks at the level of cell lines, then uses the known line pattern and the space links between nuclei to track each one. A genetic search method drives the match. Tests on a long root tip imaging set, with only minor hand fixes, showed accurate tracking.
arxiv-2504-12776:
Markus Wallinger and co-authors propose, in a 2025 paper, a way to draw set data when membership is not sure. Old set charts treat membership as yes or no. Their draw, StorySets, takes a cue from storyline charts and parallel plots. Each item stands as a tall glyph split in bins, one bin per doubt level. Each set is a curve that runs left to right through the glyphs, at the bin that fits its doubt for that item. Turns and crossings are trimmed by design, so the chart stays clean to read.

Some of the best-order tasks are hard in theory. In practice, a new exact method orders curves in each glyph near the best. A small set then shows as a curve held below a big set's curve. Tests on doubt data and on plain grid data show the range.
arxiv-2504-12876:
XinXin Qi and Hao Sun present a 2025 paper on a dark matter model with two kinds of dark particles. One is a scalar particle and the other a heavy neutral fermion, held apart by a combined symmetry rule. An extra scalar field gives the fermion its mass when the symmetry breaks, and brings a new Higgs-like particle. The team scans the model's options under the known cosmic dark matter amount.

The order of the new particles' masses changes which reactions matter. When the fermion is lightest, its creation runs through normally forbidden channels. Combining limits from Higgs decays, cosmic abundance, and direct detection searches narrows the space. Direct detection gives the tightest squeeze overall. The authors map which mass ranges survive all checks. Their work guides searches for multi-part dark sectors.
arxiv-2504-12976:
Seven researchers build a data set to teach machines to draft science ideas in a 2025 paper. Strong new hypotheses are a mark of true research skill, yet current models often propose ideas that are old hat or unworkable. No data set framed the task as a language generation problem before this one.

Their set, HypoGen, holds about fifty-five hundred problem and hypothesis pairs from top computing venues. Each pair is shaped as a Bit, a Spark, and a Flip: the standard claim, the key leap, and the counter proposal. A reasoning chain links the steps. Fine tuning on the set lifted the novelty and quality of model drafts in judge scores.
arxiv-2504-13076:
Shah Faisal proves that the widest-area Lagrangian tori in a symplectic ball must hug its boundary, in work from twenty twenty-five. A Lagrangian torus carries a symplectic area set by its smallest disk. Extremal tori maximise that area among all rival tori. Cieliebak and Mohnke conjectured where such tori must live. Their question, credited to Lazzarini, is settled here affirmatively.

Every extremal torus in the unit ball lies entirely in the boundary. The proof extends to a broad class of toric domains. All compact strictly convex four-dimensional toric domains are included. Counterexamples show non-convex domains can break the pattern, though. Convexity is thus the load-bearing assumption in the result. Symplectic geometry gains a sharp extremal classification.
arxiv-2504-13176:
Fei Shen and five co-authors present a framework for generating clothing images in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Fashion designers want fine control over a garment's shape, color, and logo placement. Earlier generators took only one condition at a time, which limits design work. Their system, IMAGGarment, accepts several conditions at once. It trains in two stages to handle global look and local detail apart.

The first stage models the overall silhouette and color with a mixed attention design. The second stage adds user logos and spatial constraints with care. The two stages join into one end-to-end tool. Output images aim for high fidelity to the brief. The work serves digital apparel and personalized fashion design.
arxiv-2504-13376:
Aitor Gómez-Tejedor, Eneko Osaba, and Esther Villar-Rodriguez wrote this computer science paper, published in 2025. It studies the unglamorous step that decides whether quantum annealers succeed: squeezing a problem's variables onto the machine's fixed wiring.

Annealers solve problems shaped like their hardware easily, but foreign shapes must be embedded, chaining several physical qubits per variable. The authors first measured how embedding quality drives results on D-Wave machines. Longer average chains clearly tracked worse solution errors. They then graded the standard embedding tool, Minorminer, on random graphs for quality, robustness, and speed. A deterministic clique embedder served as the worst-case yardstick. The verdict: the standard tool leaves significant room for improvement, and embedding deserves research attention equal to the hardware itself.
arxiv-2504-13476:
Jiadong Lou, Bingqing Liu, Yuanheng Xiong, Xiaodong Zhang, and Xu Yuan use a generative model to read plankton levels in coastal water from satellite color, in a 2025 paper. Tiny floating plants tint the sea in subtle ways that sensitive space sensors can catch. Two NASA missions now gather such rainbow-rich data, but coastal water is optically messy, and one spectrum can match several plankton mixes.

Their framework is built on a variational autoencoder, a model suited to one-to-many puzzles. Tailored designs let it recover both the plankton's light absorption and its green pigment amount from reflected spectra. Against real observations, the models scored high precision with low bias, beating a leading rival approach above all on the richer data. The authors see a path to tracking coastal ecosystems from orbit.
arxiv-2504-13576:
Weiqi Qin, Yuxin Liu, Dongze Wu, Zhenkai Qin, and Qining Luo propose a traffic prediction model in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Traditional traffic flow models lose accuracy and fluctuate badly when flows show patterns at several time scales at once. Their model, MSTIM, is built on the MindSpore framework. It combines long short-term memory networks, convolutional networks, and an attention mechanism to model multi-scale temporal information.

Experiments used the Metropolitan Interstate Traffic Volume dataset. MSTIM was compared against typical hybrid baselines pairing attention with recurrent or convolutional models in various combinations. On mean absolute error, mean square error, and root mean square error, MSTIM came out ahead. The authors conclude the integrated design significantly improves both the accuracy and the stability of traffic volume prediction for transportation planning.
arxiv-2504-13776:
Aman Agarwal and co-authors test vision transformers for wildfire detection from space in a 2025 paper. Fires are growing in intensity and length as the climate warms, and response systems are strained. Neural networks trained on satellite images can spot fires, but common designs are costly and use only local image context.

Transformers train more efficiently and use both local and global context. On a published Landsat data set, a transformer beat a specialized network baseline by a small margin. Yet the team own tuned U-Net design performed best overall. The results show transformers are capable, while well tuned networks still lead.
arxiv-2504-13876:
Augusto Ciuffoletti lays out design principles for a geology tourism app in a 2025 paper. Walking natural trails is rewarding, but visitors enjoy and learn more, and stay safer, with good guidance. Signs along paths help only so far, while nearly every hiker now carries a smartphone. The paper asks how an Android app for geotourists should be built, starting from the users rather than the technology.

The method defines sample user personas, turns their needs into firm requirements, and then builds a proof of concept against those requirements. Trail setting brings its own pressures: patchy signals, battery limits, and hands busy with walking. The author presents the working concept as evidence that the principles hold up, and as a template others can adapt for outdoor visitor apps.
arxiv-2504-14176:
Yi Huang, Tohru Ozawa, and Xinhang Tong published a mathematics paper in 2025 on a one-dimensional minimization problem tied to a sharp uncertainty principle for solenoidal fields. The work builds on an expanding square argument by Hamamoto. Working in the right function space, the team recasts an interpolation-type inequality as an exact equality. The leftover term in that equality vanishes exactly at the best cases.

Those best cases are pinned down through confluent hypergeometric functions. Along the way, the authors remove some needless limits on the given parameters. The result sharpens both the statement and the description of its extremal functions.
arxiv-2504-14276:
Neutrinos may carry a faint magnetic trait tied to their mass, and a mirror-symmetric model lets two mass mechanisms play off each other. Vivek Banerjee and Sasmita Mishra compute the trait's effects in a 2025 paper. Their model has eight possible forms for a key coupling matrix. Heavy partner neutrinos can add to a known wobble in the muon's magnetism. Only two of the eight forms land in the measured range for that wobble.

Those two pin the model's new scale to a window of a few thousand energy units. A double-beta decay check, though, gives lifetimes far beyond any detector's reach. Even huge magnetic fields barely shorten them. Weak forces rule that decay, the authors conclude.
arxiv-2504-14676:
Felix Brandt and Arnab Roy build math for a rigid ball swimming in a noisy fluid in a 2025 paper. The system couples fluid flow with the ball's motion, both shaken by random forces. A drift-type noise also rides the fluid itself.

The catalog title speaks of analysis; the authors' own title claims strong well-posedness, and the work backs it. They prove sound local solutions exist, using a stochastic maximal regularity method. A decoupling trick handles the joined fluid-body operator. One key step bounds a calculus for that operator. Blow-up tests mark when solutions must end. The authors call it the first strict treatment of strong solutions for such noisy fluid-body systems.
arxiv-2504-14776:
Wang and co-authors present Script2Screen, a tool that lets scriptwriters see and hear dialogue as they write it. Scripts are text, but the final product is sound and motion, and that gap slows ideas. Their 2025 system grew from a study with professional writers, who said linking the two forms would aid drafting, above all for dialogue.

The tool turns script lines into acted scenes with emotional speech and animated characters, in step with the text. Writers can adjust gestures, speech feeling, and camera angles in fine detail. Trials with novice and professional writers showed the live previews sped revision and sharpened drafts. Users felt the tool complemented their craft rather than replacing it, the authors report.
arxiv-2504-14976:
Titova, Izmodenov, and Korolkov refine how interstellar atoms are modeled inside the solar wind's bubble in this 2025 paper. Hydrogen atoms stream into the heliosphere from interstellar space, flying far before they collide. Most models count only charge exchange with protons, and treat it as a clean velocity swap.

Real collisions also include elastic hits between hydrogen atoms and between hydrogen and protons. Charge exchange can scatter at angles, not just flip direction. The team adds those effects to the model. They trace how the atoms' spread and flow change as a result. Better atom maps sharpen readings of the sun's boundary with deep space.
arxiv-2504-15076:
Tom Banks argues in a 2025 note that a one dimensional string theory, stripped to its core algebra, matches the algebra of fermion fields on a half line. The argument uses a known procedure for carving out an algebra at infinite size. Elegant past results on the model make the match clean.

The carved algebra is of the tamest type, tied to a wedge of space in its calm state. Finite region pieces are of the wildest type, though. The model has no black hole states. Banks speculates that many copies, plus a hidden interaction, could breed black hole like states. The algebra count stays the same either way.
arxiv-2504-15276:
Apte, Lee, Marwaha, Parekh, and Sud improve approximation algorithms for the Quantum MaxCut problem in a 2025 paper. The problem asks for the best quantum state on a graph under an energy-like objective. Good guarantees are hard to come by.

Their new method partially entangles qubit pairs matched along graph edges. Single-qubit directions stay fixed while the entanglement strength is tuned. That dial interpolates between simple product states and matching-based states. The result is a stronger approximation guarantee for Quantum MaxCut. A related Hamiltonian problem gets an even better guarantee. The authors present partial entanglement as the key new ingredient. Quantum optimization gains a sharper tool.
arxiv-2504-15476:
Rohan Surana and five co-authors test whether chat based shopping guides can be raised with no chat data at all, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Such guides need domain talk logs, which are dear and rare in new fields. The team asks if scraps like reviews, item facts, and buy logs can stand in.

They forged fake chats from those scraps and picked the best with two math sieves, one for spread and one for fact worth. Grounded fake data beat plain prompting and naive fakes across models and sets. Smart picking beat random picks, and item facts plus crowd buy signs each helped. Where real chats were thin, fake ones beat them, and the two mixed well. Code is shared.
arxiv-2504-15876:
Qizhen Wu and co-authors plan robot swarm battles with a two way learning method in a 2025 paper. In a confrontation, a swarm must split into tasks and steer each robot at once. Classic planning splits those layers and lets orders flow one way, which misses how each layer shapes the other.

Their method ties commands to task assignment and actions to path choice, and lets the layers train each other. A forecast model links the abstract task view to real motion goals. In tests, the swarm won over 80 percent of confrontations and chose moves in under a hundredth of a second. Real robot runs backed the simulation results.
arxiv-2504-16076:
Claire Lamman, Jonathan Blazek, and Daniel Eisenstein sharpen tools for measuring how galaxies line up, in a 2025 paper. Galaxies are not scattered at random angles; their shapes tend to align with the web of matter around them. That alignment, called intrinsic alignment, is both a clue to galaxy growth and a nuisance for weak lensing studies.

Measuring it is tricky because redshift measures stretch positions along the line of sight. The team design estimators that gather more of that line-of-sight signal while shrugging off the stretch. Tests on a large simulated universe show their weighting beats the standard single-cut approach. They publish recommended settings for surveys spanning scales from one to one hundred megaparsecs.
arxiv-2504-16176:
Daniel Skliannyi, Yuval Oreg, and Ady Stern grow a one-line twist super state in a flake stack in a 2025 paper. One flake of a rich-pull sheet sits on a twin carbon stack in their build. Gates tune the stack into three pads of the super state in a row.

Two seams join the pads, with plain zones set in the midst of the row. Spin pull from the sheet and shifts of wave pace round the face are key traits. Wide zones of the seam dials host the twist state.
arxiv-2504-16976:
