Yves Le Jan, writing alone in 2025, studies the clusters formed by random loops sprinkled over a complete graph. On any graph, a Poisson ensemble of Markov loops, closed walks weighted by their transition steps, marks out occupied edges that split the graph into clusters. The paper first recalls the general machinery: conductances, a killing term, and a Green matrix that encodes how walks spread.

Against that backdrop, the probability that the loop partition is thinner than a named partition takes a simple closed form through those Green matrices, including versions restricted to a subset of vertices. An alternative construction builds the same clusters from primitive loops, those without a repeating period, chosen independently with matched probabilities. On the complete graph, where every vertex touches every other, the symmetry promises explicit results. The paper sets up the tools such results will need.
arxiv-2504-17076:
Jens Petersen and co-authors argue that where objects sit in a scene matters as much as how they look for training car detectors. Generative augmentation usually swaps objects into old layouts. Or it pastes them at random, unrealistic spots.

Their model learns likely placements from real scenes. It predicts where a new object can plausibly stand. A generative painter then fills that spot in. Layout realism lifts the detector's training value. Two automotive benchmarks set new state-of-the-art results. The gains beat realism-only and diversity-only rivals. Scene-aware placement is the missing third leg. It serves any detection task with structured scenes and set, fixed, known layouts.
arxiv-2504-17376:
Maoyang Xiang, Ramesh Fernando, and Bo Wang show how to run a small language model directly on an edge device. Their paper appeared in 2025. Large models strain small hardware through heavy computing, memory traffic, and power use. The team deployed a half-billion-parameter model on a chip board that pairs a modest processor with programmable logic. They shrank the model with a compression method that weighs which weights matter most.

Their setup splits work between the two halves of the board. Heavy operations go to the programmable logic, and light tasks stay on the processor. The model shrank by about 55 percent. Output speed rose to about five tokens per second, nearly double the baseline rate. The work shows that direct on-device language models are practical without a data center.
arxiv-2504-17476:
Hoang Giang Bui, Jelena Ninic, and Günther Meschke built a consistent tangent operator in 2025 for a sub-stepping method in soil modeling. When a soil model integrates stress in big load steps, the usual implicit Euler step can fail to converge on the local nonlinear problem. Splitting the step into sub-steps rescues convergence, but makes the tangent operator, the derivative the global solver needs, messy.

The paper develops that operator for two widely used critical state models, the modified Cam-Clay model and a unified clay and sand model. With it, the global Newton iteration regains its fast quadratic convergence. The method is aimed at problems with large steps, such as tunnel simulation. The catalog title appends a publication type and its creator list repeats names; the head governs. Readers get the math that makes sub-stepping practical in big simulations.
arxiv-2504-17776:
Amir Carmel, Debarati Das, Evangelos Kipouridis, and Evangelos Pipis study clustering methods for streaming data in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Fitting distances to tree metrics and ultrametrics backs hierarchical clustering and numerical taxonomy. The input is a distance function over elements. The goal is a tree whose distances near-match the ones given. In the semi-streaming model, distances come in any order. Memory is tight.

For the zero-norm, the team gives a method that runs in polynomial time, uses near-linear space, and gives a near call for ultrametrics. They prove no exact single-pass method is there, even with no time cap. Their zero-norm result gives a near call for the one-norm too, matching the offline bound in a parameter regime. For the infinity-norm they mark out ultrametric fitting: a two-approximation in one pass, best, improving with one more pass.
arxiv-2504-17876:
Dan Cunha, Mark Friedl, and Luis Carvalho build change detectors for data that arrive at uneven times, in a 2025 paper. Most methods assume tidy, evenly spaced observations; in continuous time, two close readings should rarely straddle a change, while distant ones often do. Their model is a Markov chain whose jump odds stretch with the gap, specified without informative priors.

Forward-backward algorithms then locate the changes exactly, no slow MCMC sampling required. A new loss function and its Bayes estimator suit the setting. On synthetic data and on satellite time series, with a weather-aware mean curve to suppress false alarms, the method performed well across three land-change tasks.
arxiv-2504-18176:
Kaustubh Rajwade and Aris Karastergiou wrote a 2025 paper on fast radio bursts, the brief flashes of radio waves from deep space. The authors ask whether these bursts come from a spinning magnetosphere, the magnetic zone around a compact object such as a neutron star. Past searches looked for a steady rhythm in burst arrival times and found none.

The paper offers a new test based on the angle of the waves, not their timing. If the source spins, that angle should track the spin phase, even when bursts seem to arrive at random. The test works best where time-based searches fail, so a clear or null result would both teach readers about the source.
arxiv-2504-18476:
Leonid Antipov and Stefan Kratsch wrote this theoretical computer science paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on shrinking hard problems before solving them. Kernelization is the art of trimming an input down to a small core with the same answer, but classic kernels demand a lot of global structure.

The authors propose boundaried kernelization, which trims local patches of a graph instead. The idea grows out of protrusion replacement, where a well-behaved lump of the input is swapped for a smaller stand-in. They show polynomial-size local kernels exist for a number of problems, and prove none can exist for others. The local tool also feeds back into the classic game: they use it to improve the kernel for Vertex Cover under a distance measure. The paper reframes preprocessing as a local craft.
arxiv-2504-18676:
Alexander Estornell and co-authors mix solver math with learning to build Koopman operators more cheaply, in work from 2025. Koopman analysis swaps a nonlinear system for a linear operator on observed quantities, which opens the standard linear toolbox. Exact operators are out of reach, and approximations are hard to tune.

Coder-built methods need system details and scale badly. Learning methods hinge on guesses like the size of the observation space. The hybrid uses a convex solver to find the operator's shape first. A learner then fits the maps in and out of that space. The split cuts the unknowns users must preset. The authors frame it as efficiency with fewer knobs to guess.
arxiv-2504-19076:
Laura Dietz and co-authors examine the risks of letting large language models grade the quality of search systems. Human judges once supplied those grades, and model grades often agree with them, tempting labs to drop humans entirely. The authors warn that the agreement can mislead, especially once model signals feed back into the systems being graded.

They describe repeated story patterns, or tropes, in current debate about model evaluation. In the risky pattern, the same model family helps build a system and then certifies its success, a loop that can lock in shared bias. The paper maps where validity breaks down. It urges care before human judgment is retired from evaluation.
arxiv-2504-19476:
Mina Karzand and Guy Bresler design recommendation methods that learn from both users and items in this 2025 paper. Their model serves one item per user per round and hears only like or dislike. Users and items each fall into hidden types, and tastes run by type pairs.

Most real systems lean on just one side's structure. The pair's algorithm uses both at once. They prove it nearly optimal by matching it against information-theoretic limits no method can beat. The gap left by one-sided methods is shown plainly. The result guides how streaming and shopping services should pool their data.
arxiv-2504-19876:
Mamadou Keita and four co-authors build in 2025 DeeCLIP, a detector for AI-generated images that aims to stay sharp across generators and mild image damage. Photo-real fakes grow fast, while detectors often fail on new models or simple edits. General reach and toughness are the twin goals.

A fusion module blends high and low level features from a CLIP vision backbone. Triplet loss sharpens the gap between real and fake in the feature space. Low-rank tuning adapts the model cheaply while keeping prior knowledge. Trained only on one generator family, the system averages 89 percent accuracy across nineteen test sets spanning many generators. Fewer trained weights yet top scores mark a strong efficiency claim.
arxiv-2504-20476:
Shahid Ahmad and co-authors trace how spin and orbital motion entwine across a family of oxides, in a 2025 physics paper. The compounds hold four electrons in the key orbital shell, but their metals range from iron to osmium. As atoms grow heavier, spin-orbit coupling strengthens and rewrites the magnetic order.

One unified method follows the family across that range. At one end sits a half-metal ferromagnet where the crystal field rules. At the other, strong spin-orbit coupling locks the system into a quiet state with no net moment. In between, an antiferromagnet with unit spin anchors the map. Case compounds from barium ferrate to an osmium salt mark the stops. The sweep gives a single story for magnetism in spin-orbit materials.
arxiv-2504-20676:
Shrisha Rao sets theoretical limits on explaining AI systems in a 2025 paper, using algorithmic information theory. Explainability is cast as approximating a complex model with a simpler one. Both the error of the shortcut and the complexity of the explanation are measured with Kolmogorov complexity, the length of the shortest full description. Three main results follow.

A gap theorem shows any explanation much simpler than the model must disagree with it on some inputs. Bounds show explanation complexity explodes with input dimension but grows gently with allowed error for smooth functions. Local explanations can be far simpler than global ones while staying accurate nearby. A final impossibility result says no governance scheme can have unlimited AI power, human readable explanations, and negligible error all at once.
arxiv-2504-21176: Wang wrote a solo math study in twenty twenty-five on a sum that flips sign term by term, built from factorials and a kind of Stirling count. He finds a neat rule that makes the whole set of such sums at once, and shows the sums are never below zero. The sums count a class of trees read as game trees won by the second player. He also gives plain maps among three kinds of trees and match lists.
arxiv-2504-21276:
Code written by chat models may look right and still steer a car wrong. Wanyi Chen, Meng-wen Su, and Mary Cummings graded six such models in 2025 on a task with teeth. The models had to write code for three route-planning methods, then run it on maps of three hardness grades. Route math is a fair stand-in for safety work, since a wrong turn there is a crash in the real world.

The verdict was grim. The made code held real hazards, from stalls to bad paths, that a quick read would miss. The team say known code test sets are too soft to catch such faults. Their rule for safety work is plain: no model code ships without hard tests of the kind they ran.
arxiv-2504-21376:
Ye Yan and co-authors call bound states of a proton with an anti-Omega mote, in a study from 2025. Fresh work on kin pairs, proton with Omega and with anti-Lambda, bids a look at the flip pair. Quark frames can weigh their pull ere halls can make them.

The pull twixt nucleon and anti-Omega beats the pull to plain Omega by a hair, so binds are more apt. Counts give bound states at two spin marks, bound more deep than the kin pair's best. Phase and span counts back the binds. A first read of the pair's close-pass print, the femto mark halls can now catch, ends the work. If halls print it, the call can be tried.
arxiv-2505-00276: Mishal Assif and Yuliy Baryshnikov present a computational pipeline to recover the shape of a dynamical system's state space from observations, in work from 2025. A system is watched through one output function along many paths. The hidden space in which the system moves has a topology that shapes all its behavior. Recovering that shape from data alone is the goal. The method works from samples of trajectories rather than from equations. Such recovery would help analysts infer hidden structure in systems known only through measured outputs.
arxiv-2505-00476:
Michael Hite proposes a simpler way to prepare scattering states on today's noisy quantum computers in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Current machines can only run shallow circuits before noise ruins the result, so every step must be lean.

Building on two recent methods, Hite approximates particle wave packets by pinning them down in space, which cuts the circuit depth nearly in half while keeping the rules that fermions must obey. Simulations show the approximation approaches the exact packets in weakly interacting theories. He then ran the method on IonQ's Forte 1 machine to show it works on real hardware. The approach brings quantum scattering simulations, a basic tool for particle physics, closer to practical use.
arxiv-2505-00676:
Suchismito Chattopadhyay, Soma Mandal, and Ranjeev Misra weigh a neutron star by listening to its fastest flickers, in a paper from 2025. The star pulls gas from a companion, and the hot inner flow wobbles thousands of times per second. Those kilohertz oscillations trace orbits deep in the star's gravity, so their pattern can bound the star's mass.

Data came from India's AstroSat observatory, which watched the source drift from hard to soft states. Joint fits of two instruments showed a spectrum shaped by a hot corona's reflection, a boundary layer's glow, and a soft disk. The team tracked how the flickers moved with the spectrum's shape. Such timing and color links test the models that turn flickers into a mass estimate.
arxiv-2505-00776:
Alessandro Raganato, Rafael Peñaloza, Marco Viviani, and Gabriella Pasi probe, in a 2025 paper, whether large language models truly reason or merely echo their prompts. Their new test set asks shallow logic questions about geometric figures, a bare domain where world knowledge cannot rescue a model. Only deduction from the prompt can work.

Twenty-four models of many sizes tried the questions with no examples and with a few. The largest, over 70 billion parameters, did best cold, yet all left wide room to grow. Adding chain-of-thought prompting across 22 models helped or hurt depending on whether the reasoning came before or after the answer. The results frame prompt design as part of the reasoning itself. Small wording shifts, big swings in logic.
arxiv-2505-01176:
Massimo Bilancioni and Massimiliano Esposito extend, in a 2025 paper, the theory of how energy is transduced from one process to another inside chemical reaction networks. In the classic view, one input drives one output against its spontaneous direction. Real networks, such as the core pathways of cell life, juggle many inputs and outputs through shared steps, which blurs which process drives which.

Their fix starts from elementary processes, steps that cannot be decomposed further. From those, they pick out the true set of processes at play in transduction. The method mirrors how efficiency is defined for heat engines working between several heat baths. Choosing a reference equilibrium environment shows that efficiency is relative, tied to a stored quantity called exergy. Waste outputs can be left out of the count. Applied to core cell pathways, the framework separates true efficiency from plain output share.
arxiv-2505-01576:
Rafael Castro and Alexandre Roque build, in a 2025 paper, a cheap electronic system that watches hand washing in hospitals. Clean hands are the simplest guard against hospital infections, yet rates are usually checked by people sampling wards by hand, which is slow. Their setup uses low-cost hardware with internet links at hygiene points, logging each use and feeding a live monitor for audit teams.

A trial in a real hospital in southern Brazil ran the system for three hours on a working ward. It recorded hygiene events as hoped, showing the design works outside the lab. The authors aim to give Brazilian hospitals, bound by national rules and world guidance, a fast, hard count of hygiene compliance instead of spot guesses.
arxiv-2505-01776:
Pius Privatus and Umananda Goswami compare galaxy colours across shape and setting, in work from 2025. A sky survey with integral field spectra maps nearby galaxies in fine detail. Whether shape steers how setting affects galaxy colour was the open question here.

Six shape classes split further into lone field homes and crowded group homes. Middle and late spirals favour field settings, while early spirals favour groups in the data. Colour and brightness planes answer to setting for most shape classes tested. Late spirals and irregular galaxies barely respond to setting at all in colour. Shape thus gates how much a galaxy's home colours it.
arxiv-2505-01876:
Artur Sidorenko presents a 2025 study of when singular stochastic control problems are well-posed. In such problems, the control can push the system in jumps of bounded total variation, a style that fits storage management and investing with transaction costs. Sidorenko builds an abstract framework and proves that an optimal strategy exists among randomized controls, for a broad range of goal functions.

The goals include cumulative prospect theory preferences, which weight gains and losses the way real people do. The storage result is, he notes, the first treatment of behavioral storage management with that goal. For portfolios, a topology suited to irregular paths simplifies the proofs. The framework separates what the market model must provide from what the goal must satisfy.
arxiv-2505-02076:
Industrial process plants still lean on human experts when faults strike, since fixing them needs plant-specific knowledge. Gill and co-authors propose pairing language model agents with a digital twin of the plant. The agents read the plant state and issue control actions, while the twin holds the engineering knowledge they draw on and serves as a test bed for checking their fixes before use.

On a mixing module, the setup ran the unit on its own and cleared a pipe clog after only a few reprompts. The authors present the frame as a path toward plants that handle faults with less human help.
arxiv-2505-02276:
Miguel Martin-Landrove and Embaid wrote this 2025 paper applying chaos math to the letters of DNA and RNA. The Lyapunov exponent measures how fast a system drifts into unpredictability. A multi-parameter logistic equation, tuned by symbol order, can score the stability of letter codes. The authors extend that tool to genetic sequences with four kinds of bases.

Mapping exponents across four parameters takes special charts. They built whole-sequence distributions and two-way maps that sort bases by chemical class, purine or pyrimidine. Sequences studied ranged across gene types, with and without introns, coding and non-coding. The patterns offer a fresh lens on how letter order shapes the stability of reading and protein-making processes.
arxiv-2505-02376:
Ekaterina Shemetova and seven co-authors let language models write the annotations that static analyzers need to catch memory leaks. Their paper from twenty twenty-five presents LAMeD. Tools like CodeQL, Infer, and Cooddy track data flow through functions marked as sources or sinks. Hand-writing those marks for big or third-party libraries is slow and error-prone.

LAMeD drafts function-specific marks on its own. Plugged into the Cooddy analyzer, the marks sharpen leak detection in their tests. Search paths that once exploded in count stay in bounds. The gain is scale: whole codebases become tractable without weeks of manual tagging. The authors sketch how the same trick could serve wider code analysis. It is a pragmatic bridge between model fluency and rigid program checking.
arxiv-2505-02576:
Sergio Hernández-Gutiérrez and co-authors published a 2025 paper on a divide-and-conquer method for hard reasoning problems. Language models reason step by step, but long chains scale poorly: accuracy and speed both suffer on complex tasks, and each new task tends to demand fresh examples. The authors' method breaks a problem into subproblems recursively, tracking the dependencies between them, so partial results combine in the right order.

The decomposition needs little supervision and can be applied to an entirely new class of problems without task-specific guidance. Where chain-of-thought wanders linearly, this structure branches and rejoins like a work plan. The authors present the method as generic reasoning infrastructure, in science and engineering especially, where problems naturally nest. If it holds, one solver could face many problem families without retraining for each.
arxiv-2505-02676:
Yuhan Zhao and Jun Jiang compute how often heavy quark states decay into bound lepton pairs. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, concerns leptonium, atoms made of two leptons. Such pairs bind through electric forces alone. Factories churn out huge numbers of J/psi particles, a heavy quark-antiquark state.

Decays can spit out positronium, muonium, or dimuonium plus light or extra leptons. Future facilities will make trillions of J/psi events each year. Rates for one prized channel, ortho-dimuonium, are tiny but perhaps reachable. The authors map both spin forms of the bound pairs. A first sighting of true dimuonium motivates the hunt.
arxiv-2505-02776:
Markus Bestler, Alexander Dikopoltsev, and Oded Zilberberg create exotic wave behavior from ordinary pairing in this 2025 paper. Non-Hermitian physics studies systems that gain or lose energy, where waves can pile up at edges in a skin effect. Building such systems usually takes elaborate loss engineering.

Their model uses parametric pairing, a standard nonlinear process, in a smooth continuum. Local damping keeps the system stable. Special points in the wave spectrum spawn the skin modes when boundaries open. The authors prove the bulk and edge pictures match. The recipe offers a simpler, scalable route to effects wanted for sensors and wave control.
arxiv-2505-02976:
Debris disks, the dusty leftovers of planet building, glow faintly around young stars, and the Scorpius-Centaurus group hosts many. Justin Hom and co-authors report in 2025 a survey that imaged seven targets picked for strong infrared excess, using polarized light to sharpen the view. Four disks were resolved, three for the first time ever and one for the first time in polarized light.

Shapes within the disks hint at unseen planets stirring the dust. Comparing across known disks, scattered brightness varies tenfold at the same infrared excess, so heat glow predicts detection but not brightness. The authors set these disks as benchmarks for dust studies.
arxiv-2505-03076:
Zhenyu Xu and co-authors work out the odds math for radar-style direction detectors in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The task is to spot a signal with known row and column spaces inside matrix data, while its exact coordinates stay unknown. Many detectors exist, but their hit and false-alarm rates lacked formulas.

Focusing on two adaptive detectors with a known spatial steering vector, the team derives their statistical distributions. Closed-form expressions follow for both the chance of detection and the chance of a false alarm. Computer simulations matched the theory well. The authors say the formulas let designers set thresholds on paper rather than by trial.
arxiv-2505-03676:
Arthur Satouf, Gabriel Ben Zenou, Benjamin Piwowarski, Habiboulaye Amadou Boubacar, and Pablo Piantanida present a 2025 paper on improving sparse search with ideas from linguistics. Sparse retrievers score documents term by term, ignoring how the rest of the collection shapes what a term means. The Rational Speech Acts framework asks how a speaker trims features to single out one object among many.

Adapted to search, the framework reweights each token by contrast with other documents. Representations become sharper, since common tokens count less and distinctive ones more. Added to several sparse models, the method improved results every time. On out-of-domain tests from the BEIR benchmark it reached top performance. Code is publicly available.
arxiv-2505-04876:
Tianyu Wu, Baohua Sun, and colleagues derive how protons are distributed inside stable atomic nuclei in a 2025 nuclear physics study. Elastic electron scattering measures a nucleus's charge distribution; stripping away the proton's own size yields the point-proton density, the map of where proton centers sit. The authors work through well over one hundred stable nuclei, from lithium up to thorium.

Results appear in several standard model shapes, from harmonic oscillator and Fermi forms to a Fourier-Bessel expansion that stays close to the data. A uniform proton map library feeds reaction calculations and tests of nuclear structure theory.
arxiv-2505-05276:
Adam Kisiel worked out how to extend a measurement technique called femtoscopy from one dimension to three. He applied it to pairs of protons created in heavy-ion collisions. Femtoscopy reads the size and motion of the fireball made when heavy nuclei crash, by tracking how pairs of particles move together. For pions and kaons the full three-dimensional analysis is routine. For protons only simpler one-dimensional versions existed, because protons are rarer and the theory was incomplete.

Kisiel names the specific problems that arise for proton pairs and builds both the mathematics and the practical fitting methods to handle them. Tests on simulated collisions from a standard model show the approach recovers the source properties. He warns, though, about care needed when reading the fitted radii.
arxiv-2505-05376:
Rachmadio Lazuardi and co-authors presented GeomHair in 2025, a method that rebuilds single hair strands from three-dimensional scans with no color. Hair is hard to rebuild because strands are fine and tightly packed. No past method worked from shape alone, without color or images.

Their method finds sharp surface features and reads strand direction from shaded views using a neural line finder. A learned prior, trained on made-up hair scans, then refines the result for the scan at hand. Tests showed clean rebuilds of both simple and complex styles. From it they built a public set of strand data for four hundred people, the largest of its kind.
arxiv-2505-05476:
Anthony Lin recasts attachment theory in the language of prediction, in a 2025 paper. Attachment describes how infants bond and how those bonds script later relationships. His framework joins the dynamic-maturational model of attachment with a brain model of how the body senses itself and builds emotion, called EPIC.

The merger runs both ways: neural prediction processes shape which attachment strategies a child adopts, and early bonds in turn tune those very processes. The result is a testable bridge between nursery behavior and brain computation. Clinicians and theorists gain shared terms for a field that often talks past itself.
arxiv-2505-05576:
Gonchar and colleagues argue that current world trade models cannot justify fair trade relations. Their twenty twenty-five economics paper starts from the classic comparative advantage model. That model explains gains from trade, but not how income gets shared. The authors propose a method for building balanced trade instead.

Their ideal state gives every country a zero trade balance. Prices and export mixes are built to reach that state together. The paper proves such a price set exists when supply matches demand. It also shows tariff limits push traded goods prices upward. In a balanced system, tariff wars would have no room to start. The work is theory, aimed at reshaping trade debate.
arxiv-2505-05876:
Balint Kaszas and George Haller extend a rigorous way to shrink complex dynamic models, in this 2025 paper. The method rests a system on a low-dimensional attracting surface that captures its long-term motion. Such surfaces are usually built from local series, which fail far from their start point.

The pair rework those series as ratios of polynomials, a trick that stretches their reach. With that change, shrunken models can capture wide swings and chaotic attractors in full finite-element models. Examples from solid and fluid mechanics show the gain, in both equation-based and data-based cases. The authors frame the trick as a general upgrade.
arxiv-2505-05976:
Six authors led by Chico Sundermann shrink the logic cost of testing rich product option sets. Such sets, called feature models, can hold count rules that plain logic forms blow up on. Their first fix codes the model in pseudo-Boolean form, which packs count rules small. The next fix turns that code into a firm graph form that fast check tools love.

Set tests on rich models beat the best past path by a wide gap in their runs. Once in graph form, a shelf of fast counts and checks opens for the model. Car, chip, and software kit makers all test such sets at scale. Rich rules need no longer be cut for the sake of the checker.
arxiv-2505-06176:
Niladri Shekhar Dutt, Duygu Ceylan, and Niloy Mitra teach multimodal models the craft of photo retouching through puzzles in a 2025 computer vision study. Generative editors follow words or strokes but often warp the identity of objects in the photo, an unacceptable surprise in professional work. Traditional procedural edits, the sliders in standard tools, are safe but demand skill to sequence well.

Training on retouching puzzles, where the model must find the edit steps that transform one image into another, builds procedural skill. The resulting system aims for edits that are expressive yet conservative, keeping the photograph itself intact.
arxiv-2505-06276:
Liang Shi and co-authors build a public fake data set of crashes and near-crashes for driving research. Real crash data is rare and bound by privacy rules, so few teams can use it. The source is the largest natural driving study to date, with thousands of such events. Their set holds over 1,800 crashes and 6,900 near-crashes drawn from that study.

Faces and plates were replaced by AI-made keyframes that keep the safety facts of each scene. Notes mark event type, road and traffic states, and motion data for five seconds around the event. Synced text tales aid scene reading by machines. Two benchmark tasks show how the set can test event sorting and scene sense. The authors aim to open safety work to more labs.
arxiv-2505-06376:
Jorge Vega and co-authors shake a layer of triangular prisms and watch defects form in a 2025 study. The grains, all equal-sided prisms, lie in round and square trays. Shaking sets them into a fluid state with sixfold orientational order. Tray shapes frustrate that order and spawn topological defects.

In the round tray, defect count and charge stay fixed in steady state. Only defects of one charge sign appear. In the square tray, some defects pin to corners with higher charges. Free defects also roam, merge, and split. Total charge stays conserved through every event. The contrast shows how container shape writes the rules for defect life.
arxiv-2505-06476:
Maoshui Lv and co-authors read a wide, pulsing radio burst from a sun flare and name its source engine. Such bursts at short waves have long dodged a firm call. Past tales tied them to the big spot's lead edge and clashed. Their 2025 study works a 2011 flare burst with mid-strong slant, born near a sunspot. The burst blinks, runs hot past lab scales, and stops at sharp wave caps.

Slant and place marks line up with a maser tale: electrons in a field ring sing at twice their spin rate. Down-flow electrons in a loop mock stall in a set height band, which fits the sharp caps. The fit firms maser song as the engine for this burst class.
arxiv-2505-06676:
Eason Chen and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on an open-source kit for building animated virtual tutors that speak and react in real time. Talking-head tutors promise personal feedback at scale, but older systems sound scripted, move stiffly, or cost too much to build. Their kit plugs a language model's words into speech and a lip-synced cartoon character.

An anime-like look sidesteps the creepy near-human valley. In a fifty-person study, the tutor beat a leading talking-head baseline on sync accuracy, naturalness, expressiveness, and overall preference. The authors invite the community to add characters and classroom showcases, aiming to spread cheap, likable AI tutors across web courses.
arxiv-2505-07376:
Junji Yu and co-authors test how well language models find security flaws in code written in many programming languages, in a 2025 study. Older deep learning detectors were trained per language, which limits real-world use. Large language models promise one tool for all languages. The team benchmarked pre-trained models and top large models across seven popular languages.

A pre-trained code model, CodeT5P, won overall, above all at catching the most critical flaws. The big general models did not dominate as expected. The authors discuss where large models might still help in practice and call the study a first step. Their results give future cross-language detection work a measured baseline to beat.
arxiv-2505-07476:
Wen-Mei Li, Jianbo Lu, and Shu-Min Wu study how quantum coherence of multi-part states fades near a black hole. Their 2025 paper places mixed GHZ and W states near a Schwarzschild horizon. Part of the qubit set feels Hawking radiation while the rest stays clear.

Formulas split coherence into parts an observer can reach and parts lost behind the horizon. As Hawking heat rises, the W state holds its coherence better than the GHZ state, despite weaker entanglement. More qubits make the W edge stronger still. Fermion fields keep stronger entanglement, while boson fields keep higher coherence. The contrast guides design for quantum work in curved spacetime, the authors argue.
arxiv-2505-07576:
Chip factories scan wafer images for defects, and labeling enough bad examples to train a supervised system is slow and dear. Manuel Barusco and four co-authors benchmark unsupervised anomaly detectors on electron microscope images in 2025, a route that learns only from good parts.

Visual anomaly detection trains on normal images and flags whatever does not fit, which also yields a map of where the oddity sits. The team built a benchmark from the MIIC data set of semiconductor images and ran modern methods through it. Their results show the current approaches work well in this domain. The authors offer the benchmark as shared ground for a field that had judged itself on scattered private tests.
arxiv-2505-07776:
Shared self-driving taxis could cut car counts in dense cities, if fleets can be run in real time. Xinling Li and co-authors speed up a top fleet control method in a 2025 paper. The base method pools many riders per car but strains to keep pace at city scale.

Two add-on algorithms cut that strain, the team shows. They prove the gain in math before testing it. Runs on real Manhattan demand data back the claim. Faster control means fresher matches between riders and cars. The work helps robo-taxi fleets serve more riders with fewer cars.
arxiv-2505-07976:
Kulikov and five colleagues present a 2025 physics paper on an unusual superconducting device. Their Josephson junction sandwiches a ferromagnet between superconductors and carries an extra phase shift, making it a phi-zero junction. Under a periodic drive, ordinary junctions lock their oscillations to the electric part of the signal, producing Shapiro steps in the current-voltage curve.

This junction instead locks to the magnetic part, producing a different staircase named Buzdin steps. The step width wobbles with drive strength in a pattern like two Bessel functions multiplied, with anomalies the authors explain analytically. The locking also stirs the magnetization, causing interference and reorientation effects in step with the steps. The work maps a device whose response is steered magnetically, not electrically.
arxiv-2505-08576:
Xiang Li and co-authors build a test track for machine unlearning, the techniques meant to make a trained model forget specific data on request. Their 2025 paper presents MUBox, a platform integrating twenty-three unlearning methods, six practical scenarios, and eleven evaluation metrics, built because privacy law now demands forgetting that nobody can yet measure well.

Running the field through it produced uncomfortable findings. Even celebrated methods, including competition winners, worked inconsistently once the scenario moved past the easy settings most papers use. No single metric captured effectiveness, efficiency, and preserved usefulness together. Removing poisoned data varied wildly by attack type. The platform's lesson is metrological: a field cannot improve what it grades with a rubber ruler. MUBox offers a stiffer one, plus the comparative evidence to embarrass complacent methods into harder tests.
arxiv-2505-08876:
Jin Koda and five co-authors map molecular gas in the barred spiral galaxy M83 in two thousand twenty-five. They use the ratio of two carbon monoxide lines as their probe. Fine data from the ALMA array show how the ratio shifts across the galaxy. Low values sit between the arms, high values in the bar and arms.

The shifts sync with the galaxy's rotation and its large shapes. Star forming zones push the ratio higher still in spots. The center starts very high, the bar dips, and the disk varies again. Big gas blocks with no star birth show low values. The team says bulk gas is ruled more by galaxy dynamics than by star feedback.
arxiv-2505-09176:
Ryo Terasawa and co-authors test whether slower late-time growth of cosmic structure can ease a known measurement clash in this 2025 paper. One number, S8, summarizes how clumpy matter is today. Weak lensing data put it lower than early-universe data suggest. The clash sits at two to three times the error bars. Slowing structure growth late in time could bridge it. Several extended models can produce that slowdown.

Gas feedback, neutrino mass, and modified growth each work differently. Each leaves its own pattern across scales and ages. The team confronts these options with a major lensing dataset. Their comparison shows which stories the data allow. The paper is cosmology model testing. It treats the tension as a clue, not a nuisance.
arxiv-2505-09276:
Thomas Henzinger, Mahyar Karimi, and K S Thejaswini design in 2025 ways to check that a system follows its rules without exposing its secrets. Runtime verification watches a running system against a formal specification. When a third party does the watching, two privacy problems arise: the system's data may leak, and the specification itself may be sensitive.

Their two protocols split the difference in opposite directions. In the first, the watcher learns only whether the system complies, while both sides know the rules. In the second, the system never learns which rules are being watched, and the watcher still learns only the verdict. Both adapt tools from secure multi-party computation and swap just one message per observation step. The team built the method for a class of register-based specifications and tested it in experiments.
arxiv-2505-09376: Hyunyoung Han, Jongwon Jang, Kitaeg Shim, and Sang Ho Yoon present AfforDance, an augmented reality system for learning dance, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The system turns a dance video a user picks into an interactive lesson. It builds a 3D reference avatar from the video, syncs the music, and adds adaptive visual cues that steer the learner's moves. The authors offer the design as a step toward personal, user-centered dance teaching that adjusts to each student.
arxiv-2505-09476:
Yanbing Zhou and co-authors probe the magnetism of infinite-layer nickelates, in a 2025 paper. These compounds superconduct when doped and resemble the famous cuprates. Their charge gap is larger, though, which should weaken magnetic links through oxygen. The team measured oxygen-17 nuclei in two samples with nuclear magnetic resonance.

The signals showed glassy spin behavior from the nickel-oxygen planes, placing the material near magnetic order. Their analysis found the standard nickel-to-nickel exchange through oxygen about ten times weaker than in cuprates, too weak to explain the observed magnetism. Heavy calculations point to an extra orbital near the Fermi level that boosts the coupling. The authors say nickelate magnetism runs on a different engine than cuprate magnetism.
arxiv-2505-09776:
Alberto Gómez-Espés and co-authors review, in a 2025 paper, how teaming across borders shapes computer science research, with a focus on the biggest publishing powers. China, the European Union, and the United States lead the field in output. Drawing on a broad literature review, the authors compare joint work patterns, citation impact, and retraction rates. They also weigh how a country's development level colors the results of its research.

Joint papers involving the leading regions tended to be retracted less often, hinting at stronger research standards. Countries at the highest development level produced work with more citations and fewer retractions. Other regions, meanwhile, are closing the volume gap with the leaders. The authors argue that open, ethical international teamwork lifts the whole field, and they urge practices that include rising research nations.
arxiv-2505-09876:
Takuma Isobe, Tsuneya Yoshida, and Yasuhiro Hatsugai review topology in light systems that break the standard mold. Most such work rests on the Schrödinger equation, which reduces to a plain eigenvalue problem. Some real light systems instead obey generalized or nonlinear versions of that problem. Bands there can take complex values even for well-behaved matrices.

The first part covers the generalized case, which explains odd light spread in hyperbolic materials. It also predicts guarded crossing points in crystals made of negative-index media. The second part adds helper bands to set up a bulk-edge rule under weak nonlinearity. That rule explains why edge light modes stay sturdy when material traits shift with frequency. The review ties both cases into one frame.
arxiv-2505-10276:
Quantum light sources would be far more useful if their output could be tuned on demand. Mikkel Have Eriksen and Joel D. Cox study graphene, whose response to a magnetic field is unusually strong, as a control layer placed near a tiny light emitter. Using exact models, they examine flat sheets, narrow ribbons, and small disks of the material, each of which twists the near field in a handed way once a steady field is applied.

The emission strength and energy shift of the nearby source can be tuned by changing the charge density or the field. In ribbons, the setup makes left- and right-handed emission differ sharply, a sign of promise for guiding quantum light in one chosen sense. Disks sharpen that contrast further. The pair concludes that shaped magnetic graphene offers a flexible platform for making and steering quantum light at very small scales.
arxiv-2505-10376:
Soichiro Hattori and co-authors ask whether slow star spin can be measured from TESS space telescope data, in a study from 2025. A star's spin period can be read from changes in its brightness as dark spots cross its face. TESS watches the whole sky, but strong stray light has limited most periods found so far to under about two weeks. The team test longer periods for stars in the northern zone TESS stares at most.

As a check, they built a set of 272 long periods from ground-based ZTF data, which span more than six years. They then cleaned the TESS light curves and matched periods for 179 of the 272 stars within ten percent. The match rate rose for stars with a strong signal, which shows TESS can track slow spinners too.
arxiv-2505-10476:
Urmi Ninad and co-authors wrote this 2025 computing paper on finding cause-and-effect links when each variable is a whole vector. In climate science, a variable may be a field spread over a map, and the task is to learn its causal graph. Teams often compress such fields into averages for speed and stability.

The authors show where the common shortcuts mislead compared with a fully vector-based approach. Their focus is whether an average still stands for the same cause at a higher level. They build three scores that test different sides of that question, based on how independence patterns survive averaging. The scores let analysts check an aggregation before trusting the graph built on it. The work guards a step that climate causal studies take daily.
arxiv-2505-10576:
Qifan Fu and five co-authors teach image generators to draw hands from every side at once, in this 2025 paper. Photo-realistic hand gestures are a notorious weak spot for generative models, which mangle fingers easily. Most methods coach the model with a single rendered view of a hand mesh, so fingers hidden behind the palm are simply missing information.

Their framework, MUFEN, renders six views, front, back, left, right, top, and bottom, and picks the most informative combination as guidance for a diffusion model. A dual-stream encoder reads these multi-view priors, restoring the three-dimensional relationships that one flat projection destroys. A bounding-box fusion module then ties gesture location features into the mix, keeping the generated hands where they belong. The authors report state-of-the-art results on both numerical metrics and qualitative comparisons.
arxiv-2505-11076:
Vladimír Boža and Vladimír Macko compress large language models by splitting each weight matrix into two binary ones, in a 2025 paper. Binary weights swap costly multiplications for cheap additions, but a strict plus-or-minus-one limit usually wrecks accuracy. Their double binary factorization multiplies two sign matrices, each with its own scaling vectors, softening that limit. At one bit per weight the method beats rival binarization schemes.

At two bits per weight it competes with the best quantization methods available. A side benefit is fine-grained control: widening the middle dimension trades size for quality smoothly. The authors add an algorithm that sets different compression levels per layer, guided by pruning criteria. Code is public. They aim the method at running large models on modest hardware.
arxiv-2505-11376:
Dries Dirckx, Wilm Decré, and Jan Swevers present a 2025 computing paper on keeping robots and vehicles from colliding during planned motion. Optimal control plans smooth paths, but collision rules for rounded shapes are curved and non-convex, which slows the math. A classic theorem handles the geometry by placing a separating plane between objects.

The authors recast that plane-finding step as a classification task solved by a least-squares support vector machine. The planes then enter the control problem as fixed inputs rather than variables, turning the curved rules into straight ones. A two-level loop refreshes the planes between solver passes. In tests, path planning ran 50 to 90 percent faster than a leading rival method. The approach also scaled better into cluttered scenes.
arxiv-2505-11476:
Runze Zuo and colleagues presented a wearable soft robotic arm in 2025 that carries its own air supply and control hardware. Pneumatic soft arms bend safely around people and clutter, but they usually trail bulky external pressure regulators and offer limited strength and precision. The team's design, called UMArm, mounts many modified McKibben artificial muscles on a lightweight rigid spine. Each muscle hides its own valves and controller inside, so no separate regulator box is needed.

The hybrid rigid-soft structure aims to combine the compliance of soft robots with the force and accuracy of rigid ones. Because the arm is modular and untethered, sections can be rearranged and the whole device worn on the body. The paper presents the design as a step toward soft arms that work in unstructured places, where rigid robots struggle and human contact is likely.
arxiv-2505-11576:
Wu, Alaniz, Karthik, Dayan, Schulz, and Akata argue in twenty twenty-five that neural networks are not true black boxes: their inner activity mirrors patterns in their training data. Borrowing the mind's trick of chunking, they slice the chatter of many neurons into recurring units that stand for concepts. Three extractors cover different cases, from labelled data to none, and from low to high dimensions.

The chunks captured concrete words, grammar tags, and even story schemas, across small recurrent nets and large language models alike. Pasting a chunk into a network shifted its behaviour in controlled, predictable ways, showing the units do causal work. The authors offer chunking as a fresh route to interpretability grounded in how people themselves parse streams.
arxiv-2505-11776:
Jiali Chen and Avijit Mukherjee wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It joins the two great schools of graph self-supervised learning, generative and contrastive, in one frame that uses community shape to pick its pairs.

Contrastive methods shine at node sorting, generative ones at link calls. The new build adds community-aware node contrast, graph-level contrast for broad sense, and a rich tweak plan that masks traits, stirs nodes, and drops edges. On open benchmarks it beats top rivals across sorting, grouping, and link tasks, by small but steady lifts. The frame is meant for graphs with few or no labels.
arxiv-2505-12076:
Ali Akbar Septiandri and four co-authors fill gaps in intensive care data by treating the patient's many measurements as one connected stream. Monitors record different signals at irregular times, and the timing itself can carry clinical meaning. Standard imputation usually handles each signal separately and gives no uncertainty for its guesses.

Their method adapts deep Gaussian process emulation with stochastic imputation, borrowing strength across related measurements and across time. Each filled value comes with an uncertainty estimate, which matters when clinicians act on the numbers. On a clinical dataset the approach beat common alternatives, including chained-equation multiple imputation and last-value carry-forward. The authors stress the value of modeling cross-signal relationships explicitly.
arxiv-2505-12376:
Sunil Chandran and Suraj Kumar Sahoo pin down the boxicity of zero divisor graphs of modular rings. Boxicity is the smallest dimension in which a graph can be drawn as overlaps of boxes. Zero divisor graphs come from rings and link algebra with graph theory.

In these graphs each vertex is a zero divisor of the ring. Two vertices join when their product is zero. An earlier study gave an upper bound for the ring of integers modulo N. Chandran and Sahoo now give the exact value for key cases. Their proof splits by the prime form of N. The result closes a gap in a long-studied graph family. It also adds a clean formula for future work.
arxiv-2505-12576:
Kiran Kokilepersaud, Mohit Prabhushankar, and Ghassan AlRegib study how representation size evolves during self-supervised learning in a 2025 study. A known failure is dimensional collapse, where features use only part of the space they are given. Higher effective dimension usually means richer features and better transfer to new tasks.

The authors focus on the stage where a projection head maps core features into an embedding space. Recent work casts that head as a filter removing noisy or irrelevant features. Their method adapts dimensionality during training in response to the dynamics they measure. The goal is to keep feature diversity high without wasting capacity on noise.
arxiv-2505-12776:
Kai Liang counts independent sets in king graphs with a tensor network method, in a solo work from 2025. A king graph links squares a chess king can reach in one move. An independent set picks squares with no two linked, and counting them for large boards is a hard combinatorial task.

Liang turns the count into a tiling count on a slightly larger rectangle. A tensor contraction algorithm then computes exact counts for all boards up to a set total size. For larger boards he gives estimates. He also counts sets by their size and finds which size is most common. Thousands of new terms were added to public integer sequence lists.
arxiv-2505-13076:
Three authors audit the security of browsing AI agents in this 2025 paper. Autonomous agents that surf the web for users run on shifting page content and live tools, which opens a wide attack surface that had not been mapped end to end.

The team built the first full threat model for such agents and proposed layered defenses: cleaning inputs, isolating the planner from the executor, formal checkers, and session safeguards. A white box study of a popular open source agent, Browser Use, showed how hostile page content can hijack behavior. Their finds include prompt injection, domain check bypass, and credential theft, backed by a disclosed vulnerability report and a working proof of concept.
arxiv-2505-13276:
Sebastian Barzaghi, Arianna Moretti, Ivan Heibi, and Silvio Peroni wrote a 2025 paper on CHAD-KG, a knowledge graph for cultural heritage objects. Museums and exhibitions increasingly digitize their objects, producing both descriptive metadata and paradata, records of how the digitization itself was done. Storing both in a structured, linked form makes them reusable.

CHAD-KG converts two tabular data sets into RDF, the web's linked data format, following an application profile built on standards such as CIDOC-CRM and the Getty thesaurus. A reproducible pipeline generates the graph automatically. It now serves as the main metadata source for a digital twin of a temporary exhibition, a virtual copy that mirrors the physical show.
arxiv-2505-13576:
Phones and wearables that learn together face a moving target, since each user's habits shift over time. Sara Alosaime and Arshad Jhumka address a failure mode of that setup in 2025: catastrophic forgetting, where a model loses old skills as new data streams in.

In human activity recognition, devices join and leave at random and each person's data looks different, which makes forgetting worse. Standard continual learning leans on stored memories and replay, but federated privacy rules ban keeping raw data. Their method, FlexFed, instead guards how memory is used and adjusts how often each device trains offline, based on drift, device strength, and time away. They also add a new forgetting metric and a test setup that mimics real streaming use.
arxiv-2505-13876:
Yu-Sik Kim and Jae-Young Kim (2025) tracked the jet of the blazar PKS 0735+178 around the time of a high-energy neutrino event. Blazars are galaxies whose jets point near Earth, and some may fire neutrinos across the universe. Radio telescopes with continent-wide baselines imaged this jet at two frequencies from 2020 to 2024. The data resolve features less than a parsec from the core. A neutrino recorded in December 2021 falls inside the window.

After the neutrino, the core region brightened in radio waves, grew hotter in apparent terms, and became more opaque. A new jet knot had left the core shortly before the event. It raced downstream at about four times light speed in apparent terms. Right at the neutrino's arrival, within the timing uncertainty, the knot passed a slower feature about 0.77 parsecs out. The authors propose that crossing point as the likely birthplace of the neutrino.
arxiv-2505-14276:
Tharathep Plienbumrung and three co-authors model the magnetic and charge patterns that may form in a nickel-based compound tied to superconductivity research. Their 2025 paper studies NdNiO2, a layered material with nickel and oxygen sheets. They build a two-band model, one band centered on nickel sites and one on neodymium sites.

Long-range forces between electrons turn out to be strong in this model. The team then tests which ordered patterns the forces favor. Charge ripples appear only weakly and may be an artifact of small model size. Magnetic order depends mostly on how full the nickel band is. Once quantum wobble is fully counted, the magnetic order fades at the filling that other methods predict. The two bands stay largely separate despite their links.
arxiv-2505-14376:
Chitale and co-authors build an automatic pre-review service for research papers in this 2025 paper. Getting good feedback before submission is a known bottleneck for authors. Their system, AutoRev, reads a paper as a layered graph of sections and passages, then retrieves the most telling parts to guide a language model's critique.

Graph-guided retrieval shrinks what the model takes in, which improved feedback quality in tests. The system beat baseline tools on automatic scores and fared well with human judges too. Output is structured and aimed at fixes an author can act on, not vague praise. The authors plan to release the code, positioning AutoRev as a rehearsal for peer review.
arxiv-2505-14476:
Farshad Sangari Abiz, Reshad Hosseini, and Babak Araabi make the hidden codes of an image-generating model easier to read. Variational autoencoders store what they learn in a set of active dimensions, but in the plain version those dimensions blur together. A sparse variant turns on only a few at a time, which helps, yet samples of the same class still light up in scattered patterns. Their 2025 paper adds a push toward shared structure.

The new loss term rewards samples of one class for switching on the same dimensions, so each shared dimension stands for a clear concept or factor. Older disentangling methods chase factors that hold across every class at once. This method keeps those global factors and also learns ones tied to a single class. The result is a latent space whose active dimensions line up with meaning a reader can name.
arxiv-2505-14576:
Aboard the International Space Station, the Plasmakristall-4 facility lets researchers watch dust grains suspended in a plasma, free of gravity's pull. Emerson Gehr and co-authors report in 2025 that these dust clouds organize into thread-like filaments and layered sheets that shift with gas pressure, current, and applied electric fields. The team asks whether such clouds behave like liquid crystals, materials whose particles align like a liquid yet keep some crystal order.

They measured particle correlations within filaments, across the central plane, and through the full depth, for nine settings. At low pressure the whole cloud was weakly crystalline. At high pressure, order inside filaments sharpened while filaments slid past each other more freely. The authors compare that pattern to a nematic liquid crystal, with hints of a layered smectic state elsewhere. Computer simulations of the dust and ions backed the reading.
arxiv-2505-14776:
Dalla Barba and eight co-authors study how a relativistic jet interacts with the narrow-line region of the galaxy PMN J0948+0022 in a 2025 paper. The galaxy was first classed as a jetted narrow-line Seyfert 1, a type seen face-on in the standard model of such systems.

Sharper spectra from two large instruments showed a new shape for a key hydrogen line, more like that of a mid-type Seyfert. The team argues the shape does not come from a tilt in view. It comes from the strong jet plowing into the narrow-line gas and passing part of its energy to that gas.
arxiv-2505-14976:
Roozbeh Aghili and co-authors present a learning tool that finds private facts in software logs, in this 2025 paper. Logs guide upkeep of software, but shared log sets are scarce because logs often hold names and other private data. Rule-based scrubbing takes hand work and breaks on new formats.

Their deep learning framework spots sensitive fields without hand rules. It beat the best rule sets in tests. With only 100 labeled samples from a new data set, it found 99.5 percent of sensitive fields and scored high on a balanced accuracy measure. The authors call it the first learning-based swap for rule-based log scrubbing.
arxiv-2505-15276:
Rongzhi Zhu and co-authors study why large reasoning models often keep thinking even when a prompt tells them to save effort, in a 2025 paper. These models shine on hard tasks but waste resources by overthinking. When told to stop, they frequently slip into a still-thinking mode, above all on hard questions.

The team probes the split from three angles: confidence at the point where thinking ends, inner attention patterns, and how attention spreads across the prompt. High perplexity went with later still-thinking, and those cases leaned harder on the original question. An attention intervention could suppress the extra thinking, but accuracy fell, which suggests the extra thought often helps.
arxiv-2505-16376:
Zijia Lu, Gaurav Mittal, and their colleagues find moments in long videos from text queries without paying full price for every second, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The task, temporal grounding, asks a system to point to the exact span a description refers to, and long videos make the naive approach ruinously expensive.

The naive approach cuts the video into clips and runs a heavyweight encoder on each one. DeCafNet instead delegates the first pass to a light sidekick encoder. The sidekick scans all clips cheaply and draws a saliency map of likely matches. Only the most promising clips go to the full expert encoder for careful processing. Features from the two passes are then combined for the final answer. The delegate-and-conquer split aims to keep accuracy while slashing compute. It targets search and retrieval over the long videos that dominate real collections.
arxiv-2505-16476:
Patryk Tajs, Mateusz Skarupski, and Jakub Rydzewski presented a software package in 2025 for drawing maps of molecule motion data. Studies of molecules produce huge, high-dimension records of how atoms move. A method called t-SNE can flatten such records into maps that people can read, and a neural version of the method works even better.

Their package, NeuralTSNE, builds that neural version in Python on top of PyTorch tools. It can be loaded as a module or run from the command line. The authors show that the tool is easy to set up and use on real motion data. They offer it as a handy route for labs that want clear maps of complex molecule behavior without building their own code.
arxiv-2505-16576:
Spencer Hong, Meng Luo, and Xinyi Wan present a 2025 paper on checking single small claims for truth. Fact-check systems often fetch proof from a search engine, then ask one big model to judge. People do not work that way; they search, sift, and read in steps.

Their system, EMULATE, splits the work among a team of small agents. One agent ranks search hits by set rules, another reads page content, and others weigh the proof. Tests on several standard claim sets showed clear gains over past methods. The authors argue that copying human steps, not just human answers, makes checks stronger.
arxiv-2505-16776:
Vladislav Popkov, Xin Zhang, Carlo Presilla, and Tomaž Prosen set out the firm state of spin chains that can be solved in full. Strong loss at the ends drives those chains. They bring in grains whose spread law is re set, or dressed, by the loss it self. The firm state's range then comes from Bethe rules for a kin set that sings in tune. That set shares the same base states.

The team works out clear dressed strength scores for the XXX and XXZ chains. Those chains have loss led end fields that run straight. They grow the finds to XXZ and XYZ chains with end fields that do not run straight. In each case the dress adds a sharp point to the spread law. That point by much re shapes the firm state range next to the tune model.
arxiv-2505-17176:
João D Álvares and Alex Vaño-Viñuales present a 2025 arXiv paper on simulating Einstein's equations together with electromagnetic and scalar fields. Their setup uses hyperboloidal slices, surfaces that reach future null infinity, the one place where radiation such as gravitational waves is sharply defined. The team reports the first run of this system under a standard common formulation.

Tests in spherical symmetry cover a charged scalar field perturbing calm spacetime and one near a charged black hole. A third run follows the collapse of a charged scalar field into a Reissner-Nordström black hole. The work shows the code can extract clean signals at infinity.
arxiv-2505-17576:
Doncey Albin and co-authors release a dataset in a 2025 paper on robot teams. Robots that work together must align what each of them saw, across place and time. Tests of that skill usually fake a team by chopping one robot's path into pieces, which misses the natural variation of real separate runs.

Their dataset, CU-Multi, was gathered over several days at two campus sites. One robot ran four synchronized routes with planned amounts of overlap. Sensors include color and depth cameras, GPS with heading, and labeled laser scans. The controlled overlap and dense labels make the set a sharper test bed for matching data across robots. Access instructions and support code are public.
arxiv-2505-17676:
Kai Pischke, Jake Masters, and Nobuko Yoshida give full proofs for a theory of asynchronous communication protocols in a 2025 paper. Session types check that distributed parts follow a shared global protocol. Their top down method starts from the global rules, projects them to local specs for each part, and then lets each part reorder its own actions.

The paper defines fresh operational rules that capture safe reorderings in message passing without synchrony. It also proves, for the first time, that the most expressive projection method in the field is correct. Main theorems link the global and local views in both directions. As a payoff, key guarantees such as deadlock freedom and liveness carry over to the optimized local parts. Each part can thus be built alone, then joined safely.
arxiv-2505-18176:
Jonathan Tammer Eweis-Labolle, Tyler Johnson, Xiangyu Sun, and Ramin Bostanabad ask whether engineers should tune several computer models at once instead of one by one. Designers often hold a shelf of models of the same system, cheap rough ones and costly precise ones, and in the past calibrated each separately against trusted data. The authors build a probabilistic framework, based on tailored neural networks, that calibrates any number of models at the same time.

The framework handles models with several outputs and differing parameter sets, learns a probability distribution for every calibration parameter, and trains against all data sources at once. It also shapes a readable latent space where model-form errors can be spotted. Tests on analytic and engineering problems show joint calibration can improve predictive accuracy. Its weakness is identifiability: in higher-dimensional input spaces, parameters can trade off against each other unless physics pins them down.
arxiv-2505-18476:
Colin Folsom and co-authors release a free software pack for star studies in a 2025 paper. Their field reads how starlight twists as its color spreads out, a clue to star traits and magnet fields. Fresh, open tools are a must as gear and data forms keep changing.

The pack, called SpecpolFlow, runs in Python and works with data from many scopes. It cleans and scales spectra, pulls out shared line profiles, and builds the masks those profiles need. From the profiles it gauges the star's magnet pull along the line of sight. Guide lessons on its site walk users through standard jobs, and the code is fully logged for both screen and typed use.
arxiv-2505-18776:
Wilde, Gribakin, and Fabrikant propose in 2025 an explanation for why positronium vanishes so fast in halogen gases. Positronium is a short-lived atom made of an electron and its antimatter twin. In gases like bromine and iodine it disappears at puzzlingly high rates, and the team blames a sticking process that tears a halogen molecule apart.

They model the process for fluorine gas, where it releases energy and can run at room temperature. Scattering calculations reveal resonance states that boost the sticking, much like a known electron process. Feeding those resonances into a standard theory gives a very large rate, only tenfold below the rates seen for the heavier gases. The match supports their explanation.
arxiv-2505-18976:
Knowing which training examples shaped a model's answer is called data attribution, and the honest methods are expensive. Pingbang Hu and co-authors speed them up in a 2025 paper with a compression trick named GraSS. Gradient-based attribution needs a gradient for every training sample, which devours memory and time on large models.

GraSS exploits the fact that those per-sample gradients are mostly zeros. Sparsifying them and projecting them into a smaller space cuts the cost below linear growth. A variant tuned for plain linear layers, FactGraSS, ran up to 165 percent faster than the best prior methods on billion-parameter models. Accuracy of the influence estimates held up across experiments. The authors release their code openly for other teams to use.
arxiv-2505-19076:
Charts pack dense data into small spaces, and AI models often misread them when they reason in words alone. Muye Huang and eight co-authors present ChartSketcher in 2025, a method that lets a model draw on the chart as it thinks. Using a sketching library, the model marks its steps right on the image and reads those marks back in.

Training came in two stages: first the model learned the sketching style, then a form of practice learning sharpened its self checking. The team report strong scores on chart tests and on general vision tasks. Because each step leaves a visible mark, people can follow how the model reached its answer. The authors offer it as a more open way to read charts.
arxiv-2505-19176:
Zhuo Liu and four colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on a flaw in how AI judges are trained. Many labs use a strong model to grade answers, then train a cheaper judge on those grades. The authors name a hidden catch in this plan: teacher preference bias.

A judge trained this way learns to favor answers from its own teacher model. That skew makes scores unfair for other models. The team adds an assistant model that has no tie to the teacher. Its grades balance the training data. Tests check whether the fix cuts the bias while keeping the judge sharp. The work matters wherever cheap AI judges stand in for human review.
arxiv-2505-19376:
Ying and a team of colleagues studied in twenty twenty-five how people attribute beliefs to others. Explaining someone's actions often means guessing what they believe. Yet people could attribute many possible beliefs, and the team asked which ones they actually pick.

They built a computer model scoring a belief statement on three factors: accuracy, how much it tells, and causal relevance to the action. People watched an agent collect keys hidden in boxes to reach a goal. They then ranked statements about the agent's beliefs. Accuracy and informativeness together predicted the rankings fairly well. Causal relevance alone predicted them best. The results suggest people favor beliefs that actually explain why the agent acted.
arxiv-2505-19476:
Ziqian Wang and co-authors present FlowSE, a generative model that cleans noise from speech in a single swift pass. Their 2025 paper works in speech enhancement, the task of turning noisy speech into clear speech. Past generative tools have flaws. Word-based models lose speaker likeness through coarse coding, while diffusion models train hard and run slow. Flow matching instead learns a smooth path from noisy to clean sound.

Training uses noisy sound maps plus, when present, the spoken text. The model learns the shape of speech over time and pitch, and how text aligns with sound. At run time it works with or without a transcript, and scores rise when text is given. Tests beat leading generative rivals across the board. The team shares code, trained models, and samples for others to check.
arxiv-2505-19676:
Lachlan McGinness and Peter Baumgartner test whether frontier language models got better at formal reasoning across nine months, and find a stall, in a 2025 paper. Their testbed is PRONTOQA steamroller problems, logic puzzles of the kind automated theorem provers tackle. Models from December 2023 and August 2024 faced the same set.

Accuracy barely moved. By tracking how many tokens the models spent, the authors show that nearly all gains since GPT-4 trace to hidden system prompts or to built-in chain-of-thought habits, not deeper reasoning. Of the prover strategies tried, models handled bottom-up forward chaining best. Worryingly, a response with correct reasoning steps only weakly predicted a correct final answer.
arxiv-2505-19776:
Akram Elbouanani, Evan Dufraisse, and Adrian Popescu measure political bias in language models through sentiment in a 2025 paper. Older bias tests ask models questionnaires or let them grade themselves, which can echo their own leanings. The new idea watches a plainer signal: the same sentence should not change emotional tone just because the politician named in it changes.

The team inserted over thirteen hundred diverse politician names into 450 political sentences and scored the tone across seven models and six languages. Every pairing showed inconsistencies, with warm bias toward left figures and cold bias toward the far right. Bigger models leaned harder and more steadily, and Western languages leaned most. Swapping in invented names partly steadied the scores.
arxiv-2505-20276:
Shrinking a language model by quantization saves memory and time, but what does it cost on long documents? Five authors run the first systematic test of quantized models on tasks with very long inputs and long-form answers. They cover about 9,700 test cases, five quantization methods, and five models from two families, in sizes from 7 to 72 billion parameters.

Eight-bit versions held up well, losing under one percent of accuracy on average. Four-bit versions hurt much more, with drops reaching 59 percent on long-input tasks. Damage grew when the input was not English. The same method could leave one model nearly untouched and cut another's score by a third, so the team warns that results depend on the exact mix of method, model, and task. Careful testing, they conclude, must precede any real deployment.
arxiv-2505-20476:
Jihao Jia and co-authors measure tiny shape flaws in optical nanofibers in their 2025 arXiv paper. These tapered fibers guide light for quantum and nanophotonics work, where stable polarization is vital. Even angstrom-scale deviations from a perfect circle can rotate polarization within millimeters of travel.

They used two methods inside the setup itself. First, the split resonance frequencies of hundreds of bending modes revealed an elliptical cross-section whose semi-axes differ by only about two angstroms. Second, imaging light scattered from the fiber showed periodic polarization changes that matched the same tiny ellipticity. The work matters for quantum memories, frequency conversion and lasers needing controlled light-matter interaction.
arxiv-2505-20676:
Sadaf Safa, Ali Abedi, and Shehroz Khan present a video method to measure student engagement in online classes in a 2025 paper. Engagement drives how well online programs work, and automated measures help teachers spot fading attention early. Two hurdles stand out: engaged and disengaged students appear in uneven numbers, and engagement comes in ordered levels, not mere labels.

Their method learns from labeled videos by pulling same-level examples closer and pushing others apart, while respecting level order. It draws on face and behavior cues drawn from each video. The design aims at fair scores across the full scale, from checked-out to fully absorbed. Virtual schools get a tool that flags disengagement in time for teachers to act.
arxiv-2505-20776:
Jungyoub Cha, Hyunjong Kim, and Sungzoon Cho stretch speculative decoding to long documents in a 2025 paper. The trick pairs a small draft model with a big one: the small model guesses ahead, the big one verifies, and answers come faster. On long inputs the gains melt early, a weakness few had examined.

SpecExtend bolts on fast attention machinery to speed both the first pass and verification. Its novel move evicts memory smartly: the big model's own attention scores choose which context the small drafter keeps, sharpening guesses without retraining either model. On sixteen-thousand-token summaries the speedup neared three-fold, and on long reasoning nearly four-fold, while short inputs kept their usual pace. The authors release the code as a drop-in upgrade for existing frameworks.
arxiv-2505-21076:
Cities change over years, and satellite archives hold that story, but image-reading models usually see only one or two moments in time. Weihao Xuan and co-authors built a benchmark suite in 2025 for long-term city understanding from remote sensing images. The suite holds nearly fifteen thousand sharp images from forty-two major United States cities, spanning 2005 to 2023.

Six tasks range from spotting pixel-level change to writing scene-level accounts of growth, disaster damage, and environmental strain. Testing eighteen leading models exposed weak long-term reasoning and poor quantitative skill. The team then built a training set for this work and a baseline model that answers questions and marks change in the images. The suite gives the field a shared yardstick for time-aware Earth observation.
arxiv-2505-21276:
Wang, Guo, and Zhou show that axion interactions with kaons heat axions in the early universe far faster than past estimates said. The axion heating rate sets the hot dark matter limit on axion mass. Standard rates counted only the channel where an axion and a pion trade into two pions. Above 100 MeV, that channel alone badly understates the rate. The team computed axion scattering with light mesons in a chiral framework. The kaon channel, axion plus kaon to pion plus kaon, proved much larger.

Resonances inside that channel swell its cross section. Near 130 MeV its share dominates the total rate. Dark matter bounds built on the old rate need revisiting.
arxiv-2505-21676:
Yufeng Yang and five co-authors report real trials of a cloud-based driving system for driverless vehicles, in a 2025 study. Cars that sense only for themselves can miss hazards hidden by crowds or walls. The system adds fixed sensor posts at key spots, each with cameras, laser scanners, and small computers. The posts send tidy summaries to a cloud hub over fast 5G links. The hub merges the views into one shared scene picture.
