Two field sites tested the setup: a busy urban roundabout and an indoor space like a hospital. Shared sensing helped the vehicles keep track of people and other movers around blind spots. The authors report gains in safety and smooth coordination between vehicles. They present the design as a general frame for indoor and outdoor fleets.
arxiv-2505-21876:
Zun Wang and a team of co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on teaching video generators to move their cameras on command. Current methods render a rough anchor video from estimated point clouds to show the desired motion, but estimation errors make the anchor misleading, and the model wastes capacity forgiving it. EPiC builds anchors differently, with no pose or point cloud estimation at all.

Masking a source video by what its first frame can see yields anchors aligned by construction, from any ordinary footage. A small add-on module, Anchor-ControlNet, feeds the anchor into a pretrained diffusion model using under one percent extra parameters. Training then needs fewer steps and less data, yet the model still obeys point-cloud anchors at test time. The authors claim precise, three-dimensional camera control at a fraction of the usual cost.
arxiv-2505-22076:
Stahl, Ziegenbein, Park, and Wachsmuth present a study from twenty twenty-five on training language models for argumentation tasks. General instruction tuning leaves models weak on tasks that need domain knowledge. Argumentation, with tasks like claim and fallacy checks, is one such domain. The team craft plain instructions for one hundred five argumentation tasks from past research. They build a benchmark to grade models across those tasks. They then synthesize tens of thousands of training instructions by a self-instruct method.

Fine-tuning on that set lifts scores on both seen and unseen argumentation tasks. General language task scores stay stable in parallel checks. The authors say domain instruction sets can specialize models safely. Their benchmark gives the field a shared yardstick.
arxiv-2505-22176:
Vihang Pancholi and colleagues grade machine-made tables the way a careful teacher would: first check the structure, then read the content, then explain the grade. Standard metrics miss small structural and factual slips that make a table misleading. Writing in twenty twenty-five, their framework begins with a rubric mixing multi-level structural descriptors with fine-grained contextual signals. A first phase aligns the candidate table against the reference table's layout; a second compares meaning and wording cell by cell, producing interpretable, detailed feedback rather than one opaque score.

The system was tested on a new benchmark spanning many domains, with realistic table corruptions and human annotations. A sensitivity and specificity analysis backed its robustness across table tasks. Code and data are public. The work targets the growing pipeline of generated reports and data summaries, where tables carry the facts readers trust most.
arxiv-2505-22276:
Mohammed Alghadeer and co-authors build a quiet quantum chip lattice in 2025. Superconducting circuits lead the race for quantum machines, but scaling brings crosstalk and build flaws. Stray microwave modes and qubit cross-talk spoil accuracy as arrays grow.

Their four-by-four grid holds sixteen fixed-tone qubits with neighbor-only links. A tileable 3D design with off-chip shunts damps the stray enclosure modes. Tests showed tight spread in device values and low gate errors when all qubits ran at once. The team offers the design as a path toward larger, low-crosstalk lattices for error correction and simulation.
arxiv-2505-22476:
Altmann and co-authors present a 2025 paper arguing for Civil Clauses that keep university science peaceful. After the Second World War, many institutes wrote such pledges into their charters. Fresh government and European reports now question their reach, blurring the line between civilian and military work. A panel of the Science4Peace Forum supplied the reflections gathered here.

Clause adoptions across countries are reviewed one by one. Challenges already pressing on the clauses get documented. Arguments for holding the civilian line close the case. Dozens of signatories from the physics community back the statement. The paper speaks to rectors and funders weighing dual-use drift in public research.
arxiv-2505-22576:
Qing-He Ni and seven co-authors present ExoPhoto, a store of data on how molecules break apart in ultraviolet light at a range of heat levels. Such data are a must to model the air of planets round other stars, and of stars too, with care. One gap has been the short end of the ultraviolet band.

ExoPhoto grows out of the known ExoMol frame. It pulls in theory from three data stores built on computers, plus tests done by lab groups. It now holds twenty molecules, from water and carbon dioxide to ones that bear metals. For each heat level, its files give cross sections by wavelength, set out in the ExoMol way, with ExoMol names. For some sets it adds branching ratios and quantum yields. Growth plans call for more molecules and for data on states out of balance.
arxiv-2505-22976:
Kewei Lian and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on a test for world models that must keep space straight. A world model fakes how a scene shifts as an agent moves. If it forgets where things are, plans built on it fail. Past test sets stress looks, not long range space sense. Their set, LoopNav, is built on loops.

Agents walk loops in the game Minecraft and come back to the start. The set holds a vast span of video with the moves logged. A new score checks if the model's inner scene graph stays in line on the loop. It shrugs off pixel level noise. Data, tests, and code are open for later work.
arxiv-2505-23676:
Piotr Bartman-Szwarc, Adil M. Bagirov, and Anna Ochal present a 2025 math paper on contact problems, such as parts that press or slide against each other. Such problems are written as hemivariational inequalities, a class of hard math statements with rough, non-smooth terms. Smooth tools fail on them, so the team builds a method that works with rough slopes called subgradients.

Their hybrid method first searches widely to find good starting points, then refines them with a local search. Each step uses just two slope estimates to pick a direction, which keeps the cost low. Steps either improve the answer or add new slope data for later use. The team tests the method on a sample contact problem and compares it with other solvers.
arxiv-2505-24376:
Wei-Han Tan and co-authors use a classic method to study excited light mesons in a 2025 paper. Mesons are short-lived bits made of a quark and an antiquark. The team built forms of them with an added twist, a math step that stands for extra motion, and asked what masses and decay rates follow.

Twelve such forms were built, and ten were worked through in full number detail. The quark mixes covered plain, strange, and mixed pairs, forming sets of nine related states. Results support one known set of four mesons as such a family. The team also predicts new excited states, with masses and decay rates for hunters to test.
arxiv-2505-24876:
Ashraf and co-authors present Agent-X, a 2025 benchmark for testing AI agents on hard visual tasks that take many steps. Older benchmarks lean on made-up, single-turn questions and judge only the final answer. Agent-X holds 828 tasks with real images, image sets, videos, and written instructions. The tasks span six settings, among them web browsing, driving, sports, security, and math.

A scoring framework grades each step of the agent's work, not just the outcome. It checks whether each step was right, whether the chain of steps made sense, and whether tools were used well. Even the best current model families solved fewer than half of the tasks end to end. The authors point to weak multi-step reasoning and tool use as the main bottlenecks.
arxiv-2506-00276:
Jiawei Fang and co-authors let language models co-design robots in a 2025 paper. Building a robot means shaping its body and its control rewards together. Fixed reward rules often trap the search in mediocre designs, since each body shape moves best under different incentives.

Their framework works in two stages. First, a reflection step proposes many varied body-and-reward pairs and samples the promising region broadly. Next, top candidates are refined by alternating model-guided updates to rewards and body shape. The loop discovers both efficient forms and the motion styles that suit them. Results show strong designs without task-specific prompts or preset reward formulas. The method treats reward design as part of the invention, not a given.
arxiv-2506-00476:
Abhisek Ray and Lukas Esterle introduce ModelNet, a data set for testing privacy-preserving federated learning on image tasks, in a 2025 paper. Federated learning trains across sites without moving raw data. Benchmarks for it often lack realistic differences between clients. That weakness lets weak privacy claims pass untested. A harder, more varied benchmark was needed.

ModelNet rebuilds a classic image set from the embeddings of a pretrained network. Three client splits mimic uniform, mixed, and random domain shifts. Graph-based private methods can then be graded fairly. The authors frame it as infrastructure, not a new algorithm. Federated learning researchers gain a sterner test bed. Privacy methods must now prove themselves under client diversity.
arxiv-2506-00576:
Fatemeh Lotfi and co-authors blend language models with learning agents to manage open radio networks, in work from 2025. Open network designs split the radio system into parts that smart controllers can steer. Slicing the network for mixed services is a hard, fast-changing task.

Learning agents struggle with raw, messy inputs such as signal traits and traffic trends. The design uses two language models to enrich the agent's view of the state. A domain-tuned model turns control data into clear, structured prompts. Those prompts merge with learned tokens before choices are made. The goal is faster, more general control choices in networks whose state is only partly visible.
arxiv-2506-00676:
Fine-tuning a large language model can weaken the safety training it started with, and each research group tests that risk in its own way. Saad Hossain, Samanvay Vajpayee, and Sirisha Rambhatla built a shared toolkit for the task in 2025, called SafeTuneBed. It gathers fine-tuning datasets for tasks from sentiment to open-ended instruction, and can make harmful variants of them.

The toolkit plugs in defenses applied before, during, and after tuning, and scores both safety and usefulness with the same measures for all. Its design uses plain Python settings and plugins, so new methods need little extra code. The authors show it at work on several defenses under varied poisoning attacks.
arxiv-2506-00876:
Teaching a language model to forget private or copyrighted text usually scrubs whole documents, including harmless common words that carry general knowledge. Yixin Wan and co-authors argue for a finer eraser in a 2025 paper. Their method picks out only the tokens that truly encode the unwanted material and unlearns those.

Across two benchmarks and six standard unlearning methods, the selective version forgot the target content just as well while keeping the model's usefulness on everything else. The point is surgical: forgetting should cost the model as little general skill as possible. The approach plugs into existing unlearning pipelines rather than replacing them.
arxiv-2506-00976:
Jonathan Bobrutsky and Amit Moscovich tackle a costly math problem in a 2025 paper. The Wasserstein metric compares shapes and data sets, and it is widely used in learning tasks. Its exact value is often too slow to compute. Faster shortcuts exist, but they do not promise that the result is above or below the true value.

Their method shrinks data onto a coarse grid and solves the problem there in full. A fix-up stage then turns that result into a strict upper or lower bound. Tests on a standard image set showed speeds about ten times faster. Bounds matter because users can trust the range, not just a rough guess.
arxiv-2506-01076:
Sergey Goncharov, Pouya Partow, and Stelios Tsampas give a general proof that two styles of program meaning agree, in a 2025 paper. Programming languages are defined by operational rules. Small-step rules describe one move at a time. Big-step rules jump straight to the final result. Both styles are used everywhere in practice. Their agreement is usually proven case by case, from scratch. A shared abstract argument was missing.

The authors work inside a higher-order mathematical framework. They define an abstract notion of big-step semantics there. It complements an existing abstract small-step notion. A general construction derives the big-step version from the small-step one. An abstract equivalence theorem follows. The result is proven once, for all languages fitting the frame. The paper is aimed at semantics researchers. It promises to retire repetitive proof work. Language designers gain a reusable guarantee.
arxiv-2506-01176:
Adyan Dordzhiev proves a finite form, in a 2025 preprint, of a deformed version of de Finetti's theorem. The classic theorem says an endlessly exchangeable random sequence is a blend of independent, identical draws. A q-analogue replaces plain symmetry with a deformed one, tuned by a parameter q between zero and one. Dordzhiev states an asymptotic version of that analogue. The proof leans on the convex shape of the set of q-exchangeable probability measures.

The main payoff is a sharp speed limit. The gap between a finite q-exchangeable law and its limiting blend shrinks at a rate of exact order q to the n. No better rate is possible in general. Results of this kind matter wherever symmetry arguments justify simple models for complex data. The finite rate tells users how much data the idealization needs before it can be trusted.
arxiv-2506-01476:
Fei Guo and co-authors gauge, in a 2025 study, how long a light-struck electron takes to leave a solid, and how that span ties to the solid's symmetry. Time at the quantum scale is still poorly understood. The team use a method based on spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy to clock the delay, down to attoseconds, spans far below a trillionth of a second.

They test solids of different dimensionality: flat layered crystals, a near one-dimensional crystal, and plain copper with full three-dimensional depth. The flat crystals took about 150 attoseconds. The line-like crystal took over 200. Pure copper took just 26. The split maps cleanly onto the dimensionality, or symmetry, of the solid. The authors say symmetry may be a key dial for quantum time scales.
arxiv-2506-01676:
School subjects trip multimodal models in ways adult benches miss, and Chong Li and co-authors built a vast Chinese school test to find the cracks, in work from twenty twenty-five. Their set holds tens of thousands of questions across five core subjects, from primary to high school. Three question kinds are mixed in.

Right answers alone were not enough for them. They also graded the steps: a giant scored set of model reasonings, each judged step by step, trains a grader model. A small human-checked bench tests the graders. Top models still showed real flaws on school reasoning, the team reports, and the tools are posted free.
arxiv-2506-02076:
Christian Marius Lillelund and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on forecasting decline in ALS, a disease that wastes the motor nerves. Patients lose skills such as speech, swallowing, hand use, walking, and breathing at varied rates. Knowing when each skill may fail helps time care and aids.

The team framed the task as a multi event survival problem. Five models, one per skill, were trained on a large trial data set with 3,220 patients. Each model gives a personal curve for when a skill is likely to fall to a low level within 500 days. The models beat a standard baseline curve. The method also lets doctors test what if cases for a single patient.
arxiv-2506-02176:
Miha Nemevšek and Yue Zhang propose that dark matter was frozen into being by a cosmic blast: a first-order phase transition in the early universe. Such transitions bubble through many theories beyond the Standard Model, and here one also grants dark matter its mass. The particle flips from radiation-like to a heavy relic far faster than the universe expands.

That sudden freeze stamps strong oscillations into the density ripples that seed galaxies. If the transition struck not long before matter overtook radiation, the pattern sits where coming surveys can see it. A discovery would do double duty, revealing both the ripples' origin and where dark matter's mass came from.
arxiv-2506-02276:
Saurabh Singh and Dmitry Lagun move a generative modeling technique into latent space in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Stochastic interpolants bend one probability distribution into the next in a free way, powering today's generative models. To use them in jointly trained latent variable models was unexplored. The method needs straight access to samples from both distributions. Latent Stochastic Interpolants solves this, learning the encoder, decoder, and the latent interpolant as one, end to end.

The training goal is an evidence lower bound set out straight in continuous time. Joint tuning lets the model learn latent forms that are of use. The interpolant turns a free prior into the encoder's aggregated posterior. This dodges the tight simple priors of normal diffusion models. It dodges the heavy cost of working in high-dimensional data space too. Tests on the large-scale ImageNet generation test show the way works at scale.
arxiv-2506-02876:
Luis San Martin Fernandez and co-authors study the shape of stellar motion spreads in a galaxy's bulge in a 2025 paper. Using a simulated barred galaxy that grows a boxy bulge, they measure velocity ellipses, the directional spread of star speeds, and how those ellipses tilt and stretch.

The galaxy's bar stamps a four-lobed pattern on the ellipse measures, stronger in young stars. Projected as an observer would see, key measures flip sign with height above the plane and peak at different heights for young and old stars. Real survey stars from APOGEE and Gaia, split by iron content, follow the same trends. The agreement backs the picture of our own bulge as bar-shaped and mixed in age.
arxiv-2506-02976:
Rachid Zeghlache and a large group of co-authors sum up, in a 2025 preprint, a contest on using AI to track an eye disease. The disease is age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of vision loss. Doctors track it with layered eye scans. The MARIO challenge, held at a 2024 medical imaging conference, asked teams to automate that tracking. Data came mainly from a clinic in Brest, France, with an extra set from Algeria.

Thirty-five teams took part, and the top twelve presented their methods. One task asked whether disease activity changed between two scans. The other asked teams to forecast the disease three months ahead for patients on drug therapy. On the first task, AI matched doctor-level skill. On the forecast task, no team did well yet. The paper lays out the data, rules, and winning methods as a benchmark for the field.
arxiv-2506-03076:
Paul Davies and Philip Tee propose that a grainy spacetime could explain a stubborn mismatch in particle physics, in a 2025 paper. The muon's magnetic moment, measured with extreme care, refuses to match the value standard theory predicts. If space itself has a smallest length, the way light's carrier particle spreads changes slightly, and that change feeds into the muon's magnetism.

Working inside a framework called doubly special relativity, the authors compute the grain size that would erase the gap. It lands far above the Planck length, the usual guess for nature's pixel, yet within reach of the next generation of colliders to confirm or refute. The idea turns a nagging anomaly into a testable claim about the fabric of space, and it gives experimenters a concrete energy at which to look.
arxiv-2506-03176:
Bin Wang and co-authors argue that tuning a strong forecasting model beats building a new one from scratch, in work from 2025. Time series are hard to predict, and no single design rule fits all cases. A shared tuning step could lift many models at low cost.

They first name a conflict that arises when one tuning process serves many future time steps at once. That conflict wastes the model's learning power. Their Socket and Plug method keeps the trained core frozen. Each target gets its own small tuner with its own optimizer and stopping check. The design aims for broad gains with little extra resource use.
arxiv-2506-03276:
Jay Gopalakrishnan and Michael Neunteufel compute how light and sound modes travel through a coiled waveguide in this 2025 paper. A helix bends every mode's path, and finding the modes means solving a wave equation inside a twisting tube. Brute force in three dimensions is costly.

Their path runs through three equivalent problems. A traveling-wave guess turns mode hunting into a quadratic eigenvalue problem in the coil. An untwisting map straightens the tube, keeping the same mathematical shape. Finally the helix's steady curvature lets them collapse the problem onto the tube's cross-section, a two-dimensional problem with the same answers at a fraction of the cost. Filters remove fake, non-traveling solutions. In a coiled optical fiber, modes shifted away from the coil's center as geometry demanded, and the authors chart how pitch changes move them.
arxiv-2506-03476:
Chuyuan Li, Raymond Li, Thalia Field, and Giuseppe Carenini use language models to spot Alzheimer's disease in patient writing in a 2025 paper. Early help matters, and odd patterns in speech and text can warn of the disease. Their approach teaches the model by example: a few sample cases are placed in the prompt, a method called in-context learning.

Picking those samples by likeness worked poorly for this task. Their method, Delta-KNN, scores each training case by how much it lifts results, then picks stand-ins close to the new case. On two data sets and three open models it beat standard choices. With one model it even topped systems trained the full supervised way.
arxiv-2506-03676:
Zachary Crawford and co-authors present a 2025 model of how charge moves through solids made of tiny crystal dots. Such dot solids could push solar cells past the best rate of today's silicon cells. To work, the dots must fuse into a solid that acts like a metal, a step no team has yet reached.

The model builds on 3D scans of real dot solid samples and adds mess in both dot sites and the hops charge makes between them. Math tools that track charge flow and scale it by size map out when the solid acts as metal or blocker. For much of the range, the shift point breaks the value long thought standard. A cross zone links two known classes of shift, shaped by weak mess in the hops.
arxiv-2506-03776: Chiara Gambicchia and co-authors prove a sharp stability law for nonlocal perimeters of convex shapes in a 2025 paper. The classic isoperimetric law says round shapes enclose the most area for their boundary. The nonlocal twist replaces boundary length with a long-range interaction energy. For convex sets, the team tie the energy surplus to how far the shapes center of mass sits from its ideal spot, with best-possible constants. The result mirrors a known 1993 theorem, now in fractional dress.
arxiv-2506-03876:
Yuke Peng and co-authors present a 2025 paper on a new operating system built in the Rust language. The system works with Linux programs and keeps its trusted core small and sound. Past Rust systems used unsafe code in ways that broke that aim. The team proposes a new frame, called a framekernel, to split rights inside the kernel.

Their base tool, OSTD, supports safe system building in Rust. The full system, Asterinas, runs more than 210 Linux calls. Its speed is on par with Linux in their tests. Only about 14 percent of its code must be trusted for memory safety. The work shows a safe design can still be fast and full.
arxiv-2506-04376:
Emiliano Acevedo, Martín Rocamora, and Magdalena Fuentes find that background noise wrecks zero-shot sound classification by audio-text models, and fix it without retraining. Their 2025 paper starts from the models' appeal: they sort sounds from text prompts, needing no labeled examples. In real scenes, though, a backdrop soundscape sits under every target sound.

The damage tracked the loudness of the background, not its kind. Their method measures the background's share and folds it into the classification itself, lifting accuracy across backgrounds and noise levels. A second thread studies the gap between the audio and text embedding spaces; narrowing it also helped. The fix carried across leading prototypical methods, which the authors read as scalability.
arxiv-2506-04476:
Nilson C Bernardes Jr, Antonio Bonilla, and João V A Pinto study weighted shift acts built from maps in a 2025 paper. The acts blend a map's shift with a weight, run on spaces of spread or fade-out maps. Five traits are at stake, from tame size growth to two forms of chaos.

Broad results sort the acts by those traits in a clean way. Worked cases then apply the sort to weighted shifts on known list spaces. Shift acts on plain map spaces get the same care, which rounds out the chart.
arxiv-2506-04876:
Massimo Bianchi, Donato Bini, and Giorgio Di Russo compute how a small object scatters off an exotic star-like body, in a 2025 physics paper. The body is a topological star, a smooth solution of gravity theory that mimics a black hole but has no horizon. The probe is a neutral scalar particle on an unbound path. Its scattering angle is worked out with self-force corrections, which account for the probe's own small effect on the field.

The authors also name the electromagnetic-like source behind the background and check it fits the spacetime symmetries. They study the star's curvature, how objects are transported along special curves, and its gravity energy using super-energy tools. Such calculations may one day let telescopes tell a topological star from a true black hole.
arxiv-2506-04976:
Matthias Ehrhardt, Zeljko Kereta, and Georg Schramm wrote a two thousand twenty-five paper on making PET scan images faster. They study math methods that rebuild a scan image while using a prior rule to keep the image clean. Such prior-based methods are widely used in clinics and tend to beat older ones.

Tests used both fake data and real brain scans from a two thousand twenty-four contest. The key finding is that the prior rule must be built into the early step of the method for fast, stable results. Two methods, SAGA and SVRG, beat plain gradient descent, and their design helped win that contest.
arxiv-2506-05276:
Hao Yu and co-authors introduce CocktailEdit, a 2025 framework for editing generated time series. Making new sequences is now feasible, but precise editing, changing chosen points or segments while keeping the whole coherent, remains hard. Current methods struggle to honor both point-level and segment-level controls at once.

The diffusion-driven framework combines two control mechanisms, including a confidence-weighted anchor for point constraints. Together they allow simultaneous, flexible control across constraint types. Edited series matter for simulation, testing, and what-if analysis, where users need data that meets exact conditions rather than plausible averages.
arxiv-2506-05476:
D Langis and co-authors compile a catalog of tidal disruption events, where a star is torn apart by a black hole, in work from two thousand twenty-five. Such events let astronomers study quiet black holes, but few had been seen. The catalog lists over a hundred confirmed events found through the end of two thousand twenty-four.

Light records span X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, and heat bands, with spectra shared in public. Most events fell in one spectral class tied to stars like the Sun. Three new cases may repeat, with second flares shaped much like the first. Heat and X-ray output seemed linked, which the team explores.
arxiv-2506-05576:
Six roboticists release a dataset and method for teaching robots to grasp objects the way a task demands. Picking up a knife by the handle differs from picking it up to hand over, and models need data that records those affordances. Their TD-TOG set holds 1,449 real depth-camera scenes across thirty object categories, with hand-drawn masks for objects, usable parts, and flat grasp rectangles.

Their companion method splits the problem in two. A zero-shot step names the target object from a text prompt, with no example image needed. A one-shot step then learns the usable part from a single example. In crowded scenes the pipeline reached about sixty-nine percent task-correct grasps. A built-in test asks systems to tell apart close subcategories of objects. The authors also compare one-shot and zero-shot learning head to head, as a guide for future builders.
arxiv-2506-05676:
Graph neural networks learn from connected data, but on directed graphs they tend to blur the sharp, fast varying parts of a signal. Those parts matter most for flows, where direction is everything: a network that cannot tell forward from reverse cannot model a current. Haoyang Jiang and co-authors build a framework to fix this. It adds explicit difference matrices that encode directional gradients, so the network can see which way a signal is climbing.

It also adds physics based constraints that keep the messages passed between nodes consistent with natural laws. The team tested the framework on two real directed networks: a water flux network and an urban traffic flow network. In both cases the topology aware, physics guided model predicted the flows better than standard graph networks. The authors present the design as a way to make learned models respect the structure and physics of flow problems.
arxiv-2506-05776:
A forecast that changes its mind every week is hard to plan around, even if each version is accurate. Marco Zanotti studies in 2025 how often global forecasting models should be retrained. These are single models serving many series at once. He weighs stability alongside accuracy across three large datasets and ten models.

For probabilistic forecasts he proposes a new stability score, the Scaled Multi-Quantile Change, which needs no distributional assumptions. The headline result runs against habit: retraining less often kept forecasts steadier, and it often improved stability outright. Accuracy did not have to be sacrificed when one global model does the work. Zanotti argues for stability-aware practice — measure the flip-flopping, publish it next to the error, and retrain on the schedule the evidence supports.
arxiv-2506-06076:
Julio Silva-Rodríguez and co-authors tackle trust in medical AI in a 2025 paper. Large models that pair images with text are now used to read medical scans. Their raw skill is well studied, but their reliability is not. A method called split conformal prediction can promise a set rate of errors. It does so by checking the model on a labeled test set first.

The catch is that such models are often tuned on a few examples, which clashes with the method's strict terms. The authors propose tuning and checking at the same time, test point by test point. They add a fast, training-free solver to keep costs down. Across three medical models and nine tasks, their sets of answers grew up to 27 percent more efficient at the same error promise.
arxiv-2506-06476:
Pushyami Kaveti and co-authors give underwater robots richer spatial perception in a 2025 paper. Murk, backscatter, and fading light break the camera based mapping that surface robots take for granted, and many vehicles carry several cameras that standard pipelines cannot use. Their system fuses cameras with inertial and acoustic sensors.

Both geometric and learned methods feed a simultaneous localization and mapping core, enriched with semantic reading of the scene. Field runs with a work class vehicle in a Norwegian fjord produced real time position estimates and clean three dimensional reconstructions in poor visibility. The authors close with open problems in calibration and learned method limits for large scale ocean work.
arxiv-2506-06876:
Mahdi Shahabi and co-authors use deep reinforcement learning to split network functions in hybrid space-ground radio networks in work from 2025. Open radio access design lets operators divide central and distributed units in flexible ways.

Satellites and high-altitude platforms face tight power and capacity limits, so the split must adapt. Their Deep Q-Network agent picks the split in real time as traffic, channel state, and power change. Results show the policy tracks traffic flow and chooses efficient splits that meet data rate and delay needs. The work aims at lower energy use without loss of service.
arxiv-2506-07576:
Boyu Chen and co-authors build a Super Encoding Network for video understanding in a 2025 paper. Video understanding is a key step toward machines that model the world. Foundation models already align image, text, and audio encoders with contrastive training, but complex motion and varied scenes demand deeper mixing between those channels.

The network treats each trained encoder as a super neuron inside a larger system. A recursive association block then fuses the channels step by step with the incoming video, integrating, distributing, and prompting knowledge among the super neurons. This builds richer cross-channel interaction for downstream video tasks. Wide experiments show clear gains over standard alignment, suggesting recursion is a strong way to deepen multimodal models.
arxiv-2506-07676:
Quantum systems that leak energy to their surroundings behave in ways closed systems do not. Moein Ivaki and co-authors study what such leaky systems can learn and remember in this 2025 paper. The systems are called non-Hermitian, and they pass through phases marked by a symmetry that holds or breaks. That shift changes how tangled and how pure their states are, which in turn sets their memory power.

The test case is a web of interacting spins placed on random graphs. The authors find that the first special point, where the system's spectrum turns from real to complex values, matches a sharp drop in learning power. Tuning disorder and spin coupling moves that point, so the learning threshold can be dialed. Inside the learning phase, the system holds information in a usable way.
arxiv-2506-07876:
Seven authors present ReLIC in 2025, a learned limb plan for robots that walk and grab at once. Past work locks limbs to set jobs, which bars flex use in wild spots. Their lead splits into a gait part and a task part that trade off by need.

Each limb is dealt a walk or grab job on the fly, and the pair of parts keeps steps firm. Task feeds span paths, touch points, and plain word briefs. On 12 real tasks the rig won about 79 percent of runs. The plan was taught in a fake world first, then moved to real bots.
arxiv-2506-07976:
Junhong Shen and co-authors argue for a new way to make computer agents better in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Most gains now come from longer chains of thought before acting. But an agent that only thinks cannot learn new facts from the world or change its plan as it goes.

The team proposes scaling the length of contact with the task itself, so one run can include exploring, backtracking, and fresh planning. Simple prompting with longer contact already raised success on web tasks. Their training method then adjusts run length as the agent learns. The trained web agent set a new best among open models on two web benchmarks, and it balanced exploring and settling in a flexible way.
arxiv-2506-08576: The BESIII Collaboration reports a measurement tied to how a short-lived particle called the eta changes form. The measurement uses a decay of its heavier cousin into two charged pions and an eta. The work appeared as a particle physics paper in twenty twenty-five. The record's evidence is limited to the title and the collaboration's long author list. The methods, data, and results therefore cannot be described from what is given here.
arxiv-2506-08976:
Yu Wang and six co-authors package a strong nonlinear filter as an easy computer tool, in a paper from 2025. The Yau-Yau filter can track hidden states in noisy complex systems, but its math has kept many would be users away.

Their tool, written in a common stats language with fast code at its core, solves the key equation by grid steps in a stable way. A point and click screen lets users tune values and watch results live, with no need to code or solve equations by hand. The open, modular build invites tweaks for fields from signals to finance and health.
arxiv-2506-09076:
Haley Stone and co-authors gave a probabilistic method to fill missing genetic distances in pathogen models in two thousand twenty-five. Genome data help map how disease spreads in space and time, but many cases are never sequenced. Gaps limit what spatial models can learn.

Their method estimates how far an unsequenced case sits, genetically, from known sequences in a transmission chain. It uses collection dates and observed divergence patterns, with no need for sequence alignment or known chains. They applied it to highly pathogenic bird flu in wild birds in the United States. The approach adds biologically plausible data with stated uncertainty, at a scale suited to larger studies.
arxiv-2506-09176:
Haoyuan Cai, Zhenghao Peng, and Bolei Zhou let the robot itself ask for help while learning from a human teacher. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works in interactive imitation learning. A supervisor watches and steps in to show the right move. Constant watching taxes the human, though. Their AIM method learns when a demo is worth requesting.

A proxy value function mimics the teacher's rule for stepping in. It scores states high when the agent strays from expert conduct. As the agent improves, those scores fall on its own. Requests thus cluster on states where help counts most, including safety-critical ones. Tests in continuous and discrete control show less takeover cost than an uncertainty-based rival. Learning ran faster too, with fewer demos and fewer world steps. Code and a demo video are public.
arxiv-2506-09376:
One-step image generation may come from a light touch on a ready-made model, argue Bowen Zheng and Tianming Yang in a 2025 paper. Diffusion models paint in many slow steps, and shrinking them into fast one-step students usually costs heavy training and quality.

The authors trace the failure to a mismatch: teacher and student take different step sizes and sizes of network, so they settle into different solutions and imitation misfires. A contest-style objective alone, with no imitation loss, dodges the trap. Viewing diffusion training as general pre-training, they fine-tuned a model with eighty-five percent of its weights frozen, using little data, and reached near-top results. A frequency-based analysis backs the story.
arxiv-2506-09476:
Tianxiang Hao and co-authors build tools to read 1960s satellite photos of cities, in work from 2025. Spy satellite archives hold the earliest overhead views of urban growth. The images are warped, misaligned, and label-free, which has blocked large-scale study.

Their benchmark offers expert labels for four city land types across four cities on two continents. Coverage spans near a thousand square kilometers of varied city shapes. A companion method segments the photos with no labels at all. It copes with the grain and single-tone limits of the old film. Historians and planners gain a way to measure how cities grew over sixty years.
arxiv-2506-09576:
A superconducting qubit forgets its state on a timescale set by its surroundings, and that timescale itself wanders. Fabrizio Berritta and co-authors built a controller, running on programmable hardware, that tracks the wandering in real time for two fixed-frequency qubits. The setup improved time resolution a hundredfold over stop-and-measure routines.

It caught relaxation times leaping nearly tenfold within tens of milliseconds, far faster than the minutes-to-hours changes reported before. The statistics point to tiny two-level defects flipping up to ten times per second. Calibration schedules for quantum processors, the team argues, must respect this much faster clock.
arxiv-2506-09676:
Satabdwa Majumdar and three co-authors hunted for the settings that make a leading solar wind model miss at Earth. The model chain starts with maps of the Sun's magnetic field and predicts the wind that later sweeps past a monitoring point between the Sun and Earth. The team studied fifteen solar rotations in detail, with a close look at one, testing grid fineness and the height of the model's source surface.

A finer grid sharpened the boundary between open and closed magnetic regions, which improved forecasts of when fast wind streams arrive and how long they last. Tuning the source surface height into a band between 1.8 and 3.1 solar radii helped further, because that height shifts where field lines root and so changes the near-Sun wind speed. The authors also argue that coronal hole observations, now underused, could guide these choices.
arxiv-2506-10076:
Pablo Sala, Frank Pollmann, Masaki Oshikawa, and Yizhi You build a holographic picture of entanglement in symmetry-protected topological phases. In these phases, the state of a region can be summed up by an entanglement Hamiltonian. The authors ask how that lower-dimensional object encodes the phase as a whole.

By copying the reduced state many times, they rebuild the full fixed-point wave function and link it to a known bulk measure. The copies show long-range order along the copy direction, which they present as a universal mark of these phases. They extend the idea to warm and open systems and to mixed states, with new measures for their topology.
arxiv-2506-10376:
Fan Wu and co-authors teach a vision-language model to turn web page images into working code without losing the layout. Their 2025 paper, built around a framework named LayoutCoder, tackles a slow, hands-on step in web building. Past learned methods need heaps of labeled data and falter on unseen designs. Big multimodal models help, but they misread tangled page layouts and drift from them in code.

Three parts attack that flaw: one groups like elements by their links, one parses the page into a layout tree, and one fuses code under that tree's guide. A new test set of hundreds of real sites, split into seen and unseen, checks the work beside a known set.
arxiv-2506-10576:
Muskan Dosi and co-authors adapt in 2025 diffusion image models to data that live on hyperspheres. Standard diffusion adds round noise in flat space, which warps angle-based class shapes. Many face and object sets carry just such spherical structure.

Their method swaps in directional noise that respects the sphere. Theory and tests agree that class geometry survives the process better. Six data sets span objects and faces for the trials. Outputs track the true manifold more closely than flat-space rivals. Angular doubt is the extra signal the flat models throw away.
arxiv-2506-10876:
Pritam Chattopadhyay, Avijit Misra, Tanmoy Pandit and Goutam Paul review the Landauer principle and the thermodynamics of computation, in their 2025 arXiv paper. Landauer's principle says any logically irreversible step, such as erasing a bit, must release a minimum amount of heat. Real erasure still wastes far more than that bound.

The review covers recent classical and quantum experiments approaching the bound, plus theory for finite-time erasure, small heat baths and environments with memory, where fluctuations and correlations matter. It also surveys energy bounds for whole computations and the thermodynamics of error correction, closing with an outlook for the field.
arxiv-2506-11076:
Minyu Chen, Guoqiang Li, Ling-I Wu, and Ruibang Liu sic language models on dead code, in a 2025 paper. Dead code, instructions that never run or results never used, bloats programs, misleads maintainers, and can hide malware tricks. Compilers catch simple cases, but sophisticated dead patterns slip through, and cleanup usually demands tedious manual work.

Their framework pairs a compact code model, which flags suspicious lines through attribution scoring, with large language models fine-tuned on a big annotated dataset. The large models judge each suspect, explain why it is dead, and write the patch. Scores for finding unused and unreachable code exceeded ninety-four percent, beating a leading general model by about thirty points. The system spans several languages and closes the loop from detection to correction automatically.
arxiv-2506-11176:
Anatoly Krasnovsky offers a light path into chaos engineering: discover the service graph, then simulate failures on it. The paper from twenty twenty-five notes that live fault injection is costly and risky to run often. Hand-built dependability models, the safer rival, rot fast and take scarce expert time. His claim is that a connectivity-only model suffices for availability estimates under fail-stop faults.

The discovered model is just the dependency graph plus replica counts. Traces, mesh telemetry, and config files feed an automatic discovery step that fits into delivery pipelines. A DeathStarBench social network case tests the idea. Graphs pulled from Jaeger traces track live injection results closely across failure rates. Replication cases land near zero median error. The pitch: triage chaos tests with cheap models first.
arxiv-2506-11476:
Tom Baker and Javier Nistal present a lightweight control add-on in 2025 for music generation models. Text-to-audio diffusion models make varied, high-quality music, but most lack fine, time-varying control that producers need. The standard control method clones much of the model, which is heavy and locks users to a fixed control set.

Their design cuts the parameter count sharply while matching the standard method on audio quality and on following the given controls. Controls can be trained and loaded separately, which lowers memory use and raises flexibility. Wide tests, both by metrics and by listeners, back the claims, and the team posts many audio examples online.
arxiv-2506-11576:
Baptiste Claudon and co-authors design quantum circuits for the Metropolis-Hastings method, a workhorse sampling routine used across science. A known quantum trick turns a random walk into a quantum walk whose key gap grows with the square of the classical one, hinting at faster sampling. Older ways to build that walk must compute transition chances in a reversible way, which eats up many extra qubits, a real problem when machines have few to spare.

The new construction follows the classical logic of the method instead: propose a move, then accept or reject it, step by step inside the quantum walk. Each step uses a fixed small number of such rounds, so the qubit cost stays lean. The team also compares their design with a second route to the same gap gain. They argue the end result should keep the promised speedup for sampling tasks on near-term machines.
arxiv-2506-11676:
Sumedha Biswas, Peter Jonker, M. Coleman Miller, Andrew Levan, and Jonathan Quirola-Vásquez wrote a 2025 paper on fast X-ray flashes in space. These flashes last minutes to hours and their source is still unknown. One idea says they come from magnetars, young neutron stars with strong fields, born when two neutron stars merge.

The team compared how many flashes are seen with how often such births should happen. Mergers of two neutron stars look too rare to explain all the flashes, even if each one made a flash. So they checked other birth paths, such as the collapse of a white dwarf and mergers of white dwarfs. Counting these rates helps narrow which sources could plausibly power the flashes.
arxiv-2506-11876:
Christina Selby and co-authors set out ways to judge the sharpness of 3D maps built from satellite images, in a 2025 paper. Such maps serve scene modeling where ground surveys or aircraft scans cannot reach. Knowing their true resolution tells users what missions the data can support and whether new methods are really improving.

The team covers three data forms: point clouds, surface models, and mesh models. They describe tools and workflows that score each form against high-grade airborne laser scans used as reference truth. Their checks run largely on their own once set up. They then show results across datasets of mixed quality, showing how the scores separate sharp maps from coarse ones.
arxiv-2506-12276:
Sihan Chen and six co-authors traced chirality transfer in two thousand twenty-five from single cells to whole tissues. Many living processes lack mirror symmetry, from molecule choice to body layout, yet how small-scale twist becomes large-scale flow stayed unclear. Their test case is tissue flow driven by uneven cell growth in fibroblastoma cultures.

They built a microscopic graph model whose coarse form cannot be written as energy descent, a break from standard models. A new inference algorithm fits model settings from noisy snapshots despite big cell position swings. The calibrated model matched the large-scale flows seen in experiments. The tool may serve other noisy living and non-living cell networks.
arxiv-2506-12376:
Zhaochen Hong, Haofei Yu, and Jiaxuan You test whether language models stay consistent over chains of changes in 2025. A user may ask a model to translate, edit, or code in many steps. Small drifts at each step can add up. Past self checks miss fine shifts in sense. Their tool builds a tree of states linked by paired reverse steps.

Scores rest on how alike states stay at each tree depth. Test sets are made fresh, in part by models, to avoid leaks of known tests. Eight models from many families were tested. The tool split their performance clearly. Scores matched a known translation rank list well, though no paired test data were used. Code is shared in public.
arxiv-2506-12876:
Yan Sun and co-authors present MaskPro, a way to slim large language models under a strict pattern, in this 2025 paper. The pattern keeps a fixed count of weights in every small block, which suits fast hardware. Older methods either greedily pick weights layer by layer, and err, or learn the picks at huge training cost.

MaskPro instead learns a probability for each block, then samples which weights to keep. A new update rule, tracking a moving average of loss changes, steadies training in the huge choice space. Tests show strong accuracy with small memory use, and the method held up when training data changed.
arxiv-2506-13076:
Maria Yampolskaya and Pankaj Mehta wrote a 2025 review on Hopfield networks as models of how function emerges in biology. Hopfield models began as a theory of memory in neural networks, where stored patterns are retrieved from partial cues. Their math has since proved handy far beyond brains.

The review teaches the models from a biophysics angle. Three readings build intuition: the dynamics as noise filtering, as a geometry that gives pattern space natural coordinates, and as a slide down an energy landscape. The authors then survey recent uses across biology. Applications include cell differentiation and epigenetic memory, molecular self assembly, and the brain's spatial maps. The piece is written as a pedagogical entry point for biologists and physicists alike.
arxiv-2506-13476:
Tiny defects on printed circuit boards are easy to miss because inspection photos are small and blurry, so flaws blur into noise. Xiem HoangVan and three co-authors build ESRPCB, a system that first sharpens the image and then hunts for defects. Their super-resolution step is guided by edge information, so the fine lines and borders that define a board survive the enlargement.

A modified deep network with a new residual design rebuilds the high-resolution picture. A team of detection models, combined through ensemble learning, then examines the sharpened image together. The authors argue that keeping structural detail through the enlargement is what lets very small defects stand out. The framework is presented in a 2025 paper on automated board inspection.
arxiv-2506-14176:
Renao Yan set out a steadier way in twenty twenty-five to search for neural network architectures. The search is for pathology image classification. Off-the-shelf vision models fit medical images poorly. Hand design has tight limits. Plain architecture search is shaky in its results. Yan gives an initialization strategy. It is guided by network similarity. It seeds the one-shot search so the search converges in a more reliable way.

Domain adaptation is woven into the search too. It deals with gaps in staining between pathology data sets. It deals with semantic scale variation as well. On the BRACS breast pathology benchmark, the method beat the approaches that exist in classification accuracy. It put a focus on clinically relevant features too. Pathologists need that trait in a model to trust it. The work aims at use in practice. It holds edge computing settings, where compute is scarce.
arxiv-2506-14276:
Jack Cole and Mohamed Osman argue for deep learning as the way to crack the ARC reasoning test, in this 2025 paper. The test asks AI to infer abstract rules from a few examples, and most systems score poorly. Deep learning, though, has trained skillful networks across vision and language. The authors bet that same strength can learn fresh abstractions.

Their method trains networks on the fly at test time, starting from a pretrained language model. Two tricks add gains: fine-tuning during the test itself, and a voting scheme over augmented views. Accuracy rose several-fold with each trick. An early version won a 2023 ARC contest, and the final one set the best private test score at the time. The paper names test-time training as a core ingredient for reasoning in new domains.
arxiv-2506-14576: Nouha Oualha surveys privacy enhancing technologies for AI in a 2025 paper. As AI spreads into sector after sector, guarding personal and sensitive data grows more urgent. These technologies form a suite of tools that let data be gathered and used while privacy stays intact. The paper maps the current state of data privacy in AI, reviews how the tools are woven into AI systems, and weighs wins so far against the hard parts that remain.
arxiv-2506-14876:
Xiyuan Gao and Ulrich Nierste check the math behind a Japanese lab's rare-decay surplus in 2025, a hint of a ghost particle that slips away unseen. The catalog's title field carries raw formula code; the head gives the clean decay name used here. Their stage is a full model with two Higgs fields and a lone extra one, the home of the ghost, an axion-like particle.

A shortcut used in past work, swapping the ghost for the model's heavy twin, works at the first loop of the math and breaks at the second. Worse, the second loop is not the small fry the shortcut implies: for a wide swath of settings it rivals the first. The pair map where the ghost can still live and urge sharper hunts.
arxiv-2506-15076:
Ruihan Wu, Konstantin Garov, and Kamalika Chaudhuri ask how the way a fact is taught to a large language model affects how well that fact can later be removed. Such removal, called unlearning, is needed for privacy, for fixing stale facts, and for wiping harmful content.

Past work took the training path as fixed. Their tests vary it. Facts taught through reworded versions of the same point were easier to unlearn. By contrast, pulling one fact out of a chunk of text proved hard to unlearn cleanly. The authors argue that choices made at teaching time may be central to sound removal.
arxiv-2506-15476:
Star-forming clouds churn with turbulence that should die out quickly, yet the churn persists, and no driver has fully explained it. Shibo Yuan and Hua-Bai Li revisit gravity's role in this 2025 paper. An older landmark simulation found that self-gravity does not change the cloud-wide decay rate. That result seemed to rule gravity out.

The new work splits the cloud into its diffuse bulk and its dense cores. The bulk sets the global decay rate, which gravity leaves alone. Inside dense cores, though, decay nearly stops when gravity is present. Control runs without gravity lacked that effect. The cores were mostly in balance, not collapsing, so infall motion does not explain it. Energy freed as cores form seems to feed their churn. Gravity can thus sustain turbulence where stars are born.
arxiv-2506-15876:
Nicolás Barnafi, Alberto Martín, and Ricardo Ruiz-Baier propose an adaptive finite element method for deformable image registration. Registration warps one image onto another, a core task in medical imaging. Fixed meshes waste effort where images are smooth and under-resolve where they are not.

The authors pair the method with a residual-based error estimator whose efficiency and reliability they establish theoretically. The estimator guides adaptive mesh refinement and coarsening, concentrating computation where the registration is hardest. The nonlinear equations behind the method are solved with a pseudo time-stepping fixed-point scheme, accelerated by Anderson acceleration. An efficient data structure based on forests of octrees with space-filling curves supports the implementation. Numerical results on application-oriented problems illustrate the performance gains. The work gives imaging scientists a registration solver that spends its budget where the anatomy demands it.
arxiv-2506-16076:
Oscar Bruno and Daniel Leibovici present the core of a shock solver that works on complex shapes in a 2025 paper. Shock waves in gas flows demand methods that stay sharp without ringing. Their scheme blends smooth spectral math with a neural net that spots shocks so fake thickness lands only there.

A patchwork of overlapping tiles lets the solver fit curved, complex domains under any edge rules. No hand-tuned knobs or fix-up limiters are needed, and the layout runs well in parallel. Tests on standard 2D flow cases show the method at work. A second part extends it to sharp-cornered obstacles.
arxiv-2506-16176:
Adway Kumar Das, writing alone, studies how a disordered quantum system settles into equilibrium when it obeys a flip symmetry, in a 2025 paper. The symmetry splits the system's space into two separate sectors. The model, a random matrix with matching symmetry, has an energy spectrum that mixes the two sectors' spectra.

Das computes how different starting states evolve and how long their memory lingers. Some low-energy states barely decay, and a vanishing fraction of the matrices break the symmetry on their own. Comparing equilibrium values of local measures against standard statistical ensembles gives a nuanced verdict. Whether an observable's long-run value remembers the starting sector depends on whether the observable itself respects the symmetry. Yet fluctuations shrink with system size, and equilibrium values match the canonical average, so thermalization wins in the end.
arxiv-2506-16276:
Ming-Qiang Ren and co-authors report a 2025 finding of clean superconductivity at the border between two materials. They grew a single layer of a barium arsenide compound on top of films of an iron-based superconductor. Borders between unlike materials often breed new behavior, and here the pair produced a full superconducting gap, with no leftover normal electrons at low temperature.

The gap held up to a top temperature of twenty-six kelvin in their spectra. It stayed strong even when the film below was thinned to a single layer, unlike the bare film, whose transition fades fast when thin. The authors credit the near-perfect crystal quality of the stack, uniform in both shape and electronic behavior. The result shows how a well-made border can protect and even host superconductivity.
arxiv-2506-16376:
Kristof Cools wrote a 2025 paper on a faster equation for modeling waves that scatter off mixed material bodies. The base equation handles bodies made of chunks, each with its own traits. Where three or more chunks meet along a line, past fixes either fail or double the work.

Such systems are solved step by step, and the step count hinges on how the matrix values spread. Cools builds a single trace form of the equation that stays local in spirit. Its step count grows only slowly as the mesh gets finer. He works out the discrete form in full. Broad tests back the method's accuracy, settling, and speed. The equation also shows no false inner echoes.
arxiv-2506-16676:
Mark Adams, Jin Chen, and Benjamin Sturdevant sped up in 2025 the math solver inside a major fusion simulation code. The code models plasma inside tokamaks, the donut-shaped machines chasing fusion power, and spends most of its time solving one hard momentum equation over and over. The old solver slowed as the machine's simulated slices multiplied.

The team adapted multigrid methods, which attack errors at many scales at once, to the code's magnetic equations. Part one of their report covers the design and first results. Faster solves mean longer, finer fusion experiments on the same computers.
arxiv-2506-17076:
Ziv Aharoni and Henry Pfister build neural decoders for DNA data storage in a 2025 paper. DNA stores bits in base strings, but build and read steps drop or add bases. Such slip faults break plain codes, and best-fit decoders cost huge compute. Their neural polar decoders learn the fix from raw samples, no channel model in hand. Cost grows near the code length times its log, scaled by one dial.

On fake slip channels the decoders near the best known grades. They also gauge channel room with true aim. Real pore-read data and many-read sets join the tests. There the decoders match or beat past tools with far fewer parts. The team pitch the craft as a cheap, firm read path for DNA vaults.
arxiv-2506-17276:
Alexandre Le Nepvou puts forth a new modal logic built on layers of becoming, not on whole possible worlds. In the old Kripke view, each world in the set is fully formed and fixed. That view, he says, misses how things come to be, step by step and place by place, in an uneven way.

His Stratified Actualization Logic tags its signs with levels of how stable a thing is, and he calls these levels admissibility regimes. Each level works on a layer of what could be, and shifts link one layer to the next. The work sets out the syntax and the rules for what signs mean, states the axioms, and proves the system is sound and complete. He sketches uses for time and becoming, for quantum decoherence, and for modal metaphysics.
arxiv-2506-17476:
Jonathan Kho and six co-authors use space simulations to ask how the birth of black holes marks a well known pattern. The pattern ties a galaxy's core black hole mass to how fast its stars swirl. New space telescope finds show early black holes that look heavy for their galaxies. Their 2025 work tests seed rules in the BRAHMA simulation set.

Each seed rule leaves its own stamp on the pattern at early times. Lenient rules, which plant many seeds, keep the pattern near flat across time. Strict rules start low and climb toward today's line. Growth by mergers rules in small galaxies, while gas feeding rules in big ones. Loose scatter in the pattern also grows under strict rules. Future sky data could pick the true rule, the team says.
arxiv-2506-17776:
Dyuman Aditya, Colton Payne, Mario Leiva, and Paulo Shakarian wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It wires machine learning models into a logic engine, so that what the models see can drive clear, stated decisions in work flows.

The engine, PyReason, uses a form of logic that holds real-valued scores as truth ranges. Model outputs such as probabilities thus turn into logical facts. The system polls the models, refreshes the facts, and reworks the least model at once, so calls can be made in real time. Time sense, knowledge graph ties, and full trace of the reasoning are built in. The fit suits plants, clinics, and office flows where steps must be both fast and open to audit.
arxiv-2506-17976:
Ashley Dickson and co-authors worked out in 2025 how much energy it takes to knock oxygen atoms out of place in a high temperature superconductor. That material is a candidate for magnets in future fusion reactors, where neutron hits will slowly damage it.

Knowing the knock out threshold for each atom type lets engineers predict damage from a single neutron. The team simulated all four oxygen sites in the crystal with two methods, one fast and one based on quantum forces, and the two agreed. Runs were done at the cold working temperature of the magnets and at the warmer temperature of past neutron tests. The data feed into larger models for shield design and magnet life.
arxiv-2506-18076:
Yuqi Qing, Yu-Qin Chen, and Shi-Xin Zhang study entanglement growth in a quasiperiodic quantum system. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses the generalized Aubry-André model, which holds a mobility edge for single particles. At that edge, some states spread wide while others stay pinned in place.

Coexisting free and trapped states make the system a rare lab for quantum dynamics. The team tracks how entanglement, the quantum link between parts, grows over time. They also weigh the information capacity the system can hold. Mixed state types may store and spread information in ways pure systems cannot. Results speak to quantum memory design and to how disorder can help or harm it.
arxiv-2506-18176:
Shervin Safavi and co-authors review in 2025 perceptual multistability as a window into mental disorders. Some images or sounds flip between two reads over time, across species and senses. The pace and mix of those flips often differ in clinical groups.

Two computing frames guide the synthesis the authors build. One treats perception as hidden inference under uncertainty. The other treats each flip as an inner action in a learning loop. The review links human and animal work and ties behavior to brain paths. The authors back such flips as a gentle tool for clinic and lab study.
arxiv-2506-18276:
Quantum batteries store energy in quantum systems, but charging one is useless if the energy sloshes back out. Songbo Xie, Manas Sajjan, Ashok Ajoy, and Sabre Kais propose a control trick in 2025 that stops the flow without ever switching the charger off.

A helper qubit, the modulator, sits beside the charger and battery. Repeated quick operations on that helper reshape the system's rules through a Zeno-like effect, effectively turning the coupling on or off from the side. The trick works in a three-body model and survives slower, realistic control speeds. Scaled to many battery units, it keeps the collective charging boost, and the authors sketch a diamond-based spin setup that could host it.
arxiv-2506-18476:
Yaokun Zhong and co-authors present a learning method from 2025 for finding the moments in a video that match each sentence of a paragraph. Only a few time labels are given, which makes the task a semi-supervised one. Older methods leaned on agreement between a teacher and a student model, plus contrast at the whole-video level, but they rarely shook up the text itself.

Their method removes sentences from the paragraph to make harder training cases. The student model must still locate the remaining parts, guided by strong signals from the teacher. The team then retrains the model on its own best guesses. Mixing text shake-ups with teacher guidance gave the student stronger lessons than either trick alone.
arxiv-2506-18576:
Hate speech has no single agreed definition, and that fuzziness leaks into the AI systems asked to detect it. Matteo Melis, Gabriella Lapesa, and Dennis Assenmacher broke the concept into parts in 2025 and tested what the choice of definition does to detection.

From published definitions they built a taxonomy of fourteen building blocks, such as who the target is and what harm is claimed. They then fed definitions of varying detail to three language models in zero-shot mode, across synthetic, partly human-made, and real-world data sets. Fuller definitions changed performance, but not in the same direction for every model. The authors argue that definition choice is a hidden dial in content moderation research.
arxiv-2506-18876:
Daniela Saadeh, Kazuya Koyama, and Xan Morice-Atkinson emulate altered gravity at field level in a 2025 paper. Some gravity theories hide their effects in dense regions by a screening trick, which makes them hard to test. Their framework starts from a standard gravity simulation and predicts the correction field that altered gravity would add. Positions and velocities of matter both enter the training.

The method builds on a power spectrum trick and lifts it to full fields. A neural network learns the correction for theories whose linear behavior matches the standard one. Coming sky surveys will map the cosmic web in fine detail, and field level tools let analysts squeeze those maps for gravity's signature.
arxiv-2506-18976:
Ballar Trigueros and Marín Guzmán study how noise affects a quantum resource called nonstabilizerness, or magic, in many qubit circuits. Magic is required for quantum advantage, and noise usually degrades such resources. Their 2025 paper asks whether some noise types can instead create magic, and what happens at the scale of the whole system.

One noise type, amplitude damping, can generate or boost magic locally, while depolarizing noise provably cannot. In an encode and decode test, no sharp magic shift appeared where decoding fidelity shifted sharply. Locally injected magic washed out at the collective level after decoding and selection. The authors say realistic noise can suppress many body magic even while creating it in small spots.
arxiv-2506-19076:
Carlos Hernandez-Suarez gives a fast, accurate algorithm for reconstructing the generator points of a Voronoi tessellation. The 2025 paper solves an inverse problem: given the diagram, find the sites that produced it.

The method picks one interior cell and solves a small linear system. That recovers the cell's own generator plus those of its neighbors in a single step. All remaining sites then follow by repeated geometric reflections. Total running time grows only linearly with the number of cells. In a thousand simulations on diagrams of ten thousand cells, the average reconstruction error was tiny. The method is both efficient and robust.
arxiv-2506-19276:
Mihailo Stojnic studies rare dense clusters of solutions in the asymmetric binary perceptron. His twenty twenty-five paper uses local entropy to probe why this learning model is hard to solve. Most solutions sit alone in the feasible phase, which once suggested no fast method could work.

Yet fast methods do find solutions fairly near the limit. A proposed answer is that rare, large, dense clusters exist and methods home in on them. Stojnic applies a fully lifted random duality theory, with a large deviation upgrade, to judge such atypical clusters. Whether their local entropy thins or breaks may settle the paradox of easy search in a hard space.
arxiv-2506-19576:
Martina Amongero and Pierpaolo De Blasi work on finding groups inside networks in a 2025 paper. In many networks, points in the same group link to each other more often than to outsiders. A common model captures that pattern but leaves open how many groups there are.

Their approach uses flexible Bayesian methods that let the group count stay unknown. The new twist is forcing the model to respect the within-group linking pattern from the start. They study when that extra rule actually helps compared with the standard model. A broad set of simulated tests shows the cases where the gain appears, giving network analysts clearer guidance on when to use it.
arxiv-2506-20076:
Sharif and co-authors grow in 2025 thin films of copper selenide in two crystal forms that bulk material cannot hold at room temperature. Using a beam growth method on a sapphire base, they froze in the high heat cubic form far below its normal change point. The rhombohedral form grew beside it for comparison.

In the cubic films, resistance spiked near one hundred forty kelvin with a lag on warming, and X-rays showed the cell doubling along one axis, both hallmarks of a charge density wave. Math models tied the wave to matching curves on the electron energy surface. The other form showed no such wave, giving a clean contrast.
arxiv-2506-20176:
Yuri Andriaccio, Vincenzo Ciancia, Diego Latella, and Mieke Massink test a checker for three-dimensional mesh models. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Meshes, made of triangles or solid blocks, are the standard shape format in graphics and engineering. Their checker tests whether a mesh meets properties stated in a spatial logic.

The authors add a twist: the result of one check can be fed back into the model as a new fact. That shortens later formulas and makes pictures of the results clearer. The same trick lets them shrink a model while keeping its key spatial traits. That smaller model is easier to grasp and to display. Work was done with their own checker and viewer tools, tested on chosen examples.
arxiv-2506-20376:
Lingyun Chen and six co-authors taught robots in 2025 to navigate rooms where obstacles can be soft or hard. A robot that treats every obstacle as a wall wastes paths; one that pushes through everything breaks things. The team learned motion skills from human demonstrations, then added a live adjustment layer that senses which regions may be entered.

Soft zones can be crossed gently while hard zones are routed around, with speed and path both under control. Tests in simulation and on real robots crossed cluttered, squishy settings. The approach suits warehouses and homes where not every obstacle is solid.
arxiv-2506-20476:
Tong Zhou presents a 2025 competition paper on answering questions with retrieved documents. The LiveRAG contest at a top retrieval conference tested systems on machine-made questions across many topics and styles. Systems had to fetch support from a 15-million-document slice of a web corpus. Zhou's pipeline, built for a team entry, reranks fetched documents with two aims at once.

Knowledge awareness guides which facts a question needs. Diversity keeps the top documents from repeating each other. That pairing won first place in the contest. The evaluation set was built by an automatic generator to span question types, phrasings, and audiences fairly. The paper is a solution report, so it centers on the pipeline's design and its winning run.
arxiv-2506-20776:
Cancer cells often burn sugar in a wasteful way, even when oxygen is plentiful, a puzzle known as the Warburg effect. Vibishan, Mohit Kumar Jolly, and Akshit Goyal review that puzzle in this 2025 paper, placing cancer alongside microbes and healthy tissue. Similar shifts toward fast, wasteful fuel use show up in yeast and in normal cells, and the review asks what all of them share.

Faster growth explains the shift in some cases, the authors find, but not in all. Cells seem to weigh many goals at once, trading energy cost against other gains in each setting. The review puts forward a budget view of the cell, in which proteins and fuel are shared out like money. That view pairs well with math models and may guide new tests of why cells pick one fuel plan over another.
arxiv-2506-20876:
Automatic fact-checkers promise verdicts on medical claims, yet clinics barely use them. Sebastian Joseph and co-authors study how experts actually check such claims in a 2025 paper. They watch clinicians work real social media claims against trial evidence.

Three walls appear at once. Wild claims rarely line up with tidy trial questions. Many claims stay too vague to test fairly. Verdict labels themselves carry judgment calls. The team argues for checkers that converse instead of pronounce. Systems should ask, clarify, and show their evidence trail. Medicine, they say, needs dialogue, not oracles.
arxiv-2506-20976:
Aida Abiad and Reijnders study a coloring problem for graph edges in a 2025 math paper. The rule is strict: any two edges within a set distance of each other must get unlike colors. The question is the least number of colors that can work for a given graph and distance.

The pair derive sharp lower bounds from algebra. Their bounds use the eigenvalues of a derived graph, plus a polynomial found by an integer search method. Some graph families meet the bounds exactly, and computer runs show how the bounds fare more broadly. The authors also probe what their method says about a long standing guess in the field, and when a counter case could arise.
arxiv-2506-21076:
Hongyu Yan and co-authors presented in 2025 a single framework that poses a three-dimensional character directly, instead of posing a flat image first and lifting it up. The older two-step route stacks errors and limits pose variety. Their system, described under a fuller title in the text, unifies styling and 3D generation.

Guidance comes from a true 3D skeleton rather than a flat skeleton drawing, which captures depth and joint links far better. The result is cleaner poses with more range. Character artists gain a tool that takes one image and a target pose and returns a posed 3D figure.
arxiv-2506-21476:
Srikumar Sastry and co-authors teach sight-and-word models the ladder of life in a 2025 paper. Such models can name a beast, but they strain to hold the tree that ranks a kind inside a clan inside a realm.

Past fixes taught a kind of follows-from link, yet they left the chain rule of that link loose: if A sits in B and B in C, then A sits in C. The new frame, built on a round spread of codes, writes that chain in stone. A base model trained with it then holds the whole tree of life as its map. On kind sorts and on hunts that must climb the tree, the model beat the best past tools. The code and models are set free.
arxiv-2506-21876:
Do today's vision-language models carry an inner picture of how the world works? Qiyue Gao and a large team of co-authors build a benchmark, WM-ABench, to test that question piece by piece. Their framework borrows from psychology and splits world modeling into perception skills, like judging space, time, quantity, and motion, and prediction skills, like simulating mechanisms and chaining inferences.

The benchmark spans twenty-three fine measures across six simulated worlds with controlled what-if scenarios. In 660 experiments on fifteen leading models, the systems showed striking gaps. Nearly all scored close to chance at telling motion paths apart, and some displayed odd biases, such as treating blue objects as faster than green ones. The authors argue current models lack the disentangled grasp that real planning needs.
arxiv-2506-22076:
A supernova split into multiple images by a galaxy's gravity is a rare cosmic gift, and catching one early enough to study takes fast eyes on survey photos. Satadru Bag and co-authors train a neural network for that hunt in a 2025 paper, feeding it film strips of sky in several colors. The network learns both the look of a field and how it changes night to night.

Trained on realistic simulated survey images, it flags most lensed explosions within the first week or so of sightings while keeping false alarms tiny.
