Four-image systems and wide splits are caught best; ordinary supernovae in red galaxies fool it most. The method fits the coming Rubin Observatory survey.
arxiv-2506-22176:
Holly Dinkel and co-authors present a robot method for tying knots in a rope with one hand in 2025. The rope is a soft linear object whose shape shifts as it moves. Their method, called KnotDLO, needs no human demos and no training. It plans grasp points and target points from the rope's current shape.

The shape is tracked as a chain of short line pieces. Grasp spots come from that chain and stay smooth as the shape changes. Mid points are computed from the shape now and the shape wanted next. Sight and control are kept apart in the design. In sixteen trials, the robot tied a simple knot half the time from new start shapes.
arxiv-2506-22276:
Reuth Mirsky argues for a fresh look at how much say smart software should have inside a human team, in a solo paper from 2025. Most team software today obeys orders without question. Mirsky notes that blind obedience can be wasteful or even unsafe when an order rests on a mistake.

The paper sets out a scale of agency levels for such systems. At each level, it asks when a system should push back, warn, or act on its own call. Worked examples show how pushback could help a team rather than hinder it. The paper ends with first bounds and open questions for studying wise disobedience as a skill that team software should be built to have.
arxiv-2506-22376:
Youkang Wang and co-authors put inference-time scaling of language models on a probability footing. Their twenty twenty-five paper, OptScale, asks how many parallel answers a model should draw before picking the best. Heuristic habits rule this choice today, wasting compute or starving hard questions.

Assuming samples are independent draws, the authors derive a floor on the count needed for a target success level. Their algorithm then sets the sample number on the fly per question. Easy prompts stop early; hard ones earn more tries. A principled dial for test-time compute helps labs spend GPU hours where they buy real accuracy.
arxiv-2506-22576:
Hunter La Croix and Alan E Lindsay adapt a fast corner-friendly solver to the heat equation. The lightning method writes solutions as sums of polynomials and rational functions, placing special terms where sharp corners make solutions spike. Their 2025 paper extends the idea from steady problems to heat spreading over time.

A Laplace transform first turns the heat problem into a modified Helmholtz equation at each transform value. The lightning method solves those, and Talbot integration converts the answers back to real time. Boundary conditions are enforced at chosen points through an overdetermined system. Tests against known results and hard cases showed spectral accuracy with root-exponential convergence. The method stayed robust across time spans and shapes.
arxiv-2506-22776:
Sen Fang and co-authors ask in a 2025 benchmark whether shrinking a language model by quantization makes its code writing more fragile. Quantization trims the numbers inside a model to save memory and speed it up. They tested four model families, from small to large, under hostile prompts and under noise in the weights.

Against the common guess, the trimmed models often held up better than the full ones. In just over half the attack trials the trimmed model proved tougher. It also bore stronger weight noise. Shrinking, they conclude, can add sturdiness as well as thrift.
arxiv-2506-22976:
Ronald Orozco Lopez builds in 2025 a new calculus that works on number sequences rather than smooth curves. He sets out a matched pair of steps, one like a slope step and one like an area step. A main claim links the two steps, as in the classic case.

Lopez gives a set of base functions that fit the new slope and area steps well. He lists the traits of that base set and shows how it can be used. He then proves a form of the classic series rule for functions in this frame. The work gives sequence work a full calculus of its own.
arxiv-2506-23176:
A dense star can ring like a bell when waves from space shake it, and that ring holds clues to what the star is made of. Zhiqiang Miao and co-authors study that ring in a 2025 work with full gravity maths. They beam a wave of one tone at the star and read how it scatters.

The scatter pattern hides a factor that sets how loud each ring tone can sound. With that factor, the team works out how a close pair of stars can pump a tone as they spiral in and cross its pitch. Their frame swaps the old Newton based split for a gravity true one. They also tie the scatter shift to the full energy of the scene and set out a tide energy for the star.
arxiv-2506-23276:
David Guzman Piedrahita and co-authors test how language models behave in public goods games, where cooperation must survive free-riding. Models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents, so how they balance self-interest against the group matters. The team adapted a game with institutional choice from behavioral economics. Models repeatedly decided whether to pay a cost to reward cooperation or punish defection.

Four behavior patterns emerged. Some models built and held high cooperation. Others swung between engagement and withdrawal. A third group slid downhill over time, and a fourth stuck to fixed strategies whatever happened. The surprise was that strong reasoning models, such as the o1 series, cooperated badly. Some plain models cooperated consistently well. The authors warn that sharpening a model's reasoning does not by itself make it a better team player. Their code is public for others to test deployment risks.
arxiv-2506-23476:
Yi-bo Shen and co-authors used correlation functions to probe what two exotic particles are really made of. Over twenty years, experiments have found many hadron states that do not fit the simple quark model. A leading idea is that some are loose molecules of two ordinary hadrons. The team focused on the Ds0*(2317), testing four possible recipes for its makeup, each built around a bound pair of a D meson and a kaon.

Each recipe predicts a slightly different fingerprint in the correlation between a D meson and a kaon produced together. The fingerprints separate cleanly when a bare compact state is mixed in. The same approach applied to the famous X(3872) particle also distinguished its internal mixtures. Future collision measurements can read these fingerprints and settle the recipes.
arxiv-2506-23576:
Jailbreak prompts talk language models out of their safety rules, and one defense is to staff the gate with more models. Maria Wit and Jun Pang test that defense in this 2025 paper, reproducing a published multi-agent setup and trying it against three known attacks. They compare one, two, and three agent configurations.

Teams of models did resist jailbreaks better, mainly by missing fewer attacks. But the shield's strength swung with the attack style, and it came at a price: more harmless prompts wrongly blocked, and more computing spent. The authors say today's automated defenses remain limited and point to where alignment needs to harden.
arxiv-2507-00176:
Kiminad Mamo reframes quark confinement as a surface effect in this 2025 paper on quantum chromodynamics. Confinement keeps quarks and gluons locked inside particles like protons. Mamo places their shared information on a sphere around the hadron. At that radius, the split between inside and outside reaches peak entanglement, a linked quantum state.

Lattice results for gravity-related form factors fix both the sphere's radius and a density tied to the trace anomaly. From those, Mamo derives a slope and an entropy that grows in a straight line with rapidity. The entropy push flips sign at the sphere, holding colored parts on it. World scattering data are checked against the idea. The test adds to, rather than replaces, the classic area-law test.
arxiv-2507-00276:
Hidetoshi Nishimori, Masayuki Ohzeki, and Manaka Okuyama proved a link in twenty twenty-five between two odd effects in spin glasses. Spin glasses are magnetic alloys with frozen, disordered spins. In temperature chaos, a tiny temperature shift completely rearranges the spin state. In the reentrant transition, cooling drives the system from an ordered phase back into a less ordered one.

Working in the finite-dimensional Edwards-Anderson model, the authors add correlations among the disorder variables. Assuming a spin glass phase exists at finite temperature, they show temperature chaos follows logically from reentrance. The two effects, long treated as unrelated curiosities, turn out to be two faces of one structure. The result offers a new view of spin glass physics beyond the standard mean-field picture.
arxiv-2507-00376:
Manohar and Mallikarjunaiah studied adaptive simulations of cracking in strain-limiting solids in twenty twenty-five. Phase-field models smear a crack over a small zone, using a damage variable. This avoids direct tracking of crack surfaces. The AT1 variant is popular for quasi-static brittle fracture. But proving that adaptive mesh refinement converges is hard.

The authors study an AT1 model inside elasticity theories with algebraically nonlinear stress-strain laws. They propose two refinement algorithms driven by local error indicators. Minimizer sequences from the first converge to a set tolerance. Sequences from the second are proven inherently convergent, needing no stopping rule. Simulations of an edge crack under anti-plane shear loading checked bulk, surface, and total energies. They showed both algorithms outperform standard approaches.
arxiv-2507-00576:
Research data often sit in storage systems spread across sites that use different tools and login rules. Dante Sanchez-Gallegos and co-authors presented DynoStore in 2025, a system meant to manage data across such mixed storage. Its core idea is the data container, a standard interface that hides the details of each storage system below it.

Linked containers form one wide-area storage network, with coding methods that keep data safe when parts fail. A load-balancing method spreads work fairly across sites. In tests with medical and satellite data, DynoStore ran about ten percent faster than a central cloud setup. It also survived more failures than the rival systems tested.
arxiv-2507-00776:
Yang and co-authors explore stars made of quark matter that also switch between quark phases inside, in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Ordinary hybrid stars mix a quark core with a nuclear shell. These hybrid quark stars instead jump from one quark phase to another. The team first map the possible shapes of the mass-radius relation for such stars, then build models with sharp first-order transitions.

Real observations fence the models in: the heaviest known pulsars pass two solar masses, and a 2017 gravitational wave event bounds how squishy a star can be. Some settings produce twin stars, pairs with equal mass but different size. The transitions can also break a relation between merger ring frequency and squishiness once thought universal. The work widens the menu of possible compact stars.
arxiv-2507-01076:
Vanja Stojanović and Bor Pangeršič give the mutual-visibility problem its first empirical workout in a two thousand twenty-five algorithms paper. The problem asks for the largest set of graph vertices that can pairwise see each other along paths avoiding other chosen vertices.

The problem is NP-complete, and theory had outrun practice. The authors implement three methods: a direct random heuristic, a hypergraph-based approximation, and a genetic algorithm. On smaller graphs all three match known theoretical values. On larger instances, solutions diverge from theoretical limits and loose bounds make quality hard to judge. On graphs with known optima, the genetic algorithm and heuristics performed best.
arxiv-2507-01176:
Zachiri McKenzie works in set theory, the branch of logic that studies the base on which the rest of math stands. The 2025 paper takes up a weakened form of the standard system, with two of its tools trimmed back, and a rule about grouped sets cut down to simpler cases. The question, named for Kaufmann and Clote, asks how far such a system can stretch.

McKenzie proves a transfer result about models of that weak system. Take a richer model that grows out of a poorer one in a set way. It has new ranks, but no first new rank. Then a grouped-set rule at the next level must already hold in the poorer model. From that, the smallest model of the weak system, with one such rule added, can be shown to admit no growth of the kind in question. The answer to the posed question is no.
arxiv-2507-01276:
Some decays are banned in the Standard Model, so seeing one would point to new physics. The four authors study tau lepton decays into an electron plus a pair of mesons within a supersymmetric model that adds a local B-L gauge symmetry. The three channels are tau to electron with two pions, with a pion and a kaon, and with two kaons. They ask how the predicted rates for these flavor-violating decays respond to the model's parameters.

Using the latest experimental data, the authors trace which parameters move the branching ratios most. The numerical work shows the main drivers are the non-diagonal elements that link the starting and ending leptons. The paper offers the analysis as groundwork for experiments hunting these decays, since a future detection would signal physics beyond the Standard Model.
arxiv-2507-01476:
Cooper and co-authors show how printed surface patterns can help quantum gear stay small and light. Tools like atomic clocks need a near vacuum inside. Any stray gas spoils their work, so the gas must be pumped away. The team printed vacuum parts with fine, complex surface textures.

A special coating on the parts acts as a pump when gas hits the surface. The rough texture gives gas far more chances to strike and stick. In tests, the patterned parts pumped gas several times faster than flat parts of the same size. Computer models of the flow matched the tests and point to even larger gains. The parts can sit close to the heart of a device.
arxiv-2507-01976:
Sivaroopan and colleagues survey in twenty twenty-five how researchers fake network traffic for testing and training. Real traffic data is scarce, private, and sometimes impure, so generated copies that keep its character are valuable. The survey maps the field from classic statistical models through modern deep learning generators, including commercial tools.

It compares approaches side by side on data types and model families, and ships an AI tool that applies the comparison to any new paper. The authors then list open problems, from realism checks to privacy risks. They close with future directions, aiming the survey at both researchers and practitioners who need a structured map of the area.
arxiv-2507-02276:
Oplisstilova and co-authors report telescope observations of a bright star in Orion's Belt in a 2025 paper, where the lead author's name is spelled with diacritics in the byline. Massive stars shape the universe, but distant ones cannot be observed in fine detail. The team turned to the nearest massive stars, using a large interferometer array plus spectrum data from two observatories. Their target is a blue supergiant at the center of the Belt.

Interferometer data show the star is not round: it spins near its break up speed, which flattens it. Their best fit model gives its mass, size, and surface temperature, along with a spin period of about four days. The preferred distance matches the typical distance of its star group. Some tension remains between the shape data and the spectrum data. The authors present the model as a compromise that fits most evidence.
arxiv-2507-02576:
Dima and co-authors propose in 2025 a framework that unifies three ways to represent blood vessels in one trainable system. Voxel grids are common, but meshes and parametric models serve key uses, and they are usually built apart. Their method joins them through differentiable voxelization.

Vessels are modeled as centerlines and radii with smooth spline curves. Shape parameters are learned by fitting to segmentations, with no need for ground truth shape values. Meshes are then drawn from the learned parameters in a differentiable way, so they can be edited after fitting. Tests on aortas, aneurysms, and brain vessels showed accurate volume fits.
arxiv-2507-02776:
Jiaming Chen and Vlad Margarint present a way to draw random curves from a growth process in a 2025 paper. The Loewner process grows a curve in the plane driven by a random path, and it models many rough shapes in physics. Simulating those curves fast and faithfully is a standing challenge.

Their splitting algorithm breaks the growth into steps that can be handled in a stable way, and they prove it converges in two senses. They extend the method to variants with memory, driven by fractional noise or by reinforced noise. Those extensions let them predict fractal dimensions and other statistical traits of the curves.
arxiv-2507-02876:
Erden argues that artificial intelligence can borrow its next design leap from evolutionary biology, in a 2025 essay. He compares today's AI landscape to the Modern Synthesis in twentieth-century biology, a framework later enriched by evolutionary developmental biology. That later shift, he suggests, shows how a mature field can be deepened rather than replaced.

Synthesizing ideas from both fields, he proposes a path past current AI's limits toward its larger goals. On this view, the technological singularity stops being pure speculation and becomes a grounded prospect to reason about. The paper is a critical, conceptual examination rather than an experiment.
arxiv-2507-02976:
Amirali Sajadi, Kostadin Damevski, and Preetha Chatterjee run a large study of security flaws in code fixes written by AI tools, in work from 2025. Such tools now repair real software bugs on their own. Prior checks of their safety used small or toy tasks, not real repairs.

The study drew on over twenty thousand real GitHub issues from a known benchmark. It compared fixes by human developers, by one large model alone, and by three agent systems. The lone model added many new flaws, in patterns unlike human ones. Agents added flaws too, above all when given more freedom. Risky fixes shared telling traits and arose more on issues missing certain facts. The authors urge care in how repair tools are deployed.
arxiv-2507-03376:
Simon Divilov and eleven co-authors report a new class of materials that can manage heat with light, in a research paper from 2025. The materials are carbides that mix four or more metals in equal shares. Good heat control at very high heat is a key need for energy and aerospace work.

Lab tests and theory together show these mixed carbides respond to light in a useful way at room heat and at heat above a thousand degrees. Their response can be tuned by choice of metals, and it holds up over repeated heating cycles. The authors say this opens a fast path to designing heat-proof optical materials.
arxiv-2507-03576:
Tienkamp and co-authors measure speech changes around tongue cancer surgery in a 2025 study. Removing part of the tongue can limit its motion and muscle bulk, which may blur speech. The catalog record lists first names only, while the text byline gives the team's full names.

Eleven patients read sentences before surgery and six months after, joined by eleven matched typical speakers. Two measures were tracked: how spread out the vowel space was, and how much vowel sounds varied from repeat to repeat. After surgery, the vowel space shrank compared with each patient's own baseline, yet stayed within the typical range. One vowel grew more variable after surgery. The results suggest clarity largely held, while steadiness of articulation slipped.
arxiv-2507-03676:
Peter Allen, Julia Böttcher, Yoshiharu Kohayakawa, and Mihir Neve prove a hardier version of a classic graph embedding theorem, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Sauer-Spencer theorem says a dense enough host graph swallows any guest graph of bounded degree. The new result asks whether a randomly thinned host, keeping each edge with some small chance, still contains the guest.

Above a probability threshold their answer is yes, and the threshold is best possible apart from a log factor. They also soften the host's degree demand to a new boundary value, which they bound and guess exactly, tying it to a famous open conjecture. A sharpened blow-up lemma, proved along the way, may serve other problems, the authors note.
arxiv-2507-03876:
Alyssa Loo and co-authors test whether large language models learn rules the way people do in this 2025 paper. Cognitive science has long debated whether neural networks can capture abstract thought. The team ran several language models on a classic task where people infer rules built from logical ideas. A Bayesian model of thought, the past champion, set the bar.

Across four experiments, the language models fit human choices at least as well. Yet the rules they seemed to use differed in kind from the Bayesian model's. That gap suggests the models are not just copying the older solution in new dress. The authors argue these systems may offer a fresh account of how logical concepts arise.
arxiv-2507-04176:
Carlo Nicolini and co-authors present skfolio, an open-source Python library for portfolio optimization, in a 2025 paper. Building investment portfolios demands tools that marry sound statistics with code practitioners will actually use.

The library plugs into the scikit-learn ecosystem and follows its fit, predict, and transform pattern throughout. Strategies range from classic mean-variance methods to modern clustering-based allocation. Financial estimators ship with native interfaces, and cross-validation tools respect the order of financial time series. Machine learning workflows thus carry straight into portfolio construction. The authors pitch reproducibility and transparency as the payoff: researchers and traders share one tested base instead of private, unverifiable scripts.
arxiv-2507-04376:
Georgios Ioannides and co-authors propose MOD-X, a framework for AI agents to work together across different designs, in a 2025 paper under the head title on a modular open exchange. AI systems are moving from single models to ecosystems of specialist agents, which need standard ways to talk. Existing protocols have key limits that the new frame aims to fix.

Its layered design adds a universal message bus, full state handling, translation between formats, and blockchain based security. Innovations include publish subscribe messaging, semantic discovery of capabilities, and dynamic workflow orchestration. A worked example shows rule based, neural, symbolic, and legacy systems integrated as agents in one flow.
arxiv-2507-04476:
Researchers including J. Richard Bond present a cosmology paper, published in 2025, on how hot gas in galaxy clusters reveals the push back of ordinary matter. Ordinary matter, called baryons, can blow gas out of clusters and shift the spread of matter in the universe. Precise surveys must model that feedback well or their measures of the cosmos will drift.

The team fits a flexible halo model to clusters found by the Atacama Cosmology Telescope through the Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect, with masses checked by weak lensing. The cluster data pinned down several feedback settings in the model. Results favor middling to strong feedback, in line with computer simulations of galaxy formation.
arxiv-2507-04776:
Jun-You Wang and Li Su teach a music model by corrupting its homework. Their 2025 paper pre-trains a BERT-style model on symbolic music with two new objectives, aiming at broad understanding across tasks from chord guessing to genre labeling.

First, some note tokens are deliberately noised, and the model must restore them, a denoising drill that forces it to learn pitch relations. Second, it must predict piano-roll summaries, at whole-bar and local scales, from the corrupted sequence. Together the tasks build musical knowledge into the weights before any fine-tuning. On a twelve-task benchmark the authors built for the purpose, the pre-trained model proved competitive across the board. They credit the corruption-based objectives for the transfer.
arxiv-2507-05276:
Hassan Khandani presents a 2025 study of fixed point results for a class of shrinking maps set out by Kirk. Such theorems show a map must leave some point unmoved, but past proofs leaned on a bounded orbit term that is hard to check. That term was long seen as a must-have for the result.

Khandani shows each such map is in fact a Leader contraction, a class that brings bounded orbits on its own. The bounded term can thus be dropped. He also weakens a smoothness term on the control curve, which settles an open guess, and joins many past results in one frame.
arxiv-2507-05576:
Mehdi Elahi, Mohamed Elshamy, Abdel-Hameed Badawy, and Ahmad Patooghy wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It studies a sly chip attack, the intermittent thermal Trojan, which twists a processor's heat data at random times to stay hid.

Multi-core chips lean on heat reads to stay safe and fast. A Trojan that fires in bursts slips past threshold checks with ease, the team shows. They map how start time and burst length change the harm. Their guard is a set of tiny learned classifiers that watch for odd heat signs at run time. Catch rates jump by wide margins over past methods. Any twist past a tight band is caught every time.
arxiv-2507-05776:
Théophile Chaumont-Frelet and co-authors present a mathematics paper, published in 2025, on how to judge error in a hard type of equation problem. The work deals with the biharmonic problem in two dimensions, solved with a method called a symmetric interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin method. The core tool is a generalized Hessian, a matrix of second derivatives.

The authors prove that their error measure splits into two parts, one for how well the method fits together and one for where it does not. From that split they build a new error estimator that needs no extra stabilization term. Tests with numbers back the theory, and the estimator can be tied to the standard residual based measure.
arxiv-2507-05976:
Alessandro Umbrico and co-authors improved in 2025 the readability of rule-based explanations from a medical prediction model. The test case was judging the risk of arm swelling after lymph node radiotherapy in breast cancer care. Raw rules from an explainable model can still baffle users. Their method borrows scoring ideas from information retrieval to rate how much each attribute drives a prediction.

Those relevance scores are shown to users as plain evidence about which risk factors mattered. A user study compared the enriched output with the model's raw rules. Readers rated the new output as clearer and more useful. The authors present the trick as a general layer for explainable systems in health care. Better explanations matter because doctors must trust and check model advice before acting on it.
arxiv-2507-06076:
Dominique Guillot and co-authors classify the functions that preserve a matrix's positivity when applied entry by entry. Feed a positive definite matrix through such a function, cell by cell, and the result must be positive definite exactly when the input was. Earlier classics solved the question when all sizes are allowed at once; this work fixes the size, the harder case.

For matrices of size three or more, the answer is stark: only positive multiples of the field's own continuous symmetries qualify. Size two breaks the pattern, allowing power functions to sneak in, which the team charts over wide complex domains. Extensions cover matrices with forced zeros and a cousin problem about monotone maps, rounding out a complete census of these cell-wise guardians.
arxiv-2507-06376:
Elisavet Lydia Alvanaki, Kevin Lee, and Luca Carloni introduce SLDB, a benchmark suite for language-model-aided chip design, in a 2025 paper. Language models now write correct hardware description code, hinting at AI help for real design work. Yet current benchmarks stop at single components, while real chips are systems of many parts.

SLDB targets that system level. It offers ten baseline system-on-chip designs whose parts can combine into a vast number of tile-based chips through a synthetic library. Full configurations ship with the set: accelerator hookup code, communication settings, and test programs, all built for the ESP platform. The suite lets researchers judge whether models can handle integration and setup, not just small coding puzzles.
arxiv-2507-06576:
Sina Kalantarzadeh and Nikhil Kumar improved lower bounds in twenty twenty-five on the gap between multiflows and multicuts in planar networks. Given many source-sink pairs, a multiflow routes goods for all of them at once, while a multicut removes edges to disconnect every pair. The cut always costs at least the flow; their ratio is the gap.

For a single pair the gap is one, but in general it can grow without bound. For planar graphs, the best lower bound had stood at two for decades. The authors raise it to sixteen sevenths. More importantly, they develop fresh techniques for proving such bounds, which they expect to transfer to other network problems. The work sharpens knowledge of how far flow and cut can diverge on flat networks.
arxiv-2507-06876:
Adrian Rauchfleisch, Joshua Suarez, Nikka Sales, and Andreas Jungherr read millions of posts to see how the world greeted ChatGPT, in a 2025 paper. A big product launch works like a spotlight, drawing out a society's hopes and fears about change. The team gathered about four million posts from over a million users in 117 lands after the 2022 launch. They sorted speakers by job skills and by home-country values.

Writers, coders, and math-heavy workers did not meet the tool alike. Tech-skilled users posted early and warmly, while writing-heavy users came later and cooler. Lands high in self-reliance posted early yet more coldly, and lands that shun doubt showed fewer warm posts. The day's overall mood hid these currents. The authors say who gains and who fears loss writes the public story of new tech.
arxiv-2507-07576:
Mohamed Siala, Jordi Planes, and Joao Marques-Silva examine rule-based machine learning in a 2025 paper. Rule-based models, such as decision trees and rule lists, are favoured in high-risk fields because people can read them. Their explanations, though, are trusted only if the rules themselves are clean and sound.

The authors link explanation quality to known flaws in rule sets, such as rules that overlap in harmful ways and several forms of redundancy. They develop algorithms that can detect those flaws in a given model. Their conclusion is pointed: widely used tools for learning rule models will produce rule sets with at least one of these flaws. The paper argues that checking a model's rules should be a standard step before its explanations are trusted.
arxiv-2507-07676:
Eve Dones and Laura Bernard work out how tides bend the waves from merging neutron stars, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their setting is a scalar-tensor theory, a variant of gravity with an extra field. In such pairs, each star is squeezed both by its mate and by that field. The squeeze depends on what the star is made of, so wave shapes can betray its inner makeup.

The pair compute the squeeze's mark on the total energy flow and on the wave's phase with high care, well past the first rough terms. Three kinds of give in the star feed the signal at that level. They also give the full set of wave shapes, a base for reading future detector data and for telling new gravity from plain star stuff.
arxiv-2507-07776:
Dren Fazlija and co-authors launch SCOOTER in a 2025 paper, a framework for judging trick images that fool vision models without small-pixel limits. Such attacks may recolor an object, so old norm-based checks cannot say whether humans would notice.

The framework gives rules for crowd study size, pay, and fair score bounds. In a large study with hundreds of people, six attack types all failed to make images that look real. A top language model gave a fair first screen but missed some attacks. Free tools, with a browser task form, are shared. Safety teams get a sound way to compare attacks by human eyes.
arxiv-2507-07876:
Timur Aslyamov and Massimiliano Esposito develop a unified theory for time-averaged correlations in systems held away from equilibrium, in a research paper from 2025. Near that state, a classic theorem governs the symmetric part of these averages, and the antisymmetric part is zero. Far from that state, no such tidy rules held.

The authors derive exact, computable formulas for both parts in steady nonequilibrium states. Both are written through excess observables, quantities drawn from statistical physics and learning theory. They also bound that part using entropy-like costs. A final result limits how driving speeds up self-averaging. The whole approach serves jump processes and diffusion alike.
arxiv-2507-07976: Zehua Lai and Lek-Heng Lim prove the Pierce-Birkhoff claim for splines, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Splines are smooth piecewise polynomials laid over a flat-cut split of space. The claim says each can be written as a finite lattice blend of plain polynomials. A pure existence proof comes first, then a deeper pass that yields workable bounds.
arxiv-2507-08076:
Aryaman Bhutani, Nirmal Raj, and Zenia Zuraiq ask whether dark matter could crack a neutron star in a 2025 paper. The dense core of such a star may hold the stablest form of matter, a strange quark phase. A shift to that phase needs a seed, and a high energy wall may block it. The team show that hits from a hidden sector of particles could clear that wall.

A sparked shift could crush the star into a black hole or set off a gamma-ray burst. Old neutron stars still shine, and bursts stay rare, so such hits must be rare too. That fact lets the team set tight bounds on dark matter hits, decays, and self-loss. The bounds beat lab searches by many orders in size. For low walls they also bound how long a nucleon can live, at near 10 to the 64th power years.
arxiv-2507-08276:
Ana Djordjević, Marija Dimitrijević Ćirić, and Vladimir Juričić built a theory in 2025 for fermions on crystals that live on a curved, hyperbolic surface. Such lattices have been made in the lab, sparking interest in their physics. A key missing piece was how fermions couple to the curvature, which theory says must occur through the spin connection.

Starting from the symmetries of the curved disk, they worked out the matching theory for free fermions. It predicts a non-zero density of states at low energy wherever the curvature is finite. They then built the matching lattice factor and tested it on a finite lattice by computer. The lattice results backed the prediction, giving a base for later work on interacting phases.
arxiv-2507-08476:
Designing a particle beam line means tuning many settings at once, and slow search methods scale badly as settings multiply. Francisco Huhn and Francesco Velotti explore a smarter route in this 2025 paper: simulations that hand back exact gradients. They built their own such code using automatic differentiation and tested it against the usual trial-and-error gradient estimates.

Two test cases anchor the study, a literature cell with space charge and a realistic future beamline at CERN. The differentiable code matched estimates while running far more cheaply per gradient. Plugged into gradient-based optimizers, it beat gradient-free methods on the tuning tasks. The authors frame the work as a first careful benchmark for this approach in accelerator physics.
arxiv-2507-08576:
Four authors study the hidden ocean of Ganymede, the largest moon of Jupiter, in this 2025 paper. Flows in that salty ocean should stir a faint magnetic field. Space probes may soon read that field, so the team asks what it could reveal.

Their math shows a simpler form of the field rules is accurate enough for the task. Most of the signal is steady and comes from one part of the flow meeting the moon's own field. If the ocean is thick and salty enough, the signal should be readable at the surface. Its pattern could name the flow style and gauge ocean depth. The authors propose a score to judge such reads.
arxiv-2507-08676:
Universal quantum computers need two resources: entanglement and a second one called magic. Pablo Martinez-Azcona and co-authors show how to brew magic steadily, using dynamics that leak energy by design. Unlike closed systems, leaky ones can pull every starting state toward one chosen target state.

Working with a single leaky qubit, they find the best settings to settle into two prized magic states. No special starting state is needed, since all starts converge to the target. Added classical noise still allows high-magic results within mapped limits. They also design a fully dissipative version and compare it with a known cultivation method. A concrete design uses a cat qubit, a device already studied in labs. The work offers a hands-off way to stockpile a scarce quantum resource.
arxiv-2507-08876:
Zhao Song, Chen Shen and The Anh Han model how empty promises can still grow cooperation when people interact on a network in 2025. Players may signal that they intend to cooperate before a donation game, but the signal costs nothing and binds no one.

In mixed, anonymous populations the talk changes nothing, matching experiments. On structured networks, though, cooperation emerges. Conditional players, who answer signals but pay a small thinking cost, act as catalysts: shifting patterns of dominance among strategies shelter the unconditional cooperators. The authors offer this as an evolutionary explanation for why cheap talk matters in real communities, where relationships repeat and reputations linger.
arxiv-2507-08976:
Matthew Evans imports the idea of nilpotence into BCK-algebras, an algebraic setting far from the groups where nilpotence is classical. He begins with the derived subalgebra and builds a derived ideal from it. That construction quickly pays off in category theory.

Commutative BCK-algebras turn out to form a reflective subcategory of all BCK-algebras. Evans then defines central series and nilpotence, and proves basic properties. Within any variety, the nilpotent members form a sub-pseudovariety but usually not a variety. Algebras of nilpotence class at most c form a variety only when c equals one. A closing result says every finite BCK-algebra is nilpotent.
arxiv-2507-09276:
George Andrews and Mohamed El Bachraoui study a family of q-series, infinite sums built from a variable q, that depend on two whole numbers, k and m. For the first few choices of those numbers every term of the series is positive, but for larger choices nobody knows whether positivity still holds. The question matters because these sums also count certain two-color partitions.

A partition splits a whole number into parts, and here the parts come in two colors, with each arrangement weighted by a sign that depends on how many even parts it has. If the generating sums stay positive, that fact turns into inequalities comparing counts of these partitions. The paper works out that link and draws the inequalities from it, while leaving the general positivity question open.
arxiv-2507-09476:
Xu Chen and co-authors study how a magnetic field can steer electric flow in quantum materials in this 2025 paper. The flow they study is not the simple kind that grows in step with voltage, but a bent kind tied to the geometry of quantum states. That geometry has become a central topic in this field.

Using a standard transport framework, the team looks at flat systems with varied forms of spin-orbit coupling. The bent flow depends strongly on field direction and varies across directions in space. Those direction patterns differ by coupling type. The bent flow can also be told apart from the plain flow by sign and pattern. Exact formulas match the team's numeric results.
arxiv-2507-09776:
Mihir Kavishwar and Naresh Shanbhag tackle the energy cost of analog in-memory computing in this 2025 paper. Such chips compute inside memory arrays and sip power, but their analog-to-digital converters burn much of that saving. Lowering the converter's precision saves energy, yet it also blurs the results, so the team asked how low the precision can safely go.

Earlier work estimated the needed precision with a noise model the authors show is too crude, since it treats errors as unrelated to the input. They derive formulas for a truer accuracy measure, the compute signal-to-noise ratio, and give an algorithm, CACTUS, that picks converter settings to optimize it. In a circuit-level model of an SRAM chip, their settings cut the needed precision by three bits while gaining accuracy over older methods. They also map when their approach beats the older design rule.
arxiv-2507-10076:
Anna Rapberger and co-authors grade argument strength in a logic framework in a 2025 paper. Assumption-based argumentation builds arguments from assumptions and rules. Classic semantics sort arguments into accepted or rejected piles, a coarse verdict.

Gradual semantics instead assign each part a strength score on a scale. Such scores exist for abstract and bipolar frameworks, but not yet for this one. The paper defines a family of gradual semantics for assumptions themselves. Borrowing bipolar machinery, it scores how support and attack balance out. Finer grades help systems explain why one claim outweighs another.
arxiv-2507-10376:
Mohammadhossein Talebi and four co-authors build Raci-Net, a learning tool that tracks a self-driving car's own move in bad weather. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Cars lean on cameras, laser scans, and motion sensors to sense the world and gauge their move. Sight-based sensors sit open to harsh weather and faults. Past tools cope with faults such as a turned mount or a lost link, but fade in snow, rain, and poor light. Raci-Net joins sight, motion, and radar data. It leans on each sensor's strength, and shifts each one's weight as the state of the world changes. The aim is a move gauge that stays true when the sky turns bad.
arxiv-2507-11276:
Stefan Rohshap and co-authors unveil a fresh way to spot phase shifts in quantum matter in a 2025 paper. The usual lens is how parts of space tangle with each other. Their lens is how time scales tangle, read from how hard a time record is to compress.

Across a spread of test systems, from ring models to the classic Mott shift, this time tangle swells near a shift point. At the sharpest points it stops changing with zoom, a mark of true critical behavior. The swell shows up in near any measured trait, which makes the test a broad, even handed probe of change.
arxiv-2507-11476:
Esteban Román Catafau and Torbjörn Nordling present a fast circle finder for blurry images in this 2025 paper. Finding circles in degraded pictures matters for medical scans, robots, and factory checks. Their method, 3C-FBI, joins edge sampling with a convolution trick that piles up votes in parameter space.

Tests covered Parkinson's assessment videos, synthetic benchmarks, and images with shrinking size and growing clutter. The method scored near the top on accuracy while running at real-time speed on a plain processor. It stayed almost perfect at high resolution and held up well at small sizes with a fifth of points corrupted. The authors pitch it for hard imaging conditions.
arxiv-2507-11676:
Chris Heunen and co-authors offer a 2025 paper on a simpler way to write quantum programs. Most quantum code today works at a low level, much like circuit plans. That low level makes large programs hard to read and hard to check. The authors build a small syntax based on one core idea: phase.

Their language pairs a phase step with a choice step that picks out parts of a state. From these two parts they can build a full set of quantum gates. Well known methods such as Grover search and the Fourier transform come out short and clear. Formal meaning comes from work in category theory.
arxiv-2507-11876:
Wang and co-authors run computer simulations of breaking waves coated with surfactants, in a 2025 study. Surfactants are soap-like compounds that ride on a water surface and cannot dissolve away. Ocean waves often carry such films. The team asked how the films change the way waves break, in both gentle regular breakers and spilling ones.

Their three-dimensional simulations track the wave surface and the stresses the film creates. Regular breakers barely changed when the film was added. Spilling breakers changed a lot: the crest shape shifted, swirls grew stronger, and strong film stress could push a spiller toward plunging. The authors also extend a math frame based on circulation to count the film's push. They conclude the stress, not lower surface pull, drives the effect.
arxiv-2507-11976:
Jana-Rebecca Rehse and five co-authors organize the jobs that process analysis displays must do, in a 2025 paper. Their field, conformance checking, compares recorded process traces against a model to find where real work departs from the plan. Companies use it to check rules and spot improvements. The results are complex, so visualizations carry the insight, yet vendors built those views without a shared map of what analysts actually need them for.

The authors build a task taxonomy: a systematic list of the analytical purposes such displays serve. With that map, tools can be judged by whether their views match real tasks, and gaps become visible. The taxonomy gives designers and buyers a common language for a part of process mining that had grown by improvisation.
arxiv-2507-12076:
Khatua, Krishnamoorthi, Koo, and a large team study a magnet built on a chiral trillium lattice. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. In such a lattice, magnetic ions sit on a three-way web of shared triangles that twists in space. Webs of this kind are a hot test bed for odd quantum states.

They probe one iron-based compound with heat, resonance, and muon tools. Two stages of magnetic link growth show as the sample cools. A weak order sets in at very low heat, and a small field can wipe it out. Muon tests show the spins keep moving, with no freeze. Weak order and liquid-like motion thus live side by side.
arxiv-2507-12276:
Donia Besher, Anirban Sengupta, and Tanujit Chakraborty forecast climate policy uncertainty in a 2025 paper. The text carries the fuller title naming macro-financial drivers and Google search data; the catalog title is shorter and carries stray journal text.

Uncertainty about future climate rules can delay green investment, so predicting it matters. The authors hunt for drivers among household finances, housing, business confidence, credit conditions, and market mood, finding those five the strongest. Search data add an early read on public attention. Their Bayesian time series model then produces probability forecasts for the United States and global indices. Careful testing shows the version with steady driver weights forecasts best. The drivers, they argue, explain the win.
arxiv-2507-12976:
Kostiantyn Milkevych and co-authors speed up in 2025 the exact placement of quantum circuits onto real quantum hardware. Layout synthesis maps a circuit's logical qubits onto a chip's physical ones, and the optimal map minimizes size and depth, which is precious because today's machines are noisy. The catch: optimality is NP-hard, so tools map onto a subset of the chip, yet proving nothing better exists seems to require checking exponentially many subsets.

Their method enumerates only the relevant subarchitectures, the subsets that could plausibly host an optimal layout, given a fixed budget of spare ancilla qubits. That pruning also slashes expensive pattern matching checks. Optimality is still guaranteed within the chosen ancilla bound. Benchmarks against leading optimal tools, with and without subset tricks, favor the new enumeration. Exact methods that finish sooner widen the range of circuits that can be laid out provably best.
arxiv-2507-13276:
Siyao Li, Masahide Yamaguchi, and Ying-li Zhang study in a 2025 paper how a partner field drains long lived field lumps called oscillons. These round, pulsing lumps arise in shallow field theories and form as the early universe reheats. Their lifespan in isolation is long, but partner fields complicate the count.

The team compute instability bands of the partner field over one lump's bumpy profile. Resonance strength shifts in intricate ways with coupling strength and lump shape. Distinct drain routes rule in different coupling ranges, the analysis shows. When a lump is too small, resonance fails to start at all. Simulations show growth of the partner field can halt before the lump hits collapse energy.
arxiv-2507-13376:
Dong Xiao, Zahra Sharif-Khodaei, and their co-author build a physics-guided method to find impacts on composite plates. Knowing where a plate was hit, and how hard, helps crews judge hidden damage. Their 2025 paper blends a plate theory called First-Order Shear Deformation Theory with machine learning. Traits of the plate and its edges are read from wave and vibration patterns.

The physics model fills gaps where test data are sparse, which steadies the learning step. It also sharpens the estimate of impact force. Doubt about the hit spot is carried through into the force result, so outputs come with a measure of trust. Tests on real plates back the method's accuracy and low data needs.
arxiv-2507-13576:
Hunter Monroe's 2025 paper in logic and computer science asks when one formal theory can stand in for another as a proof system. The yardstick is p-simulation, which says one system can turn any proof from the other into a short proof of its own. Monroe proposes a way to pin down when this happens between two theories.

The proposal rests on how well one theory can interpret the other inside its own language. Monroe shows the link runs both ways for a theory extended by one extra claim. The paper also states stronger conjectures that would imply open results, such as Feige's hypothesis and the existence of one-way functions.
arxiv-2507-13776:
Di Hou, Tianyun Tang, and Kim-Chuan Toh present a 2025 paper on a faster solver for hard planning problems that mix yes-no choices with continuous amounts. Such problems appear in scheduling and design. A strong relaxation gives good lower bounds on the best answer, but solving that relaxation is itself heavy, and the right rank for the answer is unknown ahead of time.

Their solver works on curved spaces of low-rank matrices and alternates two phases: one glides downhill on the curved space, and the other nudges the rank up to escape false resting spots. They also prove their relaxation equals a smaller known one. Wide tests showed the solver is fast and robust.
arxiv-2507-13876:
Sahabub Jahedi, Yi Liao, and Xiao-Dong Ma open a new line of work in this 2025 arXiv paper on dark matter. Most searches assume dark matter keeps the flavor of the particles it touches. The authors instead study cases where it changes flavor, letting one kind of charged lepton turn into another while a pair of dark matter particles carries off energy unseen.

Working with a general theory framework, they work out the energy pattern of these three-body decays. The pattern can reveal both the shape of the interaction and the mass of the dark matter. Present limits on muon and tau decays already set tight bounds on how strong such effects can be. They also study light cast by a rarer muon decay and the silent decay of muonium, an atom-like pair.
arxiv-2507-14176:
Andrés Morales-Forero and co-authors introduce predictive representativity, a fairness audit for AI skin cancer detection, in a research paper from 2025. AI tools increasingly guide medical choices, yet bias against groups with less historic representation persists. Most audits check who is in the training data, not whether predictions stay fair in use.

Their case study tests classifiers on a widely used data set and on an independent clinical set from Colombia. Scores fell sharply for people with darker skin, even with balanced sampling in source data. The framework measures how well fairness travels to new groups and settings. A formal criterion sets thresholds for that travel. Post-use audits are urged.
arxiv-2507-14376:
Osman Erman Gungor and co-authors present a schema matching system built on off-the-shelf language models in this 2025 paper. Matching fields across databases is essential for merging data, yet it is slow and hungry for labeled examples. Their framework, SCHEMORA, works prompt by prompt without training data.

The system first enriches schema metadata, then retrieves candidates by both meaning-based and word-based search. Multi-stage recommendation narrows the field before the model judges matches, avoiding exhaustive pairwise checks. On a clinical benchmark it beat the previous best by clear margins at two cutoff ranks. The authors release the code openly, a first for this approach. Their analysis stresses that retrieval quality drives the gains and guides model choice.
arxiv-2507-15176:
Jason Gaitonde and Elchanan Mossel study how badly an attacker can warp a Markov chain's long-run behavior, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Markov chains wander between states by fixed odds, settling into a stationary pattern. Corruption here rewrites the exits from a small share of states, chosen adversarially.

For chains with a spectral gap, PageRank-style variants prove robust. The corrupted chain's settled pattern stays close to the original, within a polynomial of the corrupted share. The bounds need no dimension terms and scale gracefully. PageRank thus acts as a simple regularizer against broad, realistic tampering, they argue.
arxiv-2507-15576:
Nicolas Poggi, Shashank Agnihotri, and Margret Keuper point general-purpose vision-language models at terahertz security images, in work from 2025. Terahertz scans can reveal hidden objects, but labeled examples are scarce and the pictures are blurry and ambiguous.

Instead of fine-tuning, the authors use in-context learning: the model gets a prompt with modality-matched guidance, plus zero or one example. Two open-weight models were adapted to the terahertz domain this way. Showing even a single example improved classification and made the models' reasoning easier to read. The authors present this as the first use of the approach for terahertz imaging, suited to scientific fields where data is thin.
arxiv-2507-15876:
Eric Benhamou and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on trend following funds, known as CTAs. These funds ride price trends, from slow breakouts to fast momentum bursts. Which horizon pays best, and how the two mix, stays in dispute. The team splits fund returns into short trend, long trend, and broad market parts.

Their split uses a Bayesian graphical model that updates over time. It shows how each part drives the funds' gains and risk. The mix of horizons shapes the risk adjusted score in clear ways. The work gives allocators a fresh lens on an old debate in managed futures.
arxiv-2507-15976:
Aaron Ho and co-authors describe a smarter way to build training data in a 2025 paper on fast stand in models for plasma flow in fusion machines. Running the full physics code is slow, so labs train quick models on its output. The catch is choosing which runs to pay for, since each run costs time.

The new method lets the model flag where it is unsure, then asks the physics code to label just those cases. After many rounds, the data set grew from a small start to ten thousand cases. The trained models sorted flow types well and matched outputs fairly on fresh tests. The approach should help labs that face even slower codes and tight budgets.
arxiv-2507-16076:
Marlene Lutz and co-authors test how persona prompts shape AI simulations of social groups in a 2025 paper. Researchers often ask language models to answer as if they were members of a demographic group. Wording choices in that request may distort the portrait. The team varied two levers: how the role is adopted, and how the group identity is primed.

Five open models faced open and closed tasks across fifteen intersecting groups. Models struggled most with marginalized groups. Interview-style prompts and name-based priming reduced stereotyping and improved fit. In a surprise, a small seven-billion-parameter model beat a giant seventy-billion one at the task. The authors turn those findings into practical guidance for anyone simulating public opinion with AI.
arxiv-2507-16276:
Lambard Maxence, Bertelle Cyrille, and Duvallet Claude model smart contracts as multi level state machines, in a 2025 paper. Smart contracts automate clauses on a blockchain, but writing them takes advanced coding skill, which slows uptake. A formal model that hides the technical depth could open the tool to non programmers.

Their model tracks contract execution as states within states, which adds modularity and traceability. Reusable parts ease the step from a legal contract to working code. The authors review past methods and tools, detail the generation process, and run a security analysis of the model. The aim is robust contracts that business users can shape themselves.
arxiv-2507-16476:
Ardhendu Sekhar and colleagues proposed in 2025 a modular framework to predict cancer survival directly from whole slide pathology images. Whole slides hold rich signs of tumor form, but picking the regions and patterns that matter is hard. Their pipeline runs in four stages, each aimed at one part of that problem.

A filtering stage keeps tissue patches with prognostic value. A graph clustering stage groups patches by form while respecting space. A hierarchy stage then learns links within and between those groups. A mixture density model with expert guidance turns this into survival curves. On lung, kidney, and breast cancer cohorts, the model beat prior approaches on concordance scores.
arxiv-2507-16576:
Ahmed Lekssays, Husrev Taha Sencar, and Ting Yu present a security tool named AZERG in two thousand twenty-five. Analysts write threat reports in plain text, but sharing threat data in the standard STIX format still takes much hand work by experts. AZERG aims to turn report text into structured STIX data on its own.

The tool splits the task into four steps: find entities, name their types, find linked pairs, and name each link type. The team fine-tuned language models for each step. They also built a data set from one hundred forty-one reports, with thousands of marked entities and links. Their scores beat other models they tested, by two to twenty-five percent across tasks.
arxiv-2507-16976:
Alessandro Summer and co-authors unify a family of odd relaxation effects under one theory. The classic Mpemba effect says hot water can freeze faster than cold. Cousins of it appear in quantum systems, where symmetry returns at surprising speeds. The team shows resource theories, tools from information science, frame them all.

Heat effects fall out of the theory of athermality. Symmetry effects fall out of asymmetry theory. In each case, one slow mode in the system sets the pace. Overlap with that mode at the start decides who relaxes first. The shared math also splits thermal change into parts that keep and break symmetry. Disparate puzzles turn out to be one pattern.
arxiv-2507-17076:
Juan Ardila-Garcia, Juan Sierra-Jaraba, and Herbert Vinck-Posada weigh three pulse plans for quantum light makers in 2025. Short laser pulses set emitter states, and the glow must split clean from the drive light. Plans in view are plain swings, slow-pass flips, and a notch-cut slow-pass form.

Maps of safe zones come first in a closed frame, then glow spectra are worked out with wear in play. All three plans can make the same clean, sharp photons. The notch form alone pairs flip strength with built-in glow split, a lead for next light sources.
arxiv-2507-17476:
Alexander Fabbri and co-authors build a reasoning test for language models that starts in other languages instead of translating English items, in work from 2025. English benchmarks grow fast, but translated tests carry English culture in their bones. Fair multilingual checks need native material.

Native speakers wrote over one thousand questions in French, Spanish, and Chinese. Four kinds appear: language-specific word logic, wordplay and riddles, culture and tradition, and math dressed in local life. For two kinds, hand translations into English allow a direct cross-language score gap check. The set is pitched as hard on purpose. Results can show where a model's skill is English-deep only.
arxiv-2507-17676:
Sandip Aryal, Enrique Batista, and Gaoxue Wang compute how stray atoms affect germanium detectors, in a 2025 paper. Pure germanium detectors read particle events with fine energy detail, which makes them prized for rare-event hunts such as neutrinoless double beta decay. Flaws in the crystal can trap charge, blur that detail, and weaken the detector.

Using a refined form of density functional theory, the team weighed which flaws form most easily. Phosphorus, arsenic, and antimony enter the crystal readily and make shallow traps near the band edge, unlike nitrogen, which makes deep traps. The added atoms can also pair with missing-atom flaws to form deep traps of their own. The results name which flaws most hurt detector output.
arxiv-2507-17776:
Jie Fan builds a formal logic for a layered kind of not-knowing made famous by a public remark about unknown unknowns. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. In logic terms, Rumsfeld ignorance means not knowing, and not knowing that you do not know. A recent paper by Kit Fine drew striking results about such states.

Fan notes a snag: in Fine's setup, Rumsfeld ignorance can be defined from plain ignorance, which makes some results too easy. The fix is to let the two hidden knowledge links differ, with one a subset of the other. That change keeps most of Fine's valid claims while blocking the shortcut. Fan then gives full rule sets for the logic over several classes of frames. The framework is used to recheck Fine's results one by one.
arxiv-2507-17876:
Rıza Özçelik, Sarah de Ruiter, and Francesca Grisoni flipped molecule design on its head in 2025. Chemists want new molecules with good traits, but examples of good molecules are scarce, while poor examples abound. Training only on rare winners wastes most available data.

Their trick trains a generator on the plentiful poor examples to learn which way in model space means worse. Then they steer the model the opposite way to create good designs, with no winner examples needed. Across dozens of design tests with small molecules and proteins, the reversed models made more varied and more successful candidates than winner-trained ones. The method also handled two goals at once and few-shot jobs well.
arxiv-2507-17976:
Maria Vlachou studies how to spot, in advance, when a chat-based image search will fail to find what the user wants. Her paper appeared in twenty twenty-five. In this task, a user views a shown image, gives word feedback, and hopes the next turn brings the right item. If the item is not in stock, more turns just waste time and raise stress.

Vlachou builds tools that read the top shown items turn by turn and flag likely fails. Tests used shoe and dress data sets, with two fail types split apart. Flags worked well when the system itself was at fault. Flags worked less well when the item was simply not in stock.
arxiv-2507-18076:
Haomin Qi and co-authors test cheap ways to fine-tune large language models, in a 2025 paper. Full fine-tuning strains memory and time, so lean methods train only a small add-on. The study weighs known add-ons, among them LoRA and BOFT, and adds two fresh twists. One twist mixes two add-ons layer by layer, steered by each layer's gradient size.

The hybrid reached close to full fine-tuning quality across test suites for language, math, chat, and code. It cut training time to about half and peak memory by nearly half as well. A second twist borrows unitary tricks from recurrent networks to steady the gradients in Transformers. The team also ran a small test on low-resource tongues with few examples per tongue. Gains held there too, which the authors call a path to wider access.
arxiv-2507-18376:
Farms generate too few labeled photos to train good vision models, and diffusion models, the generators behind modern image AI, may fill the gap. Xing Hu and co-authors review their use across smart farming in this 2025 paper.

The survey covers disease and pest spotting, sharpening satellite views, forecasting crop growth, and managing resources. Diffusion models beat the older generator style on stability and image quality, and they shine at making training data where little exists. Heavy computing needs and shaky transfer between regions remain the main brakes. The authors see steady real-world gains as the tools mature.
arxiv-2507-18876:
Hybrid control trials add outside control patients to a randomized trial, but the shortcut rests on a strong assumption: that the two control groups are comparable once measured traits are accounted for. Alissa Gordon and co-authors study what happens when that assumption fails. They treat the failure as omitted-variable bias and build a sensitivity analysis for the standard doubly robust estimator used in such trials.

Their method gives sharp bounds on the bias that unmeasured traits could cause, expressed through two sensitivity parameters describing how much those traits could explain. For any chosen values, it produces valid bounds and contour plots showing how strong hidden confounding must be to overturn a finding. Simulations show the bounds hold, error control is restored, and power gains survive moderate violations. The team illustrates the approach on a phase three diabetes trial and offers design guidance.
arxiv-2507-18976:
Costanza Conti, Sergio López-Ureña, and Dionisio Yáñez design refinement rules for noisy data on triangle meshes. Their 2025 paper builds subdivision schemes that fit a tilted plane through nearby points with weighted least squares. The fit smooths noise while the mesh doubles in detail.

The rules work on any triangle grid, even ones with odd vertices. The team proves the schemes copy simple shapes exactly, approach data at the right rate, and clean noise as promised. On some regular grids they also prove convergence. Tests matched strong regression methods. The subdivision form adds a multiresolution bonus for geometry work.
arxiv-2507-19176:
Weijun Chen and co-authors design a language where every program runs in feasible time in a 2025 paper. Checking that code halts fast enough is a classic hard chore in verification. Instead of checking after the fact, their language bakes the limit into its type system.

Two directions form the core claim about the language. Every program it accepts is guaranteed to finish in polynomial time. And every problem solvable in that time can be written in the language. Proving that match is far from trivial, the authors stress. A language with built-in limits could streamline how feasible software is certified.
arxiv-2507-19276:
Zibo Wu, Bohan Zhang, Wei-Hai Fang, and Zhendong Li mix tensor networks with neural networks for quantum chemistry in this 2025 paper. Neural network quantum states are flexible tools for many-body problems, but molecules have proved harder than simple models.

The authors add three ideas. Two hybrid state forms ease starting problems and add expressiveness, one built on graph recurrent networks and one inspired by Boltzmann machines. A semi-stochastic method then cuts the cost of energy evaluation while keeping accuracy high. The combined approach reached chemical accuracy on hard test systems, including a fifty atom hydrogen chain and an iron-sulfur cluster. The work widens what these states can handle.
arxiv-2507-19576:
Byungmin Kang and Patrick Lee propose a resonance test for a quantum spin liquid. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, targets kagome antiferromagnets, magnets on a corner-shared triangle lattice. Spin liquids hide fraction-like excitations called spinons, which carry no charge. Normal resonance couples to charge, so spinons seem out of reach.

Two paths let an outside field still stir the spinons. One works through the emergent fields that spinons do feel. The team computes the absorption for Dirac-type spinons in Landau levels. Per layer the signal is small, but no skin depth limits the stack. A named new material could give a signal on par with graphene.
arxiv-2507-19676:
Brown and Wolynes extend a leading theory of glasses to network liquids in a 2025 physics paper. The random first order transition theory explains how the motion and heat behavior of glass-forming liquids track together across many materials. It also offers a route to compute slowing dynamics from microscopic forces.

Network liquids, held together by long-lived covalent bonds, pose a harder case. Breaking a bond and rearranging many particles cost competing amounts of energy. The authors show microscopic calculations for this class, helping explain why bonded liquids such as silica freeze into glass the way they do.
arxiv-2507-19876:
Quantum chemists use the random phase approximation to estimate how electrons correlate, but systems needing several reference states have lacked a unified treatment. Wang, Fang, and Li extend a diagram framework so that single-reference and multi-reference versions of two more variants fall out of one set of equations. The two variants work in the particle-hole channel with exchange and in the particle-particle channel.

Tests on sample systems show a pattern: particle-hole versions overshoot the true correlation energy while the particle-particle version undershoots it. Error cancellation between second and third orders proves key in both. The authors suggest merging the two channels for better accuracy.
arxiv-2507-20076:
A conjecture by Colliot-Thélène predicts the shape of a certain algebraic group attached to smooth projective surfaces over p-adic fields. The part the Albanese map misses should split into a divisible piece and a finite piece. Evangelia Gazaki and Jitendra Rathore prove the conjecture travels along maps: if a surface dominating another satisfies it over every finite extension of the base field, so does the surface below.

Building on earlier work, they settle the conjecture for surfaces geometrically dominated by products of curves, under assumptions about the reduction of the relevant Jacobians. Their method swaps the classical Chow group for Suslin's singular homology on open parts of the surface. The paper appears in 2025.
arxiv-2507-20176: Yan Ning, Xing Wang, and Daowei Lu link three group algebra structures in a short note from 2025. Hopf group braces, post Hopf group algebras, and Rota-Baxter Hopf group algebras extend three classic Hopf ideas to the group graded setting. Under a cocommutative rule, the first two forms can be built from each other in both directions. Rota-Baxter versions then yield brace forms by a direct step. The note maps those bridges so later work can move results across the three frames with care.
arxiv-2507-20276:
Donatella Iacono and Marco Manetti build in 2025 the algebraic machinery that governs how a geometric space, a sheaf on it, and a chosen section can all deform together. Deformation problems ask which tiny changes to a structure stay consistent. Triples of this kind appear across modern geometry, yet a single controller for all three parts was missing.

A differential graded Lie algebra is shown to steer the joint deformations, encoding both the allowed changes and their obstructions. The pair then apply the machinery to pairs of a variety and a divisor, a classic test case. Such control algebras let geometers compute, rather than guess, how families of spaces and their extra data can bend.
arxiv-2507-20876:
Aleksei Bykov and Ekaterina Sysoeva find a hidden modular pattern in the exact answer of a supersymmetric gauge theory. Their 2025 paper studies the instanton partition function of a theory with maximal flavor symmetry, where computing term by term across all instanton numbers is hopeless. A recurrence relation would generate the whole series from a seed.

The obstacle is the partition function's behavior when the Higgs field's expectation value grows large. Using saddle point analysis and a character technique, they show the function is governed by the quantum Seiberg-Witten curves, up to a constant. With that anchor, the recurrence closes, and the effective infrared coupling falls out: it is the inverse of a modular function for a certain triangle group. Such results turn infinite computations into finite ones, and keep revealing that quantum field theory's answers speak modular arithmetic.
arxiv-2507-20976:
Spotting cars from the air helps traffic watch and city planning, but a detector trained in one place often fails in another. Xiao Fang and co-authors tackle that drop in a 2025 paper. Light, layout, road style, and car types all shift between regions, and those shifts drag scores down. Their fix uses AI-made aerial images, with labels, to widen the training set.

A multi-stage transfer framework fine-tunes image-making models to close the gap between source and target areas. Tests across many aerial domains showed steady gains over several rival methods. Gains ranged from a few points to more than half again on one rival class. The team also adds two new test sets to the field. The work suits defense and civic uses alike.
arxiv-2507-21176:
Farzana Islam Adiba and Rahmatollah Beheshti present a method for revealing subtle biases in medical language models, in a paper from 2025. Models used in care can carry unfair patterns that harm decisions. Those patterns are often hidden and hard to trigger with plain test questions.

Their framework pairs knowledge graphs with helper models that act as agents. Adversarial prompts are crafted to provoke biased answers, in the style of red teaming. The graph structure lets the tests trace multi-step links between concepts, so complex bias patterns surface. Trials covered three datasets, six models, and five bias types. The method revealed more of the hidden bias, and at larger scale, than common approaches. The aim is to find flaws before clinical use.
arxiv-2507-21576:
Some control problems scale neatly: stretch the state and the controls stretch the same way. Ying Hu, Xiaomin Shi, and Zuo Quan Xu study optimal control of such homogeneous stochastic systems in 2025, with controls confined to a cone and costs that need not be quadratic.

As in the classic linear-quadratic case, the answers run through backward stochastic differential equations, here a new, highly nonlinear family. The authors prove those equations have exactly one solution under three different condition sets, using truncation and log transforms as tools. Feedback formulas for the optimal controls and value then fall out of the solutions. The framework recovers many known linear-quadratic results, standard and singular, as special cases.
arxiv-2507-21676:
Mohsen Abedi and three co-authors work out how many access points a high-speed wireless site needs, and where to put them, so each user keeps a clear line of sight. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

New bands give huge speed, more users, and sharp place sense. But their signals fade fast when the line of sight is blocked, and stray paths are weak. The site here is one where blocks sit at chance places and can move. The team casts the place as a graph, whose nodes are small cells of ground. On that base they seek the least count of points, in the best spots, that keeps the line of sight sure.
arxiv-2507-21776:
Masoud Sadeghian, Angel Lozano, and Gabor Fodor find a ceiling on what a reconfigurable intelligent surface can do for a wireless link when it is tuned only on statistics. These surfaces, walls of adjustable reflectors, bounce signals toward receivers. Tuning them slowly, from channel averages rather than instant measurements, saves overhead. The intuition is that more elements should mean more gain.

The paper shows the intuition half fails. The power a surface can capture does grow in step with its element count. The beamforming gain on re-radiation, though, saturates quickly as elements are added, across a wide family of signal spread patterns. How fast the gain flattens is set by how quickly the incoming power decays across angles. The authors spell out what this limit means for realistic surface deployments.
arxiv-2507-21876:
Raeed Mundow and Adi Nusser compare a neural network with a classic statistical method for weighing galaxy clusters, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Cluster mass is a key cosmic quantity, yet the galaxies around a cluster mix members with stray passers-by that fool simple counts.

The network, an autoencoder with convolutional layers, learned from mock galaxy catalogs. The classic method assumes clusters of like mass share one galaxy pattern. Tested on simulated clusters, the network's mass guesses scattered about a third less than the classic method's when using galaxy positions. It also won with velocity-based inputs, despite a bias that distorts distant samples. The authors present machine learning as the sharper scale for clusters.
arxiv-2507-21976:
Tanvir Khan, Aranya Saha, Ismam Swapnil, and Mohammad Haque wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It tests ways to shrink large multimodal language models, which read both images and text, so they can run on modest hardware in medical settings.

Big models are costly to run, a real barrier in clinics. The team fine-tuned a vision-language model for medical use, then pruned parts of it and rounded its numbers down with care for which parts matter most. They also add a new way to pick which layers to prune. The squeezed seven-billion-parameter model fits in four gigabytes of graphics memory, a seventy percent saving. It also scored slightly higher than models shrunk by older methods at the same size. The paper maps the trade-offs of a prune, fine-tune, then quantize pipeline.
arxiv-2507-22076:
Mohammad Abdul Hafeez Khan and co-authors refine the text prompt of an image making model at the time of use, in a loop that needs no new training of the model. Such models are touchy: a small change in the words can give a wrong or shaky image.

Each round, a large model that can see reads the fresh image next to the user's words. It spots what is off, like a missing object or a wrong trait, and writes a better prompt grounded in the real world. The loop runs again until the image fits. Tests across data sets show gains in fit and in how well the image hangs together.
arxiv-2507-22176:
Avrachenkov and Freidovich estimate slopes from coarse, uneven, noisy samples with a likelihood and spline method, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Many sensors report rarely and at irregular times, with noise on each read. Finding the rate of change from such data is hard. Classic observers struggle when sampling is coarse and noise is high.

Their estimator caps the size of a higher slope to keep fits stable. The solution takes the form of a smooth spline curve. A fresh parameterization yields fast online updates as data arrive.
