Two variants trade smoothness against computing speed. Simulations beat high-gain observers and twisting methods under coarse, noisy sampling. The gain helps systems that cannot sample faster.
arxiv-2507-22376:
Byeongsu Yang and co-authors lay out an experiment, RENE, built to hunt a ghost particle that may not exist. The quarry is a sterile neutrino, a shy cousin of known particles that would explain odd reactor readings. Their 2025 report covers the detector build, the simulation work, and what the team hopes to see.

The detector sits by a power reactor, whose flood of antineutrinos gives the hunt its raw stream. Past hunts have ruled out parts of the map where the ghost could hide. Two joint studies hint the ghost may lurk in spots still open. RENE aims its search at just those spots. The paper gives the full technical base for the run, from parts to forecasts.
arxiv-2507-22476: Dow and Guzmán present a 2025 set theory paper on covering the remainder of the natural numbers with thin P-sets. The setting is the Cohen model, built by adding Cohen reals to a universe where the continuum hypothesis holds. The theorem says that when fewer than a certain large count of such reals are added, no family of nowhere dense P-sets covers that remainder space. A matching form of the result guarantees an ultrafilter on the natural numbers that holds no tower inside it.
arxiv-2507-22776:
Tim Flühmann and co-authors tackle how to judge a medical AI's accuracy when no labeled answers exist for new data, in this 2025 paper. Hospitals need to watch model performance after deployment, yet fresh scans rarely come with truth labels. Older tricks infer accuracy from the model's own confidence scores. The team extends those tricks to estimate the full confusion matrix, not just one score.

They test the methods on chest X-rays under real site shifts and under simulated shifts in scan style and disease rates. The matrix estimates tracked clinically relevant counts well on real shifts. Simulated shifts exposed failure modes in current techniques. The authors warn that monitoring tools must be matched to the true deployment setting before use in safety oversight.
arxiv-2507-23376: Alice Miller, Ivaylo Valkov, and R. Julian Abel solve scheduling puzzles with design theory, in a 2025 paper. The Social Golfer Problem asks how to split golfers into weekly groups so no pair repeats across weeks. A variant allows group sizes that sit side by side. The authors build optimal schedules from resolvable designs, balanced block designs, and latin squares and rectangles. A general algorithm finds an optimal solution for any setup. Full solution sets cover fields of up to one hundred fifty players.
arxiv-2507-23476:
Shuochong Han and co-authors test how the changed odds of two nucleons colliding inside dense nuclear matter steer the outcome of heavy-ion crashes. Their 2025 paper uses a transport model that tracks each nucleon as two nuclei smash. The collision odds in the medium come from a many-body theory, not a free-space table.

The team reads a slate of signals: how much the nuclei stop each other, the balance of neutrons to protons, flow gaps between particle kinds, and how many pions fly out. Bigger in-medium odds mostly boost free nucleon spray and stopping. The mass shift of nucleons in the medium cuts the other way and rules the outcome. The authors warn that the bounce size and pair speed matter too, and that stopping is the most touchy signal.
arxiv-2507-23576:
Michael Li and co-authors explain a synapse that learns a thousand times too fast in a 2025 theory paper. Electrochemical synapses store memory as ion counts in a channel; conductance reads the count. Textbook wisdom said slow ion drift should cap the switching speed.

One proton device broke that cap, switching linearly in nanoseconds. The authors show the trick is control of the interface where electrolyte meets the tungsten oxide channel. Past studies differed in the channel's crystallinity, which reshaped its thermodynamics. A multiphase polarization picture then explains the linear, symmetric updates. The result points device builders at interface engineering, not faster ions, as the lever for brain-like memory chips.
arxiv-2507-23776:
Yunxiang Yan, Tomohiro Sawada, and Kartik Goyal propose a staged way to test the problem-solving skill of language models in a 2025 paper. Standard question tests grade only the final answer, which is a rough proxy for the thinking behind it. A model can guess right for wrong reasons, or fail despite sound steps.

Their frame reveals a question in stages, each stage adding part of the facts. At each stage the model answers, exposing how its reasoning builds as facts arrive. Across varied reasoning and knowledge test sets, the staged grades separated models more sharply than plain test scores did. The staged prompts also drew out better step-by-step traces from the models. The method keeps the scale and automation of standard tests.
arxiv-2508-00076:
Sarah Barbosa and co-authors train a neural network to read the air of distant Earth-like planets from their reflected light, preparing for a future flagship telescope. Their paper appeared in 2025. They generated nearly one hundred ten thousand synthetic spectra for planets with atmospheres like Earth's three great eras: early, middle, and modern. The network learned to recover gas amounts under two telescope designs, with noise and model variation separated.

Oxygen recovery faltered for the middle era's thin air, and methane read reliably only when plentiful. One ultraviolet band pinned modern ozone almost perfectly. The network leaned mostly on visible light, with the ultraviolet decisive for ozone and the infrared for methane and carbon dioxide. Skill faded past about 1.7 micrometers, a design hint for the telescope.
arxiv-2508-00376:
Cassiopeia A is the wreck of a star that blew up centuries ago, and its jets carry matter forged deep inside the star. Vincenzo Sapienza and co-authors study one jet in a 2025 paper using X-ray data from the Chandra observatory.

The team focused on three finger-like parts of the northeast jet. One spot held the highest ratio of chromium to iron yet seen in the wreck, a clue that it came from a deep layer where silicon burned fully. The three fingers differ in makeup and motion; one moves toward Earth at high speed. Mixing of layers is needed to explain the mix. The findings show how unevenly a star can throw its deepest matter into space.
arxiv-2508-00476:
Jeongwoo Kang and co-authors document a system in 2025 for answering questions from meeting transcripts. The work was a submission to a shared task on automatic minuting. Their approach combines retrieval-augmented generation with abstract meaning representations of the transcript text.

Three system variants mix the two approaches in different ways. Adding meaning representations gave high-quality answers for about a third of questions. Gains were notable for questions that require telling speakers apart, such as who said what. The team reports results from the shared task evaluation at a 2025 workshop.
arxiv-2508-00776:
Dieter van Melkebeek shows how simple greedy rules can grow out of full planning tables for classic tasks. His 2025 paper treats three schoolbook cases: picking time slots, filling a knapsack, and finding short paths. In each case a general dynamic program solves all inputs, while a greedy rule solves a narrowed case.

By unfolding the core equations step by step and using plain monotonic facts, the greedy choice falls out on its own. One case even flips its sort order, from first start to first finish, along the way. The author offers the route as a clean way to teach these rules and prove them right in class. No new algorithm is claimed; the value lies in the shared logic.
arxiv-2508-00976:
Yjan Gordon and co-authors census flickering radio sources in the sky in a 2025 paper. Many cosmic objects vary in radio brightness over a few years. Two passes of a large sky survey, years apart, let them count the changers. Thousands of compact sources shifted clearly between the two passes.

Brighter sources varied more often than faint ones in the census. Most changers matched the known profile of blazars and quasars. Blazars also produced the largest absolute swings in brightness. Sources inside our own galaxy showed the largest swings relative to their size.
arxiv-2508-01176: A sharper shape-aware bound for a classic function inequality is proven by Youjiang Lin, Jinghong Zhou, and Jiaming Lan in a 2025 paper. The Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality caps how two functions can interact through a decaying kernel. Their affine version covers two different functions at once and beats the classic bound. Reverse forms of the new bounds hold for log-concave functions. Affine upgrades matter since they stay unchanged under volume-preserving shape stretches, which sharpens use in shape analysis.
arxiv-2508-01376:
Gustavo Diniz, Silvio Quintino, and Vivian França review how electrons move through a single quantum dot, from gentle flows to far-from-equilibrium drives, in a 2025 paper. Quantum dots, tiny islands that hold a few electrons, display rich effects like the Kondo phenomenon, where electrons act in concert. Calm, near-equilibrium behavior is well charted by established methods.

Pushed hard, though, dots enter regimes where strong correlations and fast dynamics tangle, and simple theory fails. The review gathers newer tools built for that frontier, including nonequilibrium Green's functions and time-dependent simulation methods, alongside lab advances in fabrication and measurement. The authors close with open problems and prospects for devices that exploit these effects.
arxiv-2508-01576:
Jeanelle Dao and Jadelynn Dao present a smartwatch, in a 2025 preprint, that alerts deaf and hard-of-hearing wearers when their name is spoken. Hundreds of millions of people live with serious hearing loss. Catching a spoken name in a busy room is a daily problem for them. Their device, Lumename, listens on the watch itself and answers with vibration plus a visual signal. The model must be tiny and quick on cheap hardware.

Training data was the bottleneck, since one user's voice samples are few. The authors reshaped those samples with audio tricks to mimic other ages and voices. A search over model settings found a compact design with low power use. The finished watch ran on an Arduino-based board. Its name detection stayed above ninety percent accurate. The paper frames the device as a low-cost aid that works without a phone or cloud link.
arxiv-2508-01676:
Shai Kimhi, Avi Mendelson, and Moshe Kimhi map in 2025 where small adversarial patches hurt vision models most. A patch covering two percent of an image can flip a confident label. Where the patch sits may matter as much as what it shows.

Their benchmark, PatchMap, runs over 150 million forward passes across ImageNet validation images. Hot spots emerge where patches reliably tank confidence. A simple trick uses segmentation masks to place patches on weak regions, with no gradient queries at all. Attack success rises eight to thirteen points over random or fixed spots across five model types. The full map is slated for public release to spur location-aware defenses.
arxiv-2508-02176:
Andrew Tropin, in a solo paper from twenty twenty-five, built a test library for live coding setups. Such setups let a coder grow a program without pause, with fast checks of guesses. But tests are oft run apart, by command line, cut off from live tools like debuggers and value views. Coarse runs and lost context slow the loop and break focus.

Tropin's library gives tests a runtime form inside the live setup. On failure, the coder gets the full tool kit at the fail point at once. Workflows built on it rerun tests in less than a second. Readers who build code tools learn how to keep test speed inside the flow state that live coding sells.
arxiv-2508-02276:
Xiangru Tang and a large team build CellForge, a crew of smart agents that design models of how single cells react to change. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Told how a cell will act when its genes or drugs shift is a core task in disease work. It needs skill from many fields at once. CellForge takes a data set and a task, reads the past work, parses the data, and finds past models to beat. Its agents, each with a bent for data, cell life, or deep learning, then shape a model plan through talks checked by a critic. The aim is a plan that can be run and tested, not just a claim on paper.
arxiv-2508-02376:
Matus Krajcovic, Peter Demcak, and Eduard Kuric test, in a 2025 preprint, whether a lifelike virtual person can run an online survey better than a chatbot. Text surveys suffer from careless, skimpy answers, since no one feels present. The authors built a tool that puts a photorealistic avatar into a survey. It speaks, listens by speech recognition, and converses through a language model. Eighty British participants took psychometric surveys one of two ways: talking with the avatar or typing to a chatbot.

Over two thousand responses were collected. Avatar interviews drew more informative, detailed answers than the chatbot. Engagement ran higher yet took less time. Satisfaction, though, did not clearly improve. Interviews blamed taste, pauses in turn-taking, and unease at near-human faces. The authors read the results as a promise: survey talk with embodied agents feels closer to a real interview, if the rough edges are smoothed.
arxiv-2508-02576:
Nicolás Kurtovic and co-authors use a space telescope to read the warm glow of disks around three young pairs of stars. Their 2025 paper, part of the MINDS program, splits the light of each primary and companion disk. The aim is to see how having a stellar partner shapes the chemistry and physics of a disk's inner zone. Past telescope data on the same systems give a base to spot change over time.

Primary disks shone rich in water lines, while companion disks were mostly bare of lines. One primary's line glow had swung a lot since past reads, and another's base glow had too. All three systems showed jets, and some showed spread gas likely stirred by flows and close passes.
arxiv-2508-02776:
Low-mass dark matter haloes are a sharp test of what dark matter is, and strongly lensed arcs can reveal them through tiny bends in the light. Earlier work reported such haloes in ALMA observations of SDP.81, a lensed dusty star-forming galaxy. The authors reanalyze those data to check how sturdy the claims are. They find the data do support extra angular structure in the lens mass beyond a smooth elliptical profile.

But they find no evidence for the two previously reported sub-halo detections. Mock data show they would have caught a reported halo of about a billion solar masses if it were real. Testing systematics, they conclude the earlier claim was likely spurious, caused by a smooth model that fit the multipole structure poorly. They urge future searches to include multipoles up to fourth order and to demand a well-fitting smooth model first.
arxiv-2508-02876:
Binder, Lazarus, Thoresen, Laycock, and Bhattacharya chart X-ray binaries in a nearby dwarf galaxy over two decades in a 2025 paper. Chandra telescope observations of the starburst galaxy IC 10 were combined. Its massive binary systems shine in X-rays.

A couple dozen likely binaries were catalogued inside the galaxy's bright region. Their flare ranges and duty cycles fit a young population fed by supergiant stars. Brighter systems stayed on more persistently than fainter ones. Variability ran stronger than in comparable Milky Way systems, perhaps due to lower metal content. Foreground stars were weeded out with parallax data. The resulting luminosity function implied a recent burst of star formation. The galaxy's history is read from its binaries.
arxiv-2508-02976:
Hanwen Ren, Ruiqi Ni, and Ahmed H. Qureshi presented a method in twenty twenty-five that helps robots move objects to a target pose in cluttered rooms. Robots in warehouses and hospitals need this skill, but older methods are slow, need expert demos, or learn by trial and error. The team's method uses a neural network shaped by physics rules.

The network learns to solve the Eikonal equation, which gives the fastest path time through a space. No expert data is needed. While moving an object, the robot can also change its grip on the fly when the plan calls for it. Tests in simulation and on a real robot beat leading rivals on planning time, path length, and success rate across many objects.
arxiv-2508-03076:
Sylvain Attan and Nabil Oro Djibril build a cohomology theory for pre-Jacobi-Jordan algebras in this 2025 paper. These algebras twist a classic structure with a weaker identity. Cohomology is the bookkeeping tool that classifies how such structures can bend.

With the theory in hand, the pair study straight-line deformations of the algebras. They also define a special operator named after Nijenhuis for this setting. Bending an algebra along that operator turns out to change nothing essential. Such triviality results tidy the landscape of possible deformations. Pure algebra papers like this lay track for later geometry and physics. The new cohomology gives others a ready tool to reuse.
arxiv-2508-03276:
Terra Blevins, Susanne Schmalwieser, and Benjamin Roth ask if language models bend their style toward the user they talk with. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. In human talk, people tend to match each other's words and tone. Whether models do the same, and by the same means, was not well tested.

They set model replies to real dialogues next to the true human replies, across many models and three dialogue sets. Models match the talk style strongly, in fact more than humans do. The match shifts by trait. Tuned and larger models bend less than raw and smaller ones. The authors doubt the same inner drive lies behind human and model acts.
arxiv-2508-03376:
Jun Wu and colleagues introduced a quantum computing method in 2025 called CutVQA. Today's quantum machines have too few qubits for many useful tasks. One workaround cuts a large circuit into small parts that fit, but stitching the parts back together can demand a huge number of repeat runs.

CutVQA searches for good circuit designs with the cuts already in mind, then tunes each small part on its own. On two standard test tasks it matched the accuracy of full circuits. At the same time it cut the repeat-run cost by a very large factor and at least halved training time. The work shows design and cutting work best together.
arxiv-2508-03876:
Zach Cutler and co-authors present a full framework for online user studies of data displays in 2025, using the byline given in the text head. Such studies are common in visualization research. Running them well is still a heavy load. Past tools cover only parts of the life cycle, or make repeat runs hard.

Their system, called reVISit 2, spans design, pilot, data gathering, analysis, and sharing. It can replay each person's actions for review. A support community is part of the design. The system has served in published quality studies. The team shows this through repeat runs of past experiments. They also reflect on design through interviews and a tech review.
arxiv-2508-04376:
Eva Gallardo-Gutiérrez and Javier González-Doña wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five. It studies local spectral traits of operators built by subordinating a semigroup, a flow of operators over time, against a measure.

The authors show such an operator lacks the single valued extension property, and that its local spectral subspaces are dense, while the adjoint has the Dunford property and trivial subspaces. They then apply this to the classic Cesàro operator on Hardy spaces, where the local spectrum at any non-zero function matches the full spectrum. A last part treats semigroups of composition operators, where the traits hinge on the shape of the linked Koenigs domain.
arxiv-2508-04876:
Patrick Bieker wrote a mathematics paper in 2025 on shapes known as Schubert varieties inside twisted affine Grassmannians. These shapes arise in the study of groups and their symmetries. The central question is when such a shape counts as normal, a basic test of how smooth and well behaved it is. The paper works in the tamely ramified case.

Bieker proves a test for normality based on the size of a key group tied to a smaller subgroup. He then applies the test to local models in two settings, one with equal and one with mixed type. The result sorts which Pappas-Zhu local models are normal in the cases covered.
arxiv-2508-04976:
Sakib, Hu, and Abdelzaher extend a way to fit sharp object finding into the tight time and compute bounds of small edge machines. Their paper, from two thousand twenty-five, is called CSRAP.

The past way gathers the parts of a frame that count into a small canvas, which can be worked at the needed rate. The new way lets the canvas change size, and lets its rate part from the rate of the source frames. The team runs a known finder on a small board, over road video from a known set. The new freedoms give a better trade of quality for cost at each point. That means a higher mean quality for the same spend.
arxiv-2508-05176:
Designing a wiretap code means knowing how much information leaks to an eavesdropper. Guessing wrong in either direction is costly: too low, and secrecy fails; too high, and the system wastes capacity. The authors build a neural estimator for that leakage, improving a contrastive bound framework for both discrete and continuous signals. Their estimator uses a mixture of Bernoulli experts, each a small neural network, so it can handle systems that apply complex processing such as universal hash families.

Older estimators, they show, badly understate leakage once hashing is used at longer blocklengths. Their method stays reliable up to a blocklength of 255, and they argue it should scale further with more training data and bigger models. They also show how to turn the estimator around and design the hash family itself with it. The authors offer the package as a practical tool for physical-layer security design.
arxiv-2508-05276:
Phone firewalls block much scam traffic, but the texts that slip through are the ones that reach people. Agarwal, Suarez-Tangil, and Vasek worked with a major mobile operator to study 1.35 million user reports sent in over four months, asking what gets past the filters. Most reports, about 89 percent, were text messages, with the rest split between odd calls and links.

Sorting the unique texts, the team classed about 35 percent as spam and 40 percent as outright scams, then split the scams into 12 types led by wrong-number cons. The study also maps the phone and hosting services scammers lean on, and reads the lure texts closely to show how victims are pushed to hand over money or details.
arxiv-2508-05476:
Chaohui Gong, Zhiying Wu, and four peers make CT-like scans from MR scans by joining two kinds of MR views. The work came out in 2025. Fake CT scans spare sick folks the rays of a real CT scan. They also dodge some blur from moves. That makes them of use when staff plan care.

Most past ways worked from one MR view at a time. This way, MM2CT, joins T1-weighted and T2-weighted scans. Those two views light up not-quite-the-same flesh. Its core is a Mamba build, picked since it tracks wide links at low cost. That cost is less than big shift-based builds need. A small shift step adds fine grain work. The parts join traits from both views while they keep place links whole. The aim is a fake CT true enough for real care work.
arxiv-2508-05976:
Zhihao Zhu and four co-authors teach robots to connect what an object looks like with what it is for, in a 2025 paper. A robot needs to know both the shape of a tool and which part to grip or press. Vision-language models can guess such uses, but their guesses float free of exact geometry and often rely on hand labeling.

Their framework, called PASG, works in a loop. It pulls basic shapes, key points, and axes out of images on its own, then asks a vision-language model to anchor those shapes to uses and task words. The team also built a test set for this skill and fine-tuned a model on it. In real robot tasks across varied scenes, the system matched the quality of hand-labeled guidance, which the authors offer as a bridge between geometry and meaning.
arxiv-2508-06176:
Marco Bertuletti and co-authors design a many core chip for 5G base stations in a 2025 paper. New radio links push base station math loads up while power and delay caps stay tight. Software defined gear must chew tens of gigabits a second under ten watts and stay easy to reprogram.

Their cluster packs 1024 lean RISC-V cores with float units tuned for radio work and a shared memory block. It handles the uplink shared channel at rates well past the bar for high end cells. Speeds on core tasks beat custom rival chips ten fold, and energy per bit stays in the same league on a routed 12 nanometer build.
arxiv-2508-06276:
Juan Heredia, Christian Schlette, and Mikkel Baun Kjærgaard release EcBot, an open MATLAB library that learns how much power a robot arm uses, in a 2025 paper. Older power models were mostly checked on heavy industrial robots and often miss the mark. EcBot builds its model from real running data instead.

The user supplies the arm's geometry, link masses, and centers of mass, plus logged joint motion and power traces. The library then fits a data-driven model automatically. Tests on four light robots from three makers gave errors of only a few watts on both training and fresh data. The authors offer the tool for energy-aware planning and greener automation.
arxiv-2508-06676:
Watermarks let model owners prove a neural network is theirs, but a new network family breaks the usual tricks. Chia-Hsun Lu and co-authors design a watermark made for Kolmogorov-Arnold networks in a 2025 paper.

These networks learn their own activation curves, which is exactly where the new method hides its mark. It perturbs activation outputs through a frequency transform, leaving the model's task behavior almost untouched. Because the mark rides on activations rather than task data, it works across many uses. In tests, the mark survived fine-tuning, pruning, and retraining after pruning, the standard attacks owners fear. The authors frame the method as a guard for models shared across networked applications.
arxiv-2508-07076:
Valeria Aloisi and nine co-authors mine pattern rules to explain where forest species grow in Italy, in a paper from 2025. Knowing which species co-occur and under what climate and soil helps planning and conservation as conditions change. Rule mining, common in other fields, is new to this type of ecology work.

They merged records for many plant species across thousands of plots with climate, soil, and satellite data. A fast pattern algorithm found strong rules linking species to set bands of temperature and rain swings. One spruce showed a very strong tie to cold, highly seasonal places, which marks its narrow needs.
arxiv-2508-07276:
Shilling and co-authors find that bright radio afterglows of gamma ray bursts fade faster in a 2025 paper. The link between a burst's glow strength and its decay pace was known in light, X-rays, and high energy rays, but untested in radio.

Sixteen bursts with radio glows at a standard waveband show the tie clearly: stronger ten day glows decay faster afterward. Chance and selection were ruled out by simulation past three sigma. Slopes match those in other bands. Viewing angle and shifting microphysics are the favored explanations, now backed in radio too.
arxiv-2508-07776: Paweł Duch, Martin Hairer, Jaeyun Yi, and Wenhao Zhao wrote a paper from 2025 on the long-run behavior of a classic quantum field model in three dimensions, over all of space. They show the dynamics are well posed for all time. At high temperature, any two solutions driven by the same noise draw together at an exponential rate. That pull lets them name a single steady distribution for the system, which meets the standard axioms of a healthy field theory.
arxiv-2508-08076:
Four authors survey mixed-form entity match in a 2025 paper with test runs. Match work finds rows in split banks that name the same real thing, a base task for data joins. Banks clash in form, tongue, and sense, which the team calls the mixed case.

A two-part kind map splits form mix from sense mix for the field. FAIR rules both show the snags and hint at fixes in the frame. Tests of top tools under sense mix show firm caps that still stand. Next steps span sight-and-word match, human loops, and fair grades.
arxiv-2508-08176:
Mladen Dimitrov and Andrei Jorza construct p-adic L-functions in a 2025 math paper. These functions extend classic number theory objects into the p-adic world, where distances are measured by divisibility. Their objects attach to automorphic representations of a large matrix group that admit a special model named for Shalika. The representations are allowed a parahoric level of symmetry at every prime, a looser condition than full symmetry.

New local tools do the heavy lifting: improved functionals and test vectors that tie local integrals to the global function. A factorization formula for local coefficients, generalized from older theory, holds the proof together. The authors also build the functions in families over a geometric space. Family versions let number theorists vary the object and watch the function move.
arxiv-2508-08376:
Qi Zhang and Wen-Tao Xu prove that two distinct quantum phases can melt into each other continuously, settling a long-standing question. Their paper appeared in 2025. The phases are the toric code and the double semion, both carrying the same basic topological order yet genuinely different. Earlier work found only abrupt transitions or a phase in between. Both phases can be born from a richer parent order, so the team perturbed that parent model.

They confirm a direct continuous transition of the XY-star type, by mapping it to two coupled Ising models. At the transition, exotic parent-order particles become free, revealed by order parameters and loop measurements. The authors say the result opens a theory of phase changes beyond the standard condensation story.
arxiv-2508-08976:
Ziyi Guo and Yan Wang build a model to predict how disasters reshape commercial land use in a 2025 paper. Hurricanes and wildfires disrupt economic activity more and more, and shops and services can be hit hard because they depend on customer visits. Past models capture poorly how people and land change affect each other.

Resilient urban planning theory captures those links better. The authors design a spatio-temporal attention model based on that theory and tune it for post-disaster settings. Planners could use such models to guide aid to rebuild toward the commercial areas most likely to recover or fail.
arxiv-2508-09076:
Timothee Benard, Weikun He, and Han Zhang wrote this mathematics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five. It asks how well numbers can be approximated by rationals when the numbers are drawn from a fractal measure. Classic results by Khintchine and Schmidt settle the question for ordinary volume. This work moves it to self-similar measures in any dimension.

The bridge is a random walk on a space of lattices. The team shows the walk spreads out evenly in a strong, effective sense. New tools include a bootstrap scheme that pushes the walk past algebraic roadblocks. They also refine Dani's classic link between approximation and dynamics. Along the way they prove that self-similar measures do not clump near algebraic surfaces. The outcome extends both the yes-or-no law of Khintchine and the counting estimates of Schmidt to fractal settings.
arxiv-2508-09176:
Hazem Shalby and four co-authors present a training method that lets neural networks switch precision on the fly, in a 2025 paper. Shrinking a network's numbers to few bits saves power on small devices. Giving hard inputs more bits than easy ones is smarter still, but old methods paid a heavy toll each time they switched.

Their trick nests the numbers: a low-precision value sits inside the high-precision one, bit by bit. Switching then costs a simple shift, with no float conversion at all. A light controller picks the width for each layer at run time. The method hit top scores on standard image tests at low bit widths, pointing to faster, thriftier on-device intelligence.
arxiv-2508-09276: Andrada Pojar splits companion matrices into two special parts, in a 2025 paper. A companion matrix encodes a polynomial in a standard block form. One part is p-potent, meaning its p-th power returns itself. The other part is nilpotent, meaning some power of it vanishes. The work sits over a field of odd prime characteristic p. The claimed split holds exactly when the matrix trace is a whole multiple of the field's unit, the author proves.
arxiv-2508-09476:
Yuji Wang and co-authors tackle a weak spot of video generation in a 2025 paper: keeping a face the same person when the head turns far. The head byline names their method CoFE, short for Collaborative Face Experts Fusion, though the catalog title differs. Three expert modules inside the model each handle one part of the job.

One expert locks onto traits that stay fixed across poses, one reads broad scene meaning, and one keeps fine skin detail. The experts blend their signals as the video is built. The team also built a data pipeline that stresses large poses and steady identity, yielding 180,000 annotated clips. On standard tests, the method beat prior work on face match and image quality scores.
arxiv-2508-09576:
Laura D'Angelo, Francesco Denti, Antonio Canale, and Michele Guindani present a statistical model that reads teams of neurons from glowing calcium signals, in a 2025 paper. Calcium imaging films hundreds of neurons at once in moving animals, but the glow only hints at the spikes beneath. Their Bayesian model infers spikes and groups neurons into ensembles at the same time. Each neuron's firing odds follow a smooth hidden process, and grouping favors neighbors, matching anatomy.

A flexible prior handles the wide range of spike sizes while filtering out negligible blips. Applied to mouse hippocampus data recorded as the animal circled an arena, the model found spatially structured groups firing together. The groups shifted with the animal's position, as expected for a brain area that maps space. The authors offer the model for studies of learning, memory, and brain disorders.
arxiv-2508-09676:
Vishal Khare and co-authors built an AI helper for code review and tested it at a large firm, in a 2025 paper. Code review at the firm was slow, with waits of days before a change was picked up, checked, and closed. Long talks back and forth added to the delay.

The helper, named DeputyDev, reads the code change in context and writes a first review on its own. In a controlled test with more than two hundred engineers, review time fell by about a quarter per change. Time per line of code fell by about two fifths. After checks for odd cases, the tool was rolled out across the firm and later sold to other firms as a service.
arxiv-2508-09776:
Mahdi Dhaini and co-authors test whether explanations written by large language models can teach smaller models to classify better in this 2025 paper. Rationales that read like human reasoning help explain predictions and enrich training data. Writing them by hand is slow and costly, which limits how much training data can carry them.

Their framework asks several top language models to write the rationales automatically. Quality was scored with a suite of text measures. The team then trained classifiers with and without the machine-written notes on two reasoning benchmarks. Models fed the generated rationales performed on par with those fed human ones. The authors call this a scalable path to explanation-rich datasets. If machines can draft their own teaching notes at human quality, the cost of interpretable training data falls sharply.
arxiv-2508-09976:
Robots are starved for training data, and Marion Lepert and co-authors raid the world's supply of human videos to feed them. Their method, Masquerade, edits first-person human footage into robot demonstrations: it estimates 3D hand poses, paints out the human arms, and overlays a rendered two-armed robot tracking the same motions. Pre-training on 675,000 edited frames, then fine-tuning on just 50 real demonstrations per task, produced policies that generalized far better than prior work.

On three long kitchen tasks in unseen rooms, the system beat baselines five- to six-fold. Both the robot overlay and the co-training proved indispensable.
arxiv-2508-10176:
Shihang Liu and six co-authors use a faint radio signal from the young cosmos to bound a soft form of dark matter. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The signal comes from the dawn of stars and the age when their light lit gas anew. Its strength across scales holds facts on how mass clumped, which dark matter rules. The team runs full models of that age with the soft form's traits built in. They find the soft form cuts small clumps, which delays the key ages and makes them shorter than in the cold form. Early on, the signal's shift is ruled by the soft form's smooth spread.
arxiv-2508-10276:
Weightings sort the points of a space by layers, and a 2025 arXiv thesis by Daniel Hudson carries the theory into the world of Lie groupoids and their infinitesimal partners. He starts from weighted manifolds, adding weighted submanifolds, maps, and normal form theorems, then builds linear weightings for vector bundles.

Three equal definitions of a multiplicative weighting for a groupoid follow, through structure maps, the multiplication graph, and deformation spaces. The last chapters pass to algebroids, tie the notions to Poisson structures, and solve the lifting problem along wide subalgebras. Hudson also sorts groupoid weightings along the units by filtrations of the algebroid.
arxiv-2508-10376:
Yu Chen, Zihan Tan, and Hangyu Xu tackle an open problem in computer science in this 2025 paper. A tree cover is a small set of trees drawn over a set of points, so that some tree always gives a short route between any two points. Such covers have served graph algorithms for decades, and builders want few trees with little stretch.

For two or more trees, the best stretch anyone could build and the lowest stretch anyone could prove sat far apart. The authors narrow that gap with a stronger lower bound, proved on a simple grid-like graph. Their proof leans on fixed-point theorems from combinatorics, tools they expect will help study other tree-like structures too.
arxiv-2508-10776:
Juchan Kim, Inwoo Tae, and Yongjae Lee rethink how to build the calmest stock portfolio in a 2025 paper. The global minimum-variance mix leans wholly on how stocks move together, a matrix that must be guessed from the past. Standard guesses chase low forecast error, which need not mean good portfolios.

Their method learns the matrix with the final choice in the loop: the loss grades the portfolio, not the forecast. They derive the math for that direct grading and lean on the matrix's main axes. Wide tests show forecast-first methods can mislead, while decision-first learning gave steadier, better mixes again and again.
arxiv-2508-10876:
Karim Carrion presents a thesis from 2025 on speeding up cosmic inference for a model where dark matter and dark energy trade motion. Modern surveys map the large scale web of the universe in fine detail. Testing models beyond the standard one needs both accurate forecasts and fast ways to fit them to data.

The work focuses on a model called Dark Scattering, set by one strength value. Carrion computes its nonlinear matter pattern with a halo based method and checks it against full simulations. Effects from normal matter and from heavy neutrinos are added as well. Neural emulators, trained to mimic the slow forecasts, then speed the fitting by a factor of about ten thousand. Shear data from a large sky survey is used to bound the model.
arxiv-2508-11676:
Maksym Shamrai and Vladyslav Hamolia build a map of the world's languages from the inner weights of large language models, in work from 2025. Older maps rely on features chosen by hand by linguists. The pair instead let the model itself supply the features.

They score which weights matter most for each language, using a pruning method adapted for the task. Those scores form a vector for each language, and distances between vectors place languages in a shared space. The study covers 106 languages and several multilingual models. The map matches known language families well. It also shows surprise links that may hint at past contact between peoples or shared paths of change. Code, vectors, and a viewing tool are public.
arxiv-2508-11776:
Arpan Das and Arpan Kanrar settle an open case in brace theory in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Braces are algebraic structures tied to set-theoretic solutions of a famous equation. Recent work classified braces for several families of groups with a large cyclic subgroup; the count settled down as groups grew.

The modular maximal-cyclic family was the leftover case. The authors show these braces allow only one non-cyclic way to add elements. Unlike the earlier families, their number keeps growing with the group's order instead of stabilizing. That contrast makes the family a genuine exception. The paper closes a classification thread opened by a conjecture of Guarnieri and Vendramin.
arxiv-2508-12176:
Zhiwei Zheng and co-authors introduce a system that simulates radio signals inside computer-generated rooms with moving people, in a 2025 paper. Radio sensing can track people without cameras, which guards privacy. Real training data from varied rooms is hard to gather, though.

Their framework builds four-dimensional scenes from text prompts, with human motion guided by spatial paths rather than hand-drawn routes. A physics-based tracer keeps signal phase steady across space and time. Simulated signals matched both real recordings and a commercial solver closely. When added to training data, the fake signals improved imaging and activity recognition, with gains growing as more data was added. The authors release code for others.
arxiv-2508-12476:
Haojie Chen and Yang Yang introduce a new kind of eigenvalue in their 2025 paper on Hermitian tensors. A tensor is a grid of numbers with many indices, a step beyond a matrix. Eigenvalues are the special scale factors that reveal a tensor's core behavior, and this new type, written with a hat over the H, fits tensors with complex entries.

The authors give easy-to-check sets that must contain these values. From them, they derive tests for when a Hermitian tensor counts as positive in the math sense. They then apply the tools to a curvature question in complex geometry. Their method re-proves the algebra behind recent results by two other teams, which supports the new definitions.
arxiv-2508-12576:
Like Jian and Dong Liu analyze in 2025 how widening a neural network affects federated learning, where many clients train a shared model without sharing their data. Client data differ from each other, which makes a single global model hard to train well. The authors study the convergence of the standard averaging method when the network is overparameterized and trained by gradient descent.

They prove that the harm from data differences shrinks as width grows and vanishes in the infinite width limit. In that limit, both global and local models behave like linear models, and the federated method matches centralized learning. Experiments across architectures, losses, and training methods support the theory.
arxiv-2508-12776:
Rajabinasab and co-authors propose a forest-based method for spotting outliers without labels in this 2025 paper. Their approach grows from randomized principal component analysis, a fast approximate method. A related forest structure had already sped up nearest-neighbor search.

The new method builds a forest of these randomized projections. It derives an outlier score from the forest's own structure, with no training labels. Across several benchmark datasets, the method beat classical and recent rivals on some and matched them on the rest. The authors also stress-test its robustness and speed. They present it as an efficient, dependable choice for unsupervised outlier detection in practice.
arxiv-2508-12876:
Pieter Vanmechelen, Geert Lombaert, and Giovanni Samaey compare three ways to write down random fields in a hard inverse problem. Their 2025 paper uses the head title, which frames the task as Bayesian parameter identification in finite element elasticity; the catalog title differs in wording. The goal is to find how material traits vary across a part, from fine displacement data.

The three methods are a Karhunen-Loève expansion, a wavelet expansion, and local average subdivision. All three gave similar end estimates in a plane stress test. Yet they differed in sampling speed and cost as the grid grew finer. Local average subdivision mixed better and cost less per unit of error at fine scales, despite using more parameters.
arxiv-2508-12976:
Jan Albrecht and co-authors study uneven motion in a 2025 paper on beads pushed by living cells. Even cells with the same genes move in varied ways. Beads they carry thus move in varied ways too, and that spread is hard to measure from short, sampled paths.

A likelihood based method estimates the spread and gives honest error bounds for the estimate. It works even when data are scarce, a common case in lab films. With that tool, the team found that the spread in this system changes over time rather than staying fixed. The finding warns against treating cell driven motion as steady.
arxiv-2508-13076:
Isaiah Andrews, Jiafeng Chen, and Otavio Tecchio rethink estimation in economics in twenty twenty-five. In over-identified models, the model is usually wrong in some way. Misspecification is the norm, not the exception. Then different estimators stop being rival routes to one target. Each estimator defines its own estimand, its own answer.

The authors review recent use of generalized method of moments in a top journal. Formal specification testing is rare there, they find. Estimators that would be inefficient under a correct model are widely used, including hand-picked moments. They synthesize recent theory into guidelines for transparent, robust work. A new result shows Hansen's J-statistic measures the range of estimates reachable at a given precision. Readers get a clearer contract between method and meaning.
arxiv-2508-13176:
Simon Hosemann and co-authors ask how hard it is to fit a logical theory to example data, in this 2025 paper. Given a finite structure marked with positive and negative examples, fitting means finding an ontology or constraints that accept the good and reject the bad. The languages range over two description logics and several families of tuple-generating dependencies, the rules behind database constraints. Complexity is pinned down exactly for each.

The authors also design algorithms, measure how large the fitted theories must grow, and ask when a finite basis of rules exists for a set of structures. Fitting is the logical face of learning from examples, and exact complexity maps tell tool builders where automation is feasible and where it will bog down.
arxiv-2508-13276:
Jinhui Guo and co-authors propose a purely inelastic scalar dark matter model in a 2025 paper. Dark matter would be a light scalar particle with a slightly heavier partner. The two interact with ordinary matter only through the Higgs portal, and only in inelastic ways, which helps evade strict direct detection limits.

Joint annihilation of the pair in the early universe yields the observed dark matter abundance. The same interactions can drive a strong first order phase transition, producing gravitational waves that future observatories could detect. The heavier partner would live long enough to leave displaced muon jet signatures at a major collider.
arxiv-2508-13576:
Meng-Ping Lin and co-authors present in 2025 an end-to-end system that uses both sound and video to improve cochlear implant coding. Implants let people with severe hearing loss perceive sound, but noisy settings remain hard. Lip and face cues can help separate speech from noise.

Their system joins a speech enhancement module with an implant coding model, trained together. In simulations, the joint system raised objective speech clarity scores. A signal quality measure improved by a large margin over a standard coding strategy. The authors present the result as a step toward better implant listening in noise.
arxiv-2508-13876:
Katharina Stein and five co-authors improve a pipeline that lets language models write one program solving a whole family of planning problems, in this 2025 paper. A generalized plan is a single strategy, expressed as code, that handles every task in a domain, from any number of blocks to stack or packages to deliver. Earlier systems had the model draft a strategy in prose, then code it directly. One wrong strategic idea poisoned the result.

The new approach writes the strategy as pseudocode first, a sketch that can be machine-checked and debugged before any real program exists. A reflection step then asks the model to explain each failed plan, and several candidate programs are generated so the best can be picked. Tested on seventeen benchmark domains with two reasoning models, the repairs steadily raise the share of domains solved correctly.
arxiv-2508-13976:
Carlo Mazzola and co-authors argue robot trust should be built through live exchange, not traits alone. The work dates to 2025. As robots join homes and work sites, users must trust them in line with what they can do. Too much trust can bring harm, while too little wastes their worth.

The frame rests on two posts. One is the robot's skill at reading human acts with care. The other is clear talk about its aims and next steps. The authors add four parts that bridge felt trust and true skill. They say this mix keeps user hopes in line with robot acts, while users keep a grip on the work.
arxiv-2508-14176:
Zúñiga-Fernández and co-authors report two warm Earth-sized planets around TOI-2267, a close M5 and M6 star pair about 8 au apart. TESS and ground data confirm both planets. Which star each planet orbits is unknown. One planet takes 2.28 days per orbit, and the other takes 3.49 days in total.

The first planet measures 1.00 to a larger 1.22 times Earth's radius, and the second measures 1.14 to a larger 1.36 times that radius, depending on the host star. TESS shows a third signal: a candidate on a 2.03-day orbit, near Earth's size. Tests show all three cannot circle one star. The most stable setup puts the pair, near a 3:2 resonance, on one star and the candidate on the other. That would make TOI-2267 the most compact planet-hosting binary known, with worlds transiting both stars. It is a test case for planet formation and change in tight pairs.
arxiv-2508-14376:
Engineers and mathematicians need tests that tell whether a system built from matrices will stay stable. Zixiang Ni, Yongjian Hu, and Xuzhou Zhan offer such a test in 2025 for a broad class of matrix polynomials. Older tests assumed the leading term was the identity matrix, which many real problems do not satisfy.

Their method first reshapes the problem through column reduction, then rebuilds key parameters with a splitting scheme that adapts column by column. From those parameters they form two structured matrices with rectangular blocks. Stability, they prove, can be read off from whether those matrices pass a positivity test. The result extends a classical criterion to the nonmonic case in a natural way.
arxiv-2508-14576:
Abdalwahab Almajed and co-authors show that fair marks for score tools can flip with the craft picked to weigh crowd rates. Bias in learn tools is a live ill, and fair in score calls is a hard call. One fresh road casts fair as a rate-rate weigh, run by a sort tool. Their 2025 study swaps the weigh core through a flock of rate crafts and re-runs the fair marks each time.

The core pick bends the end mark by wide spans. Rank of tools by fair grace can even flip with the core. Such marks thus rest on a hid pick, a flaw for law and shop use both. Fair craft needs a core-truth check ere its marks are trusted.
arxiv-2508-14876:
Benjamin Church settles a long standing guess in algebraic geometry in a 2025 paper. A 1977 conjecture by Shioda claimed a certain kind of surface must be buildable from a plain projective space by a rational map. Church builds a surface over a finite field closure that breaks the claim.

The surface is supersingular, meaning its key cohomology is fully spanned by algebraic cycles, and its loop group is trivial. Yet Church proves it cannot be unirational. The proof rests on new obstructions for surfaces formed as quotients of a product of curves. The result closes a question that stood for near fifty years.
arxiv-2508-14976:
Chandra and three co-authors build a bot test that shifts with the user in this twenty twenty-five paper. Word tests for bots grow weak as solver tools learn their set forms. A test that breeds fresh trials can stay a step past those solvers.

Inside, a breed net makes fresh sight trials while a sound twin runs in sync. A learn agent sets the trial's grade from how the user acts in real time. Rule and net checks then split man from bot in the end call. Tests show more true folks pass and more stock bots fail than past tests. Big new aid bots can still crack it, the team says in plain words.
arxiv-2508-15176: Wei and co-authors present a 2025 group theory paper on how Sylow numbers shape a finite group's structure. They study groups built as a product of two subgroups that permute with each other. From the Sylow counts of the two parts they derive fresh bounds on several length measures: the p-length of p-solvable groups, and the nilpotent and derived lengths of solvable ones. The results extend work by Zhang from 1995.
arxiv-2508-15276:
Zhongjun Ding and co-authors build an interactive helper that spots and clears ambiguity in database questions. Their 2025 demo paper targets text-to-SQL systems, which turn plain questions into database code. Even strong language models stumble when a question can be read two ways.

Their system, AmbiSQL, flags fine-grained ambiguity from both database parts and model reasoning slips. It then walks the user through simple multiple-choice prompts to pin down intent. Answers feed a rewrite of the question before code is made. The demo plugs into a commercial text-to-SQL backend. Forty tricky queries from two real benchmarks let attendees test the gain. Users can also try the system on their own databases and questions.
arxiv-2508-15376:
Cong Wang and colleagues rebuilt dynamic driving scenes with neural Gaussians in a 2025 paper. Simulators and autonomy stacks need faithful three-dimensional reconstructions of real streets, but driving scenes mix static backgrounds spanning huge depth ranges with cars and pedestrians moving in complex, sometimes non-rigid ways. Earlier Gaussian splatting methods worked at small or object scale. DriveSplat handles the whole scene in one Gaussian representation, splitting the treatment: backgrounds get a learnable level-of-detail scheme that allocates Gaussians adaptively across near, middle, and far depth ranges.

Moving actors are modeled object by object, with rigid global motion plus a two-stage deformation that first shifts anchors, then updates the Gaussians, capturing bending and articulation. Extra regularization steadies the optimization. The unified design aims at city-scale, dynamic reconstruction rather than curated clips.
arxiv-2508-15676:
Elif Konyar, Mostafa Reisi Gahrooei, and Kamran Paynabar propose a personal modeling method for mixed populations in a 2025 paper. People differ in traits and behavior, so one model fits all poorly, yet fully separate models waste shared structure. Their approach learns many tasks at once while a low rank tensor split captures what tasks share and where they differ.

The split breaks the full set of task parameters into a compact form that shows common patterns and sub group variation. Tests on simulated and case study data beat several benchmarks, above all when sub groups varied a lot. The method also aids reading of results, since the split reveals the patterns behind personal fits.
arxiv-2508-16076:
Tariquzzaman and co-authors teach vision-language models to explain Bengali sign language, gesture by gesture, in a 2025 paper. Step-by-step written guides let hearing people copy signs and truly talk back. The team built BdSLIG, the first dataset for this task in Bengali sign language, a language the big models almost surely never saw in training.

Their prompting trick folds the classic parts of a sign, hand shape, motion, and orientation, straight into the prompt. The guides came out more structured and easier to copy than free-form answers. The work aims at learning tools for the many sign languages that AI has so far skipped.
arxiv-2508-16176:
Ryan Niu, Shoichi Koyama, and Tomohiko Nakamura personalize spatial audio from body measurements in this 2025 paper. Head related transfer functions describe how ears and head color sound by direction. Measuring them per person is costly, so datasets stay small. Recordings differ in source positions across datasets, which blocks pooling.

Their method first learns a latent code for the sound magnitude pattern. An autoencoder conditioned on source position makes codes comparable across datasets. Body measurements then predict the code for a new listener. Merging datasets makes neural training feasible at last. Tests beat current network methods on estimation accuracy. Personal spatial audio could reach headphones without a lab visit.
arxiv-2508-16476:
Maryam Ghasemzadeh and Anton van Beek present an optimization framework in 2025 for experiments that are noisy, sparse, and scarce. Tuning several goals at once is hard when each test costs much and repeats give different answers, as in drug trials and molecular simulations. Standard methods assume neat, plentiful data and waste budgets.

Their framework, named NOSTRA in the paper, folds known measurement noise into the surrogate models and searches inside trust regions near promising designs. On two test problems with varying noise, it beat existing methods in finding the best trade-off frontier. It steers samples to where they sharpen the frontier most, which suits tight experimental budgets.
arxiv-2508-16576:
Anyu Ying and nine co-authors benchmark how to train speech recognizers for children, whose voices differ sharply from adults and whose labeled data are scarce. Fine-tuning adult models is the common shortcut, but training from a flat start on child speech had never been compared systematically. The team ran the comparison inside the open ESPnet toolkit.

Self-supervised speech representations, they found, lean toward adult speech, and flat-start training on child data reduced that bias. Scaling the model helped steadily up to a billion parameters, then flattened. Age-by-age analysis of recognition and speaker verification exposed weaknesses in proprietary systems like Whisper. The public benchmark aims to make child speech research more reliable and open.
arxiv-2508-16676:
Jiacheng Li and a large team of co-authors rescale network weights mid-training to steer large language models onto better paths. Their paper from twenty twenty-five presents WISCA. Most training gains come from architecture or optimizer tweaks. Weight patterns, the spread and relative size of the weights themselves, get less systematic care. WISCA rescales weights while keeping model outputs unchanged at the swap.

The output-preserving trick bends the training trajectory without a restart. Gains show in loss and in zero-shot validation across several builds. Grouped query attention models profit most clearly. LoRA fine-tuning runs gain as well. The method is light: no structure change, no new data. The authors frame weight hygiene as a free lever that training pipelines have left idle.
arxiv-2508-16976:
Bin Pan and four colleagues present Joint Parameter Selection, a fine-tuning method that protects domain generalization, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Domain generalization means doing well on new target domains after training on few source domains. Large pretrained vision models are the usual starting point. Full fine-tuning, though, can damage the generalization built into them.

Some methods tune only a subset of parameters. That balances fitting the task against keeping generalization. Joint Parameter Selection limits updates to a small, sparse subset. The authors prove a generalization error bound that reflects update sparsity in a direct way. A selection mechanism with dual operators picks parameters. It looks for gradients that are steady and strong across source domains. Tests on benchmarks showed scores above leading domain generalization methods. The results back selective fine-tuning as both efficient and effective.
arxiv-2508-17076:
Pierre Lubitzsch, Olga Ovcharenko, Hao Chen, Maarten de Rijke, and Sebastian Schelter argue in a 2025 paper for a real-world benchmark for unlearning in recommender systems. Such systems lean on user data to tailor their picks. Privacy law gives users a right to be forgotten, so a model must be able to drop a person's data after training.

The main past benchmark missed that real task, they say. It stuck to one method type, left out tasks such as next-basket picks, and asked for drops far larger than real ones. Their plan ties the test to true loads and time caps.
arxiv-2508-17376:
Jiali Cui, Yan-Ying Chen, Yanxia Zhang, and Matthew Klenk present ShaLa, a 2025 generative framework for learning one shared latent space across data types like images, text, and audio. Many multimodal methods record every combination of details, which can bury the high-level concepts the modalities share. Classic multimodal autoencoders aim at that shared core but often infer it weakly and synthesize poorly.

ShaLa pairs a new inference architecture with a second-stage diffusion prior over the shared code. Across benchmarks, it beat leading multimodal autoencoders on coherence and synthesis quality. It also scaled to more modalities, where earlier designs faltered as the shared space grew complex. The authors pitch clean shared codes as the route to cross-modal generation and inference that actually hang together.
arxiv-2508-17476:
A dark kind that spurns the light specks may still be caught by the sky's own hum, if its birth broke a deep rule in a flash change. Taramati and co-authors work that catch in a 2025 study of a build where the count of stuff is a gauged law. New specks make the build sound; the least of them is the dark kind.

When the law breaks, foam walls in the young sky ring with a hum that next age ears can hunt. A wide dice sweep finds the live zone past all bars. Dark weights sit in one set band. The law's own post sits in a high band, and the break's ware in a low one. Low bands are barred by late dark hunts.
arxiv-2508-17676:
Zhongyi Bai and co-authors published a computing paper in 2025 on sending a virtual stand-in to meetings you cannot attend. In their SEAM design, an embodied agent represents the absent person in a virtual reality meeting. Attendees can address the agent during the session. The absent user later watches the recording from the agent's viewpoint and replies.

Two studies with forty-five participants, run with a hidden human operator, tested both sides of the experience. Attendees easily pulled decision-relevant information from the stand-in and felt the absentee's presence strongly. Absent users felt included when rewatching, thanks to the attention aimed at them. The authors offer the work as proof of concept for richer asynchronous meetings.
arxiv-2508-17776:
Ashay Burungale and co-authors prove a new structural result for p-adic representations, in this 2025 paper. Their objects are two-dimensional Galois representations with a symplectic self-duality. The team show that the first cohomology of such families splits in a clean way.

The split yields free rank-one parts that mirror the symplectic form and encode how key subgroups vary, via completed epsilon constants. Consequences reach both local and global number theory. One settles a compatibility question posed by Mazur and Rubin. Others give new cases of a parity conjecture for certain modular forms and a p-adic L-function for a special elliptic curve case.
arxiv-2508-18476:
Hesham Abdelfattah, Sameh A Eisa, and Peter Stechlinski extend two practical tools: a test for what can be observed, and a filter for estimating it. Their targets are systems with kinks, in this 2025 paper. The systems are differential-algebraic equations, part dynamics, part constraint, of index one, in both smooth and nonsmooth flavors. Nonsmoothness breaks classical calculus at exactly the points engineers care about.

The observability test adapts a sensitivity-based rank condition using lexicographic differentiation, a machinery that keeps derivative information alive through kinks. Uniquely, it works state by state, declaring which variables are observable and which are hopeless, rather than grading the whole system. Beside it sits a new extended Kalman filter built on the same sensitivities, able to track states through nonsmooth events. The demonstration target is a wind turbine power system, estimated in real time by the new filter.
arxiv-2508-18576:
Databases grind when many transactions fight over the same hot records, and classic locking drowns in deadlocks and aborted work. Farzad Habibi and co-authors propose Brook-2PL, a two-phase locking scheme designed to stay deadlock-free under exactly that pressure. It precomputes a graph of lock dependencies so transactions take their locks in a safe, predetermined order. It also releases some locks early, by chopping transactions into pieces more cleverly than older methods allowed.

On a standard commerce benchmark and a synthetic game-store workload, the protocol beat state-of-the-art rivals. It ran nearly three times faster on average in the benchmark and cut worst-case waiting times almost in half. The authors aim it at game stores, ticketing, and other hotspot-heavy services.
arxiv-2508-18676:
Chufan Gao, Jintai Chen, and Jimeng Sun teach language models to reason over tables by learning from their own training mistakes, in work from twenty twenty-five. Fine-tuning learns one data set deeply but travels poorly to new tables. Prompt-only agents travel well but waste the training data at hand. Their method, LRTab, blends both strengths without any weight updates. First the model drafts step-by-step answers across the training tables.

Wrong drafts trigger a second prompt that names conditions to avoid the error. Those prompt conditions are checked on held-out data for trust. At test time, the most relevant conditions are fetched as extra context. Two table benchmarks test the approach against strong baselines. Results beat prior methods while staying readable and cheap to run. Analysts gain table skill that carries across data sets.
arxiv-2508-18976:
Stephen Meisenbacher and co-authors study a privacy risk in cleaned text in a 2025 paper. Word-level differential privacy scrambles words to give provable privacy, yet the cleaned text can keep contextual clues from the original. Large language models can exploit those clues to rebuild private details.

The authors call this power a double-edged sword: the same reconstruction skill that fixes garbled text can undo privacy work. They examine the vulnerability and ways to reduce it. Their findings matter for anyone publishing sanitized text, from hospitals to social platforms, under a privacy promise.
arxiv-2508-19176:
Ian Cavey rebuilds a counting algebra for lattice shapes in a 2025 paper. Ehrhart theory counts the lattice points inside stretched copies of a polytope. Reiner and Rhoades enriched that count into a series and a matching harmonic algebra.

Cavey first shows the algebra is a graded shadow of the polytope's semigroup algebra. A natural filtration links the two objects step by step. He then views the algebra through toric geometry, as sections on a blown-up variety. That view settles a chief conjecture: the algebra is not finitely generated in general. Pretty counting objects can hide wild algebraic behavior.
arxiv-2508-19276:
Marcos Guillermo Lammers, Federico Hernán Holik, and Alejandro Fernández present a 2025 paper on managing scarce quantum computer resources. Today's machines, in the noisy intermediate-scale era, have few qubits, high error rates, and short coherence times. Those limits make smart scheduling of hardware and software resources essential.

The authors survey how resources matter across current uses of these devices. They sketch a vision of runtime-aware quantum software that can inspect its own state as it runs. Obstacles include weak introspection tools and tight timing limits on present platforms. As a proof of concept, they built Qonscious, a prototype that runs quantum programs conditionally. The work speaks to software engineers building for quantum hardware.
arxiv-2508-19376:
Dikshant Sagar and co-authors fine-tune a vision-language model for neutrino physics in a 2025 paper. Particle detectors record interactions as pixelated images, and sorting those events is core work for experiments hunting the ghostly neutrino. The team adapted a large multimodal model, built on a recent open language model, to classify the images.

Its scores were compared with a standard convolutional network used by major experiments. The vision-language model matched or beat that baseline on accuracy, precision, recall, and a ranking measure. It also reasons in words, so extra text context can join the image evidence. The authors propose such models as a general backbone for event sorting across high-energy physics.
arxiv-2508-19576:
Sining Zhoubian and co-authors introduced ReST-RL in 2025, a training frame to sharpen how large language models reason through code. The leading training method in this area has had strong wins, yet its reward signals can be too weak to guide much growth. Models then sample many tries that teach them little.

ReST-RL joins self-training with a value-guided search, so the two parts feed each other. A tuned self-training step spreads the sampled paths wider, which makes rewards vary more and teaches more per round. It also shows the model more half-finished states worth learning from. The aim is more exact code reasoning from the same training budget.
arxiv-2508-19676:
Georgy Lukyanov and Anna Vlasova published a research paper in 2025 on when cheaper effort backfires for experts who vouch for clients. An expert can issue a favorable certificate that a client needs, but the outcome also depends on the client's own effort. The expert cares about client gains and about a reputation for ability that even they do not know.

Making the certificate cheaper to use always helps in their model. Making effort cheaper can hurt: harder-working clients make failure more damning, so the expert may stop advising altogether. At equal starting reputation, public learning and client gains can vanish. The reversal disappears if effort is held fixed, and rare outside reports soften it.
arxiv-2508-19776:
Liding Zhang and co-authors present, in 2025, a robot path planner that repairs failed connections instead of starting over. Planning from both ends at once is fast, but the two search trees often fail to join, forcing a restart. Their method grafts the broken links at both ends to restore a continuous path.

A greedy rule picks the smallest search region that can improve the path, and sampling shifts between regions based on past gains. Those choices keep the search growing toward its partner tree while preserving a guarantee of eventual optimality. Tests from flat spaces to eight dimensions, plus real robot trials, beat existing planners on speed and path cost.
arxiv-2508-19876:
Sepideh Shafiei and Shapour Hakam present an open data set for the computer study of Iranian classical music, in a 2025 paper. At its center is the radif, a fixed body of melodic units that students learn and performers draw on. Such material had lacked a structured digital corpus.

The data set pairs audio with symbolic MIDI files, aligned phrase by phrase, plus written transcriptions and comparison tables drawn from many performers and scholars. Sections cover one master's full radif, material from a second, and samples of a florid vocal ornament sung by noted twentieth-century singers. Each unit carries a code for easy reference. Parts are openly licensed, while some recordings are cited so users can find the originals. The authors invite wider collaboration.
arxiv-2508-20176:
AI built with communities, not just for them, still struggles at the first step: getting the right people in the room. Eugene Kim and co-authors study that recruitment step in this 2025 paper. Participatory AI promises systems that fit stakeholders' needs and values. Yet identifying and engaging every affected group remains a practical weak point.

The team assembled thirty-seven participatory projects and documented how each recruited. Strategies varied widely, and reporting was often thin. Patterns in the corpus show where projects reach broadly and where they default to the easy crowd. Recruitment choices shape whose values the final system reflects. Better methodology here is cheap influence over everything downstream.
arxiv-2508-20776:
Kuniko Paxton and co-authors make skin lesion AI safer by checking its work across all classes at once. Their 2025 paper notes that top models now beat doctors on some tests, yet trust lags. Older explanation tools wobble between runs or look at too few classes at a time.

Their method builds a chance map for every class, pixel by pixel, in one view. That unified picture of the decision helps cut the risk of a missed call. A safety layer called SafeML flags likely wrong calls and warns doctors and patients when needed. Tests use public lesion image sets with two model types, a compact network and a vision transformer. The aim is clearer, safer support for real diagnosis.
arxiv-2508-21176:
Thiago Domingues and co-authors report a pattern in particle collisions, in a paper published in 2025. When nuclei crash at near light speed, they form a hot fluid whose behavior is read from the particles that fly out. The team rescaled those particles' momentum patterns by removing two global measures: how many particles formed and their average push.

After rescaling, the patterns from many setups nearly overlapped, from central to glancing crashes and even in small systems. Simulations of fluid-like flow showed the same overlap, which points to collective motion as its source. The pattern also tightened estimates of the fluid's traits and exposed weak spots in current models. The authors plan a fuller statistical analysis as follow-up work.
arxiv-2508-21376:
Tony Lee and co-authors build a broad report card in 2025 for AI models that listen and talk. Such audio-language models take mixed sound and text and answer in text. Past tests each checked a skill or two, though. They skipped fairness and safety, and used mismatched settings that block fair comparison.

Their bench merges many data sets and adds two new ones: one probing whether models dodge stereotypes, one testing reasoning over spoken chats. Ten aspects are graded, from hearing and knowledge to bias, robustness, and safety, they report, all under one prompt and scoring rulebook. Fourteen open models took the test. A shared report card is what turns model claims into something a buyer can check.
arxiv-2508-21576:
Zhijie Zhang and ten co-authors use detailed simulations to trace where the hot gas halo around Milky Way-like galaxies comes from. Their paper came out in 2025. Such halos glow faintly in X-rays, and their origin tests theories of how galaxies form.

In every version of their simulation with star feedback, the total X-ray brightness matched observations of the Milky Way and similar galaxies. But the simulated glow faded too fast with distance from the center, falling well short of the extended emission recent observations show. Star feedback, from winds, radiation, and supernovae, shaped only the inner halo. The authors conclude that extra heating is needed, perhaps from gravity, from the central black hole, or from cosmic rays.
arxiv-2508-21776:
Akram Alishahi and co-authors define colored knot Floer homology in a 2025 paper, a richer knot invariant built from link Floer homology. The idea mirrors colored versions long used in other knot theories.

The colored form comes from cables of a knot, taking more and more full twists and passing to the limit. The limit forms a module over the colored homology of the unknot. The authors give an explicit account for L-space knots, a tractable class. They also build maps for crossing changes, a key move in knot study. Topologists get a new invariant with first computations and tools to compare knots.
arxiv-2509-00176:
Muhammad Ali and Salman Khan present Waste-Bench in 2025, a benchmark for vision-language models in cluttered waste scenes. Such models join sight and text and shine on standard photos. Waste in the real world is messier: piles are cluttered and objects are deformed, which strains visual understanding.

Their data set targets waste classification under those hard conditions. A deep evaluation method then probes the robustness and accuracy of current models on it. Results expose a clear need for stronger robustness before such models can sort waste reliably. The set and study give builders a hard, realistic test for the next round of model gains.
arxiv-2509-00276:
Yuxiang Liu leads a team of nine authors who present RITE in 2025, a text embedding method that builds reasoning into search. Embeddings turn text into vectors for dense retrieval, which finds documents by meaning. Encoder models do this well for surface matches, but complex queries need reasoning past word overlap, where they fall short.

Large language models reason strongly, yet prior embedding uses of them stress context over reasoning. RITE first generates intermediate reasoning text in token space, then computes the embedding from that enriched input. The simple change lets the model's logic shape what gets retrieved. Zero-shot tests, with no task training, are the target setting for the gains.
arxiv-2509-00476:
Omar Khalid Ali Mohamed, writing alone, builds a malware detector meant to work across data sources, not just one dataset. Malware is harmful software, and detectors trained on a single source often fail on new kinds while also costing much compute.

Mohamed trains separate LightGBM classifiers, fast decision-tree models, on three datasets that cover fixed file traits, call behavior, and memory patterns linked to hidden code. He keeps only top features, then blends the models' probability scores with weights found by grid search, a scan of options. The blend reaches a macro F1 score, a balanced accuracy measure, of 0.823 on cross-domain checks, beating single models with low overhead.
arxiv-2509-01476:
