The authors define success differently: censorship works if users cannot restore the original state using free operations, the moves that create no resource. They investigate when such censorship is secure and when it fails. They also study account sharing, where outside parties help censored users move resources, linking censorship to quantum catalysis and assisted communication. The result is a network security viewpoint distinct from cryptography.
arxiv-2510-12976:
Blassel, Boussau, Lartillot, and Jacob present a likelihood-free way to infer evolutionary trees in this 2025 arXiv paper. Phylogenetics reconstructs how related sequences evolved from common ancestors. Standard Bayesian and maximum likelihood methods must compute likelihoods. That is costly and only feasible under simple assumptions, such as sites evolving independently.

Their method, Phyloformer 2, skips likelihoods entirely. A novel encoding of sequence pairs makes it scale better than earlier attempts. The model outputs a probability distribution over trees, built as a sequence of subtree merges. That lets it express full posterior uncertainty rather than one best tree. The authors report that the network estimates posteriors accurately. It beats both leading maximum likelihood methods and a previous likelihood-free method at point estimation. This opens a route to fast inference under realistic evolution models.
arxiv-2510-13076:
Burgin proves a Sárközy-type theorem for primes with restricted digits in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Write primes in some base and keep only those whose digits come from an allowed set. Burgin asks whether a large set of integers must contain two elements separated by one less than such a prime, extending classical results about forbidden differences.

The theorem says yes: any set of natural numbers with positive upper Banach density, a strong notion of being large, contains two elements differing by a shifted restricted-digit prime. The proof combines the Furstenberg correspondence principle, which translates density problems into dynamical systems, with a Maynard-style discretized circle method. As byproducts, Burgin proves a Dirichlet-type theorem on how these primes distribute among residue classes. He also proves a Vinogradov-type decay estimate for the associated exponential sums, driven by Fourier transforms that factor as Riesz products.
arxiv-2510-13176:
Pan and colleagues auto-tune compiler pass sequences with clustered evolutionary search in this 2025 arXiv paper. Choosing and ordering compiler optimization passes for each program can beat one-size-fits-all heuristics, but iterative search is far too slow and learned models often fail on unseen programs. Their framework, GRACE, attacks code size reduction for LLVM intermediate representation.

GRACE first exploits pass synergies with a weighted scoring method to seed high-quality candidate sequences and a pass pool. Contrastive learning over augmented pass sequences then produces program embeddings, and programs are clustered by similarity. Evolutionary search inside clusters yields a small coreset of specialized sequences meant to transfer, and at test time the best coreset sequence is refined lightly. Across seven datasets, GRACE cut instruction counts by about ten percent beyond the standard size optimization level on two LLVM versions, with modest average tuning time.
arxiv-2510-13276:
Zhou and colleagues benchmark whether vision-language models stay faithful over long multimodal contexts in this 2025 arXiv paper. Modern models advertise huge context windows spanning text, images, and video, but a large window does not guarantee the model actually uses distant evidence correctly. Existing faithfulness evaluations cover text-only settings or only short multimodal contexts.

Their benchmark, MMLongCite, spans eight distinct tasks across six context length intervals. It mixes text, image, and video inputs, including a grounding task where evidence must be located inside composite images of scalable difficulty. Evaluating leading models revealed limited faithfulness in long multimodal contexts overall. The analysis further showed how context length and the position of crucial content within the context systematically affect faithfulness, giving developers concrete failure patterns to target.
arxiv-2510-13876:
Laitenberger, Kopiczko, Snoek, and Asano let each token skip layers it does not need, gated by learned valves on the residual stream. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces GateSkip for decoder-only language models. Every token normally pays full depth at every layer, wasting compute on easy steps. Router and early-exit rivals proved unstable or demanded retraining from scratch.

Each attention and feed-forward branch gets a small sigmoid gate on its output. Gates squeeze branch contributions before they rejoin the residual stream during training. At inference, tokens rank by gate value and the least important skip under a per-layer budget. Smooth differentiable gates fine-tune stably on top of pretrained models. On long reasoning tasks, the method saves up to fifteen percent of compute. Over ninety percent of baseline accuracy survives those savings. Instruction-tuned models even gained accuracy at full compute in their tests.
arxiv-2510-13976:
Yihao Zhou and co-authors report the present-day results of ASTRID, one of the largest cosmological simulations, in this 2025 arXiv paper. ASTRID follows a third of a trillion particles in a box 370 megaparsecs across. It tracks how galaxies and their central black holes grow together. The growth runs from the early universe to redshift zero, the present day. Its black hole population spans a huge mass range.

The simulation reproduces the observed links between black hole mass, galaxy mass, and stellar velocity spread, Its scatter around those links matches observations better than earlier simulations. That suggests more realistic variety among black holes. Its galaxy population also matches observed counts, and with dust dimming applied, the brightness distribution and the two-peaked pattern of galaxy colors come out right. ASTRID contains thousands of groups and clusters, and massive black holes and galaxies trace the universe's large-scale structure well.
arxiv-2510-14176:
Roger Creus Castanyer and co-authors automate the design of reward functions for reinforcement learning using foundation models, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning agents learn from rewards, and setting those rewards is a central challenge. Reward machines offer a structured answer: they encode the objective as an automaton whose states track task progress, but writing them by hand is slow work.

Their framework, ARM-FM, uses foundation models to generate reward machines from natural-language task descriptions, marrying the structure of the automata formalism with the reasoning of pretrained models. Embeddings are attached to each automaton state, enabling generalization across tasks that share named subgoals. The authors test the framework on a suite of environments. They report evidence that it works, including zero-shot generalization. Machines built for stated tasks transfer to new ones without extra examples. The aim is to make reward design accessible from instructions.
arxiv-2510-14376:
Dongnam Byun and co-authors present DOS, a fix for a failure of text-to-image generators, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Prompts naming several objects come back with objects missing or blended into each other. Through studies, the team identifies four problematic scenarios, similar shapes, similar textures, biases from dissimilar backgrounds, and many objects, where relationships between the objects trigger the failures.

Their method exploits two observations about CLIP embeddings, the representations that guide image generators. It modifies three types of those embeddings, to push the objects' directions apart in embedding space: Directional Object Separation. Experiments show DOS improves the success rate of multi-object generation and reduces object mixing. In evaluations across four benchmarks, DOS outperformed four competing methods, receiving more votes, in some comparisons over forty percent more. The authors offer DOS as a model-agnostic remedy that requires no retraining of the generator.
arxiv-2510-14676:
Lerma and Peñaloza propose, in a 2025 arXiv paper, an ethical framework for artificial agents that does not put humans at the center. Most AI ethics borrows human moral intuitions and builds them in. The authors argue this limits what machine ethics could be. Their framework, NAEL, treats ethical behavior as an emergent property of an intelligent system, not a list of human rules.

NAEL grounds behavior in active inference, the idea that agents act to minimize expected free energy, a measure of surprise and risk, in a changing multi-agent world. A neuro-symbolic architecture lets agents weigh the ethical consequences of their actions under uncertainty. The behavior that results is context-sensitive, adaptive, and relational. A case study on distributing resources shows the system dynamically balancing self-preservation, learning about the world, and collective welfare, without assuming human-like moral intuitions.
arxiv-2510-14876:
Goldshmidt and co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, collision prediction models trained on real dashcam footage, judged by a stricter standard than usual: does the crash involve your car? Existing methods often cannot tell a threat to the driver's own vehicle from an accident happening nearby, so they cry wolf in deployment. The team built the first benchmark designed for this ego-centric evaluation, from a dashcam collision dataset.

They re-annotated major benchmarks to mark ego involvement, added agreed alert-time labels, and synthesized negatives where needed. Their BADAS models use a V-JEPA2 video backbone trained end to end. One variant trains on fifteen hundred public videos; a stronger one uses forty thousand. Across four datasets, BADAS set the state of the art, beat a forward-collision driver-assistance baseline, and estimated time-to-accident more realistically. The open model, code, and re-annotations are released.
arxiv-2510-15076:
Sami Davies, Benjamin Moseley, and Heather Newman study how to group similar items when the data arrive one piece at a time. Their 2025 arXiv paper concerns online correlation clustering, where each new point must be placed before the rest are known. A single scoring family creates tension between minimizing total disagreements overall and treating every single node fairly.

Remarkably, the authors give one algorithm that does well on all of those scores at once, the first such result in an online setting. It works in a model where the algorithm first sees a small sample of the incoming data, which helps it plan. They also prove that the plainer random-order model cannot deliver the same fairness guarantee, separating the two settings. Matching lower bounds show their performance ratios are nearly the best achievable in the sampled model.
arxiv-2510-15276:
Gnanasekaran Shanmugasundaram and Jitraj Saha analyze equations that model organisms moving toward or away from chemical signals, a behavior called chemotaxis. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies a class of these systems where interactions can be lethal, diffusion spreads unevenly, and the organisms also produce the signal. Such models raise a basic fear: solutions might blow up in finite time instead of settling down.

The authors settle that fear for two versions of the system, one fully parabolic and one mixing a parabolic equation with an elliptic one. Both sit inside a smooth bounded region with no-flux boundaries. Under stated conditions, they prove unique, globally bounded classical solutions exist in any spatial dimension. They then build Lyapunov functionals, energy-like quantities that decrease over time, to prove the solutions remain stable in the long run. The work extends the safety guarantees available for this family of models.
arxiv-2510-15476:
Hanbin Hong leads a large team that maps the young field of prompt security for large language models. Their 2025 systematization paper notes that jailbreak prompts, crafted inputs that trick models into harmful outputs, have spawned a flood of attack and defense studies. Definitions, threat models, and scoring rules differ from paper to paper, which blocks fair comparison and steady progress.

The team answers with five contributions. They propose a multi-level taxonomy organizing attacks, defenses, and the vulnerabilities both sides exploit. They formalize threat models and cost assumptions as machine-readable profiles, so evaluations can be reproduced exactly. They release an open-source toolkit for standardized, auditable comparison of attacks and defenses. They also publish JAILBREAKDB, described as the largest annotated dataset of jailbreak and benign prompts to date. A public platform and leaderboard for leading methods rounds out the package, aimed at making future prompt security work cumulative.
arxiv-2510-15676:
Single atomic defects can act as tiny light sources inside two-dimensional semiconductors. Lysander Huberich leads a fourteen-author team mapping such defects in monolayer MoS2, in a 2025 arXiv paper. The group combines scanning tunneling spectroscopy with tunneling-driven light emission measurements on the same defects. A thin boron nitride layer separates the material from its graphene base, widening the band gap. This setup keeps defect charge states alive long enough to record sharp emission lines.

The team identifies optical fingerprints of sulfur vacancies, oxygen substitutions, and charged carbon-hydrogen complexes. Only the carbon-hydrogen defects create bound exciton emission, about two hundred millielectronvolts below the main exciton. Maps show large spectral shifts near charged defects, matching expected band bending.
arxiv-2510-16176:
Soumak Bhattacharjee and two co-authors explain a curious reversal inside stably stratified turbulence, the kind found in oceans and atmospheres where density layering resists mixing. At small scales the buoyancy flux flips sign, so turbulent potential energy converts back into kinetic energy instead of the usual forward flow, and the effect strengthens as the Prandtl number grows.

Through filtering analysis, the authors tie the flip to ramp-cliff structures in the density field, sharp fronts already known to explain odd dissipation trends. Their math shows this local mechanism dominates at the smallest scales and drives the reversal, while larger scales also carry a non-local contribution. Direct numerical simulations of strongly stratified turbulence confirm the picture.
arxiv-2510-16476:
Xiaozhe Li leads six co-authors in a 2025 study on hard puzzle-like tasks for language models. NP-hard tasks are ones where good answers are hard to find but easy to check. Their frame, NP-Engine, trains and tests models on ten such tasks from five fields. Each task has a maker for new cases and a rule-based checker.

A rough solver gives near-best answers to train against. Their test set, NP-Bench, scores both if an answer works and how good it is. A model they trained beat GPT-4o on the bench at the same size class. Training on these tasks also helped on logic, maths, and plain tasks. Rich task mixes may be a strong path for training.
arxiv-2510-16576:
Zijian Zhang and Mingyao Cui sharpen channel reads for smart walls in a 2025 paper. A reconfigurable intelligent surface, or RIS, is a wall of tiny parts that bounce signals. Phones and base stations can steer signals with such walls. Good steering needs a sharp read of the air channel. Their plan designs the test patterns used to probe that channel.

A chance-based search picks patterns that share the most facts with the channel. A step-by-step solver then tunes the wall parts and the receiver in turns. A self-tuning step updates the channel spread model with no extra probes. Test runs show large gains in read sharpness over top past methods. Sharp reads unlock the full speed such walls can give.
arxiv-2510-16976:
Daniele Sepe and Susan Tolman widen a connectedness result for a class of systems in a 2025 paper. These systems, called integrable, keep many quantities fixed as they evolve. Their fibers are the sets of states that share the same fixed values. Whether each fiber forms one connected piece matters for sorting such systems.

An earlier paper by the same authors proved connectedness under strict rules. Those rules barred the rougher singular points of a system. The new paper relaxes that demand in a real way. It allows a new class of brief, fading singular points. Examples come from resonance cases and special geometric settings. A new family of examples shows the wider reach is genuine. More real systems now fall under the connected-fibers result.
arxiv-2510-17276:
Rishi Jha and three co-authors break and then fix guards for agent teams in this 2025 paper. Hijack attacks bend team control flow to force unsafe acts. A recent guard checks that each agent call fits the main goal. The team shows such checks can be dodged with ease.

Even strong chat models miss dodges when they grade the calls. Goal fit is vague, and the guard sees too little of the run. Their new guard draws a fixed graph of allowed call paths. All runs must stay on that graph, with per-call rules as well. Tests show the graph guard blocks the dodges that fooled the old one.
arxiv-2510-17576:
Cansu Erdogan, with Cesar Alan Contreras and three co-authors, plans robot teamwork for battery recycling in a 2025 arXiv paper. Taking apart an electric vehicle battery needs many steps in the right order. Parts can sit in varied positions, and two robot arms with different tools must share the work. A human operator guides the job with simple spoken or typed instructions.

Their pipeline turns camera views into text scene notes. Several language models then draft removal sequences that match the operator's intent. A checker model enforces format and step order rules. A final filter rejects parts that were never in the scene. Trials on 200 real scenes showed reliable, safe plans with low user effort.
arxiv-2510-17676:
Luc Dessart and W. V. Jacobson-Galan model exploding giant stars wrapped in their own shed gas in a 2025 arXiv paper. Red supergiants are huge, aging stars that end as supernovae. Many explode inside circumstellar material, meaning gas the star lost before dying. Fast sky surveys will soon catch more of these blast breakouts as they happen.

The pair built a regular grid of models spanning explosion energies and gas layouts. Their calculations follow the first fifteen days with radiation hydrodynamics and detailed light transport. Compact gas boosts ultraviolet brightness and shortens the visible rise. Gas interaction also reshapes the spectra, broadening lines in changing ways. Without surrounding gas, motion broadening dominates right after breakout instead. The model treasury will help read future observations.
arxiv-2510-17976:
J Gabriel Richardson and four co-authors build a full modeling stack for a practical source of entangled light. Chained entanglement links are a base part of future quantum networks, yet lab demos often ignore deployment concerns. The ZALM source was designed for real systems, with clean heralding signals and smart use of power.

The toolkit models the source mode by mode, alone or inside a full network test bed. A mixed math form balances speed against accuracy and makes key scores cheap to compute. Network builders get a way to test designs on screen before spending on hardware.
arxiv-2510-18176:
Soumya Rani Samineni and four co-authors inspect the middle steps of math reasoning after verifiable-reward training, not just final answers. Such training is praised for better reasoning, yet most checks still score only the last answer or pass rates. The team asks whether the trace itself stays locally coherent and globally valid.

Their setup trains a small model on grade-school math with a group-based reinforcement method. A logic-based measure flags step errors and separates trace validity from trace coherence. The study gives the field a direct way to test claims that reward training improves thinking, rather than merely improving answers.
arxiv-2510-18576: Qiyu Yang and Shengbo Zhao prove a lower bound in a short paper. They study the Riemann zeta function. They look at its derivatives along a vertical line. The points on that line are spaced evenly. The zeta function lies at the heart of deep questions about primes. The authors use the resonance method. They show a clear result for a fit range of the real part. At these discrete points, the largest values grow just as in the continuous case.
arxiv-2510-18876:
Haochen Wang and his fifteen co-authors teach multimodal models to read image regions in context. Models grasp whole scenes well. Dense scenes are weaker ground. A question may target one region among many. Earlier region models read each given region alone. The global context that gives it meaning was ignored.

Their system is called Grasp Any Region. A feature replay technique is aligned to each region of interest. The model can consult the full scene while answering about a part. It models interactions between several prompted regions at once. It moves from passive description to free-form questions about regions. A new benchmark tests single-region understanding. It also tests multi-region interaction and reasoning. The smallest model kept leading captioning performance. It beat far larger rivals on multi-region question tasks.
arxiv-2510-19076:
Yuting Wu and fifteen co-authors work to improve superconducting half-wave resonators for the Facility for Rare Isotope Beams, where more than two hundred such cavities operate. Their goal is a very high quality factor at a strong accelerating gradient, beyond what the standard chemical polishing of production cavities achieved.

Electropolishing plus a low-temperature bake reached higher gradients, though quality still fell short, and trapped magnetic flux during testing emerged as a main culprit. The team tried several strategies to cut that trapped flux. The lessons apply to any accelerator that needs efficient superconducting cavities.
arxiv-2510-19176:
Yuqiao Tan and three co-authors study how reasoning models choose between long and short chains of thought, framing that choice as an early exit problem. Step-by-step thinking makes these models strong at math and logic, but it also causes overthinking, where simple questions burn far more computation than they need.

Mode selection decides up front between long and short thinking modes, while early exit picks a stopping point midstream. The authors argue mode selection is the harder variant, since the decision comes before reasoning starts. Their empirical study clarifies when each strategy saves cost without giving up answer quality.
arxiv-2510-19276:
Smayan Agarwal and Aalok Thakkar settle when weighted automata and cost register automata define true probability distributions. Such machines assign weights to behaviors, and knowing whether those weights form a proper distribution, called the stochasticity problem, is basic to trusting them as probabilistic models.

For cost register automata in general, checking stochasticity is undecidable, the authors prove. In the fully linear fragment, though, the check runs in polynomial time through spectral methods, and every valid model can be rewritten with locally sub-stochastic updates. That local test gives a clean algebraic picture of the fragment's meaning.
arxiv-2510-19376:
Fabian Schaipp benchmarks optimization algorithms for training diffusion models on dynamical systems, a setting missing from most optimizer comparisons. Diffusion models are usually judged on text or images, so claims about new optimizers may not carry over to denoising tasks on flow trajectories.

Two newer methods, Muon and SOAP, prove highly efficient substitutes for the standard AdamW, reaching notably lower final loss. Schaipp also rechecks known training phenomena in this setting, including how learning-rate schedules shape training and how large the gap between adaptive methods and plain gradient descent really is. Practitioners get guidance grounded in their own task type.
arxiv-2510-19476:
Julian Schulz lays out a concrete roadmap for building safety cases for advanced artificial intelligence systems based on monitoring their chain of thought. When systems may become too capable for arguments that they simply lack dangerous abilities, overseers need another route: watch the model's written reasoning and catch dangerous plans there.

The proposed case has two parts. First, show the model lacks dangerous capability without its chain of thought; second, show any capability that reasoning unlocks is detectable by monitoring. Schulz then examines threats to that monitoring, including hidden encoded reasoning in linguistic drift, steganography, and alien forms, and sets a research agenda.
arxiv-2510-20176:
Yuhang Zhou and fourteen co-authors propose Mixture-of-Minds, a multi-agent system for answering questions over tables with large language models. Fine-tuned models reason well but make arithmetic slips and invent facts, while tool-based methods compute precisely yet follow rigid schemas and miss meaning. Their framework splits the job among three agents with distinct roles: planning, coding, and answering.

Code execution gives the team exact table handling while the language agents supply semantic understanding. A self-improvement stage uses Monte Carlo Tree Search rollouts to create training trajectories, then tunes the agents with reinforcement learning. On TableBench the system reaches a score above sixty-two percent, passing a strong commercial model baseline.
arxiv-2510-20776:
Binbin Huang, Haobin Duan, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, and Shenghua Gao introduce Cupid, a generative system that rebuilds three dimensional objects from images while also solving for the camera pose. Pose and shape are usually handled apart, which lets errors in one corrupt the other.

Cupid first drafts a coarse shape and image to space matches to lock a sound pose estimate. Guided by that pose, a second stage feeds pixel aligned image features straight into generation for sharp faithful detail. Scores beat leading reconstruction methods by wide margins on image quality and shape distance. Because shape and pose stay separate inside one model, the same system extends to multi view and full scene tasks without extra tuning.
arxiv-2510-20876:
Mohammad Ali S Afshar leads five co-authors in testing radiatively corrected inflation models against new sky data and swampland rules from quantum gravity theory. The swampland program claims many seemingly fine early universe models cannot arise from a full quantum gravity theory.

Two models face three swampland tests alongside data from the Atacama telescope, Planck, and baryon acoustic signals. The Higgs based model passes observations and one conjecture but fails two gravity conjectures, limiting its theoretical standing. The second model, with added scalar sectors, passes all three tests while fitting the data, though its success depends sensitively on coupling and scale choices, a map of where corrected inflation stands.
arxiv-2510-20976:
Jiyu Cui leads six co-authors on a large language multimodal model for metal organic frameworks, porous crystals prized for carbon capture and gas storage. Their design space is vast, with countless three dimensional atomic arrangements governed by strict coordination rules that plain text describes poorly.

The model is built to read multifaceted representations beyond language, so structure and property information can guide generation and prediction together. Language reasoning is paired with geometric and chemical encodings suited to framework rules. The aim is faster discovery of frameworks tuned for capture, storage, and separation tasks that matter for energy and climate.
arxiv-2510-21076:
Xinyi Ma leads nine co-authors on backmapping the solar wind, tracing plasma measured in space back to its source region on the Sun under several magnetic field models. Backmapping links in situ readings with remote solar observations and underpins space weather analysis.

Uncertainty from model choice, especially for high latitude wind, has been poorly quantified. Two heliospheric field models, Parker spiral and Fisk type, are crossed with three coronal field models to map the spread of answers. Knowing which configurations agree or diverge tells forecasters how much trust a traced source deserves.
arxiv-2510-21376:
Lukas Möller and Simon Stellmer report the first laser cooling and magneto-optical trapping of zinc atoms. They cool the atoms on a transition in the deep ultraviolet, at a wavelength of 213.9 nanometers, the shortest ever used for this kind of trap, which makes the technical feat notable on its own.

The trap holds every stable isotope of zinc, including a fermionic one whose very narrow transition could anchor an optical atomic clock. The authors map how different settings change the number of trapped atoms and how fast the trap loads. They frame the result as a first step toward using zinc for high-precision spectroscopy, which measures light absorbed or emitted by atoms, and for quantum information work.
arxiv-2510-21476:
Liubov A. Markovich and three co-authors build a bridge between two dialects of quantum information: discrete systems like spins, and continuous systems like light modes. Each dialect assigns different meanings to shared notions, so moving states and measurement data between hardware of the two kinds has lacked a clean dictionary.

Their bridge uses the tomographic picture, where a quantum state is described by plain measurement probabilities, together with two classic maps between spins and oscillators. They show explicitly, for the first time, how those maps act on tomograms and on Wigner functions, the phase-space portraits of states. A built-in compression step selects only the sector of the larger space that the target needs, so a target portrait can be computed straight from experimental data without rebuilding the full state.
arxiv-2510-21676:
Akash Shukla and four co-authors remove a coordinate headache from simulations of tokamaks, the magnetic bottles built to hold fusion plasma. Plasma structures stretch along magnetic field lines. Codes therefore prefer coordinates aligned with the field. At the X-point, though, the sideways field vanishes. The hot core also meets the exhaust region there. Aligned coordinates blow up at that spot.

Their algorithm computes the needed geometric quantities for a standard field-aligned system while stepping around the singularity. It enables two-dimensional axisymmetric simulations that cover core and scrape-off layer together in X-point geometry. A demonstration run uses the design of the Spherical Tokamak for Energy Production. It shows the method working in a realistic device layout. That clears a practical obstacle for whole-device fusion modeling.
arxiv-2510-21776:
Junhao Cai and four co-authors, Yuhan Li, Yunqiao Liu, Benlong Wang. Mingbo Li, study how the chemistry of water changes the moment a focused laser pulse breaks it down and forms a bubble. Their experiments separate two influences that are usually tangled together: how many ions the water holds overall, and which specific ions are present.

Stronger salt content always lowered the energy needed to start the bubble. At equal strength, though, acid solutions held cavitation back while alkaline solutions encouraged it. The authors trace the split to short-lived electrons in the water, which acid ions quickly capture and hydroxide ions spare. Bulk electrical conductivity barely changed, so the effect sits in tiny electron reactions rather than in charge flow through the liquid.
arxiv-2510-22176:
Junho Park, Taehan Kim, Mohammad Ali, and Di Liang make computer-designed light circuits explain themselves. Inverse design lets an algorithm sculpt photonic structures that are tiny and high-performing but look like abstract art. When fabrication wobbles, even experts cannot tell which pixels of the layout carry the performance and which are decoration.

The workflow paints a sensitivity map straight onto the design's binary mask. A light convolutional stand-in model learns to predict the device's measured quality figures, and an attribution method then credits each pixel with its share of the prediction. Tested on wavelength-splitting devices working at two telecom wavelengths, the hotspots the method flags line up with substructures that carry real physical meaning, and the maps were checked experimentally. Designers gain a diagnostic for robustness instead of a black box.
arxiv-2510-22276:
Issa Sugiura leads a six-author team asking whether global training data is enough for one culture. Vision-language models keep improving at multicultural tasks. But native fluency in a single culture's objects and customs may need native material. Japan is the test case here.

The team built WAON, the largest public Japanese image-text dataset. It was drawn from native Japanese web pages in Common Crawl. It holds roughly one hundred fifty-five million examples. A hand-curated benchmark, WAON-Bench, spans three hundred seventy-four cultural classes. Fine-tuning comparisons used several Japanese datasets. Models trained on WAON did better on Japanese cultural benchmarks. Global pretraining alone did not match them. The dataset is offered as evidence and as infrastructure for culture-aware adaptation.
arxiv-2510-22376:
Zirui Pang and five co-authors work on making large language models forget harmful or unwanted knowledge while keeping their general skill. The simplest method, gradient ascent on the data to forget, is unstable and can badly damage the model. Their smoothed version mixes the forget data with several sets of normal data at a chosen rate.

Theory guides how to pick that smoothing rate, balancing forgetting against keeping useful skill. Tests on three benchmarks, covering fake author facts, a book series, and news, show the smoothed method beats plain gradient ascent on all measures. It also ranks near the top among rival methods.
arxiv-2510-22676:
Climate models approximate small ocean processes they cannot resolve directly, and those approximations cause biases. Laure Zanna, with twenty five co-authors, introduces a framework in 2025 for building hybrid physics and artificial intelligence ocean models that learn those unresolved processes from data.

The framework supports parameterizations, meaning stand in rules for missing physics, that are aware of scale and physical structure. Examples range from deep learning models to interpretable equation based ones, placed in ocean and sea ice parts of a leading climate model. Prototype fully coupled simulations run successfully. The tools are open source, aiming to make hybrid modeling usable by other teams.
arxiv-2510-22776:
A microquasar is a small system that shoots out powerful jets. SS 433 is a well known example. Zhen Xie, Zhipeng Zhang, and Ruizhi Yang study it in 2025. They ask what the future LACT telescope array can see. Their work rests on detailed simulations.

A detection at five sigma needs about thirty hours. Sigma here measures detection confidence. Good angular resolution should split the east and west jets. About one hundred hours could isolate a central hadronic part. Hadronic means tied to protons and nuclei. The array could also tell rival spectral models apart. Results point to strong gains for PeVatron studies.
arxiv-2510-22876:
Fast decoding methods can silently corrupt model outputs. Ranran Haoran Zhang leads a team with five co-authors. In 2025 they audit batch speculative decoding. Speculative decoding drafts tokens, then verifies them. Several common implementations reported good speed. Yet they produced repeated tokens and unknown symbols.

The root cause is the ragged tensor problem. Variable acceptance desynchronizes batch data. Position IDs, attention masks, and caches fall out of step. The team formalizes invariants that valid batches must keep. Two fixes are proposed, EQSPEC and EXSPEC. EXSPEC groups same length sequences to skip realignment. It reached high throughput with near exact matching.
arxiv-2510-23276:
Thai-Binh Nguyen and five co-authors introduce a cocktail-party benchmark for the ninth CHiME Challenge. The task, Multi-Modal Context-Aware Recognition, asks who speaks when, what they say, and with whom, in a single room with overlapping casual conversation. Recordings show extreme overlap up to one hundred percent and highly broken turns.

Systems must fuse audio, visual, and contextual cues to transcribe each speaker and cluster their speech. Unscripted group chat makes the data far harder than clean studio speech. The benchmark pushes meeting transcription toward real social settings where everyone talks at once.
arxiv-2510-23576:
Anqi Li and seven co-authors present UrbanVLA, a model that steers small delivery robots through real city streets by following route instructions. City navigation is hard because streets are large, busy, and unstructured, while most earlier systems were built for short trips in calm, controlled settings. A good city navigator needs both low-level skills, like reaching a point and dodging obstacles, and high-level skill at matching a planned route to what it sees.

UrbanVLA lines up noisy route waypoints with live camera views, then plans the path to drive. Training came in two stages: supervised fine-tuning on simulations and web video routes, then reinforcement fine-tuning on mixed simulated and real data for safety. On the SocialNav task in MetaUrban, it beat strong baselines by more than fifty-five percent. Real-world runs also held up well, showing the model can scale to big city areas.
arxiv-2510-23676:
Luís Daniel Abreu and two co-authors prove quantum large sieve inequalities, bounds that limit how much a signal can concentrate on a region of phase space. Their setting upgrades Fourier analysis to operators, using a phase-space transform modeled on the short-time Fourier transform. The inequalities govern the Rayleigh quotient of restricted phase-space representations of higher-rank operators.

Building on work of Donoho and Stark, the authors show these bounds guarantee recovery of an operator when its phase-space information is missing over a sparse region. The recovery runs through an L1-minimization program, an operator version of Logan's phenomenon from signal processing. The results act as a cousin of low-rank matrix recovery and compressed sensing. They derive concentration estimates for Cohen's class distributions and the Husimi function, and they weigh the trade-off between sparsity and concentration that the method creates.
arxiv-2510-23776:
P. Ranaivomanana and six co-authors use unsupervised machine learning to hunt variable stars in Gaia DR3 data. They focus on the valley between the main sequence and white dwarfs on the color-magnitude diagram. Telescopes now deliver more photometry than humans can sift, and odd systems hide in regions that targeted catalogs skip. The authors selected over thirteen thousand sources in that valley region and let the data sort itself.

Their pipeline clusters statistical features from Gaia's epoch photometry and maps them with the t-SNE algorithm. Distinct groups emerged: hot subdwarfs, cataclysmic variables, eclipsing binaries, and stars in crowded fields such as Andromeda. Some stars labeled RR Lyrae sat in unexpected places, hinting at bad astrometry or alternate evolution paths. The authors stress that the method scales to large populations without pre-picked catalogs, and it flags instrumental false alarms alongside real variables.
arxiv-2510-24176:
Tatiana Nizkaia and five co-authors look again at a test reaction that labs use to rate catalysts. The reaction turns 4-nitrophenol into a new product with the help of sodium borohydride. Most labs treat its speed as if it followed one simple rule. In fact, two things happen at once. The borohydride breaks down in water, and free hydrogen gas in the liquid drives part of the change.

So the flow of hydrogen can shape how fast the test seems to run. The team looked at past data on small platinum and silica grains with pores of different sizes. When hydrogen moves by slow spread, the simple rule holds. When it escapes as bubbles, hydrogen is lost and the change stops short. Their model of the rates captures this switch and fits all the data in one frame.
arxiv-2510-24376:
K. Yu. Povarov and five co-authors used spin resonance tests to study a soft mode in a magnet made of manganese and tellurium. The material is an altermagnet, a new class of magnet. They placed it in fields up to sixteen tesla, along its easy axis. Below its order point of 310 kelvin, one resonance line shows up. That line is the pseudo-Goldstone mode of the antiferromagnetic resonance.

The mode acts the same in all directions. Its effective g factor is near two, which fits a full quench of orbital motion for the manganese ions. At five kelvin, the line is very narrow, about fifty millitesla wide. As the sample warms, the line grows much wider. The team explains that growth by magnons scattering off each other, which shortens the mode's life at high heat.
arxiv-2510-24576:
Erick Gordillo Herrerías and Nolwenn Le Quellec, two authors, study flute surfaces. A flute surface is an endless surface built from cuffs in a row. Fenchel-Nielsen coordinates give each cuff a length and a twist. A surface of the first kind has geodesics that reach every end. Geodesics are the straightest paths that a surface allows.

The pair extend results of Pandazis and Šarić on these surfaces. They give exact conditions on the coordinates for the first kind. From that, they characterize parabolic flute surfaces in one case. Parabolic here means the geodesic flow is ergodic, fully mixing. The case covers twist values of zero and one half. Ergodic flow means one path over time samples the whole space. The work sharpens how coordinates predict a surface's dynamics.
arxiv-2510-24876:
Abhishek Chaudhary, the sole author, works out a code plan for the best control of a wave rule driven by chance. The task pairs a cost with a wave state that shifts with a noise term tied to the state. A known max rule lets him mark the best pair by a joined front and back system of such rules.

His code uses shaped parts in space and a mid point rule in time, and he proves strong rates for how fast the code pair nears the true pair. No heavy chance tools are needed for the proof. A slope step method with exact means in place of fake draws keeps each step cheap. Code tests back the rates and the low cost.
arxiv-2510-25076:
Yanfang Zhang and Shu-Qin Zhang pin down when a self like sponge shape has a bend size of zero. Such sponges are built by a named rule that scales each part in its own way. A space that sits in far split parts is known to have bend size zero, but the sponge case needed a full mark.

First they mark just when a sponge of this type sits in far split parts. With that mark in hand, they show the sponge has bend size zero if and just if it sits in that split way. No in between case is left. The claim caps a known line of work on such sponges.
arxiv-2510-25176:
Mohammadreza Doostmohammadian, Zulfiya R Gabidullina, and Hamid R Rabiee join two tasks in one plan. They train a shared model across a web of compute hubs. They also split chip time among the hubs in the best way. Data sit spread on the hubs, and each hub trains on its own share. The web links can shift with time, yet weights stay in step.

Their plan keeps the chip use and need in match at each step, so no step is out of bounds. All hubs tend to one shared model as steps go, a pact type end. Log scale short codes for shared facts can also be fit in. Speed and scale both gain from the joint plan.
arxiv-2510-25376:
Talia Meir leads four co-authors on laser acceleration. Kale Weichman, Alexey Arefiev, and John P Palastro helped. Ishay Pomerantz closes the five-author team. Their 2025 physics paper studies direct laser acceleration. It offers compact sources of energetic electrons. Those electrons can generate secondary radiation or neutrons.

High-density plasma improves energy transfer from laser pulses. But it worsens nonlinear propagation effects like filamentation. Filamentation can disrupt the acceleration process badly. The team test superluminal flying-focus laser pulses. Such pulses mitigate nonlinear propagation in plasma. 3D particle-in-cell runs compared pulse types directly. A Gaussian pulse had equal energy and intensity. The flying-focus pulse produced far more energetic electrons. It yielded about eighty times more above threshold. Electron cutoff energy rose by twenty percent. High-energy x-ray yield tripled in runs.
arxiv-2510-25576: Julian Pozuelo, Simone Verzellesi, and Giacomo Vianello study total inverse mean curvature. Their 2025 paper works in the plane. Curves have prescribed edge in the half-plane. They characterize when critical points with prescribed area exist. They also show those critical points are strongly stable. As an use, they prove a local minimality trait. The paper is a compact variational study for readers in geometric study and calculus of variations.
arxiv-2510-25676:
Teena tom Dieck led five co-authors on cell-like senders for molecule-based signals. Lukas Brand, Sebastian Lotter, and Kathrin Castiglione helped. Robert Schober and Maximilian Schafer close the six-author team. Their 2025 paper deals with signals sent as small molecules. Most past work used senders that were far too simple. Real senders built from cells lag and add noise.

Their sender is a small fluid sac, made to act like a real cell part. Release of signal molecules comes with a lag in this model. Noise from the cell parts is built in as well. Lag and loose control leave a memory trace that is hard to read. They give two new ways to shape the sent stream. Both ways cut the memory trace at the source. The far end can then stay simple in build. Sums on a grid show the new ways read more truly.
arxiv-2510-25876:
Jason L. Sanders, working alone, gives exact formulas for how the chemical mix of a galaxy changes when star yields depend on the mix itself. A yield is the amount of a new element that stars return to gas. For elements such as aluminium, the yield grows with the metal content already present, which helps observers separate stars born in the Milky Way from stars it captured.

Sanders assumes steady star making and outflow rates and solves the single zone model in closed form. The metal link acts like an extra delay, set by how fast the system uses its gas. He compares the model with APOGEE survey data and maps how in place and captured groups split in aluminium and magnesium measures.
arxiv-2510-26476:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports precision measures of top quark production at the Large Hadron Collider. The events of interest hold a charged lepton, missing sideways momentum, two jets from bottom quarks, and two light jets. That mix matches a final state with two W bosons and two bottom quarks, where one or two top quarks may form and decay.

ATLAS used a large proton collision data set recorded from 2015 to 2018 at an energy of thirteen tera-electronvolts. The team unfolded the measures to particle level across many traits and three regions of the data, tuned to sense how the one-top and two-top routes interfere. Clear gaps showed up against theory in the regions most sensitive to that interference. The results should help improve the computer models used to simulate such events.
arxiv-2510-26576:
Filippo Scaramuzza, with four co-authors, designs a way to audit AI systems without exposing them. Laws such as the EU AI Act demand that AI be checkable, but owners must guard private data and trade-secret models. Classical audits are costly, manual, and poorly suited to black-box models.

Scaramuzza and the team present ZKMLOps, which weaves zero-knowledge proofs into machine learning operations. Such a proof can convince a checker that a claim is true while revealing nothing about the claim itself. The framework yields repeatable cryptographic evidence about a model and its inputs for auditors to use. Tests show its overhead stays bounded and stable across different proof backends and growing model sizes. The authors find full zero-knowledge auditing fits best when audits happen on demand.
arxiv-2510-26676:
Samiha Shimmi, Nicholas M Synovic, Mona Rahimi, and George K Thiruvathukal study how security flaws sneak back into fixed software. A vulnerability that returns after a patch points to deeper habits in how a project evolves. Code metrics alone miss those habits, so the team turns to process metrics, measures of how the work itself is done.

Shimmi and her three co-authors run a case study on ImageMagick, an image software project, at the level of single commits. They track seventy-six cases of reintroduced vulnerabilities against measures such as bus factor, issue density, and issue spoilage over time. Returns often lined up with rising issue spoilage and swinging issue density, signs of strained issue handling. The authors frame the work as a base for wider studies that mix process and code signals to flag risky fixes early.
arxiv-2510-26976:
J. W. Zhou and Sami Dib compare star-forming clouds in three nearby galaxies and the inner Milky Way. The pair identify molecular clouds, the cold gas clouds where stars form, in carbon monoxide data taken at two wavelengths. When the data share similar sharpness, clouds of the same mass range show broadly similar traits and star formation rates across all four settings.

Care is needed because a wide telescope beam can make clouds look larger and distort size and density estimates. After removing beam-affected clouds, the match holds, though some clouds in one galaxy move more wildly inside. Milky Way clouds with dense clumps prove heavier and denser, and clump mass tracks cloud mass closely, linking cloud state to star-forming power.
arxiv-2510-27176:
Pouya Hamadanian leads seven co-authors in presenting Glia, an AI system that designs computer systems mechanisms like a human expert team. Prior machine learning for systems mostly tunes black-box policies, leaving designs opaque. Glia instead uses language models in a multi-agent workflow where specialized agents reason, run experiments, and analyze results under an evaluation framework grounded in empirical feedback.

Applied to a distributed graphics processor cluster serving language model inference, Glia creates new algorithms for request routing, scheduling, and auto-scaling. The designs perform at human-expert levels in far less time and remain interpretable, exposing the reasoning behind each choice. The work also surfaces fresh insights into workload behavior, suggesting structured experimentation plus reasoning models can yield creative, understandable systems designs.
arxiv-2510-27576:
Leatile Marata and six co-authors survey threats to satellite navigation in 2025 and the role of smart methods in defense. Systems that guide cars, planes, and sensors rely on faint signals from space. Jamming and fake signals can harm safety and trust in those readings. Classic fixes use physics-based models, which can miss complex attack forms.

Methods that learn from data can join physics models to spot odd patterns. The authors map key tasks for safe position fixes and set out a research path. Their vision stresses robust design as self-driving and smart sensing spread. The survey helps teams plan stronger guards for vital location services.
arxiv-2511-00376:
Nitin Kumar, Nicholas Jerla, John Ponis, Sarbajit Banerjee, and G Sambandamurthy study a layered crystal with a mouthful of a name, beta sodium vanadium oxide, prized for switching its electrical resistance. They track how charge order, a patterned arrangement of electrons, shows up in transport and in low-frequency resistance noise as the crystal cools through two transitions.

Above the transitions, noise behavior points to electrons hopping between near neighbors. Below the sodium-ordering transition, sodium ions settle into a zig-zag pattern that reshapes the electronic state. Below the charge-ordering transition, noise drops sharply, a sign of correlated electron motion. A strong electric field can break the ordered state and flip the crystal into a conducting state, with switching across a wide cold range driven by electronics, not heating. Stable, quiet states hint at uses in cryogenic memory.
arxiv-2511-00476:
Ghazal Kalhor and Afra Mashhadi test whether large language models remember scholarship fairly. As these models move into search and discovery tools, they increasingly answer questions about who worked with whom. The authors ask three prominent models to reconstruct coauthor lists for researchers, then compare the output against bibliographic reference data across disciplines and world regions.

A systematic pattern emerged: highly cited researchers were recalled far better, so memorization favors scholars who are already visible. The tilt was not uniform, though. Clinical medicine and parts of Africa showed more balanced reconstruction than the global trend. The findings warn that discovery tools built on model memory can quietly amplify existing inequalities, and they argue for careful auditing of memorization-driven bias before such systems are trusted.
arxiv-2511-00676:
Easton Huch, Fred Feinberg, and Walter Dempsey build a Bayesian approach for causal effects that leans on randomization itself for strength. Instead of modeling how outcomes arise in a whole population, they fix the observed potential outcomes. The likelihood is built from the randomization distribution of a statistic, the distribution created by the experiment's own assignment lottery. A treatment effect model is still needed, but marginal outcome distributions often are not.

The weaker assumptions buy provable strength: a Bernstein-von Mises theorem and large-sample behavior for posterior means are proved. The posterior mean matches classical Hodges-Lehmann estimators in the large-sample limit, bridging to weighted estimators of the inverse-probability and Hájek kinds. Posterior randomization tests allow model checking in the same language. A nutrition case finds strong effect variation that moderation checks had missed.
arxiv-2511-01176:
Wenqing Zhu and colleagues test how well large language models detect code clones, duplicated code fragments that maintenance tools need to find. Earlier studies reported strong results, but left open whether performance holds across data sets and whether the models answer the same question the same way twice.

They built seven clone data sets from the CodeNet and BigCloneBench collections, sampling code pairs by their text similarity, and evaluated five language models under four published prompts. Models did well on CodeNet derived sets, with one reaching a high F1 score, but performance fell greatly on BigCloneBench derived sets. Consistency was a bright spot: over ninety percent of judgments stayed the same across repeated submissions, and score fluctuations from inconsistency were tiny.
arxiv-2511-01276:
Yiyao Ma, Kai Chen, Kexin Zheng, and Qi Dou generate dexterous robot grasps by transfer. A multi fingered hand must grasp stably and adapt to the task, yet analytical methods are slow and generative methods, trained on limited data, generalize poorly to new objects and tasks.

Their idea is to transfer a high quality grasp from a shape template to a new object in the same category. That is reformulated as generating the object's contact map. A conditional diffusion model does the work, seeing shape similarity and task requirements. A dual mapping mechanism handles complex shape differences, and two extra maps encode contact parts and directions for stability. A cascaded diffusion framework transfers all three maps consistently, and a recovery step picks reliable contact points and optimizes the final grasp.
arxiv-2511-01876:
Peter Ván writes a short note on Korteweg-type fluids. These are fluids whose stress depends on density gradients. They serve to model capillarity and phase interfaces. Two schools build their theory in unlike ways. One, from Dunn and Serrin, rests on the entropy principle and one line of argument about objectivity. A newer school uses weakly nonlocal thermodynamics.

Ván compares the two schools head-on. Their unlike objectivity arguments, he finds, lead to the same constitutive functions. So the seeming clash is not there. The real split lies in the pressure tensors each school allows for perfect Korteweg fluids. That split traces back to unlike symmetry demands made along the way. The note sorts what is mere convention from what is physics.
arxiv-2511-01976:
Yifan Zhang and Sarang Gopalakrishnan ask whether ordered phases of matter survive when a system is lightly disturbed by noise. Their setting is quantum and classical matter in thermal balance, described by Gibbs states, and the disturbance is weak local decoherence, which scrambles nearby information. The question matters near phase transitions, where correlations stretch over long distances.

The pair prove that, below a certain noise strength, the damage can be undone by local operations they call decoders. One consequence is that heat-stable quantum memories keep a working threshold even close to the critical temperature. A parallel result points to fast local denoisers in the late stages of diffusion models.
arxiv-2511-02076:
Carlos Lopetegui-González, Massimo Frigerio, and Mattia Walschaers develop a geometric way to describe entanglement in states of light that go beyond the familiar Gaussian family. Their objects are bosonic states of finite stellar rank, a measure of how non-Gaussian a state is. The framework breaks the state's stellar polynomial into atomic pieces and draws a structural graph from those pieces.

The graph's connected parts reveal the state's mode-by-mode entanglement and every way it could be split apart by passive optical operations. A key notion, essential variables, counts the minimal effective modes in a core state. From this the authors derive complete separability tests for two-mode states and for rank-two states across any number of modes, and they show how the method measures preparation difficulty on examples.
arxiv-2511-02376:
Aashray Reddy, Andrew Zagula, and Nicholas Saban automate the kind of patient, multi-turn manipulation that coaxes harmful answers out of language models. Most safety evaluations test one prompt at a time, but real attacks unfold over a conversation, adapting to each refusal. Their training-free framework, AutoAdv, runs such attacks automatically, combining three adaptive mechanisms that learn as the conversation proceeds.

A pattern manager reuses tricks from successful attacks, a temperature manager adjusts randomness in response to failure modes. A two-phase rewriting strategy first disguises the harmful request, then refines the disguise turn by turn. The system reached attack success rates up to ninety-five percent against one open model within six turns, a large gain over single-turn baselines. Tests across commercial and open models found multi-turn attacks consistently stronger, which the authors frame as an urgent case for conversation-aware defences.
arxiv-2511-02976:
Leopoldo Diaz, Harold Hjalmarson, Jesse Lutz, and Peter Schultz present AIDE, a method that feeds atomic-level defect data into device models of semiconductors. Radiation-born defects shorten device life, but their chemistry runs too fast and too dilute for direct measurement. Their 2025 case study uses silicon-doped gallium arsenide as the test material.

The model tracks the Fermi level and its electron and hole parts as charges settle, using an arsenic vacancy as the worked example. It settles at a Fermi level near 1.32 electron volts, where the triply negative vacancy is the most common charge state, as expected. It then follows a diffusion-driven reaction in which a gallium interstitial and the vacancy, pulled together by charge, form a gallium antisite. The method reaches regimes experiments cannot.
arxiv-2511-03076:
Jungjun Choi and Ming Yuan build a framework for pricing errors in asset markets, where a factor model says what returns should be. Their model mixes hidden latent factors with firm traits, and splits mispricing into two parts. Inside alpha is explained by firm traits but runs against factor exposures. Outside alpha stands apart from both. Their 2025 paper generalizes two recent approaches and fixes their orthogonality and scaling issues.

Estimation uses low-rank methods with explicit debiasing and closed-form answers, backed by inference theory that allows many firm traits. On United States stock returns from 2000 to 2019, they find strong signs of both alphas. Inside alpha moved by industry, while outside alpha looked like firm-specific shocks beyond the listed fundamentals.
arxiv-2511-03276:
Jinjie Ni and colleagues report a surprise lead for diffusion language models when training text is scarce. Models that write one token at a time usually dominate, but diffusion models build text by cleaning noise step by step. Under matched training, the diffusion models pulled ahead once the same small data set was read many times over.

Three traits drive the edge: reading in any order, heavy compute from two-way cleaning passes, and a built-in form of data variety. Adding noise helped the usual models yet never closed the gap. At larger scale, a diffusion coder passed its matched rival on a fixed budget drawn from ten billion fresh code tokens. The finding hints that scarce, high-grade data may favor diffusion designs.
arxiv-2511-03976:
Xu Zou, writing alone, introduces PETRA, a pretrained evolutionary transformer for predicting future mutations of SARS-CoV-2, the virus whose rapid, uneven evolution keeps challenging public health and vaccine design. Raw genomic sequences are noisy, so PETRA trains instead on evolutionary trajectories drawn from phylogenetic trees.

Tree-based training captures the hierarchy of viral change and reduces sequencing noise, while weighted training counters geographic and temporal imbalance in global data. Recall scores for nucleotide and spike amino-acid mutations far exceeded the best baseline reported. PETRA also helped track major recent clades in real time. Code was released openly for others to test and extend.
arxiv-2511-04076:
Hao Li, Haotian Chen, Ruoyuan Gong, Juanjuan Wang, and Hao Jiang propose Agentmandering, a game-theoretic approach to fair electoral redistricting that uses language model agents. Ensemble methods generate many lawful maps but ignore the strategic selection step, letting partisan actors cherry-pick a compliant map that still favours them.

Two agents for opposing interests negotiate in turns under a Choose-and-Freeze protocol, alternately selecting and freezing districts from a small candidate set. Choices stay constrained and interpretable as the state is partitioned step by step. Tests on post-2020 census data across all states showed significantly reduced partisan bias and unfairness in the abstract's reporting, treating selection itself as part of fairness.
arxiv-2511-04576:
Zhuo Zhang leads five authors reviewing neural methods for parametric partial differential equations. Such equations pervade science, and their solutions shift with physical properties, boundaries, and shape. Classic solvers must rerun for every new parameter set, which blocks wide exploration.

Two paradigms are compared in depth. Physics-informed networks embed the laws as soft constraints and suit inverse problems with sparse data. Neural operators, like DeepONet and Fourier operators, learn maps between function spaces directly. The review weighs where each approach wins, giving practitioners a map for choosing tools in parametric studies.
arxiv-2511-04676:
Ahmad Nouri-Zonoz and three colleagues present KGB-evolution, a simulation code for kinetic gravity braiding. The code extends an existing relativistic N-body tool with an effective field theory description. K-essence models appear inside it as a limiting case.

This first step implements the linearized dark energy stress-energy and scalar field equations. Power spectra match the hi_class linear predictions closely on large scales. Agreement holds at low redshift there and across all scales at high redshift. The runs also show small-scale growth pushing the dark energy field into nonlinear clustering, groundwork for a fuller Horndeski extension.
arxiv-2511-04876:
Catrin Harris leads four authors measuring how flow rate changes capillary trapping of a stored non-wetting fluid. Heterogeneity trapping isolates fluid upstream of rock contrasts, beyond ordinary pore-scale trapping. The setting matters for carbon dioxide storage underground.

Residual trapping barely responds to flow regime, but theory says heterogeneity trapping should. Steady drainage and imbibition runs at varied rates test that claim on layered Bentheimer sandstone. Medical X-ray scanning watches the fluid in place during each run. An analytic model accompanies the data, giving storage planners a rate-aware view of how much carbon dioxide stays put.
arxiv-2511-04976:
Xin Nie and co-authors report iFlyBot-VLM, a vision and language model built for robots that must see a scene and then act in it. Its aim is to close the gap between rich sight of the world and low-level motion control.

The model turns sight and space facts into a shared action language that is not tied to one robot body. It is built for four skills: grasp of space and size, finding named targets, turning acts into control values, and planning task steps. Tests on ten current embodied tests check how far this one model can stretch.
arxiv-2511-05076:
Raju Biswas and a co-author define pre-Schwarzian and Schwarzian derivatives for log-harmonic mappings that are locally one-to-one on the unit disk. These maps extend classic analytic ones, and their derivatives gauge how far a map bends from simple forms.

The authors study traits and uses of the new derivatives in geometric function theory. They give an exact test for when a non-vanishing log-harmonic map has a finite pre-Schwarzian norm. They also link that norm to the norm of a linked analytic function, which ties the new theory back to known results.
arxiv-2511-05176:
Soham Chatterjee and co-authors give a deterministic method to list-decode Reed-Solomon codes over any finite field. Past landmark methods were either random in their runs, or fixed but with cost tied to the field's characteristic, which can be huge.

Their method decodes from a set level of agreement in time that grows in a tame way with code length and field size. Reed-Solomon codes guard data in many systems, and list decoding can fix more errors than unique decoding. A fixed method with clean bounds makes that power safe to rely on.
arxiv-2511-05976:
Seyit Okan Kara completes a model with a new force that acts only on leptons, fixing a consistency flaw in earlier versions. The added symmetry charges all leptons equally and leaves quarks neutral. Such a symmetry normally breaks gauge consistency through anomalies, unless extra particles cancel them.

Kara adds one vector-like lepton family and singlet scalar fields. Their vacuum values break the symmetry and give mass to the new boson and the heavy leptons. He derives compact anomaly conditions, the boson's couplings and decay widths, and shows a trace condition suppresses mixing with ordinary forces. The setup also fits a standard neutrino mass mechanism and offers a stable dark matter candidate. Constraints from colliders are worked out across the parameter space.
arxiv-2511-06076:
P Michel and co-authors make lenses and gratings out of gas itself, using a pattern of entropy rather than sound. Gas optics can steer intense laser light that would damage solid optics. Older designs paired a standing sound wave with an entropy mode to carve periodic structures, but the sound wave limited lifetime and steering angles.

Dropping the acoustic mode entirely frees the design. Lifetime and time profile become controllable, and arbitrary patterns become possible, including chirped gratings and lenses with stronger contrast. The wider operating range covers larger diffraction angles. It also fits laser pulses from femtoseconds to microseconds. The authors present entropy-mode optics as a flexible new class of diffractive elements for high-power laser work.
arxiv-2511-06276:
Fernando Rodriguez Avellaneda and Paula Moraga sharpen estimates of aerosol optical depth, a measure of particles in the air tied to climate and health. Satellites report this quantity only at coarse scales in space and time. Finer maps would let officials target air quality policy and health interventions far more precisely.

Their Bayesian model treats the true field as a smooth process in space and time seen only through averaged readings. Covariances come from a diffusion-based partial differential equation, and fast approximate inference keeps the computation practical. In an India case study, the method tripled spatial detail and cut the time step from three hours to one.
arxiv-2511-06376:
Qian Ma, Ruoxiang Xu, and Yongqiang Cai examine what positional encoding really buys a transformer during in-context learning. In practice, context arrives as tokens from a finite vocabulary rather than as smooth control signals. The question is whether a single-layer transformer can still approximate any target function from such token context.

Without positional encoding, the authors show, vocabulary in-context learning lacks the universal approximation property. Adding positional encoding restores it, and they give several sufficient conditions that a positional encoding can satisfy to do the job. The findings explain, from approximation theory, why a component often treated as bookkeeping is actually load-bearing for in-context learning.
arxiv-2511-06476:
Mulan Wu, Mengyu Xu, and Dongyun Kim improve confidence intervals for clinical studies that can only enroll few patients. Small samples arise from tight budgets, scarce volunteers, and rare conditions. The usual normal approximation then gives intervals that miss their stated coverage, which can mislead treatment decisions.

Their method builds intervals from a quadratic-form statistic tied to a modified chi-squared distribution, yielding tighter accuracy for small samples and proportions. The authors recommend which sample sizes and proportions suit the method in practice. Worked examples use real clinical trial data, showing how the intervals behave where the standard approximation struggles most.
arxiv-2511-06676:
Subhojit Ghimire measures dialect bias in a popular toxicity filter and builds a teaching tool that makes the bias tangible. Automated moderation now scans everyday speech, and a post flagged as toxic may simply be written in a dialect the model misunderstands. The study compares scores for African-American English against Standard American English.

On average the model rated the African-American English text about one point eight times more toxic and nearly nine times higher for identity hate, a systematic skew. The interactive tool lets users drag a sensitivity threshold and see the real lever of harm. The harm is not just biased scores, but the neutral-looking policy cutoff a human sets, which turns skew into silencing.
arxiv-2511-07076:
Leander Grech and six co-authors use reinforcement learning to design the control pulses behind perfect entangling gates, the two-qubit operations at the heart of universal quantum computation. Shaping electromagnetic pulses by quantum optimal control can push gates toward their theoretical limits, but calibration is laborious and fragile under noise. The team instead trained a collection of reinforcement learning agents inside simulation settings built to be robust.

The agents discovered near-optimal pulse shapes that realize perfect entangling gates even under noisy conditions. Chosen agents were then validated on higher-fidelity simulations, confirming the plans were not artifacts of the training setting. Because the approach makes no assumption about the underlying hardware, it could transfer across quantum computing platforms while reducing the calibration overhead that optimal control demands.
arxiv-2511-07276:
Salem AlMarri and five co-authors confront a useful weakness of multimodal anomaly detection: the real world's inputs arrive corrupted. Systems that fuse video and audio beat video-only models in the lab, but environmental distortions can damage one or both modalities after deployment, and nobody had systematically measured the damage. The team built RobustA, a curated evaluation dataset that applies controlled audio and visual corruptions so the effects on detection can be observed.

They also propose a detection method built for this reality. It learns a shared representation space across modalities and, at inference time, dynamically weights each modality according to its estimated corruption level, leaning on whichever channel is cleaner. The dataset, with its extracted features, will be public, and the method showed notable resilience against corrupted inputs.
arxiv-2511-07376:
Jiewei Feng, Ken R Duffy, and Muriel Médard squeeze more accuracy out of a guessing-based error correction decoder by feeding it correlated noise patterns. Modern guessing decoders can decode almost any code structure, and one variant, ORBGRAND-AI, already exploits channel dependencies that other decoders ignore. This paper integrates that decoder as the pattern generator inside Guessing Codeword Decoding, a related universal decoding scheme.

A direct integration slightly worsened the block error rate while reducing the number of patterns queried. A more nuanced approach that leverages total correlation in the noise did better on both axes: it improved the block error rate by about 0.75 decibels while keeping the reduced query count. The work shows correlation in channel noise is a resource that universal decoders can spend for accuracy and speed at once.
arxiv-2511-07576:
James Miley, Grant Kennedy, and Alvaro Ribas resolve a giant dust belt around the star HD 126062. Intermediate-mass stars host bright debris discs and, unusually often, leftover gas long after planet-forming discs fade. Such systems are prime places to watch discs and planets interact.

First ALMA observations at millimeter wavelengths image the thermal glow of the belt in detail. Nearby extended gas emission also comes into view. Measuring the belt size and structure tests how planets or collisions maintain it. The system joins a small set where dust, gas, and possible planets can be studied together around an A-type star.
arxiv-2511-07676:
Ziqing Guo, Jan Balewski, and Wenshuo Hu present a quantum algorithm for learning patterns hidden in classical data. Trigonometric encodings map data into quantum circuits, but variational training by blind gradient search offers no guarantees about what the measured outputs mean. Existing methods stall on that gap.

Their quantum oracle stays traceable to the classical data, with circuit depth growing only linearly in qubit count. Approximate result patterns become learnable with structure intact. The Quantum Approximate Walk Algorithm aims to keep the link between data and quantum outcome auditable. Such traceability matters if quantum learning is to be trusted on real datasets rather than demos.
arxiv-2511-07776:
Gina Sohn, Genghan Zhang, and Konstantin Hossfeld give spatial dataflow accelerators a language for programs that change shape at run time. Machine learning models increasingly use data-dependent tensor sizes and control flow. Older abstractions for these chips force dynamic behavior into static, unoptimized molds.

Streaming Tensor Programs introduce flexible routing operators, an explicit memory hierarchy, and symbolic-shape semantics. Dynamic data rates and dimensions become visible to the compiler instead of hidden. Programs can then adapt tile sizes and flows as data demands. Efficient dynamic execution could let accelerators serve modern models without falling back to general processors for every irregular step.
arxiv-2511-07976:
Seyedehanita Madani and Vishal Patel address misaligned satellite image pairs used to spot land changes over time. Change detection compares images taken months or years apart, but seasons and shifts can break exact alignment. Many joint registration methods need retraining and transfer poorly to new places.

Their modular pipeline leaves existing detection networks untouched. A diffusion module creates in-between morphing frames, dense registration links those frames step by step, and a small U-Net refines the combined flow. On three public data sets, the method improves both registration accuracy and later change detection across several model types.
arxiv-2511-08076:
Yoshihito Kuno and Ikuo Ichinose map the mixed state phases of gauge Higgs subsystem codes under decoherence that preserves logical information. Some lattice gauge models double as quantum error correcting codes, with logical qubits stored apart from gauge degrees of freedom. Local decoherence respecting gauge symmetry can still disturb the stored information in subtle ways.

The authors clarify the full phase diagram and find an unusual critical mixed state where logic survives while the rest turns critical. Mapping to a decohered toric code helps explain the behavior. Tests with specific unitary couplings between logical and gauge qubits show robustness depends strongly on the starting mixed state.
arxiv-2511-08376:
Ozay Ezerceli and co-authors introduce TurkEmbed, a Turkish language embedding model built to beat current options on inference and similarity tasks. Turkish models often train on machine translated data sets, which can blunt accuracy and semantic depth. TurkEmbed instead combines diverse data sources with advanced training methods, including matryoshka representation learning, which packs useful information into embeddings of several sizes for resource limited settings.

On the Turkish semantic similarity benchmark, correlation scores improve clearly over prior models. The model also passes the previous state of the art system, Emrecan, on Turkish natural language inference and similarity sets, with gains of one to four percent. Faster coding adds practical value for downstream Turkish applications.
arxiv-2511-08476:
Hadi Ghaemi, Lauren Snyder, and Markus Stocker present ORKG reborn, a digital library built for machine readable research knowledge rather than papers alone. Leading archives organize story papers, so reusing a given finding still needs manual pulling and sorting by a reader. ORKG reborn instead publishes fine grained, reproducible knowledge expressions that link research statements to their supporting data and code evidence, inside papers designed from birth for reuse.

Retrieval can then run by statistical method, software package, variable, or data constraints, which document search cannot offer. Demonstrations with published papers from computer science to soil science show practical viability against state of the art archives. The work argues research knowledge databases carry enormous untapped potential.
arxiv-2511-08676:
