In the Jacobi case, ratios of derivatives and norms converge to constants independent of parameters. The results unify spectral changes and Sobolev orthogonality.
arxiv-2604-10376: Tang, Kresin, Baeumer, and Wang back frequency tools for multi stream Hawkes event flows. Hawkes flows model bursts where past events spur new ones across linked streams. From cluster bounds on cumulant measures, they prove a central limit law. That law yields a steady Whittle gauge under stationarity alone, even for heavy tailed excitation. A plain frequency test for joint independence of streams rounds out the work.
arxiv-2604-10476: Marchesi flips the tale of Kleiber's law from still pipes to pulsing waves. The three quarters scaling rule long rode on viscous loss in fractal nets. He ties local branch tuning to whole body size, forcing three quarters in three dimensions by wave impedance match. The rule then forecasts a shift to steeper scaling near nine tenths in small mammals and spineless animals. Tests across nine living systems in five phyla back the wave account and fault the old WBE proof.
arxiv-2604-10576: Maksimov, Shvanskaya, Volkova, and Vasiliev model a manganese phosphate magnet. Its trimer lattice yields a one third magnetization plateau for spin five halves ions. Fitting magnetization data gives an exchange Hamiltonian with the observed field steps. Both biquadratic coupling and single ion anisotropy prove necessary for the phase shifts. The spectrum matches low temperature heat data well.
arxiv-2604-10876: Wang and Wu test whether two relativistic point-particle Lagrangians claimed alike truly are, showing sameness hinges on the external potential V. Both give Hamiltonians meeting the mass shell rule, so they match when V is zero or electromagnetic. They differ, since only the first builds in the rule. In a Schwarzschild model with a fake potential, the first gives chaotic motion; the second, integrable motion. The first is urged for strength and breadth; the second fits low-energy weak-gravity cases and strong-field black-hole cases.
arxiv-2604-11176: Liu and six colleagues introduce DIReCT, a model synthesizing several PET tracers from MRI plus clinical information. Alzheimer's testing relies on neuroimaging. PET use is limited by cost and dose, blocking screening. New models can make PET from MRI, but personal precision remains a challenge. The approach joins a 3D architecture linking tracer relationships. A tuned vision model, BiomedCLIP, gives text output. Tests on several datasets show quality and accurate disease patterns. With MRI, made PET allows stratification of cognitive impairment.
arxiv-2604-11376: Kline and four colleagues anonymize medical images without wrecking downstream analysis. Standard de-identification often strips useful non-identifying content. Their end-to-end pipeline first detects and redacts regions likely to hold protected health information, such as burned-in text and metadata, then inpaints those areas with plausible anatomy via a latent-diffusion model. Tests on privacy, image quality, and task metrics show visually coherent de-identified volumes that keep fidelity for downstream models while substantially cutting re-identification risk, easing large-scale sharing.
arxiv-2604-11476: Perradin and three colleagues present Nexus-CAT, a Python toolkit for cluster analysis of trajectories. Standard tools like pair distribution functions miss link changes behind glass transitions. Nexus-CAT reads XYZ trajectories and identifies clusters via Union-Find with path compression. It offers clustering strategies. Checked and applied to silica, ice, and silicon, it observes a percolation transition before crystal growth in silicon. That suggests pressure-induced crystal growth begins with an amorphous change. In plain terms, the tool watches clusters link up as disordered matter changes.
arxiv-2604-11576: Xing and five colleagues propose AdvFLYP, an adversarial fine-tuning plan that follows CLIP's pretraining recipe. Prior methods fine-tune CLIP's encoder on adversarial examples from a proxy dataset, ignoring data mix and learning goals and thus weakening zero-shot ability and robustness transfer. AdvFLYP fine-tunes on adversarial images built from web image-text pairs, matched to their texts by contrastive loss, with a penalty on drift in adversarial image features. Logit-level terms aid robustness and feature-level terms aid clean accuracy. Tests on 14 downstream datasets beat practices.
arxiv-2604-11676: Nakamiya and 23 colleagues build a system at ELI-NP for sub-eV axion-like searches with a tenth-PW laser. The search uses four-wave mixing at the focus of two combined laser beams. Subsystems for vacuum pressure, area size, overlap, and trigger patterns serve the tenth-PW area. The system targets background sources from residual atoms and optical elements. Commissioning with 20 mJ pulses at 1.3 times ten to the minus seven mbar showed the system fully functional, supporting studies and scale-up from 20 mJ to two point five J.
arxiv-2604-11776: Kaoui and four colleagues test how leaflet length affects bicuspid efficiency against reflux. Crescent leaflets in lymphatic vessels and veins stop reflux and ensure unidirectional flow to the heart. Passive valves work from interplay between leaflet traits and flow. Under backward gravity-like flow, flux through the orifice is reported versus valve length, leaflet length, and rigidity. Varying leaflet length alone drives a transition from reflux to blockage, with threshold set by valve shape and stiffness. The study explains reflux in incompetent immature valves, especially short-leaflet ones.
arxiv-2604-11876: Müller, Pappalardi, and Fazio demonstrate a quantum Mpemba effect in two chaotic spin chains with conservation laws. Closed chaotic systems settle into a Gibbs ensemble after a quench, with late relaxation set by conservation laws and hydrodynamics. Pairs of starting states can therefore reach the same final ensemble at very different speeds. In their chains, a state initially closer to equilibrium relaxes more slowly than one starting farther away, giving a simple, robust realisation of the effect.
arxiv-2604-11976: Lampart, Pickl, and Spruck derive the effective dynamics of a Bose polaron, a dense gas of bosons moving around an impurity particle. In the joint limit of high density and large volume, volume cubed stays far below density. The microscopic motion then reduces to a translation-invariant Bogoliubov-Fröhlich Hamiltonian coupling the excitation field linearly to the impurity. The result gives a rigorous bridge from many-body quantum motion to a tractable model.
arxiv-2604-12176: Fesser and four colleagues define relational complexity as the smallest number of entities that must be bound at once to apply a relation. They build REL, a benchmark spanning algebra, chemistry, and biology that varies this number within each domain. Across frontier models, performance falls steadily as complexity rises, even with entity counts held fixed. The failure persists under more test-time compute and in-context learning, pointing to a limit tied to binding arity itself.
arxiv-2604-12376: Ziyang Liu proposes cooperative paging for long chats that outgrow a language model's working memory. Evicted passages are replaced by short keyword bookmarks. The model calls a recall tool to fetch a full passage when needed. On ten long multi-session conversations, the method beat truncation, search, and full context. Answer quality led on all four models tested. Picking the right bookmark remained the weak point, however.
arxiv-2604-12576: Daniel Miller and Jens Eisert detect entanglement from few partial transpose moments. The p3-PPT test relaxes the positive partial transposition criterion for lab use. Broader moment families beat it but usually need every moment up to some order. The team shows any three moments can suffice instead. A state meeting a three-moment inequality must be entangled. Depolarized GHZ states reveal the most promising variants. Moments up to order five reproduce the full PPT test for globally depolarized stabilizer states. Quantum weight enumerators track moment decay under local noise.
arxiv-2604-12776: Shiyu He and four colleagues sustain long stories in multi-agent story worlds. Generative emergence is stochastic, causing two failures. Social memory piles up clashing states without resolution. Place logic drifts from plot. EvoSpark counters with a layered memory that digests experiences into living thought. A staging mechanism aligns role, location, and plot. An engine turns random sparks into lasting characters. A tiny premise thus grows into an open-ended story world. Tests show EvoSpark beats baselines across diverse paradigms.
arxiv-2604-13076: Brazilek and Tidmarsh test whether value tuning sticks through midtraining, using animal compassion as a test value apart from existing alignment work. Their ANIMA test spans 26 questions across 13 ethical dimensions, and training on 3,000 synthetic texts reaches 77 percent, against 40 percent for instruction tuning. Later unrelated tuning erodes the gain, wiping it out after 5,000 samples, so such value shifts may need explicit upkeep.
arxiv-2604-13176: Celi and nine colleagues model how quasiparticle bursts after particle impacts degrade superconducting qubits, a barrier to reliable quantum computing. They measure quasiparticle recombination across several transmon qubits, sorting trapping decay channels from recombination, and find relaxation dynamics depend oddly on deposited energy. Linking joint relaxation events to fast phonon travel, they pin down deposited energy, matching Monte Carlo models, and frame transmon subsets as energy-sensing particle detectors.
arxiv-2604-13676: Mishra and Roy study how a settling spheroid orients itself in simple shear flow. The motion pits Jeffery torque from shear against inertial torque from settling. When gravity lies in the shear plane, one effective parameter governs the dynamics, and a saddle-node bifurcation at that parameter equal to one switches sustained rotation to steady equilibrium. When gravity aligns with vorticity, the attractor stays a periodic orbit, and noise drives phase slips whose rate depends sharply on the Peclet number.
arxiv-2604-13776: Nemecek and four colleagues expose a fairness gap in AI content watermarking. How strong a watermark is, how easy it is to spot, and how well it holds up depend on the content itself. Content differs by language, by cultural visual tradition, and by demographic group. Yet reviewing major benchmarks for text, image, and audio, they find almost none report results across those groups. They propose three checks: parity of detection across languages, broad cultural coverage, and metrics split by group. Evaluation, they argue, must precede deployment.
arxiv-2604-13876: Foo and colleagues generate short-lived entanglement between two quantum nodes linked by a chiral one-dimensional channel. Continuous driving plus a ground-state start lifts peak transient concurrence above the undriven benchmark in a simple emitter model. A fuller spin-chain treatment shows the nonsecular TCL-2 equation tracks the concurrence envelope and first peak, with leftover gaps traced to system-bath correlations beyond the Born picture.
arxiv-2604-14476: Mohammed and six colleagues apply prototypical networks to angle-of-arrival estimation, a wireless function used for localization, beamforming, and interference control. Deep-learning methods beat traditional noise sensitivity and array-generalization limits but demand large data campaigns, so the team trains class prototypes from complex IQ samples on a software-defined-radio testbed. Prototypes learned from a few examples then classify new, unseen angles. Training on only 23 percent of angle classes reaches a mean absolute error of 3 degrees with 4 shots on unseen angles, and 2 degrees with 32 shots.
arxiv-2604-14676: Arya, Sarkar, and Sethi offer a fast zero-dimensional model of how the gas between galaxies ionizes and cools over cosmic time, metals included. It follows one parcel of gas under a changing ultraviolet background, solving stiff rate equations for hydrogen, helium, and 107 metal ions. Temperature updates run alongside through heating and cooling processes. Checked against full three-dimensional simulations, it matched thermal and ionization histories well. Its predicted carbon-IV density then implied metallicities broadly in line with published constraints.
arxiv-2604-14876: Panda and Agrawal study regret tails for asymptotically optimal bandits. Such algorithms can show heavy regret tails, landing regret with real probability, while existing characterizations stay parametric. They extend KLinf-UCB to a nonparametric class under assumptions, proving optimality in expectation. They derive an upper bound on regret-tail probability. Special cases recover guarantees for bounded-support and heavy-tailed models, and for finitely supported rewards the bound matches the lower bound. The work gives a tight characterization of regret tails for KL-based UCB algorithms beyond parametric models.
arxiv-2604-15076: Meliani, Slimani, and Khoulji borrow brain navigation cells to steer robots through changing rooms. Their system, NEAT-NC, evolves recurrent neural nets that stand in for the hippocampus, fed by place, grid, direction, border, and speed signals. Tests in still and shifting scenes probe how well the evolved nets find paths. The study highlights how such brain-like cells help the method adapt to varied, complex settings.
arxiv-2604-15176: Wang and others slim down ALADIN for real-time spread-out tuning across many nodes. Adjoint SQP methods work out Jacobian data inside the embedded quadratic program, cutting message costs. An event-based update rule skips some Hessian and Jacobian refreshes, cutting compute cost. The method keeps local convergence and strong results while running much faster in urgent tests.
arxiv-2604-15376: Kim and Chelikavada turn a discarded byproduct of multi-step zoom-in grounding pipelines into a free confidence signal. Zoom consistency, the gap between a model's second-step guess and the crop middle, provably estimates step-1 spatial error under ideal conditions and tracks correctness across two vision-language models. Routing between specialist and generalist models on this signal captures 16.5 percent of the available oracle headroom.
arxiv-2604-15576: Mosso and three colleagues steer probability densities for nonlinear stochastic systems with Gaussian mixture Schrödinger bridges and multiple linearizations. Boundary distributions fit as Gaussian mixtures split the problem into Gaussian-to-Gaussian covariance steering subtasks, each solved by local straight-line fits around the mean path between parts. The multi-fit bounds beat single-fit bounds broadly, shown on an Earth-to-Mars transfer.
arxiv-2604-15676: Fu and seven colleagues build EvoRAG, a graph search tool that learns from its own hits and misses. Scores for answers point back to the paths that gave them, and each fact link gains or loses weight from that score, so the graph gets sharper with each round. Tests show right answers up 7.34 percent over the best past graph search tools.
arxiv-2604-15876: Quantschnig and three colleagues present QGas, a web toolkit for viewing, building, and jointly extending mapped gas network data. Gas data for energy planning often sit scattered across maps, plan images, and tables, making consistent network models slow and error-prone to build. QGas pairs GIS geometry editing with graph operations that preserve network topology, so users can digitize plans, edit elements, and manage attributes in one place. A demo extends a natural gas dataset with hydrogen and CO2 lines, showing its use for multi-carrier planning.
arxiv-2604-15976: Zhu, Wang, and Liu show how the phase of a stripe charge density wave can switch a magnetic vortex between topological and trivial regimes. Charge density waves and superconductivity interact in quantum materials, yet how wave phase textures steer vortex topology remains unclear. In a direct-modulation picture, the wave acts as a periodic potential that retunes band parameters, but cannot reproduce the symmetric node-antinode trend without tuning. In an inversion-symmetry-breaking picture, a wave node there mixes spin-triplet pairing, giving a transition when it dominates.
arxiv-2604-16076: Colamonaco and three colleagues introduce Prototype-Grounded Concept Models, which ground concepts in learned visual prototypes, image parts serving as explicit evidence for concepts. Concept Bottleneck Models structure outputs through plain concepts but offer no way to verify that learned concepts match human intent, hurting clarity. Prototype grounding enables direct inspection of concept semantics and human intervention at that level to correct mismatches. In tests, PGCMs match leading rivals on accuracy while greatly improving transparency and intervenability.
arxiv-2604-16276: Xue and five co-authors challenge Aziz and Howl's claim that a classical gravitational field can entangle quantum systems through a quantum-field-theoretic channel. They argue the claimed channel is better seen as semiclassical wavepacket motion in a gravitational field. It is not a new quantum effect. They also find their math overstated the effect. It used a discontinuous wavefunction carrying infinite kinetic energy as a stationary initial state. With a correct Gaussian wavepacket treatment, the effect becomes negligibly small.
arxiv-2604-16476: Kornai proposes ClawXiv, a signed archival workflow for research produced jointly by humans and AI. The problem is not just posting preprints, but moving fragile chat sessions and mixed LaTeX working folders into durable, signed, inspectable artifacts. ClawXiv tracks four states: legacy seed, normalized project, signed bundle and published artifact. Local author-side scripts import and normalize work, compile and sign it into a content-addressed bundle, then verify and publish it. Version 4 adds utility scripts, figure handling, configuration and a top-level build file.
arxiv-2604-16576: Li and colleagues present the first careful study of toughness in LLM-based dense search models. Decoder-only models are taking over from BERT-style backbones with large gains and broad use. For breadth across four benchmarks and 30 datasets, tuned models excel, but reasoning-optimized models pay a focus tax in broader contexts. They resist typos and corpus poisoning better than older rivals, yet stay open to word swaps. Vector shapes predict lexical stability, and larger models mostly prove more robust.
arxiv-2604-16676: Couvreur and Ludhani classify the minimal codewords in projective Reed-Muller codes of order two. That problem equals identifying quadrics over finite fields whose rational point sets are maximal under inclusion. Except one particular case over the field of two elements, any two absolutely irreducible quadrics with nested rational point sets are equal as projective varieties. The authors work out a precise characterisation of the minimal codewords and their exact number for each possible weight.
arxiv-2604-16776: Li and colleagues open SAVE, a unified generative framework built on conditional Transformers for multi-set single-cell modeling. Old methods treat genes as solo tokens, missing higher-level biological links and doing poorly. SAVE groups meaning-wise related genes into blocks, catching higher-order dependencies among gene modules. Flow Matching and condition masking enable free sim and generalization to unseen condition mixes. Across set making, batch effect fixing and shock guessing, SAVE beats state-of-the-art methods in lean settings.
arxiv-2604-17276: Li, Wei, and Zhang propose gCARPA, a flexible projection algorithm for finding a point shared by two closed convex sets in Hilbert space. It blends Douglas-Rachford and projection-reflection dynamics through outer averaging and internal relaxation, covering several classic methods as special cases, with a version whose parameters shift across iterations. For subspace problems they derive an explicit spectral recipe for choosing parameters, and experiments show the tuning can match or beat baselines.
arxiv-2604-17576: Denter studies fuel pricing under Germany's April 2026 rule that bars more than one price rise per day. With demand uncertain across two periods, flexible pricing lets a firm simply charge the static monopoly price each period. Under the rule, by contrast, the firm may price high early to keep room to move later. Denter shows the rule weakly raises expected average prices, strictly so when high future demand is likely enough and the high-low demand gap is large. Consumer surplus rises only when expected prices do not.
arxiv-2604-17676: Yang and Sandberg study a failure of subsample-based estimation in dynamic models. Even knowing where contamination sits, removing tainted points does not restore the clean goal. Contamination spreads through the residual filter, distorting the rule, so subsample-based methods are wrong for the clean-data value. The authors call this a clash between point-by-point subsampling and residual spread, arising when contamination spreads through steps feeding the rule. They propose a spread-friendly change of index sets, leaving the method the same in the limit.
arxiv-2604-17976: Plum and ten colleagues present ltzGLUE, the first natural language understanding benchmark for Luxembourgish, a national language often overlooked although tasks exist for many European tongues. They build new tasks and reuse old ones, covering binary and multi-class settings, including named entity recognition and topic and intent sorting. The paper also evaluates various pretrained encoder models on Luxembourgish, giving an overview of current model skills in the language.
arxiv-2604-18276: Petrič and Zander present the BlockEncoding interface in Eclipse Qrisp, a tool that makes block-encodings usable for quantum coding. It tucks a non-unitary operation inside a bigger unitary matrix, driving methods like singular-value transforms. It hides build details and qubitization behind simple builders and math tools. Code samples show matrix inversion, polynomial filtering, and Hamiltonian simulation, plus cost estimates for hard routines.
arxiv-2604-18376: Yuan, Zhao, Xu, and Niu tackle text-to-image person retrieval, where phrasing gaps make matching wordings look distant in embedding space. Their MVR system rewrites queries from several viewpoints, mixing key-feature guidance with varied phrasing. A training-free fix-up step pools multi-view signals to suppress noise, while a vision model adds multi-angle image captions. The method lifts the base model without training and leads on three person-matching data sets.
arxiv-2604-18476: Vo and seven colleagues present SemLT3D, a camera-only 3D detection framework that serves rare road users better. LiDAR-free detection is cheap and scalable, yet children, strollers, and emergency vehicles appear so rarely that learning skews against them. A language-guided mixture of experts routes queries to specialists by semantic affinity, while a distillation pipeline matches 3D queries to CLIP-informed 2D semantics. The design also hardens performance under varied appearances and corner cases.
arxiv-2604-18576: Murphy offers the Bayesian Linguistic Forecaster, a ReAct agent for binary forecasting with a belief state: an odds estimate and a tidy summary. The belief update is Bayesian-flavored rather than exact Bayesian math, versus a direct Bayesian approach using LLM chances. On 400 ForecastBench cases, BLF tops Brier Index among outside agents, the only method to clearly beat a crowd-plus-data standard. Backtests join date-aware search tools, leakage checks, and paired matchups, giving a strict setup for judging rivals.
arxiv-2604-18676: Olejak and Stegmann ask whether mass flow in binaries can fake signs of the pair-instability limit in black hole masses. A flip in mass ratio at the first Roche-lobe spill, then a wasteful second flow, caps the first-born hole's mass and makes a cutoff. Accretion in the first flow lifts the heavier hole's top mass, while the lighter hole stays capped at the stripped first star's mass. So systems where the lighter hole tops 45 solar masses stay rare, under one in ten thousand in base models.
arxiv-2604-18776: Tyagi and three colleagues tackle multiscale structural reliability for composites, where small scale material uncertainty must be carried to the large scale. Standard methods solve coupled partial differential equation systems again and again across scales, which is too costly in many dimensions. Their framework pairs a physics augmented neural network, which gives homogenized stiffness fast and within physical bounds, with a tensor train transport method that estimates the chance of failure. On a 3D benchmark, it gives steady failure estimates in dimensions up to 150.
arxiv-2604-19076: Dao and four colleagues build an automated recommender for quantum encoding circuits using meta-learning. Picking a circuit for a data set usually means costly evaluation of many candidates. Their tool predicts the best circuit from the data set's own traits, with no quantum evaluation. Nine candidates were assessed with 24 complexity metrics as features, across two training approaches and 14 machine learning models. Both approaches reach Top-3 accuracy up to 85.7 percent in naming the best circuit, showing complexity metrics carry enough signal.
arxiv-2604-19276: Kang, Hwang, and Lee build GenSync, a chat tool that helps family members across generations understand each other by showing translation openly. In a controlled study with 16 family pairs, they compare no translation, hidden translation, and open translation showing both the original and the interpreted text. Open translation supports conversation quality, closeness, and ease of use. Hidden translation, by contrast, often breaks the flow of talk.
arxiv-2604-19376: Tokunaga and colleagues report a low-temperature nuclear magnetic resonance study of the heavy-fermion compound CeIrIn5 in high fields near the crystal c axis. A field-driven transition was previously reported near 28 tesla for this orientation. The team sees no change in the spectrum above the transition, yet line strength drops sharply as the T2 relaxation time shortens greatly. The inverse T1 rate peaks sharply at the transition, which the authors read, with earlier high-field results and band calculations, as a move into an antiferromagnetic state.
arxiv-2604-19576: Ivanyuk and colleagues solve Langevin equations for the time evolution of shape parameters of a fissioning system. At each integration step, they compute the neutron emission odds and judge whether a neutron would be emitted. If so, they lower the nucleus excitation energy by the separation energy plus the emitted neutron's average energy. They then move to a potential energy layer with one fewer neutron and keep integrating. At scission, they count emitted neutrons, defining pre-scission multiplicity as total emitted neutrons over total fission paths.
arxiv-2604-20076: Acero and nineteen colleagues report the first radio detection of Type II supernova SN 2007it, some 12.2 megaparsecs away in NGC 5530. The April 2026 observation, over 18 years after explosion, comes from RISE monitoring nearby supernovae for late interaction with dense circumstellar material. The supernova shines at five and a half and nine gigahertz, while January 2026 ASKAP data at lower frequency show nothing. Rising emission or strong internal absorption may explain the low-frequency absence, and follow-up is urged across radio, optical, X-ray, and gamma-ray bands.
arxiv-2604-20176: Dizabadi and Kaya present a low-power cache built from standard six-transistor SRAM cells wired in series within each column. The serial layout exploits the stacking effect to cut leakage current during hold, without adding transistors to the cell itself. Matching changes to addressing and sensing, including column organization and the readout path, support the new topology. Transient simulations in Keysight ADS show lower leakage than the conventional wiring scheme, with the standard cell design preserved.
arxiv-2604-20376: Barral and eleven colleagues design a hybrid key delivery service linking isolated quantum key domains over classical wide-area links. Keys made in one domain travel safely to other domains with post-quantum Kyber relay, dynamic routing, and system-level management. The service runs on a testbed of three regional subnetworks, with design principles, deployment notes, and measured performance reported. The work shows a scalable path for wide-area quantum networking despite strong trust demands and low key rates on long links.
arxiv-2604-20476: Rossi, Giovannini, and Koch tackle a flaw in density functional theory, the workhorse method for electron behavior in molecules. Where two energy surfaces meet, a conical intersection, the usual split treatment of ground and excited states breaks the surface shape. Their Convex DFT forces its core math problem to stay convex, bowl-shaped with one clear low point, inside a chosen space. That yields one smooth electronic answer across regions where states share an energy, and checks against richer wave-function methods show smooth, sensible seams.
arxiv-2604-20776: Pachon and Gomez develop a path integral representation for quantum systems with a finite Hilbert space in a discrete phase space. Starting from the Wigner function and the Weyl transform, they derive an exact kernel that propagates the Wigner function in time. Iterating its composition law gives a sum-over-paths expression weighted by a phase-space action. Applying the formalism to one and two interacting qutrits, they show that full entanglement dynamics needs every fluctuation sector working together. The boundary-term sector fails to reproduce it.
arxiv-2604-21076: Sanjoy Pator asks whether the way patient records are formatted changes how well language models reconcile medication lists at handoffs between clinicians. Testing four formats across five open models and 200 synthetic patients, he finds plain clinical narrative wins for models up to 8 billion parameters, while raw JSON wins at 70 billion. Missed drugs, not invented ones, dominate errors, so safety checks should hunt omissions first.
arxiv-2604-21276: Srishti Ginjala and three colleagues ask whether model decoders make speech recognition fairer or more biased across groups. Testing nine models across three generations on 43,000 utterances, they find LLM decoders do not amplify bias: Granite-8B leads on ethnicity fairness, with a max-to-min error ratio of 2.28, while audio compression predicts accent fairness better than model scale. Severe degradation compresses gaps as all groups fail alike, but silence injection amplifies Whisper's accent bias, and masking traps it in loops that LLM decoders largely avoid.
arxiv-2604-21776: Paliwal and four colleagues solve a data bottleneck for reshooting dynamic video. Paired multi-view footage of non-rigid scenes is scarce. Their self-supervised system creates pseudo multi-view triplets from single internet videos. It uses smooth random-walk crops as source and target views and a warped first frame as a geometric anchor. Forced to route textures across times and viewpoints rather than copy frames, the model learns 4D structure. It achieves strong temporal consistency and camera control.
arxiv-2604-21976: D'Eramo, Manconi, and Sassi present a framework in which three classes of number-changing processes affect relic abundance via thermal freeze-out and indirect cosmic-ray signals. The classes are direct annihilations into Standard Model final states, annihilations into metastable mediators, and semi-annihilation with a dark matter particle in the final state. They show how injection spectra for gamma rays, neutrinos, and cosmic-ray antimatter vary with the importance of the three classes. They evaluate gamma-ray fluxes from dwarf spheroidal galaxies in the GeV-TeV window.
arxiv-2604-22076: Chen and six colleagues present PrivUn, a test setup judging unlearning strength with three-level attack cases: direct retrieval, in-context learning recovery, and fine-tuning restoration. Their study finds flaws in current unlearning methods, with two findings. First, unlearning spreads in waves along gradient links, not along meaning links like knowledge graphs. Second, most methods forget at the surface, leaving private facts spread over many deep model layers.
arxiv-2604-22376: Koshihara and Yuasa prove a no-go theorem for quantum heat engines powered purely by measurements in the steady regime. Their engine uses a finite-dimensional working substance, driven by bare measurements with no feedback control or thermal contact. By a Poincaré-like recurrence theorem for general quantum channels, they show measurements in the steady regime become nondisturbing and inject no energy. No work can therefore be extracted. The result shows work extraction in steady cycles needs an entropy-decreasing process, such as feedback or thermal contact.
arxiv-2604-22676: Xiong, Yeap, and Ban propose WG-SRC, a white-box probe. It swaps message passing for a fixed dictionary of raw traits, row- and symmetric-normalized low-pass flows, and high-pass gaps. It joins Fisher coordinate picks, class PCA spaces, multi-alpha ridge sorting, and score fusion, resting calls and study on spaces, energy-set sizes, and closed-form verdicts. This matters since strong networks' message passing tangles ego traits, local smoothing, high-pass gaps, class shape, and boundary effects darkly, hiding node sorts and dataset needs.
arxiv-2604-22776: Radzikowski and Chen show that a chef's sense of flavor, texture, and cultural fit, hard to put into words, already lives inside ingredient vectors learned from recipes and food chemistry. With language-model help, they clean 6,653 raw FlavorGraph entries down to 1,032 standard ingredients. From the cleaned set, they recover at least fifteen dimensions covering taste, texture, geography, processing, and culture. The result turns a scattered cook's intuition into a measurable structure for studying how ingredients relate.
arxiv-2604-22876: Gabrick and three colleagues model competition between two epidemic strains in a Susceptible-Infected-Recovered framework, where standard theory says the basic reproduction number alone decides the winner. They show random fluctuations can overturn that deterministic advantage, even far from the near-neutral regime. Chance also shrinks fixation times from years to days, under a scaling law tied to noise intensity and distance from neutrality. Even when one strain leads, noise can push the system across the barrier linked to coexistence.
arxiv-2604-23176: Andrews, Li, and Shang study optimal estimation when the likelihood may be misspecified, building on choice theory under uncertainty. They analyse axiom-based optimality rules nesting several current misspecification-robust goals, and introduce the constrained multiplier rule for flexible misspecification views. A local asymptotic minimax result extends a classic efficiency bound to a limit experiment with moment-limited misspecification. Asymptotically optimal estimators emerge as Bayes rules under a flat prior and a tilted likelihood with moment limits. Feasible plug-in versions are also asymptotically optimal.
arxiv-2604-23276: Liu and four colleagues build a lightweight production PDF parser that detects figures, tables, and forms and links captions to the right elements. Spatial heuristics, layout analysis, and semantic similarity replace parsers that miss complex visuals, grab watermarks, fragment elements, and misplace captions. On benchmarks and internal data, it reaches at least 96 percent visual detection accuracy and 93 percent caption association accuracy. As a preprocessing step for multimodal retrieval, it beats leading parsers and large vision-language models while cutting latency by over two times. It already runs in production.
arxiv-2604-23376: Richard and Yafaev carry the hybrid conjecture, which unifies two major conjectures about special points in Shimura varieties, into the mixed setting. Departing from the usual strategy, they combine equidistribution with o-minimality to prove the conjecture for the universal abelian scheme and its base. Their result also yields the mixed André-Oort conjecture, the Manin-Mumford conjecture for arbitrary abelian varieties, and a case of Mordell-Lang.
arxiv-2604-23476: Liao, Li, Huang, and Xiao sharpen quantum sensing by gauging a phase and a correlation factor at once from one shared squeezed reservoir. They show the squeezing phase is key: tuning it to fit the correlation factor gives the best precision for each value and for the pair. Gauging both at once then saves quantum effort while staying precise, even though the two values fight each other.
arxiv-2604-23576: Narava and colleagues propose CAPSULE, a safe way to train agents in complex systems whose physics are unknown. It first learns a probabilistic model of the system offline. From that model it builds safety barriers that allow for model error, setting cautious limits. An online fix-up step enforces those limits while the agent explores, matching baseline rewards on control tests while cutting safety breaches sharply.
arxiv-2604-23976: Xu and four colleagues study how robots might strengthen parent-child bonds instead of replacing human contact. After home probes with six families pointed to robot initiative and message timing as key choices, a lab study with twenty families tested those dimensions. Families bent the robot exchanges to their own habits, wrestled with who should start a message and when, and imagined everyday uses for staying connected.
arxiv-2604-24176: Bailleux and four colleagues recast explanation assessment as ranking, not generation. Instead of emitting one best explanation, they train reward models to order candidates by graded quality. Listwise and pairwise ranking losses keep ordinal structure and avoid score compression from pointwise regression or binary preference goals. Ranking losses beat regression on score separation everywhere, with listwise methods best on clean tiers and pairwise methods tougher on noisy annotations. Small encoders on curated data even match far larger models, and ranking rewards stabilize policy optimization where regression rewards fail.
arxiv-2604-24276: Kundu and five colleagues extend instance-sensitive segmentation losses to multi-class problems, where rare classes get too little signal. Blob and CC losses were built for single-class segmentation so small lesions match large ones. A one-vs-rest decomposition repurposes them for class imbalance, since uniform averaging lets each class contribute equally. Inverse-size weighting, unstable globally, works when confined inside each component's loss. On BraTS-METS 2025, multi-class CC loss lifts foreground Dice to 0.64 with rare-class gains, while blob loss leads on Panoptic Quality and recognition.
arxiv-2604-24376: Bao and three colleagues tackle classification of 21 depression symptoms from the BDI-II survey. Common methods struggle with steady fit rules, since the task is fine-grained and highly uneven. They propose Symptom Induction, packing cases into short guidelines stating what counts as evidence for each symptom. Those guidelines guide classification. Across four model groups and eight models, Symptom Induction tops weighted F1 on BDI-Sen, with large gains for rare symptoms. Induced guidelines carry over across diseases sharing symptoms, like bipolar and eating disorders.
arxiv-2604-24476: Choi, Espinoza-Rojas, and Hekker hunt for pairs of red giant stars whose blended light tricks astronomers into treating two pulsing stars as one. Using Kepler light curves, they compare mixed and separated pulse patterns for stars with close neighbours pulsing at similar rates. They name six hidden pairs whose mixed patterns skew mass and size estimates. Mass runs off by up to about three times and size by up to about two times, and all six are chance line-ups rather than true bound pairs.
arxiv-2604-24576: Richardson, Hong and Abalkina assemble BuyTheBy, a dataset of 18,710 text ads for paper-mill services, drawn from seven businesses in seven countries. Of these, 15,839 carry prices. They cover 20,598 positions for sale across 5,567 products in 14 categories, with 51,812 timestamped price points. The authors present basic analyses showing how the collection can support quantitative study of markets for academic fraud.
arxiv-2604-24676: Gautam classifies corefree fusion systems, without exception, on a Sylow 3-subgroup of the sporadic groups Fi22, Fi23 and the Baby Monster, denoted B. He shows that the 3-group in each case supports no exotic fusion systems. The paper is the first of two that will finish classifying corefree fusion systems, without exception, on Sylow p-subgroups of sporadic groups for odd p. The result thus closes the p equals 3 case for these three groups within the larger program.
arxiv-2604-25076: Powell, Yu and Tokekar address zero-shot coordination for sparse-reward tasks with varied reward shapings. Learning agents often fail to cooperate with partners sharing objectives but different details. Zero-shot coordination trains agents to cooperate with unknown partners. Existing solutions assume identical rewards for trained agents and future partners. That is unrealistic: partners may share sparse objectives yet shape rewards differently. The authors train an ensemble using randomized shapings chosen with 4 algorithms. Overcooked experiments show consistent gains by about 62 to 119 percent in sparse reward over baselines.
arxiv-2604-25276: Zheng and four colleagues introduce OmniVTG, a large data set for open-world video temporal grounding plus a Self-Correction Chain-of-Thought training paradigm. Open-world grounding struggles because data sets are small and narrow, leaving gaps between common and rare concepts. OmniVTG is built by finding vocabulary gaps and collecting videos likely to contain target concepts. The paradigm trains models to predict, then reflect on and refine predictions. Experiments show strong open-world grounding on OmniVTG and state-of-the-art zero-shot results on four benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-25376: Chen and three colleagues put forth Concept-Reasoning Expansion, or CoRE, joining image traits with set concepts. Sound brain lesion marking in MRI matters, but high marking costs and strict privacy rules call for Continual Learning that adapts with no loss of old skill. Past Continual Learning schemes hit size caps or swell with spare parts. By matching image tokens to a concept list, CoRE steers expert routing. Model growth rests on clinical priors. Over 12 linked tasks, CoRE tops past results.
arxiv-2604-25476: Menta presents PSP, an accent benchmark for Indic text-to-speech. Standard TTS evaluation gauges intelligibility and naturalness, but not accent. PSP splits accent into six dimensions: retroflex collapse, aspiration, vowel-length, Tamil-zha fidelity, Frechet Audio Distance, and prosodic divergence. Version one benchmarks five systems on Hindi, Telugu, and Tamil sets, plus an R5-to-R6 Telugu case study. Findings: retroflex collapse grows with difficulty, Hindi below Telugu below Tamil, near 1, 40, and 68 percent; PSP ordering diverges from word-error ordering; no system leads across all six dimensions.
arxiv-2604-25576: Perviz and Cammarata investigate what sets lattice heat flow in pristine and doped transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers. They solve the linearised Boltzmann transport equation in phonon and relaxon bases. Pristine bilayers show isotropic in-plane heat flow with ordering preserved across temperature. Relaxon analysis links it to phonon group velocity and layer localisation. Lighter atoms tend to raise heat flow, but a large mass contrast is needed to localise key vibrational modes. Doped bilayers instead show lower anisotropic heat flow, and setup and temperature set the direction of peak transport.
arxiv-2604-25676: Lee, Song, and Kang introduce CORAL, a retrieval method that adapts its sources and its query while answering culturally grounded questions in many languages. Fixed retrieval often pulls evidence from the wrong language or region, even with strong tools. CORAL picks sources, fetches documents, checks them for fit, and rewrites the query when evidence falls short. On two cultural benchmarks, it raised accuracy on low-resource languages above the best baselines.
arxiv-2604-25776: Wong and three colleagues survey speech emotion recognition research to test whether stated motivations match actual practice. Critical analyses have raised ethical concerns about task validity and downstream impacts, urging alignment between goals and methods. The survey finds appealing goals, such as voice-activated systems and healthcare uses, but datasets that do not reflect those deployment settings. That gap between motivation and practice, the authors argue, breeds ethical concerns. They call for concrete use cases to prevent misinterpretation, misuse, and downstream harm.
arxiv-2604-26176: Sun and Chen argue that model question answering over knowledge graphs suffers because planners rebuild retrieval plans from scratch, like a database without a plan cache. That invites schema hallucinations and thin coverage. Their CacheRAG architecture caches past plans with a schema-agnostic natural-language interface, a varied two-layer cache index, and bounded subgraph expansion with strict complexity limits. Experiments show large gains over leading baselines, including about thirteen percent higher accuracy and about eighteen percent higher truthfulness on a hard retrieval benchmark.
arxiv-2604-26276: Jiang and Xu investigated non-abelian extensions of Lie algebras equipped with derivations, from several viewpoints at once. The theory is captured by second non-abelian cohomology, the Deligne groupoid, strict Lie 2-algebras under strict derivations, and kernels. Within that unified frame, they tackled when a pair of derivations on the two ends lifts to the middle algebra, supplying an obstruction class for the lift.
arxiv-2604-26976: Grosser and Lutz study fitting description-logic ontologies to mixed examples as an ABox plus a Boolean query. Work covered the logics ALC and ALCI; they focus on the Horn logics EL and ELI and their extensions with the bottom concept. They characterize when a fitting ontology exists via simulations, build decision procedures, and pin down complexity. For atomic queries the problem lies in PTime for EL and ELI. For conjunctive queries and unions it is Sigma-2-P-complete for EL and ExpTime-complete for ELI, with bottom irrelevant.
arxiv-2604-27376: Bai, Lyu, and Zhao propose domain walls that collapse, made by an axion-like field, as a route to electroweak baryogenesis, the matter-antimatter imbalance. In their picture, the walls replace bubble walls from a strong first-order phase change, splitting regions into electroweak phases until a crossover bias makes them collapse. One-way wall motion acts like a baryon chemical potential and, through sphaleron effects, builds the asymmetry, either from late entropy input or sphaleron suppression. The collapse leaves a stochastic gravitational-wave background with marks unlike electroweak spectra.
arxiv-2604-27476: Deng and fourteen colleagues present EdgeFM, an agent-driven inference framework for vision-language models for edge use. Existing frameworks bloat general designs or lock developers into closed ecosystems. EdgeFM strips non-essential features to cut request latency, and packages agent-tuned kernel optimizations as a library of reusable skills that can be invoked directly. It supports x86 and Orin platforms, claims the first full VLA rollout on Horizon Journey, and in most cases beats vendor toolchains, with speedups up to 1.49 times over TensorRT-Edge-LLM on Orin.
arxiv-2604-27676: Alashwali offers a balanced view of users' activity logs: the good, the bad, misconceptions, and the disastrous. Most prior work stressed the negative side, such as low awareness of privacy controls and privacy concerns about own data. Through a case study of Google's controls, based on interviews with 30 account holders in Saudi Arabia, she sorts views into four themes. The study finds new themes and use cases and closes with practical tips for providers, researchers, experts, and users.
arxiv-2604-27876: Wang, Toussaint, and Gibaud test how sound changes thickening in dense, sticky cornstarch mixes. Such mixes jam through weak load-bearing force webs in patchy density waves, and work says ultrasound thins them. With a rheo-ultrasound rig, they find sound does not thin the mix but pushes the jump toward faster shear rates. Stress patterns fall onto shared curves, showing a smooth drift to fluid states. The team reads this as sound shaking force webs loose through slip, drag wobbles, and streaming, so bigger stresses must hold a jam.
arxiv-2604-28076: Ji and colleagues introduce TopBench, a benchmark for table questions that require predicting unseen answers from past patterns rather than looking values up. Its hundreds of samples span single-point prediction, decision making, treatment effects and complex filtering, with outputs mixing reasoning text and structured tables. Current models often default to lookup and stumble on intent, and accurate intent recognition proves the prerequisite for good predictive behaviour.
arxiv-2605-00076:
Tom Sorger, Eric Cornelissen, Aman Sharma, Javier Ron, Musard Balliu, and Martin Monperrus present zkSBOM, a way to share software bills of materials without exposing them. Regulators increasingly mandate these component lists, yet sharing forces a bad choice: full disclosure reveals attack surface, such as a vulnerable dependency, while full opacity lets suppliers misrepresent what they shipped.

zkSBOM uses zero-knowledge sets to commit cryptographically to an SBOM's components. A consumer can ask whether the described artifact is hit by a known vulnerability and receive a proof of the answer, learning nothing else about the list. The authors quantify the leakage from inclusion and exclusion proofs, then test the mechanism on realistic scenarios and measure its operating costs. They conclude it protects suppliers and consumers from each other at once.
arxiv-2605-00176:
Eichi Uehara builds a statistical estimator for dose-response curves that can survive badly contaminated data. Standard double machine learning relies on local smoothers, and a single outlier inside a smoothing window can bend the whole curve there. Heavy tails make that weakness serious in practice.

His estimator, SHIFT, combines cross-fitted orthogonalization with a robust second stage and a careful refit on inliers only. The cutoff for inliers is scaled by a robust spread measure taken after the robust fit, a choice that sharply cut error in a focused contamination test. Across many simulation fits, SHIFT recovered the set of true outliers almost exactly while staying competitive on curve shape. A diagnostic suite helps users judge which robust method their data calls for.
arxiv-2605-00276:
Tiejin Chen and 4 co-authors build an agentic AI system for trip planning for intelligent vehicles, where the goal is the best route, not just a workable one. Travel time, energy use, and traffic interact, so a merely feasible plan can be far from optimal. Older benchmarks also lack true best answers, which blocks fair scoring of optimization quality.

Their framework uses an orchestrating agent that coordinates specialist agents for traffic, charging, and points of interest, refining the plan as conditions change. Alongside it they release a dataset of trip planning problems with definite optimal solutions and labeled task categories. The system scored well above single-agent and fixed-workflow rivals on that benchmark, which the authors read as evidence for orchestrated teamwork among agents.
arxiv-2605-00776:
Scott Friedman and eight co-authors introduce Directed Social Regard, a method for finding mixed feelings aimed at specific targets in online text. Ordinary sentiment tools give one overall score, so they miss cases where praise and blame appear together, or who each feeling is aimed at. The team grounds its three scoring axes in social science ideas about moral framing and disengagement.

Two transformer models first find the text spans that receive sentiment, then score each span in context from negative to positive on each axis. The authors describe how they built and checked the training data. Applied to six outside datasets, the outputs line up in meaningful ways with existing labels and topics.
arxiv-2605-00876:
Duaa Alim, Mogtaba Alim, and Liam Chalcroft present GAZE, a framework that lets a medical vision-language model inspect rare brain MRI cases in steps, as radiologists do. Instead of reading an image in one pass, the model can call viewer tools for zoom, windowing, contrast, and edges, plus retrieval tools backed by PubMed and Open-i. Outputs are checked against a schema and every tool call is logged.

On a benchmark of more than nine hundred cases covering hundreds of rare conditions, GAZE improves lesion localisation and diagnostic accuracy without task-specific training. Tool use helps rare disorders most, and gains track how much the model engages the tools. Diagnosis and localisation can trade off, so joint scoring matters.
arxiv-2605-01176:
Yi Wang and Takashi Hasuike explain why one popular way of training portfolio models can inflate return signals and cause excessive trading. The approach, decision-focused learning with the SPO surrogate, trains a predictor by the quality of the final portfolio choice rather than by forecast accuracy alone. That is attractive, but in practice the trained portfolios can swing too much between periods.

Using the KKT conditions, the authors show that portfolio choices under this training act like a ranking of assets by scores adjusted for risk and trading cost. This ranking view explains both the inflated signals and the high turnover. Tests on SPO-trained portfolios then weigh three fixes: clipping, min-max rescaling, and partial adjustment of the portfolio. Realistic output limits and direct control of turnover made the strategies easier to carry out in practice.
arxiv-2605-01276:
Davide Palitta, Catherine E Powell, and Valeria Simoncini design faster ways to solve a class of large matrix equations that show up in control, fluids, and models with random inputs. The equations are nonsymmetric, so many classic fast solvers do not apply directly.

Their method builds short recurrences, step-by-step formulas that reuse only the last few steps instead of a growing history, which saves memory. Low-rank tricks keep the stored answer small, and random sampling methods cut the cost further. Tests on a benchmark problem and on a hard mixed model of diffusion with random inputs show the approach can handle problems that strain older solvers. The work grows out of a recent subspace method for symmetric cases.
arxiv-2605-01376:
Ahsan Adeel warns that today's AI systems, built on a thin view of the brain, may blur the line between true and false. Systems that chase reward boost attention to whatever scores well, with no built-in check on whether the content is valid or worth heeding, so volume and bias both grow.

Adeel calls the end state the mind-reality overload dilemma: people and systems swamped by doubtful content, with worse judgment as a result. The proposed fix is wider public access to AI built on the physics of pyramidal neurons, the cells behind waking thought. In that design, a precision mechanism tests proof for coherence before it is attended to or passed on. Adeel does not claim biology hands us moral rules, but argues such systems could support clearer beliefs and steadier judgment.
arxiv-2605-01876:
Kuoye Niu and colleagues release BadmintonGRF, a data set for estimating ground reaction force in badminton without markers on the body. Badminton is fast and non-repeating, and few public sets pair force data with video. The team recorded eight synced video views, four force plates, and motion capture for ten subjects, then aligned the streams with checked events and time offsets.

A public tier gives pose, aligned force data, and splits, while raw video and full motion files sit under controlled access. The release holds more than seventeen thousand impact segments before filtering. The authors also supply code, leave-one-subject-out splits, and ten baseline methods for the pose-to-force task.
arxiv-2605-02076:
Subarna Pudasaini, Parker Smith, and Daning Huang optimise flight paths for aircraft whose wings can morph in flight. Morphing can improve manoeuvrability and fuel use over fixed wings, but the balance between gains and control cost in unsteady moves was unclear. The team couples a trajectory optimiser to a mid-fidelity model that joins nonlinear structural dynamics with an unsteady vortex lattice method.

A physics-based cost model counts the energy needed to overcome aerodynamic hinge moments at each instant. On a flexible, high-aspect-ratio aircraft with morphing winglets, morphing widened the flight envelope by separating lift and pitch demands. A pull-up move gained about twenty-nine percent more altitude at higher control cost, while a banked turn showed its own trade-off.
arxiv-2605-02176:
Mateusz Kwaśnicki and Jack Thompson prove density bounds for weak solutions of nonlocal mean curvature equations. Those equations govern nonlocal minimal surfaces. Their results give bounds that hold at all scales and for a broad class of kernels. The kernels need only be comparable to the fractional Laplacian, a standard nonlocal operator.

A second result concerns solutions whose density is low, below a fixed constant. Such solutions must have a fat boundary. That means the boundary carries positive area in the Lebesgue sense. The outcome is striking, since a boundary is often expected to be thin. Both claims use the viscosity framework, the standard weak setting for these equations.
arxiv-2605-02476:
Shiheng Zhao and Pierre A. Haas extend the theory of odd elasticity from small bends to large shape changes. Odd elasticity describes active solids, such as living tissue, whose response does not conserve energy in the usual passive way. Most past work stayed in two dimensions and near the rest shape, where linear theory applies.

The authors set up large, nonlinear deformations for uniform two-dimensional Cauchy elastic solids. They test the frame on the Rivlin problem, where a square is pulled by fixed loads. Oddness, they find, removes the sudden shape branches a passive square would show. A three-dimensional cube keeps its branches, even though no odd linear form exists in three dimensions. The results ground later work on active and living solids.
arxiv-2605-02776:
Paolo Pin studies how strategic talk shapes the networks people form to share information. Agents build costly links, each holds a noisy private signal about a shared state, neighbors exchange cheap-talk messages, and actions reward both accuracy and coordination. Talk is cheap, so truthfulness cannot be assumed; it must survive each agent's incentives.

Pin shows full revelation can be sustained exactly when every connected part of the network is a clique, a fully linked group. The core of the network game, with varied signal quality and mildly convex link costs, is then characterized. Every core outcome is truthful and splits into exclusive, like-sorted information clubs, built by a recursive rule weighing precision against cost. Stable clubs need not be best overall: sorting can hoard the sharpest signals in one group.
arxiv-2605-02976:
R. Trasarti-Battistoni, M. Pszota, and P. Ván compare three classic formulas for where the energy of Newtonian gravity resides. Maxwell, Bondi, and Ohanian each proposed an energy density for the gravitational field. The authors show the three cannot be told apart by boundary conditions, and that their energy balance equations come out identical, despite the formulas themselves differing.

Equivalence of balances, though, is not equivalence of meaning. Judged on thermodynamic grounds, the Ohanian density stands apart from the other two. The paper is brief and conceptual, aimed at readers in gravitation theory and thermodynamics who care which local energy story a balance law really supports. It is a useful reminder that matching totals can hide distinct local claims.
arxiv-2605-03076:
Adnan Ali, Jinlong Li, Syed Muhammad Israr, Guanghua Yang, Ali Kashif Bashir, and Mohammed Ameen improve graph contrastive learning by scheduling which negative examples a model sees, and when. Negatives drive this self-supervised method, yet past work focused on picking them, not on controlling exposure during training.

Their AdNGCL framework keeps a bounded pool per anchor and rechecks hardness as representations change. A scheduler adjusts exposure to easy, medium, or hard negatives by category response, while refresh steps drop suspect items and add variety. Across ten benchmarks it led on eight datasets by mean score.
arxiv-2605-03176:
Kevin Batz, Benjamin Lucien Kaminski, Lucas Kehrer, Gerwin Klein, Todd Schmid, and Henning Urbat present an algebra for reasoning about fixed point iterations without tracking step indices. Fixed points built as iteration limits pervade computer science, from program semantics to software verification.

Their algebra of iterative constructions works purely with equations on complete lattices and continuous maps. It yields algebraic proofs of classic results, including a generalization of Kleene's theorem and of k-induction, plus a new theorem using lattice limit inferiors and superiors from any seed. Mechanized in Isabelle, the proofs can be found automatically, and completeness limits are pinned down.
arxiv-2605-03276:
Andong Deng, Dawei Du, Zhenfang Chen, Wen Zhong, Fan Chen, Guang Chen, Chia-Wen Kuo, Longyin Wen, Chen Chen, and Sijie Zhu introduce VEBench. It is a benchmark for real video editing by large multimodal models. Editing needs film craft plus reasoning. A good editor selects, aligns, and combines clips into a coherent story.

The set holds thousands of edited videos. It also holds human-checked questions in two tasks. One task names editing techniques from mixed cues. The other simulates edit work, picking and timing clips. Tests on leading models show a large gap to human editing skill.
arxiv-2605-03876:
Owen Sheekey and ten co-authors demonstrate a remote way to measure entropy in coupled quantum dots, tiny semiconductor structures that confine individual electrons. Recent experiments showed that entropy changes when electrons are added to a dot reveal the spin and orbital degeneracy of the states involved. More exotic entropies, though, require probing a whole system, not just the dot receiving the particle.

The team uses a pair of capacitively coupled gallium arsenide quantum dots. Charge measurements on one dot reveal entropy changes of the entire two-dot system. The surroundings respond to the added electron through Maxwell relations. The method works both at weak coupling, where microstate counting applies, and at stronger coupling, where numerical renormalization group calculations are needed.
arxiv-2605-03976:
Xiaochen Liu, Jean-Paul M. G. Linnartz, and Thiago E. B. Cunha model optical wireless communication links whose bandwidth is limited by components rather than by regulation, unlike radio systems. They review the bandwidth limits of physical-layer components, which typically make the gain-to-noise ratio decay with frequency in a low-pass pattern describable by a pole-zero transfer function. The goal is to squeeze more throughput through that decaying channel.

The authors optimize the signal power spectrum of DC-biased optical OFDM, allowing modulation beyond the three-decibel end-to-end bandwidth, and express the optimized throughput as a function of the maximum modulation frequency. A new Newton-based algorithm is compared with an accelerated Hughes-Hartogs algorithm for finding near-optimal spectra under theoretical, measured, and simulated channel responses.
arxiv-2605-04376:
Zheng Ma and three co-authors present a graph-based method for protein inference, the task of working out which proteins are present in a sample from the peptide evidence a mass spectrometer reports. Deep learning has been held back here by the cost and scarcity of well labelled data.

Their system links proteins, peptides, and spectrum matches into one graph and classifies the protein nodes. It trains on public data with labels borrowed from an existing inference tool, then refines those labels by self-training on confident cases. Because its input features are well normalised, the model works across data sets without retraining for each one.
arxiv-2605-04676:
Anis Bara and four co-authors ask whether vision-language models can learn to read radio frequency spectrograms from synthetic training data alone. Spectrograms are the pictures engineers use to inspect wireless signals. Understanding the spectrum is essential for intelligent communications, but extracting physical attributes from a spectrogram is a skill traditional machine learning has not achieved.

They build a platform that pairs live spectrum captures from a software-defined radio with model interpretations. That allows direct tests on real over-the-air signals. A model trained only on synthetic spectrograms is compared with general-purpose baselines. The comparison uses a shared benchmark. It probes whether the synthetic skill transfers to the real radio environment.
arxiv-2605-05276:
Joonas Lahtinen extends a theory of unbiased source finding to unbiased parameter estimation and signal reconstruction for any number of active settings. The topic touches exact recovery, studied in compressed sensing and multi-source fitting across imaging problems. Unbiased methods are prized because they avoid steady shrinkage, but their noise behaviour had an open puzzle.

Lahtinen derives upper bounds on how many settings can be recovered in the noiseless case and defines a chance measure for recovering all active parameters in the correct size order. The theory explains the noise toughness question for standardised and fair methods and reveals a trade-off between sensor count and signal-to-noise ratio. Computer tests confirm what the theory predicts.
arxiv-2605-05476:
When a knowledge graph is built automatically from text, errors creep in everywhere. Othmane Kabal and four co-authors introduce a benchmark that judges graph building and graph learning together. Without that pairing, a poor result could come from the graph, the learning model, or both, and nobody could tell which.

Their benchmark uses one biomedical text collection and three graphs: two built by different automatic methods, and one curated by experts as a quality ceiling. Models are tested on node classification under a shared protocol. The setup gives future extraction methods and learning models a fair, reproducible yardstick.
arxiv-2605-05576:
Magnon polaritons mix magnetic waves with microwave light inside a cavity, creating a hybrid excitation. L. Hackner, A. R. Myatt, W. Wustmann, and N. J. Lambert reshape that hybrid's spectrum by shaking the cavity instead of the magnet. Modulating the magnon frequency directly needs a varying magnetic field, which is technically awkward.

They modulate the microwave cavity frequency, reaching large depth and bandwidth. Two drive tones, at twice and three times a base frequency, produce spectra that depend on their relative size and phase. New anticrossings appear between sidebands that single-frequency driving leaves uncoupled.
arxiv-2605-05876:
Inverse rendering works backward from photos to shape, material, and light. Mae Younes and Adnane Boukhayma present 3D Surface Splatting, the first differentiable surface-splatting renderer built for physics-based inverse rendering. Their insight is that the surface separation problem at splatting's heart can be written in terms of the reconstruction kernels themselves.

A coverage-based compositing model follows, with opacity arising from summed reconstruction weights. That yields smooth silhouettes and useful visibility gradients at sparse edges. Combined with microfacet shading under learned environment lighting, the system jointly recovers shape and look from multiple views.
arxiv-2605-05976:
Na Li and six co-authors introduce community-to-vehicle, a plan for charging electric cars inside local energy communities. Rules often keep community energy systems and public car charging apart. That split wastes surplus solar power made within the community boundary.

Under their design, that surplus goes first to car charging inside the boundary, offered to outside users at a community price. The study builds on Switzerland's new local electricity community framework and compares stages from full separation to coordinated charging. Coordinated charging raised local solar use and improved economic results for both sides. Drivers paid less than at commercial chargers, and the community gained a new revenue stream.
arxiv-2605-06176:
Antoine-Marie Bogso and three co-authors solve a stochastic optimal control problem whose dynamics can jump and drift unevenly. The systems studied have piecewise smooth drift with discontinuities triggered at thresholds, a pattern outside classical maximum principle results that assume global smoothness. Such dynamics arise naturally in insurance surplus management, where dividends and capital injections switch on at set safety levels.

The authors establish both necessary and sufficient conditions for optimal control in this class. Their approach joins a Sobolev type representation of the first variation process with smooth approximations and a variational principle. As the application, they study optimal premium adjustment and reserve management for an insurer. The surplus there follows threshold based dividend and capital injection policies of exactly the studied form.
arxiv-2605-06376:
Tao Liu and ten co-authors move distribution matching distillation for diffusion models from fixed timesteps to continuous time. Step distillation speeds image generation, but the leading matching approach supervises only at a few preset points along the sampling path. That sparse anchoring, joined with a mode seeking divergence, tends to leave visual artifacts and over smoothed outputs. GANs or reward models must patch the quality back, the authors argue. Their method removes the need for those patches.

A dynamic schedule of random length enforces matching anywhere along trajectories, not just at anchors. A second objective matches latents extrapolated off the trajectory through the student's own velocity field, preserving fine detail. Across two modern image architectures the method delivered highly competitive fidelity for few step generation. No complex auxiliary objectives were required.
arxiv-2605-06576:
Xiaoguang Guo and seven co-authors introduce GRL-Safety, a benchmark for the safety of graph representation learning under deployment stress. Graph methods now range from topology-only embeddings to reusable graph foundation models, but evaluations mostly measure clean transfer. It was unclear how they behave when graph signals, contexts, labels, groups, or evidence are stressed.

The benchmark tests twelve methods on twenty-five datasets across five axes: corruption robustness, out-of-distribution generalization, class imbalance, fairness, and interpretation, reporting per-axis results rather than one score. Safety depends on how representation design meets the stressed factor, foundation models win only on specific axes, and some regimes defeat every method tested.
arxiv-2605-06876:
Yongjae Lee and four co-authors introduce AdpSplit, a smarter splitting operator for 3D Gaussian Splatting, the technique that renders scenes from clouds of soft three-dimensional blobs. Training grows the blob population by splitting, but the standard operator splits blindly and needs many rounds to reveal fine detail, slowing schedules that aim for fewer iterations.

AdpSplit decides how many children each split should produce and initializes them from pixel-error statistics of the region, so effort goes where the image is wrong. Across three standard scene datasets it cuts training time for several accelerated pipelines by roughly a tenth to a fifth. Paired with one fast pipeline it matches full-schedule quality while training far faster.
arxiv-2605-06976:
Dongqing Li and three co-authors infer hidden partial orders from data that only show a full ordering. Rankings and agent work traces often list steps in one line, even when some steps have no required order between them. Treating that line as the true structure can mislead analysis of prerequisites.

The authors build a smooth, differentiable version of a partial-order model, replacing hard rules with soft approximations that support gradient-based sampling and inference. They prove the soft version recovers the hard model in the sharp limit. Tests on synthetic data, animal dominance records, and cloud agent traces show accurate recovery with better speed and accuracy trade-offs on larger problems.
arxiv-2605-07076:
Zekun Wang and three co-authors study how language models can keep new knowledge instead of merely seeing it in a long prompt. Long context windows show a model more evidence, but useful facts may not be preserved or reused later. Their framework writes current context into the model's own weights.

Called SCoL, the system learns to generate instructions saying which of its own layers should update. Meta reinforcement learning trains those choices, since each update changes the model making later choices. Tests on question answering and long-context work beat prompting, summarization, and fine-tuning baselines. Learned updates stayed sparse and landed on sensitive layers.
arxiv-2605-07276:
Jia Li and five co-authors improve reinforcement learning for code-fixing agents when feedback is weak. Build outcomes are reliable but only capture surface success, not true correctness. The authors argue group comparisons in GRPO training are meaningful only after three signals are reshaped: rewards, process credit, and rollout comparability.

Layered rewards rank trajectories by both compiling and meaning, step-level scores assign credit inside a run, and failure-aware governance keeps compared rollouts alike. Together they lifted strict accuracy well above the base model and cut evaluation steps. A comparison shows token-level distillation from privileged prompts cannot substitute for those reshaped signals.
arxiv-2605-07376:
Iván Alfonso and three co-authors present BESSER, an open-source low-code framework for building smart web applications with AI agents inside. Low-code tools reduce handwriting code by modeling components and generating applications automatically. Most existing platforms are commercial, bringing vendor lock-in and limited room to extend.

BESSER instead offers a freely accessible web editor where users design, generate, and deploy applications, with transparency and extensibility guaranteed by its open-source nature. The paper positions the framework against rising demand for agent-containing web apps. It aims to give developers and organizations a way to build such applications without surrendering control to a platform vendor.
arxiv-2605-07476:
Jung Min Choi, Vijaya Krishna Yalavarthi, and Lars Schmidt-Thieme forecast multivariate time series with a hierarchical patch-mixing network. Forecasting must capture both local patterns and dependencies across variables at several scales. NPMixer opens with a learnable wavelet transform that splits signals into trend and detail parts, adapting its filters to the data.

Mixer blocks then learn patterns within and across non-overlapping neighboring patches, widening the view step by step. A channel-mixing encoder handles the high-frequency detail while the global trend stays stable. Across seven benchmark datasets and twenty-eight setups, the model beat leading rivals in most configurations on squared error.
arxiv-2605-07676:
Xavier Sumba and two co-authors try to give flow matching the structured latent representations that latent-variable models enjoy, without losing flow matching's sample quality. Ordinary flow matching starts from an unstructured source distribution, so its latent space carries no interpretable structure. Latent-variable models capture structure but often generate worse samples.

Their method, Structured Coupling for Flow Matching, puts structured latent variables and extra noise into the source. It learns a structured prior and a transport map together, sharing one recognition network between them. The result is a simulation-free flow model whose latents support clustering and disentanglement. In experiments it learned meaningful structure while staying competitive with plain flow matching on sample quality.
arxiv-2605-07776:
Nils Grünefeld and seven co-authors study what a language model's uncertainty does while it reasons its way through a problem. The intermediate token stream, the so-called reasoning trace, is treated as an evolving state. Each trace is summarized by a small profile of features describing how its uncertainty signal moves, such as slope and linearity.

Across five models on math and logic benchmarks, these profiles predicted whether a trace ended with a correct answer, with discrimination well above recent related work. Using only the first few hundred tokens already worked nearly as well, so errors can be flagged early. Correct traces showed a steeper, less linear decline in uncertainty than wrong ones, giving a principled lens on the generation process.
arxiv-2605-07876:
Chandrachud Pati and Yogesh Simmhan pinpoint where quantum compilers lose fidelity. A compiler translates an abstract circuit into hardware instructions through several phases. Standard benchmarks report only overall quality after the whole pipeline, hiding which phase did the damage. Their HBR breakdown assigns fidelity loss to high-level decomposition, basis translation, and routing separately.

Testing three real toolkits on eight methods and two hardware topologies, they find the dominant bottleneck depends strongly on circuit class. Routing eats up to sixty percent of the loss in search circuits, while the build step dominates Hamiltonian runs. Rankings between toolkits even reversed between test and production optimization settings. The model predicted rankings in noisy simulation and on real IBM hardware.
arxiv-2605-07976:
Rosa M. Mérida and four co-authors put a proposed explanation of the little red dot galaxies to a full spectral test. In the BH-star model, a V-shaped spectrum comes from an accreting black hole wrapped in a dense neutral gas envelope that re-radiates as a cool blackbody. The ultraviolet light comes from a small, primitive host galaxy. The model helped define the class but had never faced detailed fitting.

Fitting the complete JWST spectrum of The Cliff, a pivotal example at redshift about three and a half, yields a BH-star-like solution naturally, even under broad priors.
