The fit uses a code allowing stellar, nebular, black hole, and blackbody parts. The host emerges as low-mass, star-forming, and metal-poor with real dust attenuation. One tension stands out: the black hole outweighs what host scaling relations predict.
arxiv-2605-08176:
Raul Felipe-Sosa, Angel Martin del Rey, and Maria Flores Ceballos introduce neural networks whose hidden layers are dynamical systems. In their Dynamical Physics-Modeled Neural Networks, each layer is the solution of an ordinary differential equation rather than a fixed activation function, which gives the layers a biologically flavored, time-evolving behavior.

The framework is grounded in reproducing kernel Banach spaces, where the networks appear as finite-dimensional solutions of an abstract training problem linked to standard networks. A concrete build uses the FitzHugh-Nagumo model of neuron firing, with numerical solvers placed inside the computation graph through Euler-type steps. Weights and the dynamics' own parameters are trained together.
arxiv-2605-08476:
Mila Marcheva, Suchir Salhan, and Weiwei Sun turn two theories of child grammar into competing computer experiments. Maturational accounts disagree on the order in which children gain syntactic categories: growing accounts say lexical and inflectional structure comes first, while inward accounts predict early access to discourse-related categories.

The authors operationalize both orderings inside a statistical grammar induction system, holding the input and the learning algorithm fixed so only the staging differs. Each ordering defines what can be learned at each stage, and the induced grammars are scored on three evaluation metrics. The growing account significantly outperformed the inward account throughout, evidence that the bottom-up developmental sequence is the more learnable one.
arxiv-2605-08576:
Dalale Mhamdi, Amine Bouali, Taoufik Ouali, and Tiberiu Harko test a gravity theory built from two connections rather than one. In biconnection gravity, the gap between the two connections carries extra geometric degrees of freedom, while their average matches standard relativity. The team derives expansion equations for a flat universe where the extra geometry can act like dark energy.

Five standard forms for that extra energy are checked against recent telescope and supernova data. Two forms earn strong statistical support and rival the standard model. All forms enter cosmic acceleration at nearly the same era. Gravity research gains a well tested alternative account of why the universe speeds up.
arxiv-2605-08676:
Shachar Lovett, Raghu Meka, and Yimeng Wang coin moonflowers, a loose kin of sunflowers in set theory. A moonflower asks just one thing. Each set holds at least one item found in no other set. The team finds, near exactly, how big a family of small sets can grow with no such pattern.

That bound feeds code thinning, a way to shrink error codes while they still work. The team sharpens fresh bounds on block length. The cost drops from a high log power to a plain log. They also show this cost is a must. Set theory gains a new key object. Coding gains a near best bound.
arxiv-2605-09076:
Haejoon Lee and three co-authors study teams of language model agents that check each other's work over a network. Such teamwork can raise reliability, but it also opens the door to faulty or hostile agents that spread wrong answers through the group.

Their protocol, Self-Anchored Consensus, has each agent swap answers with peers, filter out messages that look unreliable, and refine its own answer, with no central controller. The authors give conditions on the network shape under which honest agents keep and spread sound information despite the bad actors. Across math and common-sense tests with many models, the method held up under attack where earlier methods fell apart.
arxiv-2605-09176:
Aditya Ranganath surveys the tools that train large language models, focusing on the step-by-step update rules called optimizers. Adam and its variant AdamW still dominate, but recent work has rethought nearly every part of the process. His 2026 review sorts the field into families, from classic first-order methods to lean versions that save memory and newer matrix-based methods such as Muon.

Along the way, the survey covers memory use, curvature, sign-based updates, low-rank structure, and stability with large batches. It also questions how methods are compared, urging fair tuning and checks at real scale. Ranganath argues the field is moving away from single speed claims toward careful tests that weigh speed, stability, memory, and ease of use together.
arxiv-2605-09276:
Liu and four colleagues tackle token reduction in spiking transformers, whose multi step processing still brings redundancy and cost. Existing methods judge tokens by response cues like activation size, firing statistics, or feature similarity, missing how class evidence evolves over time. In spiking transformers, tokens build up across spiking steps, so importance should reflect temporal uncertainty patterns, not just instant responses.

The team finds tokens show varied uncertainty paths over time, and their pooled uncertainty stats separate useful tokens from redundant ones. Their framework, Uncert, models each token's class evidence with a Dirichlet distribution. It sums up temporal uncertainty by mean and fluctuation across spiking steps, giving an uncertainty aware score for token reduction at inference time. Uncert needs no training and plugs in anywhere, and tests on static and neuromorphic benchmarks show good accuracy efficiency trade offs, with clearest gains under token pruning.
arxiv-2605-09376:
Lyu and a colleague tighten safety constraints for bicycle-model trajectory optimisation in autonomous vehicles. Planned paths can break safety limits under true dynamics with slip, tyre stiffness, and yaw-lateral coupling. They derive a characteristic speed splitting two regimes: below it the bicycle oversteers inward and stays safe, above it the bicycle understeers outward into danger. They prove the peak outward deviation follows an exact T squared horizon scaling and give a simulation-free coefficient from vehicle parameters and horizon length alone.

Together these give Mismatch-Aware Adaptive Constraint Tightening, replacing a fixed margin with a state-dependent one. That margin grows at high speed and curvature but nears zero on gentle paths. Eight experiments confirm the scaling laws. MACT hits 100 percent safety with 84 percent less wasted margin than a fixed baseline, and cuts the applied margin by 34 percent against tube MPC with the same safety.
arxiv-2605-09476:
Hilasaca and two colleagues report an experimental study assembling sentence-aligned corpora for multilingual text simplification. Text simplification matters for language learners and readers with limited literacy, yet large-scale, high-quality training and testing datasets remain scarce beyond English. The team collects and processes crowd-sourced simplification data from comparable corpora.

They report ways to align sentences from document-level data, covering Catalan, English, French, Italian, and Spanish. The resulting dataset of aligned sentence pairs is publicly available, suited to both training and testing simplification systems across all those languages.
arxiv-2605-09576:
Forstnerič and Kalaj settle an extremal question about harmonic maps that are conformal at a point. For a domain and a marked point, they consider the largest possible stretch of the differential at that point among harmonic maps from the unit disc sending the center to the point. A conformal map onto the domain always attains at most that supremum. Earlier work showed equality for the disc itself, raising the question whether equality forces the domain to be a round disc.

Their answer is no. Among bounded convex pointed domains, and up to translation, rotation, and reflection, equality holds exactly for images of the disc under a specific family of holomorphic maps with a rational derivative form. That family contains strongly convex shapes that are not round discs. The classification is sharp, giving the full list of extremal domains in this class.
arxiv-2605-09776:
Dann and two colleagues proved that a floating convex polytope can be recovered from surprisingly thin surface data. Take a convex polytope of uniform density between zero and one, floating in liquid of density one. Its surface of flotation, the locus of waterline centers, fixes the shape uniquely whenever the density differs from one half.

Likewise, the buoyancy surface, the locus of centers of buoyancy, fixes the shape for any density in the open interval. The results sit where mechanics, harmonic analysis, differential geometry, and classical convexity meet, and they echo Ulam's question about bodies floating in equilibrium in every orientation. Within the polyhedral class, flotation and buoyancy surfaces encode rigid geometric information.
arxiv-2605-09876:
Li and two colleagues ran numerical simulations to gauge how well Neptunian mean motion resonances trap small bodies while Neptune moves outward. Resonant trans-Neptunian groups preserve clues to the early migratory past of the Solar System, so trap rates help pin down migration settings and the first planetesimal disk. The study used a flat model of outer resonances.

For a set p:q resonance, capture needs eccentricity past a cutoff e_min. That cutoff rises with faster migration, greater orbit distance, and higher order. The 1:q cases show a notably higher e_min from their own dynamics. Once eccentricity suffices, trap rates barely hinge on migration rate. They hinge mainly on p and heliocentric distance, falling exponentially as either grows. Trap counts from 1:2 out to about 1:4 track what is seen, but far regions fall short, hinting other causes like resonant sticking matter there.
arxiv-2605-10876:
Edward De Brouwer and eleven colleagues introduce AssayBench, a benchmark for the virtual-cell dream of predicting cell responses without running the lab experiment. The test asks models to predict phenotypic screens, the visible outcomes of gene perturbations, from mixed text and assay inputs.

AssayBench builds on 1,920 public CRISPR screens across five broad phenotype classes. Each screen becomes a gene-ranking task, scored with an adjusted ranking metric that stays comparable across unlike assays. Extensive trials show where language models and agents stand today on this drug-discovery-relevant task. Builders of virtual cells get a standard, phenotype-first yardstick where none existed.
arxiv-2605-10976:
Oem Trivedi and Abraham Loeb build a sky test for negative mass, the exotic idea that some matter could pull with a negative charge. Bondi's classic work showed positive-negative pairs would run away together, yet the idea keeps resurfacing in dark-energy and rival-cosmology proposals.

Their joint framework pairs charge-level bounds with motion probes: radiation limits demand one universal charge, while negative-mass pairs would generically give anti-chirps, dispersal, and runaway motion. None of those signs appear in current gravitational-wave sightings, giving a robust exclusion path that does not lean on rival-gravity assumptions. Gravity physicists get a clean way to rule negative mass in or out.
arxiv-2605-11076:
Chandana Rao and five colleagues show that the internal structure of circuit building blocks controls entanglement and scrambling speeds, even inside a fixed random-circuit architecture. Random circuits usually model local dynamics with generic two-qubit gates, suggesting gate details matter little for coarse-grained diagnostics.

The team builds Clifford circuits from fixed graph-state blocks placed at random spots along a qubit chain. Graph states that local Clifford changes cannot equate yield sharply different entanglement speeds and butterfly speeds, the rates of entanglement growth and operator spreading. Circuit designers learn that block choice, not just layout, sets dynamical speed limits.
arxiv-2605-11176:
I. Kharuk presents a neural-network pipeline for Baikal-GVD that speeds event rebuilding and neutrino candidate selection. The pipeline has three stages: fast cutting of extensive air shower events, cutting of noisy optical module hits, and picking out high-confidence neutrino candidates.

All three networks use a transformer design that exploits inter-hit links through attention. Applied in sequence, the pipeline runs far faster than the standard chain. Its noise-cutting network beats algorithmic noise cutting in accuracy and estimates time residuals of signal hits, crucial for spotting track-like hits. Domain adaptation bridges the gap between Monte Carlo simulations and real data. Astroparticle physicists get near-real-time event sorting for multi-messenger alerts and diffuse neutrino flux work.
arxiv-2605-11476: Hong and Grigas develop a barrier-metric method for linearly constrained bilevel optimization. Active-set changes can roughen the upper objective, and hypergradient methods need costly linear solves. They smooth the lower problem with a log barrier, then build a proxy-gradient algorithm from upper and lower gradients plus the barrier Hessian. Near the boundary, Euclidean smoothness constants blow up, so Dikin geometry gives a curvature scale. Stationarity rates reach K to the minus two thirds deterministic and K to the minus two fifths under noise.
arxiv-2605-11676: She Yang and Aoyang Zheng advance the dynamical Mordell-Lang conjecture for curves under regular endomorphisms of complex affine space with a degree gap. They prove the conjecture holds when the gap exceeds twice the largest multiplicity at periodic points at infinity, and show every periodic curve is then a straight line through the origin. They also give examples showing the bound cannot be weakened.
arxiv-2605-11876: Dimpi Thakuria and three colleagues map which covariance matrices a finite position-momentum pair can attain. The pair is linked by the discrete Fourier transform. They combine pen-and-paper math with convex shapes and matrix methods over joint number ranges. They describe the allowed region through unitary markers such as trace and determinant. This pins down edge states, extends states of least uncertainty, and yields bounds for multi-knob sensing and tests for whether two-part systems split apart.
arxiv-2605-11976: Lutz Recke proves an implicit function theorem for blending nonlinear non-smooth elliptic systems. For Dirichlet problems with semilinear systems and non-smooth data, he assumes spread tensors H-converge as the blending knob tends to zero. For small knobs, exactly one weak answer exists near a given healthy weak answer of the blended problem. Proofs use Meyers gradient bounds in 2D and Morrey bounds for three-sided tensors.
arxiv-2605-12076: J. C. R. de Souza, A. F. Santos, and R. Bufalo ask whether closed timelike curves can exist in curvature-squared gravity. They study axially symmetric, Gödel, and Gödel-type world models. The Gödel and Gödel-type models turn out to be causal, so such curves are not allowed there. Surprisingly, every Weyl tensor term drops out of those models. A third model then shows Weyl terms feeding energy density and shifting the weak energy rule.
arxiv-2605-12376: Liu and seven colleagues automate the messy work of cleaning and reshaping tables for data pipelines. Their ProfiliTable framework centres on live profiling. A Profiler explores the data, a Generator pulls curated operators to write task-aware code, and an Evaluator-Summarizer loop feeds back scores and diagnoses for another round. That closed loop targets a common failure: code that runs cleanly yet means the wrong thing. Tests across eighteen tabular task types show the approach handling vague instructions and complex task shapes.
arxiv-2605-12476: Ahrac, Hochwald and Geva uncover a geometric link between routers and experts in sparse expert models. For one token, router weights for the chosen expert and expert weights that process it share an input direction for their gradients, differing only in scale. Matched router-expert directions thus build up the same routed token history. In practice too, a one-billion-parameter model trained from scratch shows higher router scores predicting stronger expert activation. Auxiliary load-balancing losses, they show, disturb this coupling.
arxiv-2605-12576: Yrievich breaks the shared-fault trap in backup computing with Divergent Multi-Version Execution. Lockstep and triple-backup systems run the same binaries with the same memory layouts, so one corrupted program counter or data pointer can mislead every replica down the same wrong path. His runtime checker compiles each replica on its own, giving different code and data layouts while keeping meaning identical. Faults surface by comparing standard traces of opcodes and values, while layout-dependent addresses are discarded.
arxiv-2605-12776: Ando and Goldbring apply model theory to Connes' bicentralizer problem, a long-standing open question about von Neumann algebras, structures used in quantum theory. Building on Houdayer and Marrakchi, they show selfless probability spaces can be described by a certain logical form. They extend the key equivalence to all diffuse spaces without assuming separability. They also introduce pseudoperiodic factors and prove each has a trivial bicentralizer.
arxiv-2605-12976: Weinberg sets out CLOUDBURST, the first formal taxonomy and gauge for cloud-native passive beacons that catch data theft. Thieves steal presigned URLs, container images, secrets and tokens that older honeytoken tools miss. Across 21 live beacons and 205 mock callbacks, IAM Canary Roles top the new Cloud Attribution Score, while fast churn in short-lived infrastructure sharply decays attribution within 48 hours. The scores hold up just as well across clouds.
arxiv-2605-13276: Guo and colleagues present D-VLA, a distributed training framework for vision language action models in robots. Training such models clashes with high fidelity simulation over memory and bandwidth, choking throughput. D-VLA separates fast training data from slow weight control and runs sampling, inference, gradients and weight sharing in parallel lanes. Tests show large gains in throughput and sampling efficiency, with stable near linear speedups at trillion parameter scale.
arxiv-2605-13576: Haocheng Zhong addresses the open type III cases of the algebraic reconstruction theorem, mixing crossed product algebras with semiclassical approximations. He first shows relative entropy in crossed product algebras splits into parts from the base algebra and observer waves. Making holographic crossed product algebras for bulk and boundary type III factors, he extends the theorem to include the algebraic Ryu-Takayanagi formula. That gives a full algebraic account of the theorem as a built-in framework for bulk-boundary match in holographic duality.
arxiv-2605-13976: Sarkar and four colleagues show how to transfer quantum states over distance in semiconductor hole-spin qubits using only electric control. Spin-orbit coupling normally hinders such transfer through anisotropic exchange, but tuning the electric field strength hits discrete phase-matching conditions that restore near-perfect transfer regardless of rotation axis. Steering the field direction as well aligns the spin-orbit axis, suppressing unwanted processes and enabling robust transfer without fine tuning.
arxiv-2605-14076: Pereyra proves the 2-quasi-regularizability conjecture for Wp graphs. Hoang and co-authors had asked what shape rules make the independence polynomial of a Wp graph log-concave or at least unimodal. They guessed that a connected W2 graph is 2-quasi-regularizable exactly when its order is at least three times its alpha. The proof hinges on a local expansion theorem. Every non-maximum independent set in a connected W2 graph has a neighborhood at least twice its size. Coefficient tests for both traits follow.
arxiv-2605-14276: Yao and Paulin propose MM-SOLD, a training-free particle sampler enforcing target moments throughout sampling. Score matching smooths the empirical score, promoting generalization via low-dimensional data geometry. In the large-particle limit, particle density converges to a fixed limit: a Gibbs-Boltzmann density from exponentially tilting a naive smoothed diffusion target. Experiments on 2D distributions and latent images show fast, robust, training-free CPU sampling, with fidelity and diversity matching neural baselines.
arxiv-2605-14476: Acclavio and Manara give proof nets for PiL, a logic that extends first-order multiplicative additive linear logic. New operators in PiL encode pi-calculus processes as formulas in a shallow way. The paper sets out a test for when a net is correct, a way to turn nets back into proofs, and a way to translate proofs into nets. Proof nets then give one canonical form for all sequent calculus derivations that differ only by the order of rules.
arxiv-2605-15076: Zoë Webb-Mack and Natalie Klco lay base quantum circuits for SU(2) lattice gauge theory warped by quantum groups. Local truncation plus deformation gives a tower of finite-dimensional groups nearing endless gauge links. It brings back unitarity of a plaquette diagonalization. The authors extend that unitarity across the full compute space with gauge-variant completions, yielding well-defined time unitaries. Gate counts for CX gates fall from order d to the eighth down to d to the fifth, a three-power saving.
arxiv-2605-15276: Camilo las Heras and Ignacio Ruiz study bordisms bridging between nine-dimensional gauged supergravities from type IIB string theory curled on a circle with a nontrivial duality bundle. Such bordisms realize needed loops through stacks of seven-branes or gravitational solitons of nontrivial topology. Soliton bordisms grow more and more tangled for large loops and face arbitrary suppression, driving a refinement of the Swampland Cobordism Conjecture tied to commutator widths of duality groups. Tests across duality groups support the idea.
arxiv-2605-15476: Hanyu Wang, Mingfei Yu, Xinrui Wu, and Jason Cong attack the cost of fault-tolerant quantum circuits, where T gates supplied as magic states dominate expense. Standard flows minimize a proxy count that ignores phase cancellation, so the team formulates exact T synthesis, groups Boolean functions under Clifford equivalence, and precomputes optimal implementations up to seven variables. Their mapper cuts T counts by up to 14.3 percent on standard benchmarks and by up to 40 percent on several cryptographic modules.
arxiv-2605-15576: Zhong-Wen Feng, Hong-Lin Liu, Yi Ling, and Qing-Quan Jiang build a regular black hole with a flat Minkowski core. It has a normal outer horizon and a degenerate inner horizon with zero surface gravity. At large mass the peak curvature tracks the inner-horizon radius, not the mass. That gives a plain test for curvature to stay below the Planck scale. The inner scale also sets the late-time mass in two dynamical models. That mass stays bounded and nears half the inner radius.
arxiv-2605-15676: Yichen Zhu, Xiaoming Shi, Peng Zhao, Weiyu Chen, Debing Zhang, and James Kwok replace positional blocks in diffusion language models with content-defined chunks. Position blocks split coherent tokens and lump unrelated ones. Their DCDM routes tokens into clusters via Chunking Attention, shaped by the diffusion goal. The clusters yield a chunk-causal attention mask, so a denoiser factors likelihood step by step over semantic chunks. On downstream tests up to 1.5B parameters, DCDM beats unstructured and positional-block baselines, with gains stable across scales and clear early in training.
arxiv-2605-15776: Xin Jiang, Peng Wang, and Haitang Yang report an exact AdS/CFT pairing for a CFT on an open solid torus. The Weyl-frame two-point function pairs with a finite bulk geodesic, needing no large N, strong coupling, or heavy operators. Conformal kinematics alone makes it exact, with no bulk dynamics assumed. The boundary-anchored relation emerges as its singular limit. Scalar modes along S1 yield a tower of masses on H whose propagators resum to the same geodesic expression.
arxiv-2605-15876: Hanxun Yu and four colleagues turn a vision-language model into a dense depth predictor with DepthVLM. Such models do well at 2D grounding and captioning but stay weak at 3D understanding, since text-only training under-constrains fine visual perception. DepthVLM adds a light depth head to the language-model backbone and trains under a vision-text regime in two stages, giving full-resolution depth maps beside language outputs in one pass. It beats rival vision-language models more efficiently, tops pure vision models, and lifts 3D spatial reasoning.
arxiv-2605-15976: Ernesto Garcia-Estrada, Carlos Escolano, and José A. R. Fonallosa fine-tune encoder-decoder translation models with reinforcement learning that needs no reference translations. They apply Group Relative Policy Optimization to NLLB-200, rewarding outputs with LaBSE and COMET-Kiwi scores, and test 13 languages. Gains appear in every language, largest where the starting model is weakest, and the method rivals supervised fine-tuning where parallel data is scarce.
arxiv-2605-16076: Koli and Jely build AgriMind, an ensemble that spots plant disease from leaf photos for growers in Bangladesh, where inspection is still largely manual. Three pretrained networks trained on 20,638 PlantVillage images cover fifteen pepper, potato, and tomato disease classes. Averaging their outputs reached 99.23 percent on held-out tests, about two-thirds fewer errors than single models. Pepper and potato classified perfectly, tomato reached 99.01 percent, and the full ensemble ran at 53 frames per second on a T4 GPU.
arxiv-2605-16576: Arias Junior and Ascanelli consider third-order evolution equations whose leading coefficient vanishes at the start time with finite order. That degeneracy breaks standard theory. They give sufficient conditions on the lower-order coefficients, as time nears zero and space grows large, that guarantee well-posedness in three function spaces. Those spaces cover square-integrable, smooth, and Gevrey-type functions, which allow controlled growth of derivatives.
arxiv-2605-16776: Yang and colleagues propose Distinguishable Deletion, an approach that unifies knowledge erasure and refusal for language-model removal. Erasure struggles with biased erasure from hiding token strings, while refusal risks harmful knowledge coming back because it stays intact. It restricts the response spread in latent space rather than set tokens, splitting dropped from kept knowledge so refusal can handle dropped inputs safely. An energy index tracks knowledge amount and gap, driving energy-based tuning in training and energy-based refusal at use. Tests show it clearly beats prior methods.
arxiv-2605-16976: Qu's team argues securing language-model agents starts with stating when execution truly reflects user intent. Agents turn natural-language prompts into tool calls, API requests, and code, yet most defences trust tools, a view open skill ecosystems and system access now break. Like compilers, where security lapses are mis-runs that stray from intent, they name two sources, untrusted data intake and untrusted tool runs. They derive four integrity properties jointly called intent-to-execution integrity. Current defences cover these only partly and not as a whole.
arxiv-2605-17076: Khan builds a middleware layer that keeps teams of language-model agents from corrupting shared state over the web. His S-Bus tool watches web requests to rebuild what each agent read, then enforces a consistency rule called Observable-Read Isolation. Formal proofs, exhaustive checks of over twenty million states, and nearly nine hundred thousand trial commits back its safety claims. The rule helps split workloads but can hurt joint writing on one shared store, he finds.
arxiv-2605-17176: Sun and colleagues introduce CAREBench, a benchmark that judges language models' grasp of emotion through the reasoning behind feelings, not just final labels. Built on appraisal theory, it annotates full inference chains from first- and third-person views on real stories. Tests across six models find strong systems match or beat human observers on some tasks yet lag on appraisal reasoning and positive emotions. Headline scores, the findings suggest, overstate true understanding.
arxiv-2605-17276: Li and colleagues map scaling laws for heart-trace models by training over 120 models, from 20 thousand to 200 million parameters, on a large set of heart-trace records. Models taught with labels hit a data wall on familiar data, while models taught without labels scale steadily with size and data. ResNets beat transformers on parameter efficiency on new data, and label-free training wins on data efficiency and transfer to unseen clinical tasks.
arxiv-2605-17476: Gogoi and colleagues study Joule-Thomson expansion and extended thermodynamics for a deformed AdS-Schwarzschild black hole with quintessence. The deformation and control parameters shift the temperature minimum, widen the cooling region and lift the inversion temperature. The third exerts a weaker steady influence. Heat-engine analysis finds deformation boosts efficiency, whereas higher values of the other two reduce it.
arxiv-2605-17576: Rodgers and colleagues show the absolute stability limit is met in rich hypoeutectic aluminum-silver alloys. Growth rates stay well below the one meter per second typical of additive manufacturing. Dynamic transmission electron microscopy of laser spot melting, plus postmortem checks, is set against phase-field simulations. A sharp-interface check uses a speed-based phase diagram. Predicted limits track the miscibility gap trend. They agree with sim runs across the range and experiments on three alloys.
arxiv-2605-17976: Xinzhe Yuan and six colleagues propose LLM-Guided Bayesian Optimization, a framework for discovery. Bayesian optimization balances exploration and exploitation but starts slowly and scales poorly as dimensions grow. Unlike work using language models for warm starts or candidates, LGBO embeds preferences into iterations through region lifting. Proof shows it never performs worse than Bayesian optimization, while converging faster when preferences align with the goal. In tests on iron-chromium battery electrolytes, it reaches 90% of the best value within 6 iterations, versus over 10 for baselines.
arxiv-2605-18076: Yoav Tsori and Hannes Uecker present a method for one-way ion flow under cross magnetic fields. From the Navier-Stokes equation coupled with the Poisson-Nernst-Planck model, the problem admits a decoupling. The Stokes equation comes first, giving the speed profile and a flow potential for ions. This potential fights electric pull and greatly alters ionic patterns. In planar Couette shear, it gives a clumping transition in one line, absent classically. An eigenvalue equation predicts a threshold between ion gain and loss at the charged wall.
arxiv-2605-18276: Thibaut Germain and four co-authors present DOODL, a 2026 dictionary method for dynamical systems. It treats related systems as lying near a curved surface in spectral operator space. Learned dictionaries of spectra give compact, clear embeddings of each system. On Langevin and turbulent plasma runs, DOODL beats solo operator fits by one to two orders of magnitude where data are scarce.
arxiv-2605-18376: M Daniel Ranjan, Soumya Chakrabarti, and Sanjit Das explore traversable wormholes in a higher-derivative gravity theory built on the Ricci scalar and its d'Alembertian. The theory extends general relativity with quantum corrections, as set out in 2026. Solving the field equations for a static, spherically symmetric wormhole, they study whether such wormholes can exist. They find the extra curvature terms can supply part of the stress-energy at the throat, reducing or in some cases removing the need for exotic matter.
arxiv-2605-18576: Xichen Yan and ten co-authors present scHelix, a 2026 dataset-adaptive system for single-cell RNA sequencing integration. It splits genes at input into domain-invariant Anchors and domain-sensitive Variants, processed by a dual-stream sparse diffusion encoder. An asymmetric Align-Refine-Fuse protocol aligns the Variant stream to Anchor topology, then lets Anchors absorb denoised details through bounded residual gating. The design prevents shortcut learning and removes batches robustly without harming biological clusters.
arxiv-2605-18776: Payel Santra and three co-authors propose Mask-to-Correct, a 2026 training-free framework for faithful fact correction. Misinformation spreads fast, but existing methods need scarce annotated pairs and overlook faithfulness. Their method masks to spot erroneous claim spans and judges faithfulness against retrieved evidence. Since retrieval quality varies by retriever, they add M2C-Plus, an ensemble combining corrections across rankers to cut bias and lift robustness. Across benchmarks, the frameworks beat all baselines, gaining up to fourteen percent in SARI scores without gold evidence.
arxiv-2605-18876: Amit Surana and Brandon Allen refine statistical quantum phase estimation for early fault-tolerant machines that are short on qubits and circuit depth. Their method estimates a Hamiltonian's ground-state energy from the first jump of a spectral distribution, using short circuits and few extra qubits. The paper extends random compilation to negative Pauli weights and replaces the need for a good overlap estimate with changepoint detection. Fourier symmetry halves the number of circuit runs at the same accuracy, as shown in numerical tests with a Qiskit simulator.
arxiv-2605-18976: C. Marrero-de la Rosa and twenty-two colleagues study why massive pure-disc galaxies exist and what drives scatter in their mass-size relation. They analyze 22 nearby bulgeless BEARD galaxies with deep Isaac Newton Telescope imaging, measuring R1, the radius where stellar surface density hits one solar mass per square parsec. The bulgeless galaxies follow that tight relation with similar scatter. IllustrisTNG50 comparisons link the scatter to morphology and central density, and to merger arrangement rather than frequency, with bulgeless systems favoring slightly higher-spin halos.
arxiv-2605-19276: Maosong Cao and colleagues present OpenCompass, an open platform for judging large language models across many fields at once. Existing benchmark suites vary in task type and scoring, and their scattered workflows make large cross-domain comparisons slow. The platform couples a modular design with high concurrency, splitting work into configuration, task splitting, scheduling, execution, and display. It supports rule-based, judge-based, and staged scoring, helping teams spot a model's strengths and gaps before further tuning.
arxiv-2605-19376: Baek and team turn recursive thought into a chance-based process. Earlier models of this kind follow one fixed hidden path to one answer, which limits search. Their GRAM design treats thought as a random hidden path, so a system can hold several guesses, try other plans, and scale compute by depth and by parallel runs. Trained with a variational method, it beats fixed-path recurrent and recursive baselines on set reasoning tasks and multi-answer constraint tasks, and it can also generate with no input at all.
arxiv-2605-19476: Chen and Zhang test whether strongly lensed gravitational waves can measure the cosmic dipole independently of microwave background motion and radio galaxy counts. Lensed waves arrive as multiple time-delayed images, giving lens and source distances for matching to galaxy-catalog redshifts. Rebuilding a sample of doubly lensed events under a standard lens model, they forecast detection within ten years of Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer running. Adding triply and quadruply lensed events tightens the estimate, reaching about 2.45 thousandths in the most optimistic case.
arxiv-2605-20176: Juncheng Wu and eleven co-workers build ClinSeekAgent, an agentic framework that actively seeks multimodal evidence for clinical reasoning. Given raw data, it queries health records, uses imaging tools when relevant, refines hypotheses, and integrates evidence into decisions. Their ClinSeek-Bench pairs curated input with raw data across task categories. Without specific curation, it beats curated input for GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5 on multimodal tasks. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on its trajectories yields ClinSeek-35B-A3B, top among evaluated open-source models on AgentEHR-Bench.
arxiv-2605-20476: Bendel and four co-workers fight drift in long video-to-video generation with Anchored Tree Sampling. Drift degrades quality over time, while continuity slips show as objects changing color or style between frames. Their training-free scheduler swaps sequential rollout for a tree of sparse-to-dense, anchor-bounded fills. It beats two autoregressive baselines on Wan 2.1 plus VACE across five conditioning modes and holds stable generation past 40 minutes on LTX-2.3.
arxiv-2605-20676: Mozhgan Nasr Azadani and seven colleagues present VistaQA, a benchmark that ties visual answers to pixel-level proof. Current tests check text answers or object locations alone, leaving reasoning and grounding unlinked. VistaQA holds 1,157 expert-checked samples across six task types and six visual domains, from direct perception to relational reasoning. Models must answer correctly and supply precise segmentation masks that back each answer.
arxiv-2605-21076: Abdullah Al Zubaer and four colleagues investigate automated grading for German legal cases with GradeLegal. Grading German legal exam solutions meets growing volumes and a lack of qualified graders, slowing feedback and creating a bottleneck. It is also a high-stakes skilled task, since state exam grades deeply influence career outcomes in Germany. Despite that practical relevance, literature skilled systematic studies on effective grading deeply. The authors test whether large language models can support machine grading of German legal case answers in criminal and public law.
arxiv-2605-21376: Anna-Maria Gueorguieva and co-authors assess data broker compliance with California privacy law, covering the 2018 Consumer Privacy Act and the 2023 Delete Act. The Delete Act requires brokers to register with the state and report consumer rights request metrics annually. Only nine percent of five hundred twenty-two registered brokers were fully compliant with transparency requirements after the Delete Act took effect, though slight improvements appear over time. Broker heterogeneity in request volumes is wide, with many reporting none.
arxiv-2605-21976: Anya Zorin and co-authors present TacO, a benchmark for tactile sensors in robot manipulation. Vision-based learning from demonstrations handles many manipulation tasks, yet it falls short for complex, contact-rich work, with no guide saying which tactile sensors suit which tasks. TacO tests sensors across tasks, measuring how modality, shear sensing, tactile representation, and material friction affect performance. Its results show tactile usefulness depends strongly on sensor type, material properties, and the task itself, rather than helping uniformly. Sensors, code, data, and the hardware setup will be public.
arxiv-2605-22076: John Stachurski and Junnan Zhang study links between dynamic programs using conjugacy ideas from dynamical systems theory. When two programs are connected by an order isomorphism, optimality properties pass from one formulation to the other. Applied to Epstein-Zin preferences with time shocks, this yields a sharp characterization of when it holds. The authors also show multiplicative Kreps-Porteus preferences and risk-sensitive ones are isomorphic, so the latter's results transfer to the former. Finally, such transformations can improve value function accuracy by two orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2605-22176: Si Shen and co-authors propose LLM-Metrics, a research-impact metric drawn from large language model memory. Citation counts suffer lag, disciplinary bias, and Matthew effects, so the authors test whether high-impact papers leave stronger parametric memory through greater exposure. Four probe types cover title, author, method, and venue recognition across 549 papers from 2023-2024 and 17 models. Fifteen models give positive predictions, with overall Spearman correlation 0.1495 against citations. Author-recognition probes prove strongest, and a 3B model beats most larger ones, supporting a selective-memory account.
arxiv-2605-22276: Lu and Shi study ultracold polar molecules held in optical traps as carriers of quantum information. Molecular motion in the trap usually counts as a source of wobble in dipole interactions. Here it can realise an asymmetric quantum Rabi model. The same motion can trigger a trap-dipole resonance that leaks population into uncoupled states, so controllers should avoid it. The authors also design two gates, a fast iSWAP and a controlled-phase gate, and find both can reach high fidelity.
arxiv-2605-22576: Bor and others model fleet harm and money loss from a rare once in a century solar particle storm. Their chain runs from storm hazard and shielding shifts through radiation dose to failure odds for about 10,650 United States satellites. About 100 craft sit at critical risk, mostly in high low Earth orbit and stretched elliptical paths, while middle and geosynchronous craft face negligible risk. Expected capital loss totals about 5.2 billion dollars, with daily harm from about 70 million to 1.3 billion dollars across three failure cases.
arxiv-2605-22676: MacArthur and others compare probabilistic nowcasts and forecasts of SARS-CoV-2 variant shares built from hierarchical multinomial logistic regression. Using two years of weekly retrospective predictions through the United States Variant Nowcast Hub framework, they test 12 model variants against a baseline. The hierarchical models beat the baseline on both probabilistic accuracy, measured by energy score, and point accuracy, measured by Brier score. Gains grow with data volume and model complexity in data rich places, while simpler variants win where data are thin, and no single model leads on every metric.
arxiv-2605-22976: Chenail-Larcher and four coauthors consolidate the idea of LLM code smells, poor patterns in how language model inference is wired into source code. They present a self-contained taxonomy and catalog of nine such smells, plus SpecDetect4LLM, a static analysis tool that detects them. Evaluated across 692 open-source projects and over 171,000 files, the smells touched 73.5 percent of systems. Detection precision reached 91.3 percent, with recall of 71.8 percent.
arxiv-2605-23076: Liu and Raviv improve torn paper coding, where a codeword shatters into fragments that arrive unordered at the decoder. Prior interleaved-pilot schemes achieved vanishing error but relied on global statistics, requiring long fragments and dropping short ones, yielding rates far below capacity. Their local alignment approach finds global alignment bits within each fragment using local information only, so shorter fragments become usable. The decoder thus extracts far more output, raising rates. The method extends to channels with lost pieces, approaching capacity as the length threshold grows.
arxiv-2605-23476: Ghosh explains training instabilities in deep networks, loss spikes, wobbly convergence, and gradient pathologies, through non-normal operator theory. The linearized update operators for common optimizers are generically non-normal. For Adam, non-normality tracks the commutator between the Hessian and the adaptive preconditioner, while for momentum SGD it comes from the augmented state-space form. A pseudospectral precursor bound warns of transient growth even when the spectral radius stays below one. Tests on two-layer networks confirm the indicator separates stable from unstable phases by about tenfold.
arxiv-2605-23676: Sekwenz and colleagues study LLM aids for illegal content reports under the Digital Services Act. In a study with 450 users under varied AI error regimes, they compare unaided reporting, a standard aid giving one category with reasons, and a balanced aid showing balanced cases across provisions. Balanced AI lifts provision scores under AI error and cuts error distance versus standard AI, for near-miss errors. When AI output is correct, standard AI decides faster, but neither form lifts write-up quality over unaided reporting.
arxiv-2605-24076: Fokoué argues that causal logic is AI's statistical conscience, setting genuine intelligence apart from correlation machines that are brittle under shift. He proves a Statistical Necessity Theorem: out-of-distribution generalization demands encoded causal structure, telling prediction apart from intervention. A unified frame joins Pearl's do-calculus, Potential Outcomes, Double Machine Learning, and Invariant Risk Minimization as one family of causal statistical tools. Three flaws, language-model hallucination, reward hacking, and shift decay, are then read as causal blindness, each with a sound statistical remedy.
arxiv-2605-24176: Navard and Lim present Loki, a portrait-animation system that moves a driver clip's expression and pose onto one reference photo, keeping its identity. Leading diffusion systems stack modules for expression, pose, and identity, paying in parameters and tangled controls. Loki instead encodes driver expression and pose with a face model whose axes stand orthogonal to identity, then maps them for the backbone to read natively. Identity flows separately through backbone features. Cross-identity reenactment then needs a coefficient swap, and Loki uses about 43 percent fewer parameters than rivals.
arxiv-2605-24376: Fukuta and three co-authors study magnetism and edge states in monolayer tin monoxide. Using density functional theory, they dope the layer with manganese, iron, cobalt, and tungsten, and every dopant creates a localized moment from d-orbitals. Those states form nearly flat bands near the Fermi energy, shown for cobalt-doped material. In nanoribbons, edge-localized states appear regardless of width. For chiral ribbons, oxygen-rich edges stay semiconducting, while tin-ended edges carry conduction channels. Doping plus edge engineering offer a route to tune the layer.
arxiv-2605-24576: Elias Stenhede and four colleagues ask what heart traits an AI electrocardiography model for heart failure is picking up. They applied a validated AI-ECG model to 8,147 patients who had ECG and echocardiography within three days at one hospital. Global longitudinal strain showed the strongest link to predicted risk, followed by mitral annular plane systolic excursion and ejection fraction. The pattern held in patients with preserved ejection fraction, with diastolic measures weighing more. The team validated the findings on 36,286 external pairs.
arxiv-2605-24676: Ge Ren and others build a unified scheme for sorting bubble-like nuclei in the extended quantum molecular dynamics model. They relax cluster shapes for every nuclide in the AME2020 database. Four numbers sort the shapes: B counts density-profile inflections, marking droplet, bubble, or toroidal bubble forms. H, T, and U gauge central depletion, surface thickness, and inner low-density size. Light nuclei stay droplet-like, medium-mass nuclei mostly show bubbles, and toroidal bubbles gather near charge 25 and in heavy systems. Bubbles also prove widespread among superheavy nuclei.
arxiv-2605-25376: Kolawole Quadri presents KYA, a trust and governance layer for autonomous systems that answers whether actions were approved, fit policy, and can be checked afterward. Five parts cover pipelines, tightening-only permission rules, trust scoring, audited amplification, and delegation records. The layer adds to observability tools not replacing them and ships adapters for over 15 agent frameworks. All 36 cells of a test matrix pass, the scorer runs sub-millisecond at the 99th percentile, and the system sustains 1,800 operations per second. It also catches 89 percent of adversarial probes in testing.
arxiv-2605-25576: Das studies Lie-Yamaguti algebras, systems where grouping changes results and which extend Lie algebras and Lie triple systems alike. He tackles splitting through bicrossed products, then lists all complements of a small algebra. Each other one, he shows, arises from a deformation map. He further shows deformation maps unify several known maps, defines their cohomology, and gives a Maurer-Cartan account with a ruling algebra for linear changes.
arxiv-2605-25676: Yang and colleagues release Llamion, open-weight language models with 14B parameters built by converting Orion-14B into the standard Llama-family architecture. Their KEPT recipe maps unchanged modules, starts LayerNorm-to-RMSNorm conversion with a provably optimal training-free setup, and distills the converted model against the frozen source teacher. Llamion recovers Orion's behavior on H6, MT-Bench and KoMMLU, using about 123M tokens on one A100 in four days. Its base version reaches 66.87 percent on KoMMLU, beating the next-best open Korean entry by over seven points.
arxiv-2605-25876: Qian and colleagues present DyCoRM, a dynamic rule-aware reward model for image making. Static dimensions miss the fine-grained tests users actually apply. DyCoRM grounds task tests and compares preferences by rule. The team builds DyCoDataset-20K with dynamic tests and annotations, plus DyCoBench-1K, a benchmark for such tests. DyCoPick applies it to selecting images. The work is the first reward framework for fine-grained evaluation in image making.
arxiv-2605-25976: Bu, Pădurariu and Toda split derived categories of sheaves on quasi-smooth derived stacks into ordered pieces. Such a split has vanishing maps in one direction between pieces. Here weight conditions fix the pieces, and parabolic induction gives the inclusions. The pieces take their labels from the component lattice of the stack, a key combinatorial object in Donaldson-Thomas theory. Examples cover semistable bundles and Higgs bundles on a curve, plus de Rham and Betti local systems, for reductive groups beyond type A.
arxiv-2605-26176: Liessens Dujardin and four colleagues measure pitch hearing in audio-language models, a basic musical skill other benchmarks probe only indirectly. Audio-language models increasingly tutor, transcribe, caption, recommend and produce music, so reliable sound perception is a prerequisite. A model that cannot hear pitch structure cannot be trusted to teach, transcribe or act on audio. Existing evaluations test pitch mainly through higher-level tasks and multiple-choice formats, leaving fine-grained pitch across instruments unmeasured. PitchBench fills that gap with direct tests of pitch hearing.
arxiv-2605-26576: Yuyang Tan and four colleagues segment 3D objects from queries without manual annotation using TrackRef3D. Referring 3D Gaussian Splatting lets AI pick objects by words, but older methods need costly per-scene labels and per-view pseudo masks. TrackRef3D decouples object discovery from semantic grounding through a track-then-label pipeline. A Trajectory-Aware Semantic Consensus Module merges cross-view predictions via clustering and voting into one canonical semantic identity. Visibility-aware descriptions cut ambiguity, and Hybrid Training jointly tunes coarse and fine cues. Tests report top performance.
arxiv-2605-26676: Safarov and six colleagues tackle anomaly detection when training images contain hidden defects, a common flaw in industrial inspection data. Their method, MeDS, builds an ensemble of partial memories by random subsampling, uses the ensemble distances to train a reconstruction scorer, then fine-tunes on data the scorer deems clean. It reaches 99.16 percent image-level AUROC on MVTecAD at 40 percent contamination and leads on VisA and Real-IAD under noisy conditions.
arxiv-2605-26976: Aditto, Ifty, and Zahin review microwave-to-optical quantum transduction, the conversion of microwave photons from superconducting processors into optical photons for fiber transmission. They compare optomechanical, electro-optic, and magneto-optic platforms on efficiency, bandwidth, added noise, and temperature, and propose normalized metrics for fair comparison. Optomechanical devices reach 93 percent internal efficiency with sub-quantum noise, electro-optic devices approach 99.5 percent, and magneto-optic devices lag far behind but offer non-reciprocity.
arxiv-2605-27076: Ledford and Regli frame learning under hidden feedback as TAC-MAB, a threshold bandit where tasks pay only when a team meets an unknown size threshold. A central method achieves log-scale total regret, split into a structure-search term for settling feasibility and a stats term for value guesses. A spread-out rule syncs only when structure beliefs change, cutting talk 23-fold against the central base while keeping alignment.
arxiv-2605-27176: Sourav and co-authors ask which facts in a knowledge graph actually shape hypotheses about battery materials. They vary graph density, ontology richness, topology, and control structure across three language models, and they score outputs against both the given graph and a fixed reference. Graph context shifts outputs, but models also recover much graph content from prior knowledge alone. Compact top subsets often match full-graph behavior, and even random or topology-based subsets recover much signal, so useful signal is redundant rather than tied to one ranking rule.
arxiv-2605-27276: Prannay Hebbar and colleagues build a loop in which one language model agent improves another agent on two fronts at once. The feedback agent rewrites the task scaffold and retrains the model weights, instead of changing only one side. Tested on legal classification, GPU kernel tuning, and single-cell RNA cleanup, the combined approach beats updating the scaffold alone on every test.
arxiv-2605-27476: In their 2026 paper, Hyunmin Cho and colleagues treat attention as a form of memory. They split the pre-softmax matrix into symmetric and skew parts, linking the first to the energy landscape and the second to circulation. Measures of stability drawn from the symmetric part track how well the model balances faithful recall against varied output, and tweaking circulation gives a control knob for it.
arxiv-2605-27676: Ciaran Gilligan-Lee, Joseph Egan, Yuchen Zhu, and Michael O'Riordan identify spurious correlations in fine-tuning from the weights of a naive LoRA tune, without supervision. Their GRASP method projects gradients to stop new reliance on an identified latent factor while preserving pretrained content along it. The method fully removes misalignment in insecure-code tuning, cuts it about fivefold in bad-medical-advice tuning, and more than halves political drift.
arxiv-2605-27776: Elham Matinpour studies free-boundary minimal T-surfaces inside the unit ball, built from one tetrahedral vertex, six faces, and four triple-junction arcs. The flat T-cone itself comes from a conformal minimal immersion, and rigidity criteria hold without matching conformal parametrizations. Every regular surface of this type has index at least n, with equality only for the flat T-cone, which is locally rigid modulo orthogonal transformations.
arxiv-2605-27876: Jian-Tang Lu, Xing-Xing Lu, and Zhi-Tao Wen extend a classic theorem about polynomial zeros to the world of q-differences, where steps multiply rather than add. They define a new q-weight for zeros and a matching q-radical, recovering the classical Stothers-Mason result as q approaches one. The machinery then handles polynomial solutions of q-difference Fermat-type equations.
arxiv-2605-27976: Ye and colleagues benchmark audio-language models on hour-long speech, where current tests use only short clips. VoiceGiraffe poses fifteen hundred curated tasks spanning perception and multi-step reasoning across real scenarios and languages. Models struggled throughout, especially at tracking sparse events over long spans, while humans showed the opposite strength.
arxiv-2605-28276: Onno Eberhard, Claire Vernade, and Michael Muehlebach learn optimal reactive policies where agents see only features, not full states. Their Committed Q-learning sticks to one action per feature until the feature changes, converging almost surely under a weak rewire-robustness assumption. The analysis introduces quasi-Markov environments and weakens prior realizability demands.
arxiv-2605-28376: Qian Wan and five colleagues model how thin disks around Kerr black holes with synchronized scalar hair would look to a telescope. Weak hair leaves images close to the familiar Kerr case, while stronger hair shrinks and warps the photon ring and shadow. In the strongest regime, lensing splits the shadow into separate pieces, adds crescent shapes, and shows chaotic patterns, with near edge-on views producing nested rings.
arxiv-2605-28776: Partha S. Dey and Grigory Terlov derive spread guesses for triangle counts in the linear rich-get-richer attachment model. The final distribution shifts phase from Gaussian to another odd shape, which they map in full. The long-run pattern is governed by the mix between the hidden random setting and the mean-field link effect. Their work also yields a smooth phase shift in the mean number of triads as the growth knob varies.
arxiv-2605-28876: Bowen Qin introduces LogDx-CI, a benchmark comparing 11 log-reduction tools for LLM diagnosis on cases. CI failure logs are large and noisy, and debugging agents need a tool to shrink them. Yet no public comparison of reductions exists. Hybrid grep-plus-tail routers lead on cost and quality, scoring about 0.670 per case with fewer tokens than standalone grep. In agent-loop use the quality range collapses sevenfold, though weak contexts force more calls. A cross-family summary pair beats the same-family pair, falsifying the self-call bias hypothesis.
arxiv-2605-29476: Blai Puchol and three colleagues compare three ways to translate text inside images, a job joining vision and language skills. Modular pipelines first detect and read the text, then translate it with multilingual language models. Multimodal models handle image and words together, while Translatotron-V turns one image straight into a translated image. On parallel multilingual sets with standard scoring measures, modular pipelines beat the end-to-end model, but multimodal models came out on top for flexibility and context.
arxiv-2605-29876: Colton R. Feathers and four colleagues run a Cosmic Dawn model where star birth is tuned to two fluid models and handled by neural nets in halos. Galaxy maps feed forecasts of the 21-cm glow and power spectrum across runs. Stronger second-generation birth deepens Lyman-alpha coupling and leaves a wider, shallower dip, while first-generation stars rule earliest and widest, and halo merger histories drive the switch. The core signal should show in a thousand HERA hours; a miss would point to a long gap between generations.
arxiv-2605-29976: Renu Singh and seven colleagues test two weather-trained models as long-run climate simulators. ArchesWeather gives single forecasts, while ArchesWeatherGen gives spread forecasts from flow matching, letting ensembles gauge uncertainty. Both are refitted as forced air models fed by monthly sea-surface warmth and sea-ice cover, under a shared climate-skill protocol. Forced runs stay stable over decades, hold a steady yearly cycle, and track drift in many climate variables. The models mirror a leading reanalysis climatology, large-scale winds, and year-to-year swings.
arxiv-2605-30076: Yingdong Shi and six colleagues present UniSteer, a text-guided way to steer language models by shaping inner activations. Older tricks use fixed directions or one-off modules, weak on fine-grained ideas and combined demands. UniSteer learns one conditional flow over residual-stream activations from plain-language conditions, then moves and rebuilds a source activation under a target instruction. The same model classifies by picking the label with the lowest rebuild cost. Tests on three models cover behaviour, truthfulness, fine concepts and combined instructions.
arxiv-2605-30276: Evgeny Skvortsov and Richard Van Dongen build the Fefferman-Graham growth and map for self-dual theories of any spin, a step toward self-dual holography. Self-dual theories, UV finite, should have AdS/CFT twins, and higher-spin versions make the twins simpler. Chiral higher-spin gravity stands as the top self-dual theory, twin to part of Chern-Simons matter theories. They find bulk propagators and four-point AdS/CFT links in slimmed Chiral higher-spin gravity, a higher-spin form of self-dual Yang-Mills theory.
arxiv-2605-30376: Haochen Yuan, Yichen Song, Yunbo Wang and Xiaokang Yang introduce Unicorn, a tool for training on many time-series sets. Solo models scale well but miss links across channels, while Linked models are strong but stuck in one size. At Unicorn's core is a codebook of latent prototypes that splits link modeling from channel names. By mapping mixed channels into one shared latent space, Unicorn learns link patterns across fields. Tests show Unicorn beats leading forecasters, most of all in few-shot transfer, pointing to time-series base models.
arxiv-2605-30576: Abouelazm and colleagues make reinforcement learning safer for self-driving cars by guiding exploration with expert advice only when uncertainty runs high. Advice triggers when epistemic or aleatoric uncertainty, gaps in knowledge or noise in the world, crosses thresholds that adapt as the agent gains confidence. A commitment-and-cooldown rule paces guidance so maneuvers stay coherent without draining the advice budget, and expert and agent experience share one replay buffer. In CARLA intersection tests, the method beat its baseline with higher success and fewer failures.
arxiv-2605-30876: Feng and colleagues fix a mismatch in diffusion language models that use expert layers to scale up. Each pass reads many tokens at once, while old expert routing picks experts token by token, so far too many experts fire and memory use balloons. Their dMoE groups token expert votes inside each block into one block vote, then routes by that shared vote. Tests show far fewer experts fire, memory use falls sharply, and almost all of the base score is kept.
arxiv-2605-31076: K. C. and Mishra prove operator-norm bounds for exponential-map parameterizations on se(3). They give an intermediate-growth example. Using the contraction of the SO(3) Jacobian, they show the exponential norm is bounded by one plus the Frobenius norm. They derive a quadratic upper bound for the Lipschitz constant over four. They construct an objective with a quadratic lower bound for radius at least two. These results place se(3) between compact algebras, where the constant stays bounded, and hyperbolic algebras, where it grows exponentially.
arxiv-2605-31176: Stouras and colleagues swap the single retriever in retrieval-augmented generation for a small set picked for the query mix. One retriever and one setting cannot serve short fact questions and long multi-hop reasoning equally well. The authors frame the choice as an expected best-of-k goal and give a build method with near-optimal guarantees. Learned sets beat single retrievers and naive multi-retriever baselines on question-answering tests. Fixed sets also cut delay and token cost compared with tuning settings at run time.
arxiv-2605-31276: Morales and Sheppard learn nitrogen fertiliser response curves for crops with no set form in mind. Their neuro-symbolic regression finds shared symbolic skeletons across management zones. A transformer-based search drives the hunt, and a genetic algorithm fits the skeletons to data. First tested on made-up problems, the method recovers true expressions even when data are scarce. On real winter wheat data it learns distinct curves per zone. It beats quadratic-plateau and exponential models on fit and captures varied behaviour across the field.
arxiv-2605-31376: Schieber and colleagues present LiftNav, a hybrid routing tool for robots in unknown indoor settings. Older TSDF maps support safe planning but lack meaning, while Gaussian Splatting gives rich looks yet soft geometry that limits precise obstacle dodging. LiftNav builds on a dual map joining TSDF and Gaussian Splatting, adding YOLO detectors, lifting via TSDF into 3D, and B-spline path tuning. A hinge-loss crash penalty improves path smoothness and safety. In Replica tests, it achieves a 100 percent success rate with shorter paths than a leading radiance-field baseline.
arxiv-2605-31576: Al-Najjar and team present a two-stage system for joint camera and LiDAR extrinsic calibration. Most methods treat each camera and LiDAR pair alone, ignoring rigid coupling across cameras, so estimates may be accurate yet inconsistent. First, CMRNext runs on each camera to produce initial extrinsic estimates plus dense 2D-3D correspondences. Those predictions are then refined through multi-frame bundle adjustment with reprojection and pose prior terms. Tests on KITTI and Walkley show better accuracy and consistency, with 0.89 cm error on KITTI and a sharp drop on Walkley.
arxiv-2606-00176:
Mishra, Copeland, and Green build a new way to map chance in early cosmos growth. In growth models, wild swings can seed black holes at birth. The chance curve for growth length solves a known spread law. Past routes to that curve were pieced together from parts.

Their route rests on eigenvalues, the core modes of the spread law. They first test it on flat ground with no drift. The route gives back the known curve, with its long tail and mid-range shape. Next they add a steady drift, in tight-well and broad-well forms. Tight wells match the bare case with a trimmed tail. Broad wells need a split build of modes and show a raised peak with a much weaker tail.
arxiv-2606-00376:
Guo, Wu, and Yiu mark a depth past which long thought chains fail at state-track tasks. Such tasks need exact tabs on things as they shift step by step. More thought steps can hurt scores on them, not help. The team trace that drop to hard caps in how watch heads hold state.

Their read bounds state room in bits by head count, head width, and span. Room as a whole is not the tight bind, they find. A fault law with a depth-squared term fits how errs grow. A drift gauge tracks how far a model's state strays. A depth mark, the Deterministic Horizon, sits where sound scores cross half. Tool-aided thought beats plain chains by wide spans on their probe.
arxiv-2606-00476:
Wang asks if chat agents do what they say, or just what they claim to think. Faith in an agent's acts rests on that match. No gold act exists in most fields to check it by. Wang builds a test bed where each call has a known right act.

A Texas poker sim gives that gold frame for the test. The gap is split in two steps for a clean read. Step one checks if a stated call tracks the agent's own thought. Step two checks if the act tracks the stated call. Step two proves firm when calls are read from a clear tag. Free-text reads swell the gap with noise. Step one frays in split ways, not one mode. Rule slips lean to the safe side near all the time.
arxiv-2606-00576:
Yan and co-authors give a mobile arm bot a live scene memory that stays true as rooms shift. Such bots need a scene view that is firm in shape, rich in sense, and cheap to hold. Pre-made maps and still-scene takes go stale when things move. Pose fixes can also knock past reads out of line.

Their frame, DREAM, builds a voxel sense map from depth shots on the fly. A mixed SLAM back end logs those shots in place. A prune tool rewrites past reads when poses are fixed. It keeps the long log bound in size as it works. Hunt for a named thing joins word-led 3D search with sight checks. Real tests in four lab rooms lift long task wins past a kin tool.
arxiv-2606-00676:
Scarlat and co-authors build farm data from space images in this 2026 paper. They use Sentinel-2 satellite images and EuroCrops records, which list what grows in each field. Their pipeline turns mixed field records into matched image and mask pairs that a model can learn from.

The pipeline harmonizes labels, picks images, aligns them in space, and cuts them into patches. It then filters weak patches and balances the crop classes. The result holds 67,337 patches from five European countries, with ten crop classes plus background. A U-Net model trained on ten spectral bands scores 0.7665 mean overlap on the home test split. On new data from Belgium and other sets, scores drop a lot. The authors say the gap shows how hard real shifts in labels and coverage are. Maize and wheat still transfer well.
arxiv-2606-00776:
Mukherjee and co-authors teach models the shape of crystals in this 2026 paper. Fast, sound forecasts of crystal traits drive the hunt for new materials. Graph networks and Transformers read the local setting of atoms well. But they need much labeled data, and labels for crystal traits are scarce.

Their frame, CrysLDNet, pretrains with latent diffusion to ease that lack. A variational autoencoder maps 3D crystal structures into a smooth latent space. The diffusion process then runs inside that space, on large sets of unlabeled crystals. This teaches the encoder rich facts about structure and chemistry before any trait labels are used. The model is then fine-tuned for the trait at hand. On the JARVIS and MP datasets, the authors report gains of 4.26 and 4.90 percent over strong baselines. The learned features also hold up when labels are sparse.
arxiv-2606-01076:
Ferreiro and co-authors cut the cost of run time checks in Prolog in this 2026 paper. Prolog checks types and properties while a program runs, which costs time. Assertions let programmers state rich properties, from plain types to general claims. Abstract interpretation can prove some of them early, at compile time. The rest must still be checked live, or flagged for more work.

Their first move folds run time assertion semantics into an abstract interpreter. The interpreter is multivariant, top down, and goal directed. Their second move exploits the many calling patterns the analysis infers. Each pattern can discharge checks that a single pattern view would leave in place. The work is built into the Ciao system. Performance tests show better results than prior techniques, they report. Fewer live checks mean faster programs with the same safety net. Unproven properties still surface as guidance for testing and refinement.
arxiv-2606-01176:
Sandfelder, Cucuringu, and Dong hand graph networks a small set of motif counts in this 2026 paper. Temporal interaction streams hide signal in short patterns: repeats, replies, star shapes, and three way flows. Plain temporal graph networks often fail to show those patterns to their edge scorers. The structure sits in the data, unused.

On MOOC interaction prediction, a four feature family of past window star counts already takes most of the lift over a strong static baseline. Across many real and synthetic sets, motif activity sorts along three stable axes. They cover dyadic recency and reciprocity, star diversity, and triadic flow. The team builds a compact map of 13 motif coordinates per candidate edge. It is leakage safe and local, and it plugs into any encoder with no architecture change. Tests span link prediction, edge classification, and graph classification. The same features lift scores across all of them, they report.
arxiv-2606-01476:
Zhou and co-authors distill teacher models without access to their logits. On-policy distillation trains a student on its own outputs. A stronger teacher gives dense token-level feedback. Standard versions need the teacher's logits directly. That excludes many capable proprietary models as teachers. Logit signals are also brittle and noisy. They hinge on a narrow overlap of plausible next tokens.

OmniOPD replaces logit matching with chunk-level supervision. Monte Carlo rollouts approximate the teacher's local preferences. A semantic similarity metric scores multi-token chunks. A peak-entropy scheduler audits the student at uncertain forks only. Bayesian priors and a KL anchor bound the variance. Math scores beat standard OPD by up to 28 point 64 percent.
arxiv-2606-01676:
Fraislebem and co-authors study what blocks teams from joining Agile and DevOps. Both aim to ship software faster and with better quality. Agile stresses short cycles and customer response. DevOps stresses automation and smooth operations in production. In practice, joining them hits structural and technical hurdles. The study is qualitative and rests on interviews. Six seasoned professionals from Brazil and Germany took part. Each had deep experience in both fields.

Four groups of challenges emerge from the interviews. Cultural and organizational barriers lead the list. Structural limits and process complexity follow close behind. Technical limits round out the four groups. Four solution domains answer them, from team autonomy to automation and infrastructure. Culture alignment and proactive monitoring stand out as key fixes.
arxiv-2606-01876:
Kang and Oh build a micro-level theory of heat flow in chiral Mott insulators. The thermal Hall effect probes neutral excitations in insulators. A charge gap blocks normal electronic transport there. Phonons can drive a Hall signal as large as spin's. Their role in thermal transport is thus central.

The pair derive the Raman interaction in exact form. Its strength scales with scalar spin chirality. They then show the phonon Hall effect on a kagome lattice. Isotope swaps cause a crossover in transport behavior. That crossover shifts with temperature in their model. A scaling law splits the phonon part from background. The work gives a first full micro derivation.
arxiv-2606-02276:
Tayebi Arasteh and co-authors audit a privacy risk in clinical vision-language models. Such models train on paired chest X-rays and radiology reports. They learn a shared embedding space from those pairs. Instance level links between image and report can persist there. That is a risk when images and reports are shared apart.

A de-identified image might be re-linked to its report. Cosine similarity alone could perform that re-linking. The task is formalized as image-to-report retrieval. Public paired cohorts give ground truth pairings for the audit. Models of increasing clinical specialization are evaluated. The cohorts hold 406,241 paired examples from 126,804 patients. MIMIC-CXR and CheXpert Plus supply the pairs. Linkage risk is measured rather than assumed.
arxiv-2606-02676:
Mackay and co-authors build new diagnostic plots for extreme value regression models. Such models extrapolate far beyond observed data. Convincing checks of fit matter greatly there. Few diagnostics exist for these models. Those that do are hard to read or scale poorly. Most also give one global verdict. Poor fit in one region of the covariate space stays hidden.

Two visual tools are proposed. The standardised tail plot and the normalised residual plot form the pair. Their uncertainty bounds barely depend on sample size. That fact comes from the asymptotic distribution of normalised exceedance probabilities. Global and regional fit can thus be compared fairly, even where sample sizes vary. Summary statistics for both levels are discussed. Two applications show the plots at work. One compares thousands of candidate models. The other yields actionable findings for model design.
arxiv-2606-02776:
Neplenbroek and co-authors test what really drives uneven advice from language models. In high-stakes settings like legal, medical, and financial advice, one conversation history can shift outcomes between users. Past work showed disparities between sociodemographic groups. The team asks whether models infer group membership from a single conversation. They find models actually struggle at that inference. Group disparities exist, but they are minimal in size.

The stronger driver is conversation topic. Topics are compared against a range of linguistic features, including emotions and readability. Topics predict the advice a model gives better than the rest. They act, in part, as proxies for sociodemographic groups. Their effects on advice are often unpredictable. The authors flag this as a concern for high-stakes deployment. Future work must map how conversational context steers model outputs.
arxiv-2606-02976:
Qin and co-authors build a memory system for long dialogue that tracks changing user preferences. A dialogue system must decide when to consult memory and which past turns matter. Past methods use heuristic retrieval signals or keep memory always on. Both fail when preferences shift or contradict themselves over time.

The team frames retrieval as evidence about a user's latent preference state, not as surface similarity. Each past turn is scored by a Bayes factor: how much it raises the model's likelihood of the reference response when added to context. That score gives one unified signal for both access and selection. The model learns to pick salient turns and to regulate memory use by expected utility. Tests on four heterogeneous memory benchmarks show gains over embedding-based retrieval on long, preference-heavy tasks. The method stays competitive where preferences are sparse and simple similarity suffices.
arxiv-2606-03076: Suzuki studies optimal constants and extremizers for smoothing estimates tied to quantum harmonic oscillators. Smoothing estimates bound how solutions spread over time. Knowing the best possible constant, and which functions attain it, sharpens such bounds. Suzuki establishes harmonic oscillator versions of known free-particle results. Those results are due to Simon, and to Bez and Sugimoto, and to Bez and co-authors. The paper thus carries a line of sharp analysis from free particles over to the oscillator setting, where the confining potential changes the picture.
arxiv-2606-03476:
Huang and co-authors transfer human motion onto humanoid robots without paired training data. Retargeting matters for teleoperation, imitation learning, and human-robot contact. Bodies differ in skeleton shape, limb proportions, and joint counts. Paired examples of the same motion on both bodies are scarce. Their framework, Human2Humanoid, works in that unpaired setting.

A CycleGAN design carries the transfer between domains. A skeleton-aware graph network reads features that depend on body topology. A special loss aligns end-effector paths after scale is factored out. That keeps the sense of a motion across very different bodies. Physics-based limits push the output to copy the source's contact patterns. Tests send human motion to a Unitree G1 humanoid robot. The method beats prior work on later controllability and on physical feasibility. Robotics teams get a path to reuse human motion libraries at scale.
arxiv-2606-04076:
Shenghan Luo leads a team that presents SkySense in 2026, a system for locating drones from radio channel fingerprints in sensing-and-communication networks. Labeled examples are scarce, and reflections off buildings make the radio signature of a position ambiguous.

SkySense first learns from long unlabeled flight recordings, using the smoothness of flight paths to build stable features. A generative model then maps those features to coordinates, fine-tuned with only one percent labeled data, and predictions from several base stations are fused.
