Priyanka Surve, Asaf Shabtai, and Yuval Elovici introduce CEDAR-42001 in 2026, a method that deepens audits of AI management systems built on the ISO/IEC 42001 standard. A plain conformity check says whether a rule is met, but not which system layer is affected or what to fix first. CEDAR keeps that verdict, then adds layer attribution, a five-part maturity profile, a risk-based target, and a rulebook action for each audit row.

Tested on a synthetic autonomous-fleet audit, 89.9 percent of rows conformed, yet only 34.3 percent of those reached the baseline high-assurance class. A retrospective run on the 2023 Cruise robotaxi incident mapped documented concerns to governance, perception, decision, and oversight layers. The method points auditors toward deeper testing rather than replacing it.
arxiv-2606-21776:
O'Rourke, Trisovic, and Bertsimas propose, in 2026, a new way to create synthetic training data for classifying multivariate time series. Foundation models that learn in context need example datasets drawn from a prior, a generator that decides what realistic data looks like. Existing generators produce unlabelled series, so they cannot teach a model to assign class labels.

Their generator samples a causal graph, a network of directed arrows showing which variables influence which others, over typed nodes spanning tables and time series. Each synthetic dataset therefore carries cross-channel and cross-time causal structure plus labels. Fine-tuning TabPFN on this data beat both the unmodified model and a version trained on a tables-only prior across 75 benchmark datasets. The gain isolates the value of the temporal causal structure itself.
arxiv-2606-21876:
Thorstenson shows, in 2026, that protein contact maps can be read straight from a protein language model's attention, in a single pass. The standard tool, the Categorical Jacobian, perturbs every residue with every alternative amino acid and needs about nineteen passes per position. That cost makes it slow, even though the contact signal it recovers turns out to be concentrated in a few attention heads.

Averaging only the top contact-relevant heads, chosen using as few as ten labelled proteins with no fitted weights, matched or beat the Jacobian on every bidirectional model tested except the smallest. On a leakage-clean CAMEO test set, the head readout beat the Jacobian on the large ESM-2 model by nine points. Ablations credited labelled head selection, not averaging, for the gain. Both methods lost the signal on the two causal language models tested, hinting the effect depends on bidirectional pretraining.
arxiv-2606-21976:
Baier, Klüppelholz, and Spork ask, in 2026, whether a compact automaton model can serve probabilistic model checking, computing how likely a random system is to satisfy a logical property. Families of deterministic finite automata describe infinite-word languages by testing their repeating tails, and they can be far smaller than standard automata. The paper first settles whether probabilities against such specifications can be computed efficiently.

The authors give the first polynomial-time algorithm for checking a discrete-time Markov chain against a property given as such a family. They then relax determinism to unambiguity, where each word has at most one accepting run. These can be far more succinct than the deterministic families or Büchi automata. Translating linear temporal logic into the new model costs only a single exponential, beating a double-exponential lower bound for the deterministic version.
arxiv-2606-22176:
Saini studies, in 2026, whether dilation theorems for representations extend from single correspondences to product systems over the two-dimensional natural numbers. A dilation embeds a compressed object into a larger, nicer isometric one. Muhly and Solel proved that a pure completely contractive covariant representation of a single C-star correspondence always dilates in this way.

The pair case is the open question Saini addresses. For product systems, two commuting structures must dilate simultaneously, which is where single-variable arguments break down. The study constructs product-system representations of that kind which do admit pure isometric dilations. That gives an affirmative answer for the pair question posed. The work sits in operator theory, among Wold decompositions and the model theory of commuting isometries.
arxiv-2606-22576:
Chenxing Zhong and five colleagues, including He Zhang, characterize a software architecture smell in this 2026 paper. The smell, called PairSmell, flags pairs of software entities whose placement looks wrong: two entities separated into different modules that perhaps belong together, or collocated ones that perhaps do not. The reference is an apt modular relation agreed by several modularization tools.

The team explain the smell through pair characteristics instead. A rapid literature review collected nineteen features describing relationships between two entities. Machine learning models trained on those features predict both forms of the smell, using over six million entity pairs drawn from eleven open-source Java projects. The models improved ROC-AUC, a ranking quality score, by up to about fifty-nine percent over baselines. Interpretation shows outgoing dependencies and shared terms dominate one form, while semantic similarity and ingoing dependencies matter for the other.
arxiv-2606-22676:
Dongyub Jude Lee and seven colleagues introduce a diagnostic for fragile safety alignment in this 2026 paper. Alignment tuning teaches language models to refuse harmful requests. Yet fine-tuning on a few benign examples can erase that refusal, so a model passing release tests may later lose its guardrails.

Their tool, Skin-Deep, reads the model's hidden-state activations before any attack is attempted. It compresses the layer-by-layer safety geometry into one number, the Geometric Fragility Score. Across twenty-one instruction-tuned models and six alignment recipes, it found a recurring low-rank safety subspace. Removing directions in that subspace weakened refusal, giving causal evidence the geometry underlies the behavior. The score also identified in advance which safe model would keep the most refusal after small LoRA fine-tuning. They offer it as a pre-deployment check for fragile refusal, with no attack needed.
arxiv-2606-22976:
Vansh Bansal and colleagues use random walks on graphs as a test bed for masked diffusion models in a 2026 machine learning paper. Masked diffusion models generate data by gradually unmasking hidden pieces. Many pieces can be revealed in parallel, and which ones go first matters. The team trains a model on walks across a fixed graph. The graph stays hidden, acting as secret structure inside the sequences. Validity is easy to check, much like a Sudoku grid.

Bansal and colleagues prove that a popular unmasking rule based on lowest uncertainty is not always better than random choice. Which sampler wins depends on the graph's shape. They also design a bisection sampler that finishes in logarithmically many steps, provably exact when training is perfect. Experiments confirm that different graphs favor different samplers. Early tests on a text model show the new sampler also improves the speed and quality balance.
arxiv-2606-23376:
A. Telveenus extends quaternions beyond the real numbers in a 2026 algebra note. Quaternions are Hamilton's four-part numbers, famous for multiplication that does not commute. Classically they are built over the field of real numbers. This note defines them over a class of commutative rings with identity instead, a far broader base. Several familiar properties are then generalized to that setting. The norm and conjugate machinery that makes quaternions useful is part of what carries over.

Telveenus also studies the unit group, the elements with multiplicative inverses, over such rings. Special attention goes to halidon rings, a class singled out in the paper. The note is a brief generalization exercise. It maps how much of the classical theory survives when the scalar base changes from a field to a ring.
arxiv-2606-23476:
Saikat Das, Nayantara Gupta, and Siyao Xu model diffuse high-energy emission across the Galactic plane in a 2026 astrophysics paper. The LHAASO observatory measured diffuse gamma rays at tera- to peta-electronvolt energies from the Milky Way's plane. The team models that glow as two parts. One part is faint emission from pulsar wind nebulae, driven by electrons. The other is emission from cosmic-ray protons injected by supernovae. A key uncertainty is the infrared radiation field inside the Galaxy, which absorbs gamma rays en route. The authors test profiles with enhanced infrared density toward the inner Galaxy.

Das and colleagues find the other profiles change the diffuse fit only modestly, since the analysis masks bright sources and excludes the Galactic center. The matching neutrino emission agrees with IceCube's all-sky measurement. Point sources near the center change more, above ten tera-electronvolts.
arxiv-2606-23576:
Waugh and Jardine model how corotating interaction regions change over the life of a Sun-like star, in a 2026 stellar astrophysics paper. Such regions form where fast stellar wind streams crash into slower ones, as the star rotates. They can drive shocks and spray high-energy particles outward. Those particles may erode planetary atmospheres and shape space weather, yet most studies cover only the present-day Sun.

Coupling the wind model to how stars spin down with age, the authors track where the regions form and how their particle output shifts. Young, fast-spinning stars form them close in, and they migrate outward as rotation slows. In the Hadean period, such shocks may have produced a thousand to ten million times more energetic particles than today's Sun makes. For stars below a stated mass limit, the regions can sit inside the habitable zone while their shocks form beyond it.
arxiv-2606-23776:
Gomez, Jusinskas, Lipstein, and Lopez-Arcos show that gluon interaction data in curved anti de Sitter space can be rebuilt entirely from flat space scattering data, in a 2026 paper on theoretical physics. Correlators in AdS space sit at the heart of the AdS CFT correspondence, which links gravity in a curved bulk to a quantum theory on its boundary. Computing them diagram by diagram is laborious.

They prove that every tree level gluon correlator breaks into a sum over energy poles. Each pole's residue gives a flat space scattering amplitude: the full one, or a lower point amplitude with merged external data. The merging rule mirrors the Berends Giele currents, carried into AdS. The formulae hold at every multiplicity and are checked against Feynman diagrams up to five points.
arxiv-2606-23976:
Metsch proves a smoothing theorem for functions defined on spacetime, not flat space. Lasry-Lions regularization is a classic trick. It smooths a rough function by averaging its forward and backward evolutions. Weak KAM theory supplies those evolutions. Writing from Cologne in 2026, Metsch asks when the trick yields a function whose derivatives are Lipschitz continuous, the class called C1,1. The setting is Lorentzian, so time has a direction.

Suppose the forward evolution of a function is locally semiconcave near a point. Suppose also that its superdifferentials point only toward the future. Metsch shows a double evolution, forward then regularised, is then locally C1,1 near that point. He gives conditions that guarantee the hypotheses hold. A use follows for optimal transport, the maths of moving mass at least cost. Between any two intermediate measures along a displacement interpolation, a nicely regular maximising pair exists in the dual Kantorovich formulation.
arxiv-2606-24676:
L. Kardum, G. Premec, N. Šantić, and D. Aumiler measure how warm rubidium vapour bends light. Rubidium vapour in small glass cells now serves quantum sensors, quantum memories, and quantum fluids of light. Laser control of its atomic states lets workers tune the refractive index with precision. Still, only a handful of studies had measured that index for this vapour. The team covers both the linear index and the nonlinear one.

The authors model six level rubidium atoms struck by a probe laser. They solve the optical Bloch equations for both indices. They then compare the results with measurements from an interferometric technique. Theory and experiment agree very well in quantitative terms. The Kerr nonlinear index reaches ten to the minus four square centimetres per watt. The team also shares Python scripts for every calculation, covering Doppler broadening, pressure broadening, saturation, optical pumping, and spin exchange collisions.
arxiv-2606-24776:
Zixiang Xu disproves the uniform witness conjecture, a recent proposal in extremal combinatorics. The background is the study of uniform set families whose VC dimension stays small. In 2025, Chao, Xu, Yip, and Zhang suggested the conjecture as the right extension of the Erdős Ko Rado theorem. It says that if every set in a uniform family misses a trace of one fixed size, the family cannot exceed a stated bound.

Xu fills in the missing half of the picture, and the picture contradicts the conjecture. For dimension at least four and mid range trace sizes, he constructs families larger than the proposed bound. The construction works for every ground set size from twice the set size upward. The counterexample sizes are given by an exact formula. So the uniform witness conjecture fails exactly where it had remained open. Earlier partial results for the smallest cases still stand.
arxiv-2606-24876:
Orest Kupyn and five colleagues, several at Google Research, generate explorable 3D scenes from a single image using flat triangles instead of blobs. Video diffusion models generate high quality footage and quietly encode multi view geometry in their latents. Existing feedforward decoders turn those latents into volumetric 3D Gaussians. Gaussians render well but have no clean surface, which limits simulation and standard graphics use. FLAT asks whether the latents can be decoded directly into surface aligned primitives in one pass.

Two ingredients tame the triangles, whose orientation errors easily ruin gradient flow. A ray centred rotation parameterisation steadies triangle regression. A product window function improves gradients during differentiable triangle rendering. In benchmark tests FLAT reaches much better geometric accuracy than feedforward baselines, at competitive visual quality. A light test time refinement then converts the predicted triangle soup toward clean geometry.
arxiv-2606-24976:
Sana Ayromlou, Purvi Sehgal, and Pradyumna Narayana ask why debate style AI agents fail at persuasion and propose a fix. Multi agent debate works in deterministic domains, but in subjective tasks like persuasion agents drift and start pleasing each other. The authors identify semantic leakage in standard retrieval as the trigger. Ordinary retrieval ranks by word overlap rather than logic, feeding agents material that pulls arguments off track. Their remedy is Taxonomic Strategy RAG, which routes strategies through a discrete bottleneck.

The bottleneck splits argument structure from topic content. Zero shot cross domain tests show the method moves abstract logic where ordinary retrieval collapses. It also bridges a capability gap: small persuaders using it consistently beat stronger opponents. Win rates rise from about 71 to about 79 percent, and arguments reach their point faster. Ayromlou and colleagues argue strict routing rules are needed, since default agent behaviour slides toward sycophancy.
arxiv-2606-25076:
Peter Dueben and four colleagues argue that machine learning's revolution in weather forecasting is about to change how forecasters work, not just what forecasts say. Machine learning systems now rival traditional physics based models in skill. This article, a perspective piece, turns from outputs to practice. The authors contend that learning methods and digital technology will reshape the forecasting value chain. Coding, observations, data management, verification, and services are all in scope.

Six areas of change are surveyed. Agentic software engineering, shared verification workflows, open and compressed data, interactive computing, and generative methods could make modelling, evaluation, and service creation faster and more accessible. The authors are clear on the burden this places on weather and climate centres. Infrastructure, data stewardship, quality assurance, skills, and service delivery all have to adapt. Scientific understanding, operational reliability, human expertise, and the public service role must survive the transition.
arxiv-2606-25476:
Safety testing for language models works better when the tester is itself a team of models with opposed jobs. Abrar Alotaibi, Raed Mughus, and Moataz Ahmed build such a red teaming framework in 2026. Attacker models craft ever sharper adversarial prompts, and a target model answers them. Jury models then grade the answers for accuracy and consistency. A case study aims the machinery at faithfulness, whether a response stays true to its source material and itself.

Exploitative prompts raised attack success on question answering by up to about eight percent, exposing real reliability gaps. Format limits in summarisation tasks, by contrast, measurably improved faithfulness, suggesting design choices matter more than raw model size for safety. The framework adapts across tasks and languages, from English questions to Arabic summaries, though subtle unfaithfulness without outright contradiction still slips past.
arxiv-2606-26476:
Libo Sun, Po-Wei Harn, Zewei Zhang, Peixiong He, and Xiao Qin ask a diagnostic question about warmed-up reasoning systems. Their system pairs an energy-based diffusion model with a memory of past solution paths. Diffusion models refine an answer step by step. A warm start begins from a retrieved earlier path. Speed gains are real, but which part causes them is unclear.

The authors built a five-arm ablation method to find out. An ablation removes or scrambles one part at a time. Their arms separate three effects: a shift in class odds, random warm starting, and reuse of values aligned to each graph. On a graph reachability task, alignment alone explained a swing of thirty-five points in balanced accuracy. Random starting did worse than starting cold. A second task, Sudoku, failed at a different point: the quality of its retrieval keys.
arxiv-2606-26576:
John W. Appel and twenty-eight colleagues describe the detectors of CLASS-W2, a new telescope receiver for cosmology. CLASS, the Cosmology Large Angular Scale Surveyor, maps polarisation in the cosmic microwave background. That faint glow carries clues about cosmic inflation and the first stars. A second receiver at the ninety-gigahertz band speeds up the mapping.

The focal plane holds two hundred ninety-six detectors. Each is a transition edge sensor bolometer, a device that measures heat from incoming light with extreme sensitivity. Feedhorns funnel light onto the sensors in four modules. The sensors were fabricated at NIST in Boulder and the receiver was commissioned in August of the year before publication. Laboratory tests showed highly uniform sensor properties across the array. The report details the detector design, test results, and readiness for sky observations.
arxiv-2606-27076:
Yadav and Guha Sarkar explore cosmic structure growth when dark matter slowly decays and dark energy is read off the expansion record. In their setup, heavy dark matter particles turn into fast dark radiation over time. Dark energy is not fixed as a constant either; its behaviour is rebuilt from how the universe has expanded. The authors then carry the fitted background into nonlinear collapse calculations for 2026 halo forecasts.

Spherical collapse, the standard model of a round cloud caving in, gives a collapse threshold close to the usual prediction. The rebuilt dark energy pressure ratio still strays from the constant-value benchmark. Clearer fingerprints appear in counts of the most massive halos, the giant dark scaffolds holding galaxy clusters. Matching those counts from imaging surveys with the expansion data jointly bounds the decay lifetime. Halo abundance thus becomes a sharp extra probe of unusual dark-sector physics.
arxiv-2606-27476:
Raul leads a survey of ten evolved planet-forming disks in the Upper Scorpius region, reading their inner chemistry with the Webb telescope's mid-infrared spectrograph. Most such surveys target disks only one to three million years old; these are two to six. In the 2026 astrophysics paper, each disk is classified two ways, by water richness and by its dominant non-water chemistry.

The sample's chemical diversity is unexpectedly high. Carbon-bearing molecules glow at markedly lower excitation temperatures than in younger regions, hinting at colder reservoirs. Water luminosities run systematically lower, by factors from ten to a thousand across the sample in the reported analysis. Disks with strong carbon features but no water defy the usual explanations of dust cavities or low gas-to-dust ratios. An outer-disk dust trap, the authors argue, largely controls the chemistry of the terrestrial planet-forming zone.
arxiv-2606-27576:
Ordinary cameras lose detail forever when lighting goes wrong. Flare, glare, flicker, and overexposure can wash out part of a frame. Bartosz Stachowiak and Dariusz Brzezinski propose DeLux in 2026. DeLux borrows a second sense, a neuromorphic event stream, to guide the repair. Event streams record brightness changes pixel by pixel. They keep structure that damaged colour video has lost.

DeLux works in stages. It first rebuilds an event-based view of the scene. It then detects which regions the lighting artifact corrupted. It fuses the two sources and paints the damaged spots back in. Tests used synthetic benchmarks and real car footage. The pipeline suppressed artifacts and restored the regions well. It beat colour-only repair methods and event-guided high-dynamic-range models. Its structural similarity score stayed above 0.99 across all artifact types. In driving footage, artifact severity fell by as much as eighty-eight percent.
arxiv-2606-27976:
Dense embeddings power semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation. A leaked vector store can hand the underlying text back to an attacker, though. Sergey Kurilenko shows in 2026 that modern inversion attacks share one weakness to exploit. They all rely on the store being a single global geometry. Any single geometry can be aligned with a known geometry. Even a secret global rotation falls once enough known pairs are gathered.

His transform, SHARD, removes that weak axis. The embedding is split into a short public prefix and a private residual. The residual is sharded into cells, each rotated under its own secret key. Reranking runs under encryption, where the keys cancel and inner products stay exact. Retrieval quality matches raw-space scores, unlike truncation methods. Attack cost scales with the number of cells. At 256 cells, the median anchors needed rise from 200 to over one hundred thousand.
arxiv-2606-28176:
Young's double-slit experiment is usually watched in real space, after the waves travel. Fugui Yang and three colleagues invert that view in 2026 for hard X-rays. Perfect-crystal diffraction projects the field's reciprocal-space profile right behind the aperture. The complete double-slit fringe structure is resolved directly in momentum space. No propagation arm, focusing optics, or imaging detector is involved. The field's momentum marginal is captured as it is.

The approach is compact and lensless. It serves as a coherence diagnostic for X-ray beams. The deeper point is conceptual. Wave interference, the team shows, can be detached from real-space propagation entirely. The fringe pattern lives in the momentum distribution from the start. X-ray double-slit measurements historically lagged their visible-light counterparts by over a century. This route sidesteps the usual experimental obstacles.
arxiv-2606-28276:
Nadun Ranawaka and seventeen colleagues at NVIDIA, Stanford, and partner universities built SimFoundry, a system that turns one real-world video into a ready-to-use simulation of the scene. Training and testing robot policies in reality is slow and expensive, so faithful digital twins offer a cheaper proving ground.

SimFoundry reconstructs an interactive twin automatically, then spawns digital cousins, variations that change objects, layout, or task while keeping what the objects afford. Policies trained with cousins transferred to real robots with no further tuning, and cousin training lifted success across object, scene, and task changes. Across seven manipulation tasks and five policy designs, simulation scores predicted real-world performance closely, making the system useful for judging policies before deployment.
arxiv-2606-28676:
Sandesh Pokhrel, Hamid Manoochehri, Bodong Zhang, Beatrice S Knudsen, and Tolga Tasdizen predict whether a cancer will spread by reading the layout of the primary tumor. Multiple instance learning can flag suspicious patches in a tissue slide, but it treats patches as an unordered bag. It discards the spatial layout that may encode spread potential where the tumor meets its surroundings.

Their DTMf-MIL model boosts patch features with spatial priors. It computes signed distance functions relative to tissue types: tumor cells, linked fibroblasts, and infiltrating lymphocytes. The model learns layout signatures of spread risk straight from primary tissue. It significantly outperformed state-of-the-art methods that ignore layout on metastasis prediction. Public benchmark checks showed spatial awareness improving accuracy across varied clinical tasks. The evidence says arrangement, not just appearance, carries signal about outcomes.
arxiv-2606-28876:
Zou and Donz explore a design for language models that treats memory as something managed, not just compressed. Long-context models must squeeze history into an efficient state, yet that alone does not decide when a fact should be written, overwritten, shielded from distractors or dropped. Their proposal pairs a fast recurrent or sparse backbone with editable memory slots tied to the current request, plus a sparse fallback search at query time.

Across structured synthetic tasks and small controlled models, single-approach systems failed some overwrite, versioning or anti-pollution cases, while the hybrid covered both routes. One stress test spanning about two million tokens scored perfectly with few active chunks. A tiny trained model got nearly all of six hundred cases right under light write supervision. The authors are careful: choosing what to store in open domains remains the main unsolved bottleneck.
arxiv-2606-28976:
Grinberg and Hamesh ask when a matrix keeps a special property after being raised to powers. The property: every principal minor equals one, meaning every determinant computed from a diagonal block of the matrix, using the same rows and columns, comes out as one. Over a field, powers inherit the property automatically, but over a general commutative ring they need not.

The authors show inheritance holds over any regular ring, over the integers modulo any integer, and in further settings involving quotients of Prufer domains and normal domains. Their result generalises a problem from the 2021 Putnam competition about integer matrices with odd principal minors. For arbitrary rings, they identify a stronger property that powers always inherit: all diagonal entries are one, and all cyclic products of entries around a loop vanish. Those products are shown to be integral over the ideal that the principal minors minus one generate.
arxiv-2606-29176:
Shirodkar builds an optimiser that respects the hidden symmetries of deep networks. A network's loss does not change under certain reparameterisations: shifting logits, rescaling ReLU units, scaling normalisation layers, or rotating attention heads. Standard optimisers like Adam drift along these flat symmetry directions, wasting motion and blurring measurements taken at the solution.

His Dead-Direction Conditioner lifts a base optimiser into a symmetry-respecting one, conditioning its state within the orbit structure of an invariant metric. The construction handles four gauge families and is proved exactly equivariant on an Adam base. In tests, the conditioned Adam resisted the over-training collapse that plain AdamW suffers, and read a key geometric rate in far more layers. A vision transformer trained from scratch reached lower validation loss, and with a Muon base the method solved a grokking task on ten of eleven seeds where plain Muon never succeeded.
arxiv-2606-29576:
Fernandez and five colleagues compute what quark stars and hybrid stars would look like under an improved theory of dense matter. Their starting point is the pressure of cold, dense quark matter from perturbative QCD, quantum chromodynamics, sharpened by renormalization-group-optimized perturbation theory. That improvement makes the pressure less sensitive to arbitrary scale choices.

Imposing beta-equilibrium and charge neutrality, the conditions matter settles into inside a star, yields an equation of state, the relation linking pressure and density. A compact pocket fitting formula summarizes it for two-plus-one massive quark flavours at several scale settings. Pure quark stars matching observations arise for a middle range of that scale parameter. Hybrid stars, with quark cores inside hadronic shells, follow from three representative hadron models. Stable hybrid stars matching the massive pulsar PSR J0740+6620 appear, with quark cores ranging from small central kernels to large cores several kilometres across.
arxiv-2606-29876:
Patel asks whether the reasoning of large language models is consistent, not just accurate. Models reach 60 to 70 percent accuracy on hard clinical case benchmarks, but a right answer can hide unstable pattern matching.

Patel converts free-text reasoning into clinical reasoning graphs, structured maps built with a medical scheme of five node types and seven edge types. The analysis covers 750 traces from five models on 50 published case-conference cases under three prompting styles. Graph similarity is nearly the same for similar and dissimilar cases, and no comparison survives statistical correction, so no stable diagnostic schemas appear. Structured reflection makes traces discuss distinguishing features more, but not more consistently.
arxiv-2606-30176:
R. Montenegro-Filho, D. Silva, D. Cogollo, and M. Coutinho-Filho probe a magnetic phase in a chain of three-site units. The system is the extended Hubbard model at half filling. Lieb's theorem guarantees an insulating ferrimagnetic phase for the basic model. Adding nearest-neighbor Coulomb repulsion might destabilize that phase. The authors raise that coupling and watch what survives.

Doublon density, the share of doubly occupied sites, climbs with the coupling. Despite that climb, the ferrimagnetic insulator stays robust for a while. It survives up to a phase separation line near a quarter of the local repulsion. Beyond that line, two phases coexist in the chain. One phase concentrates doublons on a single sublattice. Its partner is metallic and ferromagnetic, or a singlet, depending on coupling strength. Density matrix renormalization group calculations map the boundary lines.
arxiv-2606-30276:
Elana Todd-Miller and Eva-Maria Graefe build a semiclassical propagator for the two-mode Bose-Hubbard system, a workhorse of cold atom physics. Even this dimer shows breakdown, revival, and tunnelling effects. The basic mean-field picture treats the state as a coherent state on a sphere. Mean-field trajectories alone miss the interference between paths. Their construction sums those trajectories with their phases kept.

Each trajectory contributes with a phase given by its mean-field action. The resulting propagator approximates the full many-particle state over time. Breakdown and revival dynamics are reproduced by the approximation. A time-slicing procedure layered on top improves it further. Many-particle tunnelling effects are then captured accurately as well. The focus stays on the Bose-Hubbard dimer throughout the analysis. The methods extend to more general two-state Hamiltonians. Larger symmetry groups are reachable by the same ideas.
arxiv-2606-30376:
Zheming Fu and six colleagues speed up reinforcement learning for flow-based image generators. Flow models generate along continuous trajectories, not discrete tokens. Their step-by-step likelihoods cannot be computed exactly. Existing fixes use stochastic samplers that clash with training. Others correct the velocity field by a fixed heuristic amount. FlowAWR replaces heuristics with a derived optimum.

The method starts from the best policy under a divergence penalty. It derives the optimal velocity field for that policy. The field takes a rectification form weighted by advantage. Better samples get stronger corrections, scaled by their quality. Optimization needs no stochastic differential equations at all. Generation needs no classifier-free guidance either. On a mid-size image model, alignment scores improve clearly. Convergence runs two to five times faster than the main rival. Multi-reward tests keep quality while obeying structural rules.
arxiv-2606-30576:
Liyao Wang and five colleagues work on cross-view object geo-localization, finding a ground-level or drone target inside a satellite image. Older methods match appearances in images and are held back by datasets lacking geometry details, varied prompts and normal camera views. The team built CMA-Loc, a building dataset with over two hundred twenty thousand ground-satellite and drone-satellite pairs.

Their framework, GAGeo, builds on a three-dimensional foundation model that treats image order symmetrically. It fuses visual features, prompts given as points, boxes or masks, and task tokens in one pass. That pass predicts bounding boxes, segmentation masks and camera poses together. A contrastive loss, which pulls matching views together and pushes others apart, uses the satellite view as a shared anchor. This enables zero-shot ground-to-drone matching with no three-way training data, and tests beat prior methods on unseen scenes.
arxiv-2606-31176:
Medler and colleagues analyse new infrared spectra of the Type II supernova SN 2022acko taken with the James Webb Space Telescope. This exploding star was the first supernova watched in detail by that telescope. The team studies spectra from days 259 and 368 after explosion, when the fading debris enters its nebular phase.

Strong hydrogen lines appear alongside lines from intermediate-mass and iron-group elements, the heavier atoms forged in the explosion. Those middle elements move near 300 kilometres per second, much faster than hydrogen and iron near 100, a pattern the authors link to a two-sided bipolar outflow. Carbon monoxide emission is seen, while silicon monoxide and dust are not, and a velocity offset points to a kick given to the newborn neutron star.
arxiv-2606-31376:
Liu and three colleagues pin down the exact threshold for rainbow stackings of random edge-colourings. A rainbow stacking layers several random colourings of a complete graph through vertex permutations so that no two edges of one colour overlap. Alon, Defant, and Kravitz began the study and located the transition within a constant-size window.

Liu determines the constant term in that transition. Above the stated palette size a stacking exists with high probability, and below it none does, with the gap closing as the graph grows. For a density-one set of graph sizes the threshold is exact. The proof expands a chromatic polynomial for an auxiliary conflict graph and refines a weighted sum over permutations, settling the problem their predecessors opened.
arxiv-2606-31576:
Winther, Jeha, Dieleman, Mnih, Opper and Dittadi offer a self-contained introduction to the stochastic differential equations behind modern generative machine learning, the methods that generate images, video and biomolecules. Most accounts assume a strong background and apply core results without deriving them. This tutorial rebuilds the foundations informally, starting from finite differences rather than heavy stochastic calculus.

Central pieces include the Fokker-Planck equation, which tracks how probability mass evolves over time, and a derivation of the evidence lower bound, a tractable stand-in for the log-likelihood. Diffusion models, score matching and flow matching then appear as other parameterizations of one general variational approach. A one-dimensional density problem runs throughout as a concrete test case comparing the parameterizations side by side.
arxiv-2606-31976:
Chen and three colleagues automate a slow expert labeling task in forestry: classifying why tree height measurements disagree. Field crews, lidar and canopy height models each err differently, and experts sort individual trees into seven bias types using a rule-based diagnostic. Each tree takes three to five minutes of expert time, and experts disagree often enough to noise the reference data itself.

TreeAgent orchestrates compiled expert rules with vision-language models. A transpiler turns natural-language rules into validated decision graphs over a fixed inventory of primitives, so rule changes become configuration edits. Vision models handle only the perceptual nodes, with multi-agent voting to damp their randomness. The system beats supervised baselines on the testbed while cutting expert labeling effort.
arxiv-2608-00076:
Hasic and co-authors ask which modality drives a multimodal model's decision. Such models now aid high-stakes choices from images and text. Existing explainers flag key regions or tokens. They cannot say if the image or the text drove the call. A model may answer right while leaning on the wrong evidence.

Their Counterfactual Modality Attribution method fills that gap. It builds image-only, text-only, and joint counterfactuals with coupled diffusion priors. Shapley values turn those cases into principled modality scores. On controlled benchmarks with known ground truth, it named the driving modality in 98 percent of cases. It also beat baselines on a real clinical data set. Failures hidden by accuracy alone came into view. The method aids audits of safety-critical multimodal systems.
arxiv-2608-00176:
Psaltis builds a framework for gamma-ray feeding probabilities in nuclear decay schemes. It rests on absorbing Markov chains. Excited nuclear states act as transient states in that frame. Long-lived levels act as absorbing states. Feeding fractions then follow exactly from the transition matrix.

Uncertainties spread via Monte Carlo sampling from Dirichlet distributions. That sampling keeps branching-ratio vectors normalized to one, as physics demands. The test case is a key resonance in the magnesium-proton reaction. It governs aluminium-26 production in hydrogen-burning settings. The ground-state feeding probability found is 0.68, plus or minus 0.06 at one sigma. The method also names the transitions that drive its uncertainty. It extends readily to other nuclei, he notes.
bentham-theory-legislation-hildreth-1876:
Bentham's Theory of Legislation reached English readers through R. Hildreth's translation. Bentham himself never wrote the book in this form. His French editor Dumont built it from Bentham's manuscripts into a French redaction. Hildreth then carried that version into English for this edition.

Inside stands the utilitarian science of law: how to frame codes that raise happiness and cut pain. Civil and penal law both receive rules drawn from the one great principle. Legislators across Europe and Latin America studied the work for generations. It spread Bentham's name wider than his own tangled English prose could. The system here is clear, bold, and practical.
bonatti-astrologers-guide-1676:
Guido Bonatti was the most famed star man of the 1200s in Italy. His aphorisms, short sharp rules of the craft, came to England late. William Lilly turned them into English in 1676 as The Astrologer's Guide. The Latin name of the work is Anima Astrologiae.

One hundred and forty-six rules guide the star man in his work. They tell when a chart speaks true and when it lies. The rules draw on Arab craft passed down through Spain. The book forms a bridge from the old Arab art to the English school of Lilly.
bradley-ethical-studies-1876:
F. H. Bradley published Ethical Studies in 1876, a set of essays on moral philosophy. Bradley attacks hedonism, the view that pleasure is the good, and Kantian duty done for duty's sake alone. Against both he sets self-realization: the self grows whole by taking its place in a moral community. My station and its duties is his famous phrase for that view.

Morality, he argues, lives in the customs and roles of a real society. Yet the self must also go beyond mere social rules toward an ideal. The book is the great statement of idealist ethics in English. It shaped welfare liberalism through readers like T. H. Green.
britten-art-magic-1876:
Emma Hardinge Britten said a sage's ghost taught her the lore in Art Magic, her dense tract of 1876. The ghost bears the name Cheval Louis de B. Through her hand he maps the schools, rites, and laws of the occult from old Egypt to her own day.

Ranks of spirits, charms, and the risks of rite fill the book. Britten casts it as fact, not tale. Groups in the United States took it as a core text of rite. It is a ground stone of magic in that land. Britten had a flair for the grand claim, and she backs it here with dense lore. Fans must sift her zeal from her facts with care.
britten-ghost-land-1876:
Tales of hunts for truth in far lands fill Ghost Land, Emma Hardinge Britten's book of 1876. It is the mate to her Art Magic of the same year. Britten tracks adepts, bands, and marvels through Europe and past it. She writes as one who claims to have seen much at first hand.

Ghost lore here mixes trek tale with creed. Dark rooms, odd cures, and bands with hid names crowd the pages. Britten kept the teller's name hid at first print. The pair of books maps the hid world she claimed to know. Her claims drew both faith and scorn in her own day. That split still marks the book, which fans read as trek tale and creed at once.
burton-two-trips-to-gorilla-land-1876:
Richard Burton, the boldest traveler of his age, went after the gorilla in 1876. Two Trips to Gorilla Land and the Cataracts of the Congo tells his search in Gabon. Burton had crossed Africa and Arabia; the great ape still drew him on.

He tells of rivers, trade, fevers, and the falls of the Congo, with the gorilla as his grail. His pen is dry, learned, and full of the lore of the coast. The book adds his great name to the gorilla shelf of his century. Few explorers wrote with his mix of grit and wit.
cia-0000009376:
Japan's strategic importance is spelled out in a CIA paper dated April 1948. Japan then sat under American occupation, three years after its defeat in the Second World War. Planners were deciding whether Japan would stay a ward or become an ally.

The paper weighs Japan's ports, industry, and position off the Asian mainland in Cold War terms. An anchored Japan guarded sea lanes and faced the Soviet Union across narrow waters. Judgments like this one fed the policy turn toward rebuilding Japan as a partner. The file shows that turn being reasoned out on paper.
cia-0000009676:
Six American prisoners were held at the Krong R'buk detention camp, a March 1971 item reports, in a Cambodian district the title cuts short. Detention camps in Cambodia's east held men captured as the war spread across the border in 1970. Conditions in such camps were rough and poorly documented.

Naming the camp and its count of Americans gave officials a concrete target for follow-up. Six men at one site could be checked against recent border losses. The report also shows captivity becoming a Cambodian story, not only a Vietnamese one. Its details preserve a camp that few outsiders ever saw.
cia-0000009876:
Four American prisoners were seen on May 15, 1968, walking north near a Laotian village. The title cuts the village name off at Ban Nath, and the report was filed that June. A precise date stands out in files where many sightings float undated. Walking north suggested movement toward central camps or toward Vietnam.

Dated sightings let analysts build timelines no memory could blur. Four men on a road on a known day could be matched against camp movements. The northward direction fit the prison system's known flow. This file preserves the day, the direction, and the number, a small hard point in a soft record.
cia-0000010476:
Britain's position in Egypt is examined in a September 1951 CIA paper. British troops still held the Suez Canal Zone, and Egyptian nationalists demanded they leave. Egypt's government was weeks from scrapping the old treaty that kept them there.

The paper weighs the canal's strategic worth against the rising cost of holding it. Suez guarded the sea road to Asia and Middle East oil routes alike. Within five years, the Suez crisis would humiliate Britain before the world. This file catches the position early, as analysts measured an empire's slowly loosening grip in the autumn of 1951.
cia-0000012276:
Joseph Bulik, a CIA officer on the Soviet side of the house, wrote a memo for the record in July 1960 about a briefing of Mr. Helms. Richard Helms then ran the agency's clandestine side, and briefings to him carried weight. The memo sits in the Penkovsky file, among the earliest papers of the case that would define Helms's watch.

A memo for the record fixes what was said while memory is fresh. This one preserves an officer's account of decisions taken near the top. For readers, it shows the great case being weighed at the level where careers and policy met.
cia-0000012376:
Soviet intelligence had to be told, formally, that the United States cared about Oleg Penkovsky, and an April 1963 plan works out how. Informing the KGB and GRU of American concern was a signal, not a courtesy. Washington hoped open concern might soften the colonel's treatment, or at least mark that his fate was watched from the highest level.

Signaling games like this were planned as carefully as operations themselves. Draft messages to Moscow were weighed word by word for tone and leverage. For readers, the plan preserves the endgame's strange diplomacy, where even grief was expressed by design.
cia-0000014776: A printed protest from Haditu fills a CIA file dated June 5, 1953. The group spoke out against the death sentence passed on the Rosenbergs. Haditu sought freedom for its own land, per the title's plain words. The Rosenbergs died later that same month. Small groups far away still took up their cause in print.
cia-0000015276: Flying saucers are the clipped subject of a CIA file dated August 2, 1952. The name at the head of the title is cut out as deleted. The summer of 1952 was the peak of the first great saucer wave. A file from those weeks belongs to the season when Washington itself reported lights overhead.
cia-0000015376: A flying object was observed near a deleted place, in a CIA file dated September 6, 1955. The source date is marked unknown in the title. With the place cut out, little can be checked or weighed. The file still marks that a sighting claim reached the agency and was kept. The sighting claim is kept in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015476: Non-orbit sightings of unidentified flying objects, from December 10, 1953, into March 1954, fill a CIA record filed in 1954. The odd label non-orbit sets these reports apart from satellite tracking. Winter sightings across three months were bundled for review. Such dated bundles were the bookkeeping of the saucer watch, letting staff count and sort claims season by season.
cia-0000037176:
An American man was sighted hiding in the southern part of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, a CIA record dated March 2, 1980 reports. A man in hiding was a stranger claim than a man in a camp. The report raised questions the file itself could not answer at once.

Inside, the sighting is recorded with the odd detail that made it memorable. Was the man a prisoner, a deserter, or someone else entirely? The record leaves the question open. Files like this show the wide range of stories the postwar search had to sort, from solid leads to tales that never found an explanation.
cia-0000042676:
Further reportage on the murder of Jesuit priests fills a CIA record dated October 4, 1989 in the catalog. The title links the coverage to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. The killings in San Salvador shocked readers far beyond El Salvador.

Inside, more reporting on the murders is gathered as it appeared. Each new account added names, places, and claims to a fast-growing file. The record shows an atrocity becoming a world story in print. Priests killed at a university drew the eyes of churches, parliaments, and editors onto one small country's war.
cia-0000042876:
El Salvador: Update on Jesuit Killings, 4, is a CIA record dated February 4, 1990. The fourth update came a month after the third in the series. That slower pace marked the case's move into legal channels.

Inside, the investigation's February position is set down in brief. Court steps, rather than fresh accusations, fill updates of this stage. The file shows the probe becoming a court case in form. Its dry entries are the sound of a scandal turning into procedure. Hard cases are usually won or lost in that dry country, far from the headlines that opened them.
cia-0000045276: President Jose Napoleon Duarte spoke in 1985 about his armed forces backing peace talks with El Salvador's rebels. A CIA item dated September 6, 1985, preserves the president's remarks. Army support mattered because the military held real power beside the elected government. The short report catches a president trying to show that his generals stood behind a negotiated end to the civil war.
cia-0000049076: Actions taken by El Salvador's minister of defense against officials accused of wrongdoing are recorded in a CIA item from 1983. Discipline from the top was the rarest commodity in the armed forces, so each move drew close reading. The item survives in the Truth Commission files, beside the many records of discipline refused.
cia-0000049176: A trace reply on Francisco Antonio Moran is preserved in a CIA item from 1990, kept with the Truth Commission records. Moran is a common name in these files, attached to officers and suspects alike, which made exact traces matter. The reply gathers what the system held on this one man of the name.
cia-0000049276: Representatives Frank McCloskey, Barbara Boxer, and colleagues sat for a CIA briefing in 1989, and the session is preserved in this item. Members who fought over Central America policy armed themselves in such rooms, fact by fact and map by map. The record sits among the congressional paper in the Truth Commission files.
cia-0000049376: Managing the Salvadoran military is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049376, dated April 1, 1988. Marked for the Truth Commission, the paper takes up the handling of El Salvador's armed forces. It remains a short declassified item whose title states its managerial focus, part of the later record on the military question in El Salvador.
cia-0000096476: Views of Prime Minister Jagan on British Guiana elections are recorded in declassified CIA document 0000096476, dated October 5, 1964. The heading names Jagan and the election as its paired subjects. The brief file preserves the premier's outlook as reported, filed the same day as the agency's item on the colony approaching its critical election.
cia-0000102976: USSR: Irkutsk Labor Camp for Juvenile Offenders Detailed is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000102976, dated August 2, 1983. The title promises detail on one camp near Irkutsk that held juvenile offenders. Young prisoners are the stated subject, set apart from adult camp reports nearby. The brief record is a single camp detail item from Soviet Siberia.
cia-0000106276: Communist Activity in the Laos Panhandle is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000106276, dated September 5, 1965. The heading names a region, the southern panhandle of Laos, and an activity, communist activity. No group, town, or incident is named in the title itself. The brief record is a regional activity item from the Vietnam War years in Laos.
cia-0000107976: Japan's Economic Role in the Development of Free Asia is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000107976, dated April 3, 1967. The heading places Japan inside a regional story, the development of Free Asia. Free Asia is the title's own label for the region it covers. The brief record is a regional economy item from the spring of 1967.
cia-0000108476: Weekly Situation Report on International Terrorism 20 August 1980 is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000108476, dated July 3, 1980. The title dates its week to August 20, 1980, weeks after the July file date. That gap stands on the face of the record itself. The brief record is one weekly issue in the long terrorism series from 1980.
cia-0000111776: Blank and Use of Forced Labor on the Soviet Siberian Gas Pipeline are the two numbered items in declassified CIA document 0000111776, dated March 1, 1985. The catalog marks the first item blank in the title itself. The second item returns to forced labor on the Siberian gas pipeline. The brief record is a two-item cable with one item withheld in its heading.
cia-0000119676:
Dated around February 1969, this CIA item is headed U.S. Marine Deserts: Letter Explains Action. It preserves a letter in which a Marine explained why he deserted, as the report of it reached the agency. The Marine's name does not appear in the heading.

Desertion letters drew attention because they spoke to morale and to opinion about the war. Officials clipped and filed such reports to track how the conflict was playing at home and abroad. The item keeps that explanation in the record. Read with the Sweeney statement filed the same month, it shows the agency gathering the words of men who walked away from the war.
cia-0000124276: A January 1958 CIA item lists Soviet stations for watching artificial earth satellites by eye, with their map coordinates, drawn up for the International Geophysical Year. That year-long science campaign ran through 1957 and 1958 across the world. The item preserves the station list as filed. Visual tracking by volunteers armed with telescopes filled gaps that radar could not, and station lists like this one organized that worldwide amateur watch into data.
cia-0000126876: An August 1968 CIA report surveys how the world's communist parties reacted to the invasion of Czechoslovakia. Parties from Rome to Hanoi had to choose between condemning Moscow and defending it. The paper collects those reactions as they came in during the crisis. The split among parties mattered beyond the bloc, since Western communist parties lost members and standing over their answers to the invasion for a decade.
cia-0000126976: Dated October 1975, this CIA Weekly Summary covers Angola after independence, a companion to the Weekly Review's treatment of the same subject that month. The summary gives the week's condensed picture of the Angola watch for busy senior readers. Companion products served different desks, the summary condensing for general readers what the review argued at length for specialists following the same African war.
cia-0000132276:
A Soviet peace plan for the Gulf is the subject of Situation Report 582 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series. The report is dated January 1, 1991. Moscow was still working the diplomatic track while the coalition prepared for war over Kuwait.

The report examines the Soviet proposal and the shuttle diplomacy behind it. A Soviet envoy moved between Baghdad and coalition capitals carrying the plan. It looked like the last peaceful exit before fighting began. Readers can see how one final diplomatic option was weighed, day by day, inside the crisis reporting that reached American decision makers at the time.
cia-0000132776:
Regional fear shapes this CIA paper on Cuba and the Caribbean, dated August 4, 1960. Castro's example, analysts worried, was spreading encouragement to movements across the islands and coasts nearby. Washington watched Cuba's neighbors almost as closely as Cuba itself.

The Caribbean framing returns here after appearing in the spring papers, now with exile training under way. The briefing treats one revolution as a possible spark for others, the core Cold War fear in the hemisphere. Its declassified text, held through the CIA Reading Room mirror, preserves that worry in the language of the time.
cia-0000134276: Strain across the Caribbean that would not lift fills a CIA paper dated November 3, 1959. Ten months into the revolution, the neighborhood had yet to calm down. Cuba was the source of the strain, and the whole island chain felt it. The short paper surveys the tensions island by island as analysts mapped them that fall.
cia-0000135676: A Spanish-language paper dated 4 November 1960, from the declassified 2506 Brigade collection. The brigade of Cuban exiles was training that fall for the landing it would make in April 1961. The catalog record for this item is minimal, with no subject or author stated. Among the hundreds of Spanish texts in this release, this one is identified by its date alone. It is held in its original language through the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000136276: A cable dated 1 May 1954 is among the declassified CIA papers on the need for consolidation phase policy plans, planning for the day after the victory. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136676: A document in Spanish dated 4 February 1961, held in the CIA's declassified 2506 Brigade files. The brigade, made up of Cuban exiles, was in the last phase of preparation for its April landing. The catalog record carries no subject for this item. It is kept in the original Spanish, one of many dated February records in the brigade's archive, and described here on that basis alone.
cia-0000136776: A Spanish-language document from the 2506 Brigade, dated only to 1961 in the catalog record. That year covers the brigade's final training, its April landing in Cuba, and the operation's aftermath; the record does not place this item within the year. No subject is stated for it. The text is in Spanish, preserved as released through the CIA Reading Room, part of the exile force's declassified archive.
cia-0000138976: Russian behavior in Harbin mirrors Mukden, this March 1946 report relates from a hotel manager who left Mukden in October 1945 and stayed in Harbin until March 1946. Russian forces acted as badly in Harbin as in Mukden, he states: looting, raping, and shooting at night were very common. Economically Harbin is comparatively comfortable since food is available, the excerpt adds before breaking off. The sub-source is considered fairly reliable. It is occupation reporting from Soviet-held Manchuria, months after Japan's surrender.
cia-0000139476: Father Lawrence Jenco's second debriefing leads this task force report. It covers 9-15 August 1986. Jenco was a released hostage. David Jacobsen would likely be the next one freed, he said. The captors believe Thomas Sutherland is a CIA case officer. They see Terry Anderson as a rebellious captive. A captor known as Hajj spoke in early June. All Americans would soon be released, he said. Jenco added detail on his south Beirut site. He could not identify its exact location.
cia-03020476:
Libya opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 5 January 1956. The USSR reportedly asked for use of an airstrip, ostensibly for ferrying diplomatic staff and supplies. The American embassy in Tripoli views the report with considerable reservation. Such a field could also watch Western forces and support North African nationalists. Libya's dependence on Western base payments frames the comment.

Ethiopia, in the second item, makes an oil agreement with Czechoslovakia. Bloc trade with Ethiopia had been tiny, about a hundred thousand dollars in half a year. Czech interest is growing, shown by a large trade mission and a costly fair exhibit. Rising political tension in Paraguay closes the issue. Leaders of a failed December rebellion walk free, and Communist chiefs have reappeared in Asuncion.
cia-06485476:
Dispatch from April 1968 forwards statements on the death of Martin Luther King for headquarters retention. Attachments named are statements by the Dominican Communist Party, the Communist 14th of June Revolutionary Movement, and various trade unions. All are said to have appeared in the 7 April 1968 issue of El Nacional.

The dispatch summarizes the Dominican party statement at some length. It made reference to Stokely Carmichael's visit to a Latin American solidarity conference, quoted Fidel Castro on Carmichael and Black Power, and voiced solidarity with Black Americans. The movement's statement, available only in gist, is summarized as saying King's death showed a deep crisis in American society. It claimed racist forces treated violence as the only law, at home and abroad.
cia-06568476:
Intelligence assessment dated June 1986, marked Top Secret, studies Warsaw Pact military perceptions of NATO nuclear initiation. The Directorate of Intelligence paper was prepared by the Office of Soviet Analysis. It states that information available as of 1 April 1986 was used in the report.

The assessment reconstructs how Pact planners expected a NATO nuclear opening to look. Middle pages state that most Pact discussions expected limited NATO use to stay, at least at first, within about 30 km of the forward line of troops. That depth matched NATO nuclear artillery range and the depth of attacking first-echelon Pact divisions. Strikes up to about 1,000 km were discussed, reaching the Soviet-Polish border. No strikes on the Soviet homeland were expected before an initial massed NATO strike, the paper reports.
cia-06929976:
Memorandum for the Director of Central Intelligence, dated 27 August 2002 and marked Secret, is headed Biweekly Developments in Iraq. Its opening section, 'No summer doldrums,' states September would be busier still. The Administration was rolling out its case for attacking Iraq, with the agency's assessment of Iraqi weapons programs as its centerpiece.

The memo offers a reminder of issues raised by allies and regional states when America had made such arguments before. It recalls 1998, when UN inspectors unearthed Scud warhead fragments that tested positive for breakdown products of the nerve agent VX. That finding contradicted a long-standing Iraqi claim never to have weaponized VX, the memo states. France and Russia had tried to discredit those test results, it notes. A later passage urges showing allies that a campaign would target Saddam and his regime's linchpins, with impact on Iraqi people kept as limited as possible.
coley-clavis-astrologiae-1676:
Henry Coley was a London astrologer and mathematician who succeeded William Lilly as the art's leading English teacher. His Clavis Astrologiae Elimata, published in 1676, is his complete textbook of astrology. The Latin title promises a key, filed smooth for the student's hand.

Coley teaches the casting of charts, the judgment of questions, and the reading of nativities in plain, ordered lessons. He trims Lilly's vast practice into rules a beginner can actually carry into a consultation. The Clavis served English astrologers as their standard manual into the next century. His almanacs kept his name before the public year after year.
europmc-pmc10344776:
Prjibelski and colleagues built IsoQuant in 2023, a tool for long-read RNA data. RNA carries gene messages out of DNA, and one gene can make many message forms. Long reads can span a full message, but errors make the forms hard to rebuild. IsoQuant maps the reads to a genome and traces the joins between gene parts.

The tool works with or without a known gene list. Prjibelski found that it cut false finds fivefold when a gene list was used. In free mode, with no list, false finds fell by a factor of 2.5. It links splice joins, the cut points in a message, into a graph. Paths through that graph give the full message forms and their counts.
europmc-pmc10435576:
Agu and co-authors reviewed in 2023 a computer method that helps find what food compounds do in the body. The method is molecular docking. It predicts how well a small compound grips a target protein. Food-derived compounds with health effects are called nutraceuticals.

Docking can reveal which proteins a nutraceutical may act on. Agu covers the main software tools and the basic steps of a docking run. Scores from the method can mislead, so lab proof must follow, the authors warn. Case work spans sickle cell disease, cancer, heart disease, gut and womb health, and brain decline. New paths found this way may seed fresh drugs.
europmc-pmc1088276:
Okada and colleagues filmed immune cells meeting inside living lymph nodes in this 2005 study. B cells make antibodies, the proteins that tag germs, and they need help from T cells to do it well. How the two cell types find each other was unclear. The team used a laser microscope that can image deep in intact tissue.

After B cells met their target germ part, they moved toward the T cell zone, the authors found. A signal receptor called CCR7 guided that drift. Paired B and T cells stayed joined for ten minutes to over an hour and kept moving as a pair. Pairs with the wrong target broke up in under ten minutes. The work gives early proof of directed immune cell movement inside the body.
europmc-pmc1189076:
Hannah, Heyer, and Hincha charted cold response genes in a small plant in 2005. The plant, Arabidopsis thaliana, can gain freezing tolerance after chilly days. That gain is called cold acclimation. Hundreds of genes shift activity while it happens.

Earlier work tracked only a few genes at a time. Here, genome-wide chips followed 14 days of cold exposure. Data from two chip types and past studies were merged. The result is a database covering more than 22,000 genes. Hannah gives plant science a shared map of cold response over time. The team also tracked which pathways matter most at each stage of the cold response.
europmc-pmc12230676:
Blin and many co-authors released version 8 of antiSMASH in 2025. Microbes make small active compounds that shape soil and microbe life. Many such compounds become drugs or farm chemicals. Their recipes hide in gene clusters inside microbe genomes.

Since 2011, antiSMASH has been the lead tool for finding those clusters. Version 8 detects 101 cluster types, up from 81. Support grew for terpene compounds and for tailoring enzymes. Big builder enzymes also get sharper analysis. Blin keeps the tool current as genome data floods in. It appeared in Nucleic Acids Research in 2025. The tool scans genomes from both bacteria and fungi for these clusters.
europmc-pmc1420676:
Some cancer cells switch off genes that would curb growth, without changing the DNA code. Pruitt and co-authors probed one such switch in 2006, a protein called SIRT1 that trims chemical tags from gene packaging. They found SIRT1 sitting on the start sites of silenced tumor suppressor genes in breast and colon cancer cells.

Blocking SIRT1 woke those genes back up. The genes spoke again even though a dense methyl tag layer, long blamed for the silence, stayed in place. Pruitt also saw shifts in cancer cell traits after the block. The work points to a fresh drug target for turning curbed genes back on.
europmc-pmc1525176:
Older women in Spain use health care more than older men. Redondo-Sendino and co-authors asked why, in a 2006 survey of 3,030 people aged 60 and over. Women saw doctors more often, got more home visits, and took three or more drugs more often. Hospital stays and flu shots showed no gap.

Much of the gap shrank once illness was taken into account. Women carried more chronic diseases and worse quality of life, classed as need factors. Schooling, marital status, and social ties also explained part of the gap. Redondo-Sendino concludes the higher use largely reflects greater health need, not waste.
europmc-pmc1877876:
Mosher, Ostrander and colleagues found in 2007 a gene fault that makes whippets both bulkier and faster. Double muscling, seen in cattle and sheep, comes from faults in the myostatin gene, which normally limits muscle growth. In whippets the extreme form is nicknamed the bully whippet.

Bully dogs carry two copies of a two-letter deletion in the gene's third section, which stops the protein early at amino acid 313. Dogs with one copy were on average more muscular than normal dogs. They were also significantly faster in competitive racing events, a measured link between this fault and athletic performance. It is the first time a myostatin mutation has been tied quantitatively to racing success. Two copies overshoot into the bully form, while one copy hits a racing sweet spot.
europmc-pmc1899176:
Lee, Jayaraman and Wood demonstrated in 2007 that indole, a chemical E. coli bacteria pour out in rich food, acts as a signal between species that shapes biofilms. Biofilms are surface communities of bacteria, and indole was known to control several genes and drug pumps. Its effect on biofilm building had not been well studied.

Gene activity scans, microscopy, and mutant strains showed indole is a non-toxic signal that represses swimming, switches on the sensor protein SdiA, and boosts acid resistance. A mutant lacking SdiA formed 50 times more biofilm, tying the sensor directly to the effect. Indole flattened biofilm shape from scattered towers to even colonies. In mixed films, partner bacteria engineered to destroy indole let E. coli grow 12-fold more, confirming the signal crosses species lines.
europmc-pmc1968876:
Levine delivered the 1993 Walter Hubert Lecture, published in 1994, on p53, the gene most often broken in human cancer. The p53 gene is mutated in about 60 percent of human tumors. Its protein normally restrains cell division by switching on other genes.

Raising p53 levels either halts cells in the G1 resting phase or triggers apoptosis, their orderly death. DNA damage raises both the amount and the activity of p53, which likely protects the body from mutation buildup. After radiation, some cell types arrest while others, such as thymus cells, die. Cells lacking p53 lose that checkpoint and pile up damage-driven mutations on the road to cancer. Losing p53 also speeds tumor growth and alters responses to DNA-damaging treatment. Radiation therapy, Levine argues, should account for a tumor's tissue origin and p53 status.
europmc-pmc1974776:
Thibault, Gant and Landfield expanded in 2007 the calcium hypothesis, which blames faulty calcium control for brain aging and Alzheimer's disease. Two decades of work had tied faulty calcium control inside neurons to aging and dementia. In rodent and rabbit memory circuits, aging raises calcium-driven aftereffects, calcium currents, and L-type calcium channel activity, and several changes track memory loss.

One version of the hypothesis blames those surface channels for most other calcium changes. The authors shift focus to the cell's internal calcium store and its release channels, the ryanodine receptors. Those channels amplify incoming calcium by releasing stored calcium in response, and they work in series with the surface channels in heart and some brain cells. Evidence links altered store release to cell toxicity, aging, and Alzheimer's models. Minding the store, their title urges, is essential to the full picture.
europmc-pmc2073776:
THOMLINSON and GRAY studied the structure of human lung cancers in 1955 and its meaning for radiotherapy. These squamous tumours grow in solid cords of cells fed by surrounding tissue, not by vessels between cells. Large cords have dead centres ringed by living tumour cells. The authors reasoned that oxygen must fall from the cord edge toward its centre. Cells starved of oxygen resist radiation damage far more than well-oxygenated cells.

Simple calculations showed the oxygen drop could be large and significant. At the centre of a cord just 150 micrometres in radius, complete oxygen absence was expected, using average tumour oxygen use. The team then measured many tissue sections quantitatively. Most tumours studied were poorly differentiated squamous cancers, a pattern in about 40 percent of bronchial cancers examined.
europmc-pmc2125376:
Harry C. Schmeisser of Johns Hopkins pathology reported in 1915 on leukemia of the fowl, spontaneous and transmitted. That myeloid leukemia occurs naturally in chickens he confirms. That it can be passed by injecting an emulsion of diseased organs, into the vein or the belly, he confirms too, after Ellermann and Bang's first success.

The independence of his stock is his emphasis. Across his experiments a hundred and five fowls were used; twenty-two developed leukemia, four more looked likely but could not be diagnosed with certainty. The simple transmission series are counted plainly: forty injected chickens, thirteen leukemic, about a third. Three years of observation stand behind the paper. Readers get a transmissible blood cancer in birds established on a second, separate pedigree, strengthening the case that something in the tissue carries it.
europmc-pmc2126276:
Theobald Smith described a shape-shifting bacillus found in the pneumonic lungs of calves, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1918. The germ appeared alone in pure culture with an extensive lobar bronchopneumonia, and under the microscope and in cultures it mimicked Actinomyces, the ray fungus, closely enough to risk a wrong name.

In lung fluid the germ sits as a tiny bacillus in small groups. In culture it takes three forms: a rod form, a round spore-like form, and, in serum tubes, a clustered flake ringed with clubs like Actinomyces. The round form likely holds a spore inside a shell of leftover material. Sealed tubes were essential for growth, and cultures died off within days unless renewed. Most of the flake's bulk seems to be capsule material the germ overproduces in serum and scarcely makes on agar.
europmc-pmc2128576:
Michael Heidelberger and Oswald T. Avery returned to the pneumococcus's soluble specific substance with better purification, in a second paper on the subject. It appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1924, from the Rockefeller Institute hospital. Their first paper had found the Type substance to be a polysaccharide; now Types II and III stood side by side.

The improved method recovered the Type II substance in high purity. It came back essentially unchanged after being thrown down by immune serum, by uranyl nitrate, by basic lead acetate, or by safranine dye. Type II and Type III substances both react as polysaccharides, yet they differ markedly in chemistry. The balance of evidence, the authors judge, favors the strong claim: the specific substances of these pneumococcus types are themselves polysaccharide derivatives, sugar chains carrying type identity. They close by weighing what that means for immunity theory.
europmc-pmc2131476:
Kenneth Goodner continued experiments in 1928 on pneumococcus infection placed in the skin of rabbits. Type I pneumococci set in the skin give a disease that mirrors human lobar pneumonia in many points. This report adds further proof of that likeness and turns to treatment with antiserum, asking how dose and timing shape the cure.

The amount of antiserum needed for success rose as the disease progressed, and it rose in a definite mathematical pattern. Goodner reads that pattern as the steady buildup of some toxic or opposing substance. Seven lots of serum were tested in rabbits: their healing value did not match their mouse-protective value. He suggests the rabbit test as a fair, simple standard for ranking such sera.
europmc-pmc2131776:
Hideyo Noguchi wrote part two of his comparative studies of herpetomonads and leishmanias in 1926. Both are small flagellate parasites, the leishmanias in man and animals, the herpetomonads mostly in insects and plants. Telling them apart matters for naming what infects a patient. Noguchi applied serum reactions and sugar fermentation tests to a set of strains.

Twelve herpetomonad strains from insects and plants proved unrelated by serum tests to any leishmania, and their sugar behavior also set them apart. Seven strains from milkweeds and the bugs that feed on them fell into just two kinds, named for the bugs they first came from. The two kinds showed some group reaction in serum, but split cleanly on carbohydrates.
europmc-pmc2247476:
Drummond and Rambaut presented BEAST in 2007, a software package for Bayesian evolutionary analysis of DNA sequences. Evolutionary questions are statistical, and Bayesian methods combine prior knowledge with data through sampling. BEAST implements many stochastic models of sequence evolution, plus tree-based models for data within and between species. Its features include relaxed molecular clocks, population history analysis and handling of sequences sampled at different times.

Version 1.4.6 comprises 81,000 lines of Java code in 779 classes and 81 packages. The design is object-oriented and modular, making it a platform for developing new models. It offers a wide range of prior distribution options. The source is freely available under an open licence. The authors describe BEAST as a powerful, flexible framework for analysing molecular sequence variation and testing evolutionary hypotheses.
europmc-pmc2265676:
Fierro and co-workers evaluated methods in 2008 for reconstructing time profiles from complex two-colour microarray designs. Two-colour arrays compare two samples per slide, and alternative designs beat the standard reference design in theory. Their measurements, however, give ratios that must be mathematically converted into the true expression profile. The team compared how far different linear models agree in reconstructing ratios and time profiles from one complex design.

Estimated ratios correlated highly on average, and all methods predicted the same profile for most genes. Agreement was best for genes with large expression swings across time points. Methods sharing underlying principles gave the most similar results. Models including a dye effect proved more robust against array failure, compensating for dye-related inconsistencies. Normalisation choice mattered less, and its impact did not depend on the method.
europmc-pmc2360676:
Gray-Schopfer and co-authors examined how moles avoid becoming melanoma in 2006. Melanoma is a deadly skin cancer, and moles are its common starting point. Cells can enter senescence, a permanent stop to division, and the authors asked whether this stop acts as a barrier in real tissue.

In lab-grown human pigment cells, switching off a protein called p16 was required, alongside telomerase, for cells to divide forever. Staining of real moles showed wide p16 presence and signs of senescence, without rises in two other markers, p53 and p21.
