Early melanomas had less p16, while advanced melanomas lacked both p16 and p21 in most areas. A faulty growth gene, BRAF, found in about 80% of moles, switched p16 on. The authors concluded senescence blocks melanoma, which explains why p16 loss promotes it.
europmc-pmc2365976:
Forche and co-authors mapped a shortcut life cycle in a yeast-like fungus in 2008. Candida albicans is a fungus that lives on humans and can cause thrush and worse infections. It mates to form cells with double the usual DNA, but no true meiosis, the division that halves DNA in sex, had ever been seen in it.

Instead, doubled cells shed whole chromosomes at random until they return near the normal count. Using DNA arrays, the team showed the offspring carry shuffled mixes of the eight chromosomes. Many also swapped segments between matching chromosomes, including multiple small patch events. Removing a gene called SPO11, normally a meiosis gene in other fungi, stopped that swapping. Offspring colonies looked visibly different from parents, proving the cycle creates real variety without meiosis.
europmc-pmc2408576:
Riker and colleagues profiled gene activity in skin tumors and spread melanoma in 2008. Melanoma is a skin cancer that turns deadly when it spreads, or metastasises, to other organs. The team compared 42 primary skin tumors with 40 metastatic melanoma samples using gene chips that measure thousands of genes at once.

Primary tumors, including thin melanomas, ran high in skin-identity genes such as keratins and the gene LOR. Metastases instead ran high in a different set, including MAGE genes, the survival gene BCL2A1, and a matrix-cutting enzyme, MMP14. The switch between the two patterns happened as melanomas grew thicker, but each gene flipped at its own thickness. That makes the switch zone a window where spread begins. The authors listed candidate driver and brake genes that changed across it, checked by targeted tests.
europmc-pmc2430176:
Rehak and Rehak reviewed a blocked retinal vein condition in 2008. In branch retinal vein occlusion, a vein in the retina, the eye's light-sensing layer, is squeezed where an artery crosses it. Wall damage and abnormal blood factors complete the block, cutting blood drainage from part of the retina.

The outlook is often fair: 50% to 60% of eyes end with vision of 20/40 or better even without treatment. Vision at first presentation is the strongest clue to the final result. The main treatment problem is macular edema, swelling at the centre of vision. A grid pattern of laser burns is the established fix for a defined patient group. Injections of steroids or of new vessel-growth blockers showed promise, and surgery to free the vein helped some eyes that laser could not treat.
europmc-pmc2447176:
Driemeyer, Boyke, Gaser, Büchel, and May revisited how fast learning reshapes the adult brain in 2008. An earlier study from the same group found that three months of juggling practice grew gray matter in a motion-sensing brain area. Gray matter is the brain tissue packed with cell bodies. The open question was the time scale.

They rescanned 20 healthy adults learning the three-ball cascade, using a 3 Tesla scanner to track whole-brain structure. The growth in the occipito-temporal cortex, at the back underside of the brain, was already detectable after just seven days of training. Neither raw performance level nor sheer exercise amount explained the change. The authors concluded that the qualitative step of learning something new, not continued drill, is what drives structural change. The effect had earlier proved temporary once practice stops.
europmc-pmc2561076:
Caulfield and a large team of collaborators tested in 2008 whether a gene found in genome scans, SLC2A9, actually moves uric acid in the body. Uric acid levels track with gout, blood pressure, and diabetes, and scans had tied variants of this gene to higher levels. The gene makes a transporter protein in the kidney, where uric acid is handled, but its cargo was unproven.

Expressed in frog eggs, both forms of the protein carried uric acid fast, at rates 45 to 60 times faster than its known cargo, glucose. A gout drug blocked the transport, and human kidney cells given the gene took up at least twice as much uric acid. In men, gene variants matched reduced uric acid clearance in urine. However, meta-analyses found no link to blood pressure.
europmc-pmc2600276:
Zilberberg, Shorr, and Kollef documented in 2008 the rapid rise of Clostridium difficile disease in American hospitals. This gut infection, usually triggered when antibiotics clear normal gut bacteria, kills more Americans than all other intestinal infections combined. Using national hospital data from 2000 to 2005, the team asked whether more patients were being hospitalised and whether each case had grown deadlier.

Adult hospitalisations for the disease doubled over the period. The rate climbed from 5.5 cases per 10,000 people in 2000 to 11.2 cases five years later. The age-adjusted case-fatality rate climbed from 1.2 percent in 2000 to 2.2 percent in 2004, so the average case became more lethal as well as more common. The authors link the trend to hypervirulent strains and resistance to widely used antibiotics, and frame the infection as a growing public health hazard.
europmc-pmc2690576:
Bradley and colleagues argued in 2009 that health care improves fastest by studying its own stars, an approach called positive deviance. Decades of quality campaigns had left poor care stubbornly common, and under one percent of medical research money targeted delivery itself. The approach starts from a bet: somewhere, an organization already performs exceptionally with the same resources as everyone else.

The method runs in four steps. Find the consistently top performers. Study them closely, with interviews and observation, to form guesses about the practices behind their success. Test those guesses statistically across a broad sample. Then spread what survives, working with the very people expected to adopt it. The authors illustrate with hospital care for heart attacks, where speed of treatment varies hugely. The approach suits problems where the knowledge exists but sits trapped in a few bright spots.
europmc-pmc2729376:
Ji and co-authors showed in 2009 that restoring microRNA miR-34 shrinks the tumor-initiating cell pool in pancreatic cancer. MiR-34 is a small RNA switched on by the tumor guard p53. Pancreatic cancer cells that had lost p53 also lost miR-34, which normally lowers Bcl-2 and Notch proteins that help cells survive and self-renew. A small stem-like cell group drives new tumor growth in this cancer.

Restoring miR-34 in two human pancreatic cancer lines lowered Bcl-2 and Notch, slowed growth and invasion, and made cells more sensitive to chemotherapy and radiation. The stem-like cell group, rich in Notch and Bcl-2 and lacking miR-34, fell by nearly nine tenths. Sphere growth in dishes and tumor formation in animals also dropped sharply.
europmc-pmc2761376:
de Jager and co-authors set out in 2009 the prerequisites for measuring cytokines in clinical trials. Cytokines are immune signal proteins. Multiplex immunoassays read many cytokines from one sample. Such measures can track whether antibody drugs hit their immune targets in patients. Trivial handling steps, they warn, can badly distort the low natural levels.

Spiking known cytokine amounts into blood samples, they found recoveries mostly within eighty to one hundred twenty percent. Most cytokines stayed stable for up to two years frozen, but several fell sharply by four years. Only two of fifteen cytokines survived repeated freeze-thaw cycles well. They also demonstrate an internal control, and stress tube choice and storage rules for trials.
europmc-pmc2785876:
Kretschmer and co-authors traced in 2009 how fungicide use drives multidrug resistance in Botrytis cinerea. This grey mould fungus rots fruits, vegetables, and ornamentals worldwide. Yearly monitoring in French and German vineyards found three distinct resistance types rising fast. All resistant strains pumped fungicides out of their cells faster and overproduced the pump genes.

One type carried activating mutations in Mrr1, a switch gene for one pump. The second type owed its resistance to a rearranged control region before another pump gene, reshaped by inserted jumping-gene DNA. The same rearranged version appeared in both countries, suggesting migration from France to Germany. Crossing experiments showed that combining both changes yields a third, broader resistance. In field trials, fungicide sprays selected the combined strain over sensitive ones. Growers then lose spray tools they still need badly each year.
europmc-pmc2841576:
Carlsen and a large team built a worldwide antioxidant food table in 2010, measuring over thirty-one hundred foods, drinks, spices, herbs, and supplements. Antioxidants are plant chemicals that neutralize damaging free radicals, and plant-rich diets are tied to lower chronic disease. Samples were gathered from many countries and tested with one standard assay so the values could be compared fairly.

Scores ranged over several thousand-fold between foods. Spices, herbs, and supplements packed the most antioxidants, some exceptionally high, while berries, fruits, nuts, chocolate, and vegetables led the everyday foods. Plant foods delivered far more antioxidants than animal foods. The authors say such a full table is essential for diet studies to register foods correctly.
europmc-pmc2848976:
Halaban and colleagues reported a troubling paradox in 2010 for PLX4032, a drug built to block the mutant BRAF kinase that drives many melanomas. In tumor cells carrying the V600E or V600K mutation, the drug shut down the ERK growth pathway as designed. In cells with normal BRAF, however, it did the opposite.

Working through a partner kinase called RAF1, the drug switched ERK on persistently in normal-BRAF cells. Those cells changed gene activity widely, stuck less to surfaces, moved more, and in some cases multiplied faster. The authors warn the drug may hand an advantage to normal-BRAF tumor cells in patients, so treatment should target only mutation carriers, with monitoring for new growths.
europmc-pmc2871176:
Marre and the LEAD-1 SU study group tested in 2009 whether adding liraglutide, a once-daily copy of a gut hormone, beats other add-ons for type 2 diabetes. Over one thousand adults whose sugar stayed high on a standard pill, glimepiride, joined the twenty-six-week trial at sites in twenty-one countries. Extra arms added a rival drug, rosiglitazone, or a placebo for comparison.

The two higher liraglutide doses cut the long-term sugar marker far more than placebo or the rival drug did, with gains visible within two weeks. Patients on liraglutide also lost weight, while those on the rival drug gained, a double advantage for a disease tied to weight. Nausea was the main added side effect, and it faded with time on the drug.
europmc-pmc2887476:
Okagaki and colleagues showed in 2010 that the yeast Cryptococcus neoformans grows giant cells during infection, and that the size change reshapes the disease. Normal cells span a few micrometers, while the giants can reach ten times that width. Enlarged cells were found in infected tissue and studied for how they interact with host defenses.

Giant cells were swallowed far less by immune cells, tying size directly to survival in the host. They also resisted chemical attack by oxygen and nitrogen stress better than normal cells, though they crossed into the central nervous system less readily. Each giant carried many copies of the genome in a single nucleus and still budded off daughters. Living alongside the opposite mating type boosted enlargement, and mutant strains missing a pheromone sensor enlarged less.
europmc-pmc2924276:
Croset and colleagues demonstrated in 2010 that the smell and taste receptors of insects descend from an ancient family far older than insects themselves. The receptors, called ionotropic receptors, are variants of channels best known for carrying signals between brain cells. A cousin family, the odorant receptors, exists only in insects and was assumed to be the original animal smell system.

Surveying genomes and gene activity across the protostome branch of animals, arthropods, worms, and mollusks included, the team found ionotropic receptors switched on in smell organs throughout. A conserved core set, the antennal receptors, likely formed the first smell system of the protostome ancestor. Insects later bolted on their private odorant family, while the ancient system still handles acids, amines, and taste.
europmc-pmc2928176:
Kim and colleagues fed in 2010 silver nanoparticles to rats for thirteen weeks to set safe limits for a material now common in antibacterial consumer goods. The study followed international test guidelines, with groups receiving daily oral doses from low to high or a plain vehicle. The particles averaged fifty-six nanometers across, the size class used in sprays, fabrics, and medical products.

Males on the higher doses gained weight more slowly from the fourth week, though they ate and drank normally. Blood chemistry, tissue examination, and silver measurements in organs showed dose-dependent changes, with silver accumulating chiefly in liver and kidneys. The authors derive the dose levels that produce no observable harm, numbers regulators need as nano-silver spreads through homes and clinics.
europmc-pmc2944076:
Anenberg and co-authors estimated the worldwide death toll from human-made air pollution in a 2010 modelling study. Ground-level ozone and fine particles have risen since pre-industrial times and are tied to heart and lung deaths.

Using a global atmosphere model to contrast past and present air, they paired pollution levels with risk figures from health studies. Their estimates linked man-made ozone to hundreds of thousands of yearly respiratory deaths, and fine particles to several million heart, lung, and cancer deaths. Adding assumed safe thresholds cut the totals by roughly a third, showing how sensitive such counts are.
europmc-pmc3012676:
Du and co-authors compared two ways of summarising DNA methylation readings from a popular array platform in a 2010 study. The Beta value reads as a simple fraction methylated, while the M value stretches the same data on a log scale, and users lacked guidance on choosing.

They show the two are linked by a standard mathematical transform, but the Beta value's scatter balloons at the near-full and near-empty extremes. In a mixing experiment with known answers, the M value found truly differing sites far more reliably at both extremes. A minimum gap threshold helped the M value further. Intuition favours Beta; statistics favours M.
europmc-pmc3022776:
Buchon and coauthors studied in 2010 how the gut of the fruit fly rebuilds itself after a bacterial infection. Eating a mild pathogen had earlier been shown to trigger a sharp rise in stem cell division in the fly gut. The team measured gut cells and shapes in detail to see how new cells form, mature, and replace damaged ones.

One growth signal pathway, centered on the epidermal growth factor receptor, proved central at every step. It drove stem cells to divide, guided new gut cells to take proper shape, and helped push damaged cells out to die. A second pathway worked alongside it to boost division. Flies lacking the receptor could not keep the gut sealed and died easily from infection. The work shows gut repair is one coordinated program, not separate fixes.
europmc-pmc3053476:
Heeb and coauthors reviewed in 2011 the double life of quinolones, a family of ring shaped compounds found across nature. Relatives of quinine, the fever tree drug, these compounds show effects from allergy relief to killing cancer cells and microbes, and they inspired a major class of synthetic antibiotics. One notorious bacterium makes several quinolones of its own, not mainly as weapons but as signals.

In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, these signals report how crowded the population is and switch on attack genes accordingly. The review covers the family's naming, chemistry, and making, plus side roles such as grabbing iron and blocking energy systems in rival cells. It also traces how the signals plug into the bacterium's wider control network. Understanding the signal system could suggest ways to disarm this hospital pathogen without classic antibiotics.
europmc-pmc3084176:
Russell and colleagues documented in 2011 how a decade of rising bed net use in rural Tanzania quietly rewired malaria mosquito behavior. Nets and indoor spraying work because local malaria mosquitoes bite people indoors late at night. The team compared hourly biting patterns from before nets arrived with two later milestones of community net coverage, during which malaria transmission had fallen dramatically.

By the final survey, one mosquito group bit less at night and had shifted toward a sibling species that bites earlier and more outdoors. The other group bit indoors only half as often as before. Overall, the share of human mosquito contact happening indoors fell sharply for both. The remaining transmission now happens where nets and sprays cannot reach. The authors call for new tools aimed at outdoor biting mosquitoes, as adults or as larvae, to finish the job.
europmc-pmc3176276:
Tiago dos Santos and colleagues probed how plastic nanoparticles enter human cells in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Particles sized like natural cell cargo are candidates for delivering drugs and genes, but their entry route decides where they end up inside. The team fed two particle sizes to three human cell lines while blocking known entry pathways one at a time.

Entry always needed cell energy, never passive drift. Beyond that, routes diverged sharply by cell type. Two lines leaned heavily on the cell skeleton's actin mesh, while lung cells suffered most from blocked microtubule tracks and from blocking one entry portal. A third blocker hit only the brain tumour line. The same particle, in short, sneaks in by different doors in different cells, a warning for delivery design.
europmc-pmc3180276:
Andrew Gaudet, Phillip Popovich, and Matt Ramer reviewed inflammation after peripheral nerve injury in a 2011 paper in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. Unlike spinal cord axons, peripheral fibres can regrow, and that success depends on a well-run inflammatory cleanup in the severed stump. The review opens with history, then walks through the response stage by stage.

Damage signals open the blood-nerve barrier and wake support cells, which shed their insulation, multiply, eat debris, and call in blood-borne scavengers. Those cells finish the clearance within days and leave once re-insulation begins. The spinal cord runs the same programme badly, with lingering toxic inflammation and scarring. Comparing the two, the authors argue, points to ways of coaching the cord to behave more like the periphery.
europmc-pmc3261976:
Nicole Janssen and colleagues evaluated black carbon as an extra indicator for air quality policy in this 2011 paper in Environmental Health Perspectives. Standards regulate particles by total mass, yet combustion particles are thought to be the most harmful fraction, and traffic measures barely move the total mass figure. The team systematically reviewed studies that measured both black carbon and particle mass.

Per unit of mass, black carbon showed larger health effects than the standard particle measures, and in studies modeling both at once, its effect held up more robustly. A worked example of traffic reduction suggested the gain in life expectancy looks four to nine times bigger when counted in black carbon than in fine particle mass. The authors recommend black carbon as a valuable additional indicator where combustion dominates.
europmc-pmc3297576:
Eizirik led a team that cataloged which genes are active in the human pancreatic islets, reporting in 2012. These cell clusters house the insulin making beta cells that the immune system destroys in type 1 diabetes. Using RNA sequencing, the team listed the genes switched on in healthy islets and in islets exposed to two inflammatory signals.

Nearly thirty thousand gene transcripts showed up in the islets, roughly doubling what was known before. Inflammatory signals changed about a fifth of them, including many alarm chemicals that call in immune cells. Many genes known to raise diabetes risk were active in the islets themselves. The signals also reshuffled how genes are spliced together, suggesting the islets talk back during immune attack.
europmc-pmc3335876:
Neal, Ahmad, Gordon-Weeks, and Ton showed that maize roots use a defense chemical to recruit helpful bacteria, in a 2012 study. Maize releases compounds called benzoxazinoids from its roots, known for fighting pests above ground and microbes below. The team asked what these chemicals do to Pseudomonas putida, a soil bacterium that colonizes maize roots and benefits the plant.

One compound, DIMBOA, proved to be the main form in root secretions. The bacterium tolerates it by breaking it down, and exposure switched on its genes for chemical sensing and movement. In swim tests the bacteria actively moved toward the compound. In soil, wild type maize roots, which make the chemical, drew far more of the bacteria than roots of a mutant that cannot. The authors cast the chemical as a recruitment signal protecting young, vulnerable maize.
europmc-pmc3338676:
Delhaes and colleagues mapped the full community of microbes living in the airways of cystic fibrosis patients, in a 2012 study. Cystic fibrosis thickens airway mucus, trapping bacteria and fungi that drive lung decline. Standard cultures catch only part of that community, so the team used high throughput gene reading on sputum from four adult patients, alongside normal cultures.

Sequencing revealed complex fungal communities, with most kinds missed entirely by culture, alongside the expected bacterial diversity. Patients with worse lung function and poorer clinical scores harbored noticeably poorer communities, with fewer kinds of both fungi and bacteria. Certain pairings recurred, such as a yeast appearing alongside the notorious Pseudomonas bacterium. The authors argue the whole community should be treated as one disease entity, and that fungi deserve a real place in care decisions.
europmc-pmc3445676:
Elwyn and a large team offered a practical model in 2012 for shared decision making between doctors and patients. The approach, where patients help choose their care, was well described in principle but rarely translated into routine steps a clinician can remember. Their answer is a three-step conversation built on relationship first.

Step one is choice talk, signaling that options exist. Step two is option talk, laying out the alternatives, often with patient decision aids. Step three is decision talk, drawing out what matters most to this patient and settling the choice together. The model treats decisions as the fruit of informed preferences, carefully explored, and doubles as a guide for training the skill.
europmc-pmc3447976:
Friedman and Alm exposed a statistical trap in 2012 lurking in microbial survey data, then built a tool to escape it. Surveys report each species as a share of the whole, not a headcount, and correlation on shares is notoriously unreliable, a warning going back to Pearson. Using simulated data and Human Microbiome Project samples, they showed how badly the standard approach misbehaves.

Many apparent links between species were artifacts, and some true links appeared with the wrong sign. Diverse communities softened the distortion; sparse ones suffered most. Their method, SparCC, estimates true correlations from share data anyway. Judged against its network, the standard approach invented roughly three false links per true one in gut data and missed most real ones.
europmc-pmc3518876:
Brains constantly predict, and the mismatch signals called prediction errors steer far more than reward learning, argue Hanneke E. M. den Ouden, Peter Kok, and Floris P. de Lange in 2012. Their review gathers prediction error findings from perception, attention, decision-making, and motivation studies across many brain regions.

Error signals everywhere share a computation: incoming input is compared with a top-down prediction. Beyond that common form, content and job differ sharply by circuit, and signed errors, which carry direction, behave differently from unsigned ones, which flag surprise alone. Where a signal sits in the wiring decides what it means. The review offers a map for a concept at risk of meaning everything and nothing.
europmc-pmc3598076:
Gizem Donmez and Tiago Outeiro reviewed two sirtuin enzymes as drug targets for brain disease in EMBO Molecular Medicine in 2013. Sirtuins strip chemical tags from proteins and depend on the cell fuel NAD. The family first drew fame through links between one member and longer life under calorie restriction. Seven sirtuins exist in mammals, working in different cell compartments, and this review covers the two with the strongest brain connections, SIRT1 and SIRT2.

Both enzymes touch the core damage of Alzheimer, Parkinson, and Huntington diseases, from protein clumps to failing energy systems, though not always in the helpful direction. SIRT1 also steers how young neurons mature, which matters for repair hopes. The authors sort the targets each enzyme acts on, disease by disease, and weigh what blocking or boosting each one might do. The closing outlook judges both druggable, with care about timing and place.
europmc-pmc3603976:
Monique Williams and colleagues dissected electronic cigarettes in PLoS ONE in 2013. E-cigarettes heat a nicotine fluid into an aerosol without burning tobacco, and use was climbing worldwide with almost no testing of what the aerosol holds. The team examined the combined fluid-and-heater unit, the cartomizer, under microscopes and chemical analysis, then tested the aerosol itself, including its effect on human lung cells in dishes.

Inside, a nickel-chromium filament wire joined silver-coated copper by tin solder joints, and every unit showed burn marks from before packaging. Tin particles and whiskers floated in the fluid, which harmed lung fibroblast cells in tests. The aerosol carried particles of tin, silver, iron, nickel, aluminum, and silicate, plus nanoparticles of tin, chromium, and nickel; nine of eleven elements measured ran higher than in comparison smoke or air. The hardware itself, they conclude, seeds the aerosol with metal.
europmc-pmc3632776:
Koste Yadeta and Bart Thomma reviewed vascular wilt diseases in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2013. Wilts rank among the most destructive plant diseases, in farm crops and trees alike. Their agents, soil bacteria, fungi, and oomycetes, enter through roots and colonize the xylem, the water pipes of the plant, multiplying until flow is blocked. Leaves starve of water and the plant can die. Sprays and soil treatments barely reach an enemy living inside the plumbing.

Genetic resistance in the host is the one control that works, which puts the science focus on recognition and defense inside the vessels. Chapters cover how these pathogens live in the xylem, what they secrete, and how plants detect and answer them, from vessel-blocking gels to chemical counterattacks. The authors argue that only a molecular grip on this hidden battleground will yield new control strategies beyond breeding.
europmc-pmc3639376:
A weak alternating current passed through the scalp can tune brain waves, and Neuling, Rach and Herrmann test how long the effect lasts in a 2013 Frontiers in Human Neuroscience study. Their tool, known by the short name tACS, sends current at a set wave rate. They guessed that after-effects would hang on how strong a person's own brain waves were at the time.

In two tests, people sat for 20 minutes of current tuned to their own alpha wave rate, with eyes open or shut to keep alpha power low or high. After-effects ran at least 30 minutes when alpha power began low. When alpha power began high, the current added nothing more. Brain state, not just dose, sets what this kind of tuning can do, a point that matters for its use as a therapy.
europmc-pmc3657176:
One switch protein turns nerve helper cells into a repair crew, Arthur-Farraj and a large team show in a 2012 Neuron study. When a limb nerve is cut, helper cells called Schwann cells drive the clean-up and regrowth, a response named Wallerian degeneration in the text. The switch, c-Jun, sits inside those cells. This study tests how far its rule reaches.

With the switch on, helper cells make growth foods, grip molecules and clear tracks, and clear away old insulation. Without it, the repair cell that forms is faulty. Regrowth then fails in practice, and nerve cells die. A single glial switch, the authors say, runs the change of both insulation-making and spare helper cells into dedicated repair cells. That makes c-Jun a prime target for boosting nerve repair.
europmc-pmc3708876:
Santiago and colleagues validated the CDC's real-time RT-PCR assay for dengue, a test that detects the virus's RNA and identifies which of its four types is present. Dengue patients usually carry virus in their blood when symptoms start, so a direct molecular test can confirm cases early. The assay had recently been cleared for diagnostic use in the United States.

In confirmed dengue cases, the assay found viral RNA in about ninety-eight percent of acute samples, and it agreed with sequencing at a similar rate in suspected cases. Results were reproducible across three testing sites, with no false alarms from other fever-causing agents. The authors certify it as a reliable platform for dengue diagnosis.
europmc-pmc3741576:
Marco Meraz-Ríos and four co-authors wrote a review in Frontiers in Integrative Neuroscience in 2013 on inflammation in Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's is the most common form of dementia. Its brain marks are tangles of altered tau protein inside nerve cells and plaques of amyloid-beta outside them, ringed by activated support cells called astrocytes and microglia.

Whether inflammation helps or harms is disputed. Early on, activated microglia and astrocytes may help clear amyloid. But long-term activation has been tied to more amyloid and to changes in tau. Alzheimer's brains show raised levels of many inflammation signals. Trials and animal work with anti-inflammatory drugs suggest they may lower risk and cut amyloid buildup, but the authors say more study is needed before such treatment can be recommended.
europmc-pmc3811976:
Kang and colleagues reported in PLoS ONE in 2013 that vesicles shed by gut bacteria can calm inflammation in the colon. They used mice given dextran sulfate sodium, a chemical that triggers colitis much like human inflammatory bowel disease.

Sequencing stool samples showed that the mix of bacteria-derived vesicles shifted more sharply during disease than the mix of bacteria themselves, with vesicles from Akkermansia muciniphila dropping away. In cell tests, vesicles from that species cut the inflammatory signal IL-6 raised by E. coli vesicles. Fed to mice, they also eased weight loss, colon shortening, and inflammatory cell invasion, leading the authors to propose bacterial vesicles as a route to protect gut health.
europmc-pmc3873676:
Ali Adem Bahar and Dacheng Ren review antimicrobial peptides in Pharmaceuticals in 2013. Drug-proof infections keep rising, and even the strongest antibiotics can fail against so-called superbugs. Peptides, short protein chains made by many life forms, offer a fresh line of attack.

The review traces the history of these peptides and sorts their main types. Their targets span viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites. Some tear germ walls, others jam inner processes. Germs have evolved a few counter-moves, which the authors list. Design rules for stronger lab-made versions get close care. Two hard cases close the review: biofilms, germ cities shielded in slime, and dormant persister cells that shrug off drugs.
europmc-pmc3923676:
Mitesh J. Borad and a large team read the genes of a rare bile duct cancer. Their paper appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2014. The cancer is intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. It has few treatment options once advanced. Six patients joined a trial that sequenced whole genomes and RNA from their tumors. The goal was to find changes that drugs could target.

In three of the six tumors, the FGFR2 gene was fused to a second gene. Two patients then got FGFR-blocking drugs. Both showed early anti-tumor effects. One stayed stable on a second such drug after the first failed. A fourth tumor had a broken copy of ERRFI1, a brake on the EGFR pathway. That tumor shrank fast on an EGFR blocker. The authors call for larger trials of both drug types.
europmc-pmc3928676:
Berit Carow and Martin E. Rottenberg review a brake on immune signaling in Frontiers in Immunology in 2014. The protein, SOCS3, is switched on by infection and inflammation in many cell types, and it damps the cytokine signals that drive those responses. It binds both the JAK enzyme and the cytokine receptor, blocking activation of the STAT3 signal and sometimes sending the receptor for destruction.

That braking usually protects the body, limiting damage from its own defenses, but in some settings it worsens disease by weakening needed responses. SOCS3 also reaches beyond STAT3 into other pathways. The review assembles evidence from infections and autoimmune diseases and argues that this one protein runs a wider program for keeping immune balance across many tissues.
europmc-pmc3930676:
Daniel Jolley and Karen M. Douglas test how anti-vaccine conspiracy claims affect plans to vaccinate, in PLoS ONE in 2014. In their first study, British parents answered questions about belief in anti-vaccine conspiracy theories and about vaccinating a made-up child. Stronger conspiracy belief went with weaker intention to vaccinate, a link explained by seeing vaccines as dangerous and by feelings of powerlessness, disillusionment, and mistrust of authorities.

In the second study, volunteers read material that supported such theories, material that refuted them, or neutral control material. Those who read the supporting material showed less intention to vaccinate than the other groups, through the same feelings. The authors warn that conspiracy content can quietly shape health choices.
europmc-pmc3938676:
Jeffrey C. Glaubitz and colleagues present TASSEL-GBS, software for turning raw genotyping-by-sequencing data into genetic markers, in PLoS ONE in 2014. Genotyping by sequencing reads a reduced slice of the genome from many individuals at once, cheaply scoring large numbers of SNP markers. It is popular in crop breeding and ecology, but the flood of raw reads needs heavy computing to become usable genotypes.

The pipeline was built to run on the modest desktops and laptops, with 8 to 16 gigabytes of memory, that small breeding and ecology programs actually own. It scales from small studies to programs scoring millions of markers in up to 100,000 individuals, and it is designed for the fast turnaround accelerated breeding demands. A reference genome is required.
europmc-pmc4011876:
Robert Bain, Ryan Cronk, Jim Wright, Hong Yang, Tom Slaymaker, Jamie Bartram, and Paul R. Hunter pool studies on faecal germs in drinking water, in PLoS Medicine in 2014. Global goals track access to safe water by counting use of improved sources, such as piped water or protected wells. Those sources are built to shield water from outside dirt, in particular from faecal matter.

The team reviewed and merged studies from low- and middle-income countries that tested water for faecal germs. Improved sources did carry less contamination than unimproved ones, so the label gives some real protection. Yet improved water often carried germs. The gap means the global count of people with improved sources overstates how many drink safe water. The authors argue that safety claims need water testing, not source type alone. Their merged data give a firmer base for judging progress toward safe water for all.
europmc-pmc4059276:
Thomas J. Sharpton wrote an introduction to the analysis of shotgun metagenomic data, published in 2014. Metagenomics reads DNA taken straight from a mix of microbes, rather than growing each one in a lab. His guide explains how researchers turn those short reads into a picture of a microbial community.

Sharpton walks through the main choices: measuring which microbes are present and how common each is, sorting reads into taxonomic groups, and piecing reads together into genomes. He also covers tools for judging what the community can do. Many of the tools he surveys run from a command line and demand strong computing. The guide gives new users a map of the options and their trade-offs.
europmc-pmc4075476:
Charlotte Zenner, Solveig Herrnleben-Kurz, and Harald Walach reviewed studies of mindfulness programs run in schools. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in Frontiers in Psychology in 2014. School mindfulness courses were popular, but the evidence for mental benefits in children and teenagers needed pulling together.

Searching twelve databases plus unpublished sources in 2012, they found twenty-four studies, most with control groups. In total, well over a thousand students from grade one to grade twelve took part in mindfulness training. Overall effects were positive and clearest for thinking skills, stress, and resilience. Effects on emotional problems were smaller and not firm. The authors call the results promising while noting that study designs varied widely in quality and program shape.
europmc-pmc4192676:
Gili Ben-Nissan and Michal Sharon reviewed a shortcut in the cell's waste disposal in Biomolecules in 2014. Most worn-out proteins are tagged with ubiquitin and fed to the 26S proteasome, a barrel-shaped shredding machine. Its core alone, the 20S proteasome, can also destroy some proteins with no tag at all.

The tag-free route suits proteins with loose, disordered stretches, whether born that way or damaged by oxidation, mutation, or age. The review gathers what is known about how this pathway is governed: gate-keeping proteins that open the barrel, activators that speed it, and signals that raise it under stress. Compared with the tagged route, control of the 20S path is poorly mapped, and the authors mark the open questions.
europmc-pmc4200776:
Kendra Elizabeth Brett, Kristi Bree Adamo, and three co-authors reviewed how the placenta feeds the fetus in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2014. A growing fetus can only use nutrients the placenta ferries across from the mother's blood. Transporter proteins in the placenta do that ferrying, and their numbers shift with conditions.

The review covers transporters for glucose, amino acids, and fatty acids, and how they change in troubled pregnancies. In growth restriction they may fall short, while in diabetes and obesity they may oversupply, leading to oversized babies. The placenta seems to tune transport to match what the mother's blood offers, and male and female fetuses follow different strategies. Better maps of these controls could guide treatments that keep fetal growth on track.
europmc-pmc4310776:
Dorian V Ziegler, Christopher D Wiley, and Michael C Velarde review how mitochondria drive cellular senescence, the permanent growth arrest of stressed cells. Their review appeared in Aging Cell in 2015. Senescent cells build up with age and feed many age linked diseases, and worn mitochondria are one proven trigger of the arrest.

The old free radical theory blamed reactive oxygen alone. The review shows several other mitochondrial routes to senescence: changes in how mitochondria split and fuse, flaws in the energy chain, shifts in fuel balance and redox state, and calcium mishandling. Together these paths give a wider view of how cell powerhouses lock cells into old age, and more points where intervention might work.
europmc-pmc4317176:
Thomas E. Sussan and eleven co-authors exposed mice to electronic cigarette vapor and found their lungs defended themselves worse against infection. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE in 2015. E-cigarettes had surged in popularity on a healthy image, yet direct tests of their effects in living animals were almost absent.

The vapor carried a very large load of free radicals per puff, and exposed mice reached blood nicotine levels like those of human users. Two weeks of exposure raised oxidative stress and mild lung inflammation. Challenged with bacteria and flu virus afterward, exposed mice cleared the bacteria more slowly and fared worse against the virus. The results challenge the harmless label on vaping.
europmc-pmc4365176:
Aleksandra Duda-Chodak, Tomasz Tarko, Paweł Satora, and Paweł Sroka reviewed how food compounds meet gut microbes, in the European Journal of Nutrition in 2015. The gut microbiome changes many food chemicals in ways human enzymes cannot, since bacterial work in the gut runs without oxygen. Their review centers on polyphenols, plant compounds whose health effects depend heavily on what gut bacteria make of them.

Bacterial change usually lowers a compound's activity, but at times it creates a product with stronger effects. The review maps the paths polyphenols take through gut bacteria and the active products that result. It also covers how diet and age reshape the gut community, and why balance between the immune system and gut microbes matters for health. The message is that food effects cannot be judged apart from the microbes that process them.
europmc-pmc4414376:
Ben Sadd and a large consortium sequenced two bumblebee genomes, reported in Genome Biology in 2015. Bumblebees live in small, primitively social colonies, between solitary bees and the vast honeybee societies, so their genomes can show how social life evolved. They are also vital pollinators in nature and farming, with worrying declines in some species. The team produced high-quality draft genomes for Bombus terrestris and Bombus impatiens, two dominant, much-studied species.

Compared with the honeybee, bumblebees share many features once thought to underpin advanced social life, pushing those traits earlier in bee evolution. Both lineages carry sparse detoxification and immune gene sets, a shared vulnerability. Differences include a tilt in smell-and-taste genes toward taste, and striking divergence in microRNAs, small regulators that may shape caste and behavior. The genomes give decline research a firm base.
europmc-pmc4419676:
Yoshimi Nakano, Masatoshi Yamaguchi, Hitoshi Endo, Nur Ardiyana Rejab, and Misato Ohtani reviewed plant cell wall control in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2015. All plant cells build a primary wall, but only some add a stiff secondary wall, as in the vessels that carry water and the fibers that hold a stem upright.

That second wall gains its strength from ordered cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, each made by enzymes switched on for that task. The review centers on two families of gene switches, NAC and MYB proteins, and the chain of command between them. It traces how land plants evolved this network to build strong, water-resistant support tissue.
europmc-pmc4425176:
Mayu Kasubuchi, Sae Hasegawa, Takero Hiramatsu, Atsuhiko Ichimura, and Ikuo Kimura reviewed short-chain fatty acids in Nutrients in 2015. Gut microbes make these small acids when they ferment dietary fiber. Acetate, butyrate, and propionate serve the host as fuel, and they also act as signals in the body.

The acids switch on cell receptors and can change how genes are read by blocking enzymes that tighten DNA packaging. Newer work, surveyed here, shows fiber and these acids do more than improve the gut itself. They affect tissues across the body and help control energy balance. The review gathers what is known about their roles in obesity, diabetes, and wider metabolic health.
europmc-pmc4490476:
Jana Orsavova, Ladislava Misurcova, Jarmila Vavra Ambrozova, Robert Vicha, Jiri Mlcek, and Cenk Suphioglu measured the fatty acids in fourteen vegetable oils in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2015. Oils differ greatly in their mix of saturated, monounsaturated, and polyunsaturated fats, and that mix shapes their place in a healthy diet. The team analyzed oils from safflower, grape, hemp, sunflower, sesame, olive, coconut, and other seeds and fruits by gas chromatography.

Three fatty acids dominated across the oils: palmitic, oleic, and linoleic, in widely varying shares. The authors calculated how much of the recommended daily energy from each fat class a gram of each oil supplies, giving a nutritional ranking. They then compared reported fat intakes and heart disease deaths across twelve countries. The expected relationships were not confirmed by correlation tests. That is a caution against simple country-level claims about dietary fat and mortality.
europmc-pmc4493776:
Markus Dietlein and a team of co-authors compared two imaging tracers for recurrent prostate cancer in Molecular Imaging and Biology in 2015. Both tracers home to PSMA, a protein abundant on prostate cancer cells, and light it up on PET scans. The established tracer uses gallium-68; a newer one uses fluorine-18, which promises easier supply, larger production batches, and sharper images.

In a small group of men whose blood marker signaled relapse after treatment, each patient was scanned with both tracers. The team compared the number of suspicious lesions found, their tracer uptake, and their contrast against background tissue. Both agents revealed the recurrent disease, letting the authors weigh whether the fluorine compound's practical advantages come with equal detection performance. Such head-to-head data guide hospitals choosing which tracer to adopt for routine relapse imaging.
europmc-pmc4499176:
Steven Frese, Kent Parker, C Chris Calvert, and David Mills tracked piglet gut microbes through nursing and weaning in Microbiome in 2015. A newborn mammal is colonized within days by a complex microbial community whose assembly shapes later health. Pigs are a good stand-in for nursing humans. Pig and human milk are alike in makeup, and pigs are easy to study experimentally. Yet modern molecular data on nursing piglets were scarce.

Fecal microbes were profiled from birth to seven weeks of age, as piglets moved from sow milk alone to a starter feed of plant and animal ingredients. Communities were stable while diet held steady and shifted clearly with the change. Deeper sequencing of a subset found sugar-breaking pathways that differed between diets, with enzymes for milk sugars prominent before weaning. Diet, the authors conclude, is the dominant sculptor of the early gut community.
europmc-pmc4568976:
Assaf Ben-Meir leads a twelve-author team restoring egg cell youth with a dietary compound, in Aging Cell in 2015. Women's fertility falls steeply in the fourth decade of life as egg quality and supply drop. The causes of that aging were elusive. The team traced it to the egg's mitochondria, its energy units, which falter with age.

Old eggs in mice and humans made less of two enzymes needed to build coenzyme Q10, a molecule the energy chain requires, and their energy output fell. Giving CoQ10 reversed the decline in egg quality and number in older mice. Knocking out one enzyme in young eggs copied the aged state, down to infertility and early ovarian failure, and CoQ10 prevented that failure.
europmc-pmc4581176:
Andre Gross and six co-authors survey the machines that pick out single cells, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2015. Isolating one cell at a time underpins cell line building, cancer research, and new diagnostics. A dedicated market survey, reported here for the first time, ranked what labs actually use.

Fluorescence-activated sorting led with 33% usage, followed by laser microdissection and manual picking at 17% each, dilution seeding at 15%, and microfluidic chips at 12%. The review explains each leading method and the performance factors that matter when choosing. A search of 179 patents, 25 examined closely, previews tools now emerging. Interest in single-cell isolation, the survey says, keeps climbing.
europmc-pmc4582176:
Paul Blakeley leads a ten-author team charting the first cell lineages of the human embryo, in Development in 2015. Days after fertilization, the blastocyst sorts its cells into three lineages, including the epiblast that becomes the body proper. Human embryos are scarce and regulated, so this sorting was mapped mostly in mice, with real differences suspected.

Reading RNA cell by cell in human and mouse embryos, the team found shared programs and human-specific ones, then confirmed key patterns at the protein level. Several genes marked only the human epiblast, including the factor KLF17, and the TGF-β signal pathway was enriched there; blocking it erased a core pluripotency gene. Mouse lineage markers, by contrast, were absent or differently placed in humans.
europmc-pmc4585776:
Xu Zhang leads an eight-author team comparing two diabetes drugs through the gut, in Scientific Reports in 2015. Metformin is the world's standard type 2 diabetes drug, and berberine is a plant compound with similar effects. Both had recently been shown to work partly by reshaping gut microbes, which help drive obesity-linked metabolic disease.

In rats made obese on a high-fat diet, both drugs shifted the whole gut community back toward the lean pattern and cut its diversity. Of 134 microbe groups responding to treatment, 60 fell under both drugs. Groups that produce short chain fatty acids, a beneficial microbial output, rose markedly, more with berberine than metformin. The shared microbial signature tracked the animals' improved obese traits.
europmc-pmc4621876:
In 2015, a review of how hyaluronic acid shots might help in knee osteoarthritis was published by Roy D. Altman and colleagues. The acid occurs in knee joint fluid and gives it spring. Shots of it are a common cure, but how they work was spread across many basic studies. The team searched the lab literature for work on the mode of action.

Guarding cartilage was the action named most often. Other named actions were boosting joint building blocks, calming swelling, easing pain, and helping the bone under the cartilage. Binding to a receptor called CD44 was the trigger named most. Heavy forms of the acid beat light ones, and forms made by fermentation looked safer than forms from birds. The pooled proof backs the claimed gain for patients.
europmc-pmc4633676:
Working with colleagues, Bo-Zong Shao published a 2015 review of the NLRP3 inflammasome and drugs that block it. Inflammasomes are protein assemblies of the innate immune system that switch on inflammation. NLRP3 is the best studied member and reacts to many danger signals. The review appeared in Clinical and Experimental Pharmacology and Physiology.

NLRP3 activity is tied to metabolic disorders, multiple sclerosis, inflammatory bowel disease, and inherited fever syndromes, among others. The authors explain the complex's structure and what sets it off, then survey known blockers, some already promising in clinical testing. Autophagy, the cell's cleanup process, also features as a natural brake. The review gives drug developers a single map of the target and the compounds chasing it.
europmc-pmc4670676:
Jing Wang and colleagues published a 2016 review of how sugar chains called polysaccharides fight oxidative harm in lab tests. These long chains come from plants and other natural sources. Too many reactive oxygen and nitrogen species hurt cells and feed disease, and the chains are said to blunt them.

Across studies, the chains mop up free radicals, give up electrons, and bind the iron that would else spur more harm. Yet reports clash at times, and the ways of action had not been set in order. The authors sort the newest finds by mode of action and show how chain make-up, branching, and source shift the strength. Their account gives food and drug researchers a firmer base for judging claims made for these natural chains.
europmc-pmc4685976:
Sheila Cyril, Ben J. Smith, Alphia Possamai-Inesedy, and Andre M. N. Renzaho reviewed community engagement in health programs in Global Health Action in 2015. Programs often claim to involve local people, yet which parts of that involvement actually improve health was poorly understood. The review focused on disadvantaged groups, including ethnic minorities. It asked how large the benefit is and which design choices make engagement work.

Of twenty-four studies that fit the review, twenty-one improved health behavior, planning, service access, or health knowledge. Features linked to success included real sharing of power, partnerships that learn both ways, and bicultural workers who deliver the program. Many studies measured engagement weakly, though. The authors call for better measures so future programs can prove what involvement adds. Their findings give program designers a practical checklist.
europmc-pmc4689276:
Haji Bahadar, Faheem Maqbool, Kamal Niaz, and Mohammad Abdollahi reviewed how nanoparticle toxicity is tested, in the Iranian Biomedical Journal in 2016. Tiny engineered particles are spreading into medicine and industry, and their safety is debated. Labs test harm to cells, immune responses, and DNA damage with a set of standard assays. The authors survey those assays and the cell models behind them, and find the results often conflict.

One problem is that the particles themselves can disturb the tests, skewing readings. Different labs using different models reach opposite verdicts on the same particle. The reviewers argue that cell-only evidence cannot settle safety rankings. They call for agreed, unbiased testing models with more weight on studies in living animals. Regulators weighing nanoproduct risks, they note, need firmer ground than the current patchwork gives.
europmc-pmc4707776:
Marc Haber, Massimo Mezzavilla, Yali Xue, and Chris Tyler-Smith reviewed ancient DNA findings in Genome Biology in 2016. Geneticists once inferred the human past from living people's DNA, favoring the simplest story that fit. Ancient DNA changed the method: samples from before, during, and after key events let researchers watch change directly. The review revisits the peopling of the world with that direct evidence in hand, and warns against cutting corners with Occam's razor.

Again and again, the old bones tell messier stories: migrations layered on migrations, mixing with archaic humans, and replacements that simple models missed. Modern humans left Africa and interbred with Neanderthals and other archaic groups along the way. Selection, too, left marks the simple stories skipped. The authors' moral is methodological: when direct evidence exists, prefer it to elegant guesses. Human history, measured rather than modeled, keeps turning out stranger.
europmc-pmc4736276:
Ghoneim and O'Hara review what depression does to patients who face surgery. Low mood is common before and after an operation. It can make pain feel worse, slow healing, and raise the risk of infection. The pair search the past work on this link across many fields of surgery.

The pattern is grim and clear. Depressed patients report more pain and use more pain drugs. They stay in hospital longer and face more problems after heart, gut, and back surgery. Mood also shapes how well patients cope with care in intensive units. The authors urge surgical teams to screen for depression and treat it as part of care.
europmc-pmc4739776:
Ji, Song, Regev, and Struhl, with Sonenberg, use a new tool to ask which RNAs in human cells are truly read into protein. They scan data that tracks ribosomes, the cell's protein-making machines, as they sit on RNA strands. Long non-coding RNAs and pseudogene RNAs were long thought to be skipped by ribosomes.

The data say else. About 40 percent of these RNAs are in fact read. So are stretches before the main gene in about 35 percent of genes, and past it in 4 percent. Most of the small proteins made this way are likely short-lived waste. But a share look kept by evolution across species, and some may do real work.
europmc-pmc4786676:
Defang Li leads a broad author team in Nature Communications in 2016 on a signal that slows bone building. Bone stays in balance because the cells that eat bone and the cells that build it talk to each other. The team found the eater cells send a brake signal: a small RNA, miR-214-3p, packed into tiny parcels they shed.

The signal ran high in older women with fractures and in mice stripped of estrogen, in step with low bone building. Mice bred to make extra signal in eater cells built less bone, and a targeted blocker restored it. In dishes, the parcels passed the RNA into builder cells and damped their work. Blocking the signal in aging mice raised bone formation, marking it as a drug target for bone loss.
europmc-pmc4853476:
Neil Justin and co-authors solved the crystal structure in 2016 of a human gene-silencing complex caught by a cancer-linked histone fault. The complex, PRC2, switches genes off by marking a histone spot called H3K27. In some childhood brain cancers, that histone carries a change, K27M, and the mark fades across the cell. How one faulty copy could stall the whole complex was unclear.

The structure shows the faulty piece lodged in the complex's working pocket, sitting where the normal target amino acid should fit. Binding tests back a trap model: the faulty histone jams the machine. That grip explains the wide loss of silencing marks and suggests where a drug might free the complex.
europmc-pmc4880076:
Ho Namkoong and co-authors updated the count of lung disease from nontuberculous mycobacteria in Japan in a 2016 letter in Emerging Infectious Diseases. These germs are kin to the tuberculosis germ but spread from the environment, not between people. The last survey put new cases at 5.7 per 100,000 people in 2007. The team surveyed all 884 certified respiratory hospitals in Japan on new cases in early 2014.

Rates had climbed sharply, and the disease may now outpace tuberculosis in Japan, among the highest rates worldwide. Two species groups drove the rise, while a third stayed flat. Aging, better scans, and wider awareness may all play a part. A lifelong, incurable infection at this scale is a major public concern.
europmc-pmc4891876:
Laura Perna and co-authors reported in Clinical Epigenetics in 2016 that a DNA-based age clock foresaw death in a German cohort. The clock reads chemical marks on DNA in blood to estimate body age. When that estimate runs ahead of calendar age, called age acceleration, health may be failing. Marks were read in 1,863 older people under a case-cohort design.

Faster clock age predicted higher death rates from cancer, heart and vessel disease, and all causes together. Two clock versions, Horvath's and Hannum's, both held up. The gap between DNA age and real age thus works as a broad risk sign in older adults. Such a blood sign could flag hidden wear before disease declares itself.
europmc-pmc4945876:
Hai-Long Qian, Cheng-Xiong Yang, and Xiu-Ping Yan grow chiral covalent organic frameworks and use them to sort mirror image molecules. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. Covalent organic frameworks are porous crystals built only from organic parts. Chiral versions, which favor one handedness over its mirror twin, could sort drug like molecules, but few existed and they were hard to make. The team built the handedness into one building block from the start.

They then grew the chiral framework inside thin capillary tubes in place. The coated tubes served as columns for gas chromatography, a method that separates gases. The columns split pairs of enantiomers, mirror image forms of the same molecule, with high resolution. Results repeated well from run to run and column to column. The authors offer the bottom up route as a general platform for chiral frameworks and their use in separation science.
europmc-pmc5029576:
Ö. Tunçalp and eleven co-authors set out a World Health Organization vision for care in pregnancy and birth, published in BJOG in 2015. Deaths of mothers and newborns had fallen under the Millennium Development Goals, but the numbers stayed unacceptably high. More births were now taking place in health facilities. Skilled attendance in developing countries rose from 56 percent in 1990 to 68 percent in 2012, which moved the problem of poor care inside facility walls.

The authors argue that counting visits and procedures is not enough; the quality of what happens in the room decides outcomes. Quality spans buildings, supplies, staffing, skilled and respectful treatment, and fast action when complications strike. Their vision is that every pregnant woman and newborn receives quality care through pregnancy, birth, and the days after. The piece ties that vision to two global action plans and calls for research on the gaps that remain.
europmc-pmc5030376:
I. De Kouchkovsky and M. Abdul-Hay review acute myeloid leukemia in the Blood Cancer Journal in 2016. This cancer of immature white blood cells is the most common acute leukemia in adults, with over 20,000 new cases a year in the United States alone. Gene faults stall blood cell growth at an early stage, and the stuck cells crowd out healthy blood.

The review sorts patients into favorable, middle, and adverse risk groups by their chromosome patterns, refined by single-gene faults such as FLT3-ITD, NPM1, and CEBPA. Standard care still rests on two drug families plus stem cell transplant for those who can take it, but older patients, who make up most cases, often cannot and fare poorly. New targeted drugs offer gentler, more precise attacks, though the disease's variety means no single drug will serve all. Better gene profiling, the authors argue, is the path to steady gains.
europmc-pmc5040976:
Flora Guerra and Cecilia Bucci review the small GTPase Rab7 in Cells in 2016. Rab7 is a molecular switch that steers cargo inside cells toward late endosomes and lysosomes, the compartments where material is broken down. Its work in that delivery pathway was already well mapped. The review gathers the many further jobs that study of its partner proteins has revealed.

Rab7 helps build and position lysosomes, routes signaling receptors to their destruction, and so shapes how long signals last. It also serves in autophagy, the cell's self-eating cleanup, and holds special roles in neurons. Faults in Rab7 are tied to the nerve disease Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 2B, and its levels matter in cancer. The authors argue that tuning Rab7 could one day help counter such diseases, though the fine detail of its wider actions is still being worked out.
europmc-pmc5052976:
Charlotte Beaudart and a large working group of co-authors give practical guidance on sarcopenia in BMC Geriatrics in 2016. Sarcopenia is the age-linked loss of muscle mass, strength, and performance, and it raises the risk of falls, fractures, frailty, and death. Lab-grade tools measure it well but fit poorly into busy clinics. The group, drawn from a European osteoporosis and osteoarthritis society, reviewed the literature and met to agree on workable methods.

They suggest cheap, quick checks for people at risk, including a red-flag review, the short SARC-F questionnaire, and simple prediction formulas. Care should center on the patient, pairing resistance and endurance exercise programs, with diet support where needed. Drugs are in development but not yet standard. The paper urges primary care in particular to screen people whose symptoms or conditions put them at risk, since early action can slow the slide into disability.
europmc-pmc5093776:
Hengyun Lu, Francesca Giordano, and Zemin Ning reviewed a pocket-sized DNA sequencer in Genomics, Proteomics and Bioinformatics in 2016. The MinION, released in 2014 by Oxford Nanopore Technologies, reads DNA by sensing shifts in electric current as strands pass through a tiny pore. The review weighs what such long-read machines mean for putting genomes together.

Short-read machines are cheap but stumble over long repeated stretches, leaving assemblies broken into pieces. Long reads can span those repeats, though they carry more errors per base. Lu and co-authors describe how the MinION's low cost, speed, and small size suit field work such as tracking outbreaks where labs are scarce. They set its promise beside Pacific Biosciences machines as third-generation sequencing moves toward human-sized genomes.
europmc-pmc5096676:
David A. Van Valen and ten co-authors reported a methods study in PLoS Computational Biology in 2016. Live-cell imaging tracks living cells over time, but first someone must outline each cell in every frame, a slow manual job called segmentation. The team tested whether deep learning networks could do that outlining on their own.

Their networks outlined glowing cell nuclei and, from plain phase-contrast images, the bodies of single bacterial and mammalian cells without any added dye. They could also sort apart different mammalian cell types growing together in one dish. Measured against older methods, the networks were more accurate and cut the hand-checking time sharply. The authors share design rules from building the system, arguing the approach can widen live-cell imaging to mixed cell cultures.
europmc-pmc5143676:
Elizabeth A. Miller, DeAnna E. Beasley, Robert R. Dunn, and Elizabeth A. Archie asked why the human vaginal microbiome is unusual, writing in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2016. In women, Lactobacillus bacteria dominate and make the vagina acidic, which is thought to block infections. In other mammals these bacteria rarely exceed one percent of the community.

Comparing data across 26 mammal species, they found vaginal acidity peaks with estrogen in all species, yet never reaches human levels elsewhere; human samples center near pH 4.5 against 5.4 to 7.8 for other mammals. Measures of disease risk and birth injury risk did not explain the gap. The authors float alternatives, including the idea that starch-rich farm-based diets raised sugar stores in the vaginal tract and fed the bacteria's rise.
europmc-pmc5187776:
Eneko Axpe and Michelle L. Oyen reviewed alginate inks for 3D bioprinting in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2016, with Hermann Ehrlich also named in the text's byline. Bioprinting lays down living building blocks layer by layer to fabricate tissue, and few materials meet a bioink's demands; alginate, a seaweed sugar, is the commonest choice.

The review weighs alginate's advantages and drawbacks and sums up recent work printing blood vessel tissue, bone, and cartilage with it. It also covers tricks to improve the material, such as blending and chemical tweaks that adjust stiffness and breakdown rate. The authors aim to spur new alginate ink recipes for research, drug screening, and regenerative medicine.
europmc-pmc5226976:
Eiko I. Fried, Claudia D. van Borkulo, Angélique O. J. Cramer, Lynn Boschloo, Robert A. Schoevers, and Denny Borsboom reviewed the network view of mental disorders in Social Psychiatry and Psychiatric Epidemiology in 2017. That view treats a disorder not as one hidden cause but as a web of symptoms that trigger and sustain each other. The field began in 2008 and grew fast after 2010.

The review covers network studies from 2010 to 2016 under three themes. For comorbidity, networks help explain why some disorders co-occur so often. For prediction, symptom webs of ill people look measurably different from those of healthy people, and healthy webs may show early warning signals before a shift into illness. For treatment, the most studied idea is centrality: symptoms at the web's hub may be the best targets. The authors see study of single patients' networks as a path toward personal care.
europmc-pmc5320276:
A. J. C. Hamilton, a surgical tutor at the Royal Infirmary in Edinburgh, reported a rare hernia case in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1926. An intersigmoid hernia slips into a funnel-shaped pocket of belly lining at the root of the sigmoid colon. Its rarity and its odd signs made a clear case worth putting on record.

The patient was a woman of forty-three who also had a swollen aorta. Six weeks before surgery she began to have attacks of cramp-like belly pain with trapped wind. Each attack lasted days, kept her awake, and ended in vomiting. In the last and worst attack, her bowels stopped passing anything at all. Hamilton gives the exam findings and the operation in full. He then weighs how the pocket forms, with views from past writers on the pull of the aging colon on the belly lining.
europmc-pmc5321676:
Arata Takeuchi and Takashi Saito reviewed a lesser known group of immune cells in Frontiers in Immunology in 2017. Most CD4 T cells help other cells rather than kill. A subset, called CD4 CTL, breaks that rule. These cells carry the killing tools granzyme B and perforin, and they kill target cells that show the right class of marker.

Once dismissed as a quirk of long lab culture, such cells are now found in living bodies. They help fight viruses and tumors, and they also feed harmful swelling in some tissues. Their growth path is still murky. They sit close to the Th1 helper type, and two switch proteins seem to guide them. The authors found a surface marker that flags cells with the power to become CD4 CTL, even among fresh naive T cells. They close with a model of how these killers arise.
europmc-pmc533876:
Mahmood Saghaei built a free program for fair trial grouping in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2004. Trials that run groups side by side must assign people to groups by chance. Good software for that step should let users shape the blocks, the ID codes, and the output form. No tool at the time joined all of those controls in one package.

His Random Allocation Software does. Users can pick plain or blocked chance plans, set how ID codes look and run, and name more than two groups as they wish. Output can be shaped to suit the team's needs, and a session can be saved for later use. A list from the program can go straight to the trial coordinator, ready to label drugs or tools for each group. The paper walks through the settings and how a team would use them.
europmc-pmc5340776:
Kathrin Renner and co-authors reviewed fuel use by tumor and immune cells in Frontiers in Immunology in 2017. Killer T cells and NK cells hunt tumor cells, and their counts in a tumor track a patient's outlook. New immune drugs build on that hunt. Yet most tumors still escape, and fuel use is part of the reason.

Both tumor cells and woken killer cells crave sugar and protein parts to grow and work. Side by side in one tumor, they fight for the same fuel. Tumors also flood the space with waste, such as lactate, that dulls immune attack. Other tumor-linked cells strip key protein parts from the area, which starves the hunters. The review maps this shared fuel web and asks if tumor fuel paths can serve as drug targets to free the immune response.
europmc-pmc5340976:
Tom Smith, Andreas Heger, and Ian Sudbery improved counting in gene reading in Genome Research in 2017. Many tests tag each starting molecule with a random barcode, called a UMI, before copying it many times. The tags let labs tell true copies from mere echoes of the copy step. But the tags are read with errors, and past tools fixed those errors by rough rule or not at all.

The team showed tag errors are common, then built network methods that group tags by likely shared roots. In fake data and in real sets from single-cell and binding studies, the network fix gave truer counts. Repeat runs agreed better, and cell groups in single-cell data sorted more cleanly. The methods ship in a free package called UMI-tools, ready for wide use in reading labs.
europmc-pmc5405076:
Marco Corazzari, Mara Gagliardi, Gian Maria Fimia, and Mauro Piacentini review cell stress and cancer fate in a 2017 paper in Frontiers in Oncology. The endoplasmic reticulum is the cell's workshop for folding proteins. When folding goes wrong, the cell mounts a rescue program that tries to restore order. Tumors often live under exactly such strain, from low oxygen, low fuel, and fast, sloppy growth.

Parts of the rescue program run off track in many tumor types and help cancers start, grow, and resist drugs. Yet if the strain runs too long or too hard, the same program can order the cell to die. The review tracks how that life-or-death switch is set. The authors say learning its rules could help drugs kill tumor cells and beat resistance.
europmc-pmc5407976:
Louise M. Burke leads a large author group in a 2017 study in the Journal of Physiology on diet and race walking. Elite endurance athletes sometimes switch to a ketogenic diet, very low in carbohydrate and high in fat, hoping to burn more fat. The team put world-class race walkers through three weeks of hard training on one of three diets with equal energy: high carbohydrate, timed carbohydrate, or the ketogenic plan.

Peak aerobic power rose in all groups after training. The ketogenic group burned fat at far higher rates, as hoped. But that diet also raised the oxygen cost of walking at race pace, wiping out the gain from training, while the high carbohydrate group raced better. The authors warn that fat adaptation can cost top athletes real performance.
europmc-pmc5408676:
Evelien M. Adriaenssens and J. Rodney Brister offer an informal guide to naming and classing phages in a 2017 paper in Viruses. Phages are viruses that infect bacteria. After a new phage is found and read, its finder must give it a sound name. The finder must also fit it into the official virus family tree, run by an international virus taxonomy body. A poor name can stick in databases and official lists for years.

The guide walks the finder from a single isolate upward: what to check, what to send in, and how the expert groups judge each case. Virus classing has moved from shape and gene content toward full genome reading, and the guide reflects that shift. It aims to spare both new and seasoned phage workers the common traps in this stage of the work.
europmc-pmc545776:
Honys and Twell chart gene expression across pollen development in Arabidopsis. Their transcriptome study appeared in Genome Biology. The male gametophyte is a stripped-down lineage. Two or three cells make up a pollen grain. It delivers two sperm cells at fertilization. No genome-wide view of its development existed. Earlier tools covered only part of the picture. Low RNA yields forced biased amplification steps.

The authors built isolation methods for precise stages. They sampled from unicellular microspores onward. Mature pollen grains closed the series. Developing grains sit isolated from parent tissue. That isolation yields clean cell populations. Expression profiling then ran stage by stage. Distinct temporal classes of genes emerged. Some switched on early, others late. The dataset opens the regulatory wiring to study. Pollen ontogeny becomes a tractable development model.
europmc-pmc5488176:
Růžička and co-authors report a plant study in The New Phytologist. It hunts for the proteins that place m6A marks on messenger RNA. This mark is the most common internal edit in such RNA. It shapes growth in plants and animals alike. Yet the full writer team in plants was unclear.

Using genetics, proteomics, and RNA tests in Arabidopsis, they find a core writer set. The set holds MTA, MTB, FIP37, VIRILIZER, and the ligase HAKAI. Lowering any of them cut m6A levels, they report. The plants also shared growth faults, such as odd root vessels. HAKAI's role was new and is conserved across species.
europmc-pmc5532176:
Zárate and co-authors present a review in Clinical and Translational Medicine on long-chain omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids. These fats, named EPA, DHA, and ARA, build cell membranes and spawn signal molecules. New lipid-profiling tools have revived interest in their health roles. Western diets tilt the omega-6 to omega-3 balance far upward. Cancer tissue shows that same tilt in reverse form.

Higher omega-3 intake links to lower risk of several cancers, they report. A ratio near 2 to 4 to 1 looks protective. Omega-3 fats also guard the heart and feed the brain. DHA dominates the cortex's omega-3 supply. Advice still needs tailoring by age and condition.
europmc-pmc5555476:
Hart and co-authors present a methods study on CRISPR knockout screens. Such screens switch off genes across the whole genome in human cells. They show which genes cells need to stay alive. Results vary a lot with library design and protocol, though.

The team reanalyzed 17 genome-scale screens from three research groups. Their work expanded the set of human core essential genes from 360 to 684. They also studied what makes a guide RNA work well. From those lessons they built an optimized library, Toronto KnockOut version 3. That library performed strongly in fresh screens. Readers get both a reference gene set and a better tool for cell studies.
europmc-pmc5754376:
Olechnowicz and co-authors review how zinc status ties to inflammation and metabolism. Zinc helps regulate cytokine signals and damps inflammation. It is also needed to switch on antioxidant enzymes. Those enzymes clear reactive oxygen that harms cells.

Zinc also shapes lipid and glucose handling, including insulin work. Added zinc has improved blood pressure, glucose, and LDL cholesterol in studies. Low zinc shows up in metabolic syndrome, diabetes, and high blood pressure. Yet some studies link high zinc to worse lipid profiles. The authors call for deeper work on zinc as a predictor of metabolic trouble.
europmc-pmc5787076:
Tracey and co-authors review lipid metabolism in neurons, with a focus on ALS. Lipids serve neurons as fuel, as building blocks, and as signals. The brain holds the body's second highest store of them. In ALS, faults in lipid handling may help drive the disease.

The review sorts the five lipid classes and their roles in nerve cells. It links aberrant lipid paths to nerve ending loss, energy failure, and inflammation. Other links run to transport faults and reduced signal release. Tuning these paths may open fresh treatment options for ALS, the authors suggest.
europmc-pmc5789076:
Wu and co-authors solve how a human RNA binding protein, hnRNP A2/B1, grips its RNA targets. The protein helps mature, move, and process RNA messages. It carries two grip domains, each reading short letter motifs. The team froze both domains with several RNA pieces and solved the structures.

Each domain reads its own motif, they show. AGG goes to the first domain and UAG to the second. Further tests reveal shifting grip modes for varied sequences. The pattern supports a matchmaker model of the protein's work. A marked RNA may act through a switch, not direct reading.
europmc-pmc5795276:
Sekine and Youle review how the protein PINK1 senses mitochondrial stress. PINK1 and its partner Parkin drive the cleanup of damaged mitochondria. Faults in this path may underlie some inherited Parkinson disease. PINK1 switches on only on damaged units, which raised the question of how it knows.

The switch rests on controlled import, the authors explain. Healthy mitochondria pull PINK1 inside and cut it down. Damaged ones stall the import, so PINK1 piles up on the surface and calls Parkin. The review details each compartment step. It also weighs drug ideas to fire this path on purpose.
europmc-pmc5812476:
