Zahran and co-authors track childhood asthma in the United States. Asthma is the most common long-term lung disease of childhood. About 6 million children live with it. The CDC team studied survey data from 2001 to 2016.

Rates rose to 9.4 percent in 2010, then fell to 8.3 percent. Boys and Black children had higher rates than girls and white children. Puerto Rican children also faced high rates. Poor families saw more asthma than rich ones. Attacks grew less common over the period. Young children still landed in emergency care most often. Readers get the trends and the gaps that remain.
europmc-pmc5871676:
Skaper and co-authors review neuroinflammation as a driver of brain disease. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience. Short inflammation helps heal injury and fight infection. When it drags on, it can damage tissue instead. In the nervous system, long inflammation feeds many disorders. These range from Alzheimer disease to depression and autism. Immune signals from non-neuronal cells sit at the centre.

Microglia and mast cells are key sources, the authors say. Astrocytes and other glia also take part. Talks between mast cells and glia can start and prolong flares. The mast cell holds a key niche in that process. The review ends with therapy ideas drawn from cells' own controls.
europmc-pmc5876976:
Raghupathi and Raghupathi chart chronic diseases across the United States. Their study appeared in an environmental and public health journal. They used data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Visual and descriptive analytics guided the work. Variables fell into five groups, from disease states to behaviour. Mental health and demographics were also included.

The team compared regions and states for shared patterns. Disease rates varied widely from state to state. Hospital stays, diagnoses, and deaths also differed sharply. About 45 percent of Americans live with a chronic disease. Such diseases drive most national health spending. The authors say spotting links can guide targeted policy. Prevention and management can then focus where need is greatest.
europmc-pmc5895776:
Albini and co-authors review how innate immune cells feed tumour blood vessel growth. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. New vessels are vital for tumours to grow and spread. Tumours vary widely in vessel growth and drug response. Immune cells inside the tumour help drive that growth. They release chemokines, cytokines, and enzymes that build vessels. VEGF is both a vessel factor and an immune modulator.

The review works through each major cell player. Macrophages, neutrophils, and mast cells all feature. Natural killer and dendritic cells get chapters too. Blocking VEGF could shift the setting toward immune attack. The authors propose pairing such drugs with checkpoint inhibitors.
europmc-pmc5910376:
Protopopoff and co-authors tested new malaria nets and indoor spraying in Tanzania. Their trial appeared in The Lancet. Mosquitoes there resist standard pyrethroid sprays. One net type added piperonyl butoxide, a booster chemical. Spraying used a long-lasting non-pyrethroid drug. Forty-eight village clusters were split into four groups.

Both new tools cut malaria in children, they report. At nine months, booster nets lowered infection versus standard nets. Spraying lowered it too, by a similar scale. Using both together added no extra gain. The booster net effect still held at 21 months. Either tool alone could be deployed well, they conclude.
europmc-pmc5944976:
Burns and Kakara track deaths from falls among older adults in the United States. Their report appeared in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. It covers the years 2007 to 2016. Falls are the largest share of injury deaths in this age group. About one in four older adults reports a fall each year. The authors used death certificate data from all states.

Deaths rose from 18,334 in 2007 to 29,668 in 2016, they report. The age-adjusted rate grew by about 3.0 percent per year. Rates rose in 30 states and the District of Columbia. The steepest yearly rise hit people aged 85 and older. The authors urge providers to discuss fall prevention at wellness visits.
europmc-pmc5963076:
Rangaraju and co-authors identify a pro-inflammatory subset of disease-associated microglia in Alzheimer's disease. Their study appeared in Molecular Neurodegeneration. Disease-associated microglia show a distinct gene profile in neurodegeneration. Their meaning for Alzheimer's was unclear. The team applied network analysis to microglial gene data from mouse models. Flow cytometry then checked the predicted cell groups.

The analysis split these microglia into pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory types, they report. The pro-inflammatory group arose earlier in Alzheimer's mouse models. It carried markers such as CD44 and the Kv1.3 channel. Two drug strategies shifted cells toward the calmer state in tests. One used LXR agonism, the other blocked Kv1.3.
europmc-pmc5992476:
Francisco and co-authors review obesity, fat mass, and the immune system, with leptin at the centre. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Physiology. Obesity brings chronic low-grade inflammation and faulty fat tissue. Fat is now seen as an active endocrine organ. It secretes hormone-like adipokines that bridge metabolism and immunity. Leptin is one of the most important of these signals. Its receptor is found across the immune system.

Leptin shapes both innate and adaptive immune responses, the authors explain. The review covers its part in metabolic disorders tied to obesity. Autoimmune and inflammatory rheumatic diseases also feature. Leptin anchors the young field of immunometabolism.
europmc-pmc6061876:
Hemani and co-authors examine pleiotropy in Mendelian randomization studies. Their review appeared in Human Molecular Genetics. The method uses genetic variants to test cause and effect. It treats nature's gene shuffle like a randomized trial. Pleiotropy means one variant touches several traits.

One form of pleiotropy is harmless to the method. The variant acts through the trait under study. The other form breaks the core assumption. It reaches the outcome by a separate path. New methods can flag and correct much of that bias. Used together, they make results more trustworthy. Readers get a guide to safer causal claims from genome data.
europmc-pmc6115776:
Khomich and co-authors wrote a review in Viruses on redox changes during respiratory virus infections. These viruses cause the common cold and, at times, severe lung illness. Infection shifts the balance of reactive oxygen species in cells. That shift is tied to inflammation and tissue damage.

The review sums up what is known for flu, RSV, rhinovirus, and kin. It covers how each virus stirs up oxidative stress. It also covers how cells try to fight back. Young, old, and weak patients face the highest risk. The authors say this knowledge can guide diagnosis and new treatments.
europmc-pmc6123676:
Salami and co-authors present a research article in Communications Biology on a new way to attack prostate cancer. The androgen receptor drives this cancer. Drugs like enzalutamide block it, but most patients grow resistant in time. The team tested a degrader called ARCC-4 instead.

ARCC-4 tags the receptor for destruction by the cell. It wiped out about 95 percent of receptors in lab models. It also broke down mutant receptors seen in patients. Unlike enzalutamide, it kept working when androgen levels were high. The authors say degrading the receptor may beat merely blocking it.
europmc-pmc6152076:
Lee and Kim wrote a review in Molecules on blocking the p38 MAPK enzyme as a way to treat Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's is marked by amyloid plaques and tau tangles in the brain, plus steady loss of neurons. There is still no cure. The enzyme p38 MAPK is a known target in long-term inflammatory diseases.

Studies in cells and animals link p38 MAPK to key steps in the disease. These include tau phosphorylation, nerve cell toxicity, brain inflammation, and failing synapses. The review sums up recent work on drugs that block this enzyme. The authors weigh its promise as a core treatment strategy. Readers see both the biology and the drug hunt in one place.
europmc-pmc6189176:
Young and co-authors present a methods article in Nature Communications on a machine-learning tool for untangling brain diseases. Neurodegenerative diseases vary widely between patients. Study groups mix different forms on different trajectories, which confuses research and drug trials. Standard studies capture each patient at just one time point.

The tool, called SuStaIn, infers both subtype and stage from such cross-sectional data. Applied to imaging in genetic frontotemporal dementia, it found subgroups with distinct patterns of brain shrinkage. It could even identify the genetic type from imaging alone. Work in Alzheimer's disease data showed the same skill. The method promises cleaner groups for trials and for tracking disease over time.
europmc-pmc6209676:
Stebegg and co-authors review how germinal centres are controlled. Germinal centres form in lymphoid tissues after infection or vaccination. Inside them, B cells mutate their receptor genes. The best mutants become plasma cells and memory cells. The review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology.

That mutation process is risky. It can create B cells that attack the body itself. Many cell types work together to prevent that. Stromal cells guide antigen flow and cell traffic. Helper T cells give B cells key support. Regulatory T cells keep the response in check. The authors outline new findings on each cell type. They explain how strong protection and self-tolerance are both kept.
europmc-pmc6245676:
Rajpurkar and co-authors tested a deep learning program on chest X-rays against working radiologists. Their study appeared in PLOS Medicine. The program is called CheXNeXt. It reads frontal chest images and flags fourteen diseases at once. Targets include pneumonia, fluid on the lung, masses, and nodules. The team trained it on a large public image set.

Testing used 420 held back images, each checked by a panel of three chest specialists. Nine radiologists also read the same images. The authors report that the program matched radiologist level results on eleven diseases. It fell short on three, where radiologists scored higher. Chest reading is slow work, and experts are scarce in many regions. Tools that match experts on most targets could ease that load.
europmc-pmc6366976:
Lu and co-authors present a research article in Aging on a DNA methylation clock called GrimAge. Earlier clocks estimate age from methylation marks alone. This team first built methylation-based stand-ins for seven plasma proteins and for smoking pack-years, then combined them into one lifespan predictor.

Validated in thousands of people, GrimAge predicted time to death better than existing epigenetic clocks. It also tracked heart disease, cancer, fatty liver, and comorbidity counts. Its age-adjusted form linked to many age-related conditions and to lifestyle factors like diet and education. The authors expect the biomarker to serve anti-aging studies and risk assessment.
europmc-pmc6367276:
Stankovic and co-authors map immune cells in human lung cancer, writing in Frontiers in Immunology. Non-small cell lung cancer is the top cause of cancer death worldwide. Knowing which immune cells sit inside a tumor may predict how a patient will do.

Using flow cytometry, the team sorted immune cells from tumors, lung tissue, lymph nodes, and blood. They named thirteen cell types, covering almost all immune cells found. T cells made up about forty-seven percent of immune cells in tumors. CD4 T cells were the largest group. The map gives a base for judging immune therapy responses.
europmc-pmc6375876:
Stein and Granot present a review in Frontiers in Plant Science on sucrose synthases in plants. These enzymes split sucrose, the main sugar moved through plant veins, into fructose and activated glucose forms. The products feed energy use, starch building, and cell wall synthesis in growing tissues.

Plant gene families for the enzyme are small, with four to seven genes in three ancient groups. Plants with reduced enzyme activity grow poorly and make less starch and cellulose. Plants with extra activity grow larger with more wood and wall material. The review also covers new roles in shoot meristems and sugar signaling. The authors flag the genes as crop improvement targets.
europmc-pmc6393476:
Angelidis and co-authors present an atlas of the aging lung in Nature Communications. Aging lungs lose function and face more chronic disease. The team mapped that change cell by cell in young and old mice.

Single-cell RNA reads covered thirty lung cell types. Protein measures from deep tissue samples ran alongside. Aging raised noise in gene activity, a sign of loose gene control. Fat-making paths rose in some support cells, and airway cell mixes shifted. Protein data showed the lung's outer scaffold being rebuilt. The atlas gives lung aging research a shared reference map.
europmc-pmc6400876:
Ong and co-authors review the prefrontal cortex in pain, in Molecular Neurobiology. This front brain region is known for planning and control. It also helps process pain, through links to many other brain areas.

During lasting pain, the region changes in signals, genes, and cell activity. Its structure and links to other areas shift as well. One part of it can also damp pain, through a deep brain relay. That dual role makes the region both part of the problem and a possible fix. The review maps these circuits in detail.
europmc-pmc6411676:
Oleszkiewicz and co-authors update smell test reference values in the European Archives of Oto-Rhino-Laryngology. The Sniffin' Sticks test checks smell threshold, discrimination, and naming. Doctors compare a patient's score with norms from healthy people.

Past norms rested on small samples, above all for older people. The new norms draw on 9,139 healthy subjects aged five to ninety-six. People aged twenty to thirty scored best, the data show. Children under ten and adults over seventy-one scored about half as well. A score below 30.75 marks reduced smell in their scale.
europmc-pmc6421076:
Matthews and co-authors report a mosquito genome study in Nature. Female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes infect over 400 million people a year with dengue, Zika, yellow fever, and chikungunya. A poor genome map had slowed work on this pest.

Joining several sequencing methods, the team built a far better genome, called AaegL5. The map doubled known smell and taste receptors that guide mosquitoes to hosts. It also clarified the sex-determining region and copy changes in key genes. The authors offer the genome as a base for vector control tools. It is freely shared.
europmc-pmc6424576:
Schmidt and co-authors test whether mouth microbes commonly travel down and settle in the gut, using strain-level data from 470 people in five countries. Textbooks long treated such movement as rare and as a sign of disease. The group compared saliva and fecal samples across 310 microbial species to track shared strains.

Most oral species turned out to be transferable, and healthy people carried many gut strains that matched their own mouths. Transmission ran higher in colorectal cancer and rheumatoid arthritis patients, and in species known as opportunistic pathogens. The mouth thus acts as a steady internal source of gut microbes, shaping the digestive microbiome in health and illness.
europmc-pmc6432076:
Rizwan and co-authors review pH-sensitive hydrogels, water-swollen polymer networks that release drugs where acidity suits the payload. Many medicines dissolve poorly, break down in stomach acid, or absorb unevenly along the gut. A gel that stays shut in the stomach and opens in the intestine can protect a drug and target its release.

The history of hydrogels runs from 1894 colloidal gels to modern cross-linked networks. Sections explain how ionizable side groups make a gel swell or shrink as pH changes, and how pKa values guide material choice. Worked examples show release kept negligible in simulated stomach fluid yet maximal at intestinal pH.
europmc-pmc6441076:
Zou and co-authors put numbers on the triboelectric series, the ranking of how strongly materials gain or lose electrons when rubbed together. Static electricity from contact is universal, yet the series existed only as a qualitative list with no standard measurement. Energy harvesters and self-powered sensors need real values to design against.

Their method touches each test polymer against liquid metal under tightly fixed conditions and records transferred charge as a normalized density. Applied across a wide range of polymers, the scale exposes each material's intrinsic tendency to donate or accept electrons. The authors offer the quantitative series as a textbook standard for the field.
europmc-pmc6447676:
Bloom and Cadarette assess whether today's global health system can handle the infectious disease threats of this century, from Ebola, Zika, and MERS to rising drug resistance. The system is a patchwork of formal and informal networks across governments, charities, and industry, each with its own goals and no single line of answerability. Recent outbreaks exposed the seams.

More people in regions with weak systems, growing cities, a shifting climate, and closer animal-human spread all raise the pressure. Lab accidents or planned attacks add a human-made edge. The authors propose a standing Global Technical Council on Infectious Disease Threats, staffed across fields, to align watch systems, research, funding, and supply chains before the next emergency hits.
europmc-pmc6480976:
Allen and co-authors introduce raincloud plots, a chart design meant to end the quiet dishonesty of bar graphs with error bars. Bars hide distributions, bury outliers, and lean on assumptions the reader cannot check, all while looking authoritative. A raincloud instead shows the raw points, a density curve, and a summary box together, inference at a glance without the concealment.

The tutorial walks through building the plots in R, Python, and Matlab, with open code and interactive notebooks readers can run in a browser. Variants for repeated measures and different data shapes are demonstrated. The aim is minimal redundancy: every mark on the page earns its place statistically.
europmc-pmc6481276:
Zhao and co-authors follow melatonin across deep time, from its probable debut as a free radical scavenger in bacteria some 3.0 to 2.5 billion years ago. When early eukaryotes swallowed melatonin-making bacteria, the guests stayed on as mitochondria and chloroplasts and kept producing it, which is why the molecule turns up nearly everywhere life is tested.

Receptor-based jobs arrived later: sleep and circadian timing, immune support, and anti-cancer effects in animals; germination, growth, and stress resistance in plants, where a single known receptor also closes leaf stomata. Synthesis routes diverge slightly between kingdoms but always start from tryptophan. The review assembles the molecule's full evolutionary résumé.
europmc-pmc6566176:
Lee, Harris, Khanna and Hong review the state of peptide drug development, writing in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Peptides sit between small molecules and antibodies. Small drugs slip into cells but cannot grip the flat surfaces where proteins meet. Antibodies grip well but cannot cross cell walls. Peptides promise both reach and grip.

Over 60 peptide drugs are already approved, with hundreds more in trials, from insulin onward. The review covers the core craft: protecting peptide ends from breakdown, stiffening shapes through cycles, and sneaking cargo across membranes. Its second half turns to computation, comparing docking methods that predict how a peptide will sit on its protein target — the planning step behind rational design.
europmc-pmc6629176:
Huang and co-authors show that silencing one circular RNA helps injured mouse hearts regrow. Their research article appears in Circulation. Adult heart muscle barely replaces cells lost in a heart attack. Circular RNAs are stable rings that can steer gene networks. The team hunted for one that gates regeneration.

Superenhancer maps flagged circNfix, a ring enriched in adult heart muscle. The factor Meis1 drives its production through that enhancer. Lowering circNfix freed the protein Ybx1 from destruction. It also rescued the microRNA miR-214. Treated mice grew new heart muscle cells and new vessels. Scar area shrank after infarction, and heart function recovered better. The authors name circNfix a fresh target for repair therapy.
europmc-pmc6659376:
Bowden and co-authors improve the weighting used in two-sample Mendelian randomization. Their methods paper appears in the International Journal of Epidemiology. The technique pools causal estimates from many genetic variants. Each variant's ratio estimate needs an inverse-variance weight. Standard first-order weights can fake heterogeneity that is not there. Second-order weights can hide heterogeneity that is real. Both flaws trace to the NOME assumption. The team derives modified weights to fix them.

Monte Carlo simulations favoured the new weights. They quantified heterogeneity more accurately than either rival. They also removed regression dilution bias from weak instruments. That gain costs some precision with few weak instruments. An example revisits blood pressure and heart disease. The authors recommend pairing the schemes in practice.
europmc-pmc6669976:
Chen and Zhao review next-generation sequencing in liquid biopsy for cancer screening. Their article appears in Human Genomics. Tumours shed DNA fragments into the blood. Sequencing that circulating tumour DNA profiles the cancer. The approach is noninvasive and repeatable. Its greatest promise lies in early detection. Catching cancer early improves survival and lowers burden. Modern methods detect extremely rare mutations. Population screening still poses hard problems, though.

Healthy people carry only tiny ctDNA amounts. Normal blood cells add look-alike DNA noise. False positives rise as a result. The review covers methylation and mutation strategies together. It summarises recent progress and open challenges. Future directions for real-world screening close the piece.
europmc-pmc6701376: Designing health programs is harder than it looks - good intentions flop without method. This guidance distills a consensus exercise into principles and actions for building complex interventions. Researchers get a practical checklist for the messy work between idea and trial.
europmc-pmc6724476:
Kim and co-authors review plasmonic photothermal nanoparticles for medical use. These metal particles respond strongly to light and turn it into heat. The heat output can be tuned and switched by an outside light source. Most medical work so far has used them to cook tumors, a method called photothermal therapy.

The report argues that sensing, imaging, and drug delivery deserve equal attention. Heated particles can boost test signals far beyond standard methods. One test gained a 100-fold better detection limit than a common rapid test. The authors map the basic physics that still needs control. They close with directions for therapy that pairs diagnosis and treatment.
europmc-pmc6773876:
Ulgen and co-authors present pathfindR, an R package for pathway analysis of omics data. Pathway analysis is often the first step in explaining a biological difference. Standard methods ignore how proteins interact with each other. That leaves conclusions incomplete. Earlier tools that used interaction data did better, and pathfindR joins that line.

Starting from a gene list comparing two groups, the package finds active subnetworks inside a protein interaction network. It then tests which pathways those subnetworks enrich. Results can be clustered to simplify the picture. A scoring function estimates each pathway's activity in each sample. Tests on three gene expression datasets, against three rival tools, showed results well supported by the literature.
europmc-pmc6854376:
Ma and co-authors review CAR-T cell therapy for solid tumours, in the International Journal of Biological Sciences. In this treatment, a patient's T cells are engineered to hunt cancer. Two such products, Kymriah and Yescarta, won United States approval for blood cancers. Solid tumours, which make up most cancers, have resisted the same approach.

The review explains why. Engineered cells struggle to enter solid tumours, and the tissue around them suppresses attack. Targets shared with healthy tissue add risk. Most current work tries to strengthen the cells or disarm that hostile setting. The authors also cover the diagnostic tests that travel with these therapies, a topic they find neglected.
europmc-pmc6888476:
Lim and co-authors estimate how common self-harm is among the young, in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. Suicidal behaviour, deliberate self-harm, and non-suicidal self-injury overlap but differ. Figures varied wildly between single studies. The team searched databases for work published between 1989 and 2018 and pooled the results.

The analysis covered 686,672 children and adolescents in total. Lifetime rates of suicidal thinking ran higher in non-Western countries, at 18.7 percent, than in Western ones, at 17.6 percent. Gaps were wider for suicide plans. The authors present the pooled rates as a baseline for prevention policy, while noting the wide spread behind every average.
europmc-pmc6896676:
Chen and co-authors review electrical stimulation in tissue engineering, in Biomaterials Research. Passing mild electric signals through tissue is drawing wide attention. It shows promise for wound healing and for steering cell behaviour in lab-grown tissue. Currents can switch on signalling pathways inside cells and reshape their surroundings. Migration, growth, and specialisation all respond.

The review surveys the materials and devices used to deliver stimulation safely. Conductive, body-friendly scaffolds let engineers combine a physical support with an electrical cue at once. Cells align and migrate toward one pole under a field, a trick for organising regrowth. The authors close with the gaps between striking lab results and clinical use.
europmc-pmc7017576:
Holland and co-authors present a benchmark study in Genome Biology. They test tools that infer pathway and transcription factor activity from gene data. Those tools were built for bulk samples, which mix many cells. Single-cell RNA sequencing is noisier and sparser, so it is unclear whether the tools still work there.

The team benchmarked three bulk tools against tools made for single cells. They used simulated data, real data after gene knock-outs, and a mix sequenced with 13 protocols. The bulk tools matched their bulk-level performance, the authors report. At times they beat the dedicated single-cell tools. Results depended more on the gene sets used than on the statistics. The benchmark data were released for other researchers.
europmc-pmc7212476:
Lv and Guo review the widening list of benefits claimed for metformin. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Endocrinology. Metformin has treated type 2 diabetes for over 60 years. It is a biguanide drug prized for safety and low cost. Its glucose-lowering power made it a first-line therapy worldwide.

Later research found effects far beyond blood sugar. Studies link it to lower risk in several cancers, from breast to colorectal. Obesity, liver disease, heart disease, and kidney disease also feature. Even aging itself is now discussed as a target. The drug acts through several signaling pathways. Which pathway drives which benefit is still unresolved. The review gathers the claims and the mechanisms proposed so far.
europmc-pmc7218176:
Trache and co-authors review nanocellulose, from its basic science to advanced uses. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Chemistry. Nanocellulose is plant fiber shrunk to nanoscale threads and crystals. It is abundant, renewable, and safe for living tissue. Its strength and high surface area attract materials scientists. Surface chemistry lets researchers tune it for many jobs.

The review covers how nanocellulose is made and modified. Cellulose nanocrystals receive special attention. New uses include stabilizing emulsions without soap-like chemicals. Some versions switch stability with a change in acidity. That trick opens doors in catalysis and oil recovery. Packaging, medicine, and water treatment also feature. The authors present nanocellulose as a flagship green material. Its rise rests on turning the world's most common natural polymer into high-tech forms.
europmc-pmc7364176:
Chen and co-authors review functional near-infrared spectroscopy in Frontiers in Neuroscience, a method that watches brain activity using light. Like fMRI, it tracks blood hemoglobin changes, but through optical absorption rather than magnets. Near-infrared light passes through tissue, so sensors on the scalp can read the brain beneath.

Portability is the method's great advantage, allowing bedside and long-term monitoring. Simple setups already help critical care teams track brain oxygen in stroke and head injury patients. Finer uses need better spatial and time resolution, and the authors survey current efforts toward that goal. Limits holding back wider clinical use get an honest look. Readers get a guide to a gentler brain scanner.
europmc-pmc7401976:
Haarman and co-authors pool the evidence on complications of short-sightedness in Investigative Ophthalmology and Visual Science. Myopia is common, but its risks for sight-threatening disease are often quoted loosely. Their systematic review and meta-analysis gathered studies published before June 2019 and graded risk by degree of myopia.

Every complication grew more likely as myopia deepened. For myopic macular degeneration, odds rose from about 14-fold in low myopia to a striking 845-fold in high myopia. Retinal detachment, two forms of cataract, and open angle glaucoma all climbed in step as well. The authors quantify a gradient clinicians can use: even mild short-sight carries measurable risk, and high myopia is a major eye-health burden.
europmc-pmc7449476:
Ssentongo and co-authors pool studies on prior health conditions and death from COVID-19. Knowing which conditions raise risk can guide protection for high-risk groups. The team searched major databases for work from December 2019 to July 2020.

The analysis covered 11 conditions across 25 studies. Heart and vessel disease, hypertension, and diabetes each linked with a clearly greater risk of death. Congestive heart failure, chronic kidney disease, and cancer also raised risk. Brain vessel disease, liver disease, lung disease, asthma, and HIV/AIDS were tracked as well. The authors urge tailored prevention and treatment for patients with these conditions. Such care, aimed at the highest-risk groups, might improve survival in future waves.
europmc-pmc7464276:
Snetkov and co-authors review hyaluronic acid and how its molecular weight shapes its traits. This natural long-chain sugar was first found in tissues in 1934. It is safe in the body and breaks down well, so uses are wide.

Hyaluronic acid serves in skin cosmetics, joint fluid implants, scaffolds, and wound dressings. Its healing effect depends straight on the weight of its chains. The review collects data on how weight links with structure and physical traits. It covers behavior in water solutions and how fast the polymer degrades. Short and long chains can act in opposed ways in tissue. Readers in bioengineering and medicine gain a guide for picking the right form. Weight choice, the authors stress, is a design choice.
europmc-pmc7497176:
Vollmer and co-authors review chemical recycling as a route beyond melting and re-extruding plastic waste. Only a slice of plastic gets recycled today. Chemical routes could lift that rate a lot.

The review sums up the main chemical recycling paths. It weighs them with life-cycle analysis, which tracks costs to nature end to end. A long list of company processes shows how far industry has moved. Each current process fits certain waste streams best. No single one can solve the plastic problem alone, so mixes are needed. Research should shift to dirty, mixed, real-world waste. Better collection and sorting, backed by firmer rules, must grow too. The goal is quality products fit for reuse in a circular economy.
europmc-pmc7526376:
Jiang and co-authors review the tumor microenvironment and new blood vessel growth. Tumors need angiogenesis to keep growing and spread. Nearby cells and secreted factors shape that process.

The review explains how each part of the setting acts. High levels of growth factors help vessels form. Inflammation and low oxygen also drive vessel growth. Those same traits can blunt current anti-angiogenic drugs. The authors suggest pairing vessel drugs with other agents. Options include drugs that cut inflammation or block low oxygen effects. Readers get a clear account of why vessel therapy often falls short.
europmc-pmc7545176:
Hasell and co-authors build a cross-country database of COVID-19 testing. Case and death counts need testing data for meaning. A country that tests less will find fewer cases.

The database gathers official PCR testing data over time. It covers 94 countries in its first form. Daily series show tests done or people tested. Notes flag quality and comparison issues for each series. Sources are given for each observation. The set is updated by scraping and manual checks. It aims to help studies track pandemic spread. It also tracks a key part of national response to COVID-19.
europmc-pmc7616976:
Collier and co-authors test how vaccine antibodies handle a SARS-CoV-2 variant strain in the lab. The variant had spread to fifty countries by the time of the study work. It was not clear if vaccines built on the first strain would still work.

The team studied blood responses after the BNT162b2 mRNA vaccine in volunteers. They used lab-made viruses with the wild-type spike or the variant spike form. The variant in question is the lineage first found in the United Kingdom. Vaccine blood samples neutralized that variant a bit less well than the wild type. The drop was modest across a broad range of antibody levels measured. Blood from recovered patients showed a like drop against the variant strain. Adding one more spike change, called E484K, caused a larger loss of effect. The authors flag that added change as a threat to vaccine power.
europmc-pmc7666276:
Korte and co-authors argue that reduced brain blood flow is an early driver of Alzheimer disease. Drugs aimed at late events, such as amyloid and tau clumps, have mostly failed in trials. The authors point to blood flow as the earliest sign seen on biomarkers.

Small vessels narrow when support cells called pericytes contract, likely in response to amyloid fragments. Trapped white blood cells and clots cut flow further. Low flow then boosts the enzyme that makes amyloid and drives tau change. The authors urge treatments aimed at this early step rather than at late damage alone.
europmc-pmc7681076:
Li and co-authors review how cells pick and recycle worn-out inner parts. The process is selective autophagy, in which the cell digests chosen organelles rather than bulk contents. Targets range from mitochondria and ribosomes to fat droplets and the nucleus itself. This cleanup keeps cells in balance.

The authors set out a cargo, ligand, and receptor model for how targets get chosen. They detail two cases in depth: disposal of mitochondria and of the endoplasmic reticulum. Faults in this system link to nerve diseases, cancer, and heart failure. The review ends with open questions that mark where the field should look next.
europmc-pmc7686876:
Pollard and co-authors give an overview of COVID-19 as a global health crisis. The virus, SARS-CoV-2, was first found in Wuhan, China, in December 2019. The World Health Organization declared a pandemic on March 11, 2020. Illness ranges widely with age, genes, ethnic group, and place.

Severe disease can destroy lung cells and trigger clots and vessel leaks. This can lead to acute respiratory distress and later lung scarring. Heart disease, high blood pressure, and diabetes raise risk. The virus enters cells through the ACE2 receptor and disrupts its normal work. The authors discuss vaccines and other treatments that this biology suggests.
europmc-pmc7745176:
Salari and co-authors pool studies on mental strain in front-line COVID-19 health workers. Staff who cared direct for COVID-19 patients faced long hours, risk, and grief. The team searched many databases for work from December 2019 to June 2020. They combined rates of stress, anxiety, and depression.

The pool held 29 studies with 22,380 workers. Depression appeared in 24.3% and anxiety in 25.8% of staff. Stress ran highest, at 45%. Rates varied much between studies. Larger studies tended to report lower depression rates. The authors call for support systems for front-line staff in future outbreaks.
europmc-pmc7758876:
Nove and co-authors model how many deaths wider midwife care could avert by 2035. It uses the Lives Saved Tool across 88 nations. Those nations hold the vast bulk of world maternal and newborn deaths and stillbirths. Four paths for coverage growth were tested, from decline to universal reach.

A large rise in midwife-delivered care could avert 41% of maternal deaths and 39% of newborn deaths each year. Stillbirths would fall by 26%. That sums to 2.2 million deaths averted per year by 2035. Even a modest rise averts 1.3 million deaths a year. Universal coverage at 95% would avert two thirds of maternal deaths.
europmc-pmc7763876:
Charkhchi and co-authors review the CA125 blood marker in ovarian cancer. Ovarian cancer is the second most lethal cancer of the female reproductive tract. CA125 has been its main marker for four decades. Yet screening healthy women with it does not save lives, and no major society backs such screening.

The aggressive type II tumors cause most deaths but are seldom caught early. The authors suggest new uses for the marker. Test people with symptoms, not the general public. Raise the cutoff level, and run the test at point of care. Such shifts could catch low-volume type II cancers while surgery can still remove them fully.
europmc-pmc7789076:
Li and co-authors study how social support and resilience shaped mental health during COVID-19. A pandemic is a heavy stress event. Older adults face special risk. The team compared three age groups, from emerging adults to older people.

The authors tested the separate effects of support and resilience. They also tested how the two factors interact. Different sources of support were counted apart. Family, friends, and other sources may not act the same way. Age groups may rely on them in different measure. The results speak to who needs help most in a crisis. They also hint at which support protects mental health best.
europmc-pmc7798376:
Cockram and co-authors review how ubiquitination controls inflammatory cell death and cancer. The ubiquitin system tags proteins for removal or new roles. Three enzyme classes, E1, E2, and E3, attach the tags. Other enzymes, called DUBs, remove them.

TNF signaling shows the balance at work. Adding and removing tags compete to set the signal. Inflammasome activity can rise or fall under the same control. Faults in this system feed disease. The authors list the enzymes and targets that matter most. They also highlight drugs in early and clinical testing. Those drugs aim to restore balance in the ubiquitin system.
europmc-pmc7852776:
Gilmer writes on chronic mouth infection and its link to disease in other body parts. The talk was read before the Toronto Dental Society in January 1916. It was printed in Oral Health that February. The idea of focal infection was not new even then.

Doctors long before germ science saw a pattern. Some chronic patients could not be cured. Their health turned only once the mouth was cleaned of infection. Gilmer gathers the case for that view. He treats mouth and jaw infection as a body-wide cause. The article is a period statement of focal infection belief. It shows the roots of an era that prized pulling bad teeth.
europmc-pmc7868676:
Bulcha and co-authors survey viral carrier platforms across the gene therapy field. The field spans a 40-year history of swings. Big wins for patients mix with harsh setbacks. Some trial patients suffered grave harm or died. Viral carriers sit at the heart of both.

These carriers ferry gene fixes into cells. The last 5 years brought a wave of approvals. Designs treat cancer and single-gene diseases alike. Three platforms lead the field. They rest on adenoviruses, adeno-associated viruses, and lentiviruses. The authors explain how each one works. Their roles in past wins are set out. Limits that still cap the field get frank review.
europmc-pmc7889876:
Nouvellet and co-authors report a modelling study of movement and COVID-19 spread. Countries curbed the virus by limiting how much people move and meet. Movement data can stand in for that social distancing. The team studied the link between mobility and transmission across the world.

They analysed data from 52 countries. Transmission fell with the first drop in mobility in 73% of the countries. After strict measures eased, the link weakened in most places. Mobility still explained a large share of the change in spread in many settings. Where the link held after easing, lower mobility still meant lower transmission. The authors say lasting distancing habits kept real value. The study helps officials judge what movement data can and cannot predict in a pandemic.
europmc-pmc7904376:
Hayashino and co-authors report a methods study comparing three statistical tests for publication bias. Publication bias skews meta-analyses when positive studies are more likely to reach print. Funnel plots can hint at the bias, but reading them is subjective. The team tested how well formal tests do the same job.

They used 130 reviews from the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. Observer judgements on funnel plots served as the reference standard. At a fixed false positive rate, Egger's method reached a sensitivity of 0.93. Begg's method reached 0.86, and Macaskill's method only 0.43. Raising the cut-off p-value lifted sensitivity with little cost in false alarms. The authors conclude that Egger's and Begg's tests clearly beat Macaskill's. The study gives meta-analysts hard numbers for a routine check.
europmc-pmc8022876:
Vahratian and co-authors report on adult mental health during the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States. The CDC and the Census Bureau ran the Household Pulse Survey to track the crisis in near real time. The survey asked adults about symptoms of anxiety or depression in the past 7 days. It also asked about counseling or therapy wanted but not received. Data ran from August 19, 2020 to February 1, 2021.

The authors report that symptom rates rose from 36.4% in August to 41.5% by February, across the survey window. Unmet need for counseling rose from 9.2% at the first measurement to 11.7% at the last one. The largest increases hit adults aged 18–29 years. Adults without a high school diploma also saw steep rises. The report aims to guide help toward the groups hit hardest.
europmc-pmc8128876:
Wu and co-authors turn nitrate pollution into ammonia with a single-atom iron catalyst. Ammonia feeds fertilizer plants and chemical works worldwide. The Haber-Bosch route makes it under brutal heat and pressure. That process eats 1 to 2% of the world's energy supply. Electrochemistry offers a cooler path if selectivity cooperates. Nitrate, a common water pollutant, can serve as feedstock instead of nitrogen gas.

Isolated iron atoms anchor the team's catalyst surface. With no neighboring metal sites, nitrogen atoms cannot pair off into N2 gas. The reaction is thus funneled toward ammonia instead. Peak ammonia efficiency reached about 75% of the charge passed in their tests. Quantum calculations traced the steps and the bottleneck. The yield per milligram of catalyst ran high as well. One waste stream becomes a product stream here. Distributed, renewable ammonia production is the larger dream.
europmc-pmc8166576:
Brueggemann and co-authors track invasive respiratory disease during the early COVID-19 pandemic. Three bacteria spread by droplets cause much invasive illness, from pneumonia to meningitis. The team asked whether pandemic controls changed their spread.

Labs in 26 countries and territories on six continents sent case data. The data ran from January 1, 2018 to May 31, 2020. Cases covered Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Neisseria meningitidis. The group compared pandemic months with the years before. Their analysis shows how broad infection controls can ripple into other diseases. The initiative pooled routine lab reports across its network. The labs that took part all used the same plain rules for how a case was counted, so the sums can be set side by side and read as one set.
europmc-pmc8257776:
Moujalled, Strasser, and Liddell map the molecular routes of cell death in neurological disease. Programmed cell death builds the nervous system early in life. It runs in tight spatial and temporal patterns then.

When those cascades misfire, nerve disease can follow. Apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, and ferroptosis all appear in the review. So does death tied to autophagy, plus plain necrosis. Cell stress and inflammation can trigger each route. Faulty activation is common across degenerative diseases. The authors sort triggers, steps, and possible drug points for each path. Each death route gets its own mechanistic walk-through.
europmc-pmc8331176:
Karlinsky and Kobak build the World Mortality Dataset to track excess deaths in the pandemic. Comparing COVID-19's toll across countries is hard. Reported deaths bend with testing and policy.

Excess mortality offers a firmer measure. It counts all deaths above the expected level. No global, updated store of such data existed. The authors gathered weekly to quarterly data from 103 countries and territories. The dataset stays open and regularly updated. Their analysis shows the pandemic's true spread of death. Other researchers can reuse the same base. Open access is part of the dataset's design.
europmc-pmc8459376:
Nakhaei and co-authors review liposomes, tiny fat-based spheres used to carry drugs and genes. A liposome wraps its cargo in a phospholipid membrane. Uses span drug and vaccine delivery, sensors, diagnosis, and food products. Weak physical stability limits many of these uses.

Cholesterol holds a key role in that stability. It controls membrane fluidity, leak, strength, and stiffness. It also shapes drug retention and how long liposomes last in blood. The review sorts liposomes by structure, size, and build method. It then treats stability factors one by one. The best cholesterol amount is still unsettled, which keeps research focus on it.
europmc-pmc8719276:
Global Burden of Disease 2019 Cancer Collaboration presents a systematic analysis of cancer burden across the world from 2010 to 2019. The group measured new cases, deaths, and years of healthy life lost for 29 cancer groups. Results were split by level of social and economic development. The aim was a fair global picture of change over the decade.

Cancer deaths reached 10 million in 2019. Lost healthy years came to an estimated 250 million that year. New cases, deaths, and lost years all rose since 2010. Absolute burden increased in every development group. The largest percentage increases occurred in the low and low-middle groups. The authors call for stronger prevention and control efforts, shared fairly across countries.
europmc-pmc8749476:
Leuzy and co-authors review blood-based biomarkers for Alzheimer disease. Brain disorders like this one are hard to diagnose from symptoms alone. Spinal fluid and brain scan markers exist, but cost and invasiveness limit their use. New ultra-sensitive tests can now measure brain-linked proteins in blood.

Plasma P-tau looks like the best marker for symptomatic disease. Paired with a ratio of amyloid forms, it also suits early, silent stages. Blood NfL is not specific to Alzheimer disease, but it flags nerve damage well. It may also track the effect of new therapies. The review maps uses and unsolved problems for each marker.
europmc-pmc8910576:
Divekar and co-authors review plant secondary metabolites as built-in defenses against insect herbivores. Plants cannot flee their attackers. Chemistry is their armor. When insects feed, plants brew defensive compounds fast. Hormone signals coordinate the brewing. Volatile scents can call in the herbivores' enemies. Some compounds poison the feeders directly. Others make the plant unappealing. The review gathers this defense science for crop protection.

The authors sort the metabolite types and their making. Phytohormone control of induced defense follows. Insects fight back with detox systems and sequestration. Those adaptations get a clear-eyed section. Multi-party interactions close the survey. Pollinators and natural enemies both enter the picture. The authors point to gene-level knowledge as the next step. Engineering these pathways could harden crops sustainably.
europmc-pmc9388376:
Todo and co-authors report a phase 2 trial of a cancer-killing herpes virus for stubborn glioblastoma. The virus, G47-delta, carries three mutations that aim it at tumor cells. Nineteen adults with leftover or returned tumors got up to six injections into the tumor. All had prior radiation and temozolomide therapy.

One-year survival after treatment start was 84.2%, with 16 of 19 patients alive. That beat the preset target, and the trial stopped early. Median survival reached 20.2 months from treatment and 28.8 months from first surgery. Fever was the most common side effect, in 17 of 19 patients. Scans showed a repeating pattern of swelling then clearing inside the lesion. Biopsies found rising immune cell entry into tumors. The results led to approval in Japan, a first for such a product.
europmc-pmc9684076:
Galeano Niño and co-authors study how microbes inside tumors shape the space and cell mix of cancers. Tumor bacteria were known as bulk tissue signals before. Bulk reads hide where microbes sit and what they touch. The team brought spatial tools to oral and colorectal tumors.

They adapted a spatial transcript platform to find microbial spots in place. A second profiler showed bacterial zones had odd traits. Those microniches had fewer blood vessels than clean zones. They also held strong immune suppression in their cells. Cancer cells there bore lower Ki-67 growth marks. A new single-cell method, INVADEseq, found bacteria inside host cells. It showed which host programs shifted near the microbes. Inflammation, spread, and dormancy paths all moved. Tests showed infected cancer cells invade as single cells. They also draw myeloid cells toward bacterial zones.
europmc-pmc9812776:
Msemburi and co-authors present the World Health Organization estimates of excess deaths from the COVID-19 pandemic. Reported COVID-19 death counts were shaky in many countries. Testing access, diagnosis skill, and death papers all varied. Collateral harm from the crisis also killed people unseen.

The team estimated excess deaths month by month for two years. The window covered 2020 and 2021 across the globe. A Bayesian count model filled gaps where data were missing. Global excess deaths came to more than 14 million people. That toll ran nearly three times the reported COVID-19 deaths. Estimates varied widely across the six WHO regions. The authors describe their data and methods in full. They warn against ranking countries by these numbers. Better death reporting is their closing call to governments.
europmc-pmc9825576:
Alcock and co-authors report the 2023 state of CARD, a curated database of antibiotic resistance genes. It pairs a shared scheme for naming resistance traits with gene records and the mutations that confer them. Software built on the records reads new genomes and names the resistance they carry.

The build holds 6,627 terms in its naming scheme and 5,010 reference gene sequences. It holds 1,933 curated mutations and 5,057 detection models for the partner search tool. Curation widened on several fronts since 2020, with deeper coverage of a major drug breaking enzyme family. Records for tuberculosis drug resistance grew, and disinfectant resistance joined the scope of the database. Resistance blocking agents were curated in a systematic pass as well. Predicted resistance profiles now span 377 pathogen species in the system. Each gene also gained a short standard name to support machine learning work. A live collection gathers resistance data sent in by the wider community.
europmc-pmc9931576:
Cao and co-authors ask why new Omicron variants converged on the same spike changes. Many variants grew faster than the prior dominant line at the same time. Their paths differed, yet changes in the receptor-binding domain hit the same few hotspots. The team traced the force behind that pattern.

The shared changes helped variants evade antibody drugs and plasma from recovered patients. They kept strong binding to the ACE2 receptor at the same time. Tests of escape profiles used antibodies from people with breakthrough infections. Prior infection had narrowed antibody range through immune imprinting. That focus pushed viral change toward the same escape sites. Deep mutation scans predicted the shared changes well. The authors warn that current herd immunity and boosters may not block these variants.
europmc-pmc9960276:
Sun and Shahrajabian survey phenolic compounds in medicinal plants as natural health products. Phenolics and flavonoids may stand in for some bioactive drugs. They occur widely in fruits, grains, and herbs. The review searched Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, and PubMed.

Reported effects span antioxidant, antibacterial, and anticancer action. Heart protection, immune support, and anti-inflammatory effects are also covered. Skin protection from ultraviolet light appears as well. The authors sort groups such as tannins, coumarins, and lignans. Each class is linked to plant sources and health claims. Future research directions close the survey. The work maps a large field of plant-based candidates for new drugs.
frus-1861-d176:
Writing on 15 August 1861, William H. Seward kept Carl Schurz inside his single linked plan. The letter is document 176 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Mid August found Seward writing to Madrid in the same steady round as London and Paris. Each court got its own page, cut to its own needs. The letter to Schurz shows Spain held firmly inside the Secretary's single, linked plan. The single linked plan kept small courts from being played off against great ones. Small courts, held in one plan, could not be bought one by one by the South.
frus-1861-d276:
30 May 1861 is the date on a dispatch from Mr. Angel to William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 276 in the President's message volume for 1861. By then, in the opening months of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d76:
Writing to London on 7 September 1861, William H. Seward kept Charles Francis Adams to the autumn plan. The letter is document 76 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward kept up a near weekly rhythm of orders to London that autumn. Each letter bound Adams tighter to the cabinet's shared plan. For readers, the steady dates themselves tell a story: a government holding its nerve by routine. Routine was itself a message to London: the Union meant to outlast the crisis. The Union meant to outlast the crisis, and its mail said so in its steady dates.
frus-1862-d176:
The second Adams report of 24 October 1862 is printed as Document 176 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain, sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Late October 1862 was a turning point in the war's foreign side: the French truce plan was taking shape, and Britain had to choose. Adams's twice-weekly reports were Washington's best window on that choice. This dispatch, read in sequence, shows the care with which he tracked each shift in British thinking. Adams held the London post from 1861 to 1868, the longest run of any Union envoy in Europe.
frus-1862-d276:
On 8 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William L. Dayton a dispatch printed as Document 276 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister to France, posted in Paris.

Early May brought word of the French defeat at Puebla and the Union hold on New Orleans, both useful to Washington's case in Paris. Seward's letters that month pressed a simple theme: the rebellion was failing, and friendship with it would cost France more than it could gain. This dispatch is one of the spring's many statements of that theme. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d376:
Viscount Treilhard wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 August 1862, in a letter printed as Document 376 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. He wrote on the second day of the Bull Run battle.

Few dates in the file carry such a charge: while Treilhard wrote, the Union army was being beaten thirty miles away. The defeat would embolden those in Europe who wanted to act on the war. This letter, and the exchange around it, belongs to the record of how Washington's foreign dealings absorbed the shock in real time. Seward tested what Mercier said against what Dayton reported from Paris, week by week.
frus-1862-d476:
On 13 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to James E. Harvey in Lisbon. It is Document 476 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

By October 1862 the Confederate cruiser Alabama was loose on the Atlantic. Neutral ports from the Azores outward had become part of the war at sea. Seward's autumn orders to Lisbon kept the pressure on Portugal to hold raiders to the letter of neutrality law. Harvey's post, quiet in most histories, sat on a real front of the war. The dispatch closes the year's printed instructions to Portugal, a small file that shows how global the blockade's paper war had become.
frus-1862-d576:
On 21 July 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to James Watson Webb in Brazil. The instruction is Document 576 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Seward's July orders everywhere carried the government's account of a hard summer, and the Brazilian instruction was no exception. Webb also needed the Department's current line on the cruiser war, since Confederate raiders would soon be working the South Atlantic and seeking Brazilian ports. By the time the letter reached Rio, the season it described had passed, which is why distant ministers held such wide discretion. The document shows the system working at its longest range.
frus-1862-d676:
Anson Burlingame sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 May 1862. Burlingame was the American minister to China, and his mail formed the China section of the year's file. The letter is document 676 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Spring reports from China dealt with the state of the ports and the mood of the Qing court. Burlingame also had to weigh the moves of Britain and France, whose fleets and envoys loomed large there. His letter is a working part of that watch. It helped Washington hold a steady course in East Asia with few ships and fewer men to spare.
frus-1862-d76:
Writing from Washington on 2 June 1862, William H. Seward addressed Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The printed record keeps it as Document 76 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d176:
On 30 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this dispatch from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 176 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Britain had declared itself neutral in 1861, yet many in its government and press leaned toward the South. Adams watched Parliament, the cabinet, and the newspapers for any sign of a shift. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d276:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 2 September 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 276 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Orders crossed the Atlantic by steamship and took ten days or more to arrive. By the time Adams acted, events in London could already have moved on. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d376:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, on 29 January 1863. The note is document 376 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Lyons reported everything to London, so Seward wrote knowing his words would be read there too. Each note spoke to two audiences at once. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d476:
On 23 April 1863 a formal note passed from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d576:
Under the date 22 June 1863, the record holds a letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d676:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, sent this dispatch to London on 24 November 1863. It went to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister there. The text is document 676 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that covers foreign affairs for 1863, part one.

Britain was the foreign power Washington watched most closely during the Civil War. Its ships, ports, and trade could help or hurt the Union cause. Adams had to press the American view in person, using notes like this one as his guide. The letter shows high-level orders moving from a desk in Washington to an envoy abroad, in plain official words.
frus-1863p1-d76:
Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 12 February 1863. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 76 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Mid-February mail from London took stock after the opening of Parliament. Adams wrote on the tone of the houses, the press, and the South's men in the city. His reports let Seward judge whether the calm of the Queen's speech would hold. This dispatch is one of a pair sent that day, in the legation's usual split of topics.
frus-1876:
Grant's eighth and last message opens the 1876 volume. He reviews eight years and admits errors of judgment. Appointments, he says, caused most of them. The country files follow their settled order. Britain's section turns legal this year. An extradition treaty fills the longest run. Court argument over surrendered fugitives fills its pages.

Spain's file returns to the Virginius aftermath. It prints General Burriel's trial under the settlement protocol. Three appendices close the book. One reports the Alabama claims court. Another covers the Mexican claims commission. A Canadian case, Ex parte Bouvier, stands first. The volume's tone is valedictory. An administration ends by settling accounts. Its claims machinery fills the back pages.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d176: A third Roosevelt letter to Hull dated October 30, 1943 in the Moscow section stands as Document 176 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Repetition at this scale marks a day when much had to be settled at a distance: results weighed, thanks sent, and next steps set. The record gives the parties and the date and no subject. The letter is part of the Foreign Relations series' Moscow record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d276:
A secret memorandum of conversation at Cairo on 26 November 1943 records a meeting at half past eleven that morning. American and British information and public relations officers settled how conference photographs and films would be handled. Army colonels sit alongside staff of the British and American information services.

The agreed rules are practical. Each side processes its own still photographs in Cairo under security conditions and exchanges material. American film goes unprocessed to Washington, while British film is processed in Cairo. No picture of any kind may be released before the final release date, given the secrecy of the Tehran leg. All conference pictures, still and moving, are pooled for every party and carry one credit line: United Nations Photographic Pool.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d376:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record a luncheon at Tehran on 1 December 1943, at one in the afternoon, dominated by the planned meeting with Turkey's president. The text of a telegram inviting President Inönü to Cairo for 3, 4, or 5 December was discussed and agreed.

Hopkins insists the allies must first settle exactly what military help Turkey would get if she entered the war. Churchill's offer stands at twenty squadrons, mostly fighters, and three anti-aircraft regiments, with no land forces and no promises beyond that. His prize would be Turkish air bases for steady bombing of the Ploesti oil fields, and he wants landing craft only for a temporary Rhodes assault in March. Roosevelt, caught between the Italian, French, and Overlord demands on the same craft, asks for military advice before anything is sandwiched in.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d476:
On December 4, 1943, the opening day of the Second Cairo Conference, the Combined Chiefs of Staff sent a message to General Dwight D. Eisenhower at Allied Force Headquarters. Eisenhower then commanded Allied forces in the Mediterranean, based in North Africa. The State Department printed the chiefs' message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Traffic from the Combined Chiefs to a theater commander carried the alliance's decisions out of the conference room and into the field. Eisenhower stood at the receiving end of Cairo's choices about where Allied strength would go next. For readers, the message marks the point where summit strategy began turning into orders for the armies.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d576:
J. Leighton Stuart, the American ambassador to China, wrote to Secretary of State George C. Marshall on September 24, 1948. Stuart, a missionary educator born in China, was the last American ambassador to serve the Nationalist government on the mainland. His report is the final document in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

By September 1948 the Chinese Communists were winning the civil war, and the China that the Cairo Declaration had promised so much was disappearing. An editor's choice to end the volume here is pointed: the story that began with Chiang at Cairo closes with his government's collapse. For readers, Stuart's report is a somber bookend to the whole record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d76: On October 30, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, the day the Moscow Conference formally ended. His message is Document 76 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. London had its own reading of the Moscow results, and the prime minister kept his channel to Washington warm as ever. The record gives the date and the names and nothing narrower. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series with the day's other traffic.
frus-1944-quebec-d176:
No official account survives of the dinner meeting on September 12, 1944, at the Governor General's residence. The editors reconstruct it from General Arnold's memoir. Messages from the Russians and from Harriman about the Polish patriots in Warsaw had arrived, and aid to Poland came up at the table. Marshall and Arnold talked the problem over at length.

Arnold records that helping Warsaw was a large problem never completely solved. Churchill also produced new ideas about winning the war: getting more British planes, ships, and soldiers into the final battle against Japan. Arnold answered that the Pacific lacked land masses for Europe's heavy bomber fleets. Even 1,500 of 3,500 bombers would be lucky to be usable, and B-29s were preferred anyway.
frus-1944-quebec-d276:
Somervell and Leathers, the American and British transport chiefs, reported on September 15, 1944, on the personnel movement problem after Germany's defeat. Their appendices size the task for the first year, assuming Germany fell on October 1. American operational movements alone totaled about 3.6 million men, including replacements, build-up, and redeployment for the war against Japan, plus 1.7 million for demobilization and repatriation.

British operational movements came to about 2.1 million, with nearly a million more to demobilize or repatriate. A precise analysis, the authors warn, was impossible until combined agencies studied the problem against the chiefs' strategy decisions. They recommended the Combined Administrative Committee take it up with the planners, the transportation committee, and the shipping authorities.
frus-1944-quebec-d76:
James W. Riddleberger wrote to Harry Hopkins on September 1, 1944. Riddleberger headed the Division of Central European Affairs. Hopkins served as President Roosevelt's special assistant and closest aide. The State Department printed the letter in the Quebec 1944 volume.

Central European questions sat near the heart of the Quebec agenda. Germany's defeat raised hard choices about occupation and borders. A division chief writing to Hopkins put expert views near the President. For readers, the letter shows how regional knowledge reached the summit's inner circle. It arrived eleven days before the conference opened.
frus-1945-50-intel-d176:
The meeting named in the title took place on 7 November 1946, and these minutes are its formal record. Readers meet it as document 176 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

As minutes, the text sticks to the business of the meeting: items raised, views stated in brief, and the choices the group reached. The brevity is the point: what the group did not settle, the minutes do not claim it did. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d276:
A memorandum dated 19 May 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Kennan). The reader was the Under Secretary of State (Lovett) and Secretary of State Marshall. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 276 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The young CIA was still defining its job, while the Council weighed how far secret action abroad should go.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d376:
On 22 March 1949, staff wrote up the discussion at the 36th Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. Readers meet it as document 376 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The Dulles Report had landed in January 1949, and Washington was arguing over which of its fixes the CIA should adopt.

A memorandum of conversation is the note a participant or aide wrote after a talk, setting down who was there and what was said. The writer's own views may color a line or two, which is part of what makes the form honest to read. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d76:
The Department of State sent a circular telegram to certain diplomatic missions on 22 October 1945. Circular telegrams carry one message to many posts at once. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A circular on intelligence business told embassies around the world how to handle the new order of things after the OSS. Posts had to know which secret duties were ending, which were passing to State, and what to tell host governments. Readers can see the change reaching the field here. It is not a plan in a Washington office. It is an instruction landing on desks from London to Chungking. The volume's State thread widens from an office to a worldwide service in papers like this.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d176:
King Peter gave his guarded yes to the Tito–Subasic draft, and Ambassador Patterson cabled the royal statement to Washington on 11 January 1945. The communiqué of the Royal Yugoslav Court is quoted in full. Patterson's cable is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

The King has studied the draft closely, the statement says. He approves its basic proposals, under which Yugoslavia's future constitution and form of government rest solely on the free decision of her peoples. He will accept that decision. But as a constitutional monarch, he calls it his sacred duty to see the people truly consulted and their will fully respected. He also welcomes the widest grouping of democratic parties, from left to right, as the only sure ground of free expression.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d276:
Moscow's draft of a prisoners-and-civilians agreement is printed here in the Malta and Yalta volume. The Soviet text answers a British note of 11 December 1944. It proposes the principles that should govern Soviet citizens and British subjects freed from the Germans by each other's armies.

The Soviet government is ready to conclude such an agreement, the note says, but its reach should be extended. It should cover not only prisoners of war but citizens interned or deported by force into Germany. Some paragraphs of the British draft should also be widened and defined. The first principle follows. All freed Soviet citizens held by the western allies are to be parted from enemy prisoners without delay. The same holds for freed British subjects in Red Army hands. Each group is kept apart in camps or gathering points until it is sent home.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d376:
Before sending his famous letter on Poland, Roosevelt's staff drafted it, and the draft survives here dated February 7, 1945. The President tells Stalin he has given much thought to their meeting that afternoon. He wants to say frankly what is on his mind. On the Polish government, he is greatly disturbed.

The three great powers, he writes, have no meeting of minds about Poland's political setup. Moscow backs one government while Washington and London back another in London. That split puts all of them in a bad light before the world. People might think a breach had opened between the allies. The draft lets readers compare the plea planned with the plea sent.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d476:
Stettinius asked questions home in this cable of February 4, 1945. He wanted a summary of the Mikolajczyk memorandum shown to Bohlen. He also asked Grew to keep the delegation promptly informed on the Associated Nations. What was the present status of each of the five Latin American countries, other than Ecuador, and when might each act?

He further asked for at least a summary of the Department's cable to Moscow cited in an earlier message. The code words "Allstate Horseshoe" closed the wire. Read beside Grew's digests, the cable shows the two ends of the State Department working one set of files from Washington and Yalta at once.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d76:
Geneva, Prague, or somewhere new? This 15 November 1944 paper to the President weighs where the United Nations should make its home. Acting Secretary Stettinius reports that the question was never formally debated at Dumbarton Oaks. The memo is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

The Soviet delegates objected to Geneva, and one informally suggested Prague. Britain and China raised no objection to Geneva. An American study group reviewed six options, from Vienna to a district near Lake Como. Its pick was a neutral district joining the Swiss strip that held the League buildings with the French Pays de Gex next door. The memo urges the President to back that plan.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d176:
