Ambassador Lord Halifax proposed adding war criminals to the summit agenda in a letter dated June 29, 1945. The letter is document 176 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It follows up the British agenda list delivered a month earlier.

Four-power talks on war criminals had begun in London on June 26, Halifax notes, among American, British, Soviet, and French representatives. Even so, London expects some war crimes matters to remain unresolved by the time the heads of government meet. A brief review of the position by the leaders would be valuable in any case. The suggestion helped push the prosecution of the top Nazi leaders, then being negotiated in London, onto the Potsdam program.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d276:
Winant set down the U.S. caveat on Austrian reparations in a cable from London on July 4, 1945. The cable is document 276 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It gives the words he used that day on signing the pact on control machinery for Austria.

In the talks on a reparations desk in the pact, he told his colleagues, the group had not weighed the real question of what Austria should pay. His government accepts in principle that Austria owes reparations, he said, but holds that the four powers should fix the form and sum in light of Austria's economy and its prospects. The British and French said much the same. The Soviet member, Winant notes, had long fought any such U.S. caveat.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d376:
A progress report by the American delegation to the Reparations Commission, dated July 14, 1945, sums up what Moscow had settled and what it had not. Pauley had asked on July 3 for clarification of the open problems before the heads of government met. The supplement answers him point by point, with appendices for each topic.

On July 13 the delegations agreed the relative shares of the participating governments, and agreed rules for smaller nations' claims. No agreement came on defining reparation, restitution, and war booty, since the Soviets were not ready to discuss booty. General principles were settled except one: whether needed exports rank as a prior charge.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d476:
British hopes for a lasting combined command fill Kirk's top secret cable from Caserta of July 1, 1945. From talks with the chief of staff and other high British officers at Allied Force Headquarters, Kirk gathers what Field Marshal Alexander will do in England. Alexander will urge Churchill to persuade Truman, and senior American officials, at the Big Three meeting.

The aim is to maintain a combined command in this theater as long as possible. The British will hold out for maximum retention of a supreme commander, though they know America probably will not go along. They have therefore prepared fallback plans for an inter-allied service committee, to carry on functions of an allied character until a peace settlement is made.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d576:
Acting Secretary of State Joseph Grew sent a memo to Secretary of State Byrnes on July 12, 1945. It is document 576 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Grew passes on a message for the President from China's leader, Chiang Kai-shek.

Chiang thanks Truman for his June 15 wire, which sketched a proposed deal between China and the Soviet Union. He says he has sent T. V. Soong to Moscow to negotiate with the Soviet government. He will keep Truman informed through Ambassador Hurley in China. Chiang calls the matter grave for world peace as well as for China and Russia. He asks Truman to keep close watch on the talks and to share his views over time. The memo went by pouch, not wire, to keep the line to Potsdam free for urgent traffic.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d676:
An extract from Villard's Paris wire of July 13, 1945, reports Britain's private plan on Tangier. It is document 676 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The extract is drawn from a longer report sent over Ambassador Caffery's signature.

Villard cites Peake, the British team head, on London's intent. Britain will not raise at Berlin any question of how far Russian participation should run. That participation is accepted in principle, Peake says. Any British-Russian talk on Tangier would be limited to a bargain. London would seek something in exchange for Russian admission to the conversations. Peake also held that France would accept putting the talks off until the first week of August. The extract lays bare the bargaining beneath the formal notes.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d76:
President Truman denied a press story in a top secret telegram to Churchill on June 18, 1945. The message is document 76 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Churchill had asked about reports that Truman planned to stop in Paris and meet General de Gaulle before the Berlin conference.

Truman says the press reports Churchill mentioned are not authentic. He will keep the promise Roosevelt made to Churchill, he adds, if conditions at the time make it workable, a careful hedge. He ends by hoping the contents of the message will not get into the papers. The brief exchange shows both leaders managing the press, and French feelings, while the Berlin trip was being planned in secret.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1076:
Prime Minister Churchill circulated this extract of his Greece memorandum at Potsdam on July 22, 1945. The full text appears just earlier in the volume. Annexed to it is a report by Field Marshal Alexander, dated July 21. Alexander answers Soviet charges about Greece point by point, from the mood of the Greek people to the balance of forces on her borders.

Most Greeks, he writes, feel relief from terror thanks to British troops, and UNRRA relief now works where it could not under ELAS-EAM rule. Any Greek threat to Albania and Bulgaria is unfounded. Greece has one division, still training, against 52 Yugoslav, 18 Bulgarian, and 7 Albanian divisions nearby. A loud propaganda campaign from those three neighbors, he adds, poisons the air.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1176:
Winant cabled from London yet again on 18 July 1945. During the summit he filed almost daily. His reports built Washington's picture of British thinking piece by piece: politics, press, and the official mood in a capital awaiting an election count.

No single cable carried the whole story. The value lay in the stream, each report testing and adding to the last. This dispatch is one more layer in that piling up of detail. It shows the London embassy's steady work while the leaders bargained abroad. Readers who follow the sequence watch an ally's mind being read in real time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1276:
The United States Chiefs of Staff proposed this text on 21 July 1945. A proposed text from the chiefs put draft words on the table for the talks to accept or amend. Wording from the military staff could end up in the summit's own papers.

Drafting was power at Potsdam. The side that wrote the first text set the terms of the argument that followed. This entry preserves the chiefs' draft at its date, midway through the talks. Primary papers like this one let readers see the settlement being built from the staff level up, one clause at a time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1376:
Ambassador Edwin Wilson cabled the acting secretary of state from Turkey again on 27 July 1945. His earlier cable in the volume is dated 19 July. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Two cables, eight days apart, let readers watch an ambassador build a case over time. Turkey's spot between the Soviet Union and the Mediterranean kept Ankara in the summit's shadow talks as well as in its own file. Wilson's second report shows what had changed, or failed to change, while the leaders met in Germany. Posts like his supplied the facts on which the men at Potsdam judged the straits and the lands beyond them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-76:
Swedish requisitioning of shipping was the principal subject of a conversation that left no official record. An editorial note in volume two names that subject and marks the gap. It is the seventy-sixth unnumbered item following document 710, in the conference sequence of July 1945.

That question was expected to come up at a forthcoming meeting of the United Maritime Authority. The authority was the Allied body that allocated merchant shipping in the war's last phase. No official record of this conversation has been found, and the note gives no names or date beyond its place in the file. Entries like this one mark how much conference business ran through unminuted side talks. The editors preserve the topic and the gap together.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d776:
Byrnes wrote to Ambassador Winant in London on July 20, 1945, in document 776. The Secretary kept the London embassy close through the conference. Winant's post made him a key partner in all Anglo-American work. This letter entered the second Potsdam volume, among several Byrnes-Winant exchanges.

The London channel carried more than news. Winant had to act on the conference's drift with his own hosts. Readers see a secretary managing an alliance by letter. The document shows Potsdam's work spreading outward in real time. Each such letter turned talk in Germany into action in a capital that had to live with it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d876: American drafters prepared this undated working paper on Article 19 during the Potsdam talks, filed with papers dated July 23, 1945. Reparations must leave Germans enough to live on without outside help. Paying for imports approved by the Control Council would be a first charge on export proceeds. If the council failed to agree, each zone commander could import supplies his government deemed vital, claiming first charge on his zone's exports.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d976: Secretary of State James Byrnes wrote to Molotov on August 1, 1945, now that a tripartite reparations plan stands agreed at Potsdam. The remaining work, he says, is carrying the deal out. The key task is deciding what will be removed from the western zones, and arranging Soviet deliveries of needed products in return. Byrnes therefore urges that the Allied Commission on Reparations assemble in Berlin at once, to work with the Control Council. He asks Molotov to instruct the Soviet representative accordingly.
frus-1958-60v09-d176: A telegram from the United States delegation at the Paris summit reports the foreign ministers' meeting of May 17, 1960. Herter, Lloyd, and Couve de Murville drafted a joint statement for use if the Soviets refused to attend. The French draft was accepted once one phrase was cut. Lloyd asked why the President could not voice regret for the U-2 flight. Herter answered that the President was not sorry, and could not promise to meet Khrushchev after such insults.
gao-gaoreports-b-297176:
Raloid Corporation protested a Navy award for plane adapters in GAO decision B-297176, dated November 10, 2005. The winner was DE Technologies. The job held a test unit and runs of full units. The firm hit marks for both bids. It also hit a cap on sub work in the call.

GAO denied the protest. Marks fit the tests in the call and were sound. On the sub cap, the winner's bid did not on its face show a breach. Whether it would breach in the work is a fitness or job-run point. Those points are not for GAO to judge here. The award thus stood on the marks made.
gao-gaoreports-b-298276:
King Construction protested the terms of a lease call in GAO decision B-298276, dated July 17, 2006. The buyer was the General Services Administration. The tenant was the Federal Bureau of Investigation. The site was Louisville, Kentucky. The block was to be built to suit the tenant. Terms asked for skill in top grade office builds and in green design work.

GAO denied the protest. The agency showed a sound base for its path. Skill terms for a top grade, green build track the need for such a block. Twin skill asks for team staff were also tied to the job. Strict lease terms can stand when the build grade is high.
gao-gaoreports-b-298576:
Singleton Enterprises protested a General Services Administration award to Chezcore, Inc. The contract covered exterior masonry repair on a federal building in Battle Creek, Michigan. Past performance counted far more than price in the best-value call. GAO ruled in B-298576 on October 30, 2006.

The dispute turned on one clause about past performance. The clause spoke of an offeror's acts under past contracts. The agency read it as the firm's own record only. Singleton read it to cover key subcontractors as well. GAO found the text open to both readings. That hidden flaw in the terms tainted the scoring. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299076:
Fantastic Data protested an Army call not to fund its phase I proposal. The plea arose under the Defense Department's Small Business Innovation Research program. Phase I awards test the merit of a new concept. GAO ruled in B-299076 on February 5, 2007.

The firm faulted the review that left it unfunded. GAO read the full record of that review. It found the scoring fair and well grounded. The program sets aside funds for small-firm research each round. Not each sound proposal can be funded. A loss at the funding line does not prove a bad review. No flaw in the process was shown. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299576:
Meeks Disposal Corporation protested a Navy award to Dorado Services. The contract covered refuse collection and recycling services. The sites sit at Navy facilities in the Hampton Roads area of Virginia. GAO decided B-299576 and B-299576.2 on June 28, 2007.

The agency marked the firm's bid unfit on approach and management. The terms asked how a firm would hire and keep skilled staff. The bid gave a brief, broad note on that point. GAO found that note too thin to judge. A firm must show its staffing path in real terms. Vague pledges leave the panel with nothing to weigh. The unfit mark stood. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-308476:
A court-ordered payback to a truck safety agency may not be kept in this GAO decision, B-308476, dated December 20, 2006. A federal court told a wrongdoer to pay restitution to the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration. The agency asked if it could hold the cash. GAO said no, the cash must move on.

Cash got for the government goes to the Treasury by law. A slim carve-out covers true repayments of agency outlays. GAO held this award does not fit that carve-out. No law gives the agency power to keep it. The agency must deposit the award in the Treasury's general fund.
gao-gaoreports-b-310976:
Para Scientific Company saw its protest thrown out. GAO decided B-310976 on February 25, 2008. The Geological Survey sought lab and water test chemicals. It ran the call with no set-aside class. Para said the buy must be set aside for small firms. Mid-fight, the Small Business Administration ruled on Para's own size class.

GAO dismissed the protest. The size rule put Para past the small class for this trade code. A firm that is not small in the code lacks a stake to press the claim. Class fights need a firm that fits the class at stake.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-176:
Head Start, GAO-05-176 of February 28, 2005, asks if the watch on grant cash is strong enough for a vast preschool plan. In fiscal year 2004, Congress gave $6.8 billion to serve 919,000 poor children through 1,680 local grantees. News of cash abuse at a few sites raised hard claims about the federal watch.

GAO tests two links in that watch. It tests if the agency in charge spots weak cash control at each site in a steady way. It tests if fixes land fast and in full once flaws are found. A full risk plan could stop flaws before they grow, GAO urges.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-276:
Information Technology, GAO-05-276 of April 15, 2005, grades the budget office's own watch list for weak tech builds. Of nearly 1,200 major tech projects in the fiscal year 2005 budget, the Office of Management and Budget flagged 621. Those builds held about $22 billion. Each had known flaws that put its task at risk.

GAO asks how a project lands on that list. It asks how the office tracks the fix steps it sets for each flagged build. The list is a strong tool, the text shows. Its force fades when the chase on fixes lacks bite. Sharper use of the checks is the charge.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-376:
Environmental Information, GAO-05-376 of September 2, 2005, checks if the data streams that track the land's health will hold their course. Scores of federal plans count the state of air, water, soil, and life. Their counts feed a famed study of the nation's living world. Chiefs at each tier of rule use them to pick where to act. A break in a stream blinds that work.

GAO read 20 such plans. It asked their hosts if cash shifts or new aims in fiscal years 2005 and 2006 would bend the counts. It asked if the counts would still match the past, and still feed the grand study.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-876:
The money behind rebuilding Iraq is tallied in GAO-05-876, a report from July 28, 2005. The effort is the largest U.S. aid program since World War II. Funds flow from the United States, Iraq, and donors worldwide. GAO counted pledges and spending to date. It then tracked work in oil, power, water, and health. Challenges in each sector are named.

As of March 2005, over $60 billion was pledged or made available. The United States gave about $24 billion for fiscal years 2003 through 2005. About $18 billion was obligated and about $9 billion paid out. Some $4.7 billion was shifted from big power and water jobs to security and quick-impact work. The old occupation authority had controlled $23 billion in Iraqi funds. Donors pledged $13.6 billion over 4 years, mostly as loans.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1076:
Building security control centers are measured in GAO-06-1076, a report dated September 29, 2006. Four centers back the Federal Protective Service around the clock. They monitor alarms, monitor radios, and dispatch officers and contract guards. Their fiscal year 2006 budget is $23.5 million. They watch alarms at over 8,300 federal sites. GAO identified the services, judged how performance is assessed, and compared the centers with like bodies.

GAO found managers assess the centers by volume and timing data, call sampling, and informal feedback. Formal measures exist but are of limited use, GAO said. They are not always clearly stated or measurable. They skip government-wide tests like efficiency, cost, and outcomes. One key span goes unmeasured: the time from alarm to dispatch. That link would tie center performance to service-wide results. Better measurement is the report's charge.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-176:
Job services for veterans under a 2002 law are reviewed in GAO-06-176, a report dated December 30, 2005. About 700,000 veterans were out of work in recent months. That figure may swell as more troops leave active duty. The Jobs for Veterans Act aimed to improve state job services and push employers to hire veterans. It set new staff roles, performance measures, incentive awards, and priority service for veterans. GAO tracked how the Labor Department and states have carried the law out.

GAO checked what is known about services and results since the law took effect. It also judged how program accountability has changed. The title signals the verdict: more action is needed. States need more help to put the reforms in place. The department needs tighter accountability so Congress can see what the money buys. The report speaks to a basic pledge, that service in war should lead to work at home.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-276:
Budget triggers to tame mandatory spending are designed and tested in GAO-06-276, dated January 31, 2006. Mandatory programs grow on autopilot, outside the yearly budget vote. A trigger would force action when spending runs past a set line. GAO studied whether such devices can be built to work. It also dug into why forecasts missed the mark in seven mandatory accounts. The study covers fiscal years 2000 through 2004 and flows from GAO's duty to watch the nation's finances.

For each account, GAO split the forecast gaps into their causes. Technical factors explained much of the spread between guesses and results. It sketched sample triggers and the responses each might force. A good trigger must bite without wrecking the program it guards. It must also rest on data that arrive in time to act. The report gives Congress a toolkit and a caution in one: design decides whether a trigger guides or merely alarms.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-376:
A company can be formed with very little said about who owns it. In GAO-06-376 (April 7, 2006), GAO studies company formation across all 50 states and the District of Columbia. Shell companies have no operations. They can still be used to launder money or hide other illicit acts. Some states faced criticism for asking so little.

GAO describes what states and third-party agents collect when firms form. It reports law enforcement concerns about hidden ownership. It also weighs how state records help or hinder investigations. The study then tests the effects of requiring more ownership data. The core finding is in the title. Only minimal ownership information is collected.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-476:
Government phone and data services had to move to new contracts without breaking service. In report GAO-06-476 (June 6, 2006), GAO reviews telecommunications transition planning. Current government-wide contracts were set to expire. The General Services Administration and its customer agencies had to prepare the switch. The last such federal transition proved large and complex. That history shapes this review.

GAO checked whether selected agencies used sound practices in preparing. It judged whether the agency's technology service was ready. That check covered lessons from the past move and guidance given to agencies. Full use of sound planning practices could improve the work, GAO said. Readers get a readiness grade.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-676:
Outsourcing of health data by public health plans is surveyed in GAO report GAO-06-676, issued on September 5, 2006. Contractors and state agencies run the daily work of Medicare, Medicaid, and TRICARE. These operators hire vendors for tasks that use personal health data, at home and abroad. GAO surveyed all federal Medicare and TRICARE contractors and all state Medicaid agencies about this practice.

GAO found wide use of domestic outsourcing of work involving personal health data. More than 90 percent of Medicare contractors and state Medicaid agencies reported some in 2005. So did 63 percent of TRICARE contractors. Direct offshore outsourcing, by contrast, was rare. The report maps where health data flows and why privacy safeguards matter.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-76:
Cargo carried on airplanes is the focus of GAO-06-76. GAO released it on October 17, 2005. In 2004, an estimated 23 billion pounds of air cargo moved within the United States. About a quarter of it rode on passenger aircraft, beside travelers' baggage. The Transportation Security Administration guards this system inside the Homeland Security Department. GAO judged how far the agency had come in securing domestic air cargo.

GAO found that the agency had built a risk-based strategic plan. But it had not finished assessing the terrorist risks the cargo system faces. Actions taken to strengthen security could be limited by several factors. Putting the agency's plans into practice also posed challenges for it and for cargo firms. GAO called for federal action to finish the risk work and tighten security.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-276:
Toxic solvents reached drinking water at a Marine base decades ago, and the health study is still running. GAO chronicled the case in GAO-07-276, issued May 11, 2007. Solvents TCE and PCE turned up in two base water systems in 1982 and 1983. The systems served the Hadnot Point and Tarawa Terrace areas. A health agency began a study in 1999. It asks whether exposure before birth raised some cancers and birth defects.

Ten tainted wells were shut in 1984 and 1985, GAO recounts. Officials at the time took few steps. No rules then set limits for these chemicals. Both sites joined the cleanup list in 1989. The cleaner is the likely source for one housing area. Its contamination may date to 1957. The health study's finish was projected for December 2007. GAO used an expert panel to judge the study's design. Claims and inquiries continue alongside cleanup.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-376:
The Army's flagship modernization program has spent about $8 billion on knowledge it does not yet have. GAO gave the annual verdict in GAO-07-376, a report dated March 15, 2007. The Future Combat System links 14 weapon systems through one network. Congress will decide in early 2009 whether it continues. GAO reviewed requirements, technology, software, and costs. The program is classed high risk.

The Army calls about 80 percent of its technologies mature, GAO reports. That is double last year's share. But the Army grades by a looser standard than best practice. This year's scoring was not independent. Software size estimates have doubled since the start. The Army's cost estimate sits at $160.7 billion. Outside estimators put the bill at $203 billion to nearly $234 billion. The Army will buy fewer systems and slow output. It is the second restructuring in 4 years.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-76:
War costs for fiscal year 2006 are counted in GAO-07-76, a report dated November 13, 2006. Congress gave the military $93.3 billion for the Global War on Terrorism that year. GAO compared that funding with what the services said they had obligated by June 2006. It also checked the services' forecasts for the rest of the year. Past GAO work had faulted the reliability of war cost data. This report tracks steps taken to fix those flaws.

By June 2006, the services had obligated about $51.6 billion, or 55 percent of the funds. Personnel and operations spending ran within the year's funding levels. The Army ran hot on personnel costs, driven by recruiting bonuses and death benefits. It planned to shift about $591 million from other accounts to cover the gap. Large multiyear procurement funds would likely roll into fiscal year 2007. GAO suggested Congress require year-end data on those balances. The Defense Department disagreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-276:
Brain injury screening for war veterans is reviewed in GAO report GAO-08-276 (February 8, 2008). Blasts from roadside bombs have made traumatic brain injury a signature wound of the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. Mild cases can be hard to spot. Left unfound, they can shadow a veteran for years. The veterans' department has set up screening for these troops.

GAO describes how the screening works in practice. It traces the steps that follow for veterans flagged at risk, from full evaluation to treatment. It studied nine medical centers for the review. Screening and evaluation are in place, the title reports. Hard challenges remain in catching every case.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-76:
Who pays for air traffic control, and how much, turns on how costs get split among users. The aviation agency assigned its fiscal year 2005 costs to user groups in a January 2007 study. GAO-08-76, dated October 19, 2007, checks that method against federal cost standards.

The main design fits the standards and world guidance, GAO found. But some choices and guesses need stronger proof and clearer write-ups. Users cannot judge the split without them. GAO also warns that adding planned capital costs to the base can skew the shares. It urges the agency to track gaps between first splits and real costs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-976:
In September 2008, report GAO-08-976 looked at how the Veterans Health Administration books advance estimates for goods and care it plans to buy. Such entries, called miscellaneous obligations, totaled over $6.9 billion in fiscal year 2007. Most paid for medical care by outside providers, plus drugs and medicines. Rules for who may approve them were the core question.

GAO found the rules poorly built. They gave contract staff too little oversight, let one person both set up and approve entries, and asked for weak proof of need. Checks at medical centers in Pittsburgh, Cheyenne, and Kansas City showed the same flaws. The report lists steps to tighten control and cut the risk of fraud and waste.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-1-1776:
Edward Gibbon published Volume 1 of The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire in 1776. Gibbon tells the story of Rome from its height under the Antonines to the age of Constantine. Armies, emperors, frontiers, and the rise of Christianity fill the narrative. His irony and learning made the book an instant classic.

Famous chapters on early Christianity blamed the new faith in part for Rome's decay. Churchmen attacked him, and Gibbon replied with relish. The prose is stately, balanced, and often quietly mocking. Many call the History the greatest work of history in English. Volume 1 alone would secure Gibbon's fame.
gill-myths-and-songs-from-the-south-paci:
William Wyatt Gill collected Myths and Songs from the South Pacific in 1876 from his years as a missionary in the Cook Islands. Mangaian traditions fill the volume: creation, the gods, and Avaiki, the underworld beneath the sea. Songs in native verse, Englished by Gill, carry the tales as the islanders themselves sang them.

Gill wrote down what elders told him before the old religion faded from living memory. Heroes, cannibal gods, and voyages of the soul pass in strange, splendid procession. The book remains a first source on Polynesian myth, gathered at the last moment it could be.
gray-darwiniana-1876:
Asa Gray was America's leading botanist and Darwin's chief ally across the Atlantic. His Darwiniana, from 1876, collects the essays and reviews he wrote as evolution fought for a hearing. Gray knew Darwin's work before most Americans did.

Gray explains natural selection in clear terms and answers its critics one by one. He also argues that faith and evolution need not clash, a view Darwin himself welcomed. The reviews trace the debate from the first shock of the Origin to wider acceptance. They show science being argued out in public, in real time. Gray wrote as both a working scientist and a man of faith.
hansard-suez-canal-shares-1876:
The House of Commons took up the Suez Canal share deal in its supply debate of February 14, 1876. Hansard holds the whole talk, word for word, in its record of that day. The deal had been struck in haste in the fall of 1875, with Rothschild cash.

The Prime Minister's men tell the House that the Rothschilds paid the Khedive near four million pounds at once. The price on the record is 3,976,582 pounds, with a fee of two and a half per cent. The debate is the chief first hand record of a deal that gave Britain a stake in Suez.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
Chapters forty-one and forty-two of John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands open a new reign. The death of Queen Elizabeth ends the old alliance's personal bond. Legations go to James I from Spain and the provinces alike. Motley then shifts the scene to Ostend, where the siege enters its famous third year.

The Marquis Spinola takes command of the besieging army in this portion. The Genoese banker-general undertook to furnish the money himself, Motley explains, on condition of supreme command. His family's wealth and credit with Genoa's money-lenders made the extraordinary bargain possible. Discontent among the unpaid troops complicates his task. The chapter introduces the last great Spanish commander of the war. Spinola's purse, as much as his sword, would bring the republic to the truce table.
io-chrysippi-faniani-de-arte-metallicae-:
Joannes Chrysippus Fanianus wrote De Arte Metallicae Metamorphoseos, printed at Basel in 1576. The single book claims to describe all that belongs to the work of the philosopher's stone, most openly. A second part gathers judgments of old authors and lawyers. Their question is whether alchemy is a lawful art.

Fire must be gentle and mild at the start, the Latin text warns. Too strong a fire binds matter rather than dissolving it. The making of calx, or lime, needs that care. Fanianus joins practice to law, asking courts to judge the art as well as furnaces.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abbasi-jacob-be:
Jacob ben Moses ibn Abbasi was a translator and scholar who flourished in the second half of the thirteenth century at Huesca, in Spain. His father was Moses ibn Abbasi the Martyr. About 1298 Jacob turned Maimonides' commentary on Seder Nashim from Arabic into Hebrew. Solomon ben Adret, the top Talmudic authority of the time, praised the work in a letter Jacob placed at its head.

In his preface Jacob draws a sharp line between two kinds of knowledge. Worldly knowledge is bounded by the limits of the human mind. The study of the Law, by contrast, stands open to every person. His Hebrew is judged weak but clear, and he left no Arabic word standing untranslated, unlike the translators of the other parts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abiel-father-is: Abiel was the father of Kish and of Ner, and so the grandfather of Saul, by First Samuel. A second account in Chronicles makes him Saul's great-grandfather instead. In that form, Ner is the father of Kish, not his brother. The entry lays the clash to a slip by a scribe. A second Abiel also stands in the entry. He was one of the thirty men of David, in First Chronicles. In Second Samuel the same man is called Abi-Albon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-abraham:
Abraham Abraham was an English author and communal worker who died at Liverpool on March 31, 1863. He lived in that city for forty years. For thirty of them he led in Jewish affairs, held synagogue posts, and headed the Philanthropic Institution and the Jewish school.

Trade kept him busy, yet he still found time for study and writing. His chief mark came from pushing regular English sermons in synagogue worship. A pulpit rose at Liverpool in 1827, and the plan spread to other towns, then London. He also turned French works into books of moral tales for young Jewish readers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-jos: Abraham ben Joseph Solomon Hahazan was a Karaite rabbi at Koslov, now Eupatoria in the Crimea. He served in the first half of the nineteenth century. His father, Joseph Solomon, taught him Karaite writing and science, and Abraham followed him in the rabbinate. Six Hebrew poems by him sit in the Karaite Liturgy, Vienna edition. A poem there honors Simha Bobowich, head of the Koslov community. In it he calls himself Ibn Yashar, from his father's name in initials.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adda-776: Adda is a name shared by two amoraim with no added family name. The elder was a Palestinian of the first line, in the third century. He worked alongside R. Jonathan. The younger learned under Raba. He lived in the days of R. Ashi. The hosted text is brief. It sorts the two men by land, by age, and by the teachers and peers named with each. It gives no sayings of either man and no works under the name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-afendopolo-cale:
Caleb Afendopolo was a Karaite scholar of wide learning. He was born at Adrianople before 1430. He died about 1499 at Constantinople. He was a brother-in-law and pupil of Elijah Bashyatzi. He learned science under Mordecai Comtino. He taught in private for his bread, by one account. His large library held rare scripts, bought and copied by his own hand.

In 1490 his teacher left him a work on Karaite law to finish. Afendopolo took it up but died with it still undone. His own chief work is "Gan ha-Melek," finished in 1495. It is a set of poems and essays on love, medicine, and the mind. He wrote guides to two great Karaite books. He wrote talks on Passover, the Song of Songs, and Psalm cxix. His first discourse treats the split between Karaites and Rabbinites and the points at stake.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahijah-the-prop:
Ahijah the prophet came from Shiloh. He told Jeroboam that he would become king. Later he foretold the fall of Jeroboam's house and of the kingdom of Israel. The entry notes that both tales may come from a set of prophet stories by various hands.

Rabbinic tradition made him one of seven long-lived saints. Their lives, linked in a chain, span the whole history of mankind. Ahijah, in this view, lived more than six hundred years. He took the sacred lore from an earlier saint and passed it on. The same tradition explains his part in raising Jeroboam. Idolatrous friends tricked him into signing their paper, it says. He trusted his pupil, and his trust proved a kind of blindness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-albas-samuel-10: Samuel Albas was a rabbi at Fez, born in 1697 and dead in 1749. He was well read in the Talmud and in rabbinical writing. Contemporaries such as Hayyim ibn Atar held him in high esteem. He wrote novellae on the treatise 'Abodah Zarah of the Babylonian Talmud. Those notes have never been printed, and they exist only in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexandrians-in:
The Alexandrians in Jerusalem were Jews from Alexandria who settled in the holy city for good. Close ties bound Alexandria's Jews to Palestine, and many made the move. In Egypt they had heard the synagogue service in Greek. They had also picked up customs of their own. So in Jerusalem they formed a separate community. They built a synagogue for themselves.

Two witnesses support this. The Book of Acts names a synagogue of the Libertines, Cyrenians, and Alexandrians, among others, in its account of the young Christian congregation. Rabbinical sources add a plainer proof. Rabbi Eleazar, son of Zadok, bought a synagogue of the Alexandrians in Jerusalem. A Babylonian passage speaks of another such synagogue, but its wording is disputed. The entry holds that the Tosefta and the Jerusalem Talmud give the reading to trust.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-almanza-aron-de:
Aron de Almanza was a Marano born at Salamanca in Spain. His parents were Jews. His first wife brought a large dowry in 1696. The sum ran to 70,000 florins in money alone. Jewels worth 19,000 florins came with it. After her death he wed a Christian woman.

He moved to England in time. In 1703 he printed an account of his change of faith. The book came out in English and Spanish. It was addressed to the bishop of London. In it he struck hard at his former faith. A note at the end fights a London rumor. The rumor held that he had been a Catholic in Spain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ambron-shabbeth:
Shabbethai Ambron was a writer on the scheme of the world. He lived in Rome early in the eighteenth century. His life work bore the grand title Pancosmosophia. In it he set out to refute three great star men. Ptolemy, Copernicus, and Tycho Brahe all came under his fire. His own scheme held that the earth was flat.

He backed that claim with Jewish lore. He had made some hundred copper plates for the book. Rome then barred the work from the press. A send to Venice met the same block. A German printer pledged to print it, yet never did. The draft and plates are lost to view.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antibla-1576:
Antibla was a family of proselytes living at Jerusalem in the first century before the common era. They had once been rich, then fell into poverty. Four Talmudic passages mention them, with the family name spelled in corrupted forms.

Unable to keep their old standard of life, they planned to emigrate. Jewish leaders, glad to welcome converts in that age, did not want them driven off by want. The case went to the rabbis, who awarded the family a sum of support. One passage gives 600 talents of gold, which the entry calls hard to believe. Another gives 600 gold shekels, about 2,000 dollars, and the entry finds that figure more likely.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aquin-louis-hen: Louis Henri d'Aquin, also called Aquinas and Aquino, was a writer and translator of the seventeenth century, son of Philippe d'Aquin. He was converted to Christianity at Aquino, in the kingdom of Naples. He left many works on Hebrew language and letters. Among them was a Latin version of the commentary on Esther by Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, with added extracts from the Talmud and Yalkut, printed at Paris in 1622. He also turned the first four chapters of Levi ben Gerson on Job into Latin, at Paris in 1623.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arithmetic-1776:
Reckoning, the entry notes, was familiar to the ancient Hebrews, whose sacred books name large sums and even fractions. Like the Greeks, they used the letters of their alphabet as figures. Letters in order stood for units, tens, and hundreds up to 400. Later, final letter forms were added, raising the range to 900, though the entry says they seem not to have been widely used.

From that base the account moves to named Jewish arithmeticians. Skilled figures appear by the eighth century, among them Sahl Rabban al-Tabari. About 997 Bisher ben Pinhas ben Shubeib wrote a treatise on reckoning. Josephus Hispanus is linked to the spread of Arabic numerals in Europe. Abraham ben Hiyya and Abraham ibn Ezra follow, Ezra's Sefer ha-Mispar being the oldest Jewish arithmetic still extant. About twenty such treatises survive in Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asaph-mar-rab-1: Mar Rab Asaph, to judge by his title, was one of the Geonim, the heads of the Babylonian academies. He seems to have lived about the middle of the ninth century. His name turns up in a fragment from the Cairo Genizah, possibly written by Judah ben Barzilai of Barcelona. He may match an Asaph named among the transmitters of the Massorah traditions, though the entry warns that a misprint may lurk in that text. No ground links him to the physician Asaph.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-judah:
Judah ben Joseph Ashkenazi was a Turkish Talmudist. Born at Smyrna, he rose to be chief rabbi of that city and died there about 1812. Four books of his are listed, all printed at Salonica. The first, Mahneh Yehudah, Judah's Camp, came out in 1793 and argues points in the Tur and in the Hoshen Mishpat section of Bet Joseph.

The later books followed after his death. Yad Yehudah, Judah's Hand, of 1816 gives notes on Shebuot and parts of Megillah, Yoma, Pesahim, and Baba Batra. Gebul Yehudah, of 1821, treats Gittin, Ketubot, and Baba Kamma. Kehal Yehudah, of 1825, holds new readings on the Yoreh Deah and several Talmudic treatises. The entry also points readers to Raphael ben Judah Ashkenazi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-atel-idl-itil-e:
Atel was the capital of the Chazars in the tenth century. It stood about eight English miles from Astrakhan, under mounds on the right bank of the Volga. Arabic writers place it about sixty miles from the river's mouth. Its western part had a wall with four gates. The ruler, the ḥakam, lived there in the city's only brick building, a palace.

Most people in Atel lived in huts or felt tents. The eastern part, Khazaran, held merchants of many nations. Muslims, Christians, and Jews all lived in the city. The ḥakan and his court were Jews, and his suite numbered fully 4,000 persons. In 969 the Russians destroyed the city. The entry draws its picture chiefly from Arab writers such as Mas'udi and Ibn Ḥaukal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-avila-samuel-be:
Samuel ben Moses ben Isaac de Avila was a rabbi and preacher. He served at Mequenez in Morocco, then at Salé. He was born at Mequenez in 1687 or 1688. His book "Ozen Shemuel" gathers his sermons. Five treat repentance, preached before the Day of Atonement. Ten treat the Sabbaths of the Lord, preached before Passover and the feasts. Sixteen are funeral speeches for men of his own time.

The sermon book was printed at Amsterdam in 1715, with approvals from three rabbis. Samuel also published "Keter Torah," The Crown of the Law, at Amsterdam in 1725. That work pleads for freeing scholars from taxes. It gathers older rules on the same point, sets out rules for conduct, and adds notes on Rashi and on the treatise Nazir.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baba-ben-buta-2:
Baba ben Buṭa was a teacher of the Law in the time of Herod. He may have belonged to the family called the Sons of Baba. That family resisted the surrender of Jerusalem to Herod in 37 B.C. and hid from his wrath for ten years. A Talmudic tradition tells a different survival. In it, Baba alone of the teachers was spared by Herod.

The tradition, which the entry prints at length, brings the blinded teacher and the king face to face. Herod, not naming himself, asks Baba to curse a wicked slave, meaning himself. Baba refuses at every turn, citing verses against cursing kings, the rich, and rulers. When Herod at last owns who he is, he asks how such a man can repair his wrong. Baba's answer points him to rebuilding the Temple, in atonement for his crimes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baja-2376:
Baja is a city on the Danube in Hungary, busy with trade by the end of the eighteenth century. Jewish families settled there toward the middle of that century. A fire on May 1, 1840, burned the synagogue, the school, and the community records, so its first years are dim. The oldest entries in the burial society book date to March 6, 1791.

The entry names the early rabbis in turn. Meïr Ash gave up the post in 1815 so his friend Götz Schwerin could have it, and the community grew under Schwerin. The 1840 fire left all but three members destitute and 2,000 houses in ruins. Schwerin raised funds far and wide, and a new synagogue was dedicated Sept. 26, 1845, with a modern order of service. Schools and charities close the account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barabas-2476:
Barabas is the chief figure in Christopher Marlowe's play "The Rich Jew of Malta." It was first staged at the Rose Theater, Bankside, London, in 1591. Edward Alleyn created the role. A revival at Drury Lane in 1818, with Edmund Kean, failed to please. The entry calls Barabas an inhuman fiend with rare lapses into humanity, marked by cunning, vengeance, and a lust for gold.

Stripped of his wealth by Malta's governor, Barabas sends his daughter Abigail, feigning conversion, into his old home to fetch his hidden hoard. Then the murders pile up: two lovers set to duel by a forged letter, the nuns poisoned, two friars killed or framed, and blackmailers poisoned by flowers. Taken and left for dead, he betrays the city to the Turks and is made governor. His last trap, a floor over boiling oil, catches him instead when the rope is cut.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baruch-jacob-25: Jacob Baruch was president ("Baumeister") of the Jewish congregation of Frankfort-on-the-Main at the beginning of the nineteenth century, and father of Ludwig Börne. His father had been financial agent of the elector of Cologne. Contemporaries called Jacob "a man of sense, a courtier, sometimes orthodox, sometimes modern." In October, 1814, the community chose him as its representative at the Congress of Vienna, carrying a memorial on the rights of Frankfort's Jews. The community offered him 8,000 gulden for his services, and he refused.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bausk-or-bauske:
Bausk is a district town in Courland, Russia, counted in the census of 1897 at 6,543 people. About three thousand of them were Jews. Their chief work was trade and crafts, with 295 Jewish artisans named in the count.

The entry notes schools, a Talmud Torah, and aid for about 150 poor families at Passover. It then lists six rabbis of the town across the nineteenth century. The last named, in office from 1895, is Abraham Isaac Kook. A famed cantor and a medal winning teacher close the account. Two schools under government control and three private schools served the town, beside private teachers at home.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-behrend-israel-:
Israel Behrend was a German physician and medical writer born at Wittenburg in 1804. He died at Rostock on March 13, 1867. He took his medical degree at Rostock in 1827 and practiced in that city for forty years, building a large practice there.

His chief works treat a remedy against cholera in 1831 and a settled fever in 1853. Essays on homeopathy and facial pain ran in leading journals. Behrend also wrote in 1843 on the Jews of Mecklenburg and their claim to equal civil rights. His cholera book still holds value for its picture of care in that early year, as the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-michae: Michael Henry Benjamin, a South African politician, was born in London in 1822 and died on June 11, 1879. About 1849 he went to Cape Colony and spent ten years at Graaff-Reinet, where he promoted useful bodies. He then moved to Port Elizabeth and spoke for it in the Cape assembly from 1864. He pushed a courts bill, brought in a stamp act, and helped found a bank. Back in England from about 1869, he worked for many Jewish communal bodies in London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beryl-3176: Beryl is a stone that ranges from blue to pale yellow. The entry says it is found all over the world. It names three kinds of the stone. They are beryl, aquamarine, and emerald. In Exodus, beryl held a place on the high priest's breastplate. It stood first on the fourth row. The entry also lists later mentions. Ezekiel and Daniel both name it in vision passages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bick-jacob-samu: Jacob Samuel Bick was an Austrian author. He died at Brody in 1831. He wrote satire with force and skill. He was a leading pioneer of the haskalah. That movement spread culture among Galician Jews. His essays pleaded for secular knowledge and industry. Like other Maskilim, he favored farm work for Jews. Cholera killed him in 1831. His manuscripts burned four years later. A great fire at Brody destroyed them. Contemporaries mourned that loss deeply.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blindness-3376:
Blindness presents statistics on blindness among Jews. Rates run higher for Jews than neighbors. In Bavaria Jews showed 13.81 blind per 10,000. Protestants there showed only 7.84. Prussia in 1880 showed a similar gap. Congenital blindness also ran higher among Jews. The United States shows little Jewish blindness. Strict immigration bars explain that, the entry says.

Causes puzzle the entry's author. Newborn infection drives much blindness elsewhere. That cause is rarer among Jewish mothers. So lower Jewish rates might be expected. Consanguineous marriage was blamed by some writers. Careful investigators reject that explanation. Eye diseases and heredity carry the weight instead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boil-3476:
Boil renders the Hebrew word shehin, from a root meaning to warm. The entry says the word marks an inflamed spot. In the Bible it names two forms of disease, both with painful swelling and discharge.

One form is the simple boil, limited to one spot and not catching. The other is the eruption linked with elephantiasis, a form of leprosy. Job's sore boils are placed with the second form. Leviticus gives priests tests for hard cases. A white-haired, sunken scar meant leprosy, while no spread in seven days meant clean.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-born-gustav-jac:
Gustav Jacob Born was a German histologist and medical author born at Kempen on April 22, 1851. He studied at Breslau, Bonn, Strasburg, and Berlin. He took his medical degree at Breslau in 1876.

Born rose at Breslau from assistant prosector to professor in 1898. His chair joined histology with comparative anatomy. New methods in microscopy and embryology made his name known. One method rebuilt small body parts in enlarged plastic form. He wrote about fifty essays and works. His chief work, on grafting experiments with amphibian larvae, came out at Leipsic in 1897. That same year he received the Prussian Order of the Red Eagle of the fourth class.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-breier-eduard-3: Eduard Breier was an Austrian writer born at Warasdin in Croatia on Nov. 3, 1811. He died at Zaiwitz near Znaim on June 3, 1886. His first novel, written in eleven days on furlough as an artilleryman, appeared in 1840. Its success turned him to journalism and fiction for good. He edited the Prager Zeitung till it was suppressed in 1848. In Vienna he became a popular writer of Jewish and Austrian tales. Wien und Rom and Kaiser Joseph are named as his most characteristic works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brussels-french:
Brussels, capital of Belgium, has no record of when Jews first settled there. The entry supposes they came soon after the city's founding in the seventh century. Jews there shared the fortunes of Belgian Jews in general. Crusaders left bloody marks, yet under later rulers the community prospered in the thirteenth century.

Disaster came in 1370, when a stolen host charge led to burnings and banishment, remembered as the miracle of St. Gudule. No trace of Jews appears again until after the Peace of Utrecht in 1713. Banishment decrees in 1716 and later were not enforced. Free settlement came only after 1794 under French rule. The entry follows chief rabbis and lists the city's many Jewish charities, schools, and aid societies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-byron-george-go:
George Gordon, Lord Byron, was an English poet born in London on Jan. 22, 1788. He died at Missolonghi, Greece, on April 19, 1824. The entry treats only one part of his work: the Hebrew Melodies. Those lyrics are the sole Byron work tied to Jewish topics. He wrote them in 1814 to please his friend Douglas Kinnaird.

The melodies were set to music by Isaac Nathan, drawn from airs sung in Jewish worship. The entry judges them uneven: some have little that is Hebrew at all. She Walks in Beauty came from a ball, not a Bible scene. Others, like Oh Weep for Those, strike it as truly Jewish in subject. Byron himself was never pleased with the set and joked about it to Moore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cantarini-3976: Cantarini was a noted family of Italian Jews whose line the entry traces to one small child. Gherescion Cantarini, at one year old, was driven from his home town of Asolo. He was taken to Padua in 1547. There his descendants led the Jewish community for the next 300 years. The entry itself is only an introduction. It promises a sketch pedigree of the best known members and then stops. Separate entries in the encyclopedia carry the single lives.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carregal-carega:
Raphael Ḥayyim Isaac Carregal, a traveling rabbi and preacher, was born in Hebron, Palestine, on Oct. 15, 1733. Ordained at seventeen, he set out in 1754 on long voyages. Stays included two years in Constantinople, two in Curaçao, two and a half in London, and a year in North America. He died at Barbados on May 5, 1777.

At Newport, Rhode Island, in 1773, Carregal formed a close friendship with Ezra Stiles, later president of Yale. They studied together, argued over Messianic passages, and wrote to each other, mostly in Hebrew. Stiles left a warm, detailed memoir of his friend in his diary. Carregal seems to have printed only two brochures, both sermons issued at Newport in 1773.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chuetas-pork-ea:
Chuetas, a name meaning pork-eaters, was forced on the descendants of secret Jews in Majorca. To pass as good Christians they ate pork in public while staying loyal to Judaism in private. Neighbors shunned them. At church they sat apart, and even their dead lay apart in the cemetery, the entry says.

When the Inquisition reached Majorca in 1488 it first offered amnesty, taking back 680 people for a heavy fine. Burnings began in 1509. A failed escape by sea ended in 1691 with more than fifty people garroted and burned. Relief came only with a royal decree of Dec. 16, 1782. Their descendants, the entry closes, now hold respected places on the island.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-henri-447:
Henri Cohen, a French composer and numismatist, was born at Amsterdam in 1805 and died at Bry-sur-Marne on May 17, 1880. His parents moved to France in 1811 and gave him fine music training. He studied harmony with Reicha and singing with Lois and Pellegrini. Stays at Rome in 1832 and 1838 produced two stage works.

Settled in Paris from 1839, he taught and sang at concerts with success. A directorship at the Lille Conservatoire ended in friction with the administration. Back in Paris he directed the Cabinet des Medailles at the Bibliotheque Nationale and published on coins and bibliography. His music includes the lyric poem Marguerite et Faust of 1847 and a harmony treatise praised by Fetis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cross-4776:
Cross carries two senses in this entry. The first is the stake used by the Romans at crucifixion. Jews of New Testament times spoke often of men carrying their cross to execution. The second sense is the Christian symbol itself. Jews called it warp and woof, or simply an idol. Law on its use turns on worship. A cross worshiped by Christians counts as an idol and is barred.

A cross worn as a plain ornament, with no religious aim, may be used. Still, Jews have shunned the sign as a Christian emblem. Pious Jews refused badges that bore it. Liberal Jews wore the Iron Cross as soldiers. Jewish artists could embroider crosses on dresses for Christian ladies, one ruling holds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-daniel-hayyata-: Daniel Ḥayyaṭa, the Tailor, was a Palestinian teacher. Only two of his readings of Scripture survive in the Midrash. One treats a verse in Genesis, on the herdsmen of Isaac. The other treats a verse in Ecclesiastes, on the tears of the oppressed. His time can only be guessed. The rabbis named around him belong to the third and fourth centuries. The teacher cited after him, who builds on his views, is of the fourth generation of amoraim. So Daniel can not be placed earlier than that generation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-samuel-49:
Samuel David was a French musician born in Paris on November 12, 1836, and he died there on October 3, 1895. He studied at the Conservatoire under Bazin and Halévy. In 1858 he won the Grand Prix de Rome for his cantata "Jephtha." In 1872 he became musical director in the synagogues of Paris.

David composed a string of operas and operettas performed in Paris, among them "La Peau de l'Ours" and "La Fée des Bruyères." His ode-symphonie "Le Triomphe de la Paix," from 1878, was his most popular work. He also wrote four symphonies, choruses, songs, and several operas that were never performed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dembo-isaac-507:
Isaac Dembo was a Russian physician born at Poneviezh, in the government of Kovno, in 1846. He studied Hebrew and rabbinical books until age fourteen, then turned to secular study. He took his medical degree at St. Petersburg in 1870. He served in hospitals and in the army during the Russo-Turkish war, winning a medal.

Dembo became known for a study of ritual slaughter. Campaigns in Switzerland and Germany sought to ban the Jewish method as cruel. After comparing methods in Russia and abroad, Dembo concluded the Jewish method caused less pain than any other. Leading scientists agreed with him. He published his findings in two German books at Leipsic in 1894.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dick-isaac-maye:
Isaac Mayer Dick was a Russian Hebraist and novelist born in Wilna in 1808. His father, a cantor, gave him a Talmudic schooling, and a Catholic priest secretly taught him German. He also learned Russian and Polish. In 1841 he became Hebrew teacher in the new government school for Jewish boys in Wilna.

Dick helped found a reform-minded synagogue in Wilna and argued for lifting up Russia's Jews. In later years the Romm publishing house paid him a small weekly wage to write Yiddish stories. Those tales, of many sizes, are said to number nearly three hundred. He was famed as a wit far beyond Wilna. He died there on January 24, 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-duty-hebr-mizwa:
Duty is what a person owes to God, to other people, and to himself. In Hebrew it is mizwah, commandment, and later hobah, obligation. The word itself is too abstract for the Bible, the entry says. Its idea runs through the Bible in other forms.

Micah sums duty up as doing justice, loving kindness, and walking humbly with God. Philo makes man's highest duty the imitation of God. Jewish tradition grounds every duty in the Law as God's fixed will. Thinkers split duties into acts of the body and duties of the heart. The entry warns that viewing each rite as a debt can harden into legalism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eichenbaum-jaco:
Jacob Eichenbaum was a Russian educator, poet, and mathematician. He pioneered modern schooling among Russian Jews. He was born at Krasnopolie, Galicia, on Oct. 12, 1796. He died at Kiev on Dec. 27, 1861. His father helped him master mathematics early.

At Zamoscz Eichenbaum joined a circle of progressive young Jews. He read the Bible rationally and studied Hebrew, German, and philosophy. In 1819 he rendered Euclid's Elements into Hebrew for his own use. Years of tutoring in rich houses followed. In 1835 he opened a modern Jewish school at Odessa. His Hebrew poems, Kol Zimrah, appeared at Leipsic in 1836.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-of-york-: Elijah of York was a tosafist in England. Men suppose he died in the York massacre of 1190. Old glosses call him by a place name read as York. That town was Eboracum in Latin in his day. The word the Saint stands after his name in one gloss. That word marks a martyr in most cases, the entry notes. From it men infer he fell in the killings. He learned under Isaac ha-Zaken as a pupil. Samuel ben Solomon may have taught him as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-enoch-ben-judah: Enoch ben Judah Lob was a German Talmudist and rabbi. He served the town of Schnaittach as its rabbi. His time was the start of the eighteenth century. He studied with his father and with Abraham Broda. His own writings do not stand alone in print. They are bound in with works of his father and grandfather. Two books of responsa hold that shared matter. One of them came out in the year 1708. No life facts beyond his studies are given here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-esthonia-5876: Esthonia was a government of Russia and one of its three Baltic provinces, the entry says in a very short notice. Its total population in 1897 was 404,709, of whom 1,468 were Jews. The province lay outside the Pale of Settlement. Jews began settling there only in the last quarter of the nineteenth century. Those who came were artisans and others with special privilege. The entry gives no towns, institutions, or named persons. Its whole content is the province's status, the 1897 counts, and that late start to settlement.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fadl-da-ud-abu-: Da'ud Abu al-Fadl was a Karaite physician born at Cairo in 1161 and dead there about 1242. He studied medicine under two Jewish doctors named in the entry. He became court physician to Sultan Al-Malik al-Adil, brother and heir of Saladin. He also served as chief teacher at Cairo's Al-Nasiri hospital. One pupil, the historian Ibn Abi Usaibi'ah, called him the most skillful doctor of the age, with near-miraculous cures. His one named work is an Arabic drug book in twelve chapters, chiefly on antidotes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fenyes-fischman: Adolf Fenyes, born Fischmann, was a Hungarian painter born at Kecskemet on April 28, 1867, son of the town's rabbi. He first drew notice as a caricaturist. He then studied law at Budapest for two years, dropped it, and turned to art. He trained at Budapest, Weimar, and Paris. His chief works, prize winners in Paris and Budapest, are named as Prattling, The Quarrel, The Life of the Poor Man, and The Old Man. The entry gives nothing more about his life or later work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frangi-hayyim-s: Ḥayyim Frangi, surnamed Ḥayyim Menahem, was a Turkish rabbinical author born in 1833 at Constantinople. He died there in 1903. He published two Hebrew works of his own. The first holds responsa and sermons in two volumes, printed at Salonica in 1867-83. The second, printed at Constantinople in 1902, gathers his legal decisions. They cover the twenty-five years in which he presided over the rabbinical tribunal. He also edited a work of one of his teachers, Eliezer of Toledo. It came out in two volumes in 1853.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedlander-lud:
Ludwig Friedländer was a German scholar of the classics, born at Königsberg on July 16, 1824. He studied at Königsberg and Leipsic from 1841 to 1845. In 1847 he began to teach classical language study at Königsberg. He became assistant professor in 1856 and full professor in 1858. In 1892 he retired to Strasburg, where he is an honorary professor. His chief work shows Roman manners from Augustus to the last of the Antonines.

It filled three volumes between 1862 and 1871. The entry calls it one of the finest works of its kind in its century. It was turned into French, Italian, and Hungarian. He also edited Martial, the feast of Trimalchio, and Juvenal, with notes. He has embraced Christianity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-galina-moses-be: Moses ben Elijah Galina, a Greek scholar and translator who lived at Candia in the fifteenth century, is best known for Toledot Adam, printed at Constantinople in 1515. That work treats palm reading and face reading. It draws chiefly on Ali ibn Abbas and on a book ascribed to Aristotle. A shorter form later came out with a Judeo-German version. Galina also put Arabic works on stars and on geomancy into Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goldziher-ignaz:
Ignaz Goldziher was a Hungarian Orientalist. He was born in Stuhlweissenburg on June 22, 1850. He studied at Budapest, Berlin, Leipsic, and Leyden. He took his doctorate in 1870. In 1873 the Hungarian government sent him through Syria, Palestine, and Egypt. He spent months at Cairo's Azhar mosque hearing its sheiks lecture. In 1894 Budapest made him full professor. He was the first Jew admitted to its faculty.

His fame rests on a critical history of Arabic traditions. His "Muhammedanische Studien" gave that field its base. He also set Islam's theological movements in their true light. Ancient Arabic poetry was another strength. For Jewish science he traced Hebrew myth in the Bible. He compared Jewish and Arabic folk-lore of the Middle Ages as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gregory-xiii-ug:
Gregory XIII, born Ugo Buoncompagni, was pope from 1572 to 1585. He was born at Bologna on Feb. 7, 1502. He died at Rome on April 10, 1585. The entry paints him as kindly by nature but warped by intolerance. He let Jews return to Venaissin after their 1569 banishment. In 1581 he gave Jews safe-conduct through Italy. He also lifted the ban on interest.

His hostile acts were many. In 1578 he made Rome's Jews pay 1,100 scudi for the converts' home. In 1581 he barred Jewish doctors from Christian patients. That year he ordered all Talmud copies surrendered to inquisitors. In 1584 he forced Jews to hear missionary sermons each Saturday in their own synagogues.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-habakkuk-book-o:
The Book of Habakkuk is one of the twelve minor prophetical books. It falls readily into two parts: chapters one and two, then chapter three. The first part is a massa, a condemning prophecy, cast as a dialogue. The second part is a psalm.

In the dialogue the prophet laments moral corruption, hears God announce judgment through the Chaldeans, and protests the enemy's pride and cruelty. God answers that evil will not triumph and lists five woes against the oppressor. Chapter three sings of God's warlike power over earth, rivers, sun, and moon. The entry stresses the book's striking images and its core question: why God tolerates tyranny and wrong.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-haidamacks-1457:
The Haidamacks were Russian brigand bands of the eighteenth century. In a disordered Poland, Greek Orthodox peasants and Cossacks formed bands of runaway serfs, Saporogians, and Cossacks from Russian Ukraine. Stirred by priests, they struck at their Catholic masters, the Polish nobles, and at the Jews. In 1734 and again in 1750 they sacked towns across Kiev, Volhynia, and Podolia, killing many Jews and nobles.

The worst blow fell in 1768. A forged decree in Catherine II's name, ordering the killing of Jews and Poles, was spread abroad. Under Zhelyeznyak the bands swept the Kiev region. At Uman, the Cossack Gonta betrayed the city's trust and joined the attackers. Jews and Poles fought side by side on the walls, then died together in the streets and the synagogue. About twenty thousand Jews and Poles were killed at Uman alone.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halafta-of-kefa: Ḥalafta of Kefar Hananiah was a tanna of the second century, junior to R. Meïr. In Meïr's name he hands down a maxim about conditions: a condition stated before the duty it hangs on is valid, but a duty stated first voids the condition. The Mishnah, at Abot iii. 6, keeps his homily on how many persons make a quorum for study of the Law. In the prayer-book Abot he is named R. Ḥalafta b. Dosa of Kefar Hananiah, though some copies drop the father's name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hananeel-ben-am: Hananeel b. Amittai was the spiritual leader of the Jewish community of Oria, in Italy, in the ninth century. He is said to descend from a Jerusalem family carried to Italy by Titus. The Ahimaaz Chronicle credits him with great learning and piety. It also says he was deep in the secret knowledge of Cabala, through which he worked miracles. The same chronicle tells of a disputation he held with the Archbishop of Oria. The brief entry rests on Neubauer and Kaufmann and adds no works or dates for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hart-hebr-ayyal:
Hart treats the deer named by the Hebrew word ayyal, listed in Deuteronomy among clean animals fit for food. Deer of this kind were served at Solomon's table. The entry admits that the exact species once common in Palestine cannot now be fixed. The fallow deer is offered as a likely match.

Much of the piece gathers Bible images built on the animal. The hart stands for speed, grace, and tender care of young. One psalm uses its thirst for water as a picture of longing. Talmudic notes add facts about antlers, hunting with nets, and skin used for parchment. A proverb about money placed on a hart's horn warns of a bad venture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-ben-isra: Hayyim ben Israel was a Spanish philosopher and author who lived at Toledo about 1272 to 1277. He came from the Israeli family. He was kin to Isaac Israeli, who wrote a noted work on astronomy called "Yesod Olam." Hayyim's own known work is a treatise on paradise. It survives only in manuscript. The entry is very brief, just a few lines. It gives no birth or death dates and names no other writings by him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hefker-7476:
Hefker is ownerless property under Jewish law. Property becomes hefker in set ways. An owner may renounce it in front of three men. A court may declare it so. The goods of a convert who dies without Jewish heirs also fall in this class. Things found in seas, rivers, or deserts count as ownerless too.

The first person to take hold of such property gains it. A renunciation must be open to all, not limited to one class such as the poor. If no one claims the goods in three days, the old owner may take back the renunciation. The article sets out how taking works, and how hefker differs from land held by long use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-henschel-elias-:
Elias H. Henschel, born at Breslau on April 4, 1755, began life as an errand-boy and a physician's valet. A professor named Morgenbesser helped him gain support for study. He began anatomy at twenty-five and took his medical degree at Halle in 1787.

Henschel focused on obstetrics and became public accoucheur at Breslau. He helped introduce vaccination in Silesia. He also gave much time to the hospital for the Jewish poor. In 1813 he cared for a lazaretto holding 228 beds. During cholera he published advice for the public in 1831. Other writings covered diseases of pregnant women and newborn care. He died in 1839.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hezir-7676: Hezir is a name the entry gives to two men, listed in numbered order. The first was a priest, chief of the seventeenth monthly course in the Temple service, appointed by David. The second was a layman, one of the heads of the people. He signed the covenant with Nehemiah. The entry rests only on verses from First Chronicles and Nehemiah. It gives no dates, family detail, deeds, or sayings for either man, and no comment beyond the two identifications and their sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hivites-7776:
Hivites were one of the Canaanite nations dispossessed by Israel, the entry states. Their name may mean the villager or the midlander, by two cited scholars. The Hivite is counted as sixth son of Canaan. Hamor, prince of Shechem, was a Hivite.

Shechemites appear in Genesis as peaceful traders and cattle raisers. Later, fearing battle with Joshua's Israelites, Hivites used a trick to win safety, much as Jacob's sons had tricked them. Their four cities are named. The Gibeonites were spared for Joshua's oath. Their main body lay under Mount Hermon toward Hamath, the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-horowitz-isaiah:
Isaiah Horowitz was a German cabalist, rabbi, and author born at Prague about 1555. He died at Safed about 1630. He studied in Cracow and married into a wealthy Vienna family. Money let him give to charity and build a large library. He soon led Jewish communal affairs in Poland.

Horowitz held rabbinates at Dubno, Ostrog, Frankfort, and Prague. In 1621 he moved to Palestine and settled in Jerusalem. A pasha jailed him for ransom in 1625, and he ended his days at Safed. His best known book, Shene Luhot ha-Berit, called the Shelah, sums up Jewish religion, law, and mystic teaching. It stayed popular for centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-illowy-bernhard:
Bernhard Illowy was an American rabbi born at Kolin in Bohemia in 1814. He died near Cincinnati on June 22, 1871. He came of a line of Talmudists and studied at Presburg under Moses Sofer. He took a doctorate at Budapest and studied further at Padua under Luzzatto. Teaching at home gave way to a search abroad for a pulpit.

Illowy crossed to the United States and served at Syracuse, New Orleans, and Cincinnati. He stood as one of Orthodoxy's ablest champions, with deep Talmudic learning and fine command of tongues. He helped call the Cleveland rabbinical conference of 1855, but its Reform leanings blunted his sway. His press pieces, above all in Hirsch's Jeschurun, picture American Judaism of his day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-eisak-ben: Isaac Eisak ben Jacob Haber was rabbi at Tikotzyn and Suwalki, in Poland, in the first half of the nineteenth century. His ritual work "Bet Yitzhak" appeared at Sudzilkow in 1836. He also wrote "Seder Zemannim," on the precepts tied to set dates, printed at Warsaw in 1844. That same year brought his commentary on the Passover haggadah, with notes by his son Joseph. Another work, "Magen we-Zinnah," defended the Cabala against the attacks of Judah de Modena.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israel-isser-be: Israel Isser ben Ze'eb Wolf was a Russian rabbi who lived at Vinnitsa, in Podolia, in the nineteenth century. He wrote "Sha'ar Mishpat," novellae on the Hoshen Mishpat part of the Shulhan Aruk, in two volumes printed at Königsberg in 1860. A second work, "Sha'ar De'ah," treats the laws of interest in the Yoreh De'ah. It was published as an appendix to the first work. The entry gives no dates or posts from his life beyond his town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jaca-hebr-8376:
Jaca is a city of Aragon, in Spain, where Jews lived as early as the eleventh century. The city became the seat of a Jewish high school. Its Jews faced close rules: the king assigned them one city mill for their grain, at a set tax, on top of the usual imposts. In 1281 they had to help pay for mending the town walls, hurt in the French invasion. In 1289 they owed the king 6,000 sueldos toward an expedition against Sicily.

Violence came twice. In the Shepherds' outbreak of 1321, no fewer than 400 Jews of Jaca were killed on July 14. In 1391 Jews there were killed or baptized by force. By 1438 the shrunken community could pay only 200 sueldos in taxes. Two scholars of the late fourteenth century, Seraiah ben Daud and Samuel Almosnino, wrote from Jaca to Isaac ben Sheshet.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacobs-joseph-k: Joseph Jacobs, known as Jacobs the Wizard, was an English conjurer born at Canterbury in 1813. He first appeared in London in 1835, when he presented the Chinese ring trick. At the Strand Theatre in 1841 he won great success with costly apparatus. In 1850 he invented a trick that produced bowls of water with goldfish from under a shawl. He performed in America in 1854 and in Australia and New Zealand in 1860, and died on Oct. 13, 1870.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jekuthiel-ibn-h: Jekuthiel ibn Hasan was a statesman and man of science in the eleventh century who lived in Saragossa. He may be the same man as an astronomer who served as a judge in Cordova and wrote on the stars. At Saragossa he held high office under the emir, and the poet Solomon ibn Gabirol praised his learning, modesty, and kindness as a patron and friend. In a revolt in 1039 the plotters beheaded King Mundhir and Jekuthiel with him. Gabirol mourned him in a poem of more than 200 verses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jezelus-8676: Jezelus is a name that appears twice in the First Book of Esdras, in lists of men who came back from captivity with Ezra. In the first place he is the father of Sechenias, head of a returning family. In the second he is the father of Obadiah, also a chief on the return. The brief entry gives no life for Jezelus himself. It only matches his name across books: in Ezra the first man is called Jahaziel and the second Jehiel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jonathan-ben-uz: Jonathan ben Uzziel was the most noted pupil of Hillel. No legal rulings of his survive, but one tale shows his selflessness. A man whose children had behaved badly left him all his wealth. Jonathan kept one third, gave one third to the sanctuary, and returned one third to the children. Tradition credits him with a version of the Prophets into Aramaic, though scholars doubt the surviving version is his. He is said to have wished to render the Writings too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kalonymus-ben-s:
Kalonymus ben Shabbethai, also called Kalonymus of Rome, was a judge of Jewish law, a Bible scholar, and a poet. He was born at Rome about 1030. His father headed the Jewish community there. Questions of law reached Kalonymus from Worms, Arles, and many other places. His name as a Talmud judge spread far past Italy.

In 1070, after the death of Jacob bar Yaḳar, Kalonymus was called to lead the rabbinate of Worms. He held it until 1096. The entry thinks he fell in the Crusader attacks of that year. With Eleazar ben Judah he ran the rabbinical school of Worms. His Talmud and Bible notes are lost as books. Later writers, Rashi among them, still quote them often.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-key-10076:
The Hebrew word for a key means "the opener." In Bible times a key worked a door bolt, not a lock of the modern kind. The bolt had holes that caught iron points in the door post. The wooden key bore nails in the same pattern. Slid in from the side, it lifted the points and freed the bolt.

The entry reads the old tales by this light. Ehud could bolt Eglon's door from inside with no key. The king's servants needed the key to get in. To bear the key on the shoulder marks high office, as in Isaiah. Four Levites kept the key of the Temple. The Talmud adds a figure of speech. Three keys, it says, God keeps in His own hand: rain, childbirth, and the waking of the dead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-korobka-meat-ta:
