Qinqin Tian and co-authors study a long non-coding RNA that seems to hold back lung squamous cell cancer. The RNA, LINC01936, does not code for a protein. Their 2023 study mines cancer genome atlases for RNAs that shift in this lung cancer. Lab tests then check what the RNA does to cell growth, death, and spread. Path and gene-set tools map the routes it touches.

Cell tests gauge growth with dye assays and spread with chamber assays. Flow checks trace cell death. The title reports the net read: the RNA curbs growth and spread. Two routes are named as likely paths, a shape-shift program in tumor cells and immune cell entry into the tumor. Partner proteins were forecast by a binding tool.
pmc-10710876:
Malan Zhang and co-authors report a 2023 study on who should rate a rehab patient's abilities: one trained rater working alone, or a team. The rating tool is a Chinese version of a world health set built for rehabilitation. The team ran both styles side by side on 193 inpatients at five hospitals in China and scored how well the two agreed.

Both styles took about the same time. Agreement ranged widely by item, from under half to over nine in ten, and the weighted scores ran from fair to near perfect. Most items landed in the strong range. The authors conclude that either style gives valid, steady ratings, so clinics can choose by staffing.
pmc-10712076:
Yan Zhang and three colleagues review machine learning tools that predict death from sepsis, a life-threatening response to infection, in a 2023 paper. Standard risk scores exist, but their forecasts are weak.

The team gathered fifty studies covering one hundred four models. Pooled scores showed solid accuracy in both training and check data, beating the usual clinical scores. Two model families, random forests and gradient boosting, stood out as most reliable. One blood measure, lactate, was used most often as an input, yet standard scores ignore it. The authors urge new tools tuned to each care setting, from emergency rooms to intensive care.
pmc-10714476:
Seda Cinar, Dilek Isik Tasgin, and Canan Unaleroglu published a 2023 study of a switch in chemical synthesis. The same starting materials can end in two kinds of ring. The substituent chosen decides which kind forms. Rings of this family sit at the heart of dyes, drugs, and light-based goods. One ring kind holds four building blocks of one sort and two of another. The other holds three and one.

The team ran the syntheses with a copper salt as the catalyst. They then traced the steps with a sensitive mass spectrometry tool that reads the mixture as the reaction runs. Short-lived intermediate forms showed up in the readings, in two-block and three-block chains. Those intermediates feed the two pre-ring shapes, the team says. The work shows how the starting choice steers the ring, with the pathway read live.
pmc-10714576:
Min Zhang and co-authors build in 2023 a score from full blood counts that grades immune state in fit adults. No firm tool yet grades immune health for well people, a gap the virus years threw into sharp light. Blood counts are cheap and wide spread, so they make a good base.

Counts from more than sixteen thousand fit adults feed the build. A mix model groups immune states, and three tree tools weigh which count traits drive the groups. A weighed sum then gives one immune score per person. The score fell with age in a clear curve, which backs the method.
pmc-10714676:
The Asian longhorned beetle is a wood-boring invader that kills healthy trees, and one defense is to find wasps that attack it at home. Seunghyun Lee and co-authors spent four years in Korea testing an improved sentinel log trap, baited with chemical cues the beetles use, to draw out such parasitoids. Two wasp species turned up in the logs. One was Spathius ibarakius, already known to parasitize the related citrus longhorned beetle. The other died before adulthood and could be identified only to superfamily level, even with DNA and larval study.

Attack rates varied sharply by place and year, from 0.3 percent in Gapyeong in 2019 to 29.2 percent by Spathius ibarakius in Busan in 2022. The team suggests future searches in the beetle's native range should chase parasitoids with high attack rates like the Busan wasp.
pmc-10714876:
Yoon Jung Jang and co-authors report a phase II trial of a radioactive form of the drug rituximab, in a 2023 study. The drug was given to people with marginal zone lymphoma. Their cancer had come back or resisted prior care. This kind of radio-linked treatment is a rare option for B-cell blood cancers.

Patients first received a plain dose of the drug, then the radioactive dose. Ten patients took part, with a median age in the late fifties. Slow enrollment cut the trial short. The main goal was the share whose tumors shrank, with side effects and survival also tracked. The small size limits what the trial can show, but readers get a careful record for a hard-to-treat group.
pmc-10714976:
Yiwei Zhao and eight co-authors review plant compounds that may help treat bone loss, in a 2023 paper. Healthy bone is kept by a balance of building and removal. When removal outruns building, bones thin and break more easily. A cell recycling process plays a part in that balance.

The review first sets out how that recycling process works. It then traces its role in both bone-building and bone-removing cells. Signal pathways that link the process to bone health are summarized. The authors collect findings on proteins and natural compounds that tune the process. Many such compounds come from plants used in traditional remedies. The review aims to clarify how bone loss develops and to seed new treatment ideas. Human proof for the compounds remains a next step.
pmc-10715976:
Ki Park and Natalie A. Bello wrote this two thousand twenty-three review of cardio-obstetrics, the field where pregnancy care meets cardiovascular medicine. They note that cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of pregnancy-related death in the United States. Maternal deaths and complications have risen over recent decades. Contributing factors include older mothers, more obesity and other risk factors, and better survival of patients with congenital heart disease.

The authors explain that most patients with heart conditions can be guided safely through pregnancy with careful risk management. The problem is a shortage of clinicians trained for this work. They call for cardio-obstetrics care teams spanning cardiology, obstetrics, maternal-fetal medicine, and family medicine, covering care from preconception through the postpartum period.
pmc-10716176:
Xing-Tian Wang and co-authors asked whether how hospitals use their beds tracks with drug-resistant infections across China, in a 2023 study. The team took national monitoring data from 2014 to 2020, province by province. The data covered beds per thousand people, bed occupancy rates, and average stay lengths. They related these to how often hospitals isolated multidrug-resistant organisms.

Provinces with more beds per person had lower isolation rates for six major resistant organisms, including MRSA. Busier beds told the opposite story: higher occupancy tied to higher rates for ten organisms. Longer average stays also tied to higher rates for several resistant types. The authors read the pattern as a warning: crowded, fast-turnover wards may foster resistant bacteria, while adequate bed capacity eases the pressure. The findings are offered as data support for infection control planning and hospital resource policy in China.
pmc-10716576:
Hendrik Jan Hummelen reports a pilot study of stubborn gut complaints in a 2023 paper. Dozens of patients with unexplained digestive trouble came to his complementary medicine practice over several years. Most had already tried standard clinics and hospitals without enough relief.

Biophysical testing with a bioresonance device guided his working diagnosis of chronic salmonella infection of the gallbladder. The study charts how these patients presented and how their treatment fared. From those cases he raises a bold claim: salmonella may play a real role in functional gallbladder disorder. A pilot from one practice cannot settle causation. It can, though, point lab research toward a testable suspect.
pmc-10716676:
Benjamin Woolf and five co-authors ask what a common drug target does beyond its known use, in a 2023 study. The target, PDE5, is blocked by drugs for erectile dysfunction, and the team wanted its wider effects on fertility, sex life, and wellbeing.

Instead of a drug trial, they used genetics as a stand-in for blocking the target, drawing on blood pressure data from about 758,000 people and UK Biobank data for outcomes. Men with the genetic pattern linked to PDE5 blocking had fathered about 0.28 more children on average. No such link appeared in women. The team found no evidence of effects on number of partners, never having had sex, or self-rated wellbeing.
pmc-10716976:
Ghaidaa Khalifa and co-authors published a 2023 survey study on how adults in Saudi Arabia view alternative medicine for autism. Autism is a developmental condition affecting social and communication skills. Alongside standard care, many families try other practices, from special diets to local traditions such as Zamzam water and black seeds. The authors asked the wider public what it thinks of these options.

An online questionnaire reached 4,311 adults across the country. Two-thirds of those who answered were women. Just over half said they knew about autism. Many believed some non-drug approaches could help, led by art therapy and physical exercise. About half doubted that traditional treatment alone can help autism. Only a fifth backed some of the other practices asked about. The study maps public attitudes that clinics and health campaigns in the kingdom need to work with.
pmc-10717176:
Tensei Suzuki and co-authors report a case of blindness caused by Lemierre's syndrome, in a 2023 paper. The syndrome begins as a throat infection that seeds clots in the neck vein and spreads infected emboli through the body. A 36-year-old woman arrived with fever, facial swelling, and failing vision in her right eye. Scans showed a throat abscess and a clot in the right jugular vein. Blood tests grew the classic culprit bacterium.

Her condition included septic shock and a bleeding disorder from runaway clotting. Doctors judged that inflammation had reached the orbital apex, the tight passage behind the eye. Six weeks of antimicrobial treatment cleared the abscess and steadied her body. Her sight, though, never returned. The authors warn that eye complications, while rare, can blind. Early recognition of the syndrome may not always save vision.
pmc-10717276:
Deborah Jael Herrera and co-authors study a cash aid program and child nutrition in the Caraga Region of the Philippines, in a research paper from 2023. The program gives cash to poor families on set conditions. Malnutrition in youth takes many forms at once, from stunting to excess weight.

The team used school data for more than five thousand children and teens aged three to nineteen. They also held group talks with parents, teachers, and school nurses. Rates of stunting, thinness, and excess weight were all high. The paper weighs how program membership tracks with each form of poor nutrition, and what families say helps or fails.
pmc-10717976:
Sabrina Horvath and Sudha Arunachalam test how eye tracking can measure verb knowledge in young children in this 2023 study. They worked with late talkers, children who develop speech slowly, and with autistic preschoolers. Children saw two moving scenes side by side, then heard a verb and had to find the scene that matched it.

In the first test, late talkers knew as many verbs as peers of the same age, but they were slower to show it. In the second test, autistic children's speed and accuracy both rose with their general language skill. The authors praise eye gaze as a tool for groups that cannot answer in words. They also warn that scoring must be tailored to each child, since gaze habits vary a lot.
pmc-10718276:
Hanlin Yin, Wanyi Lin, and Liangjing Lu present a case in French in 2023 of swollen fingers and nailfold capillary changes. A 51-year-old woman came to a rheumatology unit with hand swelling that began two months earlier. She had a five-year history of Raynaud phenomenon, where fingers react strongly to cold.

Exam showed puffy fingers, redness around the nails, dilated capillaries, and small bleeds at the nail base. Blood tests found centromere antibodies, a marker tied to limited scleroderma. Scans of heart and lungs were normal. Treatment with three drugs cleared the swelling within three months, and the bleeds partly faded.
pmc-10722276:
Hatice Karabulut and nine co-authors printed drug-loaded scaffolds in 2023 for epilepsy research. Over a third of patients gain too little relief from standard seizure drugs, and long use brings side effects. A printed implant that releases a drug at the seizure site could help, with doses shaped to the patient.

The team loaded a known seizure drug at three dose levels into scaffolds made from two body-friendly polymers. Tests then checked the scaffolds' build and release behavior. The work is an early step toward local, tailored drug delivery that spares the rest of the body.
pmc-10723076:
Danah Albarrak and co-authors survey how nicotine dependence walks with anxiety and depression in Saudi Arabia, in a 2023 study. A kingdom-wide online poll ran for six months across 2022 and 2023. It asked who smokes, by old or new means, and how hard the habit grips. Standard short scales scored each person's anxiety and low mood.

About a fifth had used e-cigarettes in the last month, and a like share had smoked tobacco. Anxiety skewed mild across the crowd, and depression sat mild to minimal for most. The tie the team hunted did show: among e-cigarette users, heavier dependence marched with higher depression scores. Men leaned into dependence more than women. The authors read a two-way street between nicotine and mental strain, and they urge care that treats the pair together rather than in split clinics.
pmc-10724476:
Vanesa Anton-Vazquez and co-authors replied in 2023 to comments on their study of bloodstream infections caused by bacteria that shrug off carbapenem antibiotics. The exchange turns on words: how to label antibiotic treatment given before test results, and what calling it "effective" should mean when timing is everything. The authors note the field has no standard terms yet for these timings.

They agree that outcome depends on the drug matching the germ, on speed, and on the patient's state, and that delay cuts a drug's power. But they resist any definition implying a late dose is useless, citing work where death risk climbs with each delay rather than switching off. Clear local definitions, they argue, let readers judge fairly.
pmc-10724876:
Cristina de Paz Poves and co-authors validated a fecal test kit for measuring an inflammation marker in chest fluid instead, in a 2023 study published in Spanish. Calprotectin is a protein released by neutrophils, and its standard test uses stool samples. The team adapted the commercial chemiluminescence assay to pleural fluid, the liquid that collects around the lungs in some diseases, and ran a full validation protocol on the automated analyzer.

The marker stayed stable for at least a week refrigerated and a month frozen. Repeated measurements varied by only about two percent within a day and six and a half percent between days, with a small negative bias. The method stayed linear up to a high ceiling, and its quantification limit was measured precisely. A carryover effect appeared after very concentrated samples but was too small to matter clinically. The authors declare the test reliable for pleural fluid.
pmc-10725576:
Lena Nenoff and co-authors review uncertainty in deformable image registration for radiotherapy in a 2023 paper. Aligning warped scans guides dose delivery across cancer care. Commercial tools make it easy, but their geometric errors can be large and hard to gauge. No shared standard exists for judging a registration.

The review sorts error sources and their clinical impact. Practical advice follows for patient-specific checks, system commissioning, and research use. Developers get recommendations too, on making uncertainty visible to users. The aim is safer, more honest use of a tool clinics already lean on daily, by naming what a good alignment must prove.
pmc-10726376:
Katharine Hopkins and co-authors find high rates of gold and acrylate allergy in people with fibromyalgia in a 2023 study. Fibromyalgia brings widespread pain with no clear cause. Contact allergies to dental materials can cause whole-body symptoms that mimic it, yet allergy rates in this group were unstudied.

Patients were patch tested with an extended dental series and compared with dermatitis and dental control groups. Gold allergy was significantly more common in the fibromyalgia group than in either control group once testing differences were adjusted. Allergy to a common acrylate and to grouped acrylates also ran higher than in dental controls. The authors suggest heavier gold exposure or an altered mouth environment drives the sensitization, and that gold may even feed some patients' symptoms.
pmc-10729076:
Gina Agarwal and co-authors build a dictionary that spots needless ambulance calls in records. Their 2023 paper links paramedic impression codes to conditions that good clinic care can keep out of hospital, plus mental health calls. Crews in the UK and Canada log such codes on every run. Experts from both countries matched code lists in rounds.

British codes proved richer than Ontario's, and some pairings clashed, yet a shared map emerged. The tool now lets researchers count how many calls were avoidable in principle. It also opens cross-country studies of where those patients travel next in the system. The authors call it a first step toward lighter emergency loads.
pmc-10729976:
John Hunyara and co-authors study a molecule that shapes how the eye connects to the brain's daily clock, in a paper from 2023. Some eye cells sense light directly and send signals to a small brain area that runs the body clock. How those wires find their target was not well known.

The molecule, called teneurin-3, is common in one cell type in the clock area. In mice that lack it, the wiring from the light-sensing eye cells to that area was reduced in one zone. Links between two cell groups inside the area also changed. Yet the mice were more sensitive to light, not less, and reset their clocks faster after a shift. The work shows the molecule both guides wiring and tunes response.
pmc-10731176:
Moonhwan Kim and co-authors present a 2023 case report on liver transplant artery spasm. Artery blockage after transplant can doom the graft. A 57-year-old man with hepatitis B liver disease and liver cancer got a living donor transplant. The blood types were incompatible, a harder setting. Right after the artery join, the pulse weakened sharply. A second join through another artery still gave a poor pulse.

Scans showed diffuse spasm along the artery, like beads on a string. The team infused a fat-carried prostaglandin drug straight into the artery. That route targets the spasm at its site. Transplant surgeons get a worked rescue for a feared early complication. Spasm differs from clot, and the fix differs too. A case that names the pattern and the response can save grafts when minutes count.
pmc-10732976:
Quan Wang and five co-authors test a ginkgo compound against harmful artery wall growth in this 2023 paper. After stent surgery for heart artery disease, the treated vessel often thickens again and narrows, a problem called restenosis. The compound, ginkgolide B, comes from the ginkgo tree and is known for effects on blood and inflammation.

In mice with an injured neck artery, the compound curbed wall thickening and kept the vessel open. Tests in human vessel muscle cells pointed to a known growth signal path, TGFβ1/Smad, as the route of action. Blocking that path with another drug removed the benefit, and mice lacking the key gene gained nothing from treatment. The authors propose the compound as a lead for drugs that guard stents, while noting that human trials lie ahead.
pmc-10733176:
Keisuke Saito and co-authors traced how a signal travels across a key gap inside photosystem II, the plant protein complex that splits water and releases oxygen. A tyrosine unit called TyrZ passes electrons between the water-splitting manganese cluster and the rest of the machinery. When TyrZ is oxidized, a proton ends up moving about eleven angstroms away, and the route was puzzling.

Quantum and molecular simulations show the message travels through water, not direct force. Oxidation breaks one unusually strong hydrogen bond. A nearby water molecule swings to donate a new bond to the cluster. That shift frees a proton to hop along a second strong bond to a distant aspartate. The authors call the linked chain a Grotthuss-like network, echoing how protons relay through water.
pmc-10735176:
Many people carrying the COVID virus have few or no symptoms, yet they can still spread it, and emergency rooms rarely test them. Judith Leblanc led a large team that ran a trial in eighteen emergency departments across the Paris area in early twenty twenty-one. In turns, each site either kept its usual testing, aimed at the sick and admitted, or added nurse-led testing offered to everyone else who walked in.

The trial covered more than one hundred and thirty-eight thousand visits across both periods. At the added-testing sites, over six thousand symptom-free patients filled in a risk questionnaire, and nurses tested more than four thousand of them. The study weighed whether that extra reach raised the share of infections found among all visitors.
pmc-10735476:
Anthony Traver and Holly Dabelko-Schoeny study, in 2023, the housing older adults live in before, during, and after homelessness late in life. The team partnered with a shelter, a meal site, and a mental health outreach team in Columbus, Ohio. Twenty-two older adults and nine service providers were interviewed.

Low or no income pushed people through shared housing, doubling up, shelters, and rough sleeping. Conflict, the death of a support person, rent rises, and isolation drove people downward. Poor housing worsened health and exposed people to harm. Ties with others, shelter services, and housing vouchers helped some find stable homes again.
pmc-10735576:
Meng Huo and Kyungmin Kim study, in a 2023 paper, how support flows both ways in couples where one partner has early Alzheimer's disease. The ill partner usually receives heavy spousal care. Whether they still give support back, and how that depends on the relationship, was little known.

The team drew on paired interviews with 37 older couples. The ill partners averaged 77 years old and their caregiving spouses 76. Those with the disease saw the relationship more warmly and less negatively than their caregivers did. Support did not flow in only one direction, the authors found. Recognizing the ill partner as a giver, not only a receiver, can reshape how couples and counselors approach care.
pmc-10735776:
Vanessa Fabbre and co-authors explore spirituality in the lives of older transgender adults in a 2023 study. Mainstream faiths have often stigmatized gender minorities, which complicates belief for trans elders. The team read life story interviews with eighty-eight trans older adults from across the United States.

Six tenets from spiritual psychotherapy framed the reading. Two strands of spirituality emerged. Implicit spirituality grows through meaning, purpose, and connection that affirm a person's gender. Explicit spirituality names the deliberate work of reshaping beliefs and practices so they validate one's place in the world. Some elders lived one strand, some both, and some neither. The authors offer the map to practitioners who support aging trans clients, so care can nourish this side of life with more skill.
pmc-10735876:
Cognitive reserve — the mind's cushion against aging — is usually judged from schooling, work, and habits, but most surveys blur youth and later life together. Stephen Aichele and co-authors built a survey that asks about life twice: as it is now, in later adulthood, and as recalled from younger adulthood. It covers social standing, leisure, social life, family engagement, and religious activity.

They gave the survey to 235 community-dwelling Italian adults aged fifty-five to ninety, alongside tests of memory, vocabulary, reasoning, and mood. Analysis confirmed the two time frames form related but distinct factors. Both linked to stronger thinking scores and to depressive symptoms, with the younger-life factor tied more to intelligence and the current one more to working memory and mood. The authors offer the survey as a reliable tool for studying how a whole life's experience shapes the aging mind.
pmc-10736176:
Wan-Tai Au-Yeung and co-authors pair home sensors with weekly surveys to study how social life sways behavior in dementia, in a 2023 conference paper. Mood and conduct symptoms shadow most dementia courses, and the home's social air may feed or calm them. Two sister studies feed the work: one tracks agitation in late-stage dementia, the other apathy, low mood, and anxiety in a wider elder group.

Small early crews, nine pairs and nine solo participants, report symptoms each week online. Bed mats, motion sensors, and wearables meanwhile log the house: time out, rooms in use at once, and how many people and pets are in. Surveys add trips away and overnight guests. By laying the two streams together, the team hunts links between company and symptoms. The design aims at care that treats the social setting, not just the patient.
pmc-10736276:
Laura Niedernhofer introduces the SenNet consortium, a national program set up to find and describe senescent cells across the human lifespan. Senescent cells, which have stopped dividing, are implicated in most age-related chronic diseases and in the aging sped up by disease treatments. Drugs that clear them are already in trials.

The network joins labs worldwide to benchmark tools and align with other mapping efforts, and it added mouse mapping to use genetic tricks. Products will include shared naming, new biomarkers, and public four-dimensional atlases for many organs. Challenges include the lack of a specific marker for these cells and scant knowledge of what triggers senescence in the body. New single-cell and spatial tools are central to the plan.
pmc-10736376:
Skye Leedahl and co-authors studied digital skill in older adults who joined a technology program in a 2023 paper. The Rhode Island program paired older adults with younger helpers to learn iPad use. The team analyzed 324 participants from 2021 and 2022, aged fifty to ninety-two.

Most participants were women, and about two thirds were White, with Spanish the main language for about fifteen percent. The authors looked for traits that predicted digital competence at entry. Knowing who starts behind helps programs target teaching where it is needed most, rather than assuming all older learners begin at the same level.
pmc-10736476:
Pablo Martinez Amezcua and co-authors (2023) tested whether hearing loss travels with frailty in older Americans. Frailty brings weakness, slowness, and exhaustion, and raises the risk of disability and death. Hearing loss touches about two-thirds of older adults and links to isolation and poorer function. The team analyzed 2,361 participants from a national aging study in 2021. Hearing was measured by tone testing; frailty by the standard five-part phenotype.

Seventy-three percent of participants had some hearing loss. Those with moderate or worse loss had notably higher odds of being frail rather than robust, with an odds ratio near 1.8. The pattern strengthened with worse hearing. The authors suggest hearing loss may be a genuine risk factor for frailty, not just a fellow traveler of age. Trials of hearing treatment as frailty prevention, they argue, could matter for public health.
pmc-10736576:
Han, Lee, and Kim present a study from twenty twenty-three on contact-free sports and self-rated health in older Korean adults. The pandemic closed sports facilities, which threatened older adults' bodies and minds. Data come from a national survey of adults over sixty-five who exercise regularly. Over eleven hundred people enter the analysis. Age links to worse self-rated health and stamina in their models. Taking part in contact-free sports changes that age link, though. The age penalty shows only among non-participants.

Participants keep steadier health and stamina ratings with age. The authors read this as a buffer against age-related decline. Contact-free activity is urged as vital during outbreaks. The findings speak to keeping older adults active when facilities close.
pmc-10736676:
Lisa Barry, writing alone in 2023, shares lessons on recruiting older adults from hard-to-reach groups into research. She notes that since 2000, the number of US prisoners aged 50 and over grew 280 percent. Older people with substance use disorders also number in the millions. Both groups carry heavy medical needs, yet studies often miss them.

Her team recruited and kept 171 prisoners aged 50 and over in a cohort study. Success took a strong partnership with the state prison system and measures that fit prison life. She also discusses snowball recruiting for people seeking addiction treatment, and how to adjust entry rules without weakening the study.
pmc-10736776:
Sophia Geisser and co-authors build a two-part aid for hospice dementia care in a 2023 paper. Family partners of people dying with dementia carry heavy stress. Hospice nurses and social workers could coach them, but few get dementia-specific training for the end of life.

The program, EDITH-HC, pairs training videos for clinicians with a worksheet used in family meetings. The worksheet helps surface a partner's stressors and concerns so they can be addressed. Development drew on a literature review, interviews with forty family partners and eighteen clinicians, and two rounds of stakeholder input. A single-arm pilot checked feasibility and acceptance. A randomized pilot comes next, the authors say.
pmc-10737076:
Minzhi Ye studies how married grandparents raising their grandchildren share the parenting, and what the divisions do to the family. Half of such American families include married couples, yet grandfathers' parenting has barely been studied. Ye interviewed 193 couples separately and used latent profile analysis to sort their joint practices into types.

Four profiles emerged, mixing strength and weakness across couples. In one, both spouses parent ideally. Another pairs an inadequate grandmother with an ideal grandfather. A third pairs an ambivalent grandmother with a highly effective grandfather; the fourth is the mirror image. The profiles predicted family outcomes even with background traits held fixed. Grandfathers in the mirror-image profile showed lower positive affect, and grandmothers in the second profile showed fewer depressive symptoms. Grandchildren in the both-ideal profile showed fewer behavior and emotion problems. Ye argues practitioners should treat the grandfather as a real force in these families.
pmc-10737176:
Grace Caskie, Benjamin Johnson, and Eve Root asked which kinds of aging knowledge, and how much contact with older adults, shape ageist attitudes in doctoral psychology students, in a 2023 study. A known model names knowledge and contact as the two keys to cutting ageism. Earlier work leaned on undergraduates and lumped all knowledge into one score.

The team surveyed 192 doctoral students with scales for contact, aging facts, and five ageism measures. Split by domain, the results surprised: knowing psychological aging tied to fewer stereotypes, while knowing biological aging tied to more ageism on every measure. Social aging knowledge tied to more kindly, patronizing ageism. More contact tied to less distance and less negative feeling. The split view shows that what students learn matters, not just how much.
pmc-10737276:
Lillian Hung and co-authors study virtual reality for social life in care homes in a 2023 paper. VR gear now fits old folk, and homes seek ways to cut lone hours. Two Canadian homes ran week VR group meets from January 2023. Twenty residents of mixed mind and body strength joined in. Staff led the meets; watch notes and talks caught the acts. Ten staff groups added their view.

Three themes rose from the reads. Tale-telling in VR built each resident's sense of self. Good moods stuck past the clip's end, even when the clip was lost to mind. VR also sparked talk mate to mate and staff to mate. Patient partners co-ran the theme work. The authors call VR a fit, warm tool for home life.
pmc-10737376:
Zainab Toteh Osakwe, Michelle Odlum, Amarilis Céspedes, and Sasha Perez study how home health aides view telehealth for patients with dementia, in a paper from 2023. The pandemic pushed home care visits onto video at speed. Patients with dementia lean on aides to voice their needs to the care team. The team asked whether remote visits truly work for that group.

They interviewed twenty-five aides from four agencies in the summer of 2020. Aides favored platforms with live video, since faces make the talk feel human. They saw telehealth as a supplement, never a swap, for in-person nurse visits. Handling a tablet while giving hands-on care added strain. Many also felt their training on the tools was too thin. The authors urge agencies to plan telehealth with aides, not around them.
pmc-10737576:
Aya Yoshikawa and Richard Fortinsky wrote this research paper, published in 2023, on pain medicine and falls among older adults who live at home. It focuses on people with arthritis, who often take pain medicine and already face a higher risk of falling.

The authors studied Medicare beneficiaries in a 2015 national survey on health and aging. People with arthritis reported far more pain and pain medicine use than those without arthritis. Among those with arthritis, taking pain medicine was linked to a higher chance of falls. Taking it every day raised the risk more. Balance problems were an even stronger factor. The paper flags daily pain medicine use as a fall risk worth watching in arthritis care.
pmc-10737676:
Pildoo Sung, Jeremy Lim-Soh, and Angelique Chan present this 2023 symposium study on whether loneliness passes from older adults with thinking problems to the family members who care for them. Loneliness can spread between people, but not every caregiver of a lonely person grows lonely. The team used paired data from 135 such adults and their caregivers in Singapore.

The older adults reported more loneliness than their caregivers, and the two scores were only weakly linked. Once other traits were held steady, no link stood on its own. But one buffer changed the picture: a caregiver's sense of mastery, the feeling of being in control. Where that sense was low, a lonely care receiver did track with a lonely caregiver. The authors urge programs that ease loneliness on both sides and build caregiver mastery.
pmc-10737976:
Seven researchers ask whether religious life leaves a mark on the body's inflammation. High levels of C-reactive protein, a blood marker of inflammation, go with risk of memory loss and dementia. Faith practice has been linked to better thinking in old age, but the route was unclear. The team studied 6,652 Americans aged fifty and older in a national survey spanning 2006 to 2014.

People who attended services more often, and who scored higher on religiosity and spirituality, carried lower levels of the marker. The link held after accounting for age, income, schooling, body weight, and illness. Age, schooling, and income also went with lower levels, while diabetes, cancer, and high blood pressure went with higher ones. The authors suggest that lower inflammation may be one path by which faith supports the aging brain, and they urge support for attendance among those who value it.
pmc-10738076:
Noelle Fields and five co-authors analyse digital stories from a telephone-based reminiscence program, in work from 2023. University students worked with older adults with cognitive impairment over six weeks by phone. Pairs then built short audio-visual stories together, choosing photos, music and narration to match a shared storyboard and script.

The study covers stories from 27 older adults in a thematic analysis. Six themes stood out: family, religion and purpose, loves and hates, career, stress and coping, and major life turning points. Sub-themes ran from childhood to faith, travel, music and resilience. The authors extend work on intergenerational programs and offer advice for practice and research.
pmc-10738476:
Delirium in older patients with COVID-19 may tie into salt and potassium balance, and Milenko Petrovic and four co-authors check hospital records to see how. They review 319 older COVID patients and a comparison group of 306 with other pneumonias, tracking four electrolyte problems and delirium in each group.

About a third of each group became delirious. Electrolyte disorders overall were actually more common in the non-COVID pneumonia group, and low potassium led there. But high sodium stood out in COVID patients, a worry because it can trigger seizures and brain bleeding. Low potassium was the single most common disorder in COVID patients with any electrolyte problem. The authors urge close sodium monitoring in older COVID care. The study appears in 2023.
pmc-10738576:
Maia McLin and Danielle Nadorff compare how a child's belief in self-control relates to grades, depending on who is raising the child. Their study appeared in 2023. About six million American children live with grandparents, many without a parent present. The team surveyed 323 caregiving grandparents and 105 foster parents nationwide. Grandchildren reported a stronger sense of control over their schoolwork than foster children did, though reported grades did not differ between the groups.

The link between control beliefs and grades was strong in both groups but stronger for foster children. After accounting for caregiver age and means, the difference between groups held. The authors say caregiver type changes how much a child's mindset matters, which interventions should respect.
pmc-10738676:
Lien Quach and co-authors map falls among older Americans in a 2023 study drawn from the Health and Retirement Study. Falls bring fractures, fear, and lost independence, and the authors wanted to know which personal and social factors most raise the risk, and whether race changes those links.

Panel data from 2006 to 2012 covered more than twenty-two thousand community-dwelling adults over sixty-five. About thirty-eight percent fell at least once in each two-year window. Each extra chronic condition raised fall risk, as did poor vision, limits on daily activities, and loneliness. Stronger thinking skills lowered risk slightly. The models account for people appearing repeatedly.
pmc-10738776:
Ellen Quillen and co-authors studied how many health problems at once affect lifespan in monkeys in a 2023 paper. Older people often live with more than one long-term illness, and that load links to shorter lives. It was less clear how a like load plays out in monkeys used to study fast aging.

The team built a score from vet records for 288 rhesus monkeys, some of which had past whole-body radiation. The score counts ills such as joint pain, weak bones, diabetes, heart disease, and tumors. All of the ills showed up in both groups, and scores rose in many paths across life. The score helps show how total illness load, not just one disease, tracks with years left.
pmc-10738876:
Erica Fan and co-authors study how living in a deprived area shapes the link between brain markers of Alzheimer's disease and thinking skills, in a paper from 2023. Most past validation of these markers came from White groups. Black adults face higher risk and more social disadvantage, so the gap matters.

The cohort held just under two hundred adults aged fifty and older, half of them Black. Brain scans measured thinning of the cortex and white matter damage, and a second scan measured amyloid, a protein tied to the disease. Higher area deprivation, more brain shrinkage, and more white matter damage each linked to worse thinking scores. The mix of deprivation and shrinkage shaped memory recall in a pattern the authors explore.
pmc-10738976:
Olivia Atherton asks whether living in the countryside raises the risk of death, in this 2023 study. Most past work on rural and urban health gaps used area-level data. Such data cannot say much about single lives or how health unfolds over a lifetime. Atherton turned instead to records that follow individuals for many years.

Her study joins two large United States surveys that tracked about fifty-five thousand adults for up to twenty-nine years. Home addresses were linked to maps that grade how rural each place is. She tested whether rural living predicted death on its own, or only through income and schooling gaps. She also checked whether the link differed by sex, race, wealth, or having a partner. The study was registered in advance.
pmc-10739276:
Bobbi Symes and Kahir Lalji draw lessons from three community programs for older adults with high needs in British Columbia. Their 2023 report covers social prescribing, therapeutic activation programs, and caregiver support groups run as demonstration projects from 2020 to 2023.

Together the programs served over four thousand people, most of them long-term clients. The pandemic forced four fifths of programs to pivot in their first year, and that freedom to pivot counted as a success. Socially isolated clients benefited most, staff said. Programs deepened ties with community organizations and care networks, each forming several new partnerships. Awareness and referral flow limited growth. The authors distill what helped and what hindered for the next wave of programs.
pmc-10739376:
Tobi Abramson, Jo Anne Sirey, and Jacquelin Berman present new ways to give mental health care to older adults in a session report from twenty twenty-three. The work deals with the triple burden of age bias, mental health stigma, and race bias. It sums up results from three service models used in community settings.

One program gave brief help to older victims of abuse or crime, and video care worked as well as care in person. A peer-led program helped most people with low food access feel less depressed. A third program placed care inside senior centers and saw clear gains in mood and less loneliness.
pmc-10739476:
Ji Hye Hwang tests the safety of a single dose of a nerve pain injection in rats, in a 2023 study. The injection is a water based form of pharmacopuncture, a method that places herbal drugs at set body points. It was newly developed for nerve pain care.

Groups of male and female rats got the drug or plain salt water into thigh muscle. Hwang watched them for two weeks for signs of harm and weight change. No rat died, and no change was tied to the drug. Tissue checks at the shot site also stayed clean. The mild cell influx seen in both groups was blamed on the needle itself.
pmc-10740476:
Marcelo Umsza-Guez and co-authors work in 2023 on turning wine waste into a useful product. Wine lees, the solid-liquid leftovers of winemaking, pile up in huge amounts and pose a disposal problem. The lees hold anthocyanins, the red pigments of grapes, which also act as strong antioxidants.

Using sound-wave extraction tuned by a formal design method, the team built a process with tight repeatability. Applied to lees from two grape varieties, the method yielded extracts rich in pigment and antioxidant power. The team also checked how grape type, ferment style, and sample handling shifted the yield. Rich extracts could serve drug, food, and health product makers while cutting waste.
pmc-10740876:
Harvey Rutland and co-authors review how machine learning is used in anaerobic digestion, the process where microbes break down waste and make biogas. Their 2023 review surveys studies from labs and full-scale plants. Interest in these tools is growing because the process is hard to run by simple rules alone.

Most studies used neural networks, the review found, trained on data from systems of very different designs. Models built on lab data often fail when moved to real plants, where microbe mixes and daily running vary a lot. Used live, the tools can predict problems and keep gas output steady. The authors point to gaps in scale and clarity as the main work ahead.
pmc-10740976:
Yhu Fhei Lee, Dayna Wei Wei Yong, and Ray Manotosh review contact lens induced limbal stem cell deficiency in a 2023 article. In this eye condition, stem cells at the edge of the cornea fail or are lost. The cornea then loses its clear surface. Causes range from birth defects and burns to long term lens wear.

Lens wear is the least well understood cause, the authors note, and it often stays hidden. They search past studies for cases and discuss risk factors, how the disease develops, and how doctors can spot it. They also review treatment choices and the gaps in current guidance.
pmc-10741076:
Comfortable-riding mules are big business in Brazil, bred by crossing gaited Pega donkeys with marching horse breeds. A nine-author team asked whether a gene variant known to shape gait in horses, in the gene DMRT3, also matters in the donkeys and mules themselves. They typed the variant in 159 mules and 203 donkeys and compared it with each animal's gait style.

Mules split almost evenly between the two main genotypes, and both appeared equally in the two gait styles, batida and picada. Donkeys were almost all one genotype, yet the rarer genotype turned up more often in picada-gaited donkeys. The team reads the pattern as the variant arriving through the horse mothers in mule breeding. Their broader point is that this gene alone does not decide gait in these animals; other genes and factors must share the job.
pmc-10741476:
An enzyme that breaks down uracil and thymine in the body tunes its own activity in response to the chemicals it works on. Daniela Cederfelt and co-authors probe how that tuning works in a 2023 study of the human enzyme. The enzyme works as a group of linked units, and its activity rises or falls as the group grows or shrinks.

The team changed single building blocks of the enzyme and imaged its shapes with a cryo microscope. Closing loops over the active site locks a key residue in place and lets units join into larger assemblies. Two residues at the joins seem to sense chemical changes and adjust the grip between units. The results explain how acidity and the shape of partner chemicals steer the balance of the enzyme.
pmc-10741876:
Christina Schröder and colleagues compare two focused radiation schedules for prostate cancer, five sessions against seven, in this matched analysis from twenty twenty-three. Nearly two hundred men with intermediate or high-risk disease were treated at two centers: the five-fraction group on a robotic platform, the seven-fraction on a standard machine. Propensity matching balanced one hundred twenty for the head-to-head.

Both schedules controlled the cancer well early, with few relapses. The difference was collateral damage in the gut. The seven-fraction patients suffered significantly more moderate bowel toxicity, acute and late, including one severe bleed in an anticoagulated man. Urinary toxicity ran similar. PSA fell further in the five-fraction group. Follow-up is short, a median of thirteen months, and the authors withhold a final verdict, but the gut signal favors five.
pmc-10742076:
Andrea Alberti and co-authors audit side effects of prostate biopsy at a large Italian center in a 2023 paper. The biopsy style studied passes the needle through the rectum, guided by MRI targets. European guidance now favors a route through the skin instead, mainly for its lower infection risk.

The center tracked 458 patients biopsied from 2020 to 2022 under a strict shared pathway. About forty-four percent reported some problem afterward. Most were mild, led by blood in the urine, while about nine percent had moderate issues such as blocked urination. The audit sets a fair baseline for judging the switch: the older route, done carefully, was safer than its reputation. Centers can weigh that record against the newer route's gains.
pmc-10742176:
Mutian Lian and co-authors review a small RNA that rises under low oxygen and drives pancreatic cancer. Their review from 2023 deals with a cancer known for late finding and few care options. Its tumors sit in a very low oxygen setting, fed by dense scar tissue, fast growth, and poor blood supply.

The small RNA, named miR-210, is switched on by low oxygen through more than one path. It shapes vessel growth, spread, and cell death, all of which feed cancer growth and drug resistance. The authors trace its controls and its targets in the tumor. They argue the map points to new care targets and to early tests, which this cancer badly needs.
pmc-10742576:
Antonia Aravantinou-Karlatou and three co-authors review, in 2023 work, how social support shapes the scores lung patients give on their own health. People with the long-term lung illness in view fill in such score forms to guide their care. Yet the forms barely ask about help from kin and friends, or about access to care.

The team screened more than two thousand papers and kept ten on support and scores in basic care. Most came from the United States and Norway. Stronger support went with better scores across the board: better life quality, mind health, self care, and day-to-day function, plus milder illness. Support took many forms in the studies. The team says the forms leave this force out, and urges that it be counted.
pmc-10742876:
Physical therapy has a branch for mental health, yet even health workers hold a fuzzy view of it. Cristina Bravo and co-authors survey Spanish mental health staff on that view in a 2023 study. The survey drew 368 replies, most from physical therapists with long field time.

Three themes stood out: what the role does, what it aims at, and how it is seen. Life quality and body ills led both the task and aim lists. Exercise was the top tool, with talk-based and body-based methods close behind. The role was called unknown yet vital and whole-person in outlook. Clear interest suggests room to grow the field.
pmc-10742976:
Julia Wittenborn and a team of co-authors piloted a new mark to triage a hard cervical case. Their pilot study, from twenty twenty-three, deals with patients whose transformation zone in the cervix cannot be seen. That type three zone brings strife in colposcopy care, since harm can hide from view. The team asked if tiny RNA bits, called miRNAs, could flag high grade cell change in such cases.

They took mucosa samples with a brush at routine visits. Patients were split by tissue and cell results and by a standard virus test. Groups with high grade change were set next to clear ones. Readers who screen for cervical cancer get a first read on a bloodless mark for a blind spot in care.
pmc-10743176:
Fenghao Liu and co-authors present a 2023 journal article on genes behind queen fertility in the red imported fire ant. The invasive ant breeds fast and spreads damage, so its reproduction is a target. The team compared gene activity across queens, winged females, and males, then zoomed in on genes loud and specific in queens. Two vitellogenin genes, egg-yolk protein makers, stood out.

Both genes ran highest in queens and winged females, above all in the thorax. Silencing either gene, or both, shrank ovaries and cut egg laying. The authors present the pair as proven fertility factors and candidate targets for ant control.
pmc-10743276:
Haakenstad and co-authors ask what keeps children indoors and what might lure them out, in a 2023 mixed-methods study. Time outside benefits children's bodies and minds, yet children of color get less of it — their neighborhoods often lack safe, welcoming green space. The study centers a racially and ethnically mixed population.

Fourteen focus groups gathered fifty outdoor educators, preschool parents, and community members, and forty-nine people answered a survey. Both streams probed barriers — safety fears, cost, time, distance — and candidate fixes, with answers compared across racial and ethnic groups. Knowing which barriers bite hardest for which families lets programs spend their effort where it frees the most play.
pmc-10743576:
Andrijana Stanisavljević Ilić and co-authors study a common psychiatric drug in rats in a 2023 paper. Long-term social isolation in rats serves as a model of depression and changes brain cells that use GABA, a calming signal chemical. The team tested whether olanzapine, an antipsychotic drug, changes counts of two cell markers in the hippocampus, a brain area tied to mood and memory.

Isolation lowered counts of one marker in several hippocampal layers and raised some inflammation and stress signals. The drug partly offset those shifts, raising the second marker in one area while lowering counts in another, and it blunted the stress signal changes. It did not change one inflammation signal. Effects varied by layer and subregion.
pmc-10744076:
Rafael Salido-Vallejo and five co-authors compare outcomes of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma in organ transplant patients versus people with sound immune systems, in a look back cohort study. This skin cancer is the second most common skin tumor, and weak immunity raises its risks. The study came out in twenty twenty-three.

Cases came from one Spanish hospital across many years, with age, clinical, and tissue data logged. Rates of local return and spread were higher in tumors from transplant patients than in others. The team also read progression free survival and hunted for risk factors within the transplant group by single factor tests.
pmc-10744576:
Manuela Manziuc and co-authors wrote a review from 2023 on a new ceramic used for crowns and other dental fixes. The material blends two known ceramics. One gives a glass-like look that suits front teeth. The other, a hard white oxide, adds strength. The mix aims to give both looks and strength in one block that machines can mill.

The team searched three large databases for studies on the material's look, strength, and gluing. Its inner structure makes it tougher than older glass ceramics but less clear, so light passes less well. Tooth color below and glue shade both shift the final look. Strength scores beat those of plain glass ceramics and hybrid types, though not the strongest oxide alone. Acid etch and sand blasting are the main ways to prep its surface for glue. The team notes that long-term mouth data are still thin.
pmc-10745076:
Young Sub Lee and co-authors present a 2023 case report on two older men with small stomach cancers. Both men had early, well formed cancers that stayed in the inner lining, the kind often treated by scope based removal. Yet cancer was also found in nearby lymph nodes in both cases, which is not expected for such low risk tumors.

The report focuses on tumor budding, small clusters of cancer cells at the edge where the tumor spreads. Both cases showed high grade budding. The authors argue that budding may warn of node spread better than standard risk signs, and they urge a fresh look at treatment rules for early stomach cancer.
pmc-10745476:
Alanazi and five co-authors review medicinal herbs as helpers of the immune system against infection, in a 2023 paper. New germs keep emerging, and many resist current drugs. Herbs have served as remedies for centuries and hold active plant chemicals.

Studies show herbs can break bacterial walls, block protein making, and slow germ copying. They also calm harmful inflammation by lowering fiery signal molecules. At the same time they raise calming signals and boost killer cells that hunt viruses. The review covers the most common herbs for infectious and other diseases. The authors see herbs as promising partners, not replacements, for standard care.
pmc-10745576:
Ina Pundienė and co-authors stir carbon nanotubes into cement and watch the foam, in this 2023 study. Air-entraining admixtures bubble cement paste on purpose, to guard concrete against frost, while superplasticizers keep it flowing. Multi-walled carbon nanotubes promise strength and structure at the nanoscale. How the three additives work together was the open question.

The team checked foam stability, viscosity, electrical conductivity, dispersion, and setting times across mixes. The tubes improved foam stability and made the paste thicker, but how much hinged on which superplasticizer rode along and whether the air entrainer was present. Those agents steered the system: the polycarboxylate and polyacrylate types shifted dispersion and setting, with effects growing stronger in the full mixture. The upshot is a design principle: in modern cement, additives are a chord, not soloists, and the blend can be tuned by choice.
pmc-10745676:
Ji Wang and Wenwu Zhang design a green laser steady enough to ride inside a jet of water and cut with it. Water jet guided lasers carry the beam through a thin stream, but the source must hold power steady across its pulse range. Their long-cavity Nd:YAG design leans on stability math to widen the stable zone and shorten the thermal cutoff. A folded resonator stretches the cavity, and mirror curvature and arm length tune the margins.

After frequency doubling, pulses ran 43 to 143 nanoseconds from 5 to 20 kilohertz. Power peaked at 25.7 watts and wandered less than 1% over 400 minutes. Coupled into a 100 micron jet, the beam traveled 60 millimeters without loss.
pmc-10745876:
Késia Silva Lourenço, Heitor Cantarella, and Eiko Eurya Kuramae study how a sugar industry residue reshapes the living soil. Vinasse, the liquid left from ethanol making, is spread as fertiliser in both natural and concentrated forms. In two field trials the team tracked bacterial and fungal communities for up to 45 days after spreading, with and without added nitrogen fertiliser, reading the microbes' DNA from soil samples.

The added nitrogen alone changed little. The residue itself acted as a strong filter, and the concentrated form bit harder than the natural one. Total fungus numbers rose while bacterial totals held; more carbon lifted bacterial variety but shrank fungal variety. Bacteria and fungi answered independently, barely tracking each other. The authors conclude that what a residue carries, and how much, selects which microbes thrive.
pmc-10746476:
Ghorban Asgari and co-authors review fresh ways to pull a weed killer out of water. Diuron washes off farms and factory yards into streams and wells. It harms health and water life at low levels. The review sorts the main removal routes, with soil like soaking and strong oxidation at the front.

New soak materials get close study, among them char made from sewage sludge and ash waste. Both show strong uptake of the herbicide. A method that uses collapsing bubbles in water is also weighed, with its pluses and limits. The authors close by rating how well the novel soaks perform and where field use stands.
pmc-10746976:
Shiyuan Deng and co-authors set out a trial plan in a 2023 protocol paper on pain care for knee surgery. Replacing a worn knee joint is the main fix for end-stage knee disease, and case counts in China rose nearly six-fold from 2011 to 2019. Pain after the work is often strong and can slow rehab and sour the result.

The trial will test a form of ketamine given by vein during surgery as part of a mixed pain plan. Patients are split by chance into drug and control arms. The team will track pain, opioid use, and side effects after the work. A sound mixed plan could cut opioid harms while keeping patients at ease.
pmc-10747076:
Ritter, Wright, and Serwer test a Trojan horse idea for how a virus of bacteria might ride its host to fresh prey, in a 2023 paper. The claim: some bacteria flee down ATP gradients to escape infection, and some phages cling on without infecting. Once the bacteria reach low ATP, a sign of dense prey, the phages switch to attack.

In gel tests, the bacteria Bacillus thuringiensis gathered at low ATP spots, just as claimed. Phage added at the start site later lysed cells at the far end with no trail of killing between. The authors suggest using artificial ATP gradients to trigger such behavior in phage therapy against biofilms.
pmc-10747276:
Georgiana Dima and co-authors design a sensor that reads how well a stuff conducts, from afar and across the full range, in 2023. Past far-off reads aimed at high conduct grades. The low end, under ten units, holds the grades of body tissue. A full-range tool could feed body scans that map the inside by such grades, with no touch at all.

The team lay out how to tune the tool for each stretch of the range. Tests pulled true grades for weak samples with a miss of less than one part in ten. That span takes in the salt and flesh grades a body scan would meet. The work sets the steps to bend the tool to a chosen use. Body imaging by induction is the draw the team name first.
pmc-10747976:
Peng Zhang, Hongyuan Wen, Zhiyong Xu, and Zhao Zhao present a noise-hardy way to measure the time gap between two sensors hearing the same sound, in this 2023 paper. That gap pins down where a sound came from, but background noise scrambles it. Their method leans on a simple split: noise splashes arrive with random delays, while true signal points share one lag.

A four-step routine roughs out the delay, rearranges the time-frequency picture to part signal from noise, keeps the points flanking the delay ridge, and then refines the estimate. A sharpened second-order variant packs the signal energy tighter. In simulations and bench tests, the approach beat existing methods on both accuracy and robustness.
pmc-10748076:
Huyen-Tram Nguyen and co-authors built this 2023 cheap version of a soil-stiffness tester for construction sites. The standard tool, a falling-weight deflectometer, checks how roadbed soil flexes, but costly closed systems keep it from small projects. Their open design reads the impact with electronic sensors and a hobbyist-grade Arduino board paired with a precision converter chip.

The kit turns raw signals into force and deflection numbers ready for soil analysis. Careful calibration and alignment, checked in field tests, kept the readings accurate. By slashing cost while holding quality, the team hopes to spread routine soil checks to builders who now skip them. Open plans invite anyone to build and improve the device.
pmc-10749476:
Kim Greis and co-authors read the infrared fingerprints of fluorenyl cations held in ultracold helium drops, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. The ions are classic cases in the old puzzle of ring systems that break the aroma rule. Bare ions were made by spray, sorted by mass, then trapped in cold drops.

A tunable laser scanned a wide infrared band at fine detail. Matched with density functional math, the sharp spectra show all ions sit in their singlet state. The result pins shapes for a textbook antiaromatic family in the gas phase. Readers in physical chemistry get clean spectra where warmth and solvent blur are gone.
pmc-10750976:
Thomas Annesi and co-authors grade the websites that young sickle cell patients find when moving to adult care in this 2023 study. That handover is a risky stretch, with more emergency visits and deaths. Most young people search online for health answers, yet no one had checked what they land on.

The team searched three engines with phrases a teenager might type and kept sixty-seven sites from health departments, hospitals, societies, and others. Each site was scored for quality, reading ease, and sickle cell content, and compared with a 2018 sweep. Results were sobering. Only one in ten sites read at or below a seventh-grade level, and the average content score was near twenty-one of one hundred. Certified sites read more easily but carried thinner content. No source type led the pack. The authors call for better patient-facing pages for this transition.
pmc-10751076:
This 2023 data report ranks the top ten drugs in Australia for the year to June 2023. It draws on national subsidy scheme records, the PBS and its veterans' twin. Three tables sort the leaders three ways: by standard daily doses per thousand people, by raw script counts, and by cost to the government.

Cholesterol drugs top the dose table, with atorvastatin and rosuvastatin first and second. Rosuvastatin also leads on script counts, ahead of heartburn and mood drugs. Cost tells a different story: a COVID antiviral tops the bill at over 660 million dollars, trailed by a cystic fibrosis therapy and eye and cancer drugs. A note explains why dose rates beat script counts for fair comparison.
pmc-10753376: John Rossi comments in 2023 on a new approach to selecting aptamers, short nucleic acid strands that bind chosen targets. Standard selection is laborious and prone to artifacts that waste effort. He highlights work by Singh and co-authors, published in a leading biotechnology journal, describing selection inside a porous hydrogel. The setup should make aptamer selection easier and cleaner, he suggests, opening the method to wider use in research and diagnostics.
pmc-10753576:
Ring-shaped molecules built from benzene loops fascinate chemists, and a counting polynomial helps predict their traits without lab work. Govindhan Murugan, Konsalraj Julietraja, and Ammar Alsinai compute that polynomial for cycloparaphenylene in a 2023 paper. The molecule is a loop of benzene rings with rich electronic behavior. Descriptors drawn from its graph correlate with real compound traits. Their version sums neighborhood degrees around each atom.

Variants of the ring get the same treatment. The authors argue such math guides design of new materials. Conductivity and light-handling traits are among the hopes for these loops. The paper stays theoretical, with formulas as the product.
pmc-10753676:
Spinal fusion fixes one level and stresses the next, a problem called adjacent segment disease. Rajendra Sakhrekar and co-authors report a 72-year-old woman whose fusion, done twelve years earlier at the bottom of her spine, had left the level above unstable and slipped. Her back pain scored eight of ten, with pain shooting down both legs.

Instead of reopening her back widely, the surgeons extended the fusion through two small portals with an endoscope. The operation took about two hours with minimal blood loss. Her leg pain vanished within a week. Two years on, her disability score had fallen from seventy percent to ten, and she rated the result excellent. The authors commend the gentle approach.
pmc-10753876:
Two researchers study vapor grown polymer film kinetics at saturated monomer levels in a 2023 paper. Initiated chemical vapor deposition grows thin films from vapor, and past kinetics work used subsaturated feeds where growth is limited by monomer adsorption. Whether that limit holds at full saturation was open.

Films of a model polymer grew at substrate temperatures from 10 to 25 degrees, at full and half saturation. Half saturation runs behaved as expected. Full saturation runs split into two regimes: an early adsorption limited phase, then a steady phase limited by reaction kinetics. That steady phase warmed with temperature at an activation energy near values for bulk polymerization of the same polymer. New operating windows for film growth follow.
pmc-10754676:
Szu-Chi Chen and co-authors present a 2023 community study from Taiwan on a blood protein and later cancer risk. The protein, called VAP-1, helps white cells stick to vessel walls and plays a part in inflammation and tumor growth. The team asked whether its level in healthy people predicts cancer or death over the long term.

The study enrolled 889 cancer-free adults from 2006 and tracked them to 2018 through registries. In about twelve years, 69 people got cancer and 66 died. Those with the highest third of protein levels faced clearly higher risks of cancer, cancer death, and death from any cause. The links held after the team weighed other factors. A cheap blood test of this kind could one day help flag people for closer watch.
pmc-10756676:
Gaurav Jyani and five co-authors ask whether people from unlike walks of life price the same health state alike, in a 2023 study from India. Health surveys lean on self-reports, and a person's station in life may tint how they rate health. The team gave a set health picture to 2,311 adults from five states and asked each how much life span they would trade to escape it.

Values did differ by age, faith, family type, state, and habits like substance use. Having an illness at the time also dragged a person's rating down. Even with the picture's severity held fixed, those gaps stayed. Younger people priced their health higher than older ones. The authors say self-reported ill health cannot be blamed on viewpoint alone.
pmc-10774776:
Jiangping Ren, Feng Ling, Ying Liu, and Jimin Sun review chikungunya cases in Zhejiang Province from 2008 to 2022 in a 2023 paper. The mosquito-borne virus is not native to the region, but a local mosquito species could spread it if imported cases seed transmission.

Twenty-nine cases were recorded, nearly all imported, with just three local ones in 2017. Over half of imported cases came from Southeast Asia, peaking in late summer. Fever was universal, with fatigue, joint pain, and headache close behind. Viral genomes matched two known global lineages. With travel rules loosening, the authors urge sharper surveillance and faster diagnosis.
pmc-10782476:
Takeru Takahashi, Koshi Nagai, and Kazumasa Kotake weigh whether a Japanese herbal formula can prevent diarrhea from cancer drugs. The diarrhea can be severe and can force treatment to stop. Past trials of the formula disagreed, so the team pooled the proof from randomized trials. Three studies, all using the same cancer drug, met their bar.

Pooled results showed no clear cut in severe diarrhea against mixed comparison groups, and no change in mild diarrhea. Against no treatment alone, though, severe diarrhea did fall. The authors judge the proof thin and of low quality, and call for larger trials before the formula is trusted for this use.
pmc-10790076:
Catherine Bollard and Andrew Weyrich, editors of the journal Blood Advances, look back on a year of cancer research in its pages, in an editorial from 2023. The journal closed its seventh year with an impact factor of 7.5. That placed it among the top 12 of 79 hematology journals.

The editors thank their associate editors and note that clinical guidelines remain among the most cited items. They then spotlight recent work with a cancer focus, alongside classic blood conditions that show up during malignancy. One featured review sorts a class of follicular lymphomas that lack a common gene swap into three broad groups. More guidelines and updates are promised for the next year.
pmc-10792176:
Emilio Gil-Martin and co-authors review melatonin as a counter to gene mark errors in oral cancer in a 2023 paper. Tumors grow when chemical marks on DNA and its packing go wrong, silencing guards and freeing growth. The sleep hormone melatonin can edit those marks, and lab work hints it can undo some cancer linked changes.

Pairing melatonin with standard radiation and drug care may blunt side effects enough to keep doses on schedule. The authors stress that most proof still sits in cell and animal studies. They urge large, careful clinical trials to test whether the hormone improves survival and quality of life. The review gathers the newest findings for that push.
pmc-10800876:
Alexandra Brakel and co-authors present a study, published in 2023, on insect peptides as possible new drugs against a deadly fungal infection. The fungus strikes people with weak immune systems and kills many each year, mostly in poorer countries. Standard drugs are few and can cause harsh side effects, so fresh options are needed.

The team screened twenty antimicrobial peptides, many drawn from insects and rich in one building block. Several well-known peptides were included, plus a mammal peptide for comparison. Against three strains of the fungus, the best peptides stopped growth at low doses. Their low toxicity in past animal work adds to their promise as drug leads.
pmc-10802976:
Shrimp-shell fiber wrapped around an extraction oil makes a green sponge for rare earths, and Byron Lapo and co-authors tuned it for yttrium, in work from twenty twenty-three. Build settings were swept by two design rounds: oil share, fiber strength, and sourness. Probes checked the sponge's build and steadiness.

It pulls rare earths across a wide sourness range and shrugs off salt. Loads filled in under five minutes, near ninety milligrams per gram. It used half the oil of classic liquid extraction, with no thinning solvents. Against calcium, gadolinium, and nickel mixes it stayed picky, and it cleaned real lamp waste well.
pmc-10806176:
Eivind Sæther and Idar Lyngstad write about outdoor life as a skill that can support health across a whole life. Their article, published in 2023, uses stories and talks with older adults who have spent much of their lives outdoors. The word they study means free-air life, or life spent outside in nature.

The authors trace how this skill grows from childhood to old age. They ask what the skill looks like at each stage and how it links to the wider idea of body skill for health. Their work suggests that time outdoors, learned young and kept up for years, can support movement, health, and well-being in later life. The piece is a discussion built on lived experience, not a trial.
pmc-10826876:
Sonakshi Jyrwa and co-authors report what a national survey found about mental illness in the Indian state of Kerala. Trained field staff interviewed 2,479 adults in households across three districts, using standard diagnostic tools. Lifetime mental illness, not counting tobacco disorders, touched 14.14 percent of adults, and 11.36 percent were ill at the time of the survey.

Anxiety and stress-related disorders were commonest at 5.43 percent, then depression at 2.49 percent, while severe disorders stood at 0.44 percent. About 2.23 percent were judged at high risk of suicide. The authors note these rates run above national figures and argue they should shape the state's service planning.
pmc-10827976:
Hach, Bertsch, and Nonell published in twenty twenty-four a study of psychiatric drug use in suicidal teenagers. Few psychiatric drugs are approved for adolescents, so off-label use is common. The team checked urine and blood samples from teens admitted for acute suicidality. Samples reflected the drugs they took as outpatients before admission. More than two hundred cases were included, most of them girls.

Over half the teens took at least one prescribed psychiatric drug. Off-label use was far more common for one drug class than for antidepressants. Depressed teens were more often treated within approved labels than teens with stress disorders. Girls showed high drug blood levels much more often than boys. The authors urge blood-level checks to improve safety. They also call for more real-world evidence in this age group.
pmc-10834876:
Jun Li and co-authors published this study in 2023. It tests a two-drug combo against acute myeloid leukemia, a fast blood cancer. The drugs are azacitidine and homoharringtonine, both already used in blood cancers. In lab leukemia cells, the pair arrested growth more than either drug alone. Formal scoring confirmed true synergy. Colonies shrank, and cell death rose sharply in two cell lines.

Gene reads traced the effect to a stress pathway inside the cells. The combo lowered a growth driver called c-MYC while raising a death chain through DDIT3 and PUMA. Blocking parts of that chain blunted the synergy, confirming the route. The authors propose the pair as a candidate regimen worth clinical testing. The paper appeared in a Chinese journal, with an English abstract.
pmc-10860676:
Marilynn Johnson wrote this philosophy article, dated 2023 in the head though the catalog lists 2024, on hidden costs in everyday talk. Relevance theory, a leading account of how hearers read speakers, assumes listeners grant beliefs once they spot a speaker's intent. Johnson argues that this ease is not shared equally by all speakers.

Some speakers, worn down by repeated unfair doubt tied to prejudice, shift from stating meaning to showing it with extra effort. Others reshape their voice or appearance to sound credible, paying costs that privileged speakers never face. Drawing on work about testimonial injustice and on accent research, the article shows how social standing bends the basic mechanics of communication.
pmc-10863776:
Researchers report 2023 results on long-term blood pressure in midlife and later risk of atrial fibrillation, a fast and uneven heart rhythm. Data come from the ARIC study, with four pressure checks in a row for each person. Total exposure was summed across the visits for 9,892 adults with no rhythm problem at the start.

Over about 15 years, 1,550 people developed the rhythm problem, and rates rose step by step with total pressure. The top quarter for total systolic pressure had about half again the risk of the bottom quarter. Pulse pressure showed an even stronger link in the same data.
pmc-10871076:
Kristin Fulgoni and Victor Fulgoni study beef intake and nutrient adequacy in US adolescents using national survey data from 2023 in the pack record. Teens need more nutrients for growth, yet many fall short of recommended intakes.

Diet recalls over many survey cycles set beef intake and usual nutrient levels for teens aged fourteen to eighteen. Beef eaters took in notably more of several nutrients, including iron, zinc and vitamin B12, than non-eaters. Fewer beef eaters fell below needs for many of those nutrients. Still, over half of all teens fell short on calcium and several vitamins, the authors note.
pmc-10877376:
Kubota and co-authors lay out a trial plan for schizophrenia care in a protocol paper. Thinking problems are a core part of the illness and linked to poor outcomes, yet drugs or social training alone help only a little. The trial tests pairing brain training with one of two drugs.

Patients will be assigned by chance to get either lurasidone or paliperidone, each paired with the same training program. The first six weeks use drug treatment alone, followed by twenty-four weeks of combined care. The main measure is change in a tablet-based thinking score. The team will also track social function, symptoms, quality of life, and safety. The plan was published in two thousand twenty-four, with the study dated two thousand twenty-three in its head.
pmc-10956576:
Guilherme Bueno and co-authors review non invasive brain stimulation for fall risk in older adults in a systematic review published in 2023. Such stimulation can shift cortical excitability and support brain plasticity, and it has lately been tied to better movement patterns after nerve injury. The review asks whether it lowers fall risk and fear of falling in older people living at home.
