Databases and trial registries were searched over three years, following a standard review handbook, with only randomized trials admitted. From more than eight thousand candidate papers, nine studies qualified for a quality focused summary. The review weighs their designs and outcomes to judge what the method can and cannot yet claim for fall prevention.
pmc-11225476:
Hand washing is the simplest guard against infections spreading in clinics, yet knowing and doing are different things. Omokhua Harrison and Enabulele Joan surveyed dental health workers in 2023 in four public hospitals in Nigeria's Edo state, during a Lassa fever outbreak. One hundred eight of one hundred twenty questionnaires came back.

Knowledge looked solid: most respondents scored good or excellent on hygiene facts. Practice lagged far behind, with most rated fair or poor and only a few rated good. The outbreak, the authors conclude, did not seem to lift everyday practice. They present the gap as a training and supervision problem that hospital managers must close, since dental work puts hands close to blood and saliva daily.
pmc-11446376:
Insects smell their way to food, mates, and danger, and the receptors behind that sense could power new farm tools if they were easier to study. Emma Elise Hoch-Schneider and co-authors worked on moving those receptors into baker's yeast, a cheap host that grows fast and suits large screens. Older test beds, from fly neurons to frog eggs, are slower and costlier. The team paired the receptors with a glowing calcium sensor to read out activity.

One partner protein that the receptors normally need stayed silent in yeast, so a full smell response is not yet in hand. Still, the authors tuned many experimental settings and mapped what must change next. They lay out the groundwork for a scalable yeast platform that could one day match unknown receptors with the odours that trigger them.
pmc-11531476:
Fei Nie and Dongpeng Yan make a new kind of glass from food proteins in this 2024 paper. They use egg white and gelatin, both cheap and widely found, to form thin sheets that bend like plastic yet feel hard like glass.

The sheets form as water dries out, with bonds between the two proteins giving both strength and flex. They also glow after light exposure, with color that shifts by the light used and by time, and the glow can last a long while. The team shows the sheets used in hidden patterns and optical codes. The work points to greener, easy to shape glass for screens and tags.
pmc-11531876:
Iara Diamela Rodriguez and Leonardo Ariel Saravia weigh the strength of links in an Antarctic food web in this twenty twenty-four study. Warming has shifted the species mix around the West Antarctic Peninsula in recent decades. Knowing which species hold the web together helps judge how the system copes with change.

The pair studied Potter Cove, off the South Shetland Islands. They estimated how strongly each species affects the ones it eats or feeds, then removed species one by one on a computer to see how stability and web break-up changed. Strong links were unevenly spread. The work names the heavyweight species whose loss would shake the cove most.
pmc-11531976:
Huang, Chen, and Lin published in twenty twenty-four an editorial on a leech-based traditional medicine for high uric acid. The medicine is a freeze-dried powder from a medicinal leech species. A recent study found its protein extract lowers blood uric acid in tests. It blocks an enzyme that makes uric acid in the body.

It also adjusts transport proteins in kidney and gut to clear more uric acid. The editorial weighs that study's strengths and weaknesses. The authors hope gut microbe targeting may extend the approach to related metabolic conditions. Their piece is a commentary, not new experimental data.
pmc-11532476:
Shijiang Wang and thirteen co-authors find a protein team that shields a fat making enzyme and speeds bone cancer growth, in a 2024 journal article. The cancer is osteosarcoma, a fierce bone tumor of the young. Faulty self eating in cells, a cleanup act gone wrong, helps it grow.

The team saw the fat enzyme run high in cancer cells with the cleanup act switched on. It fed cell growth in a way that hung on that act. A second protein guards the enzyme: it calls in a third that clips off the tags that would send the enzyme to be broken down. Blocking the enzyme or its clipper curbed the boost from the guard. The trio is put forth as a drug target set.
pmc-11534176:
Nicole Cook and five co-authors explore whether doctors' free text notes can reveal patients' exposure to gun violence beyond wounds, in this 2024 study. Research usually counts only the shot and the dead, missing witnesses and the bereaved, whose exposure never gets coded. The team worked within a large network of primary and behavioral health clinics.

From a decade of records, they sampled patients flagged by diagnosis codes or a custom field, then searched nearly ten thousand charts for gun related terms. Ninety charts were read closely by hand. Only thirteen notes, fourteen percent, truly documented exposure or injury. The rest used the words in other senses. The authors list refinements this pilot suggests for a language processing tool that could one day count the full burden of firearm violence.
pmc-11535476:
Ying Wu and co-authors assess the safety of a probiotic strain in this 2024 study. The strain, Heyndrickxia coagulans BC99, came from the feces of a healthy infant. It is a candidate for use in functional foods and medicines.

The team sequenced its full genome and ran a battery of safety tests. The strain did not break down red blood cells and stayed sensitive to many antibiotics. It caused no harm to gut-like cells in culture and stuck to them well. More than ninety percent survived lab tests that mimic the gut. Feeding studies in mice and rats showed no ill effects, which supports its safety case.
pmc-11539276:
Farah Khalida Abdul Rahman and two co-authors hunted traits that drive dengue deaths in a Malaysian state. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, deals with dengue fever. Cases and deaths have climbed in Malaysia as the disease spreads in poorer lands. Past work stuck close to the clinical signs of severe infection. This team widened the lens to traits of the person, the clinic, and the setting.

They drew data from the state's e-dengue system, a live registry. A case control design set deaths next to matched survivors. Readers who fight dengue in city states get a fuller map of who dies and why. Such maps can aim scarce care at the highest risk first.
pmc-11539676:
Richa Sharma, Rukmini Mishra, and Raj Kumar Joshi present, in a 2024 data paper, a near complete genome of the fungus that causes purple blotch, a major onion disease. The fungus is a necrotroph: it kills plant tissue and feeds on the remains. Knowing its full gene set is the first step toward resistant onions.

The isolate came from Nashik, India, and was sequenced with long read technology. The assembly spans about 33 million bases in just 20 contigs, with half the genome in pieces longer than 2.6 million bases. Its gene content checks were run against universal single copy markers. The team catalogued the fungus's carbohydrate cutting enzymes, its secondary metabolite clusters, and the proteins it secretes, including candidate effectors that manipulate the host. Their group hunts onion lines with resistance, and this reference genome lets them read the enemy's playbook while they breed.
pmc-11542476:
Yu Sun and co-authors search for protein markers of papillary thyroid carcinoma, the most common thyroid cancer. The study draws on five patients, comparing cancer tissue with nearby normal thyroid tissue from each. A tagging method called TMT proteomics measures thousands of proteins at once. The team then flags proteins whose levels differ between the paired tissues and annotates what they do.

In total, 639 proteins differ: 278 run higher in cancer and 361 run lower. Six of the higher proteins stand out as potential specific markers for this cancer. The authors argue these proteins and their pathways may reveal how the disease develops. The findings offer candidate markers for later validation in larger patient groups.
pmc-11547876:
Mohammed Al Bahri and co-authors test, by simulation, how to keep magnetic whirlpools stable at high temperatures inside nanowires, in a 2024 paper. The whirlpools, called skyrmions, are tiny swirls of magnetization that could store data at very small scales. Heat is their enemy: it can scramble a skyrmion's shape or spawn stray ones at random, corrupting stored data.

The team varied three magnetic properties of the wire material and the wire's own size. For some settings of magnetization strength and directional stiffness, the skyrmion's shape held steady above 800 kelvin, well above room temperature. Wider or longer wires also protected the structure against heat. Random skyrmions only began appearing on their own above about 700 kelvin. The authors conclude that with the right material tuning and geometry, skyrmion memory can survive the heat of real devices.
pmc-11551476:
McMullen and ten co-authors explored social prescribing for Pakistani carers in this study from twenty twenty-four. Social prescribing connects people to community support instead of medicine alone. Pakistani carers in Britain face deeper isolation than white British carers, yet services rarely fit their culture. The team interviewed twenty-seven carers and ten stakeholders in London and Sheffield.

Carer identity itself proved complicated, tangled with family duty and stigma. Many carers had never heard of social prescribing. Stakeholders cited funding gaps and weak links between doctors and community groups. Both sides wanted culturally aware staff and education pitched to the community. Two carer advisers shaped the study throughout. The authors urge collaboration to close the gap.
pmc-11552576:
Arden Aron L Asuncion and co-authors report an exploding e-cigarette injury in this 2024 case article. A man in the Philippines was using a device bought online when it blew up in his face. The blast tore his lips, tongue, and palate area, broke several teeth, and knocked him down with a brief loss of consciousness and weakness in both arms.

Scans found a shattered first neck bone and a crack in the second, with a metal shard lodged just in front of the fractures. Blood vessels were unharmed and the airway, though swollen, stayed open. The team kept him in intensive care with a neck collar, ready to open the airway at the bedside if swelling worsened. The authors use the case to flag the blast risk of unregulated devices.
pmc-11563176:
Rebecca Trowman, Antonio Migliore, and Daniel Ollendorf report, in 2024, lessons from a global policy forum on how health technology assessment bodies should collaborate. These bodies judge which health technologies are worth funding, and their work crosses many fields. A 2024 forum reviewed past joint efforts to learn what works.

Six themes stood out, from pinning down a shared purpose to funding the work properly, since time and money are routinely underestimated. Inviting the right mix of partners and giving them equal standing also mattered. Case-study pilots were suggested as a practical way to run joint work. The recommendations aim to make future collaborations deliver lasting value.
pmc-11565576:
Valentina Stampi-Bombelli and Marco Mazzotti model how to build the contact beds that pull carbon dioxide straight from the air. Their 2024 study compares two bed shapes: loose pellets packed in columns, and honeycomb monoliths with thin walls. Both run a cycle that traps the gas with heat and vacuum, then releases it for storage.

The pair varied pellet size, wall thickness, and sorbent share, and scored each design on energy use, sorbent mass, and size. Short parallel columns and high-loading monoliths needed the least sorbent at low energy. Monoliths kept improving as energy rose, thanks to thin walls that ease gas flow. For sheer compactness, a sorbent loading below full strength worked best. The authors say the best design depends on which cost a project fears most.
pmc-11570276:
Enrique Hernández-Jiménez and co-authors test a new way to predict positive blood cultures in sepsis, by gauging how worn down the immune system has become. Blood culture is the standard test for bacteria in the blood, but it is slow and can mislead both ways. Sepsis itself can blunt the immune response, a state called endotoxin tolerance, and the team reasoned that this blunting might flag true infection.

Blood was drawn from emergency patients who met the Sepsis-3 criteria, at admission. In the lab, samples were challenged with bacterial endotoxin, and the cytokine reply was profiled. Clinical facts, immune cell markers, and five cytokine levels were recorded. Patients whose cultures grew bacteria showed a clearly weaker TNF-alpha response to the challenge. A sluggish immune reply could flag true infection days before the culture dish answers.
pmc-11570676:
Madeline Hawke, Linda Sweet, and Julie Considine published a 2024 study of shared decision-making in pregnancy care. Good care should involve women in choices. The team recorded real clinic consultations in Australia. Women with higher body weight formed one group. A leaner group allowed comparison.

Trained raters scored each talk with a standard scale. Scores were low across the board. Women were rarely drawn into decisions. Body weight made no difference to the scores. A case example covered induction of labor. The findings show a gap between policy and practice. Training and time may both need attention.
pmc-11570776:
Amwas and three co-authors wrote a review in twenty twenty-four on adoptive T cell therapy for solid tumors. In these treatments, a patient's own immune cells are collected, changed or grown in a lab, and given back to fight cancer. The authors focus on why solid tumors, such as brain tumors, resist such care.

The review compares three main types: tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy, engineered receptor therapy, and CAR T cell therapy. Each type has strengths, such as hitting many tumor targets or sensing very low levels of a target. The authors then survey ways to help cells reach tumors, stay active, and work inside the harsh space around a tumor.
pmc-11574976:
Xiao Jiang Chen, Lin Song, Xing Peng Han, and Quan Wang publish the full mitochondrial genome of a freshwater goby in this 2024 paper. The fish lives in Chinese fresh waters and belongs to a large genus whose family tree is still being drawn. A complete small genome gives that work solid anchors.

Sequencing on a high-throughput platform returned a circular molecule of 16,500 bases, heavy in adenine and thymine as these genomes tend to be. The team lined it up against nineteen relatives and rebuilt the family tree two ways, by likelihood and by Bayesian reasoning. Both placed this species closest to one named cousin. The authors say the sequence enriches the genus's genetic store and that more species' genomes are needed before the tree settles.
pmc-11575076:
Qinjia Ren and co-authors show that resident immune cells decide whether transplanted eye cells live in a 2024 study. In a mouse strain that goes blind from retinal degeneration, donated light-sensing cells were injected under the retina. The same cells died in normal mice but survived in the blind strain. Microglia, the retina's own immune cells, clustered tightly around the donors.

Draining the microglia away with a drug feed made the donors die even in the blind strain. Letting the cells return restored donor survival. Gene readings suggested the local tissue pushes young neuron growth in the blind strain. The finding flips the usual suspicion of immune cells: here they act as gardeners a transplant needs.
pmc-11576876:
Ruoqi Deng, Sabri Uzuner, and Li published a study in 2024 on why removing a torn knee meniscus helps some patients and harms others. The meniscus spreads load across the knee, and cutting part or all of it shifts pressure onto cartilage. Computer models usually assume one standard knee, ignoring that real knees differ in size and shape.

The team built shape models from MRI scans of thirty-one knees and simulated standing with the meniscus intact, partly removed, and fully removed. Load shifted from the inner to the outer compartment after removal, by amounts that depended on geometry. Size changes altered pressure predictably, but shape changes produced surprises no rule of thumb caught. The average-shaped knee bore the lowest pressures, suggesting shape outliers need personal planning.
pmc-11577076:
A shrub found only in Mali's Dogon Country is a mainstay of local healing, yet science had never examined it. Mamadou Konare and co-authors interview forty-five residents across three villages about Acridocarpus monodii and test its chemistry in the lab. Most healers were older men, and malaria topped the list of treated illnesses.

Leaves were the most used part, usually boiled and drunk or used in baths. The plant proved rich in flavonoids and polyphenols, the compound families behind much plant medicine. Its extracts also quenched free radicals strongly in two standard tests. The authors warn that harvesting roots and bark, favored by more educated users, threatens the species. They present the work as a first scientific record of the plant.
pmc-11577476:
Andrew T Fithian and co-authors cut the hip's sealing ring in cadaver hips to learn which tear shapes loosen the joint most. The acetabular labrum grips the ball of the thigh bone, and its tears come in several cuts: radial splits, separations where cartilage meets labrum, and complex mixes. Twelve hips without arthritis, from donors averaging about thirty-five years, went on a loading frame.

Each hip was tested whole, then with one tear, then with the complex tear, at set twists and pushes in neutral and stretched poses. The team guessed radial tears would free the most motion. Measures of the ball's shift under torque and force carry the answer. The study aims to guide which tears demand repair to keep hips stable.
pmc-11579776:
Salt water chemistry hides a puzzle: each ion seems to bend the rules in its own way. Peter M May and Eric F May offer a new frame for that puzzle in a 2024 paper. Their frame rests on triples of ions and how they interact at higher strengths. It also settles a long fight over the activity of a single ion, a value many said could not be measured.

Two unlike tests at trace levels, they show, pin that value down in a way that fits the rules of thermodynamics. A forgotten convention does the quiet work in the proof. The gains matter most for pH, whose definition leans on single-ion values. Mixed salt systems in industry stand to gain as well.
pmc-11584476:
Ye and co-authors investigate how the chemotherapy drug paclitaxel damages the eye, and whether an existing class of drugs can prevent it. Paclitaxel can cause macular edema, swelling at the center of the retina that blurs vision. The team traced the harm to Müller cells, support cells of the retina, and to a water-handling enzyme called CAXIV.

In cell and animal experiments, paclitaxel killed retinal cells, weakened the barrier between blood and retina, and raised inflammation, while water channel proteins rose and sealing proteins fell. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors calmed the inflammation and restored fluid handling. The authors propose these inhibitors as a new treatment route for this side effect.
pmc-11584676:
Wang and co-authors present ClickGen, a deep learning model that designs drug-like molecules it can actually build, in a 2024 paper. Many computer-designed molecules fail in the lab because no one can synthesize them. ClickGen assembles molecules from modular click-chemistry reactions and steers the search with reinforcement learning.

The model beat rival reaction-based generators on novelty, buildability, and fit to known binders for three target proteins. The team then aimed it at PARP1, a cancer target, and made and tested its proposals in just twenty days. Two lead compounds killed cancer cells at nanomolar doses with low toxicity. The authors frame the system as a step toward closed-loop, automated drug discovery.
pmc-11584876:
Lulu Sun and co-authors published this 2024 study on how immune cells clear germs. One defense, called LAP, wraps invading germs so the cell can destroy them. The team found that a protein named PDCD6 holds this defense back. Mice and cells lacking the protein killed bacteria better and formed more of these germ-wrapping structures.

The study traces a chain behind that effect. When germs attack, cells raise their output of lactate, a product of sugar use. The protein named above binds an enzyme and keeps lactate low. Without it, lactate rises and changes a second protein, which then boosts the defense. The findings point to a control path that future drugs for infection might target.
pmc-11585276:
HanYu Wang and six co-authors test whether a waist index adjusted for weight predicts obstructive sleep apnea, in a two thousand twenty-four cross-sectional and genetic study. The weight-adjusted waist index is meant to capture central obesity independent of body weight.

In national survey data from two thousand seventeen to two thousand twenty, higher index values tracked higher apnea risk even after full adjustment, with the top quartile at clearly elevated odds. The index outperformed other measures as a predictor, with a saturation point in the relationship. Mendelian randomization, using genetic instruments, supported a causal reading. The authors propose the simple index as a screening aid for apnea risk.
pmc-11585576:
Jessy Slota and co-authors read single brain cells to learn why some die first in prion disease in this 2024 study. Prions are misfolded proteins that wreck the brain, much like the proteins behind Alzheimer's disease. The team pulled living neurons from infected female mice and read each cell's active genes.

Cells prone to damage shared a telling pattern: genes for synapses, the links between neurons, ran low. Scoring that pattern sorted neurons from fragile to hardy across several types. Hardy cells started with more of a protective cold-shock protein, which surged further after infection. Some fragility signs matched those seen in Alzheimer's. The overlap hints at shared weak points across brain diseases.
pmc-11585976:
XiaoLe Chen, Lili Xiao, Daozhu Wu, and Saida Pan studied predictors in two thousand twenty-four of poor fetal growth and heart reshaping before birth. They compared women with suspected growth restriction against women with smooth pregnancies, one hundred seventy-nine versus fifty-three in the first split. All had standard ultrasound and fetal heart scans, with many flow and heart measures taken.

After birth, babies were split into confirmed growth-restricted and control groups by weight. The groups differed in mother traits such as body mass, blood pressure disorders, and diabetes, and in cord and fluid findings. Heart measures from the scans added predictive value. The study helps flag at-risk babies earlier.
pmc-11587576:
Six researchers in Spain compared two lab methods for reading the outer coat proteins of a pneumonia germ, in a study published in 2024. These proteins, called porins, form gates that let drugs into the cell, and losing them helps the germ resist antibiotics. Gene reading alone cannot always say whether a gate protein is truly made. The team studied twenty-six patient samples of Klebsiella pneumoniae plus two reference strains.

A gel method and a laser-based mass method gave the same protein picture for every strain. Three main coat proteins showed up at matching weights by both routes. Gene reading, though, sometimes misled: some strains carried an intact gate gene yet made no protein, while others with changed genes still did. The authors back the laser method as reliable and warn against trusting gene data alone for these gates.
pmc-11587676:
Nine doctors led by Tomasz Czarnik set out the plan for a trial on vitamin D dosing in very ill patients whose blood is cleaned by machine around the clock. Such patients often run low on the vitamin, and the cleaning process can strip more of it away. No guide says how much to give them.

The trial, run across up to five Polish university hospitals, gives one very large single dose or a slightly smaller one, by mouth or feeding tube. It checks how many patients reach a healthy blood level three and seven days later. About one hundred thirty-eight patients will join. The plan paper explains the design and its reasoning.
pmc-11588776:
Mecca and co-authors map dust particle shifts across Turin over three years. Monitors ran from 2018 to 2021, spanning the COVID lockdown. Three particle sizes were tracked: PM1, PM2.5, and PM10. Background sites read 28 to 30 micrograms for PM10. Traffic sites read higher at 36 micrograms.

PM2.5 peaked at traffic sites with 24 micrograms. Daily peaks fell in the late morning hours. The lowest values came in the late afternoon. Source direction tests pointed to the Po Valley from the north. Saharan dust paths from the south added a second source. That long window let the team set lockdown readings against normal years.
pmc-11590476:
Yue Ma and co-authors test, in 2024, whether a vitamin-related compound can protect the ovary reserve in rats with early ovarian failure. The condition has no effective treatment, and an inflammatory cell-death pathway is a suspected driver. The compound is known to calm inflammation, making it a candidate.

Rats with drug-induced failure received the compound for three weeks. Hormone levels improved and follicle counts partly recovered, lifting the ovary index. In cell tests, the compound lowered inflammatory factors and the markers of the fiery cell-death process. Blocking a related enzyme in other arms helped confirm the pathway. The authors present the compound as a promising route, pending human data.
pmc-11590976:
Miriam Parise, Silvia Donato, and Ariela Francesca Pagani report a 2024 study of online abuse between young adult partners in Italy. They asked how a blurred sense of self and partner relates to control and intrusion online. Their sample was adults in a romantic link, most of them women in their twenties.

People who found it hard to see a partner as distinct from themselves used more control and intrusive acts online. That link held only for couples who had been together a long time. Shorter links did not show the same pattern. The authors say the work helps spot when online abuse is more likely. It may also guide steps to prevent risky acts in young adult couples.
pmc-11591076:
Sharon Ke and colleagues review a plan to fight Staphylococcus aureus with several monoclonal antibodies at once. This bacterium resists antibiotics fast and attacks with surface proteins, barrier-breaking enzymes and toxins, which is why health bodies rank it a critical threat. Single drugs keep losing ground to it.

The review argues that antibodies aimed at many targets on the bacterium can work together with greater force than one alone. Hitting several epitopes at once should also slow the rise of resistance, since the bacterium would need many changes to escape. The authors present this combined approach as a strong partner, or stand-in, for standard antibiotics.
pmc-11591576:
Fabio Casciano and colleagues published a 2024 review on exercise and cancer immunotherapy. Exercise helps prevent several cancers. It can also support cancer treatment. The biological reasons are still being mapped. The review focuses on immune effects.

Exercise changes blood flow inside tumors. It releases signaling molecules from muscle and fat. These signals can wake up anticancer immunity. They may also alter tumor metabolism. The authors assess exercise given before or during immunotherapy. They suggest where future trials should look. The goal is turning a healthy habit into a planned treatment partner.
pmc-11594576:
Malgorzata Roszkowska reviewed the many levels of cancer drug resistance in 2024. Resistance is one of the hardest problems in cancer care. It grows from linked processes at the gene, cell, and tissue levels, so a single-cause view misses much of the picture.

The review pulls together recent work on gene changes, gene control without code change, and the tumor's local setting. Up to sixty-three percent of mutations can vary within one tumor, which feeds resistance. Cancer stem cells repair DNA well and run altered fuel use. Support cells and immune cells around the tumor also help it resist. Radiation can breed resistant forms under pressure. The author argues future care should hit several paths at once, guided by markers.
pmc-11595176:
Tadeusz Strozik and co-authors probe how a light activated drug molecule binds the blood's main carrier protein, in a 2024 study. The molecule, a sulfonated porphyrin, is a candidate for light based cancer therapy. How it rides on human serum albumin shapes where it goes in the body. The team mixed light based measures with computer docking.

Three molecules could bind at once, at sites of unlike grip strength. Bound molecules kept their excited states alive longer, and the protein's shape shifted slightly. Docking pointed to the three favored pockets and the amino acids holding the guest. The authors frame the map as help for drug design.
pmc-11595776:
Emilia Irzmańska and co-authors present a 2024 study on a new way to fit 3D-printed structures onto protective gloves. Gloves are a key part of personal protective equipment, and printed polymer parts could add strength or grip, if they can be joined well to the cloth.

The joins were made by ultrasonic welding and by contact welding. A polyamide knit served as the base cloth, and a few printed plastics were tried as the add-on. X-ray microtomography then showed the weld zones. The team read the size and form of each joint, on the view that a larger contact area bodes best for use.
pmc-11596476:
Chan Ho Lee and co-authors map where kidney cancer spreads and how that shapes survival in Korea in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Spread sites have been tied to survival gaps elsewhere, but Korean data were unclear. The team drew on a national study group database.

Over seventeen hundred patients who began targeted therapy were analyzed. The lung was the most common spread site, then lymph nodes and bone. Liver, adrenal gland, and brain followed. Median cancer survival ranged from about fourteen months with liver spread to about twenty-nine with lung spread. Liver, bone, and pleural spread marked the shortest survival. The authors offer the map for prognosis talks.
pmc-11596576:
Haejin Woo and six co-authors name two new kinds of bacteria found in the soil at the roots of tomato plants. Both kinds belong to a known group, Rhodanobacter, and a full battery of tests backs their new-kind rank. The soil zone at roots is a rich hunting field for bacteria that help crops grow. Helper traits can cut the need for sprayed plant food.

Both strains shrug off wild swings in soil acidity, one surviving from pH 3 to 13 and the other from pH 2 to 13. Each makes a plant growth hormone, frees bound plant food from rock, gives off ammonia, and builds iron-gathering tools. Those traits hint at real help for crops in tough soils. The team is clear that direct tests on plants are still to come.
pmc-11597676:
Stefanie Heym and co-authors build a glowing reporter cell line in 2024 to track a human T-cell virus. The virus spreads through close cell contact and hides inside immune cells, which makes infection hard to count one cell at a time. Its key switch protein turns on a viral control region, and the team wires that switch to a green glow.

They inserted a glow gene under many copies of the switch's target into T cells and picked the best clones. When the switch was present, over ninety percent of switch-positive cells glowed. Mutant switches that lack a needed partner glowed far less. Mixed with infected cells, the reporters caught the low true infection rates, proving the tool works.
pmc-11597776:
Constantin Munteanu and co-authors review a three way link among a gas, gut microbes, and cell proteins in brain disease, in a 2024 paper. The head byline is longer than the catalog list, so team framing is used. The gas, hydrogen sulfide, is made by the body and by some gut bacteria, and it guards cells from damage.

Proteins called sirtuins help cells build power parts, fight damage, and calm swelling, and the gas can switch them on. When gut microbes fall out of balance, gas levels drop and brain harm can grow. The review ties this axis to aging and to diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, and weighs care ideas that follow.
pmc-11598076:
Supharat Inphonlek and four co-authors modify natural rubber to improve its electrical and antibacterial traits. They start with deproteinized rubber and graft a copolymer of acrylic acid and acrylamide onto it with a crosslinker. The graft helps bind silver ions and interact with titanium dioxide particles.

Silver nanoparticles form under heat and pressure inside the modified rubber. Microscopy shows silver spread well through the matrix, while titanium dioxide clumps at high loading. Modified composites resist heat better than base rubber and are stiffer, with restricted chain motion. Electrical performance rises with the graft and fillers. The materials target uses that need both dielectric function and germ control.
pmc-11600676:
Fahui Jiang and co-authors surveyed soil and tea in 2024 across Jiangxi Province in China. Selenium is a trace element people and animals need, and lack of it drives disease in many lands. Tea can help fill that gap. The team took sixty-seven paired soil and leaf samples from tea lands in the province. Jiangxi is a major tea zone with rich soils. They read what drives the element's path from ground to leaf.

Soil levels ran well above world and national means. Soil carbon, iron and aluminium oxides, and years of planting lifted soil levels. One soil nutrient pulled them down. Leaf levels were far lower and hinged most on soil levels. The team names the heart of the province as the best fit for tea. It also lists soil tweaks that raise leaf levels.
pmc-11600876:
A plant compound calms fatty liver disease in mice, Ziwen Wang and co-authors report in a 2024 study. Fatty liver tied to metabolism is now the world's most common liver illness, with few drugs. Mice fed a fatty diet for sixteen weeks got the compound during the last four.

Liver fat, oxidative stress, and a rust-like cell death all eased with treatment. Computer mapping and lab tests pinned likely protein targets. Gut bacteria and fat tissue shifts were checked as well, since the gut and liver trade signals. A multi-angle rescue in mice makes the compound worth testing toward human fatty liver care.
pmc-11603076:
Shuting Sun and co-authors study a fungus that makes a toxin in grain, in a 2024 paper. The fungus harms food safety across the world, and the toxin is called DON in short. Many control factors for DON were known, but the full chain that turns its making on and off was still unclear.

The team finds a control protein that is vital for DON making; without it, output fell by more than nineteen parts in twenty. Oddly, the genes for DON rose while their proteins fell. The control protein seems to pace protein building through cell parts that make proteins. That link may help curb toxin in food crops.
pmc-11603176:
Mengistu and three co-authors measured suicidal thoughts among pregnant women at an Ethiopian hospital clinic in twenty twenty-four. Suicide is a leading cause of death in people of reproductive age, and local evidence on pregnancy was thin. The study surveyed women attending antenatal care at Gondar's specialized hospital in twenty twenty-two.

Of one hundred sixty-eight participating women, about five percent reported suicidal ideation and about five percent a past attempt, rates the authors call low. Several factors were significantly tied to ideation: unplanned pregnancy, a history of abortion, a history of stillbirth, being HIV positive, and lifetime substance use. The authors say these predictors can help antenatal services spot women who need extra support, and they call for solution-oriented follow-up research in the region.
pmc-11603676:
Tang Feng and six co-authors review personalized nanovaccines, cancer vaccines carried by tiny particles and tailored to a patient's tumor, in a 2024 paper. Vaccines against spreading cancer have drawn interest, but fewer than thirty percent of patients respond. Particles can protect the vaccine, help the immune system spot it, and carry it to tumors and lymph nodes.

The review surveys carrier designs, from fully synthetic particles to ones built from biological material, and the traits that help them fight metastases. It also covers pairing nanovaccines with other immune therapies to strike at several steps of the spreading process at once. The authors close by weighing the hurdles that still block routine clinical use.
pmc-11603876:
Beata Borgström Bolmsjö, Emelie Stenman, Anton Grundberg, and Kristina Sundquist chart risk clustering in Swedish forty-year-olds in 2024. Heart risk factors found early can still be changed. A city screening program invited all forty-year-olds for a check, giving a clean cohort view.

More than eighteen hundred volunteers gave survey and body data. Metabolic factors such as pressure, fats, sugar, and waist size were tallied. Non-metabolic factors included family history, smoking, mental strain, and social vulnerability. A standard European score summed each person's risk. Models then tested how the two factor families cluster and link within individuals.
pmc-11603976:
Johanna Heugenhauser and nine co-authors link brain tumor images to blood immune profiles in glioblastoma, in a 2024 study. Glioblastoma is the deadliest common brain cancer, and up to a third of its mass is immune cells. Imaging and immunology each describe the disease well, but nobody had fused the two views.

The team reused data from an earlier immunotherapy trial. Seventy-six patients were screened, and forty-one had both baseline tumor scans and blood immune data. Scans yielded twenty-seven measures of size and shape under a standard visual scoring system. Blood yielded sixty-seven immune variables from cell sorting and gene tests. Cross-mapping the two sets hunts for blood signatures that mirror what the scan shows, a step toward choosing therapy from a blood draw.
pmc-11604776:
Omar Mostafa and colleagues reviewed in 2024 surgery to reverse a Hartmann's procedure, comparing a single-incision laparoscopic approach with the standard multi-port one. Hartmann's reversal reconnects the bowel after an emergency colostomy and is a hard operation. Minimally invasive routes may ease recovery, but which port style is better was unclear.

Only two observational studies fit, with one hundred sixty patients in all. The single-incision approach took notably less operating time. No clear gaps appeared in deaths, overall complications, hospital stay, injury risk, severe complications, or repeat surgery. The authors call the single cut quicker with like outcomes, but they stress that randomized trials are needed for firm advice.
pmc-11604976:
Carla Bautista and co-authors studied yeast hybrids in 2024 to learn why they adapt more slowly than their parent strains. Hybrids mix the genes of two species and have a flexible gene layout. The team grew hybrids and parents in a broth with a drug that acts like harsh light. Both groups found ways to cope, and both used changes in the same broad gene switches.

After one hundred rounds of growth, the coping changes in parents sat on both gene copies, while in hybrids they sat on one copy. Gene edits showed a change must sit on both copies to give its full gain. Hybrids lost that mixed state more slowly. The authors say an old rule that favors strong gene traits slows hybrid gains.
pmc-11605076:
Andrin Doll and co-authors show that X-rays can pick out a microwave resonance signal from the exact element it comes from, in thin films of quantum bits. X-ray methods already read the spin of single elements in films well, but the faint states used in quantum tech sat out of reach. The trick is to drive the spins with microwaves and read the echo with X-rays.

Films built from metal-bearing ring molecules, with copper or vanadium at their hearts, gave the signal. The team also spotted an X-ray side effect tied to trapped charge from the beam itself. The result opens a path to read quantum states element by element on almost any surface.
pmc-11605476:
Jinglin Wang and co-authors review a promising bacterium for blocking dengue and Zika viruses in a 2024 commentary. Both viruses spread through mosquito bites and cause many infections each year, while vaccines and treatments remain limited. The commentary discusses a study that found the bacterium living in the gut of wild Asian tiger mosquitoes in Yunnan, China.

The bacterium, a strain of Rosenbergiella, was able to block both viruses from passing through the mosquito. Wang and co-authors explain why this matters and what it could mean for dengue prevention. They present the gut microbe route as a fresh biological strategy against mosquito-borne disease. Questions of scale and field use remain, but the approach offers a new direction beyond sprays and vaccines.
pmc-11605576:
Ryosuke Matsujda and co-authors report a way to watch leg motor pathways during brain tumor surgery, in a conference abstract from 2024. Damage to those pathways can leave a patient unable to move a leg well. A strip of contacts placed in the fold between the brain's two halves can stimulate the leg area directly.

The method was used in eighteen operations on sixteen patients. A six-contact strip was placed after the skull was opened, and a standard signal method located the central groove of the brain. Stable signals from three leg muscles were recorded in most cases. A drop of more than half in signal size was set as the warning line. In the monitored cases, no such lasting drop occurred. Follow-up lasted at least three months.
pmc-11605676:
Two-dimensional materials, sheets a single atom thick, promise new electronics, but measuring their key traits is slow. Harikrishnan Sibi, Jovita Biju, and Chandra Chowdhury use a graph neural network to predict one such trait in a 2024 study.

The trait, called work function, sets how easily electrons leave a material's surface, a make-or-break value for devices. Their network reads the atom layout as a graph of atoms and bonds, needing no hand-built descriptors or extra quantum calculations. Trained on a public database of layered materials, it beat standard feature-based machine learning, with a small average error. Fast, accurate trait prediction can screen thousands of candidate sheets before any lab work begins.
pmc-11605876:
Peiyao Luo and co-authors show that a mitochondria targeted antioxidant peptide calms bacteria triggered lung injury in mice, in work published in 2024. Gene wide profiling tied the injury to immune control paths and a major inflammation pathway. Treated animals were checked with sequencing, staining, and gene tests.

The peptide lowered key inflammatory signals and reduced proteins that drive a fiery form of cell death. One alarm protein stood out as central: injury raised it, the peptide lowered it, and adding it back erased much of the benefit. The authors say the peptide works by quieting that alarm protein and the inflammasome it feeds.
pmc-11606976:
Slawomir Koziel and co-authors automate antenna design in 2024. Shaping a modern antenna takes weeks of expert trial and error. Most effort goes into the basic form that delivers traits like multi band use. Few forms get tried because each costs so much expert time.

Their procedure builds planar antennas without a human in the loop. A flexible shape description lets the computer invent varied forms. Smart search methods then tune the sizes toward the target traits. Automation could cut time to market and free experts for harder problems. The work targets a stage of design long held as pure craft.
pmc-11607076:
Ramadan A Geioushy and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-four study of antibacterial paper coated with metal-decorated zinc oxide particles. Paper for packaging and records could gain germ-fighting power from such coatings. Silver and copper were added to tune the effect.

Higher metal loadings strengthened the paper noticeably. Tensile strength, stretch, energy absorption, and burst resistance all rose. Silver versions kept the paper bright, while copper dimmed whiteness. The coating attacked Staphylococcus aureus, a common contaminant. Long-term antimicrobial behaviour was also projected over decades. The work targets sustainable paper with built-in protection for archives and hygiene uses.
pmc-11607376:
Munro and five co-authors present Pantry, a framework for pulling many RNA traits from sequencing data, in a 2024 paper. Gene regulation studies often use gene expression alone. Splicing and other RNA traits hold extra signal but are hard to extract.

Pantry builds traits from six forms of RNA control, from isoform ratios to RNA stability. It then links these traits to genetic data through several standard analyses. On two large data sets, many genes with no known expression signal gained signals in another trait. Combining traits roughly doubled gene-trait finds in one test. The authors say full RNA use can sharpen complex trait genetics.
pmc-11607876:
Juan Izquierdo-Condoy and co-authors survey smartphone use among medical students in Latin America. Their 2024 study covers one thousand five hundred ninety students from seven countries, surveyed online in late 2023 and early 2024. Phones are near-universal tools, yet their role in medical training in this region had little study.

Nearly all students owned a phone, and about eighty-eight percent used it for study. Watching academic videos was the most common use, ahead of medical apps and podcasts. Women formed about sixty-four percent of the sample, and over half attended private universities. Academic phone use tracked with progress through the program. The authors weigh how schools might build phone-based learning into formal training.
pmc-11607976:
Tao Li and colleagues published a 2024 case report on treating extra heartbeats during pregnancy. Extra beats strained the expectant mother's heart. They caused palpitations and risked reducing blood flow to the baby. Her faulty focus sat in an unusual spot. It lay within the right chamber's muscular ridges.

Doctors mapped the focus without X-ray imaging. A heated catheter then destroyed the tiny faulty site. Avoiding radiation protected the fetus during the procedure. The ablation succeeded despite the tricky location. The report details her symptoms, tracing, procedure, and recovery. Radiation-free ablation deserves wider use in pregnancy.
pmc-11608376:
Wujiang Ying and colleagues built in 2024 a new impact test rig to check how a high explosive reacts to low level hits. Safety tests for launch and penetration settings need hits whose force and length can be set with care. Their rig covers a wide range of peak pressures and pulse lengths.

They used it on a melt-cast explosive based on DNAN. How the explosive reacted turned on the peak pressure, how fast pressure rose, and how tightly the charge was confined. Ignition did not happen in a fixed pattern, so the team used logistic regression to predict it. That method forecast ignition with high accuracy, and confinement changed how well it worked.
pmc-11608476:
Hongliang Hui and co-authors published this trial in 2024 on finding small lung nodules before surgery. When a patient has many nodules, marking them all so the surgeon can cut true is hard. The team tested a new guide, electromagnetic navigation, against the standard CT scan guide. Fifty patients were split by lot between the two methods.

The new guide's marks landed about as close to target as the scan's, within the set margin for a tie. The new method also ran faster, taking about sixteen minutes against twenty-two. Patients felt less anxiety before surgery with the new guide. Harms did not differ by a clear mark. The authors say navigation marking can stand in for scan marking when many nodules need flags at once.
pmc-11609576:
Chen Feng and his five co-authors, publishing in 2024, study a protein called LMAN2 in breast cancer. The protein normally helps move and sort other proteins inside cells, but its role in tumors was unclear. The team measured it in cancer samples and cell lines, then raised and lowered its levels to watch what changed, and searched for partner proteins it touches.

They found LMAN2 levels higher in tumors than in nearby healthy tissue, and higher levels tracked with worse outcomes for patients. In lab cells, extra LMAN2 sped growth, spread, and resistance to the chemotherapy drug cisplatin, while blocking cell death; silencing it reversed those effects and even re-sensitized resistant tumors in mice. LMAN2 binds a partner called MAPK9 and switches on a known growth pathway. The authors propose it as both a warning marker and a drug target.
pmc-11609676:
Haiwei Bao, Lulu Dai, Huiyang Wang, and Tianan Jiang aim ultrasound-burst drug bubbles at transplanted hearts to fight rejection. Their 2024 study loads microbubbles with sirolimus, a drug that calms immune attack. Rats receive abdominal heart grafts and split into salt water, bubble therapy, and plain drug groups.

The bubble method packs fifteen times more drug into the graft than plain dosing. Immune cell invasion of the graft drops below even the plain drug group. A growth factor signaling path linked to scarring quiets down, while self-cleaning cell proteins rise. Rescue tests with a blocker of cell cleaning and an activator of the growth path confirm the mechanism. The authors present targeted bubbles as a stronger, more local shield for new hearts.
pmc-11609876:
Anna de Jong, Anna Von Wachenfeldt, Lennarth Nyström, and Anne Andersson wrote, in two thousand twenty-four, on how women in Sweden stick to hormone pills after breast cancer. The pills are adjuvant endocrine therapy, taken for years after surgery. In cancer that feeds on estrogen, they cut the chance the ill comes back. They help only if women keep taking them.

The team found 10,422 women with that type of cancer in two thousand eight to two thousand ten, in the breast cancer list. Drug lists showed who picked them up. Good use was 94.4 per cent at one year, 87.6 at three, and 81.6 at five years. The South scored best. Zones with a cancer clinic beat zones with none at five years. Women aged past seventy-five stuck to the pills least. Help should aim at them and at women under forty.
pmc-11610076:
Rachel Canaway and five co-authors ask whether software prompts could raise alcohol screening in Australian general practice. Their feasibility study was published in twenty twenty-four. The prompt would target patients who are pregnant or planning pregnancy, a group where drinking carries extra risk.

The team reviewed literature and interviewed twenty-three stakeholders: software vendors, clinicians, and others. At least eighteen software packages serve Australian general practice, which complicates any add-on. A further twenty-two stakeholders sense-tested the recommendations. The study weighed what a fitting tool looks like, when a prompt should fire, and what helps or blocks uptake. Its findings guide how such a prompt could be built into real clinic systems.
pmc-11610176:
Avery Paxton and co-authors mapped the world's evidence in 2024 on whether living coastal defenses, such as restored marshes and reefs, truly protect shorelines. Towns are planting nature based defenses against storms and rising seas faster than the proof of their worth accumulates.

The team swept databases, search engines, and agency sites for studies of active projects in six shallow living systems, from salt marsh to shellfish reef. They sorted what each study measured: effects on nature, on water movement, on money, and on people. Machine help sped the screening. The map shows where evidence is thick and where it is thin, guiding both builders and the next round of studies.
pmc-11611476:
Jacob Msando and co-authors survey medical staff on a blue card concussion rule in semi elite Australian football, in work from twenty twenty-four. Under the rule, umpires can send a player off for a head check. The league hoped the rule would help medical teams catch concussions.

Staff from the men's and women's leagues replied at a rate near half, split among doctors, physios, and trainers. Most did not find the rule helpful and did not want it kept. Two thirds said umpires are not trained to spot concussions on field. Only a third felt fully sure in their sideline checks. Most asked for more policy teaching before each season. Ties with other staff were not much harmed by the rule.
pmc-11612276:
Atefeh Rahmani and co-authors build a magnetic carbon powder from pistachio shells to pull an antibiotic out of hospital wastewater. Drug traces in waterways harm people and wildlife, and cefotaxime is one such drug. Their 2024 powder starts as activated carbon treated with an iron salt.

The team tuned dose, acidity, drug level, and time with a design of experiments approach. At the best settings, the powder cleared 99.1 percent of the drug. Lab checks showed a strong, even surface well suited to the task. Fit tests point to a single layer grip driven by chemistry, with a top capacity of 651.6 milligrams per gram. The authors pitch the waste based powder for wider water cleanup.
pmc-11612476:
Chenyu Liu, Dongliang Zhang, and Wankai Li improve a nature-inspired optimizer and aim it at drone route planning, in a 2024 paper. The base method mimics how snow melts and refreezes as it searches for the best answer. Their upgrade, GDSAO, seeds the search with an evenly spread starter set. It lets the melt pace adapt to how spread out the pack is, and adds a local search step for members outside the elite pool.

On thirty standard test problems, the method beat a string of rival optimizers. Turned to drones, it found three-dimensional routes that dodge all obstacles and respect turn limits. The authors judge it more reliable and steadier than the methods it faced. Reliable path tools matter as drones take on delivery and survey work.
pmc-11613476:
Li Wang and co-authors built a scoring chart to predict which belly surgery patients will develop a racing, uneven heartbeat afterward, in a 2024 study. The rhythm problem, atrial fibrillation after surgery, raises deaths and costs in hospital. It is best known after heart surgery, but it also follows open belly operations. The team gathered records from two hospitals: patients who developed the problem, matched controls, and a separate check group.

Four measures stood out as risk signs: an inflammation marker, a ratio of two white cell types, a kidney waste marker, and an index read from heart tracings. The chart built from them sorted high- from low-risk patients sharply in all three groups. Its accuracy marks were high, and a benefit check said using it would help more than harm. The authors offer it so teams can guard high-risk patients before surgery.
pmc-11613776:
Ruiyin Zeng and co-authors report a 2024 study of slow-healing wounds in diabetes. Such wounds heal poorly because new blood vessels and nerves grow back too slowly. The team built a soft gel that can be injected into the wound. The gel carries stem cells from fat tissue plus tiny packets with two active factors. One factor draws the cells to the injury site.

The gel forms under light and holds its parts through weak links. Once in place, it aims at three systems at once: defense, vessel growth, and nerve growth. The cells are guided toward nerve-like roles as healing goes on. The authors present the mix as a cocktail therapy in one dressing. Wound care teams get a single tool that tackles several blocks to healing at once. The work is a lab study, so patient use would need more tests for safety and dose.
pmc-11613876:
The first year after prostate cancer treatment is often hard, with symptoms and unmet support needs. Nazmije Kelmendi and co-authors tested a support program in Swedish primary care in 2024. Patients used an app to report symptoms and get self-care advice, and they also held health dialogues with a nurse, by video, phone, or in person.

Eleven patients joined, and all finished the four-week program and reported their symptoms in the app. Patients said the dialogues covered what mattered and that the app plus nurse felt tailored to their needs. A few technical faults came up. The authors judge the program feasible and suggest starting it right after treatment ends.
pmc-11615376:
Yuxi Chen and co-authors test a common antibiotic as a treatment for retinitis pigmentosa, a genetic eye disease, in work published in 2024. The disease kills light-sensing cells over time, and immune cells in the retina speed that loss. The drug, minocycline, calms those immune cells and protects nerves in other settings.

The trial gave 35 patients a daily tablet for twelve months, with no control group. The main test measured an electric signal from the eye. About a third of patients improved on that signal at one year. Vision measures such as field, sharpness, and colour also improved. Side effects appeared in most patients but all cleared without extra treatment, and none were severe. The authors call the results promising while noting the open design.
pmc-11615676:
Elizaveta Kuznetsova, Anastasiia Liashenko, Natalia Zhozhikashvili, and Marie Arsalidou review how gifted children differ from their peers, in a paper from 2024. Schools still debate how to spot giftedness and what marks it. A shaky picture leads to missed children and weak programs. The team gathered studies from more than twenty-five countries.

In all, they reviewed 104 papers covering more than seventy-seven thousand children. Gifted children beat peers on memory, focus switching, and shape problems. Their brains also fired faster and harder on tough tasks. They scored higher on inner drive, self-belief, and openness, and earned better grades. Tests are growing more fair across cultures, the authors note. The review gives schools a firmer base for spotting and teaching gifted youth.
pmc-11615876:
Paramesh Shamanna and six colleagues describe a digital twin platform for personalizing diabetes nutrition, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Type 2 diabetes involves insulin resistance and failing beta cells. Standard diets ignore how differently individuals' blood sugar responds to the same meal.

The platform learns from continuous glucose monitoring, dietary records, and other body signals. It predicts each patient's post-meal glucose response. Recommendations then steer meals toward better predicted control. The stated goals include improved insulin sensitivity and support for remission. The paper presents the technology's development and its application in practice. Personalized nutrition of this kind aims to replace one-size-fits-all diet sheets with feedback tuned to one metabolism.
pmc-11615976:
Georgios Barakos and co-authors report a rare case of fluid on the lung tied to blood growth outside the marrow, in a paper from 2024. The patient was a woman of forty three with a blood trait that weakens red cell output. She came in with worse short breath and a huge build up of fluid on one side of the chest.

Her past held known growth sites by the spine and a gall bladder surgery a month prior. Fresh scans showed the fluid was new and had piled up fast. A full work up pinned the fluid on the spine side growths, not on germs or heart strain. Drainage plus germ drugs cleared the fluid, and later scans stayed clean. The authors urge this cause be kept in mind for like cases.
pmc-11616176:
Janah Vandenhoeck and co-authors map DNA methylation in pleural mesothelioma to find a fingerprint that sets it apart, in this 2024 paper. This rare, aggressive chest cancer is hard to tell from other lung diseases and is usually caught late. Chemical tags on DNA may give an early tell.

Eleven tumors and twenty-nine healthy pleura samples, the largest healthy set yet, were profiled at eight hundred fifty thousand sites. Public data added other lung diseases for contrast. Wide methylation differences separated tumor from healthy tissue. The unique pattern is a candidate biomarker panel for earlier, surer diagnosis.
pmc-11618176:
Alejandro González-Muñoz and co-authors studied when suction therapy can save an infected surgical mesh instead of removing it. Mesh is often used to repair hernias, but infection can force a second operation to take it out. Suction therapy, which draws fluid from the wound under a sealed cover, offers a chance to keep the mesh in place.

The team reviewed 61 patients treated this way between 2018 and 2024. They checked patient traits, surgery details, and the germs found in each wound. The mesh was saved in about four of five cases. Smoking stood out as a strong sign of failure, raising the odds that the mesh had to go. The findings help surgeons judge who is likely to benefit.
pmc-11618376:
Ryan Feathers, Ryan Vignogna, and Christopher Fromme reveal how a protein complex switches on Rab6, a traffic controller for the Golgi apparatus. Rab proteins cycle between off and on states. The Ric1-Rgp1 complex turns them on by swapping nucleotides. How it does so had never been seen in structural detail.

Their cryo-electron microscopy structure catches the complex mid-swap with Rab6. A helical region not characterized before proves to be the exchange domain, with key residues confirmed by mutation. In a surprise, an arrestin fold grips Rab6's loose tail. That suggests activators often hold Rab proteins by their tails. The findings give a detailed picture of how cargo flow through the Golgi is controlled.
pmc-11618476:
Olivier Bakker and co-authors link in 2024 rare ill genes to the drivers of common ills through gene webs by body cloth. Broad gene hunts find marks that bare ly nudge gene work, and which genes they hit stays vague. Rare ill genes, by contrast, strike their genes head on.

Their frame reads how hunt marks shift gene co work in fifty seven cloth and cell kinds. Hit genes prove rich in rare ill genes: top height genes swell with bone flaw and joint loose genes. Most key genes sit far from the hunt spots, a sign of long range webs. Web build bars close the read.
pmc-11618876: Dieter Schollmeyer and Heiner Detert report the structure of a small selenium ring compound in a short paper from 2024, made from a semicarbazone starting material and selenium dioxide. The ring joins a ten-membered carbon loop to a selenium and nitrogen unit, with a double bond on one side. The flat parts of the molecule sit almost at right angles to each other, and the chain linking them is nearly free of strain. The note records the makeup and shape for chemists who study such rings.
pmc-11620476:
Rick Yang and three co-authors responded in a 2024 paper to a call for stronger government-academic data partnerships in health crises. The original commentary urged moving from one-off sharing during emergencies to standing collaborations. The response agrees on the goal but says the hard parts got glossed over. Privacy and security of sensitive health data form one hurdle, thrown into relief during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Standing partnerships also cost standing money: funding, staff, and training that emergency grants do not supply. The authors ask for concrete routes to long-term support, such as grants or private partners. Learning must run both ways, with governments and universities building each other's capacity. Without that honesty, they warn, the backbone stays weak.
pmc-11621676:
Jinmann Chon, Yunsoo Soh, and Ga Yang Shim review stroke-tied muscle loss in a 2024 paper. Stroke can breed muscle loss past the base age form, which sours heal paths for patients. Roots span poor food, rest waste, nerve loss, and body chem shifts in the review.

Tools to call the state span mass reads, grip reads, and walk reads at the bed side. Set rules built for age loss fit stroke folk poorly, the team holds. Fresh rules that match stroke blocks are urged for sound calls. Heal gains may hinge on those calls, since missed states slow the whole rehab arc.
pmc-11622476:
Peng Zhang and co-authors survey a seafood-borne bacterium in patients and the environment around Huzhou, China, in a 2024 study. Vibrio parahaemolyticus is now the top cause of seafood-linked infection worldwide. It lives in coastal waters and shellfish. Which strains sicken people, and how they differ from water strains, was murky.

More than one hundred strains from 2020 to 2023 were typed. Dozens of serotypes appeared, with a few dominating patient cases. Growth and swimming traits of major strains were compared across sources. Shared types between water and clinic hint at direct routes to illness. Food safety teams gain targets for monitoring harvest areas. The molecular map also readies outbreak tracing.
pmc-11622676:
Higher natural creatine levels may protect the grip strength of older adults, suggests a 2024 genetics study by Minping Hong and co-authors. Rather than feeding anyone supplements, the team used inherited variants as a natural experiment, a method called Mendelian randomization, across outcomes from arthritis to bone density.

The clear signal was grip: people whose genes point to higher creatine were less likely to show weak grip after sixty. The other bone and joint outcomes showed no such pattern in the results reported. The authors present the analysis as a causal hint, bounded by the method's assumptions, not a supplement prescription.
pmc-11623176:
Farm prices swing on weather, soil, and history together, and older forecasting tools handle that tangle poorly. Haohao Chen and Fadi Al-Turjman build a cloud-based system to predict agricultural prices more sharply. Their framework stacks three learning methods. A convolutional network extracts features from the data. A gated recurrent unit follows patterns over time. Reinforcement learning then tunes the whole model.

The inputs span historical prices, weather, soil conditions, and other drivers. On public and private datasets, the system beat traditional models. Its errors, measured two standard ways, came out lower. The authors frame the work as rural informatization: better forecasts support better planting and selling decisions. That, in turn, supports rural economic growth.
pmc-11623976:
Yi-Tse Su and co-authors report a man whose heart stopped because his breathing switched off in sleep, and whose workup ended at a lung tumor hiding in his chest. Central sleep apnea is a rare but characteristic flag of anti-Hu paraneoplastic syndrome, where the immune response to a cancer attacks the brainstem. His arrest came from carbon dioxide building up overnight.

Scans found mediastinal small cell carcinoma. Treatment combined tumor removal, chemotherapy, plasma exchange, and high-dose steroids. Against the literature's grim record of irreversible damage, his apnea resolved within about a month. Rare presentations earn case reports when they teach the diagnostic reflex: unexplained central apnea deserves a hunt for the tumor behind the antibody.
pmc-11624576:
Tami Mark and Benjamin Huber count drug overdose deaths among people covered by Medicaid in the United States. Their 2024 study links Medicaid records with the national death index for the years 2016 through 2020. No past count had tracked overdose deaths for this group on its own. The pair set the group's rates beside those of the whole country.

In 2020, the overdose death rate for Medicaid members was about twice the national rate. Members made up a quarter of the population but near half of all overdose deaths. Rates topped national rates in each age and sex group past age 15. Deaths in the group also rose by more than half across the five years.
pmc-11624676:
When the COVID-19 pandemic hit, mental health clinics had to switch visits to phone and video almost overnight. Nicholas Sims-Rhodes and co-authors review what helped or blocked that switch in this 2024 paper. Demand for mental health care surged around the world at the same time. Clinics in the United States had to follow new safety rules while keeping care going.

The team ran a systematic review under the PRISMA method. They focused on changes in how care was delivered in United States health systems from March 2020 to May 2022. Their goal was to name the barriers that slowed the switch and the supports that sped it up. Many papers had described the switch itself, but few had sorted its causes. A clear list can help clinics plan the next forced change.
pmc-11624776:
Minna Mao and co-authors build a lifestyle scale for pregnant women in 2024. Many women leak urine during pregnancy, a problem called urinary incontinence. Lifestyle change is a front line way to prevent and ease it. Yet little was known about the daily habits of pregnant women with this problem in mainland China.

The team drafted scale items from the literature and refined them with expert rounds. Further cuts came from item analysis in a second stage. They then tested the scale for structure, steadiness, and repeat scores over time. A sound scale can help clinics spot risky habits and tailor advice.
pmc-11625376:
Haidar Ali and co-authors track which dengue virus type dominated Pakistan during 2023 and 2024, and probe its coat gene for drug targets. Dengue has four types and still lacks solid antivirals or vaccines, partly because infection history can backfire. Their 2024 study tests one hundred patient samples and sequences the envelope gene of the winners.

Type two caused sixty three percent of cases, with two mixed infections of types two and three. The coat gene sequences closely matched strains from China and India. Computer models of the coat protein flagged binding pockets, and docking suggested two known compounds could block early infection steps. Predicted immune hot spots on the protein may aid vaccine design. The authors say the work sharpens outbreak planning.
pmc-11625876:
Yojiro Ishikawa and four co-authors published a case report in twenty twenty-four on a cancer side effect so rare it earned a syndrome name: tumor-induced oblique abdominal muscle paralysis. Their patient, a man in his seventies with malignant pleural mesothelioma, developed a bulge on his left side that appeared when he stood and vanished when he lay down.

Scans showed the oblique muscles wasted and the navel pulled rightward, consistent with the tumor invading the intercostal nerves. Abdominal wall paralysis is usually blamed on disc problems, shingles, or nerve injury, almost never on cancer. The authors urge positional examination, standing and supine, whenever tumor nerve invasion is suspected. A bulge that keeps office hours, they show, can be a neurological sign in disguise.
pmc-11626076:
Michael Zellner and five co-authors hunt the lowest radiation dose that still gives clear lung scans, in a 2024 study. CT scans save lives but dose adds up, above all for children. The team scanned three body-shaped dummies of unlike sizes at many dose levels. They graded each image by a math measure: how steeply the density line climbs where lung meets its lining.

Three radiologists also rated the images by eye. A sharpness cutoff matched what the doctors called good enough. At that mark, an adult scan needed an effective dose of about a tenth of a millisievert, and a child scan even less. The team says the number method can guide dose cuts without losing diagnostic worth.
pmc-11626476:
Songji Tu and co-authors test a fine tool for finding leukemia cells in spinal fluid of children. The brain and spine form a haven where this cancer often returns. Standard fluid checks can miss small numbers of cells. Flow cytometry, which tags cells one by one, may catch them earlier.

Over a thousand children in China were followed across many centers. About one in eight showed tagged cells in their fluid. Those children relapsed in the central nervous system far more often than the rest. Risk models kept flagging the fluid result at several time points. The authors back the test for sharper risk sorting and care tuning.
pmc-11626976:
Chunyan Weng and a team of co-authors review TRIM proteins in gut cancers, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. TRIM proteins tag other proteins for disposal, a system gut tumors lean on heavily. The family steers growth signals, cell death, and tumor spread.

The review lays out what each member does in gut tissue, healthy and cancerous. Some TRIM proteins act as brakes; others feed tumor growth. Their levels may serve as warning markers for diagnosis and outlook. The authors also weigh the family as a set of drug targets for future therapy.
pmc-11627376:
Zhao and co-authors study the skin of fish as an immune organ, using zebrafish as their test animal. Fish live surrounded by germs in the water, and their skin is the first barrier those germs meet. The team looks at what happens in the skin after the fish are immunized by immersion in water containing a vaccine component.

The vaccine used a surface protein from a carp virus, and the researchers tracked gene activity in the skin afterward. They found responses involving a heat shock protein and the MAPK and JNK signaling paths, which help cells react to stress and infection. The findings support immersion vaccines, an easy way to protect farmed fish without injecting each animal.
pmc-11628176:
Huanhuan Li and co-authors fed zinc oxide nanoparticles to rare minnows to test their value as a feed additive. The particles are prized for being easy for the body to absorb, but their effects on fish growth and health are little studied. The team measured growth, zinc buildup in tissues, blood cells, and gene activity over sixty days.

The supplemented fish ended lighter, with zinc levels and a liver injury index clearly above the control group. Blood cell counts first rose, then fell. In muscle, growth genes were dialed down after sixty days, while liver tissue switched immune genes up. The authors read a split story: short feeding may help growth and immunity, but long feeding lets zinc build up and harms both.
pmc-11629676:
Ming-yu Zhao and co-authors ask what patients value when replacing one missing tooth in China in a 2024 paper. The two standard fixes are a fixed partial denture, a bridge anchored on nearby teeth, and an implant-supported crown. Past studies compared them in mixed ways, so the team used a choice experiment: patients picked between options that varied on five features.

Nearly three hundred people took part. The five-year complication rate mattered most, taking over forty percent of the decision weight, ahead of cost, survival rate, treatment time, and the procedure itself. Patients would pay a large sum for a ten-point cut in complication risk, and a smaller one to avoid invasive work. The authors say cutting complications should lead prosthetic research, and that the rankings can sharpen talks between dentists and patients.
pmc-11629776:
Regina Treudler and co-authors set out diagnostic criteria and guidance for anaphylaxis that strikes on the job, in a 2024 position paper from a German allergy society. Severe allergic reactions at work follow workplace exposures, and bee or wasp venom leads the trigger list, ahead of foods and drugs. Latex, chemicals, and animal contact trail far behind.

Beekeepers, outdoor workers, food handlers, and health staff carry the highest risk. The paper reviews how common the problem is, what sets attacks off, and how exposure route and cofactors shape each case. It recommends detailed histories plus skin and blood tests for diagnosis, and covers prevention and management.
pmc-11630776:
May van Schalkwyk and co-authors published a 2024 essay on how harmful industries pollute public debate. Companies whose products damage health and the environment do not just sell goods; they sell stories. Those stories shape science and policy in their favor. The authors name the effect discursive pollution, drawing a parallel with the physical pollution the same industries cause.

The piece catalogs the tactics across industries: casting doubt on evidence, framing regulation as overreach, and presenting industry-friendly claims as common sense. It also exposes contradictions inside those stories. The second half turns to defense. The authors propose how the health community can push back: naming the tactics, refusing the loaded terms, and building clearer counter-narratives. The essay adds a cross-industry lens to research on the commercial drivers of health.
pmc-11631776:
Muthukumar Santhanakrishnan and three co-authors set three tooth root set times head to head in the front top jaw. Their trial appeared in twenty twenty-four. Seventy-five patients were split by lot to fast set, fast set with a socket shield, or late set. Scans and pink gum scores tracked bone and soft gum shifts for a year.

The shield group lost the least bone rim girth by far at one year. Late set lost the most. Pink scores ran best in the shield group, then fast set, then late set. Pain and joy marks were taped too. The team backs the shield path when front bone is thin.
pmc-11631876:
Cuiwen Zhang and colleagues identify a single enzyme gene as the disease factor of a bacterium causing potato common scab. Their 2024 study examines a Streptomyces strain whose suspect gene switched on during potato infection.

The gene was cloned and shown to encode a protein of over four hundred building blocks in an enzyme family that breaks down pectin. The purified protein alone caused disease when placed on healthy potatoes. Deleting the gene slowed bacterial growth and shrank the clear zone the mutant formed on pectin plates. Colony appearance and pigment stayed unchanged in the mutant. Gene loss also reduced the strain's ability to infest potatoes, confirming the enzyme's central pathogenic role.
pmc-11632476:
Kunal Aneja, Ravi Rudraraju, and Ashok Shyam survey, in a 2024 editorial, how robots are changing total knee replacement surgery. Traditional methods rely on jigs and the surgeon's eye, while robotic systems plan the cut from scans and guide it with live feedback to sub-millimeter accuracy.

The authors highlight gains in fit and alignment tailored to each patient, with better function, fewer repeat surgeries, and faster recovery, above all in hard cases. One system built in India is presented as a lower-cost answer shaped to South Asian anatomy. Hospitals may save over time through fewer revisions, though the editorial weighs cost against these promised gains.
pmc-11632976:
Liu and co-authors use in 2024 large public cancer datasets to weigh the worth of a protein that helps tumors hide from the immune system. The protein sits on tumor cells and on immune cells that gather inside tumors. The team asked if its levels track with survival and with immune cell counts.

Levels of the protein were off normal in many cancers and linked to how long patients lived. Levels rose and fell with counts of a key immune cell type, and the protein was widely found on tumor linked forms of those cells.
