Its level on those cells also tracked with response to immune care in some cancers.
pmc-11634076:
Bengen Li and co-authors study sex hormones and gene variants in men with enlarged prostate plus low late-life testosterone, in a research paper from 2024. Both conditions are common in aging men and may share roots. Genes that handle sex hormones vary across people, and those variants may shape who gets both conditions.

Records for more than eight hundred middle-aged and older men, from 2017 to 2022, were reviewed. Men split by whether they had the paired diagnosis. The team compared hormone levels and variant patterns between groups. The aim is to clarify risk and guide screening for men who carry both conditions as they age.
pmc-11634176:
A large team of co-authors presents a study from two thousand twenty-four building a rat model of combined scalp and skull wounds. Such composite defects, where soft tissue and bone are missing together, are hard to rebuild in layers. A good animal model is the first step toward testing engineered repairs.

A three-dimensional printed plug kept the scalp wound open and slowed its healing, preserving the skull defect and mimicking a chronic wound. Alongside, the team set up a repair using the animal's own tissue as a positive control. That control healed its skin reliably within three weeks, with varied bone integration, matching clinical experience.
pmc-11634376:
Rafael Pitta and co-authors link physical activity with urinary symptoms in more than twenty thousand Brazilian men. Their twenty twenty-four cohort study uses health screening data from twenty oh eight to twenty eighteen. All men were forty or older.

Lower urinary tract symptoms include weak flow, night trips, and urgency. A logistic model weighed activity against these symptoms with other traits held steady. Low mood, age, erection trouble, and a prostate blood marker each raised the odds. Higher activity, by contrast, linked to lower odds of symptoms. The huge sample gives the activity link weight, and it points to a low-cost habit that may ease a common burden of aging.
pmc-11634976:
Yao Wu, Guiding Li, Chang-hai Lyu, Ni Zhou, and Hai Ming Wong compare mouth bacteria in preschoolers with severe tooth decay in this 2024 study. Rampant decay spreads fast, hits many surfaces, and infects the pulp early. The team matched eighty-eight young children with and without the condition.

Children with decay had more acidic saliva, brushed less well, and ate sugary snacks more often. Certain bacteria marked each group: some thrived in healthy mouths and tracked with higher pH, while others rose with candy intake in decayed mouths. Three species, including a gut bacterium rarely reported in mouths, stood out as possible markers. The authors call for follow-up studies on how gut bacteria may reach the mouth.
pmc-11635076:
Pranita Rananaware and co-authors build a hybrid cage material for dual drug delivery in a 2024 study. Metal-organic frameworks offer vast surface area and tuned pores for cargo. Control of release and safety, though, remain hard. Gold nanoparticles add imaging and therapy traits to the mix.

The team wrapped gold particles inside two joined frameworks by a simple precipitation route. Folic acid on the surface aims the carrier at cancer cells. Two anticancer drugs, curcumin and a classic fluorinated drug, ride inside. A battery of imaging and analysis tools confirmed the structure stayed intact after loading. The platform targets combined diagnosis and treatment in one unit.
pmc-11635176:
Five authors test whether a movement limiting tissue response changes how fish spread in this 2024 study. Dispersal shapes both personal fitness and whole population change, and peritoneal fibrosis, scar tissue from inflammation and repair, is known to restrict movement in threespine stickleback.

In an Alaskan lake, the team injected some captured fish with a compound that triggers fibrosis and others with saline or nothing. They released all at one point and resampled across the lake for eight days. Of 123 recaptured fish, fibrosis itself did not change dispersal. Early inflammation showed hints of an effect that did not reach significance, a lead the authors flag for future work rather than a result.
pmc-11635276:
Hayley Barnes and a large team test whether washing out the lungs can help workers sickened by dust from artificial stone, in a 2024 study. Silicosis from this stone is rising, and no treatment is proven to halt or reverse it. The wash, called whole lung lavage, floods the lungs with fluid to rinse out silica grains and harmful cells.

Eight patients with worsening disease and ground-glass scan changes went through the wash between 2021 and 2022. Scans, lung function, and exercise tests were repeated six months later. Five patients showed better scan scores and more even air flow after the wash, while lung function measures barely moved. The team reports the program ran safely and may offer modest benefit, though the group was small.
pmc-11635576:
Yu Zhang, Xiaoyu Ji, Xialing Zhang, and Yu Wang study spread of thyroid cancer to neck lymph nodes in a 2024 paper. Papillary thyroid cancer is the most common form, and its outlook hinges on whether it reaches the nodes at the side of the neck. Spread patterns there have stayed unclear.

They reviewed 486 patients whose side nodes held cancer and who had full neck surgery from 2019 to 2021. Node level three, at the mid-neck, emerged as the central hub of spread. Knowing which traits predict spread at each level helps surgeons plan how much neck to clear and spare patients unneeded dissection.
pmc-11638076:
Prerana Shrikant Chaudhari and Maria A. Ermolaeva review whether longevity treatments still work when started late in life, in a 2024 paper. Aging brings metabolic failures, and poor metabolism in turn speeds up aging. Drugs and diets that fix metabolism can extend lifespan and keep organs working better. The open question is whether age limits those gains.

The review sorts common metabolic remedies by the ages at which they help. Some work best in young and middle-aged animals. Others keep working well even in old age. The authors explain the biology behind each pattern. Their map helps readers judge which treatments merit trials in older adults.
pmc-11638276:
Omkar S Anaspure and six co-authors pool the evidence on smoking and hip arthroscopy outcomes in this 2024 systematic review. Surgeons wanted to know whether smokers fare worse after this keyhole hip operation, in particular whether more of them end up needing a full hip replacement or a repeat arthroscopy. The team searched four databases for studies on the question.

Twenty observational studies covering more than one hundred fifteen thousand patients met their rules. The pooled analysis found no statistically firm link between smoking and conversion to hip replacement, and none for repeat arthroscopy at two years either. Still, raw conversion rates ran higher in smokers, and several studies tied smoking to complications such as surgical failure, heavier opioid use, infection, and vein clots. The authors advise surgeons to weigh those trends in decisions even though the headline links stayed unproven.
pmc-11638476:
Xueni Cheng and eight co-authors review what red blood cell measures can tell doctors about rheumatoid arthritis in a 2024 paper. Rheumatoid arthritis is a long-term disease where the immune system attacks the joints. Red blood cell counts and related measures shift as the disease moves. The review pulls past studies into one account of those links.

The authors link cell count, hemoglobin, and cell size spread to disease activity. They also link the measures to other health problems and to outlook. Red cells may shape the disease too, through surface proteins and small particles they shed. The review aims to help doctors track and treat the disease. It also points to new study paths on red cell immunity.
pmc-11638776:
Emily Greenfield, Natalie Pope, and Tonya Roberts ask what age-friendly community drives change, read as system change. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Since the early two thousands, a world move has pushed towns to fit old age in built space, social life, and services. Proof of what such drives yield is still young.

They read talks with key staff at eight grown drives in the northeast of the United States through a six-part lens of system change. Strong proof shows for office practice, resource flow, ties across groups, and views of older adults. Proof for shifts in power and in policy is thin. The lens can guide how drives are judged and led.
pmc-11639076:
Sanni Ruotsalainen and a FinnGen team map the inherited side of female infertility. Their 2024 genome-wide study covers 22,849 women with infertility and nearly 199,000 controls from the Finnish FinnGen cohort. Infertility is common, yet in fifteen to thirty percent of cases no cause is found, leaving room for hidden genetics.

A recessive scan found a rare stop-gain variant in the gene TBPL2, carried by about one percent of the population. Its effect size rivaled classic single-gene disorders: women with two copies averaged 0.16 children, against 1.75 for others. The same gene sterilizes knockout mice by blocking ovulation. Those rare women who did give birth had all received infertility treatment. The study delivers a genetic landscape for a condition long short on mechanism.
pmc-11639776:
Emily Jessop and co-authors test whether blocking an enzyme can make an aggressive breast cancer cell less able to invade. Their 2024 paper studies triple-negative breast cancer, a subtype with no hormone targets and high spread rates. Soft nuclei help these cells squeeze through tight spaces, so stiffening the nucleus could slow them.

The team blocked the enzyme SIRT2 with a specific drug in a standard cell line. Treated cells built a more organized cage of fibers around the nucleus. Their nuclei resisted collapse under osmotic shock better than untreated cells. In scratch tests, the treated cells showed polarity faults that hamper directed movement. Confined models showed reduced invasiveness. The work is cell-level, but it names a mechanical route against metastasis worth testing further.
pmc-11639876:
Kobelyatskaya and co-authors build in 2024 a gene based model that sorts a severe form of ovarian cancer into its four known subtypes. The subtypes differ in growth, survival, and response to care, so exact sorting matters for tailored treatment. They drew gene data from six groups, with 535 samples in total.

They found 357 genes whose levels split the four subtypes, each with its own marker set. A neural network built on those genes forms the model, named in the title. Work of this kind could help doctors match care to subtype and design drugs aimed at the traits that set each subtype apart.
pmc-11639976:
Dried tangerine peel is a valued traditional product, but moldy stock is sometimes cleaned and resold. Huizhen Tan and co-authors build a test that spots the fraud without damaging the goods. A portable near-infrared scanner reads light bounced off the peel's outer and inner surfaces. Statistical models learn to tell sound peel from mold-damaged peel. Picking the best wavelengths sharpened the models further.

Outer surface readings beat inner ones. With scatter correction, the model scored perfect accuracy on both the test set and a fresh set collected a month later. A robustness check held up as well. The authors offer the method for market inspection.
pmc-11640176:
Dongjie Zhang and co-authors study miR-26a, a small RNA that curbs fat formation in pigs. Past work from the group linked miR-26a to fat build-up. Here they raise and lower its levels in pig preadipocytes, the cells that can become fat cells, and watch growth and change.

More miR-26a sped cell division but blocked the shift into fat cells. It acts by binding the ACADM gene and the ACSL1 gene, both tied to fat work. Gene sequencing found 337 genes that changed early in fat formation, many tied to the cell cycle. Nine stood out as likely direct targets, adding new detail on how fat formation is controlled.
pmc-11640276:
Evangelista, Lughezzani and their co-authors test a PSMA PET and CT scan for first staging of intermediate-risk prostate cancer in 2024. The scan uses a labeled marker that sticks to a protein found on prostate cancer cells.

Records from three centers covered close to two hundred patients staged before treatment. Scans found the main tumor in all patients and spread to nodes or distant sites in a small share. Spread was more common in the unfavorable risk group. Accuracy for spread topped ninety percent in both groups on follow-up. Scan results changed care plans in about one case in eight, the team reports.
pmc-11640376:
Laetitia Cloutier and co-authors compare feeding plans for pregnant sows across three cycles. Their 2024 study tests precision feeding against simpler constant plans. Two standard plans kept feed mix fixed, with amounts flat or bumped late in pregnancy. Two precision plans tuned the mix to each sow's parity or weight.

In the first cycle, piglet deaths before weaning ran lower under precision feeding than under bump feeding. The second cycle showed no litter gaps between plans. By the third cycle, stillbirths were lowest under one precision plan. Precision plans also cut nitrogen intake by about a tenth and phosphorus by slightly less. The results favor tailored feeding for both piglet survival and lower waste.
pmc-11640676:
A research team fermented enzyme-treated skim milk with a helpful bacterium to cut bitterness and add antioxidant power, in a 2024 study. Breaking milk proteins down deeply lowers their allergy potential but often leaves a bitter taste. Fermentation was the team's tool for fixing flavor while boosting health traits.

They screened lactic acid bacteria for antioxidant strength and picked a Lactiplantibacillus plantarum strain as the best all-rounder. It beat a rival strain at easing bitterness and improving flavor in the treated milk. A tuning method found the best recipe: five percent starter, eighteen hours at thirty-seven degrees, and a set acidity level. The finished milk scavenged harmful radicals at high rates and scored well on taste. Bitter amino acids fell while antioxidant ones rose. The work offers dairies a route to gentler, functional milk drinks.
pmc-11641176:
Yogurts made with plant and hybrid palm oils could carry better fats without hurting heart markers, this 2024 pilot trial suggests. Ruby-Alejandra Villamil and co-authors fed 47 healthy adults one of three yogurts daily for three months: one enriched with sacha inchi oil, one with hybrid palm oil, or a plain control. Blood fats and related proteins were checked monthly.

No group's overall lipid profile shifted clearly. Small within-group drops in total and LDL cholesterol showed in all three arms, including the plain one. The enriched yogurts did raise intake of unsaturated fats and vitamin E. The authors read the result as a safety pass: the oils can upgrade yogurt's fat profile without worsening blood markers in healthy people.
pmc-11641276:
Ricardo Domingo-Breton and co-authors benchmark nanopore sequencing choices for fish farm microbes in a 2024 study, based on the head byline. The portable sequencing method profiles farm water and fish microbes fast, yet its many method options were not fully tested side by side. Library kits, primer spans, and basecalling accuracy modes were compared on water, feces, skin, and gut mucus samples.

Some sample types amplified only with the slower library kit and longer primers. Full length primers gave the deepest naming of microbes, though database matching ran thinner for some groups. The most accurate basecaller gave the cleanest reads but took far longer. The study tunes the full workflow for farm use.
pmc-11641376:
Akihiro Itoigawa, Tomoya Nakagita, Yasuka Toda, and Diego Guidolin review the wide variety of bitter taste receptors across vertebrates. Tasting bitter helps animals avoid plant toxins and other harmful compounds. The receptors form a family on taste buds that has changed a great deal over evolution.

New gene and lab studies have mapped these receptors in many species. The family shows frequent gene births and losses, shifts in what each receptor detects, and differences within species. The authors link this diversity to diet and habitat, and sum up how ecology and evolution have shaped the sense of bitter taste.
pmc-11641476: Kan Katayama and Kaoru Dohi introduce a set of new findings on kidney diseases in this 2024 editorial overview. The piece frames chronic kidney disease as a lifestyle-related condition affecting about nine percent of the world's population as of 2017. Beyond that framing line, the hosted text carries only the opening of the overview, so the specific new insights it announces are not set out in the text provided here.
pmc-11641576:
The authors review how hormone-disrupting chemicals harm the lungs in a paper from 2024. These chemicals are widespread in the environment and in food. They interfere with the body's hormone system and can raise the risk of diseases such as asthma, chronic lung disease, and lung scarring, with exposure before birth a special concern.

The review lays out the ways these chemicals act inside lung tissue. They can drive oxidative stress, change how cells grow and mature, slow repair, and stir inflammation. They can also weaken the barrier between blood and air, letting harmful substances reach the lung. More work on mechanisms and prevention is urged.
pmc-11641676:
Yoonju Oh and co-authors review bandgap engineering in stacked two-dimensional materials through density functional theory. Layered materials can be stacked into structures with tuned traits. Their combined properties can beat any single layer alone.

The review covers stacks of graphene, boron nitride, and related sheets. Transition metal compounds and blue phosphorus also feature. Bandgap tuning serves transistors, light sensors, and solar cells. Theory predicts band structure before costly lab synthesis. The authors sort methods for engineering the gap by design. They also weigh current limits of the theory approach. Future prospects for devices close the survey. The piece guides materials teams planning new stacks for devices.
pmc-11641776:
Enzymes from heat-loving microbes keep working where ordinary proteins melt, which makes them prized for industry. Zahra Naz and co-authors characterize in 2024 a phosphopentomutase from Thermococcus kodakarensis, an archaeon that thrives near boiling. The enzyme swaps a phosphate between two forms of ribose sugar, though it closely resembles enzymes that act on larger sugars.

The team measured its behavior and solved its three-dimensional structure by X-ray diffraction. The structure revealed a fresh catalytic motif, seen in no relative, that likely explains why it chooses five-carbon sugars over six-carbon ones. It is the first such portrait of a phosphopentomutase from a hyperthermophilic archaeon.
pmc-11642276:
A hole between the food pipe and the airway is a dreaded turn in advanced esophageal cancer, and the standard patch, a covered stent, has a habit of slipping. Yuya Nishio and co-authors describe a double-stent fix in 2024 for cases where the first stent slid out early. Their method layers an uncovered metal stent with a fully covered one, each canceling the other's weakness.

In two patients at their hospital, the paired stents held the fistula sealed for the rest of the patients' lives, and both could eat by mouth again. The authors review the literature alongside their cases and argue the trick is simple, adaptable, and worth reaching for when a lone stent migrates.
pmc-11642376:
Jessica Cusato and co-authors wrote a study from 2024 on whether gene variants in the vitamin D pathway predict who answers to two biologic drugs for bowel disease. Vitamin D helps steer the immune system, and its handling genes vary from person to person. The team followed just over a hundred patients with Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis on one of the two drugs. They checked responses at three and twelve months and a stool marker of gut healing.

One drug answered more often at twelve months. An early response strongly foretold a late one. One variant in a vitamin D carrier gene marked most patients who failed to respond at a year. Another marked those who missed the gut healing target. The team offers the variants as leads for personal drug choice.
pmc-11642476:
Boris Straumal and seven co-authors review mixed titanium oxide materials that kill germs and suit the body, in a paper from 2024. Simple oxides of this family are already used in filters, food packaging, implants, and scaffolds. Mixing several metals into one oxide could widen those uses.

The review covers how such materials are made, from wet chemistry to powders and pounding methods, and the shapes they take, from thin films to porous scaffolds. It then sorts lab tests on germs and on stem and bone-like cells. Animal tests that check real use follow, since dish results alone can mislead.
pmc-11642676:
Miralem Jasarevic and co-authors compare multi artery bypass surgery in diabetic and other patients in a 2024 study. Using several arterial grafts can extend life after heart bypass, but diabetes might erase the edge. One center's twenty year records covered two hundred fifty six diabetic and eight hundred non diabetic patients with multi arterial grafting.

Diabetic patients arrived riskier and got fewer double chest artery grafts. Early complications matched between groups, yet over follow up the diabetic group suffered more heart failure shocks, dialysis, and sternal infections. Median survival ran about fourteen and a half years against nineteen and a half. The authors say diabetes should weigh in when surgeons pick a grafting strategy.
pmc-11642976:
Meijing Ren and six colleagues model how short-range order changes crystal plasticity in a chromium-cobalt-nickel alloy, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Medium-entropy alloys have become a materials research hotspot. Recent work shows they contain short-range order, which alters how they deform. The team built that effect into a crystal plasticity framework.

Their non-local constitutive model evaluates short-range order effects within mesoscale continuum mechanics. A slip model incorporating order was combined with nanoindentation and multi-level grain tensile simulations. Load-displacement and stress-strain curves showed order increases the alloy's hardness. Shear strain and dislocation distributions revealed growing heterogeneity as order increased. The study enriches crystal plasticity theory. It also offers guidance for tuning microstructure and performance in multi-level grain materials.
pmc-11643076:
Juan Xia leads a team studying diet and health among breast cancer survivors in China, in this twenty twenty-four paper. Survivors face a raised risk of other long-term diseases. Gaps in food knowledge and diet quality may add to that risk.

The team surveyed more than fifteen hundred women in a Shanghai cancer recovery club. Most were in their mid-sixties, and food knowledge was low in about half of them. The study linked food knowledge and diet quality to the chance of having other chronic diseases at the same time. The findings point to diet teaching as a fair way to protect survivors' long-term health.
pmc-11643176:
Barbara Sciandrone leads a team that tests a plant compound's safety in worms. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with justicidin B. The compound is a lignan with anti cancer traits in cells.

Finding safe new cancer drugs is a clear need, they note. Worms got two doses of the compound in tests. The low dose did not harm worm life, short or long term. The high dose cut life span in short daily use only. Build up in throat granules may explain that harm. Chem tests found changed forms of the compound too.
pmc-11643276:
Iustina Grosu and co-authors review the tangled link between vitamin D and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Their 2024 review starts from a hint: places with less ultraviolet light show higher cancer rates. Pancreatic cancer has grim prospects, so a safe, known compound draws interest as a helper.

The team searched the medical literature and kept ninety-seven studies for the final text. Population studies gave mixed results on risk and outlook. Lab work, though, showed the vitamin can slow cancer cell growth, push cell death, and curb spread, both directly and by reshaping nearby tissue. The authors call for a clearer picture of what vitamin-driven changes in the tumor setting would mean for care.
pmc-11643376:
Grzegorz Łysiak and Ryszard Kulig published a study in twenty twenty-four on what happens inside the press when farm waste is squeezed into pellets. The waste is the solid left from biogas making. Pellets store and ship well and can serve as food for soil or as fuel. The snag: once the press lets go, the pellet springs back a bit, and that spring can spoil its strength.

The pair pressed samples at five levels of wetness and five force levels, ten squeeze cycles each. Spring-back grew with wetness and force, and shrank with each added cycle. Yet spring-back barely tracked pellet strength. The energy locked in for good was the true mark of a strong pellet. The authors say watching the squeeze-release loop is the best way to judge a batch.
pmc-11643476:
Paired-ring molecules called biaryls sit inside many drugs, dyes, and natural products, and making them cleanly is a standing goal in chemistry. Xiaohui Di and co-authors report a green route in a 2024 study, using a cheap copper-loaded stone sponge as the catalyst. The stone can be fished out and used again, unlike dissolved metal salts.

Two starting families feed the pairing: simple phenols and a class of boron-linked rings. Warm alcohol or even plain water carries the phenol runs under open air. The boron runs need no additives at all. Both routes tolerate a wide mix of side groups, yielding a shelf of products. One run chained the pairing into a second classic reaction in the same pot, giving rich ring systems in a single pass.
pmc-11643676:
Ewelina Szaniawska-Białas and co-authors review work from two thousand twenty-four on membranes made of tiny tubes of titanium oxide. The tubes are grown in neat rows by a process called anodizing. When the layer is lifted free and its tube ends are opened, liquids and gases can flow through it.

The review covers how the membranes are made, what shapes the tube growth, and how the freed films are treated for different uses. It then surveys recent work that uses them to make hydrogen, clean polluted water, store energy in cells and batteries, sense chemicals, and serve medical aims. The authors weigh what helps the material work and what still limits it.
pmc-11643776:
Nayara Tamayo-Fonseca and a large team of co-authors report, in a 2024 study, expert views on healthy eating policy in Latin American and Caribbean cities. Global agencies urge policies to improve diets, but local context often decides whether they work. The team asked which actions local actors should put first in the cities of that region.

A panel of twenty-one experts from thirteen countries judged twenty-one candidate actions over two rounds of the Delphi method. Eight actions won high-priority status, eight ranked low, and five stayed debatable. The panel noted local snags, such as informal street food stalls, which make zoning rules near schools hard to enforce. The results give city actors a ranked menu shaped by regional reality.
pmc-11644176:
María Mondéjar-López and co-authors field-test garlic extract in chitosan nanoparticles as a seed treatment for cereals. Their twenty twenty-four study coats seeds before sowing in rain-fed fields. The particles are round, near two hundred nanometers wide, and stable in cold storage.

Garlic brings pest and microbe defense at a very low dose; chitosan carries and guards it. Treated fields were scored for growth and health beside gene activity reads in the plants. The transcript data hint at which defense paths switch on. A plant-based nano-primer that works in real fields, not just pots, fits the shift toward greener crop care.
pmc-11644276:
Mesfer Al-Zahrani and Antonio Pantano test how new-generation glass fiber polymer bars hold their shear strength through a year of harsh soaking. These bars replace steel in concrete where rust is the enemy, but alkali, acid, and heat can eat their strength. Two surface types, sand-coated and ribbed, face the baths beside older generations of the same bars.

Their 2024 study finds the new bars clearly hardier, keeping most of their strength where the older ones sagged under the same abuse. The ribbed new bar proved the steadiest of all. A neural network model then learns the retention pattern and forecasts it far better than a straight-line fit, giving engineers a predictor for design life in hostile settings.
pmc-11644376:
Raluca Marinica Albu and co-authors tune plastic light filters by changing the liquid used to cast them. Their 2024 study mixes polyvinyl alcohol with crystal violet dye. Filters that pass one band of light serve in signals work and chemical sensing.

Water, a common solvent, and peroxide gave unlike films. Water and the solvent kept the dye's absorption and created new band edges, narrowing the energy gap. Peroxide bleached the dye and raised transparency instead. The water films blocked green-to-red light while passing over 90 percent of the rest. Surface scans showed how dye changed roughness. The team offers the recipe for cheap band-pass filters.
pmc-11644776:
Lucia Cavigli and four co-authors test sound-based detection of a seed pathogen in a 2024 paper. A bacterium that wilts common beans rides inside seeds and is quarantined in many regions. The standard test grinds up seed and runs slow lab assays, which cannot screen harvests at scale.

The bacterium's colonies come in distinct colors, and that pigmentation suggests an optical fingerprint. The team measured the colonies' light absorption, then built a stand-in infected seed to trial a photoacoustic method, where light pulses make tiny sound waves that reveal what absorbed the light. The technique detected the bacterium inside the mock seed without harming it, and it could tell apart strains by color. Early detection that leaves the seed intact could speed border control checks and help farmers plant clean seed, the authors argue.
pmc-11645076:
Daniel Geneau and co-authors studied how to fit radar data for sprint modelling in 2024; the catalog lists one further author absent from the head byline. Radar gives precise speed traces for building force-velocity profiles of athletes. Different curve fits, though, can shift the resulting numbers.

Forty-seven university athletes ran two forty-metre sprints each while radar recorded their speed. Five fitting methods were compared, from standard models to a polynomial and a sigmoid curve. Fit quality and derived force-velocity measures differed significantly across methods. The sigmoid and polynomial fits matched the data best. The authors warn that comparing athlete profiles across studies is unsafe when the fitting method differs.
pmc-11645276:
Violeta Raverdy and co-authors used data-driven grouping to show that fatty liver disease tied to metabolic problems comes in two distinct types. The disease, shortened to MASLD, affects many people with obesity but follows very different courses. Working from six simple clinical measures in nearly fourteen hundred patients, the team found two clusters, then checked them in biopsy cohorts and a national biobank.

One type is driven mainly by the liver itself, progresses fast toward chronic liver disease, yet carries limited heart risk. The other is cardiometabolic, marked by blood sugar problems and high triglycerides, with higher risks of heart disease and diabetes. Gene, tissue, and blood profiles differed sharply between the types, which suggests treatment should be tailored to each.
pmc-11646376:
Orthorexia, an unhealthy fixation on eating only foods seen as pure, may be fed by heavy social media use. Unal and Kocatepe Avcı survey 255 adults without psychiatric diagnoses, using scales for orthorexia, social media addiction, and eating attitudes. They test whether eating attitudes carry the effect of compulsive platform use onto its symptoms.

Its scores rose with every other scale, and eating attitudes predicted all parts of it. One part of addiction, conflict, predicted daily-life impairment from it. The path analysis showed both a direct link and an indirect one through eating attitudes. The authors urge clinicians to address both habits together.
pmc-11646776:
Santhosh reports a single case in 2024 of a man treated with blended old and new medicine. The man, aged sixty, had a swollen prostate gland since 2019 and was found on a routine screen to have very high blood fats. The two ills looked apart, yet an old text frame tied them through shared body paths.

Drugs were picked to ease both the fats and the weak urine flow at once. In one month his blood fats fell by near two thirds, and his flow grew less halting. Gains held and grew over the next year and a half. The case shows a blended plan at work on two ills.
pmc-11647076:
Theresa Ackfeld leads a team with a tumor that mimicked a heart attack. Their case from twenty twenty-four deals with a woman of forty-three. She came in with chest pain, head pain, and sweat.

Heart traces looked like a major heart attack at first. Yet vessel scans showed no blocked heart arteries at all. A heart chamber scan showed a balloon like tip instead. High blood pressure raised doubt of an adrenal tumor. Blood tests proved it, and surgery took the tumor out. Such tumors should be weighed in odd cases.
pmc-11647276:
Elizabeth Roberts, Mala Watts, Safiya Riley, and Kathryn Hart surveyed dietetic staffing for eating disorder care in the community in a 2024 paper. Food rebuilding is central to most therapies for anorexia and bulimia, and dietitians are trained for exactly that work. Yet their role on treatment teams is often sidelined.

The authors cite surveys showing specialists endorse dietitian input far less than patients and carers do. In one, barely half of specialists backed a dietitian assessment for every patient, against near-unanimous support from families. General clinicians also showed thin nutrition knowledge next to dietitians. The scoping survey behind the paper maps how dietetic hours are actually spread in community services, and asks what keeps the role marginal.
pmc-11647376:
Jacob Schriner and Ryan Dumas, two authors writing in 2024, comment on prep time for trauma teams. A study they discuss found a sweet spot for how long a team should have before a patient arrives. Teams that hit that window completed key steps faster.

The comment notes that more than four in five patients arrived outside that window. Transport mode and weak communication often decide the warning time in city settings. Rather than chase an ideal window, the authors urge cutting wasted steps in care. Faster blood access is one example they give, worth minutes on average.
pmc-11648076:
Mahdi Tavakol, Alexander Newbold, and Kislon Voïtchovsky use computer models in a 2024 study of salt water trapped in tiny gaps under a changing electric field. Such gaps sit at the heart of small sensors, yet ions and water act in complex ways at that scale. The team varied the gap size, the salt level, and the wall material.

Across all tests, the water and ions lined up to cancel the applied field. Ions lagged as the field flipped faster, while water moved ahead of it. Gap size changed the strength of the effect, and the wall material shaped how the fluid acted near the edge. The findings aid small-scale sensing tools.
pmc-11648776:
Lisa Maurer and her team asked if special insoles help people with Parkinson's disease walk more safely, in two thousand twenty-four. The disease often makes walking unsteady and raises the risk of falls. The insoles aim to boost feel in the foot and steady the step.

Sixteen people with the disease walked while wearing the special insoles and plain insoles in turn. The team timed their steps, tracked brain waves, and asked how steady they felt. None of the gains reached a level the team could trust. Step speed and length did not change in a clear way. The authors say the group was too small to settle the question, and longer studies are needed.
pmc-11649576:
Jiaqin Yu and five co-authors study impaired vigilance in patients with narcolepsy type 1 in a 2024 paper. Vigilance, the power to keep watch and react fast over time, is the main trait that sets how well these patients cope in the day, since the disorder brings strong sleep attacks.

A psychomotor vigilance task gave a hard score of that power. Patients and healthy controls were set side by side, next to scores for night sleep, daytime sleepiness, thinking, mood, and self-control. The team read how far the patients' task scores fell, and hunted brain paths that might lie behind the gap.
pmc-11649676:
Rodrigo Vieira, Plinio Moreno, and Athanasios Vourvopoulos test brain signals for predicting human action in a 2024 pilot study. The setting is human-robot teamwork, where a robot that sees a move coming can work more safely. Brain waves, read by EEG sensors on the scalp, can show signs of a planned move more than a second before it happens.

The team trained deep learning models on a data set where people imagined movements. Their best model sorted the signals with accuracy near eighty-one percent. In a live pilot test, actions were forecast a few hundred milliseconds before they were carried out. The authors say pairing brain signals with modern learning methods could make shared tasks smoother. They frame the work as an early step toward safer joint work with robots.
pmc-11650076:
Karin Hammarberg and co-authors make and test four short animated videos that coach midlife women toward healthier habits. Midlife health sets the slope for later aging, yet clear guidance often misses women with low literacy or other first languages. Short cartoons on a free platform can cross those bars.

Two videos cover menopause self-care and two cover joint health, built with clinicians and a production firm. Nearly five hundred women watched and rated them in an online survey. About nine in ten called the content very easy to grasp. Between a third and two thirds found fresh facts in each video, by topic. Most said they would likely use the tips. Scores held up across schooling and income levels, which backs cartoons as an equal-access health tool.
pmc-11650176:
Shadi Ghaemi and three colleagues pool clinical trials to ask whether vitamin D supplements ease depression, in a meta-analysis published in two thousand twenty-four. Earlier trials disagreed, leaving the dose question open. The authors searched three databases for randomized trials in adults through December two thousand twenty-two.

Thirty-one trials with 24,189 participants qualified. Each extra thousand international units of vitamin D3 per day slightly reduced depressive symptoms. The effect appeared in people with and without diagnosed depression and grew more pronounced at higher doses in some groups. Certainty of evidence was graded moderate. Anxiety outcomes were also examined. The authors present vitamin D as a modest adjunct, not a stand-alone antidepressant.
pmc-11651676:
Suzanne Jan de Beur and co-authors review what health care patients with tumor-induced osteomalacia use and endure, in a review from 2024. The ultra-rare syndrome comes from tumors that leak a hormone, FGF23, which wastes phosphate and softens bone. Early signs are vague, so diagnosis often comes late.

The review gathered 414 papers, most of them case reports covering 621 patients. The mean wait from first symptoms to diagnosis was 4.6 years. Patients averaged 4.1 imaging tests where reported, and half had suffered a fracture. Surgery to remove the tumor was tried in 81 percent and worked in 67 percent. Longer waits tied to worse surgery results and more tumor return. The authors urge faster recognition of the disease.
pmc-11652176:
Rocío Fernández-Jiménez and co-authors test simple bedside measures as sarcopenia detectors in lung fibrosis patients, in a 2024 paper. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis scars the lungs, and muscle wasting rides along, worsening survival. Full body-composition workups are impractical in clinic, so cheap proxies matter.

Eighty-four patients, mostly men, were graded by the European sarcopenia criteria using impedance scans, handgrip strength, a timed stand-and-walk test, and ultrasound of the thigh muscle and belly fat. About one in five met the sarcopenia bar. The team derived cutoff values for the thigh muscle's cross-section and the walking test, then checked them against survival curves. Two quick measures, one image and one stopwatch, may flag the patients most at risk.
pmc-11652676:
Bleeding inside the brain is hard to treat, and few drugs protect nerve tissue afterward. The authors test esketamine, a drug known for blocking a brain receptor, in mice with this kind of hemorrhage. They trigger the bleed by injecting collagenase into a deep brain region, then track weight, movement, and behavior. Gene-reading and drug-target analyses point to a growth factor, neurotrophin-3, and a signaling pathway called PI3K/AKT as the drug's likely route of action.

Mice given esketamine show better function and less nerve damage. A virus-based step that raises neurotrophin-3 in the same brain region supports its central role in the benefit. When the team blocks the PI3K/AKT pathway with a specific inhibitor, the drug's benefit largely fades. The authors conclude that esketamine protects the injured brain mainly through this factor and pathway, suggesting a possible treatment direction.
pmc-11652876:
Siyi Chen and co-authors study a 2024 question about how the gut handles a choline-bearing compound sold as a supplement. The compound, called GPC, has been studied as a source of choline inside cells and has been hoped to guard the brain. Yet high intake of choline compounds is tied to making a liver product, TMAO, that is linked with artery disease.

The team focuses on an enzyme in the gut, Gpcpd1, and its role in breaking down GPC. In lab tests with a layer of gut-like cells, added GPC was split into choline on the outer side, and the choline then crossed into the cells. Tracing that path helps explain how much of a supplement turns into the raw material for TMAO, and where control points may sit.
pmc-11653576:
Jiaqi Zhang and co-authors published a 2024 study building a questionnaire to measure how much patients feel they gain from China's family doctor contracts. Under the scheme, residents sign with a family doctor team and receive broader primary care. Whether patients themselves feel better served was unmeasured: no instrument captured their sense of medical gain. The team set out to build and test one.

Scale development followed the standard craft: draft items from the concept, refine them with patients and experts, then check the questionnaire's structure and consistency in survey data. Preliminary validation asks whether the scale hangs together and measures one thing rather than noise. Such a tool lets managers compare districts and programs by the patient's own ledger, not just visit counts. The authors frame felt gain as a missing metric in judging a flagship reform: a service can be comprehensive on paper and thin in experience.
pmc-11653676:
Nursing students across the Arab world will graduate into hospitals where artificial intelligence is spreading. Omar Al Omari and co-authors surveyed in 2024 more than seventeen hundred such students in ten countries about their readiness to use it.

Most students scored in the middle on knowledge, attitude, perception, and intention toward the technology. The four measures moved together: knowing more and feeling positive predicted stronger intention to use the tools. Understanding the technology, seeing oneself as tech-savvy, and strong clinical grades stood out in the analysis. The authors call for tailored teaching that builds skill and confidence before students reach the ward.
pmc-11654076:
Juan Wei and co-authors studied nutrition and chemo side effects in stage IV stomach cancer in a 2024 paper. Poor nutrition is common in these patients and harms tolerance and survival. The team asked whether pre-treatment nutrition scores predict early bone marrow suppression.

The study covered one hundred two patients treated from 2012 to 2021 at one centre. Half were malnourished at the start and about half had low muscle mass. Patients with low scores on two nutrition indexes, or low muscle index, had more strong marrow suppression after the first cycle. Muscle index and a blood protein level were the clearest predictors in adjusted analysis.
pmc-11654176:
Weiyi Wang surveyed young men in China about backing HPV vaccination for women, in a study published in 2024. HPV is a common virus that can cause cervical cancer, and vaccines can prevent much of that harm. Partners can shape a woman's choice, yet men's support had drawn little study. Wang asked what men had done, and what they would be willing to do.

About one thousand men at eight universities in Zhejiang took part in early 2021 surveys. Less than half had shared vaccine facts with loved ones, and fewer had urged vaccination. Most of those who had not helped said they were willing to start. Good views of the vaccine's benefits and active fact seeking went with stronger support.
pmc-11654276:
Dawson and a large team studied how health and social services work as partners for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander clients in twenty twenty-four. Many clients deal with several groups at once. When services work in silos, on their own, clients can find care hard to get. The study was set on Kaurna Country in northern Adelaide, Australia.

Fifty-nine service providers took part, through interviews and yarning circles. Yarning is a discussion method grounded in the culture. Two thirds of participants were Aboriginal. Acts of partnership included advocacy, referrals, shared information, and case meetings. People said these acts improved client access and how staff felt about work. Keen staff, shared goals, and formal agreements helped. Racism, red tape, short-term funding, and high staff turnover got in the way. The authors list reforms, from steady funding to coordination led by Aboriginal people.
pmc-11654376:
Astrid Devulder and co-authors present a woman whose hidden seizures turned out to be the first sign of Alzheimer's disease in this 2024 case report. She arrived in her sixties with acute confusion. Her scalp brain-wave test looked normal, yet scans showed swelling in the right inner temporal lobe and a sugar scan found that area burning hot.

Electrodes placed deep through small skull openings told the true story: continuous seizure activity in the inner temporal lobe, invisible from the surface. Fluid tests then confirmed Alzheimer's disease. A tau scan showed the protein damage heaviest on the same side as the seizures. Months later that hippocampus had shrunk. The authors argue overexcited neurons are not a side note in early Alzheimer's but part of its engine, and that hidden seizures deserve a hunt when confusion appears.
pmc-11654676:
Craig Cameron wrote an editorial in 2024 marking his first year as section editor for biomedicine and life sciences at Science Advances. The section now handles close to forty percent of the journal's twenty-eight thousand yearly submissions. His piece tells authors and readers what the section prizes.

Getting past the first editorial screen is the high hurdle, with about a quarter of manuscripts moving forward. Nineteen editor teams, all staffed by working scientists, cover the section's breadth. Cameron wants direct submissions that matter deeply to their own fields and, where possible, to a wide audience too. He also flags topical areas where the journal hopes to grow, and commits to keeping standards high as volume climbs.
pmc-11654776:
Agathoklis Vallas and co-authors review artery variants that complicate thigh flap surgery in a 2024 paper. The gracilis flap borrows thigh muscle on its feeding artery, the medial circumflex. Sixteen studies charted how that artery varies: split and double pedicles, differing lengths, and branching patterns. Each variant changes the harvest and the vessel joining.

Short or branched pedicles carried higher risk in the gathered reports. The review's advice is consistent: image precisely before surgery and stay adaptable during it. Reconstructive success often hinges on anatomy known before the first cut. A variant map turns surprises into plans for this common flap.
pmc-11654876:
Acid wears tooth enamel down, and a protein from sugarcane may armor it. Carolina Ruis Ferrari and co-authors tested CaneCPI-5, a cystatin protein, alone and blended with a phosphate compound, on bovine enamel samples in the lab. Nine treatments competed, including plain water and a commercial erosion-protection rinse.

After three days of treatment cycles ending in a citric acid bath, the blend with the strongest phosphate dose protected hardness best, beating the protein alone. For calcium loss, the protein alone and its mildest blend matched the commercial rinse. The authors conclude the pairing strengthens protection against early erosion, at least in vitro. Human mouths are the next test.
pmc-11655076:
A licorice-root compound that gels in water can also kill bacteria, but only when the chemistry of the water is right. Mathieu Joos and co-authors map that dependence in a 2024 study. The compound carries three acid groups that take on protons as acidity rises, and its gel state changes with them.

The team tested the gel against a panel of hospital bacteria, including resistant staph and several gut and lung pathogens. Killing power grew as acidity increased and the compound protonated. Some bacteria fell even to the fully deprotonated gel, while others needed the most acidic form. The results tell designers of antimicrobial dressings exactly which pH window each target demands.
pmc-11655176:
Jaclyn Harris, Celine Goulet, and David Chapple ask what a trip by plane or car does to a stowaway lizard, in a 2024 study. Hitching rides with people is a chief way that foreign beasts reach new lands and spread once there.

The team sent delicate skinks, a known pest abroad, on a short flight with trips to and from the airport, or on a three-hour drive. Heat in transit swung more than at rest but stayed in the band the skinks can bear. Flight changed neither how much the skinks moved nor how boldly they poked about. The drive made them more active but no bolder. The authors say such toughness is part of why stowaways thrive, and they urge more work on the trip stage of an invasion.
pmc-11655776:
Gashaw Arega and co-authors report a rare tumor in a baby's brain and eye in a 2024 case report. The tumor is a germ cell growth that most often sits in the sex glands; in the brain with a reach to the eye it is all but unheard of.

Such a growth can look like a host of more common eye ills in a child, which can stall the call and cost dear time. Scans size the mass and map its reach. Blood and spinal fluid marks, plus a slice read, seal the call. The child, ten months old, bore a mixed mass above the brain's core with a reach into the eye. The team took the eye and much of the mass out by surgery. Marks in blood and the slice read bore out the call. Care rests on surgery, drugs, and rays as a team.
pmc-11655876:
Zengzhuang Yuan and co-authors show how a gene called ELF3 helps lung cancer grow when a guard gene is missing, in this 2024 study. The guard gene, PTEN, is often lost in tumors. A cell death route named ferroptosis can block cancer, and the team asked how ELF3 affects it. Extra ELF3 alone in mouse lung cells caused overgrowth but also more ferroptosis.

With PTEN removed as well, tumors formed and ferroptosis dropped. The reason was a gene, SLC7A11, that ELF3 switches on and that holds ferroptosis back. A drug blocking that gene restored cell death and curbed tumors. Human lung tumors showed matching patterns, and high ELF3 with its partner gene tracked with worse survival. The authors propose triggering ferroptosis as a treatment angle.
pmc-11655976:
Breno Sousa and co-authors release real-device datasets of flooding attacks on car-to-car networks, in a 2024 paper. Cars that swap safety messages need those channels clear. A flooding attack chokes them with junk packets, which can hide true warnings and risk lives. Most past attack data came from simulators, which miss the quirks of real gear.

The team ran the attacks on three true MK5 on-board units, the radios cars use to talk. They logged the traffic as the floods hit, in varied runs. A learning model was then set loose on the logs for a first read of their depth. Scores for accuracy, precision, recall, and their blend are reported as a base line. The authors offer the sets so defense tools can train on real, not fake, floods.
pmc-11656376:
Yuta Yamanaka and co-authors compare two immune drugs paired with chemotherapy for advanced small cell lung cancer in a 2024 study. This fast-growing cancer is usually treated first with chemo plus an immune checkpoint drug. Two such drugs are in common use, and no clear winner between them had been shown.

Records covered 100 patients split across three drug pairings. Survival without growth and overall survival were much the same for both immune drugs. Age, fitness, and spread to liver or bone did not change the picture. One patient with spread to the brain did notably well on one pairing. The authors suggest that pairing may deserve preference when the brain is involved, while noting the small, backward-looking design.
pmc-11656576:
Tara Anderson and co-authors set out a study protocol on the support needs of families facing pancreatic cancer, in a 2024 paper. The disease is aggressive and often found late, so survival is low. Family members often become the patient's main support. Many feel unready and carry heavy unmet needs of their own.

The planned study uses mixed methods in three phases. A survey will map family members' needs and wellbeing first. Interviews will then dig into lived experience. A third phase will weigh the role of support services. The fast decline in this cancer strains families in a short span. Knowing what families need can shape services that reach them in time.
pmc-11656876:
Pernille Gram and co-authors survey medical interns in Denmark about their ultrasound training and skills, in a 2024 national study. Bedside ultrasound is now used across many specialties, so training must keep pace. The team ask what training interns received, how skilled they feel, and how much they expect to use scanning later.

A questionnaire was built from a theory model, interviews, and focus groups, then pilot tested. It went to all 1,231 medical interns in Denmark. Results are summarized with comparisons between universities. The findings can help tailor ultrasound education in specialty training to real gaps and expectations.
pmc-11656976:
Zhibo Hu and co-authors present a 2024 study of a plant compound that shields kidney filter cells in diabetic mice. Diabetes can drive a fiery form of cell death in these cells, speeding kidney failure. The compound comes from a traditional medicinal root.

Treated diabetic mice showed better kidney measures and less tissue damage. A death pathway chain, from a stress sensor through an inflammasome to a pore forming protein, was dialled down. Cell tests confirmed each link by silencing and boosting steps. Filter cell markers recovered. The authors pitch the compound as a candidate to slow diabetic kidney disease, pending much more work.
pmc-11657176:
Okagbue and nine co-authors review whether Nigerian girls in villages reach puberty later than girls in cities. Ages at first menstruation are falling worldwide, faster in poorer countries. The review gathered studies spanning 1976 to 2023 under standard reporting rules.

Ten studies qualified, with a low overall risk of bias. First periods came at about 13.4 years in rural areas and 13.0 in urban ones. The gap, though, was not statistically firm, and it seems to be shrinking over time. The authors note the steady downward trend in both settings. They frame the work as a base for health planning for adolescent girls.
pmc-11657376:
Jana Turzakova and co-authors review the links between climate change and patient health from a nursing angle in a 2024 paper. Climate change threatens health in many ways, and nurses stand on the front line of care. Yet what nurses think and know about these risks was scattered across studies. The team set out to gather that evidence in one place.

Their mixed-methods review searched six databases and kept eighteen studies, mostly quantitative. Three themes stood out. Nurses grasp how climate and health intertwine, and students could act as agents of change if taught well. At the same time, daily practice throws up barriers to sustainable care. The authors urge nursing schools to teach climate content and hospitals to back greener practice.
pmc-11657576:
Suzanne Cosh leads a team that sets cut scores for climate anxiety. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with eco anxiety in young adults. Fear and worry on climate change are seen world wide.

Such anxiety can be helpful at times, but can also harm health. No good way yet flags who needs support for it. A large sample of Australian young adults filled forms. Distress scales scored low mood, anxiety, and stress in each. Those scores set what counted as a true case. Cut scores on the climate scale were then derived.
pmc-11657776:
Maria Correa and co-authors check insecticide resistance in malaria mosquitoes on São Tomé and Príncipe in this 2024 study. The islands cut malaria sharply over twenty years of spraying and net programs, but cases rose again in the last year, threatening their elimination goal. The team collected mosquito larvae in rainy and dry seasons from 2022 to 2024 on both islands.

The local mosquito stayed fully open to one newer insecticide, but showed strong resistance to the pyrethroid class and to DDT, worst in the rainy season on São Tomé. Even five to ten times the normal dose did not fully restore kill. A booster chemical partly reversed resistance, hinting at enzyme-based defenses in the mosquitoes. A known resistance mutation was common on São Tomé and rare on Príncipe. The authors urge non-pyrethroid tools.
pmc-11657976:
Yue Liu and co-authors report a 2024 study of a switch that can turn a cell therapy on and off. The therapy trains immune cells to attack blood cancers and works well, but it can trigger dangerous swelling or nerve harm. A way to pause or stop the cells would make the treatment safer.

The switch rests on a building block that human cells do not use. Without it, the attack protein cannot be fully built, and the cells stay off. Feeding the block turns protein building on. The team tested whether dose of the block could tune cell activity up and down. Such control could cut the risk of severe side effects.
pmc-11659776:
Chantal Oderbolz and co-authors used brain recordings to ask how the brain tracks the rhythm layers of speech in a 2024 paper. Speech melody is organized in a hierarchy of units, from syllables to phrases, that stands apart from sentence grammar. How the brain parses that hierarchy was unexplored. Thirty young adults listened to German sentences that were manipulated at different levels of the rhythm hierarchy.

Two brain measures were used: how well brain waves lock to the speech rhythm, and how slow waves steer faster activity. Both showed that the brain keeps the hierarchy's structure during listening. The faithfulness of that tracking depended on how intact the hierarchy was in each sentence. It also varied with each listener's sense of rhythm and timing skill. The authors cast rhythmic brain mechanisms as core to how speech is understood.
pmc-11659976:
Kuang-Yu Wei and a large team compare two transplant drugs in rats in a 2024 paper. Both drugs are calcineurin inhibitors that affect how the kidney handles salts and blood pressure. The newer drug, voclosporin, seems to disturb magnesium and calcium less than tacrolimus, but lab proof was missing.

Rats received one of the drugs or a plain vehicle for 28 days. The team tracked salt handling, blood pressure by telemetry, and the levels of transport proteins in the kidney tubule. Tacrolimus raised calcium loss more than four-fold and lowered blood magnesium. Voclosporin did not. Tacrolimus also cut several transport proteins that voclosporin spared.
pmc-11661976:
Yeji Lee and co-authors merge two T cell tests into one assay in a 2024 paper. T cells drive much of the adaptive immune response, and labs gauge them by markers that switch on after a trigger or by the signals they release. Running both tests at once has rarely been tried, though it could save scarce samples.

Blood cells from seven healthy donors met virus peptide pools and control mixes. One marker pair for helper cells of the CD8 line gave cleaner reads with less background noise than its rival pair. Taking half the fluid mid test did not warp the results. The joint assay thus reads both switch on state and signal release from one small sample.
pmc-11662176:
Zahra Baghani, Malihe Karrabi, and Hossein Assarzadeh pool trials of light-activated disinfection for deep tooth decay, in a 2024 review. Antimicrobial photodynamic therapy promises to cut bacterial load in deep cavities, but baby teeth and adult teeth differ in tubule structure, so the therapy may not work equally on both.

Searching five databases through April 2022, three reviewers screened the literature and kept seven studies. The meta-analysis compared bacterial counts before and after treatment in primary versus permanent teeth, tracking cavity germs overall and key species like Streptococcus mutans. Random-effects models and bias checks framed the verdict. Whether dentition type changes the payoff decides where dentists aim the light first.
pmc-11662676:
Devashish Tripathi and co-authors build a deep learning tool that spots many-gene adaptation in human genomes, in this 2024 paper. Traits shaped by hundreds of small genetic nudges leave faint traces. Older statistics often miss them or cry wolf under tangled population histories.

Their two-stage tool, RAISING, tunes its network first, then selects features and predicts. On published and fresh simulations it beat three rival methods, with far higher true detection and sixty times less compute than one deep rival. A sliding window version scanned four continental population groups. It flagged many regions under adaptation while staying robust to history and selection quirks.
pmc-11663376:
Yajing Liu and seven co-authors test two blood markers for early warning of kidney injury in sepsis patients, in a 2024 study. Sepsis in intensive care often harms the kidneys, and the standard marker rises late. Records and blood samples from 197 patients were tracked over the first two days. One hundred four patients developed kidney injury.

Both new markers rose before the standard one did. From six hours on, their levels ran far higher in the injury group. Curve tests gave the second marker the stronger score of the two. The authors back both as early flags that could speed care. The study was retrospective, so wider checks are still owed.
pmc-11663576:
Pablo Calzadilla and Fernando Unrein present a study the catalog lists under 2025. Cyanobacteria harvest light in waters where light swings wildly. Clouds and wind stir shallow lakes, so cells spend long spans in dark water. Brief trips to the bright surface punctuate that darkness. Too much light can damage the harvest machinery. Cells must balance capture against protection as light jumps.

The study centers on a protein called RppA in that balance. Pigment production is regulated in tight coordination during acclimation. The authors trace how the protein helps cells adjust to dark-light cycles. Lake ecology and biofuel work both care: pond-grown cyanobacteria face the same swings. A strain that acclimates fast wastes less light and survives gusts of sun. The work speaks to basic photosynthesis science in a realistic light regime, not steady lab lamps.
pmc-11663876:
Katharina Gryksa and seven colleagues compare social and emotional behavior in two common lab mouse strains, in a twenty twenty-four study. The strains, a black line called BL6 and a white line called CD1, differ in genes and in stress responses. The team tested males as teens and as adults on anxiety, fear, social acts, and pain sense. They also mapped the oxytocin system, a hormone web tied to social behavior.

BL6 mice were more anxious, less social, and more shaken by trauma at both ages. CD1 mice calmed with age, while BL6 mice grew more fearful. Oxytocin receptor patterns differed by strain and age. The authors urge care in picking strain and age for stress research.
pmc-11663976:
Grass carp farming loses many fish to bacterial disease, and heavy antibiotic use brings its own harms. Penghui Yu, Mengzhen Feng, Jianguo Su, and Gailing Yuan tested two plant-based compounds in 2024 as a cleaner option. Both compounds raise levels of hepcidin, a natural peptide that fights bacteria and controls iron in the body, which is costly to make as a drug.

In cells, the two compounds raised hepcidin and related gene activity and killed bacteria directly. Fed to carp together, they improved growth and survival, raised immune markers in blood, and lowered bacterial counts in organs after infection. Gut tissue damage was also less severe. The pair worked better together than either alone.
pmc-11664176:
Shijie Fu and nine co-authors screen bile microRNAs that predict how bile duct cancer near the liver responds to chemotherapy. Infusion chemotherapy into the liver artery helps many patients with this advanced cancer, but survival gains vary a lot. Bile offers a nearby fluid where markers might be found.

Sequencing linked levels of three microRNAs in bile to survival after treatment. Only one of the three, when raised in cancer cells, made them resist the two drug regimen, and lowering it restored sensitivity. Lab work shows it acts by suppressing a target protein called SPARC. The three markers may help forecast outcomes, and the lead marker points to a route to reduce drug resistance.
pmc-11664276:
Wang and eight co-authors pinpoint which chemicals give stored grass carp its spoiled smell. Freshwater fish spoil fast at room temperature, and the smell drives buyers away. The team measured odor chemicals in fresh, spoiled, and badly spoiled fish cubes.

Nineteen odorants mattered across the stages. Mixing and removal tests confirmed five key culprits in spoiled fish, including trimethylamine and ammonia. Badly spoiled fish added five more, among them putrescine and histamine. Twelve amino acids and ten fatty acids fed the formation of these smells. The authors say the map of odor sources can guide fresher storage methods.
pmc-11664576:
Five researchers in the United Kingdom simulate chitosan sticking to silica in a 2024 paper. Chitosan is a nontoxic natural polymer from shell waste, valued for drug and food uses. How it coats silica at the molecular scale guides the design of coated particles.

Full atom simulations with boosted sampling give the sticking energy per unit of polymer. The value sits near the scale of thermal jitter at room heat, so the coat is loose and reversible. Surface load came out low and is ruled by charge balance. Hydrogen bonds do most of the grip, through the polymer's nitrogen and hydroxyl oxygens. The team offers the map for particle design.
pmc-11665776:
Yunhan Wang and colleagues published a plant biology study in 2024 on how a potato viroid copies itself. Viroids are tiny circular RNA strands that infect crops. They carry no protein-coding genes of their own. Instead they borrow the host plant's machinery to multiply.

One borrowed enzyme joins the cut ends of viroid RNA into circles. The team tracked that enzyme and the viroid inside plant cells. Both gathered together near the nucleolus, the cell's dense core region. The viroid RNA itself was highly condensed in that same spot. The authors argue the pair forms a droplet-like condensate for processing. The finding extends condensate biology to these minimal pathogens.
pmc-11665876:
Somya Mehra and four co-authors model how sleeping malaria parasites wake in the liver, in a paper published in twenty twenty-four. One malaria species, Plasmodium vivax, hides as dormant forms called hypnozoites. They can stir weeks or months after a bite and cause fresh illness. What sets their timing was unknown.

The team fitted a simple math model to a rich cohort study on the Thailand-Myanmar border. Over thirteen hundred children were watched daily for twenty-one months, logging thousands of malaria bouts. A model where each sleeper wakes at a steady random rate fit the relapse patterns well. It put the average dormancy near six months. The team also tested what a blood test for hidden infection could add in quiet regions.
pmc-11668576:
Antonia Wambsganz and co-authors published this health psychology study in 2024. Only about half of Germans meet the World Health Organization's activity recommendations, despite exercise preventing many illnesses. The team surveyed 1,119 mentally healthy adults online to find what separates regular exercisers from the rest, hoping to spot levers for public health.

Regular exercise went with stronger motivation of both kinds, inner and outer, plus higher self-efficacy, resilience, and belief in one's own control. Exercisers also scored higher on conscientiousness, extraversion, and agreeableness, and they took more risks. Circumstances mattered too: money, sports facilities nearby, and having active family members in childhood. Many people preferred outdoor group exercise yet actually trained alone indoors. The authors recommend cheap, low-threshold exercise options in public spaces and childcare settings, aimed at disadvantaged groups.
pmc-11669776:
Ailbhe McKinney and five co-authors study camouflaging in girls at the start of adolescence in this 2024 paper. Camouflaging means hiding one's neurodivergent traits to pass as neurotypical, at real effort. The project was co-produced with fifteen neurodivergent women, who ranked this topic first. The main study covered 119 girls aged eleven to fourteen, seventy neurodivergent and forty-nine not. Girls rated their camouflaging, anxiety, and depression. On masking and compensation, the two groups scored alike.

They split on assimilation, the felt sense of pretending to fit in, where neurodivergent girls scored higher. Older girls camouflaged more. In both groups, camouflaging strongly predicted anxiety and depression. The harm link is thus present by age eleven, not a late teen development. The authors argue adults should not read a socially smooth girl as a thriving one. The effort to blend in may be the very thing draining her.
pmc-11669976: Chun-Han Cheng, Wen-Rui Hao, and Tzu-Hurng Cheng comment on evidence that a diabetes drug class protects the diabetic heart before symptoms start. The drugs, SGLT2 inhibitors, block a kidney protein that reclaims glucose. Their 2024 editorial discusses a study of patients with type 2 diabetes and silent heart failure, in whom the drugs improved heart function, eased oxidative stress, and quieted inflammation. The editors argue for starting the drugs early, at the silent stage of diabetic cardiomyopathy, rather than waiting for symptoms.
pmc-11670276:
Jordyn Stoll, James Larson, Sean Bailey, Christopher Blackwood, and David Costello test in a 2024 study what feeds algae in two Great Lakes bays. Harmful blooms hinge on which nutrients limit growth at each site. Big nutrients get most study, while trace metals that power cell engines get less.

Bottle tests used water from two blooming and two clear sites in Lakes Erie and Michigan in late summer. Three of four sites were limited by more than one nutrient at once. Blooming sites answered most to added nitrogen, while clear sites answered most to phosphorus. Three sites also grew more with a trace metal mix added. Nitrogen boosts fed a toxin making alga most, while phosphorus fed other groups.
pmc-11671276:
Silva Wolters and co-authors study rubber particle proteins in Russian dandelion latex in a 2024 paper. The plant is a hopeful source of natural rubber. Rubber forms on tiny balls in latex, the cell fluid of a set of plant cells.

The team found the full gene family for these proteins and mapped where each is active. They fished out partners for the three most common proteins in latex. Lab checks in yeast and under the microscope tested select links. The network tied the proteins to stress response and to making other plant compounds, well past rubber itself.
pmc-11671776:
Huihui Xiang and co-authors build a gene signature for lung adenocarcinoma outlook in a 2024 study. Amino acid metabolism in tumor cells shapes how this lung cancer grows and responds to treatment. A score built from those genes might sort patients by risk and therapy fit.

Nine genes formed the signature, drawn from a national cancer atlas cohort. High-risk patients died sooner, and two outside data sets confirmed the split. Risky tumors carried more faults in a famous guardian gene. The score also hinted at who benefits from chemotherapy and immune therapy, a hint borne out in a treated patient cohort. Immune cell mixes differed by risk as well.
pmc-11672076:
Chen and a large team target an RNA editing enzyme in liver cancer in twenty twenty-four. The enzyme, FTO, removes a chemical mark from RNA and drives several cancers. Its role in liver cancer was unclear. The team also asked how it relates to small vesicles that cancer cells release.

FTO levels were higher in patient liver tumors than in normal tissue. It boosted cancer cell growth, movement, and invasion in lab tests and in animals. Lowering FTO helped immune T cells enter tumors and attack them. A protein called GPNMB was found to be a key target of FTO. Vesicles carried GPNMB to T cells and damped their activation. An FTO blocker curbed cancer growth and improved response to other drugs.
pmc-11672476:
Christopher Everett and co-authors print magnetic films from a polymer loaded with two kinds of nanoparticles. Their 2024 paper uses a block copolymer as a template holding iron oxide and nickel particles at once. Mixed films like these suit magnetic sensors and data storage.

A slot-die printer laid the films in one pass, a method fit for scale-up. X-ray scattering watched the film form as it dried, and the mixed film set in four stages against five for the plain polymer. Surface scans tracked how particle load changed the texture. All films were magnetic, and more nickel tuned the response while the iron oxide share stayed fixed across the sample set.
pmc-11672676:
Mark Arnold and four co-authors modeled in 2024 what Great Britain would miss if it stopped extra testing on farms with atypical scrapie. Scrapie is a fatal brain disease of sheep and goats, and the atypical form seems not to spread between animals. Farms where it appears now face two years of testing on all animals that leave. The European Union ended that rule in 2021, but Britain kept it.

Mixing statistics with spread modeling, the team estimated about one case every three years would be missed. Other routine checks, at farms and slaughterhouses, find about ten cases a year. Losing the extra farm tests would thus dent the data only slightly. The study gives officials a measure for judging whether the rule is worth its cost.
pmc-11672776:
Connie Allen Wild, Lisa Yon, and Peter Henzi wrote this commentary, published in 2024. It looks at how group mates in social mammal species gather around and support a female while she gives birth.

Such support has been seen in primates, elephants, whales and dolphins, and bats, in groups with very different social setups. In humans, support during birth is known to help both mother and baby. The authors ask whether the same holds for other mammals. A calmer birth may lower the risk of a hard delivery and help the mother bond with her newborn. Both factors shape whether the young survive. The paper weighs ideas such as kin selection to explain why helpers might gain from lending support.
pmc-11672876:
A microwave device that melts local fat and smooths cellulite without surgery has spread quickly through clinics. Klaus Hoffmann and a large international board of co-authors gather the field's best practice for using it. The device, sold as Onda Coolwaves, targets local fat deposits, cellulite, and loose skin. Demand for noninvasive body shaping has grown fast, and treated patients and studies have multiplied.

What the board supplies is a compendium of recommendations from the most experienced users: ideal settings, patient selection, and treatment method for safe, effective sessions. The authors are frank that one thing is still missing — solid evidence on long-term efficacy and safety. Their guidance rests on the most recent data available, and they note that future research may change the recommendations. The review serves clinics adopting the device now.
pmc-11673076:
Fenglan Wang and co-authors compare chrysanthemum flower extracts in 2024 for antioxidant power and skin whitening effect. The flower is a traditional Chinese medicinal herb rich in active compounds, yet its whitening action was little tested. Petal extracts from five cultivars grown in Guangdong were put through a battery of lab measures.

Cultivars differed widely on enzyme blocking tied to pigment, radical clearing, sun absorption, and protection scores, as well as on levels of flavonoids, phenolics, and chlorogenic acid. One cultivar led on nearly every count, with the richest levels of all three compound groups. Deeper chemical profiling of three cultivars flagged a set of compounds that tracked with the strongest effects. The authors aim the results at cosmetic and herbal makers screening flower types for skin care use.
pmc-11673176:
Yangyang Wang and co-authors study whether watering wheat before a spring cold snap saves yield, in a 2024 paper. Cold events in spring are growing more common with climate change. They strike wheat at the jointing stage, when stems rise. Northern China faces a real threat to its harvests.

Four wheat varieties were tested over two years. Plants faced five cold levels, down to minus ten degrees, with or without prior watering. Watered plants showed less leaf wilt, stem breakage, and grain loss. Cold cut yield per plant across the board, but watering softened the blow. The work explains the protection in plant terms, which can guide farmers bracing for late frosts.
pmc-11673276:
Eleonora Fini and a large team of co-authors study clotting risk in endometriosis in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The chronic inflammatory condition affects women of reproductive age and has been tied to thrombosis. The molecular link was unclear.

Seventy-one patients and matched controls were compared. Patients showed higher oxidative stress across blood cell types and in plasma.
