Their fibrinogen, the protein that builds clots, was oxidized and structurally altered. That damage made clots form oddly and resist breakdown by the usual enzyme. The authors read this as a pro-clotting state driven by oxidative stress. They propose the fibrinogen changes as a target to cut cardiovascular risk in these patients.
pmc-11673376:
Chang-Hong Wu and co-authors review mental fatigue in sport, published in 2024, covering what it is, what causes it, and how athletes can fight it. Mental fatigue is the drained, unfocused state after long hard thinking, and coaches have long suspected it dulls performance. The review gathers Chinese and international research into one account.

Four theories compete to explain the mechanism, from motivation control to waste buildup in the brain. Effects show up in endurance, decision making, tactics, and technique. Countermeasures split into body based routes, such as caffeine, scents, and gentle brain stimulation, and mind based routes, such as music and positive thinking. Readers get a full playbook for a hidden factor in athletic results.
pmc-11673476:
Haima Yang and co-authors build a computer model that sorts vaginal lesions in medical images, in a paper from 2024. The lesions, linked to a common virus, are often missed when doctors inspect the cervix and focus less on the vaginal area. Missed cases can delay care.

Their model, called DLRNet, was designed to learn from small sets of images. One part finds the lesion in the image. A second part then reads both the raw image and the marked map to make its call. A third part guides focus to the right features. The team built the model on a known image network and tuned it at several levels. By reading cervical and vaginal signs together, the model aims to sort lesion types more exactly than a single-path model.
pmc-11673576:
Ellen Wrobel and co-authors probe how a cup-shaped carrier molecule interacts with model cell membranes in a 2024 study. Drug carriers must slip into cells without wrecking the membrane, so their surface behavior matters.

The carrier, a water-soluble calixarene called SCX4, met single-layer lipid films mimicking healthy and cancerous cell surfaces. It spread the films out and softened them in every recipe, changing their look under a special microscope. Infrared measures plus computer simulation showed the carrier grips cancer-model films at charged lipid heads through electric attraction. On healthy models it mostly clung to cholesterol instead. The contrast hints at selective entry into cancer-like membranes.
pmc-11673876:
Larissa M Pires-Teixeira and co-authors study how two invading corals reshape food webs on tropical rocky shores, in this 2024 paper. The corals, both named Tubastraea, arrived from elsewhere and now spread through the Caribbean, the Gulf of Mexico, and Brazil's southwest Atlantic coast. They fight hard for space, but their feeding ties were barely known.

The team read chemical isotope signatures in shore life to map who eats whom. Invaded communities showed less feeding variety, with species bunched into similar feeding roles. The invaders occupied the same feeding niche as native filter feeders, which helps explain their success as rivals for food. Local conditions, such as water movement and human pressure, seemed to help some communities resist. The work adds diet to the list of invasion battlegrounds.
pmc-11673976:
Han Sol Kang and colleagues present ARS, an artificial intelligence driven recovery controller that helps a quadruped robot get up after falling. Their 2024 study addresses a basic problem, since falling is inevitable for legged robots on rough terrain.

A single neural network model was trained in two steps in simulation using reinforcement learning. It was then applied directly to a real quadruped robot with twelve degrees of freedom. Experiments showed recovery within five seconds from varied postures, even when the robot was completely turned over. The robot also recovered after a fall caused by a disturbance. The approach avoids separate controllers for each fall type.
pmc-11674076:
Liya Kondratyeva and co-authors map the early immune response to the BCG vaccine in mice in this 2024 paper. The vaccine protects against tuberculosis and also trains the innate immune system against other germs, an effect called trained immunity. The team asked what happens in bone marrow and spleen in the first days after a local dose.

Three days after vaccination, mice showed more natural killer cells and monocytes in the spleen. Gene activity shifted in killer cells, monocytes, and bone marrow cells, mostly in immune control genes. Two killer-cell signals and two marrow receptors stood out. Neutrophils showed no change in count or gene activity. The authors frame the results as an early map of trained immunity.
pmc-11674276:
Florin Froimovici and co-authors set out a three-phase technique for fixed full-arch restorations on implants, along with a proposal to improve it. Full-arch zirconia restorations are popular for their strength and looks, yet they still suffer fractures, misfits, and complications around the implants. Their 2024 plan is driven by the final restoration from the start: first data acquisition, then restoration design, then manufacturing and delivery. Intraoral scanning and photogrammetry pin down the true positions of the implants.

Design software tests function and appearance before the final piece is milled. A dual software approach reverse-engineers a titanium bar from the finished restoration design rather than working forward. A zirconia-titanium hybrid structure balances strength, flexibility, and weight. Passive fit and biological and mechanical principles guide the whole process. The authors hold that this should reduce the record of fractures and sore complications.
pmc-11674376:
Federico Costa and co-authors review lung ultrasound in 2024 for newborn breathing trouble. Preterm babies often lack the lung coating that keeps air sacs open, a dangerous state long checked by X-ray. Ultrasound at the bedside offers a radiation-free rival, and the review gathers ten years of studies on its worth.

The method beats X-ray and CT in accuracy for this diagnosis, judges the need for the missing coating, and predicts when breathing support will fail. Scores built on its images guide care. The authors flag uneven training and scoring as the main barriers, and see AI help as the path to wider, steadier use.
pmc-11674676:
Luca Gammeri and five co-authors review what mast cells and basophils do in four major viral diseases. The viruses covered are SARS-CoV-2, influenza A, HIV, and dengue. These innate immunity cells bridge innate and acquired immunity. They can drive damage during infection, yet they also help spark humoral and cellular immune responses.

In some cases the cells act as reservoirs that help a virus copy itself and spread through the body. Knowing these roles could aid therapy, diagnosis, and prognosis alike. The review also notes the promise of artificial intelligence and machine learning tools for building sharp diagnostic and prognostic aids.
pmc-11674976:
Marie Quiriny and a large team build a molecular signature to sort thyroid nodules before surgery. Their prospective study was published in twenty twenty-four. Needle biopsies leave many nodules in a grey zone, and surgery is often the only way to know.

Biopsy samples were taken from nodules during thyroid removal, across all biopsy categories. Tiny RNA molecules and gene mutations were measured in each sample. The true diagnosis came from the removed tissue. Learning algorithms trained on half the samples classified the rest. The best model leaned mostly on the small RNAs, reaching high accuracy with strong specificity. The signature could cut unneeded thyroid surgery.
pmc-11675176:
Hans Fuchs, Elisabeth Dumont, and Federico Corni revisit Sadi Carnot's waterfall picture of heat, two centuries on. Their essay appeared in twenty twenty-four. Carnot, founder of thermodynamics, pictured heat as a force of nature that works like falling water.

In his image, heat's drop from hot to cold drives an engine the way a waterfall drives a wheel. The authors read the picture as an archetype: a deep pattern in how humans grasp causes. They show how the same pattern maps onto fluids, electricity, magnetism, gravity, and motion. From it they build a unified way to talk about power and energy across physics. The essay honors the analogy as a tool for building theories, not a mere metaphor.
pmc-11675476:
Aristeidis Mystakidis and co-authors use math planning to build nurse rosters in a 2024 case study. Rostering in a cancer ward is hard, since patient needs are sharp and hard to predict. Bad rosters tire staff and can lower the quality of care. The team built a model based on integer programming, which picks the best whole-number plan under set rules.

The rules cover legal work hours, staff skills, and personal wishes. In a real clinic trial, the model spread work more fairly among nurses. It met most wishes and kept all rosters within the law. Staff satisfaction rose along with smoother running of the ward. The authors present the model as proof that operations research can aid daily health care management.
pmc-11675876:
Adla Hassan and co-authors count fractures tied to weak bones in Bahrain, in a 2024 study. Such breaks are rising worldwide as people age. The team wanted a national picture to guide prevention and care.

They reviewed bone density scans from four large centers for the years 2016 to 2018. Among more than four thousand scanned patients, about four hundred had suffered a fragility fracture. Nearly all were women, with an average age near sixty-four. Spine, thigh, and wrist breaks were most common, though foot and ankle breaks also ranked high. Links with age, sex, body mass, and vitamin D were also tested.
pmc-11675976:
Endre Csaki, Antonia Foldes, and Daniel Campos present open questions about anisotropic random walks, a topic in probability theory. Their 2024 article gathers intriguing unresolved problems and the background needed to understand them.

Between twenty oh seven and twenty eighteen, the authors collaborated extensively with two senior colleagues on many of these problems. Over the following six years they continued exploring the same issues. The article compiles key results from a dozen of their previous works. That compilation frames the open questions for other researchers. Readers get both a progress report on anisotropic random walk theory and a map of what remains unsolved in the area.
pmc-11676076:
A large team studies eye infections caused by a free living amoeba in this 2024 paper from Poland. The amoeba, Acanthamoeba, can infect the cornea and cause keratitis, which may blur sight or even cause blindness if not caught.

The team checked corneal samples from cases that had resisted standard drugs, using microscopes, cultures, and gene tests to name the species. Most complex cases were tied to contact lens wearers who exposed lenses to tap or pool water. Samples held the amoeba in both active and cyst forms, along with bacteria, fungi, and other germs. The work warns that lens hygiene is key to stopping these hard to treat infections.
pmc-11676676:
Samantha Avina and co-authors review which parts of the Cryptococcus fungus could anchor a vaccine. This yeast-like fungus endangers people with weak immune systems. Global health bodies rank it among the top fungal threats.

No fungal vaccine exists for clinical use today. Whole cell and subunit candidates show promise in studies. The capsule, glucans, and chitin layers all provoke immunity. Surface proteins and shed vesicles add more targets. Tweaking these antigens can steer the immune response. The goal is lasting protection against infection. The review sorts which immunogens look strongest. It maps the road toward a first human vaccine against this fungus in people.
pmc-11676776:
Pintarič and co-authors published a 2024 study of how fertilizers shift the links between soil microbes and soil enzymes across three farming systems. Microbe and enzyme activity together signal soil health. The team sampled soils from conventional-integrated, organic, and biodynamic farms across seasons. Each soil received one of three feeds: standard fertilizer, spent mushroom substrate, or a composed fertilizer. They then tracked how microbe groups and eight enzymes moved together.

The biodynamic soil changed least under the different feeds. Standard fertilizer created negative links between one microbe group and one enzyme in the organic and biodynamic soils. Other links flipped sign depending on the feed, whatever the base soil. The authors suggest some microbe-enzyme links could serve as general soil health indicators, while others reflect the farming system.
pmc-11676876:
Svetlana Nikolaevna Nekoval and co-authors test microbe strains and bio-based products against a root-knot nematode that harms tomato plants. Published in 2024, the study targets Meloidogyne hapla, a tiny worm that forms galls on roots. Four microbe strains and three registered green nematicides were tried, next to a chemical control.

Two strains cut the number of galls by about 92 and 88 percent, close to the chemical control. Other strains raised fruit weight by about nine to ten percent and lifted yield as well. Sugar content in the fruit rose under some treatments, while vitamin C fell under others. The authors argue such bio-based tools can curb the pest with less harm.
pmc-11677076:
Qingxuan Qiao and a large team of co-authors study gut bacteria from a crop pest moth, in two thousand twenty-four. When the moth caterpillar feeds, it spits gut fluid onto the plant, and the bacteria in that fluid can sway the plant's defenses. The balance among plant, insect, and bacteria shapes who wins.

Six bacterial strains were grown from the fluid and tested on a model plant. Two strains stood out: they weakened a moth enzyme that normally helps the insect blunt plant defenses. Caterpillars with those strains grew worse on the plant, though not on artificial food. The authors suggest adding such bacteria could become a tool for pest control.
pmc-11677176:
Florian Weber and co-authors study how the fat molecules in a membrane affect its dealings with HDL particles, in a 2024 paper. HDL, the so-called good cholesterol carrier, binds membranes and swaps cargo with them. Membrane traits spring from the fats that build it. The team varied fat structure from head to tail to see what changes.

Light-based methods tracked fat domains, order, and motion in the membranes. Both fully fluid fats and some gel-phase fats interacted well with HDL. Ordered mixes with cholesterol cut both binding and cargo exchange. The results show that the whole fat molecule, not one part, sets the terms of trade with HDL. That insight may refine models of cholesterol transport.
pmc-11677376:
Nevena Todorovic and four co-authors reviewed how gut microbes split by cause in liver cancer growth. Their review, from twenty twenty-four, deals with hepatocellular carcinoma, the top form of first liver cancer. Long liver disease runs through swelling, scar, and cirrhosis to that end. Gut microbe balance is now known to sway that path in both germ and non germ causes. A newer field reads the microbes that live in the tumor it self, the oncobiome.

The team sets the microbe tale by root cause of the liver ill. That split is their core claim: one tale does not fit all roads to this cancer. Readers get a cause wise map for a hot new field.
pmc-11677576:
Anandanarayan Muruganandam and co-authors review how gut germs may trick the immune system into attacking joints in rheumatoid arthritis. The review's core idea is molecular mimicry: germ parts that look like body parts. Gut makeup in patients runs poorer and shifted. Their 2024 paper links mouth and gut bacteria to the making of anti-citrullinated protein antibodies, a hallmark of the disease.

A skewed gut also moves defender cell counts and cytokine levels, which track disease activity. Germ mix even shapes how drugs work and how toxic they run, a field named pharmacomicrobiomics. The team maps named bacteria and metabolites as leads for personal care. Gaps in proof are flagged for the next round of studies.
pmc-11677776:
Babar Shahzad and co-authors tested whether flour made from zinc-enriched wheat leaves useful traces in teenagers' blood, in a 2024 study. Zinc shortage is common and harms growth and immunity. Breeding extra zinc into wheat is a cheap fix where wheat is the staple, as in Pakistan. Blood zinc itself barely budges with small intake gains, so the team watched fat-based markers instead, using samples from a blinded trial of five hundred seventeen girls.

The girls ate the enriched or plain flour for twenty-five weeks. Nearly all fat markers and enzyme activity scores showed no clear difference. A few inflammation and stress markers dipped in the enriched group at first, but the gains faded once the many comparisons were accounted for. The authors say these markers deserve more study before they can certify that biofortification works.
pmc-11677976:
Researchers report new herpesviruses in bats on the island of St. Kitts in 2024. Mouth swabs from 66 healthy bats found virus in about a quarter of samples. Tree bats showed the top rate at 75 percent, and free-tailed bats sat near 28 percent.

Two virus groups split cleanly by host species, each a likely new member of the beta branch. One group keys to a kin virus from a near island, which hints at spread by bat travel. One strain crossed the host line, a sign the viruses can jump between bat families at times.
pmc-11678076:
Anna Dobkowska, Jiri Kubasek, and Xiaogang Li study a new way to shape magnesium alloys in a 2024 paper. Magnesium is light but hard to form at room heat, since few slip paths open in its crystal. A method that uses a shaking die can force the metal to flow without first heating the raw blocks, which could save energy and cost.

The team shape pure magnesium and three alloy families with that method and test how each resists rust in short electric tests. The method improved rust resistance for pure magnesium over its raw block. Trends differed for the alloys, and also differed from older shaping methods, so the authors urge wide study of the new route.
pmc-11678576:
Nearly every cell runs a pump that trades sodium for potassium across its wall, setting up the gradients that nerves, muscles, and kidneys depend on. Bárbara Cordeiro, Carlos Leite Fontes, and José Meyer-Fernandes review how that pump is governed in this 2024 paper. Their focus is the dialogue between hormones and a small helper protein called FXYD2.

Beyond the ions themselves, the pump is tuned by how much of it a cell makes, where it sits, and how fast it runs. Hormones reach it through their receptors and signaling chains, often by way of FXYD family proteins that get tagged by those chains. The review walks through several hormones, including insulin and dopamine, plus plant-like steroids that bind the pump directly. It closes with what pump misrule means for diseases such as high blood pressure.
pmc-11678676:
Chi-Yung Hsieh and four co-authors present a way to coat films with custom thickness patterns in a 2024 paper. Thin films with an even coat suit many uses, but some optics need thickness that varies in a planned way across the surface. Older setups need extra moving parts to shape that profile.

Their device pairs a fixed shadow mask with a rotating plate that holds the samples. The mask opening is cut to match the wanted profile. Tests produced steady slopes and wave-like patterns across the film. The team also built a variable filter from layered materials with a cavity layer of changing thickness. One coating step yields the full pattern with no added motion hardware.
pmc-11678776:
Vijayakumar and six co-authors design a circuit that lifts weak signals for a robot arm brain in a 2024 paper. Chips speak at many voltages, and a level shifter bridges them. Classic shifters mirror current between parts, but parts can fight over a shared feed and spoil the match.

Their shifter swaps the mirror for a dynamic inverter and adds a fix-up loop steered by the output. The loop steadies the outgoing level. The design targets a known flaw: current quarrels among parts on one supply. Bench results, they report, show clear gains over the standard builds.
pmc-11679076:
Sherif Fakher and others tested polymer gels for underground flow control in 2024. Directing fluids underground is technically hard and costly to get wrong. Carbon dioxide behaves compressibly down there. Water and gas flow together often. Two crosslinked polymer systems were compared. Loose sandstone formations hosted the tests.

Both polymers cut water flow more strongly. Carbon dioxide flow fell less overall. Salt levels changed performance markedly. One polymer loved salt conditions greatly. The other weakened in salty water. Oil recovery could benefit from such diversion in the field. Carbon storage could benefit as well. Future work targets storage improvement.
pmc-11679376:
Balachandran Nair Premakumari Sreeja and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four study on securing location finding in wireless sensor networks. Networks of small sensors must know where each node sits. Malicious anchor nodes can feed false positions and wreck that map.

Their algorithm borrows the bat search method from nature-inspired computing. Clustering and probability checks help it spot and isolate bad anchors. Simulations pitted it against six existing secure localization methods. It beat them across the performance measures used. The work targets safer sensing for security systems and environmental monitoring where position errors carry real costs.
pmc-11679476:
Zhichao Sheng and nine co-authors split machining surface errors into steady and random parts with a wave space method, in a paper from 2024. Surface errors on contact faces drive assembly fit and tool steadiness, so clean models of them matter.

Their method draws a cross shaped bound in wave space to split the two error kinds at the best point by wave rate. Tests on two machined faces beat common random error filters at both tasks: pulling random error out and keeping true process marks in. The authors say the split lifts model truth for later fit checks and process tuning.
pmc-11679576:
Yuliya Veryaskina and co-authors search for markers that predict the course of a blood cancer in this 2024 paper. The cancer, multiple myeloma, grows from plasma cells in bone marrow and accounts for about a tenth of blood cancers. Its course varies widely between patients, partly through gene and gene-control differences.

The team read small RNA molecules in marrow samples, then checked a panel of those and eleven genes in patient groups. Several small RNAs ran higher in cancer samples than in non-cancer ones. Most did not separate good-outlook from poor-outlook patients. Three genes did shift between those outlook groups, in telling directions. A ratio built from two of the genes showed promise as a forecasting marker. The authors frame myeloma growth as a cascade of tangled molecular paths.
pmc-11679776:
Advanced bile duct cancer now starts treatment with a standard drug trio, but later choices can be guided by the tumour's genes. Stephan Ursprung and co-authors study a German molecular tumour board that gives such advice. Their 2024 paper reviews 583 patients sent to the board and follows the 92 whose cancer was cholangiocarcinoma.

Sixty-five of the 92 carried one to three gene changes that drugs could target. Liver spread showed up more often in that group, and spread to liver or lung came with larger total tumour size. In the 25 patients with follow-up scans, the median time to growth was about 23 weeks, and growth took mixed forms, from old spots swelling to new spots appearing. The authors argue that gene boards earn their place, and that imaging patterns can hint at which tumours carry targets.
pmc-11679876:
Sato, Aoshima, and Eriksson describe a Swedish care model, adapted for Japan, that keeps patients' drug treatment continuous as they move between care settings. Breaks in medication management are a known source of harm, especially for older inpatients, and Japan lacks a system for pharmacists to lead cooperation across professions. In the Lund model, a clinical pharmacist acts as the catalyst who guides the team through a systematic medication process.

Evidence from Sweden links the model to fewer unsuitable prescriptions and lower readmission. It also links it to fewer return visits for drug problems and lower total medical spending. The authors argue that importing the framework, with pharmacists anchoring it, could give Japan a route to better teamwork among professions and steadier pharmacotherapy. The piece is a narrative review rather than a trial report.
pmc-11679976:
Fang Fang and co-authors present an interactive art system that uses brainwave data to mediate a multi-person experience with artificial intelligence, published in 2024. AI systems are now common in daily life, but research has often overlooked the philosophical and media aspects of the technology. Their system, called the Humanity Test in the text, treats emotion and consciousness as the meaning of human nature.

In an experiment, participants experienced the system with and without brainwave data feeding into it. With the data, immersion rose significantly, and emotional experience was more positive. The authors sum up three design directions: enhancing immersion, creating emotional experiences, and expressing philosophical concepts. They see brainwave data as a medium that can enrich interactive experiences and probe the line between humanity and technicality.
pmc-11680076:
Dmitry Matveev and co-authors build a fine sieve that splits carbon dioxide from carbon monoxide, in a study from 2024. The gas pair comes up in fuel and steel work, and a cheap split saves both cost and air. Their sieve pairs a thin picky skin with a loose sponge bed that must not slow the flow.

The team cast fresh sponge stock with hydroxyl ends, in a spread of chain lengths. One grade let gas through at a rate six times the trade stock rate, a record class for such beds. Two skin stuffs were screened; one was used for gas splits for the first time. The full stack kept the split keen. The work shows bed craft counts as much as skin craft in sieve design.
pmc-11680376:
Justin Smith and co-authors test vaccine antibodies in monkeys in a 2024 paper. A mucosal HIV vaccine should raise IgA antibodies that block the virus at entry sites. No immunogen had yet produced IgA that neutralizes hard-to-kill tier 2 strains.

The team purified IgA and IgG from the blood of six vaccinated rhesus macaques. The vaccine used a stabilized envelope trimer with a strong adjuvant. IgG carried more antibody overall. Yet per unit of binding antibody, IgA from some animals neutralized the matched virus as well as or better than IgG. Potency tracked with the share of certain antibody forms.
pmc-11680476:
Yao Zhang and co-authors create, in 2024, a long-lived line of rabbit bone marrow stem cells for bone repair research. A stable, standard cell source is needed before engineered bone can move toward use. The team took stem cells from New Zealand rabbits and made them immortal with a viral gene, then tested their bone-forming power.

The new line kept growing over the long term without forming tumors. A growth factor reliably pushed the cells toward bone in dishes, and a gel material boosted bone formation in animals. The authors present the line as a promising, steady supply for bone defect studies, replacing variable fresh cell batches.
pmc-11681576:
David Hanna and Carlos Rodriguez argue that a fatty particle deserves more attention in HIV care. Their 2024 commentary notes that heart disease risk runs high in people living with HIV, even on strong therapy. Lingering inflammation is one driver. The particle, lipoprotein(a), carries oxidized fats that spark inflammation and clots on their own.

They discuss a study in this journal issue that measured the particle in 117 adults with and without HIV. Levels ran higher in the HIV group despite near-full treatment use. Higher levels tied to stiffer coronary response under a hand-grip stress scan. The authors say looking past standard cholesterol to this particle may explain leftover heart risk. They frame it as the next horizon for prevention in this group.
pmc-11682776:
Manal Hadi Ghaffoori Kanaan, writing alone in 2024, tests ozone gas on retail meat in Iraq. A foodborne germ that infects meat was the target, along with total germ loads. Ozone is a promising cleaner, but the right settings for meat were unclear.

Chicken and beef were seeded with the germ, then gassed at a low dose for twenty or forty minutes in the cold. Counts of the target germ and of air-loving and air-shunning germs all fell clearly. A second twenty-minute dose deepened the drop over the next day. The author presents ozone as a workable aid for market meat safety.
pmc-11688276:
Liao and co-authors build a prediction tool for high-risk breast lesions that may hide worse disease, in a 2024 imaging study. Some lesions found on biopsy are upgraded to cancer after surgery, which leads to operations that prove needless for others. The team studied 138 patients and mined their MRI scans for radiomics features, both inside the lesion and in the tissue rim around it. Features were combined into scores and merged with clinical factors in a nomogram.

The combined model reached strong accuracy in both the training and validation groups. It beat models built on tumor features alone. Such a tool could help doctors judge which lesions truly need excision. Fewer low-risk patients would then face surgery they do not need.
pmc-11688376:
Danish, Suhail, and Farooq teach a deep learning tool to outline the gestational sac in ultrasound scans and call the age of the unborn, in a study from twenty twenty-four. The shape of the sac and its mean width help foresee miscarriage and tell how far along a mother is, early on. By hand, the measures are slow work and swing with the sonographer who scans. Five hundred scans, from four to ten weeks, form a fresh data set.

Four nets of the CNN kind, built on ResNet cores, vie in cross-check rounds. ResUNet wins, with overlap and Dice scores near the top of the scale. A new biometry trick calls gestational age by machine, straight from the outlines. Its miss next to sonographers is just seven hundredths of a week, on average. The chain can stretch with ease to other parts of the unborn.
pmc-11688476:
Wenjie Xu and co-authors report an epidemiology study, printed in 2024, charting hand, foot and mouth disease in a Chinese city across nearly two decades. The childhood illness surges seasonally and can strain clinics, so forecasting matters. The team mapped cases in Quzhou from 2005 onward and built two time series forecasting models to compare.

Tens of thousands of cases accumulated over the study years, with boys affected more than girls and two peaks each year, one in late spring and one in autumn. Yearly totals swung widely, peaking in 2016. The authors weigh the seasonal model against a modern forecasting library using standard error measures. Their aim is an early warning tool local health officials can trust.
pmc-11688876:
Jessica Benfer, Gretchen Tucker, and John Cagle ask what a good life means inside nursing homes for people with dementia, in a 2024 study. Quality care is hard to give amid staff turnover and hard transitions. The team heard views not just from residents, but from family and staff as well.

They held forty-six mixed-method phone interviews across seven homes in the United States. Residents felt days went better with a clear daily plan and warm contact with others. Family felt better when staff reassured them and they could balance care with the rest of life. Staff focused on whether residents were well cared for and their needs met. The findings point to simple steps that lift daily life for all three groups.
pmc-11688976:
Zhan Yu and co-authors study how the pandemic changed older adults' use of digital tools in China, in a mixed-methods study from 2024. China's zero-case policy leaned on mandatory QR codes, which pushed many older people online for daily needs. The team asked what that forced shift left behind.

Survey data showed internet use among older adults jumped sharply in 2020 against 2015. Focus groups in Shanghai added texture: many felt compelled to go digital to shop and stay in touch. In the post-pandemic era, some felt digital demands had invaded daily life. Belief in their own tech skill now drives whether they keep using it. Prior community tech classes shaped how people fared, a lead for policy.
pmc-11689076:
Robert Turner presented a study of Black male dementia caregivers, a group research rarely sees, in a 2024 paper. Dementia cases among older Black Americans are set to triple in a decade. Many husbands care for wives with the disease, yet Black men often do not call themselves caregivers and skip formal support.

The project measures how caregiving burden hits these men's thinking and body health. Interviews and focus groups probe their needs and their wariness of research itself, including giving blood or saliva samples. Past work shows such men feel unready for the role and lean on informal help. The author argues that knowing this hidden workforce is urgent as case counts climb. Findings should shape support that men will actually use.
pmc-11689176:
Alycia Bristol, Synneva Hagen-Lillevik, Shinduk Lee, and Nancy Allen listen to care partners who juggle a loved one's dementia and diabetes at once, in a study from 2024. The team piloted adapting Share plus, a program that pairs glucose monitoring data sharing with communication and planning skills, for these dyads. Two focus groups, nine partners in all, plus burden surveys, fed the work.

Partners voiced frustration and gaps in know-how, above all about how dementia symptoms sabotage diet, medication, and talks about care. Distress scores ranged widely; burden was mostly slight to moderate. Partners also wrestled with respecting the person's independence. The authors will fold these specifics into a tailored version of the program.
pmc-11689476:
Family caregivers of people with dementia sometimes cross lines, threatening a nursing home in a hard moment, and an eight-week course called KINDER tries to prevent that emotional mistreatment before it starts. Kylie Meyer and co-authors test whether the course is workable and promising in a 2024 pre- and post-test study. Borrowing ideas from partner-violence prevention, KINDER teaches disease knowledge, communication skills, and coping strategies over video calls and weekly practice.

Forty-five caregivers enrolled and eighty-two percent stayed to the end; the main reason for leaving was feeling the program did not fit their situation. Attendance and homework completion ran high. After the course, potentially harmful care behaviors fell significantly. The authors read the results as feasibility proven and a first efficacy signal worth a larger trial.
pmc-11689576:
Alexa Allan and co-authors link neighborhood quality with health in 2024. Where people live can shape sleep, mood, body health, and thinking. The study drew on a sleep focused group of Black and White adults from varied incomes. Both felt quality and measured quality of each area were recorded.

Felt quality covered disorder like graffiti, trust among neighbors, and shared control. Measured quality came from a national index of area hardship. Health checks spanned mood forms, sleep scores, body conditions, and thinking tests. Early results from this small group probe which side of place, felt or measured, tracks health more closely.
pmc-11689676:
Vonetta Dotson gives a career talk, in twenty twenty-four, on brain health research and outreach. Dotson is a brain and aging specialist. Her work studies what helps or harms brain health in diverse older adults. Gains come from acts such as exercise. Harms come from states such as low mood. Her aim is to cut gaps in brain and mood disorders in late life, so all can age well.

She credits two bodies, a national aging institute and a national aging society, for support across her career. That support spans early training to large grants. She also shares newer outreach: a start-up firm and a book that give the public plain, science-based facts on keeping the mind sharp.
pmc-11689776:
Jonathon Vivoda and Renée St Louis ask what moves older Americans toward or away from buying an electric vehicle, in a 2024 study. Seniors adopt EVs more slowly than younger buyers, and the barriers named in earlier work were only part of the story. The team used two survey waves from a national panel, keeping the 2,016 adults who answered both.

Likelihood of buying rose with education, liberal ideology, and trust in climate science. Believing EVs are fun, reliable, or cleaner also raised the odds, while believing they cost more lowered them. Asian and Hispanic respondents showed higher likelihood than white respondents. Change over the year, though, hinged on just three factors: party identification, income, and how much a person had heard about EVs. The authors suggest outreach and test-drive exposure may matter as much as price for this age group.
pmc-11690176:
Mishy Roy and Michael Rosenbloom report what medical students learned from a buddy program for people with memory loss, in a 2024 study. Half of patients with thinking problems go unrecognized, in part because doctors feel uneasy raising the topic. Most schools teach the biology of Alzheimer disease but give students little direct time with patients.

The program paired 20 patients with mild Alzheimer disease from a dementia clinic with first-year students at the University of Minnesota. Each student spent four hours a month with a patient family and wrote monthly journal entries on the time together. The authors read those journals for common themes. The entries show how steady contact shapes student views of dementia care.
pmc-11690376:
Sean Halpin studies how nurses teach patients in a talk-based way. The study appeared in 2024. Clear, brief facts from nurse teachers help patients take part in their own care. Yet the range of choices is hard to sort, most of all for older adults with complex illness.

Halpin taped twelve teaching visits by three nurses, with over a thousand minutes of sound in all. The patients had a blood cancer and a mid age of sixty-five. Two speech habits stood out in the tapes. Nurses reused set lines that they honed from patient to patient. They also swapped between I and we to show sole voice or team voice.
pmc-11690576:
Howard Degenholtz and six co-authors describe a state and university partnership that put data behind aging policy in Pennsylvania. The Pennsylvania Department on Aging is building a ten-year Master Plan for Older Adults called Aging Our Way. Agency leaders asked the University of Pittsburgh to run a statewide needs assessment. Community meetings were held in all 67 counties, and a telephone survey followed the Age-Friendly Community model.

The phone survey drew 900 adults aged 60 and older, weighted to match census data, while a web version in four languages drew 6950 replies. Findings went to the Long-Term Care Council, whose subcommittees shaped policy advice from the results.
pmc-11690876:
Kimberly Davis and co-authors describe dementia training for ambulance crews in a 2024 paper. EMS providers meet older adults in crisis and can link them to help. Focus groups showed they get almost no formal dementia training. A state plan in Virginia backs a public health push on dementia.

The project trains crews on two fronts. One covers life with dementia, disease course, communication, and community resources, from patient and caregiver views. The other covers advance care planning and end-of-life orders and talks. Sessions ran in seven regions and reached 275 providers so far. The model aims to make whole EMS systems dementia capable, not just keen individuals.
pmc-11690976:
William Evans asks how sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle, reached a state with no agreed definition, no diagnostic criteria, and no approved drug, in a symposium paper from 2024. Muscle is far more than a motor: it disposes of blood sugar, drives resting metabolism, supports bone, and stores amino acids for hard times.

Losing muscle therefore feeds chronic disease, disability, and death, and drug makers have chased muscle-building therapies for decades. Yet none has won approval for this condition. The symposium sets out to explain the stall. Science on muscle protein control has leapt ahead, the author notes, while the field's basic terms stayed unsettled. The piece frames the talks that follow on why translation into care has failed.
pmc-11691076:
Xiaona He and Wei Gao test whether prior depression raised COVID infection risk in older Europeans, in a study from 2024. Mental disorders and infection links drew wide interest, but population data on depression were scarce. A large aging survey offers a chance to check with proper sampling.

They used survey waves from the first two pandemic years for adults aged fifty and older across many countries. Prior depression, scored on a standard scale, raised infection odds in both years. Among depressed participants, obesity raised risk further, and unvaccinated depressed people faced the highest gap. Depression also raised reinfection risk, the authors report.
pmc-11691176:
Ling Xu and co-authors studied what young adults gain from weekly storytelling calls with older partners, in a 2024 study. College students were paired with older adults for ten weeks of phone calls. One group shared life memories in a guided reminiscence program with digital storytelling, while a comparison group followed a general wellness program.

Students were tested before, during, and after the program for loneliness, attitudes toward ageing, and knowledge of Alzheimer's disease. Attitudes toward ageing did not shift in either group. Loneliness, though, eased more over time in the reminiscence group, and their knowledge of the disease grew more as well. The authors say regular cross-generation contact can quietly help students' well-being and understanding, and they draw lessons for campus programs.
pmc-11691276:
Mohammad Hossain, Natalie Pope, and Regina George wrote this 2024 review on caring for aging parents across national borders. Migration and global aging mean more adult children support elders from another country. The team searched ten databases and, after strict screening, kept nine studies that describe what this long-distance care looks like and what it costs the carers.

Care from afar mixes money and emotion: sending funds, arranging local help, mailing gifts, making decisions, and calling often. Costs run in both countries, including trips home, and strain many budgets. Carers report guilt, worry, and distress at being absent when things change suddenly. Strict border rules, weak employer support, and thin elder care in home countries add pressure. The authors note the research base is small and mostly qualitative, and they urge deeper study of this growing group.
pmc-11691376:
Melissa Powers, a solo author, tells how her university won Age Friendly University designation the slow way, in a 2024 symposium paper. The University of Central Oklahoma's campaign began with campus groundwork. A diversity committee backed it first. Then the Faculty Senate and Staff Senate passed unanimous resolutions, each affirming that people of all ages are welcomed and valued. The request then stalled at leadership level for lack of interest.

A change of leadership reopened the door. Campus support still measured high, so the advocates went straight to the President, who approved without hesitation. His one condition set the agenda: first do an age-friendly assessment of the campus to guide priorities and programming. That assessment was underway at the time of writing. Powers offers the story as a field note for advocates elsewhere: build the base first, and be ready when the window opens.
pmc-11691676:
Jun Kitayama and Hitoshi Igawa report a small study from 2024 on how old age can shift a person's sense of self. An older thinker called that shift by a long name and tied it to a looser line between self and world. The pair asked if healthy older adults near Tokyo feel such a change now.

Eight adults, with a mean age near seventy-four, took part in talks and a short health check. Their scores showed good health. Yet most still felt rooted in daily life and had not thought much about death. A few spoke of kin who had died, or of buying less. The pair read those small signs as an early stage, not the full shift.
pmc-11691776:
Hongbo Chen links fine particulate air pollution to clinic visits for ankylosing spondylitis in Beijing, in this 2024 time-series study. Airborne particles disturb the immune system, but a connection to this inflammatory spine disease was untested. Medical claims data supplied nearly fifty-nine thousand outpatient visits from 2010 to 2017, matched against daily pollution levels.

Each ten-unit rise in particle concentration brought a small but significant same-day increase in visits, about a third of a percent. Women and younger patients were the most susceptible. The study is presented as a first signal that air quality matters for this autoimmune condition, with mechanisms left for future work.
pmc-11691876:
Wuyang Zhang and co-authors chart hearing loss across a decade among older Americans who give or receive family care. Their 2024 study joins two national surveys covering Medicare beneficiaries and their unpaid caregivers from 2011 to 2022. Hearing was self-reported for most years, with measured testing added near the end.

Self-reported hearing loss inched up in both groups, reaching about thirty-five percent of care recipients and ten percent of caregivers by the final year. Measured testing told a starker story: nearly three quarters of recipients had objective loss, more than double the self-reported share. In some pairs both sides of the caregiving relationship struggled to hear. Rates ran higher for men and for spousal caregivers. The authors argue hearing deserves attention as a caregiving issue, not just a personal one.
pmc-11691976:
Huan Liu and Hong Mi compare integrated long-term care services in Taipei and Ningbo, in a 2024 study. Both cities face ageing populations, but their care systems developed differently. The authors used literature review and field research to contrast the two models.

Taipei's system showed broad coverage, varied services, professional teams, smart technology, and strong policy backing. Ningbo stood out for family-centered care, close links between medical and elder care, and community rehabilitation. The authors judge Taipei's system more mature overall, while Ningbo leads in medical-care integration. They recommend stronger policy coordination and cooperation between departments so each city can borrow the other's strengths.
pmc-11692076:
Dao and co-authors present a 2024 study on racial gaps in advance care planning among older adults in San Antonio, Texas. Advance directives state end-of-life wishes for times when a person cannot speak. Fewer than half of older adults complete one. The team taught sessions at seven community centers, then surveyed fifty older attendees, average age near seventy-five.

Completion gaps ran along racial lines. About sixty-two percent of White respondents had a directive, versus under forty percent in both other groups. Doctor offers of help skewed the same way. Medical power of attorney forms showed an even wider split. The authors link the pattern to earlier disparity studies and urge targeted outreach.
pmc-11692276:
Louisa Holaday and co-authors studied well being in older adults who had been in prison themselves or had a close family member who had, in work published in 2024. Data came from a national survey of more than a thousand adults aged fifty five and older. About a fifth had been incarcerated, and nearly two thirds had a family member who had.

Adults with any such exposure were less likely to report thriving overall well being. They also had lower odds of strong physical health and strong social well being, even after many other factors were counted. Longer family incarceration went with steadily lower well being. The authors urge policy makers to find ways to soften these lasting harms.
pmc-11692376:
Michel Bleijlevens and co-authors look back to look forward in a 2024 nursing review. Helping older people stay in charge of their own daily care protects dignity and quality of life. Yet many nurses lack a clear picture of what autonomy means or how to support it in daily tasks like washing and dressing.

The team mined classic nursing theories for their takes on autonomy and its close cousins. Theories that shaped the field were gathered from textbooks, web searches, and expert advice. Reading them side by side shows how the idea grew over time. That history now guides training for nurses who want to support, not take over.
pmc-11692476:
Li Yao and Harue Masaki test a teaching program in a 2024 study of older Chinese migrants in Japan. Long term care planning is a hard problem for this group, who must learn a foreign care system late in life. Their program ran six modules of lectures and group talks over live video links. It aimed to raise readiness for future care needs among elders living at home in the Tokyo and Kansai areas.

Twenty-two people finished the course and all surveys, at an average age of 73. Readiness scores rose after the program and rose again a month later, both gains clear by the tests used. Attitudes toward aging, though, did not shift in a clear way. The authors say the course works for planning, even if it leaves deeper feelings about aging untouched.
pmc-11692676:
Megan Siebecker and four co-authors chart, in a 2024 study, health disparities for Native American older adults in Wyoming. Accumulated inequities leave this group at higher risk for many chronic conditions than non-Hispanic White peers. The team drew on state healthy aging reports, census data, and COVID-19 death counts to compare the state with Fremont County, home to the largest share of older Native adults.

About twenty-four hundred Native adults aged 55 and up live in the state, and over half of them live in that county. Life expectancy there runs five years below the state mean. Deaths in the COVID-19 years ran about half again as high as the state rate. Maps built with small-area methods show the gaps in place. The authors call for policy steps aimed at these disparities.
pmc-11692876:
Ray-Yuan Chung and three co-authors build a chatbot to raise technology and health literacy in a retirement community. Their study came out in 2024. Many residents struggle with digital tools, which blocks their access to information and services.

The chatbot, powered by a large language model, was designed with the residents in mind: large text, high contrast, voice input, and simple navigation. It answers practical questions such as dining menus and contact details. It also gives step-by-step guides that teach digital skills as residents ask. In trial sessions, residents completed the set tasks successfully. They reported high satisfaction and said they would recommend the chatbot to peers. The authors propose it as a friendly front door to the community's existing app.
pmc-11692976:
Natsue Shiraishi and co-authors study how older adults notice gains and losses from ageing. Their 2024 paper uses three survey waves over twelve months with 878 people aged 70 and up in Japan. Awareness of age-related change shapes how ageing feels, and learning may feed the gain side.

People with more lifelong learning started with higher gain scores. In the models, age and learning both tracked with the level of gains. Physical activity and daily-living ability tracked with the level of losses instead. No drift over time appeared in either score. The authors back steady learning and movement as buffers in old age.
pmc-11693076:
Ai Iizuka and seven co-authors describe a 2024 trial of a team form of the board game Go for older adults in Tokyo. In Pair Go, two players share one side, so wins and losses are shared too. The team built a class around the game to test if shared play could lift mood and build social ties.

Twenty-eight adults aged seventy-one to eighty-six met once a week for twelve classes of ninety minutes. Each class mixed short talks, practice tasks, and full games in pairs. Scores for loneliness fell after the course, and half the group made new friends they kept seeing outside class. The authors say shared play may help in ways that the solo game does not.
pmc-11693176:
Jooyoung Kong and co-authors take a life course view of caregiving for aging parents and early adversity in a 2024 study. Caring for aging parents is heavy work, and childhood trauma may shadow caregivers decades later.

Data from a national midlife study covered over four hundred adults caring for aging mothers. Childhood adversity patterns sorted into five classes, from low adversity to substantial adversity. Substantial adversity covered a small share, while most reported low levels. Schooling tied to class membership. Caregivers with substantial childhood adversity showed worse body and mental health than the low group throughout. The study flags trauma-aware support for adult-child caregivers.
pmc-11693276:
Haosen Sun and Brea Perry study social ties and the aging mind in a 2024 paper. Some people keep sharp minds despite brain damage, a buffer often called cognitive reserve. Ties that bridge unlike groups may build that buffer, but it was unclear which mind skills gain most, or how the gain compares with schooling.

The team used data from two hundred seventeen adults in a project on social networks and Alzheimer's disease. Brain scans gave a base line, and mind tests were compared against it. Networks rich in bridges linked to stronger reserve in general skill, planning, spatial skill, language, and memory for events. The gains matched or beat those from schooling in those areas, though not for focus or speed.
pmc-11693376:
Jennifer Jain studies, in 2024, older women who run for recreation in rural Maine. These women, aged sixty-five to seventy-eight, grew up as women's sport was transformed by a 1972 law. Thirteen runners took part in group talks, journals, and follow-up interviews, analyzed with a grounded theory approach.

Many had met unorganized sport through family as girls, and turned to running as adults for mental and physical health. Barriers included health problems, worry about how aging bodies are seen, slower pace that shut them out of club runs, and few companions in rural areas. Commitment, planning, and adaptation kept most running. The findings can guide community programs.
pmc-11694076:
Lucy E M Finnigan and co-authors test whether muscle energy faults underlie the fatigue of long COVID, in a research paper from 2024. Many patients report deep, lasting tiredness after infection. Faulty cell power plants, the mitochondria, are one suspect that magnetic scanning can probe.

The team scanned calf muscles of fatigued patients and healthy controls during exercise and recovery. They tracked fuel recovery speed and top oxygen use, and compared them with a fatigue questionnaire. Patients had normal blood tests and heart scans, isolating the muscle signal. The study design lets the authors test whether slow muscle energy recovery tracks how tired patients feel.
pmc-11696776:
Margaux Soulard and co-authors, in a 2024 study, looked at a drug choice for a rare blood problem in people whose bodies make too few antibodies. Some of these patients get immune thrombocytopenic purpura, where the body attacks its own platelets and bleeding risk rises. Drugs that raise platelet counts without holding back the immune system may suit them well.

The team gathered records from across the country for 28 adult patients who got these drugs. They tracked how many reached a safe platelet count, and how many reached a full count. Follow up after the first drug ranged from two weeks to more than ten years, with a middle value near 33 months. The report weighs both benefit and safety for this small, hard to treat group.
pmc-11698376:
Steel furnace slag is waste that might replace virgin rock in cement making. Elijah Adesanya and co-authors tested that idea in 2024 by cooking a ferrite-rich cement clinker with the slag in place of a fifth of the usual raw materials. The resulting clinker held the standard phases in unusual proportions, heavy on ferrite.

Adding a small dose of gypsum sped up the setting chemistry and produced the expected strength-giving phases. A secondary iron-rich gel formed as the ferrite reacted with dissolved silica. Long exposure to carbon dioxide curing broke down some phases, yet the mortar grew stronger as carbonate formed. The authors say slag-based clinker can work, with curing conditions shaping the final product.
pmc-11699576:
Mak-Soon Lee, Miae Doo, In-Hwan Kim, and Yangha Kim test a pepper brew on fat burn in brown fat of fat mice in a 2024 study. The brew is a thick draw from hot peppers, rich in the burn drug. Their ask is if it lifts force burn and fat stock in the brown store.

Young mice split to plain food, fat food, and fat food plus the brew for a long span. The brew group gains less weight and shows a cleaner blood fat face. Force burn runs high in that group next to fat food kin.
pmc-11700276:
Jean Louis Fobane and seven co-authors survey trees and stored carbon in Cameroon's Atlantic forests in a 2024 study. These wet forests hold rich life and lock away much carbon, yet their plant makeup and stocks were thinly charted. The team planted twelve one hectare plots in two forest zones and counted every tree past a set trunk width.

More than six thousand trees across three hundred seventeen species filled the count. A tree based sorting split the plots into three plant groups with their own species mixes and soil and climate tastes. Stand density and trunk area swung by group. Carbon stocks ran near two hundred tons per hectare with no clear gap between groups, though the split of stock shifted. The authors hand managers a base map for care and guarding.
pmc-11707376:
Gregory Piazza reviews blood thinning treatment for patients with cancer in a 2024 article. Cancer raises the risk of clots in veins and lungs, and also of an irregular heart rhythm. Both call for anticoagulant drugs, yet cancer also raises bleeding risk, so choices are delicate.

Piazza explains how inflammation, heart damage, and cancer drugs promote rhythm problems and clots. Newer oral drugs have become a more convenient option than older vitamin K blockers for many patients. The review lays out pathways for safe and effective treatment in a group where stroke and bleeding risks pull in opposite directions.
pmc-11707476:
Remmele and coauthors compare vaccine cover in twins where one has a heart defect. Children born with heart defects face higher infection risk. Long hospital stays add exposure to germs as well. Twin pairs let the team control genes and home setting.

The study recruited twins across Germany from 2019 to 2022. Ages ran from 3 to 99 years in the pairs. Vaccine records were checked against German national rules. Cover for early shots and lung germ shots was logged. Pairs showed where the heart twin lagged or matched. Gaps may guide catch-up vaccine plans for heart patients.
pmc-11709376:
India Pursell and co-authors described a new mouse model for studying Alzheimer disease in 2025. Small RNA pieces help control which proteins a cell makes, and one such piece is linked to brain cell loss and memory problems. Tools to study it in a living brain have been lacking.

The team built mice in which that RNA piece can be switched on in a set class of nerve cells. Mice aged about twenty-eight to forty-six weeks were given plain water or a drug to switch the RNA on for up to ninety days. Early results after thirty days pointed toward lower levels of some target genes. The model lets future work test how this RNA shapes memory and brain change.
pmc-11709476:
Alec McKendell and co-authors compare, in 2025, two ways to outline cells in brain tissue from people with Alzheimer's disease. Rich stained images hold clues about why some brain areas suffer while others resist. The team stained samples from a vulnerable area and a resilient area, from donors with disease, mild impairment, or no disease.

One method used a custom tool built on a common image platform, while the other used a second program with fixed cutoffs. Results differed: one method found a drop in a class of neurons early in disease that the other missed. The authors show that the choice of tool can change the science itself.
pmc-11709576:
Gonzalo Sánchez-Benavides and co-authors test whether phone-call speech can flag hidden Alzheimer's changes in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Speech shifts can be early signs of the disease. People with memory complaints but normal test scores may already carry its biology.

Forty-one such Spanish and Catalan speakers did memory and fluency tasks on an automated call. Software scored their speech on memory, executive function, and speed. Those free of the amyloid marker scored higher overall than those with it. The gap was strongest for speed and middling for executive function, with no gap for memory. Tau groups showed only a trend. The authors see a cheap, remote screening path.
pmc-11709676:
Sarah Gao and seven co-authors test a short mood-and-behavior survey in older adults in rural South Africa in a 2025 study. People with Alzheimer disease often show such symptoms, and a brief informant survey grades their weight. Whether that survey works well in a South African setting was untested.

Data came from a large aging study in Agincourt, with thinking tests, exams, and informant reports. The team set survey scores beside test results and brain scan signs of shrinkage and emotion control. The study checks how far a tool built elsewhere can be trusted in this rural group.
pmc-11709776:
Christian Haass presents a 2025 conference abstract on a gene therapy plan for frontotemporal degeneration. Too little progranulin, a growth-related protein, drives one inherited form of the disease, with TDP-43 clumps in the brain. Direct brain delivery of gene therapy spreads poorly, so Haass's team aimed a virus at the liver instead.

The virus makes a progranulin variant that can cross into the brain and stay there after one dose. In two mouse models, treatment eased motor deficits, TDP-43 faults, cleanup failure, and nerve loss. A human cell model showed the same rescue. The work offers early proof for this delivery route.
pmc-11709876:
Zahra Rostami and co-authors share a 2025 conference abstract on empathy-like behavior in rats given amyloid. Empathy rests on reading the feelings of others, a skill that frays in brain disease. The team injected amyloid into the hippocampus of rats and tested whether they still worked to free a soaked cage mate.

Fourteen rats took part, tracked over twelve days of the helping task. The time to open the door fell in the amyloid group, both when the soaked mate reacted and when it did not. The authors read the shift as a break in picking up social cues. The work probes how disease proteins warp social behavior.
pmc-11709976:
Nimisha Basavaraju and Reddy Peera Kommaddi study a receptor that may help explain why brain connections vanish early in Alzheimer's disease. Loss of synapses, the junctions between brain cells, tracks closely with memory loss in the disease. A signaling pathway called Wnt helps build and keep synapses, and its Frizzled receptors sit at both sides of the junction.

Working with mice bred to mimic the disease, the team measured one receptor, Fzd7, in synapse samples from the brain's cortex. Levels of the receptor were clearly lower in the diseased mice at nine months of age. They also tracked changes in a partner protein's tagging and breakdown marks. The work shifts focus toward receptors themselves, after years of study on other parts of the pathway.
pmc-11710076:
Edoardo Marcora and Hao Sun share a 2025 conference abstract on fine-mapping gene control sites in the human brain. Small DNA variants can tune how genes switch on, how their messages are spliced, and how chemical marks sit on DNA. The team used new math tools to pin down which variants drive these effects at single-letter detail.

The team found variants that play two or three roles at once, tuning marks and gene output across nearby genes. They also sorted splicing events that doom a message to decay, and tied one such event to an Alzheimer's risk signal. The results show how gene control layers interact in brain tissue.
pmc-11710176:
Clumps of misshapen protein, called oligomers, are suspects in several brain diseases. The normal prion protein on cell surfaces has been accused of passing their toxic effects to neurons. Gianluigi Forloni and fourteen co-authors test that charge for tau oligomers, the form linked to Alzheimer's disease. Earlier work by the group had cleared the prion protein in the cases of amyloid-beta and alpha-synuclein oligomers.

Tau behaved differently. The oligomers bound the prion protein tightly and gathered on cells in proportion to how much prion protein the cells carried. They impaired memory in normal mice but not in mice lacking the protein. They also blocked a strengthening of synapses linked to learning, only when the protein was present. The authors conclude that this partnership is real for tau and could make a drug target in Alzheimer's disease and related tau disorders.
pmc-11710276:
Maria Eduarda Barbosa and ten co-authors ask whether the makeup of fatty plaques in neck arteries mirrors the lesions of Alzheimer's disease in the brain. Their 2025 study draws on 237 donors from a São Paulo aging biobank, averaging seventy-nine years old. Earlier work tied artery disease to Alzheimer's broadly, but no one had compared plaque ingredients with the brain's plaques and tangles directly.

The team measured blockage, cap thickness, and cell content in the carotid arteries, and graded the brain changes by standard criteria. Two patterns emerged. Where smooth muscle cells filled more of the segment, tangle load in the brain was lower. Where the fibrous cap covered more area, tangle load was higher. Since a thick cap marks advanced artery disease, the authors read the pair of results as one story: as atherosclerosis advances, tangles in the brain accumulate.
pmc-11710576:
Justine Debatisse, Fangda Leng, and Paul Edison examine a brain scan measure that may flag early Alzheimer's damage before tissue visibly shrinks. The measure, cortical mean diffusivity, tracks how freely water moves in grey matter; freer movement hints that the tiny barriers inside tissue are breaking down. The team combined several scan types for ninety participants grouped by amyloid status and diagnosis.

Diffusivity ran higher in amyloid-positive patients with mild impairment or Alzheimer's than in cognitively normal peers, across wide cortical areas and memory regions. It also tracked cortical thickness only in people without amyloid buildup. The authors argue the measure captures early microstructural injury that unfolds alongside amyloid deposition, before gross shrinkage takes over. That timing could make it useful for early detection research.
pmc-11710776:
Sterre de Boer and co-authors tackle a hard diagnosis problem in a 2025 multi-center study. One form of frontotemporal dementia changes behavior early and is often mistaken for a late-life psychiatric disorder. No reliable marker separates the two, so the team pools 508 dementia cases and 152 psychiatric cases to find the sharpest clinical clues.

They test thinking scores, brain shrinkage ratings, and two blood markers in turn, then jointly. Some thinking patterns, such as stronger word fluency and screening scores with weaker attention, pointed toward a psychiatric cause instead. The study is the largest of its kind for this dementia form. Its models aim to seed diagnostic tools that spare patients years of wrong treatment.
pmc-11710876:
Omar Namiq and Namir Al-Tawil report a rare case of a rib broken by coughing, in work from two thousand twenty-four. A woman aged fifty-four had a dry cough for sixteen days after a chest infection. Sharp pain then set in on the right side of her chest.

The break sat in her right fifth rib, caused by the force of hard coughing. Her bone health showed no clear signs of the thinning disease often blamed for such breaks. Care without surgery led to a good outcome. The authors urge doctors to weigh rib breaks when a long, hard cough pairs with chest pain.
pmc-11712076:
Arshia A Khan reports a 2025 study of a smart home built to help people with dementia. The work was done in a lab space with healthy volunteers. The home mixes robots, worn sensors, and room sensors to watch mood, movement, and safety through the day.

Sensors in chairs and a robot that reads faces judged mood and matched what people said they felt in most cases. Door sensors caught every exit event in the tests. Wall sensors picked up wandering, and worn sensors tracked body changes during tasks. Robot contact showed the strongest effect on body signals. The results suggest such a home could help guard quality of life.
pmc-11712176:
Elizabeth A Boots and co-authors pilot a self-run thinking test in people with progressive supranuclear palsy in a 2025 Mayo Clinic study. The disease, called PSP, is a rare brain disorder that affects movement and thought. Self-run tests work well in Alzheimer's disease, but their fit for other diseases was untested. The platform, Mayo Test Drive, runs on phones and tablets.

Eleven patients took both the self-run test and standard paper tests. Ten finished the self-run test in about twenty-two minutes on average. Users rated ease of use near nine out of ten, and all said they could manage alone, though some needed help with links or codes. Those with the worst movement symptoms struggled most with tablets. Score links with the standard tests were also checked.
pmc-11712376:
Kaj Blennow studies a blood marker for Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 paper. The marker, a changed form of tau protein, is read as a ratio against its unchanged form in some tests. That ratio was hoped to sharpen detection of Alzheimer's-type change.

Blennow shows that fast brain cell loss and sudden injury can skew the ratio in both spinal fluid and blood. The unchanged form rises with general cell damage, dragging the ratio with it. Data came from large groups with Alzheimer's, a prion disease, and acute injury, read by two methods. Clinics should read the ratio with care when other brain harm is present.
pmc-11712476:
Karina Leal and co-authors describe a center that builds open tool kits for new Alzheimer's drug targets, in a 2025 paper. Dementia touches tens of millions of people, and fresh targets are badly needed. Many candidate proteins lack the probes and tests that let labs judge them.

The center runs a pipeline that ranks targets and builds a package of reagents for each. Packages hold chemical and cell probes that are checked and shared freely. Targets came from large disease consortia lists of understudied proteins. New methods speed ranking, antibody checks, and probe hunting. The authors argue that open tools will hasten the search for drugs against this varied disease.
pmc-11712576:
Yuqing Chen and four co-authors gather trial evidence on traditional Chinese medicine as a treatment for Alzheimer's disease. Their 2025 review and pooled analysis search four major databases for studies that meet set quality rules. Standard drugs for the disease help only modestly, so older herbal and combined approaches draw interest.

Thirteen studies with 1,183 patients in total passed the screen. Patients on the traditional treatments scored better on two standard thinking tests than control groups. Scores for behavior problems and daily-living skills, though, showed no clear gain. The authors suggest these treatments may work best as add-ons beside standard drugs. They call for bigger, stricter trials with longer follow-up and checks against brain markers of the disease.
pmc-11712676:
Chanchal Sadhu and co-authors charted in 2025 how a tau-targeting antibody moves through mice and monkeys ahead of human trials. The antibody, VY-TAU01, grips the bad form of tau, a protein that tangles in Alzheimer brains, and blocks tangle seeding in dishes. Its parent form was dosed in gene-tweaked mice that grow such tangles, and the human form in macaques. Blood and spinal fluid levels were tracked, along with free tau in the mice.

Levels rose in step with dose in both fluids, then fell in the usual two-phase way. No sign showed the target soaking up the drug in bulk. Free tau reads gave the action arm of the study. The team offers the data as the base for first human dosing.
pmc-11712776:
Dementia care strains families hardest where services are thin. Gabriela Novotni and co-authors test NOMAD, a home-based program in North Macedonia where a nurse and social worker team visits people with dementia and their caregivers. The trial compares the program against usual care across twelve GP practices in the Skopje region.

Over four home visits, the team builds a personalized care plan with the family doctor and dementia experts, and hands caregivers a manual plus teaching sessions. The study tracks caregiver depression, burden, and quality of life, plus the daily functioning and service use of the person with dementia. Acceptability is assessed alongside outcomes. The authors frame the model as a template for low-resource settings.
pmc-11712976:
Alexandru D Iordan and co-authors present a 2025 study of mild behavioral impairment, a pattern of new behavior symptoms in older adults that can appear before memory loss. The team asked how this pattern links to Alzheimer's disease markers and to the way brain networks divide their work.

They studied 128 people with mild memory problems or mild dementia, using PET scans for amyloid and tau plus scans of network activity. People positive for both markers showed a less sharply divided salience network, and that weaker division went with worse behavior symptoms. The results suggest tau may drive the symptoms by loosening this network's borders.
pmc-11713076:
Stefanie Tremblay and co-authors studied the brain's white matter in older adults whose families include Alzheimer's disease, in work published in 2025. White matter carries signals between brain areas, and changes there may start early in the disease, yet it is little studied.

The team used scans from 134 adults with no thinking problems from a Montreal area cohort. They blended several scan measures into one score for how unusual each tiny brain spot looked. They then linked that score to test scores and risk factors, for men and women apart. In men, one clear pattern tied widespread white matter change to the measures studied. The work treats white matter as a mix of changes, not one.
pmc-11713176:
Ramachandra Reddy and a large team study the safety and composition of an Ayurvedic herbo-mineral tablet proposed against COVID-19. Their 2024 study follows laboratory evidence that the tablet kills the virus in cell assays.

Safety was tested in fruit flies and their larvae, which stayed healthy and active at tested doses with normal activity rhythms. Elemental composition was measured with several spectrometry methods. Microscopy and diffraction examined the tablet's microstructure. The tablet proved safe in the fly model up to the highest dose tested. The authors argue the findings support an accessible, safe traditional therapeutic approach, with composition data guiding quality control.
pmc-11713276:
Neda Rashidi-Ranjbar and co-authors test shining near-infrared light through the skull to help fading memory, in a 2025 pilot study. Mild cognitive impairment often precedes Alzheimer's dementia, and failing mitochondria, the cell's power plants, are part of the story. The light therapy aims to recharge those power plants without drugs or surgery.

Fourteen patients at a Toronto memory clinic were randomized to real or sham treatment, using a home headset daily for six weeks. The team measured thinking tests before and after, alongside safety and practicality of the routine. A pilot this small cannot prove the therapy works, but it can show whether patients tolerate and complete it, and hint at which abilities move. Positive hints would justify a bigger trial of light as a gentle lever on the aging brain.
pmc-11713376:
Aparna Kanmani and co-authors build a caregiver-led brain training program for dementia in India in a 2025 paper. Standard cognitive training often sidelines the family caregiver. Their program trains caregivers as co-therapists, guided by neuropsychologists, using nine tasks that span attention, thinking, memory, and language.

After a small pilot, thirty-two patient-caregiver pairs took part, half with training and half with usual care for five weeks. The training group gained in attention, executive function, and memory, plus daily independence and quality of life. Caregivers felt more confident and rated the plan highly feasible. Readers get a home-grown model for dementia care where specialists are scarce.
pmc-11713476:
Ece Bayram and co-authors report a survey study from 2025 on the daily concerns of people who care for a family member with Lewy body dementia. The work was done with a community group linked to the Lewy Body Dementia Association. It asks what worries caregivers most and where care falls short.

The team surveyed 832 current and former caregivers in the spring and summer of 2021. Most cared for a spouse or partner. Many said they worried each day about handling care alongside other duties, about what the illness would do next, and about changes in behavior. The authors argue that better support and clearer guidance would help both caregivers and the people they care for.
pmc-11713576:
Lan Zhang, Lin Li, Denglei Ma, and Weipeng Wei test a plant extract in rats with high blood pressure in a 2025 study. High pressure damages small brain vessels and the white matter that links brain regions. The extract comes from a herb used in Chinese medicine. Rats with inherited high pressure serve as a model of this early vessel disease.

The rats got the extract for three months. Treated rats learned and remembered better on object tests. Scans and tissue checks showed less white matter damage and less loss of the fatty coating on nerve fibers. Brain support cells also calmed down, and gene activity in a key tract shifted. The extract may guard the brain by quieting swelling and feeding growth signals.
pmc-11713676:
Machelle Wilchesky and Stephanie Ballard describe, in a 2025 methods paper, how to catch harm caused by screening itself. Their setting is a pilot of an elder abuse screen for long-term care homes. Asking about abuse can stir bad memories or distress, so safety checks matter as much as accuracy checks. The pair built a system to spot and judge any harm the screening might do.
