Their plan draws on methods from partner violence research and drug trials. Harm reports come from many sides: residents, the study social worker, home staff, and research staff, plus chart reviews. A safety committee led by a specialist reviews progress after set numbers of residents take part. Social work teams stand by to step in, and every resident gets a card with phone numbers for instant help.
pmc-11713776:
Tyler Lewis Stevens and co-authors study a calcium sensor inside mitochondria in a 2025 Alzheimer's paper. Mitochondria supply cell energy and also take up calcium, a signal that can harm them in excess. Earlier work from the lab showed that calcium overload alone can trigger damage much like Alzheimer's. Patient brain samples showed low levels of one sensor, named MICU3, that helps control the uptake channel.

The team tested what happens when this sensor is lost. They drew on tissue from patients who did not inherit the disease and on animal models. Loss of the sensor appears to be part of how the disease advances, not just a side effect. The result names a fresh target for drugs that protect the cell's power supply.
pmc-11714076:
Howard Chertkow wrote a 2025 discussion paper on the friction that can arise between clinicians, researchers, and care partners in dementia work. Involving caregivers in research and care planning is essential to good medicine. Yet the parties can honestly disagree, and those disagreements deserve realistic handling rather than slogans.

One example is Alzheimer trial enrollment. Caregivers rarely join from pure altruism, and a failed or placebo-arm trial can push them to withdraw. Balancing their autonomy with a trial's need for completion is delicate. A second example is prognosis: who shapes the story told to the patient, especially where medical assistance in dying is legal, as in Canada. Chertkow sketches approaches for each clash. The paper argues candor about disagreement strengthens partnerships.
pmc-11714276:
Blood tests for Alzheimer's markers are easier than brain scans, but their meaning may differ across racial groups. Antoine Trammell and ten co-authors studied 3,035 adults in 2025 from a health disparities cohort, comparing blood marker levels with the volume of white matter damage seen on MRI. The group spanned white, Black, and Hispanic participants, with and without thinking problems.

Black participants carried the most white matter damage, while white participants showed the highest levels of two blood markers. Links between the markers and damage volume appeared mainly in impaired Hispanic participants. The authors say blood markers cannot be read the same way in every group. They call for more work on what drives these gaps.
pmc-11714476:
Yuhui Huang and co-authors search blood chemistry for signs that flag fading memory and thinking in older adults. Their study draws on the Rugao Longevity and Ageing Study, a community cohort in China. Blood samples were read by nuclear magnetic resonance, and thinking was scored by two objective tests.

In a first stage with 1,643 people, the team found 28 metabolites tied to severely impaired thinking. A second stage followed new cases over two years, matched against healthy controls. Pathways linked to the flagged chemicals were mapped as well. Models built with the markers predicted new cases better than standard risk factors alone. The work hints that a blood test could one day help flag early decline.
pmc-11714576:
Pablo Garcia-Gonzalez and co-authors mine spinal fluid data for patterns in Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 study. The disease stays partly unknown, and fluid from the spine holds clues in its proteins and fats. The team merged both data types to find hidden structure.

Samples came from 1,121 people at a Barcelona center, across stages from early worry to full dementia. Each data type was shrunk to its main axes on its own first. The top axis held about 40% of the fat spread and 60% of the protein spread. Those two top axes tracked each other closely across people. Later steps tie the axes to known risk factors and disease stage, in search of cleaner patient groups.
pmc-11714776:
Payton White and ten co-authors probe, in 2025 work, a link between a blood mark of Alzheimer's disease and a sleep rhythm in older Black Americans. The rhythm, brief bursts in deep sleep, helps fix memories and may flag the illness before signs show. The blood mark tracks a protein that tangles in the ill brain.

Seventy-five healthy older adults from a long health study gave blood and wore a sleep band at home for two nights. pmc-11715776:

pmc-11716176:

pmc-11716276:

pmc-11716376:

pmc-11716476:

pmc-11716576:

pmc-11716676:

pmc-11716776:

pmc-11716876:

pmc-11716976:

pmc-11726876:

pmc-11727876:

pmc-11728676:

pmc-11730776:

pmc-11744376:

pmc-11825476:

pmc-11886876:

pmc-11894576:

pmc-11970176:

pmc-11996776:

A sulfur compound rich in skin proteins blocked spore making in normal strains only. Host skin chemistry may thus mute spore spread through Rac.
pmc-12082676:
Chukwuma, Adetukasi, and Opeodu surveyed school students in 2024 in Ibadan, Nigeria, about sugary food habits and oral health knowledge. Sweet refined carbohydrates feed tooth decay and gum disease when hygiene lags. Two hundred forty-eight senior secondary students from public and private schools answered a structured questionnaire.

Knowledge looked strong: over ninety-four percent scored well, and nearly all agreed sweet food causes decay and twice-daily brushing matters. Girls scored slightly better than boys. Yet eating patterns told another story, especially in public schools, where over a third reported high refined carbohydrate intake and about half moderate. Knowing and doing diverged, and the authors call for stronger oral health campaigns in schools.
pmc-12086676:
Caroline Signori-Müller and a large team compared the stored carbohydrate reserves of tropical lianas and the trees they climb, in a study published in 2024. Lianas, woody vines that compete with trees for light and water, are growing more abundant in some forests. The reserves in question, non-structural carbohydrates held in stem wood, fuel growth and help plants survive stress, yet little was known about how they differ between growth forms.

The team measured total reserves, split into starch and soluble sugars, in uninfested trees, in trees whose canopies were more than half covered by lianas, and in the lianas themselves. Sampling covered a moist site in western Amazonia and a drier site in the south. As their title reports, the lianas held greater concentrations of these carbohydrates in their stem wood than the trees did.
pmc-12091076:
Seyed Jafari and five co-authors examine what makes research on human dignity so easy to get wrong. Their 2024 study holds that dignity research underpins the ethics of human rights, so its flaws carry weight. Sloppy work can entrench discrimination, distort how schools of thought view dignity, and weaken rights talk as a whole.

The team sorted the pitfalls they found into two groups. One group concerns material: studies may ignore the history and culture that shape a view of dignity. The other concerns method: studies may miss the range of voices needed for a full picture. Both flaws fall hardest on people at the margins. The authors urge researchers to guard against these traps so their work defends the rights of all.
pmc-12099076:
Shota Fukuda and five colleagues published a 2024 study on friendly mouth bacteria that block a gum disease germ. The germ, Porphyromonas gingivalis, invades gum cells and drives periodontal disease. Healthy mouths host many harmless bacteria, but their protective roles are rarely tested in the lab.

The team focused on Neisseria, a common harmless mouth resident. They built a flow-based test to count how many germs get inside gum cells. Neisseria cut that invasion down in their tests. The result suggests some mouth residents act as guards, not just bystanders. Harnessing such guards could add a new line of defense against gum disease.
pmc-12110476:
Yusuf Karaşin and Yalçın Karagöz build a survey scale for abortion attitudes in Turkey, in work from 2024. Abortion is lawful there under set terms, and views on it split by culture and era. A shared scale can make those views plain to study. The team drafted items, took expert notes, piloted the draft, and tested it on three hundred three women in Istanbul.

The final scale holds twenty-three items in three groups. The groups were named stigma, exclusion, and heed for respect. Fit scores for the three-group shape passed standard bars. The authors offer the scale as a sound tool for future work on this charged topic in Turkey.
pmc-12284476:
Rubromycins are bacterial aromatic polyketides with a signature spiroketal core, known for killing cells and germs by striking nucleic acids. One member bears a ring change that an amide bond synthetase installs. The six authors mined genomes for clusters with that enzyme but without the usual ring-building enzymes, in hope of finding a new compound. One strain, Lentzea tibetensis, was the hit.

Grown in culture, it made a new family member fused to an aminocoumarin group, which the team named coumarubrin. Mass spectrometry and NMR pinned down its structure, and its absolute configuration matches the family. First assays show strong activity against Gram-positive bacteria. The head dates the paper to 2024, though the catalog lists 2025.
pmc-12324076:
Verónica Dubois and co-authors check whether yeast fungi live in gum biofilms of people with HIV in Buenos Aires, in work from 2024. Mouth thrush is common in this group. Lasting growth of the fungi on mouth surfaces can help thrush take hold.

The study covered 51 patients on HIV treatment, with checks of teeth and gums. Staff took samples from under the gum line and from the mouth lining, 255 samples in all. Lab tests using DNA methods named each fungus found. Men made up most of the group, with a mean age near 41 years. The results show where the fungi hide, which can guide dental care for these patients.
pmc-12367976:
Yuwei Liao, Zhifan Lin, Siyu Li, and Xiaolei Yin report a 2024 method to grow pancreatic ductal organoids with high efficiency. Organoids are small 3D cell cultures that mimic an organ, and they help model pancreatic disease, but making mature ductal cells this way has been hard.

A cocktail of small molecules tunes the culture so more organoids form and more of their cells are ductal cells. The cultures grow from Sox9-positive ductal cells, hold a mix of ductal and acinar cells, and stay stable over long growth. The authors point to drug screening as a prime use for the system.
pmc-12480076:
Kyeong-Ah Lee and co-authors review lab tests for scrub typhus in Korea from 2019 to 2023. Scrub typhus is a mite-borne illness that brings fever, chills, rash, and a dark bite mark. Data came from the national control agency and regional health institutes.

Of more than two thousand suspected cases, about one in eight tested positive. Many patients had both a gene test and an antibody test, letting the team compare the two. The gene test found more cases than the antibody test in this data. Patterns by sex, age, and region are also traced. The findings can guide which tests labs reach for first.
pmc-12660876:
Cedric Foucault and co-authors published this 2025 brain study on how people hold the odds of what comes next. Judging chance guides seeing and acting, yet how the brain stores a probability value was unknown. Past scans tied some regions to surprise or uncertainty, but not to probability itself. The team used a strong 7-tesla scanner to hunt for the code.

They found the signal in two areas, the side frontal lobe and a parietal region. The code surprised them: it was not a simple rising line. Instead, different cell groups tuned to different probability ranges, like notes on a scale. The code for confidence, by contrast, rose in a mostly straight way. The authors urge the field to expect richer codes in future work.
pmc-12661676:
Grace Kemigisha and co-authors report a 2025 survey on mosquito repellent use for malaria control in Nangabo Ward, Uganda. Repellents could add to nets and sprays, yet they are little used in places where malaria is common. The team asked household heads what they know, feel, and do about repellents, and what drives use or non-use.

Most people had heard of repellents and viewed them in a good light, but steady use was very low. Many did not know if the products were safe for young children or for pregnant women, and cost was a key block. Older heads and large households used them less, while more schooling and good attitudes raised use. People also said they would prefer natural options over made ones.
pmc-12661876:
Xianwei Han and co-authors report in 2025 a rare, harmless bone growth in an unusual place: the sacrum, at the base of the spine. The growth, called florid reactive periostitis, usually forms on the small bones of the hands and feet. Their patient, a girl aged twelve, had unexplained pain and swelling near her tailbone.

Scans showed bone loss and surface reaction that first looked like cancer. Tissue tests, plus a gene test that helped rule out cancer, confirmed the harmless growth, which mixes young bone, fiber tissue, and long-standing swelling. Simple drugs and rest eased her pain, and scans improved within two months.
pmc-12662776:
Thomas Scruby, Kae Nemoto, and Zhenyu Cai weigh a shortcut for fault-tolerant quantum computing, in work from 2025. Hard gates on error-corrected qubits are usually made with magic state distillation. That process is costly and factory-like.

The team shows how a looped pipeline design can run a published non-Clifford gate between surface codes. The design shuttles qubits over short ranges on a two-dimensional chip. Its scheduling is only slightly more complex than the plain code. Honest accounting, though, favors distillation for now. The gate's decoder is weak, forcing very large code sizes to keep errors low. The authors argue that better decoders could flip the comparison.
pmc-12663276:
Niloufer Dumasia and Prasad Pethe study how a signaling pathway guides stem cells toward becoming pancreas cells. Human embryonic stem cells can be coaxed into the pancreatic line in a dish, offering a model of early development. Two proteins, RING1B and BMI1, tag genes to keep them switched off during this process.

A signal called sonic hedgehog must be quieted for pancreas formation to proceed. The team asked whether that signal also directs the two proteins onto pancreas genes. Using a method that fishes out protein-bound DNA, they compared cells given the signal with cells given a blocker. The signal changed both the activity of key pancreas genes and how much the two proteins sat on their control regions. Occupancy tracked two genes closely, yet the master pancreas switch stayed unchanged, showing the pathway steers gene silencing in this step.
pmc-12663376:
Cristina Cairone and co-authors study self-injury in a Milan prison in a 2025 paper. Among seven hundred twelve men held before trial, eight percent hurt themselves without suicidal intent during detention. Records ran from February to October 2023.

Nearly ninety percent of episodes involved men from North Africa, often tied to requests for a cell move or medication, which points to a communication role. Youth and past self-injury raised risk in that group. Elsewhere, mental illness and past attempts mattered most, while children and schooling protected. Readers get a case for culturally aware mental health care behind bars.
pmc-12663476:
Krishna Kumar and co-authors (2025) propose a hybrid scheme for encrypting images that repairs the known weaknesses of the RC4 cipher. RC4 is fast, but its keystream is biased and its key scheduling weak, so it is unsafe alone. The scheme starts by deriving a strong 256-bit key from a password using standard tools, then builds a modified keystream reinforced with a second pseudo-random sequence to reduce bias.

Encryption then works in stages. Pixel values are substituted using the S-box of the PRESENT cipher. The image is shuffled spatially with a chaotic cat map. A diffusion step then spreads each change across the picture. Test measures such as entropy and standard attack statistics came out at desirable levels. The authors conclude that the layers wash out RC4's weaknesses while keeping strong encryption performance for uses like medical imaging and surveillance.
pmc-12663576:
Marta Grabowska and co-authors track testis changes under immune suppressing drug plans in a 2025 study. Transplant patients take drug mixes for years to keep organs safe. What those mixes do to male gonads over time is poorly known. Rats followed six drug plans for six months in the experiment.

Every drug plan disturbed the sperm making tissue lining to some degree. Tubes shrank and dividing germ cells fell below control levels. Two plans raised the share of germ cells with broken DNA. Switching to a single newer drug softened some measures but not all.
pmc-12664276:
Min Yi Sum and co-authors report a 2025 study that tracks, moment by moment, how slights, mood, and odd beliefs link in people with a first bout of psychosis. Slights are the subtle, mild form of stigma these patients meet in daily life. How a slight is taken may rest on mood at that moment and on a belief that events refer to oneself.

The team used phone prompts at 28 time points over two weeks, with a full clinic check at the start. Records from 36 patients who kept up most prompts fed the study. Low mood and self-referring beliefs each linked to more felt slights. A data-driven search found two paths: low mood feeds self-referring beliefs, which feed felt slights, and low positive mood feeds slights on its own. Paths split a lot by person.
pmc-12664876:
Gene activity in a key memory area of the brain is the focus of a 2025 study of Alzheimer's disease by Tayani Pour and co-authors. The disease still has no firm cure, in part because its gene changes are not well mapped. The team studied gene data from the CA1 part of the hippocampus, an area hit early in the disease.

More than a thousand genes differed between sick and healthy samples. Paths tied to fats rose, while paths tied to cell storage fell. Five hub genes stood out, and three of them link to how cells make energy. The authors say these genes and paths are fresh leads for drugs and tests.
pmc-12666176:
Sameer Parpia and co-authors set out a plan to compare two ways of analyzing a kind of clinical trial in this 2025 protocol. These trials test whether a new treatment is no worse than standard care. Two analysis styles are common: one keeps all patients in their assigned groups, and one counts only those who followed the plan.

Current thinking holds that the first style may be too lenient when patients break the plan. The review will gather 390 such trials published before the end of 2024 from three databases. It will compare effect estimates and the width and bounds of their ranges between the two styles. It will also test how the share of excluded patients affects the gap.
pmc-12684376:
Sassi Siddiqui and co-authors replace a harsh acid with a homemade green liquid to help turn used oil into a cleaner product. Their liquid is a deep eutectic solvent, two cheap solids that melt into a liquid when mixed, here in five ratios. Tests showed it was gentle: no harm to lab cells and no effect on five microbes.

Used as the catalyst for joining oil with methanol, it reached 96.3 percent conversion in ten minutes at mild heat under tuned conditions. A planned set of experiments found the solvent dose mattered most. The authors scored the method's greenness against the classic acid route and report a cleaner profile.
pmc-12687076:
Nacul and co-authors review the add-on treatments tried when septic shock refuses to yield to standard care. In refractory cases, blood pressure stays dangerously low despite fluids and first-line drugs, and death rates are high. The team searched four databases for randomized trials of newer interventions published between 2000 and 2024. Twenty-four trials qualified, covering drugs such as methylene blue, vasopressin, and terlipressin, plus vitamin and steroid combinations.

Some treatments bought real gains short of survival: methylene blue freed patients from pressure drugs a day sooner, and terlipressin improved kidney blood flow. But no single therapy consistently saved more lives. The authors conclude that the add-ons can steady the circulation without yet proving a mortality benefit. They call for bigger trials and combined approaches aimed at inflammation itself. For intensive care teams, the review is an honest ledger of hope and evidence.
pmc-12690976:
Jun Yen Ng and co-authors report, in a 2025 paper, only the third published adult case of an acute myeloid leukemia carrying a rare gene fusion, DDX3X joined to MLLT10. This fusion arises from a swap between chromosomes X and 10, and almost nothing is known of its adult behavior.

Their patient, a twenty-seven-year-old woman with the myelomonocytic form of the disease, resisted several rounds of chemotherapy. Pooling all three cases exposes wide genetic variety, stubborn chemoresistance, and poor outlooks. The authors argue this rare entity carries unmet clinical needs and should inform how future leukemia classification and risk systems treat it.
pmc-12691176:
Piotr Cierpikowski and Julia Bar review heat shock proteins as possible drug targets in head and neck cancer, in a 2025 paper. These proteins rise when cells are stressed by heat, inflammation, or toxins, and many tumors overproduce them. Inside cancers they shape the tumor's surroundings and help cells survive.

Trials against these proteins are running in breast, prostate, colon, and lung cancers, but head and neck tumors have been left out. The review gathers what is known about the proteins' normal roles and their behavior in this cancer type. The authors argue the gap is an opportunity: the biology is mapped well enough to justify dedicated trials.
pmc-12692276:
Eight researchers study how melatonin protects goat fertility cells from heat in a paper from 2025. Heat stress is a growing threat to male fertility in livestock as the climate warms. Sertoli cells support sperm production but are easily hurt by heat. The team exposed goat cells to heat and tracked gene activity and carbon flow through cell metabolism.

Heat damaged the cells' energy hubs and slowed the main energy cycle. Pre-treatment with melatonin restored hub function and chemical balance. It also shifted metabolism into a protective pattern and kept more cells alive. The authors say melatonin could help protect breeding animals in hot climates. The work also informs human heat and fertility research.
pmc-12694076:
Joan Josep Sirvent-Verdú and co-authors test lenses made by holography for see-through screens in a 2025 paper. Such lenses can steer light into a guide plate, a role key to glasses that lay text and images over the real world.

Making many such plates at once is the hard part. One route shifts the color of the record light, which drops the need for prisms and gels at record time. The team asks how far that route can go when lenses, not plain grates, do the steering. A lens can also rule scale and blur, which a grate cannot. The paper weighs how the film shrinks as it sets and what that warp does to grade, for two record setups and a range of lens strengths.
pmc-12695476:
Shintaro Yamagami and co-authors check whether slow blood flow in a heart pouch predicts clots after a rhythm procedure in a 2025 study. Atrial fibrillation lets blood pool in the left atrial appendage, a small pouch where clots form. Ablation can restore rhythm, but stroke risk may linger. The speed of flow in that pouch, seen on an ultrasound through the esophagus, was already known as a warning sign before treatment.

The team reviewed more than fifteen hundred ablation patients who had that ultrasound first. About one hundred had reduced flow speed; the rest had preserved speed. They then tracked clot events, rhythm relapse, and major heart outcomes over the long term. If a slow pouch still warns after ablation, those patients may need longer clot protection than the standard plan.
pmc-12695676:
Kruthika Reddy and co-authors report an unusual case of Wilson disease in a 2025 article. Wilson disease is an inherited disorder where copper builds up in the body and can damage the brain. It usually shows with tremor, stiffness, or behavior change, which makes it easier to suspect.

Their patient was a twenty-four-year-old Indian man whose only problem was nine months of slurred speech, plus drooling and trouble moving food with his tongue. He had no tremor, stiffness, or thinking problems. Eye rings typical of copper buildup, blood tests, and brain scans pointed to the diagnosis. Treatment with copper-removing drugs and speech therapy brought marked improvement by his own account. The authors urge a full work-up when slurred speech stands alone.
pmc-12695876:
Seigan Hayashi and co-authors chart the full vibration landscape of a tiny self-oscillating beam by experimenting directly on it, in work from twenty twenty-five. Micro devices behave strongly nonlinearly, which can help performance. Ordinary tests only watch forward motion and miss hidden states. Experimental continuation instead tracks steady and repeating responses in hardware. The method had never probed micro systems at such fast timescales.

Their active cantilever self-oscillates near a hundred kilohertz naturally. Forced responses are mapped across frequency and drive strength grids. Stable and unstable periodic orbits both appear on the response surface. The surface folds in ways unlike the classic Duffing oscillator. A multi-valued landscape emerges from the careful experimental sweep. Designers gain a truer map of micro device dynamics.
pmc-12696276:
Maxime Bertrand and co-authors argue that invasive blood pressure should be read as a full monitoring tool in a 2025 review. Such monitoring is a base part of care for critically ill patients. Each part of the pressure wave, top, bottom, mean, and pulse spread, carries its own clue about heart and vessel function, beyond a single number.

Pulse spread can stand in for stroke volume and flag fluid response in ventilated patients. Bottom pressure reflects vessel tone and can guide when to start vessel tightening drugs. Two newer ratios are offered as sharper markers of tone and drug response. The review urges a physiology driven, personal approach to intensive care.
pmc-12698376:
Hong Sun and co-authors study a supplement that eases nerve damage from a cancer drug in a 2025 paper. The drug, a packaged form of a classic chemotherapy agent, often causes painful tingling and numbness in hands and feet. Alpha lipoic acid is known to protect nerves, but the route of its action was unclear.

In rats given the drug, the acid eased the nerve injury. Network analyses of drug and gene data pointed to several pathways, with one immune signaling route standing out. Docking checks supported a direct link to that route. Lab tests then showed the cancer drug switches the route on, while the acid calms it back down. The work gives a firmer base for trials in patients.
pmc-12698476:
Siqi Wang and co-authors profile myasthenia gravis patients who carry two antibodies at once. The disease, an autoimmune attack on the nerve-muscle junction, is usually tracked by anti-receptor antibodies; some patients also carry anti-titin antibodies. Reviewing 35 hospitalized patients in Southwest China, the team compared 18 with the single antibody against 17 with both.

The double-positive group skewed more severe: nearly half sat above class II on the standard scale, against far fewer in the single group, and half also had thyroid trouble. Onset tended later, though not significantly. Symptoms, thymus findings, and treatment results otherwise matched. Dual testing, the authors suggest, flags patients headed for generalized disease.
pmc-12698576:
Congling Wang and co-authors show that the path of a metabolic index, not just its level, forecasts artery clogging. The index joins blood fat, sugar, and body mass into one insulin resistance gauge. Their 2025 study follows 2,329 Chinese adults through repeat health checks over about five years. Path modeling split the group into two tracks: a stable track and a rising track for the index. Neck artery scans tracked clog growth.

Clogs grew in nearly half the group. The rising track grew them more often. Its risk stayed higher after full adjustment, and ran highest in the young and in women. Adding the track to standard models sharpened forecasts. The team urges repeat metabolic checks, not one-off reads.
pmc-12699376:
Asma El Kaourat and eight co-authors published a 2025 study making silver nanoparticles the green way, from argan oil waste. Saponins drawn from argan press cake, the residue of oil making, drove the synthesis of silver and silver chloride grains. A battery of instruments confirmed the product: round grains 12 nanometers across on average, with the expected light absorption band.

The grains killed both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria in standard assays. They also showed moderate toxicity against three cancer cell lines, breast and cervical among them. The authors present the waste-to-grain route as sustainable and biocompatible, with medical promise. Turning a regional waste stream into a medical material is the study's wider pitch.
pmc-12699676:
Fatima Nazir, Sameera Rizvi, and Tahir Munir link mothers' minds to birth weight in Karachi in a 2025 study. Low mood, worry, and stress in pregnancy are common in Pakistan, yet birth care rarely treats them. The team asked whether such strain raises the odds of a small newborn, and whether felt support blunts that risk.

Mothers were signed up within two days of a live birth at two large Karachi hospitals. The case group held 196 mothers of small babies, matched by 196 mothers of sound-weight babies. Set forms logged strain, support, and home facts for each mother.
pmc-12700976:
Zhaofei Shi and co-authors build in 2025 a scan-based model that spots dry uric acid kidney stones without surgery. Four hundred sixty eight patients across centers give plain scan data. More than twelve hundred image traits shrink to six key ones by selection.

Image scores join clinic traits in one combined model. Test scores top ninety four percent area marks in training and outside sets alike. The model beats image-only and clinic-only rivals by clear margins. Urine acidity, blood uric acid, and the image score drive the calls. Outside validation guards the scores against one-site quirks.
pmc-12702276:
Yueping Zhou and colleagues compare three ways of preparing the womb lining for a frozen embryo transfer in women whose ovaries respond poorly, in this study from twenty twenty-five. Over four thousand six hundred women with diminished ovarian reserve had their first transfer between twenty sixteen and twenty twenty-four. The options were a natural cycle, hormone replacement, or hormone replacement preceded by a drug that quiets the ovaries first.

The pretreatment won. Women who received it had better live birth and clinical pregnancy rates than hormone replacement alone, with the clearest gain in those thirty-five and older. Natural cycle and hormone replacement performed alike. Babies born as singletons fared similarly whichever route was used. The authors suggest the quieting pretreatment deserves a place for older patients with low reserve, while noting the evidence is retrospective.
pmc-12705676:
Evelyn Muñoz-Núñez and co-authors made camphor derivatives and tested them against cancer cells in a 2025 study. Modifying natural products is a classic route to new drugs. Camphor offers a rigid, well-known scaffold that chemists can decorate with new groups to tune its action.

The team attached ring structures containing sulfur and nitrogen to the camphor frame. They measured killing power against cancer cells and antioxidant activity in lab tests, and modeled the compounds on computers to explain the results. One thiophene-bearing compound stood out in the panel. Such screens do not make a drug, but they reveal which decorations deserve the next, costlier round of testing.
pmc-12705776:
Georgine Szipl, Anton Baotic and Kurt Kotrschal study contact calls in jackdaws, highly social crows that form lifelong pair bonds, in 2025. Their short tchak calls may help birds keep in touch while feeding out of sight of each other.

Calls from nine adult males during natural foraging were recorded and analyzed with standard and machine learning methods. Two forms appeared, a harmonic form in most males and a noisy form in fewer birds. Both forms carried cues to individual identity, and spectrogram methods read those cues best. The authors say the two forms show flexibility in jackdaw vocal life.
pmc-12706076:
Polish lakes have been warming for two centuries, and Mariusz Ptak and co-authors reconstructed just how much using a global weather reanalysis. Because lake surface temperature tracks air temperature closely, the Twentieth Century Reanalysis let them rebuild seven lakes' thermal history from 1806 to 2022, long before direct records. The lakes warmed by about 0.081 degrees per decade on average.

The record breaks into phases, with turning points in the 1840s, the 1940s, and the late 1980s. Recent decades brought the fastest warming, and the authors expect it to continue. They call for coordinated strategies to protect lake ecosystems.
pmc-12706176:
Zhilong Huang and co-authors model where a carnivorous pitcher plant lived, lives, and may yet live. Nepenthes mirabilis, a vulnerable species of Southeast Asia, was mapped from 513 records with the MaxEnt method across past, present, and future climates. Annual rainfall proved the strongest single driver of its range.

The model points to Wallacea and New Guinea as the cradle, with spread over glacial land bridges into the Sunda lands, the Philippines, and Indochina. Under warming, good habitat slides toward higher latitudes and low-latitude groups face growing risk, with the sustainable-development path kindest. The authors pair the maps with in-place and backup conservation advice.
pmc-12706876:
Tadesse Sheleme and co-authors ran a cluster randomized trial of medication therapy management in southwest Ethiopia. Their 2025 study took in adults who had both diabetes mellitus and hypertension, and who went to outpatient clinics.

Hospitals were placed by chance in a group that got the new care or a group that did not. Each group had two hundred one patients. The new-care group got medication therapy management as well as the usual care. Staff gauged how well patients stuck to their drugs with the Adherence in Chronic Diseases Scale. In the new-care group, the share who stuck to their drugs rose by fifty percent. The control group showed a unlike result. The trial tests if set, pharmacist-led help can keep people on long-term drugs.
pmc-12707076:
Dewa Wardhana, Cindy Soetomo, Agung Satyarsa, and Rohadi Rosyidi review blood clot risk after surgery for tumors near the pituitary gland in a 2025 paper. Such surgery is complex, and clots in deep veins are a known risk after brain surgery. The team ask when risk peaks and what body shifts drive it.

They searched major databases and kept three studies that fit their rules. All pointed to the first ten days after surgery as the peak risk window. In that window, hormone and fluid shifts swing salt levels and strain vessel walls, making blood more prone to clot. The authors urge early, tailored steps to prevent clots.
pmc-12707676:
Ma and Gurkan-Cavusoglu model how cancer cells move through their division cycle under chemotherapy, in a 2025 paper. Their probabilistic framework follows many generations of cells, tracking how drugs trigger checkpoints, cell death, and a risky workaround in which damaged cells slip past checkpoints and pass harm to their offspring.

Calibrated against real cell measurements, the model links its parameters to DNA repair quality and cell fate choices. Sensitivity analysis shows that sloppy repair under certain drug classes drives later predictions most. Across three drugs, higher doses disrupted cycle dynamics more strongly. The authors aim to guide dosing and treatment design.
pmc-12709776:
Maryam Khakbaz and co-authors pool, in 2025, the evidence linking vitamin D levels to frailty in older adults. Studies had disagreed, so the team gathered forty-one of them, covering cohorts and one-time surveys, and rated the certainty of the evidence. The blood marker for vitamin D status was compared between highest and lowest groups.

In forward-looking studies, the highest vitamin D group had about twenty-nine percent lower frailty risk. One-time surveys showed an even stronger link. Each step up in blood level brought a steady step down in risk. The authors conclude low vitamin D tracks with frailty, while noting most evidence is observational.
pmc-12711876:
Prediabetes warns of diabetes ahead, but only some people cross over, and Luo and co-authors built a way to tell who is at real risk at the moment prediabetes begins. From health records of more than seventy-four thousand patients, they carved a clean cohort of 14,436 whose onset met strict blood sugar criteria. A gradient boosting model read routine facts, from blood sugar and body mass to lipids, medicines, and lifestyle. It then scored each patient's risk.

Trained on one period and tested on patients from later years, the model reached an area under the curve of 81.6 percent. Its high-, medium-, and low-risk groups followed clearly different paths toward diabetes. The split held up in the later cohorts too. The authors argue that risk scoring at the first sign of prediabetes could aim early help at the people most likely to benefit.
pmc-12712676:
Aleksandra Nurzynska and seven co-authors created a 3D-printed wound dressing insert from a natural gel, in a 2025 paper. Heavily weeping wounds heal slowly and risk infection, so dressings must drink up fluid and support repair. The team printed inserts from curdlan, a bacterial sugar polymer, enriched with calcium ions. The dry inserts are small and compact, easy to slot into layered dressings, yet swell to absorb large amounts of fluid.

Tests confirmed the material's heat stability and safety: it did not poison cells, damage blood, or cause mutations. It also encouraged skin cells to multiply. The authors aim the inserts at hard wounds such as venous leg ulcers, where fluid loads are heavy. They present the work as a step toward dressings that manage fluid actively instead of merely covering the wound.
pmc-12713676:
Claire Pearce and co-authors review how Australia's allied health assistant workforce is being put to work, in this 2025 paper. Assistants support therapists in fields from physiotherapy to speech work, extending scarce professional hours. Big reforms in disability and aged care funding have raised demand for the role faster than the evidence about it.

The review gathered thirty-eight studies and eighteen policy documents from 2007 onward. Four themes stood out. Assistants improved access and service flow where they were used well. Training and supervision shaped to each setting made the difference. Local structures, such as funding rules, decided how far the role could stretch. Tension also ran between freeing assistants to innovate and guarding professional boundaries. Evidence on outcomes is still thin in mental health, disability, and aged care. The authors call for workforce plans that back the role with training and clear structures.
pmc-12714076:
Mayowa Omotosho and co-authors report a newborn infection traced to a home remedy in a 2025 case study. In many communities, families rub shea butter on a baby's umbilical stump to help it heal, a custom that can instead seed dangerous germs.

The patient, a ten-day-old boy, arrived irritable, refusing the breast, with a red and tender stump. Blood culture grew Leclercia adecarboxylata, a normally mild environmental bacterium that can turn deadly in the vulnerable. pmc-12716576:

pmc-12716976:

pmc-12717076:

pmc-12717276:

pmc-12717976:
N van der Windt and co-authors present a 2025 study of the microbes that live in sponges of one widespread family, and whether a sponge's family tree predicts its microbial tenants. pmc-12718176:

pmc-12718276:

pmc-12718376:

pmc-12718576:

pmc-12720476:
Bethany Davey and colleagues pool trials on whether numbing a nerve can spare hip fracture patients the confusion of delirium, in this review from twenty twenty-five. pmc-12721076:

pmc-12721876:

pmc-12721976:

Imaging advances get attention throughout, as do links between structure and disease signs. pmc-12722176:

pmc-12722276:

pmc-12722376:

pmc-12722476:

pmc-12722776:

pmc-12723076:

pmc-12723176:

pmc-12727176:

pmc-12727576:

pmc-12727776:

pmc-12727876:

pmc-12728076:

pmc-12729076:

pmc-12729276:

pmc-12729576:

pmc-12729976:

pmc-12730876:

pmc-12731976:

pmc-12732176:

pmc-12732676:

pmc-12732776:

pmc-12732976:

pmc-12733076:

pmc-12733176:

pmc-12733276:

pmc-12733976:

pmc-12734176:

pmc-12734376:
A team in Korea links blood calcium levels to recovery after cardiac arrest in a 2025 paper. Death and brain damage stay common after out of hospital arrest, and calcium imbalance marks the post arrest syndrome. The study reviewed 421 patients given targeted temperature management from 2011 to 2023.

Ionized calcium, adjusted for blood acidity, was tracked at five points over three days. Higher levels tied to better brain outcomes and lower thirty day death rates, whatever the patient's other traits or calcium infusions. Each small rise cut the odds of a poor brain outcome by about seventeen percent. Adding the time course lifted prediction accuracy markedly. The authors propose serial calcium checks as a prognostic tool.
pmc-12734776:
Szczygiel and Radon-Kobus test how print orientation affects a steel-filled plastic composite made by filament printing, in a study from twenty twenty-five. The composite holds ninety-five percent steel powder by weight, far above typical loadings. Such heavy filling may behave very differently by print direction. Samples are printed flat and upright for comparison.

Tensile tests measure strength in each orientation. Surface roughness is read with a contact profilometer. Wetting is judged from contact angle, and size accuracy from caliper checks. Results link orientation to both strength and surface traits. The data guide printing choices for metal-rich polymer parts where direction cannot be ignored.
pmc-12735176:
Tanya Pereira-Riveros and colleagues grow a finicky gum bacterium using extract from another bacterium. Their methods paper from twenty twenty-five targets Tannerella forsythia culture. The periodontal pathogen cannot make a key wall ingredient itself. Pure cultures need that ingredient supplied from outside.

The team extracted wall material from a staph strain instead. Measurements standardised the extract strength with calibration curves. Plates seeded with the extract went into an oxygen-free chamber. The target bacterium grew on those plates over a week. Results confirm the substitute source supports isolation work. Simpler culture opens this pathogen to more labs. Gum disease research depends on growing such organisms reliably.
pmc-12735276:
Boyanka Angelova and co-authors map the bacteria that live at the edges of three glacial lakes in the Rila Mountains of Bulgaria, in work from twenty twenty-five. High lakes are rich in life yet hard to reach, so their microbes stay poorly known. Seasons and warming may reshape those small communities fast.

Water samples came from ice free months in twenty twenty-three and twenty twenty-four. Gene reads found more than a thousand bacterial groups across the lakes. Richness peaked in June, just after ice melt, most of all in the highest lake. Warmth and carbon in the water drove the main shifts. The study warns that cold loving types may fade as the region warms.
pmc-12735676:
Weiwei Wang and a large team of co-authors review vaccines against a poultry disease in a 2025 article. Infectious bursal disease attacks the immune organ of young chickens and costs the poultry industry heavily. Vaccination at large scale, alongside strict hygiene, is the main defense, and many vaccines already protect well against classic and very strong strains.

The problem is that the virus keeps changing in the field, and fresh variant strains have appeared in recent years. Older vaccines can lose their grip on these new forms. The review traces vaccine design from traditional whole-virus products to modern molecular platforms. The authors argue the next generation must be safer, stronger, and able to keep pace with the virus as it drifts, and they map the strategies most likely to get there.
pmc-12735776: Wen-Hung Wang, Arunee Thitithanyanont, and Sheng-Fan Wang wrote a 2025 review on African swine fever and its growing threat in Asia. The disease was first identified in Kenya in 1921 and stayed mainly a sub-Saharan concern for nearly a century. The review traces how that picture changed as the disease spread, and what its evolution means for pig farming and control efforts across Asia.
pmc-12736076:
Hakan Ogutlu and co-authors survey non medical staff in mental health services in Turkiye about eating disorders in a 2025 study. Such disorders are serious, often start in the teen years, and carry high risk. Most past work asked medical staff what they know. This study asked 42 non medical staff in community services in Ankara.

Each person read one of six short cases, spanning eating disorders, depression, and diabetes, then answered questions on what the illness was, its causes, and their views. Only 28.6 percent named the disorder in their case correctly. Many held stigmatizing views, such as blaming the person, and many thought the disorders mainly affect females and respond poorly to care. The authors call for better training.
pmc-12736176:
Kristina Feizer and co-authors study chiral nematic droplets in polymer films in work from 2025. These droplets twist light and can switch under voltage, which makes them useful for displays and optics.

In flattened droplets, the team find a twisted structure with two stable states that differ in axis direction. A small voltage turns the axes to align with the field, and a strong field unwinds the twist. Cells reach high transparency in the on state with low control voltage. Contrast grows with a chirality measure, which helps explain the optical behavior seen.
pmc-12736376:
Sofía Fernández-Godino and co-authors report a small study from two thousand twenty-five on diet and daily function in multiple sclerosis. The disease inflames and damages nerves in the brain and spinal cord, often in young adults. Diet may shape its course, since foods differ in how much they stir inflammation.

The team studied nineteen patients, scoring their diets with an index of inflammatory potential. They also rated function with a scale made for this disease. Patients on the more inflammatory diet reported a heavier symptom burden, with more fatigue and more muscle and gut complaints. Those on the calmer diet reported fewer symptoms and more energy. The authors treat the work as a first step that needs larger samples.
pmc-12736876:
Some mosses can dry out completely and come back to life, and Pragya Singh and co-authors study how one such moss, Hedwigia ciliata, handles the swing between wet and dry. In controlled conditions they tracked water content and photosynthesis over forty-eight hours of drying after full hydration, then through rewetting. The moss drinks fast when water returns, yet it also holds onto water longer than its surroundings would suggest.

While drying, the moss delays its shutdown: photosynthesis keeps running into the early dry phase, and its light-harvesting machinery stays intact. Protective measures against light damage stayed quiet during drying, while recovery signals after rewetting were strong. The authors read this as preparation in advance — the moss readies itself for the dry state before it arrives. They offer the species as a useful model for drought stress in mosses.
pmc-12737076:
Sérgio Ivan Lopes and co-authors published a 2025 perspective article on low-cost air sensors for indoor rooms, and how to build and trust systems around them. Tight new buildings hold air in, saving energy but fouling the air people breathe. People spend most of their lives indoors. A sick building syndrome grew from that: illnesses with no single cause, tied to time spent in a place.

Low-cost sensors can now monitor indoor air in real time, at fine detail. They flag pollution sources and help cut heating and cooling use. They do not match the reference instruments, and the team is plain about that. The article gives a shared design model for such sensor networks, from the sensing head to the network link. It then weighs the strengths and weaknesses of the cheap path, and looks ahead to how their reliability can be proven.
pmc-12737276:
Yongqi Hu and co-authors use an ultra-thin, high-density brain surface array to watch how long-term caffeine rewires mouse cortex activity. The sixty-four-channel device records with fine spatial detail while barely disturbing the brain. Caffeine sharpens alertness briefly, but its lasting effects on sleep structure and brain connectivity are murky.

Recording mice through baseline and recovery, the team finds chronic caffeine lowers overall signal power and sleep spindle strength. At the same time, regions fire more in sync, and spindles change in length and number. Sleep deprivation, by contrast, raises power. The contrast shows caffeine's long shadow differs from simple tiredness, and validates the array.
pmc-12737576:
Xianghao Xiao and co-authors present a 2025 animal study on whether a vitamin A compound fed to sows can protect their piglets' lungs. Breathing diseases cost pig farms heavily, and newborn lungs set the stage for later health. The team tested all-trans retinoic acid, a form of vitamin A, in the mothers' diet.

Fifteen sows were split among five diets with rising doses, fed from day 12 to day 95 of pregnancy. Lungs from the newborn piglets were then examined and sequenced. At the lowest dose, piglets had more air sacs with thinner walls and more helpful microbes. Harmful bacteria also fell. The authors note one caution: resistance to a class of antibiotics rose. Dose choice will matter.
pmc-12738076:
Chowdhury and coauthors give a lab method for sharp imaging of cell fibers. A method called expansion microscopy puffs samples up for fine views. It lets plain lab scopes show tiny cell parts. Fiber labels can blur or shift during sample prep, though.

The new method strips cell fluid and skins while it keeps fibers intact. Growth steps then cut fibers into small bits for dye tagging. Dyes tag the cut ends, so no antibody step is due. Tag shift stays at about one nanometer or less. The method works for lab-grown fibers and for fibers in cells.
pmc-12738576:
Azine Datlibagi and a team of co-authors built a lab model of a scarring eye disease, in two thousand twenty-five. The disease grows membranes inside the eye that can harm sight. Their model uses a human retinal cell line grown in a dish, with or without a water channel protein added.

Certain treatments pushed the cells to change type, stretch out, and move more, like cells in the disease. Cells with the added protein, under the harsh treatment, matched real patient membranes most closely in gene use. The protein also seemed to aid cell movement and invasion on its own. The authors offer the model as an easy tool for study.
pmc-12738676:
Maria Emmerich, Benjamin Liertz, and Robert Wille release an open-source slicer tuned for printing microfluidic chips, in a 2025 paper. Such chips route tiny fluid volumes through fine channels. Resin printing can make them fast, but standard slicers favor outer surfaces. Inner channels end up clogged or rough as a result. Their tool detects chip features automatically before slicing.

The chip is then oriented and sliced dynamically to protect those features. Cross-sections are rasterized for the printer. Several chips can be arranged on one build plate automatically. A single calibration step sets exposure times for a resin and thickness pair. The modular code is public for others to extend. Cleaner channels should improve flow and experiment quality. The authors target labs that print their own devices.
pmc-12738776:
Hui Huang and co-authors assess wildfire risk to power lines in a 2025 study set in Guangdong, China. Fire near high voltage lines can weaken air insulation through heat, smoke, and flame. That can trip a line and cause wide outages. Climate extremes and human activity are raising fire risk.

Their framework joins two parts. A Bayesian network estimates ignition odds from place, weather, fuel, and human factors. A physics model then judges insulation failure from flame and smoke. Distance to settlements, vegetation type, and monthly rainfall stood out as top factors for ignition in the grid studied.
pmc-12739176:
Louis-Marie Paget and four co-authors published a check-up study in twenty twenty-five on how well code-based rules spot mild head injury in French emergency rooms. France has no dedicated watch system for these injuries. A large ER data network could fill the gap, if its diagnosis codes can be trusted.

The team read over five thousand charts by hand and scored each rule against the charts. Rules worked well in children but fell short in adults, and none met the bar set for a watch system on its own. Scores shifted with age and other traits of the patients. The authors show both the promise of the data and the work still needed before it can count cases with care.
pmc-12741076:
Lauren Mottel, Brennagh Shields, and Brian Kwee review biomaterials designed to calm and steer the immune system so badly injured muscles can regrow with blood vessels and nerves, in a 2025 paper. Severe muscle wounds, from lost tissue to cut nerves, heal poorly, and cell therapies often vanish from the site or lack donor tissue. Implanted materials can also stir the very inflammation that blocks repair.

The review walks through strategies that work with immunity instead of against it: surface chemistry, slow release of calming cues, and materials drawn from nature or built in the lab. Each is weighed against the needs of muscle, nerve, and vessel regrowth together, since working muscle needs all three.
pmc-12742076:
Tianzheng Zhong, Feng Wang, Jianfeng Qiu, and Weizhao Lu study brain size changes in ADHD in a 2025 paper. The condition affects behavior, focus, and self-control in many children. Scans show that gray matter volume differs from that of other children, but the order of change is unclear. The team asks whether some brain changes drive behavior or follow from it.

The study used scans from 135 children and teens with the condition and 182 without it. A sorting method grouped patients by brain shape to handle wide variety. The team then lined up the scans by symptom scores to mimic change over time. Their network method traced which regional changes likely came first. The map may help explain how symptoms unfold as children grow.
pmc-12742176:
Bin Gao and a large team define a liver disease where metabolism and alcohol team up in this 2025 paper. Fatty liver from metabolic problems is now called MASLD. Some patients also drink at levels below classic alcohol disease but above abstinence, and their condition needed its own name.

MetALD covers patients with at least one metabolic risk factor who drink 140 to 350 grams of alcohol weekly for women, or 210 to 420 for men. Heavier drinking counts as alcohol disease proper. The paper reviews how this mixed group differs in course and care. Clear borders help trials enroll the right patients and doctors give honest advice.
pmc-12743076:
Javier Millán and co-authors survey lung and heart worms in Spanish wild carnivores in a 2025 study. These nematodes are among the most harmful parasites of wildlife, yet records for the Iberian Peninsula were thin, and none existed for the European wildcat. The team examined road-killed animals from Navarra, mostly wildcats, across ten species.

Fifteen of thirty-three wildcats carried the worms, with three species identified by shape and gene checks. Badgers, martens, and polecats also hosted several species. One wildcat worm had never been recorded on the peninsula before, and the team deposited fresh gene sequences for poorly known types. The survey gives a baseline and a prompt to check pet cats roaming the same ground.
pmc-12743476:
Eddie Nagadi and co-authors published a 2025 study of how to rinse the root canals of a tooth so a deep bacterium dies in the walls. The bacterium in view often feeds root infections. The rinse is a mixture of three fluids, activated in the canal by one of three ways: sonic shaking, ultrasonic shaking, or a laser beam. A plain needle rinse was the control.

Nearly forty extracted teeth were seeded with the bacterium and split into four groups. Live-dead dye and a fine microscope measured how deep the kill ran. The laser way won by a wide gap: its kill depth ran past a thousand tiny units, micrometers. The sonic way came next, then the ultrasonic. The needle control ran least by far. Statistical checks held the gaps as firm.
pmc-12744876:
Sachin Talwar and a large team of co-authors report two infants whose heart repair was undone by abnormal veins. The Kawashima operation links the upper body's great vein to the lung artery in babies born with a blocked lower vein and a single pumping chamber. Their 2025 report covers two girls, twelve to thirteen months old and weighing six kilograms, who had the operation. Extra veins that reroute blood around the repair grew early and starved the lungs of flow.

Imaging by cineradiography found the malformations. A literature review places the pair among known cases. The warning is practical: even a perfect repair can fail fast if these veins open. The authors urge early imaging when a baby fades after this operation.
pmc-12745276:
David Ballesteros and co-authors review a blood-filtering treatment in 2025 for septic shock with kidney failure in a Colombian intensive care unit. A special membrane can both replace kidney function and soak up toxins and inflammatory signals from the blood. Data from poorer countries are scarce, so the team studies fifty patients treated in a public hospital.

Over seventy-two hours, blood pressure rose and the need for pressure-raising drugs fell to near zero. Still, sixty-two percent of patients died in hospital, with deaths tied to worse severity at arrival. Among survivors, about two-thirds left hospital free of dialysis. Covid-related sepsis fared worse, the authors note.
pmc-12745876:
Muhammad Ahsan Jamil and co-authors review side effects of a bone drug in cancer patients in a 2025 report. Zoledronic acid guards bones when cancer spreads and tames high calcium in blood. Yet it can also drop calcium too low and strain the kidneys.

Records covered four hundred adults treated at a cancer hospital in Lahore during 2024. After treatment, average kidney markers rose sharply and average calcium fell sharply. About three in ten patients crossed into poor kidney range, and a small share fell to very low calcium. The team calls for routine checks of kidneys and calcium, plus supplements, to keep treatment safe.
pmc-12746076:
Alexander Clark and co-authors report a 2025 study on leg bones and tendons in hawks and owls that hunt with their feet. Birds of prey seize and carry prey with their back legs, so those parts hold clues to how each kind hunts. One shin muscle lifts the ankle, and its tendon bears the load when prey is grabbed.

The team compared the shin bone anchor point for that muscle and tested how far its tendon stretches. Owls had a stouter bone and an anchor set farther out, which gives them more leverage at the ankle. Tendon stretch strength did not split the two groups, yet owls need about half the twist force to lift a set load. Their tendons are springy, which may soak up shock and store energy in flight.
pmc-12746576:
Piotr Panek and co-authors compared two stomach tests in a 2025 study of patients set for weight-loss surgery. Work-up before surgery often includes a scope test of the stomach, with checks for Helicobacter pylori, a germ linked to stomach pain and ulcers. No rule says which of the two common tests to trust more, so the team looked back at past cases.

One test checks a small tissue bit for a fast color change, and the other checks the tissue under a scope for the germ itself. The authors compared how often the two tests agreed and how much infection they found. They also weighed whether the scope and tissue checks help spot stomach swelling in this group.
pmc-12748576:
Patoo Withatanung and co-authors characterize a new virus that infects a staph bacterium in this 2025 paper. The host, Staphylococcus pseudintermedius, infects animals and can pass to humans. Drug resistant forms with strong biofilms are a growing problem. The virus, called VL4, was isolated from sewage using a resistant clinical strain.

Its genome holds 68 reading frames and no toxin, resistance, or virulence genes. Family analysis placed it as a new species in its genus. The virus reproduced fast and stayed stable at body temperature and neutral acidity. It suppressed host growth and attacked 27 of 31 clinical isolates. It also blocked new biofilms and partly broke down mature ones. Such phages may become backup treatments.
pmc-12748676:
Bin Wu and four co-authors design a power supply controller for pulsed laser diodes, in a 2025 paper. Switching supplies are compact and efficient, but laser pulses demand a hard trio at once: fast rise, flat current top, and high accuracy. The team interleaves several circuit branches in parallel and mixes control modes.

At light load, a burst-mode voltage control speeds the response and trims extra current. During pulses, a dual-loop current control takes over: an inner loop evens out the branch currents, while an outer loop regulates the total output. Switching between modes follows the control signal's demand for a pulse. Simulations and a built prototype confirmed the scheme. Rise times fell and the output current stayed stable, which is what precision laser driving needs.
pmc-12748776:
Reenu Rajpoot and co-authors describe XTC-Net in 2025, a deep learning model that finds atelectasis on chest X-rays. Atelectasis means a lung has partly or fully collapsed. Early detection can prevent worse lung problems and guide quick care.

XTC-Net joins three parts in one system. Xception pulls out rich spatial features from each image. A Transformer tracks long-range links between distant parts of the image. A Capsule Network adds care for small shifts in shape that mark collapsed regions. Trained on a public chest X-ray set, the model scored near perfect marks on accuracy and related tests. A check on a second large data set from the NIH also held up well. The team presents the system as clear and fit for clinic use.
pmc-12748876:
Animals differ widely in how well they regrow lost body parts, even among close relatives. Sergio Campos and co-authors compared regeneration across species of Hydra, a small freshwater animal known for rebuilding its whole body. Most species regrew feet readily, but Hydra oligactis and its relatives were much slower. Looking at gene activity during regrowth, the team found that the weak species barely switched on Wnt signaling after injury. In a related species, that signal is required for foot regrowth.

A brief treatment with a drug that boosts Wnt signaling switched on the foot program in the weak species and raised its foot regrowth rate sharply. The profiling also pointed to a gene called dlx2 as a likely high level regulator of foot regrowth, acting under Wnt control. The authors offer the comparison as a framework for studying how regenerative ability evolves and is lost.
pmc-12749076:
Minglin Zhou, Zhikui Liu, and Hanying Bai test how layered fill over soft river soil carries heavy loads, in a 2025 study. Storage yards on soft ground are often built by draining and piling weight on top. Shallow fill layers act like soft clay. How stress spreads through such a base was unclear.

A large field test piled bulk minerals in steps. Sensors tracked stress and strain inside the ground. A fill band three to four and a half meters down spread the load like a hard crust. That crust formed and adjusted as loading grew. Knowing where stress goes helps engineers design yards that settle evenly instead of failing in patches.
pmc-12749276:
Peemongkon Wattananon and five co-authors study a deep back muscle in a 2025 lab study. The muscle helps hold the trunk firm in still poses and in motion, yet its motor unit acts have been little probed. The team asked how sound repeat measures of those acts are, and how speed and load change them.

Twenty-nine adults with no back pain bent their trunks forward for 60 seconds at a time. Two speeds and two loads were mixed across sets. Fine wire-free sensors split the muscle signal into single motor units. The study shows which measures stay steady on retest, a base for later work on back pain.
pmc-12749976:
Murata and co-authors wrote a study from 2025 on delayed bleeding after removal of bowel growths in patients on blood thinners. The drugs, a class of direct oral blood thinners, are gauged poorly by standard tests. Their strength in the blood varies a lot from person to person. Delayed bleeding days after the snip is a known risk of the procedure. Whether the drug's measured strength predicts that bleed was unknown.

Centers across Japan followed users of these drugs through the procedure over four years. About one in ten suffered delayed bleeding. Blood levels of the drugs swung widely between patients on the same dose. A lab gauge of the drug's anti-clotting action tracked the blood levels closely. In the pooled math, patients whose drug action ran high faced far greater odds of a delayed bleed. The team advises care with patients whose readings run strong.
pmc-12750076:
Paula Collazo-Castiñeira and nine co-authors study phone health apps for older adults in a 2025 paper. Mobile health tools could support healthy aging, yet older people adopt them far less than the young. The team asked retirement age adults what would make such tools welcome. Their focus was design persuasion and behavior change methods.

Nineteen Spanish participants from Madrid community settings joined focus groups. Most were women, with an average age near sixty two. They favored simple designs that ask little time. Barriers surfaced too: low digital skill and fear of leaning too hard on technology. Transcripts were coded against two known frameworks plus fresh themes. The results guide apps built for older users first, not adapted as an afterthought.
pmc-12750276:
Zihan Sun and co-authors make a sodium battery electrode film without the harsh chemistry its crystal form usually demands, in work from 2025. The gamma-prime phase of vanadium pentoxide has wide layers that suit sodium ions, but making it normally takes temperatures above 600 degrees and toxic reagents.

Their route combines gentle heating with electrochemical treatment to convert a thin film into the desired phase. The film delivered an initial capacity slightly above the theoretical value, at a healthy voltage. Its charge efficiency reached 98 percent, far above the roughly 50 percent reported before. Cycling stayed stable at a fast rate, and the film matched powder performance, opening a cleaner manufacturing path.
pmc-12750776:
Mia Fowler and co-authors ask which patients truly need long antibiotic cover after revision joint surgery, in a 2025 paper. Extended oral antibiotics grew popular after one study showed a steep drop in joint infections for high-risk patients. Later results conflict, the risk is higher in revision surgery, and long antibiotic use clashes with stewardship goals.

The team reviewed 1,995 consecutive aseptic revision hips and knees, flagging each patient's listed comorbidities from diagnosis codes. About half the hips and three in five knees carried at least one flagged condition. Simply having a flagged condition did not significantly raise infection risk on its own. The paper pushes for a sharper definition of high risk before antibiotics are handed out.
pmc-12750876:
A large French research team tested the national rare disease registry in this 2025 paper. Rare diseases have become a public health priority in many countries, yet basic counts of who has them are still missing. France built its registry, the BNDMR, in 2013 to fill that gap.

Doctors enter patient data at each visit, and each disease gets a standard ORPHA code. A diagnosis can be marked confirmed, probable, or under investigation, and family links can be stored. As a test case, the team estimated how common one rare disease is: TNF receptor associated periodic syndrome, an inherited fever disorder. They aimed to judge whether the registry's data are sound enough for epidemiology. Good registry data can guide clinics, research, and funding for rare diseases.
pmc-12751676:
Francesca Conca and a large team mapped how the brain supports picture naming in people with brain disease that gets worse over time. Their 2025 study had 178 patients in the frontotemporal dementia group and the Alzheimer's disease group. Each patient took an Italian picture naming test and had an FDG-PET brain scan. The team cut ten word traits, such as word length and how often a word is used, down to four groups. They linked naming scores to brain use in eleven zones on the left side of the brain.

Short, plain word forms went with better naming. One brain zone, the fusiform gyrus, backed both the look and the sense of the pictures. Front and side zones linked word sense and word sound. The two disease groups used distinct zones for the same traits. That hints each disease finds its own way to make up for loss.
pmc-12751976:
Xue Zhong and co-authors mine health records for conditions that precede Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 study. Some conditions are known to raise risk, but a systematic scan had not been done. The team used two huge record databases, covering 153 million people, and tracked the ten years before diagnosis.

They found over forty-four thousand cases matched against hundreds of thousands of controls. Hundreds of conditions appeared more often in future patients, led by mental and nerve disorders. More than seventy conditions repeated in both databases, including depression, sleep disorders, artery hardening in the brain, and type two diabetes. Nineteen of them tied to known genetic risk signals for the disease. The authors see chances for early action in the list.
pmc-12752176:
Mohamed Ismail and co-authors pool studies on an eye disease of early babies in sub-Saharan Africa, in a 2025 review. The disease can blind preterm infants, and better newborn care means more such babies now survive in the region. Yet local data on how common it is were patchy and disputed.

Twelve studies from nine countries, covering more than eleven thousand infants, met the bar. About twenty-two percent of at-risk babies had the disease, with rates from under six percent in Uganda to forty-seven percent in Nigeria. Low birth weight, young gestational age, oxygen use, and infection raised risk, while breast feeding seemed to protect. The authors urge fast screening programs.
pmc-12752876:
Beyyumi and co-authors report in 2025 on child kidney transplants at one center in Abu Dhabi from 2010 to 2024. Transplant is the best care for end stage kidney disease. The study covers 69 children aged 1 to 16, with 36 grafts from living kin donors and 33 from deceased donors.

Mean age at transplant was near ten years. Birth defects of kidney and urinary tract were the top cause of failure. Most children had dialysis first, while 13 had a graft before dialysis. Rejection hit 45 percent of children, most in the first year. Donor antibodies were a strong sign of rejection risk, which guides closer watch for those children.
pmc-12752976:
Jing Lin and four co-authors ran a trial on pain relief after womb surgery in a 2025 paper. Deep internal pain after keyhole removal of the womb remains hard to control. A neck nerve block, guided by ultrasound, is used for other pain but was little tested for this kind. The team split ninety patients into three groups.

One group got both blocks, one got a belly wall block alone, and one got no block. The combined group reported much lower deep pain in the first hours and needed rescue pain drugs far less often. Cut pain did not differ between groups. The authors back the neck block as an addition to standard pain plans.
pmc-12753176:
Heitor Teixeira Alves Carvalho and co-authors report a 2025 study of wrist surgery at a public hospital. The work looks at breaks of the far end of the radius bone, fixed with a locked plate on the palm side. The team asked how often the bone loses height after that fix.

Charts and scans for 65 wrists treated from 2020 to 2024 were checked for change over time. The mid loss was small, at 0.60 mm, yet 13.8% of cases lost more than 2 mm. Most cases lost less, and sex did not shift the rate. Loss was worse in older patients with hard breaks, though the plate still held the bone well in most cases.
pmc-12753476:
Megan Wolfe and co-authors compare glucose in spinal fluid with glucose in blood, in healthy dogs and dogs with brain and cord disease. Spinal fluid glucose is easy to measure and might track inflamed disease of the central nervous system. The team used the ratio of fluid glucose to blood glucose. Records came from one hospital.

The study held 41 healthy dogs and 359 with nervous system disease. In healthy dogs, fluid glucose averaged 78.4 milligrams per deciliter and the ratio 0.80. In healthy dogs the ratio rose with age. Dogs with non-inflamed structural disease had higher fluid glucose than healthy dogs, near 87.8, but a like ratio. Dogs with epilepsy had a like ratio too. Dogs with inflamed disease had a mean ratio of 0.70, significantly lower. A cheap fluid test will not name a disease, but a low ratio adds a clue for inflammation.
pmc-12753576:
Liou Zhang and co-authors trace a protein that helps liver cancer resist a standard treatment in a 2025 study. The treatment threads chemotherapy into the tumor's blood supply, but many tumors stop responding. The protein SERPINA1 was known to be off balance in cancers, yet its role here was unclear.

Blood levels of the protein rose after treatment in patients who did poorly. In cells starved of oxygen or dosed with drugs, the protein sped growth, movement, and invasion, and animal tumors backed its role. It works by gripping a partner protein and shielding it from a tagging enzyme that would mark it for destruction. Blocking that grip is a proposed target.
pmc-12753776:
Jui-Chi Lin and co-authors grow two-metal framework crystals on a liquid metal surface, in work from 2025. Framework crystals are porous lattices prized for catalysis, sensing, and light devices. Mixing two metals widens their tricks, but classic cooking is slow and hot, and electric methods use solid posts that passivate.

A fluid gallium alloy post solves the sticking problem, since its skin heals itself. Electric pull and surface flow spread the first metal evenly as it leaves the liquid. It then builds the lattice with a second metal from the bath. At a mild voltage, the sheets came out crisp and evenly mixed. A baked version showed promise as an oxide.
pmc-12753876:
Souleïmen Jmii and co-authors map in 2025 where a light sensing protein grips the heat response switches of plants, to guide future engineering. Heat stress costs crops growth and yield. When heat hits, switch proteins rush to protect the cell's proteins, and the light sensor helps move them into the nucleus.

The team joined computer structure predictions with lab tests that detect binding between proteins. They confirm the sensor's main domain grips many of the switches across a shared region. That shared grip makes the interface a platform: mutants can be designed or selected to tune the heat response. Stronger heat tolerance bred this way could protect harvests in a warming climate.
pmc-12753976:
Lingang Xu and four co-authors build a machine learning model to forecast how well stem cell care will work in plastic surgery. The care shows promise, but results vary a lot by person and no trusty forecast tool exists. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Records of hundreds of patients treated over three years were split into training and test sets. The team screened traits by single factor checks, then by joined models and a shrink method that picks key traits. Three learning models were built and checked on the held back set. About three in five patients in both sets had good outcomes, which sets the base the models must beat.
pmc-12754176:
Hai-fei Zhou and colleagues find a way to grade stomach cancer from scans alone, without a blood draw, in this study from twenty twenty-five. Doctors can estimate how much of a tumor is fluid space outside cells, a clue to how nasty the cancer is. The standard method needs the patient's blood count from a lab sample, which is not always on hand at scan time.

The team used one group of patients to build formulas that infer the blood value from plain CT images of two large vessels. In a second group with stomach cancer and dual-energy CT scans, the inferred values matched the lab-based ones closely. Both versions sorted tumors by their grade under the microscope about equally well. The authors say the scan-only method can stand in when blood results are missing, keeping the grade clue available for care planning.
pmc-12754776:
Rongxin Zhang and Jean-Louis Mergny study folded DNA shapes near gene switches in a 2025 paper. The shapes are called G-quadruplexes, where DNA folds into a stacked, four-strand knot. A gene can have more than one promoter, or start switch. Which switch a cell picks shapes the mix of message copies it makes. Whether these knots sway that pick was the open question.

The team joined two data types from two cancer cell lines. One mapped fresh messages and their starts, the other mapped where the knots sit. They found 573 switches whose use changed a lot between lines. About a quarter sat near a knot, and knot-linked switches mostly grew more active. Drugs that steady the knots sparked fresh switch use, the team reports.
pmc-12754876:
Elif Varli Tekingur and Gul Yildiz Telatar published a research paper in 2025 on a Turkish version of a questionnaire that asks dental patients how they perceive oral illness. Tooth decay is widespread, and care plans work better when staff grasp how patients see their condition. No checked Turkish version of the oral-health form existed.

Over four hundred adults with tooth decay at a university dental clinic filled out the translated form. Statistical checks trimmed six weak items, leaving thirty items across seven themes that hung together well. Repeat and split checks supported the form's steadiness. The authors judge the Turkish version fit for use in clinics and studies.
pmc-12754976:
