Sarper İçen and Arif Hüdai Köken explore in 2025 how AI chat models guide clinicians who face hard ethical choices in child and teen psychiatry. Such choices are complex: young patients are vulnerable, their say grows with age, and duties to the patient, the family, and the law can pull apart. Cases about secrecy, parental rights, and forced reporting are among the hardest.

Most past study of AI ethics help comes from Western settings. This study sits in Türkiye and uses a qualitative method. It asks how several large language models handle ethical, legal, and emotional sides of set cases. Their answers are weighed for soundness and fit to local law and culture. The work helps judge whether such tools are ready to sit beside clinicians in tough calls, and where they fall short.
pmc-12756476:
Xinyuan Han, Zhijun Huang, Jing Ning, and Wenhui Shang published this case report in 2025. It describes a 47-year-old man with high blood pressure who fell into a coma from bleeding inside his brainstem. Scans showed a bleed of 10.3 milliliters, a size that usually ends in death. The report follows the mix of treatments the hospital team used over the following weeks.

Doctors drained the pooled blood through a small guided puncture and opened a breathing tube in his neck. Care also covered drugs to stop bleeding, steps to lower pressure inside the skull, and treatment for repeated infections by drug-resistant bacteria. After two months the man woke up and regained some limb strength, though speech and swallowing stayed impaired. The authors present the case as a sign that combined care can save some patients, while noting that one case cannot prove the approach.
pmc-12757176:
Indra Maulana, Iwan Shalahuddin, Theresia Eriyani, and Sandra Pebrianti mapped what kinds of support help health workers protect their own mental health. Their 2025 scoping review starts from a known risk: nurses, doctors, and aides face high rates of stress, worry, low mood, and burnout, worse since the pandemic. The team searched five databases for studies from 2000 to 2025 and kept only trials that passed a strict quality check.

Fifteen trials made the cut. Six tested calm-focus training such as meditation. Five used phone apps or online therapy. Four used coaching or computer-aided training in bouncing back. Calm-focus work cut stress and worry by up to thirty percent. App-based help aided sleep and eased burnout. Coaching lifted engagement and cut exhaustion. The authors call for trials in poorer settings next.
pmc-12757276:
Jared Hobson, Allison E. Garda, Jonathan Ticku, and Abigail Stockham report a full response in a rare ovarian cancer under a novel drug mix in 2025. This cancer type shrugs off standard chemo and carries a poor outlook. The patient reached two targeted drugs plus a shaped radiation method. Access took fights with cost and system blocks along the way.

Lab checks after care showed no live cancer. The case adds proof for the novel mix in this cancer. It also spotlights money strain and uneven access in cancer care. Trial rules and drug spread come under fire. The authors ask how new cures can reach patients fairly. Chronic style care for cancer frames their plea.
pmc-12766476: Ryan Buckner and a large team of co-authors report in a 2025 paper the genome of a virus that infects soil bacteria. The virus, named IsHungry, was isolated on a strain of Arthrobacter globiformis and has the long tailed shape typical of its group. Its genome spans 40,628 base pairs and holds 61 likely genes plus three transfer RNA genes. All but four genes point the same way for reading, a pattern that matches its cluster of kin viruses.
pmc-12766576:
Jens Bager Christensen and co-authors published this developmental neuroscience study in 2025. The cerebellum, the brain's coordination center, builds its inhibitory neurons late in development from a pool of stem-like progenitors. How those progenitors choose the inhibitory path was unclear. Using single-cell RNA sequencing in newborn mice, the team traced the progenitors' trajectories and found a two-step relay of gene regulators.

One factor, ASCL1, starts the program, then hands over to a second factor, FOXO1, which drives the final differentiation. A signaling pathway called WNT pushes cells from the first state into the second. Both factors also run separate side jobs in cell division and survival. The same WNT-to-FOXO1 relay promoted neuron production in human progenitor cultures. The authors say the conserved program may matter for disorders where these neurons are overproduced.
pmc-12766776:
Siri Schøyen Seterelv and six colleagues ask why trusted global treatment guidelines often stall on the way into local practice, in a 2025 study. Their case is a rapid recommendation series from a major medical journal.

Citation tracking and a survey found thirty-three uses across rich and poor countries alike. Twelve users were interviewed in depth, surfacing fourteen obstacles grouped under trust, clarity, and practical fit. Formal appraisals scored the guidelines high on validity but low on ease of use and measurability, echoing the interviews. Tensions emerged between rigor and credibility, and between novelty and fitting current practice. The authors say naming these tensions early could improve guideline uptake.
pmc-12767376:
Researchers build in 2025 a tool to flag brain-ill patients in intensive care who face high risk of dangerous blood clots. Clots in veins pose a grave threat in brain units, yet few risk tools fit those patients well. A tailored score could guide preventive care.

Charts of 605 patients from 2022 to 2024 feed the work, split into training and test sets. Eight factors enter the final model, among them age, unit stay length, clot blood tests, and lung infection. A chart form of the model sorts high from low risk with fair strength. Checks suggest the score could help teams target clot prevention where it counts most.
pmc-12767576:
Yirgalem Melkamu and co-authors document local knowledge of fodder trees and shrubs in the dry Metema District of northwestern Ethiopia. Livestock raising is the main livelihood there, and wild trees and shrubs form a major share of animal feed. Yet this plant knowledge was poorly recorded.

The team surveyed three hundred eighty-five informants across eight villages through interviews, field walks, and group talks. They recorded forty-six fodder species, with the pea family richest. Goats, the most kept animals, browsed every species listed. Leaves were the part used most, and one species topped both citation and preference ranks. Skilled informants knew significantly more species than general ones.
pmc-12768676:
Aline Toledo and co-authors price the first ward year of pre-term babes in Brazil, in a study from 2025. Born-early babes drive three in four new-born ills, and their care bills run past the birth ward. The team asks which traits of the babe and birth drive those bills.

Birth and ward banks were linked for near two hundred thousand such babes born from 2017 to 2022. Each week of growth in the womb cut the bill, the math shows, while low first-breath scores and birth kind each swayed it. The view is the state's: what the public purse pays. Maps of cost by trait, the team says, can steer funds to the wards and weeks where a real buys the most health.
pmc-12768776:
Adson José Moreira and co-authors wrote a 2025 study on the budget effects of a new HIV drug plan in Brazil. The standard first treatment pairs three drugs, made in Brazil through a public production partnership. That partnership also builds national industry skill, so any switch has stakes beyond price.

A review body weighed a rival three-drug pill and asked what its uptake would do to budgets and to the partnership. Data came from the 2022 national HIV monitoring report, which set the pool of patients. Prices came from a health price database and the review report. The model assumed the new pill would gain ten percent of the market each year, reaching half by year five. The study tests whether the new plan stays sound for both care and industry.
pmc-12772176:
Nichol and co-authors study seed pods that refuse to open in a 2025 plant paper. Plants in the mustard family fling seeds when dry pods split, a trait breeders bred out of crops like canola. Shattering at harvest still costs growers a large share of yield in bad years. The team traced how one gene, switched on by the hormone ABA, controls the woody layers that let pods spring apart.

The gene works through two partner factors that drive production of lignin, the stiff plant polymer. Pods failed to open at both extremes: too much woody tissue and none at all. Only a middle band of lignin let drying forces build and release as planned. The result names a Goldilocks zone that breeders can aim for when they want pods that hold seeds until harvest.
pmc-12775376:
Philipp Wanner and co-authors test whether a bout of cycling after practice helps people with Parkinson's disease learn a balance skill, in work from 2025. Motor learning is blunted in Parkinson's, yet exercise near practice is known to prime the brain for plasticity.

Twenty-four patients practiced a new balance task over six sessions, then either cycled at moderate intensity or sat resting. The exercise group learned significantly more, with the gap clearest in the fourth and fifth sessions. Gains seemed to grow during practice itself rather than between sessions. Fitter participants benefited most, in exploratory analysis. The authors pitch post-practice exercise as a cheap addition to rehabilitation, deserving a larger trial.
pmc-12780176:
Ana Raquel Cruz and co-authors wrote a study from 2025 on gut bacteria that cling to the bowel wall and help train the immune system. The bacteria grow first as single teardrop cells, then stretch into long threads. The tip of the young cell is the part that grips the gut wall. The team froze the bacteria and viewed them with a fine electron scope to see that grip up close.

Young cells wear a neat, tiled coat. At the tip, it gives way to a messy fringe of hairs. As the cell grows into a thread, a new hair-like coat takes over. The same switch showed up in bacteria from mice and rats. One key protein sits all over the wall but can be reached by immune cells only at the tip.
pmc-12780276:
Amirhosein Maharati and eight co-authors hunt, in 2025 work, for early signs of bowel cancer in gene activity. The cancer kills many people each year, in part because it is often found late. The team mixed large public data sets with lab tests on paired tissue samples.

Three lead marks stood out: a cell growth gene, a long non-coding RNA, and two small RNAs. One long RNA split tumour from normal tissue with great force, beating a blood mark now in use. Some marks also tracked with tumour size, spread to nodes, or poor response to a drug plan. None of the marks tracked with how long patients lived. The team presents them as tools for early spotting, not for judging outcome.
pmc-12780376:
Li and a large team build in twenty twenty-five a scan-based model to spot hidden air trapping in lungs that standard breathing tests miss. Trapped air signals small-airway trouble, defined here by an inflated leftover air volume. In a single-centre group of several dozen adults, each person had low-dose scans at full inhale and exhale plus breathing tests within a week.

About a third met the trapping definition. Their scans showed distinct density ratios and more very-low-density lung area than the rest. A model built on scan measures sorted the groups well in training and fairly in internal checks, led by three measures. The authors say paired-phase scans could aid early risk sorting and follow-up.
pmc-12781576:
Lishen Liu and co-authors pooled twenty trials to check whether the blockbuster drug tirzepatide harms heart or kidneys, in a 2025 meta-analysis. The trials covered 15,905 people with type 2 diabetes or obesity, against placebo or other treatments. Heart attacks, strokes, heart failure, kidney impairment, stones, and infections all counted as adverse events.

No significant link appeared either way: the heart event ratio sat at 0.83 and the kidney ratio at 1.22, both with wide intervals crossing safety. Subgroups by disease, dose, and comparator told the same story. Within trial horizons, the drug's powerful benefits arrive without a proven organ penalty, the authors conclude.
pmc-12783076:
Kim Yao Ong and co-authors report a single skin case in this 2025 letter. A man aged forty-eight had annular pustular psoriasis, a rare form of the disease that spreads in rings edged with small sterile blisters. His rash began under one arm and spread over four months, settling in body folds and around the elbows and knees.

Creams for fungus did nothing, and steroid pills helped only until the dose dropped. A skin sample confirmed the diagnosis, so the team started risankizumab, a drug that blocks a key inflammation signal, plus strong steroid creams. Peeling began within two days, the skin looked far better within a month, and it was fully clear at fifteen weeks. The authors note this drug is seldom reported as the first main treatment for this condition.
pmc-12783176:
Guoshan Li and six colleagues engineer a nerve repair tube loaded with a drug and stem cells, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. Peripheral nerve injuries after fractures often heal incompletely. A guidance conduit that also delivers therapy could close the gap.

The scaffold electrospins polycaprolactone with collagen into a tube. Inside sits a collagen gel carrying vinpocetine nanoparticles and menstrual blood-derived stem cells. Laboratory tests checked structure, mechanics, cell survival, and blood compatibility. Rats with severed sciatic nerves then tested real recovery. Motor and sensory function, muscle preservation, and axon regrowth were measured. The menstrual blood cells are an accessible, ethically simple stem cell source. The design stacks several healing aids into one implant.
pmc-12784276:
Silas Furquim and co-authors review how a failing heart can partly heal, and how doctors should treat a heart that looks healed, in a 2025 paper. The healing, reverse remodelling, shrinks the stretched heart and restores its squeeze. It is not one thing: a heart may improve for a spell, rest in remission on its drugs, or truly recover. Drugs and devices can each coax the turn in the right patients.

Scans, tissue signs, and blood marks sort who is likely to heal and who may relapse. The open fight is over the group whose pumping score has climbed: pull the drugs back, or hold the line? Stopping all therapy invites high relapse, yet careful partial cuts look safe for select profiles. The authors make reverse remodelling a central goal of care, with follow-up tuned to each heart's depth of healing.
pmc-12784676:
Cancer low in the rectum can spread to lymph nodes along the pelvic sidewall, and East and West have long disagreed about what to do. Dai Shida reviews the divide in a 2025 paper. Japanese guidelines treat those nodes as regional disease to be cut out. Western practice long treated them as body-wide disease, favoring drug and radiation therapy before surgery without the extra clearance.

Trial evidence has since shown the dissection sharply cuts local relapse, especially with enlarged nodes, and 2025 European guidelines now endorse selective removal after drug treatment. Robot surgery suits the hard-to-reach area, with steady 3D vision and wristed tools across four defined tissue planes. Shida frames robotic dissection as a meeting point of Eastern surgical craft and Western combined therapy.
pmc-12784876:
Aleksandra Studzińska and co-authors show that a mere fragment of an antibody can fight a dog's lymphoma as well as the whole molecule. The target is a surface marker found in excess on canine diffuse large B-cell lymphoma cells. Earlier work showed full antibodies against it kill the cells; what was unclear is whether the killing needs the antibody's tail, which recruits immune help, or just its grip. The team tested the full antibody and two fragment forms on lymphoma cell lines and in mice carrying the tumours.

Even the smallest fragment, a single-armed Fab piece, killed cells in the dish and slowed tumours in mice. Treated mice went about 19 days before the disease progressed, against under 10 days for controls, matching the full antibody's 19.5 days. The authors conclude the fragments kill directly, without calling in the immune system.
pmc-12785276:
Murat Uztimür and co-authors ask whether a gut virus in calves also harms the lungs and liver. Their 2025 study deals with rotavirus, a common cause of diarrhea in newborn calves. In human care the virus is known to reach past the gut, but in animal care its wider effects are less clear.

The team studied 52 young Simmental calves: 40 sick with the virus and 12 healthy. Some sick calves died and were examined after death, while blood tests tracked a set of markers tied to cell stress, cell death, and organ strain. Tissue checks confirmed harm in both the lungs and the liver of sick calves. The results argue that the damage in calves is not confined to the gut.
pmc-12785576:
Longer fibres make poplar wood worth more, but the gene switches that set fibre length are little known. Guhang Shi and four co-authors track one such switch pair in a Chinese poplar in 2025. A tiny RNA holds down a gene that helps steer early wood growth.

The team first mapped the tiny RNA's whole family and found its members split in role. Link tests tie the pair to fibre length. A glow test in cells, gene counts, and deep reads of both genes and their decay all point one way: the tiny RNA reins the gene in. That gene, in turn, steers genes that build cellulose, the fibre's frame. The pair is a fresh target for breeders who select trees by gene marks.
pmc-12785676:
Xinzhu Cai, Wanfu Hou, and their co-authors compared six varieties of white radish for texture, taste, and flavor. Their 2025 study notes that a full picture of how varieties differ was missing. Such knowledge helps growers and food makers pick the right variety for each use, from pickling to fresh eating.

One variety led on hardness and chewiness, while another was the most brittle. The sweetest variety carried the most total sugar. Two varieties stood out for savory and bitter notes. Chemical analysis found 43 volatile compounds in all, and one variety was richest in the sulfur compounds behind radish bite. Two named compounds were identified as the key flavor substances. The team tied the sensory traits to cell wall, amino acid, and volatile chemistry.
pmc-12785776:
Małgorzata Dylewska and co-authors study a DNA lesion left by acrolein, a pollutant also made inside stressed cells. Their 2025 study looks at the mark acrolein leaves on cytosine, one of the four DNA letters. Such marks can cause mutations if the cell's repair crews miss them.

In tests, the mark mostly turned a C into an A when the DNA was copied. One repair enzyme, AlkB, cleared the mark well even without a stress alarm. A second enzyme, AlkA, could not cut it out, though it handles a sister mark on another letter. Models of the enzyme pocket explain the split. The bond in the cytosine mark is far harder to break with water.
pmc-12786576:
Mostafa Sadeghian and three colleagues review how pairing machine learning with image-based strain tracking improves damage detection in materials, in a 2025 paper. Engineers watch cracks form under load, but manual reading of the images is slow and error-prone.

Digital image correlation maps how a surface deforms frame by frame. Machine learning layers on top can flag damage automatically and nearly in real time. The review compares classic learning models with deep networks across composites, metals, and other materials. It weighs open challenges, from data needs to complex loading, and sketches future directions. The authors conclude the pairing beats either method alone on accuracy, speed, and reliability.
pmc-12786676:
Deepinder Kalra and co-authors use NMR scans to learn what form nickel and copper ions take inside a common cell culture fluid. Their 2025 study cares because the ions' chemical dress, called speciation, decides how cells take them up and whether they help or harm. Both metals are needed in traces as enzyme helpers, yet both turn toxic in excess.

The fluid, a standard growth medium, is full of biomolecules eager to bind metals. Proton NMR, a gentle method that leaves the sample intact, watched those bindings form. The work grounds later toxicity claims in the actual chemistry cells meet, rather than in the dose printed on the bottle.
pmc-12787076:
Yang Hou and co-authors crush-test printed titanium lattice blocks in a 2025 study. The blocks use a gyroid pattern, a smooth, repeating curved surface that packs strength into little weight. Such porous metals suit aircraft and medical implants, where light weight and load bearing must coexist.

Samples with varied openness were printed by laser melting and then tested by pressing, simulation, and theory. Strength barely cared about loading speed but depended strongly on how much solid the block held. Damage patterns mixed ductile tearing with brittle snaps. Simulations traced how damage grows and how the blocks soak up energy. The team also tied the flat stress plateau during crushing to the solid share, which aids design.
pmc-12787176:
Dariusz Lesniak, Konrad Laber, and Jacek Madura study how tubes of a strong aluminium alloy are formed by extrusion. The alloy, grade 7075, resists shaping and rubs hard against the press tools. In practice the force needed nears the limit of the press, and cracks can form on the tube surface.

The team tests three math models for how the metal stress changes with heat and speed of shaping. They fit the models to lab test data and run computer simulations of tube extrusion at two billet heat levels. They then check the simulation results against real press trials. The best fit model helps engineers pick heat and speed settings that cut force and reduce cracks.
pmc-12787376:
Dimitra Apostolidou and co-authors combine lab measures and simulations to judge heat treated 3D printed plastic without cutting it open in a 2025 study. The printed polymer, PLA, changes stiffness as it is heated. Sound speed tests, both along and across the material, gave elastic constants and related values.

Two simulation routes were checked against the lab data, and a circuit based method matched far better than a wave based one. Both data sets showed chains packing tighter and stiffening up to two hours of heating. Longer heating brought clear decay. Spectra of light absorption backed the same story, and one ratio stayed steady throughout.
pmc-12787476:
Jie Zhang, Yingguang Zhou, and Naixia Lv use computer models to tune single-atom catalysts, in a 2025 study. Such catalysts park lone metal atoms on a support sheet, which wastes no metal and can speed chemical reactions. Their sheet is boron nitride, and they test what happens when carbon atoms are mixed into it.

The models place silver or gold atoms on plain and carbon-mixed sheets, then check how well each grabs oxygen. One form of oxygen bound in a way that stretched its bond more, a sign of stronger activation. Sheets with four carbon atoms per patch worked best, lifting the energy of the metal's outer electrons so they pass more charge to oxygen. The results give designers a recipe for stronger catalysts built on this sheet.
pmc-12787776:
Tarik Akan and co-authors teach machine learning models to predict how a magnetic alloy film behaves at high heat, in a 2025 study. The film is a thin layer of nickel-iron alloy, the kind used in sensors, and the team measured its resistance under magnetic fields from room warmth up to three hundred fifty degrees. Beyond that range, direct measurement gets hard.

Several learning models trained on the lab data then forecast resistance at still higher temperatures. The best model matched held-back measurements closely and even let the team estimate the alloy's Curie point, where magnetism fades. Reliable forecasts past the lab limit help engineers design sensors and devices for hot settings, from engines to industrial plants, without destroying samples in extreme tests.
pmc-12788076:
Haichuan Li and co-authors test a probiotic strain in ageing mice in a 2025 study. The strain, a type of Lactobacillus, was studied for whether it can ease oxidative stress, a form of cell damage that grows with age. A sugar compound was used to induce ageing like changes in the mice.

Fifty mice were split into control, model, vitamin, and low and high dose probiotic groups. Treatment lasted eight weeks. Samples from blood, liver, colon, and stool were then checked. The probiotic curbed tissue shrinkage and inflammation signals, and helped restore gut microbe balance, the authors report.
pmc-12788476:
Urmila Keshari and co-authors compare three bedside tests for spotting a hard airway before surgery, in a study published in 2025. Placing a breathing tube can turn dangerous when the airway is unexpectedly hard to reach. Doctors use quick checks of the mouth and neck to warn of trouble, but the checks vary in accuracy.

The team tested 150 adults set for planned surgery under full anesthesia. One doctor ran all three checks: a mouth-opening score, an upper lip bite test, and a neck distance measure. The view seen during the procedure served as the standard. Twenty patients proved hard to tube. The lip bite test caught the most cases while keeping false alarms low, beating both rivals. The authors recommend it as the best single bedside screen.
pmc-12788576:
Mohammed Rashid and colleagues measured jaw bone density during orthodontic treatment sped up with low-level laser light. Laser treatment can move teeth faster, but its effect on the dense outer bone of the lower jaw was unclear. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team ran a randomized study of adult patients with fixed braces. Half received laser sessions on alternating days during the first month, aimed at the lower jaw bone. Three-dimensional scans at the start and after twelve weeks gave density readings near a molar and a canine tooth.

The laser group lost clear density at both sites by twelve weeks, while the control group barely changed. Lower density fits the idea that light loosens bone so teeth can shift sooner. The authors present the finding as support for laser-assisted treatment, within the short window their scans covered.
pmc-12791176:
Nilesh V Joshi and six colleagues review what happens when dental implants sit very close to natural tooth roots, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Spacing between implants and neighboring teeth guards gum health and prevents iatrogenic harm. The team searched seven databases under standard review guidelines. Eleven studies covering over two thousand implants qualified.

Pulp and root-tip disease were the commonest harms reported. In proximity-contact cases, a fifth to a quarter of affected teeth needed root canal treatment. Bone loss and implant gum disease appeared in up to four percent of very close placements. Cavities and structural defects were reported less consistently, mostly in back teeth. The pooled risk was low yet clinically relevant. Implant survival still exceeded ninety-five percent overall. Evidence certainty was moderate for some outcomes and low for others.
pmc-12797676:
Hlulani Nghayo, Khabiso Ramphoma, and Ronel Maart ask rural South Africans how they see mouth health. Mouth disease hits rural areas hard, since clinics are far and health drives rarely reach them. The team held five group talks with 50 people from five rural villages in Limpopo province. Talks were taped, typed out, and coded for shared themes with no set list in advance.

Three themes led the talks. Blocks to care, such as distance and cost, came first. Weak spread of mouth health advice came next, since few drives reach these villages. Last came home factors, such as daily habits and beliefs about teeth. The team urges that mouth care join main health policy and that staff posts be shared more fairly. Local voice, they argue, must shape the fix.
pmc-12800176:
L. Szelerski and colleagues compared surgical techniques for healing upper arm bone breaks that had failed to knit, using an external frame method named for Ilizarov. The frame slowly adjusts bone position while new bone forms. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the Warsaw team reviewed about a score of patients treated over more than a decade for post-injury nonunion of the humerus. Records before and after surgery included X-ray classifications and validated shoulder function questionnaires, plus standard scoring systems for bone and function.

About nine in ten patients achieved bone union that held over a year of follow-up. Shoulder scores improved by large margins on every scale used. The most common problem was infection around the frame wires. The authors recommend the frame especially when nonunion comes with deformity or shortening, and favor a closed approach for chronic cases at risk of wound trouble.
pmc-12801476:
Mannose, a sugar used in food and health products, is usually made by reshaping other sugars rather than by brewing it with microbes. Sijia Zhao and co-authors change that in a 2025 study, rewiring a sturdy yeast long used as a factory for proteins. They feed it two fuels: one to grow the yeast, one to turn into the sugar.

Key valves in the yeast's sugar pathways were cut, pinched, or boosted to pool a mid-step compound. Genes for two side products were removed to stop waste. A borrowed gene from a gut bacterium finished the path to free mannose. In large fed tanks the strain poured out more of the sugar than any microbe brew before it. The team frames the design as a template for brewing other rare sugars.
pmc-12801576:
Wan, Hamid, and Krishna study mental health and identity growth among medical students in Singapore, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Becoming a doctor shapes values and self-image, but the strain can harm mental health. Local non-Western evidence on that clash was scarce. The team interviews students on a cancer care posting.

Ten students share their experiences in deep interviews. Stress comes from exams, clinic work, extra activities, and relationships. Those clashes test students' inner compass, meaning their core belief system. Students with a mature compass and strong support cope in healthy ways. Those without support fall into harmful coping and deeper strain. The team urges long-term, personal support over brief fixes.
pmc-12802776:
Aravind Nehrujee and nine co-authors test whether stroke survivors in India can train at home with a hand robot. Robot-assisted therapy can rebuild hand movement after stroke, but home use is little studied, above all in poorer countries. Their pilot study used PLUTO, a robot built for hand training, in patients' own homes.

Seven chronic stroke survivors were recruited, and five completed the program. Engagement was high: participants trained for about 1,660 minutes over roughly 25 days on average. They rated the device easy to use and viewed it warmly. Hand and arm function scores rose by more than the smallest change that matters in practice, and daily-living scores improved as well. The authors call home robot training feasible and promising for widening access to rehabilitation, while calling for larger controlled trials.
pmc-12803876:
Taisuke Yoshinaga and co-authors report a rare cause of leg nerve squeeze in a case study from 2025. The patient was a woman aged 54 years with numbness and weakness in her left lower leg for six years. The nerve at fault, the common peroneal nerve, usually gets squeezed near the knee by bands or muscle sheets.

Standard care did not help her, so the team operated. Surgery showed a vein passing through the nerve and pressing on it. The surgeons sealed and cut the vein, which freed the nerve. Her symptoms cleared after the operation. The report warns surgeons to count veins among the possible causes of this nerve problem.
pmc-12804676:
Dyes that glow for a long time after excitation let microscopes sort cell parts by glow length, and new members of one dye family widen that trick. Carmen Viedma-Barba and co-authors cook the dyes faster with microwaves, in a 2025 study. Two dye branches were made in several forms and their light traits measured in full. Solvent effects on color were traced with computer chemistry help.

One branch gathered in cell power plants, where its glow shortened sharply. The other lit up cell nuclei and ride-along pockets. Those glow-length contrasts split cell compartments cleanly in lifetime imaging. Super-resolution views were also taken. The authors pitch the dyes for mapping cell interiors by lifetime.
pmc-12805776:
Linghui Kong and co-authors published this questionnaire study in 2025. Older patients with chronic musculoskeletal pain often move less, and pain and exercise behavior feed on each other. A questionnaire called BioPMovQ was designed to measure that relationship from a biological and behavioral angle. The team translated it into Chinese using standard translation principles. They then tested it on 526 elderly pain patients at a large hospital in Shanxi Province.

The final Chinese version kept sixteen items. Expert ratings of content quality were high. Factor analysis found four themes: disability, confidence for physical activity, movement avoidance, and self-perceived ability. Together they explained about sixty-nine percent of the variation in answers. Consistency and repeat-test scores were all solid, above 0.84. The authors conclude the translated scale is reliable and valid for studying how pain relates to movement behavior in this patient group.
pmc-12807976:
Anna Braspenning and seven colleagues interview users of a blended phone-based fatigue program for young patients, in a study from twenty twenty-five. The program, PROfeel, samples experiences by phone, then reviews them face to face. Fatigue in chronically ill youth responds to daily-life factors. No such blended program had yet reached pediatric care.

Eleven patients, eleven close others, and twenty professionals were interviewed. Patients wanted improvement yet found the sampling burdensome. Three themes ran through their accounts. Families valued the insights the sampling produced. Support and ownership shaped how the program landed. The study maps what implementation must solve. Effort must be balanced against insight for young users.
pmc-12808376:
Shanshan Dong and co-authors report a case of dangerous bleeding during heart support in this article, published in 2025. A 49-year-old man with a weak, stretched heart waited for a transplant while a balloon pump helped his heart. An infection and unstable blood flow then set off a state where clots break down far too fast.

His blood tests showed very high levels of clot breakdown products, and blood kept oozing at the pump entry site. The team gave a drug that slows clot breakdown, aimed at the measured fault. Bleeding stopped and the blood values settled, with no harmful clots forming. The man stayed stable until his transplant. The authors urge teams to watch for this fault when pump patients get infections.
pmc-12808776:
Eyu E, Wending Liu, and Yuanzhe Li report a 2025 qualitative study of anxiety about asking questions among Chinese postgraduates in TESOL programs in the United Kingdom. Many such students hold back from posing questions in class, even with strong English, and past work has paid more mind to formal speaking tasks than to this daily act.

Small-group interviews with a set of students dug into the mind, culture, and setting sides of that anxiety. Their school past and cultural norms shape how risky a question feels. The study aims to fill gaps on how these forces act at the graduate level.
pmc-12809676:
Narsireddy Amreddy and co-authors build targeted vesicle carriers for lung cancer drugs in a 2025 study. Chemotherapy remains frontline care despite collateral toxicity. Off-target exposure limits how hard clinicians can dose. A carrier that homes to tumors could ease that tradeoff.

Natural cell vesicles were loaded with gold-bound cisplatin. The drug linkage releases faster in acidic conditions. A targeting protein on the surface seeks a receptor tumors overexpress. The finished carriers measured about one hundred forty nanometers. High-receptor cancer cells died far more readily. Low-receptor cells and plain carriers fared worse by design. Cell death and DNA damage rose in both cancer lines. Normal lung and kidney cells were largely spared. Free drug, by contrast, hurt the normal cells. The authors claim selective, enhanced tumor killing. Animal studies would be the next gate.
pmc-12809976:
Jianyu Pang and co-authors characterize worn-out killer cells inside hard-to-treat breast tumors, in a 2025 study. The cancer type lacks the three usual drug targets, so immune therapy matters yet often disappoints. Natural killer cells should attack tumors, but a tired subset gathers inside them instead. The team used single-cell gene reads to define these tumor-linked killer cells.

The tired cells showed weak killing power and strong stress signals across many cancers. In this breast cancer type, more of them meant worse patient outlook. A six-gene score built by machine learning measured their level and predicted survival well. Tumors with high scores gained little from immune checkpoint drugs. Screening by computer then found a dozen candidate drugs, including some already in clinics.
pmc-12810176:
Marshal Lucas, Annapurna Kannan, and Vignesh Kailasam systematically review whether jaw length predicts dental crowding across malocclusion types, in a two thousand twenty-five orthodontic meta-analysis. Crowding against skeletal base size is a daily treatment-planning question.

Seven databases were searched through April two thousand twenty-four; five studies qualified and two entered the meta-analysis, most at low bias risk. In class two malocclusion, patients with heavier lower crowding had mandibles about four millimeters shorter than lightly crowded peers. Crowding ran moderate to severe with short class two bases and minimal with the longer bases of class three. The authors frame jaw length as a diagnostic input for tailored orthodontic plans.
pmc-12811976:
Adibul Chowdhury and four co-authors report a liver illness that mimicked an autoimmune disease, in this twenty twenty-five case paper. A man in his early sixties with HIV had taken the same drug, efavirenz, for years with no trouble. New blood tests then showed raised liver enzymes, though he felt well.

Tests found immune markers and tissue signs that pointed to autoimmune hepatitis. Yet he lacked other traits of that disease, and his virus stayed controlled. A team of specialists judged the long-used drug the true cause and swapped it for another. The case warns that drug harm can arrive late and wear a good disguise.
pmc-12812576:
Jian-Peng Wang and co-authors report a study, published in 2025, on a group of immune cells inside stomach tumors and how they help cancer evade attack. These cells, tumor associated macrophages, shape the local immune scene. One subtype, marked by a lipid link, is the focus here, along with a signaling pair that may drive its effect.

The team mined single cell and bulk gene data from public sets to profile the tumor scene. They sorted macrophage subtypes, traced how the cells change over time, and modeled how they talk to other cells. A prediction model was built from the subtype's genes. Lab tests then checked one key gene's effect on a brake protein that tumors use to blunt immune attack. The work aims to give prognosis clues and fresh treatment targets for stomach cancer.
pmc-12813276:
A Chinese herbal formula called Huanglong Zhixiao is tested in asthmatic mice in a study by Yong-xia Chen and co-authors, published in 2025. The work asks whether the formula calms asthma by restoring balance among gut microbes and aiding immune function through the gut-lung link.

Female mice were split into three groups of fifteen: a healthy group, an asthma group, and a group given the formula each day before an asthma trigger. The team sequenced fecal samples to map gut microbes and checked lung and gut tissue for damage and for proteins that seal the gut wall. The design lets them test whether shifts in the gut track with less lung harm and a stronger gut barrier.
pmc-12815276:
Terenzio Cassina and co-authors tested the hearing of the orchestra at Milan's La Scala opera house in 2025. They asked whether a career inside loud music wears the ear the way factory noise does. Opera pits are loud by any standard measure.

Musicians' average hearing sat slightly below that of a healthy unexposed public, yet clear impairment was rare: under three percent in both ears. Four violinists showed loss in the left ear only, the ear nearer the instrument. The damage rate ran well below what the standard industrial noise model predicts for the same exposure. Ten year comparisons showed decline on par with plain aging. The authors judge the risk real but modest.
pmc-12815476:
Chaimae Bekhakh and co-authors present a rare chest tumor that hides behind common ones in a 2025 case paper. These cancers have lost a gene called SMARCB1, also named INI1, and the World Health Organization now lists them as their own entity. They grow fast, shrug off standard reads, and mimic other high-grade chest tumors under the microscope.

The report follows one tumor in the central chest, the mediastinum, through the full naming process. Shape study, a broad panel of stains, and proof of total gene loss had to agree before the label stuck. Look-alike cancers get a careful sorting in the discussion. Naming the entity early matters: it steers therapy and opens doors to trials aimed at cancers missing this same gene family. The authors call the group rare, aggressive, and overlooked.
pmc-12816576:
Shehla Yasmeen, Aaron DiFilippo, and Marius Orlowski explain a strange effect in copper-based memory devices: stopping a reset halfway makes them conduct better. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. The devices store data in a tiny metal filament whose shape sets the resistance.

The authors model the filament as it rebuilds under strong electric fields and intense local heating at its tip. Copper atoms drift and migrate, reshaping a cut cone into an hourglass with lower resistance. Their model matches the measured drop, up to about elevenfold for the weakest filaments. They also split the reset into two phases, strengthening then rupture. Slow voltage ramps give atoms time to move, which explains the timing effects seen in tests.
pmc-12817776:
Mingming Fan and co-authors showed surgery stress can spread liver tumors in two thousand twenty-five. Cutting blood flow then restoring it injures the liver. That injury is common in liver surgery and transplants. It has been linked to tumors returning as metastases. The team used mouse models of two cancer types. White blood cells and vessel walls were the focus.

Injury boosted spread to liver and beyond. A sticky vessel protein helped tumor cells latch on. A common statin drug blocked that protein's action. Removing the white cells also cut metastasis. Human patient data tied the protein to prognosis. Blocking the pathway may prevent recurrence after surgery. The work reframes a surgical side effect as treatable.
pmc-12819476:
J Alabbad and co-authors ask, in a 2025 cohort study, whether giving antibiotics after draining an anorectal abscess lowers the chance of a fistula forming later. Draining the abscess is the core treatment. Whether a week or more of antibiotics on top changes the fistula rate has stayed controversial.

The study reviewed every adult treated for this kind of abscess at one university hospital from 2011 to 2024. Records supplied demographics, clinical details, and culture results. In all, 770 patients entered the analysis, the segment shown begins. The main comparison was fistula formation within twelve months, between those who got the antibiotic course and those who did not. Secondary analyses hunted other factors tied to fistula risk. A fistula means another operation, so even a modest protective effect would change routine practice; a null result would spare many patients needless antibiotics.
pmc-12821176:
Plants ship tiny bubble-like parcels between cells, and those parcels carry microRNAs that may even speak to animal cells. Yang Xiao and co-authors build a better way to harvest the parcels from a tough source: the tuberous roots of a medicinal lily relative, Ophiopogon japonicus. The roots are dense and full of starchy contaminants that spoil standard preparations.

Their recipe pairs enzyme pre-treatment, which loosens the root's cell walls, with spinning steps refined beyond the usual protocol. A dense-liquid layer step with an early clearing pass removed debris best. The winning method gave more parcels and cleaner ones than the standard routes. Sequencing the parcels' small RNAs then profiled their cargo. The authors offer the pipeline to other hard plant tissues.
pmc-12821276:
Tianci Yao and a team of co-authors studied how changes in frailty link to new chronic disease, in two thousand twenty-five. Frailty is a state of weakness that grows with age. The team used a large Chinese study of adults aged forty-five and older, with frailty checked twice, two years apart.

Adults who moved from strong to weak faced higher risks of nearly all diseases studied. Adults who were weak and then grew stronger faced lower risks of about half of them. Heart disease, stroke, and memory disease all showed that kinder pattern. The findings suggest that frailty is not fixed, and that recovery may cut future disease risk.
pmc-12821876:
Shaoxi Pan and co-authors quantify the cost of polypharmacy in older adults in the United States in work from 2025. Polypharmacy means taking five or more medicines, and it raises the risk of adverse events.

Using a national survey from 2018 to 2021, the team matched about five thousand older adults with polypharmacy to a like group without it. Annual health spending averaged about fourteen thousand seven hundred dollars with polypharmacy versus about eight thousand nine hundred without. The gap covered drugs, office visits, and hospital stays. Polypharmacy also linked to a higher risk of skipping care for cost.
pmc-12822076:
Mohamed Rakab and ten co-authors pooled studies on when to pull chest drains after heart surgery, in a 2025 review. Nine studies covered over eight and a half thousand patients. Day one removal was compared with day two. Fluid around the heart was the main worry with early pulls. Hospital stay and death rates were tracked as well.

Early removal raised the risk of fluid around the heart. Fluid around the lungs trended the same way. Patients still left hospital about a day sooner. Intensive care time did not differ meaningfully. Deaths, infections, and rhythm problems matched between groups. The authors deem early removal broadly safe. They advise risk-based selection and watchful follow-up after pulling. Effusion checks should be routine in early-removal pathways.
pmc-12822176:
Flu and pneumonia fill wards each winter, and dirty air plus cold may fill the bill as well as the beds. Huanhuan Jia and six co-authors price that weather-and-air share in 2025, in Changchun, a cold factory city of China. Ward records from 2017 to 2020 meet daily air and weather logs.

Among 162,621 breath-related stays, flu and pneumonia made 75,113, near half, and drew 990 million yuan in costs. Flexible curve models, with lagged effects spread over days, tie each pollutant and the cold to the daily bill. A priced share of the burden can be argued over in budgets, not just in clinics. Cold cities carry a double load; the study sizes it.
pmc-12822276:
Safoura Ghodsi and co-authors compare two ways to fix crowns on dental implants in a study from 2025. One method holds the crown with a screw alone. The other, called dual-retained, adds cement to the screw. Fit, screw tightness, and strength all matter for long implant life.

Twenty metal-ceramic crowns were split into two groups of ten. One group sat on ready-made titanium posts, the other on cast posts. The team checked fit and torque loss before and after heat and chewing cycles. Half a million load cycles mimicked long use in the mouth. Fracture tests then showed how each design breaks. Dentists can use the results when they choose a fixing method.
pmc-12823576:
Laura Gómez-Consarnau and nine co-authors track a light-eating pigment in rich coastal waters in a 2025 study. Ocean microbes with rhodopsin, a pigment akin to the eye's, are the most common light users at sea. Old work cast them as dwellers of starved waters, where sunlight pays when food does not.

Month by month off southern California, the team read the pigment's key part in sea water. Levels crested in spring, at the height of the algal bloom and its green peak, not in lean times. A class of bacteria famed for riding blooms rose with the pigment. Feast, it seems, suits these sun eaters too.
pmc-12824176:
Yuhong Ma and co-authors build a speech test that spots early Parkinson's disease from a Chinese tongue twister. Their 2025 paper starts from the slurred speech and sound slips that mark early cases. The twister stresses sounds these patients find hard. Recordings from a hospital clinic for older adults formed the test library. A math transform then turned each clip into a wave whose peaks mark each syllable.

Peak height, place, width, and area, plus total clip length, formed the feature set. A support vector machine read those features best of three models tried. In clinic trials the full system flagged patients with high scores and fast, steady replies, which the authors pitch as an aid for remote screening.
pmc-12824276:
Woosub Roh and co-authors published a study in 2025 checking a new satellite's cloud motion measures against a global storm-resolving model. Vertical air motion in clouds is key for weather and climate models but hard to observe. The EarthCARE satellite's Doppler radar now measures how fast cloud particles fall worldwide. The team compared its data with high-resolution simulations for two rain cases.

Simulations matched the overall vertical patterns seen by the satellite. Gaps in Doppler speed, above all in convective zones, point to model bias and measurement uncertainty. The authors say the satellite gives physically consistent data that can tighten how models treat cloud particles and motion.
pmc-12824376:
Xiaoxin Zhang, Bin Chen, Jiafu An, Chen Lin, and Peng Gong count forest lost to mining worldwide in a 2025 study. Mining chews forests, but sloppy records of where digging happens have hidden its true bite.

A fresh inventory maps over two hundred thirty six thousand mine sites with checked accuracy. Between 2001 and 2023, mining cleared near twenty thousand square kilometers of forest and released three quarters of a billion tons of carbon dioxide. That toll runs two to three times past older counts. Over half the loss traces to unrecorded digs, a plea for tighter watch.
pmc-12824976:
Ralph Lamson, a retired psychologist, reports using his own case to build a self-assessment tool for spine fusion surgery. His 2025 case report starts from his own state at age 79: a narrowed spinal canal, a collapsed disc, and crushed nerve roots. He asked whether a model would advise surgery for a patient like him.

He coded the test in Python, with a boosted decision tree at its core and two backup methods. Real data from his case were mixed with made-up data to widen the set. The tool reads a patient's survey answers and returns a call on surgery. Lamson is frank about the limits: one case and fake data can only go so far, and the tool is meant to aid talks with doctors, not replace them.
pmc-12827176:
Zhen Wei Sun and co-authors, in a study published in 2025, ask whether immune cell counts can forecast survival in advanced lung cancer treated with radiation, chemotherapy, and then immunotherapy. The patients had stage III non-small cell lung cancer. Blood lymphocytes often plunge during radiation, and the team tracked those counts at three points in care.

The study covered 139 patients, nearly all men, most with the squamous form of the disease. Counts fell and partly recovered across treatment. Patients whose lymphocyte count one month after radiation stayed above a set line lived longer. So did patients with certain sizes of drop and rebound during treatment, and those with higher counts of CD8 killer T cells after radiation. The authors suggest that watching immune recovery could help judge who benefits from the follow-up immunotherapy.
pmc-12827976:
Janik Fechtelpeter and co-authors test in a 2025 paper which models best forecast mental health paths in phone apps. Daily phone check ins track mood and conduct in fine grain. Good forecasts of those states can steer timely, adaptive help for each user.

Three 40 day trials with 145 people in all feed the contest of model types. Linear network models face two bendy rivals, a piecewise neural net and a transformer. The piecewise net gave the most accurate forecasts of both calm drift and shifts after prompts. Its hidden web also made sense in mind terms, with calm mood as a high impact node. Shocks could then be simulated ahead, a direct bridge to care choices in apps.
pmc-12829076:
Mahnaz Fosouli, Jalil Khataei, and Farshad Riahi report unusual jugular vein anatomy in a teenager with a facial birthmark, published in 2025. A seventeen-year-old Iranian girl with a large skin hemangioma on her face was scanned before dental work. The CT angiogram found two surprises in the neck's main drainage veins. Her right internal jugular vein was missing along its whole neck course.

Her left one ran as two separate channels that kept their flow and size. Such variants matter because the jugular is a highway for central lines, neck surgery, and clot-busting treatments. Paired with the facial hemangioma, the pattern hints at a shared developmental origin in the branchial arch system. The authors urge procedural teams to image first when anatomy may stray from the textbook.
pmc-12829276:
Shengbing Li and five co-authors build a lab model of kidney scarring in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Fibrosis is a hallmark of chronic kidney disease, but its causes and reversibility are only partly understood. A human model in a dish could help test treatments.

They grew kidney organoids from human induced pluripotent stem cells. Injury came from low oxygen, an inflammatory signal, or both together, with the pair giving the strongest scar response. Scar markers rose and mature kidney markers fell. Over two weeks, some tubular traits recovered alongside growth of progenitor cells, while the filtering structures recovered little. The platform can now be used to test anti-fibrotic and regenerative strategies.
pmc-12830576:
Meihong Zhao, Zhengxiao Han, Ende Wang, and Jiageng Liu protect car navigation from fake GPS signals, in a 2025 study. Spoofing attacks feed a vehicle false satellite signals, dragging its reported position off course. In dense city streets the harm can mean wrong turns, failed deliveries, or unsafe driver-assist choices.

Their system watches for spoofing in three adaptive modes and models both normal motion and attack patterns. A split-form Kalman filter then blends sensor data into a position estimate that resists the fake signals. Computer trials and real field tests in complex urban areas kept accuracy high under attack. Stronger defenses matter more as cars lean harder on satellite guidance.
pmc-12830676:
Maciej Rybiński and co-authors watched how vitamin D3 rewires immune cells inside a living person, not a dish. Lab studies had hinted the vitamin works partly by opening or closing stretches of DNA. This study followed one strong responder who took large monthly doses for three months. Blood immune cells were sampled before dosing and one and two days after.

More than 3,500 DNA regions opened up after the dose, mostly at gene start sites. The opened regions carried marks of immune control switches, though not the vitamin's own receptor, which points to indirect teamwork. Some 380 genes changed their activity over the two days, many tied to front-line immunity and interferon signaling. Linking the two datasets tied 306 changed genes to vitamin-sensitive DNA regions. The picture is of a broad, fast epigenetic response in real human blood.
pmc-12830776:
Junwei Fang and co-authors profile in 2025 the stem cells inside pancreatic cancer and build a score to forecast how patients will fare. This cancer has a bleak outlook, and its stem cells are thought to drive its spread and its shrug off of drugs. Yet the mix of those stem cells inside a tumor was poorly mapped.

The team joined single cell data with large bulk data sets from cancer atlases. They found the malignant cell groups and rated how stem like each was. Other tools traced how the cells change over time, how they burn fuel, which switches they use, and how they talk to nearby cells. From those traits they built a stem based score. A score tied to the tumor's most stubborn cells could help sort patients for trials and point to new drug targets.
pmc-12831376:
Huijie Wei and Wubin He published a consensus study in 2025 on a nurse-led exercise plan for breast cancer patients during chemotherapy. Treatment often brings nerve damage in the limbs and deep fatigue, which hurt daily life and care adherence. Exercise helps, but no standard nurse-led protocol existed. The team used a Delphi process to build expert agreement.

Twenty-two experts from nursing, cancer care, rehabilitation, and patient advocacy took part in three rounds in early 2025. They agreed on forty-two items. The plan starts checks and exercise orders at the first treatment cycle, mixes aerobic, strength, and balance work, and adjusts load to daily symptoms. Digital tools support tracking and records.
pmc-12831476:
Miguel Tenreiro and co-authors use human cerebral organoids to show that the gene MeCP2 shapes early forebrain growth. Loss of this gene causes Rett syndrome, long seen as a postnatal disorder. Organoids and joined telencephalic assembloids modelled early cortical growth with and without working MeCP2.

Without MeCP2, gene programs for cortical excitatory neurons went off track, and cell form and function matured late, though the basic layout of the tissue held. Cortical interneurons were made in excess, moved in an overactive way, and drove lasting over-synchronised network activity in the joined structures. Early, prenatal roots of Rett-related faults are the clear message.
pmc-12834976:
Gökhan Yüksek, a solo author, designs a motor controller that bakes time delay into its own rule, in a 2025 engineering study. The target is the brushless DC motor, a workhorse in robots and vehicles, whose speed must hold steady when signals lag. The controller blends the present error with a weighted delayed error, and two knobs reshape how it chases the set speed. A physics-inspired search method tuned the gains.

On a standard test rig, the tuned design settled eight percent faster than rival tuned controllers and cost less on a mixed score. Overshoot stayed under three percent. Lab runs on a real drive kept the edge under noise, drift, and outside pushes. The author offers the design for motion jobs where lag cannot be dodged.
pmc-12835076:
Six authors, led by Ahmed Ramady, model in 2025 how waves move through a heat stretched material that also feels gravity. The material has tiny stretched fibers and conducts heat with a time lag, not at once. Their model adds a fractional math twist that gives finer control over how heat relaxes.

The team shrank the linked equations for motion, stress, heat, and fiber stretch into a form they could solve in part. Computer runs then showed how each knob changes the waves. Gravity shifted wave height, speed, and fading in a clear way. The refined lag model gave tighter control over heat behavior.
pmc-12835176:
River gauges that touch the water can be risky to run in mountain floods, so radar that reads surface speed from the bank is gaining ground. Abhishek Kumar and Manoj Kumar Jain tested ways to turn those surface readings into full two-dimensional flow maps in 2025, at two Himalayan river sites in India. They compared two entropy-based methods, each with a unlike way to correct for the dip of fastest flow below the surface.

Both methods were checked against a standard current profiler at several river stages. The second method won on both rivers, with clearly smaller errors on one of them, and it located the fastest thread of flow correctly. Discharge estimates matched as well. The authors recommend the second method for like settings, with more tests on other river types.
pmc-12835476:
Chenchen Yang and four co-authors mined single-cell data for a prognostic gene in pancreatic cancer in a 2025 paper. Pancreatic cancer is among the deadliest cancers, and chemical tags placed on proteins after they are built may drive its course. One tag, S-nitrosylation, had never been profiled in this disease.

The team combined bulk and single-cell data from several cohorts and raced 101 machine learning combinations to build a survival model. Their winning model split patients into high- and low-risk groups across nine cohorts. Among tag-linked genes, LAMC2 tracked the risk score most strongly. Lab tests in a pancreatic cancer cell line backed its role. The authors propose LAMC2 as a key driver worth targeting.
pmc-12836976:
Henrik Thomassen and Villy Våge report one center's results with a repair for reflux after weight-loss surgery, in a 2025 paper. The surgery, sleeve gastrectomy, is the most common weight-loss operation, yet it often leaves patients with heartburn. The usual fix is a gastric bypass, but some patients still need daily acid pills.

The Hill repair rebuilds the valve area between stomach and food pipe without wrapping the stomach around it. Ten patients had the repair between 2019 and 2022 for reflux after sleeve surgery. Symptom scores improved at one and three years, and pill use fell from all patients to under a third. Pressure at the valve rose sharply after surgery. Two patients later needed another operation for returning symptoms.
pmc-12837176:
Niall O'Boyle and five co-authors present a 2025 paper on a training program where pharmacy and medical students swap roles in simulated care. From 2026, all new pharmacists in the United Kingdom will prescribe on their own. Both professions need sharper skills in taking histories and judging patients.

The program ran in a teaching hospital for final year students of both kinds, from January to March 2025. In role exchange sessions, each side played the other's part in admission cases. That swap builds respect for the partner's skills and habits. The paper describes how the program was built and what the first run showed about joint prescribing readiness.
pmc-12838476:
Klaus Widhalm, Sebastian Durstberger, and Peter Putz report a two thousand twenty-five crossover trial on downhill walking and knee control. Poor leg alignment while walking can feed into knee osteoarthritis. Live visual feedback might help walkers correct their movement.

Twenty-eight healthy adults aged eighteen to thirty-five walked on a sloped treadmill. Conditions mixed self-paced walking, inward focus, and screen feedback, plus a matched-speed repeat. Feedback changed left knee sideways motion and load balance between the legs. Effects were moderate to large. The findings support testing feedback training for people who need better knee control.
pmc-12838776:
Xia Yang and co-authors present a review, published in 2025, on a traditional medicinal herb as a source of new kidney drugs. Kidney disease is rising with modern lifestyles, and current medicines leave many patients sliding toward organ failure. The review gathers evidence from several databases on Scutellaria baicalensis, a flowering plant long used in Chinese medicine, and its protective effects on the kidney.

Its flavonoids calmed inflammation and oxidative stress, curbed cell death, and slowed scarring in study models. Four compounds, baicalein, wogonin, baicalin, and wogonoside, carry most of the credit. The authors argue these plant molecules are promising starting points for kidney therapies, while noting how much work remains before any reach the clinic.
pmc-12840076:
Awele Ndubisi, Felix Agyapong-Opoku, and Belinda Agyapong review past reviews on social media use and sleep quality in teens and young adults, in a paper from 2025. Heavy social media use is now a normal part of young life. Many studies link it to poor sleep, through late use, light, and mental arousal.

The team used a five-stage scoping method and searched five databases for reviews from 2020 to 2025. Ten reviews met all the rules and were studied. Across them, social media use had a small but steady negative link to sleep quality. Problem use, where habits feel out of control, linked more strongly than normal use. Some platforms tied more to short sleep and late bedtimes than others. The authors map gaps for future studies.
pmc-12840776:
Tatiana Tikhonova and five colleagues turn a drop of finger blood into a calcium measurement using a smart gel, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. Blood calcium flags parathyroid, kidney, and bone disorders. Point-of-care testing needs methods without a full laboratory.

Their platform is gelatin hydrogel loaded with Arsenazo III, a calcium-sensitive dye. A blood drop placed on the gel separates into plasma and cells as it soaks in. Calcium binding shifts the gel's absorption spectrum, readable optically. Six candidate gel materials were compared; only gelatin performed suitably. The approach promises rapid total calcium readings at the bedside or clinic. Simplicity is the selling point: no centrifuge, no large analyzer.
pmc-12844876:
Regev Cohen leads a large team in a 2025 case report on botulism from an unknown source. The disease paralyzes nerves through a bacterial toxin and can kill. This adult patient had no foodborne source that anyone could find, a rare path that points to the gut itself hosting the germ.

Stool tests and a mouse assay confirmed the toxin-making germ in the gut. The patient, short of breath with dry mouth and failing eye nerves, improved fast on a seven-part antitoxin. Oddly, the blood held antibodies tied to a kin nerve syndrome. The authors weigh whether the toxin can spark such look-alike immunity.
pmc-12846476:
Mario García-González and four co-authors report a detailed guinea pig case in a 2025 paper. Diseases of the reproductive tract are common in pet guinea pigs, but two conditions found together are rarely written up. Their patient was a two-year-old female with a tender belly.

Ultrasound showed cysts on both ovaries and a thickened, cyst-filled womb lining. Surgeons removed the ovaries and uterus under combined pain control, and lab tests confirmed both diagnoses. The guinea pig healed fully within 21 days. The authors also stress the value of writing up animal cases under standard reporting guidelines, so other vets can trust and reuse the details.
pmc-12847876:
Gholam Hossein Hamedi and co-authors test whether two nano additives guard warm-mix asphalt against water harm as it ages, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Twenty mixes faced freeze-thaw rounds in a strength test, with surface energy reads beside. Warm mixes age less in laying but still fear water.

Both additives raised the energy cost of water-driven peeling, in fresh and aged states. Self-grip energy of the binder jumped by over half in the two binders tried. Grip on stone rose about a tenth on average. Lab strength and energy reads agreed strongly in late freeze rounds. Readers in road work get a physics-backed case for nano lime and chalk.
pmc-12847976:
Orsola Mocellin and co-authors grow liver tumors on chips, blood vessels and all, to screen drugs against them. Hepatocellular carcinoma thrives inside a busy microenvironment that shapes how it grows and answers treatment. Their chips carry patient-derived tumor tissue with its stromal partners under flowing liquid, about twelve hundred of them in one campaign. Twenty-eight treatments were tried across eight primary tumors and two cell lines.

The standard drugs sorafenib and lenvatinib cut overall culture viability and wrecked the vessel layout, yet left the tumor cells themselves standing. A statin, atorvastatin, hurt viability without touching the vessels. Other drugs dialed down IL-6, a marker tied to outlook. The authors offer the platform for early, patient-real drug hunting.
pmc-12848076:
When a honey bee smells alarm pheromone, the colony braces for attack. But which scent receptors catch that signal was unknown. Benjamin Andreu and co-authors hunt them down. They expressed bee odorant receptors in a fruit fly test system, an 'empty neuron' setup. Calcium imaging and electrical recordings then showed which receptors fired for which compounds.

Two receptors stood out, named AmelOR136 and AmelOR109. Both detect parts of the alarm pheromone. The first is narrowly tuned, a specialist suited to a clear alarm channel. The second responds broadly, to many odorants including pheromones. The contrast is elegant: one receptor whispers 'danger, specifically,' while the other keeps general watch. The findings open the molecular black box of bee social communication.
pmc-12849076:
A gout flare burns hot, and then, in a sound joint, it cools down. That cooling is an active step, and it is run by specialized pro-resolving mediators. Ismael Bermejo-Álvarez and his co-authors test whether stem cells can speed that resolution. In their 2025 study in rabbits, gout was set off by shots of urate crystals in the joint. Human stem cells from fat were then given in one dose.

The team took counts of the mediators in the joint lining with precision mass spectrometry. They also counted prostaglandin E2 and the action of linked genes. The stem cells pushed the making of that compound into overdrive. That super-induction fed the making of the mediators. Tests in the lab with macrophages probed the path more. The results cast the cells as things that speed the cooling, not just things that damp the flare.
pmc-12849176:
Amira A Helaly and co-authors report a 2025 study on a plant disease of cucumber. A germ called Pantoea causes leaf spot and cuts yield. Heavy use of chemical sprays harms soil and health, so growers need safer guards.

The team tested a broth from helpful root germs and tiny zinc oxide grains, alone and mixed. In lab dishes, the grains blocked the germ more as dose rose, and the broth alone made a wide clear zone. Chemical scans named the active parts in the broth. In a greenhouse, the team tracked disease level, plant health traits, and fruit yield. The mixed guard aims to cut sprays while keeping plants strong.
pmc-12849376:
Factory-made foods crowd older adults' diets, and heavier intake may track with frailty. Jamal Hallajzadeh, Parasto Yousefi Tanha, Arian Azadnia, Alexei Wong, and Sajjad Moradi test that link in a 2025 study. Three hundred sixty-eight older adults in Maragheh, Iran, filled a long food questionnaire. Body makeup and activity were measured, and blood was drawn. About a quarter of the group met the frailty bar.

The highest processed-food third faced about double the frailty odds of the lowest. Among men the link ran stronger still, while women showed no clear link. Models adjusted for the usual health traits. The authors write for community-dwelling elders, not care-home residents.
pmc-12849476:
Yuanli Chen and co-authors build a model for elder care in China in a 2025 study. China has the world's largest aging population, and national strategy pushes sports and medicine to merge in community services. The team coded hundreds of thousands of characters of policy texts, reports, and cases using grounded theory software.

Thirteen core categories emerged, and the authors propose four service models: sports-led, medicine-led, technology-driven, and talent-driven. Each comes with its own strengths, bottlenecks, and operating path. Foreign models are compared with Chinese practice along the way. Readers get an actionable blueprint for community elder health.
pmc-12852076:
Haiming Ye and co-authors review fracture care, published in 2025, tying treatment choices to how broken bones heal. Fractures are common, and their numbers are rising with traffic crashes, sports injuries, and an aging population. Surgeons work from shared principles, including the AO approach and a later biological approach that stresses blood supply and soft tissue.

The review sums up recent work on the healing process itself, from the first blood clot to new bone taking shape. It weighs long used concepts against new views drawn from clinical practice, and notes problems that remain, such as bones that fail to heal and infections at the break. Readers get a clear map of where fracture theory stands and where it is moving.
pmc-12853876:
Sara Larsson and colleagues ran a two-year trial on wrist arthritis exercise in two thousand twenty-five. Wrist arthritis causes lasting pain and weak grip. Education and exercise help other joints first-line. Proof for the wrist stayed thin. Patients joined a twelve-week self-management program. Half trained nerve and muscle control. The rest did motion-only exercises.

The team tracked wrist scores, grip strength, and pain. They also counted who later chose surgery. Follow-up lasted a full two years. Such long tracking is rare in wrist research. Results guide a real choice patients face. Many hope to delay or avoid an operation.
pmc-12853976:
Neah Albasha and six co-authors explore what helps and what blocks fall prevention for older adults in Saudi Arabia. Their qualitative study was published in twenty twenty-five. Falls lead injury and hospital use in this group, and local barriers tied to culture, schooling, and resources were underexplored.

The team interviewed sixteen health professionals, nurses, therapists, and doctors from public and private hospitals. Talks ran in Arabic and were analyzed with a mix of open coding and a theory framework. Themes covered knowledge, beliefs, setting, and means. The mapping gives structure to scattered complaints. The authors aim to guide fall programs that fit Saudi homes and clinics rather than copying foreign models wholesale.
pmc-12855176:
Xiangyi Li and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on how years of coal dust exposure reshape the microbes of miners' throats and the fats in their blood. Dust harms miners' lungs over a career, and throat microbes help guard respiratory health. The team studied twenty-two Tangshan miners grouped by exposure length, plus unexposed controls.

Gene sequencing of throat swabs and blood fat profiling tracked the changes. The variety of throat microbes thinned steadily as exposure years grew. Short exposure already shifted some measures, while longer exposure rewired more of the microbial community and lipid pattern. The authors argue these timelines could flag damage earlier than symptoms do.
pmc-12856576:
Fran Oficial-Casado, Jose Ignacio Priego-Quesada, and Pedro Pérez-Soriano built a 2025 formula to forecast Valencia marathon times from half marathon results. The hosted text dates the work to 2025, though the catalog lists 2026. Pacing may sharpen forecasts, but few studies had tested that idea. The team used 8,261 runners who ran both Valencia races in the same year, in 2022 or 2023.

They fit three formulas, adding age group and then pacing spread to half marathon time and sex. Adding pacing did not improve the forecast, which explained most of the spread in times with a modest average error. A classic system matched theirs overall, though each did better for different runner levels. Coaches can use the formula to set training paces.
pmc-12857076:
Joshua Okyere, Castro Ayebeng, and Kwamena Dickson examine the town-country gap in blood pressure medicine use in Cape Verde, in a 2025 paper. Fewer than half of adults with hypertension there take their medication, the team found in a national survey of 468 adults. Urban residents were nearly twice as likely to take it as rural ones, and women more likely than men.

Diabetes and excess weight also raised the odds of taking medication, while eating little fruit lowered them. A decomposition analysis then traced how much of the urban-rural gap came from differences in traits like schooling and wealth between the groups. The authors say closing the gap needs policies aimed at the rural shortfall in access and support.
pmc-12858676:
Shahed Salehzehi and co-authors build a graph neural network that reads breast MRI scans and patient facts together to assign several cancer labels at once. Care teams judge receptor status, tumor stage, and grade side by side, not one by one. The authors turned five kinds of MRI volume into 3D graphs. Each voxel and each clinical variable became a node, with radiomic features and patient data as its traits.

Edges link nodes by closeness in space and by likeness in brightness. A graph isomorphism network then sharpens each node's profile by pooling its neighbors. Rare classes were balanced with synthetic samples, and five-fold cross-checks tested firmness. The labels sought were HER2 status, TNM stage, and the parts of histological grade. A model that gives these jointly, with an eye on structure, fits how oncologists in fact weigh a case.
pmc-12858976:
Seunghun Song, Jueun Baek, and Sangjae Seo present a 2025 journal article introducing LNP Atlas, a dataset of lipid nanoparticle recipes for delivering genetic medicines. These fat bubbles carried mRNA vaccines to fame, yet design knowledge lies scattered across papers. The team extracted formulations from the literature with an AI-assisted workflow, then standardized everything with automated checks.

Each entry holds lipid types and ratios, chemical codes, particle size and charge, synthesis settings, and biological results. The authors expect the shared resource to speed data-driven design of delivery particles for vaccines and gene therapies alike, replacing scattered reading with searchable evidence.
pmc-12860076:
Hongyan Liu and co-authors review how chemical marks on RNA steer immune cells and shape the terrain around tumors. Their 2025 review works in epitranscriptomics, the study of those marks. Several mark types are now known, each laid down, read, and erased by its own enzyme set.

Through that system the marks tune how immune cells grow, mature, switch on, and do their work. Inside a tumor they help cancer hide from the immune system and blunt immunotherapy. The enzymes themselves double as forecast markers and as targets for drug pairs. New detection tools are revealing how the marks vary across space and cell type. The authors also flag the mark types whose control paths remain murky.
pmc-12860576:
Eleftheria Dampa reviews the proof for creams that loosen rough skin in keratosis pilaris, a common and harmless condition of bumpy hair follicles. Her 2025 review covers three groups of skin creams: alpha hydroxy acids, beta hydroxy acids, and urea. The bumps most often appear on the upper arms, thighs, and buttocks, and they trouble many people for how they look and feel.
