All three cream types showed potential benefit, and they remain sensible first choices for easing symptoms. Yet the proof base is thin. Trials were small, measured results in unlike ways, rarely hid who got which cream, and seldom followed patients for long. Little is known about keeping gains over time, or about which cream suits red versus rough forms. Dampa calls for stronger trials before firm guidance can be given.
pmc-12863376:
Melissa Clarkson and Kristen Platt survey how artists and anatomists have drawn the human kidney over past centuries, in a 2025 paper. Kidneys filter blood and carry urine through a web of vessels and tiny tubes. Many of those structures can be seen in dissection with the naked eye or weak magnification, so early illustrators could record them faithfully.

Most modern textbooks show the kidney in one standard frontal slice. The authors argue that this view hides much of the organ's inner layout. Their survey gathers older, varied ways of depicting the kidney, offering today's medical illustrators richer options for showing how the organ is built.
pmc-12866476:
Barış Boza, Fırat Ersan, and Verda Alpay test a birth-hold drug's marks on the unborn heart in a 2025 study. The drug is a top pick to hold early birth and stretch the term at hand. Proof of its marks on the child heart stays thin in the field, they note.

Over one hundred with-child cases split to drug care and calm terms in the work. Sound reads give heart form, flow marks, and a work score for the child. Birth ends join the checks for both arms of the run.
pmc-12868276:
Qiuju Yang and co-authors profile the first Brucella canis strain ever isolated from a human patient in China's Yunnan Province. The dog bacterium causes brucellosis in people, yet its evolution is barely charted. Their patient arrived febrile with sweats and fatigue after frequent contact with dogs and livestock, and the isolate, YN20042, was confirmed by culture, biotyping, and a species test.

Whole-genome sequencing placed it in sequence type twenty-one, matching its reference strain almost base for base, with strong structural conservation. The genome carries a dozen predicted virulence factors across seventy-one genes, several bearing mutations, plus signs of horizontally acquired DNA. Tree analysis clustered it with strains from Zhejiang and Beijing. The authors read a complex evolutionary path of variation and recombination.
pmc-12876176:
Gloria Okpala, Anna Walker, Craig Brideau, Pina Colarusso, and Lisa Gieg tested two chemicals against microbes that live in slime layers on pipes and tanks. The head dates their study to 2025. These sulfate-reducing microbes sour stored fluids and eat away at metal. Chemicals that kill free-floating cells may fail once the microbes settle into a biofilm, a sticky shared shelter.

The team grew biofilms in flow cells and dosed them with each chemical for ten to fourteen hours. Free cells died at low doses. The films only paused at those doses and bounced back. One chemical needed the highest doses tried to stop sulfide output for good. Under the lens, low doses left most cells alive, while high doses left none. Gene reads showed which kinds survived each dose. Dosing must rise for films, the authors warn.
pmc-12876876:
Xiaofeng Peng and eight co-authors published a 2025 mouse study on a diet trick that protects kidneys from a common injury. When kidney blood flow is cut and restored, the rebound damage, called ischemia reperfusion injury, is a leading cause of acute kidney failure and a threat in transplants. No good preventive treatment exists.

Across tissue, blood, and gene data, one metabolite stood out: SAM, tied to the amino acid methionine. Its blood level rose sharply in acute kidney injury, flagging it as a possible diagnostic marker. A short diet stripped of methionine lowered SAM and made kidneys far hardier against the injury. Tracing studies showed the diet retunes the kidney to burn more glucose and fat ahead of time.
pmc-12883376:
Yan Xu, Hongtao Cui, Xinna Wang, and Fang Liu review how doctors should handle early breast growth in young girls, a condition called isolated premature thelarche. Published in 2025, their review notes that the condition looks much like early puberty, which does need treatment, so families and doctors often feel torn.

The authors propose sorting girls by risk rather than treating all of them or none of them. Girls with normal growth, no jump in bone age, and low hormone levels can be watched with regular checks. Strong drug treatment is saved for the few whose bodies keep changing in a puberty-like way. The plan aims to spare most girls needless drugs and cost.
pmc-12883776:
Yu Xu and colleagues built prediction tools for death within twenty-eight days among intensive care patients. The SOFA score, which grades organ failure, is widely used to judge outlook in critical illness. Whether tracking how the score changes over time, alongside age, sharpens prediction was the open question behind the study of several hundred patients at one hospital.

Change in SOFA between early time points added real predictive value, especially for patients whose starting scores sat in the middle range. A simple chart tool combining change and age gave an easy bedside estimate, while a machine learning model also performed well. Outside testing showed more multi-centre work is still needed.
pmc-12913576:
Xiaoyan Zhao and co-authors compared the chloroplast genomes of slipper orchids to trace how the group evolved and adapted, in work the text head dates to 2025. These orchids span temperate to tropical homes, yet the molecular roots of their spread were little known. Chloroplast genomes, which run photosynthesis, offer a clean system for such questions.

The team assembled the full chloroplast genome of one species and joined it with 47 public genomes from all four genera of the group. They compared genome structure, codon use, repeat patterns, and signs of selection. A family tree built from 81 protein-coding genes anchors the study, which weighs drift against natural selection in shaping these genomes.
pmc-12915676:
Sivasankar and Markkandan present a 2025 paper on keeping wireless links private with the help of intelligent reflecting surfaces. These surfaces are panels of many small elements that bounce signals in chosen directions. The risk is that a stray listener may catch the signal while conditions change as users move. The authors propose a hybrid method with the short name SGP-DARE that tunes both the sender's beams and the panel's settings.

One part of the method handles the joint tuning at low computing cost. The other part guards against errors in channel knowledge and user movement. The scheme works within hardware limits such as fixed phase steps. In simulations it beat rival methods on secrecy and energy use. The authors aim at networks where eavesdropping risk and power cost both matter.
pmc-12920676:
Ahmed Abdelmoaty, Maha Alsadik, and Khaled Abdel-Sater wrote a review in two thousand twenty-five on lung problems in celiac disease. Celiac disease is a long-term gut disorder set off by gluten in people with a genetic risk. It mainly harms the small intestine, but signs keep appearing in other organs.

The review gathers evidence that the lungs are one of those organs, a link summed up as a gut-lung axis. It covers lung conditions reported in celiac patients, from asthma to rarer lung disease. It also lays out the paths that might connect gut harm to lung harm, and what the link means for doctors and for future studies.
pmc-12946076:
Lindiwe Modest Faye and four co-authors study community-led governance for tuberculosis care in a rural district. Their paper is dated two thousand twenty-six in the pack, while its text head says the year before. The district, in South Africa's Eastern Cape, bears a high TB load with few means. Their frame blends clinic rules with community voice.

They use patient data from twenty eighteen to twenty twenty. Treatment success climbs from about two in five patients to about two in three across those years. Machine learning models are used to explain, not to forecast, and they mirror the governance marks by design. Scenarios show a steady pace could hit the world target of ninety-five percent success by twenty thirty, while a slow pace would fall short.
pmc-13001676:
Jared Zhao and Bryan Ward present a 2025 case report on a hard ear procedure. The task is to widen a blocked ear tube with a small balloon, normally slipped in through the nose. In some patients, odd nose or tube shapes block that path, and the standard try fails.

In the case they report, doctors placed a mouth tool and guided the tube in through the mouth instead. A camera through the nose let them watch as the tool curved around the soft palate to the tube mouth. The angle from below made entry easy, and the patient could clear the ears well after care. The authors offer the mouth route as a backup when the nose route cannot work.
pmc-13018376: Monika Gandhi and co-authors published a 2025 study of three infusion plans for patients fresh from abdominal surgery. Sharp pain after surgery slows recovery and triggers stress. Two drugs were in view: a sedative and a numbing drug, each given by infusion. The team compared them head to head, and as a pair. Ninety patients were observed, with pain and recovery scores taken at one and two days. The combination group showed the lowest pain scores, used the least backup pain drug, and led in recovery.
pmc-13064776:
Alberto Carrara traces how the idea of the human mind has changed in Western thought. The head text dates this article to 2024, though the catalog lists 2025. It follows the concept from ancient Greece through Plato and Descartes to the present day. Schools like empiricism and functionalism each reshaped the idea in turn.

Modern brain imaging and holistic views now push toward a joined picture. The author stresses ties among mental life, the brain, and the world around a person. Ties to other people get special weight in that picture. Such a view could help psychiatric care and mental assessment take a fuller approach. The paper argues for a view that bridges inner experience and outer measures.
pmc-13082476:
Rim Laaboudi and co-authors present a case report, published in 2026, on a rare ovarian growth made mostly of thyroid tissue. Such a growth, called struma ovarii, turns cancerous in only a small share of cases, most often into papillary thyroid carcinoma. The patient was a woman aged forty who arrived with sudden pelvic pain and a large mass on one ovary.

Emergency surgery removed the affected ovary and tube, and lab tests found a small thyroid cancer inside the growth, with no spread beyond it. Her own thyroid gland tested normal afterward. Advised to have more surgery, she chose watchful follow up instead, and the authors stress both standard cancer protocols and respect for patient choice.
pmc-13094576:
Debra Winberg and co-authors interview diabetes patients about taking their medicines in this 2026 paper. Type 2 diabetes control depends on steady medication use. Some health plans now offer a zero dollar copay for these drugs. Whether cost is the main barrier, and what else helps or hurts, was the focus.

Semi structured interviews were held with plan members with and without the zero copay benefit. The interview guide was built with patients, clinicians, and plan leaders. Barriers named went beyond price, into routines, side effects, and beliefs. Supports included reminders, family help, and trust in the care team. Comparing the two groups shows what a copay waiver alone cannot fix. Plans can target the remaining barriers directly.
pmc-13098876:
Cynthia Lilieholm and a large team of co-authors test whether the choice of radioactive payload changes how well radiation therapy wakes up the immune system, in a 2025 study. The therapy targets a marker on neuroblastoma tumors and was paired with immune checkpoint drugs.

Mice with marked tumors received an antibody carrying one of three radionuclides, at two dose levels, with or without the immune drugs. All versions homed to tumors. The alpha emitter at the higher dose, plus immune drugs, gave the best survival and strong interferon-driven activation. A beta emitter instead thinned regulatory immune cells, lifting the killer-to-regulator balance. The authors conclude payload and dose must be tuned together.
pmc-13114676:
Baohong Wei and co-authors test in 2026 whether cuttlefish ink can ease ADHD-like traits in mice through immune paths. The disorder affects five to ten percent of children worldwide. Current drugs carry side effects and unclear long-term risk, which spurs a hunt for gentler options.

A drug-induced mouse model shows less hyperactivity and better learning after ink treatment. Brain cell harm and swelling fall, while immune organ suppression reverses. Gene, blood, and gut data join to trace the immune rebalance behind the gains. Blood counts and immune cell mixes in key organs also return toward normal.
pmc-13116276:
Pedro Ramalho and co-authors run a small randomised trial of exercise breaks for the imaging staff who spend their days scanning others, in a 2026 study. Radiologic technologists face heavy occupational stress and burnout, yet workplace exercise evidence in this exact group is thin. Nineteen technologists at a Portuguese health unit were randomised: ten to a six-week programme of exercise sessions during work hours, nine to carry on as usual.

Stress, burnout, and quality of life were measured before and after. The trial's scale is modest, a pilot in spirit, but its design is the real thing: random assignment, a control group, and validated questionnaires. The authors offer the protocol and results as groundwork for larger trials, and for managers weighing a simple, cheap intervention against the cost of losing experienced staff to burnout.
pmc-13120676:
Yugo Kato and a large team explain how a marine worm armors its jaws with zinc. The green worm Nereis aibuhitensis hunts and burrows, so its jaws take a beating. Zinc concentrates near the jaw tip, and the team mapped exactly where and how it binds.

X-ray tests showed the zinc sits in no crystal at all. Instead it grips organic molecules rich in the amino acid histidine. One histidine-heavy protein appeared only in the zinc-rich tip. The design hardens the jaw without brittle mineral. Engineers could copy this trick for tough, light materials.
pmc-13127676:
Cammies, Cavaciuti, and Montgomery build a hands-on class to teach brain size scale rules. Scale rules sit at the core of how brain form shifts by kind. Yet the rules prove hard for class youth to grasp cold. They force a merge of growth thought with math ties. Part-wise scale shifts through deep time add more load still. Few lab tasks let youth probe the rules in brain terms.

Their task pairs sheep and pig brain cuts with plain dye steps. Free scan tools let youth view and weigh part shares in shots. Youth can trace scale ties in one kind and cross kinds. Test scores on scale asks rose sharp past the lab meet. That rise hit a firm mark by test norms in class. Most youth, 93 percent, urged the class stay on.
pmc-13128376:
Li Huang and Hao Li describe a lung cancer patient treated with dual checkpoint blockade despite drug-resistant tuberculosis, in a 2026 case report. A fifty-six-year-old man with advanced squamous lung cancer had already failed several regimens when he developed multidrug-resistant TB, a combination that trials normally exclude. His TB was first stabilized with an all-oral drug regimen, alongside radiation to a growing metastasis.

He then received QL1706, a single antibody blocking both PD-1 and CTLA-4. The cancer stayed stable for about eleven months, the TB never reactivated under close monitoring, and no severe immune side effects appeared. The authors present the case as first evidence that such dual therapy can be feasible when TB is tightly controlled.
pmc-13130276:
Cajsa Aranäs and co-authors report a rat study from two thousand twenty-four on pairing two gut-hormone drugs to cut alcohol drinking. Alcohol use disorder has tangled brain roots, so combining drugs may help where single ones fall short. Two gut-brain peptides, amylin and GLP-1, each reduce drinking in rodents on their own.

The team paired activators of both receptors in rats of both sexes, in two drinking experiments. Adding the amylin drug to ongoing GLP-1 treatment lowered intake in males and females. Starting both at once cut intake at first, but tolerance then developed. Food intake and body weight fell consistently in both sexes. Inflammation markers did not change. The results support combined gut-hormone treatment as a lead for alcohol research.
pmc-13130576: A correction notice fixes typographical errors in a study that models Anopheles mosquito numbers across Madagascar. Missing stage labels in the model description are restored. The path from eggs to larvae, pupae and adult females now reads in full. Adult search, feeding and egg-laying steps are named rightly. A simulation sentence gains the full list of life stages counted in each commune. The validation text is also corrected, and the acknowledgements are updated. The science of the model is not changed.
pmc-13134976:
Tugba Barlas and seven co-authors compared MRI measures in thyroid eye disease across thyroid function groups, in a 2026 study. Most such patients have overactive thyroids, but some do not. Seventy-four patients with orbital scans were split by function. Eye protrusion, muscle thickness, and fat swelling were measured. About four fifths were in the overactive group.

Protrusion ran greater in the overactive group. Fat swelling behind the eye was worse in the normal or underactive group. Muscle thickness and asymmetry did not differ between groups. An antibody level predicted total muscle thickness in their model. Activity scores did not explain the imaging traits. The authors conclude function status colors the disease's look on scans. Treatment planning should weigh that difference. Larger cohorts could sharpen the antibody finding.
pmc-13135576:
Mustafa Ozan Atasoy and co-authors screen in 2026 backyard chickens in Türkiye for a group of small viruses called gyroviruses. Such viruses infect poultry widely, but their mix in backyard flocks was poorly known. Tissue samples from one hundred healthy chickens in five provinces, taken in 2020 and 2021, were tested for six virus types.

Nine in ten samples held at least one type, and mixed infections were common. Two types were found in chickens in Türkiye for the first time, which widens their known range. Family tree analysis showed most strains matched global lines, with some variation. The authors call for continued watching of backyard flocks.
pmc-13136776:
Takeshi Yamamura, Masanao Nakamura, and Hiroki Kawashima discuss a sedative for gut endoscopy in a 2026 article. Sedation helps patients accept scope exams and helps doctors work well. Common drugs in Japan include midazolam, the top choice, and propofol, which gives fast recovery. Each carries drawbacks, from slow wake-up to tight use rules.

The article presents ciprofol as a useful new option for this setting. It sits in a line of agents that act on GABA receptors, like propofol. The authors weigh benefits and safety in light of Japanese guidelines. Better sedation may raise repeat exam uptake and disease spotting, they argue.
pmc-13141176:
A large team studies what happens when melanoma patients stop combination immunotherapy in this 2026 paper. The two drug combination is standard care for melanoma that has spread to the brain, but guidelines say little about when responders can safely stop.

The study gathered 465 patients: 392 who stopped within twenty-four months for reasons other than disease growth, and 73 who kept going past that mark. Survival, response, time without growth, and side effects were compared across the groups. Many stops came after complete response. Work like this helps doctors weigh the burden of long treatment against the risk of stopping for patients whose disease has melted away.
pmc-13141476:
Orlando Fernandes and co-authors use machine learning to flag suicidal thoughts in university communities in this 2026 study. Depression and such thoughts often occur together, but the thoughts can also appear when mood scores are not high. The team looked for the wider set of factors that separate people with these thoughts from those without.

Their data came from an online survey of 3,828 members of the Brazilian academic community. A learning method that weighs each questionnaire source on its own sorted the two groups with about seventy-eight percent balanced accuracy. Depression scores were strong predictors, as expected. Even so, optimism, loneliness, emotional mistreatment in childhood, and background traits together carried half the weight of the model. The authors argue that screening in academic settings should look beyond depression scores, so at-risk people are not missed.
pmc-13141676:
Tetsuya Muto, Shigeki Machida, Shinichiro Imaizumi, and Tetsuju Sekiryu study the effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on retinal artery occlusion in a 2026 paper. The condition blocks an artery in the retina and can harm sight, in branch and central forms.

The team split new patients in Japan into groups before and after the state of emergency was declared in April 2020. They compared how often the blockage was found, plus sex and age splits. Rates of two other eye conditions were checked the same way. No clear change in the rate of retinal artery occlusion was found.
pmc-13142776:
Bolong Wu and co-authors find a brake on a key immune cell type in this 2025 study. A form of ATP, the cell's energy carrier, acts as a danger signal outside cells and shapes immune responses. T cells store and release this carrier through a transporter, but that side of the process was poorly known.

The transporter is high in one helper T cell type and limits its growth and function. When T cells are triggered, the transporter helps load ATP into storage sacs and release it. The released ATP then sets off a chain of signals that cuts the cells' output of a key defense protein. Blocking the transporter boosted these cells against infection and tumors in tests.
pmc-13143076:
Rachel Berns and co-authors published a survey study in 2026 comparing young and master runners on injury limits and training habits. Two hundred and seven runners answered an online questionnaire built on a standard overuse injury tool. Over a third of young runners and half of master runners reported injury limits on their running.

Master runners also reported more arm and shoulder injuries, longer histories, and higher weekly mileage. Smoking, gravel surfaces, and owning many shoes tracked higher odds of limitation for masters, with no protective habits found. For young runners, coaching, off-road tracks, and varied surfaces lowered the odds. The authors argue injury prevention should be tailored by age group.
pmc-13143276:
Francisco Heras and co-authors argue that eyes are shaped by a budget fight between lenses and light sensors. Their 2026 study measures both parts in one currency, specific volume, so costs can be compared fairly.
