Erin McCloskey reports in 2024 on patient and public input in the DynAIRx study of medicine reviews. The study serves people who live with many long-term health problems and take at least five drugs each day. Such reviews aim to check that each drug still helps and does no harm.

DynAIRx uses artificial intelligence and data from health records to flag people who need a yearly review. The team then builds clear visual dashboards to guide staff during those reviews. A public group of people with lived experience helped shape the work, so patient views stay at the center of the design.
pmc-13179176:
Dang Ma and co-authors compare in 2026 two ways to reach a broken wrist bone for plate repair. The standard route cuts a tendon sheath near the wrist. The changed route keeps that sheath whole while still giving the surgeon clear access to the bone.

The study looked back at one hundred sixty five patients with unstable breaks treated over about two years. Both groups healed with like bone alignment on scans. The group with the sheath kept whole had less pain at each check and better hand scores for the first six months. Grip strength and wrist motion were also tracked for a full year.
pmc-13180176:
Kyle Cox and six co-authors present a 2026 lab study comparing two ways to repair a torn knee meniscus root. The meniscus is a cartilage pad in the knee, and a tear at its back root leaves the joint in a bad state for wear. Many repair methods can restore near normal mechanics, but no single best method has won out.

The team tested ten matched pairs of donor knees in three states: intact, torn, and repaired. One knee of each pair got the classic fix, a stitch pulled through a bone tunnel and tied over a button. The mate got a knotless all stitch anchor. Loads and shifts were compared across the states.
pmc-13180876:
Veerapaneni, Delhibabu, Subbotin, and Zhukova built a fast in-memory database in twenty twenty-six for smart video surveillance in critical patient care. Hospital video systems produce data at high speed. Standard databases can be too slow, delaying decisions about patients who need urgent care.

Their system, named SubDataBase-0.91s, keeps all data in memory and saves to disk in the background. They tested it against six major database products using scripts that mimic video data streams. It read and wrote far faster than the slowest rival and beat the fastest commercial in-memory rival on some tasks. Dropping strict safety rules of general databases gave the speed. The authors offer it as a base for smart hospital systems.
pmc-13181876:
Giovanni De Antoni and co-authors wrote a study from 2026 on access to rare disease drugs in Switzerland. The drugs, called orphan drugs, treat diseases that few people have, among them faults in body chemistry passed down at birth. The team looked back at adults cared for at one Swiss center over five years. They tracked who was offered such a drug, who got it, and how long the wait was.

Of one hundred and ninety patients, forty-one had a reason to get an orphan drug, and thirty-nine did get one. The wait from need to first dose was about a month in most cases. It stretched to more than six months for drugs not yet cleared for sale in Switzerland. Swiss clearance also came close to two years after clearance abroad. The team urges simpler pay and approval paths so care is not held up.
pmc-13182176:
Qiang Chen and Gaoshang Zhu studied a tiny RNA as a possible marker for kidney injury in sepsis in a 2026 paper. Sepsis can damage the kidneys fast, and early warning has real value. The team enrolled just under two hundred sepsis patients, about half with kidney injury.

Levels of the RNA were higher in the injury group and rose with standard signs of kidney strain and illness severity. It split the two groups well and stood as a risk factor on its own. Higher levels also linked to higher death rates. In a lab model of kidney cells, blocking the RNA undid much of the injury pattern. A gene it targets was pinned down by a reporter test. The authors propose the RNA for diagnosis and outlook.
pmc-13182276:
Ziyi Yuan and co-authors build in a 2026 study a new kind of X-ray detector that glows with twisted light. Normal detectors give plain, unpolarized glow, so images rest on brightness alone. Their design pairs tiny perovskite crystals with a spiral liquid crystal that steers the glow's twist.

The twist measure passed 0.7, a strong mark, and the device sensed faint X-ray doses with sharp detail. It could read hidden twist patterns under a surface, which suits security marks and medical scans. Live, twist-tuned imaging adds a fresh channel of data to a century-old tool.
pmc-13182376:
Osebo and co-authors track system delays and outcomes for bone and joint trauma care in Tanzania, using a live registry at five hospitals. Road injuries drive much of this trauma, yet data on patterns and delays were scarce. Their 2026 study enrolled patients from mid 2023 to late 2024 and followed early outcomes.

The cohort held 7,121 patients, most of them men, with a median age of 31. Fractures appeared in about seven in ten patients, half of them open wounds. Death within fourteen days hit about eleven in a hundred, and was far higher for open fractures. Transfer between hospitals, rural home, and long prehospital delay each raised death risk. Timely surgery lowered it, the authors found.
pmc-13182576:
Keisuke Ohtani and co-authors present a 2026 case report of nose route brain surgery that freed a man from seizures. A pouch of brain tissue had slipped through the skull base into a sinus near the temple. Such pouches are now a known cause of drug resistant temple epilepsy, yet proof of which tissue sparks the fits is hard to get.

The 41 year old man had fits that drugs could not stop. Scans showed the pouch, and scalp wires pointed to the front temple zone. Through the nose, the team laid depth wires into the pouch and near cortex and saw spikes in both. They cut the pouch plus a small rim of cortex and rebuilt the skull base. He had no harm from the surgery and stayed seizure free for 48 months.
pmc-13182876:
Mariana Girão Carrilho and co-authors present a large literature review, published in 2026, on artificial intelligence in health promotion. Health promotion helps people and communities stay well through behavior change and supportive settings. AI tools promise timely, personal, and scalable help, yet past research has grouped them by technology labels rather than by what they aim to do.

The team used language processing and machine learning to map more than six thousand peer reviewed articles. Topic modeling sorted the field into clusters by purpose, target users, and delivery setting. Three broad settings stood out, with AI tools built into daily life, care services, and wider public programs. Readers get an organized view of a scattered field.
pmc-13182976:
Oskar Szelest and co-authors study how cells repair single-strand DNA breaks across the cell cycle, in a 2026 paper. They image two repair proteins as they gather at a set number of induced breaks. Short-patch repair stayed active through the whole cycle and fixed breaks in over sixty percent of non-dividing cells. Long-patch repair ran in about thirty percent of such cells, paused early in the copying phase, then resumed later.

The team also find a ceiling on the response. If the total breaks induced within seconds pass about 110, no more repair protein is recruited. Within less than a second, a cell commits part of its available protein pool to the damage site. They suggest the cap may come from a limited supply of a tagging molecule.
pmc-13183076:
Shihu Gan and co-authors review plant compounds against lung cancer in this 2026 paper. Non-small cell lung cancer is a top cause of cancer death, and drugs often fail through resistance. A signaling route called PI3K/AKT acts as a hub that drives tumor growth.

The review covers monomers from traditional Chinese medicine that tune this pathway. Some block core parts of the route directly, while others act on receptors above it. Some work through microRNA networks or by raising oxidative stress in tumor cells. Lab evidence for tumor control is strong across many compounds. Gaps in human testing still block clinical use, the authors note.
pmc-13183676:
Heyu Zhao and co-authors reveal how a gene-silencing complex reads its landing sites in a 2026 study. The Rpd3L complex strips chemical tags from histones, the spools DNA wraps around, to keep genes off. How the surrounding chromatin switches its cutting activity on was unclear, so the team froze the complex on its targets for electron microscopy.

Near-atomic images show a lopsided machine gripping two DNA spools at once. One cutting module anchors the first spool while arm-like domains hold the bare DNA between them, swinging the second spool within reach of the far cutting module and waking its dormant activity. Lab tests confirmed that gripping both spools boosts the cutting and widens what it can cut. Promoter control works by this two-point grip.
pmc-13184176:
Limei Jiang and co-authors study pain and low mood in arthritis patients in a 2026 paper. Arthritis brings joint pain and stiffness that limit daily life, and patients face a higher risk of depression. The team used a large Chinese ageing survey to measure how strongly pain links to depressive symptoms.

Among 1,020 patients, those with pain had much higher odds of depressive symptoms than those without. The link was strongest in men, in patients under 65, and in those with less schooling. Several factors protected against low mood: more education, good self-rated health, internet skills, and keeping the ability to do housework. The authors urge clinics to flag high-risk patients early and support both pain control and mental health.
pmc-13185676:
Jiying Ling, Ethan Yaroch, Yingcen Xie, Kenneth Resnicow, and Jennifer Baumgartner present a study dated 2026 on family body measures and preschoolers' social behavior. A child's behavior at school reflects home life, and the team asked whether parents' and children's body and health measures track with how the children act.

Data came from 168 preschoolers, about forty-seven months old, and 154 parents at sixteen Head Start centers in the Midwest. Parents and teachers rated behavior problems and social skills. Trained staff measured height, weight, body fat, skin carotenoids, and parent blood pressure. Children's body mass scores linked positively with teacher-rated social skills. Other links, including parents' body mass with self-centered behavior, were explored in the full analysis.
pmc-13185976:
Karan Khadayat, Morgan House, Vasudeva Tati, and Amit Joshi give a step-by-step protocol for testing whether a protein sticks to a fat membrane, in a 2026 paper. Such sticking drives much of cell metabolism, transport, and signaling.

The method uses purified protein and shop-bought fats formed into bubbles called liposomes. The team shows how to make the bubbles and check their size. Protein and bubbles are layered into a sugar gradient and spun. Bubbles float upward, carrying any stuck protein with them, and the layers are then sampled and read. By changing the fats in the bubbles, the same steps can test many proteins. The protocol points readers to an earlier study for full detail.
pmc-13186076:
Huiyuan Ye and co-authors build a tiny delivery system to treat lupus, an immune disease that attacks many organs, in a paper from 2026. Current drugs can cause harm with long use. The team sought a gentler option that calms inflammation and clears harmful oxidants.

Their system starts with very small particles of a dark polymer. Immune cells of a calming type take the particles in as they mature, then shed them inside small parcels called exosomes. Those parcels carried a rich protein load and entered target cells well. In tests they cut oxidant stress and inflammatory signals better than plain parcels from the same cells. In mice with lupus, kidney damage eased and disease markers fell, with no clear toxicity.
pmc-13186176:
Pfeil and six colleagues give a protocol for preparing mouse bladder and urethra for microscopy in twenty twenty-six. Seeing cells in their three dimensional tissue setting aids understanding. Whole mount preparation keeps the organ intact instead of slicing it. Their method starts with mice perfused through the heart.

Steps cover dissection, tissue clearing, and antibody labelling. Cleared tissue becomes transparent for confocal laser scanning microscopy. Three dimensional processing of the images is also detailed. The protocol suits the urethra and urinary bladder of mice. It lets researchers map cell networks across whole organs. The authors point readers to an earlier study for full usage details.
pmc-13186276:
Takahiro Hadano and two co-authors report a 2026 pilot study from a Japanese university hospital on pain diagnoses that are easy to mix up. Many patients sent in with diagnosed or suspected fibromyalgia may in fact have myofascial pain syndrome, a muscle pain condition with tender trigger points. The team re-read the charts of patients seen from 2018 to 2022 and checked each final diagnosis.

Of the patients in the final set, the large share were judged to have the muscle condition, not fibromyalgia. That group was older, felt less fatigue, and responded better to local care. Yet many also had upper back pain and wide pain, traits linked to fibromyalgia. Careful exams and response to local care may help sort the two apart.
pmc-13186476:
Endobronchial ultrasound lets doctors sample chest lymph nodes through the airways, and a large series asks how safe it is under conscious sedation. Ram and co-authors reviewed 3,454 procedures done over fourteen years at their center. About 2.2 percent of patients had complications, and just 0.3 percent were major. The major events included severe bleeding, two breathing arrests, an infected chest cavity, and one death.

The team also pooled seven large published studies covering 27,560 patients. That analysis put the overall complication rate near 1.2 percent. The authors conclude the procedure is safe, with serious harm rare but real.
pmc-13188076:
Payam Riahi Samani, Ali Hajihashemi, and Ramin Jokari report a rare bowel injury after colon surgery, in work from twenty twenty-six. Most cases of ischemic colitis come from poor artery flow to the bowel. A blocked vein is a much rarer cause, above all after surgery. Their patient was a man in his sixties who had elective removal of the left colon. Six days later he came back with belly pain, cramps, and loose stools.

Scans with contrast dye traced the cause to a blocked vein above the rectum. The bowel wall nearby was swollen and thickened in a ring. Tissue tests confirmed the type, showing dead support tissue and clots in small vessels. Care stayed conservative, with fluids and bowel rest as the core steps. The man recovered fully with no need for a second operation. The case urges teams to check veins when bowel pain follows surgery.
pmc-13189076:
Zhujing Zhu and Huanru Qu report a case linking a VIM gene variant to a rare trio of signs in 2026. The patient is a thirty seven year old man with a skin vessel disease that causes painful leg ulcers. He also shows early gray hair and early cataracts. That trio had not been tied to this gene before.

His mother shares the same three signs, hinting at inheritance. Gene testing found the variant in both mother and son, but not the father. After three months on a drug called tofacitinib, his skin ulcers improved markedly. The authors call the drug result early and in need of more study. The case may widen how this gene's faults are recognized.
pmc-13189476:
Wen-Tao Xiang and co-authors pool decades of studies on brucellosis in Chinese deer, in a 2026 review. The disease harms livestock and spreads to people. Deer farming, especially sika and red deer, has grown fast in China. Reports of infection in deer have risen with it.

Five databases yielded forty-seven studies and 54,699 samples from 1978 to 2025. The pooled share of positive tests was 16.3 percent, with wide variation. Rates climbed after 2000 and ran higher in the northern farming belt. Red deer, adults, and females tested higher than their counterparts. The map helps target testing and control where deer farming is densest.
pmc-13190276:
Chia-Yuan Chang and colleagues audit antibiotic prescribing for migrants in British Columbia, in this population study from twenty twenty-six. Migrants face language and access barriers that can skew care. The team used province-wide health records to grade each outpatient antibiotic course as fitting, maybe fitting, or never fitting its diagnosis.

Prescribing fell by nearly half between the year two thousand and twenty twenty-two, for migrants and non-migrants alike. But migrants still got a higher share of never-fitting prescriptions and a lower share of fitting ones, even after accounting for patient and doctor traits. Bad fits clustered in the youngest patients, the poorest groups, and prescriptions from surgeons and urologists rather than family doctors. The authors say stewardship programs should watch equity, not just totals, and coach the specialties and clinics where poor fits concentrate.
pmc-13190776:
Ahmed and coauthors study word use in young patients with a brain tumor. The tumor sits in the back lower part of the brain. Some patients find it hard to pull up the right word. Few past studies test word skill before surgery or probe speech in depth.

The team tested 38 patients aged about 3 to 18, before and after surgery. Each child named pictures in a timed word game. Scores tracked both right words and speed of speech. The team also sought speech traits that flag who will struggle. Their aim is care that spots word loss early and plans speech help.
pmc-13191276:
Myers and Subramaniam developed signal markers for spotting sleep apnea events in brain recordings. They worked with overnight sleep study data from 25 adults held by a Dublin hospital. Using a nonlinear band-pass filter, they extracted the dominant waveforms tied to apnea events and wrote an equation describing the amplitude part of those waveforms. They then tested how well amplitude and phase features could locate events of different apnea types.

For central sleep apnea events, the method reached about 82 percent sensitivity with about 71 percent specificity and precision. Thresholds marking the start and end of events fit across all apnea groups with a good match. The authors conclude that within the theta frequency band, the amplitude of the brain signal is the main sign of an apnea event, and adding phase sharpens the timing.
pmc-13191776:
Muhi-deen Wonwana Mohammed and co-authors map gaps in proof on control of leishmaniasis, a neglected tropical disease. Their scoping review from 2026 joins global work on spread, tests, and care outcomes. The disease has many forms and a patchy map, and proof on it is split.

The review held 118 studies from work dated 2000 to early 2026. Seventy five of them fed the spread analysis, covering fifty three countries, and the rest fed test and care checks. The skin form was the most wide spread, while the organ form clustered in East Africa, South Asia, and Brazil. Gene based tests beat other tests in the checks. The authors list where trials and field data are still missing.
pmc-13193676:
David Duncker, Henrike Hillmann, and Philipp Sommer introduce the best case reports of 2025 from a heart journal. Their 2026 piece covers the European Heart Journal Case Reports. Case reports rarely give firm proof from numbers. Still, they capture care as doctors live it: one patient, a hard choice, or a rare illness.

Winning cases were picked across the journal's areas. They span rhythm care, heart failure, valve work, and artery work. One told of ablation in a patient in shock with a heart pump in place. Another told of heavy calcium in the heart that led to a transplant. The editors say careful watching and clear writing turn single cases into shared lessons for other doctors.
pmc-13193976:
Qizhi Tan and seven co-authors mapped the worldwide literature on osteoporosis biomarkers as a knowledge graph built with language models, in a 2026 study. They gathered 1,595 core papers from two decades across two major databases. Word embeddings from a large model placed keywords in a semantic space, reducing confusion between terms with several meanings.

Network methods then found nine major research themes and the topics with high promise but low development. Three stood out: inflammation and immunity, detection technology, and gut microbes. Oxidative stress emerged as a bridge concept linking several systems. The graph also flagged rising nodes outside the usual hotspots, including specific RNA molecules and a cell-derived preparation, as candidates for clinical value.
pmc-13194376:
Ayumu Kubaru and Hiroki Murakami ask which side of mindfulness guards against internet addiction in a 2026 paper. Mindfulness training is known to go with lighter internet overuse, but which part helps most was unclear. The team tested 134 Japanese university students with standard tests for addiction tendency and for five mindfulness facets, such as observing, describing, and acting with awareness.

The total score tracked lower addiction scores, as did two facets: non-judging of inner experience and acting with awareness. When all five facets were tested in one model, only acting with awareness stayed a clear predictor. The authors suggest that training aimed at those two facets, above all aware action, may work better against compulsive internet use.
pmc-13194476:
Shuqi Ding and co-authors study how planting density steers sugar use in maize stalks, in work from 2026. Crowded fields change how each plant grows and stores energy. The team grew two maize types at two densities and sampled stalks at two growth stages.

Gene reads and focused chemical tests ran side by side on the stalk samples. As density and stage rose, stalk parts and sugar stores grew, they report, while one key enzyme's work fell. Another enzyme split by maize type. Tens of thousands of genes shifted with type, density, and stage together. Maps of those shifts can guide breeders and farmers who must pick a density that keeps stalks strong without wasting seed or yield.
pmc-13194576:
Huiru Chen and co-authors build machine learning models to predict recovery after stroke clot treatment. Their 2026 study covers patients given a low dose of alteplase between four and a half and nine hours after symptoms began. That late window is riskier, so a good forecast of function at ninety days has real value.

Records came from patients treated between 2019 and 2023, split at random into training and validation sets. A shrinkage method picked the best input traits, and five learning algorithms were compared. Judging used accuracy curves, calibration, and a tool that shows which traits drive each prediction. Two hundred two patients took part, and poor outcomes were common in both sets.
pmc-13195376:
Public health teams need small-area counts of disease, and electronic health records may offer a sharper lens than the census. The authors compare three sources for Minnesota: records from a statewide health consortium, the 2020 census, and the CDC's PLACES small-area estimates. The consortium's records cover 5.27 million people, about 92 percent of the census count. Coverage ratios vary: women and older adults are captured at or above parity, while children and American Indian residents fall well below.

For disease rates, the record-based figures put adult diabetes at 9.5 percent and hypertension at 32.2 percent, close to the PLACES figures of 9.9 and 29.9 percent. Agreement at the census-tract level is weaker, with only about 40 percent of tracts landing near the PLACES values. The authors conclude that health records can complement census data for local planning, while warning that tract-level estimates still diverge often.
pmc-13195776:
Shakhawat Tanim and co-authors showed in 2026 that math can nearly double the reach of mobile health clinics without adding a single vehicle. They studied a South Carolina program screening for hepatitis C. A location model chose parking spots that maximized uninsured residents within a five-minute drive or ten-minute walk of each stop.

Optimized sites expanded the covered population by about ninety percent for drivers and 135 percent for walkers. Overlap between stops shrank and average travel times fell. In rural areas, bigger coverage clearly meant more clinic use. Small shifts in where a clinic parks made outsized differences. The team applied the framework with local partners to guide real deployments, and offers it as a reusable planning tool.
pmc-13196176:
Mustafa Al-jarshawi and colleagues offer a 2026 projection for oral semaglutide in the United States. Semaglutide is a drug for type 2 diabetes that also protects the heart. The team applied results from the SOUL trial to national survey data to estimate broad impact.

They estimate about six point one million adults would qualify for the drug. Over four and a half years, wide use could prevent about 118,664 major heart events. Those events include heart-related death, heart attack, and stroke. Gains held across sex and race groups. Even at half uptake, tens of thousands of events could be avoided. The authors argue that better access could bring large public gains.
pmc-13196476:
Madhan Kumar Murthy, Vivek Kumar Gupta, and Anand Prakash Maurya review diagnosis of non-tuberculous mycobacterial infections in a 2026 article. These germs live widely in the environment and strike people with weak immunity or lung damage. Lung disease from them can scar tissue and lead to breathing failure. Early diagnosis is key to good care.

Current tests have clear limits, the authors note. Metabolomics, the study of small chemicals in the body, may fill some gaps. Artificial intelligence can sharpen those chemical methods further. The review weighs the promise and the hurdles, and sketches how the combined approach could move into practice.
pmc-13196776:
Jian Wang and co-authors present a battery fluid that revives dead lithium, in this 2026 paper. Lithium metal batteries promise high energy, but spiky growths called dendrites and crusts of dead lithium shorten their life. The team suspended tiny catalytic particles, each holding single cobalt atoms on zinc oxide, in a standard battery fluid.

The particles eased lithium ions out of their solvent shells, so plating came out smooth and dense. Test cells ran sixteen hundred hours, and a full cell kept nearly all its capacity over a thousand cycles in the cold. The authors frame the fluid as a practical route to durable lithium metal cells.
pmc-13197376:
Albrecht Lindemann and colleagues report a 2026 case series on stopping leukemia therapy after remission. Older patients with acute myeloid leukemia often get two drugs long term until the disease returns. Past work hints that stopping in deep remission may not hurt survival, so the team offered a fixed six-month course.

Seven patients reached full remission and chose to stop therapy. Five cleared their mutation traces to very low levels. Six of the seven stay in remission, from seven to fifty months so far. One patient relapsed after fourteen months and regained remission once therapy resumed. The authors suggest time-limited therapy may suit select patients, though the group is tiny.
pmc-13197476: Xiaoming Wang and colleagues issued a 2026 author correction to a study on forecasting the strength of permeable cement road base. The original source data file was an older, less complete version. The notice explains how one figure's results were built, adding nine outside strength values to three lab values for one mix design. It gives the full value list, the mean and spread used, and why a population formula was chosen for that larger set.
pmc-13197676:
Martin Schwer and six co-authors present a 2026 study of a second generation library of small chemical fragments that bond permanently to proteins. Such fragments can reach pockets that normal drugs cannot, including flat or hidden sites. A well profiled library saves discovery teams months of screening.

The new library holds 81 fragments across five reactive classes, from epoxides to sulfur reactive rings. The team measured each fragment's physical traits and its speed of reaction with sulfur groups, a common anchor in proteins. One test case revived a broken tumor suppressor protein, p53, in its mutant form. The paper reports which fragments reacted cleanly and which were too hot.
pmc-13199876:
Sarah Schulenberg, Michelle Loeser, and Michael Schmueck-Henneresse (2026) publish a protocol for profiling CAR T cell products, the engineered immune cells used against cancer. Judging a product takes more than counting cells: makers need to know what the cells are and how well they kill. The workflow combines two views. One is full-spectrum flow cytometry with thirty-three markers, which reads each cell's identity. The other is live-cell imaging of serial tumor killing, watching them attack target after target.

The protocol walks through preparing the cells, staining them with antibodies, running the cytometer, setting up the killing assay, and analyzing data streams. It is written so other laboratories can reproduce the pipeline, and the authors note it adapts to other engineered T cell therapies. Standardized profiling matters because these drugs vary by batch, and clinics need comparable measures of potency.
pmc-13200676:
Yu Fu and co-authors run a trial of a new pain drug against oxycodone after womb removal by keyhole surgery. Their trial from 2026 deals with post surgery pain and sickness, both common in this operation. The new drug acts on the same receptor as classic opioids but in a biased way, which may keep pain relief with fewer side effects.

The plan enrolls sixty six women at one center, split by chance between the two drugs in a blind design. Each drug is given by vein twenty minutes before the end of surgery, at a set dose by weight. Checks over two days cover sickness rates and grades, pain relief success, and blood pressure at set times. Standard anesthesia and surgery apply to all.
pmc-13200976:
Xun Huang and co-authors mapped two decades of research on college student suicide with bibliometric tools. They gathered 2,262 publications from 2002 to 2022 and charted who publishes, where, and on what themes. Output grew fast and may keep growing steeply. The United States led the field, and the ten most productive institutions were all American, yet cooperation between institutions was weak. Two journals carried the most work in the area.

Hot topics included suicidal thoughts, prevention, medical students, mental health, stigma, and mobile health approaches. The most published and most cited authors were identified for newcomers. The authors conclude that interest in student suicide research is rising, but the field needs stronger collaboration across countries, institutions, and authors. Their maps are meant to guide researchers choosing directions, showing both the crowded centers and the thinly studied edges of the field.
pmc-13202076:
Dementia care research rarely asks which questions matter most to affected families, and a 2026 plan by Elena Michel sets up a partnership to do exactly that. The plan presents GenderDem, a priority setting study on diversity-sensitive psychosocial programs for behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia.

Following the James Lind Alliance approach, people with dementia, caregivers, and health professionals will serve together on a steering group as co-researchers. Two rounds of online surveys will gather and rank candidate research questions from wider participants, supported by a literature review. A final workshop will settle a top ten list meant to guide future dementia care research funding.
pmc-13202276:
Zohaib Khurshid and co-authors prepare camel dentin as a graft material in a 2026 paper. Stripping mineral from dentin leaves a collagen scaffold rich in growth proteins, prized for bone repair. Camel teeth offer a fresh source. Granules are soaked for a day in two acids at varied strengths: EDTA and citric acid. Microscopy, element scans, and light based chemistry checks grade the result.

Treated dentin turns porous and rough, a sign of mineral loss, they report. Calcium and phosphorus levels drop sharply. Spectra confirm phosphate and carbonate bands fade while protein bands grow. The team weighs which acid mix best readies camel dentin for dental tissue engineering.
pmc-13202476:
Martina Vachtlová and ten co-authors make six new light-switch compounds in a 2026 chemistry paper. The compounds are halogenated azobenzene acrylates, which change shape when light hits them. Adding fluorine, chlorine, or bromine atoms lets chemists tune how they switch. The team made the compounds in three steps and tested them in depth.

Single-halogen types switched best in liquid, with up to 93 percent shape change. Types with two halogens switched less, due to their bent shape. One fluorine type kept a clear color change in a plastic film for over 90 days. The team says halogen choice is a strong tool for tuning such materials. Uses may include heat sensors that change color and light-run devices.
pmc-13202676:
One molecule hitting two cancer targets is the design goal of a 2026 study by Joydeep Chatterjee, which synthesizes eighteen new imidazoquinoxaline compounds. The research article uses a Pictet-Spengler route to build carboxamide-bearing molecules aimed at both the EGFR growth signal and the tubulin skeleton of cells.

Two compounds beat the approved drug erlotinib against breast cancer cells in culture and blocked EGFR enzyme activity at low concentrations. One of them also stabilized microtubules much like paclitaxel, raised reactive oxygen species, and arrested cells before division. Docking and dynamics simulations showed both compounds sitting stably in the two target pockets, supporting the dual-action design.
pmc-13202976:
Matthew Chen and four co-authors use language models to sort mild from severe symptoms in cancer patients on radiation care. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Symptom watch during and after such care is key, but past machine tools cost much to retrain and give no clear reasons.

They frame the task as anomaly spotting and write six prompts with a chance-based design. The models read scant patient data and call each symptom mild or severe. Tests on prostate patients cover bowel pain, low mood, and sexual trouble. Scores are checked by standard marks and charts, and sample reason chains are shown so staff can see how a call was made. The path offers live, explainable watch.
pmc-13203076:
Huanhuan Zhou and five co-authors published a pig study in twenty twenty-six on a gene that helps muscle stem cells turn into muscle. The cells came from week-old piglets and were grown in dishes. The gene, TEAD4, rose step by step as the cells matured, in step with known muscle genes.

When the team shut the gene off, the cells still grew at the same pace. But they failed to fuse into muscle tubes, and their muscle genes stayed low. Gene-wide reads pointed to energy balance as the weak spot, with one energy-sensing path turned up too high. The authors say TEAD4 keeps the cells' energy use in tune while they build muscle, a hint for both farm and basic science.
pmc-13203876:
Fernandes, Fernandes, and Gehrke set out a score tool in twenty twenty-six to guess if a tooth implant will do well before surgery. Implants last long in most cases, but body, habit, and build flaws still cause strife. Their tool sums six fields into a score out of one hundred.

Fields cover body health, habits, hard jaw bone, soft gum, the implant, and the false tooth plan. High scores mean a bright outlook and low scores mean high risk. Chart views let a dentist read the result at a glance. The tool is a design plan for now and needs clinic tests to prove it.
pmc-13204876:
Jonas Wallinder and co-authors ask whether gene traits tied to belly artery swell split by sex. The study appeared in 2026. The swell is far more common in men than in women. Smoke and such can part-way tell why, but kin risk hints genes play a role too.

The case set held women and men with the swell plus matched peers. Thirteen gene spots were read, picked from past work and from paths tied to sex salts. Two spots split firm by sex in the full model. One spot sat in the start zone of a gene whose blood levels tied to the swell. No spot split in both sexes at once.
pmc-13205476:
Vanessa Talavera-Cobo and co-authors put data care first in a small neural test for prostate cancer risk, in a proof study from 2026. Risk class steers all care in this ill, and a wrong class costs dear. Smart tools could help, but small banks make them shaky.

The crew built a strict care frame for the bank: checks for truth, fit, and form till the rows were AI-ready. From 76 souls, the frame kept a clean 49. A plain net then learned risk from eleven facts, tried at three train-test splits. The pitch is the frame, not the net: grade the rows ere you grade the tool, and small banks can still bear fair proof.
pmc-13206176:
Daiyi Zhao, Kaiyue Bi, Dongsheng Niu, Xuewen Li, and Feng Li track how 'French' plums change as they ripen. Plums are sold fresh, but softening and rot after harvest cost growers money. The team read fruit at six stages of growth, checking firmness, sugars, acids, color, and health-linked compounds. Firmness fell as fruit ripened, while sugars rose and acids dropped. Skin moved from green to deep purple-red.

Two health-linked compounds peaked mid-way, before the skin turned. At the purple stage the fruit struck the best balance of sweet, tart, and firm. At full ripeness the walls of the fruit cells broke down. The paper pins the best stage to pick and eat.
pmc-13206576:
Engineers predict when a wearing part will fail by watching it degrade, often under stress tests that speed the wear up. Li and Yan propose a model for that job built on a generalized Wiener process, a random-walk style description of decline. The drift of the walk depends on stress, and its noisiness is allowed to differ from unit to unit through random effects.

Parameters are fitted with an expectation-maximization algorithm. From the fitted model, the authors derive the full distribution of failure times under normal use, not just an average life. They test the model on simulated crack growth and on real wear-scar measurements from an alloy product. Predictions of lifetime and reliability sharpened against simpler models. The authors offer the framework for industries that must schedule replacement before failure, from machinery to electronics.
pmc-13206676:
Fatma Soylu Çakmak, Yeliz Yıldırım Varışoğlu, and Meserret Aslan study menopause symptoms, faith-based coping, and resilience in a 2026 paper. They asked whether resilience, the ability to bounce back from strain, carries the effect of religious coping onto how strong symptoms feel. The study surveyed postmenopausal women in Türkiye aged forty-five to sixty.

Negative religious coping, such as feeling punished, went with lower resilience. Resilience itself did not link clearly to symptom strength, and positive coping showed no clear link to resilience either. The model explained only a small share of why symptoms differ. No carrying effect of resilience was found. The authors say symptoms likely depend more on body and life context, and they urge studies that follow women over time.
pmc-13207176:
Rui Mao and co-authors published a research paper in 2026 on emodin, a plant compound that protected fatty livers at one dose yet harmed healthy livers at a higher one. The team gave three doses to mice with metabolic fatty liver disease and to normal mice, then profiled tissue, blood chemistry, metabolites, and gut microbes.

A middle dose gave the best liver protection in diseased mice, while the top dose visibly damaged normal livers. The split tracked changes in gut microbe products that feed the liver, plus shifts in cell-death balance genes. The authors propose the gut-liver axis as the likely switch and the middle dose as the plausible therapeutic window.
pmc-13207576:
Esmeralda Melgoza, Madeline Feldmeier, and their co-authors studied why ambulances wait at emergency department doors in California. Their 2026 paper measures offload time, the gap between ambulance arrival and transfer of care, across 310 emergency departments. The data predate a state law that set reduction targets.

Records came from the state EMS authority, local agencies, and a health care data department. The main measure was the time within which ninety percent of transfers finish. A selection method picked predictors, and count models weighed them. Urban sites and departments with more treatment stations waited longer. Predicted times ran from about ten to nineteen minutes at rural sites and nineteen to thirty nine minutes at urban ones. The findings frame the policy debate.
pmc-13208376:
Yuhan Li, Henggen Zhang, and Xujiayin Zhao turn tunnel-boring waste into a durable building material. Their 2026 study tackles shield tunnel spoil, the soil dug out by tunneling machines. They set the spoil with a low-carbon binder made partly from industrial waste, and stir in basalt fibers to toughen it. The team then cycled the samples between wet and dry states to mimic weather wear.

At the best dose, fibers lifted early strength by about 13 percent and slowed cracking as cycles mounted. Scans after eight cycles showed one percent fiber cut pore volume by 54.3 percent and crack volume by 63.2 percent. Damage came from binder loss as water moved, plus swelling and shrinking of clay minerals. The fiber web held the material together by pulling out slowly and soaking up energy.
pmc-13209476:
Evidence favors cemented hip implants for broken femoral necks, yet surgeons rarely use them, and a 2026 study authored by Hamed Tayyebi quantifies the gap. The retrospective cohort covers 4,407 patients over fifty who received partial hip replacement for intracapsular fractures across a hospital system between 2009 and 2018.

Only about one patient in nine received a cemented implant, despite cemented cases showing significantly fewer fractures around the implant during and after surgery. Surgeon background predicted the choice: trauma specialists used cement far more often than arthroplasty specialists in the data. The authors call the mismatch a stubborn evidence-practice gap needing stronger guideline uptake.
pmc-13209576:
Yin Shang, Fengqin Li, and Chunhong Yang model electric-driven flow of an elastic fluid in a tiny channel in a paper from 2026. The channel walls carry a polymer brush and a charge pattern that varies along them. A time-varying electric field drives the fluid, a Maxwell fluid with spring-like behavior. The team solves the governing equations with a superposition method. They track how oscillation strength, elasticity, and electric parameters shape speed and solute spread.

Wall charge patterns plus the pulsing field create swirling, back-and-forth motion. Moderate pulsing boosts both flow and transport. Stronger pulsing, though, makes transport less efficient. The results give design guidance for lab-on-chip devices that move samples electrically.
pmc-13210176:
HIV infections among people who inject drugs in Kyrgyzstan have fallen sharply, and a 2026 modeling study authored by Ainura Moldokmatova asks what really drove the drop. The research article runs a deterministic compartmental model under three scenarios, switching needle programs, substitution therapy, prevention, and antiretroviral treatment on and off.

The simulations point to a shrinking population of people who inject drugs as the main engine of the decline. Prevention programs and treatment still reduced the overall burden meaningfully, the model suggests, even if they were not the primary trend drivers. Reported case patterns, meanwhile, likely mirror changing testing behavior more than true swings in new infections.
pmc-13210576:
Meimei Luo and co-authors profile a medicinal plant's leaves across the seasons, in a study published in 2026. The plant's stems are widely used, but its leaves are thrown away as farm waste. The team asked what useful compounds the leaves hold, when they peak, and whether any could calm swelling.

Leaves picked at six times of year held about 6,750 distinct compounds, rich in building blocks and in plant defense chemicals. The six harvests fell into three seasonal stages, and winter leaves were richest in the defense group. Computer screening picked eighty-three likely active compounds and mapped how they might act on swelling pathways, with lab-style docking checks. The authors say the leaves deserve use rather than the waste pile, with winter harvests the prize.
pmc-13212876:
Douglas V. D'Agati and Donald C. D'Agati write in 2026 an essay on living well with a bipolar temperament, drawn from the lives of six exceptional historical figures. Their subjects, who lived before psychiatric medicines existed, achieved greatly while suffering severe depressions.

The figures range from Samuel Johnson and Winston Churchill to explorer Meriwether Lewis and physician William Osler. Five of them wrote down lessons from their experience in strikingly similar terms. Each, the authors argue, found rescue in total commitment to a demanding, absorbing, spiritually satisfying challenge. That devotion seemed to both soothe and prevent depressive collapses, for reasons science still cannot fully explain.
pmc-13213076:
Cong Gao and co-authors review in 2026 how a nerve-signalling molecule called CGRP steers immune behaviour throughout the body. Sensory nerves release this peptide where they meet immune cells, shaping defence against microbes, tumour control, and the steady state of barrier tissues such as skin and gut.

Effects swing with context: the microbe involved, the tissue niche, and other signals present all change what the peptide does. The review dissects how different cell types decode its message through receptor variants and switching adaptor proteins. Drugs that block or mimic the signal, including antibodies already used for migraine, may treat inflammatory disease or cancer. Two puzzles, a receptor code and feedback loops with microbes, await answers.
pmc-13213276:
A Dutch priority-setting partnership led by Carsten F J Bakhuis presents a two thousand twenty-six agenda for research on breast cancer in pregnancy. The condition is rare but rising. Diagnosis often comes late, and care involves hard choices for mother and baby.

Patients, clinicians, and researchers met in moderated focus groups. Lived experience guided the talks, held in a questioning dialogue style. Participants then submitted research questions and ranked them by weighted voting. The result is a shared list of what science should answer next. Funders get priorities set by the people most affected.
pmc-13213476:
Rezvan Rajabzadeh, Seyed Hamid Hosseini, and Aioub Sofizadeh forecast a skin disease carried by sand flies in one Iranian county, in a 2025 study. Zoonotic cutaneous leishmaniasis is entrenched in Maraveh Tappeh County, and its case counts swing with the weather. The team gathered sixteen years of monthly cases, 1,301 in all, alongside temperature, humidity, and rainfall records, and fitted time series models that allow for seasons.

Cases peaked in November and bottomed out in June. One combined ARIMA-SARIMA model predicted the monthly pattern best, and climate factors linked to cases at lags of up to five months. The authors offer the model as a planning tool for local control programs.
pmc-13213676:
A bikini-line scar hides better than a long one, but hip surgeons worry about wound trouble in the fold. William Crockatt and co-authors reviewed nine hundred twenty-five front-approach hip replacements in three flavors: standard long incision, bikini incision, and long incision with a single-use tissue protector. Overall, four percent of wounds had complications, nearly all superficial, and under one percent needed a return to the operating room.

Raw rates favored bikini and protected incisions over the plain long cut, though adjusting for the surgeon narrowed the story. The large series reassures patients who prefer the discreet scar.
pmc-13214876:
Anna Popova and a large team of co-authors measure immunity to hepatitis A and E in Belgrade's population. Their study appeared in 2026. In May 2024 they tested blood from 2,533 healthy volunteers for antibodies showing past infection or vaccination. Recruitment was voluntary and online, so women and middle-aged adults are overrepresented and children scarce; the authors warn the rates cannot be read as the whole city's.

The hepatitis E estimate rests on a single test without confirmation, a second stated limit. Within those bounds, antibody rates were linked to age, social, and clinical factors. The authors say even an imperfect snapshot helps target vaccination and food and water safety where immunity is thin.
pmc-13214976:
Ning Song and co-authors dissect in 2026 single cells from osteosarcoma, a bone cancer whose spread to distant organs drives most deaths. They hunted for the molecular switch that lets tumour cells migrate and invade.

Ten cell clusters emerged, with immune cells more plentiful in metastatic samples, and five malignant subpopulations appeared on closer inspection. One gene, BAMBI, faded as tumours shifted from contained to spreading states. A regulator called JUN seems to control it, and losing BAMBI unleashes a growth pathway that boosts movement and invasion. Checks in a public dataset and in cell experiments backed the chain. The pair offers candidate targets against metastasis.
pmc-13215576:
Hanna Lagerlund and co-authors present a 2026 qualitative study of staying active after a mobile health program for people recovering from stroke or transient ischemic attack. The question was what helps or hinders activity once structured support ends.

Twelve participants were interviewed twice, three and six months after the program, and shared photographs that captured their daily activity between interviews. Three themes emerged around building knowledge, coping within a complicated life situation, and the role of surroundings. Participants used personal strategies and social support to stay active despite health barriers. The authors compare sustained activity to a soap bubble that needs both persistence and a supportive environment.
pmc-13215976:
Dongsu Lee and Wonseuk Jang present a 2026 survey study of what makes Korean internet users willing to share health data they generate themselves, such as readings from wearables. Two privacy theories frame the analysis.

The authors modelled responses from 4,518 people in a national 2023 panel survey. Perceived risk was the strongest brake on sharing and perceived benefit the strongest push, with moral motivation and interpersonal trust adding smaller effects. Digital literacy cut both ways: the understanding side of it lowered perceived risk, while heavier use raised risk concerns. The authors recommend trust-based, user-centred strategies as digital health services expand.
pmc-13216376:
Gobinath Rajendran and co-authors present a 2026 study of nano zinc oxide as a leaf spray for rice growing in zinc-deficient soil. Zinc shortage limits rice yields and leaves grain low in a nutrient people need.

The starting point is the weakness of conventional zinc fertilisers, which crops use at under five percent efficiency. Nano zinc oxide particles, highly reactive and readily taken up, are proposed as a more effective carrier of the nutrient. The study set out to compare how well this foliar nano treatment performs, with yield, the plant's antioxidant defence, and the zinc content of the crop as the outcomes in view. The work speaks to fertiliser strategies for zinc-poor soils.
pmc-13216676:
Sinda Zarrouk and Josef Finsterer question a case report's diagnosis in a 2026 letter to the editor. The original report blamed a mild Chiari malformation for a spinal fluid cavity spanning a woman's whole cord after tuberculosis. The letter writers find that explanation too thin and press for missing workup details.

A mild Chiari rarely fills the entire cord, they argue, and recent tuberculosis is itself a rare cause that must be excluded with fluid tests and cultures. They also flag an internal contradiction about the patient's standing and walking, and ask why arm weakness stayed absent when the cavity ran strongest in the neck. The letter asks the original team to answer before the cause is settled.
pmc-13217476:
Meihua Xiong, Yong Luo, and Shiping Hu build, in twenty twenty-six, a prognostic signature for head and neck squamous cell carcinoma from single-cell and bulk gene data. This cancer is highly varied, with poor prognosis and uneven therapy response. Good biomarkers are scarce. The team dissected the tumor microenvironment with single-cell data, and found gene modules tied to lesion progression using network analysis. Those modules merged with differential expression and genomic data. Many machine learning models were tried for prognosis; the best was validated in independent cohorts.

A nomogram combined the risk score with clinical features, showing high predictive accuracy. High-risk tumors showed more hypoxia, sugar-burning, and invasion programs, plus greater genomic instability. Immune profiling of the risk groups followed.
pmc-13218176:
Cilia Naaman and co-authors hunt for genetic variants that influence both kidney filtration and albumin leakage, in a 2026 large-scale European study. Chronic kidney disease is a major burden, especially in type 2 diabetes, and its two markers are the estimated filtration rate and the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio. Earlier work mapped genes for each marker separately, leaving their shared genetic basis unclear.

Using 432,451 UK Biobank participants, mostly of European descent, the team tested 423 variants previously tied to filtration rate for links to both markers. A subgroup of 16,265 people with type 2 diabetes was analyzed separately. Nearly all the variants related to filtration, 75 also related to albuminuria at a loose threshold, and twelve survived strict correction. In the diabetes subgroup only one variant survived correction. Two shared loci, near the genes GSTA2 and USP2-AS1, hinted at effects specific to diabetes, pointing to common pathways behind both kidney markers.
pmc-13218476:
Aboa Paul Koffi and a field team report active case-finding surveys for yaws across fifteen districts of Côte d'Ivoire in a 2026 public health study. Yaws is a neglected tropical disease tied to poverty in hot, humid regions, and children bear most of the burden. Côte d'Ivoire is among the few countries where yaws remains endemic, and planners needed its extent measured to aim at eradication.

Teams visited 3,870 villages and hamlets across 345 areas, examining children aged two to fifteen in schools and households, targeting nearly half a million children. About sixty-six thousand children had skin lesions. Rapid tests flagged 291 yaws cases, and a confirmatory dual test verified 146, most of them children aged five to fourteen. Traumatic wounds and fungal infections were more common than yaws itself. Treating confirmed cases with single-dose azithromycin on the spot, the survey gives the country a map for the eradication plan.
pmc-13219376:
He-Xue Yuan and six co-authors frame age-split care for kids' rear abscess care on a growth heal line. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-six. Such sores are common yet thin known, and kids' soft cloth and age-split heal ways make calls hard. Cut and drain gives fast ease but may raise the risk of a fist path, most in old kids.

Drug and watch care oft works in babes and young kids, whose heal force runs high. Age splits in shield acts, germ mix, and gland form steer the course. The team urge age-fit plans and name gaps for set rules.
pmc-13220576:
Xiaoman Suo, Yingnan Liu, Guofang Zhang, and Yang Li write a 2026 perspective on why cancer immunotherapy keeps stalling before the clinic. Marrying nanoparticles to immune therapy promises precise, safer cancer treatment, and animal studies deliver. Human translation, though, is throttled by problems that appear inside a body.

The authors organize the obstacles as a barrier-strategy framework. A protein corona coats nanoparticles in blood and rewrites their identity. Tumor barriers blunt how well the drugs act once delivered, and how the body metabolizes and excretes the particles decides long-term safety. Against each barrier they set strategies: designing from mechanism rather than trial and error, artificial intelligence assistance in optimization, delivery systems, and safety-by-design from the first sketch. Their roadmap asks the field to invest in integrated technologies, translational models, and scalable manufacturing, arguing that nanoimmunotherapy's clinical potential will not realize itself.
pmc-13220776:
Chaowei Wang, Yunqing Mao, Shuo Wang, Li Liu, and Guang Yao test whether three blood markers can jointly predict sleep trouble after stroke. Sleep disorders strike many patients after an acute ischemic stroke and slow recovery. Their 2026 study drew on 256 patients, split by sleep quality scores a week after onset. Blood taken at admission was checked for hypocretin, a nerve fiber marker, and an inflammation marker.

About sixty-three percent of patients had sleep disorders. Nine traits raised the risk on their own, among them age, snoring, and prior stroke. Each marker alone predicted sleep trouble fairly; the three together did far better. Re-sampling checks kept the score high. The authors offer the panel as a tool to flag high-risk patients early.
pmc-13221876:
Pelliccia and a large registry team compare two drug plans after a heart valve procedure in twenty twenty-six. The procedure, called TAVR, places a new aortic valve through a leg vessel. Guidelines advise one antiplatelet drug for most patients after the procedure. Two drugs may raise bleeding risk, but past data on death rates were mixed.

The registry held more than ten thousand patients, and the study kept five thousand five hundred fourteen for review. One group left the hospital on one drug, and the other left on two drugs. Death and major bleeding at six months were lower with one drug. The gap in deaths was still present at two years. The authors link two drugs with higher death risk at both time points.
pmc-13221976:
Yoshitaka Yamamoto and co-authors review heart valve surgery in patients with brain bleeding in a 2026 study. The patients had infective endocarditis, a heart valve infection that can send clots and bleeding to the brain. Surgeons must weigh the risk of operating soon after a brain bleed against the danger of delay.

The team reviewed 54 valve surgeries from 2015 to 2024, focusing on 13 patients with bleeding inside the skull. Those cases ranged from tiny microbleeds to larger hemorrhages. Surgery came after a median of one day for microbleeds and twenty days for larger bleeds. After surgery, bleeding worsened in three patients, and one patient died in hospital, though no death was blamed on brain complications. The authors map how timing varied by bleed size.
pmc-13222176:
Cher-Hui Koh and co-authors compare two single-incision routes for minimal access nipple-sparing mastectomy, in a 2026 retrospective study from one institute. Operations between 2012 and 2025 used either an armpit crease incision or a lateral chest wall incision, by endoscopic or robotic technique. The series held 371 cases, split between the two placements.

For endoscopic surgery, the chest wall route cut operating time by nearly an hour on average. Robotic cases showed no such time difference. Delayed wound healing was more common with the chest wall incision, while pain, sensation, and satisfaction reports were comparable. Both routes remain viable, with trade-offs surgeons can match to the patient.
pmc-13222376:
Harshitha B. Tyagaraj and co-authors build a cobalt-based nanomaterial into a sensor for the antibiotic nitrofurantoin, in a 2026 study. The hybrid mixes a metal-organic framework with nitrogen and selenium, forming mixed rods and sheets rich in active sites. Such trace drugs pollute water and food chains, so sensitive testing matters.

The sensor found nitrofurantoin down to about one nanomolar, with a strong response per unit area. Repeat runs agreed closely, and common background compounds barely disturbed readings. Spiked environmental and body samples gave accurate results. Fast charge transfer through the doped material explains the results, suggesting a practical tool for tracking this drug outside the lab.
pmc-13222976:
Casey Aveggio and co-authors set out a 2026 framework for pairing new tools in life science with safety. Artificial intelligence now helps design and test biological work at high speed, but the same speed raises the risk of misuse. The authors argue that safety and progress should be built together, not traded off against each other.

Three case studies show where joint funding can pay off. Shared data systems can open access while guarding sensitive files. Tracking the source and history of AI-made tools can aid both review and repeat work. Tests that grade tool skill can lift quality while warning of rising risk. The paper closes with funding and policy steps to support this shared approach.
pmc-13223076:
Jared Wilsey and eight co-authors set out a safety frame for medical tools that rot in the body in a 2026 paper. Such tools, made of polymers that break down, defy the usual lab playbook. The standard full-soak test fails, since the tool falls apart in the very fluids used to strip its parts.

Their frame starts by counting each polymer in the tool, then takes the worst case: full break-down into its base bricks. A vessel closure tool made of a three-part polymer serves as the test case. The frame ties dose to break-down speed, for fair risk calls.
pmc-13223976:
Juan Zhang and colleagues investigate a 2026 ovarian cancer study on why tumours stop responding to cisplatin, a widely used chemotherapy drug. Attention falls on ESM1, a gene whose activity rises in resistant cells. The team combined earlier sequencing data with protein-interaction measurements to trace what ESM1 controls.

Experiments in cells, including electron microscopy, showed that a small heat-shock protein called HSPB1 sits at the centre of the resistance effect. ESM1 binds the ERBB2 receptor and raises HSPB1 production, switching on FAK, SRC, and NF-kB signalling. That chain blocks ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death, and helps cancer cells survive cisplatin exposure.
pmc-13224376:
Raimunde Liang and colleagues evaluate a 2026 hospital study of a scanning method for spinal infections, a condition called spondylodiscitis that is very hard to confirm. Symptoms are vague, standard MRI can be inconclusive, and the original source of infection often stays hidden. The scan in question uses a radioactive sugar tracer that lights up active tissue.

Records covered 191 patients scanned for suspected spinal infection between 2016 and 2023, with infection confirmed in 160 of them. When MRI was unclear, the scan changed the diagnosis in nearly half the cases. Combined with MRI, detection improved further, and the whole-body view uncovered 23 previously unknown infection sites elsewhere, helping guide treatment.
pmc-13226976:
Tyler J Snow and colleagues reanalyse a 2026 trial dataset from active-duty service members with chronic pain, testing a urine marker of oxidative DNA damage as a signal of recovery. Participants completed a six-week interdisciplinary pain programme and gave urine samples at the start and end. Sleep-related function and physical abilities, including treadmill and lifting tests, were tracked alongside.

Function and sleep both improved during the programme, while the damage marker fell. Falling marker levels went with better sleep-related function at three and six weeks, and changes in physical function also tracked the marker's movement. The authors present the marker as a candidate objective companion to self-reported recovery, though the analysis was exploratory and used a lenient significance threshold.
pmc-13227176:
Kyoko Yamamoto and colleagues present a 2026 emergency case in which a painless cheek abscess turned out to be cervicofacial actinomycosis, a slow bacterial infection known for forming drainage channels. A woman in her seventies was found immobile at home after an estimated six days and arrived with a broken thigh bone. Staff noticed red, swollen skin over her right cheek, yet she felt no pain there.

Scans showed a gas-containing abscess under the cheek skin, and mouth examination revealed poor oral hygiene plus a fistula leaking pus. Cultures grew Actinomyces alongside three other bacteria, pointing to a dental source. Treatment combined surgical drainage with a long antibiotic course, planned at six months, reflecting how stubbornly this infection can persist.
pmc-13230076:
Guangyu Chen and Jinyuan He study digital skills and health gaps in China in a 2026 paper. As daily life moves online, people with weak digital skills may fall behind in health as well. Access alone no longer tells the whole story once most people are connected.

Survey data from a 2023 national Chinese sample drive the analysis. Digital literacy linked positively to both physical and mental self-rated health. The link survived controls for schooling, income, and social status. It ran stronger for mental health than for physical health. Among people already online, skill level still separated health outcomes. The authors argue policy should build capability, not just access, to narrow health gaps.
pmc-13231776:
Maria Madeleine Ruthrich and colleagues study in 2026 how sex and stress shape common cold and flu-like illness in two groups. One group held two hundred seventy-three healthy adults, while the other held one hundred ninety-four stem cell transplant patients. Everyone reported airway symptoms and stress on a short standard scale.

Healthy women reported worse symptoms and higher stress than healthy men, with stress tracking symptoms only lightly. The patient group flipped the symptom gap, with men reporting more symptoms than women. Stress there tracked symptom load closely, most of all in women, and stress levels barely differed by sex. Illness burden itself predicted stress in patients, so support should fit health status rather than sex alone.
pmc-13231876:
Xiaoqiu Wu and colleagues study in 2026 how body appreciation shapes weight control habits in overweight teenagers. Two hundred ninety-four students aged thirteen to sixteen from three schools filled in scales on body appreciation, weight control practices, and daily lifestyle. Eighty-six students fell in the overweight or obese range by body mass index.

Overweight students scored lower on body appreciation and on healthy weight control habits, yet higher on unhealthy habits. Model testing showed body appreciation linked to lower body mass both directly and through healthier habits. A therapy-based promotion model built on those links fit the data well. School programs that rebuild body respect may steer habits better than weight lectures alone.
pmc-13232876:
Yuhang Liu and colleagues review in 2026 how gut microbes in obesity can damage the tiny vessels feeding the heart muscle. Coronary microvascular dysfunction blunts blood-flow reserve and seeds later heart disease, and obese patients show sharply reduced reserve. The gut-heart route runs through chemicals that microbes make from food and from the gut wall itself.

One metabolite drives fat deposition and inflammation, while falling short-chain fatty acids weaken vessel lining control. Bile acids tune vessel tone, bacterial wall fragments spark body-wide low-grade inflammation, and several newer metabolites speed hardening or clotting. Each pathway suggests a matching countermeasure, from blocking a metabolite to targeted diets. Trials built on these mechanisms are the stated next step.
pmc-13233276:
First-year medical school can wear students down, and those who rate themselves low may burn out fastest. Shoukai Yang and five co-authors followed new medical students across three survey waves in 2026 to trace that path from self-evaluation to learning burnout.

Nearly 4,900 students answered surveys six months apart, rating their core self-evaluation, anxiety distress, digital media habits, and burnout. Once starting burnout was accounted for, the direct link from self-view to later burnout faded. Two indirect paths carried it instead: students with lower self-evaluation felt more anxiety distress and used digital media in more troubled ways, and both predicted higher burnout later. The authors point to those middle steps as places to intervene.
pmc-13233376:
Sihan Yang and co-authors track fats in human milk and their links to infant brain growth in a 2026 study. Phospholipids build nerve cell membranes, yet population proof tying milk content to development was scarce. Fifty mother infant pairs at a Beijing hospital gave milk at four stages across the first six months.

One hundred forty eight lipid species in thirteen classes were measured. Total amounts fell from early milk to mature milk, with each family following its own path. Higher levels of three lipids in early milk tracked with better development scores at six months, while one family tracked lower. The authors argue the first days of feeding carry outsized weight for the links studied.
pmc-13233976:
James F Howard and colleagues published a 2026 subgroup analysis of the ADAPT trial, which tested the drug efgartigimod in generalized myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune disease that weakens muscles. The original phase 3 trial enrolled patients whose muscles carry antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor. This analysis re-examined the data by treatment history, other medicines in use, age, sex, body mass, disease duration, and prior thymus surgery.

Across every subgroup, patients on efgartigimod answered treatment at higher rates than those on placebo, on both a daily-living scale and a strength scale, during the first two treatment cycles. Side effect rates stayed similar between drug and placebo groups whatever other treatments patients used. The authors conclude the drug's benefit is broad rather than confined to one kind of patient.
pmc-13234176:
Tony Hauptmann and Stefan Kramer published a 2026 statistics study on fixing biased survey samples without wrecking the good parts. Social science datasets often need reweighting so they match a trusted reference sample. When only a few variables are badly skewed, standard debiasing distorts everything else. The authors' method, feature-weighted maximum representative subsampling, trims a sample toward representativeness while deliberately going easy on the worst-biased features.

Weights for each feature come from a classifier trained to tell the two datasets apart, so important differences still count. On eight artificially biased datasets, the method kept more usable records, and downstream prediction quality showed no significant loss. A real social science dataset confirmed the approach. The code is public, and the authors frame the trade-off as keeping data that heavy-handed correction would throw away.
pmc-13235076:
Felicia Jia Hui Chan and co-authors interviewed in 2026 people in Singapore about health care for adults with intellectual disabilities. Focus groups gathered nineteen professionals, while interviews paired sixteen adults with their caregivers. Questions covered barriers and helpers when seeking care or entering the health system. pmc-13236676:

pmc-13236876:
Priya Sharma, Nipin Kalal, and Nimarta Rana review, in a 2026 paper, why organ donation lags behind public support, and which fixes work. pmc-13237476:
Farah Demachkieh and colleagues surveyed 400 users of a charity service in Tripoli, Lebanon, in 2026 about palliative care awareness. pmc-13237576:
Mehrabian and colleagues report a hard case of Hailey-Hailey disease eased by an unexpected drug. The patient, a man of sixty-five, had endured three years of burning, itching, and splitting skin in the groin area. pmc-13237976:
Brusco and colleagues cost out a new infection-tracking programme for Australian aged care homes. The programme, NISPAC, gives homes a standard, streamlined way to log infections and antibiotic use. Three coordinating bodies share the running of the programme, and their costs count too. A clear price tag lets funders judge the programme fairly, and lets other regions copy it with eyes open about staff time and money.
pmc-13238576:
Rowena Boyd and team analyzed emergency department visits across all six public hospitals in Australia's Northern Territory from 2001 to 2023. They asked how dry and humid heatwaves each affect demand. A case-crossover design compared each patient's visit day with nearby control days, using two heatwave rules: temperature alone, and temperature combined with humidity. pmc-13239176:
Ruixian Li, Ying Han, and co-authors test a blood tau mark for Alzheimer disease in older adults in China, in work from 2026. The mark is strong in past work, but its path over time and a fit cut point for this group were not set. More than five hundred folks joined the study.

pmc-13239976:
Lon Schneider and two co-authors wrote a 2026 letter urging caution about claims for the Alzheimer's drug lecanemab. The writers ask for full data before such claims are accepted.
pmc-13240576:
Yuya Aoki and co-authors describe a 2026 case report on safer tube handling during a bedside tracheostomy procedure. The procedure opens the windpipe for patients who need long-term breathing support. Moving the breathing tube carries risks such as cuff damage or accidental removal.

Their two-step method first measures an individual withdrawal distance using light passed through a bronchoscope. The same light signal then confirms the final tube position at the incision site in real time. In the reported patient, the whole procedure finished within twenty minutes and caused no complications. The report offers clinicians a simple, repeatable way to lower tube-related risk during this common procedure.
pmc-13240776:
Fadi Zaiem and co-authors report a 2026 case that weighs two deadly risks against each other. A transplant of the lungs usually demands a cancer-free waiting period, in case the cancer returns under immune suppression. Their patient was a sixty-six-year-old man whose lungs were failing fast from scarring, while he had just been treated with curative intent for liver cancer.

The team listed him at once and transplanted both lungs thirty days after the cancer therapy. MRI checks over more than four years found no return of the liver cancer. He died four years after the transplant from a chronic failure of the donated lungs. The authors argue the choice was sound: near-term death from breath failure outweighed the cancer risk in a carefully picked case.
pmc-13240876:
Wu's team at Jining exposed autism-model brain organoids to two gut fatty acids and read the gene readout. Short-chain fatty acids are thought to stir inflammation and metabolic trouble in autism. pmc-13241376:

Heart, lung, liver, kidney, skin, and peritoneum each get a section.

Tags on metabolic enzymes, including the newly recognized lactylation, recur as control knobs. Some enzymes push fibrosis through side jobs unrelated to their chemistry. The authors close with therapies already aiming at glycolysis and lipid pathways. Targeting metabolism, they argue, could sit beside current anti-scar care.
pmc-13241776:
Cristina Di Giorgio and co-authors report a 2026 study of bile acid signaling in stomach cancer. A receptor called FXR senses bile acids and shapes the tumor surroundings. Tumors often use such signals to hide from the immune system.

Blocking FXR improved the effect of anti-PD-L1 therapy, suggesting a combination route.
pmc-13241876:
Yuxin Wang and co-authors describe a 2026 method that uses sound-driven cell rotation to sharpen weak signals from living cells. Early Alzheimer disease may alter calcium handling and membrane fluidity in single cells long before symptoms. Those signals are faint and hard to measure reliably.

The authors pitch the approach for preclinical studies of early cell stress.
pmc-13242076:
Filis and a large team checked in twenty twenty-six if doctor grades of drug side harms match what breast cancer patients feel. pmc-13242276:

pmc-13242776:
Sabrina Brinkmöller and co-authors publish a 2026 claims data analysis of opioid formulation and opioid-related disorders in German primary care. pmc-13242876:

pmc-13243276:

pmc-13243376:
Yanyan Lan and co-authors test wrist-ankle acupuncture against nerve pain from chemotherapy in 2026 mouse work. pmc-13243876:
Alberte Aspaas Lundquist and colleagues add two patients to the tiny known group with disease caused by faulty MRPS34, a mitochondrial protein. Their report appeared in JIMD Reports in 2026. pmc-13244076:

pmc-13245076:

pmc-13245376:

pmc-13245576:

pmc-13245676:

pmc-13246176:

pmc-13246776:

pmc-13246876:

pmc-13246976:

pmc-13247976:

pmc-13248276:

pmc-13248376:

pmc-13248876:

pmc-13248976:

pmc-13249076:

pmc-13250176:

pmc-13250876:

Job title, department, training in leading, workplace quality, and self-belief each lifted the scores. Workplace and self-belief linked most strongly with the ratings. pmc-13251076:

The editors state they have lost confidence in the results and conclusions. The notice adds that none of the authors replied to letters about the retraction.
pmc-13251476:
Kourosh Azizi and colleagues compare two fly species for maggot therapy of infected burn wounds, using a rat model in 2026. pmc-13252976:
Meijun Jiang, Shaoyun Zhang, and Cong Xiao review electrical stimulation around flap surgery in this 2026 article. Skin flaps moved to cover wounds from cancer or injury can partly or wholly die, and no drug has reliably prevented that loss.

Because one drug usually hits only one part of the failure process, the authors argue that a physical method touching many steps at once holds real promise.
pmc-13254576:
Ashley H. Clawson and colleagues show that what happens at home outweighs community smoking norms for Arkansas youth nicotine use in a 2026 study. pmc-13254876:
Ahmadreza Afshar, Ali Tabrizi, and Mohammad Javad Shariyate describe a diagnostically elusive vascular malformation in the palm in a 2026 case report. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a tidy, circumscribed lesion in the first web space but could not reliably reveal its vascular nature. The team proceeded to complete surgical excision on suspicion. Microscopy delivered the answer: a tangle of arterial and venous channels within fatty fibrous tissue, matching a type B malformation. The authors urge clinicians to keep this diagnosis in mind for atypical hand masses that imaging cannot settle.
pmc-13254976:
Lomous Kumar and co-authors present a 2026 genetic study of skeletons from a cave site in Ladakh, in the Indian Himalayas. pmc-13255176:

A block-selection step picks trustworthy stretches of the biased run for rebuilding free energy profiles. The team tested the recipe on three different enzymes, including a viral protease, and saw repeated reactive events within feasible times. pmc-13256176:
