pmc-13276376:

pmc-13276676:

pmc-13277276:

pmc-13278476:

pmc-13279276:

pmc-13279876:

pmc-13280376:

pmc-13281776:

pmc-13284776:

pmc-13285676:

pmc-13286076:

pmc-13286776:

pmc-13286876:

pmc-13286976:

pmc-13287276:

pmc-13287976:

pmc-13288376:
Mary E Carrington, Michael S Ross, and Suresh C Subedi tested a shortcut used in forest science in 2026. The shortcut reads forest ageing from a row of sites of different ages. It avoids waiting decades for one site to age. Dry tropical forest plots in North Key Largo, Florida, were measured in 1993 and again in 2013 to check the shortcut.

Real change inside each site matched the pattern read across sites, for both species mix and leaf traits. Early fast-growing leaf-shedding species gave way to tougher evergreen kinds, as expected. One surprise stood out: leaf traits spread widest late in ageing, not narrowest. The authors blame crowding and scarce resources as unlike evergreens meet at high numbers.
pmc-13288676:
Shaista Rehman leads a 2026 study of colon cancer risks in Oman. The study ran at two Muscat hospitals. It compared 166 cancer patients with 166 controls. A survey tapped habits and body measures. Family history and other illness were also logged.

Smoking stood out in the results. It meant roughly four times the odds of cancer. Higher body weight also raised odds. Polyps, diabetes, and high blood pressure raised them too. Bowel inflammation raised odds as well. Family history more than doubled the odds. That held for close and distant kin. The authors press for risk-based screening. Quitting help and weight care should join it.
pmc-13288876:
Rutakayile Bizoza and colleagues follow long-acting schizophrenia shots in Rwanda in 2026. Five centers hosted the work. It held 93 adults aged eighteen to thirty-five. Usual oral drugs ran for twenty-four weeks. Monthly paliperidone shots came next. A three-monthly form followed later.

In all, 86 people finished the study. That is 92.5 percent of those enrolled. Severity scores barely moved on oral drugs. They improved clearly once shots began. Social performance scores rose alongside. Three-quarters reported at least one side effect. Most effects were mild or moderate. Weakness and nasal infections were common complaints.
pmc-13288976:
Mi Mi Ko and colleagues profile a Korean aging cohort in 2026. The KoMAC study tracks adults aged 50 to 65. It blends standard care with Korean medicine views. Recruitment began in August 2023. Sites span city and rural areas.

The goal is 1,000 adults in all. Early data show town and country gaps. Rural adults drank and smoked more. City adults had weaker lung scores. Hearing also ran worse in city adults. Aging cut body and social function for most. Women showed the steepest drops. Korean pattern checks shifted with age too. Yearly follow-ups will track risk over time.
pmc-13289076:
Taalke Maria Sitter and colleagues study drug links to force and relapse in Sweden. Their 2026 study deals with forensic mental care. It covers all new patients from 2009 to 2024. In all, 2,690 patients were tracked. Each patient was compared with themselves over time.

About one in four faced force at least once. About one in four also relapsed into crime. Newer antipsychotic drugs tied to less force. They also tied to less relapse. Drugs for addiction tied to less force too. Clozapine showed the largest drops of all. Shot, pill, and mixed plans did not differ. The authors urge care in reading cause and effect.
pmc-13289176:
Goodluck Willey Lyatuu and colleagues introduce a 2026 project plan in Tanzania. The ENGAGE project deals with young mothers with HIV. It aims to stop HIV passing to infants. Teen girls face high pregnancy and HIV rates. Their care dropout risks infant infection.

Phase one will study a cohort of 10,147 young women. They all use routine mother-to-child prevention care. Phase two will probe social drivers by talks. An evidence scan will hunt for fixes. Phase three will co-create a care package. Young women and staff will shape it in workshops. A test version will run at picked sites. Later work will pilot it in full.
pmc-13289276:
Anil Alp and Mevhibe Irem Yildiz write to a journal editor in 2025 about a brain illness after weight loss surgery. The illness stems from a lack of vitamin B1 and can harm memory for good if missed. It is most known in heavy drinkers, yet cases after stomach surgery have risen in recent years.

Their letter tells of a 26 year old woman who fell ill one month after her stomach was made smaller. She had been holding back grief, which the authors link to poor intake after surgery. Risk factors they list include vomiting, fast weight loss, and missed supplements. They urge full checks of mind and mood before such surgery.
pmc-13289376:
Owen Hibberd headed a 2026 survey on measuring and replacing calcium in children with major trauma. Low ionized calcium can worsen bleeding by hurting clot formation, vessel tone, and heart squeeze. Guidelines say to keep calcium normal, yet they do not say when to test or top up in injured children, leaving practice unclear.

Answers came from 67 emergency departments and 99 clinicians across 19 countries via research networks. Most departments had a major bleeding protocol, but nearly a quarter left calcium out entirely. Timing for replacement was missing or vague in most protocols that did mention calcium at all. Clinician views on a sample case, stable versus unstable, showed wide variation in when to act.
pmc-13289576:
Toshinao Kawai headed a 2026 randomized, blinded trial of thalidomide for bowel inflammation in chronic granulomatous disease. That rare immune defect, present in about 1 in 225,000 births, impairs germ killing and sparks excess inflammation. Nearly half of patients develop bowel disease with diarrhea, bleeding, pain, and fever, resembling classic inflammatory bowel disease in symptoms.

Patients aged one year or older received thalidomide or placebo under double-blind conditions for comparison. The abstract reports potential benefit with acceptable safety and no added infection risk signal in this first controlled trial of its kind. Standard options include steroids, immune suppressants, and biologics, all with trade-offs. A repurposed oral option would matter for families facing limited choices.
pmc-13289676:
Yuto Shiozaki and co-authors ask whether strong communities recover better after disaster in this 2026 study. The team surveyed older residents of a Japanese city in 2010, then again two and a half years after the great earthquake and tsunami of 2011. More than three thousand people across ninety-eight districts took part.

Towns with more social participation before the disaster saw better recovery of daily life afterward. Local activities also softened the blow for people whose homes were badly damaged. Heavy housing damage and loss of loved ones dragged recovery down. The authors say building social ties in calm times is a practical way to prepare for disaster.
pmc-13289776:
Humphrey Deogratias Mazigo led a 2026 report on building an endoscopy unit for liver and spleen harm from schistosomiasis in northwestern Tanzania. That parasite disease is a common cause of severe illness and death in adults locally, yet treatment capacity was very low. A needs check at Nansio District Hospital confirmed demand, missing skills, and building needs before work began in earnest.

The unit opened in August 2023 and has seen 666 patients so far, about two thirds of them men. Belly swelling, vomiting blood, and black stools were common reasons for care. Ultrasound found scarring around liver vessels in 71.5 percent, and most scoped patients had severe esophageal varices needing banding. Follow-up showed strong early success.
pmc-13290876:
Dental implant surgery quietly lowers pain thresholds in the face for weeks, Kiyomi Uehashi and colleagues report in an exploratory study from 2026. Why some patients develop lasting nerve pain after implants is unresolved, and no objective test exists, so the team tracked heat pain thresholds around surgery in 76 outpatients in Osaka.

Thresholds were measured before and after surgery in the cheek, jaw, and neck regions the trigeminal and cervical nerves serve. On the operated side, the share of patients showing a threshold drop ranged from about 29 to 49% at one week, then shrank steadily to near zero by twelve weeks. The changes were subclinical: sensation shifted without patients reporting pain. Uehashi and colleagues read the pattern as a common, transient nerve response worth monitoring in implant care.
pmc-13290976:
Zhenzhen Dou heads a 2026 nationwide study of brain abscess in children in China, covering the years 2016 through 2023. Brain abscess is rare in children yet can threaten life, and large studies of its changing pattern have been scarce, so the team used discharge records from 33 tertiary children’s hospitals.

Altogether 799 children were identified, with yearly rates staying broadly flat across the study span. After 2020 the age mix shifted away from toddlers toward older children and teens. Infections spreading from a nearby site also became more common in the later years, while heart defects present at birth held steady as a risk factor. Surgery, complications, hospital stay length, and costs all ran higher after 2020 in adjusted comparisons.
pmc-13291076:
Which needle points work best in electroacupuncture for bowel inflammation is probed in a 2026 mouse study led by Jiayin Lu. Three points used in Chinese medicine, Dachangshu, Tianshu, and Shangjuxu, were compared in mice given a chemical that triggers inflammatory bowel disease, with body weight, colon shape, and inflammation signals all tracked.

Needle treatment at all three points eased tissue damage and slowed weight loss, and each point lowered one key inflammation signal, IL-6, with the strongest drop at Dachangshu. A second signal, IL-1β, barely moved under any point tested. Gut microbe mixes and body chemicals also shifted after treatment, mostly along lipid, amino acid, and energy pathways, which may explain why point choice changes the result.
pmc-13291476:
Patients and dentists in Saudi Arabia judge AI tools for teeth. Shimaa Rifaat leads a 2026 survey in the eastern province. Smart tools are entering dental care fast. Their success rests on trust from both sides of the chair.

A self-filled survey ran in English and Arabic. It held 38 questions in five parts. Topics spanned tech comfort, AI awareness, and worries. Both patients and dental staff took part. Views were compared across age and job traits. Few past studies set both groups side by side. Local culture shapes how new tools land. Results can guide a smoother rollout in clinics.
pmc-13291776:
Bao-Hua Wei and Hong-Ju Da report a 2026 case report and literature review on purulent pericarditis caused by mouth bacteria. Their patient was a 66-year-old man with no known gum disease or recent dental work. He arrived with pus around the heart plus an abscess below the diaphragm.

Gene sequencing of the pericardial fluid found three periodontal pathogens together: Tannerella forsythia, Fusobacterium nucleatum, and Porphyromonas gingivalis. Doctors drained the fluid, gave targeted antibiotics, and supported his organs until he stabilized. The authors argue that oral bacteria can travel through the blood and seed distant sterile sites even without obvious mouth disease. They also praise broad molecular testing for naming hard-to-grow organisms in infections of unknown origin.
pmc-13292376:
Elsa-Rush Eyang-Assengone and a large team survey a 2026 rural Gabonese village, Dienga, for filarial worm infections using molecular tools. Control programs lack current local data, and Loa loa co-presence makes mass drug campaigns risky. Ninety volunteers gave blood in August 2021 for microscopy and qPCR testing, plus questionnaires on symptoms and knowledge.

PCR found infections in 23.33 percent of volunteers, well above the 13.33 percent microscopy caught, confirming its edge for hidden cases. Loa loa dominated, with Mansonella perstans at just 1.11 percent of those tested. Men were hit far harder than women, 40.5 against 11.32 percent in the survey, and rates peaked past age 61. Itching, Calabar swelling, and eyeworm together strongly predicted infection. Only 10 percent of villagers knew the vector.
pmc-13292576:
Youngsu Kim and co-authors explore a 2026 home-dialysis reality: peritoneal dialysis sells freedom from the clinic, but patients must turn their houses into safe treatment rooms. Semi-structured interviews with 43 patients at a South Korean tertiary hospital asked how they judge and manage the spaces where dialysis happens. Thematic analysis sorted their answers inductively.

Patients described three kinds of space. Hospitals meant delegated safety, trusted to professionals. Homes meant internalized safety, where they rearranged routines and storage to keep sterile control. Everywhere else brought a paradox: travel is theoretically easy, yet unpredictable environments triggered such careful risk checks that many simply narrowed their world. Control over the surroundings, more than the place itself, decided whether a space felt safe. The authors urge educators to teach the spatial work honestly.
pmc-13292676:
Mihiprabha Rathnayake and co-authors spray a 2026 shortcut onto incubating chicken eggs: probiotics misted over the shell so chicks hatch with a head start on gut microbes. First they timed Enterococcus faecalis sprays across embryo days, checking colonization by culture and genome sequencing. Then five probiotic strains, alone and mixed, were sprayed and the chicks' jejunal communities tracked to thirty days after hatching.

Spraying on days 15 and 17 of incubation colonized embryos best. Ligilactobacillus salivarius, Lactobacillus plantarum, and the full mixture pushed gut communities toward the mature profile significantly faster than oral dosing did. Group differences peaked at day two after hatching, then communities converged, with the sprayed mixture staying distinct longest and richest early on. The authors call coarse spraying a practical, industry-ready delivery route.
pmc-13293476:
Mary Kamillah Grace Reyes and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how artificial intelligence tools help people manage stress on their own, outside clinics. Stress is widespread, yet therapist-led care is limited by capacity, cost, and stigma.

Following standard review steps, the team searched six databases for English studies from 2000 to 2025 and kept 35 of 3008 records found. Quality was checked with a mixed methods tool. Five core roles emerged: direct therapy support, behavior support, teaching, companionship with emotional support, and stress tracking with triage. Early proof looks promising, though the authors stress that evidence is still taking shape.
pmc-13293576:
Mingyue Fan and Binbin Gu build, in a 2026 study, a chart tool to predict when hands-on realignment of a broken wrist will fail. Wrist breaks are very common, and knowing failure risk early can steer patients to the right first treatment.

Records covered 822 patients whose breaks were classed by whether manual realignment worked or failed. Eight factors entered the final model, from break type and swelling to drinking history and time since injury. The tool sorted risk well in internal checks and matched observed outcomes closely. The authors suggest it can support personal treatment choices, though outside testing is still needed to confirm its worth.
pmc-13293776:
Masamitsu Eitoku and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, Japan's notebook health record system for retired workers once exposed to hazardous agents, including migrant workers. Japan's aging population draws more migrant labor, and past exposure can sicken workers long after jobs end.

The scheme, set in law, gives former workers a personal record book and free checkups for 15 named agents or jobs. New books issued for major agents have slowly fallen in recent years. Over two decades, three more agent types joined the scheme, and asbestos rules widened. Public hospitals may serve as checkup sites in workers' home countries, the authors suggest.
pmc-13293876:
Yuan-Hao Mao and coauthors describe a 2026 advance in ring laser gyroscopes, devices that sense rotation from tiny frequency shifts between two beams. At very slow rotation the beams lock together, a flaw that blocks precise sensing. Past fixes add moving parts or extra optics, which hinder small designs. The new approach needs no inserted elements.

Inside a helium-neon device, chiral symmetry breaking and nonlinear pulling bias the system on its own. Experiments showed beam direction switching that followed rotation direction, with a linear response near zero rate. Bias instability reached 2.2 × 10−2 degrees per hour at a 10 s integration time, pointing toward compact high-precision sensors.
pmc-13294176:
Pietro Figueiredo, Guilherme Dotto, and Edson Foletto turn quarry waste into a sponge for dye polluted water, in a 2026 study. Granite and quartzite scraps were fused with alkali until their crystals collapsed into glassy solids with richer pores. The quartzite product took up more dye and became the focus.

Tuned to pH 9 and a set dose, the material soaked up a crystal violet dye to about eighty six milligrams per gram and settled within ninety minutes. It kept working after four wash and reuse cycles. Heat measures showed the uptake is spontaneous and releases heat, driven mainly by electric attraction.
pmc-13294276:
Zhenyue Qin and colleagues test a uterus-sparing plan for severe adenomyosis in a 2026 retrospective case series. Care choices hinge on fertility wishes and disease pattern, and the Kishi scan classes sort cases by where growth sits. Their patients wanted no future pregnancy but wished to keep the uterus. Partial removal of diseased tissue was paired with hormone device and drug steps afterward.

All 34 patients treated from December 2017 to October 2022 completed surgery. Pain scores, bleeding scores, hemoglobin, a blood marker, and uterine size all improved clearly after treatment in the reported comparisons. One hormone device slipped downward. Longer follow-up will judge lasting relief.
pmc-13294376:
Niousha Sadjadi and coauthors test how far a species' word-pattern fingerprint stretches across its genome in a 2026 study. Short DNA word frequencies form chaos game pictures that identify species without alignment. Complete chromosome sets from humans and three other eukaryotes from distinct kingdoms were scanned, hunting spots where the local fingerprint strays from the genome-wide one.

Most regions matched the home fingerprint closely. In humans, 80% of half-million-letter segments sat within 0.24 of the chosen reference on a zero-to-one scale in the reported metric. Stray segments clustered where short and long repeat runs pile up. One short reference stretch can thus stand in for most of a genome in sorting tasks.
pmc-13295376:
Laura Franziska Flach, Emilio Sabia, and Thomas Zanon study dairy goat farms in South Tyrol in a 2026 article. Mountain goat keeping supports rural income, old landscapes, and farm diversity under hard conditions. How profits and environmental costs interact on such farms was little documented.

Ten alpine farms shared interview answers and accounting records for the analysis. Full-cost accounts measured money performance, while life cycle methods scored impacts per litre of corrected milk and per hectare. Joining the two views exposes trade-offs that single scores would hide. The framework aims to guide support that lifts both earnings and environmental care in mountain systems.
pmc-13295776:
Katarina Ulfsdotter Gunnarsson, Martin Henriksson, and Marcus Bendtsen simulate lifelong gains from a digital alcohol programme in a 2026 study. Online help for risky drinking can shift behaviour, but whether shifts pay off in health and costs over decades was unclear. A person-level model followed two virtual groups through life.

One group received the digital programme and the other usual care, with ten alcohol-linked diseases tracked. Lasting effects gave the programme group fewer illnesses, slightly more quality-adjusted life years, and lower healthcare costs per person. Gains shrank as the assumed effect faded faster, and vanished when fading ran quickest, stressing proof of lasting change.
pmc-13296276:
Alina Arabela Jojić and co-authors examine, in a 2026 laboratory study, how solvent choice shapes extracts from common juniper cone berries. Different solvents pull out different plant chemicals, so the team split one alcohol extract into separate fractions. Each fraction was then profiled for polyphenols and tested for biological activity.

The ethyl acetate fraction held the most polyphenols and was richest in hyperoside, a plant compound linked to antioxidant effects. That fraction also acted most strongly against melanoma cells in culture while sparing normal skin cells more. Both fractions showed antioxidant action and weak to moderate effects against bacteria, notably Streptococcus pyogenes. The results guide researchers who want to concentrate juniper compounds for further drug development work.
pmc-13296876:
Rita Domingues and José C. M. Pires present SOMBA, an easy-to-use program for reading microbe community data from gene sequencing, in a 2026 paper. Two marker genes name the bacteria and tiny algae in water and soil samples. The tools for such data are split up and hard for non-experts to set up, though.

Their single program with a visual layout chains the steps in order: joining paired reads, trimming, quality checks, and error cleanup. It then groups like sequences and names them from curated banks for each community type. Added modules gauge variety within and between samples. Two matched workflows keep the two markers on the same footing, giving a standard route from raw output to clear findings.
pmc-13297076:
Anamaria Violeta Țuțuianu and colleagues examine, in 2026, the home lives behind 333 Romanian children treated for dental neglect between 2020 and 2024. Records from a city hospital and a private practice profile caregivers' age, schooling, income, substance use and family stability.

Most caregivers were young adults, many with little schooling, and nearly half used alcohol. Low income, present in most families, tied closely to dropping out of the treatment plan. Children of drug-using caregivers arrived years later than others, and over half lived in disrupted homes. The authors stress neglect's many-sided roots.
pmc-13297576:
Baglan Kazhiyakhmetova and a large team hunt blood proteins that could flag radon-linked lung cancer early, in a 2026 study from Kazakhstan. Radon gas is the second cause of lung cancer after smoking, and early disease gives no clear signs. Home radon levels were measured across two seasons in the north of the country, and blood from fifty-seven patients and seventy-three controls was profiled.

Several settlements showed radon above world reference levels, with levels shifting by season. Protein scans found clear differences tied both to cancer and to radon exposure. The flagged proteins serve inflammation, fat handling, oxidative stress, and immune control, among them ORM2 and PRDX2. Such markers may one day support early checks for exposed communities.
pmc-13297876:
Rui Li and colleagues turn soy whey wastewater, a food industry by-product, into beads that pull copper from dirty water, in a 2026 study. The beads blend the wastewater with alginate and cellulose, set by a slow calcium release that gives an even, porous gel. Copper pollution from plating shops is the target.

The beads beat plain alginate on surface area and uptake. Binding followed the pattern of a single chemical layer, with capacity rising as the water warmed. In real plating wastewater the beads removed over ninety-two percent of the copper and kept most of their power after six reuse cycles. Waste thus cleans waste, at low cost.
pmc-13298076:
Pierina Visciano reviews how climate change may raise marine biotoxin risks, in a 2026 survey. Warming and nutrient enrichment favour harmful algal toxins such as brevetoxins, palytoxins, pinnatoxins, and cyclic imines. Toxins once confined to tropical waters, including tetrodotoxins and ciguatoxins, now appear in fish and shellfish from temperate regions.

These compounds can build up in seafood and reach people through the food chain. Visciano connects the ecological drivers to human health concerns and argues for joined-up science, updated regulation, and proactive public health management. Readers get a broad warning about a moving hazard rather than a single toxin case study.
pmc-13298276:
Chun-Heng Hung, Chung-Ta Lee, and Po-Chuan Chen present a 2026 case of chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction with an unusual appearance. The condition mimics a mechanical blockage even though no physical obstruction exists. Their patient, a man in his late thirties with no prior abdominal surgery, arrived with high-grade obstruction and early signs of reduced blood flow.

Emergency surgery revealed a braided, dough-twist pattern in the distal small bowel, and the segment was removed. Tissue analysis showed severe wasting of the outer muscle layer with nerves intact, confirming the muscle-based form of the disease. He recovered well with improved nutrition. The authors highlight surgical judgement and full tissue profiling.
pmc-13298776:
Bone density can be read from ordinary chest scans if the calibration holds up, and Yizhang Tong with colleagues validated an automated phantom-less system in a 2026 prospective study. Among 252 people having routine chest CT, the system measured spinal density at T11 to L1 without a physical reference phantom.

Against phantom-based measurement, results correlated strongly, with r = 0.867, and the system detected osteoporosis with an AUC of 0.962. Manually chosen visceral fat calibration beat the automatic subcutaneous fat choice for spotting early bone loss. Readings stayed consistent across five different scanners. The authors endorse the approach for opportunistic screening during scans done for other reasons.
pmc-13298876:
Alberto Aimo and co-authors check in 2026 whether patients in heart failure trials have grown less sick over twenty years. Better background drugs should lower event rates in the untreated arm, which would change how new trials are sized. They gathered phase three trials in one top journal from 2004 to 2024.

Thirty-eight trials fit, most on the weak-pump form of the disease. Control-arm patients had a median age of sixty-seven, and about a quarter were women. Pump scores and a blood strain marker set the group's risk level. Yearly event rates were weighed by trial size and follow-up length. A clear trend, either way, tells trial planners how many patients they must enroll to see a drug's effect.
pmc-13299476:
Cell-shed specks are the skin trade's new hope, and Candelaria Contreras and Amin Ariza-Donado grade that hope in a 2026 review. The specks, sold as exosomes, pass proteins and gene bits from cell to cell.

Trials hint at gains for skin youth, hair growth, wound mend, and dark spot care. Gains may flow through fresh skin frame, new blood paths, and calmer immune fire. The team also asked twelve skin doctors in Colombia how the tools feel in real work. Their word is care: goods swing wide in source and make, hard trials are few, harm has come from goods with no stamp of law, and rules are far from set.
pmc-13299576:
Women may break down one common mood drug through a liver path more fast than men. Janina Eiberger and her team hint at that in a 2026 blood-level study. They mined past blood checks from sick people on one of three mood drugs and set drug break pace by sex, grouped by gene type.

For two drugs worked by the CYP2D6 path, no sex gap showed in 117 and 73 blood sets. For the third drug, escitalopram, worked by CYP2C19, men with the plain gene type held more drug per dose in the blood than women. That hints women clear it more fast. With just 51 sets for that drug, the team call the find a first hint, not a fact, and ask for a big check.
pmc-13299876:
Vid Duplančić and colleagues estimate the wider societal cost of breast cancer in working-age Croatian women, in a 2026 multicentre study. Quality-of-life and work productivity questionnaires plus informal care reports came from 271 women in outpatient oncology care. Health utility sat well below the general population average.

Lost productivity among employed women formed the largest cost piece, followed by unpaid caregiving from family and friends. Combined economic indirect costs approached nine thousand euros per patient-year, with a separate monetised welfare loss reported on top. An extended national estimate reached tens of millions of euros yearly. The authors urge planners to count these hidden burdens in policy.
pmc-13299976:
Sichen Liu, James Townley, and Chuen-Yen Lau survey radiolabelled antimicrobials as infection imaging agents, in a 2026 scoping review. Pathogen-specific imaging could improve outcomes, yet no antibiotic-based tracer has reached sign-off despite decades of work. Searches spanning 1970 to 2025 gathered well over one hundred lab-stage and a smaller set of clinical articles.

Most clinical tracers showed weak infection precision, though some helped describe drug behaviour in the body. A few preclinical candidates combined many preferred traits. Good tissue penetration often came with poor washout, which blurs target contrast. The authors see pharmacokinetic uses during active infection as the most promising near-term direction.
pmc-13300276:
How stem cells guard their glutathione supply changes as they turn toward neurons, Nobuko Matsumura and colleagues show in a 2026 cell study. Working with mouse bone-marrow mesenchymal stem cells and neuron-like cells derived from them, the team tracked the cysteine transporter EAAC1 and its brake protein, GTRAP3-18.

Undifferentiated stem cells held more glutathione yet kept EAAC1 mostly off the cell surface, while the derived neuron-like cells relied on it more directly. Removing GTRAP3-18 lowered glutathione in stem cells but raised both EAAC1 and glutathione in neuron-like cells. The split shows redox control is rewired by lineage, a point that matters for stem-cell therapies aimed at nerve repair.
pmc-13300576:
Carbon dioxide calms bees for handling, yet its inner effects vary with age, Ying Wang and two colleagues show in a 2026 proteomics study. They exposed honey bee workers at three life stages, newly emerged, nurse, and forager, then compared protein patterns in hemolymph and brain tissue.

Newly emerged bees proved the hardiest, leaning on chemical defense pathways in both blood and brain. Nurse bees mounted weaker blood responses but guarded the brain first. Foragers instead favored blood detoxification paired with brain energy control. Across all ages, bees shifted energy use to ride out the stress, a finding with practical value for transport and colony care.
pmc-13300876:
In a 2026 retrospective study, Zeynel Mert Asfuroğlu and colleagues find that rebuilt web spaces between fused fingers generally serve patients well for decades. They assessed fifty-three people and ninety reconstructed web spaces after congenital syndactyly surgery. Appearance, hand function, and psychosocial state were scored with the Withey scale, QuickDASH, and a purpose-built survey.

Median follow-up reached ten years, and the typical scores, Withey 2, QuickDASH 14, and psychosocial 29, all sat in the favorable band. Complicated syndactyly fared worse on every measure, and girls reported weaker function and psychosocial results. Surgery between ages one and five and repeat operations also tracked with poorer appearance, guiding family counseling.
pmc-13301176:
Should every aortic repair patient get a heart artery check first? Marwan Hamiko and colleagues examine that habit in a 2026 study of 177 elective thoracic aortic repair patients treated between 2015 and 2025. Half the group received coronary angiography before surgery; survival was tracked for a median of 4.9 years.

The test uncovered new or worsening coronary disease in 44.7 percent of those tested, and 13.6 percent of all patients had their heart arteries treated before repair. Yet hospital deaths and major cardiac events matched the untested group, and long-term survival did not separate either. Coronary disease itself looked deadlier before adjustment, a gap the authors trace to wider artery disease across the body.
pmc-13301376:
As grassland turns to desert, the fungi nursing plant roots swap identity, Xue Wang and colleagues show in a 2026 field study. Along a drying gradient, they sampled rhizosphere soil around Stipa breviflora and Artemisia frigida, sequencing fungi and scoring root colonization. Network analysis and path modeling traced how the community rebuilt itself.

Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, the classic root partners, lost diversity and root foothold as dryness deepened. Dark septate endophytes moved the other way, gaining ground in roots and inferred abundance. Fungal networks broke into looser fragments, a shift the models tie to the guild swap itself. Soil usefulness fell too, marking wider decline beneath the visible plants.
pmc-13303376:
Ya Wang, Fangqiu Yu, and Wei Wang published a case report with a literature review in 2026 on brucellosis with kidney injury and a rare immune complication. The infection, from Brucella bacteria, often hits many organs with vague signs. Their patient was a man aged fifty-one with unexplained fever, falling blood counts, and rising kidney failure markers. Blood culture confirmed the infection.

Scans showed kidney surface changes, and the picture fit haemophagocytic syndrome, where immune activity runs wild. Combined anti-Brucella therapy plus a chemotherapy drug brought clear improvement in symptoms and kidney function. The authors stress detailed history taking and lab proof when fever has no clear source.
pmc-13305176:
Mei An and co-authors review sulfur movement in coal chemical looping combustion in a 2026 synthesis. The clean coal method captures concentrated carbon dioxide with low nitrogen oxide output, but sulfur in coal poisons the oxygen carriers and dirties the gas stream.

Sulfur release during coal heating and gas steps is mapped for two looping styles, and paths that spread sulfur through the system are traced. Rather than merely tolerating sulfur, the authors urge carriers designed to grab it on site. Multi-job oxygen carriers could protect themselves while cleaning the stream, speeding real-world use.
pmc-13305676:
Humphrey P. K. Addy, David Amedorme, and co-authors predict, in a 2026 study, what the microbes in West African fermented maize foods can do, not just who they are. Six products from Ghana, Nigeria, and Benin, including mawe and ogi, were studied from archived gene-sequencing data. Software predicted what the microbes can do from which bacteria were present in each food.

Firmicutes dominated every sample, and Lactobacillus ruled most, reaching over eighty percent in some mawe. Predicted functions followed the leading genus: transport proteins, gene control, and DNA copying. Other genera chipped in specialty pathways, from lactate production to cell-membrane fat building. Shop-bought mawe showed extra predicted activity in energy use and cell-wall building. The authors frame the predictions as a baseline needing lab checks.
pmc-13305876:
Hero Mohammed, Ayesha Rahman, and Malgorzata Wiench report in 2026 that sugar alcohols can strengthen the antiseptic chlorhexidine against mixed oral biofilms. Their lab model mixed three streptococcal species with the fungus Candida albicans, a blend linked to tooth decay and gum disease. Biofilms were grown under plain, sugar-rich, and fake saliva settings.

Chlorhexidine alone cut biofilm mass sharply, while xylitol, maltitol, and sorbitol needed much higher doses on their own. pmc-13307076:

pmc-13308676:

pmc-13310576:

pmc-13312176:

pmc-13323776:

pmc-13328176:

pmc-13328576:

pmc-13329376:

pmc-13330176:

pmc-13331176:

pmc-13332476:

pmc-13333376:

pmc-13333476:

pmc-13333676:

pmc-13333776:
Tim Ho and Mark Ryan propose a new model of chronic pain in a 2026 narrative review, treating it as a state-constrained disorder of brain networks. pmc-13333876:

pmc-13335076:

pmc-13335676:

pmc-13336676:

pmc-13336876:

pmc-13336976:

pmc-13338276:

pmc-13338676:

pmc-13339876:

pmc-13340076:

pmc-13340476:

pmc-13340676:

pmc-13340776:

pmc-13341276:

pmc-13341376:

pmc-13341476:

pmc-13341776:

pmc-13342076:

pmc-13342576:

pmc-13342876:

pmc-13343576:

pmc-13343876:

pmc-13345376:

pmc-13346676:

pmc-13346976:

pmc-13347076:

pmc-13347176:

pmc-13347776:

pmc-13348076:

pmc-13348576:

pmc-13348676:

pmc-13348876:

pmc-13350476:

pmc-13350676:

pmc-13351276:

pmc-13351476:

pmc-13351576:

The team compared general health outcomes between vulnerable and other children and probed how family structure shapes the gap. Hard numbers on where the gaps are widest can steer aid, school health services, and family support to the right levers.
pmc-13351876:
Hua Sun and co-authors compare two ways of clearing older patients for lung surgery in a 2026 cohort study. Many patients are turned down because breathing tests look poor. From 2022 to 2024, patients first had standard breathing tests, and those with weak results went on to exercise testing before a decision.

In total, 130 older patients had surgery, with 71 in the breathing-test group and 59 in the exercise-test group. Complication rates were close, at 23.94 percent versus 25.42 percent, with no clear difference. Hospital stay and chest tube time did differ between groups. Results suggest exercise testing can safely widen access to surgery for patients with weak breathing tests.
pmc-13352176:
Ding-Tian Yu, Si-Si Xie, and Cheng-Guo Duan study how chromatin changes steer immune gene switching in Arabidopsis in 2026. Plant defence depends on fast rewriting of gene activity, but the chromatin controls behind it stay unclear. The team combined RNA, chromatin, and access profiling after treatment with salicylic acid or the peptide flg22.

Each signal reshaped chromatin and gene activity in its own broad pattern. Salicylic acid raised two activating histone marks together at defence sites, while flg22 worked mainly through one mark. Open chromatin tracked closely with active defence genes. Network checks highlighted NPR1, ICS1, and PR1 as hubs. Results show two signals can reach defence through partly separate chromatin routes.
pmc-13352376:
Hongqiang Li and co-authors profile the chemistry of eggs from five poultry species in 2026. Eggs are a rich nutrient source, and knowing species differences can guide production and new products. Chicken, duck, goose, quail, and pigeon eggs were split into yolk and white and screened with untargeted metabolomics.

Analysis found 519 differing compounds in yolks and 312 in whites across species, spanning lipids, ring compounds, and benzenoids. Yolk networks showed tighter grouping than white networks. Transport and amino acid pathways stood out as enriched routes. Machine learning picked 9 candidate markers that may separate species, though the authors say outside validation with targeted tests is still required.
pmc-13352476:
Jingnan Xue and colleagues report a 2026 surgical case of thyroid tissue found beside the bile duct. Misplaced thyroid tissue is uncommon, and spots near the gallbladder are extremely rare, yet such lumps can mimic bile or gallbladder tumours. A 50-year-old woman had 2 years of on-and-off pain in the upper right belly.

Scans showed a dense lump of 22 by 14 mm at the liver hilum next to the gallbladder neck. She declined further imaging for cost reasons and asked for surgery. Keyhole removal took the gallbladder and lump together, and tissue study showed benign mature thyroid follicles. Her own thyroid gland was normal, and she stayed symptom-free after surgery.
pmc-13352676:
Ki-Woong Nam, Hyung-Min Kwon, and Yong-Seok Lee link a red cell index to stroke associated pneumonia. The pneumonia is a common infection after acute ischemic stroke, and many prediction models exist. A more objective and easy marker would help clinicians flag risk early from routine blood tests.

The study looks at 500 consecutive stroke patients, of whom 62, or 12.4 percent, develop it. The index puts red cell count and hemoglobin over lymphocyte and platelet counts. After adjustment, each rise in the index carries 46 percent higher odds of it. Age, swallowing difficulty, impaired consciousness, white cell count, and inflammation markers also predict it on their own. High index patients with pneumonia need intensive care and intubation more often.
pmc-13352776:
Aygül Karaca tests a seed treatment for peppers facing cold starts in a 2026 study. Low soil warmth is a chief barrier to sprouting and even seedling stands in warm-season crops sown early. She soaked pepper seeds before sowing in proline, an amino acid that helps plants handle stress by guarding membranes and fighting cell damage.

Seeds soaked at four strengths were tested at warm and chilling temperatures. Cold cut sprouting sharply in plain seeds. The strongest soak gave the best sprouting and emergence under cold, and its seedlings showed less cell damage plus stronger defense enzymes and more green pigment. Karaca concludes that a proline soak is a cheap shield for early sowing.
pmc-13353876:
Ayako Ijuin and colleagues test a multi-constriction nanopore called Epx4 for single-molecule protein reading in 2026. Nanopores sense molecules label-free as they pass through, and extra narrow points can sharpen signals. Epx4 is a pore-forming toxin with two separate barrels and up to four constrictions along its path.

In single-molecule runs, Epx4 caught positively charged polypeptides more often than the standard alpha-hemolysin pore. Machine learning on its signals reached an area under the curve of 0.82 and an F1 score of 0.72, both above the standard pore. Geometry checks confirmed the multi-grip layout. The authors propose Epx4 as a strong base for accurate protein sensors.
pmc-13354576:
Nidal H Abu-Hamdeh and co-authors used computer models in 2026 to test ways to speed up cold storage freezing. Their design used a ring-shaped tank, metal foam, a fluid with tiny mixed particles, and heat rays to move cold through the space. A math model tracked the line between liquid and solid as freezing went on.

Metal foam gave the biggest gain, cutting freezing time by about 79 percent in the model. Heat rays cut the time by about 23 percent, and the special fluid added a smaller gain. The work points to foam as a strong tool for fridges, air cooling, and other cold storage uses.
pmc-13355276:
Avinav Bharati and co-authors tested three AI chatbots in 2026 on questions about medical physics in cancer care. Experts wrote 11 questions and put each to ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Gemini, asking each one twice. Three experts then scored the answers for correctness, completeness, ease of reading, trust, and fit for local practice.

DeepSeek scored highest on correctness and gave the most complete answers, at ten of eleven questions. Still, no chatbot matched human skill on any measure, and scores for real-world use did not differ much. The authors argue that chatbots should support medical staff, not replace them, in a paired way of working.
pmc-13355376:
Camilla A Cascardo and Severine Cao told of a modern case of scurvy diagnosed partly through twisted hairs, in 2026. Vitamin C deficiency, once thought rare, has re-emerged among people with highly picked diets and brain-growth problems. Early recognition matters because scurvy is readily treatable yet mimics infectious, vascular, and rheumatologic disease.

A man in his twenties with autism and notice-deficit/overactivity illness gave with unilateral bruising, and trichoscopy showed twisted hair shafts, an atypical finding that pointed toward scurvy. Machine factors helped explain the one-sided spread. The case shows how hair check can unmask a food deficiency hiding behind an unusual presentation.
pmc-13356876:
Imran Ahmed, Kunjan Chadha, and Keshab R Paudel wrote a 2026 review of irritable bowel syndrome. The disorder brings repeated belly pain and changed bowel habits, with no visible damage to the gut. Its care stays hard because causes are mixed and response to treatment varies from person to person.

The review sums up current care, from diet and drugs to brain-gut therapies, and weighs their limits. It sets out the tangled drivers now accepted: altered gut motion, a tender gut lining, faulty gut-brain signals, low-grade immune activity, microbe shifts, and a leaky gut barrier. The authors close with the directions they judge most promising for future care.
pmc-13357076:
Ming Yan and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how targeted drugs perform when bowel cancer spreads to the liver, a leading cause of death in these patients. Such targeted therapy is now common, but its exact gains in survival, shrinkage, and surgery chances were unclear. They pooled randomized trials and cohort studies found in four databases through July 2025.

Thirty-four studies with 12,084 patients showed targeted therapy lengthened overall and progression-free survival and raised response rates. It also increased the chance of surgery to remove liver tumors, most clearly in first-line and marker-selected patients. Severe side effects were more common but manageable. The authors support targeted drugs within team-based, precision care.
pmc-13358476:
Ya Wang and co-authors present a 2026 review of breathing support for acute respiratory distress syndrome, a severe lung failure. Machines that breathe for patients can also harm the lungs if each breath is too big. Doctors already use small breaths; the team asked if even smaller breaths help more.

They combined six studies with 1,102 patients that compared ultra-low with low breath sizes. Most patients on the smallest breaths also used life-support machines that take over gas exchange for the lungs. The review weighs the gain in lower lung stress against the risks of extra machines, to guide care in intensive care units.
pmc-13358576:
Xuanyu Zhu and co-authors present a 2026 study on a warning sign in early lung cancer. Some tumors shed cells into nearby air spaces, a pattern called spread through air spaces. It raises the risk of the cancer coming back, yet doctors can only confirm it after surgery. The team built computer models to predict it before the operation.

They used records and CT scans from 445 patients with the earliest stage of non-small cell lung cancer. Machine learning models weighed scan traits and patient facts to sort likely cases. A good forecast matters because it can steer the choice between a small, lung-saving cut and a larger, safer one.
pmc-13360476:
Ju-Ho Song and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on knee alignment math for a bone-cutting operation. High tibial osteotomy straightens bowed legs, but a tilted joint line predicts poor results. The standard knee classification computes joint tilt from two bone angles and ignores the joint line convergence angle, which shifts under load.

The team reviewed 323 operated knees with X-rays before surgery and one year after. Their modified tilt value, which adds half the convergence angle, matched the true joint orientation more closely than the standard value. Knee scores also improved a great deal after surgery. The authors propose the modified scheme for planning.
pmc-13360676:
Yosta de Stigter and eight co-authors reworked a glowing DNA test so it can run in one pot alongside DNA copying, in this 2026 paper. Their earlier dyes, called LUMIDs, light up when they bind copied DNA, giving a simple readout for infection tests. The dyes fell apart at the warm temperatures that fast copying methods need, which blocked one-pot use.

The team swapped in a heat-tough glowing enzyme and added a second heat-tough binding protein. A caged fuel that leaks out slowly keeps the glow going long enough to watch. The combined test detected cancer-linked papillomavirus types at extremely low levels within about thirty minutes. A plain digital camera read the results, even in patient samples, which suits clinics with little equipment.
pmc-13361176:
Li-Min Zhang and others critically surveyed magnesium-based thermoelectrics, in 2026. Magnesium compounds have emerged as a key direction for large-scale thermoelectric uses, thanks to elemental abundance, low cost, green compatibility, and competitive work at low to mid temperatures. Rapid progress called for a full survey.

Three typical classes were covered: Mg3X2 compounds, MgAgSb, and Mg2X compounds, with emphasis on crystal structure, electric bands, phonon transport, and carrier scattering, plus bulk and thin-film developments. The review maps work limits and design strategies. Thermoelectric teams gain a consolidated account of a lasting items family.
pmc-13362776:
Maryam Choulli and a large team report a 2026 study of throat cancer patients at three Barcelona hospitals, asking whether nutrition at diagnosis forecasts early response to curative treatment. The virus HPV splits this cancer into types with different outlooks. The team measured body size, muscle from scans, fitness tests, blood markers, and a standard nutrition score in 101 patients before therapy began.

Among virus-positive patients, the nutrition score split outcomes clearly: about three quarters with good scores cleared the cancer early, versus a third with poor scores. Among virus-negative patients, fitness level and age split outcomes instead. Muscle scans and blood markers added nothing once nutrition and fitness counted. Diet care at diagnosis may thus help, the authors suggest.
pmc-13363576:
Xiangjun Kong, Xia Wang, and Wulan Zeng present a 2026 review of nanostructured catalysts for clean energy conversion, covering both electric and light-driven reactions. These tiny engineered materials sit at the heart of water splitting, fuel cells, and carbon dioxide reuse. The review follows five catalyst families, from single metals to single-atom designs, and the recipes that shape them with care.

Five levers for better performance get close treatment: shape, doping, layered junctions, defects, and supports. For each key reaction, the authors name the measures that best predict success. Their verdict is pointed: raw activity is rarely the bottleneck now; holding performance under harsh, factory-grade loads is. Earth-abundant stand-ins for precious metals get special attention.
pmc-13364176:
Kam Hang Chan and co-authors watch an antimicrobial lipid meet live bacteria in real time, in a 2026 paper. Staphylococcus epidermidis causes many hospital infections, building biofilms on medical devices and shrugging off antibiotics. A skin-secreted lipid, cholesteryl linoleate, kills this bacterium, but how it engages the cells was unclear.

The team built a surface plasmon resonance microscopy protocol to film the encounter. Bacteria stayed alive through the imaging procedure. Liposomes carrying the lipid bound the cells directly and far more strongly than plain liposomes, with binding rising as dose rose. The grip varied across a single cell, patchy rather than uniform, matching the mixed state of resting cultures. Seeing the contact directly sharpens ideas for lipid-based defenses.
pmc-13365476:
Udomsak Saengow and co-workers set in 2026 how folks with long ills in south Thailand smoke, by zone: leaf grow zones and plain zones. They ask 879 patients face to face from care lists in both zone types. Hand rolled leaf rolls rule use, more so in grow zones.

Near one in five had smoked at some point, and all but a few past smokers were men. Smokers show high lung ill rates and more care stays per year. Grow zone life and more house cash lift smoke odds, while women smoke far less. Rules must face cheap leaf reach in farm towns.
pmc-13369476:
Annabel Lim and co-authors map the forests hiding inside Southeast Asia's farm and logging concessions. Across four countries, some forty two million hectares of natural tropical forest sit inside land licensed for logging, palm oil, timber, and rubber. Clearing them would endanger key wildlife areas and release over a billion tons of carbon dioxide across thirty years.

The team prices rescue through carbon markets. Break even prices span a wide range, from modest to steep per ton. At strong prices, large tracts could pay for their own protection. The authors stress that carbon cash alone will not suffice; finance partners and firm policy must join.
pmc-13369976:
Nasrin Alamdari forecasts in 2026 how United States land use may change by twenty sixty-seven, using seven decades of agriculture department records. Three methods are compared: a Markov chain model, curve fitting chosen by information criteria, and scenario versions for business as usual, faster urban growth, and conservation. Under the baseline path, cropland and forest shares shrink while pasture and special uses grow.

Curve fitting independently favors saturating logistic curves for several land types, suggesting transitions are leveling off. State models converge at different speeds. Alamdari offers the framework to any country with periodic land inventories.
pmc-13371876:
Amaya Daniels and co-authors tell of a huge gallstone that moved in an odd way in a 2026 case report. An 82-year-old woman had a drain tube path from her gallbladder to her skin. Such paths are used when surgery is too risky for a sick patient.

A stone about 65 mm long moved through the path and got stuck just under the skin. Scans can miss how much hard stone sits in such a lump, the team warns. They cut the path open and took the stone out, and her symptoms eased fast. The case is said to be the first of its kind with a stone this large.
pmc-13372376:
Eanna Johnston and co-authors built a fine eye scan to track burns in a 2026 study. Alkali burns are a harsh type of eye harm and can blind. Plain scans see shape well but miss tiny shifts in the clear front window of the eye.

The new scan reads light in a way that picks up shifts far below the plain scan's limit. The team used it on a burn model and on care with cell-based drops. Scan shifts tracked harm and heal steps as they changed. A tool that watches heal steps without touch could help eye teams time care and test new drops in trials.
pmc-13373276:
Gina Chowa and others centre the lived experience of adolescent girls and young women in Burundi in a 2026 study of mental health. The work moves beyond counting cases to trace the conditions that shape well-being in a low-resource, conflict-affected setting, using phenomenological qualitative methods. Structural inequality, gender norms, economic precarity, and violence contact all feature.

The study also identifies barriers to care and locally grounded facilitators of resilience, from community ties to social protection systems. Its help is practical: actions should be culturally responsive, gender-sensitive, and built into existing community structures. The authors present the voices of Burundian girls and young women as the foundation for fairer mental health policy and programming.
pmc-13373676:
Shuroog Nabhan and co-authors summed up switch data for a gut drug and its copies in a 2026 review. The drug calms bowel swelling, and cheaper copies are now in wide use. Doubts stay on what switch steps do to health in daily care.

The search found seven studies with 5,721 adults in all. Three were planned ahead, three looked back, and one took a one-time snapshot. Watch time ran from six months to just over two years. The sum-up weighs if health held firm after a switch, and in which ways. Such proof helps clinics and patients trust a switch made to cut costs.
pmc-13374176:
Li Zhang and co-authors mapped a view-sort method in long ill work in a 2026 review. The method asks people to sort views into piles, which shows how groups truly see a point. It suits the mix of tales that long ills bring, where one fixed plan fits few.

The team used firm review steps and searched four data banks to late 2025. Each past use was logged for its ask, its craft twists, and its gains. Use has spread across many long ills, from pain to heart and mind care. The map shows where the method shines and where reports are thin, to guide new work.
pmc-13374276:
Caiping Liu and co-authors linked long calm-drug use to thought skill in a 2026 study in China. The drugs in view calm nerves and aid sleep, and are often used long in mind care. The group came from a large watch study of a grave mind ill.

Fifty-seven long users were matched to 57 non-users by age, sex, ill span, and main drugs. A set test scored thought, and scales scored signs, weight of ill, and daily life skill. Long users scored worse on thought tests in the match. The team says long use should be weighed with care, and thought should be checked in this group.
pmc-13376376:
Qiaoli Wei, Junwei Yao, and Weitao Zheng present a 2026 decision method for rating sports performance, tested on soccer players. Rating a player means weighing many unlike skills at once, under doubt about each score. Their method uses a kind of fuzzy number that can hold both support and doubt for a claim in a single value.

The authors set new rules for working with those numbers and build fair combining tools that weigh gains and losses in an even way. Expert scores for goals, assists, tackles, and passing were combined into player ranks. The ranks were checked against a known ranking method, and the match supports the new tools for hard, multi factor choices.
pmc-13376576:

Tuo Han and seven co-authors test that ratio in 2026: lactate, a strain mark, over albumin, a health mark. Their pool is 731 gravely ill patients of this heart type, drawn from a large care database.

The patients split into three bands by the ratio's size. The team then tracked death within twenty-eight days, with models that bend to fit the link's true shape. Past work had tied the ratio to death in sepsis and in mixed grave illness. This study asks whether the tie holds in this one heart group. A two-value blood read that sorts risk could guide care where time is short.
pmc-13376676:
Alexandra N Bancos and seven co-authors compare two groups whose adrenal glands no longer work. Some patients lose the glands to surgery on both sides; in others, the immune system destroys them. Both groups must take hormone replacements for life, and both face sudden adrenal crises.

Their 2026 study surveyed adults at two centers: 203 with the autoimmune form and 139 after surgery. Quality of life scores came out nearly equal. Yet the autoimmune group reported more crises in the past year, 25 percent against 13 percent. After adjusting for age, sex, and dose, only the cause of the condition predicted crisis counts. Within the surgery group, quality of life was better when surgery treated a tumor than excess hormone disease.
pmc-13377376:

These brain responses fire automatically when a rare sound breaks a run of repeated sounds, and they index auditory discrimination and sensory memory. Their 2026 review synthesizes 55 studies comparing autistic and non-autistic people across childhood, teen years, and adulthood. A summary framework without pooled meta-analysis structured the work.

Responses also arrived later more often, tied to language difficulties and sharper hearing. Some gaps converged with age in later childhood or adolescence. pmc-13379376:

The plastics covered are polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, polystyrene, nylon-6,6, and PET. Graphs comparing the plastics show how the measures grow and differ, which can help predict material properties from structure alone.
pmc-13379976:
Yecheng Chen and colleagues present a 2026 study of blood sugar stress measures in critically ill patients with heart failure. Illness can push blood sugar up sharply, and that rise is linked with worse outcomes. One measure corrects the rise for a patient's usual sugar level, but people differ in how their blood sugar marks long-term control.

Records for 2,488 patients came from three intensive care databases. The team grouped patients by a glycation index, which captures that personal difference, and tracked how the stress measure changed over time against death rates. The link between the stress measure and death differed across the groups, so the same reading may not mean the same risk for every patient.
pmc-13380376:
Zhongshu Li and six co-authors build copper complexes where two metal atoms sit close enough to interact, in a 2026 chemistry paper. Their starting ligand is a bulky phosphorus compound whose three arms each carry a carbon double bond that can grip metals. In single-copper complexes, though, the arms barely engage, and the ligand acts mostly as a large shield.

Adding a second copper source changed the structure entirely. The phosphorus atom now bridges both coppers, and the double bonds grip the pair much more strongly. The team made a small family of these paired complexes with different partner anions. Experiments and quantum calculations agree that taking up the second copper is both fast and favorable. The work shows how a reluctant ligand can switch roles when a second metal arrives.
pmc-13381676:
Xiaojuan Cui and co-authors traced a path from long parental lectures to self-harm in Chinese pre-teens, in a 2026 study. Self-injury without intent to die is rising in this age group, and early onset predicts later harm. The team recruited over fourteen hundred fifty children aged ten to twelve, plus parents, from eight schools in Tianjin. Parents reported on their discipline style. Children reported their focus on negative events and their own self-harm.

About one in four children reported self-injury, a high share. A chain analysis linked heavy parental verbosity to self-harm through two ordered steps. First came a stronger focus on negative over positive events. Then came worse emotional symptoms, which fed the harm. Data on feelings came from both children and parents to cut bias. The authors urge discipline that reasons briefly and warmly, rather than at length.
pmc-13382776:
Eric N. Enyong and co-authors examine caveolin-1 outside its usual membrane pockets in retinal support cells in 2026 work. In Müller glia, the main support cells of the retina, caveolin-1 is plentiful while its pocket-forming partner is scarce. Microscopy confirmed that the flask-shaped pockets themselves are almost absent in these cells.

Without pockets, caveolin-1 boosted signals from a bacterial sensor and raised levels of the messenger IL-6 after stimulation. Silencing the protein, or forcing pockets to form, calmed that response. In vessel cells where pockets are normal, silencing had the opposite effect, a contrast that may guide care for inflamed eye disease.
pmc-13383376:
Abel Nhama and five co-authors pool in 2026 the evidence on artemether-lumefantrine, the standard malaria drug pairing, in Mozambique. Malaria still burdens the country heavily, and control depends on the frontline drug keeping its edge. Trial after trial has tested the pairing in children and adults under World Health Organization protocols.

The review gathers those studies and pools cure rates, with and without genetic correction for reinfection. Day-three parasite clearance and early and late failures were tracked as warning signs. Checking risk of bias kept the summary honest. Knowing the drug still works, or catching the first slide toward resistance, shapes national treatment policy for millions of infections each year.
pmc-13385576:
Zheng Wei's team observed coupled Kondo clouds in a mirror-symmetric nanotube-molybdenum device, in a 2026 physics study. Magnetic impurities in metal are screened by conduction electrons into a spin cloud, but detecting that cloud in dilute alloys stayed hard. The team built mirror-symmetric carbon nanotube arrays separated by a molybdenum strip.

The Kondo effect hinged sensitively on strip width. Widths of roughly one-third to just over one micrometer gave a Kondo temperature plateau near 108 kelvin, while one and a half to three micrometers gave about 16 kelvin. A two-spin model reproduced both plateaus and their crossover, explained by intra-edge and inter-edge cloud coupling. The result opens routes in spintronics and quantum computing.
pmc-13385776:
Jessica Gianopulos and co-authors pin drug resistance in pancreatic cancer on a gene regulator in a 2026 paper. This cancer swaps between classical and basal subtypes. The protein ZNF274 tracks with subtype and guards the off state of many genes. When ZNF274 is lost, cells shift classical to basal, grow invasive arms, and gain a weakness to CDK7 blocker drugs.

Two arms drive the shift, they find. A gene called ZEB1, normally held down, rises and brings mesenchymal traits. Silenced viral leftovers in the genome also wake, and their double stranded RNA alarms the cell, locking the new subtype in. The liability may be reachable in the clinic.
pmc-13385876:
Anh Cong's team solved structures of protein kinase C-beta and its allosteric regulation, in a 2026 structural study. The team determined structures of human PKC-betaI and PKC-betaII.

The work gives a foundational model for second-messenger control of PKC function.
pmc-13386676:
Bilal Aygün's team tested serum TIE-2 as a diagnostic marker in newly diagnosed multiple myeloma, in a 2026 case-control study. Angiogenesis drives myeloma pathophysiology, and TIE-2 regulates vessel growth, but its diagnostic value was unclear. The team compared 38 newly diagnosed, untreated myeloma patients with 37 healthy volunteers at Adana City Hospital.

Serum TIE-2 ran significantly higher in myeloma patients at 1.4 versus 0.9 nanograms per milliliter. Receiver operating analysis gave about 76 percent area under the curve for distinguishing patients from controls. TIE-2 shows promise as an adjunct blood marker, pending validation in larger cohorts.
pmc-13386776:
Trent Benedick's team built and validated a radiotherapy planning aid that matches new cases to similar past cases, in a 2026 paper. Radiotherapy planning still leans on individual experience plus dose-based tools, and finding a good reference case can guide plan creation. The team built a multi-step method that measures geometric similarity between cases from overlap volume histograms and spatial target signatures, comparing features with Earth Mover's Distance and a hybrid cluster-then-predict machine-learning model.

Validation on 192 head and neck cancer cases showed a strong link between the model's geometry score and actual dose similarity, with a correlation of about four-fifths. Clinical review plus receiver operating analysis gave an area under the curve of about 88 percent for spotting cases clinicians judged useful as planning templates. The tool aims to standardize plans, raise plan quality, and help clinicians at the first planning step.
pmc-13386876:
Benjamin Hafey and Liangqi Xie review hybrid viral-human DNA circles in HPV-driven cancers in a 2026 article. When human papillomavirus integrates into host DNA, it can spawn circular elements mixing viral and human stretches. Such hybrids appear in roughly 30 percent of HPV-linked throat cancers, with parallels in cervical cancer models.

The circles amplify viral drivers together with captured human genes and build new enhancer hubs from scratch. They also drive very high gene output and can act as roaming activators elsewhere in the genome. The authors discuss how these traits may open treatment angles tailored to hybrid-carrying tumors.
pmc-13386976:
Erasmus N. Kotey and a large team build a glowing, traceable version of a monkey virus related to Epstein-Barr in 2026 work. Rhesus lymphocryptovirus mirrors human EBV infection in macaques, making it a prized vaccine test model. Until now it lacked the green fluorescent tag that speeds EBV cell tracking in the lab.

The engineered virus kept its full genome intact and infected blood cells from several primate species. A mutant missing the entry protein gp350 infected B cells and surface cells far less well in their tests. That result confirms gp350 as the key to entry, matching its human counterpart.
pmc-13387676:
Rifyal Muhamad, Anis Widyasari, Diannisa Sangun, and Fitriana Ekawati surveyed men's role in care before pregnancy in Indonesia in 2026. Such preconception care aims to improve a woman's health before pregnancy, and it works best when the partner takes part. Male involvement in the country is rare and little studied.

One hundred men at three primary care centers in the Bantul region answered the survey in 2024. Involvement was high in forty-six percent, moderate in twenty-eight, and low in twenty-six. Men who knew more took part more. Warm attitudes and good talk with a spouse also tracked with engagement. Time pressure, money limits, and cultural barriers held some men back.
pmc-13388776:
Andrea Delbarba's team reviews how low testosterone reshapes male body makeup and how dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, the standard bone-density scan, can track it. Testosterone loss cuts lean mass and raises fat mass, especially around the organs. It weakens muscle, feeding frailty and heart-metabolism-linked risk through disrupted signals between bone, muscle, and fat.

The review explains the scan's three-compartment model, which quantifies fat, lean tissue, and bone with low radiation. It weighs evidence that testosterone replacement partly reverses the changes. Practical guidance covers reading scans in hypogonadal men so clinicians can spot osteosarcopenic obesity, the joint loss of bone and muscle with excess fat.
pmc-13388976:
Joshua Conrad Jackson's team tracked sixty years of civil rights lawmaking in the United States with text analysis of legislative archives, asking whether support grew gradually or in bursts. Civil rights bills became more common over time, but sponsorship split sharply by party.

Divergence sped up in the early 1990s and again in the mid-2010s, the second surge driven by racial minority Democrats as the Black Lives Matter movement rose. pmc-13409976:

pmc-13410376:

pmc-13410576:

pmc-13411776:

pmc-13413476:

pmc-13413976:

pmc-13415476:

pmc-13418276:

pmc-13418476:

pmc-13419176:

pmc-13419476:

pmc-13420176:

pmc-13421476:

pmc-13421576:

pmc-13421676:

pmc-13421776:

pmc-13423076:

pmc-13424076:

pmc-13424276:

pmc-13424376:

pmc-13424476:

pmc-13424576:

pmc-13424876:

pmc-13425576:

pmc-13425876:

pmc-13425976:

pmc-13426376:

pmc-13426976:

pmc-13427076:

pmc-13427476:

pmc-13427576:

pmc-13427776:

pmc-13427876:

pmc-13428176:

pmc-13428776:

pmc-13429276:

pmc-13429876:

pmc-13430176:

pmc-13430776:

pmc-13430876:

pmc-13431176:

pmc-13431576:

pmc-13434276:

pmc-13435476:

pmc-13435676:

pmc-13435776:

pmc-13436776:

pmc-13437676:

pmc-13439476:
Cristina Valares-Masa's team studied student teachers in 2026 on outdoor learning in early childhood schooling, where gains for children are clear but teacher training lags. pmc-13441776:

pmc-13442876:
Jiaxu Zhang and colleagues cut the squeeze that solid-state lithium-sulfur batteries need in a 2026 paper. pmc-13443676:
Chenwei Zhou and colleagues untangle how two gene-on marks share control of a gene's start zone in a 2026 study. pmc-13443876:
Chaudhry and Ehtesham present a 2026 commentary on expanding molecular oncology testing in Africa and other lower-income countries. pmc-13444176:
Piotie and colleagues published a 2026 report on building a diabetes registry in South Africa. Type 1 diabetes needs lifelong insulin, yet national data on it stay thin. pmc-13445076:

pmc-13445376:

pmc-13445776:
Paola Ferri and colleagues examine a 2026 quasi-experimental study of how team-based learning builds evidence-based practice competence in second-year nursing students. pmc-13445876:
Zeinab Habibpour and coauthors explore a 2026 interview-based study of final-year nursing students' placement time at Khoy University in Iran, where new placements aim to close the theory-practice gap. pmc-13446176:
Esther Soler-Climent and colleagues probe how body makeup, metabolism, and muscle function hang together in diabetic foot disease, in a 2026 case-control study. pmc-13446576: The publisher issued a correction in 2026 covering 99 abstracts whose PDF versions were wrong when first posted. pmc-13447376:

pmc-13447976:

pmc-13448076:

pmc-13448476:

pmc-13448676:

pmc-13448876:

pmc-13449576:

pmc-13449676:

pmc-13449776:

pmc-13450576:

pmc-13452176:

pmc-13453976:

pmc-13454176:

pmc-13454276:

pmc-13455276:

pmc-13457076:

The findings support careful donor selection and long-term kidney monitoring.
pmc-13474576:
Mary E Hackbarth and co-authors model a rare storage disease in mice in 2026 by copying its most common gene fault. The disease blocks exit of a sugar acid from cell recycling units, harming the brain over time. Mice with two copies of the fault built up the sugar acid as patients do. They showed unsteady gait, tremors, seizures, and shorter lives.

The model gives drug tests a faithful test bed.
pmc-13474676:
Zhenning Feng and colleagues probe blood antioxidants and thinking skills in 2026 in people with schizophrenia who had never taken antipsychotic drugs. Just over two hundred patients and about one hundred healthy peers gave blood for four antioxidant measures. Thinking was scored with a standard battery, and symptoms with a standard rating scale. Models tested links while accounting for age, sex, and clinical traits.

Within patients, higher levels of the two protective measures tracked with lower odds of impairment. Diet and metabolic care may deserve a place beside drug care.
pmc-13474776:
Uhawenimana and colleagues asked eye care users in Rwanda in 2026 how primary eye services felt after the country folded them into performance-based financing, a system that pays clinics partly on results. The team ran six focus group talks at six health centers with 72 people, including older adults and people with disabilities. They asked about travel, cost, quality, and how satisfied users felt with the care they received.

Cost still blocked many people, mainly the price of eyeglasses and some medicines that community health insurance did not fully cover for them. pmc-13474876:
Batuhan Aydın and co-authors test a dissolving membrane in 2026 for guiding bone regrowth in rat skull defects. The membrane layers two plastics, one slow to dissolve and one fast, printed in three dimensions. Twenty-four paired defects were split across four setups, mixing membranes with graft types or blood alone. Bone growth was measured at four and eight weeks.

The layered membrane with blood alone led all groups at four weeks by a clear margin. At eight weeks it still beat two groups and tied the control. Early speed matters where a membrane must hold space before it dissolves. The design earns larger animal tests before human use.
pmc-13475276:
A chemical that clears plastic in food packaging needs a careful safety check before approval. Tests showed the substance moves into food only in amounts below measurement limits, and the same held for its altered forms and impurities. Lab studies cleared it of gene-damage concerns, and computer checks agreed for the minor forms. The panel concluded it raises no safety concern at the proposed level.
pmc-13476076:
Ellison and colleagues measure how fast liver cells clear 207 chemicals, data needed to set an internal safety threshold for exposures. Safety limits today rest on doses fed to animals, but harm depends on the level that reaches blood and tissue. Their 2026 study uses frozen, thawed liver cells from several species at two low doses. pmc-13476576:
Kinan El Husseini and co-authors chart research themes in 2026 for chronic lung transplant failure, the top cause of late death after transplant. pmc-13477076:
Harrison R Herrera and co-authors show in 2026 how follow-up quality warps reported harms after mechanical aortic valve surgery. A group of 558 patients from 2000 to 2023 split into local and referral patients by distance from the center. Bleeding and clot events were counted by chart review and by billing codes. Matched groups of local and distant patients were compared.

Local patients were followed far longer and showed higher raw event rates. Careful time-based math shrank but did not erase the gap. Billing codes stretched the gap wider than chart review did. Distant patients are not safer; they are simply watched less closely.
pmc-13477776:
Singh and co-workers in India reported in 2026 a rare appendix cancer that wore the mask of plain appendicitis. Their patient was a woman of 64 with right low belly pain for a week. Scans showed a plump appendix with small stones, a classic sign of a blocked, sore organ. The team took the organ out, as is standard for such a case.

Stains for three marks came back plus, and a fourth came back minus, a code that points to the lower gut as the source. The cut edges still held tumor. The authors stress that each removed appendix needs a full tissue read, since this fast cancer needs more care than the first cut.
pmc-13478176:

Fibre layout decisively shaped wear resistance, with the multi-direction stack showing the lowest wear rate, about 44 percent better than the one-direction layout. It also showed lower friction, minimal roughness growth, and higher cross-section hardness, pointing to better load sharing. Microscopy showed mainly abrasive wear with less damage in multi-direction panels. The work links structure to wear performance for lightweight design.
pmc-13479476:
Peng and co-workers in China sifted in 2026 what shapes a heart patient's full day of motion, rest, and sleep. Street traits, like how green or dense the home zone was, also tracked with day shape. No study tied state rules to the day at all. The authors urge plans that push rehab sign up and home backing first.
pmc-13479576:
Jun Liu, Jun Sun, Huanyu Li, and Jingyu Zhao published a 2026 systematic review and network meta-analysis comparing physical activity programs for people with autism spectrum disorder. Exercise is a promising drug-free support, yet families face a confusing menu of types and doses. Seven databases were searched through December 2025 for controlled studies.
