Network methods let the authors rank programs that were never tested head-to-head, by borrowing strength across the whole evidence web. The ranking approach gives therapists and parents a comparative map for choosing activity type and dose, rather than another single-program verdict.
pmc-13479976:
Chenxi Jin and coauthors published a 2026 retrospective MRI study checking whether jaw disc positions after surgery are actually sensible. The operation, arthroscopic disc repositioning done on both sides, treats jaw joints where the cushioning disc has slipped forward and will not return. Ninety consecutive patients with scans were screened for the analysis.

After exclusions, fifty-nine surgical patients covering 101 joints were compared with thirty-one symptomatic patients whose discs were not displaced. Scans at one, three, and six months after surgery measured both disc position and joint mobility. The authors call their yardstick rationality: a disc can sit correctly yet still fail to move with the jaw. The graded follow-up shows whether early good positions hold or drift.
pmc-13480076:
Fumio Kurosaki and co-authors present a 2026 review of an inhaled drug used for stubborn lung infection with Mycobacterium avium complex. The drug, a liposomal form of amikacin breathed in through a nebulizer, serves patients whose infection resists standard care. The team read charts for 27 patients treated for at least six months at one centre between late 2021 and mid-2025.

Faulty use also mattered, covering stretched-out dosing gaps and late swaps of nebulizer parts. Voice hoarseness was the most common side effect and at times drove the dosing gaps. Teaching patients steady technique and checking their routine often may lift success rates without new drugs.
pmc-13482576:
Alshammari and colleagues show in 2026 that how you brew a medicinal plant changes what you get from it, comparing three methanol extraction methods for the herb Onosma rechingeri. The methods were sound-wave extraction, plain soaking, and heated Soxhlet extraction, Each yielded a different chemical mix. The heated Soxhlet method pulled out the most plant compounds overall and the most rosmarinic acid, and it led the electron-transfer tests. Plain soaking won elsewhere, carrying the most luteolin-7-glucoside of the three and blocking the brain enzyme and the starch enzyme most strongly of all. Computer docking backed the chemistry, flagging luteolin-7-glucoside as a strong binder of the starch enzyme, with rosmarinic acid favored for the brain targets.
pmc-13482876:
Gider and colleagues asked whether newer deep-learning tools beat a standard method at spotting the rare crashes that kill people. Their 2026 study used 5,676 crashes recorded in Batman province, Türkiye, from 2013 to 2022. Fatal crashes made up only 0.8 percent of records, so a lazy model could look accurate while missing every deadly case. The team compared XGBoost with two neural designs, TabNet and FT-Transformer.

FT-Transformer won, reaching the strongest discrimination scores and catching about 44 percent of fatal crashes among its top-ranked cases. Its precision-focused score ran nearly four times the random baseline the authors computed for comparison. XGBoost and TabNet trailed close behind each other. Gider warns that with so few fatal cases, scores that reward overall accuracy mislead, so rare-event measures should guide model choice for road safety work.
pmc-13483376:
Zirui Wang and others build a prediction model for recurrence in triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive form that lacks three common treatment targets. Their 2026 study joins medical and pathology data with quantitative traits from magnetic resonance imaging in a cohort of seven hundred patients. The model adds two novel elements: variation inside the tumour and traits from tissue just around it.

The merged model outperformed standard staging in ranking patients by risk, and it held up when tested for disease-free lives at one, three, and five years. By capturing tumour variety that staging systems miss, the tool aims to help doctors tailor treatment intensity and follow-up schedules to each patient. Oncologists gain a fuller picture of biological aggressiveness from scans they already collect.
pmc-13483576:
Karen Redhead and co-authors separate the effects of sleep apnea and low mood on pregnancy outcomes in a 2026 observational study. One hundred twenty-two women late in pregnancy at a large maternity hospital completed overnight breathing and oxygen monitoring and reported depressive symptoms. Chart review then recorded outcomes for mothers and newborns.

Babies of mothers with sleep apnea had much higher odds of a low Apgar score five minutes after birth, even after mood and body size were accounted for. More frequent oxygen dips were linked to higher birthweight babies. Depressive symptoms, in contrast, were linked to preterm birth rather than to newborn condition at delivery. The authors argue that both breathing treatment and mental health care deserve attention in pregnancy.
pmc-13483676:
Hou and colleagues filmed pelvic organs in motion to map how prolapse actually unfolds inside the body. Pelvic organ prolapse means organs such as the bladder sink from their normal places, and doctors usually grade it while the patient lies still. Their 2026 study scanned 63 women with advanced prolapse using MRI while they strained, then tracked each organ's center point across three pushes.

Each organ followed its own segmented path rather than sliding straight down as textbooks imply. The bladder traced a reversed C shape, bending at three turning points as its angle shifted. The uterus traced a reversed S with four turning points. By the third strain, the uterus had traveled about 83 percent of the reference line's length, far beyond its first-push distance. Hou argues surgical planning should respect these organ-specific routes.
pmc-13484876:
Zheng Cao fabricates a conductive heart patch that copies the layered, aligned fiber architecture of natural heart muscle. Published in 2026, the patch weaves oriented nanofibers into a gel matrix laced with dopamine and polypyrrole for electrical conduction. Fiber direction gives each layer one-way electrical character and guides heart cells to line up along the fibers.

In rats after heart attack, implanted patches improved heart function, limited wall thinning and scarring, and reduced cell death plus oxidative stress while new vessels grew into the damaged zone. pmc-13484976:
Sangrim Lee coats traditional mulberry paper with a conductive nanomaterial to build a flexible pressure sensor for wearables. Published in 2026, the design stacks several coated sheets so their rough, porous fibers compress and change electrical contact under load. Paper type, stacking pattern, and coating amount are tuned systematically for best response.

Sensitivity exceeded 15 per kilopascal across an unusually wide span from gentle touch to a full megapascal of pressure. Response was fast, output stayed consistent, and the device survived more than a thousand loading cycles. Built into gloves and wristbands, prototypes tracked finger bends, wrist pulse, and touch strength in real time. Wireless links even carried Morse code taps and CPR training feedback. pmc-13485076:
Lasrado and colleagues surveyed in 2026 how eye doctors in India manage optic neuritis in children, a sudden inflammation of the optic nerve that harms vision. Care for this condition varies, and the team wanted to map current practice and spot gaps. The authors call for shared practice guidelines.
pmc-13485676:

Two pressures compete, since reuse aids learning while distinct forms prevent confusion.

Sharing of meanings proved highly systematic at both levels, even though the particular meanings involved differed between levels. pmc-13487276:
Virginia Mares links automated fluid measures in the aging retina to the health of the light-sensing layer beneath. Automated numbers let clinics compare eyes and visits without reader drift.
pmc-13487976:
Iversen and team studied how stroke patients travel through Norway's emergency call system, then tested an artificial intelligence assistant on recorded calls. It rescued nine of fourteen strokes that human operators had missed in the error subgroup. Iversen calls the results promising but exploratory, demanding larger and more varied call collections before live deployment.
pmc-13488676:
Fanghong Nie and four co-authors rethink basic nursing care in an age of AI and robots, in a 2026 review. Ageing populations and staff shortages push technology into wards fast. Most writing judges the tools by speed and safety alone.

The authors propose judging technology by relational augmentation instead. Does a tool strengthen relationships, recognition of need, and a caring setting? pmc-13489076:
Maruša Škrbec leads a team that probes a parasite in pet rabbits. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with Encephalitozoon cuniculi. The parasite infects many mammals, with rabbits as main host.

Pet rabbits in Slovenia were tested over two years. Urine from random pet rabbits went to gene based tests. Microscope checks sought spores in the same samples. Gene material showed in a share of the urine set. Blood tests found both early and past infection marks. Types and clinical signs of infection were mapped. pmc-13490376:

pmc-13490576:

pmc-13491676:

Narcissism linked to problematic use both directly and through those two outlooks, while sadism showed only a small overall link. Among women the narcissism path ran fully through competitive individualism, and among men psychopathy pulled in opposite directions along different paths. The author advises caution because the measures did not behave identically across sexes.
pmc-13491776:

Microbial diversity fell step by step as syndrome components accumulated. Women with the syndrome carried more Lactobacillus, Roseburia, and Escherichia-Shigella, and less Akkermansia, a microbe often tied to metabolic health. pmc-13491876:

The sensor measured hCG across a wide range with a detection limit low enough for early pregnancy, and it ignored other hormones while distinguishing the pregnancy-specific subunit. Tests in urine worked directly without sample cleanup. The authors pitch the platform for quantitative point-of-care testing beyond pregnancy as well.
pmc-13493776:

As chopping proceeds, xylose builds up and the enzyme works less well, a problem known as product inhibition. The structure showed a single xylose molecule sitting in one pocket of the enzyme, held by hydrogen bonds and contacts with five conserved building blocks of the protein. pmc-13493976:

No deaths, fluid buildup, or visible damage to the abdominal lining followed, and microscopy showed the surface cell layer intact apart from mild flattening and slight scarring beneath. pmc-13494076:

pmc-13494476:

In mice, tumors with more of the strand grew less. Patient tissue checks backed the pattern. The authors propose the strand as a partner that deepens the drug's lethal effect.
pmc-13495076:

It charged a small capacitor in three minutes and survived thirty thousand cycles unchanged. It also sensed vibration frequency and pressure without outside power. The authors aim it at monitoring buried infrastructure.
pmc-13495376:

Instruments led the top hundred, then fixation devices, healing biologics, implants, access tools, and computer-guided systems. Fixation patents drew the most citations and the fastest yearly citation rate. Across eras the mix shifted: instruments dominated the earliest years, then shrank in share, while implants and biologics climbed. Near half the patents had expired at the time of study. The authors read the map as a record of where shoulder scope invention has concentrated and where it is heading.
pmc-13495476:

Single-port surgery took about ten minutes longer, yet patients lost less blood and left hospital about seventeen hours sooner. Complication rates and bladder control at three months did not split. pmc-13498476:
A large team studies thyroid problems in people with acromegaly in this 2026 paper. Acromegaly is a hormone disorder that enlarges body parts, and it has been linked to goiter and perhaps to thyroid cancer, but care for the main disease has improved in recent years.

The team first looked back at 92 patients over 28 years, then scanned the thyroid in 74 of them. Most patients had inactive disease at the last visit. Four cases of thyroid cancer were found, only one in a patient with active disease. The two stage design lets the authors ask whether thyroid risk stays high now that hormone control is better than in the past.
pmc-13498776:
Tetsuo Kon and his team review how chromosome-level genome assemblies are changing life science. Their review from twenty twenty-six marks a shift in genomics. The review steps through the making, checks, and marking up of assemblies. Case studies show four big gains from this way of work. Structural variation and deep chromosome change over ages come into view. Doubled genomes of tangled build can at last be sorted. Traits tie to genome layout in new ways. Life forms far from the pet kinds gain study tools of the same rank. The authors cast assemblies as base tools for new finds.
pmc-13499176:
Christian Summa, Daniel Swink, Joseph AbouAyash, and a wider team wrote this case report, published in 2026. It describes a full repair, done entirely through the leg artery, of a torn and bulging aorta in a sixty-six-year-old man.

Because of an earlier neck bypass, the team avoided arm access and worked only from the leg. An electric cutting step opened a controlled channel between the tear's two layers so the graft could pass. All gut branches received stents through nested tubes. Final imaging showed no leaks. The authors present the case as proof that even complex aortic repairs can be done from the leg alone.
pmc-13499676:
Hamzah M Javed and colleagues describe in 2026 a delayed, whole-body collapse after a large overdose of a common HIV treatment tablet that combines four antiviral drugs. pmc-13500376:

They sat within a few dozen DNA letter differences, hinting at recent shared ancestry across the human-animal boundary. pmc-13501576:

Of these, 62 received percutaneous endoscopic lumbar discectomy through a single channel, and 60 received unilateral biportal endoscopy, which uses separate viewing and working channels. Everyone was followed for at least twelve months.

Both groups improved markedly in pain and disability. The biportal operations took longer, averaging about 132.77 minutes against 86.61 minutes in clock time, and involved more blood loss, near 270 millilitres against roughly 37 millilitres on average. Long-term pain scores, disability scores, and excellent-or-good outcome rates, 91.9 percent against 93.3 percent, were comparable. A cumulative sum analysis placed the learning curve turning point at 24 cases for the biportal method and 38 for the single-channel one.
pmc-13501776:
Tianlong Wang leads a twenty-three-author team reporting a 2026 multicentre validation of a transfusion risk score for heart surgery on bypass. The FW-TRIC score was built earlier at Fuwai Hospital to forecast which patients will need red blood cell transfusion, a common event tied to worse outcomes. This study tested it externally in 3,287 adults operated on at nine Chinese cardiovascular centres during 2024, excluding transplant, mechanical support, and pre-transfused cases.

The overall transfusion rate reached 40.1 percent, giving the test plenty of events to judge. Discrimination was good, with an area under the curve of 0.713, and calibration was excellent, meaning predicted rates matched observed ones closely. Every single ingredient of the score, from age to surgery type, predicted worse alone than the combined score did. Performance held across all nine centres, with each centre's area above 0.65 on that measure. The authors back its use for blood management planning.
pmc-13502576:
Arpan Mondal and Richard A. Layfield report a 2026 study in which rare-earth complexes chop white phosphorus step by step. White phosphorus, the P4 molecule, is industry's gateway chemical, but rare-earth reagents stop at cage anions that resist use. The team's yttrium and gadolinium dinitrogen complexes, sources of divalent reactivity, instead cleaved P4 into a series. First came a four-atom dianion, then a two-atom dianion, then a phosphorus atom carrying an electron.

Structures and spectra characterized each stop. The four-unit ligand adopts a bicyclobutane-like shape, the two-unit ligand binds side-on as a double bond of the element, and the atom behaves as an element-centred radical. Paramagnetic resonance confirmed coupling to the element and yttrium, while the gadolinium version showed antiferromagnetic exchange with the radical. Calculations placed the spin on the element, extending its multiply bonded chemistry into the rare earths.
pmc-13502776:
Wang and colleagues described a sixty-one-year-old woman with breast cancer that spread into the membranes around her spinal cord. She regained leg function and nearly three and a half years of disease control, in a 2026 case report. Her tumor was triple-negative, lacking the drug targets, and had returned after two quiet years, paralyzing both legs.

Wang profiled her genes and found an mutation in PALB2, a DNA-repair gene that makes tumors vulnerable to a drug class called PARP inhibitors. After chemotherapy and a checkpoint immunotherapy drug had failed, they added the PARP inhibitor olaparib. Her leg strength improved from paralysis to partial movement, and scans showed shrinkage of the spinal-membrane and bone lesions. Progression-free survival reached forty months with side effects. The authors caution that one case cannot separate drug's contribution, but argue the strategy merits study in patients.
pmc-13503276:
Emma Elizabeth Sabu Kattuman leads an eight-author team with a 2026 melanoma study that unmasks an inflammation receptor as a self-fuelling tumour driver. Mining TCGA data, the team found the cysteinyl leukotriene receptor CysLT1R far higher in metastatic than primary tumours. In mouse and human melanoma cells, activating the receptor with leukotriene D4 drove growth and invasion through two pathways, ERK and YAP. Crucially, the melanoma cells make their supply: they express the synthase and secrete the leukotrienes themselves.

That autocrine loop keeps the receptor switched on without help from surrounding tissue. Deleting the receptor, or blocking it with the drug MK571, clearly slowed tumour growth in animals and shut down the YAP-LOXL-2 axis. Experiments in receptor-deficient mice showed the host's own receptor in nearby tissue contributes too. The authors nominate CysLT1R as a druggable target in a cancer starved of options.
pmc-13503476:
Basri and a large team review how bile acids, the detergents the liver makes to digest fat, may help or harm the brain in Alzheimer's disease. Beyond digestion, bile acids act as hormones, and gut bacteria constantly remodel them before they circulate to distant organs. Their 2026 narrative review pulls together biochemical, animal, and clinical findings on two bile acid receptors that sit at the crossroads of metabolism, inflammation, and brain health.

People with Alzheimer's or mild cognitive impairment show altered bile acid profiles. The review sorts the family into villains and protectors. Water-hating secondary bile acids are linked to blood-brain barrier leaks and direct nerve toxicity, while water-loving types appear anti-inflammatory and protective in the cited evidence. Bile acids also trigger gut hormones, including GLP-1, the target of blockbuster diabetes drugs, giving them indirect routes to the brain.
pmc-13503876:
Chao Ma leads a team that glued crystal sponges into gas-sorting sheets with a plastic-like bond, in a 2026 study. The crystals, called metal-organic frameworks, sort gases by pore size and chemistry. Sheets made from them leak through gaps where grains meet, which ruins the sorting.

Heat and a helper compound triggered a linking reaction right at the grain faces of one crystal type, UiO-66. The sheets ended up almost all crystal by weight, with few leak paths left. They passed carbon dioxide fast while holding back nitrogen, beating a known quality line for that pair. The sheets also shrugged off damp air and could be refreshed. The same trick worked for three more crystal types of the same family.
pmc-13504376:
Amanda Östensson and Joakim Jonsson evaluate an artificial intelligence workflow that plans prostate radiotherapy from MRI scans alone. Their 2026 study explains the appeal: MRI shows soft tissue far better than CT, but standard planning needs both scans, and aligning them adds positional error. The AI system outlines organs and fabricates a synthetic CT from the MRI, skipping the alignment step entirely.

The team tested the system on nineteen patients with both scans on file. Its outlines matched expert hand-drawn ones about as closely as experts match each other, scoring above 0.9 overlap for prostate and bladder. The synthetic scans stayed close to the real ones in density and structure. Recomputed radiation doses on the synthetic scans agreed almost perfectly with the original plans, and every clinical dose limit still held. The authors back the workflow for clinical use in pelvic radiotherapy.
pmc-13504476:
Timothy Chizmar argues that the coordinators behind ambulance blood programs are the mission-critical role nobody sees in a 2026 commentary. Over four hundred civilian EMS systems now carry whole blood to give bleeding patients transfusions before hospital, where each minute of delay raises the odds of death. Hemorrhage is the leading preventable killer after injury.

Coordinators run the clinical and logistical machinery: cold-chain storage, waste control, partnerships with blood banks and hospitals, and data that guides the program. New coordinators mostly learn on the job from distant mentors, the author notes. A published framework now spells out the knowledge and skills the role demands. The piece calls for treating coordination as a profession in its own right, since the lifesaving promise of field blood stands or falls with it.
pmc-13504776:
Nan Sun and others propose a federated distillation model for cell type classification from medical single-cell transcriptomes. In 2026, the plan, called scKSFD, lets institutions collaborate without pooling raw patient data, a constraint imposed by privacy rules such as GDPR and HIPAA. Standard federated learning exchanges model parameters; this approach instead shares probability-level soft labels on a reference data set.

Stratified proxy sampling preserves rare cell groups, while probability-level aggregation mitigates batch-specific levels shifts without explicit feature correction. Across forty-two medical data sets, the method matched or beat centralized and current federated baselines under heterogeneous settings, with clear paired improvements. A multi-hospital COVID-19 case study improved classification over local-only training without sharing patient-level levels data.
pmc-13505076:
Yaodong Zhang leads a team testing a newer anesthetic against propofol for preventing sickness after surgery, in a 2026 trial. Nausea and vomiting after operations strike about a third of patients and most high-risk ones. Propofol helps but can sting on injection and drop blood pressure.

The trial enrolled 334 women having keyhole gynecologic surgery, split between the two drugs for sleep induction and upkeep. Sickness rates in the first day were near equal, at about 58 percent in each group. The new drug did not prove itself no worse within the set margin. It did win on safety: far less injection pain, less early low pressure, and less slow heart rate during surgery. Pain scores and satisfaction matched. The authors offer it as a gentler option.
pmc-13505176:
Denzel L Q Drop leads an international team that tested a virtual reality video made to help intensive care survivors understand what happened to them. Many survivors develop stress symptoms, anxiety, or low mood after critical illness. Across eleven hospitals, 344 adults who had spent at least three days in intensive care were split among standard care, an early video viewing, and a late viewing.

Six months later, stress symptom scores did not differ between either video group and standard care. Anxiety, depression, and quality of life also showed no group differences. Patients still rated the video highly, giving it a median eight out of ten for improving understanding and for satisfaction. The authors warn that a single viewing should not be expected to work like longer, guided, or personalised programmes, and they suggest future trials focus on high-risk patients.
pmc-13506576:
Kanako Kasuya and colleagues review, in a 2026 study from Japan, how often older patients with womb lining cancer received care that matched national guidelines. Records covered 130 patients aged 70 or older treated between 2010 and 2019 at one hospital. Guideline care meant main surgery, node checks when needed, and added chemotherapy based on risk.

Patients aged 75 or older met the full standard far less often than those aged 70 to 74, mainly through fewer node checks and less added chemotherapy. Missing the standard linked to worse outcomes even after other factors were counted. The authors advise judging fitness by full assessment, not age alone.
pmc-13506976:
Tsuboi and a large team offer a simple bedside test to split two look alike tremor diseases in twenty twenty-six. Dystonic tremor and Parkinson's disease can be hard to tell apart when signs are mild. A brain scan can help, but it is costly and not always at hand. The team measured tremor with motion sensors in one hundred two patients.

Tremor while drawing a spiral ran higher in dystonic tremor, while tremor at rest ran higher in Parkinson's. Posture tremor did not split the groups. A plain rule, spiral shake beats rest shake, named the disease with high accuracy. Three blind raters using their eyes alone matched the sensors well. The authors urge wider testing of the rule.
pmc-13507076:
Nandang Permadi and co-authors report a plant science study, published in 2026, protecting banana plantlets from a browning problem in tissue culture. Laboratories grow banana plants from small tissue pieces, the fastest route to many identical plants, but enzymes brown the tissue and stall growth. Lime peel extract fights that browning with antioxidants, yet it breaks down and washes out too fast to last.

The team sealed the extract inside tiny beads of alginate and gelatin, which released it slowly over weeks and stayed stable in storage. In two banana varieties the beads cut browning more than free extract did. Readers get a practical delivery trick that could raise success rates in commercial banana propagation.
pmc-13508276:
Asima Khan and six co-authors map how proven type 2 diabetes care gets put into practice at primary clinics in poorer countries, in a 2026 scoping review. Diabetes is rising fast in low- and middle-income nations, where tight budgets make clinic care uneven. The team searched eight databases for studies from 1996 to late 2024. Papers had to describe rolling out, adapting, or judging evidence-based diabetes care in primary settings. Ninety-two articles covering 85 studies in 27 countries qualified.

Rollout tactics clustered most often around engaging patients, changing clinic infrastructure, and using feedback to adjust course. Tactics tailored to local context appeared less often. The team also coded what helped and what blocked progress, using a standard framework. Readers get a map of which strategies clinics actually use, where the gaps lie, and which hurdles planners must clear before diabetes care can improve at scale in resource-poor settings.
pmc-13508376:
Sofia Kaloper and four co-authors study how accurately people report the places tied to HIV risk and care in Los Angeles, in 2026 work. Prevention programs lean on location data to find hotspots, yet self-reported places carry error. Data came from a long-running study of gay, bisexual, and other sexual minority men in the city. Mapping checks and statistical models then weighed which traits, activity types, and areas predict reporting accuracy.

Personal traits, the kind of activity reported, and geography each shaped accuracy in a meaningful way. Places inside a person's home region were reported more accurately than places outside it. That regional tilt could quietly bias hotspot maps built from surveys alone. The authors plan sharper models with confidence ranges around reported points. Their goal is fairer targeting of prevention work, so that areas with fuzzier reporting do not get overlooked in funding maps.
pmc-13510376:
S. Fouziya Sulthana, U. Mohammed Iqbal, B. S. Sreeja, and Rajesh Anbazhagan review flexible wearable sensors that track body chemistry and body signals at the same time, in 2026 work. Most wearables today cover one side only, either movement and electrical signals or chemical measures such as glucose and lactate in sweat. Joining both sides in one soft, skin-fitting patch could give a fuller picture of health between clinic visits.

The review covers new flexible materials and building methods, then weighs progress in physical sensing, chemical sensing, and ways to merge them on one platform. Gains include steady tracking of chronic conditions and earlier warning of changes. Hurdles remain in accuracy over time, power, data handling, and the step from lab demos to approved medical use. The authors close with directions for the next wave of combined wearables.
pmc-13510576:
Marinos Chatzikonstantinou, Kyriaki Michailidou, Marios Pantzaris, Gavriella Alexandrou, Charalambos C. Charalambous, and Dimitris Sokratous pilot a two-arm exercise program for people with progressive multiple sclerosis, in 2026 work. Five participants with primary or secondary progressive forms took part in a twelve-week program of in-phase movements, where both arms move in the same pattern together. Sessions ran thirty to sixty minutes, and the study used a single-case design with staggered starts.

The program proved safe, workable, and well tolerated across the group. Three of the five participants showed clear gains in the excitability of pathways from brain to muscle, plus gains in some clinical measures. Earlier work had shown similar gains in the relapsing form of the disease. The authors call the low-cost program a candidate for routine and group rehabilitation, while stressing that five cases can only point the way.
pmc-13510876:
Natasha Hockaden and co-authors grow brain cancer cells at body like oxygen levels in a 2026 study. Glioblastoma lives in a low oxygen pocket, yet labs usually grow it in room air, far richer than any tissue. Patient derived tumor models sat for at least a week at five percent oxygen against the usual twenty one. Migration, growth, cell cycle, and signaling were then compared.

The realistic oxygen setting reprogrammed the cells: they migrated more and answered drugs differently. If lab air has been quietly flattering drug candidates, this helps explain glioblastoma's grim trial record. The study makes a simple plea with data: test brain cancer drugs under the air the tumor breathes.
pmc-13512776:
Koraj and colleagues redesigned inhibitors of ST6GAL1 to fix their flaw: they could not cross cell membranes. ST6GAL1 is an enzyme that decorates cell surfaces with sialic acid and helps cancers spread and hide from immunity. Their 2026 medicinal chemistry study started from a known non-sugar inhibitor bearing a sulfonic acid group. They replaced that group with look-alike substitutes called bioisosteres.

Koraj found that sulfonylurea substitutes restored passive membrane crossing in an artificial membrane test while keeping enzyme inhibition. An expanded series improved potency, with the best compound reaching low micromolar strength. Binding measurements confirmed the new compounds engage the enzyme at similar strength to the parent. Magnetic resonance mapping showed which parts of the molecule touch the enzyme, with the strongest inhibitors making extra contacts through their aromatic arms. The work supplies a design framework for cell-permeable versions of this cancer target.
pmc-13514676:
Teresa Sinicropi and four co-authors present a 2026 case report of a giant desmoid tumour in the small bowel of a 27-year-old man. Desmoid fibromatosis is rare, grows invasively where it starts, and almost never spreads, yet its behaviour is unpredictable and no standard treatment pathway exists. The patient arrived with fever and worsening abdominal pain five years after sleeve gastrectomy weight-loss surgery, and a CT scan revealed a large abdominal mass arising near the small intestine.

Surgeons removed the mass along with the right colon and the end of the small intestine, and laboratory examination confirmed the desmoid diagnosis. The man left hospital on the fifth day after surgery in good condition, with no sign of the tumour returning at the time of writing. Sinicropi's team reviews the wider literature and finds their full-removal approach matches current thinking.
pmc-13515676:
Wheat straw rots slowly because its cell walls are built tough, yet the right microbe can dismantle them. Tingyao Lv and co-authors characterize such a microbe in 2026, a heat-loving Streptomyces strain pulled from finished compost in Anhui, China. Over twenty-eight days it visibly shredded the straw surface and broke down about a third of its mass.

Cellulose and fiber sugars fell sharply, and the strain's cutting enzymes peaked a week in. Its genome carries many genes for those enzymes. Gene activity scans after three days on straw showed over sixteen hundred genes switching level, most wall-cutting genes switching on. The authors back the strain as a candidate for turning straw waste into useful products.
pmc-13515876:
Mikołaj Maga and six colleagues translate and validate a Polish version of the Walking Impairment Questionnaire in a 2026 study. The questionnaire scores walking distance, speed, and stair climbing for people with intermittent claudication, the leg pain of narrowed arteries that strikes during walking. One hundred patients lined up for vessel-opening treatment completed the Polish form, two quality-of-life surveys, and a six-minute walking test.

Scores on the Polish questionnaire lined up with both quality-of-life surveys across every domain. They also tracked the distance walked before pain began and the maximum distance reached. Repeating the test gave near-identical results, and the questions hung together strongly as a set. Maga's team concludes that the Polish version, built on metric units, is a reliable and clinically useful gauge of walking limits in this patient group.
pmc-13515976:
Gulnur Nakhanova leads a twenty-two-author team developing a quality-control test for a brucellosis vaccine candidate, in a 2026 study. The vaccine uses a lab-made protein, superoxide dismutase, as its antigen. Standard antibody tests can misread such proteins after the chemical steps used in vaccine making, so the team built an older-style diffusion assay instead. First they raised rich antibody serum in sheep, comparing two booster additives.

The aluminium-based additive produced far stronger antibody levels than the rival by day forty-two. With that serum, the diffusion assay formed rings whose size grew in a straight, predictable relation with antigen amount. It detected the protein down to a fraction of a microgram per millilitre, measured precisely, and ignored unrelated proteins. Nakhanova's team presents the assay as a sturdy tool for checking antigen strength in future vaccine batches.
pmc-13516676:
Rejoice Nyarku leads a ten-author team validating a rapid Salmonella test for poultry settings in a 2026 study. Salmonella in chickens is a top food-safety threat, and knowing which strain is present guides the response. The platform, GenoPATHX, runs two multiplex gene panels, one tuned to chickens and one to turkeys, each spotting priority strains plus a general Salmonella marker in a single same-day workflow.

Bench validation showed strong, straight-line readings and detection down to tens or hundreds of genome copies per reaction. The panels caught every target strain in the test set and excluded off-target germs cleanly. On naturally contaminated farm samples, the direct workflow reached about eighty-one percent sensitivity and ninety-one percent specificity against the reference culture method used by United States inspectors. Nyarku's team presents the assay as ready support for poultry surveillance and risk-based food safety action.
pmc-13518476:
A short strand of synthetic RNA that silences hepatitis B's messages is through its first human tests. Wen Wang and co-authors report the phase one study of AHB-137 in this 2026 paper. Fifty-two healthy Chinese volunteers formed the safety stage. Then came twenty-two treated patients with chronic hepatitis B, whose virus was already suppressed by standard pills.

Six under-skin doses were spread over four weeks, at two dose levels. No serious harms, deaths, or dropouts occurred; most reactions were mild, sore injection sites, fever, and quiet lab blips. One patient's liver enzymes spiked as the viral surface protein fell fast, a flare the field reads with interest. Blood levels rose in proportion to dose and cleared on schedule. The study's job was safety, and the drug passed to fight another day.
pmc-13518776:
Inka Romero-Ortells, Manuel Perea, Eva Gutierrez-Sigut, and Jon Andoni Duñabeitia report 2026 eye-tracking experiments on how subtitles steer attention in bilingual teaching videos. University students watched two-speaker lessons while researchers varied the spoken language and the subtitle language. The learners were Spanish speakers studying English, with native English speakers as a comparison group.

Dubbing the audio into Spanish shifted gaze from speakers' mouths toward their eyes, while comprehension rose compared with original English audio. Once subtitles appeared, viewers in both language groups spent most of their looking time on the text itself, whatever language it used. Comprehension stayed equally high with first- or second-language subtitles, a useful lesson for video designers.
pmc-13518876:
Yue Li and eight colleagues profile the immune landscape of high-grade serous ovarian cancer in 2026, a disease that recurs often and shrugs off checkpoint immunotherapy. Sequencing single cells from tumors of eight untreated patients, covering 84,065 cells, they mapped six major cell groups and traced how killer CD8 T cells wear out into exhausted states.

Exhausted T cells stood out for producing CCL3, a signal that talks to macrophages through the CCR1 receptor. Fluid from exhausted cells pushed macrophages toward the tumor-friendly M2 type far more strongly than fluid from active T cells, and added CCL3 boosted that shift further. Blocking this axis, the authors propose, might warm up cold ovarian tumors.
pmc-13518976:
Gaoyuan Fu proposes a 2026 network model, CT-GCN, that predicts how productive Chinese manufacturing firms will become while separating true causes from mere correlations.
