The framework estimates productivity with the Levinsohn-Petrin method, identifies causal effects with double machine learning, and maps firms into graphs built from supply chains, distance, and technology similarity. Prediction error fell by more than 19 percent versus baselines. Research spending, digital transformation, and human capital emerged as genuine drivers, with effects varying by sector, size, and region. Tailored strategy advice follows from those differences.
pmc-13520276:
Erenoğlu and Kılıç ask whether nursing students who cannot put their phones down also experience more abuse inside online dating relationships. Cyber dating abuse covers partners monitoring messages, controlling contacts, and attacking through digital channels. Their 2026 cross-sectional study surveyed 224 nursing students at a state university in southern Turkey, most of them women and nearly all single, using validated addiction and abuse questionnaires.

Every abuse dimension moved with phone addiction, always weakly but always significantly: students scoring higher on addiction reported more monitoring and control by partners, and more direct digital aggression. They also admitted doing more of each themselves. Nearly two thirds of the students said they felt lost without their phones, and a third reported low mood when not using them. The authors argue nurses are well placed to teach young people to spot digital abuse early.
pmc-13520376:
Bereket Yilma Beshah and colleagues map in 2026 where young children in East Africa miss their third diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis vaccine dose, and which local factors track with missed doses. Survey data covered 14,200 children aged 12 to 23 months in seven countries from 2018 to 2023.

Missed doses clustered geographically rather than scattering evenly. The strongest cluster centred on central and northern Mozambique, where risk was nearly four times the background level. Having no maternal schooling and fewer than four antenatal visits tracked with missed doses, though strengths varied by place. Maps of this kind help outreach teams target cold spots first.
pmc-13521776:
Fear of movement, called kinesiophobia, keeps many people with inflammatory bowel disease inactive even when exercise would help. Xinyi Gao and five co-authors surveyed 249 patients at a Shanghai hospital, scoring their fear of movement, their independence in daily tasks such as bathing and dressing, and their fatigue. More than half the patients scored at or above the fear threshold, with an average score near thirty nine on the scale used.

Two factors dominated the analysis. Patients who were less independent in daily life feared movement far more, and this link was the strongest in the model; greater fatigue also raised fear, more modestly. Female sex, insurance type, and moderate disease activity played smaller roles, while severe activity oddly did not. The authors suggest that restoring daily independence and easing fatigue may be the most direct ways to lower this fear and get patients moving again.
pmc-13521876:
Yang and team surveyed family caregivers in China in twenty twenty-six. They care for disabled older adults at home. Such care brings heavy strain and can feed low mood. The team surveyed three hundred fifty-three caregivers in two eastern cities. Set scales gauged resilience, burden, low mood, and family function. About a third of caregivers showed signs of depression.

Greater resilience linked to fewer signs of low mood. Burden carried part of that link, as a go-between. Family function changed how strong the go-between path was. In strong families, resilience cut low mood more, through lower burden. The team urges help that builds both resilience and family function. Backing the whole family may ease burden more than aiding one caregiver. The one-time design limits claims of cause, but the patterns held.
pmc-13521976:
Magdalena Benda and colleagues review in 2026 infection risk from T-cell redirecting cures for relapsed myeloma. The set held 123 studies, mostly early phase. Cures cover engineered CAR T cells and bispecific antibodies. These cures changed care, yet infection load stays high.

Any-grade infection rates ran from about 40 to 80 percent in most reports. Risk peaked early after cell dosing or in early antibody months. Severe infection topped half in some antibody groups. Fatal cases arose under both cure types. Viruses and bacteria led the germ lists. Fungal disease and one pneumonia type arose where preventive cover was absent.
pmc-13522176:
Jialu Chen and co-authors study a protein called BpdE in Brucella abortus, a germ that lives inside host cells and causes brucellosis. Published in 2026, the work asks how BpdE, an enzyme that breaks down a key signal molecule, shapes the cell cycle of the germ. Little was known about such enzymes in this species before.

Deleting the bpdE gene made the germs grow faster in the lab and survive better inside host macrophages, the immune cells they infect. The changed germs also held more DNA than normal. The team found that BpdE lifts the activity of the minCDE genes, a set that helps control cell division. In short, BpdE acts as a brake on growth.
pmc-13522276:
Yousef Hawas and colleagues present in 2026 a 54-year-old postmenopausal woman with lobular breast cancer in both breasts. Spread reached the stomach. An eye socket lump first feared as spread proved to be plain inflammation. Lobular cancers reach gut and orbit more often than other breast types do.

Biopsy showed hormone-sensitive, HER2-negative disease in both breasts. Scans found gut wall thickening and belly fluid. Lungs and liver stayed clear. Drug care then hormone upkeep held disease stable. Fresh eye checks after droop and vomiting named a steroid-responsive false tumour. Nerve harm from drug care needed plasma exchange. Bone scans showed no bone spread.
pmc-13522776:
Dongxu Li and colleagues build a membrane-based nanoplatform for painful tendon disease in a 2026 study. Tendinopathy causes long-term pain, driven by an inflamed environment that draws in pain-sensing nerves and weakens tendon stem cells. The platform fuses membranes from immune cells and sensory nerve cells and combines them with cleaned tendon matrix material.

The hybrid membranes soak up multiple inflammatory signals and pain-related molecules, calming the local environment and protecting stem cells from aging. The tendon matrix pushed those stem cells toward tendon identity and movement. In animals, treatment improved collagen alignment, eased pain, shifted immune cells toward healing, and restored tendon function. The authors present the design as a way to break the inflammation and aging cycle while rebuilding tendon.
pmc-13522976:
Junjie Wang and co-authors link extreme heat to depressive symptoms among teenagers in China, in a 2026 study. Heat waves have grown more frequent as the climate warms. Their effect on young minds is less studied than their effect on bodies. Sleep, exercise, and self-rated health may sit on the path between heat and mood.

The team drew on four waves of a large national family panel study. Records ran from 2016 to 2022 and were matched with a standard index of extreme hot days. Analysis tested both the direct link and the possible pathways. Results matter for schools and health planners in a warming climate. They also flag groups that may need extra support during heat waves.
pmc-13523276:
Shuang He and co-authors review ten years of severe face and neck infections in a 2026 hospital study from western China. Such infections fill deep spaces in the face and jaw, and they can turn life-threatening. The team pulled records for 542 patients who had open surgery at one large hospital. They tracked germs found, drug response, and how patients fared.

Germs grew from samples in 400 cases, just under three quarters of the total. Two germ groups, Streptococcus and Klebsiella, showed up most often. Five drugs still worked on many samples, led by levofloxacin. Case counts fell early in the decade, then rose again. Patients treated during and after the COVID-19 years faced far higher odds of problems in hospital than those treated before.
pmc-13523376:
Ayse Sena Manzak Dursun and colleagues trial a home exercise program for women with asthma in a 2026 randomized study. Thirty women were assigned to a training group or a control group receiving a general activity booklet. The training group met a physiotherapist weekly for eight weeks and exercised at home three days a week, following a standardized, low-cost routine.

Compared with controls, the training group improved significantly on one breathing measure, walking distance in six minutes, an activity-related quality of life subscore, and leg strength measured by repeated standing. Other outcomes, including overall asthma control, did not separate clearly in the reported results. The authors present the program as an accessible alternative where advanced rehabilitation centers are out of reach, particularly for reducing sedentary behavior.
pmc-13523476:
Chunlan Yu and others assess, in a 2026 mixed-methods study, whether maternity care stakeholders in China would accept a midwifery continuity of care model. In that model, a known midwife or small team follows a woman through pregnancy, birth, and the postnatal period. Chinese maternity care remains largely led by obstetricians and split across many hands, so acceptance is a key test.

Surveys reached 896 maternity providers across China, and focus groups added views from providers and childbearing women. About 93 percent of them said they would accept and use the model, with midwives most willing and obstetricians least. Leadership backing was the strongest helper, followed by obstetrician endorsement and women's buy-in. Group discussions showed unmet needs for relational continuity alongside practical barriers the authors say planning must address.
pmc-13523576:
Jose de Melo Junior and co-authors report the findings and outcomes of repeat ablation procedures for atrial fibrillation in patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a thickened heart muscle. Such patients commonly need a repeat catheter ablation, yet why the fibrillation returns was poorly defined. Their 2026 study takes 45 such patients at one center from 2015 to 2023. Each was matched one to one with controls without the thickening, and full heart maps were compared.

Pulmonary vein reconnection led the findings: 86.7 percent in the thickened-heart group against 75.5 percent in controls, a gap short of significance. Over a median follow-up of 456 days, fibrillation returned in 57.8 percent of the thickened group and 51.1 percent of controls, again short of significance. Large atrial size and fast recurrence tied to return at first analysis, then lost the tie in adjusted models. Repeat ablation outcomes match those of controls, the authors hold.
pmc-13524376:
Tess Cherlin and six co-authors examine how much pain women with polycystic ovary syndrome experience, in a two thousand twenty-six study of electronic health records. The condition, recently renamed polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, is common, yet its pain burden is underexplored.

Drawing on a network covering over one hundred million women, the analysis found about twenty-one percent of women with the syndrome had recorded pain. Prevalence was highest among Black and White patients. Both the syndrome alone and the syndrome with pain carried higher relative risks for conditions including infertility, ovarian cysts, and obesity. Women treated with syndrome-related medications showed fewer pain diagnoses afterward, and the authors urge clinicians to address pain directly.
pmc-13524676:
Kanita Mankan and others pool, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, how well standard kidney function equations perform in kidney transplant recipients. Knowing the filtration rate matters after transplant, and cystatin C depends less on muscle mass than creatinine. Guidelines endorse cystatin C for chronic kidney disease mostly, with little guidance for transplant care.

Twenty-six studies met the bar, and fourteen gave usable bias data on 4,041 adult recipients with repeat measures. An equation using both creatinine and cystatin C showed the smallest average bias against measured filtration. Rules using creatinine alone tended to underestimate true filtration, while rules using cystatin alone overshot it. Accuracy within set margins was also pooled. The authors support the joint equation for transplant follow-up while noting studies varied.
pmc-13524776:
Patricia León-Cabrera and co-authors find that very slow brain waves track how hard a learner is mining a text in this 2026 study. Learning a new word from context means picking the useful clues out of a sentence and ignoring the rest. The team wondered whether slow electrical drift at the scalp could mark that effort.

Volunteers learned new words from sentences that gave away a lot or a little about each meaning. A slow negative wave built up while they worked. Its size did not follow how helpful the sentence was. Its slope, though, told on the learner: people who learned better showed a steeper slope, above all when the context was rich. The authors read the slope as a sign of deep engagement with useful information. They propose these ultraslow signals as markers of information sampling during learning.
pmc-13524876:
Poirot, de Médina, and Silvente-Poirot propose in 2026 a new way to think about cholesterol production. The pathway that builds cholesterol runs more than twenty steps and makes many distinct intermediate molecules, called sterols, which seems wasteful if cholesterol is the only goal.

The authors argue that the intermediates are products in their own right, each with its own effects on membranes, signals, and oxidation chemistry. Their framework, sterol flux rewiring, says that what matters is how the flow through the pathway is redistributed. The redistribution creates whole sterol states rather than piles of single molecules. That view ties together findings long kept apart, from inherited pathway disorders to immune and brain biology. It also suggests treatments that reshape the sterol state instead of simply blocking cholesterol production.
pmc-13524976:
Magdalena Kloc and nine co-authors review compounds from fungi as candidate weapons against skin cancer. Their review appeared in two thousand twenty-six. Skin cancers are common, invasive, and often outlast standard treatments. Fungal chemistry offers a deep shelf of molecules that kill cells in useful ways.

The compounds surveyed attack on several fronts: forcing cell suicide, starving tumors of blood vessels, and stirring the immune system. Named examples include cordycepin, a ganoderma acid, and immune-active polysaccharides like lentinan. Evidence spans dish tests, animal studies, and early human trials. Production, delivery into the body, and toxicity remain the main hurdles. Pairing fungal agents with chemo, radiation, or immune therapy looks promising. The authors call the field promising but still largely preclinical.
pmc-13525176:
Andri Burger and colleagues survey, in a 2026 snapshot study, student wellbeing supports in medical schools across Australia and New Zealand after new guidance appeared. Medical students report more psychological distress than peers, with effects on learning and patient safety. National documents now urge safe learning environments and wellbeing-oriented curricula, and accreditation standards were revised.

All 24 accredited schools were invited to an online survey between February and May 2024, distributed through dean and wellbeing networks. Sixteen responses came from fourteen schools, representing 58 percent of the sector, after duplicate entries were merged. Respondents were educators and administrators working in student wellbeing or medical education. Their answers reflect personal institutional views, not formally endorsed positions, a caveat the authors state plainly while assessing alignment with the guidance.
pmc-13525476:
Keneilwe Bowane and co-authors record nursing students' experience of emergency online learning in a 2026 paper. When COVID-19 lockdowns hit, the University of Botswana moved teaching online almost overnight. Nursing is a hands-on field, so the shift raised sharp questions. The team interviewed sixteen nursing students in late 2023 and sorted their accounts by content analysis.

Five themes emerged: the chances online learning opened, how students performed under it, its challenges, what needs improving, and the fit between nursing as a profession and remote study. Students valued continuity and flexibility, yet wrestled with the loss of clinical feel and the strain of remote work. The authors offer the findings to planners who must keep nursing education running through future crises.
pmc-13525876:
Eduardo S Farinazzo and colleagues studied how unequal hearing deprivation shapes results after second-ear cochlear implants. Published in 2026, the retrospective study followed postlingual patients implanted in sequence between 1990 and 2021 at a tertiary center, tracking hearing over two years after each implant activation. The ear deaf for less time, the ear deaf longer, and both ears together were compared.

The shorter-deprivation ear beat the longer-deprivation ear in quiet and in noise at two years, while both ears together beat either ear alone by wide margins. Longer gaps between implants tracked with better bilateral scores, yet longer ineffective hearing-aid use tracked with poorer scores. Partial electrode insertion in the more deprived ear also hurt bilateral results. The authors conclude that shorter deprivation helps, but bilateral hearing still adds value even after long silence in one ear.
pmc-13526376:
Onorhide and colleagues measure two clotting markers in sickle cell disease across calm and crisis states in twenty twenty-six. The disease makes blood prone to clots, yet marker data during pain crises are scarce in their region. Thirty patients were tested during a crisis and again when well. Thirty healthy controls joined the study.

Both markers peaked during crises and sat lowest in controls. The clotting marker also tracked with how severe the disease was. In the calm state, the two markers rose and fell together. The team says both can help gauge clot risk in these patients. Their values may warn which patients face the worst course.
pmc-13527576:
Son and colleagues test two plant compounds, alone and combined, as restorers of an immune system flattened by chemotherapy. Cyclophosphamide saves lives in cancer and autoimmune disease but leaves patients defenceless against infection. Their 2026 mouse study used extracts of two traditional medicinal sources, a bracket fungus and red sage root. It then tested their signature molecules: protocatechuic acid and tanshinone IIA, both known to prod immune pathways converging on the NF-kB switch.

In immunosuppressed mice the combined extract significantly eased weight loss and spleen shrinkage. It restored the proportions of T cells, natural killer cells, and macrophages that the drug had cut in the reported measures. Lymphocytes regained their ability to multiply, macrophages ate more aggressively, and killer cells destroyed tumour targets better. The two pure compounds each switched on the same immune pathways in cells, and together outperformed either alone.
pmc-13527676:
Leizhi Zheng, Mengyue Li, Bin He, Qiang Liu, and Chengbao Liu reconstruct, in a 2026 chemistry study, the surface of a crystalline carbon nitride polymer. Their aim is to hold ionic liquids in place for converting carbon dioxide into useful chemicals. Carbon nitride offers tunable structure and active sites but weak catalytic activity alone. Their design pairs organic superbases with hydrolyzed polymer as bonding partners.

The combined catalyst joins amino groups and hydrogen-bonding functions inside one framework, cooperatively activating epoxides for coupling with carbon dioxide. At mild pressure, ninety degrees, and six hours, the best version delivered a chlorinated cyclic carbonate in ninety-nine percent yield with ninety-nine percent selectivity. The solid catalyst was recovered by simple separation and reused. The authors present the platform as a sustainable route for green chemical transformations.
pmc-13527876:
Na-Young Kim reviews how South Korea trains and certifies people who interpret in medical care. Her 2026 study reads seven public papers, from test rules to course plans. She maps each paper against eight skill areas drawn from world standards for this work. Each area is scored by how fully it links to both teaching and testing, from no link to a full link.

Only three of the eight areas were fully linked in the papers she read. Basic areas such as ethics scored well. Skills like remote work by phone or video, and short note taking, were thin or missing. Kim ends by sketching a joint path for nurses who also train as interpreters.
pmc-13528076:
Cristina A. Smith and four colleagues analyze COVID-19 vaccine willingness across fifteen developing countries in a 2026 study. Data came from a global survey run over six months. The design used repeated snapshots rather than following the same people. Models accounted for clustering and change over time. Culture was summed into three broad components.

People aged fifty-five and over were more willing to vaccinate. Women were more willing than men, with odds about one and a half times higher. Fear of side effects cut willingness in a curved pattern. Willingness also rose and dipped across months in a shallow arc. Culture pushed both ways, with no simple leaning. The authors say campaigns must work with local culture, not against it. Simple one-message drives are unlikely to fit all settings.
pmc-13529176:
Dai and colleagues reviewed nanomaterials engineered to deliver tumor vaccines in a 2026 survey of the field. Tumor vaccines train the immune system by giving it tumor antigens, the identifying markers of cancer cells, plus helper substances, so that antigen-presenting cells can activate killer T cells. Conventional vaccines underperform because their antigens are weak and often fail to reach those presenting cells in lymph nodes.

Dai organizes the new delivery materials into four families: polymer-based, fat-based, inorganic, and biomimetic, meaning modeled on natural cells or membranes. Tiny carriers can shield antigens, travel efficiently to lymph nodes, linger there, and be taken up by presenting cells. strengthens the anti-tumor response and may prevent spread and recurrence while reducing off-target effects. The authors map design choices across these families to guide construction of more effective vaccine platforms for clinical use.
pmc-13529676:
How well top AI models do on German medical license exams is gauged by Lasse Cirkel and co-authors in work dated 2026. The team fed twenty-four real exams from six years to a set of models. Near seventy-five hundred items came with scores from vast student sittings. Eight models took the full set with images, and thirteen took a shared text-only set.

The best model scored near perfect on both exam halves. Open models ran close, and even small ones beat the mean student. Image items hurt models far more than students. Hard sets for men and models barely overlapped, a gap worth heed.
pmc-13530076:
Yun Wang and Guohua Zhu introduce a 2026 method for finding long non-coding RNAs that shape tumor immunity across many cancers. These RNA molecules do not build proteins, yet they steer immune pathways and cell entry into tumors. Few such regulators had been pinned down before this work.

Their algorithm, named LncImmune, screens 32 cancer types and combines several tools to flag candidate regulators. Core molecules split lung adenocarcinoma into two groups with cold and hot immune character. The groups differed in mutations, immune cell levels, drug sensitivity, and outlook, pointing toward fresh markers for prognosis and treatment.
pmc-13531176:
Magnesium implants that melt away in the body are attractive but dissolve too fast, and a 2026 study by Tonya D. Andreeva and co-authors coats them to slow the melt. Unchecked breakdown can also stir bad reactions in nearby tissue.

The team built nanometer-thin coats from layered charged polymers and wax on sample implants. The coats were smooth, water-shy, and under a micrometer thick, and they made the metal kinder to two cell types in lab tests. In rats, implants under the skin were tracked with fine CT scans and tissue checks. How well the coat tamed the breakdown depended on the setup, and the study maps both the gains and the limits.
pmc-13531876:
Masaaki Yuki leads a 2026 study of a small protective protein, PRELP, that fades from scarred human lungs. Tissue staining placed the protein in support regions and some air sac cells of healthy lungs, with clear loss in fibrotic disease. Mouse experiments used a drug that scars lungs to test cause and treatment.

Mice lacking the protein scarred worse than normal mice. Giving the protein through the airway before injury suppressed scarring. Dish tests showed it kept surface cells in character, slowed scar-cell movement, and worked through two signaling routes, nominating it as an inhaled therapy candidate.
pmc-13531976:
Kerstin Lillpers and six co-authors study low bone density in systemic sclerosis in a case-control paper from 2026. The disease stiffens skin and organs, and bone density runs low in its patients for reasons not fully known. The team compared 211 patients followed in Lund, Sweden, with 505 matched controls, measuring hip and spine density, blood markers, and lifestyle factors.

A heart stress marker and a sign of low-grade inflammation each linked to low bone density on their own. Disease traits such as the diffuse skin subtype and finger ulcers also linked. Weight and the heart marker best predicted hip scores in a machine learning model.
pmc-13532376:
Rui Wu and co-authors study why the food pipe narrows after a common scope procedure in a 2026 paper. The narrowing comes from excess scar tissue, as support cells turn into scar-forming cells. The gene signals that drive that change were poorly known.

Gene scans of human tissue flagged one gene, DPP4, which was raised in narrowed tissue and in a rat model. Blocking the gene's protein slowed scar cell growth and cut scar gene activity. Rats given a blocker drug healed with less narrowing and less collagen. A pig study backed the result. Changes in a growth path called Hippo-YAP moved in step, though the data show a link, not a chain of command.
pmc-13532476:
Leah M Gober and colleagues report in 2026 on early stent care for a narrowed aorta in young pigs. A narrowed aorta, called coarctation, is a birth defect that can raise blood pressure and strain the heart. New stents can be widened over time as a child grows, yet long-term effects were not known.

Eighteen pigs were split into sham, untreated narrowed, and stented groups. Stents widened to adult size, removed the narrowing, and kept heart function close to normal. Four of six stented pigs formed small bulges near the stent that needed cover stents, a risk readers should note.
pmc-13534176:
David Žižek and nine co-authors review implanted heart devices in heart failure care, in a 2026 paper. Pacemakers and defibrillators treat slow rhythms, resynchronize a faltering heart's chambers, prevent sudden death, and allow remote monitoring. The review weighs today's uses against newer options and the barriers to adopting them.

Standard right-side pacing is giving way to pacing both chambers or stimulating the heart's own wiring near the left bundle branch. Leadless pacemakers and defibrillators worn outside the veins promise fewer lead problems. Monitoring implants and new indications are widening what devices can do. The authors caution that randomized evidence is thin, procedures are complex, and access differs sharply between health systems.
pmc-13534276:
Won Myung Lee and colleagues study in 2026 whether a sticky powder can prevent a pain and fever syndrome after scope removal of growths in the upper colon. The syndrome follows a scope procedure that cuts tissue under the lining and can lengthen hospital stays. Records covered high-risk cases treated from April 2023 to October 2024 across centres.

Nine patients developed the syndrome overall. Rates were much lower with the powder than without it, and all cases settled with rest and antibiotics and no surgery. Readers see early clinical proof that a simple barrier layer may prevent this problem.
pmc-13534476:
Weber and colleagues studied in 2026 a plant membrane protein called HIR2 in Arabidopsis, a small model plant. Plant cell membranes sort their proteins into zones, but the rules behind this order are murky. HIR2 belongs to a family of membrane-organising proteins and anchors to the inner face of the cell membrane.

HIR2 was found to bind several receptors, including partners of BAK1, a core receptor in growth and immunity signalling. Plants lacking HIR2 showed impaired growth and weaker immunity, tying the protein to those pathways. Advanced microscopy showed HIR2 changes how BAK1 moves and clusters in the membrane. Computer modelling predicted HIR2 assembles into a cup-like multi-protein complex, matching large complexes seen in lab gels. The authors propose HIR2 helps build membrane sub-zones that shape receptor behaviour.
pmc-13535376:
Doris Zheng and co-authors present a 2026 study on sex differences in how the immune system guards against kidney cancer spread. Men get this cancer more often and die of it more than women. Habits explain part of that gap, but immune differences may explain the rest.

The team focused on natural killer cells, which patrol for tumors, in spread to the liver. A gene on the X chromosome that escapes its usual silencing may boost these cells in females. Males had more of the cells but weaker action. Understanding that split could lead to immune care tuned by sex.
pmc-13535676:
Harish Saluja, Anuj Dadhich, Seemit Shah, and Shivani Sachdeva report a digitally planned jaw rebuilding in a case from 2026. A young woman carried a central giant cell granuloma in her mandible. Removing such a tumor leaves a gap that breaks face shape and bite. Rebuilding the jaw's curve is among surgery's hardest puzzles.

The team planned the repair on a computer before touching the patient. A free fibula flap, leg bone with its vessels, supplied the new jaw segment. Digital simulation shaped it to mirror her anatomy. Restoring continuity and muscle anchors was the goal. Pre-planning turns a sculptural gamble into a measured build. The case shows digital rehearsal earning its place in facial surgery.
pmc-13536276:
James DeWitt Crall and Marilia Palumbo Gaiarsa argue in 2026 that differences between individuals within a species shape how plant-pollinator communities respond to global change. Forecasts based on species averages may miss gradual shifts or sudden collapse risks. The authors draw on niche theory at the species level to frame the individual scale.

Individual variation may soften responses to stress in many cases, making change more gradual than average-based models predict. Outcomes hinge on how key traits, such as stress tolerance and pollination skill, vary and pair within individuals. A roadmap closes the piece for future field studies.
pmc-13536576:
Lei Wu and colleagues report in 2026 a simple new route to substituted 2-amino-1,3,4-oxadiazoles from hydrazides and isothiocyanates. These ring compounds matter widely in drug and farm chemical research, so easier synthesis has broad value. The method uses sodium hydroxide to drive a ring-closing step that removes sulfur under mild conditions.

The team reports wide substrate tolerance, strong yields, and easy handling across many variants. Such direct access could speed library building for biological screening in medicine and crop science. An alternative regioselective path to this valued scaffold is now open to chemists.
pmc-13536776:
Agata Olearczyk and co-authors survey workplace health promotion in Poland in a 2026 nationwide poll of 1,030 full-time workers aged 18 to 60 years. Online interviews in December 2025 asked whether employers offer health activities beyond required safety duties, how often workers use them, and what blocks use. Answers were compared across company size, ownership, job type, and satisfaction levels.

Fewer than half the workers said their employer offers health promotion, split between regular and occasional offers. About half of those with access used activities often. Lack of time was the leading barrier. Access clustered in large firms, foreign-owned private firms, big cities, and among highly satisfied staff and managers. Flexible hours and shift work also tracked with access. The authors highlight wide gaps by workplace traits.
pmc-13536876:
Jie Wen and colleagues analyze peroxisome-related genes across digestive cancers in a 2026 study combining data modeling with lab tests. Peroxisomes are small cell parts that handle fats and oxygen balance, yet their cancer roles stay unclear. Gene signatures for outlook were built for eight digestive cancers, immune surroundings were profiled, and focused tests in liver and bowel cancer cells probed treatment resistance and fat handling.

Signatures predicted outlook strongly across the cancers. High-risk tumors showed a more suppressed immune setting with more regulatory and repair-type cells. One gene, PEX13, ran high in treatment-resistant liver tumors, and silencing it or a partner gene eased resistance in lab models by reshaping fat use. The authors propose targeting peroxisome function in high-risk groups.
pmc-13537576:
Stefanie Jungmann and co-authors study mental load, the invisible work of planning and tracking family life. Women and mothers carry much of this load, yet research on it stays thin. Two online surveys anchor the study. The first drew several hundred women, and the second close to two thousand mothers.

Mothers rated invisible tasks as more stressful and more unfairly shared than visible chores. Heavy mental load went with lower good mood and higher anxiety and low spirits. The top complaints were never stopping thoughts about tasks, and a sense that tasks never end. Load also rose with two traits: worry prone and dutiful streaks. Being a single mother sharpened the worry link.
pmc-13538276:
Meng-Ya Liu, Hong-Bing Yao, and Cheng Chen trace how an RNA-binding protein pushes helper T cells toward the allergy-driving type in hay fever. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. The protein, ELAVL1, steadies certain RNA messages, and one target stood out in allergic tissue.

Gene screening flagged allergic rhinitis genes, and nose tissue from forty-two child patients and forty-two healthy children was compared. The target message, CPA3, ran much higher in patients. In dish tests, the protein's grip kept that message alive longer, tilting T cells toward the Th2 type. Silencing the target eased nose symptoms and tissue damage in allergic mice and calmed the Th2 response. The chain gives a fresh drug angle on hay fever.
pmc-13538476:
Roxana Portieles and co-authors benchmark virus-derived wall-cutting proteins as antibacterials in a 2026 combined computing and lab study. Seven variants from Bacillus-infecting viruses were docked against a tiny wall fragment, simulated over long timescales, scored for binding strength, and tested against two bacterial species. The aim was to learn whether cheap fragment scores predict real killing power well enough to rank candidates.

Most variants recognized the fragment favorably, yet contact styles and stability differed widely. Lab tests crowned one variant as strongest against both species, while two others shone mainly in computing scores. Overall links between fragment scores and killing stayed modest. The authors nominate the lab winner and one runner-up for development, while warning that tiny fragments poorly stand in for whole walls.
pmc-13539776:
Kazuma Haida, Yuria Yamasaki, and Nanami Sugawara ask what home means to older adults with health woes in Japan, in work from 2026. Home is more than a care site, yet its felt sense for this group was not well mapped. More than fifty adults in town, fringe, and farm zones gave long talks.

Four themes frame their sense of home. Free choice and self rule lead, then a place that holds daily life up. A known place held dear comes next, with prized bonds to close folks last. Home spills past walls to the whole near zone. Care staff should learn each sense of home.
pmc-13539876:
Aanya Shah, Stephen Baker, and Dar Shah follow a seventy-five-year-old woman whose kidney disease refused to sit in one category for eleven years. Her biopsies showed membranous nephropathy with the full pattern of lupus kidney disease, yet her tissue also stained positive for PLA2R, the marker of the primary, non-lupus form. Two diseases seemed to share one kidney.

Twice she reached remission, first on cyclosporine, then, after a relapse a decade later, on mycophenolate with prednisone. The case adds a long, well-documented example to the small literature on this overlap, and it warns clinicians that mixed features demand flexible treatment rather than a forced label.
pmc-13540376: Renuka Kadirkamanathan and six co-authors used base editing to undo the gene fault behind a radiation-sensitive immune disorder. Children with broken DNA repair genes can develop severe combined immunodeficiency, and ordinary radiation can harm them. One such gene is NHEJ1, needed to mend double-strand breaks. In skin cells taken from a patient, the team rewrote single DNA letters to reverse the mutations. The work shows base editing can repair such faults in patient cells and can help test what individual variants do.
pmc-13540576:
Fadime Ersoy Dursun and Bilinc Doğruöz Karatekin follow patients after bone marrow aspiration and biopsy to measure a little-recognized complication: pain that lingers for months at the procedure site. They screened over two hundred adults at least three months after the procedure with pain questionnaires and, for those reporting pain, a standardized physical exam and pressure-sensitivity testing.

About six percent had chronic pain. Most showed ordinary tissue-pain features, but a substantial share had nerve-pain traits on screening scores. Some exams pointed to the sacroiliac joint. Pressure thresholds at the biopsy site were lower in patients with chronic pain, suggesting local sensitization. The authors urge systematic pain checks after biopsy, while noting the small number of cases.
pmc-13540676:
Babak Mirminachi and five co-authors report a 2026 case of a rectal tumor removed through a scope, sparing open surgery. The tumor was a stromal growth in the gut wall, found during a check in a 53-year-old man. It sat just above the dentate line, a tight spot where wide surgery costs dear.

Scans and a sample confirmed a low-grade tumor rooted in the muscle layer. The scope team cut between the muscle layers and lifted the tumor out whole, its capsule unbroken. The gap was closed with an endoscopic tool. The case shows how deep scope work can clear select tumors while saving anatomy.
pmc-13540876:
Chunfang Peng and colleagues present a new gene-picking method in 2026. The method serves single-cell and spatial gene-reading data. Analysts first pick the most variable genes. Only then can they group cells into types. Standard tools rescale the data first. That step can hide real biological differences.

Their method is called EMD-HVG. It skips rescaling entirely. It measures variation with earth mover's distance. That statistic makes no assumptions about the shape of the data. Tests on real and simulated datasets gave top scores in most scenarios. The count was twenty-six wins out of thirty. Gene sets from the method also gave cleaner cell clusters.
pmc-13541376:
Spacing out doses of a costly immune drug for children with a stubborn fever disease is studied by Akay and co-authors in a 2026 paper. The disease, familial Mediterranean fever, resists the standard daily pill in some children. Sixty such children at one center who took the immune drug were split into three groups by dosing path.

One group kept a steady spacing, one stretched spacing with success, and one tried and failed. Blood swelling markers were tracked over time with careful models. The team also hunts traits that predict a safe stretch. Longer spacing cuts cost, visits, and needle burden for families. The results help doctors judge which children can safely take the drug less often.
pmc-13541576:
Jose Carlos Pachon-M and colleagues discuss a rescue method in 2026. The method is cardioneuroablation. It can help when standard ablation blocks the heart's relay by accident. Slow-pathway ablation cures a common fast rhythm. The target sits millimetres from the AV node. Block still strikes two to three percent of cases. Block normally means a lifelong pacemaker.

The case involved a man in his early fifties. His final burn caused complete nodal block. He felt faint and breathless, with no reversal in thirty minutes. Operators skipped the pacemaker plan. They ablated a nearby nerve cluster instead. Normal conduction returned in the same session.
pmc-13541776:
Mahmut Ozturk and co-authors report, in a 2026 study, results for a delayed form of a major heart operation in high-risk babies born with a weak left heart. The standard operation is done at once, but fragile newborns may fare poorly. The delayed plan first bands both lung arteries, then does the full operation weeks later.

Twenty babies with many risk factors, such as early birth and genetic syndromes, were treated at one center. Bands went on at a median age of two and a half days, and the main operation at about five weeks. Three quarters survived the operation. Babies operated within four weeks of banding needed no further lung artery work, a point in favor of the delay.
pmc-13541976:
Thomas Berleth, Christian Hardtke, Jim Mattson, and Gerhard Przemeck look back on how plant axis research took shape in a 2026 perspective. In the early 1990s, big genetic screens began asking how plant cells set their top-to-bottom axis. Hormone based and hormone free ideas clashed for years. A study of the MONOPTEROS gene helped shift views toward self-organizing patterns steered by polar auxin flow.

That gene later proved to code an auxin response factor. Once hormone signals and transport could be tracked precisely, models of plant patterning absorbed them. The essay also reflects on hype and doubt in science, using this field's turns as a case study.
pmc-13542176:
Neha Chourasia and colleagues present a speech tool in 2026. The tool recognises emotion in spoken voices. Machines that answer human feelings need such a tool. Older systems lean on hand-crafted features. They crumble with new speakers or noisy rooms. The new design uses a one-dimensional convolutional network.

Three sound descriptors feed the network as one sequence. They cover tone texture, signal crossings, and energy. Training data pooled four public acted-speech collections. Extra training copies came from noise, shifts, and pitch changes. Stretching added still more variety. Seven emotion classes were tested at the end. Accuracy reached about ninety-five percent on test data.
pmc-13542276:
Agnieszka Gdowicz-Kłosok's team profiled the chemistry of fluid that collects where breast tissue was removed during surgery, in a 2026 study. One group of patients had breast-conserving surgery with radiotherapy given during the procedure itself, while another group had full mastectomy. Fluid from 54 patients was taken on the first and fifth days after surgery and read with nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, which found 42 small molecules.

The fluid's chemistry changed clearly between day one and day five in both groups, reflecting early wound healing. Levels of several amino acids fell while lactate and pyruvate rose in the breast-sparing group, a pattern suggesting more sugar-burning activity in the irradiated tissue bed. Ketone bodies declined across both groups. No firm chemical separation showed between the two surgery groups overall. The authors present the profiles as a baseline for future work on how wound fluid may influence leftover cancer cells.
pmc-13542376:
Pedro Acién and Maribel Acién published a 2026 review on how malformations of the female genital and urinary tracts present and get diagnosed. Because both systems develop from shared embryonic tissue, faults in one very often accompany faults in the other. The authors update their embryological-clinical classification, which sorts anomalies by their developmental origin, and discuss the mesonephric and Müllerian structures whose failed formation produces most cases.

One message runs through the review: a missing kidney on one side is the renal problem most often paired with obstructive genital anomalies. Some duct faults always come with that renal absence. Certain patterns, such as leaking urine between normal voiding in a girl, can point to the diagnosis early. Outcomes after surgery also depend on the anomaly's developmental type, so the classification is presented as a practical tool for choosing investigation and treatment.
pmc-13542476:
Listening to music stirs feelings and memories, and it also stirs the brain and the heart at the same time. Scott Leimroth, Robert Barry, Frances De Blasio, and Timothy Byron review studies that recorded both signals together in healthy adults who were not musicians. They found eighteen papers and checked how closely each followed good practice in its field.

Brain findings scattered widely, with little overlap in what the studies measured or how. Heart results were just as mixed: some studies saw heart rate rise with music, others saw it fall. Only a few studies tested whether brain and heart rhythms sync up during listening. The authors call for shared standards so this two-field research can build on itself instead of starting over each time.
pmc-13542576:
Julius Kaiser and co-authors compare habitat use of a butterfly at the north and south edges of its range. Their paper from 2026 deals with the Southern White Admiral. Numbers thin toward range edges, yet those edge groups matter most for care, and past habitat work often covers only a small part of a range.

Larvae were surveyed in the Swabian Jura at the north edge and in the Turkish Aegean near the south edge. Host plants were honeysuckle kin in both regions. The butterfly picked well lit sites with long sun and low tree shade in both places, but the pull was much stronger at the north edge. Larvae also sat higher above ground at the north edge.
pmc-13543376:
Md Iftekher Iqbal and Fariah Osman report two laser rescues of blocked glaucoma drains in a 2026 case series. Drainage implants lower eye pressure in hard glaucoma, but their tubes can clog, and the usual fix is more surgery. Both patients were one-eyed and high risk. In the first, a child with congenital glaucoma, iris tissue blocked the tube ten months after placement.

A laser opening in the iris freed the tube. Pressure settled at a healthy level for at least seven months without drops. A brief pressure spike and bleed cleared on their own. In the second case, a burn survivor's tube clogged with vitreous gel; laser cutting freed it and cut pressure within hours. His fragile eye surface later forced removal of the implant anyway. The authors back laser first where the eye can bear it.
pmc-13543476:

pmc-13543576:

pmc-13544876:

pmc-13545176:

One recipe gives the cleanest light signature of well-formed particles.

pmc-13546576:

pmc-13547376:

pmc-13547576:

pmc-13547976:
Moustafa Mansour and co-authors update in a 2026 review the care of a deadly fungal infection of the brain. The mold Aspergillus kills over half its victims, most of whom have weak immune systems. Drugs reach the brain poorly, germs grow resistant, and diagnosis lags.

pmc-13548276:
Lena Böff and co-authors survey, in 2026, infection control in health facilities across four sub-Saharan African countries during the COVID-19 pandemic. Over half of facilities reported no screening of patients or staff, and only a fifth had alcohol hand rub in every room. Mask supply was reported sufficient by about sixty-three percent of workers. The authors link compliance with hand hygiene and masking to facility and worker factors.
pmc-13548476:

Statistical profiling sorted the nurses into hidden groups rather than assuming one average attitude.

pmc-13548676:

Both predicted favourable ninety day outcome, with visual grading slightly the stronger of the two in the tests. In adjusted models visual grading stayed an independent predictor while automated grading lost its standing once collateral flow was added. The authors praise visual reading as simple and open to any centre.
pmc-13549476:

Careful filtering removed false variants caused by lab bias and sample mixing.

The authors say within-host data illuminate viral evolution even if they track spread poorly.
pmc-13549876:

pmc-13549976:

pmc-13550176:

A joint analysis pulled out the molecule sets that best separate the infections, which the authors offer as clues to each virus's strategy.
pmc-13550876:
Yao Chen, Kanghua Zhang, Yu Mu, and Xuezhen Jia published a 2026 study of cognitive impairment in schizophrenia. Schizophrenia affects thinking as well as perception and behavior, and the thinking problems strongly affect daily life. The authors asked how these problems differ between forms of the illness.

Using a standard symptom scale, they split patients into a positive-symptom group of 93 and a negative-symptom group of 67. They compared cognitive scores, symptom severity, and social functioning between the groups. The aim is to link the pattern of cognitive loss to symptom type and to how well a person manages in everyday life.
pmc-13551076:

Similar tool motion patterns across cases suggest the method can flag both normal and odd practice.
pmc-13551676:

The authors say this is the first report of a JAK inhibitor in TRAPS, and they add the tocilizumab case to limited published experience.
pmc-13551776:

pmc-13552076:

pmc-13552176:

pmc-13552476:

pmc-13552876:

pmc-13553076:

pmc-13553176:

pmc-13553476:

pmc-13553676:

pmc-13553876:

pmc-13554376:

pmc-13556376:

pmc-13556476:

pmc-13558876:

pmc-13559076:

pmc-13560276:

pmc-13562276:

pmc-13562476:

pmc-13562576:

pmc-13562676:

pmc-13563476:

pmc-13565276:

pmc-13565576:

pmc-13565676:

pmc-13568376:

pmc-13574776:
