pmc-13574976:
A sick child can be the first sign of a threat that spans farms, bugs, and weather. Daniele Zama argues in a 2026 essay that child infection care needs a joined-up digital rebuild. Dengue's spread into Italy and France in 2024 shows how fast such threats now move.

The One Health frame ties human, animal, and nature health into one view. Shared data systems, maps, gene tracking, and smart tools could link clinic notes to field signals. That link would speed outbreak spotting and safer drug use. Zama asks for systems built around children, not shrunk adult tools. The prize is earlier, fairer care for the young.
pmc-13575076:
Yuping Sun leads a 2026 early-phase trial in China testing two cancer drugs together. The pair are ceralasertib, a pill that blocks the ATR repair enzyme, and durvalumab, an immune therapy given by infusion. Patients had advanced solid tumours with few options left, many after prior immune therapy had stopped working.

Fourteen patients joined two dosing schedules. Most had some side effect, half had a severe one, yet no dose-limiting problems appeared. Drug levels in the body matched results from Western studies. Three of 13 patients checked for response saw their tumours shrink in a confirmed way, across lung and cervical cancers. The authors judge the pairing workable and active enough to study further.
pmc-13575176:
Jonathan Hunter and seven colleagues examine emergency department use by older adults with both physical and mental illness in a 2026 study. Having several long-term conditions is common in seniors, yet the added role of psychiatric illness in medical emergency visits was little studied. The cohort covered more than 2.5 million people.

At every level of physical illness burden, visits for non-psychiatric reasons rose as psychiatric severity grew. Statistical models confirmed separate effects for physical burden, psychiatric severity, and continuity of primary care. Seeing the same family doctor regularly did not soften the link between illness burden and frequent visits, a result the authors found unexpected. They call for more work on what regular primary care actually changes for this group.
pmc-13575776:
Zishuai Chou and co-authors report an inherited eye disease case in 2026. A man in his late fifties came in with bleeding under the macula of both eyes and warped vision. Odd growths of vessels under the retina caused the harm. The twin eye pattern without the usual aging deposits was atypical.

Gene testing found a harmful change in a gene that helps retinal support cells stick in place. That change is often mistaken for common age related macular disease. Care used long term injections that block vessel growth, given as needed. The case urges gene checks when vessel growth looks out of pattern.
pmc-13576276:
Petr Novak leads a 2026 study asking which thinking tests best separate mild cognitive impairment from dementia, using the first cohort from a Slovak memory clinic. The group enrolled 150 people over three years, with 84 classed as mild impairment and 55 as dementia in the main analysis. A wide battery of memory, fluency, attention, and daily-living tools was applied.

A verbal learning test and a questionnaire on complex daily activities separated the groups best. Two digit span tests, forward and backward, showed no difference between groups at all. People with dementia had more shrinkage in memory and outer brain regions, larger fluid spaces, and lower total brain volume. Schooling, vital signs, and body measures did not differ. The authors back daily-living assessment and call for sharper objective tools.
pmc-13576476:
Giulia Cheli and nine colleagues profile the ion channels of balance-sensing hair cells in chicken embryos using multiple omics methods, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Vestibular hair cells detect head movements for balance and gaze. Their ion channels are acquired during differentiation and only partly known. The team compared developmental stages up to hatching.

Two hair cell types were examined, with type one defined by a signature potassium current. In adult mice that current is carried by a known channel subunit, with a second candidate debated for immature cells. A blocker of the second candidate had no effect at any stage here. Transcript evidence found the first subunit but not the second. Patch-sequencing confirmed its expression in both cell types. Further transcripts revealed many other channel subunits shaping these sensors.
pmc-13577176:
Chongli Yu and co-authors present a study dated 2026 on bone health in psoriasis patients taking biologic drugs. Psoriasis is linked to bone problems, but long-term data on bone outcomes under these drugs are scarce. The team compared two widely used biologics, secukinumab and adalimumab.

Records from 2021 to 2024 were screened, and 364 patients started one of the two drugs. Fifty patients had repeated bone density scans, giving 128 measurements in all. Another ninety-one patients gave repeated blood marker data. Density paths at the spine and hip favored secukinumab over time. One bone-building marker rose and one breakdown marker fell on that drug, while a second marker showed no clear difference.
pmc-13577376:
When a parent is admitted to a psychiatric ward, children are usually kept away, and the separation hurts both sides. Abby Dunn and co-authors set out a study plan in 2026 to learn how family visits work in such units in England and what better rooms and support would look like. Of about 97,000 admissions in one year, a large share involved parents of dependent children.

The plan mixes interviews first, then questionnaires shaped by what the interviews find. Parents, carers, staff, and children themselves will take part, with children using drawing and writing to share their views. People with lived experience help run each stage. The findings will feed a co-produced family visit pack for wards.
pmc-13577676:
Ronan Berg wrote a 2026 commentary on how blood volume in the chest links to gas transfer in the lungs. He starts from central blood volume, the blood held in the lung vessels, the heart, and the large chest vessels. Only a small share of that blood sits in the tiny lung vessels at rest. Berg then turns to a new study in the same journal issue.

In that study, healthy people faced raised or lowered pressure on the lower body. The shifts moved central blood volume up or down. Berg explains how the team split gas transfer into a membrane part and a blood volume part. The link between the two volumes was not a straight line. Readers get a clear guide to why lung vessels open up under load, and how that shapes breathing tests.
pmc-13577976:
Cancer experts trace how two trial groups shaped the care of brain and spine tumours over decades. The groups ran large multi-site trials that set how radiation is dosed and paired with drugs. Their work spans tumours that start in the brain, tumours that spread there, and rarer kinds such as meningioma and a brain lymphoma. This review reads the trial archive to show how care rules grew, step by step.

Early trials fixed base rules for dose, target size, and dose splits. Later work showed that more dose was not always better and built tools to sort patients by risk. In the main brain tumour type, drug plus radiation became the new norm. For spread tumours, sharp focused radiation changed care. Fresh trials now sort patients by gene marks before they assign the treatment.
pmc-13578076:
Mohammad Shalmani and co-authors build in 2026 a diagnostic AI that works the way a hospital does: as a team of specialists, not one generalist. Real diagnosis is a referral journey, since no doctor masters every disease. Yet most prediction tools are a single model stretched over thousands of codes, thin everywhere and weakest on rare conditions.

Their system, CPS-Net, is a swarm of dozens of specialist transformer models, each trained on a focused slice of records from seventy-five thousand patients at one hospital system. Language model agents arranged in primary, specialty, and subspecialty tiers route cases between them, sharing a case memory so every referral is transparent and auditable. On test cases the swarm's top guesses beat a single monolith model by wide margins. The authors argue the architecture, not just the data, is the advance: mirror the referral network and predictions reason like it.
pmc-13578276:
Atefeh Zarei and colleagues ran a 2026 green wall trial in Mashhad, Iran, asking whether microbes and charred plant matter help plants grow on reused household wash water. Clean water is scarce, so the wall of Crassula plants was watered with city water or with greywater, the used water from sinks and showers. Three helpers were dosed at varied levels: blue green algae, root fungi, and biochar.

One mix more than doubled the green pigment in leaves. Another mix nearly tripled root and shoot weight next to the weakest plants. The best cleaning mix cut the waste load of the greywater by more than half. Which mix won depended on the goal, growth or cleaning, and the authors want tests in other cities before wide claims.
pmc-13578476:
Sebastián Ávila and co-authors set out a lab method from 2026 to count chromosome sets in young Atlantic salmon kept in alcohol. Farms breed sterile salmon with three sets, so each batch must be checked. Alcohol keeps samples well in the field, but counts from such samples can swing and need a steady guide.

Their method stains DNA with a red dye and runs blood cells through a beam counter. A known sample mixed in each run serves as an inner yardstick, which trims swings in the glow signal. The kit uses plain lab goods and no paid software. The steps adapt older lab methods for field-kept fry. Farms in lands like Chile and Norway must certify sterile stock, and this method helps them prove it.
pmc-13579276:
Julian Wier and co-authors link gut disease to worse joint infections in a 2026 study. Infected artificial joints are treated in stages, with an antibiotic spacer holding the gap. Germs from a troubled gut may seed these infections. A national hospital database found patients who had spacer surgery after hip or knee replacement between 2016 and 2023.

Those with chronic gut disease grew more infections with several germ species at once, and died more often. Adjusted models kept joint, sex, and sickness burden in view. The gut joint axis, once a hunch, now carries outcome numbers. Surgeons may need broader early antibiotics for this group.
pmc-13579376:
Tracy Sides and co-authors gather expert views on how Veterans Affairs research networks bring patients into research work. Patient input is a core part of learning health systems, yet networks lack firm guidance on building it. Their 2026 study ran a modified Delphi process with three panels: veterans, engagement staff, and research leaders. Panels rated forty-four promising practices drawn from network use, then met to discuss.

The panels jointly backed twenty-nine practices, grouped into five duties for networks. Some practices split the panels. Comments circled three themes: scarce resources, respect for partners, and fear of burdening veterans. The authors say engagement needs real funding, skilled staff, and planning time.
pmc-13579476:
Yue Zhang leads a large team in a 2026 study of HIV care visits and viral suppression through the COVID-19 years in the United States. Lockdowns and rules broke up routine HIV care and viral load tests, and it was not clear when visit rates and suppression got back to pre-pandemic levels.

The study sits inside a long-running North American cohort of people with HIV. Adults at many United States clinics were tracked across four years. The team read how often they came in and how often their virus stayed suppressed, year by year, next to the rules in force at the time.
pmc-13579576:
Yao Yang and eight colleagues published a study in two thousand twenty-six on a gene that may drive brain inflammation in Alzheimer's disease. Microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, fuel the inflammation, but their control switches are incompletely known. Human cell-level gene data were combined with mouse and cell experiments.

Network and machine learning analyses flagged KLHL2 as a candidate brake. Its levels fell steadily along the disease-linked microglial trajectory and in diseased mice and treated cells. Raising it cut inflammatory output through a WNK3-linked signalling chain; lowering it did the reverse. The authors propose KLHL2 loss as a driver of inflammatory microglia. The pathway offers a fresh drug target lead.
pmc-13579676:
Gideon Loevinsohn and co-authors survey every public emergency department on Kenya's coast about how they sort the sick from the sickest. Their 2026 study visits all ten public emergency departments across three counties, interviewing clinical leaders in February 2026 with a standard questionnaire. Triage decides who is seen first, and poor triage costs lives, yet its practice across sub-Saharan Africa is patchy and little documented.

The survey covers triage infrastructure, daily practice, and staff perceptions. Coastal Kenya's results give county and national planners a baseline: which departments run a formal system, with what staff and space, and where the gaps yawn widest.
pmc-13579876:
Mohammad Basheer Alameer and colleagues link daily habits to sleep and mood among medical residents in Syria, in a 2026 survey across twenty two hospitals. Just over two thousand residents answered standard scales for sleep quality, depression, and anxiety, alongside questions on smoking, coffee, alcohol, and body weight. Residency is a draining stage, and the team asked which habits track with the strain.

Smoking tied to worse sleep and higher depression and anxiety scores across the board. Among women, coffee and alcohol each tied to higher anxiety, alcohol most sharply. Underweight women, against the grain, showed lower odds on all three problems. The authors urge programs that help residents quit smoking, guard sleep routines, and keep stimulant and alcohol use modest, for the sake of both doctors and patients.
pmc-13580076:
Sarah-Jeanne Salvy and co-authors lay out a trial of early time-restricted eating during cancer therapy, in this 2026 protocol. Fasting makes tumor cells frailer while shielding healthy ones in animal work. Long fasts are hard, so the trial tests a daily eight-hour eating window placed early in the day.

The study will enroll 175 adults with breast or rectal cancer who are getting drug therapy before surgery. Half eat inside the early window; half spread meals over twelve hours or more. Main reads are full tumor clearance, organ saving, and patient-reported side effects. Tissue tests will check the stress-shield theory. Mood and habit data round out the picture.
pmc-13580376:
Mehmet Demirci, Ozge Unlu and Alpdogan Kantarci propose an anaerobic stress index for microbes on clear dental aligners, in work listed for 2026. Aligners are seen as kinder to gums than fixed braces, yet local gum swelling still occurs.

The team reanalyzed sequencing data from many samples across ten studies with a single pipeline. Saliva missed local biofilm shifts, acting like a dilution filter. Fixed braces caused a fast rise in one microbe group, while aligners drove a slow shift toward oxygen-free growth. Their index rose fourfold by six months in aligner users. They suggest it as a marker of hidden imbalance.
pmc-13580676:
Sang and colleagues studied trichostatin A, a drug that blocks enzymes removing chemical tags from proteins, in a cell model of sepsis, the dangerous whole-body reaction to infection. Their 2026 experiments used human immune cells stimulated with a bacterial toxin to mimic severe inflammation. The team focused on autophagy, the cell's recycling system, and on one protein that helps recycling compartments fuse with disposal compartments.

Sang found that trichostatin A quieted the targeted enzyme and reduced a modified form of the fusion protein. sped up the joining of recycling and disposal compartments inside the cells. Treated cells released less of the inflammatory signal TNF-alpha, a driver of sepsis damage, and cell recycling markers shifted in line with faster cleanup. Computer-based drug mapping also linked the target enzyme to sepsis pathways, together supporting this drug class as a candidate for sepsis-related disease.
pmc-13580976:
Resthie Putri and co-authors study early growth and asthma in twins in a 2026 paper. How fast babies grow after birth may shape later breathing health. Swedish twin records linked growth charts to asthma reports in childhood. Preterm and full term children were analyzed in separate groups.

Children with asthma lagged slightly in weight and height in the first half year. That gap showed mainly among children born early. Later growth up to age five looked alike across groups. Small babies who then caught up fast had higher asthma odds.
pmc-13581676:
Shengdong Chen and co-authors test in 2026 a planned way to calm sad feelings in youth who report symptoms of depression. Changing how one reads a sad scene can soften its impact, but people with low mood often struggle to do this in the moment. A plan made in advance, meant to switch on when a trigger appears, may work more smoothly.

In a blind trial in China, students with high and low symptom scores were split among three groups. One group watched passively, one reframed scenes in the moment, and one used the pre planned approach. The authors compare how well each approach lowered feelings, and whether gains lasted on a later visit.
pmc-13581776:
Zhaonan Hou and colleagues report a rare case of bladder cancer spreading to skin, first mistaken for a skin infection. The patient, a man in his seventies, had major bladder surgery years earlier for invasive cancer. He came in with a spreading rash on his right thigh that was treated as erysipelas, a bacterial skin infection, for more than two months without improvement. A skin biopsy then showed metastatic bladder cancer, confirmed by marker tests reported in twenty twenty-six.

Treatment combined a targeted antibody drug with an immune therapy drug, chosen partly because earlier standard chemotherapy had not been tolerated. Pain resolved within several cycles and scans later showed complete disappearance of the skin spread. Treatment was eventually stopped after a serious immune side effect damaged his adrenal glands, requiring hormone replacement. The authors urge biopsy of stubborn skin lesions in cancer survivors.
pmc-13581976:
Wenhao Zhong and five co-authors critically weigh a proposal to pair family constellation therapy with antidepressant drugs for depression. Their review appeared in two thousand twenty-six. Drugs like SSRIs control symptoms but act slowly and unevenly. Family constellation therapy is a group method that stages hidden family dynamics across generations.

The review first sets out the strengths and limits of drug treatment. It then traces how harsh family settings and buried trauma raise depression risk. The therapy's theory and early evidence come next: fair effects on general distress, but no trials aimed at depression itself. Joining the two fits the biopsychosocial model, calming biology while working on family roots. Direct proof for the pairing, though, is still missing. The authors sketch staged and parallel ways to combine them.
pmc-13582076:
Julianne Griffith and four co-authors wrote this 2026 study on a small parenting behavior that may shield toddlers of depressed mothers. Children of depressed mothers face higher risk of anxiety and sadness early in life. The team filmed mothers and toddlers at play and coded, in five-second slices, how quickly and warmly each mother answered her child's positive feelings.

A year later, the pattern was clear only where it mattered most. Among mothers with depression, stronger positive responsiveness predicted fewer internalizing problems in the child. Among mothers without depression, the link was absent. Other measures, like total shared smiling time, did not show the effect. The authors read responsiveness as a buffer worth targeting in early prevention: brief, warm answers to a toddler's joy may blunt the risk that depression passes down.
pmc-13582176:
Leiane Mota Costa and colleagues validate a twelve question scale that sorts why older Brazilians skip regular exercise, in a 2026 study. Two hundred adults aged sixty and up, mostly women, took the scale plus a standard activity survey. The scale splits its questions into personal barriers, like pain or low drive, and environmental ones, like no safe place or no company.

The two part shape held up well under factor checks, with clean fit scores. Personal barrier scores split active from inactive elders as theory wants. Stability over repeat testing and internal consistency both ran strong. The authors offer the scale to clinics and researchers hunting fixable barriers, while warning their convenience sample limits how far the result travels beyond like groups.
pmc-13582376:
Xiaotong Li and seven co-authors study how total symptom load relates to thinking problems in breast cancer survivors in a 2026 paper. Thinking difficulties after cancer are tangled with other symptoms, which complicates care. The team used enrollment data from a trial of two hundred sixty women with early stage disease who reported thinking problems and insomnia.

Fatigue was the most common added symptom, followed by insomnia, pain, anxiety, and depression. A combined symptom score was built from those five. Higher total burden tracked strongly with worse self reported thinking, even after accounting for age and chemotherapy. Objective memory test scores did not track the total, though insomnia alone correlated with them. The authors urge treating symptom clusters together.
pmc-13582476:
Speech betrays the state of the mind, and Junjie Wang and co-authors test whether voice measures can flag violence-linked symptoms in schizophrenia. Seventy-five people, patients with and without violent behavior and healthy controls, read numbers, poems, rhymes, and weather reports while software extracted pitch, resonance, and energy features. The three groups differed on many features after accounting for age, schooling, and sex.

Yet the two patient groups did not separate from each other on voice alone, though several features tracked symptom scale scores. Voice may serve as an objective companion measure of severity, the authors suggest, but not yet as a violence detector.
pmc-13582576:
Huimin Jie, Huaying Huo, and Jiamei Wang build an end-to-end AI pipeline for colon cancer that runs from gene signatures to drug candidates. Their 2026 paper joins two drivers of the disease that are rarely handled in one frame. One is a protein tag called succinylation that rewires cell fuel use. The other is neutrophil-led swelling in the tumor's home turf.

The team mined two big public sets of tumor gene reads to pull out genes tied to both drivers. A survival model that pairs a forest method with a ridge fit proved the best at sorting patients by risk. Map-based clustering then split the tumors into subtypes with unlike immune scenes. The pipeline pushes on to virtual tests of how cell states shift, and toward reusing known drugs.
pmc-13583076:
Joey Champigny and co-authors estimate, in a 2026 study, how common mental illness is among people receiving continuing care in three Canadian provinces, with and without dementia. Care here covers home care and residential long term care. Past counts for these at risk groups have been sparse, despite their high needs.

The team ran parallel repeated studies in Ontario, Alberta, and Manitoba, using linked health records. For each year from 2012 to 2023, they counted the share with each mental illness. Recipients were matched to comparators on demographics, dementia, and other illnesses. Proven case definitions sorted the diagnoses. Splitting by dementia status shows whether the extra burden sits with dementia itself or with the care setting. Such counts can guide staffing and services for a population often missed in mental health planning.
pmc-13583176: Cheng-En Hsieh and four co-authors report a rare belly tumor case in a 2026 paper. The tumor is a myxoid form of smooth muscle cancer found outside the uterus. It followed earlier keyhole surgery to remove uterine growths. Special staining and a gene test were key to naming the tumor type. The authors urge doctors to consider these tests for myxoid belly tumors, most of all after prior uterine surgery. The report pairs the case with a review of past writing on this rare diagnosis.
pmc-13583476:
Cysts in the spleen are uncommon, and removing only part of the organ can bleed heavily. Tze Hee Tay and co-authors describe an 18-year-old patient in this 2026 case report whose returning spleen cyst was treated with a two-step plan that spared most of the organ.

First, doctors blocked the small artery feeding the cyst's segment, marking a clear cutting line. Keyhole surgery the next day removed just that segment, with modest blood loss. Tests confirmed a benign cyst, and scans three months later showed a healthy remaining spleen and no return of the cyst. The patient was back to contact sports.
pmc-13583576:
Sless and co-authors report a heart attack with an unlikely weapon: the butt end of a hockey stick. A healthy thirty-year-old took a check to the chest in a recreational game, and chest pain began that radiated to jaw and shoulder. In the emergency department his tracing showed a major heart attack pattern, and he suffered a cardiac arrest from a lethal rhythm.

Catheter pictures revealed the cause: a tear in the left main coronary artery had blocked the front descending artery. He went for emergency bypass surgery as shock deepened. Only ten traumatic left-main tears appear in the literature, none from sport. The authors urge wide thinking when young patients arrive with chest pain after a blow.
pmc-13584176:
Alhommedi Alhabbad and co-authors document, in a 2026 study, a sharp rise in flu-linked muscle inflammation among children in Riyadh during the 2024-2025 season. This condition, acute myositis, leaves children with calf pain and trouble walking after influenza, but how often it follows infection was unknown because past reports lacked a base count.

The team counted every child with confirmed flu at one hospital across two matched winter seasons of 120 days each. Cases required calf pain, gait trouble, and a raised muscle enzyme with no other cause. Comparing seasons and flu types on a true denominator shows whether the surge was real or just noticed more.
pmc-13584276:
Xuanyu Meng and colleagues look at infection after surgery in babies with biliary atresia, a rare disease that blocks the bile ducts of newborns. The Kasai procedure builds a new drain for the liver, and keeping the child's own liver working is the main goal. Their 2026 study followed 404 children at one centre and asked how later infections lined up with liver outcomes.

Infections that began early were tied to slow clearing of bilirubin, the yellow pigment that builds up when bile cannot drain. Children whose first infection came later kept their own liver longer, with each month of delay linked to a lower risk of death or transplant. The authors warn that their design shows links, not causes, yet they argue that infection timing deserves close watch after this surgery.
pmc-13584376:
Mahtab Motevasselian and co-authors report a 2026 study from Tehran on babies whose growth in the womb sits in the low but not lowest range. Babies below the tenth percentile by weight face clear risks, yet those between the tenth and twenty-fifth may also fare worse than average. The team followed low-risk mothers and compared outcomes across these weight groups.

Mothers had ultrasound scans in late pregnancy, along with checks of blood flow to the baby. Poor outcomes such as low birth weight, breathing trouble, and intensive care stays were far more common in the lower group. Blood flow measures were more often abnormal there too, but they did not predict which babies would do poorly. Closer watch of this group may still be wise.
pmc-13584476:
Yifei Xu and colleagues tested in 2026 a nurse-led respiratory care bundle for very ill patients with abdominal sepsis. Such patients face a high risk of pneumonia from inflammation, long bed rest, and weak cough. The study compared a period of traditional care at one site with bundle care across five centers.

In all, eight hundred sixty-nine patients were included. Pneumonia struck far fewer patients under the bundle, and the bundle stayed protective after adjusting for other factors. Hospital stays were shorter, and deaths within twenty-eight days were lower. Checks with five other methods gave the same pattern, with no gaps between centers. The authors link the bundle to safer, faster recovery.
pmc-13585576:
Yuxin Zhang, Mingyu Du, Luyang Li, and Yanan Xing pooled past studies in a 2026 review of diet and pancreatic cancer. Pancreatic cancer is one of the deadliest cancers, and past work on the Mediterranean diet gave mixed answers. The diet stresses plant foods, olive oil, fish, and little red meat. The authors searched four large databases for studies that linked diet scores to cancer risk.

Fourteen studies met their rules, most of them long cohort studies. People with the highest diet scores had about ten percent lower risk than those with the lowest scores. The pattern held for both men and women. The authors warn that these studies can show links, not proof of cause, and call for stronger work ahead.
pmc-13585876:
Akram Abushamma and colleagues run a follow-up drive for patients who tested positive on a stool-based bowel cancer screen at Cleveland Clinic. A positive stool test only helps if a colonoscopy follows, yet many patients never complete that step. Their 2026 quality project worked with Ohio patients aged 45 to 75 whose positive tests dated from the year before contact, using a patient navigator to call or message them.

Of more than 2,500 patients with positive tests, about a third had not finished a colonoscopy within a year. Among those the navigator reached directly, roughly one in six completed the scope within six months, against a far smaller share for message-only outreach. The main barriers named were gaps in knowledge and transport trouble, with fear and past bad experiences also cited. Overall completion still fell short of the team's goal.
pmc-13586276:
Paweł Piłat and co-authors study how a protein joins RNA decay hubs in work from 2026. Processing bodies are droplet-like structures in the cell where messenger RNA is broken down, built around a scaffold protein called EDC4.

The protein N4BP1 binds that scaffold and three other decay factors, and sits with it in processing bodies only when both of its KH domains are intact. Its KH fold lacks the classic RNA-binding motif, and mutations in variant motifs break the complex. Yet its lowering of viral and normal transcripts does not need the scaffold, so other partners must act.
pmc-13586476:
Sian O'Gorman and co-authors ask Australian women with type 2 diabetes in 2026 what helps them exercise, what forms they like, and what they aim for. Advice lands better when it fits a person's life, so the team mixed survey counts with written answers. In all, 119 women aged twenty-two to eighty-seven took part, most with a few years of the disease.

Over half reported at least 150 active minutes a week, the team reports. Health gains drove most, above all weight and blood sugar control. Written answers reframed those gains as a way to need less medicine. Younger and older women were compared for shifts across adulthood. Counseling that starts from a woman's own goals may stick where generic targets fail.
pmc-13586576:
Yongbin Wang and co-authors take the global measure of leishmaniasis, the sandfly-borne disease the world files under neglected. Using the Global Burden of Disease database, their 2026 study tracks prevalence, new cases, deaths, and years of healthy life lost. The coverage is 204 countries from 1990 to 2021, split by age and sex.

The pattern splits in two. Prevalence crept upward at about seven tenths of a percent a year, while incidence, mortality, and disability rates all fell, mortality fastest at nearly seven percent a year. A decomposition analysis asks how much of the change belongs to population growth, to aging, and to true shifts in the disease's behavior. A Bayesian age-period-cohort model then projects the burden forward to 2036. The authors aim the whole apparatus at strategy: where the disease retreats, where it quietly holds, and where programs should push next.
pmc-13586776:
Toshiyuki Hirai and five colleagues study why patients end up with leftover drugs, using pharmacy records across the human lifespan, in a study dated twenty twenty-six. Unused drugs signal that patients are not taking medicine as planned, which weakens care and wastes money. The team drew on records for 36,340 outpatients from community pharmacies between twenty sixteen and twenty twenty-one.

About one in ten patients had leftover drugs. Those patients tended to be older, take more drugs, have longer prescriptions, and use more prescribing departments. Yet the weight of each factor changed with age group in a clear pattern. The authors say support for patients should fit their stage of life, not follow one rule for all ages.
pmc-13586876:
Sharda Salunkhe and co-authors implement and test a tuning system for nearest neighbor search in multi vector databases in a 2026 paper. Such search finds the closest data points and is core to vector databases. Its speed depends heavily on data, accuracy needs, storage, and query mix, and multi vector records make tuning harder still.

Their build follows a known framework that makes candidate indexes from the workload, estimates cost and recall by sampling, and searches for a setup that meets recall and storage limits. It was coded in Python with common data tools, building the final index only after the setup was chosen. Tests used a six column data set to judge the approach.
pmc-13587276:
Farhad Heydari and colleagues put four bedside stroke scales head to head in an emergency department study. Brain scans settle a stroke diagnosis, but they are not always at hand in the first minutes, so short checklists of face, arm, and speech signs do the early work. The team scored 655 adults with suspected stroke between 2021 and 2023 and checked every score against MRI results.

Close to three quarters of the patients truly had an ischemic stroke, a blockage type. All four scales sorted patients well, with no firm winner overall. The Cincinnati scale caught the most true strokes, which suits roadside use, while the detailed NIH scale wrongly cleared the fewest healthy patients, which suits hospital confirmation. The authors advise picking the tool by setting, time pressure, and the user's training.
pmc-13587376:
Adekunle Ayomide Adegoke and colleagues compare two immune signals in Nigerians living with HIV on treatment. Antiretroviral therapy quiets the virus but often leaves the immune system partly stirred up. One signal, IL-6, marks inflammation, while IL-10 marks the calming side. Their 2026 study drew 81 people at a Port Harcourt teaching hospital: some on treatment under six months, some for two years or more, plus HIV-negative controls.

IL-6 ran highest in the short-term group, lower in the long-term group, and lowest in controls, with each step clearly apart. Years of treatment thus cool inflammation without fully matching the uninfected state. IL-10 ran higher in treated patients than controls but did not track time on treatment. Age and sex shifted neither signal. The authors back cytokine profiling as an extra gauge of immune health on therapy.
pmc-13587576:
Khawla Abu Hammour and co-authors reviewed RSV vaccines given in pregnancy, in a 2026 paper. RSV is a top cause of lung illness in newborns worldwide. Vaccinating the mother aims to pass protection to the baby. The team gathered proof on how well that works and whether it is safe.

They searched five major databases under a registered review plan. Sixteen papers fed the review, from nine parent trials plus real-world studies. pmc-13589576:

pmc-13589976:

Alireza Shahtalab and three co-authors fed hempseed to broiler chickens and tested two additives meant to help them digest it, in this 2026 study. pmc-13590476:

pmc-13591276:
Meghan Reading Turchioe and four co-authors argue that nurses must help shape the AI tools they will answer for, in a 2026 commentary. pmc-13591576:

pmc-13592476:

pmc-13592576:

pmc-13592876:

pmc-13593576:

pmc-13593776:

pmc-13593876:

pmc-13594076:

pmc-13594476:

pmc-13594776:

pmc-13594976:

pmc-13595376:

pmc-13595476:

pmc-13595676:

pmc-13598176:

pmc-13599076:

pmc-13599876:

pmc-13600176:

pmc-13601576:

pmc-13601776:

pmc-13602376:

pmc-13603176:

pmc-13603376:
