Nour Abdelrahman and many colleagues published a 2026 study on growing crystals of a layered magnetic material. The material mixes chromium with niobium diselenide, in a one-to-four ratio. Such layered crystals host gaps where magnetic atoms can sit, which tunes their electronic and magnetic states.

Good single crystals of this mix have been scarce. Past reports on its magnetism even clash with each other. The team grew high-quality crystals and tracked how their antiferromagnetic states change. In such states, nearby atomic magnets point in opposed directions. Clean crystals let the group settle what the material truly does. That base is needed before any device use.
pmc-13636076:
Nasir and co-authors trace how one family of antibodies grew stronger against the pandemic virus, to draw rules for building better ones. Antibodies mature over time, trading weak grip for tight grip on their target. The team followed a vaccine-born line from weak early members to a very strong late one.

The strong line kept its frame steady while changing one key loop. A set anchor and a repeated block in that loop marked the potent members. The best late antibody bound about three thousand times more strongly than its early kin. Computer models showed how the small changes added up to that grip. The rules they extract can guide the design of antibody drugs. They may also help judge vaccine-born lines in future outbreaks.
pmc-13638276:
Maaike Wempe, Frits Holleman, Michiel Schinkel, and Michiel Gorzeman compare an AI self-triage program with the Dutch national standard used in emergency rooms. Patients who arrive on their own answered the digital tool after normal triage. Agreement between the two methods is the core question.

The study ran in two Amsterdam emergency departments and included 203 consenting adults. Statistical agreement was near zero: the program over-triaged about thirteen percent of patients and under-triaged about five percent against the standard. Yet the program placed more patients who later had serious outcomes into its top urgency bands. It also guessed the final diagnosis in about a quarter of cases. The authors say the tool shows promise but needs refinement.
pmc-13641676:
Wonseok Lee and colleagues review the biology of steatotic liver disease through a lens in a 2026 paper that separates subtypes. The umbrella covers metabolic dysfunction-associated disease, alcohol-associated disease, and a mixed form where moderate drinking joins metabolic dysfunction, yet the subtypes share much of their appearance. The authors argue that distinctions in pathology and molecular features are needed to build models that capture how alcohol and metabolic stress amplify each other.

The review draws on multi-omics and single-cell profiling of genes, epigenetics, spatial patterns, and proteins to map cell diversity and disease drivers. It follows progression from simple fat buildup through inflamed steatohepatitis to fibrosis, driven by fat-laden liver cells, inflammatory myeloid cells, and scar-making stellate cells. It also weighs human liver spheroids as experimental models. The result is a framework for classifying the disease and for targeting therapy to its drivers.
pmc-13642376:
Bruno Riccio and seven co-authors review a drug formulation trick for non oral delivery in a 2026 article. Amorphous solid dispersions keep a poorly soluble drug in a high energy glassy state mixed with a polymer, boosting how fast it dissolves. The approach is well studied for pills, but evidence for skin, lung, eye, and other routes is scattered and mostly early stage.

The review covers how drug and polymer interact, how molecules move in the mixture, and how water uptake can trigger crystallization that ruins the boost. Evidence is summed up route by route, including injections and implants as special cases. The authors map what blocks translation into real products.
pmc-13643176:
Zohreh Tavaf and colleagues show how the ENL protein grips three gene control partners, in work from 2026. ENL steers gene reading in growth and turns rogue in several cancers. Its grip on TAF and SNF partners was known, but the binding trick stayed unclear.

One ENL domain binds greasy motifs inside floppy regions of all three partners. The grip needs no acetyl tag, unlike classic reader domain behaviour in cells. Genome maps show ENL sharing active start sites with two partners widely. Cancer data link ENL and partner levels rising together across tumour types. Blocking that grip is a fresh drug angle against ENL driven cancers.
pmc-13644176:
Danielle Tracey and two colleagues present a 2026 study of a shared gardening program in at-risk areas of New South Wales, Australia. Shared gardens are known to help health and mood. Less clear was whether such a program can be run as planned and grown wider.

The study used thirty-three survey replies, thirty-nine talks with people, and case notes from seven sites. People in the program had strong needs tied to health and jobs. Those with disability had the most need. Turnout rose and fell, with clear aids and blocks. People liked the program and gave ideas to improve it. Delivery stayed true to the plan, the authors found.
pmc-13644776:
Siddhartha Bandyopadhyay, Joanne Baker, and Jisan Afrin examine what functional neurological disorder costs society. In this condition, patients have real symptoms such as weakness or seizures that stem from how the nervous system works rather than from structural damage. It is hard to diagnose and treat, and even counting how many people have it is a challenge.

Drawing on past studies, the authors show that most cost work counts only direct health care spending. The wider costs to families, employers, and patients themselves are likely much higher and mostly go uncounted. They also weigh whether the usual yardstick for judging value in care suits a condition like this one. When the true burden is understated, they argue, funding and new tools lag behind need. The paper appears in a themed issue on digital health care for this disorder.
pmc-13646076:
Aobo Zhuang, Bin Zhou, and Mengmeng Xiao introduce a journal collection of twenty-one articles on tumors of the retroperitoneum, the deep space behind the abdominal organs. Such tumors are hard to reach, often found late, and tangled with major vessels and nerves. The editors sort the collection's lessons along one care pathway. Six original studies, fourteen case reports, and one review make up the set.

The first lesson is that good surgery starts with sharp diagnosis, and the editors cite ultrasound scores, imaging patterns, and tissue tests that separate look-alike tumors. A deep learning model trained across twelve Chinese centers also gets attention for sorting tumor types from scans. Later pieces turn to planning operations around each patient's anatomy and matching treatment scale to tumor biology. The editorial closes by tying surgical care to long-term team follow-up for these rare cancers.
pmc-13646276:
Niamh O’Malley and five colleagues solve the three-dimensional structure of a human potassium channel called Kir7.1, in a 2026 study, to explain a rare inherited eye disease. The channel helps cells keep their electrical balance and is switched on by a membrane fat. A mutation in its gene causes snowflake vitreoretinal degeneration, which has no cure. Using cryo-electron microscopy, the team imaged both the normal channel and the disease variant.

In the variant, the swapped building block swings into the channel's pore and blocks potassium flow, which explains the loss of function. A second finding surprised the team: binding of the activating fat widened the channel's gate even without a part usually seen docked in other channels. That hints this channel opens through a halfway shape of its own. The structures give drug designers a concrete target for restoring channel function.
pmc-13646776:
Xu Li and Yuhui Ma study PINK1, a gene tied to mitochondria, in lung squamous cell carcinoma. Their 2026 paper notes that this cancer is aggressive with a poor prognosis, and that mitochondrial dysregulation is linked to it.

The team joined differential expression and survival analyses to find candidate genes from the mitochondrial unfolded protein response. PINK1, short for PTEN-induced kinase 1, stood out as a key gene. High PINK1 expression went with worse survival. Cell lines with PINK1 raised or lowered were tested with blotting, growth, colony, and invasion assays. The gene promoted progression through the FAK/AKT/RhoA/vinculin pathway, a chain tied to cell movement.
pmc-13648776:
Nicholas Summerfield and ten colleagues taught a deep learning tool to trace heart parts on scans of patients who carry heart devices. Metal in these devices blurs CT scans with streaks. The tool serves two groups: people set for heart-sparing radiation, and people set for burn therapy that stops wild heart rhythms.

The team retrained the tool with device cases mixed in, then tested it on held-out device scans. Scores rose for both the rhythm group and cancer patients with devices. Scores on scans with no device barely moved. Dose maps showed the heart's lower chambers, one valve, a key nerve node, and the left heart arteries took the most dose in rhythm cases. The authors back device-aware training.
pmc-13649376:
Haoyang Jiao and two colleagues argue that care for polycystic ovary syndrome should pivot to insulin sensitivity and weight-neutral risk checks. A world accord has renamed the ill the polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome. The swap will count for little, they say, if care still fixates on ovary shape and body size.

Weak insulin response can serve as a hub for care in a large share of patients. It is not the sole cause, though, and it should not turn into a test that gates diagnosis. Their path keeps checks on blood sugar, fats, pressure, heart risk, pregnancy plans, and mind health, open to all body sizes. Drugs keep their guidelined roles. If the new name lifts care, time will tell.
pmc-13649876:
Riaz Abbas and co-authors ran a crossover trial in 2026 on AI voice-to-text tools for medical liaison staff at a drug firm. These staff must log their talks with doctors by hand, which takes time and focus. The trial asked whether speaking notes into a system would improve the work experience and the quality of logged insights.

Each staff member used both the AI tool and normal practice for four weeks each, in random order. Satisfaction scores were higher with the voice tool across all areas, above all for speed, mental load, and shaping insights. Expert ratings of insight quality were much the same, though. Accuracy was lower for Japanese and Korean speakers, which lowered their satisfaction.
pmc-13649976:
Hao Pang and three colleagues follow patients with a form of chronic hepatitis B who receive pegylated interferon alpha, a timed course of immune-based treatment. The team tracks two genes, IFI44L and SAMHD1, measured in blood immune cells, to see whether their levels during treatment line up with later response.

Patients were treated for 48 weeks, and gene levels were measured before treatment and at weeks 12 and 24 using a standard laboratory test. Higher levels at the mid-treatment checks went with larger falls in viral markers. The week 24 readings separated responders from non-responders most clearly among the time points tested. The results point to both genes as possible early signals of how well interferon therapy is working, though the authors frame them as candidates needing further proof.
pmc-13650676:
Hongzhi Cao and five colleagues report a 54-year-old man whose liver held two cancers growing side by side: a hepatocellular carcinoma and a bile duct cancer. That pairing is called a collision tumor. They stay distinct under the microscope rather than mixing, a rare entity confused with blended tumors or spread from elsewhere.

The man, a long-term hepatitis B carrier, came in during June 2024 feeling tired, eating poorly, and with a swollen belly. Scans first suggested widespread spread of one cancer, while a specialized scan hinted at two primaries, and biopsies aimed at both lesions confirmed the split diagnosis. Surgery was ruled out because lymph nodes were involved, so the team combined artery-delivered chemotherapy for one tumor with immune therapy, a vessel-blocking antibody, and chemotherapy cycles. At the check in April 2026 he had lived over eighteen months with tumors shrunk and no severe side effects.
pmc-13650976:
Lin Guo and five colleagues ask whether rising above one's parents in education protects functional health in old age, and whether the answer depends on the country. Their outcome is intrinsic capacity, the World Health Organization's composite of thinking, movement, energy, senses, and mood, which reframes aging around function rather than disease.

Harmonized data from five national aging studies covered over one hundred thousand people past fifty, about half a million observations in all. Upward educational mobility was robustly tied to higher capacity everywhere. In China, Europe, South Korea, and Mexico, mobile adults also declined more slowly with age, a pattern of delayed aging. The United States broke the pattern: mobility raised the starting level sharply while the pace of decline matched everyone else's. Wealth, behavior, and chronic disease carried part of the effect. The authors keep mobility central to healthy longevity policy.
pmc-13651276:
Hui Liu and co-authors listen to parents of children with cerebral palsy in a 2026 interview study from China. Daily care is heavy, and caregivers often fade out of social life, yet their own experience is rarely asked about directly. Family-centered care depends on hearing it.

Twenty-six main caregivers from a large rehabilitation hospital described their lives in interviews held in person, by video, or by phone. Four themes emerged: distress pulling them out of social life, care duties crowding out chances to join in, and further strains and supports the analysis details. The findings point nurses and services toward concrete ways to keep caregivers connected.
pmc-13651576:
Li Chu and co-authors report a runner whose liver enzymes screamed far louder than his muscle damage should allow. Rhabdomyolysis, the breakdown of muscle after exertion, floods the blood with muscle contents, and liver test chaos usually appears only in extreme cases with very high creatine kinase. Their 2026 case report presents a 43-year-old man who felt fatigue, nausea, and muscle pain after a 3,000-meter run.

His kinase peaked at a moderate 2,828 units per liter, yet his liver enzymes soared past 2,200 and 1,500, while bilirubin stayed mild, clotting near normal, and the liver's protein output intact. Virus tests were negative. Fluids, urine alkalinizing, and liver-protective drugs brought every value down fast; he left the hospital on day eight and was fully normal at one year. The authors warn doctors not to rule out muscle injury when the kinase looks modest.
pmc-13652876:
Janousch and co-authors followed more than fifteen hundred young people in Zurich from childhood into adulthood to ask when teenage cannabis use leaves a mark on the mind. Participants reported how often they used cannabis at six points between the ages of eleven and twenty-four. At age twenty-four they took tests of sustained attention, spatial working memory, and memory for visual scenes. The team adjusted the results for earlier use and social and behavioral background factors.

Use at ages thirteen, seventeen, and twenty was linked to weaker attention and weaker scene memory at twenty-four. The clearest gaps appeared among near-daily and daily users. Spatial working memory showed no link. The team sorted users into four patterns over time, but those patterns did not differ in test outcomes. The authors read the results as a warning about early and frequent use.
pmc-13653176:
Qiaohui Ye and Yanfei Xu hunt for what predicts whether younger stroke patients stick to healthy behaviors in hospital, in a study from 2026. Good habits drive recovery and prevent a second stroke, but work and family pressures compete in this age group. Early flags for poor adherence would help target coaching.

Records of 298 patients treated from 2021 to 2024 were split by an adherence index into high and non-high groups. Nearly half fell in the non-high group. That group scored worse on daily function and thinking tests. The authors combined the strongest factors into a prediction model and checked its discrimination with standard curves.
pmc-13653376:
Imogen Smith and three colleagues trap light-activated catalysts inside polymer beads so oxidation chemistry can run in water, in a 2026 study. Porphyrin catalysts use light to make singlet oxygen, a selective oxidizer, but they usually demand organic solvents.

Two porphyrins were built for the job, one for stitching into gels, one for ionic assembly into beads. Both forms converted sulfur compounds, thiols, and aldehydes effectively. In heavy water, where singlet oxygen lives longer, several reactions ran to completion; sulfur oxidations stopped neatly at the middle stage instead of overshooting. Easy catalyst recovery is the selling point. Cost and slower rates in plain water point the team toward microfluidic nanobeads.
pmc-13653576:
Louis Le Moigne and nine co-authors report a 2026 chemistry study on stripping fluorine from two tough plastics. These plastics resist heat and chemicals, which makes them hard to break down or recycle. Removing their fluorine could open safer ways to handle the waste.

The team used titanium based helpers with a silicon reagent in aromatic solvents. The helpers cut fluorine from both plastics at steady rates. The left over material held as little as 0.8 percent fluorine in the best cases. The products were checked with several tools, including magnetic resonance scans of the solid samples. The work gives a lab route toward taming a stubborn class of plastics.
pmc-13653676:
A-Hyeong Choi, Seon-Yle Ko, and Young-Joo Jang study gum ligament stem cells in this 2026 study. These stem cells rebuild the ligament that holds teeth in place, partly by turning into fibroblasts, the cells that make its tough fibers. A growth signal starts that change, but the inner controls were not well known.

Using a new antibody as a probe, the team found a protein called EPLIN in the changed cells. Removing EPLIN broke the cells' inner frame, loosened the links between cells, and sped up growth. Adding extra EPLIN had the reverse effect, pushing stem cells toward the fibroblast state even without the growth signal. The authors cast EPLIN as a guard that holds the mature state in place.
pmc-13653976:
Arash Ghalyanchi Langeroudi and co-authors review two decades of a poultry virus's genetics in Iran in a 2026 paper. Infectious bronchitis virus, a chicken coronavirus, slashes egg output and growth across the industry. Iranian reports existed but had never been gathered in one place.

Thirty-two studies from 2003 to 2022 met the bar, most in broiler flocks and most using PCR-based tests. Four major lineages circulated side by side, including Massachusetts-type and QX-like strains. Reporting styles clashed between studies, and missing sample counts blocked any pooled prevalence estimate. The authors call for steady molecular surveillance, uniform reporting, and vaccines matched to the strains actually circulating in Iranian flocks.
pmc-13654176:
Aaron Rayan and co-authors audit, in a 2026 paper, whether symptom questionnaires from patients help radiologists read lower spine scans more accurately. Back pain sends many people to CT imaging, yet scans often show age-related changes that are not the true pain source. Two hundred fifty patients at a community service filled in a questionnaire before their scan was reported. The form asked about pain type and location, altered sensation, and past tests.

Most forms came back completed, and most patients reported back pain, with about three-quarters also reporting leg symptoms. Radiologists mentioned the questionnaire in the great majority of their reports. In a notable share of cases, the patient's own account pointed to a different problem than the referral note suggested. The authors judge the forms a cheap, useful aid for focused reporting.
pmc-13655276:
Hamlin and co-authors review a whole-life health program for adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities at a residential center. This group faces high rates of chronic disease, made worse by barriers in care. Most programs for them target single problems, not overall health.

The review covers 295 adults, many with autism, who took part in the program. It joins food, movement, sleep, and daily routine into one plan of care. The team set the group's disease rates against national and state figures for people with disabilities. The results suggest the group fared better than those baselines on several counts. The report argues that lifestyle care, standard for others, should be built for this group too. It offers one center's model as a start.
pmc-13655476:
Chang Kyung Kang and Jonathan Li review a tricky problem in HIV care: virus levels that stay low but never fully vanish on treatment. Modern drugs suppress the virus for most people, yet this lingering trace is common. It can mean missed doses or drug clashes, or virus leaking from hidden reservoirs with no real growth.

The review lays out a step-by-step workup, starting with adherence, food and drug interactions, and resistance tests. Fixes differ by cause: better adherence or a drug switch for true growth, but watchful waiting for reservoir leak. The authors also cover new long-acting shots and note sex transmission risk stays very low in this range.
pmc-13655876:
Jingyi Huang and Meng Wu write a letter about a study of multimodal biopsy for peripheral lung lesions under radial endobronchial ultrasound guidance. They praise the use of a tissue adequacy rate beside diagnostic yield, since modern lung cancer care needs tissue fit for molecular tests. Their concern lies with how the ultrasound patterns were read.

The split between lesions seen as within the target and those read as adjacent drove both tissue forecasts and the choice to add larger forceps or needle sampling. Yet the study gave no reader agreement figures, no set rules for freezing images, and no standard way to measure its margin threshold. Live reading also turns on motion and operator judgement, they note.
pmc-13657776:
Jan Novák and co-authors test a simpler screen for sperm DNA damage in a 2026 study. Standard sperm checks can miss hidden damage, and the most precise DNA test needs special gear, chemicals, and skilled staff. A flow cytometry test for dying sperm might stand in for it.

The team compared the apoptosis test with the reference DNA fragmentation assay in men from infertile couples. The question was whether the easy test predicts the hard one's result well enough for screening. If it does, clinics could triage patients faster and reserve costly tests for unclear cases. The study is a practical step for fertility labs.
pmc-13659676:
Christopher Ma, Giuliana Arevalo, Siobán Keel, and Cynthia Levy describe a man whose liver disease returned after a transplant because his true diagnosis had been missed. He had long been treated for erythropoietic protoporphyria, a disorder in which protoporphyrin builds up, causing pain in sunlight and, in a minority, liver failure. After the transplant his symptoms and porphyrin levels worsened, and biopsies showed heavy porphyrin deposits in the new liver.

Genetic testing during a bone marrow transplant workup revealed a faulty ALAS2 gene, which means he actually had the X-linked form of the disease. That distinction matters because iron treatment lowers porphyrin in the X-linked form but not reliably in the other. Once oral iron began, his light sensitivity eased quickly and his liver tests improved as porphyrin levels fell.
pmc-13659776:
Anna Harrison and co-authors survey kidney doctors in the United Kingdom in a 2026 study. Women with chronic kidney disease face distinct health needs, from period changes to pregnancy risks. It was unclear how ready kidney doctors feel to handle those needs in daily clinics. The survey asked about confidence, past training, and blocks to good care.

Most of those who replied felt low confidence on periods, menopause, and sexual health. Confidence ran a bit higher for birth control and pregnancy advice. Still, fewer than half felt ready to adjust drugs that can harm a fetus. Time limits, lack of training, and rare case exposure were the main blocks named.
pmc-13660576:
Hilal Hatice Ülkü, Fulya Torun, and Selcen Öncü compared feedback from two AI chat tools in a 2026 study. Medical interns now often get AI feedback on their case work. The team asked whether ChatGPT or Gemini gives better notes after a mock patient talk on iron poor blood, a common training case.

Thirty two interns were split by chance between the two tools. Interns and teaching experts scored the notes on a shared rubric for clarity, accuracy, and help with reasoning. Scores sat close, with interns rating ChatGPT a touch higher and experts near tied. Both tools were clear and kind, but both missed the patient's own view. ChatGPT gave more ordered, thoughtful notes, while Gemini gave more concrete cases.
pmc-13661276:
Pradeep K Sheokand and co-authors pin down the job of a protein whose loss causes Batten disease, a fatal childhood brain disorder. Their 2026 study concerns CLN8, a protein in the cell's membrane workshop that teams with another enzyme to build a signature fat of the lysosome, the cell's recycling unit.

The team shows CLN8 is itself an enzyme that performs one exact step in building that fat, attaching a fatty chain with the correct handedness. Atomic-scale structures reveal its active site and a ping-pong style of transfer. Disease mutations cripple the step and halt fat production in mice. Supplying the missing intermediate fat restored production in cells and mice and eased symptoms in mutant fish. The authors propose the supplement as a treatment idea.
pmc-13661876:
Ralf Porzig and co-authors test a nurse guide program for cancer patients in Germany in a 2026 trial. Cancer care can feel split across many clinics, which leaves patients stressed and unsure. Nurse guides offer steady, planned support and help link each step of care. The trial took place at six hospital centers in the state of Saxony.

Patients were split by chance into a guide group and a standard care group. The guide group got twelve months of support from a trained nurse. The main outcome was how many patients had at least one more hospital stay in that year. The trial stopped early after slow sign up, which the authors note as a limit on its findings.
pmc-13662476:
Maria Fusaro and co-authors review a rare vessel disease and a possible vitamin treatment in a 2026 paper. The disease hardens small arteries in people with advanced kidney failure, often those on dialysis. It causes painful skin sores that heal poorly and can turn deadly. A lack of active vitamin K may help drive the hardening, since the vitamin switches on a protein that blocks vessel calcium buildup.

Blood tests in patients show high levels of the inactive form of that guard protein. Case reports hint that vitamin K pills may help sores heal and slow hardening. Firm trial proof is still missing, though. Trials now under way aim to test dose, safety, and benefit.
pmc-13662876:
Tomoki Asano led a 2026 study using deep learning on CT scans to ask whether muscle quality or muscle quantity better reflects walking ability before hip fracture in older women. Muscle loss and fatty infiltration both accompany aging and fracture risk, yet which matters more for function was unclear. The team studied 170 women with intertrochanteric or femoral neck fractures, automatically segmenting muscles on the unfractured side into gluteal, adductor, quadriceps, and hamstring groups.

Pre-injury walking ranged from outdoor walking to being chairbound or bedridden. Across all muscle groups, poorer walking tracked with lower muscle attenuation, higher comorbidity burden, and lower body mass index, while muscle volume did not reach significance. The authors conclude that CT muscle quality, reflecting fatty infiltration, mirrors functional decline better than size alone. Geriatricians get support for reading muscle quality into fracture risk and rehabilitation planning, not just muscle bulk.
pmc-13666076:
Hospital stays for rare muscle inflammation diseases are tracked across fifteen years by Dutsch-Wicherek and co-authors in a 2026 study. These diseases are chronic, immune-driven, and hard to study in trials due to their rarity. The team drew on a nationwide Polish hospital database from 2010 to 2024.

More than seven thousand patients were included. Records cover age, sex, main diagnosis, stay details, and deaths in hospital. Trend models test how stay rates moved over time. A profile of the typical patient in this group is also built. Large record studies like this one can guide clinic planning for rare diseases where trial data will stay thin.
pmc-13668476:
Counting a child's hardships gives a single score meant to flag later health risks, and screening programs based on that score are spreading. Alan Meehan, Stephanie Lewis, and Andrea Danese argue in a 2026 debate piece that routine screening with the score is not ready. Group-level links to illness are strong, they grant, but the score predicts any one person's future poorly, with many false alarms and misses.

A single count also ignores context and strengths, and a positive result leads to no proven care path, while labels can stigmatize. The authors urge richer, personal measures that weigh development, social setting, and protective factors instead.
pmc-13669976:
Huang and Lunos studied whether gentle surgery protects leftover hearing in ear implant patients, in a paper published in 2026. Implants restore hearing for people with severe loss, but the surgery can destroy the hearing that remains. Soft techniques aim to spare the inner ear's delicate parts. The team reviewed ten years of adult implant cases at their center. They asked whether preservation rates changed over time and what predicted them.

Sex, age, and the type of electrode made no clear difference. Patients who got a higher dose of steroids around surgery kept their hearing more often, at 36.4 percent versus 15 percent. Rates also crept up slightly in later years. Low-frequency hearing, the range most valued for music and tone, was checked on its own. The results support steroids and refined technique as the levers that matter.
pmc-13671876:
Xiaotong Mao and co-authors survey in 2026 how shape drives reactivity in a key polymerization helper compound. The helper's active form stayed murky despite wide industry use. More than one hundred species across sizes feed the computation for this survey.

Ion strength grows more negative as the clusters grow larger. Sheet forms out-react cage forms at every size checked. Large models stretch to sizes plants actually use in production. Two reactive site types emerge at those sizes, one per break path. One sheet form matches the crystal-proven shape of the helper itself.
pmc-13672176:
Waves that ride a metal surface, called surface plasmon polaritons, power many tiny light devices. Humaira Zafar and co-authors study those waves where gold meets a thin oxide layer over silicon. They pair electron-beam measurements with computer simulations of the same layered stacks.

The simulations let them split lost energy into absorbed and scattered parts. Absorption dominates, proving the signals come from waves trapped at the buried gold-oxide boundary. Swapping the oxide for one with a higher permittivity shifted the waves' color and changed how tightly they hug the surface. Losses stayed mostly in the gold. The 2026 work links lab spectra to energy loss at hidden interfaces.
pmc-13672976:
Tarak Srivastava and co-authors hunt in a 2026 study for early urine signals that a child's kidneys are over-filtering and quietly injuring themselves. They measured eicosanoids, fat-derived signal molecules, in stored urine from three hundred eighteen children with chronic kidney disease and seventy-two children with bedwetting as a comparison group.

Most of the kidney group had birth defects of the urinary tract; the rest had glomerular disease. Across disease stages, several signals rose, including prostaglandin E2 and thromboxane products. Earlier work tied one of them to damage before protein leaked. Stage-linked urine markers could warn before standard tests turn.
pmc-13673276:
Juan Jiang and co-authors report health data from Hainan Province in China in 2026. Their study covers the year 2023 and looks at three linked conditions in adults. The conditions are high blood pressure, diabetes, and poor blood fat levels. When these cluster in one person, heart and vessel risk climbs fast.

The report finds that high blood pressure paired with poor blood fats was the most common cluster. That pair beat other pairs and the full triple cluster in how often it appeared. The authors flag groups at higher risk for checks. Their baseline data can guide joint screening and prevention plans in the province.
pmc-13673576:
Luca Troffer and nine co-authors test whether blocking cell couriers calms the prostate's squeeze in a 2026 paper. An enlarged prostate clamps the urine channel, and its muscle tightens under adrenaline-like signals. Courier proteins called Rab GTPases ferry receptors around inside cells, so blocking them might soften the grip.

The team mounted human prostate tissue in baths and provoked contractions several ways, with and without two courier blockers. Drug-driven contractions shrugged off both blockers at every dose and tissue type. Nerve-driven contractions dipped under one blocker in only one tissue group. The grip, the authors conclude, is largely maintained despite the blockade, a sobering result for that drug idea.
pmc-13674376:
Carly Moser and co-authors ask which families gain most from parent advocacy training in a 2026 study. Autistic youth often lose services when school-based support ends at graduation. A group program called ASSIST teaches parents the adult service system and how to push for access.

An earlier trial showed the program raised advocacy skill and program entry for graduates. The new study sorts families by the advocacy level they held at the start. Knowledge, felt skill, and empowerment form that starting measure. If gains cluster in one group, recruiters can aim the program where it pays most. Scarce training seats should go where they change outcomes.
pmc-13676376:
Kirsten Rodgers and a large team study memory cells that guard the airways in a 2026 paper. These T cells settle in the nose and throat, where they blunt virus spread early, and in the lungs, where they clear virus and curb harm. Past work said lung settlers need the virus on site to form, while throat settlers may not.

The team asked how local virus meets and cell signals jointly shape each settler kind. Upper and lower airway cells turned out to need distinct mixes of the two. The split helps explain why each niche guards its own stretch, and guides spray vaccine design.
pmc-13676576:
Lianjie Niu and co-authors compare two ways to treat breast cancer that has spread to the liver in only a few spots. Patients received either surgical removal of the liver tumors or focused high-dose radiation, across three centers between 2010 and 2023. From 1,055 eligible patients, the team formed 708 matched pairs of similar patients, 354 in each group, and followed them for a median of about 55 months.

Median survival was 48.3 months after surgery and 38.8 months after radiation. Time without progression was closer, at 21.8 and 19.7 months, and local failure at the treated site was similar in both groups. Hospital stays ran 8 days for surgery against 1 for radiation, and patients restarted general therapy sooner after radiation. The authors caution that hidden differences between groups limit firm conclusions.
pmc-13676676:
Clara Morato Dias and co-authors searched for a group of germs in wild cats in Brazil, in a study from 2026. House cats are known to carry these germs, which spread to people at times. Far less is known about wild cats. The team tested blood and tissue from many wild cats across Brazil, with just under three hundred samples in all.

About three in one hundred samples tested positive for the germ group. Positives came from five kinds of wild cat, from small spotted cats to the jaguar. Gene checks showed some germs matched types found in house cats. Others matched types seen in wild rodents and their fleas. The authors suggest wild cats may pick up the rodent types by eating prey, as well as hosting the cat-linked types.
pmc-13677076:
Maria Michali and seven co-authors measured how patients feel after nose-straightening surgery in a 2026 study. A bent nasal septum blocks airflow and drags down quality of life. Forty-three patients had septoplasty combined with radiofrequency shrinking of the swollen lower turbinates on both sides, and answered two validated symptom questionnaires before surgery and six months later.

Twenty healthy volunteers provided a comparison baseline. Both questionnaire scores improved significantly after surgery. The prospective design, with the same patients tracked across the operation, strengthens the reading. The authors present patient-reported outcomes as the honest test of this surgery, since anatomy alone does not say how well a nose breathes.
pmc-13678076:
Janan Arslan, Tamara Künzle, Yeşim Güner, and Agustí Alentorn published a 2026 software paper bringing standardized radiomics into a popular pathology image platform. Radiomic features turn tissue images into numbers describing organization and texture. The open source program QuPath measures shape, brightness, and classic texture features, but lacks the standardized set researchers expect, forcing exports to separate Python tools.

Their extension, QuRad, computes 119 features from cell detections and marked regions without leaving QuPath. Tested against the reference Python package on the same images, nearly all default features matched to a tight tolerance. A breast cancer tile with 410 cells matched perfectly, and melanoma tiles agreed closely. A few shape features differed because one tool traces outlines while the other builds meshes.
pmc-13678276:
Massimo D'Archivio and co-authors set out a view piece from 2026 linking a warming climate with type 2 diabetes. They argue that heat can harm how the body handles blood sugar, in part by cutting the work of brown fat that helps burn energy.

Food choices sit on both sides of the loop, since diets shape both health and gas output that warms the air. The authors join diet, sex and gender, heat, brown fat, and diabetes risk into one loop that feeds back on itself. They offer the loop as a base for new studies and for care plans that take sex and gender into account.
pmc-13678676:
Kanu Garg and colleagues published a 2026 review of ultrasound treatment for wheat proteins. Wheat feeds much of the world. Heat processing can damage its nutrients. Ultrasound offers a gentler, non-thermal alternative. Sound waves reshape protein structure and behavior.

The review covers chemical and structural changes. Function in foods can improve after treatment. Storage life may also lengthen. Evidence spans many wheat products and studies. Sustainability and precision are recurring themes. Food makers want quality without heavy energy use. Ultrasound fits that demand well. The authors map what is known and what remains untested.
pmc-13679976:
A journal's October 2026 obituary column records the deaths of Canadian doctors, giving a short entry for each. Each entry names the doctor, the city where they lived, their medical school and graduation year, and their field of practice. Most entries add the date of death, the age at death, and a link to a fuller notice. The doctors listed trained from the early 1950s to the 1980s.

Fields in the list range from family medicine and psychiatry to pathology, pediatrics, and obstetrics. Ages at death run from the early seventies to the late nineties. The column serves as a record of service for the medical community in Canada. Colleagues and former patients can use it to learn of a doctor's passing and find the full obituary. It also preserves, in brief, the training paths of a generation of physicians.
pmc-13680376:
Venkatesh Thirumalaikumar and co-authors present a 2026 dataset on how plants remember heat stress. A mild heat episode can prime a plant to survive a later, harsher one, and that primed state can last for days. The molecular steps behind that memory are still under study.

The dataset tracks Arabidopsis seedlings across the memory phase using three kinds of large scale measurement at once. It records gene activity, small molecule levels, and protein levels at set times after priming. The authors describe it as the first detailed dataset of its kind for this phase. They offer it as a resource for finding genes that build heat resilience and for breeding tougher crops.
pmc-13680476:
Nathan Vaudiau and a large team of co-authors show how two kinds of guide cells team up to train tumor-fighting cells, in a study published in twenty twenty-six. Some killer T cells settle in tumors like resident guards, and patients who hold more of them fare better. How those guards get specified was unclear.

The team used a mouse model of lung cancer and removed each guide cell type in turn. One type proved vital for making the main attacking and worn-out killer cells. Both types, though, helped shape the resident-like guards in the lymph nodes that drain the tumor. The second type shows tumor parts sparsely, which favors guard training, while the first type drives guard growth and adds a homing signal. Teamwork, not a single teacher, builds the guards.
pmc-13682176:
Esther Decabooter and Sebastiaan Nijsten audit five years of safety checks on cancer radiation plans at one Dutch center. Radiotherapy grows more complex each year, and a failure can hide in the dose, the aim, or the machine. Their 2026 audit joins three check kinds: a second dose calculation, machine log-file checks, and portal imaging reads, run both before treatment and live in the patient.

The pretreatment arm held 18,558 plans, and the in vivo arm 1,817. Nearly all high-priority failure modes could be caught, except a wrong machine output calibration. Combined checks scored far more true hits than each method alone. The in vivo arm flagged the most failure kinds and also showed where plans themselves could be sharpened. The team urges a broad net of checks, each with its own job.
pmc-13682476:
Tianhao Wang and co-authors give a recipe for growing bone organoids with plant-based ink in a 2026 protocol paper. Organoids are lab-grown mini tissues. Bone versions often lack immune signals, though immunity steers bone repair. They also rest on animal-derived gels that vary batch to batch and are poorly defined.

The team's ink mixes aloe vera gel, a printable gelatin derivative, and a clay-like additive, with no animal matrix and no added cytokines. In dishes, the ink steadily reprogrammed macrophages, immune cells that set the tone for healing. That built an immune setting in which bone organoids matured well. The protocol walks through ink preparation, organoid printing, and tests in skull bone defect models. The authors offer the platform as a defined, repeatable swap for gel-based systems. They suggest it can adapt to other immune-responsive tissues.
pmc-13683776:
Kanishka Sakthivel and Mary Rajaiah report a single case of Siddha therapy for stress related insomnia in a 2026 case report. Insomnia affects a large share of adults, and non drug options are limited. A fifty five year old woman had four months of poor sleep and daytime fatigue.

She received twenty one daily sessions of Varmathadaval therapy with a ginger oil, each lasting about one and a half to two hours. Standard sleep and stress scores improved by roughly three fifths after treatment. Time to fall asleep dropped and total sleep rose. Benefits largely held at follow up visits weeks later.
pmc-13684276:
Lisa Melber and co-authors map what is known about fighting teen nicotine use through social media itself. Their scoping review searched five databases and screened 1,626 records, keeping 18 studies. The set spans message tests, mock feed trials, and large campaigns such as Truth and The Real Cost, plus one school program teaching students to read nicotine posts with a critical eye.

Most studies found short-term gains in knowledge, in how risky teens judged nicotine, or in engagement. Proof that the campaigns cut actual use, or changed habits for long, was thin. The authors blame self-reported outcomes and brief follow-up. They call for stricter long-term studies and continued funding, and suggest pairing campaigns built for each platform with tighter rules on the marketing teens see online.
pmc-13684576:
Traenkner and co-authors report a study, published in 2026, on brain immune cells tied to mental health conditions. One gene switch is needed for a special group of these cells to work well. Mice that lack the switch groom themselves without pause and act anxious. The effect grows stronger in females after maturity. What the switch controls inside the cells was largely unknown. The switch bound thousands of spots, yet only some nearby genes changed activity. Genes it turns on were linked to immune signals and hormone response. Genes it turns off had other roles. The team sorted genes by how binding, contact, and response fit together. Their map shows how one switch runs a program in brain immune cells. It gives new leads on how faults in these cells may feed compulsive and anxious behavior.
pmc-13684676:
Michael O'Sullivan and co-authors separate the jobs of two sibling pore proteins in fruit flies, in a 2026 paper. Knocking down the second version, but not the first, made larval wings overgrow like tumors, echoing the effect of losing Polycomb silencing. Gene readouts confirmed wide loss of silencing, especially over a patch of genes that activate JAK/STAT signaling. The siblings did not differ in pore building; they differed in where they sit in the nucleus. A pore protein, it turns out, doubles as a gene silencer.
pmc-13685776:
Samantha Thomas and co-authors ask how women in Australia view the growing business around menopause. Their study appeared in 2026. Three themes stood out. First, some women welcomed the attention as a sign their experiences count. Second, many feared firms were profiting from women's weak spots, and doubted the motives behind the marketing. Third, women felt flooded by online content and struggled to judge what to trust. The authors argue that policy and health advice must reckon with this crowded, profit-driven setting.
pmc-2247476:
Drummond and Rambaut present BEAST, software for Bayesian evolutionary analysis by sampling trees. Studying how sequences change is a statistical task at its core. Use of probability models for family trees, alignments, and population genetics was growing when they wrote.

BEAST is described as a fast and flexible package that samples many possible trees and weighs each by likelihood. That approach yields not just one tree but a sense of how sure each branch is. BEAST became a central tool for dating species splits and tracing the spread of viruses through time.
pmc-3012676:
Du, Zhang, Huang, and co-authors compare two ways of expressing DNA methylation levels from microarray data. Measuring methylation across CpG sites is crucial for understanding how genes are switched without changing the DNA code. Illumina's Infinium assay offers cheap, high-throughput profiling for that purpose.

Results can be reported as Beta values or as M values, and the choice affects statistics. The authors test both methods side by side to show where each behaves well. Their guidance helps researchers pick a scale that supports valid comparisons in studies of cancer and development.
pmc-3445676:

pmc-3447976:

pmc-5340976:

The catch is that the tags themselves pick up read errors, so true groups can split or merge. UMI-tools models those tag errors and groups the reads the right way. That fix makes counts of gene activity far more true to the sample. As tagged tests spread through labs, tools like this became part of the basic kit.
pmc-6366976:

pmc-7617476:

pmc-7619276:
Dena Matalon and a large team of colleagues report clinical, molecular, and gene-expression findings from a major cohort of people with RNU4ATAC-opathy. That three-way view, covering the body, the molecule, and the transcript, sharpens diagnosis for children whose features overlap with better-known syndromes. pmc-7857476:
Jeanne Bertuit and two colleagues study how pregnancy changes walking in women with pelvic girdle pain, and whether a pelvic belt helps. The study enrolled women with the pain condition, healthy pregnant women, and non-pregnant women, measuring the timing and spacing of their steps on an instrumented walkway. Two belt designs for pregnant women were tested on the same measures.

Women with pelvic pain walked with shorter stance and cycle times than healthy pregnant women, and pregnancy itself slowed walking and shortened steps compared with the non-pregnant group. Wearing a belt measurably changed speed, single-support time, step length, and step width. Results like these let midwives and physiotherapists recommend belts on evidence about gait, and let designers see which support style changes walking the most.
pmc-9825576:
Brian Alcock and colleagues presented the 2023 update of CARD, a database that collects what is known about how bacteria resist antibiotics. CARD pairs a set of standard terms for resistance with checked gene sequences and the gene changes known to cause resistance. Together they let a lab read a bacterium's genome and say which drugs it can likely withstand.

The update adds more curated records, support for machine learning, and better tools to predict a sample's resistome, the full set of resistance genes it carries. Health teams use CARD when they sequence bacteria from hospitals and towns. Knowing resistance genes with care is key to picking the right drug and to spotting dangerous strains early.
polano-talmud-selections-1876:
Polano's Talmud: Selections, published in 1876, offered English readers early and easy access to rabbinic literature. The Talmud itself is a vast record of Jewish law and debate in Hebrew and Aramaic. Polano chose and translated passages for a general audience.

The selections range over prayer, charity, family duty, court rulings, and tales of the rabbis at work. Readers could meet the Talmud's mix of strict law and warm story without facing its full bulk. The book served as an influential introduction for English readers curious about Jewish tradition. Victorian readers met a living tradition here, not a dead code.
price-observations-civil-liberty-1776:
Price's Observations on the Nature of Civil Liberty appeared in 1776 and made him famous in a night. The dissenting minister wrote as Britain moved toward war with its American colonies. His pamphlet defended the American cause on principle, and it sold by the thousand in the year of independence.

Price defines liberty as self-government, for nations as for persons, and argues that Britain's claim to tax and bind the colonies was a form of slavery. He extends the argument to Ireland and India, which widened both the book's reach and its enemies. The government of the day considered prosecuting its author. The tract carried deep thought to the barricades across the sea, and it stands as the English voice of the American Revolution at its birth.
proudhon-what-is-property-tucker-1876:
Benjamin R Tucker published his translation of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon's What is Property? in 1876. Proudhon, a French printer and self-taught thinker, had issued the memoir in 1840 and shocked France. His answer to his own question became famous at once: property is robbery.

Proudhon distinguished property, the right to use and abuse and charge rent, from simple possession of what one works. He attacked rent, interest, and profit taken without labor. Judges and economists denounced the book, and Proudhon answered them in later memoirs. The work is widely read as the founding text of anarchism, the first time a writer claimed that label with pride.
shi-king-book-of-poetry-legge-1876:
James Legge published his complete translation of the She King, the Book of Poetry, in 1876. It forms volume three of his Chinese Classics, in a revised edition with the Chinese text, prolegomena, and notes. The Shih Ching holds 305 songs and hymns, gathered in China more than two thousand years ago.

Court odes, temple hymns, and folk songs of love, harvest, and war stand side by side. Tradition credits Confucius with choosing and ordering the collection. Legge's prose renderings favor exact sense, while his notes carry the learning of Chinese commentators. The songs remain China's oldest poetry anthology and a school text for ages. English readers meet them whole in Legge.
smith-chaldean-account-genesis-1876:
George Smith, a bank note engraver turned Assyriologist at the British Museum, wrote this book in 1876. He had taught himself to read the clay tablets of Babylon from the museum's vast store. Four years past, he had read out a flood tale from the tablets to a stunned London crowd.

The book sets the Babylonian tales of the making of the world and man by the side of Genesis. A flood tale far older than the Bible stands in its pages in clay writ form. The find shook the firm faith of Victorian Britain in the lone truth of its own text.
spina-quaestio-de-strigibus-latin-1576:
Bartolomeo Spina, a Dominican who served as master of the sacred palace at Rome, wrote his Quaestio de strigibus early in the sixteenth century. This edition of 1576 kept his answer in print. Spina writes against Ponzinibio, the skeptical jurist who had called the sabbath an illusion.

Point for point, Spina defends the sabbath's reality with scholastic logic and old texts. The witches fly in body, he insists, and their assemblies truly meet. His book is the Counter-Reformation's learned reply to early doubt. Orthodoxy strikes back here with full armor. Reading Spina against Ponzinibio shows the sixteenth-century debate at its sharpest, lawyer against theologian over the same frightened women.
taine-ancient-regime-durand-1876:
Hippolyte Taine's The Ancient Regime appears in John Durand's translation of 1876. The book opens Taine's Origins of Contemporary France, his study of the Revolution's causes. Taine applies his method of race, milieu, and moment to old France. Taxes, privilege, and a rigid central state crush the peasantry and starve reform.

He paints the court, the tax farmer, and the village in hard detail. The old regime, in his account, made revolution near certain. Taine wrote after the Paris Commune, and fear of crowds colors his work. Historians debate his science, yet respect his research. The volume is a classic of analytical history in the French style.
the-dare-boys-of-1776:
Stephen Angus Cox wrote The Dare Boys of 1776, with pictures by R. Mencl, published in New York by the Platt and Peck Company under a 1910 copyright held by the A. L. Chatterton Company. Its contents send the Dare boys through a night attack, dangerous work, spy missions, a haunted house, and the Battle of Long Island, with General Washington pleased along the way.

Chapter I, The Clang of the Liberty Bell, opens on the fourth day of July, 1776. Excitement runs through all the colonies, for on this day the people's representatives, gathered in Philadelphia, are to decide whether the Declaration of Independence, already drawn up, should be adopted and signed. In Philadelphia the feeling runs so high that business stops and crowds throng the streets, talking and waiting for the decision.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
Spain, the opening part of Spanish Passions in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, follows the 1894 London edition translated by Arthur Machen, with chapters discovered by Arthur Symons. Chapter One opens with a hard maxim: whoever punishes a knave and leaves him alive invites vengeance. Casanova has survived a den of thieves, three against one, and lost his purse. At dinner, a police agent summons him to Count Schrotembach, the governor at Vienna.

The governor shows him a watch and sets the hour: be gone from Vienna by that time tomorrow, or face expulsion. Casanova protests the injustice of the order, issued before he could lay his robbery complaint. The chapter's summary promises the empress moderating the order without annulling it, then Munich, Augsburg, and Aix-la-Chapelle. Readers see the adventurer's luck turn on official suspicion, with Spain still ahead of him.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Number 478 of the Mirror, dated Saturday, February 26, 1831, illustrates autographs of eminent persons and resumes the theme of character in handwriting. Shenstone's quaint wish, to see Mrs. Jago's handwriting and judge her temper, supplies the motto. The signatures come from an engraved plate of forty-three autographs published with the Edinburgh Literary Journal, No. 28. Anecdotical traits only are selected here.

Anne Grant of Laggan's present hand shows a little instability of advancing life, yet keeps a well-rounded breadth and distinctness matching her clear, judicious mind. General Stewart of Garth writes a free, bold, military hand, taken from a letter praising Chambers's History of the Rebellion of 1745. Allan Cunningham's writing flows easily and tastefully, the reviewer adds, from a man who handled the chisel as Hogg handled the plough. Readers are taught to read temper and trade from ink strokes.

The Mirror's number for Saturday, May 21, 1831, No. 490, records an old house in Southwark, taken down the previous autumn for the New London Bridge approach. The crazy but picturesque building stood on the High Street's eastern side. Its style belongs to Henry VII's time, with florid carvings on the first and second stories' fronts. The upper stories had later been covered with plaster, and the windows mix periods.

The house carries a historic claim beyond its architecture: it was the residence of Anne Boleyn, the article states. Its interior was finished in palatial style, with the royal arms conspicuous in one apartment. The editors regret that Southwark's ancient history remains unwritten despite the suburb's celebrity. The Mirror's stated object is rescuing such relics from oblivion, and here demolition supplies the deadline. Readers get a doomed house photographed in prose weeks after its fall.
the-old-bell-of-independence-or-philadel:
Henry C. Watson wrote The Old Bell of Independence, a book for young Americans about Philadelphia in 1776. Lindsay and Blakiston entered it for copyright in 1851. Stories of chief men of the Revolution are linked by veteran storytellers gathered around the old State House bell. The contents promise a story of General Washington, The Spy's Fate, and a story of a sermon. Watson praises devotion and resolve while calling war itself a horror.
the-principal-navigations-voyages-traffi: Volume III of Hakluyt's Principal Navigations, in Edmund Goldsmid's edition, covers North-Eastern Europe and Adjacent Countries, Part II. Other records hold Volumes II, VIII, X, and XII of the same set. The pages shown here reach only the title pages, so the Muscovy voyages themselves stay out of view.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-22:

the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-23:
Headed volume twenty-five in its own pages, though the record calls it volume twenty-three, this portion covers 1576 in chapter four. the-valley-of-fear-pg3776:
Arthur Conan Doyle's The Valley of Fear appears again in this separate edition, and its contents and opening match the other library copy of the novel. The first chapter begins with Watson starting a sentence and Holmes cutting in impatiently. Watson confesses himself long-suffering yet annoyed by the sardonic interruption. Readers get the familiar partnership at work before the Birlstone case unfolds, first in England and then in an American valley ruled by fear.

tob-4146-15476:
Books eight through twelve fill volume three of Ganguli's Mahabharata, and the war burns toward its end. Great champions fall one by one. A night attack slaughters sleeping warriors, an act the epic itself treats as shameful. Victory, when it comes, tastes of ash.

tob-4176:
Teresa of Avila, the Spanish nun and reformer, described the soul as a crystal castle in The Interior Castle, her mature masterpiece of 1577. Benedict Zimmerman translated her guide for English readers. Seven sets of mansions lead inward, room by room, toward the King who waits at the center.

Readers get both a rich portrait of a lost civilization and the background they need for the clash that follows in later volumes.
tob-9052-15476:
